en: Preface to the Newly Carved Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* Assembly:
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is truly the final testament of the Dharma King and the bequeathed charge of the Compassionate Father. As ministers and as sons, it is only right that we follow and uphold it.
In previous dynasties, its exposition was most flourishing, and eminent masters appeared in succession, establishing it as the *Nirvāṇa*.
The various schools, such as those of Hexi and Guangzhai, each produced their own commentaries; however, by the middle period of the Tang dynasty, these schools gradually declined.

Consequently, the treatises and commentaries of the various masters were also lost with the passing of time until almost nothing remained. The only work that has survived to the present day is the commentary of our Great Master Zhang’an.
It is my conviction that it must profoundly accord with the Buddha’s intent and serve as a guide for all Buddhas.

Is it not so that [the Dharma] is protected and remembered? Furthermore, through the penetration of pure sincerity, the eight obstacles and five difficulties may be worn down without being diminished;
thus, neither Māras nor externalists can obstruct or sever it. This single treatise is the life-vein of the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra, a matter of no less concern than a single thread supporting nine tripods.
Those who are its descendants ought to pay homage to it with their whole hearts, exerting effort to cherish, revere, protect, and uphold it. However—
It is regrettable that since ancient times, the various commentaries on the sutras have circulated separately, making it difficult to cross-reference them.

During the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, a monk named Yuancheng first began to synthesize them for the convenience of students. While his intention was commendable, he arbitrarily exercised editorial emendations and interpolated his own private remarks.

The Jing and Wei rivers have become conflated, leaving many later students in doubt and error. Like a cowherd adding water to the stream, he has directly contradicted the scriptures right before our eyes;
it is to be feared that his merit will not suffice to compensate for his transgression. Master Shouduchun was moved by a resolute determination to clear this grievance.

He accordingly took the individual commentaries from the Tripitaka and integrated them directly into the scriptural text, not daring to add or subtract even a single character, so as to enable others to part the clouds and see clearly.
"To see the sun and sky through the mist—is this not a source of great joy? Therefore, it has been titled the 'New Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra.

After the Master passed away, the great-hearted monastics exerted themselves with diligence to carve the woodblocks for its wide dissemination. Recently, the carving project was completed, and one copy was brought to me to request a preface.
As I stroked the scroll, I sighed and said: 'Alas! This too is surely the result of the Buddhas' protective mindfulness and the sincerity of their devotion.'"
Was it not by polishing him that he was made thus? Was it not that the Buddhas and Patriarchs employed the person Pure Gong as their instrument to accomplish this task?
If it were otherwise, how could his removal of obscurations and restoration of the correct path have been so swift and manifest?
Thus, it may be verified that Pure Gong was truly a loyal minister and a filial son. How then could I fail to assist, praise, and extol him?
"Would you not wish to join the ranks of the filial grandsons? Thus, he was subsequently included in the sequence.
Composed by Prince Kun, the former Abbot of Tiantai, who held the rank of Quansanhou Yipin, on the day before the eighth month of the year of Bingwu (the Dragon year), the sixth year of Tenmei.
The General Preface for the Newly Carved Combined Edition of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* with its Commentaries:
Regarding the undertaking of this combined edition, the primary aim is to enable students to save the labor of consulting various sources and directly perceive the essential meaning of the sūtra.

Once the drilling and churning are skillfully performed, the *amṛta* (clarified butter) may be obtained. Previously, there was a commentary by Yuancheng which specialized in synthesizing and penetrating the texts;
however, in its desire to suit the times, it rearranged, added to, and deleted from them, resulting in much damage to the original substance.

Furthermore, because it lists the names and posthumous titles of the two Patriarchs at the beginning, ignorant people have sometimes mistakenly wondered whether this [commentary] is the authentic one. Upon further examination...
The harm caused by this complete commentary is surely no small matter. I have felt deep pain over it for a long time and have long desired to revise it.
Recently, having been further encouraged by various worthies, I have ventured to undertake this task.
In its execution, I dare not arbitrarily alter or omit even a single character according to my own whims; rather, I hope thereby to dispel falsehood and delusion, returning to the truth.
It is correct.
As for the title "Collected Commentary on the Southern Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra" indicated at the beginning, this was established by me.
The "Southern Edition" is precisely that which is being explained; it is distinguished from the unrefined "Collected Commentaries. Thus, following the topical divisions, the chapters are arranged.
This preface integrates the commentary into the scriptural text.
Originally, the scripture consisted of thirty-six fascicles and the commentary of fifteen fascicles; the present integrated commentary likewise consists of thirty-six fascicles.
Although there are variations in the number of fascicles due to adjustments, it was initially arranged by following the sequential order of the scripture’s fascicles.
Therefore, there is neither addition nor omission. As for the titles on the scroll, I did not dare to let their positions deviate.

Generally, a character raised one space indicates the scriptural text (sūtra), while a character lowered one space indicates the commentary (ṭīkā). Furthermore, this applies to the punctuation of the phrases.
Instruction in reading was provided alongside, or occasionally interspersed within the circles, to facilitate the study of the young.
All the scriptural texts assembled here follow the Song dynasty editions;

however, regarding any discrepancies in characters, misplaced chapters or sections, or other points of doubt, these have been collated against the Ming and Goryeo editions and all noted in the margins for the purpose of research.

I have examined that the wording of the sutras currently being discussed may differ from what is cited in the commentary (*śāstra*). Where there exists another version that accords with the citations in the commentary,
even if it carries no additional meaning, I have nonetheless set it forth so as to enable one to recognize the differences and agreements between ancient and modern texts.
Generally, there are two editions of the commentaries circulated in our country. One is a woodblock edition from the Kwanmu era, and the other is a movable-type edition.
Although the woodblock edition contains some errors and omissions, its general structure is superior to the Song and Ming editions.
Therefore, we have adopted it as the base text; however, for those errors and omissions, we have consulted the Song and Ming editions, or—
Comparing it with the movable-type edition and consulting various supplementary corrections, a superior version has been produced.
For instance, in the first fascicle, beneath the name of the editor, there is an extraneous character "shu" (述); as this is absent in the Song and Ming editions, it is correct to omit it accordingly.

At the end of the thirty-sixth fascicle, from the phrase "following the scriptural teachings" (從經教) until the end of the commentary, there are forty-three characters; while that [edition] possesses them, this...
Where there were omissions, they have been supplemented based on the original sources. Other instances involving ambiguous readings have been noted in the margins for reference.

In all cases where the original texts of the sūtras and commentaries contained a mixture of formal (zhèng) and vernacular (sú) characters, these have mostly been revised to conform to the standard forms, except as follows: [text continues].
Regarding the inverted lustful desires and so forth in the middle section of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I have intentionally retained their original characters.

As for the prose of this commentary, if the end of a preceding section coincides with the end of a line such that no further space remains and it connects directly to the beginning of the topical outline (*ke*) of the next chapter, it may be difficult to distinguish at first glance.
I now demarcate these points with the symbol “︽” to ensure that the beginnings and endings remain clearly distinct.
Generally, in previous commentaries, the topical outlines were placed at the beginning, while the subsequent sections provided either a word-by-word exegesis or a direct explanation;

consequently, the distant and proximate connections were difficult to trace. Now, I have created a system of topical outlines and appended them to the beginning of each sentence, so that one may avoid the distress of being lost at a fork in the road.
Generally, when there are blank sections in the commentary where no scriptural text appears, or when a single passage is divided into two sections, this is logically untenable.
That such instances occur despite being empty fabrications or redundant repetitions is likely because different versions existed at the time, with varying omissions and completions of the text;
could this not also be due to later scribal omissions? For example, as in the Goryeo edition... [sentence fragment].
The substance [of this text] is quite elegant, and furthermore, many of its characters coincide with those cited in the *Shu* (Commentary).

Thus, it remains unknown whether the sutra that Zhāng'ān examined still exists in its original form today. However, since the original manuscript of that sutra was never seen by Gūshān, I have now consulted multiple editions, yet none of them correspond.

There are only two categories: the "Vast" (Xū) and the "Two" (Liǎng).
All current divisions of chapters and assignments of categories are for the most part based on the *Kējīng* (Canon of Categories) from the Yuan edition.
This *Kējīng* was compiled and analyzed by the Master Zheng of Éméi and his colleagues, and subsequently revised and edited by the Master Dù of Wǔlín; it may truly be called [authoritative].

I have examined this with great precision. However, regarding the detailed sub-sections within the commentary (*śū*), there are instances where they cannot be reconciled, or where the meaning is not fully clear;
in such cases, it is not that there is no commentary or sub-sectioning, but rather that one must cross-examine and exercise careful judgment between them.
At the end of the fifteenth volume of the original commentary (*śāstra*), there is a passage of one and a half pages remaining that begins with "from silk cords binding the body.
This is actually part of the commentary on the latter section of the sūtra, yet it is not included in the Song or Ming editions.

It ought to have been reconciled with the text of the latter section of the sūtra; however, because the text is fragmentary and incomplete, it can no longer be restored. This refers to the complete commentary.
I have searched for many years, yet I still do not know whether he lives or has passed away; it is like a calf longing for its mother’s milk.
I earnestly hope that future worthies will devote their hearts to this matter, so as to preserve this wish-fulfilling jewel.

The commentary on the "Four Reliances" chapter (Sishen-pin) in the sixth fascicle reads "qīng cōng" (輕[怡-台+藂]). Having searched through dictionaries, this character has not been found. For now, I dare not privately alter it;
I have marked it as unusual above the grid to await the broad vision of scholars. However, I suspect it may be a corruption of the character "cāo" (懆).

For instance, the character for "qīngzào" (輕躁, light and fickle) in the sutras is also written as "cāo," which is glossed as "sào" (燥, dryness/aridity). Since the pronunciation and meaning of "sào" and "cōng" are somewhat similar, [it may be that].

Alternatively, it may also be explained as "cóng" (a cluster of fire). If that is so, could it be that the original character was "qīng cóng" (light cluster), which was erroneously written as "yí cóng"?
Master Yuan of Gushan compiled and finalized the structural outline (*shu ke-wen*) for this work in ten fascicles.
As it correlates with the scriptural text, it is of great benefit to students. Were it not for this, even the *Zhigui chao* (Excerpts on the Pointing Back) could not be considered a complete work.

Since no other version exists for comparison, I have instead verified it against the [Zhengshi].

In the "Preface Chapter," the masters of former generations established a precedent by chanting directly, dissolving the text, explaining the meaning, and dividing it into sections and chapters.
Consequently, the phrases of this sutra vary in length— neither uniform nor fixed— appearing in groups of two, three, four, five, seven, and so forth.

Emperor Wu of Liang established only the "before midday" and "after midday" periods; Kaishan [Huiyuan] added only the "introduction" and "proper" sections; Guangzhai ensured the circulation of the text;
Lingwei raised the question of the "causal origin" (nidāna) and provided the answer regarding its remaining momentum; the five gates of Hexi; the seven divisions of Vasubandhu;
and the eight gates of Xinghuang—though each is as beautiful as the orchid or the chrysanthemum, the Sūtra prohibits while the Śāstra permits, and the cowherd’s addition of water is a prohibition.
This [text] is divided again into five parts, which are further subdivided into seven sections: (1) Listing the Chapters; (2) Indicating the Textual Passages;

(3) Explaining the Titles; (4) The Arising [of the Teaching]; (5) Common and Specific [Aspects]; (6) Citing Scriptural Evidence; and (7) Divergent Interpretations. First, regarding the listing of the chapters:
(1) Invoking the Assembly of Nirvāṇa; (2) Expounding the Bestowal of Nirvāṇa; (3) Manifesting the Practice of Nirvāṇa.
4. Questions and Answers on the Meaning of Nirvāṇa; 5. The Functions of Nirvāṇa in Terms of Gathering and Subduing (etc.). Second, indicating the textual locations:
first, from "Thus" (*evam*) until "blood flows and sprinkles the ground" is the Request; from Cunda until the questions of the Great Assembly is the Bestowal;
from "Manifesting Illness" until King Guṇaratna is the Practice; from the "Lion’s Roar" until the end of the chapter is the Meaning; [the section] from Kāśyapa... [is the Conclusion].
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* employs three explanations for its title. First, the Way does not operate in isolation; it awaits the proper time and relies on companions.

Now that the time of Nirvāṇa has arrived, the gateway of the face opens its illumination, and sounds are emitted according to the capacities of beings to startle them into awakening and move their hearts.

To gather those present at Kuśinagara through these conditions is called "summoning" (*zhào*); to lead them together is called "inviting" (*qǐng*). Among the assembly, there are both the provisional and the real: the real may be named as such, while the provisional is what is appropriate.
Fifty-two assemblies from the ten directions were invited to gather and collectively manifest the Great Parinirvāṇa; therefore, this is called the "Invitation to the Assembly of Nirvāṇa.
Over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Buddha cultivated the Great Nirvāṇa-treasury, which is difficult to attain.
Originally, he had no secretiveness or stinginess regarding it, yet because [beings] were not fully capable of receiving it, he first used poison as a coating and only later [revealed it].

Washing with water was the same as before, while the powdered incense differed; he waited for the opportune moment and the right time because of Cunda’s offering of food, which resulted in the constant [attainment of] physical strength and color.

Because of the bhikṣus’ request for him to remain, he rejected the false and spoke of the True; through his earnest exhortations and inquiries, Kāśyapa received his instructions and followed his questions with offerings, ensuring nothing was left out or obstructed.
Thus the rain of Dharma overflowed, filling the city of Kuśinagara, and it is therefore called "The Expounding."
Nirvana is a gift; yet the secret treasury is profound and majestic, beyond reach by mere practice.
Through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he manifested [this state] to lead others forward; thus he lay on his right side, remaining silent and saying nothing.

He manifested the conduct of illness, and only when urged by Kāśyapa did he sit cross-legged, with a serene and joyful countenance, speak of the three fingers, and teach that a bodhisattva should practice the five conducts and ten virtues.
Therefore, it is called "demonstrating the practice of nirvāṇa. Yet, the meaning of nirvāṇa is vast and inexhaustible;

to cite one instance as a cover for all is like pointing to salt while discussing the ocean. Thus, by specifically inquiring about Buddha-nature, six successive layers are addressed, and the Buddha responds to each by naming them the meaning of nirvāṇa.
However, the essence of Buddha-nature is neither good nor evil; it employs both good and evil simultaneously, pervading all things.
Boundless and all-encompassing, it briefly summarizes the general principles to encompass vast applications: when used for good, it includes Rāhula; when used for evil, it can contain Cūḍapanthaka.

Since this is the case for these two disciples, all others may be treated by analogy. Furthermore, its essence is neither heterodox nor orthodox, yet it employs both heterodoxy and orthodoxy simultaneously:
when employing orthodoxy, it first gathers the five bhikṣus headed by Aśvajit; when employing heterodoxy, it finally includes the heterodox.
The ten external factors at the beginning and end being thus, those in the middle follow the same principle. What is called "nirvāṇa" functions through four modes of arising:

it arises from the assembly of the multitude; it is established by means of giving; it arises from practice; and it arises from seeing the meaning and realizing the meaning. These functions are themselves functional because they arise from meaning;
meaning arises from practice; practice arises from giving; and giving arises from the gathering of the multitude. Thus, these factors depend upon one another in both direct and reverse order.
Thus, the sequence is established: because it begins where there was no beginning, there is invocation; because it ends where there is no end, there is great function.

When evil is exhausted and the heterodox are eliminated, when goodness reaches its limit and the orthodox comes to rest, and when the methods of subduing and gathering have ceased, one enters ultimate quiescence and nirvana.
Regarding the distinctions of the five supernatural powers, the teachings given at the beginning, middle, and end are all delivered before an assembly; were there no assembly, they would be in vain.

Regarding the teaching of whom it is bestowed upon, this applies generally to the assembly as a whole; yet, since the gathering of the assembly is foremost at the beginning, it is appropriately termed "invocation.
Generally speaking, every single word and deed is bestowed upon sentient beings.

Specifically, however, when responding to the conditions of questions and seeking, the text is extensive and the matters are clear; therefore, it is called the "Expounding of Nirvana," which generally provides instruction.

There is nothing that does not conform to the compass and square; all these practices are fully understood. To discuss them separately as the five elements and ten virtues results in voluminous texts and manifest matters;
therefore, they are called the "practices of nirvāṇa. This sutra elucidates Buddha-nature from beginning to end.

Since Buddha-nature pervades everywhere without exception, this single cycle of question and answer discusses Buddha-nature exclusively; because the text is extensive and the matters are manifest, it is named [the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*].
The meaning of "universal" (*pān*) refers generally to a single treatise that guides and benefits all sentient beings, just as the great earth and medicinal herbs serve the needs of living beings;

my Dharma is likewise thus, and for this reason it is called "universal. The Lion’s Roar says: "Buddha-nature is also called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, also called Prajñāpāramitā, also called the Vajra Samādhi, also called the Siṃhanāda Samādhi, and also called Buddha-nature.
Yet, since Buddha-nature is not one, why are there five? These five names are used to facilitate understanding; they do not imply that there are five distinct entities to be summoned."

The entire assembly consists of the Tathāgata’s fellow practitioners and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). If considered from the perspective of their roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*), they all abide in the *Śūraṅgama*;
if considered from the perspective of their manifestations, they constitute the fifty-two assemblies. Therefore, they are summoned and invited by the name of the *Śūraṅgama*.

[The author] privately maintains that the fifty-two assemblies consist of the three assemblies of bhikṣus and so forth, with the bodhisattvas constituting one; from the second [assembly] onwards, they proceed in constant succession.
There are twenty assemblies numbering in the trillions of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (sands of the Ganges), eight assemblies numbering in the *asaṃkhyeya*, and four intermediate assemblies.
There are six heavens constituting the six Brahma assemblies, one asura, one māra-heaven, one Mahāmaheśvara, and the four directions;
these together with the four combinations total fifty-two. These are the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men, the One Possessing All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

It illuminates the underlying principles such that not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy remains; it opens the eternal to reveal the nature and excavates the treasury of awakening to bestow upon the assembly gathered at this time.
If viewed from the perspective of Buddha-wisdom, it should be called *prajñā*; if viewed from the perspective of established teaching, it is called the gift of *nirvāṇa*.
One should know that the name *prajñā* can serve as a realization of the gift of *nirvāṇa*; this is called the single practice that is truly upright and straight. It cannot be... [incomplete].
It can overturn and further shatter the fetters and delusions of affliction. If viewed from the perspective of cultivation, it is called "practice" (*caryā*);
if viewed through analogy, it is likened to a vajra. One should know that the meaning of the Vajrasamādhi as a practice for realizing *nirvāṇa* is so named for this reason.
Because *nirvāṇa* is designated by a name, there is Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) beneath it; therefore, there is Buddha-nature.
This is precisely the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. This meaning is sovereign, definitive, and fearless.

Whether understood from the perspective of the metaphor—the lion’s roar—or from the perspective of that which is metaphorized—the meaning of Buddha-nature—one should know that the name "lion’s roar" signifies the essence of the attainable *nirvāṇa*.
Essence and function are mutually identical; within all phenomena, there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss.

That which is not the Buddha-nature is the very substance through which its function manifests to travel and transform the world, gathering the wicked and the heterodox so that they all return to the correct meaning.
One should know that the name "Buddha-nature" can be realized as the function of *nirvāṇa*. Now, following the sūtra, I have divided this text into chapters;

it is well-supported by evidence and is not a mere fabrication. Regarding the seven different interpretations, I have categorized them according to time into the periods before, during, and after Emperor Wu of Liang.
Regarding the division of the sutra: if it were based on the morning, noon, and afternoon, that might be acceptable;

however, how could this apply equally to the evening and midnight? In the *Jushi qingseng jing* (Sutra on the Layman Inviting Monks), it says: "Generally speaking, one complete cycle of this calendar constitutes which year?

As for the divisions into sections according to the sutra, there is no such difficulty. Kaishan [Huiyuan] established the sequence: the introduction, the main body, and the conclusion. Here, the "introduction" refers specifically to the invocation.
Thus, the four chapters of the *Guangzhai* (Light-Residing) merely utilize a small portion of the chapters for the sake of circulation;

as for the *Lingwei* (Numinous Flavor), it provides answers to inquiries regarding conditions (*yuanqi*) while retaining residual power (*yusheshi*). Since there are questions and answers throughout [the text], there must be residual power everywhere.
If Hexi takes the first two fascicles as the "Gate of Connecting the Present and Past through Conditions," this gains the real (*shi*) but loses the provisional (*quan*). Now...

Regarding the invocation, it encompasses both the provisional and the real; from the third fascicle up to the "Questions of the Great Assembly," these constitute the sections on the concise and the extensive.
This [current section], however, concerns only the quantity of the text. Now, in expounding the Nirvana Sūtra, the bestowal of gifts includes both the extensive and the concise:
the five practices constitute the gateway to the practice of Nirvana, while the ten merits constitute the gateway to the merits of a Bodhisattva. Thus, practice and...
Since both merit and virtue are causes, they are now combined into the chapter on Practice (*xingzhang*) to avoid cumbersome text.
Because the *Lion’s Roar* takes the entire sutra as the gate of the inconceivable Middle Way Buddha-nature, it is difficult to understand due to its synthetic presentation;

by dividing the application of its meanings here, the text becomes easier to clarify. Master Di considers the first fascicle to be the section on "Reversing Demonstration through Supernatural Powers" (*shentong fanshi fen*). This is correct.
The provisional has lost its substance; what is now spoken of as "invocation" is thus without partiality.

That [text] takes the second fascicle as the Section on Seed-Nature (*gotra*) for Dispelling Doubts and Eliminating Attachments, while from the third fascicle up to the Questions of the Great Assembly it constitutes the Section on the True Meaning of the Right Dharma.
Now, by establishing a single Nirvana-bestowal, both of these two sections are encompassed. That [text] takes the five practices and ten merits as the method.
He then cultivates the factors of completion; therein, the "Lion’s Roar" constitutes the section on heedfulness for entering realization.

Since the prior cultivation has already been established as the entry into realization, and realization itself is what is entered, there would otherwise be redundancy. Now, for the sake of the topical outline (*arthakāṇḍa*):
Kāśyapa represents the section on abiding in compassion, while Cunda represents the section on manifesting the characteristics. This demonstrates the transition from evil toward good.

The section on the union of the heterodox with the orthodox for practical application consists of: first, the introductory chapter on the "Gate of Past and Present Karmic Connections" (which clarifies the intent);

second, the "Gate of Dispelling Doubts and Eliminating Attachments" (which utilizes the human mind); third, the "Gate of Brief and Extensive [Explanations]"; fourth, the "Gate of Practice"; fifth, the "Gate of the Five Stages";
sixth, the "Gate of the Middle Way within Practice"—all of which clarify the intent; and finally, the "Gate of Expedient Means for the Heterodox and Orthodox."
The distinction between the "Non-dual Gate" (*Fǎn'èrmén*) and the "Opening and Closing" (*Kāihé*) of Hexi does not differ in its essential meaning or flavor.
Regarding the second, the detailed explanation: the "Chapter on Summoning and Inviting" was established by the scribe of the scripture;

it was traditionally called the "General Preface" (*Tōngxù*) because the Way is the same throughout the three periods [of past, present, and future], and the "Specific Preface" (*Biéxù*) because the teaching-gates and the capacities of the audience differ. Furthermore, now...
Because the Buddha established all [teachings]—whether Small, Great, Separate, or Perfect—in this manner at the beginning of his career, it is said to be "common" (tong).

Yet, because the specific texts (jing) that serve as the vehicles for these teachings all possess differences, they are called "distinct" (bie). Furthermore, the opening of every sutra begins with "Thus" (*evam*), which is a uniform expression intended to inspire faith.
Within this common introduction, there may be five or six elements, depending on whether the subject and the location are treated separately or combined.
Thus it is. "Thus" refers to the principle being transmitted; "I have heard" refers to the person who transmits it; "at one time" refers to the occasion when the transmitter and the transmitted meet;
"principle" refers to the time of that meeting; "Buddha" refers to the master from whom it was received; and "dwelling" refers to the place where it was heard.
In this land, the multitude of followers are those who have personally received the teachings; they attest to one another in succession, exhorting others to believe that these are not false.

This is intended so that future generations may follow them without confusion. Furthermore, at the beginning of all sutras, both great and small, there is always an exhortation to believe. Belief in the Great and belief in the Small must differ;

if they did not differ, then there would be no distinction between the Small and the Great, nor between the Common, the Distinct, and the Perfect. Since such differences do indeed exist, [the teachings must be distinct].
How are these distinguished? To state them briefly: if one says that the transmitter and the transmitted are similar, this is "as it is" (*tathatā*);

if one says that there is nothing other than the transmitter and the transmitted, this is "it is" (*asti*). This accords with the intent of the Tripiṭaka (Hīnayāna). If one says that understanding merges with reality, this is "as it is";
if one says that the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom is stilled, this is "it is. This accords with the intent of the Shared Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna). If one says that [it] accords with...
To believe that the faculties respond to things according to whether they oppose or accord with principle is the intent of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha/Śrāvaka).

To say that the realm of Māra is identical to the realm of the Buddha, such that a single form or a single fragrance is none other than the Middle Way, is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna).
Since this is the case, passages such as "Thus have I heard" are easily understood; thus, Nāgārjuna spoke of "faith."
Those who say "it is thus" do not believe that "it is not thus. If one believes the first three [sections], this is faith in the provisional means (*upāya*);
if one believes the latter one, this is faith in the perfect fusion of the single reality (*ekayāna*).

These general and specific introductions have been employed by all masters using what is commonly heard in the world; there is no need for further elaboration, as it is fully detailed [in other texts].
In the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), only the single meaning of "interpreting according to the teaching" is currently preserved; all other [meanings] are to be inferred from it.
Now, we clarify that the five phrases of the "General Preface" (*tongxu*) may also serve as the preface to the five chapters [of the *Nirvana Sutra*].

Thus, the "Preface of the Request," the "Preface of 'Thus Have I Heard'," the "Preface of the Time," the "Preface of the Place of Practice and Abode," and the "Preface of the Meaning of the Assembly" share the same function. Regarding the assembly of the *Nirvana Sutra*, indeed, one who does not... [text continues].
To say "it is different" is as if there were no such thing; to say "it is not" is as if it were "is. If one does not perceive this "difference," then difference is truly non-different;
if one does not perceive "not," then "not" is truly not "not. One who realizes this meaning finds that what is different is not different, and what is "not" is not "not.

Beginning from the various classes of insects down to the dung beetles (*gōngqiāng*), their deceptive species and extraordinary forms, and their chaotic karmic retributions, rise up to the Brahma-world, covering the great trichiliocosm.

The subtle characteristics incline toward and displace the coarse, while the coarse reflects upon and supplants the subtle. If one views this with the eyes of an ox or a sheep, there is nothing that does not mutually interact;

how could it be otherwise? To attain such realization is to know that the Mahāsattvas of the Dharmakāya dwell in Śūraṅgama Samādhi, manifesting in various ways, and to awaken to the non-difference within difference.
Therefore, it is called "suchness" (tathatā). Knowing that it is neither "is" nor "is not," one speaks of "it is. This is how it should be understood.

Thus, the introduction for the assembly’s invocation is clearly established. I have heard this introduction regarding the gift of *nirvāṇa*, which I did not hear in the past but now hear for the first time.
I see that eight *droṇas* of non-glutinous rice were distributed throughout the great assembly; I hear that the fruits of these two gifts are equal and without distinction;
and I hear of the various flavors of the Dharma—the four virtues of the new *i* [the letter *i*], the secret Buddha-nature, and so forth—which I had not heard before.
Because it is heard, one knows that the "I have heard" (evam mayā śrutam) introduction refers to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

The "one-time sequence" (*ekakāla-krama*) of the *Nirvāṇa* practitioner refers to practice at a single time, not sequential practice; it refers to realization at a single time, not realization through preceding and succeeding stages. The text states:
"Furthermore, there is another practice, which is the practice of the Tathāgata—not sequential practice, but which can fully manifest the five [perfections] within a single thought-moment."
One should know that the attainment of the body is realized all at once; it is the sequential entry into *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the meaning of "sequential entry into *nirvāṇa*":
"place" (*sthāna*) signifies the locus where the body returns to rest. The Buddha-nature is the ultimate ground of the final goal.
Expelling the heterodox and leading the unwholesome toward that Kuśinagara, it is neither withered nor flourishing—a middle state of quiescent extinction. If it were otherwise...
If one reaches the ultimate limit and stops there, one should know that the sequence of the dwelling place is identical to the sequence of the *Nirvāṇa*.

As for those who share in hearing [the teaching] (*sahāśravaṇa*), the deities of mountains, forests, rivers, and seas, as well as species such as cattle, sheep, bees, and stinging insects, constitute the assembly of co-hearers.

Thus, one knows that the three sons equally receive the teaching; they together cultivate the three fields, wherein both good and evil are gathered, and both the heterodox and the orthodox are all delivered. Therefore, it is "identical" (*tong*).

The "Hearing the Multitude" (*śrāvaka-saṃgha*) constitutes the introduction to the *Nirvāṇa* [Sūtra], used to lead into the five introductions which shall be individually assigned as they conclude. Furthermore, one introduction is explained for each of the five chapters.
Now, the "multitude" does not exceed the eight Buddhas; these eight Buddhas are no different from the manifest Buddha, for there is no one who is not a Buddha—thus they are called "the true.
Because the two types of giving are without distinction, it is said they are "identical," as they all enter the secret treasury.
Therefore, it is said that this is the practice of the Tathāgata; it is said that the single practice universally encompasses all; it is said that this is the identical Buddha-nature;
it is said that the essence of the meaning of "thusness" (tathatā) is non-dual; it is said that evil and wickedness are non-dual; it is said that there is nothing superior to "thusness";
and it is said that one should know that such is the general introduction comprising these five chapters; my hearing [of the Dharma] is likewise so.
Formerly I heard that the fourfold assembly was not the eight Buddhas; now I hear that the eight Buddhas are precisely the fourfold assembly.

Formerly I heard that there is a distinction between the beginning and the end, and that the five fruits undergo transition; now I hear that the two kinds of giving are without difference, all being eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
Formerly I heard that rivers wind and turn before reaching the ocean; now I hear that the continent of Aparagoyānī is like a straight cord.
In the past, I heard that those with physical eyes cannot even see empty space, much less perceive the true nature;
yet now I hear that practitioners of the Mahāyāna, though possessing only physical eyes, are said to have the Buddha-eye, and with this Buddha-eye they perceive the true nature with perfect clarity.

In the past, I heard that good and evil are as distinct as the Jing and Wei rivers, and that the heterodox and the orthodox follow different tracks; yet now I hear that the lowly fish and the divine tortoise are both equally within the water. This is truly so.
For my sake, listen to the five chapters of the introductory preface: First, at one time [the Buddha] received the summons of the light of sound;
second, at one time he gathered in the Śāla grove; third, at one time he revealed the Tathāgata’s secret treasury; fourth, at one time he heard of the eternal bestowal of Nirvāṇa;
fifth, at one time he heard it and reverently accepted it for practice. These constitute the single meaning of entering Nirvāṇa while abiding within the secret treasury.

At that time, having heard the two characters for "eternal abiding" (*nitya-sthiti*), one awakens one's parents, ancestral kin of seven generations, and all sentient beings—whether enemies or kin, good or evil.
This constitutes the first chapter of the general preface: "The Place of Abode.

Here, "place" refers to the Buddha’s dwelling, which is invoked through the resonance of sound and light; the Buddha bestows this dwelling place of the Buddhas upon the assembly, and the multitude follows the Buddha to abide therein.

Arising from the place where the practice of Nirvāṇa begins, seeing the Buddha’s dwelling place is precisely what constitutes "seeing" (the meaning). Because the Buddha’s dwelling place draws in and gathers even the wicked, it serves as the "dwelling place.
The five chapters of the general introduction are identical in that they all consist of hearing and seeing the constant sound and light;

this is because it is not a hearing through other expedient means, and thus they are "identical in hearing. Finally, in the question and answer, there is the constant [bestowal of] life, physical strength, and power.

They share in the hearing of unimpeded eloquence; they share in the hearing of the conduct of the straight line of the Kyōja (Kauśika); they share in the hearing of the meaning of the secret treasury of the Western Sea;
and they share in the hearing that even the wicked possess the Buddha-nature. By means of these, they constitute the assembly of those who hear together.

This concludes the general introduction in five chapters. Furthermore, the five introductions sequence the three points (*san-ten*): thus, the general introduction of the three points is neither vertical, nor horizontal, nor parallel.
Not distinguishing them separately, one refers to them as the "Thus Have I Heard" Prologue; the "Prajñā at One Time" Prologue; the "Liberation Dwelling Place" Prologue;

and the "Dharma-body Co-hearers" Prologue. Furthermore, the three dots are not in vain. Moreover, these five prologues sequence the four virtues: the "Thus" serves as the general prologue for the virtue of *catur-guṇa* (the four virtues);
"I heard" sequences the virtue of *sukha* (bliss); "at one time" sequences the virtue of *śubha* (purity); and "dwelling place" and "co-hearers" sequence the virtue of *nitya* (permanence).
I [have explained] the essential meaning of the sūtra by means of these five introductory sections; all other cases follow this same principle and need not be explained in detail.
One should reflect upon other examples accordingly.
Thus have I heard.
Regarding "I have heard": "I" refers to the self, the non-self, and that which is neither self nor non-self;
"hearing" refers to hearing, not hearing, and hearing while not hearing—that is, hearing which is not non-hearing.

These three aspects of "I have heard" represent the provisional meaning previously explained as being neither self nor non-self; "not hearing" and "not non-hearing" represent the perfect meaning of "I have heard" in the present.
The scripture clarifies the intended meaning:
"At one time.
"One time" refers merely to the worldly convention of counting as "one"; that which is "one" in terms of emptiness is precisely the meaning of the Two Vehicles.
The unification of the ultimate and the conventional is the meaning of "Bodhisattva. It is all and yet not all, not one and yet not not-one;
it is both one and all. This latter "one" is the primary intent of the present sutra at this moment.
The Buddha was staying between the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Ajiravatī River at the birthplace of the Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara.
Regarding the term "Buddha," there are three bodies and four meanings; according to the latter meaning, the former may be understood by analogy. As for the dwelling place, it is fully described here.
One should say that Kuśinagara has no equivalent translation [in Chinese], or it may be translated as "Horn City" (*Kūṭagrāma*).
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* refers to it as "South of Horn City," which is precisely this city. Some call it "Thatch Grass City" (*Kuśagrāma*) or "Reed City";

it was named after the fact that this city was covered with grass. Others call it "City of the Rishis" (*Ṛṣipattana*), for in the past there were rishis here who lived long lives and honored [the Buddha].
People name their dwellings after themselves, and they also name countries after themselves; therefore, it is called the Kingdom of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas.
Among men, these Mallas possessed strength equal to a thousand men. Altogether numbering three hundred thousand, they formed a confederation that was subject to no sovereign.
Sustaining themselves by the Dharma, they were neither violent nor chaotic; they were the indigenous people of that land, and thus it is said they were "born" there.
The Āciravatī River—translated here as "Golden Sand"—is located south of the city; it is twenty *zhang* wide, though some say forty *zhang*.
As for the twin *śāla* trees—translated as "Firm and Solid"—there are two trunks on each side, making eight in total across the four directions;
they are all five *zhang* high. Four are withered and four are flourishing, their lower roots joined together and their upper branches interlaced.

They grow together like twin branches, their flourishing and withering appearing like mutual yielding; their leaves are luxuriant and dense, their blossoms like chariot wheels, and their fruit as large as jars.
Their sweetness is like honey, and they possess color, fragrance, and flavor. Because of these eight trees, the entire grove is given a single name:
"The Firm. Within this single city alone, there are various perceptions: those who see it as earth and stone are human inhabitants.

Regarding the meaning of dwelling in the world: if one views it as impermanent, suffering, empty, subject to arising and ceasing, this is the dwelling place of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

If one views it as the place for generating the bodhicitta, the place where one encounters the Buddhas of previous lives, the place of aspiration, and the place for practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth, this is the dwelling place of the Bodhisattvas.
If one views it as the perfection of the four virtues, ultimately and fully endowed with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), [this is the dwelling place of the Buddhas].
The city symbolizes permanence; the abundant provisions symbolize bliss; the subduing of enemies symbolizes selfhood; and the absence of calamities symbolize purity.
Furthermore, each of these matters symbolizes the four virtues: the indestructibility of the city symbolizes permanence; its abundance symbolizes bliss; its defiance of enemies symbolizes selfhood;

and its lack of hardship symbolizes purity. The *ārakṣaka* (guardian) symbolizes permanence because he has no master; bliss because his mind is at peace; selfhood because his strength is robust; and purity because [he is free from affliction].
The "manifestation of my physical delight" represents purity; the "flowing river" represents constancy; the "golden sand" represents purity; the "coolness" represents bliss;

and the "auspicious fortune" represents me. Regarding the "trees," the subsequent text states: the pair in the east represents constancy, the pair in the south represents bliss, the pair in the west represents me, and the pair in the north represents purity.
Furthermore, the lush growth of the pairs represents constancy, the cool shade represents me, and the flowers represent [the same].
Pure fruits represent bliss; if one can discern these four virtues both collectively and individually, this is the dwelling place of all Buddhas.
If one says that hearing this is what is seen by those in birth-and-death—ordinary worldlings—it is what is seen by the two vehicles of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
If one says it is what is seen by Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, it refers to the eight Buddhas among the nine Buddhas. This is indeed... [the dwelling place of all Buddhas].
Regarding what the Buddha perceives, if one grasps this underlying intent, each subsequent phrase may be interpreted accordingly.
Within the assembly of those who heard the teaching together, there are two parts: first, the gathering of the assembly; second, their deportment.
At that time, the World-Honored One was accompanied by a great community of bhikṣus numbering eight billion hundred thousand people.
Regarding the initial passage, I personally maintain that, according to the intent of this school, the fifty-two assemblies must be taken as those who "heard it together" (saha-śruta).
Therefore, the term "hearing together" precedes the fifty-two. Since the bhikṣus are mentioned first here, it says "hearing together.

This "hearing together" constitutes five categories, which correspond to the number of the various classes of beings. Although the current text lacks certain groups, they should logically be included; "together" (saha) means in common.
Furthermore, the *Śāstra* explains "commonality" by means of seven points: namely, one place, one time, one precept, one mind, one view, one path, and one liberation.
Because the bhikṣus share these seven points with the Buddha, it is said that the Buddha and they are common [in these respects].
Regarding the meaning clarified in the Tripiṭaka, the Buddha of sixteen cubits and the bhikṣus were together in the same location of Kuśinagara and remained together in Nirvāṇa.

When they sit in meditation, their discipline (*śīla*) is the same; their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the same; their untainted vision (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*) is the same; and their path to *nirvāṇa* is the same.

They are all equally liberated with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-vimukti*), and in these seven respects they are all equal to the Buddha; therefore, it is said that they "share" [the path]. If one explains the meaning according to the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*), five aspects are the same while two are distinct. What are they?

Their realization of the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—that is, the wisdom that perceives emptiness within form rather than the emptiness resulting from the destruction of form—is distinct. This vision is not the same.
The Mahāyāna path differs from the narrow path; one should know these two distinctions.
If the provisional teaching clarifies the meaning of the Honored and Special Body Buddha—including its time, place, and so forth—the former two bhikṣus would not see it.
What benefit would a lamp provide to a blind person? For those without eyes, the precepts, the mind, the vision of the Path, and liberation remain as they were before.
What benefit is there in playing music for two deaf men? It profits nothing for those without ears.
Just as this Buddha does not share [the experience] with the two former bhikṣus, and these intermediate bhikṣus do not even share it with the former Buddhas, how much less so for ordinary bhikṣus?

If the meaning of perfect clarity (*pariniṣpanna*) constitutes the seventh stage of Buddhahood, all are within the realm of the Buddha; they dwell only together with the Bodhisattvas of Perfect Clarity.
Regarding the Śūraṅgama [Samādhi] manifesting in the form of a bhikṣu: even the [Buddhas of] the previous three [aeons] did not share this [manifestation], let alone a mere bhikṣu.

The reason it is said here that they "shared" it is because these were all great expedient means (*mahopāya*) and because the [teaching] has been fully revealed. The term "Great" (*Mahā*) is an exclamation of praise for his virtues.
As the *Śāstra* states: "Mahā is translated as 'great,' 'much,' 'vast,' or 'superior'—one who is revered by celestial kings and great beings."

Therefore, it is said that he is "greatly proficient" (*mahābhijñā*) in the four Vedas and the Tripitaka; it is said that he is "superior" (*viśiṣṭa*) to the ninety-five types of heterodox schools. This is the explanation based on the Tripitaka. It is said that he is "venerated by the noble ones" (*ārya-pūjita*); it is said that he is "greatly proficient" in the analytical dharma-gates of essential nature (*svabhāva-vibhāga-dharmamukha*); it is said that he is "superior" in the two kinds of liberation through the wisdom of analyzing phenomena (*dharma-pravicaya*) and the wisdom of the mind (*citta-prajñā*). This is the [explanation based on] the Śrāvaka vehicle. It is said that he is "venerated by the noble ones"; it is said that he is "greatly proficient" in the dharma-gate of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharmamukha*); it is said that he is "superior" in the liberation of the non-abiding mind (*apratisthita-citta-vimokṣa*). This is the explanation based on the Mahāyāna. It is said that he is "venerated by the noble ones"; it is said that he is "greatly proficient" in the dharma-gate of the non-arising of all phenomena; it is said that he is "superior" in the liberation of the non-abiding mind. This is the explanation based on the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). It is said that he is "venerated by the noble ones"; it is said that he is "greatly proficient" in the dharma-gate of the non-arising of all phenomena; it is said that he is "superior" in the liberation of the non-abiding mind. This is the explanation based on the Buddha-vehicle. It is said that he is "venerated by the noble ones"; it is said that he is "greatly proficient" in the dharma-gate of the non-arising of all phenomena; it is said that he is "superior" in the liberation of the non-abiding mind. This is the explanation based on the Tathāgata-vehicle. It is said that he is "venerated by the noble ones"; it is said that he is "greatly proficient" in the dharma-gate of the non-arising of all phenomena; it is said that he is "superior" in the liberation of the non-abiding mind. This is the explanation based on the Dharma-vehicle. It is said that he is "venerated by the noble ones"; it is said that he is "greatly proficient" in the dharma-gate of the non-arising of all phenomena; it is said that he is "superior" in the liberation of the non-abiding mind. This is the explanation based on the Sangha-vehicle. This is the explanation based on the Jewel-vehicle. This is the explanation based on the Vehicle of the Threefold Refuge of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. This is the explanation based on the Vehicle of the Threefold Refuge of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. This is the explanation based on the Vehicle of the Threefold Refuge of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats. It is said that he is "venerated by the noble ones"; it is said that he is "greatly proficient" in the dharma-gate of the non

The first explanation is based on the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna): because he is revered by those who are learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), it is said that he "greatly penetrates" the dharma-gates of both the Great and Small Vehicles;
because he frequently surpasses the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, it is said that he is "superior. This [second] explanation is based on the Distinct Teaching (Pratyeka-yāna):
because he is revered by those who employ the seven kinds of skillful means (*upāya*), it is said that he "greatly penetrates" both the provisional and the real.
Because it is a *dharmaparyāya*, it is said to be "numerous"; because he acts as the leader among those who are fixed in certainty (*niyata-rāśi*), it is said to be "superior.
This explanation is based on the *Yuanjiao* (Perfect Teaching). As for the "greatly empowered" manifestation as previously mentioned, the term "bhikṣu" refers to his class or category.
He is called a bhikṣu for three reasons: he neither looks up nor looks down; he is neither square nor crooked; and he maintains a pure livelihood by begging in sequential order.
Because he has received the precepts, he is called a "beggar" (bhikṣu). The seven branches of the prohibitions serve as a tether for the mind-monkey;

the fear of the wolf of impermanence causes the fat of afflictions to wither—this is called the cultivation that destroys evil. When practicing these three dharmas, the celestial Māras and their poisonous afflictions fear that he will transcend their realm and dread that he will deliver others.
Therefore, they feel sorrow and terror. The essential meaning of this Tripiṭaka is that all phenomena are neither high nor low.
Neither cardinal nor intermediate directions, one sustains the life of wisdom; knowing that evil is not evil, and there is no knower—this is called "destroying evil.
Not attaining fear or joy is called "frightening Māra.

This explanation clarifies the meaning of a *bhikṣu* (monk) from the shallow to the profound, proceeding through the three truths in succession to seek the Dharma-joy of the Middle Way; this is called "begging for food" next.
First, the destruction of the five abodes is called "destroying evil. Because one fears afflictions (*kleśa*), one fears karma; because one fears karma, one fears the aggregates (*skandha*);
and because one fears the aggregates, one fears the celestial Māras. This is what is meant by "fearing the Māras. This explains the specific meaning of a *bhikṣu*.
Within all phenomena, there exists the nature of peace and bliss (*anurakṣaṇa-dhātu*); this is called "true milk-rice," by which one sustains oneself through that nature of peace and bliss.
When that which is purely the Buddha-dharma within has no evil to be destroyed, it is called "destroying the evil Māra.
As for "Māra who fears," this explains the meaning of the term *saṃgha* (assembly). According to various sūtras, the presence of four or more individuals in harmony constitutes a *saṃgha*.
The *Śāstra* states that there are four types of *saṃghas*: those who break the precepts, the "mute sheep," those with shame, and the true *saṃgha*; these follow the latter [categories].

Regarding the two types of Saṃghas: prior to the hundred-and-one *karmans*, the first two [stages] are "having shame" (*hrīmat*), while the four fruits are "real," referring to the assembly of the Tripiṭaka.
The stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*) is "having shame," while the eight persons above that are "real," referring to the assembly of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*).
The thirty minds are "having shame," while the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are "real"; this is the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekayāna*).
The assembly of those with the ten levels of faith possesses a sense of shame, while those of the forty-one stages belong to the true, perfect teaching.

As for the remaining two types of bhikṣus, they are present within each teaching because there is no distinction between their evil; therefore, they are not separately described as having shame or being true.

Furthermore, there are four meanings: first, initiation; second, reflection; third, responding to the capacity of the audience; and fourth, forming a karmic connection. These are explained by combining them.
Regarding the phrase "the assembly (and so forth) numbering eighty billion hundreds of thousands," this refers to a numerical count.

It may count only persons, or it may count the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*), or it may count the gateways to the Dharma (*dharma-mukha*), or it may count the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). (And so forth.)
Next, "surrounded from front and back" refers to deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Being surrounded from front and back means either being moved by the respectful engagement of the three karmas, or being moved by the entry into emptiness through the four gates, or by the four... [text fragment].
One enters through the provisional gate by means of the movement of the faculty, or one enters through the middle gate by means of the movement of the faculty.
From the fifteenth day of the second month, the second distinct introduction follows; this is precisely the text for the invocation, which is divided into three parts:

first, clarifying the invoker; second, clarifying the invoked; third, concluding the invocation. The first part is further divided into three: first, invocation by voice; second, invocation by light; [and third, invocation by mind].

Regarding the six types of summoning—summoning by three movements, summoning by voice, and summoning by sound—the first, summoning by sound at one time, expresses the Dharma; the second, summoning by sound at opportune moments; the third, the beginning and end of the sounds;
the fourth, the horizontal and vertical aspects of the sounds; the fifth, the resonance of the correct sounds; and the sixth, the exhortations and proclamations within the sounds.
First, concerning the expression of the Dharma through the downward sound during the second month: [The text continues with the detailed explanation of the six types of sound-summoning.]
On the fifteenth day of the second month:
the second month is the time of mid-spring; "mid" (*zhong*) signifies the Middle Way. The fifteenth day is the time when the moon is full;
"full" (*man*) signifies the perfect and eternal. Thus, the day of the full moon in mid-spring symbolizes the Middle Way.
The Dharma of perfect luminosity.
Next, at the time of approaching nirvāṇa, when the voice descends, it accords with the occasion.
At the time of approaching nirvāṇa—

When the conditions for the Way ripen, one does not wait; at the time of arrival, as the subsequent text states, because the roots of goodness of the various seers of Mount Gandhamādana, the Mallas of Kuśinagara, Cunda, and Subhadra had matured, he proclaimed *nirvāṇa* so that they might enter the secret treasury.
The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "For those who are to be saved by means of extinction, he manifests extinction."
"To deliver and cause them to be liberated" refers precisely to this meaning.
Third, regarding the Buddha’s voice from beginning to end:
by means of the Buddha’s supernatural power, he emits a great sound.
Supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is the root and great sound is the branch; from the root, the traces are manifested so that all may attain awakening. Yet these are neither root nor branch.
Furthermore, emptiness-wisdom (*śūnyatā-jñāna*) is the root, seed-wisdom (*bīja-jñāna*) is the root, and the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the root (and so forth).
Fourth, regarding the horizontal and vertical pervasiveness of its sound:
its sound fills [the world] up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

"Fills" refers to the horizontal dimension, while "up to the Peak of Existence" refers to the vertical dimension. According to another interpretation, the Peak of Existence is merely the Brahma-world, namely the *Nirartha* (or *Niṭṭha*) heaven.

Since those in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) lack form and bodies, they should not be able to hear sounds; therefore, it cannot be that there are persons in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Someone might cite the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*), which says:
"The power of concentration in the Formless Realm can transform and produce clouds of incense, flowers, and so forth to make offerings to the Buddha.

If this is so, why can they not transform and produce bodies? This objection is indeed valid. Now, I shall provide three rounds of crosswise and vertical analysis; first, one horizontal point covers six [cases].

The vertical [axis] penetrates the three realms, while the two horizontal [axes] encompass the four modes of birth; the vertical penetrates the three vehicles, while the three horizontal [axes] encompass the ten realms.

Because it penetrates vertically up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*), one knows that the "summit of existence" (*bhavāgra*) is not limited solely to the *Nirgrantha* (the non-Buddhist practitioners).

If one takes the summit of the three existences to be the Realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), or if one takes the summit of the three existences to be the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), there is yet another summit, namely the Sublime [Tathāgata].
It is understood that while two peaks were summoned and one peak was invited, this intention is so vast that it cannot be compared to the Brahma-world.
The five [sounds] respond to the resonance of those below;
according to their respective classes of sounds, they universally proclaim to all sentient beings.
Responses vary according to the different types of beings, yet the universal proclamation is non-dual.
To respond with a non-dual voice to varied perceptions is truly inconceivable.

Furthermore, this exclamation of "Today" and the subsequent proclamation are divided into two parts: first the exclamation, then the proclamation; the exclamation is intended to inspire veneration and reverence.
The instruction on the initial lament of sorrowful attachment consists of two parts: first, a double praise of the two virtues; second, a double conclusion regarding the two virtues.
Within the first part, there is first a praise of internal virtue, followed by a praise of external virtue. Regarding the former text:

Today, although the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses immeasurable internal virtues, he praises only these three titles for the purpose of clarifying three matters. First, in praising him as the Tathāgata, it is to show that he is born like all Buddhas to inspire in others reverence and esteem;
thus, he is the Father of the World. As an Arhat, he is the supreme field of merit, capable of producing [great fruits].
Virtuous karma constitutes the World-Lord, the Truly All-Knowing One, who is able to shatter doubts and obstructions and give rise to wisdom and understanding;
he is the Teacher of the World. Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "From this day forward, we are without a lord, without a kinsman, and have no one to revere and look up to," and so forth.
Next, regarding external virtues:
he has compassion for sentient beings, protects sentient beings, and regards all sentient beings equally as he does Rāhula.
Although his external virtues are immeasurable, only these four [immeasurables] are cited here to clarify the original vows made by him in his former lives as a father, a ruler, and a teacher.

All are fully endowed with the four immeasurables; now, to benefit others and rescue them from suffering while bestowing happiness is the essential purpose. To feel pity is great loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
to have compassion is great compassion (*karuṇā*); to provide protection is great joy (*muditā*); and to regard all equally is great equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Next, there is the concluding eulogy of the lower section.
It serves as a refuge and a shelter for the world.
First, it establishes the three titles as a refuge; second, it establishes the four immeasurables as a shelter for the world.
Next, the Great Awakened One descended from above and addressed them:
"The World-Honored One, the Great Awakened One, is about to enter parinirvāṇa. If any among all sentient beings have any doubts, you may now ask them all;
this shall be your final inquiry."

He addressed them with two kinds of responses: the first response was to cause them to sever their doubts, and the second response was to inspire them to pose questions. The Greatly Awakened One, the All-Knowing, is able to sever the former doubts;

through his fourfold equanimity and great compassion, he will surely listen to the subsequent questions. Once the subsequent questions are asked, he will expound the path of instruction, enabling them to attain Nirvana.
By bestowing the severance of doubt, they shall cast off the false and obtain the true; only then will the new "I" be revealed, and the Great Voice will be proclaimed universally.
The sequence for establishing the teaching is clear from this meaning. Previously, the three titles were praised in full; now, we simply respond with "Great Enlightenment" (Mahābuddha).
"Great Enlightenment" is precisely the Omniscient Illuminating Teacher; as he is both the Master and the Father, there is no need for further elaboration.

Furthermore, "Tathāgata" is the first title and "Great Enlightenment" is the latter title. Praising the first while mentioning the last, or vice versa, cites one side [of the whole]; the underlying intent is thus...
If one were to analyze this in detail as before, each section should clarify the four meanings; however, since the intended meaning will become manifest on its own, I shall not state them again.

Next, from "At that time" onwards, the passage concerning the summoning by light is divided into four parts: first, the time of the light; second, the place from which it issues; third, the object of the light; [and fourth, the purpose].
Regarding the first passage on the benefits of the four illuminations:
At that time, during the early morning—

the hour when darkness and light intersect as the sun rises— the manifestation of the dawn symbolizes the arising of wisdom-light, the extinction of the darkness of delusion, and the attainment of nirvana.
Because this is the appropriate condition for his power, he emits them at dawn.
Next, regarding the place of light:
from his face, he emits various kinds of light; that radiance is multicolored—blue, yellow, red, white, crystal, and agate.

The face is the gateway; though the mouth is not itself the six colors, the six colors appear upon the surface of the mouth. Thus, Buddha-nature is not the six dharmas, yet it is not separate from the six dharmas.
Furthermore, blue, yellow, red, and white are fixed colors that manifest according to one’s own intention;
crystal and agate are indeterminate colors that change according to the object, manifesting according to the intentions of others. Moreover, the Great Nirvana is like a vast ocean.
The various tortoises and fish, as well as the various precious jewels, that inhabit the bodies and dwellings of sentient beings possess a radiance of diverse colors;
this should precisely symbolize this [teaching]. Furthermore, because it delivers beings across the six realms and purifies the six sense faculties, it emits light in six colors.
"The three lights shine universally upon this" clarifies that which is illuminated.
These lights shine universally upon this trichiliocosm, the world-system of the Buddha, and likewise so it is throughout the ten directions.

The "three thousandfold world" and so forth up to the "ten directions" constitute horizontal illumination; if one were to apply this analogy to sound, there should also be vertical illumination, yet it is not mentioned because height and breadth manifest reciprocally.
Fourth, as for the middle and lower grades of light benefiting others, this is judged to refer to the new assembly, since they already possess that which is "middle."
As for the question of why it is necessary to speak of "new" and the "three karmas," etc., these can be understood from the present text, which is divided into two parts.
First, the removal of the three obstacles: therein, all sentient beings of the six realms who encounter this light have their sinful defilements and afflictions entirely eliminated.
The sentient beings of the six realms are the obstacle of retribution; their sinful defilements are the obstacles of karma and afflictions, as stated in the text.
Next, these [beings] of the three lower karmas, out of longing and devotion, give rise to wholesome states.
Upon seeing and hearing this, all these sentient beings experience great distress in their hearts and simultaneously raise their voices in lamentation and weeping.
"Alas, compassionate father! How painful, how bitter! Raising their hands, they beat their heads and strike their chests with loud cries;
some among them tremble with their whole bodies, weeping and sobbing.

These things are easily seen in the *Wen* (the *Sūtra on the Removal of Obstacles and the Birth of Goodness*, where it says one quickly attains the vision of the Buddha); it refers to the invocation of light in the *Preface to the Nirvāṇa Sūtra*."
The practice of the mind lies herein.
Third, regarding the passage "At that time, the great earth and the lower realms shook," it means that at that moment,
the great earth, all the mountains, and the great oceans were all utterly shaken.

There is movement on land and movement in water; as water and earth depend upon one another, they both move. This represents how ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*) mutually depend upon each other.

To overturn the conditions of existence (*bhava-pratyaya*)—namely delusion and craving—the shaking of the earth is used to represent this. Furthermore, the term "quaking" (*kampa*) refers to its physical form, characterized by rising and surging;
"thundering" (*nirghoṣa*) refers to its sound, characterized by roaring and awakening. On a broad scale, there are six types of movement, which further expand into eighteen movements.
... (and so forth). However, as for the sounds, lights, movements, and so on—whether they appear before, after, or simultaneously—the perceptions of those who encounter them differ;
how then can one dogmatically insist upon a fixed order?

From the phrase "according to the time of the various sentient beings" onwards, the following clarifies the text regarding that which is summoned, which is divided into two parts. First, a general clarification of that which is summoned: [text follows].
At that time, these were the sentient beings [referred to]. Second, there is the specific clarification of those summoned, which refers to the general invocation categorized according to their types;

this is divided into four parts: first, the suppression of suffering; second, the arousal of a request; third, the explanation of the request; and fourth, the explanation of suffering. Regarding the first section:
At that time, all the sentient beings said to one another, "Let us each restrain ourselves for now; do not be so deeply distressed.
Hearing that our teacher and father has passed away, how could we not suffer? To drown in an ocean of grief benefits neither oneself nor others," which is why they spoke of restraining themselves.
Next, we should together descend and extend our invitation.
We shall go quickly to the city of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas, to the place where the Tathāgata is, prostrate ourselves in reverent salutation,
and entreat the Tathāgata not to enter parinirvāṇa, but to remain in the world for a kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa.
If one remains suppressing suffering, it likewise brings no benefit; therefore, it is necessary to make a formal request. Thus it is said: "One should go to the Buddha's presence.

Regarding the phrase "a kalpa or a declining kalpa" (*kalpa-kṣaya-kalpa*): if one were to request for a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*), it would obstruct the future Buddhas. Therefore, the request is made only for a small kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
This refers to the period from when the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years, gradually decreasing until it reaches ten years; this constitutes one small kalpa.

Third, regarding the mutual grasping of hands, this explains the text of the request, which is divided into three parts: first, the initiation of the request; second, the formal explanation of the request;
and third, the conclusion of the request.
[The phrase] "mutual grasping of hands" refers to the first part.
The mention of "grasping hands" merely serves as the initial occasion for mutual expressions of grief and lamentation.
The subsequent passage, "Next, he spoke these words," correctly explains the intent of the request.
Furthermore, he spoke these words: "The world is empty; the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, and unwholesome karmic actions have increased."
World-honored One!
Indeed, because the Tathāgata comes by means of the Suchness (tathatā), there is a Buddha when he is in the world; because he departs from the world, there is no Buddha.
Therefore, it is said that the world is empty. This is the desire to invite the Tathāgata, who is our father. The Buddha is the Worthy of Offerings (Arhat); he is the field of merit for offerings.

If there were no one worthy of offerings (*arhat*), good karma would be exhausted; therefore, it is said that "the merit of sentient beings is spent," expressing the desire to invite the Master Worthy of Offerings.
The wisdom of universal knowledge (*sarvajña*) obstructs evil and reveals the good; if the One of Universal Knowledge departs, there will be no one to provide guidance.

Therefore, it is said that "unwholesome states increase," expressing the desire to invite the Teacher of Universal Knowledge (*Samyaksaṃbuddha*). Since such is the intent of these invitations, one ought to act with urgency.
One must go to the Buddha without delay.
Those who have issued the threefold invitation should depart quickly.
You all must go now, go quickly! The Tathāgata will surely enter parinirvāṇa before long.
Fourth, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, he spoke these words" explains suffering.
Again, he spoke these words: "The world is empty; the world is empty. From this day forward, we have no protector and nothing to revere.
Poor, destitute, and orphaned, we are suddenly separated from the Unsurpassed World-Honored One. Should any doubts arise..."
To whom else should we now turn for questioning?

Compassion once covered the world; it rescued those in suffering and brought joy to the destitute. Now that both compassion and its counterpart have departed, everyone is simultaneously afflicted by poverty and suffering.
As they cry out together into the void—without rescue, without protection, and with no one to revere as their lord—this is what it means to be a Buddha without a master.
The suffering of being poor, destitute, and orphaned, suddenly separated from the Unsurpassed World-Honored One, Śākyamuni, who is without peer—this is the suffering of having no kinsman.
Should doubts arise, whom could one ask? Śākyamuni, who is without teacher—this is the suffering of having no master. Thus, in this succession, the meaning of sorrow and suffering is established.

Next, from the phrase "at that time" onwards, there are immeasurable [sections] which constitute the specific invocations; these are divided into two parts: first, the invocation of those in this land, and second, the invocation of those in other lands.

Regarding this land, there are three sections: first, the invocation of the assembly of Jambudvīpa; second, the invocation of the intermediate assembly; and third, the invocation of the assemblies of the higher realms.
Within the Jambudvīpa assembly, there are three types: namely, the Śrāvakas, the Bodhisattvas, and the mixed assembly. The *Śāstra* clarifies that the Bodhisattvas are present.

Because they practice the Middle Way, they occupy a position between the eldest and the youngest; this should be understood in full according to the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), which states that there are both explicit and implicit meanings (*youshi yubiao*, etc.).
Others previously divided this into two intentions: first, the enumeration by addition, and second, the enumeration by subtraction.

Regarding the first [division], the assembly of monastics and laypeople is distinguished. The present intention is as before: first, the Śrāvakas, who are further divided into two—monks and nuns. Regarding the monks: [End of excerpt]
Furthermore, regarding the two groups—the assembly surrounding the Buddha first and the assembly from outside second—they ask the Buddha why he summons them.

The answer is that although they do not actually come when summoned, the act of summoning startles them so that they may later inquire; moreover, because it is done for the sake of the majority, it can also be said that he summons them. The assembly surrounding the Buddha consists of three types:
those who are summoned, those who respond to the summons, and those who comply with the summons.
At that time, there were immeasurable great disciples, such as the Venerable Mahākātyāyana,
the Venerable Bakula, the Venerable Upānanda, and other such great bhikṣus.

Regarding the initial statement "there were at that time immeasurable [disciples]": since the number has already been established as "immeasurable" above, the term "immeasurable great disciples" here refers to the entire retinue.

Thus, it is said "immeasurable great disciples," meaning those who are like younger brothers or like sons, showing respect and yielding to one another at the two pillars, and thus designating them as a single category (and so forth).
