"Venerable" (*āyuṣmat*) is a title used by fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) to address one another with mutual respect.
Regarding the Venerable One, as in the Āgamas, from now on the monks shall address those of seniority as "Venerable" (*bhadanta*) and those of juniority as "Elder" (*sthavira*);
because their virtuous deeds are praised, they are called "Elders" (*sthavira*), and so forth.
Kātyāyana is translated here as "Fan-sheng" (Fanning the Cord); Bakula is translated as "Good Appearance"; Upānanda is translated as "Great Joy," or alternatively...
Because his physical form was upright and handsome, his parents named him Mahānanda. While living at home, he was a wheel-turning monarch;

having renounced his body, he became a Māra king. The Buddha, foreknowing future events, manifested eighteen transformations and said, "If you can leave the household life, you shall attain such [attainments] as these.
His parents granted him permission, and because he attained the three types of supernormal knowledge and the six higher powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), he was named Gaurīputra (Heavy Joy).
Next, those who encounter the Buddha’s light are those summoned.
Regarding those who encounter the Buddha’s light:
one should say that encountering the sound and the light and the shaking of the earth briefly mentions one while encompassing two.
Third, their bodies tremble and shake; this is called "summoning in accordance.

Their bodies tremble and shake, even to the point of violent convulsions such that they cannot support themselves; their minds become turbid and bewildered, and they let out loud, piercing cries, giving rise to various such forms of suffering and affliction.

In the preceding passage, it was stated that encountering light dispels the three obstructions and gives rise to the three virtues; now, for brevity, the obstructions are omitted while the virtues are retained, as in the text.

Question: Since the Arhat has exhausted all sorrow and grief, why does he suddenly reach such a state? Answer: This is residual habituation (*vāsanā*), not the active afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, it is demonstrated as a model to inspire others to aspire toward it.

Moreover, these are specific delusions (*bhinna-moha*) that have not yet been eliminated, rather than pervasive delusions (*sāmānya-moha*). As for "sorrow and grief" (*śoka-parideva*): [The text continues with the definition of these terms.]
This Dharma-realm of the Buddha encompasses all phenomena; as for the subsequent passage concerning those with sorrow and those without sorrow—all are the realm of the Tathāgata.
These shall not be discussed in further detail here, as they are already distinguished according to the four teachings.
Next, at that time, there were again eighty hundred thousand who had come from outside to be summoned;
these summoned ones were of four categories, and the initial enumeration of their praise and conclusion is understandable.
At that time, there were also eight million [monks],
who were of the same class as the aforementioned monks;
the term "various bhikṣus" is explained as before.
All three were arhats; first, he praised their own virtuous qualities:
they had attained mastery of mind, accomplished what was to be done, were free from all afflictions, and had fully disciplined their faculties.
An Arhat is one who has attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and possesses mastery over the mind; such a person is one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).

To praise their virtue of non-arising is to praise the wisdom of no-more-learning, as they have already accomplished what was to be done. To praise their virtue of being a Worthy One (*arhat*) is to praise their freedom from affliction and their taming of the faculties.
For the faculties are themselves thieves; as the *Teaching Left Behind* states, "These five faculties are thieves. Thus, it praises their virtue of having slain the thieves.
Next, as with the Great Dragon King, he praises the virtue of transforming others:
"Like the Great Dragon King who possesses great majestic power, has accomplished the wisdom of emptiness, and attained his own benefit;
like a sandalwood tree surrounded by sandalwood trees; like a lion king surrounded by lions."
Since it is said that he possesses great majestic power (*mahā-tejas*), there is no room for doubt that his own majesty is known to benefit sentient beings and is venerated by others.

Now, the elephant is used as a metaphor for the greatness of power within the stages [of practice], while the dragon is a metaphor for the greatness of power within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Alternatively, the elephant may simply be called a "dragon-elephant" (*nāga-hastin*); for example, when the divine elephant Airāvaṇa—the precious elephant of Śakra—travels through the void, he covers vast distances in a mere instant.
Suddenly transcending ten thousand *li*, he transformed his tusks into thirty-two tusks;
each tusk had seven ponds, each pond had seven lotus flowers, and each flower had seven jade maidens who offered music, bringing delight to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

If one takes the dragon-elephant as a metaphor, it is even more appropriate for transforming others; the sandalwood serves as a simile for benefiting beings through precepts, while the lion serves as a simile for wisdom.
Benefiting sentient beings by being able to act as a master for others through these two dharmas, he is in turn surrounded by a pure assembly.
(4) Thus concludes the section on his immeasurable merits.
Those who have accomplished such immeasurable merits are all true sons of the Buddha.

Since it is said that they are "immeasurable," know that these true sons of the Buddha—whether designated as such from their own side or from the perspective of others—are in their traces (traces) the true sons of the Hīnayāna, but in their essence (root) the true sons of the Mahāyāna.
By means of the true sons of the Mahāyāna, one summarizes the aforementioned merits of both self and others (and so forth).
Next, regarding the three types of summoning by means of light, sound, and movement, first is the summoning by light. This consists of two parts:
first, each [practitioner] departs from their usual dwelling place at dawn; this is the summoning by light.
Each person, at the time of sunrise in the early morning, leaves their permanent residence and encounters the Buddha’s radiance while using a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*).

"Morning" signifies the beginning of clarity; using the *yāśchi* (teeth-cleansing twig) represents the commencement of practice. It symbolizes the movement of the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) and manifests the beginning of sublime conduct.
Encountering the Buddha’s light, they then address one another, thereby complying with the summons of the light.
They said to one another, "Virtuous ones, you should quickly wash and rinse yourselves to become pure.
Having spoken these words, the hair on their bodies stood on end, blood appeared all over their limbs like *pāṭala* flowers, and with tears filling their eyes, they were overcome by great anguish.
Prior to this, there was no mention of the removal of the three obstructions, yet there was a passage concerning the virtues of the three karmas.
They said to one another: "The bristling of the body hairs is the virtue of the karma of speech; the arising of great suffering and affliction is the virtue of the karma of the mind.
*Pāṭala* is the name of a tree; its leaves are green and its flowers have three colors. When the sun has not yet shone upon them, they are black; when the sun... [shines], they become red.

When illuminated, it appears red and all red veins manifest; when the sun sets, it appears yellow, signifying that one has not yet received the summons and the three virtues have not arisen—like black.
To receive the summons is sorrowful, like red; to be without a Buddha is like yellow (and so forth).
The purpose of "excluding" (jian) is to summon [beings] in accordance with their inclinations for their benefit;
the purpose of "summoning" (shao) is to bring sentient beings to benefit and peace, to accomplish the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna, and to benefit sentient beings.

"Excluding" distinguishes this from one's own solitary practice; "accomplishing the Mahāyāna" distinguishes it from the Lesser Vehicle; and "supreme emptiness" [distinguishes it from] inferior forms of emptiness.
This practice of simplicity is not shallow; it is the meeting of the true sons of the Buddha with the text.
Next, following the manifestation of the Tathāgata, one responds to the invocation.
One manifests the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings of skillful means in order to ensure that the various modes of preaching the Dharma are never interrupted.
Furthermore, there are two aspects: first, the great voice universally proclaims and commands that at the very end one shall ask;

now, by offering this summons, it reveals the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings on skillful means, opening up the constant inquiry and manifesting the emergence of the ultimate final teaching. Next, in order to prevent interruption, the voice below follows the sound of the summons;
if one accords with the Buddha’s vocal teaching, then the preaching of the Dharma will not be severed.
Third, for the sake of all sentient beings, he went forth and invoked the earth to tremble;
for the purpose of taming all sentient beings, he quickly arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times,
joined his palms in reverence, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the second [period], when the mountains and seas shook and inverted views were overturned, the nature [of reality] was revealed;
now, following this summons, the causes and conditions for subduing [beings] arise. One swiftly arrives at the Buddha’s abode, immediately moving in accordance [with the truth].
This refers to that which can summon and that which is summoned—the profound marks of realization through wisdom, and the wisdom that knows wisdom (as described at length).
The two rows of nuns constitute the first two groups; the subsequent group of those whose traces are revealed constitutes the second.
That is to say, there are four aspects regarding those who are to be honored and followed, those who are summoned, their names and numerical positions, and their praises.
At that time, there were also the bhikṣuṇī Kauttālī-Subhadrā, the bhikṣuṇī Upānandā, and the bhikṣuṇī Sāgaramati.

Among those listed in the foremost positions, these three were the leaders; "Kauttālī" has not yet been translated [into Chinese], while "bhikṣuṇī" refers generally to both types of nuns (the *śramaṇerikā* and the *upāsikā*).
Regarding the specific designations for women: among the laity, those who have received the five precepts and so forth are called *yí* (aunt);

those who have left home are called *ní* (nun). However, within the Vinaya, they are also addressed as *ā-yí* (aunt) or *ā-jì* (elder sister), using these titles to signify kinship through the Dharma.
Together with six billion bhikṣuṇīs,
all of whom were likewise great arhats;
their status may be known.
With all outflows exhausted, their minds attained mastery, having accomplished what was to be done and being free from all afflictions;
with their faculties fully subdued like great dragons, they possessed great majestic power and had perfected the wisdom of emptiness.
In the section on praise, first he praises his own practice as described above; next, like a great dragon departing, he praises his virtue in transforming others, also as described above.
Next, he departs at the time of dawn to attend to the three summons, as explained above.
Furthermore, at the break of dawn when the sun first rises, his body hairs stand on end and blood appears all over his body like *pāṭala* flowers;

with tears filling his eyes, he experiences great anguish. Desiring to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, and to accomplish the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna, he reveals the Tathāgata’s secret teachings of skillful means, speaking in various ways so that they shall never be interrupted.
Because the Dharma serves as the cause and condition for the subduing of all sentient beings, he quickly went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and with palms joined in reverence, withdrew to sit to one side.

Next, regarding the section on the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, the departure from their traces is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the traces themselves; second, explaining and establishing them based on their original ground.

The first part concerns the traces of the bhikṣuṇīs. The second part, "all of whom are bodhisattvas," refers to their original ground. First, it indicates their general status, hence the phrase "all of whom are [bodhisattvas]," and so forth.
Next, the phrase "those of lower rank" specifically points to high-ranking bodhisattvas. While the general statement does not yet distinguish between high and low, [the specific reference does].
To further explain the vastness of his original lofty traces:
among the community of bhikṣuṇīs, there were also various bhikṣuṇīs who were all bodhisattvas, "dragons among men.
As for the initial mention of "dragons among men," this merely refers to being like dragons among worldly people; it is not particularly extraordinary. However, these [bodhisattvas] are—
A worthy and holy one, a dragon among men,
who dwells immovably in the stages of the ten bhūmis; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he manifests in a female body,
yet constantly cultivates the four immeasurable minds and possesses the power of mastery to manifest as a Buddha.
Next, regarding the stages of the ten *bhūmis*: "explaining that her fundamental nature is high" clarifies that she currently manifests in a female body;

"clarifying that her traces are vast" [is explained as follows]: why are the traces vast? Because of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). Why is the fundamental nature high? Because she has attained the samādhi of mastery (*vaśitā-samādhi*).
If she is already capable of becoming a Buddha, why could she not manifest the forms of the nine realms [of existence]? (etc. Another scholar divides this passage into two parts.
The first pair consists of the original and the trace; the latter pair consists of cause and effect. It is said that cause and effect are difficult to perceive (and so forth).

Next, the listing of the assembly of bodhisattvas is also divided into two parts (and so forth). Regarding the six aspects of what is summoned—namely, number, category, stage, name, praise, and conclusion—the first, "a single Ganges-sand [of kalpas]," refers to the number.
At that time, there were again as many [beings] as the sands of the Ganges.
There are four reasons why many sutras take the Ganges as a standard of measure: first, because many people recognize it;
second, because those who enter it obtain merit; third, because it is the largest among the eight great rivers; and fourth, because it is the birthplace of the Buddha, the homeland of the Great Sage.
Therefore, it is frequently employed; this is the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*.
Next, regarding the category of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

This is the commentary on the ten meanings of the Bodhisattva, explaining the "aspiration for the Way" (bodhicitta) and the "great aspiration for the Way": first, to exhaustively transform and teach all sentient beings;
second, to exhaustively make offerings to all Buddhas; third, to exhaustively purify all Buddha-lands; fourth, to exhaustively uphold all Buddha-dharmas;
fifth, to exhaustively ensure that the lineage of all Buddhas is never severed; sixth, to exhaustively discern... [the seventh through tenth points follow].
1. Fully knowing all Buddha-lands; 2. Fully discerning all the assemblies of Buddha-disciples;
3. Fully knowing the minds of all sentient beings; 4. Fully knowing how to sever the afflictions of all sentient beings; 5.
Fully knowing the faculties of all sentient beings—taking these ten gates as the foremost, there are further immeasurable asaṃkhyeya gates. Therefore, it is so named.
In the *Bodhisattva-mahāparipṛcchā* (Great Chapter on Bodhisattvas), the Buddha himself clarifies the meaning of "Mahāsattva" through ten gates:

first, one should don the great armor amidst immeasurable births and deaths; second, one should relinquish all that one possesses; third, one should maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings;
fourth, one should deliver all beings by means of the three vehicles; fifth, one should deliver all [beings].
1. Having delivered all beings, one forgets the merit of that deliverance; 2. One should understand that the mark of non-arising is the true nature of all dharmas; 3.
One should practice the six perfections solely with the mind of *sarvajñā* (omniscience); 4. One should study wisdom to thoroughly comprehend all dharmas; 5.
One should thoroughly comprehend that all dharmas have a single mark; 6. One should thoroughly comprehend immeasurable marks—these are the ten gateways.
The one who is foremost, named Mahāsattva Nāgārjuna, explained these ten meanings in the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*:
first, for immeasurable days, months, years, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas within saṃsāra, he benefited and liberated all sentient beings;
second, as for the relinquishing of all possessions, whether noble or lowly, internal or external, there was nothing [he did not give].
1. To cherish the impartial mind toward all sentient beings, treating them equally regardless of whether they are objects of hatred or love, or whether they are enemies or kin;
2. To deliver those of the three vehicles according to their respective capacities, causing them all to reach nirvana together;
3. To forget one’s own merit, giving rise to neither self nor other, and perceiving neither the savior nor the saved; 4. To know that which is unborn—that all [phenomena] are [unborn].
1. All dharmas are non-arising; 2. the seven practices and six perfections are performed with a pure and unadulterated mind, dedicating them toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge);
3. thoroughly penetrating all dharmas means being fully proficient in all worldly activities;
4. the gate of the single characteristic refers to ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), which is the mark of *nirvāṇa*, free from recollection and conceptualization.

Regarding the ten distinct gateways of the immeasurables: beginning with these ten gateways of progressive numerical increase—namely one, two, three, and four—there are further immeasurable gateways of dharma;
this is the meaning of "Mahāsattva. Herein, the four types of bodhisattvas should be clarified;
as noted in the separate records, this text frequently extols the virtues of the perfected bodhisattva.
The Dragon among the three persons departs for the position of clarity.
The Dragon among men occupies the rank of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), abiding immovably while manifesting his body through skillful means (*upāya*).
The Dragon among men emerges from the stage of skillful means; one who occupies the rank of the ten stages dwells in the stage of reality (*tattvabhūmi*) and remains steadfastly established therein.

The Immovable One is eternally quiescent in the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), yet through skillful means manifests his body to benefit beings throughout the lower realms of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Fourth, as for their names, the following list of names is given:
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas such as Sāgaramati (Ocean-Mind) and Akṣayamati (Inexhaustible-Mind).
He serves as the foremost leader.

Among the assembly of one *gaṅgā* river, only two individuals are listed; as for Hai-de (Ocean Wisdom), he is like the Bodhisattva Hai-hui (Ocean Wisdom) in the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, and also like the "Ocean of Great Nirvāṇa" mentioned in the following passage.
He is named "Ocean" (*Sāgara*) because he is established from these eight inconceivable [qualities].

Regarding "Inexhaustible Intent" (Akṣayamati) [and so forth]: in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, this bodhisattva himself declares his own name and elucidates eighty kinds of dharma-gates to clarify his inexhaustible intent [and so forth].
Fifth, their minds all universally extol his virtues; this section is divided into three parts: first, a general extolling of his upward seeking;
second, an exposition based on the Four Great Vows that encompasses downward transformation; third, a conclusion summarizing both upward seeking and downward transformation.
Their minds all revere the Mahāyāna, abide securely in the Mahāyāna, have a profound understanding of the Mahāyāna, delight in the Mahāyāna, and protect the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the first term, "revering," this refers to the principle as stated in the subsequent text: "That which the Buddhas take as their teacher is..."
Regarding the Dharma, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he contemplated who was worthy of veneration;
none surpassed Prajñā. 'I shall revere it'—this is its meaning. As for "abiding securely," this is discussed in terms of realization. As the subsequent passage says:
"All sentient beings as well as all Buddhas alike abide securely within the secret treasury"—this is its meaning. This is a profound understanding.
This refers to the *Jñāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom), as stated in its later sections: "It can generate the profound and vast wisdom of a Bodhisattva;

it is like a large box requiring a large lid, or a deep well requiring a long rope"—this is its meaning. As for "delighting in [practice]," this refers to the discussion of actual conduct, as stated in the following passage:
"The eight characters of the Snowy Mountains were not considered difficult; cutting off three *liang* daily, he never once called it suffering."
Regarding its meaning, "guarding" is discussed here in terms of the teachings, as illustrated in the following passage where Xianyu executed his punishment and Juede broke the enemy array;
this is precisely that meaning. When the great aspiration of the Bodhisattvas to seek the supreme reaches its limit, it is like the ocean.
Here, five meanings are briefly cited to demonstrate its characteristics.

Next, following "Well able to accord with and proceed," there is the praise of the virtue of downward transformation, beginning with a general praise of the Four Great Vows, followed by a specific praise.
[The text reads: "Well able to accord with all worlds.
The Bodhisattva has already ascended the Ten Stages and dwells therein immovably; rather than realizing Nirvana, he would willingly enter Saṃsāra."
The original vows accord with the world: two great vows arise in accordance with great compassion, and two great vows arise in accordance with great kindness;
this is a general praise of their intent.
Next, he made this vow and departed to praise [the Buddha] individually.
Having made this vow— "May all those not yet liberated be brought to liberation"— he had, throughout incalculable eons of the past,
cultivated and maintained pure precepts, properly upheld his conduct, and resolved those who were not yet resolved, thereby continuing the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it would never be severed.
"In future ages, you shall turn the wheel of Dharma.
Having separately praised his initial vow—that he would deliver those not yet delivered—he next praises his second [vow]: that in the past he maintained the precepts;

since these precepts are the antidote to the defilement of transgressions, and because one is liberated from the bonds of defilement through this antidote, he says "liberated," thereby separately praising the second [vow] for liberating those not yet liberated.
The vow "to continue the lineage of the Triple Gem" is a distinct praise of the third vow within this immeasurable Dharma-gate.

If one speaks of carving sandalwood, casting precious metal, copying the *sūtras*, shaving the head, or dyeing the robes, these merely represent the continuity of the Triple Gem through conventional signs and appearances.
However, if one gives rise to the bodhicitta, this is called the essence of the Buddha-Gem; and if one understands the Great Way, this is called the matter and principle of the Dharma-Gem.
The harmonious fusion of these is called the Jewel of the Sangha; this is precisely the non-interruption of the Three Jewels of the Principle-nature (*dharmatā*). The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"Wherever this scroll is located, there is the Buddha and his honored disciples. Furthermore, it says: "If one knows that [the Dharma] is eternally abiding, one should know that this household has the Buddha present.
Inferring from this, the non-interruption of the Three Jewels is itself the immeasurable Dharma.
The gate into the future world is the fourth vow, which distinguishes itself from the aforementioned unsurpassed Buddha-way by means of its vows;
this third section on "Great Adornment" concludes the Four Great Vows.
One adorns oneself with the Great Adornments (*mahā-vyūha*).
This also serves as a double conclusion for the aforementioned seeking of enlightenment above and transforming beings below; thus it is called the "Great Adornment.

If treated as a separate conclusion for the fourth vow, it means that in the future, upon becoming a Buddha, one will adorn the body with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and adorn the mind with the ten powers (*daśabala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

The "Great Ornamentation" (Mahāvyūha) chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* frequently employs the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) as ornaments;

the middle portion of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* takes non-ornamentation as its ornament; and the subsequent sections employ the merit of the six perfections and the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) as two types of ornaments.
The sixth section, the conclusion on the lower [stage], also has two parts: first the general, then the specific.
It concludes the aforementioned seeking of the higher and transforming of the lower through merit and wisdom; subsequently, it generally observes all sentient beings as if looking upon an only son.
The passage "The disciple descends" below refers specifically to the conclusion of the four great vows for transforming others.
Next, the phrase "also at dawn" and so forth refers to the invocation of light;
that is, also at dawn, when the sun first rises, one encounters the Buddha’s radiance.
Next, the raising of the body hairs and the departure constitute the summoning by following the light.
When the body hairs stand on end, blood appears over the entire body like *pārijātaka* flowers, tears fill the eyes, and great suffering arises,
this is likewise for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, and for the accomplishment of the supreme empty conduct (*śūnyacaryā*) of the Mahāyāna.
It preserves the body, mind, and speech, as well as the three obstacles and so forth;
it manifests the departure and reverent compliance with the invocation of sound;
and it manifests the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings of skillful means in order that various forms of Dharma preaching may never be interrupted.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he went forth to summon the earth by means of compliance;

for the sake of the causes and conditions for the subduing of all sentient beings, he quickly arrived at the place of the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times,
and with palms joined in reverence, withdrew to stand to one side.
The explanation is as above (etc.).
Regarding the section on "three times two Ganges-sands" and below, which lists the miscellaneous assemblies, it is divided into three parts: first, twenty-one assemblies with increasing numbers;
second, eight assemblies with identical numbers; third, one assembly with no fixed number. The first two [sections] regarding the Ganges-sands are further divided into three (etc.). First:
Among those summoned, there are also several categories named "Chanting the Bonds" (Jianjie).
The first two are constant enumerations.
At that time, there were further [beings] as numerous as the sands of two Ganges Rivers.
Because it is not known by the world, it is measured by constancy.
Next is the category of the upāsaka.
All upāsakas who receive and uphold the five precepts are fully endowed with dignified deportment.

The *Śāriputra-abhidharma* refers to them as "men and women free from desire" (*vītarāga-puruṣa-strī*); the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to them as "pure-faith laymen and laywomen" (*śraddhā-upāsaka-upāsikā*);
the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* refers to them as "meritorious men and meritorious women" (*puṇya-puruṣa-puṇya-strī*), or alternatively as "virtuous-lodging men and women.

Although there are many such varieties, they are collectively termed the "two assemblies of householders. If one speaks of them specifically, although their physical appearance remains that of the laity, they have never married and always follow [the path] as such.
Regarding those who come to join the two assemblies: this refers to the two assemblies of those free from desire.
If one has previously married but now upholds the five precepts, forever severing secular ways, they are of service to the Buddha-dharma and are called a *śikṣamāṇa* (vowed layperson).

If one does not violate secular laws while upholding the five precepts and further adds the eight fast-day observances (*upavāsa*), they are called a virtuous male or female devotee (*upāsaka* or *upāsikā*). Furthermore, there are those who simply take the three refuges.

One who possesses none [of the precepts] is called a nominal *upāsaka*; one who possesses one or two is called one with a small portion; one who possesses three or four is called one with a large portion;
and one who fully maintains all five is called one with a complete portion. The Sūtra states that "complete" (*paripūrṇa*) is precisely the "full portion.

Furthermore, one who merely maintains the five precepts while seeking human or celestial rebirth is one with no portion; whereas one who, in addition, fears the suffering of birth and death and aspires for *nirvāṇa* is one with a portion.

If it is for the sake of sentient beings only to a small degree, while knowing that the precepts are subsumed within the Dharma-realm and are practiced exclusively for the sake of the Buddha-way to a great degree, this is the "complete" [practice].
One who is fully endowed with dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) possesses such deportment:

they are always accompanied by propriety, always accompanied by the precepts, always accompanied by impermanence, always accompanied by compassion, and always accompanied by the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
In the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, one can manifest various forms pervading the ten realms; every lifting and lowering of the feet is endowed with the Buddha-dharma.
Even in brothels and taverns, there is nothing that is not the True Path, as one abides in the majestic deportment of a Buddha—this is what is meant by being "fully endowed.

One should know that the five precepts and the rules of deportment have both a fundamental essence and a manifested trace; being able to remain unmoved within this essence, one universally manifests before all beings.

This is called the observance of the full precepts (*upāsaka-śīla*). Regarding the meaning of the question on the *upāsaka*, if one asks how the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas further respond, the underlying principle is necessarily as follows:
I have not yet seen such a teaching in the scriptures, and perhaps some may not believe it; therefore, I shall now attempt to explain it.

The four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*) belong to those who are without [fixed] status (*aniyata-gotra*); the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) belongs to those with a limited portion; and the second and third fruits belong to those with a greater portion.
For the most part, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are "complete"; furthermore, regarding these four categories, if they pertain to the Mahāyāna, they are all "incomplete.
If one has severed as many *rajas* (dust-like afflictions) as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, it is "small"; if one has severed one or two grades of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is "much";
and if one has exhausted all ignorance, it is "complete. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Today we are truly *śrāvakas*, for by the Buddha..."
The sound of the Way is heard by all, which constitutes the majority of Śrāvakas; those at the stage of "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-vipaśyanā) are Bodhisattvas who have no portion [of realization].
From the stage of the "eight persons" up to the sixth bhūmi, the severing of afflictions is equal to that of the Han [Chinese] practitioners, which is a small portion.

On the seventh bhūmi, one cultivates the path of skillful means, which is a large portion. On the eighth bhūmi, the path and contemplation flow together as a dual stream, which is the full portion. Furthermore, there are thirty... [text continues].
The mind is "undivided" (*amśika*); the first and second stages are "partially divided" (*pradeśika*); from the third to the ninth stages it is "mostly divided" (*bhūyastva*);

and the tenth stage is "fully divided" (*paripūrṇa*). Furthermore, the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) are undivided; the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) are partially divided; the ten practices and ten transferences (*daśa-caryā-daśa-pratipatti*) are mostly divided; and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) are fully divided.
Moreover, according to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), the thirty minds of the distinct [teaching] (*viśeṣa-triṃśac-citta*) are undivided.

The completion of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) apart from the ten abodes (*vihāra*) constitutes the partial fulfillment; the completion of the ten practices (*caryā*) and the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) constitutes the majority fulfillment;

and the completion of the ten stages constitutes the full fulfillment. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet because they lack its manifestation and function, they are "Buddhas without parts.
In the first abode and the first stage, one can act as a Buddha within a hundred realms; this is the "partial Buddha. In the second abode and the second stage... [and so forth].
The above refers to Buddhas of "great portion" (bahu-bhāga), while those of "full portion" (paripūrṇa) are Buddhas of wondrous enlightenment (*vimala-jñāna*).

For this reason, every Dharma-gate possesses both the provisional and the real, as well as the original and the trace; this is precisely that meaning. Question: What is the meaning of the beetle (*gōngqiāng*) and the scorpion (*fùchài*)?
Answer: Generally, a single wholesome dharma has four aspects; by analogy, a single unwholesome dharma should also be understood in this way. Furthermore—
Setting aside the discussion of the "Teaching of Names" (mingjiao), let us speak instead of the provisional (quan). The deeds performed by a small bodhisattva constitute the "no-part" (wufen);
those performed by one at the first stage of the ten stages (dizhu) constitute the "small part"; up to those performed by one at the tenth stage and so forth constitute the "large part";
and the deeds performed by a Tathāgata constitute the "fulfilled part. Therefore, there exists the distinction between the provisional and the real.
Because this assembly truly summoned and entreated him by means of skillful means, it is called "Summoning and Entreaty.
Their names are listed in the three columns below:
their names include the Upāsaka King of Undefiled Majestic Virtue, the Upāsaka Good Virtue, and others.

Regarding the "foremost leaders," only two individuals are listed: Vimalakīrti-rāja (the King Without Stain), who was likely the one who rebuked the eight thousand [bodhisattvas] and censured the five hundred [monks], namely Vimalakīrti;
and Śubhavyūha (the One of Auspicious Virtue), who was likely the son of the householder who organized the sacrificial assembly.
This refers to those very individuals, the foremost among the two groups of *gaṅgā* [bodhisattvas].

They deeply delight in contemplation. Below are four sections praising their virtues: first, the praise of their prior aspiration; second, the praise of their subsequent vow; third, the praise of their superior seeking; and fourth, the praise of their downward transformation.
Following the thirteen points of counteractive measures, this constitutes the praise of their superior seeking.
He deeply delights in observing the various gates of antidotes, namely:

suffering and pleasure, permanence and impermanence, purity and impurity, self and non-self, reality and unreality, refuge and non-refuge, sentient beings and non-sentient beings, the eternal and the non-eternal, peace and non-peace, the conditioned and the unconditioned, cessation and non-cessation, nirvana and non-nirvana, and the supreme and the non-supreme; he constantly and joyfully contemplates these.
Regarding such dharmas as these gates of remediation, they likewise desire to hear the unsurpassed Mahāyāna;

having heard it, they are able to explain it to others, maintain pure precepts well, and thirst for the Mahāyāna. Having themselves attained fulfillment, they can further satisfy the thirst of others;
they are skillfully able to gather supreme wisdom, delight in the Mahāyāna, and protect the Mahāyāna.
The former [commentators] said: "Taking suffering as medicine to treat the disease of pleasure, and likewise with the impermanent and the permanent, etc.

Now it is clarified that this was merely the initial teaching and is not the intent of the present sutra. The former [commentators] further said: "These various remedies are the contemplation of the six aspects (*ṣaḍākāra-bhāvanā*).
Citing the following passage: "The impermanent is birth-and-death; the permanent is Great Nirvāṇa. There is no [contradiction].
"Self" refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; "self" also refers to the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.

"Suffering" refers to all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); "bliss" refers to Great Nirvāṇa. "Impurity" refers to all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma); "purity" refers to the true Dharma possessed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, these six modes of contemplation were not explained previously, but are only detailed starting from the second fascicle.
It is only within the parable of the birds that this is first clarified: their traveling together should not be used to praise the virtues of the *upāsaka*.
This is the general meaning drawn from later [sections] by the compiler of the sutra, which he then projects forward to offer praise. Xinghuang likewise stated:
"When the bhikṣus first arrived, none of them were yet arhats"; the compiler took their later realization of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and projected it forward.

The bhikṣu sighed, saying: "It is not so for the monastic assembly; how could it be thus for the laity? You should know that the Buddha’s fellow practitioners have long mastered this contemplation, which is why he sighed.
Furthermore, regarding the discernment of the one [path]: when medicine and disease correspond to one another, this may be considered a remedy;

however, when the six practices move in tandem, how can this be considered a remedy? The explanation says: when medicine and disease correspond, the disease departs but the medicine remains; this is partial.

The sixfold practice of counteracting through dual movement, where each serves alternately as medicine or illness until the illness is eliminated and the medicine vanishes, constitutes "perfect counteraction" (*paripūrṇa-pratipakṣa*).
If this is so, then for those who have long practiced alongside the Buddha and are thoroughly proficient in the six contemplations, they will not harbor doubts upon hearing this praise;

but what about other practitioners of reality? Even those who are provisionally guided toward the ultimate can attain this, as stated in the following passage: "Those who receive the preceding teachings..."

Using the medicine of impermanence to counteract the disease of permanence—though the disease of permanence may depart, one again clings to impermanence—hears the medicine of eternal abiding to destroy the disease of impermanence;
this is precisely what is employed in the present teaching. As for the three types of cultivation discussed below, using the superior to break the inferior is the same principle.
Second, those who originally did not receive the preceding teachings [are taught] through the sequence of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
First one cultivates impermanence to remedy permanence, and next one cultivates permanence to remedy impermanence;
by destroying the twenty-five states of existence, one attains the twenty-five samādhis and dwells in Great Nirvāṇa. This is the ocean of Great Nirvāṇa, which gradually becomes deeper.
Thus, it fully possesses two kinds of remedies. How can one distinguish between them? One is the former teaching, and the other is the latter teaching.

Regarding the third [aspect] of what has been taught: furthermore, there is one practice which is the practice of the Tathāgata, fully endowed with permanence, impermanence, both permanence and impermanence, and neither permanence nor impermanence.
It consists in the perfect cultivation of the six contemplations to simultaneously treat permanence and impermanence, such that the medicine and the illness act as mutual remedies;
when the illness is eliminated, the medicine perishes, and when the illness is treated, both are abandoned. Therefore, this is called the "Gate of Counteractive Treatment" (pratipakṣa-mukha). If...

Regarding the discourse on practicing all modes of conduct through a single mode of conduct, it is as clear as the noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*). As for the discourse on the dual practice, it is explained by the analogy of the bird.
It is said that the lay followers (*upāsaka*) who possess these virtuous qualities are still shallow in the first two cases, while in the latter case they are profound.

The text states: "Deeply delighting in the contemplation of the various doors of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*"); this praises the intention of the third [category]. Regarding the fifty-two types of faculties and dispositions...
The three kinds of provisional [teachings] are identical in not departing from the ultimate reality; they lead toward Nirvana so that one may enter it.

Since not even a single kind exists there, how much less could there be three? This is the meaning of the gate of true counteraction, and it also reveals the intent of the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings on skillful means (*upāya*).
Within this text, the provisional is praised precisely for its guidance toward the ultimate. If there were no practice of the ultimate, what would the provisional be?
If that which is induced lacks skillful means (*upāya*), there is truly nothing to rely upon; since one praises skillful means, one also incidentally praises reality (*tattva*).
Why, then, do you judge them as belonging to the preceding or subsequent teachings? If one were to analyze this by examining each phrase, one should say:

to sink into the conventional is suffering, while to sink into the ultimate is bliss; to sink into the ultimate is suffering, while to differentiate [the conventional] is bliss. The same applies to permanence, self, purity, and so forth.
Furthermore, to sink into emptiness is suffering while Great Nirvana is bliss; to sink into emptiness is bliss while Great Nirvana is suffering.
This applies equally to the superior and the non-superior. Question: What is the difference between "constant" (*nitya*) and "eternal" (*dhruva*)?

Answer: That which does not arise from causes and conditions is "constant"; that which remains unchanged from beginning to end is "eternal. All such [distinctions] are the maladies of the two extremes.

The mutual relationship between medicine and illness is termed a "gate" (mukha) for penetrating entry into the Middle Way; it is neither medicine nor illness, transcending both extremes and the middle.

For those who delight in hearing this, it is precisely the aforementioned meaning of revering the Mahāyāna. Like the ocean receiving all streams or space containing all forms, one who can explain this to others knows that wisdom resides in the teaching.
Such skillful wisdom understands the profound and simultaneously encompasses the transformation of those below, bringing them to equality.
This is taking principle as the intent of the Mahāyāna. Those who thirst for and yearn for the Mahāyāna correspond to those who dwell securely and are fully satisfied above;

the intent of those who additionally thirst for and yearn for it includes the transformation of others below, and those who are well able to gather [beings] in correspond to those who deeply understand and delight in it above.
As for "guarding" according to phenomena above, and "according to teaching" above, they are likewise applied.
Being well able to accord with [the needs of others] is praised as the downward transformation;
being well able to accord with all worlds to deliver those not yet delivered and liberate those not yet liberated,
thereby continuing the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it is never severed in future ages, one shall turn the wheel of Dharma.
The general and specific praises of the four great vows are as explained above.
"Adorned with the Great Adornments" is the concluding praise, also as explained above.
Being adorned by these Great Adornments, his mind constantly and deeply relishes the practice of pure precepts.
They are fully able to sever the five fetters as described in the text;

they are fully able to accomplish such meritorious qualities and give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, regarding them with impartiality and non-duality as if looking upon an only child.
Next, one also offers the invocation at dawn;
likewise, at the time when the sun first rises in the morning,
the very moment of offering the invocation constitutes the three invocations of seeing, hearing, and perceiving.
In order to perform the cremation, they called out in unison.
To cremate the body of the Tathāgata, every person took ten thousand bundles of fragrant wood—such as sandalwood, aloeswood, gośīrṣa-candana, and celestial incense;
in the grain of each piece of wood, and even in its pores, there were the seven treasures.
Subtle and wondrous light, like various kinds of multicolored painted ornaments, manifests these exquisite colors— blue, yellow, red, and white— through the power of the Buddha,
so that all sentient beings may behold them with joy. All the trees are anointed with various fragrances,
such as saffron, aloeswood, and resinous incense, and are further adorned by the scattering of many flowers, including the *utpala* lotus.

Kumuda flowers, padma flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, along with various fragrant trees, had five-colored banners suspended from them—soft and exquisite like celestial garments, kauśeya silk, or kṣauma cloth.
These fragrant trees were carried upon jeweled chariots, which emitted various lights of blue, yellow, red, and white; their axles and wheels were all [adorned with jewels].
These were inlaid with the seven precious gems; each carriage was drawn by a team of four horses, and each horse was as swift as the wind.
Before each carriage stood fifty-seven exquisite jeweled banners, covered above by nets of pure gold.
Furthermore, each jeweled carriage had fifty exquisite jeweled canopies, and from each carriage hung various flower garlands.
There were *utpala*, *kumuda*, *padma*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers,
whose petals were made entirely of pure gold and whose calyxes were made of diamond. Within these flower calyxes, many black bees gathered and congregated,
sporting and enjoying themselves, while emitting a wondrous sound— namely, the sounds of "impermanence," "suffering," "emptiness," and "non-self."

Furthermore, it is said that in the path originally traversed by the Bodhisattva, there were various kinds of singing, dancing, and musical performances—zithers, flutes, lutes, pipes, harps, and drums.
From amidst these musical sounds, this cry emerged: "Alas! Alas! The world is empty and void!
Before each chariot, an upāsaka held aloft a tray made of the four jewels; upon these trays were various kinds of flowers.
Utpala flowers, kumuda flowers, padma flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers; saffron and various other incenses,
all of which were most subtle and supreme— these were provided by the upāsakas for the Buddha and the Saṅgha as various provisions for food,
fully prepared with sandalwood, aloeswood, and fragrant fuel, and matured by water possessing the eight qualities.
The food was sweet and delicious, possessing six kinds of flavors: first, bitter; second, sour; third, sweet; fourth, pungent; fifth, salty; and sixth, bland.
Furthermore, it possessed three qualities: first, lightness and softness; second, purity and cleanliness; and third, being prepared according to the Dharma.
Adorned with various such refinements, [the meal] reached the place of birth of the Malla, between the twin śāla trees, where golden sand was spread everywhere.
The ground was covered with kāliṅga cloth, kṣauma cloth, and variegated silken fabrics, spreading completely over the sand for twelve yojanas.
For the Buddha and the Saṃgha, he prepared lion-thrones made of the seven precious jewels;
these thrones were as high and large as Mount Sumeru, and upon each throne there was a jeweled canopy from which various necklaces hung down.
The *śāla* trees were all hung with various kinds of exquisite banners and canopies;
various fine incenses were used to anoint the trees, and various named flowers were scattered among them.
What does the preceding passage reveal regarding the Esoteric Teachings (*guhyamantra*), and how is this cremation (*jābī*) to be harmonized with the renunciation of the Sangha?

The assembly directly proclaimed this: for these lay followers, phenomena are manifested through events, and the Dharma is communicated by means of material wealth. Regarding the term *jāva* (cremation), it signifies "burning";

the preparation of fragrant wood is a means of using burning to manifest non-burning, and using extinction to clarify non-extinction—thereby revealing that which is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished.
The preparation of offerings and food is a means of using food to clarify non-eating, thereby revealing that which is not [merely] non-eating.
Regarding food and non-food, through skillful means one attains the opening of the Esoteric Teaching and realizes the Manifestation;

this honoring of the invocation of fragrant wood with its various adornments signifies that while extinction is luminous, it is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished, and thus there are various sublime Dharmas.
Food possesses the three virtues and six flavors, and the jeweled canopy and jeweled throne are all exquisitely adorned; this symbolizes the vastness of compassion.
The *Jili zhong* (Essentials of the Middle Way) also contains various dharma-gates.
From the point where it says, "Each of the upāsakas had this thought," it proceeds to describe their movement toward [the Buddha].
Each of the upāsakas had this thought: "If any sentient beings lack anything—whether food, drink, clothing, or garments..."

Whether it be his head, eyes, limbs, or body, he gives them all away according to whatever is required. When practicing such giving, he is free from desire, hatred, defilement, and poisonous thoughts;
without any remaining aspiration for worldly blessings or pleasures, his mind is set solely upon unsurpassed, pure bodhi.

The previous statement, "for the sake of the causes and conditions for the subduing of all sentient beings," clarifies here that the intention is the same: to gather in sentient beings through *dāna* (generosity) so that they may be subdued.
From the passage beginning with "these upāsakas and others have all already established themselves" onwards, this follows the invocation of the Light.
These upāsakas, all of whom were already firmly established in the path of the bodhisattvas, further thought:

"Now that the Tathāgata has accepted our food, he shall enter parinirvāṇa. Having had this thought, the hairs on their bodies stood on end, blood appeared over their entire bodies like *pārijātaka* flowers, their tears filled their eyes, and they were overcome with great suffering and distress.
One should eliminate the three obstructions; now, merely generating the goodness of the three karmas is as stated in the text.
Next, "each carrying [offerings] and departing" refers to making offerings, which also constitutes the text for the ritual of summoning.
Each person brought their own offerings, loaded them onto precious chariots, and swiftly arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling with incense wood, banners, pennants, jeweled parasols, food, and drink.
Prostrating themselves at the Buddha’s feet, they presented the offerings they had brought to the Tathāgata.
They circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, wailing aloud with voices that moved heaven and earth; they beat their breasts and cried out loudly, tears falling like rain.
Again, they said to one another, "Alas, O virtuous ones! The world is empty; the world is empty!
Thereupon, each raised their own body and threw themselves before the Tathāgata, addressing the Buddha: "We pray only that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.
The World-Honored One, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept. Thus, although the upāsakas made this request three times, he did not grant it in any instance.
Their wishes unfulfilled, they remained silent with hearts filled with sorrow and distress, just like a compassionate father whose only son has suddenly fallen ill and passed away;
having returned from the funeral rites, he is overcome with extreme grief.
The upāsakas likewise wept and lamented in distress, setting aside their various offerings in one place and withdrawing to sit silently to one side.

The next three passages concerning the *gaṅgānadīvālukā* (sands of the Ganges) constitute three [sections] (*yùn*). [The phrase] "those summoned" constitutes the fourth, namely: number, category, name, and praise.
Of these, the first three *gaṅgānadīvālukā* refer to number.
At that time, there were again [as many as] three *gaṅgānadīvālukā*.
The section following "Next, the Upāsikās" is explained in the same manner as above.
These various upāsikās have received and maintain the five precepts and are fully endowed with dignified conduct.
Following the three types of longevity and virtue, the names of three individuals are listed below.
Their names were the laywoman Āyuṣmatī, the laywoman Guṇamālā, the laywoman Viśākhā, and others, with eighty-four thousand such as these as their leaders.
Because longevity was her virtue, she was called Āyuṣmatī; some say that Guṇamālā is Śrīmālā, and that Śrīmālā is [Guṇamālā].
The King’s consort should not be of such a class; Śakra is the mother of the thirty-two eggs.
From "All are able to endure" onwards, there are two sections: first, a brief praise of the virtues of seeking above and transforming those below;
second, an extensive praise of seeking above and transforming those below.
Being able to endure all things and protect the True Dharma for the sake of delivering immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, she manifests in a female body.
Her initial endurance and protection constitute a brief praise of those who seek the higher [enlightenment] and protect the teachings of the True Dharma;
as described above, those who guard the Mahāyāna uphold the affairs and principles of the True Dharma, and thus revere the Mahāyāna.
This refers to the concise eulogy of her who, out of her great love for the Mahāyāna and her vow to deliver hundreds of thousands of beings,
manifested in a female body as the result of her vast vows.

Next, following the section on reprimanding the household, there follows an extensive praise of seeking the higher [enlightenment] and transforming those below; this is an expansion upon the intent of protection and maintenance.
Within this extensive praise, there are three parts: first, seeking the higher; second, transforming those below; and third, a double conclusion of seeking the higher and transforming those below.

Regarding the first, seeking the higher, the text is divided into two sections: first, the contemplation of the matter (*vastu*), and second, the conclusion regarding the accomplishment of merit. As for the contemplation of the matter:
Second, first the object of the practice is indicated, followed by the presentation of five gates.

Regarding the "reproving of household methods," the initial reproving of household methods refers to the observation of the object; if one were to consider only the broom and the duties of a wife as "the household," [it would be insufficient].
The Dharma is too restrictive if one takes the cycle of the three realms as its home; yet it is too expansive if one takes the five aggregates as its home.

Its karmic fruits and retributions are narrow and constricting, like being confined within a cage or a pen—something nurtured and cherished by the foolish and ordinary, but despised and rejected by the sages and saints.
Therefore, it is called "reproach."
One should observe one's own body as being like four venomous snakes; this body is constantly being devoured by immeasurable worms;
this body is foul and filthy, bound by the prison of craving; this body is loathsome, like a dead dog;
this body is impure, with nine orifices constantly flowing; this body is like a city, with flesh, blood, sinews, and bones wrapped in skin, and the hands and feet serving as its gates.
The defensive towers and battlements are called the sense-faculties (*āyatana*), the head is the main hall, and the King of the Mind dwells in the center.
This city of the body has been abandoned by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, yet it is constantly relished by foolish ordinary beings.
Within it dwell the rākṣasas of greed, hatred, and delusion; this body is as unstable as a reed, an *eraṇḍa* tree, or a bubble on the water.
The plantain tree is like this body: impermanent and not abiding for even a single thought-moment. It is like a flash of lightning, a torrential flood, or a mirage;
it is like drawing on water, where as soon as one draws, it vanishes. This body is easily destroyed, like a great tree standing on a steep riverbank.
Before long, this body shall be devoured by foxes, wolves, owls, hawks, vultures, crows, magpies, and hungry dogs.
What wise person would take pleasure in this body? Next, one observes one's own body from below;

first is the contemplation of suffering (*duḥkha-anupaśyanā*), wherein the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) harm one another and various insects further gnaw at them, while the elements themselves prey upon one another, making the body a thicket of suffering.
This body is foul and impure; this is the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-anupaśyanā*), which consists of five types.
It is impure. Those bound by the prison of desire are covered by a thin skin and falsely called "pure";
because they are entangled without end, it is called a "prison. A dead dog is ultimately impure; its nine orifices constantly flow, being impure by its own nature.
Like a city, it is established as empty through false conditions—mud, wood, earth, and stone—and is filled with the evils of the three poisons. Observe this as emptiness.
A ghost stands within it, deceiving those outside while being sycophantic toward those inside; therefore, it is called "empty. That this body is not solid is the contemplation of non-self;
that this body is impermanent is the contemplation of impermanence. These two contemplations, coarse and subtle, are as explained in the text.
Next, from "How much more so than a cow's footprint," one binds the merit and binds the contemplation of the matter; these together constitute the seventh [section].
First, by means of the analogy, one binds the contemplation of the matter, observing that the faults and afflictions of this body are exceedingly vast.
It would be easier to contain the waters of the great ocean in the footprint of an ox than to fully describe the impermanence, impurity, and foul stench of this body;

it would be easier to roll the great earth into pellets the size of jujube fruits, gradually reducing them to the size of mustard seeds and even down to atoms, than to fully describe the defects of this body.
Therefore, one should abandon it as one discards snot or sleep.
Next, he raises the three samādhis to explain their underlying principles and profound subtlety.
For this reason, the upāsikās constantly cultivate their minds through the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Regarding "causes and conditions," the contemplation of phenomena consists of searching and examining both internally and externally; because they cannot be found, they are empty of emptiness, lacking the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) and even lacking the characteristic of emptiness itself.
Because they are without characteristics, there is no volitional activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*). The *Śāstra* explains:
"The two vehicles contemplate the Truth (*tattva*) through the three samādhis, while Bodhisattvas contemplate the true nature (*dharmatā*) through the three samādhis," and so forth.
Third, citing the Mahāyāna, he concludes the matter by showing that the contemplation accords with the sūtras;
[the practitioner] deeply delights in inquiring about and receiving the Mahāyāna scriptures.
Fourth, citing the one who can preach, he concludes that while seeking the higher [attainment], one does not lose the lower [capacity for] transforming others.
Having heard it, one is also able to expound it for others;
this "contemplation of the matter" (*vastu-vipaśyanā*) is the method for instructing others.

Fifth, "protecting and upholding" refers to protecting and upholding [the teaching] by summarizing the contemplation of the matter, which is the contemplation of principle (*tattva-vipaśyanā*) that remains unmoving within its original ground.
"Upholding the original vow" refers to the sixth [point],
which describes the acts of disparagement and censure; that is, it concludes the matter of the Bodhisattva’s fundamental vow by observing what is brought about by this power of aspiration.
One should disparage the female body as being extremely loathsome and its nature as unstable.
By contemplating these seven matters, one attains right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), which can destroy birth and death.
Constantly cultivating such right contemplation, one breaks through the boundless cycle of saṃsāra and yearns for the Mahāyāna.
Having already satisfied herself, she is further able to satisfy others who thirst for and yearn after the Dharma; she deeply delights in the Mahāyāna and protects the Mahāyāna.
Although she manifests in a female body, she is in truth a bodhisattva—this can be seen in the text (and so forth).
This meaning is entirely the male counterpart to the section on upāsikās as a door of remediation.
Her nature is upright and straightforward; however, because she specifically addresses the affliction of female attachment, she provides five gates.
These five gates take the true reality as their causal condition; thus, principle is present within phenomena. This is a wondrous antidote.

In the chapter on Bodhisattvas, her deep delight in the Mahāyāna and her protection of the Mahāyāna are the same as those mentioned above. Although she manifests in a female body, she is in truth a Bodhisattva.
This refers to those who securely abide in the Mahāyāna.
Next, following the praise for those who are well-able to conform [to the world] and proceed downward to transform others, the virtues are explained as above (*etc.*).
They are well-able to conform to all worlds, delivering those not yet delivered and liberating those not yet liberated, thereby continuing the lineage of the Triple Gem.
They shall ensure that the Wheel of Dharma is not interrupted in future ages, but continues to turn.
Third, through great adornment, they eliminate the two fetters, seeking the higher while transforming those below.
Adorning themselves with great adornment, they firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts and fully accomplish such meritorious virtues.
"Regarding all sentient beings, one should give rise to great compassion, equal and non-dual, as if looking upon them as an only child.
This is explained as above (*etc.*).
"Also at dawn" means to be summoned.
Furthermore, at the break of dawn when the sun first rose, they each said to one another, "Let us go; this is the time for summoning.
They each said to one another, "Today we ought to go to the space between the twin trees."
Those who were appropriate to be invited should be summoned in accordance with propriety.
They presented offerings in two portions.

The various *upāsikās* brought forth offering materials that were twice as superior as those previously prepared, and having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet.
Having circumambulated the Buddha hundreds of thousands of times, they addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, we have now prepared various offerings for the Buddha and the Sangha;
we only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our offering. The Tathāgata remained silent and did not grant his permission.
The upāsikās, their wishes unfulfilled, felt despondent at heart and withdrew to stand to one side.
[The section on] respectful demeanor (*kṛtya*) [is as follows].

Next, the four groups of *gaṅgā* beings are divided into two [sections] (as detailed below). Among those summoned, there are several categories; the praise of their names constitutes the first four *gaṅgā* numbers.
At that time, there were furthermore [as many as] four Ganges-sands [of beings].
Next were those in the city of Vaiśālī and its like;
the Licchavis of the city of Vaiśālī—men and women, great and small, wives and children, retinues—as well as those of Jambudvīpa.
The retinues of the various kings.
*Vaiśālī* is translated as "Good Path" (*hǎodào*) by Master Zào; "Extensive Purity" (*guǎngyán*) by Master Shí; and "Extensive and Broad" (*guǎngbó*) [by others].

These names all derive from the fact that the streets and lanes of the country were magnificent and orderly. *Licchavi* is also transliterated as *Lichang*, *Mili*, or *Chumi*; these are merely differences between the Chu and Xia dialects.

Regarding this, it is said that they are "border-lord rulers" (*pratyantapāladhipati*), or alternatively, "those who transmit the governance of the state. Master Guan states: "In that country, there is a tradition of yielding office;

five hundred elders take turns serving as the sovereign. Therefore, it is said that they 'transmit the governance of the state. Once their term of office has ended, they depart for the border regions to serve as border-lord rulers, and so forth.
As for the phrase "the retinues of the various kings," these are all Licchavis who successively act as one another's [rulers].
The King then had imperial kinsmen and maternal relatives who were likewise included among the royal class.

Third, regarding the quest for the Dharma, there is a praise of his virtues, which is divided into two parts: first, the praise itself, and second, the conclusion of the praise. Within the first part, there are two sections;
first, a single phrase clarifies the "aspiring upward" for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
For the sake of seeking the Dharma, the next three pairs constitute the lower transformation: first, the precept of giving;

second, the thorough cultivation of ethical conduct and the perfection of dignified demeanor; and third, subduing heterodox teachers and those who destroy the true Dharma, while constantly addressing one another as follows:
We shall use our gold, silver, and treasuries to ensure that the profound treasury of the inexhaustible, ambrosial, and sublime True Dharma remains long in the world;
we pray that we may always have the opportunity to study and practice it.
Second, regarding the methods of subduing and gathering:
if there are those who slander the Buddha’s True Dharma, one should cut out their tongues and further make this vow:

"If there are those who leave the household life and violate the prohibitive precepts, I shall cause them to be dismissed and return to lay life; yet, I shall employ those who are able to deeply delight in protecting and upholding the True Dharma."
I shall honor and serve them as I would my own parents; if there are members of the Saṃgha who are able to practice the True Dharma, I shall rejoice in it and cause them to gain power.
Listen to this third time.
They always desire to hear Mahāyāna sūtras, and having heard them, they are also able to explain them extensively for others.
As the text describes, they manifest downward transformation while simultaneously seeking upward transcendence.
Next, from the phrase "all are fully accomplished" onwards, the removal of fetters follows the text.
They have all fully accomplished such meritorious virtues.
Their names are listed as in the text:
Viśuddhavimalagarbha Licchavi, Viśuddhāpramāda Licchavi, Gaṅgā... [and so forth].
The Licchavi Śuddhaphalgu and the others addressed one another in this manner; such was their mutual exhortation.
Thus they spoke to one another: "Virtuous sirs, you should now proceed quickly to the place where the Buddha is."

If there were no summoning by invitation, how could there be compliance? By observing compliance, one knows that there is an inviting summons; thus, while the movement of compliance is clarified through the summoning, the rest may be understood accordingly.
Next, the offerings are presented.
The various requisites for the offering were fully prepared;

each Licchavi adorned eighty-four thousand great elephants, eighty-four thousand chariots drawn by teams of four horses, eighty-four thousand moon-bright jewels, and eighty-four thousand bundles of celestial *candana* and aloeswood incense, with each category numbering eighty-four thousand.
Before each elephant stood a precious banner and pennant.
Their canopies were small ones measuring a full yojana in circumference and breadth; their banners were at least thirty-two yojanas long;
and the lower parts of their precious standards were one hundred yojanas high.

Carrying such articles of worship, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we now..."
He prepared various offerings for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, saying, "I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept my offering.
The Tathāgata remained silent and did not grant his permission. The Licchavis, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress;
by the supernatural power of the Buddha, they rose seven *tāla* trees' height above the ground and remained suspended in mid-air in silence.
The respectful demeanor is as described in the text. Regarding the "seven *tāla* trees": this refers to one whose nature is upright and lofty, who does not remain beneath other things;
the Buddha’s power received him at a height of seven trees. Alternatively, it is said that this is merely according to the circumstances.
Next, regarding the five great ministers and elders, the text is divided into two parts: those summoned and those who responded to the summons.
There are several categories of praise for their names and numbers, as detailed in the text.
At that time, there were furthermore [as many as] five Ganges-sands.
The minister and the elder sighed over those in the intermediate state who seek the higher while transforming those below, as described in the text;
they revered the Mahāyāna.
If there are followers of other teachings who slander the True Dharma, these individuals have the power to subdue them,
just as a shower of hail destroys grass and trees.
[Their names are listed as follows...]
Their names were the Elder Sūryaprabha, the Elder Lokapāla, and others such as these who served as the leaders.
They departed from the place where the offerings had been prepared, proceeding in accordance with the invocation.

The offerings they prepared were five times greater than those before; together they carried them to the space between the twin trees, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, we have now prepared these various offerings for the Buddha and the Sangha;
we only pray that you will take pity on us and accept our offerings. The Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept them. The elders—

These individuals, their wishes unfulfilled, harbored grief and distress; by the Buddha’s spiritual power, they rose seven *tāla* trees’ height from the ground and remained silently suspended in mid-air.
Among the various means employed, he was summoned to the space between the twin *śāla* trees by the sound of the regular meal being prepared, which is a summoning through movement.
"To harbor sorrow and distress is to follow the summoning of light" (and so forth).
Next, regarding the listing of the *śreṣṭhins* (householders): since it is stated that they are "six times superior to the former," these must be the six *nitya-dāna-pati*s (constant donors).

However, while the number of kings can be counted, the others—excluding the single person Ajātaśatru—do not require constant measurement; therefore, their number is simply not mentioned. This is the meaning of the text.
Regarding the three types of summoning—the summoned, the respectfully summoned, and the compliantly summoned—among those first summoned there were various classes of beings with specific names.
At that time, there was also the King of Vaiśālī together with his queen, the ladies of the harem, and his retinue;
as well as all the kings within Jambudvīpa, with the exception of Ajātaśatru, along with the people of the cities, towns, and villages.
Among the aforementioned categories, King Jina is excluded as he appears later;
his name is King Vimalacandra, and so forth,
with their names listed as they appear in the text.
To mobilize the fourfold army was equivalent to issuing a formal summons.
Each king, intending to proceed to the Buddha’s dwelling, mobilized his own fourfold army; each king had one hundred and eighty trillion people as his retinue.
These chariot forces were drawn by elephants and horses—the elephants possessed six tusks, and the horses were as swift as the wind.
The ornamental offerings were six times greater than those before; among the various jeweled canopies, even the smallest measured eight *yojanas* in circumference and breadth,
while the shortest banners were sixteen *yojanas* long and the lowest jeweled standards were thirty-six *yojanas* high.
These kings praised his virtues.

These kings dwelt securely in the True Dharma, despised false teachings, revered the Mahāyāna, took deep delight in the Mahāyāna, and felt compassion for sentient beings as if they were their only child.
The fragrance of the food and drink they possessed spread forth, filling four yojanas.

The fact that the praise of his virtues—consisting of his aspiration for the higher and his transformation of those below—is presented without a fixed sequence demonstrates that there is no fixed order.
Furthermore, he was summoned at the early morning;
likewise, it was at the early morning, at the time when the sun first rises.
Holding various kinds of sweet delicacies and the like is the rite of summoning.
Carrying these diverse, exquisite, and sweet foods to the space between the twin trees, they approached the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we have prepared these offerings for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; we only pray that the Tathāgata will look upon us with compassion."
Having received my final offering, the Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, did not grant their request;
those kings, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Next, regarding the seven groups of *gandharva* consorts: the former list refers to the consorts of the present age, while this current list refers to widowed ladies, virtuous women, and the like.
This text is divided into two parts: the "Summoning" (*āhvāna*) and the "Conformable Summoning" (*anurūpāhvāna*). The summoned entities belong to several categories, which are here praised by name.
At that time, there were also queens from as many kingdoms as there are grains of sand in seven Ganges Rivers;
with the sole exception of King Ajātaśatru’s queen— who, in order to deliver sentient beings,
manifested in a female body and constantly contemplated the activities of the body, perfuming her mind with the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Within this category, the Universal Monarchs are further distinguished; those who originally manifested as the traces of the three samādhis and served as female consorts were all provisional manifestations.
Their names are listed as follows: Queen Myō (Miao) of the Three Realms, Lady Aioku (Aide) of the Heavenly Humans, and so forth, including the wives of all such kings.
The names are as written in the text.
All are established in the praise of virtues;
they all abide entirely within the True Dharma, practicing the prohibitive precepts with perfect deportment, and possessing compassion for sentient beings.
"Regarding them as equal to an only son," "seeking [enlightenment] above and transforming [beings] below," and so forth, are all as stated in the text.
As for "each addressing one another," this refers to the sequential invocation as described in the text.
They said to one another, "We should now go quickly to the place where the World-Honored One is;

the offerings prepared by the kings, devas, and humans are seven times greater than before—incense, flowers, precious banners, silken streamers, flags, canopies, and the most exquisite food and drink.
The smallest of the precious canopies extends sixteen *yojanas* in circumference, and the shortest of the flags is thirty-six *yojanas* long, reaching down to the base of the precious banners."
These [offerings] extend sixty-eight *yojanas* in breadth, and the fragrance of the food and drink pervades and fills eight *yojanas*.
Carrying such articles of worship, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we have prepared these articles of offering for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; we only pray that the Tathāgata..."
Feeling compassion for me, the Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept my final offering.
