At that moment, the ladies, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress; they tore out their hair, beat their breasts, and wailed loudly like a compassionate mother who has recently lost her beloved child, then withdrew to one side and sat in silence.

Next, the passage concerning the assembly of goddesses from the eight Ganges rivers is divided into three parts (etc.). The first part, concerning the enumeration and names of those summoned, is as stated in the text.
At that time, there were furthermore [goddesses] as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges rivers.
Next are the class of celestial maidens (*devakanyā*).
These various celestial maidens are,
for the most part, of the class of celestial maidens belonging to the realms from the third light upwards to the fourth terrace downwards.
The names of the three rows are as they appear in the text.
They are headed by the goddess Viśālākṣī.

Regarding the passage beginning with "They spoke thus," the text praising their virtues is divided into three parts; first is the praise for what is seen with the *divyacakṣus* (heavenly eye) obtained through karmic retribution.
Next, these [beings] below praise those above for seeking the three virtues;
first, as the text says, they praise those below for their transformative activity, speaking thus: "Sisters, observe closely, observe closely!

These multitudes have prepared various kinds of sublime and excellent offerings, wishing to present them to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus. We, too, shall likewise prepare such solemn offerings."
With exquisite offerings, you have made worship to the Tathāgata; having accepted them, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa.

Sisters, it is extremely difficult for the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, to appear in the world, and it is even more difficult to make an offering at the very end. If the Buddha enters nirvāṇa, the world will become empty.
These goddesses delight in the Mahāyāna and desire to hear it; having heard it, they are also able to explain it extensively for others.
They thirst and yearn for the Mahāyāna, and having satisfied themselves, they are further able to satisfy those who likewise thirst and yearn for it. They protect the Mahāyāna;
if there are followers of other teachings who harbor hatred and envy toward the Mahāyāna, their power can crush them as hail destroys grass. They maintain and uphold the practice of the precepts.
He is fully endowed with dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
Next, in praising his superior aspiration, it is said that he desires to hear the Mahāyāna; this is his profound understanding of the Mahāyāna and his being fully endowed with dignified deportment.
He is securely established in the Mahāyāna; the rest is as in the text.
The third [point] is that he is well able to accord with those below; this is the explanation of "transforming those below" as previously stated.
He is well able to accord with all the world to deliver those not yet delivered and liberate those not yet liberated.
In future ages, he shall turn the wheel of Dharma and succeed to the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it is never severed. He trains in the Mahāyāna and is adorned with the great adornments.
Having thus adorned oneself and accomplished such immeasurable merits, one regards all sentient beings with impartial compassion as if looking upon an only child;
furthermore, at the break of dawn, one should perform this invocation.
Furthermore, at the break of dawn when the sun first rises, one should each take celestial *agaru* (sandalwood) incense;
this is for the purpose of summoning [the deities] according to the text (*yathāvidhi*), and so forth.
One should each take various kinds of celestial *agaru* and other incenses, doubling the amount of all the incense woods found in the human world; the fragrance of these woods—
It can extinguish the various foul odors and impurities among humanity. There are white chariots with white canopies, each drawn by four white horses;
upon every chariot, white curtains are spread, from the four sides of which hang golden bells.

There are various fragrant flowers, precious banners, flags, and canopies, along with exquisite sweet delicacies, various musical performances, and lion thrones spread out. The four legs of these thrones are made of pure, deep-blue lapis lazuli.
Behind each of their seats there was a couch made of the seven treasures, and before each seat stood a golden table.
Furthermore, there were lamp-stands made of the seven treasures, with various precious jewels serving as lamps. Sublime celestial flowers were strewn everywhere upon the ground.
After these goddesses had prepared such offerings, their hearts were filled with sorrowful emotion, and their tears flowed freely.
Experiencing great anguish, yet for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings, to accomplish the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna,
and to manifest the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings of skillful means and to ensure that the various methods of preaching the Dharma would not be interrupted,

he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept [this]."
We, having made our final offering to the Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept [the gifts].
The celestial maidens, their wishes unfulfilled, harbored distress in their hearts and withdrew to one side, sitting in silence.
Next, the nine assemblies of *nāga* hosts are also divided into three [groups] (and so forth). There are several categories of names for those summoned.
At that time, there were further as many *nāga* kings as there are grains of sand in nine Ganges Rivers, dwelling in the four directions.
Their names were the Nāga King Vāsuki, the Nāga King Nanda, and the Nāga King Upananda, who served as the leaders.
They responded to the summons exactly as prescribed in the text.
These dragon kings, likewise at the break of dawn when the sun first rises,
prepared various offerings and summoned [the Buddha] according to the ritual text.
Having prepared offerings twice as great as those of humans and devas, they brought them to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, and circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times.
They addressed the Buddha, saying, "We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering. The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept.
These dragon kings, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to sit to one side.

Next, the passage concerning the assembly of the ten *gaṅgānadī-vāluka* ghost-king deities consists of two parts: the enumeration of the various classes of names summoned, and the statement that at that time there were further ghost-king deities equal in number to the sands of ten *gaṅgā* rivers.
At that time, there were yet again ghost-king deities equal in number to the sands of ten *gaṅgā* rivers.
With King Vaiśravaṇa as their leader—
these must be the four primary kings listed here according to their names—
do you all proceed quickly to summon them in accordance with this invocation.
They said to one another, "O virtuous ones, you should now go quickly to the place where the Buddha is.
Prepare offerings twice as great as those of the various nāgas, take them to the Buddha’s presence, prostrate at his feet, circumambulate him a hundred thousand times, and say to the Buddha:

'We pray only that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering. The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not grant permission; thus it was with these kṣetrapāla kings.
Failing to achieve his wish, his heart was filled with grief and distress as he sat to one side.
The ritual implements were arranged according to the text.
Next, twenty *koṭis* of bird-kings of the Ganges increased in number until a thousand billion *koṭis* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* spirits arrived before King Śveta.
I have merely briefly listed a few words by way of illustration.
At that time, there were also twenty *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of *garuḍa* kings, with the *Durdharṣa* (Subduer of Enemies) bird king as their leader.
Furthermore, there were gandharva kings as numerous as the sands of thirty Ganges Rivers, with King Narada as their leader.
Furthermore, there were kiṃnara kings as numerous as the sands of forty Ganges Rivers, with King Sudarśana as their leader.
Furthermore, there were mahoraga kings as numerous as the sands of fifty Ganges Rivers, with the Great King Sudarśana as their leader.
Furthermore, there were asura kings as numerous as the sands of sixty Ganges Rivers, with the King Śambara as their leader.
Furthermore, there were seventy Ganges-sands of *dānava* kings,
headed by Vimalanadīrāja and Bhadradatta; and furthermore,
there were eighty Ganges-sands of *rākṣasa* kings, headed by Bhīṣaṇarāja, who had abandoned [all attachments].
Those with evil minds no longer ate human beings, and they gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward their enemies and those they disliked;
those whose forms were ugly became entirely handsome through the Buddha’s spiritual power.
Furthermore, there were ninety Ganges-sands of forest spirit kings, with the Joyful Fragrance King as their leader.
Furthermore, there were as many as a thousand Ganges-sands of mantra-holding kings (*dhāraṇīndra*), with the Great Illusion Mantra-Holding King as their leader.
Furthermore, there were as many as one hundred million Ganges-sands of lustful ghost-demons (*piśāca*), with the King of Good Vision as their leader.
Furthermore, there were ten billion celestial courtesans, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
with the goddesses Lambā, Urvaśī, Tilottamā, and Viśākhā as their leaders.
Furthermore, there were a thousand billion earth-dwelling ghost kings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with King Śiśumāra as their leader.
Among them, some praised his virtues; all were capable of understanding [the Dharma]. This concludes the twenty-first assembly, which increases the preceding count.
Furthermore, there were a hundred trillion sons of gods, wind deities, and rain deities, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; these three groups were together.
Furthermore, there were tens of billions of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of devaputras and world-protectors, such as the Four Great Kings;
and there were also tens of billions of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* numbers of wind-deities from the four directions who blew upon the trees at both the proper and improper times.
Flowers were scattered between the twin trees.
Furthermore, there were as many cloud-and-rain-controlling spirits as there are grains of sand in ten trillion Ganges Rivers, all of whom thought:

"When the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa and his body is cremated, we shall pour down rain to extinguish the fire at that time, providing cool relief for those among the assembly who are distressed by the heat."
Furthermore, there were twenty *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* elephants, up to twenty *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* sages— five groups in total,

each numbering as many as the sands of twenty Ganges Rivers. Additionally, there were twenty *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* great fragrant elephant kings, including Rāhu Elephant King, Golden Elephant King, and Sweet [Elephant King].
Rasa-rāja-hastin, Gandha-hastin, Manojña-gandha-hastin, and others as their leaders— revere the Mahāyāna, delight in the Mahāyāna,
and knowing that the Buddha would soon enter parinirvāṇa, each plucked countless and boundless exquisite lotus flowers and came to where the Buddha was.
They prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Furthermore, there were as many lion kings as there are grains of sand in twenty Ganges Rivers, with Siṃhanāda-rāja (Lion’s Roar King) as their leader;
having bestowed fearlessness upon all sentient beings and carrying various flowers and fruits, they came to the place where the Buddha was,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Furthermore, there were kings of twenty *gaṅgā* rivers’ worth of various flying birds—
ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, gandharva-birds, kālaṇḍaka-birds, starlings, parrots, *kroñca*-birds, *vahiṅga*-birds,
*kalaviṅka*-birds, and *jīvajīvaka*-birds— and such birds as these brought various flowers and fruits.
They went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Furthermore, water buffaloes, oxen, and sheep, as numerous as the sands of twenty Ganges Rivers, went to where the Buddha was and yielded milk of wondrous fragrance;
this milk flowed until it filled all the ditches and pits of the city of Kuśinagara, perfect in color, fragrance, and flavor.
Having accomplished these tasks, they withdrew to stand to one side.
Furthermore, there were twenty times the number of *Ganges* sands of various ṛṣis from the four continents, with the Ṛṣi Kṣāntivādin as their leader;
carrying various flowers, incenses, and sweet fruits, they came to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and paid him homage.
They circumambulated the Buddha three times and addressed him, saying, "We only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept our final offering.

The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not grant his consent. Thereupon, the sages, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to sit on one side.
The enumeration of the texts is thus concluded.
Among all the bee-kings in Jambudvīpa, there is one who is the leader of countless hosts;
among all the bee-kings in Jambudvīpa, the Bee-king Wondrous Sound is the foremost, holding various kinds of flowers.
They approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him once, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Among the assembly in the second row, Jambudvīpa was on one side and the immeasurable worlds were on the other;
this intermediate space was further divided into two parts: first, those previously listed, and second, those who, out of compassion, summoned those who were near and far.
At that time, all the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs within Jambudvīpa assembled, with the sole exception of the two groups led by the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda.

Regarding the phrase "the former assembly," it refers to the previous thirty-four assemblies; the reason for singling out these two groups is that there were specific matters concerning them, both manifest and underlying.
As for Kāśyapa, he did not come because he was sustained by the meditative absorption of *nirodha-samāpatti*. Ānanda did not come because he was ensnared by Māra.

As for those who were intended to be manifested, Kāśyapa was manifested to demonstrate that he would not abandon even the minor precepts; Kāśyapa was the eldest son who was to uphold the Buddha-dharma.
If the Buddha were on the verge of passing into *parinirvāṇa*, he should have waived the minor precepts. Thus, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "When I pass away..."
After the Parinirvāṇa, regarding those who well maintain the subtle precepts and those who cannot, Kāśyapa later asked:
"What are these subtle precepts? Ānanda replied that he did not know. Kāśyapa then rebuked Ānanda, saying: "You received the Buddha's instructions directly from his presence;
how can you now say you do not know? Whether they should be abandoned or not, you have been ridiculed by the non-Buddhists and by your own teacher."
After the precepts have ceased, all shall abandon them, and yet they cannot be abandoned. Kāśyapa, if he were to come, would he truly be able to uphold this matter correctly?
Ānanda, in order to manifest [the truth], was praised by the Buddha at the very end and entrusted with it; thus the power of the divine mantra was revealed.
If Ānanda had come, he would not have asked questions, nor would he have been praised, nor would Mañjuśrī have been commanded to hold the mantra and untie the snare. II.

The fact that the assembly did not come reveals the intent of this question: the Buddha was asking Kāśyapa to relinquish the minor precepts. Why did Kāśyapa not permit his teacher and disciple to oppose one another?

The answer is: it is not so. The Buddha acted for those of sharp faculties because there was benefit to be gained, whereas Kāśyapa, being of dull faculties, returned [the matter] to its former state; therefore, it was not a case of opposition or refusal.
Next, the subsequent section is divided into three parts: first, humans and devas; second, mountain deities; and third, river and ocean deities. Regarding the first part:
furthermore, within immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there are intermediate spaces.
This refers to the gods and humans of the four heavenly kings, both above and below. Regarding the scriptural statement, "the intermediate [realms]," what is there that is not included?
Although the text does not explicitly mention the three continents or the ten billion sets of four continents, by logical inference they must be included.

For if beings from distant lands in other directions can still come here—such as those from Pūrvavideha in the east or Aparagoyānī in the west—for what reason would those from the [other] ten [directions] not arrive?

If even the hundreds of millions of the four heavens have not yet arrived, for what reason have they not come? If one were to infer from the intermediate statements, the multitudes would be most numerous;
this can only be known through the mind and cannot be recorded in writing (and so forth).
Next, there were all the mountain deities below, including every mountain in Jambudvīpa, with Sumeru, the King of Mountains, as their chief.
These mountains were adorned with lush, verdant groves and flourishing foliage that shielded the sun's rays; they were everywhere embellished with various kinds of exquisite flowers.
The flowing waters of Dragon Spring were pure, clear, fragrant, and clean;
devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, rishis, and those who employ incantations and arts, along with performers of music and dance—all such multitudes filled the area.
These mountain deities also came to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to one side.
Regarding the statement that the mountain deity of Mount He must have the form of a mountain, this is not necessarily so;

the tree deity manifests only half his body and does not take the form of a tree, while the mountain deity need not take the form of a mountain. They are simply spirits who have attached themselves to the mountains. First, the various mountains are listed;
next, their characteristics are discussed; finally, the approach to the Buddha is explained.
The ocean and river deities were likewise as described in the text.

Furthermore, there were incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) numbers of deities of the four great oceans and various rivers, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, who possessed great majesty and great supernormal powers (*mahā-ṛddhi*).
The offerings they presented were twice as superior as those of the previously mentioned deities, consisting of bodily radiance, musical instruments, and lamps.

They completely eclipsed the sun and moon so that they no longer appeared; then, scattering campaka flowers over the River Śītā, they approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Regarding the *Hiraṇyavatī*, tradition holds that it is the same as the *Jīvaka*; however, this is not so according to current accounts. The *Jīvaka* is large and the *Hiraṇyavatī* is small.
Some say its breadth is four *zhang*, others say eight *zhang*. It lies north of the city while the *Jīvaka* lies south; they are separated by one hundred *li*.
The Buddha resided between them, and at the time of his *nirvāṇa*, he was reached by the scattered flowers, though the *Hiraṇyavatī* itself has not yet been seen [by him].

[The text] is translated as follows: Next, the transformation of the forest into white [is explained]; this refers to the sorrow for those nearby. Having already summoned those from afar who have assembled, one now sorrows for those who have not yet assembled.

This is further divided into two parts: first, sorrowing for those nearby; second, summoning those from afar. Regarding the initial sorrow for those nearby, there are generally three manifested signs.
At that time, the śāla grove of the city of Kuśinagara turned white like a white crane.
Regarding the śāla trees, as previously explained, this grove which was once flourishing suddenly turned white like white cranes;

within the grove were cranes that, at the time of the transformation, were indistinguishable from the cranes themselves. This has a symbolic significance: if prosperity is certain, it will not decline.
If it were suddenly to wither, it would be a definitive withering; yet it was not like the withering of a crane. Since it was like a crane, its withering was not true withering;

since its flourishing was suddenly transformed, its flourishing was not true flourishing. That which is neither withering nor flourishing—the nirvana in the interim—manifests birth and death while signifying non-arising and non-extinction.
At the twin śāla trees, a single transformation allowed each according to their kind to understand, so that those who reached the heights realized the fundamental source.
The lower [capacity] takes pity on those who follow mere traces; those of middle capacity abide between compassion and realization. As stated in the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness":
"Those of inferior and foolish commoners always speak of *nirvāṇa*, but only Bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī can know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging.
This is precisely the meaning of this passage.
Next, regarding the "empty space halls and pavilions with exquisite ornamentation clearly defined":
within the empty space there spontaneously appear halls and pavilions made of the seven treasures, with carved and engraved patterns and exquisite ornamentation clearly defined,
surrounded by railings interspersed with various jewels.
The manifested form of the Buddha’s body is the most supreme in all the heavens above and the earth below;

now that the conditions for this physical existence have ceased, his unsurpassed wisdom no longer dwells in governance. This is what the inferior practitioners lament. Furthermore, while the hall originally rested upon its foundation, it now stands in space;
thus, within the void there is a hall, its carvings and engravings, its exquisite ornaments, all distinct and clear—neither moving nor falling, wondrous indeed.
Its magnificent adornments manifest as a treasury within space, complete and without deficiency—this is what the person of middling capacity prizes.
Furthermore, that the hall is grand and orderly, radiant and beneficial, is its aspect of existence; that it stands high in the void with no one to enjoy it is its aspect of non-existence.

If the matters of existence and non-existence are concluded, one should gather this "existence within emptiness" back into the state where there is neither emptiness nor existence; this is the path of the person of superior capacity.
Regarding the reach [of his compassion]: his compassion reaches downward, his reach extends upward, and his compassion reaches those of middle standing;
it lies between the first and the last of the three ranks. As for the many flowing springs and bathing pools beneath the hall:
beneath the hall there are many flowing springs and bathing pools filled with exquisite lotus flowers, just like those in the northern continent.
The land of Uttarakuru is also like the Garden of Joy in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
at that time, the various adornments within the śāla grove were likewise exceedingly lovely and delightful.
All these devas, humans, and asuras beheld the signs of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, and they were all moved by grief, sorrowful, and found no joy.
The Buddha’s body and speech respond to those below, flowing forth immeasurable verbal teachings, just like a bathing pool.

This bathing pool has two functions: first, it can wash away defilements; second, it can remove feverish distress. This represents how the Buddha’s teaching can exhaust adventitious dust externally and eliminate ignorance internally.

As for the presence of wondrous lotus flowers, this represents following the Buddha’s teaching, which is precisely the cultivation of causes. These causes [lead to]... (Note: The final phrase "因" (causes) appears to be an incomplete fragment in the source text.)

Because it is a fruit that transcends the world, two locations are cited as metaphors: the completion of the work of transformation is like a hall rising high, and the flowing nourishment of the verbal teaching is like a clear spring in a pond.
Regarding its essential nature, it neither departs nor remains; regarding its benefit, however, one speaks of departing and remaining.
The text says, "All behold the Tathāgata’s appearance of nirvāṇa"; this is, for the time being, the lower [view].

Regarding what the practitioner perceives: if one were to discuss this in full, there should be the upward-reaching of the superior and the downward compassion of the inferior, as previously explained.
These three characteristics, though differing in their sequence, share the same intent as before. First, by means of a great voice, one exhorts and questions;
through questioning, the secret teaching becomes manifest, just as the clear spring flows forth beneath this hall to benefit many people, with its opening facing forward.
Light of five colors shines everywhere, removing the three obstructions and giving rise to the three virtues, causing one to establish practice and advance upward.
It is like a lofty hall rising high, departing from below and ascending into the void; its exquisite adornments are distinct, with various decorations.

As the ground shakes before it and the waters move, reflecting their overturning, the nature of perception now transforms the forest into cranes, ensuring that one does not linger in decay or prosperity, but returns to the center.

Having reached the ultimate limit of what is difficult for beings to awaken to, I once again strike my palms together in lamentation. Although the "summoning the near" and "summoning the distant" differ in form, their intent is the same as before;
I merely wish to provide further clarification.
From the descent of the Four Heavenly Kings downward constitutes the "summoning the distant," while following the opening text from before constitutes the third summoning.
The various assemblies of the upper realms consist of five chapters; first, regarding the heavens of the desire realm, the Four Heavenly Kings are explained initially.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and Śakra-devānām-indra are of this same category.
They said to one another, "This is the summons.
They said to one another, "Examine how the gods, humans, and asuras have prepared great offerings;
we wish to offer our final service to the Tathāgata, and we shall likewise make such offerings. If it is my final [opportunity]..."
For one who has attained offerings, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is then accomplished and fulfilled without difficulty;
this is truly because, upon hearing the sound or seeing the light, one immediately perceives the offerings presented by others through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Having personally prepared these offerings, they came to where the Buddha was, arriving in accordance with his summons.
At that time, the offerings presented by the Four Heavenly Kings were twice as magnificent as those before:
they brought *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *karkārava* flowers, *mahākarkārava* flowers, and *mañjūṣaka* flowers.
Mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, Saṃtānikā flowers, Mahāsaṃtānikā flowers, Priyaṅgu flowers, Mahāpriyaṅgu flowers,
Samantabhadra flowers, Mahāsamantabhadra flowers, Kālika flowers, Mahākālika flowers, Gandhapura flowers, Mahāgandhapura flowers,
Nandika flowers, Mahānandika flowers, Utpala flowers, Mahotpalas, and Gandhamada flowers.

They brought various kinds of exquisite and delicious foods to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and— [offering] the *puṣpa*, the *mahāgandha-mada-puṣpa*, the *samanta-gandha-puṣpa*,
the *mahā-samanta-gandha-puṣpa*, the *divya-suvarṇa-patra-puṣpa*, the *nāga-puṣpa*, the *pārijātaka* tree flowers, and the *kovidāra* tree flowers—
the radiance of all these devas and humans eclipsed the sun and moon, causing them no longer to shine.
Having presented these offerings with the desire to worship the Buddha, Tathāgata, he remained silent and did not accept them out of consideration for the proper time.
At that moment, the devas, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Śakra Devendra merely summoned them, and they were summoned accordingly (as detailed above).

At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven prepared various offerings even more magnificent than before; the flowers they held were likewise of such subtle and wondrous fragrance.
Carrying the most delightful Hall of Victory (*Vaijayanta*) along with various smaller halls, they approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One, we deeply delight in and cherish the Mahāyāna; we only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our food.
Knowing it was not the proper time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept it. The Śakra-devas, their wishes unfulfilled, harbored resentment in their hearts.
Śocanā withdrew to one side.
Thus it continued until the offerings presented by the gods of the sixth heaven surpassed those before;
the small precious canopies covered the four continents, the shortest banners encircled the four seas, and the lowest of the standards reached as far as the Heaven of Sovereignty (Īśvara).
A gentle celestial breeze blew, causing the banners to emit wondrous sounds as they bore exquisite food to the place where the Buddha was.
They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to him, “World-Honored One, we pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.
Knowing the proper time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept it. These devas, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand aside.
On one side...
up to the sixth heaven, three intermediate heavens being omitted.
Reaching upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), all the Brahmakāyika gods gathered there; at that time, Mahābrahmā and the others...
The Brahma-hosts emitted light from their bodies that pervaded the four continents; the light of the sun and moon among the humans and devas of the desire realm no longer appeared.

Carrying various precious banners, silken streamers, pennants, and canopies—even the shortest of which were suspended from the Brahma palace down to the space between the *śāla* trees—they approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, we pray only that the Tathāgata...”
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, silently declined our final offering.
At that, the Brahmās, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.

From the bottom up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), this should be the Peak of Form (*rūpāgra*); one should list the Brahma Heaven [separately] as the text analyzes these three peaks (and so forth).

In the preceding treatise, it was stated that the Buddha’s power should penetrate all three types of peaks; here, however, the discussion of the ritual offerings clarifies only the Peak of Form (and so forth).
Next, the Asura Kings were listed.
At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra, together with an immeasurable great retinue of asuras, possessed bodily radiance surpassing that of Brahmā;
they carried various precious banners, silken streamers, flags, and canopies, some of which were small.
Covering a thousand worlds, they brought exquisite and delicious foods to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him:
"We pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering. Knowing the proper time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept it.
The asuras, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Regarding the statement that the father of Śacī’s retributive reward is inferior while his environmental reward is comparable [to that of the gods], yet his light is superior:
this is because it is the light of a Great Bodhisattva, and thus it may be said to be superior.
Next, as for the hosts of Māras: "Māra" means "the slayer," and Pāpīyān is named the "evil among evils. He dwells at the summit of the sixth heaven.
The section concerning the Lord of the Desire Realm consists of three parts.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, the King of the Desire Realm, together with his retinue of celestial maidens and an immeasurable,
boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) multitude, [arrived].
Second, he issued a general amnesty and opened the gates of hell, bestowing pure water upon them and addressing them thus: "At this moment, you have no power to act;
you must single-mindedly recollect the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and establish this final offering of sympathetic joy."
To cause you all to obtain peace for a long night, Māra Pāpīyān completely removed the swords and blades within the hells;
he extinguished the immeasurable bitter poisons and blazing fires by raining down water.

Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, he further gave rise to this thought, causing his entire retinue to abandon their swords, bows, crossbows, armor, weapons, spears, lances, long hooks, golden mallets, battle-axes, and clubs.
The wheel and the lasso:
these three are prepared as offerings for presentation.
The offerings held are twice as superior as those established by all humans and devas; even the smallest of their parasols covers a medium chiliocosm.
The offerings were presented in two parts: first, the recitation of mantras; second, the presentation of the offerings.
Having arrived at the presence of the Buddha, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One, we now delight in the Mahāyāna and protect the Mahāyāna. If there are good sons or good daughters who, for the sake of making offerings or out of fear...”
Whether out of fear, for the sake of deceiving others, for the sake of wealth and profit, or to comply with others, they may receive this Mahāyāna—whether it be authentic or spurious.
At that time, we shall eliminate the fears of such persons and recite this mantra for them.
Takki takkarākṣi lukale mahālukale āra carā tarā sāha.
This mantra is able to protect those who have lost their minds,
those who are terrified, those who preach the Dharma, and those who do not sever the True Dharma.
To subdue non-Buddhists, to protect one’s own body, to protect the True Dharma, and to protect the Mahāyāna, I shall speak this mantra.
If there is anyone who can uphold this mantra, they will have no fear of wild elephants;

even when entering wildernesses, empty marshes, or perilous places, they will give rise to no fear, nor will they suffer from water, fire, lions, tigers, wolves, thieves, robbers, or royal calamities, O World-Honored One. If there is anyone...
"World-Honored One, those who are able to uphold such a mantra will be able to completely eliminate all such fears.
World-Honored One, we shall protect those who uphold this mantra, just as a tortoise withdraws its six limbs. World-Honored One, we do not speak these words out of flattery or deceit;
we shall, with utmost sincerity, augment the power of those who uphold this mantra."
"May the Tathāgata, out of compassion, graciously accept our final offering.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Māra Pāpīyān, saying: "I do not accept your offering of food and drink;

I have already accepted the divine mantra you have spoken for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings and the fourfold assembly. When the Buddha had finished speaking these words,
When he remained silent and did not accept these three requests, and they were all likewise refused, Māra Pāpīyān, his wishes unfulfilled, was filled with grief and distress and withdrew to one side.

When the Buddha accepted the incantation but not the offering, Māra asked, "Since you are so wicked, how could you possibly have obtained a good incantation? The Buddha replied, "This incantation is..."
The Dharma of the former Buddhas was obtained by chance; it is like someone in a kingdom who encounters a treasure and returns it to the king.
This mantra is the name of a spirit-king; once its name is known, the spirit cannot cause harm. It is like a thief waiting for wealth:
if the owner knows the thief's name and calls it out, the thief will not proceed. Next, it says that the mantra is the king of spirits.

First, as for naming: if one calls out the name of the master, it will not cause harm even if one exhorts its followers. Second, as for summoning: if one summons it with the proper ritual, it will not cause harm.
Third, as for incantation: it is like a thunderbolt; spirits and ghosts fear its majesty and dare not cause harm. Fourth, as for incantation: it is an esoteric language, like a military signal;

if one responds correctly, one is released, but if one does not respond, one is punished. It is the same with spirits and ghosts: if they comply with the incantation, they provide protection; if they do not comply, their heads shall split apart.
The "Five Clouds" (Pañca-megha) mantra is a decree of the Buddha that none dare violate. Some have criticized it, saying: "This is a vidyā-mantra, a mahā-vidyā-mantra, a mantra without equal;
if it were merely the name of a ghost or the like, how could it cause people to attain the fruit of awakening?

This interpretation is not correct. If one were to interpret it exclusively [as a mere incantation], one would be unable to harmonize with the Way; therefore, it should be interpreted as a dharma-gate.
All afflictions are called "demons," and ignorance is the "king of demons. Its ability to shatter evil is like a thunderbolt;
it is true according to the facts, and this constitutes the esoteric language of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

It is the command of the Buddha that by relying on this Dharma-gate, one will certainly attain the Way. Furthermore, this expresses the intent of both the specific and general four *siddhāntas*: the first four are specific, while the last one is general.
This interpretation is not problematic.
Next, regarding Maheśvara, that is, Mahesvara, who dwells at the summit of the Form Realm and presides over the Great Trichiliocosm:
he is a manifestation of a tenth-stage Bodhisattva. As for his appearance as Brahmā, the Lord of the World, listed among the world-protectors in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this is...

What do you think? If one says that the Lord of the Sahā World is precisely Maheśvara, or if one says it is Śikhin Mahābrahmā and others, this merely cites those of the Second Dhyāna and so forth to include the Brahma-kings of the Third and Fourth Dhyanas.
Furthermore, it is said that if one speaks of him as the Lord of the World, in reality he governs only a small chiliocosm; however, because his family name is magnificent, [he is thus designated].
Regarding the statement "the Lord of the World," [the author] privately asserts that this refers to one who has attained the status of being the lord of a great trichiliocosm;
those below this rank cannot [be so called]. This text is divided into two parts: first, those of a similar class who are the objects of the invocation.
At that time, the Great Lord Maheśvara, together with his retinue of immeasurable and boundless numbers and the assembly of devas,
performed the second offering as prescribed for the ritual invocation.
All the sacrificial implements provided completely covered Brahmā, Śakra, the World-Protecting Four Heavenly Kings, the eight classes of humans and non-humans, and the celestial beings.
All such offerings as these, prepared by Brahmā and Śakra, appeared like a smear of ink beside a conch shell and were no longer visible.
Even the smallest of their precious parasols could cover a trichiliocosm.
Carrying such articles of worship, they approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we..."
The humble offerings you have presented to me are like mosquitoes making an offering to me;
it is also like someone throwing a single handful of water into the great ocean, or like a small lamp assisting the hundred thousand suns,
or like holding a single flower to augment the flourishing blossoms of the spring and summer months, or like adding a *ting-li* seed to Mount Sumeru— how could these possibly compare?
O World-Honored One, who is like a great ocean, the sun, the bright lotuses, and Mount Sumeru; even this meager offering I now present is likewise so.
If one were to fill the entire trichiliocosm with fragrant flowers, music, banners, and canopies to make offerings to the Tathāgata, it would still not be worth mentioning.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata constantly dwells upon the earth for the sake of all sentient beings.
Because they undergo various sufferings within the evil realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, may the World-Honored One look upon us with compassion and accept our offerings.
Next, at that time, [the Buddhas] from the eastern direction summoned the assemblies from other lands— or as it is said, those Buddhas whose voices and light did not reach them— [responded].

If one dispatches [a messenger] to arrive in this land according to the previous text, where the light universally illuminates these three thousandfold worlds and even the ten directions in the same manner, is this not an "invitation by light"?
Furthermore, when that Buddha dispatched [the messengers], the threefold invitation in the text was sufficient in its intent;
he offered fragrant food to the Buddha—this is "invitation by light. His journeying there to pay homage is "invitation by movement. [This is for the purpose of] requesting a definitive resolution.
The doubt concerns the sound that summons the mind. The text is divided into two parts: first, clarifying one direction, and second, applying this by analogy to the other three directions.
Regarding the eastern direction, there are three pairs: first, those Buddhas speak here, and this assembly sees that assembly;
second, the great assembly here, through the inconceivable, sees by not seeing, and thus sees that Boundless Body; third, the Boundless Body, through the inconceivable...
Regarding the three instances where those who were not invited came: first, that Buddha offered provisions to this Buddha, yet this Buddha did not accept the offering from that Buddha;
these three signs are the same as the three kinds of auspicious omens at the beginning of the sutra.

That Buddha’s speaking of this [to them] is the omen of sound perceived by this assembly seeing him; that assembly’s coming here is the omen of the earth shaking perceived by this assembly seeing him.
He made offerings to them, yet these Buddhas did not accept them; this was the first of the initial pair of auspicious lights.
Regarding that Buddha’s discourse on these Buddhas, the text is divided into four parts: first, clarifying the distance.
At that time, to the east, beyond immeasurable, incalculable, *asaṃkhyeya* worlds as numerous as the dust motes of the sands of the Ganges...
In that realm, there is a buddha-field named Manojña-svarā, where the Buddha is named Gaganasama Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi,
Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Second, that Buddha spoke thus.
At that time, that Buddha addressed his foremost great disciple, saying: "Good son, you should now go to the Sahā world in the western direction.
In that land there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

"Know that the Buddha, the World-Honored One—the one endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans—is soon to enter parinirvāṇa.
Son of good family, you may take this fragrant food from this world;
its fragrance is excellent, and eating it brings peace and security. You may present it to that Buddha, the World-Honored One, for him to eat."
"Those sons of good family who have already entered parinirvāṇa may likewise pay homage and request a resolution of their doubts.
Having spoken thus three times,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantagātra then received the Buddha’s instruction, rose from his seat, and prostrated himself.
Circumambulating the Buddha’s feet three times to the right, together with a multitude of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya great bodhisattvas,
he set out from that land and arrived here in this Sahā world.
The four manifestations of auspicious omens are as described in the text.
At that moment, the great earth of this trichiliocosm shook in six ways;
subsequently, this assembly saw that other assembly also become terrified by four things.
Thereupon, within the assembly, the Brahmās, Śakra, the Four Great Kings, Māra Pāpīyān, Maheśvara, and this great multitude, seeing this earthquake, had the hair on their bodies stand on end;
their throats and tongues became parched, and they were struck with such terror and trembling that each wished to disperse in the four directions.
They saw that their own bodies no longer possessed radiance, and all their majestic power was extinguished without remainder.
Second, the consolation:
At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat and addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Sons of good family, do not be afraid; do not be afraid. Why is this? To the east of here, beyond immeasurable and incalculable [worlds]..."

In worlds as numerous as the atoms in incalculable Ganges-sands, there is a world named Manojña-ruta where the Buddha is named Gaganasama Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.
Therein dwells a bodhisattva named Anantakāya, who, together with immeasurable bodhisattvas, desires to come here to make offerings to the Tathāgata. By that bodhisattva...
By the power of my majesty and virtue, the radiance of your bodies shall no longer appear;
therefore, you should give rise to joy and harbor no fear.
Third, he saw that assembly.
At that time, the entire great assembly saw that Buddha and his retinue from afar, as clearly as one observes one's own reflection in a bright mirror.
Then Mañjuśrī addressed the assembly again: "What you have now seen of that Buddha and his retinue is like seeing this Buddha;
by the Buddha’s spiritual power, you shall likewise come to see the infinite Buddhas of the nine directions."
A fourth time they cried out, "Alas!
At that moment, the great assembly said to one another, "Alas, alas! The world is empty;
the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa."
When the great assembly sees the Buddha, they ought to give rise to joy; why then do they cry out "Suffering"?
Upon hearing that Buddha’s teaching, this Buddha should enter into parinirvāṇa. Is it because of the preceding omen of sound that the earth shakes and trembles?
Or is it because of the preceding omen of the earth shaking that one perceives light like a mirror? Having seen and heard these preceding omens of light, that Buddha, for their sake...
This manifestation of nirvāṇa is why he uttered the cry of suffering. When asked, "Why do those in this assembly—all fellow practitioners of the Buddha—tremble with fear?
the answer is: "In discussing the ultimate reality now, my intent does not lie in the provisional. Furthermore, among the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are superior and inferior grades;
what is accomplished at the superior level is unknown to those at the inferior level. It is through the power of the Buddha that even insects can [attain] supernatural abilities."
Knowing that one cannot understand this without relying on supernatural power, and seeing that this Boundless Body manifests such an auspicious sign by receiving the Buddha’s supernatural power,
why would Śakra be further alarmed or have any doubt?

Next, regarding the first of the second pair: starting from the great assembly’s vision of the Infinite Body (Anantagātra), each and every pore of this Bodhisattva reveals that he manifests the inconceivable—seeing by not seeing.
At that time, the entire great assembly saw the Bodhisattva Infinite Body along with his retinue; this is the Bodhisattva.
From each and every pore of his body, there emerged a great lotus flower;

on each lotus flower were seventy-eight thousand cities, equal in length and breadth to the city of Vaiśālī, with walls and moats interspersed with the seven treasures, and rows of *tāla* jewel-trees in seven tiers.
They were teeming with people, peaceful, secure, and prosperous—just like Jambudvīpa.
The defensive walls are made of gold; each wall is adorned with various kinds of trees made of the seven precious jewels, their flowers and fruits flourishing.
When a gentle breeze blows through them, they produce subtle and wondrous sounds. These sounds are harmonious and elegant, like celestial music.
When the people within the city hear these sounds, they immediately experience supreme and exquisite bliss. Within these moats is wondrous water.
It is overflowing, pure, fragrant, and as clear as genuine lapis lazuli.
Within these waters are ships made of the seven treasures, upon which people ride to play, bathe, and enjoy themselves together, their happiness being limitless.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable lotuses of various colors—*utpala*, *kumuda*, *padma*, and *puṇḍarīka*—and these flowers...
In length and breadth it is like a chariot wheel; upon the banks of its moats there are many groves, and within each grove are five spring-pools.
Within these pools grow various flowers—*utpala*, *kumuda*, *padma*, and *puṇḍarīka*—each flower in length and breadth also like a chariot wheel, their fragrance rich and most delightful.
They delight in that water, which is supremely pure, clear, and soft; wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks sport within it.
Each garden contains numerous palatial residences made of various jewels; each palace is perfectly square, measuring four yojanas in length and breadth.
Their walls are composed of the four precious substances—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and are surrounded by windows and lattices of pure gold.
The railings are made of *māndārava* flowers, and the ground is strewn with golden sand; within these palaces and residences, there are many bathing pools fed by streams of the seven treasures.

Along the edge of each pool, there are eighteen staircases made of gold, and *jambūnada* gold forms the plantain trees, just like those in the Nandana Garden of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Within each city, there are eighty-four thousand such features.
Each of these kings, lords of men, has his own immeasurable number of queens and court ladies with whom he enjoys himself, delighting in pleasure;
the other people likewise do so, each enjoying themselves together in their respective dwellings.
Among these beings, no other names are heard, but only the sound of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna. Within each of these flowers...
Each had a lion throne; the four legs of each throne were made of deep-blue lapis lazuli, and upon the seats were spread soft, pure white garments.
These garments were exquisite, surpassing those of the triple world. Upon each seat sat a king who taught and transformed sentient beings through the Mahāyāna Dharma.
There were some sentient beings who copied, upheld, read, recited, and practiced according to the teachings in this manner.
While the Mahāyāna sūtras were being disseminated, at that time the Bodhisattva Anantagātra settled immeasurable sentient beings in this way;
having manifested his own body, he caused them to renounce worldly pleasures and spoke these words: "Alas, alas!
The world is empty; the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa."
To perceive a single hair-path as small is to see the minor; to perceive the magnificent adornments of the seventy-eight thousand cities within it as vast is to see the great.
Yet, the dimensions of that body are equal to empty space, which is neither large nor small—how could it be fully described?
Nevertheless, there is no impediment to coming from there, for the great and the small are mutually contained; the pore does not widen, nor do the cities narrow.
Again, they heard sounds of joy and the enjoyment of pleasure; again, they heard cries of "Alas, what suffering!
and again, they heard sounds exclusively teaching the Mahāyāna. These are the sounds of neither suffering nor pleasure, which do not obstruct one another.
The reason the Bodhisattvas manifest these matters is to signify that the present Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa is likewise inconceivable.
Next, at that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra, together with immeasurable bodhisattvas—
bodhisattvas who had come from the inconceivable realm where they do not come—
arrived. At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra, surrounded on all sides by those immeasurable bodhisattvas, manifested himself in such a manner.
By means of their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they sustain these various and immeasurable offering implements, as well as the most excellent and fragrant delicacies.
Should anyone catch the scent of this food, all afflictions and defilements are completely extinguished.
Through the supernormal power of these Bodhisattvas, the entire assembly is able to behold such transformations and the boundless bodies of the Bodhisattvas.

The body of this Bodhisattva is vast and boundless, equal to empty space; with the exception of the Buddhas, no one else is able to see it, for such is the limit of the dimensions of this Bodhisattva’s body.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra and his retinue presented offerings even more magnificent than those previously described, as they arrived at the place where the Buddha was.
Next, among the three pairs [of verses], the first offers worship to the Buddha.
Bowing at the Buddha’s feet with palms joined in reverence, they addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, we pray that you will compassionately accept our offerings.”
Next, he did not accept [the offering], as stated in the text.
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept it; thus, all three requests were likewise refused.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra and his retinue withdrew to stand to one side.
Next, the same applies to the other three directions.

In the Buddha-worlds of the south, west, and north, there were likewise immeasurable and boundless Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who, bearing offerings even more magnificent than those previously described, arrived at the place where the Buddha was and, after doing so, withdrew to stand to one side; all of this was exactly as before.
All is as stated in the text: since the body is already boundless, this land and other lands both reside upon the tip of a single hair;

why then does it suddenly come from that place to here? If it comes from that side to this side, then this assembly here sees it coming from that side, while on that side it is seen as remaining on that very side.
Because the ancient [commentators] said there is "a small portion of the boundless," they maintained that there is coming.
To depart from this is not permissible; since it is said that their measure is equal to empty space, how could empty space have a "small portion" or a "large portion"?

Since you speak of a "small portion," it is therefore not the same as space. Now we clarify that the inconceivable form of the Bodhisattva is such that the finite is the infinite and the infinite is the finite;
it is neither finite nor infinite, and the finite is itself the infinite. Its measure is equal to empty space, and there is no [distinction].
The "limit" (anta) is itself that which is beyond it; this "this" sees that "that" coming.
Although there is neither limit nor non-limit, yet because it can both be limited and limitless, it is called inconceivable (*acintya*).

If there were anything fixed, it would not be inconceivable—for example, the sixteen-foot [Buddha-body] whose crown Brahmā cannot see; it is neither seeing nor non-seeing, yet it is both able to be seen and unable to be seen.
It is like a mirror held beside the body: the body appears within the mirror; it is not "within," yet it is not not-within.

Furthermore, the sun does not descend into the pond, nor does the water rise up, yet its reflection appears therein. If even the perception of a solid, obstructive form is thus difficult to conceive, how much more so the inconceivable?
How could one grasp it with the ordinary mind?
From the departure from the twin *śāla* trees, the third major section, "The Concluding Summation of the Invocation," has two parts: first, the concluding summation of the assembly’s gathering;
second, the concluding summation of the auspicious signs. Since the assembly had already gathered and the auspicious signs had likewise concluded, both must be summarized.
The first summary of the assembly’s gathering is further divided into three: first, clarifying that the location is inconceivable; second, clarifying its... [text continues]
The first passage clarifies that the place is inconceivable through three points regarding the inconceivability of persons.
At that time, the auspicious and blessed ground between the twin śāla trees was thirty-two yojanas in length and breadth, filled with a great assembly such that there was no empty space between them.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas of Boundless Body from the four directions and their retinues sat therein.

In a space as small as the point of a needle or a mote of dust, thirty-two *yojanas* can accommodate fifty-two assemblies of long banners and great canopies; people are not obstructed and the ritual offerings remain unharmed.
Furthermore, if even a needle-point or a mote of dust can contain the Boundless Body (*Anantagātra*), how much more inconceivable is this!

As for the number of retinues, offerings, and persons of the Bodhisattvas of Boundless Bodies from the atoms of the four directions and the ten directions who possess unobstructed and uninjured faculties—
this is the inconceivable second stage of the person. First,
from "from the atoms of the ten directions" downward, it concludes that the multitudes from other directions have gathered upon the needle-point and in Jambudvīpa.
The assembly of this land gathered at the twin trees;
great bodhisattvas from Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as motes of dust all came to the gathering,
as did the entire multitude of Jambudvīpa.
This is inconceivable for humans. Second,
it is that those who should have gathered did not gather, while those who should not have gathered did gather—
except for the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Ānanda, the two assemblies, King Ajātaśatru, and his retinue.
Even venomous snakes capable of killing by their gaze, dung beetles, scorpions, and those who practice the sixteen kinds of evil deeds—all these gathered together.
Those who should gather were the two assemblies, such as Kāśyapa and others; those who should not gather were the poisonous insects, wicked people, and malevolent spirits—these three.
This assembly is inconceivable both in its gathering and its non-gathering.
The third clarity is the benefit of the assembly:
the *dānava* spirits, *asura*s, and others all abandon their evil thoughts and give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, regarding one another as fathers and mothers.

Just as sisters or younger siblings regard one another, so too do the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm direct their minds toward one another with loving-kindness, with the sole exception of those possessed by the icchantika.
This refers to the gathering and non-gathering of the assembly, from which they equally give rise to loving-kindness; in both gathered and ungathered places, they all purify their *dāna*.
The Bhava-deva is one who gathers the multitudes of sentient beings within the trichiliocosm; he is also one who does not gather the multitudes.

Furthermore, he excludes both the compassionate and the non-compassionate. The "non-compassionate" refers to the icchantikas, who do not give rise to a mind of compassion. Both the compassionate and the non-compassionate are inconceivable.
Third, from that time forth, the three-thousandfold world system—by the power of the Buddha—further clarifies the location:

at that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, the ground of the great trichiliocosm became entirely soft and supple, free of mounds, ravines, earth, sand, gravel, stones, thorns, or poisonous weeds;
it was adorned with various jewels, just like the western land of Amitāyus.

At that time, the great assembly in the Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss saw all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, just as one sees one's own reflection in a clear mirror; their vision of the various Buddha-lands was likewise so.
The three thousandfold world system is a place where the assembly gathers, while the worlds of the ten directions are places where they do not gather;

yet both are equally adorned and purified like the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore, it is said that the ten directions are likewise so. Because the assembly gathers, such benefits are brought about;

in places where the assembly does not gather, the very fact that beings do not even conceive the aspiration [for enlightenment] is already inconceivable, let alone the Tathāgata manifesting his birth there.
The manifestation of his parinirvāṇa is indeed inconceivable; this concludes the assembly of the congregation.
Next, following the descent from the Tathāgata’s face, the auspicious signs were completed.
At that time, five-colored light issued forth from the Tathāgata’s face, its brilliance illuminating and encompassing the entire great assembly.
He causes the bodily radiance of those beings to vanish entirely; having performed what was to be done, [the light] returns and enters through his mouth.
From the previous point up to this one, there are nine omens in total, which together accomplish three meanings and are thus subsumed as a single group.
This is because the sound, the light, and the wind all issue from the mouth; if the light is withdrawn into the mouth, the same applies by analogy to the wind and the sound.
When the sound ceases, the teaching ceases; when the questioner asks "Who?", this signifies that the teacher has departed and withdrawn the light. When the light ceases, the illumination ceases;

when the three obstacles darken the Way and the goodness of the three karmas does not arise, this signifies that the master has departed and withdrawn the wind. When the wind ceases, spiritual transformations cease;
when there is no means by which inversion can be overturned, this signifies that the relative has departed.
At that time, the devas, humans, and the entire assembly, including the asuras, seeing the Buddha’s radiance re-enter through his mouth, were all seized with great terror;
their body hair stood on end, and they spoke thus: "The Tathāgata’s radiance has emerged and now returns within;
this cannot be without cause or condition. It must be that what was to be done in the ten directions has been accomplished, and this is surely the sign of the final nirvāṇa."
How bitter! How bitter! How is it that the World-Honored One has suddenly abandoned the four immeasurable minds and will no longer receive the offerings presented by devas and humans?
The sun of noble wisdom shall from now on be extinguished forever, and the unsurpassed Dharma-ship shall sink here.
The great assembly saw one [of the disciples] who understood the three [vehicles], and seeing his mouth close as he drew in his breath, they knew that he would surely lose his teacher;

therefore, they wailed and wept, crying out, "He shall no longer receive the offerings of devas and humans! This weeping was for the sorrow of losing a field of merit and the grief of having no food of the Dharma.
Seeing the light being drawn back into the mouth, they knew that the Master would surely pass away; therefore, they wept, saying, "From this day forth, the sun of noble wisdom will forever..."
The three obstructions are extinguished; who shall now eliminate the three virtues? Who shall give rise to insight? The wind enters the mouth, and one knows that kin will surely be lost.
Therefore, we weep, crying: "The Dharma-ship has sunk! Who shall shatter ignorance and ferry us from this shore to the other shore of Nirvana?
These three types of weeping are for the sake of our parents, teachers, and masters.
Alas, how painful! The great suffering of the world! Raising their hands to beat their breasts, they wail and weep with cries of grief;
their limbs tremble so violently that they cannot support themselves, and blood flows from all the pores of their bodies, drenching the ground.
Alas! This mind is pained and wails; this mouth is sorrowful and cries out; this body trembles and moves.
Thus do the three karmas of compassion and longing extend even to this point. *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle One.

The Chapter on Cunda.

The "Chapter on Explanation" is divided into three parts: first, distinguishing between the sparse and the dense; second, distinguishing virtuous conduct; and third, explaining the title. Regarding the first intention:
according to the Indian text, it still belongs to the "Chapter on Life Span," where the meanings of the eternal and non-eternal, as well as the provisional and the ultimate, are analyzed.
In terms of meaning, this is "dense"; in terms of the text, it is "sparse. Master Xie followed the person and the event, titling it the "Cunda Chapter. In terms of the text, this is...
What is dense in meaning is now rendered sparse; here we clarify the chapter on the "Bestowal of Nirvāṇa," which in both the Sanskrit and Chinese texts is without loss.
Following the preceding person, the bestowal is constant life; following the subsequent matter, the bestowal is constant cultivation (and so forth).
Next, regarding the practitioner: Cunda belongs to the category of the two constants; why then is he established as a separate chapter to briefly clarify ten differences?

1. At one time, the assembly first made offerings and subsequently requested [the Buddha to remain], whereas Cunda first requested and subsequently made offerings. 2. On two occasions the assembly requested three times, yet the Buddha remained silent;

on the third occasion, Cunda requested only once, and the Tathāgata immediately accepted. 3. For three reasons he accepted the great assembly; for four reasons he opened the path of permanence through food.
4. Fifth, he himself requested to remain in the world. 6. Seventh, he relayed the request of the assembly. 7. Eighth, he praised it with his golden mouth before the great assembly.

The praise of the nine [offerings] constitutes the introductory section; the questions and answers constitute the tenth. If one asks: "Since none among the multitude possesses the vows of the past, why not establish a separate chapter for them? Furthermore, why does Cunda’s offering differ so vastly from the rest as to transcend all comparison, such that he offers later rather than before? Answer: Offering later is a matter of yielding one's own virtue to another. The ancients clarified five types of yielding: the low yields to the noble, the commoner yields to the sage, the coarse yields to the refined, the inferior yields to the superior, and the disciple yields to the master. It is because Cunda yielded his virtue to the Buddha that he offered later. Moreover, it was because he had previously received a prediction of supreme enlightenment that he was permitted to offer last. This is why he did not offer first. Furthermore, the Buddha’s body is the Dharma-body; its nature is eternal and unchanging. Because the Buddha’s body is thus, the offerings made to it are likewise inexhaustible. The subtle yield to the many, and the near yield to the distant; now, according to the text, there should be ten types of yielding.

First, the worldly yields to the supramundane, namely the community of monks and nuns. Second, the ordinary yields to the noble, namely those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Third, the shallow yields to the deep, namely all bodhisattvas.
Fourth, the lowly yields to the honorable, namely kings and great ministers. Fifth, the manifest yields to the hidden, namely...
1. Devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits yield the few and coarse to the many and subtle, namely humans and devas;
2. They yield wealth to the Dharma, namely the hosts of Māras; 3. They yield those of their own kind to those of a different kind, namely lions, birds, bees, and so forth;
4. They yield those nearby to those far away, namely the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions; 5. They yield those living near cities to those in seclusion, namely the Kṣāntivādin Ṛṣi.
The five points of the assembly’s request for the text to be concluded are roughly exhausted; ten general intentions have been briefly covered. Question:

For what reason is there a difference between the former silence and the present silence regarding acceptance and non-acceptance? Answer: The Buddha’s intention is difficult to fathom. Now, there are both general and specific explanations.

Both the former and present silences are [taught] according to the four *siddhāntas*. Regarding the silence of worldly people, there is acceptance and non-acceptance; the Buddha follows the world, and thus there are these two.
Silent acceptance or non-acceptance differs; there are cases where it is appropriate to accept silently and cases where it is appropriate to not accept silently.

Since both give rise to wholesome desire, and because that wholesome state arises therein, there are three types of silent [action]. Breaking evil and attaining the Path is likewise so. For the Noble Ones, nothing is in vain, yet this is not something ordinary people can fathom. To explain separately:
at that time, the assembly lacked extraordinary conditions and was weak in its capacity for spiritual resonance, such that they were made to pursue and examine their past causes.

This is called the world’s silent refusal. If, at the outset, one speaks and yet is not accepted, then later, when the offerings for the *śamaṇa* assembly have all gathered, one accepts them all equally.
This is called a person’s silent refusal. One who silently refuses does so to censure their inability [to eat];
by means of eating, they clarify non-eating, opening up the impermanent to reveal the permanent, and manifesting a supreme remedy.

"Power" refers to the silence of non-acceptance as an antidote. If it were a body sustained by food, one might silently accept eating; however, the Dharma-body and the eternal body have no food and no acceptance—this is called the silence of non-acceptance in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). This silence of non-acceptance is the meaning of the Buddha’s realm, which is inexhaustible; briefly stated, there are four [aspects], and explained in three ways. The sixth fascicle states that his surname was Hua and his given name was Zichun; the two characters "zi" (子) and "tuó" (陀) appear interchangeably in the texts.
Formerly it was said that his original name was Chuntuo, and later the great assembly, praising his virtue, bestowed upon him the honorary title Miaoyi (妙義). However, this is not the case.
Chuntuo is the transliteration [of the foreign name], while Miaoyi is its Chinese rendering. He was first granted an auspicious name to serve as a portent for his final act. Therefore...
The great assembly praised him, saying that his name and virtue were inseparable; Subhūti, the "Well-Born," was one such as he.
However, his wondrous meaning is profound and vast, beyond the power of words to exhaust. Herein, ten aspects are briefly indicated:

namely, the excellence of meaning, the excellence of understanding, the excellence of giving, the excellence of stage, the excellence of virtue, the excellence of response, the excellence of penetration, the excellence of teaching, the excellence of field, the excellence of benefit, and the excellence of principle. Regarding the excellence of meaning:
The three points and four virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither parallel nor distinct; both Buddhas and sentient beings all dwell securely within the Secret Treasury.
As the text says: "The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable; within all phenomena there is the nature of bliss.
One who understands this subtlety realizes the wondrous wisdom of Great Nirvana, which illuminates and exhaustively penetrates the rational nature.

The movement accords with the opportune moment, and the ultimate aspiration for enlightenment is without distinction. The text states: "As for Cunda, he is named 'One Who Understands the Sublime Meaning';

though he receives a human body and mind, his heart is like the Buddha's heart. Regarding the excellence of the *dāna* (offering), eight bushels and four pecks were sufficient to satisfy the great assembly as numerous as the tips of needles.
The text further states: "It causes you to be fully endowed with the stage of *dānapāramitā* (the perfection of giving)."
Although these individuals dwell in the household life, they are masters of all the arts and crafts of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
even Śakra and Brahmā look up to them with reverence, just as the full moon outshines the stars. These *upāsakas* are Dharma-princes;

as the text says, "Those who leave home at a young age and enter the ranks of the great Saṃgha possess wondrous virtues such as the ten extraordinary qualities and the ten acts of yielding, serving both the Buddha and the assembly."
The passage of praise states: "Namo Cunda, Namo Cunda. He is the one whom we all look up to with reverence and who has moved us with his wondrous virtue.

When the Buddha’s messenger from the East, a man of great supernatural power, brought fragrant rice for the gods and humans, he presented it while they were parched with hunger, yet [the Buddha] would not accept it.
The same occurred in the other directions. How much more so, then, when Cunda made this single request on behalf of the gods and humans? It was immediately [granted].
Out of compassion for Cunda, he knew that the food was neither exquisite nor coarse, neither gross nor subtle.

As the text says, "For the sake of the great assembly, out of compassion he accepted Cunda’s final offering. Regarding the "exquisite supernatural power," when the preparations for the offering were first made, the earth shook in six ways;
at the very moment the food was presented, he spoke thirteen verses as recorded in the sutra—this is what is meant by "exquisite supernatural power."
Regarding "Excellence in Teaching": skillfully raising the five challenges while skillfully concealing the conditioned, as in the Sūtra on the Excellence of the Field;
this refers to entering final nirvāṇa, which constitutes an excellent field of merit. As the text says: "You act as an excellent field of merit for sentient beings. Regarding "Excellence in Benefit":

because one accepts their offerings, one universally receives the great assembly, thereby benefiting all through material wealth; because one opens the eternal through food, one benefits them through the Dharma.
Because the Great Being Cunda possesses these ten wonders as well as all other immeasurable wonders, this chapter is named "The Chapter of Cunda" (*Cundavarga*).
If one follows the title of the sutra, it should be called "The Ten Greats" (*Daśamahā*); however, because it refers to the person, it is called "The Ten Wonders.
The difference between "wonder" (*miao*) and "great" (*da*) is merely a matter of phrasing. From here until the end of the section on the questions of the assembly, this is the *Nirvāṇa*.
The section on giving is divided into three parts: this chapter on giving to the permanent endowments (*sthāvarika*) and the five fruits corresponds to the various classes of beings in this land;
the chapter on lamentation (*parideva*) and the giving to the superior threefold cultivation corresponds to the assembly of *śrāvakas* in this land;
the chapter on longevity and giving according to questions corresponds to the assembly of bodhisattvas in this land (and so forth). Question: Are there assemblies from other directions?
The textual structure, beginning from the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" (現病品), further clarifies the five practices and ten virtues.
The "Lion’s Roar" (師子吼) inquiries into the nature [of reality], as well as the accounts of Kāśyapa and Ānanda, are intended to address the assembly of bodhisattvas from other directions.

Yet, since the Buddha speaks with impartiality, raining his teaching universally upon all, how could there be any partition? For the time being, the text is divided to demonstrate its beginning and conclusion, though in truth, it is without division.
Question: If that is so, since from beginning to end there is only a single Nirvana, then the "Chapter on No-remainder" (Anupadhiśeṣa) would be unnecessary.
Answer: The preceding section clarified the general meaning; thus, this statement may be made (and so forth). This chapter consists of four parts:
first, by offering food, it clarifies non-eating; non-eating is the eternal, which refutes the impermanent and opens the way to that which is neither eternal nor impermanent.
1. Regarding the two constant causes: by requesting him to remain, "abiding" is negated through "non-abiding," thereby opening the way to that which is neither abiding nor non-abiding.

2. Regarding the three causes concerning the discussion of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): for the time being, let us set these aside; by opening the way to that which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned, there are four causes. 3. Urging the offering:
clarifying that [the Buddha] is in cessation (*nirvāṇa*) when he eats, and not in cessation when he does not eat, thereby opening the way to that which is neither cessation nor non-cessation.
The four sections may be sought within the text. As for the sequence of their arising: the assembly is summoned because the intention is to reveal the secret;
because of the food, there is clarity; and because of clarity, one should abide. Because abiding is not the ultimate perfection, it is obscured by non-abiding.
Since abiding and non-abiding mutually establish gain and loss, there is the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Furthermore, let us set this aside for now; if one sets aside the non-seeking, then even "is" is without being "is," and thus it is not "is.
