Therefore, the text says: "The *upāya* of *nirvāṇa* is precisely that which is 'not,' and thus it urges one to practice giving;
now is the very time. The second and third [turnings] are likewise so. When both "is" and "is not" are negated, quiescence is bliss; when affairs reach their end and principles are exhausted.

Therefore, bowing one’s head and drinking tears, one prepares the offerings. Regarding the general and specific [aspects], although they are divided into four sections, they cannot be treated as exclusively so.
Why? Because the meaning of the perfect and wondrous teaching is inexhaustible; according to their respective classes of sounds, each attains understanding.

It is not that each individual understanding is restricted to the Perfect Dharma alone. Now, viewed from the perspective of these three meanings, one specifically raises the "constant" to refute the "non-existent."
The *Changwen* (Constant Text) says: "I now bestow upon you constant life, physical vigor, peace, and unimpeded analytical clarity.

Because there is a self within me, I therefore discourse on the self, abide in the self, and contemplate the self. If there were no self, who would abide and who would contemplate? The text further says:
"You should now observe that analytical clarity is pure with respect to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and impure with respect to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this is precisely purity."
The text states: "The Tathāgata skillfully conceals the conditioned marks" (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), specifically clarifying that bliss (*sukha*) is precisely *nirvāṇa*, for all Buddhas reach this state.
The text further states: "Having been born, they do not abide; cessation (*śānti*) is bliss.

If one follows these distinct [statements] exclusively, it results in the fault of establishing a mere antidote (*pratipakṣa*) and losing the perfect meaning (*pariniṣpanna-artha*). This principle may be understood (as elaborated in the source). Second, the clarification.
Regarding the "Pervasive One" (the *Vyāpin*), what is clarified here is that "permanence" is never spoken of as being distinct from the Self;
permanence is the Self, and the Self is also purity and bliss. The Self is permanence, and it is also purity and bliss; purity and bliss are likewise so. As the text says:

"This Seal of the Permanent Dharma (*nitya-dharmamudrā*) is precisely the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of all Buddhas. If it were merely permanence, then permanence would be deficient, for it would not possess the four [attributes].
Virtue, how could it possibly attain this Seal of the Dharma-realm? The three types of knowledge (trividyā) are neither common nor distinct, being ultimately pure.
Why is this? If it were merely "eternal," it would contradict impermanence; such a concept of relativity is refuted by the sūtras and śāstras.
The Commentary on the Śāstra states: "Impermanence is a remedial dharma, not the ultimate truth; likewise, eternity is the remedy for impermanence. Furthermore...

As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon is itself dependent. Now, regarding what is called "eternal," it is neither eternal nor non-eternal;

therefore, it is neither universal (*sāmānya*) nor particular (*viśeṣa*). If it were universal, it would be defined in contrast to the particular; since the particular has already been refuted, how could the universal be established?
One should know, then, that the eternal is neither universal nor particular. The text says: "The karmic rewards of the two types of giving..."
That which is equal, without distinction, without penetration, and without differentiation is called "self. I am also like this: neither self nor non-self. The text says:
"You should now contemplate the realm of all Buddhas. As for the Buddha-realm, it is without self and without non-self;
it is pure and yet not pure, and not impure. The text says: "Let us set aside for a moment the conditioned and the unconditioned."

The relinquishing of existence and the relinquishing of non-existence are neither pure nor impure; pleasure is likewise so, and that which is neither pleasure nor non-pleasure is called the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
As the text says: "One should not contemplate long life or short life;
being neither long nor short, it is neither pleasure nor non-pleasure. Thus, these three meanings cannot be fixed as three; they are neither vertical, nor horizontal, nor parallel.

The particular is identical to the universal, yet the particular is not the universal; the particular is not one, two, or three, yet one, two, and three must be understood as perfect and wondrous (*pariniṣpanna*) to comprehend the eternal.
Furthermore, these four passages collectively establish what precedes and initiate what follows. Regarding "establishing what precedes":
the aforementioned loud proclamation and the final inquiry were intended to reveal and manifest the esoteric teachings of the provisional means (*upāya*); now, the fruit [is realized].

To open the teaching of the "neither-nor" (ubhayānta-vinirmukta), the upper gate emits light to remove obstacles and give rise to goodness; all desire to accomplish the foremost practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-caryā*).
Now, as a result, I urge you to contemplate the realm of the Buddhas. As a result, the upper stages tremble and overturn, and all return to where the Buddha is.
Now, as a result, I show that both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) shall for now be set aside. If you wish to seek the True Dharma, you should act as follows:
Having trained in this way, one finds peace and extinction as bliss, for one reaches the same destination as the Tathāgata.

Thus, the meaning of the previously mentioned invitation and other rites is fulfilled through the gift of *nirvāṇa*. As for what follows, it teaches the contemplation of the realm of all Buddhas—that is, the virtue of *prajñā*.
Those who seek the True Dharma should train in this manner; for now, let us set aside the discussion of liberation.
The virtue of the bliss of quiescence is the Dharmakāya; wherever the Buddha goes, it is this very virtue.

Thus, the division of the text reveals that the Buddha’s words are excellent in their beginning, middle, and end, and do not merely open with a chapter. First, the offering presented at the outset consists of four parts:

1) the request, 2) the acceptance, 3) the objection, and 4) the response. Regarding the request, there are two sections: first, the narrator describes the virtues; second, the speech is uttered to present the request. [This concludes] the description.

Regarding the virtues, there are two parts: first, a description of his virtuous character; second, the respectful observance of ritual decorum. First, his virtue of yielding is described; next, the virtues of his actions are described.
At that time, in the assembly, there was an upāsaka who was the son of an artisan from the city of Kuśinagara, named Cunda, together with fifteen of his peers.
In the exposition of the virtue of yielding, ten meanings are combined; the *upāsaka* is explained as before. This constitutes the three types of yielding:
yielding the secular for the path, the ordinary for the noble, and the shallow for the profound. The city of Kuśinagara is explained as before; this refers to yielding the near for the distant.
Regarding the son of a craftsman living by the city, there are two meanings: he is either the son of one who will become a great master artisan, or [the son of] a craftsman.
Thus, the one who holds the axe is noble, while the other is base; yet it is not known which is right.

Furthermore, using the base to yield to the noble and the coarse to yield to the subtle—among these fifteen individuals of the same kind (one version says fifty pairs, another says five hundred and fifteen;
fifty according to the leaders, five hundred according to those closely associated, and perhaps the rest according to their followers)—it may well be so.

This single phrase [expresses] yielding the similar to the dissimilar in order to manifest the yielding of the manifest to the profound, and yielding the few to the many. Now, to explain the underlying intent:
this person specifically requests the Buddha to accept their offerings; this is precisely the yielding of material wealth for the sake of the Dharma.
Based on the text, the meaning is established, and the significance is naturally fulfilled.
Next, in order to cause the world to obtain wholesome fruits, he praises the virtues he has performed.
For the sake of causing the world to obtain wholesome fruits, there are many paths to such fruits, namely:
agreeable fruits, untainted fruits, partial fruits, and ultimate fruits. Among these, "agreeable" refers to...
As for "fruition," it is that which is censured by the noble ones (ārya). The text states: "I now, in this place, do not seek the bodies of humans or devas.

As for the "fruition of outflowlessness" (anāsrava-phala), it refers to the extinction-ashes of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), which is praised by the sūtra-commentators; it is certainly not the fruition of self-taming and self-purification.

As for the "fruition according to one's capacity" (yathābhāga-phala), it refers to the abiding in the fruition and retribution of the three stages of worthiness (tri-satpuruṣa-bhūmi) and the ten stages of sagehood (daśa-ārya-bhūmi), yet it is not ultimate. The subsequent text says: "I..."

Because the food now offered is intended to obtain the unsurpassed reward, it is not for the sake of inferior fruits; rather, it is to enable sentient beings to attain the ultimate fruit of the Buddha's Bodhi.
Next, setting aside the physical demeanor of the body, the following describes the ritual of reverence.
Abandoning his physical deportment, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, wept with deep emotion.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
His deportment was unlike that of others—namely, the deportment of a layperson, the deportment of a practitioner on the Path, the deportment of the Dharma-gate, and the deportment of a Buddha.
When King Prasenajit visited the various Buddhas, he set aside his five marks of majesty—his crown, sword, jade belt, shoes, and carriage;
although others did not possess these five, they likewise removed their turbans, loosened their girdles, and traveled on foot. These are all mundane dignities.

As for the dignities of the Path, they refer to such things as baring one shoulder, wearing single-layered robes, celestial crowns, and celestial garments, along with their prescribed forms and regulations. As for the dignities of the Dharma-gate, they refer to... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

This refers to various dharma-gates such as the patience of birth (*utpatti-kṣānti*) and the patience of phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*). Regarding the Buddha’s majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), it refers to qualities such as the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Alternatively, it may refer to discarding secular attire and donning the robes of the Way, or discarding the attire of worldly affairs and entering the attire of the dharma-gate.
Or, even while in secular attire, one displays the power and fearlessness by baring the right shoulder; this signifies the distinction between the secular and the Way.

There are three types of baring the shoulder: baring the real, baring the conventional, and baring the mundane. Regarding "baring," as in the scriptural account of baring one's flesh to apologize for an offense, this refers to the path.

As for "baring" in the context of a disciple serving a teacher, one bares the right shoulder and covers the left for the sake of convenience in labor; this is baring the conventional, where the conventional covers the real to facilitate the practice of skillful means.
This interpretation applies to other sutras and is not the intended meaning of the present teaching. Here, it is said that the real is bared and the conventional is covered.

Concealing the provisional nature of impermanence while revealing the reality of the "neither-one-nor-other" (ubhayānta-vinirmukta), this is precisely what accords with the capacity of the recipient and facilitates the benefit of beings according to their needs;

hence it is said that one should bare the right shoulder and place the right knee upon the ground. Since the sun rotates to the right, following the ways of the world, placing the right side on the ground corresponds to the mundane realm.
The sun is the essence of Yang (the masculine principle), symbolizing wisdom that guides practice; thus, this constitutes [the ritual posture].
The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "The right is the true path; the left is the deviant path. Using the true to eliminate the deviant is the application of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*).
The knees symbolize practice (*caryā*), and the ground symbolizes principle (*tattva*). Because practice accords with principle, one places the knees upon the ground;
this is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). This intent may be understood by applying it generally to other sūtras. However, according to the present sūtra, the knees are eternal."
To place the ground of practice upon the eternal principle means to reach that principle through practice; thus, one kneels to the ground—this is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).

As for the explanation of joining the palms (*añjali*), it need not be further explicated here, as it can be understood through its conventional sense: just as clasping the hands in the world expresses reverence, so too does this gesture signify it.
As for what is signified, two things are indicated: the two principles of provisional and ultimate. Within each of the various teachings and flavors, these two are present; now, in this sutra...
Once they have merged, there is logically no "external" [to them]. As for those who feel compassion and resonance: in compassion, they pity others; in resonance, they respond to the Buddha.
Since the practices of others differ, their compassion is likewise not uniform. If offerings are not accepted, then merit and virtue do not arise; therefore, one must be compassionate.

Since the offerings are not accepted, one cannot rely on the offerings to open up the eternal; therefore, one must be compassionate. Since the eternal cannot be opened, the two [compassion and resonance]...

It is not that they do not manifest this; therefore, there is compassion. If the Buddha were to accept the offerings, the final act of giving (*dāna*) would fulfill the vows of myself and my fellow practitioners.
Thus, through compassion, he assists others by responding to their prayers. [The practitioner] does not cease the ritual of prostrating at his feet, thinking privately:
"By placing my crown upon the Buddha’s feet, the fruits of all teachings are fully subsumed within the perfect cause."

Next, he addressed the Buddha to state his request, which consists of the introduction, the formal petition, and the conclusion. The introduction is twofold: first, the introduction of the Three Jewels as a vessel for crossing over;
second, the introduction of the seeking of deliverance for oneself and others.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "I only pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will take pity [upon us]."

First, the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus constitute two jewels. The Buddha and the bhikṣus, being fully endowed with wisdom and the abandonment of defilements, are themselves the Jewel of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the term "compassionate one" (ārya) refers to the gateway of the dharma of compassion; this single character is also the Jewel of the Dharma.
Thus, these Three Jewels serve as a field of merit for those who lack offerings, enabling them to become a community that possesses offerings. Without them, there would be none.
In making offerings, there is nothing to be offered; if there is no recipient, there is no basis for offering.
Therefore, you must accept our final offering in order to deliver immeasurable sentient beings.
"To accept us" refers to those of our own kind and class. "The last" means that from the beginning one reaches the end;
when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he first benefited sentient beings, and now as he enters nirvana, he benefits them for the last time.
Since the Buddha has no occasion to receive [offerings] again, and I have no day to offer [them] again, it is called "the last. "To deliver immeasurable [beings]" indicates others.
In this way, both self and others desire to rely upon a vessel to request deliverance.
Regarding the World-Honored One’s departure, there are three methods of requesting; these are explained through two types of analogies and their corresponding applications:

first, the request because of what is lost, and second, the request because of what is sought. Regarding what is lost, there are two parts: first, clarifying what is lost, and second, explaining what is lost. First, [what is lost]:
"Lost! World-Honored One, from this day forward we are without a master, without kin, and without a savior.
We have lost the Three Jewels: to be without a master is to lose the Buddha; to be without kin is to lose the Dharma; to be without a savior is to lose the Saṃgha."
They lack protection, having lost their refuge;
they have no protector, no home, and no destination, being impoverished and destitute.
If there is no master of loyalty, there is nothing to protect; if there is no relative of filial piety, there is no place to return; if there is no teacher of learning...
Since that which one pursues is neither a master to protect nor a master for whom one can be protected, there is no honor and no emolument;
therefore, it is called "poverty. Since there are no kinsmen to whom one may return, and even those kinsmen have departed and do not return, there is no life and no shelter;
therefore, it is called "distress. Since there is no teacher to whom one may turn, and the teacher does not show the way, there is no instruction and no accomplishment; therefore, it is called...
The meaning of the preceding section has been explained to clarify what was intended.
Next, from "From desire" down to "from the Tathāgata," this is the request because it concerns that which is sought; furthermore, this request is twofold:
first, the clarification of what is sought, and second, the explanation of what is sought. Regarding the first passage:
One seeks future sustenance from the Tathāgata;
seeking the Buddha’s very essence fulfills the three benefits. Since the Buddha is a fertile field and the one from whom one seeks a livelihood, it is said that one seeks future sustenance.
Because the Buddha can nurture the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom, it is said that one seeks life from a kinsman.
That the Buddha can instruct and guide one so that one attains the correct path is precisely seeking fulfillment through a teacher;
if one follows the Tathāgata, then all meanings are encompassed.
Next, "I only wish to depart" explains what is being sought.
We only pray that you will compassionately accept our humble offering and then enter parinirvāṇa.
Next, following the World-Honored One’s analogy of the kṣatriya, this metaphor is divided into two parts:

first, the analogy of poverty, which illustrates what was lost—namely, having neither a master nor kin—and requests [the Buddha] because he has no master; second, because he is destitute due to having no kin.
"World-Honored One, it is as if a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, or a śūdra, out of poverty, were to travel far away to another country seeking food and requesting sustenance."
Regarding the mention of the four castes (*catur-varṇa*) within the analogy of poverty: the old translation states these are the "four noble clans," but this interpretation is incorrect.

As we observe today, the four great clans are all equally honored in their respective regions and do not hold one another in contempt. However, in the present text, the four castes are distinguished by high and low status, which is inconsistent with that meaning.
We now clarify that these are the four *varṇas*: *kṣatriya* is translated as "Lord of the Fields" (*tiánzhǔ*), referring to those who love the people and govern the state.
The *kṣatriya* class corresponds to the *brāhmaṇa*, which translates as "pure conduct" and refers to those who are extensively learned and well-versed in the classics.

The *vaiśya* has not yet been seen translated [in this context], but it should correspond to commoners engaged in agriculture and trade. The *śūdra* has not yet been seen translated, but it should correspond to those of the lowest status, such as those who carry excrement or corpses.
Traditionally, the four castes have been used as metaphors for the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) and also as metaphors for the six realms of existence (*ṣad-gati*).
This interpretation is not correct. If one uses the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence as analogies, they are too narrow and fail to encompass the full meaning.

Now, let us use the nine dharma-realms as an analogy for the capacities of the faculties. By grouping these nine into four types of expedient means, we see that the bodhisattvas of expedient means possess the capacity to transform others and govern sentient beings, and thus they are likened to the Kṣatriyas.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, being equally untainted and pure, [are likened to the Brahmins].
Nirvana is likened to the Brahmin; receiving retribution in the two realms of gods and humans and the good paths is likened to the Vaiśya;
the four [realms] beginning with the hells, all being evil destinies, are likened to the Śūdra. The reason for this is that all sentient beings possess the same Buddha-nature;
its flavor is true and real, and the Three Jewels are of one essence, equal and without distinction, yet they are [obscured] by afflictions.
Enveloped and obscured by afflictions, they transmigrate through the six realms of existence, receiving various bodies with distinct boundaries and differing natures;

their experiences are intermingled—sometimes sour, sometimes salty, sometimes sweet, and sometimes bitter—lacking a master or kinsman, having lost both home and nation, while the Three Jewels remain hidden and unmanifest.
On the outside, they are far removed from the Three Jewels and have forfeited all wholesome dharmas; therefore, it is so said.
Because poverty separates one from both good and evil, it is said that [the Dharma] has come from afar; because it is not one's own original source, it is said to be another land.
The *Xingpin* (Chapter on Nature) states: "Although all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, none are able to see it, for they are shrouded by the three poisons.
Consequently, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, or are born into various families such as those of the kṣatriyas. Thus it is.

Regarding its meaning: if one examines the opening analogy by comparing the *kṣatriya* and the other castes to the four types of human faculties and natures (*indriya-gotra*), it is as if one were examining the concluding analogy which states that "the poor among the four castes" refers to my own person;

this illustrates that a single individual may possess four types of faculties and natures. Furthermore, the text also says: "to rescue and deliver immeasurable sentient beings suffering in affliction."
Furthermore, it seems to employ a simile based on many people; since there are these two textual passages, one cannot take [the meaning] exclusively in one direction.
If this intent is grasped—that as it is for one person, so it is for many—then there is no hindrance to its dual application regarding a single person.

However, the primary tenet of this sutra clarifies the permanent and discriminates the nature (dharmatā). Examining the initial teaching of the Dharma, it universally loses [the distinction of] the three natures (trisvabhāva), and thus the meaning of the three natures is not manifest.

It is said that because the nature of correctness is not manifested, it is called "lacking a correct nature"; because the nature of proximate conditions is not manifested, it is called "lacking proximate conditions";

and because the nature of a master who understands is not manifested, it is called "lacking a master. To summarize these three faults as the basis for the request, the Dharma-exposition regarding what is sought states:
"Those who seek their future food solely from the Tathāgata are like those who seek their salary solely from their master; this is true seeking."
By means of the causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*), one is able to assist in clear understanding and manifest the truth; this briefly cites one point as a request.

Regarding the loss of analogy, there is a specific request concerning the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): sentient beings originally possess the nature of the true cause (*samyak-hetu-bhāva*), which is non-different from the Three Jewels in their essential unity;
yet, being shrouded by delusions, they receive various bodies and distinctions such as the four castes. This is the meaning.
To cite the "different" as a request for the "not-different" is to separately request the Tathāgata to manifest the nature of the True Reality (*dharmatā*).
One who is far removed from their own country due to poverty is called "poor"; one who has no master is called "indigent"; and one who has no teacher is called "distressed.

This cites the poor to request the wealthy, and separately requests the Tathāgata to manifest the nature of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), such as laboring in agriculture and even clearing away weeds and filth.
It clarifies that from humans and devas up to bodhisattvas, although they partially eliminate afflictions, these are merely limited roots of supreme goodness and cannot bring about full development.
They can only hope for the rain of the heavens; yet with a single sprinkling of that celestial rain, [the potential] can be brought forth.

One must specifically request the Tathāgata to reveal the nature of the manifest cause (*vyakti-hetu*); for the three Buddha-natures are neither universal nor distinct, but accord with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.
Regarding the two types of requests—the general and the specific—the remaining text follows the sutra. In the section below concerning the Tathāgata’s acceptance, there are likewise two intentions:

"I shall now eliminate your poverty" signifies his granting of the role of master, revealing the nature of the causal conditions; "the unsurpassed rain of Dharma" signifies his granting of the role of teacher, revealing the nature of realization;
and "causing the sprouts of Dharma to grow in the field of your body" signifies his granting of the role of cultivator.
The Teacher clearly reveals that these are the three distinct causes for the Buddha-nature.

Why is this? Cunda’s offering of food has two fruits of retribution that are without distinction. How can they be without distinction? If one allows him to be the donor, he is simultaneously the teacher;
if one allows him to be the teacher, he is simultaneously the donor. These three—suchness and so forth—are equal and without differentiation. If this is revealed...

The causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*) is precisely what is manifested; when it is manifested, it is the manifestation of the causal condition. These three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) are manifestations that are without distinction.
This is the general admission regarding the nature of the three causes. Some may say: "This has not yet clarified Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
How so? This is the answer: the sutra clarifies Buddha-nature as its primary teaching. If this were not opened at the beginning, how could it be established later?

The reason for treading upon this is precisely that the Buddha of the Single Essence is requested to act as the presiding Master, the Relative of the Single Essence is bestowed as the immediate Teacher,
and the Lord of the Single Essence is bestowed to grant constant life-force and vigor; the Teacher of the Single Essence is bestowed to grant constant eloquence,
thereby causing the Three Treasures and the Three Buddha-natures of the Single Essence within one’s own body to manifest, equalizing self and other, internal and external.
For those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence who are without distinction, [the Buddha] has already acted together with Cunda for the sake of those who have not yet understood;
through the section on "Sorrowful Lamentation," he opened the secret treasury and established all his children within it.

From the *Lifespan* and *Vajra* chapters, which follow in succession, up to the *Kāśyapa* and *Lion’s Roar* chapters, he extensively revealed the Buddha-nature. If this fundamental principle were not clarified at the outset, [the teaching would remain obscured].
Regarding the Buddha-nature: for what purpose is it expounded, and what is its central tenet? Fearing that the text might become scattered, I have here cryptically indicated this meaning.
Next, from the passage "laboring in the fields" onwards, the text provides a metaphor for that which is sought.
The laborers are engaged in farming; they have well-trained oxen and excellent fields that are level and free from sand, salt, weeds, and wild growth, and they only hope for rain from heaven.
This analogy briefly illustrates that all wholesome dharmas—whether belonging to humans, devas, those of the two vehicles, or the skillful means of bodhisattvas—are entirely dependent on conditions.

Because it represents only a small portion [of the whole], this is cited as a primary illustration. For those seeking labor, the explicit purpose is to clarify the aversion toward the wretchedness of the miserable realms and poverty;
since one still values the excellence of human and celestial rebirths, the text says, "By working for hire in agriculture, one obtains well-trained oxen. This passage contains two meanings:

first, if the ox is used as a metaphor for the body, the body is a virtuous fruit that still belongs to the human and celestial realms; second, if the training of the ox is used as a metaphor for the body [itself].

The mouth represents the field of precepts; the excellent soil represents meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the level and upright ground represents wisdom (*prajñā*); and the weeding out of weeds and filth represents the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*). This also has two meanings:
if one removes the four abiding [delusions], it refers to the goodness of the Two Vehicles; if one removes the dust and sand, it refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Three [Vehicles].
Merely longing for the rain of Dharma is the seeking of the direct cause (*tathatā-hetu*); merely longing for the Tathāgata is the seeking [of the fruit].
The primary request is for the Dharma-rain; this constitutes the threefold request for a teacher.

If these are fulfilled—like a pauper finding a master, a destitute person finding a kinsman, or one who is blind finding a guide—then the Buddha-nature will manifest. The essential point of what is sought lies precisely here.

The Buddha responds to these requests according to their petitions and bestows his grace; he constantly grants life, physical form, and strength, thereby accepting them as his kin and revealing their true nature.

To bestow constant tranquility is to grant him the status of a sovereign, manifesting his nature as a condition; to bestow constant eloquence is to grant him the status of a teacher, manifesting his nature of realization.
Only when there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows does one come to know the intent of the text.
Third, following the words "taming the ox," the analogy is first applied: the application of labor is matched first, and poverty is matched afterward.

Although the sequence of the text is not [strictly] chronological—since poverty and labor are not necessarily fixed in their order, for one is poor because of labor and labor because of poverty—the point remains that from humans and devas up to the third stage of the Bodhisattva, all are equally poor;
though there are slight differences, they are all poor, whereas the Tathāgata is not.

The superior wealth and treasures do not accord with one's intent in their sequence, yet they may here accord through the application of effort; this is further illustrated by the analogy of first traversing various methods and subsequently attaining union within a single essence.
The phrase "taming the ox" is a metaphor for the body and speech; the "level and upright fertile field" is a metaphor for wisdom, which removes the saline and barren soil.
The weeds and brambles are a metaphor for the removal of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Initially, among those who encounter the Dharma, those who do not attain rebirth as humans or devas are specifically omitted from the text; this is because the sevenfold precepts of body and speech serve to guard and protect them, corresponding to the taming of an ox above.
Concentration (*samādhi*) can support wisdom (*prajñā*), corresponding to the fertile field above; as for wisdom, its distinctions are forgotten [in this context].
"Joining above, level and upright, removes the delusions of the four abodes; joining above, removing filth, removes the delusions of the dust-sands; this joins with the removal of saline soil.
Next, 'World-Honored One, my present body has... and so forth, which joins with the single essence."
World-Honored One, my body is now like a well-trained ox, a fertile field cleared of all impurities; I only hope for the Tathāgata’s rain of ambrosial Dharma.

My body possesses the precepts, which correspond to the trained ox; concentration corresponds to the fertile field; and wisdom corresponds to the clearing away of impurities. Although I am thus endowed with these virtues...
The conditions cannot manifest the truth; one merely longs for the Tathāgata to depart, which is precisely to seek the teaching of the "enabling cause" (paripūri-hetu).
As for those who depart from the four castes of the poor, this corresponds to the aforementioned poverty.
Those of the four castes who are poor are none other than ourselves; we are destitute of the wealth and treasures of the unsurpassed Dharma.
We only pray that you will take pity on us, sever our poverty and suffering, and rescue immeasurable sentient beings from their afflictions.

The preceding section, which traversed the four castes, has already been explained as being established within a single essence; this follows the intent of "rescuing" those below by merging them with the distinct categories of the four castes above.

Third, from the phrase "That which I now offer," there are two parts that together form a double conclusion, the first of which concludes the sought-after goal within the preceding metaphors of the Dharma.
Regarding this request:
although the offerings I now present are meager, I hope they may suffice for the Tathāgata and his great assembly.

In the "Request for the Dharma" (*Dharmayācanā*), it says that one should receive my humble offering and then enter *nirvāṇa*; this appears to be a request made specifically to the Buddha alone. Now, I shall conclude with a simile.

The phrase "hoping to be able to sufficiently provide for the Great Assembly of the Tathāgata" means that [the merit] does not reside solely in the Buddha, but is well able to sufficiently provide for the assembly of fifty-two [bodhisattvas].
Furthermore, it reveals his ability to universally bestow a single meal upon the vast multitude;
though the offerings are few, they suffice for the many, providing inconceivably for a multitude whose number is difficult to conceive (and so forth).
Next, I now have no master and no kinsman; having departed from the Dharma and its analogies regarding the two fetters, I have lost my way.
I am now without a master, without kin, and without refuge; I pray that you will look upon me with compassion.
Third, regarding those like Rāhula, this is a request for the removal of faults sought within the dharma-illustration of the "twofold bond.
Just as with Rāhula—
the Buddha is his sovereign as a Golden-Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), and he is also his own teacher— so it is for me and all others as well.
These three matters are identical to those concerning Rāhula.
From that time, the text regarding the second acceptance of offerings consists of three parts: first, the permission to accept the gift; second, the actual acceptance;
and third, the explanation of the permission to accept. Furthermore, there are two sub-sections: first, the narration of the permission; and second, the Buddha’s proclamation of the permission.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the All-Knowing One, the Unsurpassed Tamer, addressed Cunda, saying:

"Excellent, excellent! First, the narrator sets forth the three titles of the Buddha; yet because Cunda had made his request using these three titles, the Buddha responds and grants his consent by employing those same three titles.

By citing 'World-Honored One,' he grants him the status of Master; by citing 'All-Knowing One,' he grants him the status of Teacher; and by citing 'Unsurpassed Tamer,' he grants him the status of Kinsman."
If he granted [the request] to be his master, poverty was immediately severed; if he granted [the request] to be his kinsman, destitution was immediately dispelled;

if he granted [the request] to be his teacher, hardship was immediately eliminated. Thus the three losses were restored and the three pursuits were successfully achieved. The World-Honored One is one whom all gaze upon with reverence:
like a filial son serving his parents, like a Brahmin serving the sacrificial fire, and like the various devas [revering their lords].
Serving Śākyamuni is the meaning of filial piety; serving the sacrificial fire is the meaning of reverence for a teacher; and serving Śākyamuni is the meaning of loyalty (and so forth).
Furthermore, the World-Honored One is like the Buddha-moon gazed upon by the constellations of those in training and those beyond training;

he is like Mount Sumeru, the precious mountain, surrounded by the ocean-like waters of the four kinds of bodhisattvas; and he is illustrated by metaphors such as the sandalwood forest and the lion, which represent his precepts and meditative concentration.
Because his wisdom is revered by the world, he is called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*). Regarding "omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*):

it may refer to the fact that through his marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and form-body (*rūpakāya*), he universally faces all beings, and each being understands him individually; thus it is called omniscience.

For example, there are sentient beings in the world who serve eighty deities; for each deity there is a specific mark, and according to what they behold and what they serve, [they perceive the Buddha accordingly].
Because he comes to cause every single being to attain liberation, he is called the "Omniscient One" (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, one does not regard the physical body as the Buddha;

rather, one regards the Omniscience as the Buddha. Since this Omniscience is seen as the basis for the adornment of the marks and signs upon this physical body, it should be known that because wisdom is fully perfected, it is called the "Omniscience.
The "Tamer" (*vināyaka*) refers to one who adapts [the teaching] to the capacities of sentient beings.
Regarding the conditions that should arise and should cease, and those that should be accepted but are not—these are for the purpose of taming all sentient beings.
In other sutras, "Tamer of Men" (*purusa-damya-sārathi*) is used as two titles, whereas in this sutra they are combined into one. The text says:
"Since you yourself are a man of noble character (*puruṣa*), you further tame men; excellent, excellent! This is a seal of approval for his dual request regarding both the Dharma and the parable.
Next, "I shall now eliminate your poverty for you"—this is the Buddha’s proclamation of consent.
"I shall now eliminate your poverty; with the unsurpassed rain of Dharma, I shall rain upon the field of your body to cause the sprouts of Dharma to grow."
To sever poverty is to grant me the status of master; to provide the rain of Dharma is to grant me the status of teacher;
to produce the sprouts of Dharma is to grant me the status of kinsman. From you now, I receive this as a formal acceptance:
"If you now desire from me long life, physical vigor, well-being, and unimpeded eloquence, I shall bestow these upon you."
"Long life, physical strength, peace, and unimpeded eloquence—these are what you now seek from me.
Regarding long life, I shall fulfill your request for your father; regarding physical strength, I shall fulfill your request for your master;
regarding unimpeded eloquence, I shall fulfill your request for your teacher. When I say 'I shall bestow these upon you,' it is my granting of these three."

(As stated above... The old [interpretation] clarifies that the true essence of *nirvāṇa* is eternal (*nitya*), as it remedies impermanence (*anityatā*). Thus, the sequence of the five periods is explained:
although the *Prajñāpāramitā* elucidates the Buddha of the *viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa* (exalted marks), it is for the sake of establishing non-arising (*anutpāda*);

although the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi* speaks of seven hundred *kalpas*, how could it compare to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? Although the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* speaks of immeasurable lifespans, these are still impermanent; they culminate in *nirvāṇa*.
The teaching of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* first clarifies permanence and bliss, while distantly rejecting the Deer Park [teachings] and closely refuting the *Lotus Sūtra*.

It asserts that all paths converge in *nirvāṇa*, which is perfect, eternal, and exhausts the source and fulfills the nature. Those who speak thus selectively pluck single phrases from various sūtras suited to specific conditions and interpret them as having the meaning of impermanence;
they also selectively adopt the "permanence" of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*—which is intended to cure a specific ailment—as the ultimate essence. Both of these approaches are one-sided.
What is lost? The Prajñāpāramitā, the Mother of Buddhas; Nirvāṇa, the Teacher of Buddhas; the *Śūraṅgama*, the three Buddhas of Nirvāṇa;
the three dots (*bindu*) of the Dharma; the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; Nirvāṇa as Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*); and the One Vehicle as Buddha-nature itself.

Since all sentient beings are entirely the One Vehicle, why is the One Vehicle further used to refute the Dharma of the One Vehicle? How does one refute the Dharmakāya? How does one refute the Dharma-Buddha and the Buddha?

The Master said: "How can one destroy the Mother of Buddhas? Thus we know that those who delude themselves regarding skillful means and are confused about the teachings of the various sections (varga) fall into mutual contradictions and errors, thereby losing the correct intent;

such views are not to be employed here. Although the 'Earth' school (Dilun) does not hold to the doctrine of the five periods, their interpretation of the principle that the 'present and eternal' sublates the 'impermanent' is similar in its logical force to the old [beliefs], and thus they share the same underlying disposition as the Xinghuang school. The Xinghuang school explained it as follows: [text continues].

Regarding "the permanent and the impermanent," medicine and disease treat one another: impermanence treats permanence. If one recognizes impermanence, this is the expedient means for treating permanence;

once the disease is removed, the medicine is exhausted. If one does not recognize this, one clings to the medicine as if it were the disease, whereby the disease becomes the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

Therefore it is said: "O King, your illness is grave. To treat permanence with impermanence is likewise an expedient means; once the disease is removed, the medicine is exhausted. If [one does not understand this], then...

Those who understand realize that consciousness itself constitutes the views of permanence and annihilation; through these two skillful means, one can sever both annihilationism and eternalism, thereby transcending them.

Thus, when the wise perceive the arising of phenomena, they immediately extinguish the view of annihilation; when they perceive the cessation of phenomena, they immediately extinguish the view of permanence.

If one does not understand this, one remains within these two views. Now it is clarified that this interpretation differs from the former tradition; yet for one who grasps the essential meaning, there is nothing [to be attained].
To idly pursue thoughts arising from words is identical to the fault mentioned previously. Why? To refute permanence and impermanence is merely a provisional means of discussion;
to point to that which is neither permanent nor impermanent as the true essence is like avoiding emptiness while seeking emptiness—the further one goes, the more distant one becomes from it. Why?
For the Buddha said that the karmic rewards of the two types of giving are equal and without distinction. If [one claims] that what was previously taught regarding the five...
If the fruit is impermanent and one now says it is permanent, this may be considered a distinction;
however, if both permanence and impermanence are neither permanent nor impermanent, only then is there equal non-distinction. This also reveals the expedient means of the Esoteric Teachings.
If one grasps this intent, then the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Śūraṅgama* are nothing other than secret. Yet, the meaning of this "permanence" is the very throat of this teaching.
The heart-essence of all sutras and the dwelling place of the multitude of sages; the dharma-realm of all Buddhas is inconceivable, and the wisdom of the Tathāgata can never be fully expounded.
Whether it be the permanence of quiescence, the permanence of manifestation, or the permanence of curing afflictions, how could these possibly accord with the perfect principle?
Now, let me attempt to explain: the Buddha’s appearance in the world is fundamentally for the sake of the Great Matter.
Because the causal conditions of the Great Matter (mahā-vastu) are the eternal and constant Dharma that encompasses all, it is called "Great Eternity" (daichang).

Because it establishes all phenomena (dharmas), it is called "Eternity of Affairs" (shichang). Because the capacity [of beings] eternally responds [to it], it is called "Eternity of Causal Conditions" (yinyuanchang). There is no distinction [between these];
they are spoken of as distinct for the sake of explanation. As stated below: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma. Because the Dharma is eternal, all..."
The Buddhas likewise always do so; all Buddhas of the three periods of time take this as their teacher. This is eternally without teacher or disciple; teacher and disciple are both eternal.
Such distinctions are called the eternity of the world.

I now eliminate your poverty for you with the unsurpassed rain of Dharma, raining upon the field of your body to cause the sprouts of Dharma to grow. You now seek from me longevity, physical form, and strength.
“I shall bestow upon you peaceful bliss, unimpeded eloquence, long life, physical strength, peace, and unimpeded eloquence.
He further said, “Out of compassion for you and for all beings, I now desire to enter parinirvāṇa.
If any devas or humans make their final offerings to me here, they shall all obtain the fruit of immovability.”
All these passages clarify that the arising of eternal goodness is what is called the "eternity of the person.
Those who wish to distance themselves from the four inversions should know that this refers to eternity, bliss, self, and purity: "self" has the meaning of Buddhahood;
"eternity" is the Dharma-body; "bliss" is Nirvana; and "purity" is the True Dharma. By means of these four qualities, one destroys the four inversions. Furthermore—
It is said that the characteristics of the four dharmas previously practiced are all inverted.
Those who wish to attain the true cultivation of various perceptions should be like that wise person who skillfully cultivates the perception of self, permanence, bliss, and purity.

It is like a skilled physician who first uses salty and bitter medicines to treat a fundamental illness; although the fundamental illness has departed, the patient subsequently suffers from the salty and bitter taste, and is later treated with pure milk.
The Buddha is also like this: he first uses impermanence to treat the disease of permanence;
once the disease of permanence has departed, he further treats the disease of impermanence. Now, by using true permanence to destroy former impermanence, he says, "I am the King of Physicians.
Desiring to subdue the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), he proclaims, "There is no self and no person"; for these reasons, he speaks of existence.
My constant refutation of the impermanent is likewise so. Furthermore, the "pair" in the East refers to the permanent, which serves to refute the impermanent.
Moreover, the two birds flying together as a pair is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s non-dual yet dual functioning.

Passages such as these all clarify that the permanent dharma is presented in contrast to refute the impermanent. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) also states: "The permanent and the impermanent are opposites."
The method of treatment is not the ultimate truth; it is called "counteracting permanence. That which is the ultimate truth is neither permanent nor impermanent.

Now, this sutra also says that the karmic fruits of the two types of giving are equal and without distinction. If permanence were to negate impermanence, or if impermanence were distinct from permanence, there would be a distinction.
This is not the ultimate truth. The ultimate truth is neither permanent nor impermanent.
Because it is eternal, there is no distinction. If two birds fly together, it illustrates their dual functioning; if both birds rest together, it illustrates their mutual quiescence.
To function while being quiescent, and for that quiescence to be bliss—this is Great Nirvana. Passages such as these all refer to the ultimate truth of eternity.
One should know that this eternity is unimpeded by the four *siddhāntas*; yet even this eternity is intermittent, for it is a cause.
The Great Matter is eternally quiescent and severed, yet its ultimate wondrous principle is eternally productive;

it establishes all dharmas, eternally counteracts and destroys delusions, and possesses such mastery. Why then do you rely exclusively on this [one aspect], burying the mutual discourse of medicine and disease within the counteractive treatments?
This would ruin the comprehensive capacity of all sutras and śāstras. Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is fundamentally...
That this [Buddha-nature] exists is not a phenomenon restricted to the present alone; furthermore, all twenty-five realms of existence (*bhava*) possess it.

This "self" is precisely the Buddha-nature, and the Buddha-nature is eternal. This Buddha-nature is heroic and fierce, difficult to destroy. These many words and meanings demonstrate its manifest eternity.
Furthermore, it is said: "All who possess a mind shall become Buddhas; in the future, they shall attain the eternal, the blissful, the self, and the pure."
Passages such as these state that it is "present" and "future. Furthermore, it is impossible for dharmas to exist across the three periods of time;

since the three periods do not exist, how could there be a "present" or a "future"? The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "It is only by means of conventional words that the three periods are spoken of;
it does not mean that bodhi has past, future, or present. If one stubbornly insists that the future and the present each have their own basis...

Those of the three periods of time do not understand my intention; how could they possibly comprehend these verses? Furthermore, this "permanence" reveals the Tathāgata’s esoteric teaching of skillful means.
What was previously concealed as permanence is now revealed and distinguished as permanence;

there is no difference between the present permanence and the past, nor is the past impermanence distinct from the present permanence. Next, when I say, "I shall now sever your poverty," if it is removed—
The poverty of the four realms of existence reveals the impermanence of all evils while manifesting the permanent; as the text below states:
"Repenting the four grave prohibitions, the mind that slanders the Dharma is eliminated; the five heinous crimes are extinguished, and the icchantika state is ended"—this is precisely its meaning.
If one cuts off the poverty of humans and devas, this reveals the impermanence of all virtues while manifesting the permanent; as the text says: "I now..."
In this state, one does not seek the status of gods or humans; even if such states were attained, the mind would find no satisfaction or joy in them.
Furthermore, the statement that "by the extinction of this form, one obtains eternal form" and so forth conveys this very meaning.

If the poverty of the two vehicles is severed, the untainted (anāsrava) and impermanent is opened up to reveal the eternal. As the text says: "For the sake of the śrāvakas, he opens up and develops wisdom."

Regarding the eye (and so forth), if the Bodhisattva’s poverty is severed through skillful means, the six perfections—both general and specific—are opened, revealing the eternal within the impermanent.
The text states: "It causes all Bodhisattvas to clearly perceive the Buddha-nature," and further says:
"Prior to this, we were all called people of false views. In sum, opening all that remains [of conditioned existence] is entirely for this purpose.
Without exception, all that was previously uncomprehended is now revealed as being of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*);
this is called the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s expedient and esoteric teachings, wherein all are established within the secret treasury of the three dots and four virtues.

Furthermore, this "permanence" is precisely the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), and the Buddha-nature is permanence; since permanence is now revealed, the Buddha-nature is likewise revealed, and thus it acts for the sake of these beings.
The Master personally opens [the gate]; the Host opens it as a condition; the Teacher opens it to eliminate and sever poverty.
When the nature of the objective realm is opened, all shall attain the fruit of immovability. This is the opening of the nature of the fruit.
If one applies this principle, what person, what dharma, what teaching, what practice, what stage, or what function would not be eternal? What dharma would not be non-constant?
If it were not impermanent, how could there further be the distinctions between the two vehicles of good and evil?
It is ultimately the Great Parinirvāṇa, cut off from the path of language and extinguished as the sphere of mental activity;
inconceivable, vertically deep and horizontally vast, boundless and bottomless, capable of establishing great meaning and filling the Dharma-realm, it is inexhaustible. How could it be otherwise?
The judgment is that this [state] is the quiescent breaking of delusion; is it then the "present" or the "eternal"? This meaning of "eternal" is like empty space.
Briefly, I have contrasted the four schools to show its general outline. Next, regarding the names of the five fruits within the state of *samādhi*, they are not explained in the text;

I privately remark that since these five are all "fruits," they fully encompass both cause and effect and all myriad virtues. First, I shall eliminate the names in sequence, then contrast them accordingly.
Since the five dharmas are all eternal, it is first said that they are "eternal. To maintain [the continuity] is called "life-force" (*jīva*).
Eternal life-force is without beginning or end and is never severed. Taking what is not form as form, this body of mine is precisely the functioning of the *dharmakāya*.
Its power pervades all places; its function is inexhaustible. Being unmoving is termed "peace" (*kṣema*), even though it possesses power.
"Stability and immovability" refers to the empowerment of the faculties; "eloquence" refers to the unconditioned compassion that universally bestows the medicinal medicine of the Dharma.

Next, regarding the *Abhidharma* (the Dharma of Analysis): this is the life-force of the three mysteries. "Life" is the mystery of mind (*mantra*); "form, power, and stability" is the mystery of body (*kāya*); and "unimpededness" is the mystery of speech (*vāc*).

It is also called the four virtues: the mind is the virtue of permanence (*nitya*); the body is the virtue of bliss (*sukha*), selfhood (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*); and the speech is the virtue of purity.

If one attains this understanding that it pervades all phenomena—since there is nothing that does not possess these five Buddhas and because one bestows upon others the five constant virtues (*pañca-śīla*)—then giving is likewise inexhaustible.
What is called "inexhaustible" refers precisely to the five fruits.
Third, for what reason does "departing" mean to explain giving?
For what reason is it said that Cunda’s offering of food has two fruits of retribution without distinction? What are these two?
First, having received [the food], he shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; second, having received [the food], he shall enter *nirvāṇa*. I—
"Now, by receiving your final offering, I shall cause you to fulfill the *dānapāramitā*.

Having explained the initial [teaching] and the subsequent [teaching], the meaning of the intermediate [teachings] can be understood. This intent is not only that the later teachings reveal the eternal; the initial [teachings] do so as well.
Since the various teachings have been cited as examples, one should know that the stages of practice, the positions, and the realized persons are likewise thus—the seal of the eternal Dharma."
Sealing all things as nothing other than eternal constitutes the eternity of practice; making offerings from beginning to end constitutes the eternity of teaching;
that there must be persons for both types of giving constitutes the eternity of person;
that there must be karmic fruition constitutes the eternity of realization; and that there must be stages for realization constitutes the eternity of stage—these are equal and without distinction.
This Dharma is eternal (and so forth). Furthermore, regarding "equality without distinction," according to the explanatory text, there are various meanings:
it may mean that both the beginning and the end equally accept, equally consume, or equally do not consume; or that both the beginning and the end equally attain the five fruits;
or that both the beginning and the end equally perceive the Buddha-nature, sever afflictions, and are able to preach the Dharma.
If one relies on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, it is because both the beginning and the end are thus and empty;

if one relies on the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Shi lun), it is because both the beginning and the end are the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; if one considers the intent here, it is because both the beginning and the end are eternal;
and as for "eternal," it is the eternity that is neither eternal nor non-eternal. If one fails to understand this eternity that is neither eternal nor non-eternal...
Question: Does the eternal mind have no distinction across all dharmas, teachings, practices, stages, and persons?

Question: Are all sentient beings eternally present, or will they become so in the future? Answer: As already explained above, all three periods of time are eternal. Question: If they are eternally present, are sentient beings then Buddhas? Answer:
How could a child in the womb not share the same surname as its father? If they share the same surname as the father, [then they are indeed so].

It is better to hold one accountable for the six levels of realization: all sentient beings are the Constant of Principle; hearing the Great Nirvana and understanding and knowing the Buddha-nature is the Constant of Name;
knowing the nature and being able to practice it is the Constant of Contemplative Practice; seeing a stump at night is the Constant of Similarity;
the golden probe clearing the eye so that the three fingers are clearly seen is the Constant of Partial Truth; and there is no [Constant] of Ultimate Perfection.
Ascending to the Great Enlightenment is itself the ultimate; such is the nature of all that is eternal. Regarding the doubt as to what constitutes this eternity:

the meaning of the name *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment) may be seen as explained in the usual manner. Having received this final offering, the affairs of this one life-period are concluded and the benefit of the Dharma is fully realized.
You have heard and seen this; rely upon it and practice giving, and you will surely be complete in your generosity.
The passage concerning Cunda’s formulation of the objection consists of two parts. First, a general refutation stating that it is not so:
At that time, Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying, "Regarding what the Buddha has taught—that there is no difference between the karmic rewards of these two kinds of giving—this meaning is not so."
Later, Nan-yeh-ch’eng composed four objections separately, while K’ai-shan composed five objections; their titles differ (and so forth). Herein, we clarify the five objections:
first, there is the possession of wisdom and abandonment, and second, the absence of wisdom and abandonment.

Why is this? Because the one who first receives the gift has not yet exhausted their afflictions, has not yet attained the realization of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), and is not yet able to cause sentient beings to fulfill the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*);

whereas the one who receives the gift later has already exhausted their afflictions, has already attained the realization of all-knowledge, and is able to cause sentient beings everywhere to fully possess the perfection of giving.
Second, there are those who possess the title of "Saint" and those who do not.
The one who first receives the offering is still a sentient being; the one who later receives the offering is the God among Gods.
Third, they are endowed with four bodies or five bodies.
The one who first receives the offering has a body sustained by mixed food, a body of afflictions, a final body, and an impermanent body;
whereas the one who later receives the offering has a body free from afflictions, a vajra-body, a dharma-body, an eternal body, and a boundless body.
How can it be said that the karmic fruits of these two offerings are equal and without distinction?
Fourth, those who possess the eyes of transcendence and those who do not possess the eyes of transcendence.
The former recipients of offerings have not yet fulfilled the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*;

they have only attained the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) and have not yet attained the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) up to the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*). The latter recipients of offerings have already attained fulfillment in the *dāna*.
If the perfections from the *pāramitā*s up to the *prajñāpāramitā* fulfill the physical eye up to the wisdom eye,
why do you say that the retributive fruits of these two types of giving are equal and without distinction?
Regarding the five who obtain the five fruits and those who do not obtain the five fruits (as detailed at length):

World-Honored One, if the first recipient of an offering receives it, eats it, and it is digested within the stomach, thereby obtaining life, physical form, strength, tranquility, and unhindered eloquence,
whereas the subsequent recipients do not eat it and it is not digested, so that they lack these five fruits— how is this so?
Yet it is said that the fruits of these two types of giving are equal and without distinction.
Regarding the first objection, the discussion of self and other is presented in full; regarding the latter four objections, only the perspective of "from this" is discussed.

Since the original intent was to clarify the merit received by the recipient and the benefit to others, and because the first [objection] already exhaustively raised these points, there is no need for further elaboration in the subsequent ones; therefore, they are omitted. Nevertheless, these five objections...
The sharp points [of these doctrines] are difficult to resolve: what is the ultimate principle? It is quiescent cessation, neither great nor small.

When he manifests traces to transform sentient beings, there are those with sharp and dull faculties, and thus there must be superior and inferior [responses]. Those with small conditions see both the beginning and the end as inferior; those with great conditions see both the beginning and the end as superior.
If, at the outset, he sat beneath the tree and accepted the milk-gruel from the cowherd girl, and having eaten this food...
The Ten Powers fill this small vessel for those of inferior views; when one first sits upon the lotus pedestal, the attendant bodhisattvas all sit upon the lotus petals.

The Buddhas of the ten directions emit light from between their eyebrows, which enters the crown of the lotus pedestal, while the retinues of the Buddhas emit light from between their eyebrows, which enters the crowns of the petals.
Through the samādhi of the bodhisattva on the lotus pedestal, he receives his office and achieves fruition.

The Bodhisattva Buddhakusumapattraka attained the state of a Response-Buddha (Nirmāṇa-buddha). One should know that this great condition of seeing the victory is distinct from that of the cowherd woman and the various Buddhas;
the milk-rice and the radiance are eternally different. This is precisely the first instance of the two types of Buddhas—the Great and the Small—receiving offerings:
when the Buddha went forth to beg for food and arrived at Cunda’s house to eat the *tandula* soup during the middle of the night.
Entering parinirvāṇa, he turned toward the twin śāla trees and cremated his body; this was a minor circumstance seen by those of inferior vision.

If one sees only Cunda’s sorrowful offering of eight *hu* and four *dou* of rice, it is because they do not contemplate that this offering satisfied all beings and that the Buddhas of the ten directions dispatched great disciples to present fragrant food in their alms bowls to the Buddha at his nirvāṇa; this is the superior vision of those who perceive the great causal conditions. You should know this.
Begging for alms differs from having food sent; fragrant rice is forever distinct from coarse offerings.

Such is the nature of the final acts of receiving offerings by the Buddhas of the Great and Small Vehicles. By analogy, their wisdom and severance, as well as even their five fruits, should likewise differ.
When Cunda’s sharp-edged [offering] follows the great conditions and precedes the small conditions, one encounters the difficulty of reconciling these distinctions.

The Buddha, answering by means of what is perceived through great conditions, showed that there is no difference between the beginning and the end; thus, the distinction between the Jing and Wei rivers is as clear as day, and the beginning and the end are non-dual.
Now, I shall further cite a sutra to analyze this: in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, it is said that when [the Buddha] first sat beneath the tree, there were four kinds of manifestations:
some saw him sitting on auspicious grass, some saw him sitting on celestial robes, and some saw him sitting on the seven treasures.

In the *Jian zuo xūkōng xiàngfǎ juéyí jīng* (Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Image of Sitting in Empty Space), it is stated that when the Buddha enters nirvāṇa, there are four kinds of manifestations:
one may see Kuśinagara as consisting of earth, stones, trees, and forests; or one may see it as adorned with the seven treasures;
or one may see it as a place where the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time travel and dwell; or one may see it as the true mark of suchness (*tathatā*), a realm of pure Buddhahood.
Since the four marks manifested later are not uniform, by analogy, one should infer that his wisdom (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and even the five fruits (*pañca-phala*) must likewise differ.

Now, I shall briefly explain this further in relation to the Teacher. When the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka first received the milk-rice, he possessed neither wisdom nor abandonment and was thus unable to transform others so that they might attain wisdom and abandonment.
As long as one has not yet transcended ordinary phenomena (*laukika-dharma*), one cannot receive the title of "Noble One" (*ārya*). This is because suffering [remains].
The physical body is frail and externally requires various foods; internally, the outflows have not yet been extinguished and afflictions remain, such that the bonds of the fruit still persist.

This is the final body, destined for ultimate destruction; it is an impermanent body. Although one practices the giving of alms (*dāna*), because the transcendence through principle has not been attained, this giving is incomplete;
the same applies up to and including wisdom (*prajñā*). The bodies of parents are merely... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

Because the fleshly eye has not yet attained penetration and clarity, one lacks the four eyes; yet, once the food has been accepted, one personally attains five benefits and is able to bestow those five benefits upon others.
Observing Cunda’s words, they specifically cite the Tripiṭaka to argue that it is difficult for a Buddha to have just newly attained enlightenment.

If, however, one refers to a Buddha of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), then at the time of the Bodhisattva path, he has already severed the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), and the untainted [wisdom] manifests before him; thus, he personally attains both knowledge and severance, and likewise enables others to do so.

Having attained this, he abandons ordinary dharmas and enters the stage of the noble ones. Through his vows, he nurtures his practice and manifests sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), displaying a body that receives food;
he is no longer subject to the four abidings (*catvāra āśrayāḥ*), but possesses only residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*). This is called the "body of impermanence," the final body.
It is not the final body of the active afflictions (*kleśa*); having already perfected the three perfections (*pāramitā*) of giving, it is the final body of impermanence.

From honey up to *prajñā*, [the Buddha] has already attained the four eyes but not yet the Buddha-eye; he demonstrates the benefit of digesting solid food for others so that they may attain the five fruits.
What Cunda questioned has not yet touched upon this. When the separate and perfect Buddhas first receive offerings, it is as the Buddha answered:
"Since I attained Buddhahood, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed, and I have long been fully endowed [with these]."

The wisdom that brings about abandonment causes others to attain the wisdom of abandonment; even when food has been consumed long ago and has not yet been digested, there are no five kinds of results.

This demonstrates that what is first accomplished is received at the beginning, while what is later accomplished is received at the end. How could one use inferior views to challenge the superior views?
It is clear that there is no difference between the initial and final fruits. Thus, the meaning is evident.
The four Buddhas’ response consists of two parts: first, the direct answer to the five difficulties; second, the universal reception by the great assembly.
Regarding the initial answer to the third difficulty concerning the four bodies and five bodies, the Buddha said:
"Good son, the Tathāgata has for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas been without food."
The body of one free from afflictions is the body without end, the eternal body, the Dharma-body, and the Vajra-body.
Because bodies involve separation and union, there are four or five [types]; as this teaching is the foremost, it is answered by transcending [the categories].
However, Cunda first raised the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka, initially posing a challenge regarding the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka who underwent six years of austerity.
When the vital essence of his practice was nearly exhausted, he sustained his physical strength with milk-rice until it was fully replenished; thus, this is a "body of food.

Since such a body of food manifests due to karmic conditions, it is a body of afflictions. Through thirty-four moments of mind, the fetters of the seeds are severed and exhausted, leaving only the fetters of the fruit.
This is the final body, which must enter parinirvāṇa at its end; because it is an impermanent body, it is cited here.

I challenge the Buddha: you now refute the four [bodies] with five, asserting that because the "final limit" (paścima-koṭi) is identical to impermanence, they are combined into the "body of impermanence.
Yet you cite four bodies; this is merely what is seen through limited conditions (*parīttapratyaya*). What is perceived through vast conditions (*mahāpratyaya*) does not possess these four.
Why? That which is "light" is precisely wisdom (*jñāna*); that which is wisdom is precisely the eternally abiding (*nitya*); and that which is eternally abiding is... [the Tathāgata].

This body is not a body sustained by food; furthermore, that which is radiant is precisely wisdom. The light of wisdom destroys the darkness of afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus it is not an afflicted body.
If one were at the initial stage of severing afflictions, one would still possess the bonds of the fruit [of past karma], and that would be a "final body" (*paścima-deha*);
however, since this is not the initial severance, it is not a final body. While the bonds of the fruit of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) may be impermanent, this [body] is eternally abiding.
Because wisdom is like a vajra, it is not subject to impermanence; it is not perceived by great conditions, for there are only five [aspects] and not four.

How much more so for the Tathāgata, who, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, has been free from these four bodies—transcending both the large and the small, and simultaneously negating both four and five.
Thus, he is neither food nor non-food, neither permanent nor impermanent, and neither affliction nor non-affliction.
It is neither the absence of affliction, nor dharma, nor non-dharma; neither an extreme, nor the absence of an extreme; neither vajra, nor the absence of vajra.
It is able to respond to two conditions by performing four acts and five acts, yet with respect to the Tathāgata, it is neither four nor five—profound and yet more profound.
Therefore, it is clear that the retributive fruits of the two kinds of giving are without difference.

Next, from the passage beginning with "Good son, those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature" to the end, he answers the objection regarding the cessation of wisdom versus the cessation of ignorance.
"Good son, those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature" refers to the body of afflictions, the body sustained by impure food, and the final body.
At that time, having received the food, the Bodhisattva entered the Vajra-samādhi;

once this food was digested, he immediately beheld the Buddha-nature and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, I say that the karmic fruits of these two kinds of giving are equal and without distinction.
Cunda cited the Tripitaka, stating that when the Buddha was a bodhisattva, he took a consort and fathered a son;

he then abandoned his kingdom and renounced his kingship to sit beneath a tree upon grass, whereupon he rose to wash and received food. At that time, he had not yet severed even a hair’s breadth of afflictions (*kleśa*) and was thus unable to transform sentient beings.

Cunda used this as a challenge to the Buddha. The Buddha answered by explaining what is perceived through the "great conditions" (*mahā-pratyaya*), thereby refuting the two conditions of the Tripiṭaka and the Shared Teachings (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). Thus, the two conditions were established.
Regarding the Buddha, what are the two conditions by which he is perceived? It is not only that one does not see the Buddha-nature within the Tripiṭaka before receiving food;

even after having received it and becoming a Buddha, one still does not see the nature. This applies equally to the Universal Buddha (Samantabhadra). One should know that those who have not yet seen the nature refute both teachings.
When a Bodhisattva on the Flower-Pedestal receives the office of a Buddha, he enters the Vajra-samādhi and ascends to the office of a Buddha.
Attaining the stage of *sambodhi*, clearly perceiving the Buddha-nature—the eternal body, the Dharma-body, the Vajra-body—is what is called "wisdom.
Being devoid of the four types of bodies constitutes "severance" (*prahāṇa*). Furthermore, one is able to cause others to be fully endowed with wisdom and severance.
Moreover, entering the Vajra-samādhi, that is, the Vajra-body, destroys the impermanent body; this constitutes one instance of attaining wisdom and severance.
The three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*) are themselves the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which destroys the body of afflictions;

furthermore, the ultimate realization of the nature through wisdom and severance constitutes the eternal body (*nityakāya*), which destroys the body of nutriment (*āhārakāya*). Moreover, this wisdom and severance can also cause others to become fully endowed with wisdom and severance.

Therefore, although the two types of giving differ in their timing, there is no difference in their retribution, nor is there any distinction between wisdom and severance. Thus they receive these names according to their different temporal contexts.
Third, regarding the response to the second objection concerning whether there is a title for the Honored One or not:
At that time, the Bodhisattva destroyed the four māras; now, upon entering nirvāṇa, he likewise destroys the four māras. Therefore, I say this.
Second, the karmic rewards of these two gifts are equal and without distinction.

Cunda bases his argument on the fact that when a *tri-piṭaka* bodhisattva was still a layperson, he possessed the marks of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) and was thus a "god among men" (*manuṣya-deva*).

Yet, from the time he left the household life until the moment he received this food, he had not yet attained the Path; he was still inferior even to those reborn in the heavens. How, then, could [this gift] be considered superior?
The title [of "heavenly being"] is not that of one born in heaven, nor even that of one who has attained birth as a deity in the Pure Heavens;
