since such a title does not exist, it is said that they are still sentient beings. The Buddha now does not answer by means of the Tripiṭaka, but rather through the great conditions perceived on the lotus pedestals;
for the Bodhisattvas upon those lotus pedestals have already destroyed the four Māras. Thus, the *Śāstra* says: "They have attained Bodhi..."

The Bodhisattva path destroys the demon of afflictions (kleśamāra) by attaining the Dharma-nature body; it destroys the demon of the aggregates and death (skandhamṛtyumāra) by attaining the immovable samādhi;
and it destroys the demon of the celestial son (devaputramāra). This sutra is likewise: entering the vajra-samādhi is the Vajra-body, which destroys the demon of the celestial son;
attaining perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) upon being born in heaven is the Dharma-body, which destroys the afflictions and the aggregates, thereby enabling one to see [the Truth].
The Buddha-nature is the eternal body that destroys the Māra of Death. Since such merit exists, is this not birth in the heavens, the Pure Heavens, and the God among Gods?
Now, entering Nirvāṇa, one likewise destroys the four inversions, such as the notion of impermanence; because there are no inversions, one destroys the Māra of Afflictions.
Without the aggregates of affliction, there is no death, and thus one destroys the Māra of Heaven. This is accomplished first and then last.

Since both [the destruction of the four māras and the attainment of the title] involve the simultaneous destruction of the four māras, the simultaneous non-existence of sentient beings, and the simultaneous attainment of the honorable title "God among Gods," there is no difference between them.
From this point onward, although it is not explained in detail at that time, it serves as the answer to the fourth difficulty regarding the six pāramitās and the five eyes.

Although the Bodhisattva at that time did not extensively expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures, having already mastered them previously, he now enters nirvana to analyze and expound them extensively for the sake of sentient beings;
therefore, I say that the karmic fruits of these two kinds of giving are equal and without distinction.
Cunda, based on the Tripiṭaka, has seen only the renunciation of kingdom and throne, but not the teaching of the Dharma;

he has seen only the giving of wealth, but not the giving of principle (*dāna*). Therefore, it was said that his perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to his perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) were not yet complete.

Because he saw only that which is within the realm of obstructions, it was said that he possessed only the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) and lacked the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) up to the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*). Now, however, the Buddha—
Because of the great conditions perceived through the flower pedestal, although he does not yet preach the Dharma, he has already attained thorough penetration;
his perfection of the *dāna-pāramitā*—from material gifts (*āmiṣa-dāna*) and the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*), including both principle and phenomena—up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*, is already complete.

He surpasses what is seen by humans, devas, those of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas, and has already partially attained the Buddha-eye. Now, the Buddha answers regarding the single matter of the Dharma-gift (*dharma-dāna*), while the other perfections are implied.

The five eyes may be understood according to this principle, and thus they are omitted here and not explicitly answered. What was previously a thorough penetration is now extensively manifested for the sake of sentient beings;
therefore, the two types of giving are equal and without distinction.
Fifth, regarding the response from the son of good family concerning the Tathāgata’s body: there is a refutation of the claim that while five fruits exist, five fruits do not exist.
Son of good family, the Tathāgata’s body has already been without the consumption of food and drink for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

The śrāvakas say that I first accepted the milk gruel offered by the two cowherd girls, Nandā and Nandabalā, and only thereafter attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; however, in truth, I did not eat it.

Cunda [thought]: "According to the Three Piṭakas, one who gives food with the five virtues of giving receives five kinds of retributive fruits, such as longevity, physical strength, peace, and eloquence;
yet now I hear the Buddha say that I have truly not eaten, and thus the donor should likewise receive no fivefold fruit.
The Buddha answered him from the perspective of his original ground at the time of initial enlightenment: "Throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have neither received nor eaten."

In the minor narrative of ultimate purity, at the beginning it is seen that he received milk-rice from his mouth; in the major narrative of the initial vision, it is seen that he received light upon the crown of his head.
Yet, regarding the Dharma-body, there is neither food nor non-food. In the minor narrative at the end, it is seen that he received the offering of rice-porridge;

in the major narrative at the end, it is seen that he universally accepted the great assembly. However, for the Tathāgata, there is no begging and no receiving. Therefore, these two—the beginning and the end—[are thus].
The fruits of giving and so forth are without distinction.
Next, regarding the one who universally accepts:

from this moment forward, I shall accept these various offerings for the sake of the entire assembly of this gathering; therefore, although I accept what you have lastly offered, in truth I do not eat it.
Next, the request for the Buddha to remain is divided into four parts: first, the cause of the request; second, the formal presentation of the request;

third, the refusal of the request; and fourth, the renewed request. First, four intentions arise: the assembly all present offerings and request the Buddha to remain, but as the request to remain is not granted, they have yet to express their plea.
Because the Buddha has consented to accept Cunda’s offering, the assembly, through Cunda, requests the Buddha to remain once more; Cunda then follows this intent.

The multitude’s hearts were moved once more as the Buddha accepted their offerings; he universally revealed that the eternal Dharma is not something that abides, yet it is inappropriate to request that he abide in this eternal Dharma.
Because the profundity of this Dharma was difficult for the assembly to fathom, they earnestly and repeatedly entreated him. Master Xinghuang explained:
"The great assembly heard together the voice [of the Buddha] announcing that his parinirvāṇa would soon occur. Hearing this, they raised an objection, saying: 'The Dharmakāya is eternal.'"
Furthermore, at first hearing of extinction, one thinks it is like the extinguishing of a lamp; hearing of permanence, one thinks it means always remaining in the world.
Now, the Tathāgata is fundamentally without going or staying; how could he ever be like those who perceive staying or perceive going? Only going is staying, and only staying is going.
Without arising from quiescent extinction, he manifests his body in other assemblies; while the appearance of going remains distinct, the appearance of staying is eternally present.
If the Buddha were always departing, what benefit would there be for the assembly in his coming and staying? (And so forth.
Now it is clarified that the conditions for the Buddha’s departure and staying are not uniform; briefly, there are four types. Some, seeing him depart, rejoice within themselves, saying:
"Innumerable sentient beings have fallen away from the presence of the Buddha; I alone now have the good fortune to witness the Buddha from beginning to end," thus comforting themselves.
Seeing [the Buddha] depart for the sake of attaining this world is a departure based on the causal condition of attachment;

one may see him depart with grief, lamentation, beating one's head, and weeping—this is a departure based on the causal condition of attachment to the person. Or there may be seeing him depart as a means of destroying immeasurable evils;
even though the Tathāgata is departing, why should I cling? This is a departure based on the causal condition of remediation. Or there may be...
Seeing them depart and enter the secret treasury, reaching the Buddha’s destination, they clearly perceive their own nature and become equal to the Dharma-Princes;
this is the causal condition for the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). Regarding "seeing the departure," it may be that one person possesses all four [aspects], or only three, or only two;
alternatively, four people may each possess one, with various differences among them, yet for the Tathāgata there is neither going nor staying.
Furthermore, consider Cunda: at times he was moved by sorrow, and at times he was filled with joy;

at times he said, "The Tathāgata will not enter parinirvāṇa, yet I cannot help but harbor grief and distress"; at other times he said of himself, "I am now together with Mañjuśrī, the Prince of the Dharma, and others.
If there were no such affinity between them, how could Cunda have been thus? Therefore, we know that Cunda did [not [desire the Buddha's passing]].

All these are merely conditions. Regarding the first phrase, "going," there are four different conditions; the other phrases—"staying," "both going and staying," and "neither staying nor going"—are to be understood by analogy with this.
The initial cause for the request consists of three parts: first, the request made with joy and praise;

second, the refusal of the offering, which caused him to be choked with grief; and third, his current joy upon hearing that [the Buddha] will universally accept [the offerings], all of which stems from Cunda. Thus, his joy arises from Cunda.
Therefore, they praised [the Buddha] and made this request in order to fulfill their original intention.
At that time, the great assembly, hearing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had universally accepted Cunda’s final offering for the sake of the entire congregation,
rejoiced and leaped for joy.
He then praised him with both prose and verse; the prose portion is further divided into two parts: first, the brief, and second, the extensive.
With one voice they praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! How rare! Cunda, the name you now bear is not in vain.
One who is called 'Cunda' is named for his mastery of wondrous meanings. You have now established such a great purpose; therefore, it is according to reality."
The name "Cunda" is established based on its meaning; therefore, you have now attained great fame and profit in this present life, and your merit, virtue, and aspirations are fulfilled.
To summarize, four praises are offered: fame, profit, virtue, and aspiration. Regarding "fame," a noble name was first established, and subsequently its wondrous significance arose.
Since future events will verify that the former name was not an empty title, they praise him with one voice, saying: "How rare is Cunda! Thus he is called "Great."

"Principle" (*yi*) refers to its horizontal breadth being boundless; "wondrous principle" (*miaoyi*) refers to its vertical depth being bottomless. Furthermore, that "the permanent is impermanent" is the profound meaning;
that "one is permanent and all are permanent" is the great meaning; and that "neither permanent nor impermanent" is the wondrous meaning, as has already been explained previously.
Next, regarding the phrase "you now," those who are of lesser capacity gather from throughout the land and from the ten directions at this auspicious ground of merit.
The echoes of his assemblies resounded throughout the Brahma heavens, and his banners hung down to cover the three thousandfold world system. The Tathāgata remained silent, accepting nothing at all.

Later, Cunda came forward and requested to offer his provisions, which were accepted in their entirety. Such was his peerless reputation that surpassed the world, that the multitude sighed in admiration, saying:
"In this present life, you have attained great fame and profit. Regarding the single character 'virtue' (德), one would yield ten places to you; five [of the ten] would be reserved for you."
The fruit shall first be for one person alone, yet even eight *hu*—though slightly meager—is sufficient to fulfill the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*); this is its merit.

Regarding the three characters "wishes," "may," and "fulfill": because they satisfy and permeate the aforementioned four types of sufficiency, and because the former Buddha established his vow while the present Buddha has perfected that vow, it is said that the wishes are fulfilled.
From the words "How marvelous, Cunda! he proceeded to praise extensively, moving from the later back toward the earlier to extol the four virtues;
first, he again raised the six difficulties to praise extensively the fulfillment of the fourth vow.
"How marvelous, Cunda! You have been born among humans and have further attained this most difficult-to-attain, unsurpassed benefit. Excellent, Cunda!"

Just as the udumbara flower is rare in the world, so too is the appearance of a Buddha in the world exceedingly difficult; it is further difficult to encounter a Buddha, give rise to faith, and hear the Dharma;
and it is even more difficult to be able to perform such an act of offering at the very moment the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa. Thus it was said.
When the lifespans of the various devas are exhausted and the five signs of decay appear, the other sons of heaven offer them this prayer of blessing:

"May you be reborn in a favorable realm; may you obtain excellent benefits. Such is the benefit of the human path for one who maintains the precepts. As the subsequent passage states: "The soil of the lands of the ten directions is vast, while the soil upon a fingernail is small.
Having abandoned the bodies of humans and devas, one mostly obtains birth in the three evil realms; having abandoned the bodies of humans and devas, one sometimes obtains birth as a human."
When a deva who is about to fall from heaven attains another heavenly rebirth, the devas do not rejoice; yet when such a deva attains a human rebirth, all the devas fulfill their wishes.
It is like two people at two different Mount Sumerus: one stands upright with a needle’s eye, while the other, driven by the wind, attempts to pass a thread through that eye.
This is extremely difficult; even more difficult than this is for one among humans to be able to maintain the precepts. It is rarer still than the ocean.
It is extremely difficult for a blind turtle, emerging from the depths once every thousand years, to encounter a floating wooden plank with a single hole and enter that hole to dwell within it.

If one were to encounter a Buddha appearing in the world while existing among humans, the difficulty would exceed even this. To cast a needle upright upon the ground and have a mustard seed thrown into the air land upon its point is extremely difficult;
likewise, to encounter a Buddha and give rise to faith is even more difficult than that. Thus, one gives rise to faith.
To hear the Dharma is more difficult than this; to provide the final offering is even more difficult than that. While these six things are difficult for others, they are easy for Cunda.
Therefore, the great assembly marveled, saying: "How extraordinary! Cunda has again attained the unsurpassed benefit that is most difficult to obtain—like the *udumbara* flower.
This flower signifies the appearance of a Wheel-Turning King; likewise, by being able to provide the final offering, one attains five things."

The fruit will certainly be that of a Dharma King; having already bestowed this prediction upon the great assembly and finished his extensive praise of the fulfillment of the vow, he next offers extensive praise of virtues beginning with "Namo.
"Namo Cunda, Namo Cunda! You have now fully perfected the *dānapāramitā*."
"Namo" may be said to mean "save me," "take refuge," or "bowing the knees"—the latter referring to bending both knees.

Because he possesses the virtue of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) characterized by the ten forms of yielding and the five fruits, he is now praised. Furthermore, "Namo" encompasses three meanings:
uttering it with the mouth is the vocal action (*vākkarma*); bowing the knees is the bodily action (*kāyakarma*); and taking refuge is the mental action (*manaskarma*).
Third, following the analogy of the autumn moon, he extensively extolled its benefits:
"Just as on the fifteenth night of the autumn moon, it is pure, full, and free from all clouds and obscurations, such that there are no sentient beings who do not gaze upon it;
so too are you gazed upon by us. The Buddha has already accepted you."
This final offering shall cause you to fulfill the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). Homage to Cunda! Therefore, it is said of you:
"Like the full moon, there is no sentient being who does not look up to you with reverence."

Autumn is the season of Yin, and the moon is the essence of Yin; when its time arrives, it becomes full, outshining all the stars, solitary and preeminent, beautifying heaven and brightening the earth for all to gaze upon. Cunda was likewise thus:

possessing wondrous benefit, he met with this supreme and wondrous occasion to establish a sublime meaning before the great assembly, such that none could precede him in addressing the Buddha to reveal the Eternal.
All the great assembly, having received offerings, reverently dedicated their three karmas [of body, speech, and mind] to him.
Fourth, from "Namo Cunda, whose mind is like the Buddha-mind" downward, his name is extensively praised:
"Namo Cunda! Although you have received a human body and mind, your mind is like the Buddha-mind; you, Cunda, are now truly a son of the Buddha."
They are no different from Rāhula and others.

As stated above: "One who understands the wondrous meaning is one whose name accords with the Dharma; one whose mind is like the Buddha's mind is one whose name accords with the Buddha—truly a son of the Buddha;
one whose name accords with the Saṃgha is one who accords with the Triple Gem. This reveals that his person is the single essence of the Triple Gem.
Furthermore, it is said that [this person] possesses all dharmadhātus, such as the five fruits, the three points, the four virtues, and the five Buddha-natures, exactly as previously explained.
One praises their mastery of the mind as being like the Buddha-mind; one praises their attainment of the title of "Teacher" for understanding the wondrous meaning;
and one praises their attainment of kinship as being like Rāhula (and so forth).
In the following verses, there are two parts: the first single verse praises [the Buddha] as mentioned above, and the subsequent three verses constitute the request.
At that time, the great assembly spoke these verses:
"Though you were born into the human realm, You have already transcended the sixth heaven. I and all the multitude..."
Now, therefore, I bow my head and request:
the first passage says, "As for you," this refers to the name of Cunda mentioned above; "born into the human realm" refers to one of the six difficulties;
"the vow is fulfilled" means he has transcended the sixth heaven to equal the Brahma King; and "requesting the Buddha to reveal the eternal" is as follows:
This praises their virtues; "I and all the assembly" refers to the collective eulogy, where "all" includes those above who join in praise with one voice.
This expression, "I and all," is like a leader at the head who initiates the discussion of the principles, appearing as if Mañjuśrī were the primary petitioner.
Next, the two among the middle [pair] first performed the two acts for the assembly:
"O Most Victorious Honored One among men, you are now about to enter parinirvāṇa. You should take pity on us;
we pray only that you quickly entreat the Buddha to remain long in this world for the benefit of immeasurable multitudes."
"Proclaim the Dharma praised by the wise, the unsurpassed nectar for the sake of all beings... (and so forth).
Next is the single line of entreaty.
If you do not invite the Buddha, my life will not be preserved. Therefore, you should prostrate on his behalf for the sake of the Tamer of Men (the Teacher), who is essential to my very life.
Were the Buddha not in the world, I would not receive the nectar of the Dharma, and my life of wisdom would surely perish.
This is the entirety.
Next follows the request made by Cunda, which is divided into two parts: first, the prose section narrated by the scribe (the *jīngjiā*); second, the verse section consisting of Cunda’s petition.
Within the initial prose section:
At that time, Cunda was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, just as if someone whose parents had suddenly passed away were to be restored to life;
Cunda’s joy was likewise so.
To say "suddenly passed away" is an abbreviation; in full, one should say "the loss of their lord, kinsman, and teacher," and so forth. [He then] offered the sound [of his voice].
The great assembly rushed forward and fell prostrate, their blood spilling upon the ground;

thus, it is now said that those who had met with sudden death were restored to life, their constant vitality, physical strength, peace, and eloquence fully restored as they comprehensively mastered the Dharma-realm.
Because they were permitted to serve as masters and elders, the crowd rejoiced greatly at the time, and Cunda later felt even greater joy; this, too, was another instance of yielding.

In the subsequent verse, eighteen and a half lines are divided into two sections: the first eleven and a half lines convey the assembly’s praise, and the following seven lines convey the assembly’s request.
Within the initial section, three praises are briefly conveyed;
first, nine lines convey the praise of his excellent vows, which begins by conveying six hardships and concludes with the latter two and a half lines using a simile as a summary.
Rising again, he paid homage to the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"How wonderful it is to have gained this personal benefit! Having well obtained this human body, I have eliminated greed, anger, and the like, and am forever freed from the three evil realms.
How wonderful it is to have gained this personal benefit! I have encountered and found this heap of gold and jewels."
Having encountered the Teacher, the Tamer, one need not fear falling among the animals. The Buddha is like the udumbara flower;
it is difficult to encounter him and give rise to faith. Once encountered, one cultivates roots of goodness, forever extinguishing the suffering of the hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, one can diminish the ranks of the asuras, as easily as casting a mustard seed onto the point of a needle.
The appearance of a Buddha is rare indeed; I have already fulfilled the perfection of giving (*dāna*).
Having delivered humans and devas from birth and death, the Buddha is unstained by worldly dharmas, like a lotus flower dwelling in the water.

He has skillfully severed the seeds of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and forever crossed the stream of birth and death. To be born as a human in this world is difficult; to encounter the era of a Buddha is likewise difficult.

The initial statement regarding "attaining one's own benefit" extols the difficulty of obtaining a human body, a favorable rebirth, and the elimination of defilements—these being the benefits of virtue;
"the heap of gold and jewels" refers to what is abandoned by those who do not fear [suffering];
"the udumbara flower" extols the difficulty of generating faith; and "the needle-point" extols the difficulty of making the final offering. The Buddha is unstained.
Worldly dharmas pass away and hearing the Dharma is difficult;
it is like a blind turtle encountering a floating yoke in the great ocean.
The food I now offer is for the departed to ascend and extol his virtues.
May this food now offered by me obtain the unsurpassed reward; may all fetters of affliction be shattered and rendered without solidity.
Now, in this place, I seek neither the body of a deva nor that of a human;
even if such were obtained, my heart would find no pleasure therein. Thus does the Tathāgata accept my offering.
With immeasurable joy,
through this offering, I make a vow for the unsurpassed fruit and do not desire any further existence.
Just as the eranda flower produces the fragrance of sandalwood, may my body be like the eranda flower.
The Tathāgata accepts my offering, emitting the fragrance of sandalwood; therefore, I rejoice.

Furthermore, in the subsequent analogy within the section on "Knots," it says: "Just as sandalwood emerges from *eranda* (castor-oil) plants, though the cause is minute, it suffices for a great multitude.
Moreover, through the act of eating, it reveals non-eating; it is not that food is non-food, but rather the wind of the fragrance of the Way’s virtues is brought forth.
All things are neither permanent nor impermanent.
I have now attained manifest retribution; my departure and soaring praise for the benefit [of others] are as described in the text.
I have now attained manifest retribution in this most excellent and sublime state, equal to Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas.
All have come to make offerings to me;
having departed from all worlds, they now ascend [to this assembly] and request [the Buddha's presence].

Regarding these three initial stanzas, the first two express the intention of their sorrowful suffering, while the subsequent three express the intention of requesting his stay for the benefit [of beings]; the final two stanzas conclude these two intentions.
All the worlds are filled with great suffering and distress, for they know that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, now intends to enter parinirvāṇa. They cry out these words in a loud voice:
"The World’s Tamer should not abandon sentient beings; he should regard them as his only son."
The text says: "In this world, where there is no charioteer, no lord, no kinsman, or no teacher, great suffering and affliction arise.
The Tathāgata, dwelling amidst the Saṃgha, proclaims the unsurpassed Dharma—like the precious Sumeru mountain resting securely upon the great ocean.
With his Buddha-wisdom, he is able to thoroughly sever the darkness of our ignorance."
Just as when the sun rises, its light shines everywhere, dispelling the clouds; so too the Tathāgata is able to skillfully eliminate all afflictions.

Just as when clouds arise in the void, one attains refreshing coolness—[the subsequent passage] generally clarifies the benefits of the Triple Gem as the Tathāgata dwells among the Saṃgha, while specifically clarifying [his presence] like Mount Sumeru.
The Master benefits others like a mountain reflected in water, where the water takes on the color of the mountain; the Master benefits others by preaching the Dharma, which they practice accordingly.

Therefore, this is the benefit of the Buddha’s wisdom (*jñāna*), which is well able to sever the "half-practice" [of afflictions]. This is the benefit of the Cloud of Wisdom (*jñānasaṃbhāra*), which gives rise to refreshing coolness.

This is the benefit of the "good root" (*kuśalamūla*). These two clarify the direct benefit from the Tathāgata. Being well able to eliminate these is the benefit of the Lord regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This thief and marauder disturbs the path of men; the Buddha-sun shines forth to dispel it, rectifying the chaos and restoring the right way; therefore, he is the benefactor of the sovereign.
As for the three fetters:
these sentient beings, out of deep attachment, increase their lamentation and grief, all of which is for the sake of birth and death.

Drifting upon the waters of suffering—for this reason, O World-Honored One, you should cause sentient beings to increase their faith so as to sever the suffering of birth and death, and remain long in this world.

[This refers to the state of mind characterized by the bonds of grief and distress arising from longing when the three benefits are lost; conversely, it refers to the faith that arises when the three benefits are obtained.]
The phrase "the mind increases its fetters" refers to the request for [the Buddha] to remain.
From the point where the Buddha says to Cunda, "So it is, so it is," until the third section where the request is declined, there is a prose passage followed by verses.
The prose is divided into two parts: first, an account praising the difficulty [of the request], and second, the use of that difficulty to decline the request. Regarding the first part:
The Buddha told Cunda: "It is so, it is so, just as you have said. The appearance of a Buddha in the world is as difficult as the blooming of the udumbara flower;

to encounter a Buddha and give rise to faith is likewise exceedingly difficult. To offer the final meal at the time of a Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, being able to fulfill the perfection of dāna, is many times more difficult still."

Now, these six difficulties revolve around one another; while the three types [of practitioners] exist even when there is no Buddha, it is only when a Buddha appears that [the other three] come to be.
Herein I shall describe the three difficulties that exist when a Buddha has appeared; the remainder can be understood [thereby]. (And so forth.)

Next, the request by means of various refutations (*dūṣaṇa*) is divided into three parts: first, the request by means of various refutations; second, the request by means of the Buddha’s sphere (*buddhaviṣaya*);
and third, the request by means of the two functions. Regarding the request by means of various refutations:

"Cunda, you should not now be so deeply distressed; rather, you ought to rejoice and feel profound self-congratulation that you have encountered this final opportunity to make offerings to the Tathāgata and have thus fully accomplished the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). You should not request the Buddha to remain long in the world."
"You have ascended above the masses and uttered four praises for your own joy; these six hardships and four praises all stem from my entry into *nirvāṇa* and the granting of eternal life to you.
May these various merits extend to all beings. If I were to remain long, there would be no final offering.
If this vow is not fulfilled, the assembly will not offer praise, and my name would be established in vain. I would lose my own benefit and further obstruct [others]."
Others might suddenly rejoice at the prospect of providing for you in the future and invite you to stay long; yet if there is no provision for the future, there will be no long stay.
Since you yourself are like a spearhead [clashing with its own point], your prohibition is intended precisely for this reason.
Next, regarding the passage beginning with "Now you," which sets forth the Buddha’s realm as a refutation:
You should now contemplate the realm of all Buddhas.
The realm of the Buddhas can only be known by a Buddha; it is not something that can be measured by inferior stages, for it transcends the path of language and the sphere of mental activity.
Where extinction reaches existence, existence becomes more thoroughly non-existent; where non-existence reaches extinction, extinction becomes more thoroughly existent.

That which is neither existent nor non-existent is abiding in non-abiding; non-abiding is itself abiding. It is neither abiding nor non-abiding. Such a realm leaves the speaker speechless and causes the grasper to fail.
Because it cuts off all emotional deliberation, it is described as "that which should not be questioned. Why then, Puṇḍra, do you suddenly ask whether one dwells in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)?
To obstruct [the opponent] by treating them as an ordinary person so that they do not know how to answer—there are six such types (and so forth)—is likewise intended for those who are lowly;
it serves to suppress those who are exalted, for one who is truly noble should not lower themselves, but rather allow their own expectations to subside.
Third, "all are below" refers to citing two functions to preclude the request.
All are impermanent; the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise so.
It is only that the Buddha’s realm is profound and subtle, and the Buddha’s supreme functions are unknown to you, leading you to speak of the two birds of permanence and impermanence.
Moving together or dwelling apart as appropriate, they manifest or remain hidden according to the capacity of beings;

sometimes they employ dwelling, and sometimes they employ non-dwelling—yet this very non-dwelling is itself dwelling, being neither dwelling nor non-dwelling. Previously, by employing impermanence in giving, one obtained the five fruits;

yet all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent. If [giving] were definitively impermanent, how could the present teaching grant the five constant fruits through the practice of giving?
Since the fruit pervades all phenomena and is fully revealed as eternal, one should know that it is neither eternal nor non-eternal, yet capable of being both eternal and non-eternal.

Furthermore, whereas previously the five-gate contemplation was practiced using the discourse on impermanence—referring to the realm of others—the present teaching employs the five-gate contemplation using the discourse on eternity, which is the realm of oneself.
How could such a distinction between self and other be definitively established? Could the "self" and "other" truly act in this manner?
One should know that these are all the supreme functions of the Buddha. If he employs them through permanence, there is no need for a request;

if he employs them through impermanence, a request is likewise unnecessary. Therefore, by citing these two functions, it is refuted that one should speak of [the Buddha] as being subject to such [limitations].
The eleven and a half verses are divided into two parts: the first ten and a half lines clarify impermanence, and the final line clarifies permanence.

Within the former, there are again two sections: the first nine lines generally clarify the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), while the last one and a half lines specifically apply the principle of impermanence.
Within the former, there are again five sections; the first three and a half lines concern the contemplation of impermanence.
He then spoke these verses for Cunda:
"In all worlds, those who are born must return to death; Though a lifespan may be immeasurable, it must inevitably come to an end.
Prosperity is necessarily followed by decline; Where there is gathering, there must be parting."
Youth does not endure for long; the bloom of beauty is assailed by disease. Life is swallowed by death;
there is no dharma that remains constant. Though kings may attain sovereignty and possess peerless power, all things pass away and perish;
the lifespan is just like this.
Next is the contemplation on the suffering of conditioned existence:
The wheel of manifold sufferings has no limit; it revolves without rest. The three realms are all impermanent;
all states of existence are devoid of joy.
Next is the contemplation on the emptiness of the single line:
The essential nature and characteristics of the path Are all empty and non-existent; There is no dharma that transmigrates, yet there are always afflictions such as suffering and anxiety.
Next, two lines describe the contemplation of selflessness:
Terrorizing are all faults and evils— Old age, sickness, death, and the distress of decline.
These are boundless, easily destroyed, and invaded by enemies; Enveloped by afflictions, they are like a silkworm within its cocoon.
How could one who possesses wisdom take pleasure in this place?
[Next, one and a half lines:
This body is a collection of suffering; it is entirely impure, a yoke, a bond, an abscess, and a wound.
Fundamentally devoid of benefit, even up to the bodies of the various devas, all are likewise thus.
When asked whether the transformation-bodies of the devas are not impure, the answer is: although they lack foul odors, they are still impure as they are censured by the noble ones.
Next, the following verses clarify that all desires are impermanent:
All desires are impermanent; Therefore, I do not cling to them.
Free from desire and with skillful reflection, I have realized the true Dharma. Having ultimately severed existence, Today I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
As stated in the *Śrī-sūtra* (Ruiying jing): "Because he felt weary and disgusted upon exiting the four city gates, he did not cling to them;

through contemplation of detachment, he practiced austerities for six years and realized the True Dharma. With thirty-four moments of mind, he gave rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), and today he shall enter Nirvana—this being his final state of Nirvana without remainder."
Next, the single verse for crossing over the ocean of existence is used at all times:
I have crossed over the ocean of existence; I have transcended all suffering. Therefore, at this present moment, I experience only supreme bliss.
The "crosser" crosses to the further shore of both this and that, and also crosses to the further shore that is neither this nor that;

because one attains mastery over all such "thises" and "thats," I have not only transcended all suffering, but have also transcended all pleasure and the absence of both suffering and pleasure—this is what is called "Great Bliss.
My purity is likewise to be understood in this manner (etc.). This concludes the judgment on the preceding nine lines.
Half of this [verse] shows that the Buddha is identical to both the conditioned and the unconditioned, which is the meaning of both the real and the unreal;
the latter two lines show that all phenomena are identical to the Tathāgata, which is the meaning of both the permanent and the impermanent, and the non-real and the real.
This permanence and impermanence reveal the true Dharma that is neither permanent nor impermanent. Now, it is said: "If so, permanence and impermanence are two."

Thus, by means of these two skillful means (*upāya*), the reality is revealed; it is just as one enters the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), through the two contemplations of skillful means in the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*.
This is the meaning of the three truths in their shallow and deep aspects.
How can the realm of a Bodhisattva be the same as the realm of a Buddha? This text clearly states: "One should contemplate the realm of all Buddhas."
Regarding the "realms" (dharmadhātu): the three truths, one truth, and one truth as three truths are neither one nor three;
yet they are three, and each is one. All are empty—each of the three truths is empty, all are empty. All are provisional—each of the three truths is provisional, all are provisional.

All are the Middle—within each of the three truths there is the Middle, and all are the Middle. Only the Middle is the conventional; only the conventional is the true; only the true is the Middle. There is no [Middle] apart from these.
The two are non-different; it is precisely in this way that they are called the realm of the Buddhas. Therefore, the reason for using the Buddha-realm to decline the request is as follows:
if one is empty, all are empty—how can one request [the Buddha] to remain? Even if one is central, all are central—how can one request [the Buddha] to remain?
The intent behind declining the request lies exactly here. Why, then, use the Bodhisattva-realm?

Is this the realm of the Buddha’s teaching? If one merely follows the literal text, this meaning is difficult to perceive; therefore, I shall now further clarify this meaning by means of the verse-text itself.
The first nine and a half lines clarify that "one is empty, all are empty"; the verse on "leaving desire" clarifies that "one is provisional, all are provisional";
the verse on "my crossing over" clarifies that "one is the Middle, all are the Middle. Within these verses, [the principle] is extensively set forth and returned to.
The commentary on the prose section briefly indicates the intent regarding the Buddha’s realm, which will be further explained later (etc.).
Regarding the fourfold request: some say it is not a "repeated" request because the Buddha does not fail to respond repeatedly;

others say that from two perspectives it is a repeated request—relative to what precedes it, and relative to what follows as the opening of the discourse. Within this, there are three parts: first, receiving the intent; second, expressing humility and gratitude.
Third, the formal request.
At that time, Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is so, it is so; it is truly as the Holy One has spoken.
Having received this instruction, I shall follow it despite the difficulty of such a request, for six difficulties arise from the request. It is indeed as the Buddha has said."
My present wisdom is so slight and shallow, like that of a mosquito or a gnat; how could I possibly conceive of the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One, I am now accompanied by great dragon-elephants among bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have severed all fetters and outflows, such as Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince.
World-Honored One, it is as if a young child has just emerged [into the world].

Just as a family member, though not yet possessing the full precepts, is nonetheless included within the ranks of the Saṃgha, so too do I, by virtue of the supernatural powers of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
come to be numbered among such great Bodhisattvas.
This humility arises from the realm of the Buddhas. The realm of all Buddhas is vast and boundless; how could a mosquito or a gnat know its limits?
To discern this is not ultimate knowledge; such knowing is humility. "To express gratitude" (xie) arises from function:

having received the offerings of the Buddha, one fulfills the final act of giving (*dāna*), severing the fetters of stinginess and outflows. This is equal to Mañjuśrī’s receiving the Buddha’s [teaching].

Having received this offering, he has attained the wisdom of the other shore (pāramitā) equal to that of the Great Bodhisattvas; thus, he employs the metaphor of the dragon-elephant (*nāga-hastin*) to illustrate his wisdom and severance of afflictions.
Furthermore, he compares himself to a youth to represent his recent attainment of the precepts, while likening those who have long been established to the seniors.

That he has been able to emerge from the depths of the abyss and ascend to the heights of the clouds is due to the grace of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; therefore, one must express gratitude through constant practice.

Third, the formal request for the permanent abiding of the Dharma is capable of producing wholesome roots in sentient beings; since the great suffering of the masses has reached its peak and the Tathāgata has not yet [entered parinirvāṇa], they therefore request it again.
This consists of the Dharma, the analogy, and the application. First, the Dharma is as stated in the text.
For this reason, I now wish to cause the Tathāgata to remain long in the world and not enter parinirvāṇa.
For example, a hungry person will never vomit [their food].
Regarding the term "vomiting" in the subsequent analogy, there are two interpretations: first, it is said to be an analogy for the great assembly’s longing and thirsting [for the Buddha].
"May the Tathāgata abide forever without change or rejection. Thus the text says: "I now desire to cause the Tathāgata to abide for a long time.

From this we know that it serves as an analogy for sentient beings. Second, it serves as an analogy for the Buddha: the Buddha contemplates the capacities of beings just as one feels hunger and thirst;
he wishes for the Buddha to remain in the world likewise without change or rejection. Therefore, the analogy is joined by saying: "I only pray that the World-Honored One also..."
Furthermore, because it is thus, we know that this is a metaphor for the Buddha; for the skillful and secret words of the Sage must not be taken in a partial sense (and so forth).
We only pray that the World-Honored One will likewise remain thus in the world forever, and not enter parinirvāṇa.

Regarding the third section, the "incidental discussion" (*prasaṅga*): what is meant by "incidental"? First, the explanation of the name; second, the explanation of the text according to its sequence.
The explanation of the name has three parts: first, explaining the name; second, clarifying the intent; third, a detailed analysis. First, explaining the name:

it is called an "incidental discussion" because the previous offering of worship was the primary subject, whereas this [discussion] is incidental. Furthermore, the assembly present is incidental, as they were not yet understanding [the primary point]; thus, it is incidental.

Therefore, in the treatise, the question and answer concerning whether true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) is primary or skillful means (*upāya*) is secondary are presented as a "secondary discussion" (*pārśvavāda*) because they are a skillful expedient.
Furthermore, while the realm of the Tathāgata is primary, the two functions [of teaching] are secondary;
since the present discussion concerns these two functions, it is called a secondary discussion. This is the intention arising from the fourfold purpose (*caturvidha-saṃgraha-vastu*).
For what reason? Because the Buddha, in response to the offering of alms, used the gift of the eternal to refute impermanence.

Furthermore, he clarified that there is no difference between the two types of giving, benefiting those of profound understanding who realize that both the permanent and the impermanent are non-existent.

Yet, those who are deluded give rise to views of superiority and inferiority, disparaging the impermanent while venerating the permanent. The Tathāgata, moreover, in response to requests for him to remain, used non-abiding to refute abiding.
Furthermore, it clarifies that the inconceivable benefit of the Buddhas' realm consists precisely in understanding that which is neither abiding nor non-abiding.
Those who are deluded claim that "non-abiding" is a superior form of "abiding," yet due to their own confusion, they cannot attain liberation.

Therefore, Mañjuśrī rebuked Cunda’s request for him to remain by pointing to impermanence and non-abiding, while Cunda countered Mañjuśrī’s assertion of impermanence with the challenge of eternal abiding.
Because dwelling in resistance makes manifest its irrationality, it is said that both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) shall be set aside for now;
pointing toward the Tathāgata, this shall be explained extensively later. By citing this [the former] to reveal the non-[truth of the latter], the meaning is self-evident.
For the sake of this principle, a digression is necessary. Furthermore, above, Cunda himself spoke of Mañjuśrī as the Dharma King.
"O sons, the assembly at that time harbored doubts: Mañjuśrī is an ancient Buddha whose practice is remote and whose understanding is profound;

he is capable of both questioning and answering. Cunda, however, is at a shallow stage of initial resolve and his understanding is slight. Although he was able to question, we did not see him provide an answer. How then can they be called equals?
Therefore, by examining the text from a different perspective, Mañjuśrī is profound yet falls into defeat, while Cunda is shallow yet achieves victory. This victory of the shallow is not [the case]."
Victory over the profound and defeat by the non-defeated—only through that which is neither defeated nor victorious is their equality revealed.

By means of this principle and its application, the intent of the digression may be roughly discerned without the need for extensive commentary. The examiner asks: Mañjuśrī elucidates the samādhi of emptiness as the True Dharma;

it must therefore be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Yet, when Cunda discusses the non-existence in relation to existence, the non-existent is established only in dependence upon the existent. How can this be?
It should be that Mañjuśrī spoke of existence while Cunda spoke of non-existence. The commentary explains:

Mañjuśrī supported the emptiness of the former teachings in view of the "Great Existence" (the ultimate), whereas Cunda supported the non-existence discussed in contrast to existence within the present teachings;
thus, by negating existence, he attained this non-existence. Furthermore, since Cunda had only now fully perfected his practice of *dāna*, his cultivation was still shallow.
One should say that the Ancient Buddha Mañjuśrī is superior because he is profound; thus, one should not concede defeat. To explain:
it is merely a matter of what is appropriate for the occasion, like two pieces of wood striking each other as hammer and anvil—there is no fixed determination of victory or defeat.

Not conceding defeat does not diminish one’s profundity, and not being victorious does not increase the shallowness of the other. Let us set aside Mañjuśrī for a moment; thus, both victory and defeat are abandoned. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī...

Chen-tu maintains that the past is correct when judged by the past and incorrect when judged by the present; he maintains that the present is correct when judged by the present and incorrect when judged by the past.

If one constructs four propositions, each adhering to two functions while manifesting the essence, they are both "correct"; if each adheres to two functions while injuring the essence, they are both "incorrect.
When distinguishing essence and function individually, each has one aspect that is correct and one that is incorrect; thus, through the functioning, [the essence is revealed].
The essence is that which is neither both nor neither; this text consists of two parts: first, the ancillary discussion, and second, the return to the main thesis.

The ancillary discussion further has three sections: first, Mañjuśrī’s reprimand and exhortation; next, Cunda’s reprimand and exhortation; and finally, Mañjuśrī’s praise. Within the first section, Mañjuśrī’s reprimand and exhortation, there are two parts:
first, the reprimand, and second, the exhortation. Within the reprimand...
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, addressed Cunda, saying: "Cunda, you should not now speak such words,
wishing to cause the Tathāgata to abide forever in the world without entering parinirvāṇa, like that starving man who has no desire for food."
To cite their request and say, "You should not now speak such words," is to reprimand them.
Next, to say, "You should now contemplate; you should train yourself thus," is to exhort them.

You should now contemplate the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); by contemplating and practicing in this way, you will possess the *śūnyatā-samādhi* and seek the True Dharma.

One should train in this way. Next, Cunda’s reproachful exhortation consists of two parts: first, a dual reproach regarding the teaching of contemplation; second, a dual exhortation regarding the teaching of contemplation. Within the dual reproach, there are again two sections:
first, a reproach for the faults of the teaching of contemplation; second, a dual summary of the errors of teaching contemplation. First, the reproach of the teaching:

Regarding this contemplation, there are further two parts: first, a critique of the teaching, and second, a critique of the contemplation itself. The initial critique of the teaching has three points:

(1) one should not suppress a superior title by equating it with an inferior title; (2) one should not elevate an inferior dharma by equating it with a superior dharma; and (3) a summary of the faults incurred, which brings shame upon the former text. As for the first point:
Cunda asked, "Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is the most honored and supreme among gods and humans;
can such a Tathāgata be something conditioned? If he were a conditioned phenomenon, he would be subject to arising and ceasing."
Now, the Tathāgata is the supreme title common to all Buddhas, unchanged from antiquity to the present; thus he is called the Tathāgata.

How could one who is most venerable be equated with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)? For all conditioned phenomena are the base names for birth and death—lowly, inferior, and the weary burdens of all existence.
If one were to equate the Tathāgata with conditioned phenomena, one would be destroying the eternally abiding nature and reducing it to something transitory.
How could it be possible for Nirvana, which is the cessation of all bending and defilement, to become birth and death?
Furthermore, it is like a bubble on water; having set aside the three [inferior] views, one should not equate the inferior dharma with the superior dharma upon hearing this.
For example, just as a bubble on water arises and perishes quickly, and its coming and going revolves like a chariot wheel, so too are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Thus have I heard: the lifespans of the devas are exceedingly long; why then, World-Honored One, is the lifespan of these gods among gods even shorter, not even reaching a hundred years?
It is like a village headman who possesses sovereign power and, by the force of that sovereignty...
One who can suppress others has their merit exhausted; subsequently, they become poor and lowly, despised by others and driven into service as their subordinates.
Why is this? Because they have lost their power and influence.
The "superior dharmas" refer to the four virtues, while the "inferior dharmas" refer to the four opposites. The bubble on the water is a metaphor for impermanence.
The wheel is a metaphor for suffering. I have heard that the lifespan of the devas is extremely long;

those "extremely long-lived" devas are precisely those of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), who are formless and invisible. Therefore, it is said, "I have heard. By citing the long, the short is contrasted;
the short refers to falling from the womb or miscarriage. This raises the question of impurity regarding the formless realm: how can there be impurity there? The answer is: although it is not...
Unwholesome forms are censured by the noble ones and are likewise impure, like a village headman who has lost his power;
this is an analogy for the absence of self (*anātman*). One should know that the four inverted dharmas ought not to be equated with the four virtuous dharmas.
The World-Honored One is likewise; to depart from this would manifest his faults and bring him disgrace.

The World-Honored One is also thus identical with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). If he were identical with all conditioned phenomena, he could not be called the "God among Gods" (*devātideva*). Why is this?
Because all conditioned phenomena are, by their very nature, the dharmas of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
If one were to equate the superior with the inferior by disparaging it, one would lose the honorable title of "the Most Honored among Gods" and also lose the supreme dharmas of the four virtues.

If one were to equate the inferior with the superior by exalting it, one would disgrace the supreme name of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and also disgrace the supreme dharmas such as permanence.

From this point onward, Mañjuśrī’s subsequent discourse consists of three parts censuring that [erroneous] contemplation: (1) one should not contemplate the superior as being identical to the inferior;
the text states: "Do not contemplate the Tathāgata as being the same as conditioned phenomena."
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, do not view the Tathāgata as being identical to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Second, one should not view inferior dharmas as being identical to superior dharmas.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, whether speaking with knowledge or without knowledge, you have stated that the Tathāgata is identical to conditioned phenomena.
The text states: "If one speaks with knowledge, it is called speaking with knowledge; if one speaks without knowledge, it is called speaking without knowledge.

If one knows that the Tathāgata is not composed of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) yet forcibly asserts his identity with them, this causes the lower dharma to become identical to the superior dharma.

If one does not know that the Tathāgata is not composed of conditioned phenomena yet claims he is identical to them, this is to obscure the superior dharma through delusion and to confuse the lower dharma."
Third, it exposes his disgrace and humiliation:
if the Tathāgata were the same as ordinary practitioners, one could not say that he is the God among Gods,
the Sovereign Dharma King within the triple world.
If the Tathāgata were identical to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
he could not be called the "God among Gods," and he would lose his exalted name and exalted Dharma. If all conditioned phenomena were identical to the Tathāgata,
it would disgrace his exalted name and also disgrace his exalted Dharma (and so forth).

Next, following the analogy of "just as a king of men," the faults of both the combined meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*) and the combined verbal expression are explained. Regarding the first analogy, there are two parts:

first, the fault of the combined meditative observation, and second, the fault of the combined verbal expression. The first section further consists of two parts: first, the analogy, and second, the application (*yoga*).
For example, suppose a king of men has a great strongman whose strength equals that of a thousand others and whom no one can subdue;
therefore, this man is called "one who equals a thousand. Such a strongman is beloved by the king, who bestows upon him special honors, rank, and rewards as a matter of course;
thus he is termed "one who equals a thousand. However, this person’s physical strength does not necessarily match that of a thousand.

Because he can surpass a thousand through his various skills and arts, he is called "Equal to a Thousand. In the first parable, it says: the king represents sentient beings and the wrestler represents the Buddha. The wrestler exerts his effort for the sake of the king, while the Buddha bestows transformation upon sentient beings. When the king sees that the wrestler possesses many skills and arts, he generously grants him titles, fiefs, and emoluments. Just so, when sentient beings see the Buddha’s manifold skillful means, they all receive the great benefit of the Dharma. Therefore, the Buddha is called "Equal to a Thousand.
