That which follows the Way is the perfect function; as the text below says, "Two birds fly together.

By citing what precedes and what follows, the supreme skillful means is explained to realize the true Buddha’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity—things you do not recognize. What you do recognize, however, is the extinction into cessation through the reduction of ashes.

Although there is no perfect application prior to the Way, it is not that the supreme perfection does not exist prior to the Way; therefore, this passage refutes the failure to perceive the True Buddha.
From the words "How do you adorn [the body]? onwards, there is an extensive explanation of the failure to perceive the True Dharma.

"O bhikṣus, how shall you adorn the precious city of the True Dharma, fully equipped with the various treasures of merit—namely, the walls and moats of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom?
Now that you have encountered this precious city of the Buddha-Dharma, you should not take up these deceptive things;
it would be like a merchant leader who, having reached a city of genuine jewels, takes up shards and rubble and returns home."
You, likewise, have encountered this precious city, yet you take up false and deceptive things.
That which is the True Dharma is the arising of true, virtuous, and wondrous form; it produces sublime and wholesome nectar, being perfectly complete and without deficiency.
It is also called the "cream of cream" (*sarpir-manda*); all medicinal herbs enter into it, and it is the seed of all three trainings.
The various merits, whether horizontal or vertical, high or broad, overflow and fill completely, like the walls, moats, and battlements of a precious city;
this is what is called the True Dharma. You eliminate delusions through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); when delusions are exhausted, the contemplation itself vanishes.

Taking the wisdom of the body as "有余涅槃" (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), if one enters "无余涅槃" (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), the physical body is reduced to ashes and wisdom is extinguished, becoming identical with emptiness and eternally quiescent. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

The *Dharmasaṃgraha* states that the Dharma favored by the poor is inferior and belongs to the Hīnayāna; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* calls it a "base matter" and this scripture refers to it as "false gravel.
These are all condemnations of those who have not attained the True Dharma.

Furthermore, there are two [points] regarding the injunction: "O bhikṣus, do not, with an inferior mind, disparage the vast [teachings]," which likewise condemns those who have not attained the true Saṃgha.
"You bhikṣus, do not give rise to contentment with a lowly mind. Although you have now attained the going forth, you do not yet conceive a longing for this Mahāyāna.
You bhikṣus, although your bodies are clothed in the dyed robes of the kāṣāya, your minds are still not imbued with the pure Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
You bhikṣus, although you go on alms-round and travel through many places..."

"From the very beginning, you have never sought the Dharma-food of the Mahāyāna. Although you, monks, have shaved off your hair and beards, you have not, for the sake of the True Dharma, eliminated the various fetters (saṃyojana).
First, he generally rebukes their inferior resolve and lack of aspiration for the supreme Dharma; next, he specifically rebukes them by way of cause, effect, and merit."
One is called a *saṃgha* by virtue of the merit of cause and effect; since your causes and effects are neither true, though you wear the *kāṣāya*, you have not destroyed the evils of the five abodes;
though you fear neither internal nor external demons, though you practice alms-gathering and travel many places, you are not a mendicant worthy of offerings;
and though you have shaved off your beard and hair, you have not slain the thieves [of the afflictions]. As long as you do not give rise [to the Path], you are not a true *saṃgha*. Above.
By citing the true Buddha-dharma to refute the counterfeit Buddha-dharma, one does not manifest the characteristics of the counterfeit Buddha-dharma;

likewise, by refuting counterfeit monks, one does not manifest the characteristics of true monks. That these appear alternately before and after is because by citing the true, the counterfeit is known, and by citing the counterfeit, the true is known.
"O you bhikṣus, from now on you must truly set forth the text concerning the true Three Jewels; this consists of two parts, the first of which is the heading:
'From now on you must truly [set it forth].
O you bhikṣus, I now truly instruct and command you."
The true corresponds to the former false, and the real corresponds to the former empty.
As for the second, the direct demonstration: it is I who am present here and now.
I am now present before this assembly in harmony; the *dharmatā* of the Tathāgata is real and not inverted.
I am the Buddha Jewel; the great assembly in harmony is the Sangha Jewel; the Tathāgata’s *dharmatā* is the Dharma Jewel.
Within the Dharma Jewel, the three points (*bindu*) are complete: the Tathāgata is *prajñā*; *dharmatā* is the *dharmakāya*; and non-inversion is liberation (*vimukti*).
These three are called "treasuries" (*kośa*), for they contain all phenomena; the same applies to the Buddhas and the Sangha.
Third, from "Therefore, you all... onwards, this is the section on what should be abandoned and what should be attained; it consists of two parts:
first, exhorting the abandonment of the false, and second, exhorting the cultivation of the true. Regarding the first passage:
"Therefore, you all should be diligent, collect your minds, and with valorous effort, crush all fetters; [you are] the sun of wisdom of the Ten Powers."
Once you have already sunk into oblivion, you shall be shrouded by ignorance.
Since that which is false in essence arises precisely from ignorance, and as long as ignorance is not eliminated one cannot escape falsehood, I therefore exhort you to abandon ignorance.
O Bhikṣus, it is like this: the great earth below serves as an exhortation to cultivate the True Text, which is divided into four parts:

first, the parable explaining the Secret Treasury; second, the Dharma-exposition of the Secret Treasury; third, the interpretation of the Secret Treasury; and fourth, the conclusion of the Secret Treasury.

The parables consist of three sections: first, the parable of the great earth; second, the parable of the various mountains, medicinal herbs, and grasses; and third, the parable of being of use to sentient beings.
"O Bhikṣus, it is like the great earth and its various mountains and medicinal herbs, which exist for the use of sentient beings.
First, as for the great earth: the earth does not merely serve as a universal support; it also brings forth without being born, giving rise to medicinal herbs.

These herbs function without having a prior purpose, yet they are used for the benefit of sentient beings. That which is produced by the herbs does not exist apart from that which gives rise to them."
That which is produced is also for the use of sentient beings; although sentient beings take and use it, it is also summoned by karma and brought forth by the merit of the great earth.
Thus, the three types—the seed, the plant, and the medicinal herb—are interwoven such that they cannot be separated. They are distinct yet each possesses all three;
this can be used as an analogy for the "Secret Three-in-One," and the "Secret One-in-Three. It can be used as an analogy for how all things are secretly complete within one another.
Because it is like a treasury, this analogy is cited to illustrate the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*).
Next, from the passage "My Dharma is also thus" onwards, the teaching employs the Dharma to correspond with the analogy in order to clarify the secret treasury.

Within this, there are both sequential and telescoped correspondences intended to demonstrate that the secret treasury is sovereign, indeterminate, and inconceivable. First, regarding the self and the Dharma:
"It is likewise" refers to this correspondence:
my Dharma is also like this, producing the sublime and excellent flavor of the nectar of Dharma as a potent medicine for the various diseases of the afflictions of sentient beings.
The Dharma-body is like the great earth, and the great earth is like the Dharma-body; thus the analogy is likewise.
By citing the three aspects of the Dharma-body, it corresponds to the three meanings of the great earth as the source from which the wondrous, wholesome nectar of the Dharma-flavor arises.

By citing the three aspects of the three types of *prajñā*, it corresponds to the three meanings of the various mountains and medicinal herbs for the benefit of sentient beings. By citing the three aspects of the three gates of liberation, it corresponds to the three meanings within their function.
I shall now cause all sentient beings, as well as my sons and the fourfold assembly, to abide entirely within the Secret Treasury;
I, too, shall abide therein and enter into parinirvāṇa.
I shall now cause all sentient beings to enter the secret treasury, thereby transcending the four classes of disciples;
they shall enter the secret treasury, thereby transcending the medicinal herbs. I myself shall also enter and transcend the great earth.
Once the illness is cured, the merit of the medicine and the earth ceases; yet, by abiding in profound stillness, sentient beings derive the benefit of *prajñā*.
When merit perishes, the function of the Dharmakāya ceases; all return together to the ultimate quiescence within the Secret Treasury.

All sentient beings therein represent the stage of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), corresponding to the first *bhūmi*. The fourfold assembly represents the middle stages, corresponding to the forty positions.

The Buddha represents the final mind, corresponding to the stage of *samyaksaṃbuddha*. Together they enter the Secret Treasury and all behold their Buddha-nature. Now, as for these sentient beings who have entered:

"Is it the same as the Buddha? Answer: It is distinguished by way of six positions (and so forth). Furthermore, following from the preceding text: the great earth is likened to the Jewel of the Buddha;
the various mountains, medicinal herbs, and grasses are likened to the Jewel of the Dharma; and their utility for sentient beings is likened to the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Next, regarding the combined text: "My Dharma is also like this. This is the nectar produced by the Buddha; it is the Dharma, which serves sentient beings.
The Sangha.
Third, following us, it is called "the lower" (the section explaining the Secret Treasury). First, he presents the interpretations of others; next, he applies the text.
The people of the *Dicheng* school say that the *ālayavijñāna*, being within delusive afflictions, is termed the "Secret Treasury. The followers of the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* say:
If the Buddhas of the future were outside sentient beings, then all sentient beings would have to attain the fruit of Buddhahood; this principle would belong to persons and thus would be "internal.
If it were not yet present at this very moment, it would be "external. Because it is external, it is not internal; because it is internal, it is not external.
This is called the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*). The *Nirvāṇa-benyou-lun* states: "The Buddha exists within the bodies of sentient beings," yet even this is not "secret."

That which exists outside the body is not the body; that which exists inside the body is neither inside nor outside. That which exists as "neither non-inside nor non-outside" is not the secret (*guhya*) at all.
Because sentient beings themselves are this very [reality], it is called "secret. The first two types of interpretations are refuted by this treatise (and so forth).
As for what is taught in the ancient teachings, it is called "mysterious" (*mi*) because it is hidden, and "repository" (*zàng*) because it is covered—meaning that impermanence covers permanence.

Because they mutually conceal one another, the signless is not understood; by revealing what was concealed, the eternal and so forth are made manifest—this is called the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*).
Various analogies for this, such as those of a person with physical deformities or the treatises of non-Buddhists, are explained in detail in the subsequent text.
This is termed the Secret Treasury of the former teachings. In the present sutra, the veil is opened like the moon situated in the sky, pure and clearly revealed, unlike the former teachings.
It is simply because the True Dharma is subtle, wondrous, inconceivable, transcending names and detached from marks that sentient beings do not understand it;
thus it is called the "Secret. Because the Dharma-realm encompasses and gathers all phenomena with inexhaustible function, it is called a "Treasury" (*garbha*).
Therefore, the text below states: "Neither vertical nor horizontal, neither parallel nor distinct—this is the meaning of 'secret' (guhyaka); it is the perfection of the three dharmas."
That the feet have no deficiency is the meaning of "treasury" (*kośa*); the meaning of the text is thus radiant and clear. Why then do others offer different interpretations?

[The author] cites the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra* to refute various human teachers, and cites the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* to refute the provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*). It is like a great wind sweeping away the mist, leaving the Milky Way brilliantly clear (and so forth).
Now, the explanation of the text of the Secret Treasury is divided into three parts: first, the analogy of the three dots; second, the analogy of... [the text continues].
The three eyes, the three unions, and the three virtues—these three phrases, taken in their general sense, represent the entry into principle through phenomena;
the three dots are the written characters, which refer to verbal teaching; the three eyes are the divine eye, which refers to spiritual practice;

and the three virtues are the Teacher of Buddhas, which refers to the ultimate principle. Furthermore, these are the Buddha-seal that seals both teaching and practice; for whatever words there may be...

To speak of that which is associated with this: it is the practice of cultivation that is the secret teaching, the attainment that is the secret conduct, and the realization that is the secret principle;
thus, by way of these three, it is called the teaching, conduct, and principle according to the truth.
What is called the "Secret Treasury" is like the three dots of the letter *i*. If they are placed side by side, they do not form the letter *i*;
if they are placed vertically, they likewise do not form it.
Regarding the first three dots, how are they like the worldly letter *i*? In foreign lands, there are two types of *i*: the old and the new. The old...

The horizontal and vertical strokes are severed and separated; this is used as a metaphor for that. The horizontal stroke is like a blazing fire, and the vertical stroke is like water being dropped—each does not continue into the other.
It is not horizontal like a blazing fire, nor is it vertical like falling water.

One should understand that in this land, the characters beneath the grass have fine lines where the strokes are connected; this is the form of the new *ī*, while the old *ī* may be compared to the teachings of the past.
The *dharmakāya* of the three virtues possesses *prajñā* as its original nature; it is perfected through cultivation, and only upon entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* does it become liberation.
At that point, there is no longer a body or wisdom, which is like a vertical drop of water falling and separating from others.

Furthermore, when distinguished in terms of body and wisdom, there is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which is like a horizontal line of fire where the flames exist simultaneously yet remain distinct and unrelated to one another.
The new "I" character (*i*) serves as a metaphor for the three virtues of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) in the present teaching:

it is simultaneously illumination and simultaneously sovereignty, such that one is named as three, yet the three have no separate substance. Because they are not horizontal, they are neither before nor after;
because they are not vertical, one is three and three is one. It is like a large dot, or like fine strokes: three yet one, one yet three.
Because it cannot be described as one or three, nor contemplated as one or three, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
This "inconceivable" is neither three nor one; it is the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*), like the letter *i* of the world.
This phrase constitutes the root of this sutra; to manifest this meaning, extensive questions and answers are established, resulting in twenty-five chapters that flow forth in abundance.
"If one loses this meaning, one will be utterly deluded regarding the fundamental; toward what then shall one point as a refuge?
(and so forth). Next, to explain by way of the three eyes:
it is like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara; only then can the *ī* with its three dots (*bindu*) be formed. If they were separate, it could not be achieved.
It is established.
Maheśvara dwells at the summit of the Rūpadhātu and governs one side of the trichiliocosm. He has three eyes and one face;

these three eyes and one face cannot be described simply as "one" or "three," whether considered vertically, horizontally, together, or separately. He is able to adorn the celestial countenance and act for the world.

The Sovereign of the Realms (Dhātupati) thoroughly illuminates the three thousand worlds; if he were not both vertical and horizontal, the Sovereign of Adornment could not illuminate the world and all things would not be perfected as the Three Virtues.

It is the same here: if the vertical and horizontal were separate, the Secret Treasury (Guhyakośa) would not be established; only when it is neither vertical nor horizontal does the Secret Treasury become established (and so forth).
Next, regarding the explanation of the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyakośa*) by way of the three virtues:
I am likewise not *nirvāṇa*, and the dharma of liberation is also not *nirvāṇa*; the body of the Tathāgata is also not *nirvāṇa*, and Mahāprajñā is also not *nirvāṇa*.
These three dharmas are distinct from one another, yet they are also not *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the fact that the various virtues of the stage of fruition are spoken of as only three, this is a concise enumeration that encompasses all dharmas.

The body of the *dharmakāya* is neither form (*rūpa*) nor non-form (*arūpa*). Because it is not form, it cannot be seen through physical characteristics; because it is not non-form, it cannot be known through mental conceptualization.
Although it is not form, form fills the ten directions; the vast and the minute are mutually contained within it, being neither expansive nor narrow.
That which is not non-form can also be sought after, for it can give rise to the profound and vast wisdom of sentient beings;
therefore, it is said that the form of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible, and so forth—this refers to the merit of the Dharmakāya. Prajñā is neither cognition nor characters.

Because it is not cognition, it cannot be moved by deliberation or discrimination; because it is not characters, it cannot be expressed in speech or written upon the girdle. Yet, it is also not a lack of knowledge.
The "non-character" (a-akṣara) is not the same as the extinction of ashes because it is not due to a lack of knowledge; nor is it the same as partial emptiness because it is not a non-character.

Although it is not knowledge, there is nothing it does not illuminate; the three truths are universally radiant within the ultimate realm of the Buddha, where both the ordinary and the holy are clearly manifest.
Although it is not a character, it fully possesses all characters—those of the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane.
He fully comprehends the flow of the Dharma-realm, which is like a cascading river or the surging of the ocean, inexhaustible and boundless. As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
"He can expound the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind; all say that the World-Honored One speaks in their own language.
This is the extraordinary power of his unique dharma. Thus, the virtue of *prajñā* and liberation is neither clamor nor silence.
Neither bound nor liberated: because it is not bound, the five abodes cannot fetter it; because it is not liberated, the ten knowledges cannot leave it empty.
Though not liberated, it is liberated, being unrestrained by the two extremes, as explained in the "Liberation from the Hundred Phrases.
Though not bound, it is bound, for it is bound by those who are dull-witted, deluded, icchantikas, and non-Buddhists; thus, there is the affliction of practice.

The son’s walking and staying manifest the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; wherever he appears to tame sentient beings—whether in base circumstances—he surely bestows [benefit], like a physician treating an illness or a lotus in water, unstained and without attachment. This is the merit of liberation.
The inconceivable bodily karma of the Buddha is subsumed within the Dharma-body; the inconceivable verbal karma of the Buddha is likewise subsumed therein.
If one encompasses the inconceivable liberation of the Buddha’s mental karma (*manas-karman*), then all is encompassed; thus we know that the three virtues encompass all virtues.

Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* speaks of the purity of form (*rūpa-viśuddhi*) and the purity of the *prajñā* of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna-viśuddhi-prajñā*).

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of the "adornments of the Tathāgata" and the "purity of the six sense faculties" (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*). These are the various [teachings] found throughout the sūtras.

It is taught that all things are subsumed within the three virtues (triguṇa); encompassing both the general and the particular, and integrating both phenomena and principle, this concise summary of the vast does not exceed these three virtues.
Even if one considers them as being either separate or combined, vertical or horizontal, distinct or identical—none of these represent the secret treasury. As the text says:
"The Dharma-body is neither prajñā, nor is it liberation; nor is it that which is neither vertical nor horizontal, neither combined nor distinct."
The identity of the three within the one, the immeasurable within the one, and the one within the immeasurable—neither one nor immeasurable—is called the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*).
From the passage "From now on, I abide in... onwards, the fourth section concludes the secret treasury.
I now abide securely in these three dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, this is called "entering nirvāṇa," like the worldly letter *ī*.
Abiding securely in these three dharmas, one binds these three virtues and enters great nirvāṇa, binding the secret treasury like the worldly letter *ī*.
This consists of binding three dots; the text is abbreviated and does not bind the "heavenly eye. Nevertheless, the Buddha constantly abides securely in these three dharmas.
The statement, "I now merely act in accordance with conditions as appropriate; thus, for the sake of sentient beings, I am said to enter nirvana," refers precisely to this meaning.

Third, from the passage beginning "At that time, the bhikṣus... to the end of the section on doubt and attachment, the text is divided into three parts: first, the [erroneous] attachment; second, the [corrective] teaching; and third, the conclusion.
Regarding the "Requesting the Three Doubts about the Buddha": First, he rebukes and strips away [the claim that] what has been realized cannot be immediately relinquished;
therefore, there is the attachment that the Buddha’s teachings are new. Because one hears [the teaching] and does not understand it, one desires to study;

thus, there arises this doubt and attachment as to why, when both ancient and modern teachings are the word of the Buddha, one is false and the other is true. The text is divided into two parts: first, an account of his compassionate suffering.
Regarding the first part of the formal presentation of the thesis:
At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was certain to enter parinirvāṇa, they were all filled with grief;
their body hair stood on end and their tears flowed profusely as they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him countless times.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching that one enters nirvana by abiding in the three dharmas, they fail to contemplate the meaning of "abiding" and instead give rise to the notion of departing from here and dwelling elsewhere;
for this reason, they experience sorrow and suffering (and so forth).
Next, following the World-Honored One’s excellent discourse on "departing from this," the text records what was heard and describes it as something never before taught;

however, it merely adheres to past teachings. This adherence is divided into two parts: first, the adherence itself, and second, the praise of that adherence. Furthermore, the adherence consists of three aspects:
first, adhering to the principle by way of the teaching; second, adhering to the principle by way of practice; and third, the actual adherence to the principle.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, you have excellently expounded impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
'Excellently expounded' means that you have upheld the ancient teachings and strengthened the words; this teaching is excellent because it is capable of fully articulating the underlying principle."
World-Honored One, it is just as among the footprints of all living beings, the footprint of the elephant is supreme;

so too is this perception of impermanence the foremost among all perceptions. If there are those who diligently practice it, they will be able to eliminate all craving for the realm of desire, craving for the realms of form and formlessness, ignorance, pride, and even the perception of permanence.
Next, regarding the simile of the elephant’s footprint: because the practice of past conduct is the most excellent among all progressive practices, it is used as a metaphor for the "great footprint.

The notion that there is wisdom and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) in practice is the initial gateway to wisdom; thus, the beginning is cited as the representative term. From diligent effort onward, one grasps the abandonment of abandonment;
when thought is abandoned, knowledge is also abandoned, and false views are thereby eliminated. For this reason, [the text] speaks of the latter and does not mention the former.
Regarding the notion of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*) and the ear mentioned previously: when delusion departs, wisdom perishes.
From the World-Honored One, if one were to depart from impermanence, one would leave behind the principle of correct adherence.
World-Honored One, Tathāgata, if one were to depart from the notion of impermanence, one should not now enter into *nirvāṇa*. If not...

Regarding "detachment," why is it said that by cultivating the perception of impermanence, one becomes detached from craving for the three realms, as well as ignorance, pride, and the perception of impermanence itself?
Within this principle, it is neither detachment nor non-detachment; for if one were detached from impermanence, one would not enter nirvana. If...

If one does not depart from impermanence yet still possesses all afflictions—because it is neither departing nor non-departing—one is able to sever all afflictions, harmonize with the profound principle, and realize the Truth;

how could there be anything beyond this? To disparage this as being false (and so forth), or to claim that if one departs [from impermanence] then the former teaching is wrong, while if one does not depart then the former teaching is right—upon examining the text, such views are difficult to sustain (and so forth).
Next, following the passage from the Blessed One beginning with "It is just as a farmer," this is the praise:
"The Blessed One is like a farmer who, during the autumn months, deeply plows his field and is able to remove weeds;

so too is the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā), for it is able to remove all craving for the realm of desire (kāmadhātu-rāga), craving for the realms of form and formlessness (rūpa-ārūpya-rāga), and ignorance (avijjā)."

"O Bhagavān, regarding pride and the perception of impermanence: just as autumn plowing is the best among all forms of plowing, and just as the elephant's footprint is the most excellent among all footprints, so too is the perception of impermanence supreme among all perceptions."

The praise of the three aforementioned attachments is as follows: regarding the method of plowing in autumn, there are two capacities—one is that weeds do not grow, and the second is that the soil becomes fertile.
"Fertile" praises the teaching; "weeds die" praises cessation (*nirodha*); and "fertile" again praises the practice of agricultural methods, which praises the principle (*dharma*).
The praise of autumn plowing praises the teaching; the praise of the elephant’s footprint praises the practice; and the praise of impermanence (*anityatā*) praises the principle (and so forth).
Next, the World-Honored One said: "For example, if a sovereign emperor were to depart from here, whom would one petition to hear the new teachings for the sake of joyfully practicing and studying?

If the Tathāgata were to depart, from whom would one receive instruction? Because of this, he requested [the Buddha] to provide a superior critique of the request; within the request, there was much made of the analogy of a close relative, which the Buddha rejected as not being true.
Now, I dare not employ the analogy of a close relative, but shall instead use the analogy of a master-teacher, who is precisely the one who provides unified instruction.

This is because the meaning is broad; there should be five analogies in total. The first is an analogy for inviting the Master [of the Dharma], and the latter four are analogies for inviting the Teacher [of the Way].

Examining the text of these combined analogies, they represent the invitation to study the "new *i*" (the new character). Why is this? Arhats have already destroyed the four abidings (*catuḥ-vāsabhūmi*), yet ignorance and nescience (*avidyā*) remain undestroyed.
Since these specific delusions are now raised, it is known that the "new *i*" is being invited. The initial "pardon" serves as a general introduction.
The analogy of requesting a mantra-reciter applies to Śrāvakas who have not yet eliminated the two types of delusion; it also generally applies to Śrāvakas who have not yet eliminated ignorance.
The analogy of requesting a fragrant elephant applies specifically to those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have not yet eliminated the delusions of thought (*klesha*).

The analogy of requesting a person cured of malaria applies specifically to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who have not yet eliminated one side [of the obstructions]. The analogy of requesting a drunken man applies generally.
I act as the petitioner for all ordinary beings and sages.

World-Honored One, it is like a sovereign who, knowing his life is nearing its end, grants a general amnesty to all those imprisoned and confined throughout the realm, ensuring they are all set free before he passes away.
The Tathāgata should now likewise deliver all sentient beings.
"Those who are bound and confined by ignorance and nescience have all been made to attain liberation, and only then will you enter nirvāṇa.
We, however, have not yet attained deliverance; how can the Tathāgata now wish to abandon us and enter nirvāṇa?"
World-Honored One, it is as if there were a person possessed by a spirit who, upon encountering a skilled master of incantations, is cured through the power of those spells.

The Tathāgata is likewise; for the sake of the śrāvakas, he eliminates the spirit of ignorance and causes them to dwell securely in the dharmas of Mahāprajñāpāramitā, liberation, and so forth—just like the letter *i*.
The first two [similes] are as explained in the text.
Regarding the third, the simile of the fragrant elephant (*gandhahastin*), there is first the illustration and then the application.
"World-Honored One, it is as if a fragrant elephant were bound by a person; even though there were a skilled trainer, he could not restrain it, for it would suddenly break its bonds."
"Still bound by fetters, I wander at will; I have not yet been liberated from these fifty-seven bonds of affliction.
How can the Tathāgata wish to abandon me and enter parinirvāṇa?"

Regarding the statement in the *Compendium* (*Abhidharmasamuccaya*) that there are fifty-seven afflictions (*kleśa*), the commentators provide three ways of categorizing them: five groups of five, ten groups of ten, and seven groups of seven. The school of enumeration (*saṃkhyā-vādin*) states that in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four types of dull [afflictions]:

greed, hatred, delusion, and pride. These pertain to the five categories of existence (*pañca-gati*). Regarding these five categories: for each of the four truths (*satya*) realized through insight (*darśana-mārga*) and the one path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), there are four [afflictions] each, totaling twenty. Furthermore, in the upper realms (the form and formless realms), there are likewise four for each of the four truths, totaling sixteen. Thus, the total is thirty-six. When combined with the twenty-one [afflictions] of the desire realm, they constitute the fifty-seven. (Note:

This passage explains the numerical breakdown of the fifty-seven afflictions by first identifying the four "dull" afflictions—greed, hatred, delusion, and pride—which are present across all five destinies. It then calculates their occurrence across the paths of seeing and cultivation within the desire realm and the upper realms.)
In the twenty [afflictions] of the upper two realms, one removes anger from each, resulting in five factors; in the lower [realm], there are three for each of the five, totaling fifteen.

Thus, the two realms together constitute thirty. Adding these to the twenty of the desire realm makes fifty. When combined with the seven mental fetters (*paryavasthāna*), which are the root of the seven outflows (*āsrava*), this constitutes the fundamental [afflictions].
As the masters say: "The ten afflictions of the vision-truths (*darśana-heya*) are delusions regarding the four truths, making forty; the [ten] of the cultivation-truths (*bhāvanā-heya*)..."
The four *srotāpatti-āsravas* (outflows) are further deluded regarding the Four Truths; four times four makes sixteen.

Combined with the views regarding the Truths, this totals fifty-six, and including ignorance (*avidyā*), it becomes fifty-seven. Xinghuang says that each of the five gates of contemplation contains three inversions—namely, those of perception (*saṃjñā*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), and mind (*citta*)—making fifteen.
When these are applied to the three realms, they become forty-five. Furthermore, there are three [inversions] for each of the Four Truths.
[Reversing the order of] three, four, twelve, and ten, with the preceding [number], it totals fifty-seven (and so forth).
World-Honored One, just as a person suffering from malaria who encounters a skilled physician finds their affliction removed, I am likewise thus:
though I have encountered the Tathāgata despite my many sufferings and the fever of wrong livelihood, my illness has not yet been cured, nor have I attained supreme peace and security.
"World-Honored One, why do you, who always delight [in the world], now wish to abandon it and enter parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One, it is like a drunken man who, being unconscious, does not distinguish between kin and strangers, nor mother, daughter, or sister;
he is deluded by lust and disorder, his speech is dissolute, and he lies amidst impurity. At that time, a skilled physician gives him medicine to take; having taken it,"
He immediately vomited it up and, recollecting his own mind, felt deep shame and remorse, severely reproaching himself: "Alcohol is unwholesome, the root of all evils.
If one can sever it, one remains far removed from all transgressions. World-Honored One, I am likewise;

throughout the past, as I have transmigrated through birth and death, I was intoxicated by sensual desires and greedily craved the five objects of desire. I did not regard my mother as a mother, nor did I regard my elder sister as a sister."

To perceive as a woman that which is not a woman, or to perceive as a living being that which is not a living being—because of this, one revolves through the cycle of birth and death, suffering the pains of saṃsāra.
It is like that intoxicated man who lies amidst impurity; the Tathāgata should now bestow upon me the medicine of the Dharma so that I may vomit up the foul wine of afflictions.
Yet, I have not yet attained a mind of awakening; how can the Tathāgata wish to abandon me?
Entering into *nirvāṇa*.

The analogy of intoxication refers to the performance of the three types of unwholesome karma within the Middle Period, resulting in retribution; it is like taking medicine to purge delusions (and so forth).
Third, regarding the World-Honored One: the analogy of the plantain tree removes this doubt concerning the teaching of the past—that if it were not the Buddha, [the teachings] would not be so.

One should explain that if the former teaching were [identical to] the Buddha’s, it would not be the case that the present teaching is not [the same]; if it were [the same], why was the present teaching not taught earlier?
If it is not [the same], how can it be called "real"? Therefore, doubt arises. Regarding the text, there are three parts: first, clarifying non-self; second, citing scriptural evidence;
third, clarifying its function.
“World-Honored One, it is as if there were someone who praised a plantain tree for being solid and substantial; such a thing is impossible. World-Honored One, sentient beings are likewise.
If one were to praise the self, the person, the sentient being, the life-span, the nourisher, the knower, the seer, the agent, or the experiencer as being real, such a thing is also impossible.
We cultivate the perception of non-self in this way, World-Honored One. It is, for example, like this:”

Just as the dregs of fermented gruel have no further use, so too is this body: it is without self and without master. World-Honored One, just as the seven-leaf flower has no fragrance, so too is this body:
it is without self and without master. We shall thus constantly cultivate the perception of non-self in our minds.

The plantain tree illustrates the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); the dregs of juice illustrate the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); and the seven leaves illustrate the [remaining] three aggregates.
Next, he cites the Buddha’s teaching that all phenomena are without self or what belongs to a self:
"As the Buddha has taught that all phenomena are without self or what belongs to a self, you, O bhikṣus, should practice accordingly."
Having thus gained faith, one eliminates the conceit of "I"; having abandoned the conceit of "I," one enters nirvana.
Third, the analogy of a bird's track in the sky clarifies the absence of self-activity.
World-Honored One, it is as impossible as for the tracks of a bird to appear in the sky;
likewise, it is impossible for one who can cultivate the perception of non-self to still possess various [erroneous] views.

In the past, the teaching was able to eliminate both *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions); thus, it clarified non-self (*anātman*). When the Buddha previously taught the clarification of non-self, he said:
"I cultivate non-self; if there were such a thing as a self, that would be impossible. Why, then, do you today speak of a self?
Therefore, the absence of self is raised as the basis for the doubt regarding the teaching.
Fourth, from that time, the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus. This section on dispelling attachment and removing doubt has two parts:
first, praising the absence of self; second, refuting [the notion of self]. Regarding the first part:
at that time, the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus, saying, "Excellent, excellent! You have skillfully cultivated the perception of non-self."
There are three intentions [behind] what is stated above. Why is "non-self" alone praised? Because it is the root of attachment, doubt, and so forth. Why is it praised?
Because it is the natural order of worldly dialogue and response. Furthermore, first one uses "non-self" to refute the false;

once the [opponent] is able to accept it, one then intends to take away [their attachment], yet first gives it to them. Moreover, by grasping at the inferior, one attains the superior—this constitutes the fourth [point].
This refers to the entirety of the meaning.

Next, there are three points regarding the refutation: first, the refutation of their biased principles, as the text below states: "These three kinds of cultivation have no real meaning," thereby criticizing them;
second, the refutation of their biased practices, as the text below states: "All that was previously cultivated is entirely erroneous."
The three inversions refute their biased teachings; as the subsequent text states: "What was previously called 'cutting off the milk' is not true speech. These three points each have two parts:
first, restating their adherence to their own views, and second, responding with a refutation. Regarding the initial refutation of their biased principles, there are three sections:
first, praising and restating their adherence; second, employing analogies; and third, concluding with an expression of admiration from the World-Honored One.
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we do not merely cultivate the perception of non-self;
we further cultivate other perceptions as well, namely, the perception of suffering, the perception of impermanence, and the perception of non-self."

World-Honored One, it is like a person who is intoxicated; their mind is dazed and confused, and when they look at the mountains, rivers, cities, palaces, and the sun, moon, and stars, all appear to be spinning.
This intoxication has two faults: first, it causes disorder and confusion; second, it leads one away from what is wholesome.
The third section consists of two parts: first, a summary verse concluding the discussion on the fault of intoxication for those who do not practice.

"World-Honored One, if there are persons who do not cultivate the perception of suffering, the perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, and so forth, such people are not called noble ones;
they are full of negligence and wander through the cycle of birth and death."
Second, praising those who are faultless and well-practiced:
"World-Honored One, for this reason, we have well-cultivated these various perceptions.
Next, as for the Buddha’s refutation, he provides a response by means of refutation, which is divided into two parts; first, the refutation of that which is not inverted or confused.
The section on "Inversion, Confusion, Regression, and Intoxication" follows that [on the preceding]. It refutes the cultivation of non-virtue and establishes the cultivation of virtue;

it first refutes inversion and confusion, which is divided into four parts: (1) admonishing the listener and introducing the topic; (2) clarifying the nature of inversion and confusion; (3) presenting the absence of inversion and confusion;
and (4) concluding by attributing the fault to [the opponent].
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Listen attentively, listen attentively!
As for the analogy of the intoxicated man you have just cited, you know only the words but have not yet grasped their meaning.
Regarding the phrase 'reiterating what was previously stated' in the section on the admonition, it reiterates that very calculation; you know only the words but do not understand their meaning."

The words are the language, while the meaning is the underlying principle. Just as one who is intoxicated hears speech yet does not understand its meaning, and though he himself speaks, there is no substance to his record—so it is with you:
you hear others speak of "transmigration" and "non-transmigration," and you claim to practice well, yet in reality, you do not practice well.
What is the meaning? It is like a drunken person who, seeing the sun and moon above, perceives them as actually revolving when they are not;

sentient beings are likewise. Covered by the afflictions and ignorance, they give rise to perverted minds, conceiving of a self where there is no self, the impermanent as permanent, the impure as pure, and suffering as pleasure, because they are shrouded by these afflictions.
Although they give rise to this thought, they do not comprehend its meaning; it is like that intoxicated person who perceives motion where there is no motion.
Regarding the passage in the midst of the "inverted confusion" (*viparyāsa*) that speaks of bringing down the sun and moon, this is precisely an analogy for destroying inverted confusion.

As for the term "sentient beings" (*sattva*), others say it is specifically referring to the bhikṣus, while others say it refers to sentient beings in general. I, however, say this is not so; since the metaphor of intoxication has already been applied, it must refer to them [the bhikṣus].
To know that a bhikṣu is a sentient being and to realize that what is reckoned as "self" is actually "non-self" is to destroy one's delusions and confusion;
it is also to destroy the attachment to impermanence and non-self by taking them to be ultimate. You take impermanence and non-self to be ultimate, yet this too is not real.
It is a false construction of non-self, like a drunken man who perceives a turning point where there is none.
[The text] transforms the notion [as follows].
Regarding the third "I": that which is free from falling into error or confusion is precisely permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Self" (ātman) is the meaning of Buddha; "permanence" (nitya) is the meaning of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya); "bliss" (sukha) is the meaning of Nirvana; and "purity" (śubha) is...
This is the meaning of the Dharma. What you criticize as wrong is not actually wrong; rather, it is what you take to be right that is wrong. "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening.
He is called "Self" because of his sovereignty. He is "eternal" because the Dharma-body is not produced by conditions. He is "blissful" because he is precisely Nirvana.
Nirvana is without sensation and is called great bliss; purity is precisely the Dharma, and the Dharma is precisely without defilement.
That which you previously rejected is now affirmed as such. That you do not understand this meaning is truly due to being intoxicated. (And so forth.)
"Fourth, you bhikṣus who have severed the lower fetters and returned to the state of non-returning—
how can you say that those who possess the notion of a self wander through birth and death with arrogance and haughtiness?"

The bhikṣu says: "To claim that 'the permanent is inverted' and 'the impermanent is not inverted' is to reverse the Buddha’s teaching. The impermanent is indeed inverted and the permanent is not inverted.
It is like the sun and moon which do not revolve; those who are drunk perceive them as revolving. Are the sun and moon at fault? The fault lies solely with the drunkard.
Likewise, permanence, bliss, self, and purity are truly not impermanent; to recklessly calculate them as impermanent is the fault of the one who holds such an inverted view."

Next, regarding what you have said concerning the refutation of "going" in the passage on the well-cultivated and the poorly cultivated, the text is divided into four parts: first, the dual presentation of the two types of cultivation;
second, the dual clarification of the eight inversions; third, the dual reversal of faults and their return; and fourth, the exclusive citation of superior cultivation.
If you say, "I also cultivate the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self," these three types of cultivation lack true meaning;
I shall now explain the superior methods of cultivation.

The beginning and middle state: "If you say... This marks the fact that their cultivation lacks substantial reality, thereby refuting what is considered good as being neither good nor bad—like the false words of a drunkard, devoid of truth.
Next, it marks superior cultivation. Regarding "relative" (prati), its meaning may be broad or concise;
there are various versions such as ten gates, eight inversions, or six practices. Here, we shall briefly correlate it with three.
Next, "counting suffering as pleasure" and "leaving aside [the view that] pleasure is suffering" together clarify the eight inversions.
To count suffering as pleasure and pleasure as suffering is an inverted dharma; to count the impermanent as permanent and the permanent as impermanent is an inverted dharma;
to count the non-self as self and the self as non-self is an inverted dharma; and to count the impure as pure [is an inverted dharma].
To perceive the pure as impure is an inverted dharma; such are the four inverted dharmas.

Because people do not know how to correctly cultivate these dharmas, you practice the eight inversions—how can you establish yourself as one who is skillfully cultivating [the path]? The text says: "This person does not know the correct [method]."
Cultivating all dharmas.
Third, from you monks, these two pairs turn back the eight inversions and return to them; the text is divided into two parts:

first, turning back the four inversions of permanence and bliss to return [to impermanence and suffering]; second, turning back the four inversions of impermanence to return [to impermanence and suffering]. Regarding the first part, furthermore:
The second part consists of the initial correct reversal of misconceptions, followed by three rounds of analytical examination;

the first is as the text states: "You, O bhikṣus, give rise to the perception of pleasure within the nature of suffering, the perception of permanence within the impermanent, the perception of self within the non-self, and the perception of purity within the impure."
The next three sections refer to the mundane and supramundane, the existent and non-existent, the inverted and non-inverted, and so forth. First, regarding the mundane and supramundane:
the mundane also possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity; the supramundane likewise possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The ultimate principle is like space, being neither mundane nor supramundane. Those who are deluded by it give rise to perversions, which are termed "mundane";
those who understand it achieve virtue, which is termed "supramundane. Ignorance covers you, resulting only in perversion and not in virtue. If they were to raise this objection:
"If this is a perversion, why is it called permanence, bliss, self, and purity?"
Next, regarding mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*), there is both existence and non-existence.
Mundane phenomena possess words but lack meaning; supramundane phenomena (*lokottara*) possess both words and meaning.
Therefore, concerning mundane phenomena, one must discern between word and meaning as explained below: they merely have names, and for this reason, they are not [ultimately real].
To possess the virtue but lack its meaning.
Third, for what reason is there that which is inverted and that which is non-inverted below?
For what reason does the worldly dharma have four inversions such that one does not know its meaning? What is the reason for this? There is...

The inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), the inversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*): these constitute either four inversions or three inversions, which manifest their lack of ultimate meaning.

The ancient [commentators] stated that "the three minds are non-inverted, while the consciousness-mind is inverted," and further stated that "the consciousness-mind is non-inverted, while the other three are the three inversions. Regarding perception, there is the inversion of perception; regarding sensation (*vedanā*), there is... [the inversion of sensation].

Regarding the inversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), there is both the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*) and two further explanations—general and specific—concerning these three inversions. Generally, they exist within all four types of consciousness. To distinguish them specifically: the inversion of mind resides in the consciousness-consciousness (*vijñāna-citta*);

the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) and feeling (*vedanā-viparyāsa*) reside in the perception-consciousness and feeling-consciousness; and the inversion of view resides in the volition-consciousness (*cetanā-citta*).

Furthermore, whenever a mind takes an object as its condition, it is universally the inversion of mind; when it is a conceptualization, it is the inversion of perception; and when it is capable of discrimination, it is the inversion of view.
Furthermore, the initial false conceptualization of the mind is itself a perversion of the mind; that which conditions the mind to form perceptions is the perversion of perception;

and that which solidifies these perceptions into fixed attachments is the perversion of views. Moreover, the perversions of views reside in the minds of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), while the perversions of perception and mind belong to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), for whom such perversions no longer exist.
Now, why is it that you instead attribute these perversions back to the bhikṣus? These bhikṣus falsely claim [that they are free from them].
The mind is exhausted, yet the true mind is not exhausted; because of the empty conceptualization and biased views of the untainted mind, three inversions are formed.
Since one inversion possesses four aspects, they constitute twelve inversions. Thus, having identified the error, he returns to it by asking:

"If the world also possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and the supramundane is likewise so, then one should also say that the world possesses impermanence, non-self, and [the other two characteristics]."

Is it the same for the world? Answer: Taking the impermanence and non-self of the two vehicles as the mundane, and the impermanence and non-self of the Buddhas as the unsurpassed skillful means, this constitutes the supramundane. [Question: There are names without meaning (and so forth).
One should apply a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) to both the mundane and the supramundane, to the inverted and the non-inverted virtues, and to superior and inferior cultivation.
Furthermore, the mundane world consists solely of inversion and lacks virtue, whereas the supramundane consists solely of virtue and lacks inversion;
thus, that which is inverted is the mundane virtue, while the arising of skillful means is the supramundane virtue. This principle applies to all other meanings as well.
It is further said: "The cultivation of impermanence and non-self is inferior, while the cultivation of permanence, bliss, self, and purity is superior. It is also said:
Cultivation through a single method is inferior, while cultivation through both methods is superior; furthermore, this is not a partial or gradual cultivation, but rather a supreme cultivation.

Now, regarding which of these various modes of cultivation this belongs to, with whom is it distinguished? (etc. Cultivation through a single superior method belongs to those of the sequential type (*ānupūrvika*);
cultivation through both superior methods belongs to those of the indeterminate type (*aniyata*); and that which is neither partial nor gradual belongs to those of the sudden type (*tadātva*). (etc.)
Due to these three inversions, people in the world perceive suffering within what is pleasant, the impermanent as permanent, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure;
this is called inversion. Because of these inversions, people in the world know the words but do not understand their meaning.
Fourth, regarding "What is the meaning? this section exclusively clarifies the excellence of cultivation and consists of two parts: first, clarifying excellence by contrasting it with inferiority;
second, exhorting one toward excellent cultivation.
As for "What is the meaning?": that which is "selfless" refers to saṃsāra; that which is "self" refers to the Tathāgata; and that which is "impermanent" refers to the śrāvaka.
The Pratyekabuddhas are eternal; the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is suffering; all non-Buddhists are happiness; Nirvāṇa is impurity;
and the true Dharma possessed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is purity. These are called the non-erroneous.
Because they are non-erroneous, one knows the words and knows the meaning.

If we discuss them generally, the inferior [teachings] possess all these faults; however, we specifically refute what is most extreme: because there is bondage and attachment within saṃsāra, it is "non-self";
because śrāvakas advance further [toward liberation], it is "impermanent"; because non-Buddhists abandon suffering through [the pursuit of] suffering, it is "suffering";

because conditioned phenomena are largely defiled, they are "impure," and so forth. As for the specific citation of the superior to refute the inferior, as in the Sūtra, it is now explained comprehensively.
It is my thought that the initial passage states: "I" refers to the Tathāgata; this marks the Three Jewels as encompassing all phenomena. "Constant" refers to the Dharmakāya;
this marks the three *bindus* as encompassing all phenomena. "Bliss" refers to Nirvāṇa; this marks the four virtues as encompassing all phenomena.
"Pure" refers to the Unconditioned; this marks the Dharmadhātu as encompassing all phenomena. Now, regarding these various...
Because sound is neither vertical nor horizontal, neither one nor different, and is inconceivable, it attains this meaning and attains this excellence.
Next, regarding the passage beginning with "If one wishes," the exhortation to practice is as stated in the text.
If one wishes to distance oneself from the four inversions, one should know such [qualities] as permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Next, when the various bhikṣus departed at that time, this was intended to break their biased conduct; it is also called the "Text on Responding to the Invitation," which consists of two parts:

first, the restatement of the invitation, and second, the response to the invitation. Regarding the breaking of biased conduct, the first part—the restatement—is threefold: (1) receiving the intent and praising the Buddha, (2) based upon... [text continues].
The praise, the formal invitation, the three essentials of the command, and the conclusion of the invitation are as stated in the text.

At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, one who is free from the four inversions can thoroughly know the permanent, the blissful, the self, and the pure.
Since the Tathāgata is now forever free from the four inversions, he has already thoroughly known the permanent, the blissful, the self, and the pure."
"Purity!
Since you have already fully realized permanence, bliss, self, and purity, for what reason do you not remain for one kalpa or half a kalpa to instruct us and lead us away from the four inversions,
but instead abandon us and enter parinirvāṇa?"
If the Tathāgata would look upon us with compassion and instruct us, we would receive his teachings with a sincere heart, receiving them upon the crown of our heads and practicing them.
If the Tathāgata were to enter parinirvāṇa, how could we continue to dwell together with these poisonous bodies while practicing the holy life?
We, too, shall follow the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and enter parinirvāṇa.
From this point, the Buddha’s response to the request consists of two parts: first, a rebuke for what was improper, and second, the formal response itself.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "You should not speak such words."
Regarding the first reprimand: "The coming and going of the Tathāgata is not within your domain; since you cannot know the Buddha’s arrivals and departures, how could you possibly follow him?
Therefore, it is said that you should not do so. Next, the response is twofold:
first, responding by way of the person (pudgala), and second, responding by way of the Dharma. Your previous request for me to stay was precisely because you wished to study.

The Dharma now remains as the Dharma for people; those who have attained stability in their training—what more could they request? Regarding the person who repays [the Buddha's kindness], there are three parts:
first, the designation of the entrustment; second, the praise of that person being equal to the Tathāgata; third, the explanation of that praise.
I now entrust all my unsurpassed True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa.
This Kāśyapa shall serve as a great refuge for you all, just as the Tathāgata serves as a place of refuge for all sentient beings;
Mahākāśyapa shall likewise serve as a place of refuge for you all.
The first two points are as stated in the text.
For example, when a great king who governs many territories goes on a tour of inspection, he entrusts all matters of state to his ministers;
likewise, the Tathāgata has entrusted all the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa.
Regarding the meaning of the third explanation: it is like a king delegating a minister to go on a tour;
because the Buddha wished to travel to other regions, he entrusted Kāśyapa with this task.
From you all, it should be known that he departed to repay the invitation through the Dharma. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, repaying the invitation; second, refuting biased conduct.

The first section provides the response regarding the method for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), consisting of the analogy and its application. Within the analogy, the departure from springtime serves as a metaphor for biased conduct;

the older translation’s phrasing—“observing through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation”—does not accord with the text. Following the textual division of Master Lang of Hexi, the passage is divided into two parts:

first, clarifying the arising of delusions and the loss of the principle; second, clarifying the cultivation of study and the seeking of the principle. The first phrase refers to the arising of delusions during the "springtime."

The phrase "at the beginning of this year, things sprout" is a metaphor for the initial arising of delusion; furthermore, because understanding arises from delusion, it is said that "in springtime, there were various people," etc.
Regarding the two lines concerning the place where the pearl was lost, the old tradition says it was a great pond (*mahā-hrada*), which is a teaching on impermanence (*anitya*).

Master Lang, however, said it refers to the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra-samudra*). As for the character *yù* (bath), it is sometimes written as *zhǎo* (pond); the latter reading is more common. "Riding in boats to play" refers to the third [section].
Regarding the phrase "the cause for losing the jewel": the old commentary states that because the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) was shallow, it is called "sporting.

The [Master] of Hexi says that anger and pride are like riding in a boat, while the pleasures of the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) are like sporting. The metaphor of losing the lapis lazuli treasure represents the loss of the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).

Some of the old commentaries say this refers to losing the principle (*li*), while others say it refers to losing the understanding (*jie*). As for "sinking into deep water," sinking once does not mean a permanent loss.
It has been said of old that the perfect principle is submerged within the teachings on impermanence; thus it is said to be "sunk in deep water.

Furthermore, the principle of Buddha-nature is submerged by anger, pride, birth, and death, such that it cannot manifest. Next, regarding the passage "At this time, all people... and below, there are two parts:
first, practicing and seeking the principle based on former teachings, which constitutes biased cultivation—that is, false cultivation; second, clarifying the present [cultivation].

The "perfect cultivation" (*paripūrṇa-bhāvanā*) is the superior cultivation. First, regarding "competing to seize," this refers to the partial cultivation of the contemplations on impermanence and suffering.
The tiles and stones that cause injury are a metaphor for suffering; the grasses and trees that are hollow and floating are a metaphor for non-self (*anātman*);

and the sand and gravel at the bottom of the water, which are scattered and dispersed, are a metaphor for impermanence (*anitya*). Each person claims their own [view] to be correct, yet they do not attain the true principle.

Next, the passage "joyfully taking it out" serves as an analogy for the present teaching on the perfect cultivation [of the three wisdoms], whereas the previous [teaching] involved only the three wisdoms in a partial manner;

the present intention is not thus, as it still represents the end of partial cultivation where the clarification of principle has not yet reached its ultimate limit. Therefore, it says: "Thus one knows it is not the true [nature]. Generally speaking, there are four points: first, awakening that the former was not true;
second, by the power of the Buddha-nature, causing sentient beings to awaken; third, clear faith and understanding; fourth, [the realization of] the ultimate.

The fourth point clarifies that the vision of wisdom is precisely the attainment of the principle. Regarding the first passage, it means that only now, with the arising of the teaching, does one realize that what was previously held was incorrect.

Regarding the two previous interpretations, they rejoiced while holding [the jewel] forward and bringing it out toward the rear, saying: "Rejoicing, I hold it forward and bring it out; this is not the true [state]; it is toward the rear.
Now, all of these are taken as a single phrase. Next, from the passage "At that time, the precious jewel... onwards, it is due to the Buddha-nature.
The power first clarifies that true cultivation consists of hearing the teachings now spoken regarding Buddha-nature; by the power of Buddha-nature, sentient beings are enabled to awaken.
As for "those within the water," Buddha-nature is not distant; it resides solely within the five aggregates of birth and death.
"When the water is clear" means that by the power of Buddha-nature, sentient beings are enabled to awaken. Third, in the following section on the Mahāyāna, one point is clarified.
The previous "faith-understanding" (adhimukti) is like a conceptual knowledge and vision that has not yet attained the grasping of the moon’s form;

the Middle Way’s perfect principle is ultimately without deficiency—this is the stage of the lower wisdom-vision (*hīna-prajñā-darśana*). "Tranquil and slow" means that while abiding in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one is as if in nirvāṇa;
hence it is called "tranquil and slow. Next, O bhikṣus, you should not conflate the subsequent four [stages] with this analogy.

First, "should primarily practice" corresponds to partial cultivation; second, "should further practice" corresponds to perfect cultivation; third, "one should again know" corresponds once more to partial cultivation;

fourth, "desiring to attain the true reality" corresponds once more to perfect cultivation. Since the scriptural passages herein are points where the mind should be focused, I have retained the traditional interpretations;
please do not find them tedious. Now, in explaining this chapter: although the bhikṣus have heard the new *ī*, they have not yet eliminated [their afflictions].

The former attachment held that the Buddha was impermanent; thus, although they requested him to remain out of faith in the permanence of the Dharma, they did not yet believe in the permanence of the Buddha.
Though their mouths made the request, their minds still remained fixed on the old view. The Buddha rebuked them for this former attachment, saying:
"You should not speak such words. In response to their request, he spoke of both the new and the old, stating that all the True Dharma has been entrusted to Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata.

Because the conditions for his departure had ceased and the capacity of Kāśyapa had arisen, [the Buddha] entrusted [the Dharma] internally, which was equal to the Buddha’s own virtue, and externally, he commissioned a great minister to uphold the teachings of the True Dharma.
He then pointed to the circle of the letter *ī* as a place of reliance to fulfill the request made to him.

In this context, it is said that the Dharma was entrusted to Kāśyapa because those who study the new *ī* were intended; in the subsequent passage, it is because those who do not study the new *ī* are intended.

Therefore, it is said that Kāśyapa is impermanent and incapable of being entrusted with the teaching; each [case] serves as a specific condition. Now, regarding the first part—recompensing the request with the Dharma—it is divided into two sections:
first, the refutation through the discourse on the Dharma, and second, the refutation through parables. As for the discourse on the Dharma:
"You all should know that the previously cultivated perceptions of impermanence and suffering are not ultimately real.
Since you wish to study the new *ī*, you should reform your delusions and give rise to faith;
because you still harbor false attachments while clinging to the True Dharma as if it were defiled, it is said that the impermanence and suffering you previously cultivated are not ultimately real."

In the subsequent section of analogies, there are again two analogies that correspond to the first: the analogy of losing a treasure due to negligence before it was opened during springtime, and the analogy of opening it to seek it but not finding it;
these are also called the analogy of having skillful means and the analogy of lacking skillful means.
For example, it is like a group of people in the springtime who, while bathing in a great pond and playing on a boat, lose a lapis lazuli gem which sinks into the deep water.

"Springtime" refers to a season when all vegetation is newly sprouted and all is fresh and delightful; this is used as a metaphor for the five sensory objects and the six desires, which are objects of indulgence and attachment.
The people at that site collectively represent those who are negligent, like those bathing in a great pool. The great pool represents the river of birth and death;
bathing represents anger, pride, attachment, aversion, and the like; riding in a boat represents being carried by various karmas;
playing represents clinging to desirable fruits; and losing the lapis lazuli gem represents the lack of the cause for liberation within one's dissolute wisdom and understanding.
Because one is submerged in darkness, speech is lost; therefore, this chapter refutes the loss of practice as being more urgent than the loss of prior understanding.
Later, when attachment to pleasure obscures understanding, speech is lost. "Sinking into deep water" refers to being shrouded by the aggregates (*skandha*) of birth and death.
From that time on, those people departed; because they lacked the skillful means to seek it out, they were unable to provide a true analogy.
At that time, all the people together entered the water to search for this treasure, competing with one another to seize tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, and pebbles.
Each person individually claimed to have found a lapis lazuli gem, joyfully carrying them out.
All these people are generally deluded followers; their distinct threefold practices are all like entering the water together.

Those who believe in the meaning of the initial teaching are like those who enter the water to seek treasure. Those who perform inferior threefold practices and vie for tiles and stones are like those who mistake them for the real thing.
Claiming to have attained what they have realized, they say they have achieved *nirvāṇa*; their joyful emergence with a single phrase is a mere analogy.
The preceding praise of the elephant’s footprint as supreme refers to the thorough cultivation of non-self; because he held this realization within his heart, it is said that he rejoiced.

Because he turned toward the Buddha and offered praise, it is said that he "brought it forth. This serves as an analogy for the aforementioned state of harboring doubt due to attachment to one's own views.
Thus one knows that for those who seek liberation through expedient means because they do not yet realize the non-reality [of phenomena], an analogy is provided.
One thereby knows that at this time, although the true jewel is still within the water, by the power of the jewel, the water becomes entirely clear;
then the great assembly, seeing the jewel within the water, perceives it as clearly as looking up at the form of the moon in the sky.
At that time, there was a wise person among the multitude who, through the power of skillful means, entered the water calmly and slowly, and immediately obtained the pearl.

This is a metaphor for hearing the present teaching and thereby breaking through former principles and practices; one realizes they are not real, and understands that [views such as] suffering, impermanence, and so forth are false, being like shards and rubble.
Therefore it is said: "Only now do I know what is not true. Altogether, from the beginning up to this point, these form six points through which the meaning is collectively explained and sought.
Regarding this passage: as for the precious jewel, the jewel is inherently possessed and is not something acquired only now;

yet sentient beings, attached to pleasure, sink to the bottom of the water, and though they search with clumsy observation, they ultimately cannot find it. By means of the principle-jewel, through hearing the present teaching, one realizes that what was previously [perceived] was unreal;
by knowing the characters and knowing their meaning, beginning from this very sutra, there is the "jewel of name and word. This is it.
At that time, the precious jewel was still within the water; by the power of the jewel, the water became entirely clear and transparent.
This means that when one contemplates the principle according to the teaching—the jewel of contemplative practice—the principle is what is expressed (*vācya*).

Therefore, it is said that [the jewel] is "still within the water," for the expressive [word] is like the expressed [meaning], and the expressed meaning is like the expressive word. Thus, it is said that "by the power of the jewel, the water becomes clear. In this regard, the Great...
The assembly then sees the precious jewel beneath the water, which is like looking up at the form of the moon in the sky;
it is similar to the jewel as one looks up at the moon. Because it vaguely resembles the jewel, it is said that one "sees" [the stage] resembling the True (tathatā);

thus, the stage of resemblance is clearly elucidated. The empty sky is a metaphor for the resemblance to permanence, the full moon for the resemblance to bliss, and the moonlight for the resemblance to purity.
The analogy of "resemblance-purity" is neither superior nor inferior; by taking the superior to compare with the inferior, one attains mastery and freedom.
This analogy of "resemblance-self" (and so forth) refers at that time to a person who is like a partially realized jewel.
Because each individual person finds their own gateway, it is said that through the power of a single person’s skillful means, one who is "calm and gradual" before the Way abides in birth.

To interpret death as nirvana, to engage in subtle and correct contemplation, and to proceed with gradual, detailed, and thorough discernment—unclouded by the waters of the teachings and with the waves of the mind unmoved—one’s mind accords with principle and immediately obtains a portion of the jewel.
This is explained according to the six stages to show that for those who possess skillful means and superior cultivation, the jewel is sought and obtained;
this is based on the practical application of the meaning of their practice.
"O bhikṣus, you should combine the analogies of gain and loss. There are two [sets], each further divided into two parts. Regarding the combination:
the first part combines the gain and loss of the three cultivations, and the second part combines the gain and loss of the four cultivations."
"O bhikṣus, you should not practice the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity as if they were ultimate truths,
like those people who each took tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, or gravel for precious jewels.
You should skillfully learn expedient means and constantly cultivate the perceptions of permanence, self, bliss, and purity in every place."
Furthermore, one should know that the characteristics of the four dharmas previously cultivated are all inverted.

Those who wish to attain reality and cultivate various perceptions should be like that wise person who skillfully extracts a precious gem—namely, the perception of self, permanence, bliss, and purity.
Applying this principle, one should traverse all phenomena, for each possesses both inferior and superior modes of cultivation. Thus the text says:

"In every place and at all times, one constantly cultivates the perception of self, and the perceptions of permanence, bliss, and purity. One should reflect that it is not only in this sutra, nor limited to a single object;
rather, contemplation is established everywhere.

Third: From "At that time, the bhikṣus departed" onwards, this section on the teaching for dispelling doubts is divided into two parts: first, the presentation [of the objection], and second, the refutation.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha previously taught that all dharmas are without self, you should..."
Having practiced and studied thus, one then leaves behind the notion of a self; one who leaves behind the notion of a self leaves behind arrogance;
one who leaves behind arrogance attains entry into nirvāṇa. What is the meaning of this?
First, "ascending" refers to the complete ancient teachings; "practice" refers to the conduct of those who train as previously taught by the Buddha;

"application" refers to the removal of pride and so forth; and "principle" refers to entering *nirvāṇa*. Once practice and principle have been fully resolved, the force of the phrasing establishes the correct intent within the teaching.
If the ancient teaching were indeed the present one, it would not be non-present; if it were not the present teaching, it would not be so.
"Why did you not speak of this sooner? (and so forth).
