This scriptural passage should be interpreted according to the four *siddhāntas*. Regarding the section on "bringing others to correctness," it consists of five parts: first, the woman remains silent;
second, Kāśyapa asks, "How does one bring others to correctness? Third, when the Buddha was preaching the Dharma, a woman who was nursing an infant came forward.
Having bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and with a mind reflecting upon what he had been contemplating, he sat down to one side.
Then the Tathāgata, knowing [the answer] yet asking as a matter of form, said:
"At that time, the World-Honored One, though already aware, asked: 'Out of affection for your many children, you consumed much ghee without exercising due moderation.'"
[The Buddha spoke of] what was digested and what was not digested.
Three women praised the Buddha.
At that time, the women addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is most marvelous, World-Honored One! You are well able to know the thoughts within my mind."
Fourth, the request regarding the quantity of the Dharma:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will instruct me on the proper amount. World-Honored One, this morning I gave much ghee to my child;
I fear he may not be able to digest it and might meet an untimely death. I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain this for me."
The five bonds of her joy were sealed.
The Buddha said, "The food consumed by your child was immediately digested, thereby increasing its lifespan.
Upon hearing this, the woman’s heart leaped with great exultation, and she spoke again: "Because the Tathāgata speaks the truth, I am filled with joy."
Regarding the four ancient interpretations of this passage, the first states that this woman arrived while the Buddha was preaching the Dharma. The second says this is not so;
at that time the Buddha was already eighty years old, and how could he address a woman as "sister" when she was an elderly woman who had nursed him as an infant?
This refers to a past event. The third says the Buddha transformed himself into a woman, just as he transformed himself into a child. The fourth says there was no such woman at all.
This is a hypothetical parable.
From the passage "Thus having departed from the World-Honored One," this is used to generate wholesome roots and to harmonize with the preceding analogy.
Furthermore, it is said that women address the Buddha as "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān), or that the Buddha himself refers to himself as the "World-Honored One. Now...

This passage establishes what precedes and initiates what follows; whether it is "consumed" or "not consumed," it thus establishes the preceding discussion of impermanence and so forth, while initiating the subsequent text.
This is divided into three parts: first, establishing the preceding point of joy.
The World-Honored One, desiring thus to discipline all sentient beings, skillfully distinguishes and explains what is digested and what is not digested.
Next, he also explains the "lower" [teachings], which are precisely for the purpose of generating wholesome roots.
It is also taught that all phenomena are selfless and impermanent.
Third, if the Buddha [were to teach] permanence first— this being a detailed analysis of those who cannot be transformed by such a remedy (and so forth)—
then the disciples receiving his teachings would say that this Dharma is the same as that of the non-Buddhists.
Even if she were to abandon him, he again addressed the woman: "Going [to others] is the remedy for correcting others. This text consists of two parts: first, citing her incapacity;
second, again addressing the woman: "If the child has grown up and can come and go by himself, whatever he eats—whether it be easy or difficult to digest—he will be able to assimilate it."
Just as butter provided by my own household would not suffice for me, so it is with my śrāvaka disciples;
like your infant, they cannot digest this eternally abiding Dharma. Therefore, I previously taught suffering and impermanence.
Next, the antidotes are explained.
If my disciples, the śrāvakas, have already perfected their merits and are capable of practicing the Mahāyāna sūtras, I shall explain for them in these sūtras the six flavors.
What are the six flavors? Suffering is explained as having the flavor of vinegar; impermanence has the flavor of salt.
Non-self is the taste of bitterness, suffering is the taste of sweetness, self is the taste of pungency, and permanence is the taste of blandness.
Within that world, there are three kinds of tastes: namely, impermanence, non-self, and the absence of bliss.

With afflictions as the fuel and wisdom as the fire, these causes and conditions produce the food of nirvana—namely, permanence, bliss, and self—which I cause all my disciples to relish with sweet delight.
The three worldly flavors are countered and refuted by the three supramundane flavors. Saline, sour, and bitter are the flavors of retribution for ordinary beings;
impermanence, suffering, and non-self are the flavors of the path for the noble ones. These two combined are called the three worldly flavors.
Sweet, pungent, and bland are also the flavors of retribution for ordinary beings; permanence, bliss, and self are the flavors of the supramundane path. These are combined and designated as such.
"The supramundane samādhis have a distinct meaning [as follows].
Furthermore, he told the woman: 'This is the ultimate truth that rectifies others.
Again, he told the woman: 'If you have a reason to go elsewhere, you should drive out your wicked sons and cause them to leave the house.'"

He entrusted all his treasuries to his virtuous sons and daughters. The woman said to the Buddha, "Truly, as the Holy One has taught, the treasury of precious jewels should be shown to virtuous sons and not shown to wicked sons. Sister, I am also like this:
at the time of my parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgata’s subtle, secret, and unsurpassed Dharma-treasury shall not be given to the śrāvaka disciples, just as your treasury was not shown to the wicked."
My son, you must entrust this to the bodhisattvas, just as one entrusts a precious treasure to a virtuous son. Why is this?
Because the śrāvaka disciples give rise to the notion of change, claiming that the Buddha-Tathāgata has truly entered parinirvāṇa; yet in truth, I have not truly entered parinirvāṇa.
It is like when you have gone on a long journey and have not yet returned, your wicked son then says that you are dead.
"You are truly not dead; the various bodhisattvas declare that the Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging.
Just as you, my good son, do not say that I am dead, for this reason I entrust the unsurpassed secret treasury to the bodhisattvas."
Good son, if there are sentient beings who say that the Buddha is eternally abiding and immutable, you should know that such families possess the Buddha;
this is called "correcting others.
The text has two parts: first, [showing] that through the three *siddhāntas* they are indeed wicked sons to whom the treasure-store is not entrusted; second, the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
One who is called a "virtuous son" is entrusted with the treasure-store, whereas the śrāvakas are not; therefore, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is not taken as the primary meaning.

Furthermore, since śrāvakas are accepted as those who produce wholesome roots—and this is not exclusive to the Mahāyāna alone—it should be understood that both the Small and Great Vehicles employ these [teachings] as the four *siddhāntas* (purposes).
Thus, this household is one where there is a Buddha; "Buddha" here carries the sense of permanence (*nitya*).
Furthermore, "awakening" (jue) carries the meaning of understanding; since this person understands [the truth of] permanence, there is a Buddha in his household.

Third, regarding the ability to respond to questions according to the text, there are two parts: first, the formal explanation of the questioning and answering; second, the proclamation against eating meat.
Kāśyapa asked: "How can one provide an answer according to the question? Suppose someone were to come and ask the Buddha, the World-Honored One:
'How should I act so that, without relinquishing wealth or property, I may be called a great donor (mahādānapati) and a patron (dānapati)?"

In the initial passage, the Buddha raises a question that is not restricted by fixed categories and requires an answer that likewise transcends fixed categories; he simply takes "giving" as the primary point, and other examples follow suit.

If there were no giving, it would not be called "giving"; likewise, if there were no upholding of precepts, it would not be called "śīla," and so on, up to if there were no wisdom, it would not be called "prajñā" (and so forth).
The Buddha said: "If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who have few desires and are content, who do not accept or possess impure things, one should give them slaves, servants, and laborers;
to those who practice the pure life (brahmacarya), one should give women; to those who abstain from wine and meat, one should give wine and meat;
to those who do not eat past noon, one should give food past noon; and to those who do not wear flowers or scents, one should give these."

One who gives gifts such as these flowers and incense has their reputation for giving spread throughout the world among the śrāvakas, yet they have never expended even a hair’s breadth of their own expense;
this is what is called being able to respond appropriately to questions.
Answer: There are five propositions, which may be explained in two ways. First, one does not know that the recipient does not eat fish or meat;

if one offers fish or meat to them and they do not accept it, there is no loss to oneself, and a great act of giving is accomplished. Second, one knows beforehand that they do not eat meat, yet gives it to them specifically to manifest their virtue;
thus, while there is no loss to oneself, it would cause the recipient to become attached to fame. Furthermore, [the text] observes this.

To rejoice in the merit performed by others without creating obstacles is also a great gift; furthermore, to skillfully liberate those who suffer without depriving them of even a hair’s breadth [of their well-being] is called a great gift.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: [The following two sections establish the prohibition against eating meat through six rounds of question and answer; in the first round, the prohibition is proclaimed.]
[Regarding] meat.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, one who eats meat should not be given meat.
Why is this? I see that those who do not eat meat possess great merit."
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa, saying, "Excellent, excellent! You have now been able to well understand my intention. A Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma should act in this way.
Son of good family, from this day forward, I do not permit my śrāvaka disciples to eat meat.
When receiving offerings of food from donors with faith, one should regard that food as being like the flesh of one's own son."
There are ten points by which certain masters explain why meat should be abandoned: first, that all beings possess Buddha-nature and thus should all become Buddhas;
second, that the transformations of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are boundless; third, that [meat] belongs to one’s own kinsmen within the cycle of saṃsāra;

fourth, that it is composed of the same four elements and five aggregates as oneself; fifth, that it is impure, consisting of semen and blood; and sixth, that one cannot bear to eat it oneself, yet desires to devour it from others.
7. Clouds of resentment arise naturally when one inflicts cruel harm upon others without cause; 8. it violates the path of a Bodhisattva’s transformation of beings; 9.

one consumes little but commits great sin, and since one does not sever the eating of meat, one hopes for a share in the merit of the ten directions; 10. enmity becomes endless, for if one kills a single life, one must repay it in five hundred lives;
therefore, one should not eat meat, for it is like eating the flesh of one's own son—the father and son are of the same substance according to the Dharma.
However, when Ci (Maitreya) heard this, he wept and choked back his tears, for his heart felt as though it were poisoned.

Regarding the first [case], it is said that in the past there was a king who, while traveling on a road, ate the flesh of his own son to survive the perilous journey. Regarding the second, it is said that a son gave up the flesh of his own body to provide sustenance for his parents.

Regarding the third, it is said that he raised an analogy by speaking of eating the flesh of one's son. Regarding the fourth, it is said that it is not merely a matter of eating meat, but rather like eating the flesh of one's own son.
"One should conceive that whenever one receives an offering, as well as fruits, vegetables, and the like, they are all the property of another, just like the flesh of one's own son" (and so forth).
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, why does the Tathāgata not permit the eating of meat?"
"Good son, those who eat meat sever the seed of great compassion.

Regarding the second point—that eating meat severs the seed of great compassion—there are three interpretations: first, that the Buddha is great compassion; second, that the first bhūmi is great compassion;
and third, that the stage of nature (gotrabhūmi) is great compassion. Great compassion must necessarily rely upon small compassion as its seed.
If one eats meat, there is no minor compassion; therefore, it is said that the lineage is severed.

Furthermore, it is said that sentient beings themselves are the seeds of great compassion and must certainly attain Buddhahood. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* designates all sentient beings as "sons of the Buddha";
to eat them is thus to sever the seed of the Buddha.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "For what reason did the Tathāgata first permit bhikṣus to eat the three kinds of pure meat?
Kāśyapa, these three kinds of pure meat were gradually restricted according to circumstances."

The third [point] concerns the three kinds of pure meat, which refers to not seeing, hearing, or suspecting [the animal was killed for oneself]. There are two interpretations: first, "not seeing" means not seeing it killed for one's sake;

"not hearing" and "not suspecting" are likewise understood. Second, "not seeing" and "not hearing" mean that even if one does not see or hear it, provided it was simply killed [generally], one does not inquire whether it was for oneself or not;
however, if there is no suspicion, one must state that it was for oneself.
The fourth section clarifies the ten kinds of impure meat.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for what causes and conditions do you not permit even the nine kinds of pure meat, let alone the ten kinds of impure meat?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "This was also established gradually due to specific circumstances; you should know that this is precisely the meaning of the present prohibition against eating meat.
Regarding the passage on the "Brahma-conduct" below, it says: "Humans, snakes, elephants, horses, pigs, dogs, chickens, foxes, lions, monkeys, and *mihuo* (a type of monkey);
humans who resemble snakes, snakes that resemble dragons, elephants, and horses—these are the treasures of the state; pigs, dogs, and foxes are base and evil beasts."

The lion is the king of beasts, and humans are of its own kind; the nine kinds of purity refer to [the three types of] views, hearings, and doubts, each having their respective preliminary and subsequent applications as well as the fundamental [stage], and so forth.
The fifth section clarifies fine foods.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying: "Why does the Tathāgata praise fish and meat as fine foods?
"Good son, I do not say that things such as fish and meat are fine foods. What I call fine foods are sugarcane, *śāli* rice," and so forth.
Rice, honey, all grains and wheat, as well as black sugar, milk, curd, butter, and oil constitute fine food;
although it is taught that one may possess various kinds of clothing, what should be possessed must be of dyed colors— how much more so regarding attachment to the taste of this fish and meat?
If one follows the words of others, these are considered delicious foods; yet if one follows one's own intention, one does not say they are delicious.

Kāśyapa spoke again: "If the Tathāgata were to prohibit the eating of meat, then what of those five kinds of flavors—milk, curd, whey, fresh butter, and clarified butter—as well as sesame oil, and various garments such as those made of *kauśeya* silk, conch shells, and leather?"
One should likewise not accept such items as vessels made of gold and silver.
The sixth section states that the five kinds of dairy products from cows, up to and including basins and vessels of gold and silver, must all not be accepted.
The Buddha replied, "It is for eight reasons that one should not be the same as the Nirgranthas.
Good son, you should not share the views of those Nirgranthas.
They go naked, practice self-starvation, and consume food in excess or fail to do so; herein, one should exercise proper discernment."
Regarding precious objects, even though they give rise to strong greed, one should not keep them;
yet, as with the five flavors, since they are not part of the essential body, their acceptance is permitted—how could this be like the Nirgranthas who prohibit them categorically?
Second, it clarifies that one must understand the Tathāgata’s intention in opening the three [types of pure meat] while prohibiting the ten.
Each of all the prohibitive precepts established by the Tathāgata has its own specific intent. Because of these differing intents, he permitted the consumption of the three kinds of pure meat;

because of a different perspective, he prohibited the ten kinds of meat; and because of yet another perspective, he prohibited them all entirely, as well as the meat of animals that died of natural causes.
How could that be the same as the views of those non-Buddhist outsiders? [They hold that] sentient beings cannot be severed all at once;
first, one severs the three kinds of perceptions because they are external; next, one severs ten kinds; then, beyond those ten, one severs the perception of greed;
thus, everything is completely severed.
The third time he established the prohibition for all disciples to completely abstain from all meat was when he addressed the past by proclaiming the present:
"Kāśyapa, from this day forward, I establish a rule that my disciples shall no longer eat any meat whatsoever."

Furthermore, within the Bodhisattva precepts, even minor offenses have long been prohibited; yet, for the sake of saving sentient beings, although one may appear to eat meat, in reality one does not eat it.
Fourth, the resentment caused by eating meat persists for a long time.
Kāśyapa, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, all sentient beings who smell the odor of one who eats meat will give rise to terror.
Good son, it is like a person who has been near a lion; when others see them and smell the stench of the lion, they too become terrified.
Good son, it is like a person who eats garlic; because of its foul and loathsome odor, other people [will recoil].
Upon smelling its odor, they abandon it and depart; even those who see it from afar do not wish to look at it, let alone approach it.
It is the same for all meat-eaters: when sentient beings smell the scent of their flesh, they are all terrified and conceive the thought of fearing death.
All living creatures—whether moving in water, on land, or through the air—abandon them and flee, all saying, "This person is our enemy."
For this reason, a bodhisattva does not practice eating meat. Although they manifest eating meat in order to deliver sentient beings, even while appearing to eat it, in reality they do not eat it.
Good son, if such a bodhisattva does not even consume pure food, how much less would they eat meat?
The transformative path was not practiced and became isolated from sentient beings (and so forth).
The five schools of the Śrāvakas adhered to the Lesser Vehicle, consumed meat, slandered the Great [Vehicle], and gave rise to contentious treatises on sudden severance and evil.

"Good son, after my parinirvāṇa, when countless hundreds of years have passed and the noble ones of the four paths have all entered nirvāṇa, and after the True Dharma has vanished during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there will be bhikṣus who merely maintain the outward appearance [of the monastic life] and observe the Vinaya;

they will read and recite the sūtras only sparingly, yet they will be greedy for food and drink to nourish their bodies. Their clothing will be coarse, shabby, and ugly, and their physical appearance will be haggard and unsightly."
Possessing an air of majesty, they raise cattle and sheep and carry loads of firewood and grass; their hair, beards, nails, and body hair are all long and coarse.
Though they wear the *kāṣāya*, they resemble hunters; they gaze intently and walk slowly, like a cat stalking a mouse.
They constantly proclaim, "I have attained Arhatship," yet they suffer from many ailments and lie in filth. Outwardly appearing virtuous and good, they inwardly harbor greed and envy.

Those such as the Brahmins who receive the dharma of the mute, though they are not truly śramaṇas, manifest the appearance of śramaṇas; their false views are rampant, and they slander the True Dharma.

Such persons destroy the precepts, right conduct, and majestic deportment established by the Tathāgata, speak of the fruit of liberation while being divorced from the pure dharma, and ruin the profound secret teachings, acting according to their own whims in opposition [to the truth].
While preaching the Sūtras and Vinaya, they made such statements as, "The Tathāgata has permitted us to eat meat," and they produced their own arguments, claiming these were the Buddha's words;
thus they disputed with one another, each calling themselves a śramaṇa and a son of the Śākya.
Sixth, it is explained that consuming meat frequently gives rise to evil matters.

"Good son, at that time there were also various śramaṇas who hoarded raw grain, accepted fish and meat, prepared their own food with their own hands, and carried oil flasks, precious parasols, and leather sandals;
they associated closely with kings, ministers, and elders, and practiced divination."
They study physiognomy and astrology, diligently practice the way of medicine, keep male and female slaves, and deal in gold, silver, lapis lazuli,
tridacna shell, agate, crystal, pearl, coral, amber, jade, conch shells, and various fruits and gourds; they learn various arts and crafts, painting, masonry, calligraphy, and teaching,
as well as planting roots and saplings, practicing sorcery and incantations, performing illusions, and compounding various medicines.

Singing, music, perfumes, flowers, grooming the body, dice, go-board games, and learning various crafts—if there be a bhikṣu who can remain free from such evil matters, one should say of that person: "He is truly my disciple."
Seventh, removing the filth from vessels during years of famine.

At that time, Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās depend on others for their livelihood, if they obtain meat mixed with other foods while begging for alms, how should they eat it? It should be purified."
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa: "Pure food should be washed with water to separate it from meat before being eaten.
If a vessel has been defiled by meat, provided that no flavor of it remains, its use is permitted and incurs no fault.
If one sees that there is much meat among the food, one should not accept it; all meat that is manifest should not be eaten. Whoever eats it commits an offense."
The eight points for establishing the regulations are all as stated in the text.
I now proclaim this regulation against eating meat; were it to be explained in detail, it would be inexhaustible. Since the time for the *Nirvāṇa* has arrived, I have therefore spoken briefly.
This is what is called "being able to respond according to the question."
What is meant by "skillfully understanding the meaning of causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya)? This is the fourth characteristic.

If discussed generally, all the sutras and śāstras are teachings on the provisional names of causes and conditions. If discussed specifically, the phenomena of the Tripiṭaka are teachings on causes and conditions.

In the present text, the focus is specifically on the Vinaya: for instance, when one wishes to establish a precept, one must first provide the causal origin (nidāna) and subsequently clarify the precept itself.

Because the characteristics are extensively expounded following the substance (*tattva*), it is called "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*). Since the other two Piṭakas do not contain as much [detail] as this, they are not specifically pointed out.
Regarding the text, there are two rounds of question and answer: first, a hypothetical inquiry regarding the cause;

second, an inquiry as to why [the rules] are not taught all at once; third, an inquiry concerning falling [into offenses]; fourth, an inquiry concerning the Vinaya; and fifth, an inquiry concerning the Prātimokṣa. The first is general, while the latter three are specific.

[The Buddha replied: "It is different, Kāśyapa. How can you be said to well understand the meaning of dependent origination? Suppose there were an assembly of the fourfold community that came and asked me:
'World-Honored One, regarding such a matter as this, why did the Tathāgata, when he first appeared in the world, not preach this Dharma for King Prasenajit?'"
Regarding the profound and subtle meaning of the gates: at times it is explained as deep, and at times as shallow; sometimes it is termed an offense, and sometimes it is termed non-offense.
What is meant by "falling" (pāta)? What is meant by "discipline" (vinaya)? What is the meaning of "prātimokṣa"?

For what reason did the Tathāgata not immediately teach his disciples the five categories and seven groups of offenses so that they might practice them, but instead waited until an infraction had occurred before enacting the precepts?
King Prasenajit—translated here as "King of Harmony and Joy"—was exceedingly compassionate;

when he was not intoxicated, he always harbored thoughts of loving-kindness, and even when he deserved death for an offense, if he were under the influence of wine, he would be pardoned and spared (and so forth). The Buddha...

When he wished to establish the precept against stealing in that country, he asked the King about the laws of the kingdom: "At what amount does theft constitute a grave offense? The King replied, "Five coins.

The Buddha, following the laws of the kingdom, established the rule based on this specific circumstance. He questioned the King extensively; it was for this reason that he first cited the national custom.
The profound and subtle meaning of this is why he did not expound the *pien-zu* (sections and clusters) of the Vinaya all at once. These precepts are the eternal joy of the Mahāyāna.

Because the self is pure, it is said to be profound and subtle. Regarding the second question concerning falling [into offenses], the meanings of *śīla* (precepts) and *vinaya* (discipline) may be mutually inclusive for those who recite them.
*Prātimokṣa* (liberation) is named "liberation," while *vinaya* is named "extinction" (*nirodha*).

Here, extinction is inclusive of liberation. When asking about *prātimokṣa*, one also obtains *vinaya*. The Vinaya has two meanings: first, the weighing of lightness and heaviness; second, prohibition and restraint.
Now, taking "restraining" (śīla) as it encompasses both the sense of prohibition and the sense of precept: "precept" (śīla) refers to the Vinaya that prohibits and subsumes;
when recited from a written text, it is called "Vinaya," and when chanted from memory in the mouth, it is called "recitation" (svādhyāya). These are two names for one and the same entity.
The two Buddhas answered the four questions and then answered them again; the old tradition uses this as the "five questions" (etc.).

Within the answers, the order is not sequential: first they answer regarding the *mokṣa*, second they answer regarding the *pācittiya*, third they answer regarding the *mokṣa* again, fourth they answer regarding the *vinaya*, and fifth they answer the general question.
Regarding the first answer concerning the *mokṣa*:
The Buddha said: "Prātimokṣa is called 'contentment,' 'accomplishment of dignified conduct,' and 'having nothing to receive or store';
it is also called 'pure livelihood.
Contentment and pure livelihood are its essential meaning."
Next, the answer regarding those who fall:
"Those who fall" refers to the four evil destinies (*catur-apāya*). Furthermore, as for falling, one falls into the hells, even unto Avīci.

Regarding the speed [of this process], it is swifter than a torrential rain; hearing this, one should be struck with awe and maintain the prohibitions firmly, not transgressing the rules of decorum, and practice cultivation.
To be contented yet still accept any impure thing, and furthermore to fall [into such states], nourishes the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
for these reasons, it is called "falling."

Regarding the falling into [the realms] and the lightness or gravity [of offenses]: if one commits an offense belonging to any of the five categories (*pañcāpatti*), one falls into the four destinies; thus, the meaning of "falling" applies generally.

Furthermore, "falling" specifically pertains to the commission of grave offenses (and so forth). Moreover, as for "falling," it nourishes this general sense, yet it is specifically applied to both the light and the heavy:
the light falls into the two [upper] paths, while the heavy resides in hell.
*Prātimokṣa*: the lower three responses concerning the wooden gavel (*kaṭhina*).
*Prātimokṣa* refers to the abstention from unwholesome and perverse actions of body, speech, and mind.
*Vinaya*: the lower four responses concerning the discipline (*vinaya*).

The Vinaya consists of the entry into the precepts and dignified decorum (*vīryāpatti*), the profound sūtras and their excellent meanings, the prohibition against accepting all impure things and the causes and conditions for such impurity,
as well as the prohibition of the four *parājika* offenses, the twelve *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the two *aniyata* dharmas, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*,
the ninety-one *pāyattika*, the four *pratideśanīya* dharmas, the numerous *śaikṣa* dharmas, and the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
The first line directly follows [the sequence]: entering the three extinctions (*nirodha*), entering the precepts and dignified conduct (*śīla-īryāpatha*)—this is the Vinaya Piṭaka;

the profound sūtras—this is the Sūtra Piṭaka; and the excellent meanings—this is the Abhidharma Piṭaka. Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are ninety rules; in the Mahīśāsaka school, there are ninety-two.
First, a nun who is not ill must not go to preach the Dharma [to a monk]. Second, one must not divert the property of the Saṃgha toward oneself. Now, it is said:
The ninety-first [point] also concerns the breadth or brevity of the teaching gates.
Alternatively, there may be someone who breaks all precepts; this is the answer to the general question as to why [the Buddha] did not teach [the precepts] all at once.
Furthermore, there may be those who break all precepts—where "all" refers to the four grave offenses (*catur-antarāpatti*) up to the seven rules for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-samatha*).

Or again, there may be those who slander the true Dharma, including the profound sutras, as well as the icchantikas who fully accomplish the exhaustion of all marks (*sarva-nimitta-kṣaya*) and lack any causal conditions; such people claim of themselves, "I am wise."
Those of sharp intelligence conceal all their offenses, whether grave or light; they hide their various evils just as a tortoise withdraws its six limbs.
Thus, these many sins are not repented for throughout the long night; because they are not repented for, they increase day and night.
These bhikṣus never disclose the multitude of offenses they have committed, causing what they have transgressed to spread and entangle further. Therefore, the Tathāgata knows this.
Matters were regulated gradually and could not be established all at once.
The reason why the five categories of offenses (*pañca-varga*) could not be instituted instantaneously was the fear that people might simultaneously violate them all;

furthermore, had they been instituted all at once, it was feared that people would be unable to uphold them. Therefore, they were established progressively from light to heavy. "Complete" means to possess everything in its entirety.
To exhaust all marks of evil is to possess all goodness. To have no causes and conditions means that there are no further causes and conditions for the Buddha-dharma;
this is also to deny the existence of causes and conditions.
At that time, a son of good family departed from the second hypothetical question and asked the Tathāgata: "Why did you not explain this beforehand?"
The text is divided into two parts; first, it asks why this was not explained beforehand.
At that time, a son of good family and a daughter of good family addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has long known such matters;
why did you not establish the precepts earlier?"
The subsequent inquiry regarding the intent to cause one to fall into [hell] may be sought in the text.
It is as if the World-Honored One were about to cause sentient beings to enter the Avīci Hell;

it is like a great multitude of people wishing to reach another region who lose the correct path and follow a wrong one, and because these people do not realize they are lost, they all claim, "This is the way."
Furthermore, seeing no one to ask about right and wrong, sentient beings thus become deluded regarding the Buddha-dharma and fail to perceive the true reality (*tathatā*).
The Tathāgata ought to first preach the Right Path for them and instruct the bhikṣus: "This is a violation of the precepts; this is the upholding of the precepts.
This is how they should be regulated. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, is the Truth; he knows and perceives the Right Path alone.
There is the Tathāgata, the God among Gods, who can expound the superior merits and their profound meanings of the ten wholesome paths of action;
therefore, one should request that the precepts be established first.
The Buddha replied with two points, first answering the criticism regarding falling into ruin.

The Buddha said, "Good son, if one says that the Tathāgata can proclaim for sentient beings the superior merit of the ten wholesome paths of action, then the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings as he does Rāhula. Why do you raise the objection, saying:
'Could it be that the World-Honored One intends to cause sentient beings to enter hell? I see a person who possesses the causes for falling into the Avīci Hell'?"
For the sake of such a person, I might remain in the world for an eon or slightly less than an eon.
Since I possess great compassion for sentient beings, for what reason would I deceive those who regard me as their own children by causing them to enter hell?
Good son, it is like a beggar within a king’s realm who, seeing a hole in his robe, subsequently mends it; the Tathāgata is likewise, for he beholds all sentient beings.
There are causes and conditions for entering the Avīci Hell, which are immediately remedied by the goodness of the precepts.

Later, in responding to the meaning of "not first," there is both a simile and its application. Within the initial simile, the analogy of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) is presented, which also contains three meanings;
first, the analogy of the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) illustrates the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*).
Good son, it is like a wheel-turning sage king who first teaches the ten wholesome dharmas to sentient beings.
Next, he gradually disciplines those who commit evil, as if severing them step by step.
Thereafter, as there are gradually more who commit evil, the king accordingly disciplines them step by step according to their specific deeds.
The practice of the threefold conduct of the noble king—namely, relinquishing his throne to leave the household life—is an illustration of how the gradual approach ultimately returns to the sudden.
Having severed all evils, he then personally practices the dharma of the noble king.
The application of the analogy is likewise. Within it, there are two parts: first, the formal application; second, the citation of the wheel-treasure to clarify the intent of opening and closing.
Although there was something previously stated, that was intended to apply [the analogy] in a sudden manner.
"Good son, I am also like this: although there is something to be taught, I cannot establish it beforehand."
It is because monks must first concur in their intentions;

it is because monks must first gradually practice what is contrary to the Dharma that one can subsequently establish regulations according to the specific circumstances. Sentient beings who delight in the Dharma will then follow the teachings and practice accordingly.
Thereupon, they behold the sudden realization of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body through its harmonious integration.
It is only such a multitude as this that is able to perceive the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
Next, by raising the analogy of the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) to illustrate the inconceivability of the Three Jewels, he reveals the Tathāgata’s sudden and gradual methods of opening and closing.
Just as the wheel-treasure possessed by a universal monarch (cakravartin) is inconceivable, so too is the Tathāgata inconceivable;
the two treasures of Dharma and Saṃgha are also inconceivable; and both those who can expound the Dharma and those who hear the Dharma are inconceivable.
This is called skillfully understanding the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). In this way, the Bodhisattva analytically elucidates these four kinds [of inconceivability].
The meaning of "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) is the meaning of causes and conditions within the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Whether explained previously or not, it is beyond the capacity of sentient beings to fathom; therefore, it is inconceivable.

Next, from the section on "self-correction" onwards, this is the second [section], which clarifies the four characteristics and the single characteristic, having previously analyzed and demonstrated the Great [Vehicle].
Because of parinirvāṇa, the one characteristic and the four characteristics are clarified; now it is clarified that these are identical.

Since the one characteristic is precisely Great Nirvāṇa and they are equal without distinction, the four characteristics are clarified as being the one characteristic. If [the one] were fixedly one and [the four] fixedly four, how could one and four be attained?
Therefore, we know it is neither one nor four, yet one and four can be spoken of. This takes the Three Jewels—being distinct in essence yet one in essence—as an illustration.

Now, it is clarified that this is not so; the Three Jewels as distinct entities belong to the Hīnayāna and are not of the same category as this [Mahāyāna] teaching. The "one-four-one-four-one" [formula] all expresses the intent of the Mahāyāna.
The Three Jewels as one essence (ekakāya-triratna) can be understood by analogy with the Three Jewels being one essence.

This is just as in the preceding text, where Nirvāṇa is referred to collectively and the three virtues (triguṇa) are referred to individually (and so forth). Regarding the text, there are two parts; first, the formal explanation of the four [aspects].
First, regarding the subsequent refutation and resolution of doubts, the initial correct elucidation is as follows:
Furthermore, "correcting oneself" refers to attaining this Great Parinirvāṇa; "correcting others" refers to my speaking as a bhikṣu, saying that the Tathāgata eternally exists and is unchanging.
Regarding the "answering according to the question," it is because of your inquiry, Kāśyapa, that [this] has been attained.
He extensively expounded for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās this profound and subtle meaning of causes and conditions.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not understand such a profound meaning;
they have not heard that the three dots of the letter *i* constitute liberation and nirvāṇa, which is the secret of the Great Prajñā.
I now expound and analyze this secret treasury for the sake of all śrāvakas, opening their eye of wisdom.

To realize the name of one's own true nature (*svabhāva*) is precisely to shatter impermanence; this is the cause for correcting others. When asked extensively through questions and answers, these three points are analyzed as causes and conditions.
Because they are different names for the same substance and not separate dharmas, they constitute a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).

The *dharmakāya* is the specific term while *nirvāṇa* is the general term; now, taking *nirvāṇa* as the specific and the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyakośa*) as the general, they are therefore not the same.
However, since the manifest name is "Dharmakāya" and the hidden name is "Treasury," sometimes one serves as the general and sometimes as the specific.
Since this is equivalent to and no different from the case of *vimukti* (liberation) and *prajñā* (wisdom), the analogy should likewise apply here.
Next, within the section on counter-arguments, there are doubts, questions, answers, and explanations that may be investigated.
Suppose someone were to say: "How can these four matters be one and not false?"
One should immediately counter-argue: "In what way do these four things—emptiness, non-existence, immobility, and non-obstruction—differ from one another?
How could they possibly be called false?"
"No, World-Honored One.

These various phrases have but a single meaning, namely the meaning of emptiness. To rectify oneself and to enable others to be rectified, and to provide explanations according to questions and answers regarding the meaning of causes and conditions, is likewise thus:
it is identical to Great Nirvāṇa, without any difference."

Question: Are the four marks and the one mark the four *siddhāntas*? Answer: In principle, they should be understood as such; however, by examining the textual characteristics, they may also be categorized accordingly.
For instance, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is the *paramārtha-siddhānta*; its teaching of permanence for the sake of the *śrāvakas* is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*;
its extensive exposition based on inquiry is the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta*; and its formation through the three dots is the *lokasaṃvṛti-siddhānta* (and so forth).

The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "Regarding the second point of analysis: if *nirvāṇa* were identical to the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) and no different from them, why would one analyze *nirvāṇa* but not the four characteristics?
The names of the four characteristics differ from those of the past, whereas the name of *nirvāṇa* remains the same as before.
This is because in the past, the cessation of the bonds of causes—being without dependence and without correctness—was called *nirvāṇa*; thus, it is the cessation of afflictions."

In the former [conception of] nirvāṇa, there was no distinct nirvāṇa apart from the afflictions; in the present [conception of] nirvāṇa, the afflictions have already been extinguished, and there exists an eternally abiding dharma.

In the former nirvāṇa, all modes of existence (*bhava*) were extinguished; in the present nirvāṇa, there is a sublime existence. In the former nirvāṇa, there was no reliance upon external retribution;
in the present nirvāṇa, there is the Dharma of the Teacher. In the former nirvāṇa, there was no primary retribution; in the present nirvāṇa, there is the Tathāgata. If not...
The "Discernment" (Liaojian) is divided into four sections to distinguish its unique textual features: first, the Buddha’s discernment; second, Kāśyapa’s exposition of the doctrine;

third, the realization and understanding; and fourth, the confirmation and fulfillment. The first section, the Buddha’s discernment, is further divided into two parts. First, he provisionally formulates five challenges, the first of which clarifies the extinction of delusions.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "If there are sons or daughters of good family who speak thus, saying, 'The Tathāgata is impermanent;
how should one know that he is impermanent?'—it is as the Buddha has said: the extinction of all afflictions is called nirvāṇa.
Just as when a fire is extinguished, nothing remains, so too is it with the extinction of all afflictions; therefore, it is called nirvāṇa."
How is it that the Tathāgata is a permanently abiding dharma, immutable and unchanging?
Second, there is the existence of cessation.
As the Buddha said: "To be free from all forms of existence (bhava) is called nirvāṇa; within this nirvāṇa, no forms of existence exist."
How is it that the Tathāgata is a permanently abiding dharma, immutable?
It is the third basis for cessation:
just as when a garment is completely worn out it is no longer called a "thing," so too with nirvāṇa; when all afflictions have ceased, it is no longer called a "thing."
How is it that the Tathāgata is a permanently abiding dharma, immutable and unchanging?
The fourth [point] clarifies the cessation of suffering as correct.
As the Buddha said: "The extinction resulting from the departure from desire is called nirvāṇa; it is like a person whose head has been severed—there is no longer a head."
The same applies to the extinction of desire and the state of quiescence; because they are empty and possess nothing, they are called *nirvāṇa*.
How is it that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma, unchanging and immutable?
The five supernormal powers and the cessation of existence all cite former teachings; one may seek [the answer] by fully relying upon the Buddha’s intention.
As the Buddha has said: "For example, when glowing iron is struck with a hammer, sparks fly out and scatter; having vanished, they cannot be known where they have gone.

Attaining right liberation is also like this: having already crossed the mire of lust and all states of existence (bhava), one reaches the immovable state, and it is not known how one has arrived there.
How is it that the Tathāgata is a permanently abiding dharma, unchanging and immutable?"
Next, if someone raises such an objection, the Buddha provides the following response in three parts: first, a rebuke; second, the actual answer;
and third, a summary of the distinction. Regarding the initial rebuke, there are both general and specific aspects; the general rebuke is that [the objection] is erroneous.
Kāśyapa, if there is anyone who raises such an objection, it is called a "deviant objection.
Because one uses a partial argument to challenge what is complete, it is termed a deviant objection.
Following this, Kāśyapa, [the text] separately rebukes Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa, you likewise should not harbor such a thought as that the nature of the Tathāgata is subject to extinction.
"Should not" means that one should not allow the names to become confused by rendering [the eternal] impermanent; therefore, it is said that one should not harbor such a thought.
Next, the response is divided into three parts; first, it answers the two questions regarding the extinction of delusions and the extinction of their basis.
Kāśyapa, that which extinguishes afflictions is not called a "thing. Why? Because it is eternally ultimate;
therefore, it is called "constant. This state is quiescent and unsurpassed.

The text states: "That which is called the extinction of afflictions" refers to the fact that once the subject (the grasper) is devoid of afflictions, the subject's dependent retribution has no further locus to which it belongs;
therefore, it is not termed a "thing. If one follows the former interpretation, this absence of things is pointed to as *nirvāṇa*.
If one follows the present interpretation, it is merely that which is abandoned. Why? Because what follows immediately clarifies that the ultimate attainment is indeed [this].

"Purity, tranquility, purity, and bliss" refers to impermanence being "self" and permanence; as the text states, the nirvana currently attained—both in terms of what is abandoned and what is realized—is different from that of the past.
Next, from the passage "extinguishing all marks" onwards, this answers the two questions regarding whether cessation itself has a cessation.
The complete extinction of all marks without remainder is a state that is pure white, eternally abiding, and non-retrogressive;
therefore, nirvāṇa is called "eternally abiding. The Tathāgata is likewise eternally abiding and unchanging.

The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are precisely existence, which encompasses both the primary retribution (*vipāka*) and the secondary environment. If one follows the former sense, the extinction of existence is the extinction of its fruits, which is *nirvāṇa*.
If one follows the present sense, it refers simply to that which is to be abandoned; when there is nothing remaining to be removed, what is attained is without remainder.

This is bliss (*sukha*), for it is pure and white (*śubha*); this is purity (*śuci*). It is permanent (*nitya*) because it is eternally abiding; it is self (*ātman*) because it is non-retrogressive, and so forth.
Third, regarding the statement that "the stars flow," this answers the fifth inquiry.

To say that "the stars flow" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*). That they "disperse and are immediately extinguished so that their location is unknown" means that once the afflictions of all Tathāgatas have been extinguished, they no longer abide within the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
Therefore, the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma, free from change.
It is easy. When the stars fall, afflictions are extinguished; this is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Once dispersed, they are immediately extinguished and no longer exist within the five destinies;
this is *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. If one relies on the former meaning, it is called "nirvāṇa"; if one relies on the present meaning, it is merely that which is abandoned.
All these are eternally abiding and without change; that which is thus attained is different from what it was before.
Thirdly, Kāśyapa, the severing of fetters constitutes its distinction.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, that which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma; for this reason, the Tathāgata reveres and makes offerings to it.
Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal.
In the Nirvana of the past, there was no person of primary retribution; in the Nirvana of the present, there are the Buddhas.

In the Nirvana of the past, there was no environment of secondary retribution; in the Nirvana of the present, the Dharma serves as the teacher. In the Nirvana of the past, there was nothing [of this kind].
Among all those who have attained nirvāṇa, there is a sublime existence known as "reverence.
While in the former nirvāṇa, afflictions were extinguished and no further phenomena remained; however, in this present nirvāṇa, there exists an eternally abiding dharma.
Because this dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal. This is a brief statement; to speak fully, it is because the Buddha is characterized by dharma, bliss, self, purity, and eternity.
It is likewise so (and so forth).

Next, Kāśyapa again addressed [the Buddha] regarding the two rounds of questions and answers concerning the refutation of arguments. In the first round, there is first the question and then the answer.
Within the initial question, there are two parts, which appear as three difficulties; these seem to concern afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and existence (*bhava*).
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying: "If the Tathāgata also ceases when the fire of afflictions is extinguished, then the Tathāgata would have no permanent abode.

As for the initial statement that 'the Tathāgata also ceases when the fire of afflictions is extinguished,' it is because [the Tathāgata appears] due to afflictions; therefore, some people [hold this view]."
Since the afflictions have already been extinguished, how can there be anyone who says that the Tathāgata exists eternally and remains unchanging?
Just as when the red glow of molten iron has vanished, its destination is unknown, so too are the Tathāgata’s afflictions;
having been extinguished, they go nowhere. Furthermore, just as the heat and the red color of that iron vanish once they have ceased, the Tathāgata is likewise.
Once extinguished, it is impermanent; when the fire of afflictions is extinguished, one enters nirvana. One should know that the Tathāgata is thus impermanent.

Furthermore, it is said that when iron sparks fly up, they vanish in redness and their destination is unknown. This is precisely because of the movement of karma: once karma is extinguished, there can be no arrival.
How, then, can you speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity? As the subsequent passage states: "The red color of the heated iron vanishes."

Once this is accomplished, there is no longer anything further; it is precisely because of delusion and karma that "existence" (bhava) arises. When afflictions and karma are extinguished, how could there be "wondrous existence"?
Good son, what is called "iron" refers to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Although ordinary beings may extinguish their afflictions, they [still possess] extinction...
Because it arises again after having ceased, it is called impermanent; the Tathāgata is not so, for having ceased, he does not arise again, and is therefore called permanent.
Next, the Buddha replied: "Iron is like an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); the Tathāgata is not so. Herein, the two meanings regarding ordinary persons are clarified:

when non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) or those with worldly wisdom sever their afflictions (*kleśa*), they are subject to rebirth, which constitutes the impermanence of ordinary persons; whereas the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) sever both the common and the specific [afflictions].
"Once delusion has arisen, further distinct delusions are produced; this is the impermanence of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The Tathāgata is not thus, for he does not accord with these two extremes. Therefore, he is called 'Eternal' (and so forth).
Kāśyapa spoke again—this is the second question and answer. This inquiry traces back to the two previous points, first asking..."
Next, to answer the intent of the first question:
Kāśyapa spoke again, saying, "Just as when the color of iron has vanished and it is placed back into the fire, its red color arises once more;
if the Tathāgata were like this, his fetters (saṃyojana) should arise again. If the fetters were to arise again, he would be impermanent."

Ordinary beings extinguish delusions only to have them arise again; therefore, they are impermanent. Since the Tathāgata has likewise extinguished [delusions], he too should arise again and would thus be impermanent.
In the Buddha’s response, there are two parts: first, a refutation of the error, and second, a shift in analogy. First is the refutation of the improper [position].
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa, you should not speak in such a manner, saying that the Tathāgata is impermanent. Why?
Because the Tathāgata is eternal.

How could the Buddha—who is not one of the two types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), whose long-enduring [afflictions] have been exhausted, and who has fully realized both the general and specific [truths]—give rise to afflictions? Therefore, you should not say so."
Next follows the response by means of further analogies.
"Good son, just as when wood is burned it leaves behind ashes, so too when afflictions (*kleśa*) are extinguished, there is *nirvāṇa*.
The analogies of the worn-out garment, the severed head, and the broken jar are likewise. Such things each have their own names."
Kāśyapa said: "A ruined garment, a severed head, or a broken jar—once iron has been cooled, it can be made hot again;
but the Tathāgata is not like that. Having severed the afflictions (kleśa), he is ultimately cool and serene; the blazing fire of affliction shall never arise again.
Kāśyapa, you should know that immeasurable sentient beings are like that iron; I, with the blazing fire of untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna), shall burn those beings."
The various fetters of afflictions arise;
the body of an ordinary person is as hot as iron, difficult to melt. The wisdom of the Buddha is fierce and blazing like fire consuming wood.

Once [the wood] is extinguished, there is ash; once afflictions are extinguished, there is nirvāṇa. It is like a tattered garment, a severed head, or a broken jar—these things vanish before one's eyes.
The name arises later, and once the afflictions have been extinguished, one attains nirvāṇa; this is not as you asked.
The three Kāśyapas’ subsequent understanding is as recorded in the text.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "Excellent, excellent! I now truly know that what the Tathāgata has taught is that all Buddhas are eternal."
Fourth, regarding the establishment by way of illustration:
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa, it is as if a noble cakravartin king were staying in his inner palace or sometimes wandering for recreation in his rear gardens;
although the king is not among his ladies-in-waiting, one cannot say that the noble cakravartin has passed away. Good son, it is like this..."
The coming is likewise; although he does not manifest within the realm of Jambudvīpa when entering into parinirvāṇa, this is not called impermanence.
The Tathāgata emerges from immeasurable afflictions and enters the place of nirvāṇic peace and bliss, wandering among the flowers of awakening, contemplating, delighting, and experiencing joy.
The realm of the transformation of the inner palace is like the rear garden of Jambudvīpa;
it is a place for enjoyment and play, analogous to permanence, bliss, self, and purity (and so forth).
Kāśyapa asked again: "I have already crossed over—this is the second [point] extensively opening the secret of the body regarding the diverse forms of the six realms."
To refute the notion that these are the deeds performed solely by the noble ones and not by others, [the Buddha] now reveals the secrets of the Dharmakāya:
first, he opened up the Prajñāpāramitā as four aspects; then, he combined those four aspects into Nirvāṇa. This Nirvāṇa is itself the Dharmakāya and Liberation.
Having thus completed one cycle of revealing the "mouth-secrecy" (vāg-guhya), he now further reveals the Dharmakāya to produce various bodies, thereby harmonizing them.
The various bodies are nothing other than nirvāṇa, prajñā, and liberation. Others claim that one thing covers while another opens, one thing manifests while another conceals;
thus, each opening and each manifesting are eternally unrelated. How could such a principle be correct?

It is merely that what is covered is the opening, and what is opened is the covering. The proponents of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng lun) say this is a skillful means (*upāya*) for ordinary beings.
If one understands the present illumination as it is, how could one not understand the rest? The followers of the *Dharmadhātu* school claim that this is the function (*vṛtti*) of the *dharmadhātu*.
But how can there be a function that is separate from its essence (*svabhāva*)? Other schools explain that the large contains the small; this is the skillful art (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the sages.

Yet, in the present illumination, what single art is not based on causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? Causes and conditions are themselves emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*). Only...
Only those who are ready for deliverance can perceive this; is it not indeed due to causes and conditions?

Through the wondrous wisdom of causes and conditions, one atom can contain the immeasurable, yet the immeasurable cannot contain a single atom. One can freely and without obstruction extend or contract the past and present, or draw and cast this and that.
Zhuang Zhou attained the essence of reality and transformed himself into a butterfly; he also recognized his own dream as having traveled to the ends of the earth.
If even those who are dazed and confused remain thus, how much more so those of supreme virtue! Following the text, there are two parts: first, opening the secret of the person;
second, discussing the meaning. Opening the secret has two sections: first, the question; second, the answer. The question has four parts: first, receiving the purport;
second, the formal objection; third, concluding the question; fourth, requesting an answer. The first is as in the text.
Kāśyapa asked again: "As the Buddha has said, 'I have long since crossed the great ocean of afflictions.
To this, there is a further objection:
if the Buddha has already crossed the ocean of afflictions, for what reason did he again take Yaśodharā as his wife and father Rāhula?"
"Yaśodharā" means "fame," and "Rāhula" means "born in the palace" (and so forth).
By these causes and conditions, one should know that the Tathāgata had not yet crossed over the great ocean of the various fetters of affliction.
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain its causes and conditions.
(The third and fourth [sections] are as in the text.
The answer consists of three parts: first, a general negation; second, an exhortation to listen; and third, the actual response. The first is as in the text.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "You should not say that the Tathāgata has long since crossed the great ocean of afflictions;

for what reason did he again take Yaśodharā as his wife and father Rāhula? By this cause and condition, you should know that the Tathāgata has not yet crossed the great ocean of the fetters of affliction."
Next follows the exhortation to listen from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*:
"Good sons, this *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is able to establish the Great Meaning. You should now listen with a sincere mind and contemplate it attentively;
explain it extensively for others, and do not give rise to alarm or doubt."

If there is a bodhisattva who departs from this, it is a correct answer; and this correct answer is further divided into two parts: first, a general presentation stating that a bodhisattva dwelling in Great Nirvāṇa has eight successive stages;
second, a specific presentation explaining Śākyamuni. The first section is further divided into two: first, the seven successive stages which provide the formal explanation;
second, the final one which serves as a summary.
If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa, can take this Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains—so high and vast—and cause it to enter into a mustard seed;
yet those sentient beings who depend upon Mount Sumeru do not feel any oppression, nor do they have any perception of coming or going, being no different than before.
Only those who are ready for deliverance see this bodhisattva placing Mount Sumeru inside [the mustard seed].
The mustard seed then returns once more to its original place of abiding.
Furthermore, Son of Good Family, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Great Parinirvāṇa and are able to place a trichiliocosm into a mustard seed;
yet the sentient beings therein experience no sense of confinement, nor do they have any thought of coming or going, remaining as they were before.
There was no difference [in the world], yet only those who were ready for deliverance saw this bodhisattva place this trichiliocosm inside a mustard seed and then restore it to its original location.
Good son, furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa,
are able to enter the trichiliocosm into a single pore, and even returning it to its original place is likewise so.

Good son, furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Great Parinirvāṇa and sever [the world], taking all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—the three thousand great thousandfold worlds—and placing them upon the point of a needle as if threading a jujube leaf. They cast them into other Buddha-worlds in distant directions;
yet the sentient beings therein do not perceive the coming and going, nor where they are. Only those who are ready for deliverance can [perceive it].
Seeing them, even returning them to their original locations,
is likewise so. Furthermore, son of good family, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, abiding in the Great Parinirvāṇa,

seize the worlds of the three thousandfold great thousand-fold universe of the ten directions and place them in their right palm like a potter’s wheel, then hurl them to other directions amidst the atoms of dust.
In the world, there is not a single sentient being who has the perception of coming or going; only those who are to be delivered perceive them.
This is likewise true even regarding their original locations.
Good son, furthermore, there are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, dwelling in the Great Nirvāṇa, extract and take up all [beings] from the ten directions.
Infinite Buddha-worlds are all contained within his own body; the sentient beings therein do not feel any oppression, nor do they have any perception of coming, going, or dwelling.
Only those who are ready to be delivered can see them, and this is likewise true even for their original locations.
Good son, furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Great Nirvāṇa and place the worlds of the ten directions within a single mote of dust;
yet the sentient beings therein experience no sense of confinement, nor do they have any thought of coming or going—
only those who are ready to be saved can see them— and this is likewise true even for their original locations.

Regarding the initial and intermediate ancient interpretations that a Bodhisattva abides in Great Nirvāṇa, there are three [points]: first, it is said that this refers to a Buddha who, for the sake of Bodhisattvas, manifests as a causal person;
because he is able to abide in the fruit, it is said that he "abides in Great Nirvāṇa. Second, it is said that this is not so;
for if it were a Buddha, it would simply be a Buddha abiding in Nirvāṇa—what then would it mean for a Bodhisattva to "abide" in Nirvāṇa? As for "abiding," [it means...]
There are two types: first, abiding through faith (*śraddhā-vihāra*), and second, true abiding (*bhūta-vihāra*). Since these are states attained by persons, they are merely abidings through faith.
Some raise this objection: if he were a Buddha, he should be a Bodhisattva; yet this is still the Buddha abiding in *nirvāṇa*, which has no concern with Bodhisattvas.
If, on the other hand, it is an abiding through faith, how could one perform such a great deed? Now, as for *nirvāṇa*...
The essence of *parinirvāṇa* transcends cause and effect; although it is neither cause nor effect, it can function as both cause and effect.

If one regards it from the perspective of a person who is still on the path of causes, one says that *nirvāṇa* is the cause, because such a person abides therein. If one regards it from the perspective of a person who has attained the fruit, one says that *nirvāṇa* is the fruit, because such a person abides therein.
This is, for example, like the state of "correct nature" (*samyaktva*), which is neither cause nor fruit.

"Effect and cause" (and so forth). Here, it is clarified that because the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) constantly contemplates *nirvāṇa* while practicing the Path from the very first moment of generating the resolve for enlightenment, the previous passage states:
"All sentient beings are entirely dwelling within the secret treasury.

Why, then, is it said that the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching cannot yet dwell in Great *Nirvāṇa*? The reason for clarifying the Bodhisattva here is to cite the cause [in order to explain the effect].
If even the causes and conditions that manifest the fruit are thus, how much more so the fruit itself? This meaning is established of its own accord.
Why, then, is it said that a Buddha should become a bodhisattva? And for what reason is it said that a bodhisattva cannot perform various transformations?

The subsequent passage states: "A bodhisattva dwells in great nirvāṇa while practicing various deeds. What is the intention behind saying they cannot dwell in great nirvāṇa while performing these various [deeds]?
Because of these supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), there is no need for further explanation. These seven points, moreover, proceed from the few to the many:

first, Mount Sumeru is directly placed within a mustard seed; this is extended until the ten directions are contained within a single atom. As these instances are compared with one another, the inconceivable subtlety of the marvel becomes ever more manifest.
The conclusion may be understood as follows:
"Good son, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Great Nirvāṇa, he is able to manifest various and immeasurable supernatural transformations;
therefore, it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa. This is what belongs to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."
"You can manifest such immeasurable supernormal powers and transformations that no sentient being is able to fathom them;
how then can you know that the Tathāgata indulged in sensual desire and fathered Rāhula?"

"Good son, I have long resided [in this state]. Setting aside others for a moment, I shall take Śākyamuni as an example to explain three points: first, a brief clarification of the method of his transformative teaching;
second, a detailed exposition of the locus of his skillful means; and third, a summary conclusion. The first is as stated in the text."
"Good son, I have long dwelt in this Great Nirvāṇa, manifesting various supernatural powers and transformations.
Following this, in the section on 'Extensively Explaining Expedient Means' within the three thousand worlds, there are again three parts:

first, a general clarification of the manifestation of transformation throughout the three thousand worlds; second, a specific clarification of the manifestation of transformation in Jambudvīpa; and third, a summary of all expedient means."
Within this trichiliocosm, there are ten billion suns and moons and ten billion Jambudvīpas,
wherein various manifestations appear as described at length in the Śūraṅgama Sūtra.
Regarding the specific [analysis] of Jambudvīpa, there are again four sections: first, the manifestation of this life; second, clarifying other lives;
third, further clarifying this life; and fourth, further distinguishing other lives (and so forth).
Within this trichiliocosm, or specifically in Jambudvīpa, I manifest parinirvāṇa, yet I do not ultimately undergo parinirvāṇa;

or I manifest entry into a mother’s womb in Jambudvīpa, causing my parents to conceive the thought that I am their son, yet this body of mine is ultimately not born from the union of desire. I have long since [transcended this].
For immeasurable kalpas I have been free from desire; this body of mine is itself the Dharma-body.
To accord with the ways of the world, I manifest entry into the womb. Good son, in this Jambudvīpa, within the Lumbinī Grove, I manifest birth from my mother Māyā.
Immediately upon birth, I am able to walk seven paces to the east and proclaim these words: "Among humans and devas..."
When the asuras, gods, and humans see the most honored and supreme among them—their parents—they are filled with wonder and give rise to a sense of rarity.
These people say, "This is but an infant," yet this body of mine has long been free from such states for immeasurable kalpas.
This body is the Dharma-body; it is not established by flesh, blood, sinews, marrow, or bones. It follows...

In accordance with the ways of worldly beings, he manifested as an infant and took seven steps to the south, manifesting his desire to serve as the supreme field of merit for immeasurable sentient beings;
he took seven steps to the west, manifesting that his births were exhausted and old age and death forever severed—this was his final body;
he took seven steps to the north, manifesting that he had already crossed over all existences and the cycle of birth and death; he took seven steps to the east, manifesting...
Acting as a leader for sentient beings, he took seven steps toward the four directions to demonstrate the severance of the various afflictions and the nature of the four Māras;
he took seven steps upward to manifest the attainment of the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
he took seven steps downward to manifest being unstained by impure things, like empty space; and he took seven steps downward to manifest the rain of Dharma.
I extinguish the fires of hell so that those sentient beings may experience peaceful and secure happiness; for those who violate the prohibitions and precepts, I manifest as frost and hail.
After seven days have passed in Jambudvīpa, I manifest the shaving of my head, and all people say, "I am a newborn infant who has just had his hair shaved.
Among all humans, devas, Māra the Evil One, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, there is none who is able [to challenge me].
How much more so for one who beholds my cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa)—it is impossible for anyone to come before me with a razor to shave my hair.
Even if someone were to bring a razor to my crown, such a thing could never happen; for throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I have long since shaved off my beard and hair.
It was only because I wished to conform to the ways of the world that I manifested the act of shaving my hair. Furthermore, as soon as I was born, my parents led me into a celestial shrine.
In the midst [of that assembly], I manifested myself to Maheśvara;
when Maheśvara saw me, he joined his palms in reverence and stood to one side. For immeasurable kalpas past, I have long since abandoned such entry into celestial shrines;
yet, for the sake of conforming to worldly conventions, I manifested myself in this way, appearing here in Jambudvīpa.
Although all sentient beings pierce my ears, in reality there is no one who can pierce them;

it is only to accord with the ways of worldly beings that I manifest such a thing. Furthermore, I adorn my ears with lion-shaped earrings made of various jewels, yet I have already been free from such ornaments for immeasurable eons; I do this only because I wish to conform to the ways of the world.
I manifest entering a schoolhouse to study books and commentaries;
yet, throughout immeasurable eons, I have fully accomplished the power to universally observe all sentient beings within the three realms and find none capable of being my teacher.
Nevertheless, in order to conform to worldly conventions, I manifest entry into a schoolhouse; therefore, I am called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has practiced these studies.
My training in riding elephants, driving chariots, horsemanship, wrestling, and various other arts was likewise so.
Furthermore, in Jambudvīpa, I manifested as the crown prince of a king; all sentient beings saw me as a prince, delighting in and enjoying the pleasures of the five desires.
Yet, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have already renounced such pleasures of the five desires.
In order to accord with worldly conventions, he manifested such signs so that the physiognomists might declare:
"If he does not renounce the household life, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) and rule over all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa. Everyone believed these words;

yet, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have already relinquished the status of a Wheel-Turning King to become a Dharma-Wheel King, and have now manifested the appearance of one who has renounced rice in Jambudvīpa.

"O daughters, regarding the pleasures of the five desires, the sight of old age, sickness, death, and those who have already left the household life as śramaṇas to practice the Way—all these were said to be Prince Siddhārtha’s initial departure from home;
yet I have already left the household life and studied the Way for immeasurable kalpas.
It is only to accord with worldly conventions that I manifest such things."

Regarding the first point, concerning the name Māyā in this life: the *Xiánjié jīng* (Sutra of the Worthy Kalpa) translates it as "Extremely Sublime," while the *Xuǎnyìng jīng* (Sutra of Auspicious Responses) translates it as "Subtle.

It is also translated as "Mother of Great Wisdom. As for [the Buddha] walking seven steps in each of the ten directions: Hejixi (Dharmarakṣa) says that when an elephant king is first born, it immediately walks seven steps;
the Tathāgata manifested this by acting like an elephant king. Yecheng (Yan Fotiao) says it was to demonstrate his transcendence of the six realms of existence.

Therefore, regarding the seven steps taken [at birth], the *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya-sūtra* states that each step corresponds to one of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), because he was awakening what had not yet been awakened.
As for the statement that the south is the "supreme field of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*), the Hexi region explains that in the Sanskrit original, the south is designated as the right;

since the right hand is the hand of convenience, this clarifies that in the Buddha-dharma, pure precepts (*śīla*) constitute that which is convenient, and thus they are established as the supreme field of merit.
Regarding the statement that the south is the direction of Yang (the sun) and can thus give birth to the myriad things, it is therefore called the "Field of Merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*).
As for the demonstration of the seven steps in the west, Hexi says that the west is the rear, hence it is said that his births have ended and this is his final body.
Kaishan says that the west is the direction of autumn, meaning it is the land of death. Regarding the north, Hexi says that in the Sanskrit original it is called *uttara*, which means "victorious."
It is said that having already transcended birth and death, the eastern direction is the foremost of all directions; "growing" is taken in the sense of arising.
From me, manifesting the renunciation of household life here in Jambudvīpa, this is the second accomplishment for the sake of ending future births.

In Jambudvīpa, I manifested the renunciation of the household life, received full ordination, and through diligent cultivation of the path, attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and the fruit of *arhat*.
All people said that the fruit of *arhat* was easily obtained and not difficult to attain; yet, I had already realized the fruit of *arhat* throughout immeasurable kalpas.

If one were to show the manifestation of renunciation and the attainment of Buddhahood in this very life, then the present mention of the four fruits would imply that these occurred in a different lifetime.
