Furthermore, it is because sentient beings perceive according to their own karmic responses; even if [the events] took place in this life, such things occur.

Those of the Two Vehicles all claim that the Tathāgata is an Arhat; as the *Śāstra* states regarding the Dharma of the Śrāvakas: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
"The stage of the Arhat is called the stage of the Buddha" (and so forth).
This constitutes the third layer of exposition concerning the matter of attaining Buddhahood through this birth, intended for the purpose of liberating [sentient beings].
For the sake of delivering all sentient beings, I sat beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment with grass as my seat and subdued the hosts of Māras;
yet all people say that I have only now, for the first time, subdued the palace of Māra at the Bodhi tree in the site of enlightenment.
In truth, I have long since subdued them throughout immeasurable kalpas, doing so only because I wish to subdue those sentient beings who are stubborn and fierce.
Therefore, I manifest as a transformation body and further display the passing of excrement and urine, as well as the exhaling and inhaling of breath;
all people say that I truly possess excrement, urine, exhalation, and inhalation. Yet, this body of mine is the fruition of karmic retribution and is free from such afflictions;
it is only to accord with worldly conventions that I manifest in this way. Furthermore, I manifest as one who receives the offerings of the faithful, yet this body of mine—
I have no hunger or thirst, yet I manifest them in accordance with worldly dharmas; furthermore, I manifest being like all sentient beings by appearing to sleep.
However, I have already, throughout immeasurable kalpas, been fully endowed with unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous wisdom.

Having transcended the three realms of existence, my deportment—whether moving or staying—is such that even if my head, eyes, belly, back, or entire body were afflicted with pain, or even if I had to undergo retribution for striking others with a wooden mallet, I remain free from suffering.

I wash my hands and feet, bathe my face, and rinse my mouth with *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks) to purify myself; all people say that I perform such acts, yet this body of mine possesses none of these things.
My hands and feet are pure like lotuses, and the breath from my mouth is as fragrant as the *utpala* flower.
All sentient beings say that I am a human being, but I am truly not a human being. Furthermore, I manifest—
I currently wear rag-robes that I wash, dye, and mend; yet long ago I no longer required such garments.
All people say that Rāhula is my son, King Śuddhodana is my father, and Queen Māyā is my mother.
Having lived in the world and experienced all its pleasures, I renounced such things to leave the home life and study.
The multitude of people spoke again, saying: "This is the Prince Gautama of a great clan, who has distanced himself from worldly pleasures to seek the supramundane Dharma.
Yet, I have long since abandoned worldly desires; such matters as these are all mere manifestations.
All sentient beings say that this person is he, but in truth, O son of good family, I am not he, even though I am here within this Jambudvīpa."
He repeatedly manifests entry into *nirvāṇa*, yet I do not, in truth, enter ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Nevertheless, all sentient beings say that the Tathāgata has truly and completely ceased to exist; however, the nature of the Tathāgata does not in fact perish forever.
Therefore, you should know that this is a permanently abiding dharma, an unchanging dharma. Good son, Great *Nirvāṇa* is precisely the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
When I come to the Dharma-realm, I further manifest within Jambudvīpa as appearing in the world;
all sentient beings say that I have only now attained Buddhahood, yet I have already accomplished what was to be done throughout immeasurable kalpas.
In accordance with worldly conventions, I again manifest in Jambudvīpa, leaving the home life and attaining Buddhahood.
Śuddhodana is also called Śuddhodana, which means "Pure and White" (Bainjing), and is also called "Pure Rice" (Jingfan).
Regarding Gautama, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* translates it as "Destroyer of Evil," while the Āgamas describe him as "Pure and Virtuous."
I further manifest going to the fourth stage to distinguish other births (and so forth).
I also manifest in Jambudvīpa not upholding the prohibitive precepts and committing the four grave offenses, such that all people see it and say that I have truly committed them;
yet, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have firmly upheld the prohibitive precepts without any lapse or deficiency.
I further manifest in Jambudvīpa as an icchantika, such that all people see me as an icchantika;
yet, in truth, I am not an icchantika. How could an icchantika achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
I further manifest in Jambudvīpa as one who breaks the harmony of the Saṅgha and reunites sentient beings.
I say: "I am the one who breaks the Sangha. Yet, when I observe among gods and humans, there is no one capable of breaking the harmonious Sangha.
Furthermore, I manifest in Jambudvīpa to protect and uphold the True Dharma; all people say, "This is the one who protects the Dharma," and they are all struck with wonder and amazement.
Such is the natural law of the Buddhas; one should not be struck with wonder or amazement. Again, I manifest in Jambudvīpa as Māra Pāpīyas...
All the people of the ten directions say of me, "He is Pāpīyān.
Yet for immeasurable kalpas, I have been free from the deeds of Māra, pure and untainted like a lotus flower. Furthermore, I manifest in Jambudvīpa as a woman who attains Buddhahood;
when all people see this, they say it is most marvelous that a woman can achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Tathāgata Bodhi ultimately does not receive a female body; however, for the sake of taming immeasurable sentient beings, he manifests in female form.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, he further displays various physical forms.
I also manifest birth within the four realms of existence in Jambudvīpa, yet I have long since severed the causes of the realms through my karma.
For this reason, I fall into the four realms of existence; yet, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, I am born therein.
Furthermore, I manifest within Jambudvīpa as a Brahmā Deva King, causing those who serve Brahmā to abide in the True Dharma.
However, I am not truly so, though all sentient beings unanimously regard me as the genuine Brahmā. I likewise manifest celestial forms throughout all the temples of the devas.
In this way, I further manifest entering the houses of courtesans in Jambudvīpa;

yet, in reality, I have no thought of lustful desire, being pure and unstained like a lotus flower. For the sake of sentient beings who are attached to sensual desires and forms, I proclaim the sublime Dharma at the crossroads;
yet, in reality, I have no mind of desire or defilement. The multitude calls me a protector.
O women, I further manifest in Jambudvīpa by entering the households of maidservants, desiring to attract and transform them so that they may abide in the True Dharma;
yet, in reality, I possess no such evil karma as to fall into the state of a maidservant.
I also manifest within Jambudvīpa as a teacher, instructing and transforming the ignorant so that they may abide in the True Dharma. I also manifest in Jambudvīpa... [and so forth].
In Jambudvīpa, I enter various taverns and gambling dens, manifesting all manner of victory, defeat, disputes, and litigation in order to rescue those sentient beings;
yet I truly possess no such evil karma, though all sentient beings claim that I commit such deeds.
Furthermore, I manifest staying for long periods in cemeteries, taking on the body of a great vulture to deliver sentient beings.
When birds and all other sentient beings perceive me as truly being a vulture body, I have long since been free from such karma;
yet, for the sake of delivering those birds and vultures, I manifest myself in this way.
Furthermore, I manifest as a great elder within Jambudvīpa, desiring to establish immeasurable sentient beings in the True Dharma. Moreover—
I manifest as various kings, great ministers, princes, and counselors, each being foremost among their respective assemblies;

for the sake of cultivating the True Dharma, I occupy the royal throne. Furthermore, I manifest within Jambudvīpa during the arising of an epidemic kalpa, when many sentient beings are afflicted by disease;
first I bestow medicine, and thereafter I preach the subtle and wondrous True Dharma to them.
While abiding in unsurpassed bodhi, he causes all people to say that an age of illness has arisen;

furthermore, he manifests the arising of an age of famine within Jambudvīpa, providing food and drink according to their needs, and subsequently preaches the subtle and wondrous True Dharma to cause them to abide in unsurpassed bodhi. Furthermore, he manifests an age of weapons within Jambudvīpa.
When a kalpa arises, he immediately preaches the Dharma for them so that they may leave behind enmity and harm, enabling them to abide securely in unsurpassed bodhi.

Furthermore, he manifests as one who teaches the perception of impermanence to those who conceive the notion of permanence; he teaches the perception of suffering to those who conceive the notion of pleasure;

he teaches the perception of non-self to those who conceive the notion of self; he teaches the perception of impurity to those who conceive the notion of purity. If there are sentient beings who are greedy...
Because he teaches the Dharma to those attached to the three realms so that they may leave such places and deliver sentient beings;
because he teaches the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous Dharma-medicine to sever the trees of all afflictions; because he plants the tree of the unsurpassed Dharma-medicine;
and because he expounds the True Dharma desiring to rescue and liberate all followers of external paths—although he manifests as a teacher for sentient beings, yet...

From the very beginning, his mind has never harbored the notion that sentient beings are his teachers; rather, it is out of a desire to rescue those who are lowly and base that he manifests entry among them to preach the Dharma for them—it is not because of evil karma that he receives such a body.
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, dwells thus in the Great Parinirvāṇa; therefore, he is called eternally abiding and unchanging.
As it is with Jambudvīpa, so it is with Pūrvavideha, Aparagoyānī, and Uttarakuru.
As it is with the four continents, so it is with the trichiliocosm. As it is with the twenty-five [realms], so it is with the summit of existence.
Because it is extensively explained in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is therefore called the Great Parinirvāṇa.
If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who dwells securely in such a Great Parinirvāṇa, they can manifest such supernatural transformations and miraculous powers without any fear.
Kāśyapa, for this reason you should not say that Rāhula is the son of the Buddha. Why?
Because throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I have already been free from desire and existence; therefore, the Tathāgata is called eternally abiding and subject to no change.
Kāśyapa spoke again, and following the second discourse on doctrine, there were two further questions and answers.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "How is it that the Tathāgata is called 'eternally abiding'? The Buddha replied:
"Just as when a lamp is extinguished, it has no location; so too is the Tathāgata—once he has entered parinirvāṇa, he likewise has no location."
In this discussion, having cited the previous analogy of the extinguished lamp— whereby once extinguished it never arises again—
the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* manifests [this] to challenge the subsequent argument by means of the preceding intention.
The answer consists of three parts; first, it rebukes his question.
The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa, son of good family, you should not speak in this way: 'Once a lamp has been extinguished, it has no location;
likewise, when a Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, he has no location.'"
Second, the answer by means of an analogy:
"Good son, it is like when men or women light a lamp; whether the lamp vessel is large or small, it is filled with oil.
As long as there is oil, its light remains; once the oil is exhausted, the light also perishes. That the light is extinguished is an analogy for..."

Although the lamp and its vessel still remain even when the light that extinguishes the afflictions has been completely extinguished, the Tathāgata is likewise: although the afflictions have been extinguished, the Dharma-body remains eternally present.
(This was asked three times.)
"Good son, what do you think? Do the light and the lamp-vessel perish together?
Kāśyapa replied in accordance with the question, raising an objection:
"No, World-Honored One. Although they do not perish together, they are nonetheless impermanent. If, however, one considers them from the perspective of the Dharma-body..."
The analogy of the lamp-vessel suggests that because the lamp-vessel is impermanent, the *dharmakāya* must likewise be impermanent.
The Buddha’s response consists of four parts: first, a rebuke of the question; second, the establishment of the thesis; third, the reconciliation of the analogy; and fourth, a detailed analysis.
"Good son, you should not now raise such an objection as this: that just as the world speaks of a vessel, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is the unsurpassed vessel of the Dharma;
yet that vessel is impermanent and is not the Tathāgata."
Because among all phenomena, nirvāṇa is the eternal essence of the Tathāgata, it is called "eternal.
The first two [points] are as stated in the text.
Furthermore, son of good family, that which is called the "extinguishing of the lamp" is the nirvāṇa realized by an Arhat; it is so called because greed has been extinguished.
Because they still possess attachment to the various afflictions (*kleśa*), the *anāgāmin* is compared to the extinguishing of a lamp.
Because they still possess attachment, it cannot be said that they are identical to the extinguishing of a lamp. Therefore, in the past, I spoke with intentional ambiguity, saying:
"It is like the extinguishing of a lamp, yet not the same as Great Nirvāṇa; it is like the extinguishing of a lamp. The *anāgāmin* does not return again, nor do they go back.
When one returns for the twenty-fifth time and will never again receive a foul body, an insect-like body, a body of food, or a poisonous body, this is called an Anāgāmin.
When the lamp is extinguished at the third assembly,
it is said that this is the Nirvāṇa of an Arhat— a permanent extinction from which there is no further birth— just as the Nirvāṇa of a Tathāgata is an extinction.
Yet, without extinguishing the unborn, one is born (and so forth).
If one further receives a body, one is called an Anāgāmin; if one does not receive a body, one is called an Anāgāmin.
One who has coming and going is called an Anāgāmin; one who has no coming and going is called an Anāgāmin.

Furthermore, in the fourth of the four analytical summaries (*piṇḍoddāna*), it says: "The *anāgāmin* does not undergo rebirth. One interpretation states that this means they do not undergo rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
another states that according to the Mahāyāna, the *anāgāmin* does not undergo rebirth in either of the two extremes.

Chapter on the Four Marks, Part Two.

From the beginning of this fascicle is the third section, "The Virtue of Liberation through Opening the Secret of Intention. This text is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the opening of the secret;
second, clarifying the liberation of others. Regarding the opening of the secret of intention, Xinghuang (興皇) stated that the opening of the secret of body was not yet exhaustive;
here, it is clarified that the secret of all three karmas is universally opened. As the text says: "The words of the Tathāgata open up, develop, and reveal [the truth]. How could this be otherwise?
Is it not that the opening of the mouth is the Tathāgata-mind, free from stinginess? Is it not that the opening of the intention is the Tathāgata-Dharma-body, complete and without deficiency?
Is it not that the opening of the body is the Tathāgata-Sūtra, whose universal text requires no partial exposition? Why is this?

Because the Buddha manifests ordinary forms and teaches the "half-syllable" Dharma; according to what is appropriate for others, he employs the skillful means of the three karmas to conceal the Three Secrets.
That which the ignorant regarding karma do not understand is called a "secret treasury" (*guhya-kośa*); now, by opening the skillful means, it is revealed as the ultimate reality.

For the wise who have attained thorough penetration, there is nothing secret or hidden. This is the opening of the mystery with respect to the three types of karma; furthermore, it is the opening of the mystery with respect to the four propositions:

others open the Buddha’s mystery, the Buddha opens the mystery of others, the Buddha opens his own mystery, and others open their own mystery; others open the Buddha’s mystery, and the Buddha opens the mystery of others.
Regarding "the secret" (*mi*), at the beginning of the chapter, Kāśyapa says: "The Buddha-dharma is not like that; it causes all sentient beings to fully know and see.
'Knowing' refers to opening the secret of the mind (*manomaya-guhya*); 'seeing' refers to opening the two secrets of body and speech (*kāya-vāk-guhya*)... [and so forth].

When the Buddha opens the secrets of others, he reveals to all sentient beings the treasure-store of all-enlightenment (*sarva-bodhi-ratna-kośa*), manifesting the jewel on the forehead (*lalāṭa-maṇi*) and placing it within the secret treasury (*guhya-kośa*). This is "opening for others."
"The Secret Buddha reveals the secret of the Buddha: 'Since I attained the Way, I have constantly preached the Prajñā-dharmakāya and liberation.
This present body of mine, as well as all its various forms and images, is itself the Dharmakāya.

When my children have grown up and possess the capacity for responsibility, the Tathāgata has no heart of stinginess—this is the meaning of the Secret Buddha revealing the secret of the Buddha. Others reveal the secrets of others."
As the King of Virtue said: "I understand one phrase or half a phrase; because I understand one phrase up to half a phrase, I see a small portion of Buddha-nature.
As the Buddha has taught, I too shall attain entry into Great Nirvana," and so forth.

Furthermore, the "opening of the secret" refers to twelve phrases, meaning that within each of the four phrases, the three karmas are opened, thus forming twelve phrases for the opening of the secret.
(As stated above... Furthermore, there is no opening and no closing, no manifestation and no concealment. Why? Because the principle of Buddha-nature has never been opened; who then could cover it?
Since there is neither opening nor closing, how could there be manifestation or concealment? If not even a single phrase can be found, how much less could there be many?
It is only because sentient beings hear this and cannot understand that it is called "secret" (*guhya*); the wise, however, fully comprehend it.
Thus, there is neither manifest nor secret, yet because it is manifest and secret, it is called "opening" (kaiai). It is an opening that occurs without anything to be opened, as previously analyzed.
As the *Wen shi lun* states: "Prajñā is the manifest teaching, while the Lotus Sūtra is the secret teaching. The old interpretation explains this as follows:
the discourse on the non-abiding Great Way of Prajñā is the manifest teaching, whereas [the Lotus] is the secret teaching. However, [this view] is refuted.
To think that because the secret is not revealed, it is therefore not understood—this interpretation is incorrect. The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither manifest nor secret;
as conditions for both manifestation and secrecy, all sūtras are thus. How could the specific intent of Nāgārjuna be used to invalidate the meaning of all other sūtras?
This passage also uses impermanence to refute permanence; how could this be due to a lack of understanding? Therefore, [the previous] opening was made.

Next, the secret [teaching] explains that the two meanings of "liberation" (vimukti) are interrelated. Why is this? If one is fixedly open or fixedly covered, being thus restricted by openness or covering, it is not called liberation.
Only when one is neither open nor covered, yet is able to open and able to cover—possessing mastery over opening and covering—is it truly liberation.
Therefore, these two passages both belong to the category of the virtue of liberation; regarding the passage on "opening," they are divided into two parts.

Having previously clarified the opening of the Esoteric [teachings], the following discussion on the meaning of the opening of the text is divided into three parts: first, the question; second, the answer; and third, the acknowledgment and understanding.

The question is further divided into three sections: first, the objection that it is not the Esoteric Treasury yet claims there is nothing; second, the assertion that it is indeed Esoteric language and that there are three [aspects]; and third, the formal conclusion.

At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as for what the Buddha has said—that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a secret treasury (guhyagarbha)—this meaning is not so.
The initial text states that 'treasury' refers to principle (li). Since principle is without opening or concealing, how can it be called 'secret'? Therefore, it does not exist."
Next, for what reason? Because there is speech based on the departure from this [prior] speech, there is "instruction" (*deśanā*). Instruction is fundamentally a condition;

because there is opening and concealing based on conditions, there is "esoteric language" (*saṃdhābhāṣya*). By analogy, there are esoteric aspects of body and mind, which constitute esoteric language.
This includes the elements of the dharma, the simile, and the application (*dharmanidarśanopanaya*), and so forth. Regarding the first, the dharma, it is as the text states.
Why is this? The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess only esoteric speech, but no esoteric treasury.
It is like a master of illusions and his mechanical wooden figures; although people see them bending, stretching, bowing, and looking up, they do not know what is within that causes them to act thus.

Next, regarding the analogy: the illusionist and the mechanical device should correspond to two matters, while the illusion has two meanings: first, that it is a base art, shallow and superficial, such that one does not wish for others to see it;
second, that one fears others might emulate the art, such that one does not wish for others to see it. The mechanical device is likewise [governed by] these two matters.
Since the two matters are identical, they together constitute a single analogy (and so forth).
The Buddha-dharma is not like that; it causes all sentient beings to fully know and see it.
How, then, could one say that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a secret treasury?
[The text continues] as written, including the closing seal.
Second, the Buddha’s response consists of two parts: first, he praises the questioner and answers that there is no secret treasury.
The Buddha commends Kāśyapa, saying, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! As you have said, the Tathāgata truly has no secret treasury."
Next, the nine similes answer [the question] that there is only esoteric speech; however, among these similes, some follow the literal sense while others are inverse.

The autumn moon is a simile following the literal sense, whereas the accumulated gold is an inverse simile; this can be seen in the text (and so forth). These nine similes are divided into three parts:
first, the seven similes refute the esoteric [nature of] the three karmas and reveal the manifest three karmas; second, the elder’s instruction of his son...; third, one... [etc.].
Regarding the first passage, which explains the three analogies of the dragon kings for the causes and conditions of opening and not opening the secret: Why is this?
It is because it is like the full autumn moon situated in the sky, manifest, pure, and free from obscuration, which all people behold.
The meaning of the term "coming" (*āgama*) is likewise so: it reveals and makes manifest that which is pure and free from obscuration.
The ignorant do not understand it and call it a "secret treasury," but the wise, having fully realized it, do not designate it as a "treasury."
Autumn is the season of Yin, and the moon is the essence of Yin. When the essence of Yin resides in the season of Yin, its brilliance becomes increasingly intense.
The moon is likened to the Buddha who can respond, and autumn is likened to the capacity that can evoke; when the response and the evocation correspond, there is only opening and no concealment.
Good son, it is like a person who has accumulated immeasurable billions of gold and silver, yet whose mind is so stingy that he refuses to give in charity or rescue the poor;
such an accumulation is called a "secret hoard. The Tathāgata is not like this;
having accumulated the treasures of immeasurable sublime Dharma over countless kalpas, his mind is free from stinginess, and he constantly bestows them as gifts.
"How can it be said that all sentient beings possess the Tathāgata-garbha?
Good son, it is like a person whose physical faculties are incomplete—perhaps lacking an eye, a hand, or a foot—who, out of shame, does not wish to be seen by others;
because they are not seen, this is called a 'hidden storehouse. It is not so with the Tathāgata."
If there exists the True Dharma, complete and without deficiency, which allows people to behold it, how can it be called the "Secret Treasury" of the Tathāgata?
Son of Good Family, for example, a poor man who owes much wealth to others and fears his creditors hides himself and does not wish to appear;
therefore, it is called a "treasury. The Tathāgata is not like this; he owes nothing to any sentient beings. Although he bears worldly dharmas, he has delivered sentient beings from them.
He does not withhold even the worldly dharmas. Why? Because he constantly conceives the thought of all sentient beings as his only child and expounds the unsurpassed Dharma for them.
Regarding the fourth analogy, it says: "Though he carries the supramundane Dharma. He Xi (Hexi) says this refers to the Buddha’s original vow to deliver all [beings].
Because the Buddha enters *nirvāṇa* before all sentient beings have been exhausted, it is said that he is "in debt" (*fu*) to them. Xinghuang says:

"When the Buddha attains the fruit [of Buddhahood], it is for the sake of sentient beings; how could there be a causal practice performed for the sake of attaining the fruit without being for the sake of sentient beings?
It is only because sentient beings are not yet exhausted that it is called 'being in debt'. This meaning is essentially no different [from the former]. Hexi now provides two interpretations.
The initial resolve is "small wealth," while attaining the fruit is "great wealth. Being able to deliver sentient beings is "giving";

not being willing to deliver them is like a person who does not seek their goods from a creditor—whom should the owner give to? In principle, one is considered in debt; in reality, however, there is no debt owed.
The following parable of the dragon king further clarifies this point. Furthermore, when the Buddha first resolved his mind, he vowed to cause sentient beings to become weary of [suffering].
To abandon all states of existence is called "not failing the worldly dharmas.
It means vowing to practice the supramundane dharmas and bearing this task like the earth supporting all things, never abandoning it from beginning to end;
therefore, although one speaks of "bearing" the supramundane dharmas, this is the sense of "bearing" as in carrying a burden, not the sense of "bearing" as in a debt.
Good son, it is like an elder who possesses great wealth and has but one son;
he loves him dearly and feels no desire to part from him, showing him all his precious treasures. The Tathāgata is likewise, regarding all sentient beings as his only child.
Good son, just as people in the world, because their male or female organs are ugly and loathsome, cover them with clothing and thus call it "concealment," the Tathāgata is not so;
having forever severed these organs, and because he has no organs, there is nothing to conceal.
Good son, it is like the discourses of a Brahmin, which he never wishes to be heard by Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras. Why is this?
Because there are faults and evils within those discourses. The True Dharma of the Tathāgata is not like this;
it is good in the beginning, middle, and end. Therefore, it cannot be called a "secret treasury."
Next, the parable of the elder instructing his son is divided into two parts: first, the parable of the secret [instruction], and second, the parable of the disclosure.

The first part is further divided into two: first, the disclosure, and second, the synthesis. The disclosure consists of four sections: (1) the desire to teach the Great [Vehicle]; (2) because the conditions are unfit, he temporarily teaches the Small [Vehicle];
(3) the non-explanation of the Great; and (4) the conclusion regarding the absence of concealment. The first two correspond to the text as it stands.
Good son, it is like a householder who has only one son; his heart constantly remembers and cherishes him without end.

Desiring to have him go to a teacher to receive instruction, he fears the boy will not achieve success quickly and thus brings him back immediately. Out of affectionate concern, he diligently teaches him the "half-syllables" day and night.
"And why do you not teach him the Vyākaraṇa treatise? For what reason? Because he is still young and his strength is not yet sufficient.
"Good son, suppose a householder were to teach this child the half-syllables; would the child then immediately be able to understand the Vyākaraṇa treatise?
"No, World-Honored One."

Regarding the third point, it is stated in the *Mahāvyutpatti* that the *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra*—which is translated here as the *Mūla-akṣara-śāstra* (Treatise on the Root of Letters)—is what the Hexi region calls the fundamental scripture of worldly letters and the treatise on phonology.
It elucidates the four types of eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*), censures worldly dharmas, and praises supramundane dharmas.
Its diction is refined and elegant, and its principles are profound; although it is an external treatise, [it is nevertheless...]
Is it not the case that the absence of false teachings is the work of a Great Being (mahāsattva) of skillful means? The details of the questions and answers may be sought in the text.
The four concluding sections are as stated in the text.
"Is it so, World-Honored One, that the elder has some secret storehouse regarding this son? No, World-Honored One. Why is this? It is because the son is young in years;
he was not told [of it] for that reason, nor was it out of stinginess or secrecy that it was not revealed. Why is this?
If one possesses a mind of envy and stinginess, only then is it called a 'storehouse. The Tathāgata is not like this; how then could it be said that he has a 'storehouse'?"
"Coming to the Secret Treasury":
from the Buddha’s words "Excellent! downward, this corresponds to the first analogy. First, it describes the praise, which properly corresponds to the desire to expound the Great Teaching.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! As you have said, if one possesses a mind of anger, jealousy, or stinginess, that is called 'concealment.
The Tathāgata has no anger, jealousy, or stinginess; how, then, could he be said to conceal anything?
Son of good family, that great elder refers to the Tathāgata. Speaking of 'one son' refers to all sentient beings, for the Tathāgata regards them as equal."
Regarding all sentient beings as if they were one's only son; "teaching the only son" refers to the śrāvaka disciples;
"half-syllables" refers to the ninefold canon and the Vyākaraṇa treatises; and "Vyākaraṇa" refers to the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.
Next, because the śrāvakas are inferior, he provisionally teaches them the Small Vehicle.
Since the śrāvakas lack the power of wisdom, the Tathāgata teaches them the ninefold canon of the "half-syllables" (ardhakṣara),
but for the sake of those who are not inferior, he does not teach the Great Vehicle.
Yet they do not explain for them the *Vyākaraṇa* (grammar), the Vaipulya Mahāyāna, or the four [truths].
Sons of good family, it is like that lower class who lacks the secret treasury;
sons of good family, it is as if that elder’s son, having grown up and being capable of reading and studying, were not to be taught the *Vyākaraṇa*.

If the *Vyākaraṇa* treatises could be called a "treasury," and if there were any śrāvakas with the capacity to receive the Mahāyāna *Vyākaraṇa* treatises whom the Tathāgata withheld from teaching out of secrecy, one might say that the Tathāgata possesses a secret treasury.
But the Tathāgata is not so; therefore, the Tathāgata has no secret treasury.
Next, following the analogy of that elder teaching the half-syllables (*ardhākṣara*), this serves as a metaphor for the opening of the secret [teachings].
Just as that elder, after teaching the half-syllables, subsequently expounded the *Vyākaraṇa* treatises.
Next, as for what is called "the lower correspondence," it is as stated in the text.
I likewise, having taught the ninefold canon of the "half-syllables" to my disciples, subsequently expound the Vyākaraṇa treatise,
which is to say that the Tathāgata eternally exists and is unchanging.
Formerly, this passage was cited to prove that impermanence (*anityatā*) is [the teaching] of the Small Vehicle while permanence is that of the Great Vehicle.

Master Xinghuang challenged this interpretation, stating: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* also clarifies impermanence; therefore, it should belong to the Small Vehicle. The explanation given in response is: "Impermanence applies universally to both the Great and Small Vehicles;

likewise, the terms 'Half' and 'Full' [Teachings] should also apply accordingly. Here, we clarify that impermanence belongs to the Tripiṭaka, whereas permanence and impermanence belong to the Common and Distinct [Teachings] respectively."
That which is both permanent and impermanent, yet neither permanent nor impermanent, is the perfect application of the fourfold analysis to various sutras;
how could it give rise to one-sided disputes?
Thirdly, the passage below regarding the dragon king, clouds, and thunder serves as an analogy for those who lack the causal conditions for secrecy.

Furthermore, good son, it is like this: for example, in the summer months, when great clouds and thunder arise and heavy rain falls, those farmers who have sown seeds will reap many fruits, while those who have not sown seeds will have no harvest.
That those who have no harvest is not the fault of the Dragon King, yet this Dragon King has nothing hidden away. I, too, am like this, as I bring down the Great Dharma.
In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is said: "If sentient beings plant the seeds of goodness, they shall obtain the fruit of the sprouts of wisdom;
those who do not plant the seeds of goodness shall obtain nothing. That they obtain nothing is not the fault of the Tathāgata, for the Buddha, the Tathāgata, truly has nothing to conceal."
"Not sowing seeds" means there is no cause for secrecy; "not sprouting" means there is no cause for opening [the teaching], as stated in the text.
The three Kāśyapas spoke again, immediately understanding the meaning of the text.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "I now know with certainty that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has no hidden treasury."
Next, as the Buddha has taught, this discussion of the meaning (arthaviniścaya) is further divided into two parts: first, the discussion of the meaning, and second, the comprehension and acceptance.
Regarding the initial discussion of the meaning, there are two rounds of question and answer. The first question has three parts, the first of which is the acknowledgment of the present permanence.
As the Buddha has taught in the Vyākaraṇa-śāstra, it is said that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, exists eternally and is unchanging.
Next, you cite his former teaching on impermanence;
however, this interpretation is not correct. Why? Because the Buddha previously spoke this verse:
The Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of Śrāvaka disciples—even they must abandon this impermanent body;
how much more so the various ordinary worldlings?
(Third question: Why is this so?)
"Now you speak of that which eternally exists and is unchanging; what is the meaning of this?
The Buddha replied, "It is twofold: first, I clarify the provisional [teachings] of the past; second, I clarify the reality of the present.
The Buddha said, "Good son, for the sake of all my śrāvaka disciples, I taught the 'half-syllables' and thus spoke in this way."
Verse: "Good son, when King Prasenajit’s mother passed away, he wailed and mourned with such overwhelming grief that he could not control himself;
he came to where I was, and I immediately asked him, 'Great King, for what reason are you so distressed and sorrowful as to reach this state?
The king replied, 'World-Honored One, the Queen, my consort, passed away on such-and-such a day. Even if there were someone capable of restoring my mother to life—'"
"If you can return to your original state, I shall renounce my kingdom, elephants, horses, the seven treasures, and even my own life and body to repay you.
I spoke further, saying: "Great King, do not be distressed, sorrowful, or weep.
For all sentient beings, the exhaustion of their lifespan is called death. Even the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvaka disciples must eventually relinquish this body; how much more so for others?"
"O virtuous son of ordinary beings, I spoke this verse for the sake of King Prasenajit as a teaching on the 'half-syllables.

Regarding the name Prasenajit mentioned previously in the provisional [teachings], the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* calls him 'Harṣa' (Joy), while the *Saṃyukta Āgama* calls him 'Grandmother's Nourisher' (*Pitāmahapopa*)."
Next, from "Now I" onwards, the reality is clarified.
Now, for the sake of my śrāvaka disciples, I expound the *Vyākaraṇa* treatise, stating that the Tathāgata eternally exists and undergoes no change.
If there were anyone who said the Tathāgata is impermanent, how could their tongue not fall off?
As for those whose tongues fall out, this calamity is brought about by constantly taking the impermanent to be permanent;

Master Sōng of Pengcheng Temple said that when the Buddha’s wisdom was in flux as the time of impermanence approached, his tongue rotted within his mouth—a state which is not easily overcome even then.
Kāśyapa spoke again; this was the second round of questions and answers.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "As the Buddha has taught:
'Having nothing accumulated, being moderate in eating, like a bird flying through the sky, its tracks cannot be found.'"
What is the meaning of this? O Bhagavān, among this assembly, who is said to be one who has no accumulation?
Who is said to be one who is content with food? Who walks upon the track of space that cannot be traced, and where does such a traveler go?

This question arises immediately from the verse stating that the Tathāgata is eternally present and subject to no change; while the verse contains only three questions, the prose commentary contains four.
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa, that which is accumulated is called wealth and treasure. Noble son, there are two kinds of accumulation."
The first is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The accumulation of the conditioned refers to the practice of the *śrāvakas*;
the accumulation of the unconditioned refers to the practice of the Tathāgata. Good son, the Saṅgha is also of two kinds: conditioned and unconditioned.
The conditioned Saṅgha is called the *śrāvaka* Saṅgha; the *śrāvaka* Saṅgha has no accumulation, namely, [the accumulation] of slaves, servants, or unlawful things.
Regarding stores of goods, grain, rice, salt, fermented soybeans, sesame, and various large and small beans— if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata permits the keeping of slaves,
servants, or such things as these, their tongue would curl back and shrink;
for all my śrāvaka disciples are named "Those Without Accumulations."
The Buddha’s answer to the first question contains three points: 1. Regarding "there is no accumulation," he mentions accumulation to clarify that there is no such thing as accumulation;

this is because accumulation has two aspects, which serves to clarify that what is accumulated is itself non-accumulation. 2. "The Saṃgha is also like this" clarifies that what is accumulated is non-accumulation. 3.
"Śrāvakas are conditioned" means that because śrāvakas engage in mental application (*manasikāra*), they are conditioned; they grasp [phenomena] at the improper time.
Because it is realized, it is called an accumulation; because the bodhisattva practices within non-action, it is called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
because one does not take emptiness as a realization, it is called non-accumulation (and so forth).
Next, that which is also called "named" answers the second question.
This may also be called "knowing contentment with food": if one has craving for food, it is called "lack of contentment"; if one does not crave food, this is called "contentment.
Regarding the phrase "the tracks are difficult to trace," this answers the third question.
Those whose traces are difficult to find are close to the path of unsurpassed bodhi.
I say that such a person answers the fourth question;
I say that although such a person departs, they arrive nowhere.

Now, it is explained that the Buddha’s answers to the four questions extensively reveal that "permanence" is non-accumulation, "purity" is contentment, "bliss" is being difficult to seek, and "self" is having no place of arrival;

furthermore, "permanence" is having no arrival. Furthermore, "non-accumulation" is the absence of origination, "contentment" is the absence of suffering, "being difficult to seek" is the presence of the Path, and "having no place of arrival" is the presence of cessation. Because there is cessation, there is no suffering; because there is the Path, [there is cessation].
It is clear that the meanings of permanence, bliss, self, and purity apply equally to the Path and Cessation, as they exist eternally.
Next, when Kāśyapa speaks again, it is an expression of his understanding.
Kāśyapa further says: "If even the conditioned Saṃgha has no accumulation, how much more so the unconditioned Saṃgha? As for the unconditioned Saṃgha..."
This is the Tathāgata. How could there be any accumulation in a Tathāgata? That which is called "accumulation" is termed "concealment.
Therefore, whatever the Tathāgata speaks, he has no stinginess regarding it. What is meant by "concealed traces that cannot be sought"?
It refers to Nirvāṇa. Within Nirvāṇa, there are no sun, moon, stars, or constellations, nor are there cold, heat, or wind.
Those born from rain are subject to birth, death, and the twenty-five states of existence; they are separated from all sorrow, suffering, and afflictions.
Such is nirvana, the dwelling place of the Tathāgata, which is eternal and unchanging.
For these reasons, the Tathāgata has come to this śāla grove and entered parinirvāṇa within the Great Nirvana.
From the Buddha’s address to Kāśyapa regarding what is called "great," there is a passage where someone uses this text to establish [the meaning].
Now, following this, the second section correctly clarifies liberation (*vimukti*). This section is divided into three parts: first, a brief clarification of liberation;
second, an extensive clarification of liberation; and third, a summary of liberation. The brief section is further divided into two: first, a brief exposition of liberation; second, the discussion...
The meaning is briefly explained as threefold: first, its vastness; second, its being without blemish; and third, its being the locus of liberation.

It is called "vast" because it encompasses all without exception and one cannot find its limits or depths. It is "without blemish" because lust, anger, and delusion are exhausted and all afflictions are entirely removed.
It is called a "locus" because object and wisdom are in accord. These are the three brief explanations.
That they cannot be separated from one another also constitutes the accomplishment of essence and function, as well as the fulfillment of both self and others;
although these three points are brief, their underlying principles are comprehensive. Within this extensive text, there are both the principle and the analogy.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "That which is called 'great' has a nature that is vast and expansive.

That which is called 'great' has a nature that is vast and expansive; this is an etymological explanation according to the name, and it cannot be said to be a 'great' that exists only in relation to the 'small.
Why? Because in the preceding passage, 'great' was explained by means of 'permanence,' whereas here it is explained by means of 'vastness. [The passage continues: "...below, by means of 'not...'"
Regarding the "Great" in the phrase "The Great through Contemplation," one should know that this "Great" is an absolute, inconceivable greatness.
It is like a person whose lifespan is immeasurable who is called a "great man"; if such a person can abide securely in the True Dharma, they are called the most excellent among humans.
As I have taught, the Eight Arousals of a Great Man may belong to a single individual or to many individuals.
If one person possesses all eight [qualities], they are the most excellent.
This is like a person who possesses both vertical and horizontal intentions; though they may have many virtues, the essential point lies in their lifespan.

An immeasurable lifespan is the analogy for the "vertical" aspect, which corresponds to internal practice (*adhyātma-caryā*). Although there are many paths to practice, what is valued is the True Dharma (*saddharma*); therefore, it is said that such a person is truly human.

Regarding the phrase "Superior in the middle as I have explained," it refers to a single individual who possesses eight qualities; because such a person has great functional capacity, this explains the manifold virtues horizontally.
By correlating these with the Dharma, one uses both horizontal and vertical perspectives to explain "Great."

Next, from the passage beginning "What is called nirvāṇa," it clarifies that there are no sores or afflictions (*vraṇa*). Some cite this to translate *nirvāṇa* as "absence of entanglement" (*wú lèi*);

"absence of entanglement" is precisely "absence of sores. Master Xinghuang explained: "Nirvāṇa is a general name for liberation in the foreign land (India), whereas 'liberation' (*jiětuō*) is its specific designation here [in China].
It is logically appropriate to translate the general term with the general term, and the specific term with the specific term."
How could one take a specific synonym for "liberation" (*vimukti*) to translate a general term?

While *nirvāṇa* is translated as "liberation," here we do not translate the general term, but rather translate the specific sense as "one without sores" (*niṣkaṇṭaka*). This is because the general term inherently encompasses the specific, and the specific sense of being "without sores" is contained within it;
thus, the specific is used to explain the general. How could such a translation of terms be confused or conflated? Regarding this:
The text consists of the proposition, the illustration, and the application.
That which is called nirvāṇa is free from all sores and blemishes.
Good son, it is like a person who, having been struck by a poisoned arrow and suffering great pain, encounters a skilled physician.
To extract the poisonous arrow and apply wondrous medicine so that they may be freed from suffering and attain peace and happiness,
the physician then travels through cities, towns, and various villages; wherever there are those afflicted by illness, pain, or sores, he goes to those places to treat their manifold sufferings.
The teaching on the Dharma illustrates that one is oneself free from sores and wounds, while the parable of healing the sores and wounds of others merely serves as a mutual illustration.
Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise; having attained equal and perfect enlightenment, he acts as a Great Physician-King.

Seeing the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa suffering through immeasurable kalpas, pierced by the poisonous arrows of the afflictions of lust, anger, and ignorance, and undergoing intense and bitter pain, [he acts for their sake].

Having thus treated this [world] with the nectar-like medicinal dharma of the Mahāyāna sūtras, he proceeds again to other regions where there are the poisonous arrows of various afflictions (*kleśa*);
there he manifests as a Buddha to provide healing for them. For this reason, it is called *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Third, from the perspective of the locus of liberation, there are again two types: first, self-liberation; second, the subduing of others.
"Great Parinirvāṇa" is termed the locus of liberation.
Regarding the word "locus" (*sthāna*) mentioned in the initial passage, it refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as the locus; it does not refer to this [physical] place.
Having attained liberation, one is at peace in this place and further subdues others. The *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states:

"It is established as a place encompassed by the constant *pāramitā*. This text says: "By means of this place of true and profound meaning, it should be known that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) constitutes the place.
Thus, it is clear that the ultimate truth is taken as the locus.
Next, regarding those places where there are beings to be tamed and transformed for the sake of others:
wherever there are sentient beings to be tamed, the Tathāgata manifests therein.
Because it possesses this true and profound meaning, it is called Great Nirvāṇa.

This not only reveals the perfection [of the Buddha-nature] but also censures the Lesser Vehicle. Although the Dharma-body and Prajñā of the past transformed sentient beings, they lacked the two virtues of liberation and *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;
once these were entered, they were forever extinguished, such that they could not even transform others in a single place, let alone everywhere.
The liberation of the present, however, accords with the ten dharma-realms—the six paths of existence and the four types of noble ones.
However, for those sentient beings who must be tamed, he tames them everywhere; though they may be in hell, their bodies and minds suffer no pain;
though they may be among animals, they have no fear; though they may be among hungry ghosts, they are forever free from hunger and thirst;
though they may be among humans or devas, they are free from human and celestial affairs; and though they may be among those of the Two Vehicles, they hear the sound of the Buddha-way.
Compassion teaches and transforms in all places without any blemish or the burden of defiled attachment; for this reason, it is called the "place of liberation.

It is not merely that there is no defilement upon contact with the place; furthermore, because there is the illumination of *prajñā* and the mastery of the *dharmakāya*, these three points are fully present within the very place of liberation.
Thus, the past is rejected and the present is revealed—the meaning of this is clear.
The second part, beginning with "Kāśyapa said," is the discussion of the treatise; the preceding section clarified three meanings, whereas this section discusses only two.
The first two rounds of question and answer discuss the meaning of being "without sores," as in the text.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the physicians of the world are all able to cure and treat everything."
The sores and ailments of sentient beings, and the unwholesome men who are the sores of the world, are of two kinds: first, those that can be cured;
second, those that cannot be cured. Generally, that which can be cured a physician is able to treat, while that which cannot be cured he cannot treat.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "If it is as the Buddha has said, then the Tathāgata must have already healed the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa.
If you say they have been healed, why is it that among those sentient beings there are still some who have not yet attained nirvāṇa?
If they have not all attained it, how can the Tathāgata say that the healing is finished and that he wishes to go to another land, O son of good family?"
Within Jambudvīpa, sentient beings are of two kinds: first, those who have faith; second, those who lack faith.
Those with faith are said to be curable. Why? Because they will certainly attain nirvana and be free from all afflictions.
Therefore, I say that after I have cured the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, those who lack faith are called icchantikas. An icchantika is defined as one who...
It can be cured except for the icchantikas; all others are cured. Therefore, nirvāṇa is called "without sores.
Regarding the three subsequent rounds of questions and answers concerning the locus of liberation, the first round is as stated in the text.
“World-Honored One, what is called ‘nirvāṇa’? “Good son, nirvāṇa is called liberation.
The subsequent exchange of questions and answers consists of two parts; first, the question which presents both [aspects] together.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "Is that which is called liberation material (rūpa) or is it non-material?
In the subsequent response, there are two parts: first, a dual explanation; second, a dual conclusion. The Buddha said:
"Good son, it may be material or it may not be material. That which is said to be non-material is [the realm of] sound."
To hear the words "liberation of the pratyekabuddhas is form" is itself the liberation of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Good son, for this reason, liberation is both form and not form; yet the Tathāgata has taught it to his śrāvaka disciples as being non-form.
The ancient interpretation holds that the permanent fruit of Buddhahood possesses form (*rūpa*), citing this very passage as evidence. Furthermore, another master says:
although the fruit of Buddhahood is formless, it is called "form" because its wondrous wisdom is manifest; thus, it is designated as form. Moreover, there is another explanation:
among the three aggregates (*triskandha*), two aggregates are not form while one aggregate is form; by taking up the aggregate of form, [the Buddha] makes himself manifest.
However, regarding the analogy for the fruit of Buddhahood and liberation, Xinghuang said:

"If it were definitively with form or definitively without form, one should not establish 'either' or 'or' as conditions to constitute form or non-form. Yet the Dharma-body is neither form nor non-form;
yet that which is 'either form' is formless form, and that which is 'either non-form' is form-non-form. For this reason, there are two."

To say that those who ride [the Mahāyāna] do not understand this because it is not their realm, or that the Śrāvakas lack form because they regard form as a fetter like shackles and thus preach formlessness, or that Bodhisattvas can realize both form and formlessness and therefore speak of "wondrous form" as being serene—none of these are correct.
What is the essence of liberation? How could it ever be either form or non-form? As the text below states: "No..."
It can be said that both form (*rūpa*) and non-form are ineffable, as are emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and non-emptiness, because they function as two conditions.
Thus it is said: "Form is non-form; non-form is also form; form is also non-form; non-form is neither form nor non-form—this is inconceivable.
This third question and answer precisely clarifies this meaning: it is the realm of all Buddhas, not that of the *śrāvakas*.
This is precisely the meaning of what is known by the Pratyekabuddhas.

World-Honored One, if the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas were not of form (rūpa), how could they abide? Good son, for example, the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is both form and non-form;
I also declare it to be non-form. If someone were to challenge this, saying: "If there is no perception..."
If the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception were not form, how could it abide, come, go, advance, or halt?
Such meanings are the realm of the Buddhas, not something known or understood by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. Liberation is also like this:
it is both form and non-form, yet is described as non-form; it is both perception and non-perception, yet is described as non-perception. Such meanings are the realm of the Buddhas.
This is not something known by the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Second, at that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "I only pray that you will take pity on us," and so forth; this extensively clarifies liberation through a series of questions and answers.

At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that out of compassion you will once more deign to extensively expound the meaning of the practice and liberation of the Mahāparinirvāṇa."

Question: Is this a question regarding the two practices for *nirvāṇa*, which concerns the meaning of the cause of liberation? Or is it a question regarding the fruit, which concerns the contemplation of the master?

[The Master] says: "There is no need to distinguish between cause and fruit; it is simply a question concerning this practice of liberation. [The interlocutor] says: "Virtue (*guṇa*) is practice (*caryā*). Now, I say this is not so;
rather, it is a request to elaborate upon the three meanings mentioned above. As for the character "xing" (行), its pronunciation is "heng" (衡), meaning "to be" or "to exist."
Please elaborate upon and expound these so that they may be opened up and expanded: first, please elaborate upon the meaning of "liberation" (*vimukti*);

second, please elaborate upon the meaning of "being without blemish" (*nirjvara*); third, please elaborate upon the "state of liberation" (*vimuktisthāna*). Since these three meanings have already been briefly presented, I now request their detailed exposition.
How, then, is the remainder of the liberation explained?

Regarding the response to the subsequent question, it is traditionally transmitted that there are one hundred phrases (*śata-pada*). However, according to the calculation of the head monks (*śayanāsana-adhipati*), there are only eighty-four or eighty-five;
if one calculates by combining the major and minor categories, there are ninety-seven or ninety-eight; and if one speaks with extreme precision, there are over one hundred.
Nevertheless, "one hundred" is used because it is the name for a complete number, just as, for example, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* refers to the "one hundred [perfections]."
The *Pāramitā* [Sūtra] contains only ninety [phrases] (and so forth). Since ancient times, no one has been seen to explain these hundred phrases;

only the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha’s single-fascicle *Yìjì* provides a brief commentary, yet it is difficult to understand. The Great Master Tiantai once spent an entire summer retreat at Lingshí explaining these hundred phrases.
Within each of the hundred phrases of liberation, there are all hundred phrases—thus comprising ten thousand dharma-gates in total.

Previously, I studied this for my own satisfaction but did not record it; now that there is no means to transmit it, how regrettable, how regrettable! May future generations not remain ignorant of it.
Having briefly explained liberation through the three preceding meanings, the subsequent one hundred phrases extensively clarify it.
Within each and every phrase, both horizontally and vertically, there is no flaw or defect; reaching the state of liberation, they tame sentient beings—every single phrase is exactly thus.

What are the three points? They are the complete fulfillment of the three meanings without deficiency; they are fully present and can be contemplated from afar—how could one possibly find words to express them?
Yet, lacking the power to explain them extensively, and with an unceasing desire to study and revere them, I shall now divide the text.
It begins from the passage "named 'Distant Departure'" and extends to "like the sun and moon, which do not oppress sentient beings," broadly elucidating the preceding section on non-existence.

The Meaning of Sores and Tumors (3 sheets): From "the immovable nature of names" to "not giving rise to a single thought of goodness," this extensively explains the meaning of the aforementioned section on liberation (27 lines).

From "for example, a heap of grain" to "for example, an illusory object," this extensively explains the meaning of the aforementioned section on its vast nature (1 sheet, 16 lines). Furthermore, from "having no physical body" to "able to save all."
Regarding "those who fear," this further expands upon the meaning of being "without wounds" (one page, eighteen lines).
Furthermore, from "that which is the place of refuge" up to "returning home after bathing," this further expands upon the meaning of the "place of liberation" (two pages).
Furthermore, from "the bliss of non-action" up to "severing all craving and all signs," this further expands upon the meaning of being "without wounds" (forty-seven lines). This.
Since this is a passage providing an extensive explanation, there is no fault in restating it.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa, saying, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! One who is truly liberated is called one who has distanced himself from all fetters.
If one is truly liberated and free from all fetters, then there is neither birth nor conjunction. This is an analogy.
Just as a child is born from the union of a father and mother, true liberation is not like this; therefore, liberation is called "unborn.
Kāśyapa, for example, the nature of clarified butter (ghṛta) is pure, and the Tathāgata is likewise;
he is not born from the union of a father and mother, for his nature is pure. The reason he manifests having parents is because he wishes to transform [sentient beings].
Because they deliver all sentient beings, true liberation is itself the Tathāgata; the liberation of the Tathāgata is non-dual and without distinction.
It is like when various seeds are sown in spring or autumn: upon encountering warmth and moisture, they immediately sprout.
True liberation is not like this. Furthermore, liberation is called "emptiness" (vimala); emptiness is itself liberation. Liberation is...
Liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is neither created nor a creation.
Whatever is created is like a city wall, a tower, or a pavilion; true liberation is not like this. Therefore, liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); it is not like a potter who, having finished his work, breaks it. Liberation is not so.

True liberation is neither born nor extinguished; therefore, liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is likewise neither born nor extinguished, neither aging nor dying, neither breaking nor decaying. He is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata who has entered Great Parinirvāṇa, being neither old nor dead. What is the meaning of this? "Old" is defined as...
Transformation, the whitening of hair, the wrinkling of the face, death, the dissolution of the body, the end of life—such phenomena as these do not exist within liberation.
Because these things are absent, it is called liberation. The Tathāgata likewise has no whitening of hair or wrinkling of the face;
since he is free from the conditioned phenomena [of such states], the Tathāgata does not undergo aging. Because there is no aging, there is no death. Furthermore, liberation is...
It is called "freedom from illness. As for what is called "illness," it refers to the four hundred and four types of diseases as well as other external factors that invade and damage the body;
because these are absent in this state, it is called "liberation. To be free from illness is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Since the Tathāgata is without illness, the Dharma-body is likewise without illness. Thus, there is no illness.
That which is called the death of the Tathāgata is termed the destruction of the body and the end of life; where there is no death, that is the Deathless (*amṛta*).
The Deathless is true liberation (*vimukti*), and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Since the Tathāgata has accomplished such merits, how could one say that the Tathāgata is impermanent? To say he is impermanent is impossible.
The Vajra-body is how could it be impermanent? Therefore, the Tathāgata is not said to pass away. The Tathāgata is pure and free from defilement;
the body of the Tathāgata is not sullied by the womb, just as the *puṇḍarīka* is pure by nature.
The liberation of the Tathāgata is likewise so. Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is pure.
Furthermore, "pure and stainless liberation" means that all the sores and wounds of the outflows (*āsrava*) are forever eliminated without remainder;
the Tathāgata is likewise, possessing none of the sores and wounds of the outflows. Furthermore, "liberation" is without strife or contention.

For example, a hungry person seeing the food of another gives rise to greed and the thought of seizing it; liberation is not like this. Furthermore, "liberation" is called "tranquility. Ordinary people...
The lady said: "What is called 'tranquil and still' refers to Maheśvara; such words are themselves false and illusory.
True tranquility and stillness is ultimate liberation, and ultimate liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is named 'peaceful security.
A place with many bandits is not called peaceful; only a clear and level place is called peaceful."
Within this liberation there is no fear; therefore, it is called "peaceful security. Thus, peaceful security is true liberation.
True liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma. Furthermore, liberation has no equal.
Those who have equals are like various kings who have neighboring kingdoms as their peers; true liberation, however, is not so.
To be "without equal" means that there is no one who can equal him, just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) has no peer; liberation is likewise without equal.

One who is without equal is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata, the King who turns the Wheel of Dharma. Therefore, the Tathāgata has no equal; it is impossible for him to have an equal.
Furthermore, liberation is called being without sorrow. Those who possess sorrow are like a king who, fearing a formidable neighbor, gives rise to anxiety.
For one who is liberated, such things do not exist; it is like having destroyed an enemy, whereby there is no further worry.
Liberation is likewise free from sorrow and fear. That which is free from sorrow and fear is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is...
It is called "without sorrow or joy. For example, suppose a woman has an only son who has gone away on official service and she suddenly receives news of his death;
hearing this, she suffers in grief. Later, she hears that he is alive and thus gives rise to joy. Within liberation, however, there is no such thing.
That which is without sorrow or joy is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, as for liberation:
It is free from dust and defilement. For example, in the spring months, after the sun has set, winds may rise and stir up clouds of dust;
yet within liberation, no such thing exists. This absence of dust and mist is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
Just as the bright jewel in the topknot of a noble cakravartin king is free from all impurity, the nature of liberation is likewise so.
That which is without defilement and has no defiler is like true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Just as the nature of pure gold, unmixed with sand or stone, is called a true jewel, and someone who obtains it conceives the notion that it is wealth, so too is the nature of liberation.
That true jewel is an analogy for true liberation.
True liberation is the Tathāgata. For example, when an earthen jar is broken, its sound is harsh;
a diamond-jewel jar is not like this. Liberation likewise has no such harsh breaking. The diamond-jewel jar is an analogy for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the body of the Tathāgata is indestructible; that which has a harsh sound is not so.
Just as castor seeds placed in a great heat burst forth with a loud crackling sound, such is not the case for one who has attained liberation.

Like a vessel made of genuine diamond-jewels, which makes no sound of cracking even if a multitude of countless hundreds of thousands of people were to shoot at it together and none could destroy it—making no sound of cracking—such is true liberation; such is the one who has attained true liberation.
This is like a Tathāgata who, like a poor man, was bound by others with shackles and fetters and subjected to the suffering of whips and punishments because he owed them goods;
yet within liberation there is no such thing, for there is no debt.
It is like a wealthy elder who possesses immeasurable billions of treasures and has sovereign power, owing nothing to others; such is liberation.
It is also thus: possessing immeasurable wealth of Dharma, jewels, power, and sovereignty, one has no debts and is free from those who might demand payment;
this is like true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called being free from oppression—like crossing through the heat of spring, eating sweets on a summer day, or experiencing cold on a winter day. Within true liberation, [there is no such suffering].
There is no such unpleasant matter that causes distress, just as true liberation is free from distress;
true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, being free from distress is like a person who has eaten their fill of fish and meat and then drinks milk:
such a person will soon approach death. In true liberation, there is no such thing. If a person...
It is just as when one obtains the excellent medicine of ambrosia and the ailment is thereby removed; so it is with one who has attained true liberation.
The excellent medicine of ambrosia is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata. How could there be any oppression or lack of oppression?
It is like an ordinary person who, being arrogant and self-exalting, thinks to himself: "Among all things, who is able to harm me?"
If one were to seize a snake, a tiger, or a venomous insect, you should know that such a person would not exhaust their natural lifespan but would instead die an untimely death;
however, within true liberation, no such thing occurs. As for "not being oppressed":

it is like the divine jewel possessed by a *cakravartin* king, which can subdue dung beetles and ninety-six kinds of venomous insects and the like. If anyone should hear the fragrance of this divine jewel, [they will be liberated].
The extinction of all poisons in true liberation is likewise; it is the complete distancing from the twenty-five poisons.
That which is the extinction of poisons is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, that which is without oppression is like space; liberation is also thus. That space is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
That which is liberated is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, that which is oppressive is like various lamps burning near dry grass;
when they are close, it blazes intensely. Within true liberation, no such thing exists. Moreover, that which is not oppressive is like the sun and moon, which do not oppress sentient beings;
liberation is likewise, for there is no oppression toward any sentient beings. There being no oppression is like [the following]:
True liberation—true liberation—is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the "unmoving dharma," just as there is no distinction between enemy and friend within true liberation; such things do not exist therein.
Moreover, that which is unmoving is like a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who has no other noble king to serve as a close friend; if there were another friend...
Such a state does not exist; liberation is likewise thus, for there is no longer any kinship, and if there were kinship, such a state would also not exist.
That king having no kin is like true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, that which is immovable is like a plain white garment that easily takes dye, but liberation is not so.
That which is immovable is like the vārṣika flower; it is impossible for it to have an odor or to be blue.
Liberation is likewise: it is impossible for it to have an odor or various colors. Therefore, liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "rare," just as a lotus flower grows within water, yet is not [of the water].
It is rare for one to be born within fire; it is truly rare for someone to see this and immediately give rise to joy.
It is likewise with true liberation: whoever sees it gives rise to joy in their heart.
That which is rare is an analogy for true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharmakāya. Furthermore:
This is rare: it is like an infant whose teeth have not yet grown; only as they gradually grow larger do the teeth finally emerge.
Liberation is not otherwise; it is neither produced nor unproduced. Furthermore, liberation is called empty and tranquil, and there is no uncertainty therein.

"Uncertainty" refers to those such as the icchantikas who ultimately do not shift [from their state], or those who have committed the grave prohibitions and thus do not achieve the Buddha-way—there is no such thing.
Why is this so? If a person attains pure faith in the Buddha’s True Dharma, at that moment they immediately extinguish the state of an icchantika.
Furthermore, if they become a lay follower (upāsaka), they are likewise able to extinguish the state of an icchantika.
One who has committed a grave transgression, having extinguished this sin, shall then attain Buddhahood. Therefore, it cannot be said that [the attainment of Buddhahood] is definitively impossible.
It is impossible that one who has shifted [from this state] would fail to achieve the Buddha-way; in true liberation, there is absolutely no such matter of extinction.
Furthermore, that which is empty and quiescent falls within the Dharma-realm; as the nature of the Dharma-realm, it is true liberation.
True liberation is itself the Tathāgata. Moreover, if an icchantika were to be completely extinguished, they could no longer be called an icchantika.

What is meant by the term *icchantika*? An *icchantika* is one who has severed all roots of goodness and whose mind does not take any wholesome dharmas as an object of focus, such that not even a single thought of goodness arises.
Within true liberation, such things do not exist; because such things do not exist, it is indeed true liberation. True liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "immeasurable. For example, the measure of a heap of grain can be known, but true liberation is not like that.
It is like the great ocean, which cannot be measured; liberation is likewise immeasurable.
That which is immeasurable is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called the immeasurable Dharma.
Just as a single sentient being has manifold karmic retributions, so too is liberation: it possesses immeasurable retributions.
That which possesses immeasurable retributions is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata. Moreover, liberation is...
It is named "Vast," like the great ocean, with nothing equal to it; liberation is likewise, with nothing able to equal it.
That which has no equal is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "Supreme"; just as space is the highest and beyond compare, liberation is likewise the highest and beyond compare.
That which is unsurpassed is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "that which cannot be surpassed.
For example, wherever a lion dwells, none of the hundred beasts can surpass it;
liberation is likewise such that nothing can surpass it. That which cannot be surpassed is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "unsurpassed. For example, just as the northern direction is the highest among all directions, so too is liberation unsurpassed.
That which is unsurpassed is true liberation; that which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "the supreme of the unsurpassed. For example, just as the north is superior to the east.
The same applies to unsurpassed liberation. That which is unsurpassed and beyond the unsurpassed is true liberation;
true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called the eternal dharma (*dharmatā*).
For example, when the bodies of humans and devas perish and their lives end, this is called "eternal," not "non-eternal. Liberation is likewise not non-eternal.
That which is not non-constant is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "firmly abiding. Just as *khatāra*, sandalwood, and aloeswood are solid and substantial in nature, so too is liberation—its nature is solid and substantial.
That whose nature is solid and substantial is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "non-void. For example, the substance of bamboo and reeds is hollow and fragile;
liberation is not like this. One should know that liberation is precisely the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "incorruptible.

It is like a wall that has not yet been plastered or decorated: mosquitoes and gnats may alight upon it and sport there, but once it has been plastered and adorned with colorful paintings and carvings, they cannot do so.
When the insects smell the fragrant colors, they immediately cease to stay; this lack of staying is an analogy for true liberation.
True liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "boundless. For example, villages all have boundaries and limits, but liberation is not so.
For example, space has no boundaries or limits; liberation is likewise without boundaries or limits.
