Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "invisible";
it is like the track of a bird in the sky, difficult to see. This difficulty of being seen is an analogy for true liberation. True liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "profound. Why? Because it cannot be entered by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
One who is able to enter is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, "profound" refers to that which is revered by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. For example, the merit of a filial child nourishing their parents is profound;
this profound merit is like true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata. Moreover, liberation is named...
It is invisible; for example, just as a person cannot see the crown of their own head, so too is liberation.
It cannot be seen by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. That which cannot be seen is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "having no abode"; just as space has no abode, so too is liberation. Thus it is said.
A house is a metaphor for the twenty-five states of existence; the absence of a house is a metaphor for true liberation.
True liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "ungraspable. Just as an *āmala* fruit can be grasped and held by a person, liberation is not so;
it cannot be grasped or held. That which cannot be grasped or held is true liberation; true liberation is [the Tathāgata].
That which is thus is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "ungraspable.
For example, just as illusory objects cannot be grasped or held, so too is liberation ungraspable and cannot be held. That which is ungraspable is true liberation;
true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is bodiless. It is like a person whose body is afflicted with scabies, leprosy, various abscesses, madness, or emaciation;
within true liberation, there are no such ailments. Being free from such ailments is the analogy for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "one taste," just as milk has one taste.
Liberation is also like this, having but a single flavor. This single flavor is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called purity; it is like water free of mud, clear and still.
Liberation is also like this—clear and still, pure and serene. This clarity, stillness, and purity is true liberation. True liberation is...
Furthermore, this Tathāgata is also called liberation. Liberation is termed "one flavor," just as rain from the sky is of one flavor;
it is pure and of one flavor, and this purity of one flavor is a metaphor for true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is termed "removal," just as the full moon is free from all clouds and obscurations; liberation is likewise free from all clouds and obscurations.
To be free from all clouds and obscurations is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called tranquility.
For example, when a person’s feverish illness is cured, their body attains tranquility; liberation is likewise: the body attains tranquility.
When the body attains tranquility, that is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is equanimity. For example, in a wild field, both a venomous snake and a weasel possess a murderous intent;
liberation is not like this, for it is devoid of murderous intent. That which is free from murderous intent is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Moreover, equanimity is like the impartial heart of parents toward their children; liberation is likewise so.
That mind is an impartial mind; that which is an impartial mind is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "having no other place. For example, it is like a person who dwells only in a supreme, wondrous, and pure house, having no other place to go.
Liberation is also like this: there is no other place. That which has no other place is true liberation.
True liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "contentment.
For example, when a hungry person encounters sweet delicacies, they eat them without satiety; liberation is not like this. It is like eating milk-rice:
once one has had it, there is nothing further required. Having no further requirement is like true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, as for liberation...
It is called "severing," just as when a person who has been bound severs their bonds and attains release;
liberation is likewise the severing of all fetters of doubt. Thus, the severing of doubt is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "reaching the other shore. For example, a great river has this shore and that shore, but liberation is not like this.
Although there is no "this shore," there is a "far shore. That which is the far shore is true liberation;
that which is true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called silence.
For example, the waters of the great ocean overflow and abound with many sounds, but liberation is not like this. Such liberation is the Tathāgata. Moreover, as for liberation:
It is called "Exquisite" because it is like a mixture of various medicines with *harītakī*, which is bitter in taste;
liberation is not so, for its flavor is like nectar. Its flavor being like nectar is an analogy for true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is the removal of all afflictions (*kleśa*), just as a skilled physician compiles various medicines to effectively treat all manner of diseases.
Liberation is also like this: it can eliminate afflictions. That which eliminates afflictions is true liberation;
true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "unconfined. For example, a small house cannot accommodate many people, but liberation is not so;
it accommodates much. That which accommodates much is true liberation; true liberation is...
This is precisely the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called the extinction of all cravings and the absence of impure desire.
For example, a woman has many cravings and desires, but liberation is not so. Such liberation is the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata is thus free from the fetters of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and the like. Moreover, liberation is called "the absence of craving."
There are two kinds of craving: first, the craving of hungry ghosts; second, the craving for the Dharma.
One who has attained true liberation is free from the craving of hungry ghosts, yet possesses the craving for the Dharma out of compassion for sentient beings.
Such craving for the Dharma is itself true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is the relinquishing of "I" and "mine"; such liberation is the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata is the Dharma itself; furthermore, liberation is the cessation that is free from all craving for existence—such liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma itself. Furthermore, liberation is protection;
it is that which can rescue one from all fears—such liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma itself.
This is precisely the Dharma.
The Master [Hui]guan interpreted one or two phrases in a biased manner, saying: "Liberation is not so; although this shore does not exist, there is a 'far shore.
If these two are relative, then to negate both is like negating 'this' and 'that. Once 'this' and 'that' have departed..."

Later, it is concluded by means of "neither that nor this," as for example, when concluding with "the Great" by means of "neither small nor large," or concluding with "the other shore" by means of "neither that nor this.
Furthermore, there is an interpretation based on relative dependence (*apekṣā*):

just as falling into evil is contrasted with ascending to goodness, so too is "this shore"—which is *saṃsāra*—contrasted with "the other shore," which is named *nirvāṇa*. This is intended to disparage the inferior and to honor the superior.
Because it is supreme and exalted, it is said that although this shore does not exist, there is a further shore.
Furthermore, liberation is the place of refuge; if one has such a refuge as this liberation, one seeks no other support.
It is like a person who relies upon a king and seeks no other support; although they rely upon the king, there is still the possibility of being moved or displaced.
That which relies on liberation is without movement; that which is without movement is true liberation.
True liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma. Furthermore, liberation is called a dwelling place.
For example, if a person travels through a vast wilderness, there are dangers and difficulties; liberation is not so, for it has no dangers and no difficulties.
That which is perilous and difficult is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is fearlessness:
just as the lion king feels no fear among the hundred beasts, so too does liberation feel no fear among the hosts of Māra.
He who is fearless is truly liberated; he who is truly liberated is the [Tathāgata].
Furthermore, this Tathāgata is liberated; he is not constricted, unlike a narrow path that cannot even accommodate two people walking side by side—liberation is not like that.
Such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata. Moreover, it is not constricted;
for example, it is like a person who, fearing a tiger, falls into a well—liberation is not like that. Such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata. Furthermore...
There are those who, like one in the great ocean who abandons a ruined small boat to obtain a sturdy ship, board that sturdy ship and cross the sea to reach a place of safety;
their minds attain happiness and liberation is likewise so. When the mind attains happiness, this is true liberation;
true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is the uprooting [of all afflictions].
All causes and conditions are like this: for example, one obtains curd from milk, ghee from curd, and clarified butter from ghee;
yet within true liberation, none of these causes exist. That which is without such causes is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is that which can subdue pride; it is like a great king who holds small kings in contempt—liberation is likewise.
It is not so; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation is the subduing of all negligence; "negligence" refers to having much craving, whereas true liberation is devoid of this.
That which is devoid of this is true liberation, and true liberation is itself the Tathāgata. Moreover, liberation...
This [wisdom] can remove ignorance, just as the finest clarified butter (*ghṛta*) removes all dregs and impurities; this is called *amṛta* (the supreme nectar). Liberation is also like this:
by removing the dregs of ignorance, true illumination emerges. This true illumination is itself true liberation.
True liberation is none other than the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called tranquility—pure, singular, and non-dual—like the open wilderness.
The elephant is solitary and without peer; liberation is likewise solitary and without a second. To be solitary and without a second is true liberation.
True liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "solid and real.
Just as the stalks of bamboo, reeds, and castor-oil plants are hollow while their seeds are solid and real, none among the other humans or devas—except for the Buddha, the Tathāgata—possess this.
The firm and solid true liberation is far removed from all streams of existence (*bhava-srotas*); such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "awakening and realizing" that which increases my true self;
true liberation is likewise thus. Such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "abandoning all existences," just as...
When someone has finished eating and then vomits, liberation is also like this: to abandon all modes of existence (*bhava*) is true liberation;
one who abandons all modes of existence is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "the definitive" (*niyata*);
just as the fragrance of the *pāṭalī* flower does not exist within its seven leaves, so too is it with liberation. This liberation is the Tathāgata. Moreover—

Liberation is called the water element (*āpas*). Just as the water element is superior among the elements because it can moisten all grasses, trees, and seeds, liberation is likewise able to moisten all classes of sentient beings.
Such liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "entry," just as a gateway provides a path for entry. Gold... [text fragment]... provides a path for entry.
The liberation of one whose nature resides in gold is likewise so;
just as one who cultivates non-self enters through that gateway, such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "good," just as a disciple who follows his teacher and faithfully observes his instructions is called "good"; liberation is also like this.
This liberation is itself the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called the supramundane dharma;
among all dharmas, it is the most transcendent, just as clarified butter and milk are the most excellent among all flavors. Liberation is likewise so. This liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "immovable"; for example, it is like a door-sill which the wind cannot move. True [liberation] is thus.

Liberation is also like this; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "waveless," for while the waters of the great ocean have waves and billows, liberation is not so;
such liberation is itself the Tathāgata. Moreover, liberation is like a palace; one should know that liberation is itself [the Tathāgata].
Furthermore, this liberation of the Tathāgata is called "that which is employed," like Jāmbūnada gold, which has many uses and no one can speak of any defects in that gold.
Liberation is also like this: it has no defects; that which has no defects is true liberation.
True liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is the relinquishing of infantile conduct.
For example, just as an adult abandons the behavior of a child, so too is liberation. To abandon the five aggregates is to abandon them;
this abandonment of the five aggregates is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "ultimate," just as one who has been bound, having been released from those bonds, bathes, becomes pure, and then returns home—liberation is also like this.
Ultimate purity, ultimate purity is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the bliss of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-sukha*). One who experiences the bliss of non-action has already vomited forth greed, hatred, and delusion.
It is like a person who, having mistakenly drunk poisonous medicine, takes an emetic to eliminate the poison; once he has vomited it out, [he is restored].
Just as poison is immediately eliminated and the body attains peace and happiness, liberation is also like this:

one expels the poison of the fetters of all afflictions (*kleśa*), and the body attains peace and happiness, which is called the bliss of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-sukha*). This bliss of non-action is true liberation;
true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is named the severing of the four kinds of poisonous snakes of affliction; to sever these afflictions is [liberation].

This is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is named the departure from all states of existence (*bhava*), the extinction of all suffering, and the attainment of all happiness.
It is the eternal severance of greed, hatred, and delusion, and the uprooting of the very foundation of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
To uproot this foundation is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is defined as the severance of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and the production of all untainted wholesome phenomena (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*).
It is the cutting off of all paths—namely, the notions of self, non-self, neither self nor non-self, and neither not-self—which means only severing attachment without severing the view of self.
This view of self is called the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and the Buddha-nature is true liberation; true liberation is [the ultimate state].
That which is thus is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "not empty of emptiness. "Empty of emptiness" refers to that which has nothing whatsoever;

that which has nothing whatsoever is the liberation conceived by the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others, yet because those Nirgranthas actually possess no liberation, it is called "empty of emptiness.
True liberation is not like this; therefore, it is "not empty of emptiness."
That which is not empty of emptiness is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called "not empty.
It is like a jar that once contained water, wine, milk, curd, ghee, or honey:
even when it no longer contains water, wine, curd, ghee, or honey, it is still called a "water-jar" and so forth. Yet, one cannot say of such jars that they are either empty or not empty.
If emptiness were said to be empty, then there could be no form, fragrance, taste, or touch;

yet if it were said not to be empty, then there would likewise be no water, wine, and so forth. True liberation is also like this: it cannot be described as form or non-form, nor can it be described as empty or non-empty.
If it were said to be empty, then there could be no permanence, bliss, self, or purity; yet if it were said not to be...
Who would receive this emptiness as being permanent, blissful, self, and pure? For this reason, it cannot be said that emptiness is [the same as] non-emptiness.
"Emptiness" refers to the absence of the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), all afflictions (*kleśa*), all suffering, all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*);
it is like a jar being called "empty" when it contains no curd. "Non-emptiness" refers to true reality and goodness.
Form is permanent, blissful, self, and pure; it is immovable and unchanging, just like that jar. Because it possesses form, fragrance, taste, and touch, it is called "not empty.
Therefore, liberation is like that jar. While that jar may be destroyed when encountering conditions, liberation is not so;
it cannot be destroyed. That which cannot be destroyed is true liberation. True liberation is itself Suchness (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, liberation is called the departure from craving. For example, suppose there were a person whose heart was filled with craving and hope for Śakra Devānām-indra, Mahābrahmā, or Maheśvara; such a person would not attain liberation.
However, once one has realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one is without craving and without doubt. To be without craving and without doubt is true liberation, true liberation.
Liberation is the Tathāgata. It is impossible that one who has attained liberation could still possess craving or doubt.

Furthermore, liberation is the severing of all craving for existence, the severing of all signs, all fetters, all afflictions, all birth and death, all causes and conditions, and all karmic retributions. Such liberation is the Tathāgata. Thus it is.
Coming [to this realization] is itself nirvana.
Furthermore, liberation consists in severing the four venomous snakes and taking the four dull latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) as four serpents—namely, greed, hatred, delusion, and pride.

It is correctly said that these four pervade both the views and the afflictions (*kleśa*), capable of wounding the Dharma-body and damaging the life-force of wisdom. [The question asks: How are they severed?
Delusion is the cause and liberation is the fruit. How is liberation attained? It is by severing the four poisonous snakes.

The Kaishan school cites a sutra stating: "The power of ignorance is great; it can be severed by the Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom. Regarding the fruits, there are Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*vibuddha-bodhi*); Equal Enlightenment is that which severs [delusion]. The Zhuangyan school cites a sutra stating:
"The superior person severs the unsurpassed [ignorance]; they do not sever [it through] contemplation. Master Guan [Guanding] says: [This refers to the severing of the root of ignorance].
It is said that the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) is neither severed nor unsevered. For those whose conditions are such that they should hear of severance, it is like the Kai-shan school;

for those whose conditions are such that they should not sever, it is like the Zhuang-yang school. Now, if one relies on the meaning of the Four Teachings: in the Tripitaka Teaching, the fruit is severed while the cause is not severed;

in the Shared Teaching, the cause is severed at the time [of the path] and the fruit arises as the severance of habituation; in the Distinct Teaching, the cause is severed and the fruit is mostly severed with a remaining one part; and in the Perfect Teaching...
From cause to fruit, all are termed Buddha-wisdom; it is neither severed nor unsevered. While unsevered, it is severed; yet this severance is itself non-severance.
To sever all modes of existence is to transcend the principle of "going. Birth-and-death arises from that which lies outside this principle.

The production of untainted wholesome dharmas is precisely what constitutes nirvāṇa within the principle. As for "severing and blocking all paths," it means severing all paths characterized by "attainment. If...
The four propositions regarding self and non-self are all eliminated; yet the view of self is not eliminated, for the "self" within the principle is not eliminated.
Now I clarify that severing all existence is the refutation of the provisional; giving rise to the outflow-free is the entry into emptiness;
severing the obstructions of all paths is the simultaneous negation of the two extremes; and not eliminating the view of self is the entry into the Middle Way—this is called liberation.
The meaning of this should be clearly discerned by the wise among the various masters themselves.

Thirdly, "following the three leaps and returning to the three refuges" is a summary of liberation; furthermore, it consists of two parts: first, the summary, and second, the discussion of the doctrine.
Because all sentient beings fear birth and death as well as the various afflictions (*kleśa*), they take the three refuges (*tri-śaraṇa*).
It is like a herd of deer that, fearing a hunter, feels relieved once it has escaped; if it takes one leap, it is likened to one refuge, and three leaps are likened to the three refuges.
By means of these three leaps, it attains peace and happiness. Sentient beings are likewise: they fear the four Māras.
Because the evil hunter received the three refuges, he attained peace and happiness;
those who attain peace and happiness achieve true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata is nirvāṇa; nirvāṇa is the inexhaustible; the inexhaustible is the Buddha-nature; and the Buddha-nature is definitiveness.
That which is "definitive" is precisely *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Regarding the summary:
the three knots that eliminate fear are the "knots above" which are without sores; the three refuges are the "knots above" which are the locus of liberation.
That they are one while being three is horizontal breadth; that they are three while being one is vertical depth. This concludes the section on their nature being vast.
Because Potalaka was afraid of the hunter, he leaped three times; because he was terrified of Māra and external forces, he took the Three Refuges.

The first leap is a metaphor for taking refuge in the Saṃgha, as he was still close to the hunter; the second leap is a metaphor for taking refuge in the Dharma; and the third leap is a metaphor for taking refuge in the Buddha, whereby he finally attained peace and security.
Thus, in the passage below, it says that the frightened pigeon entered the shadow of Śāriputra, yet remained trembling with fear and found no rest. Furthermore:
Following the sequence of the Three Jewels: the first leap is a metaphor for taking refuge in the Buddha; the second leap is a metaphor for taking refuge in the Dharma;
and the third leap is a metaphor for taking refuge in the Sangha. Only by fully taking refuge in the Three Jewels does one attain fearlessness.

Some say that the preceding [leaps] constitute the three refuges as distinct entities, while the subsequent [leap] constitutes the three refuges as a single entity. This is not so; rather, within this very context, they are already a single entity.
At the time of the Three Refuges, the assembly had not yet fully understood; Kāśyapa asked again to clarify them further. Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"If the Buddha-nature is *nirvāṇa*, [the following] three matters are raised to discuss its meaning: first, the question of the Three Refuges; second, the question of unconditioned bliss;
third, the question of the non-arising and non-ceasing. Since these one hundred phrases are extensive, only these three questions are briefly cited.
I said: After the explanation of liberation, these three questions were set forth; one should believe that these three questions encompass the gateway to all dharmas.
Regarding the first question on the Three Refuges, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if Nirvāṇa, the Buddha-nature, and the Tathāgata are definitely one..."
Regarding the meaning: why is it said that there are three refuges?
Since liberation, the Tathāgata, and nirvāṇa are declared to be but a single dharma, they ought to constitute only one essence and one refuge;
why then speak of three? This is to raise three objections against the claim of oneness.
The Buddha replied that there are four reasons why it should be three: first, because its essence is sublime; second, because its names and meanings are to be distinguished;
third, because of the citation of scriptural evidence; and fourth, because of its sovereignty. Regarding the first reason—that its essence is sublime—it should be three.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "Good son, because all sentient beings fear birth and death, they seek the Three Refuges;
by means of these Three Refuges, they know that their buddha-nature and ultimate nirvana are certain."
If liberation and nirvāṇa were definitely of one essence and could not be three, they would not be wondrous or precious, nor would they be worthy of taking refuge in.
That which is three yet one, and one yet three, is truly wondrous and precious, and is thus worthy of taking refuge in.
As the text says: "Because of the fear of birth and death, one seeks the triple refuge; by means of the triple refuge, one knows that nirvāṇa is one and three."
Regarding its meaning:
next is the "Analysis of Names and Meanings.

Noble son, there are dharmas where the name is one while the meaning differs; there are dharmas where both name and meaning differ; and there are dharmas where the name is one while the meaning differs. As for those where the name is one while the meaning differs:
The Buddha is eternal; the Dharma is eternal; the Saṃgha is eternal; and Nirvāṇa and space are likewise eternal. This is called "identity of referent with difference of name.
As for the identity of referent with difference of both name and meaning: the Buddha is named "Awakened" (Buddha); the Dharma is named "Non-awakening";

the Saṃgha is named "Harmony"; Nirvāṇa is named "Liberation"; and space is named "Non-virtuous" as well as "Unobstructed. This is the identity of referent with difference of both name and meaning. Furthermore, it is also "virtuous."
The three refuges for a man are likewise thus: both name and meaning differ; how can they be one?

Liberation, the Tathāgata, and nirvāṇa are all equally permanent, and for this reason their names are the same. Yet their meanings differ. Because they share the same [quality of permanence], they are "one";

because they differ [in their specific characteristics], they are "three. Thus, although the names are three and the meanings are distinct, they may still be designated as "three" based on the names, or as "one" based on the meanings. This is how it is with names and meanings.
Since they are all distinct, how can they not be three?
Regarding the citation of the three proofs, there should be three;
therefore, I told Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī: "Do not offer worship to me; you should offer worship [to them]."
"If one makes offerings to the Saṃgha, one obtains the complete fulfillment of making offerings to the Three Refuges.
Mahāprajāpatī then replied to me, saying, "Within the Saṃgha there is neither Buddha nor Dharma;

how can you say that by making offerings to the Saṃgha, one obtains the complete fulfillment of making offerings to the Three Refuges? I further told her, "If you follow my words, you are thereby making offerings to the Buddha."
Because liberation is itself the Dharma, those who receive offerings from the Saṅgha are actually making offerings to the Dharma.
Good son, for this reason, the Three Refuges cannot be considered one.
If the Saṅgha, which possesses a distinct identity, already fully embodies the Three Jewels, how much more so must the Buddha, whose essence is one with them, not possess the Three?
"Because the four masteries are not fixed, there should be three.
Good son, the Tathāgata sometimes explains one as three and explains three as one;
such meanings are the realm of the Buddhas, and are not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

Formerly, in order to refute heterodox teachings, the One was made into Three, yet the Three did not deviate from the One; now, in order to refute sectarian views, the Three are made into the One, yet the One does not deviate from the Three.
This identity of the One and the Three is the realm of all Buddhas, not something known by those of inferior capacity.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "To inquire about 'going' and to inquire about 'non-active bliss' constitute two questions. First, this summarizes the essential meaning.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "Regarding what the Buddha has said—that ultimate peace and bliss is called *nirvāṇa*—the following objection is raised: What does this mean?
For if *nirvāṇa* involves the relinquishing of the body and the relinquishing of wisdom, and if both body and wisdom are relinquished, who then would experience that bliss?"
The meaning is this: if ultimate bliss were called *nirvāṇa*, then since there would be nothing at all, who could experience peace and happiness?
The Buddha answered in three parts: the simile, the application, and the conclusion. The Buddha said:
"Good son, it is like a person who, having eaten, feels a distress in his heart and goes outside wishing to vomit; once he has succeeded in vomiting..."
After some time, he returned once more. His companions asked him, "Has that ailment you were suffering from finally been cured, that you have come back?
He replied, "It has been cured; my body has attained peace and well-being."

The Tathāgata is likewise: he is ultimately and utterly remote from the twenty-five states of existence and has eternally attained the state of nirvāṇa, peace, and bliss, which is immovable, inexhaustible, and without cessation.
He has severed all sensation and is thus called "one who experiences non-sensation" (anupādāna-sukha).
Such non-sensation is termed "eternal bliss. It is impossible for it to be said that the Tathāgata possesses the experience of sensation.
Therefore, ultimate bliss is precisely nirvāṇa; nirvāṇa is precisely true liberation; true liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
Because of being afflicted, one vomits [it up];
because of vomiting it up, there is nothing further remaining, which is called peace and bliss. The Buddha has no sensation of pleasure.
It was also like this. Kāśyapa spoke again, saying, "Go and ask about non-arising and non-extinction. There were seven questions and answers; the first four were as in the text.
Kāśyapa spoke again, saying, "Is non-arising and non-extinction liberation? [The Buddha replied: "So it is, so it is, son of good family."
That which is neither born nor extinguished is liberation; such liberation is the Tathāgata.

Kāśyapa spoke again: "If that which is neither born nor extinguished is liberation, then the nature of empty space is also without birth or extinction and should therefore be the Tathāgata. The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "Good son, this..."

That is not so. World-Honored One, for what reason would it not be so? Good son, how could the clear and exquisite voices of the kalaviṅka and the jīvajīvaka birds possibly be the same as the cries of crows and magpies?
"No, World-Honored One. "The cries of crows and magpies compared to those of the jīvajīvaka..."
Even a hundred thousand million times [the former] cannot serve as a comparison.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "The voice of the kalaviṅka and other such birds is subtle and exquisite, yet their bodies are not the same;

how can the Tathāgata compare them? They are no different from crows and magpies. It is like comparing a mustard seed to Mount Sumeru; the relationship between the Buddha and empty space is likewise so."
The voice of the kalaviṅka bird may serve as a metaphor for the voice of the Buddha, but it cannot be used as a metaphor for the cries of crows and magpies.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You now well understand that which is extremely profound and difficult to comprehend.
There are times when the Tathāgata, for specific causes and conditions, cites empty space as a metaphor for liberation; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata."
That which is true liberation cannot be equaled by any among gods or humans; yet this empty space is truly not its metaphor.
For the sake of transforming sentient beings, that which is non-analogous—empty space—is used as a metaphor.
You should know that liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the nature of the Tathāgata is itself liberation. Liberation and the Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction, O son of good family.
That which is not an analogy is like an incomparable thing for which no analogy can be drawn; because there are causes and conditions, an analogy can be established.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "The face is as handsome as the full moon," or "the white elephant is as pure as the Snowy Mountains.
However, the full moon cannot be equated with the face, nor can the Snowy Mountains be equated with the white elephant. Good son, it is not so.

These metaphors are employed to illustrate true liberation for the sake of transforming sentient beings; through these various analogies, one should know that the nature of all phenomena is likewise so.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "Why does the Tathāgata provide two kinds of explanations?"
The fifth question asks: "In what sense does the Tathāgata make two kinds of statements? This question arises from the following:
previously, sometimes the Buddha’s body was compared to space and sometimes it was not; sometimes it was compared to clouds and thunder and sometimes it was not;
and sometimes it was said to be one and three, or three and one. Taking these as points of contention, the difficulty is raised by stating that he makes two kinds of statements.
The Buddha said, "Good son, suppose there were a person who, grasping a sword or blade with a mind of hatred, wished to harm the Tathāgata.
Would that person be able to destroy the body of the Tathāgata and thereby commit an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma)?
"No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because the constituent elements (dhātu) of the Tathāgata’s body cannot be destroyed. For what reason?"

Because there is no aggregate of a body, but only the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the principle of the nature of phenomena cannot be destroyed, how could such a person destroy the Buddha-body?

It is solely by virtue of an evil mind that one incurs the immediate retribution (*ānantarya*). By means of these causes and conditions, through the drawing forth of various parables, one comes to know the true Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! I..."
That which you wished to say has already been said. Furthermore, son of good family, it is like this:

suppose there were a wicked man who intended to harm his mother while staying in a field near a stack of grain. His mother went to bring him food, and upon seeing her, he immediately conceived a murderous intent and stepped forward to sharpen his knife.
The mother, perceiving this at once, fled and hid within the stack of grain. The man, holding his knife, circled the stack and hacked away at it everywhere as he cut.

Having already felt joy and having already conceived the thought of killing, his mother then emerged and returned home. What do you think: has this person committed an *ānantarya* (immediate) offense?
World-Honored One, it cannot be definitively stated. Why? If one says he has committed the offense, the mother’s body should have perished;
if her body did not perish, how can one say there is an offense? If one says there is no offense, yet he conceived the thought of killing after she had already been born.

With hearts full of joy, how can you say that such a person does not exist? Although this person has not fully committed the crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), they are nonetheless guilty of such a crime.
By means of these causes and conditions, various parables have been cited so that the true Dharma may be understood. The Buddha praised Kāśyapa, saying, "Excellent, excellent, good son!
For this reason, I have taught various skillful means and parables to illustrate liberation. Although...
By means of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* analogies, it is truly impossible to compare it through analogy;
yet, there are certain causes and conditions by which it may be explained through analogy, and there are certain causes and conditions for which no analogy can be cited.
Therefore, liberation achieves such immeasurable merit, and for those who proceed toward *nirvāṇa*, both *nirvāṇa* and the Tathāgata likewise possess such immeasurable merit.
Because it is fully accomplished with such immeasurable merits as these, it is called Great Parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha answered with two analogies: although the bodies of those who harm the Buddha or their mothers are not destroyed, the crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya) is already established;
thus, one cannot definitively say that the body is destroyed, yet one cannot say the body is not actually destroyed, nor can one say there is no offense, for they have indeed committed an offense.
The Tathāgata knows the proper time; he may teach definitively or indeterminately, for all four *siddhāntas* are unfailing.
The three Kāśyapas addressed the Buddha, and this was their realization.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is only now that I have come to know that the destination reached by the Tathāgata is one that has no end.
If there is no end, one should know that his life span must likewise be inexhaustible."
The four Buddhas’ praise for his departure is a statement of confirmation.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have now skillfully been able to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to sever the afflictions and all fetters of bondage, they should likewise protect and uphold the True Dharma."
The Dharma.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tiantai śramaṇa Benzhun at Riyong. Sectioned and Compiled.
Collected Commentary on the Southern Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Five;
Collected Commentary on the Southern Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Six;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Eight: The Four Reliances (Scroll Six).
Translated during the Northern Liang dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master from India, Dharmakṣema;
re-edited by the Śramaṇas Huiyan, Huiguan,
and Xie Lingyun of the Jin dynasty.

The Chapter on the Four Reliances. "Four" refers to the number. "Reliance" (niśraya) means to depend upon. Because all those in the world depend upon them to obtain benefit, they are called the four reliances.
There are two kinds of reliance: first, relying on one's own Dharma to obtain benefit; second, relying on others to obtain benefit. If one relies solely on...
The Dharma does not rely upon persons; it is not called a "reliance" [on persons]. If one were to rely on persons, one would simultaneously obtain the Dharma. As the text says:
"When four persons appear in the world, they protect, establish, and bring benefit; because their purpose is powerful, the Four Reliances are established.
This answers the previous question: "How can one attain vastness and serve as a refuge for the multitude? It refers to attaining the vast Dharma. To "attain" means to encounter a person. Directly...
The treatise states that while one may rely on the vast [teachings], it is not necessarily the case that there is a person; yet if one attains the Dharma, that person must possess the Dharma.

Since the questioner asked about attaining the Dharma and the respondent now answers regarding attaining the Dharma, we know that the names of the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*) were established based upon persons.

Furthermore, in the past, because people mixed the true with the false, one relied on the Dharma to distinguish between persons; now, because the Dharma is confused by both the Great and Small Vehicles, one relies on the person to distinguish the Dharma.
Because one relies on a true person to grasp the True Dharma, the Chapter on the Four Reliances (*Catur-pratisaraṇa-varga*) is established based upon these four types of persons.

Furthermore, in the past, when the Dharma was used to distinguish persons, it resulted in those persons having no Dharma and the Dharma itself being non-universal—like abandoning this to resort to that in order to seek empty space.

Now, it is clarified that the person is precisely that which upholds the Dharma; because one does not abandon this to resort to that, the Four Reliances are established based upon the four types of persons.
This chapter is explained according to the intent of the four *siddhāntas*. Question: The Tathāgata is a true person; why is he not depicted in the form of a Tathāgata?
Yet the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] are not true persons; why are they depicted in the forms of those four fruits? Answer:

Although the Buddha is a true person, because he appeared after the time of the Buddha [the historical Śākyamuni], he cannot be depicted in the form of the Tathāgata. As for the four fruits being called "not true persons," it refers to the four... [text breaks off].
If it is true that this is a field of merit where the path of transformation is easy to practice, one should fashion this image.

As for the question of why other images are difficult [to produce], the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* provides various demonstrations in response. To discuss this generally, all [images] may be made; specifically, there are four categories:
the Tathāgata acting as a Tathāgata, the Tathāgata acting as the Four Reliances, the Four Reliances acting as a Tathāgata, and the Four Reliances acting as the Four Reliances.
Question: The four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*) constitute the four fruits; the four fruits constitute the four fruits.

Since the four fruits cannot constitute the four reliances, although there are various meanings, we shall now follow one path: namely, that the four reliances serve as the images of the four fruits. Question:

If the Tathāgata acts as the four reliances, can the four reliances be considered as a single reliance? Answer: The aforementioned opening of one characteristic becomes four characteristics; when these four are combined, they form one.

The characteristics are one characteristic: when opened, they constitute the hundred liberations; when synthesized, they are simply the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa. Now, from this nirvāṇa, the four reliances are opened forth;
when synthesized, it is still the Buddha who constitutes the four reliances. Question: For what reason does the Buddha first command reliance on the Dharma and later command reliance on the person?
Answer: When the Buddha first appeared in the world, heterodox persons were exceedingly numerous; therefore, he caused them to rely on the True Dharma.
To exclude heterodox persons, there are no longer heterodox persons; there is only the "Small Dharma" (Hīnayāna), which one must rely upon to follow the "Right Person.

To exclude the Small Dharma, one likewise relies on the Right Person. This is because the people of the beginning [era] were sharp-witted and thus relied on the Dharma; whereas the people of the present are dull-witted and thus rely on the person. Speaking in terms of the ultimate, one relies on both person and Dharma. As the text says:
"Relying on the Dharma" refers to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena); *dharmatā* is the Tathāgata. This was previously explained as the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).

Regarding the differences in the stages and practices, according to the *Dilun* masters, the thirty minds prior to the [ten] abodes constitute the stage of the disciple (*śrāvaka*), while the thirty minds themselves constitute the stage of the teacher (*ācārya*).
From the first ground (*bhūmi*) upward is the second reliance, both of which are the stage of the teacher.

According to the *Chengshi lun* (Tattvasiddhi-śāstra) masters, the six minds prior to the ten abodes constitute the stage of the disciple, while from the seventh abode upward is the first reliance, the stage of the teacher. Furthermore, it is said that the ten...
The two moments of mind prior to these belong to the stage of a disciple; the thirteen moments of mind constitute the initial stage of relying upon a teacher.

In that vision of the *Avataṃsaka*, these thirteen moments of mind are the primary, the guide, the honored, and the supreme. Furthermore, the seventeen moments of mind prior to these belong to the stage of a disciple;
from the eighteenth moment of mind upward is the initial stage of relying upon a teacher. Moreover, those prior to the nineteenth moment of mind are...
The stage of the disciple consists of twenty mental states, culminating in the final mind of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). This is the first reliance upon the teacher’s stage.

Within the stage of the teacher, the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) do not constitute the teacher’s stage; rather, from the initial mind of the first *vihāra* up to the sixth *vihāra* is the first reliance upon the teacher’s stage.
From the seventh *vihāra* through the seventh ground (*bhūmi*) is the second reliance upon the stage. The eighth and ninth grounds constitute the third reliance upon the stage.
The tenth stage is the fourth [of the four] positions of reliance (*āśraya*). Regarding the distinctions of these positions: in the first [position], there are afflictions but no nirvāṇa;
in the latter, there is nirvāṇa but no afflictions. There is no difference between them in that both the beginning and the end possess both afflictions and nirvāṇa.

However, while "stage" (*bhūmi*) refers to the meaning of distinction, "treatise" (*śāstra*) refers to the meaning of perfection. As for the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, it does not [apply to] the thirty minds.

If one eliminates distinct delusions while remaining within the intermediate stage, neither the "distinct" nor the "perfect" [approaches] are established. Now, regarding those before the stages (*bhūmi*) who have not yet eliminated distinct delusions, this constitutes the first reliance;
regarding those on the stages who have eliminated distinct delusions, the establishment of three reliances constitutes the distinct meaning.

Regarding the ten levels of faith as the first reliance, and the elimination of distinct delusions through the thirty minds and the ten stages as the establishment of three reliances, this constitutes the perfect meaning.

Regarding the meaning of "perfect" (*yuan*), there is both a general and a specific interpretation. The general interpretation holds that the forty stages of mind (*xixin*) collectively constitute the four reliances (*sishi*).

The specific interpretation holds that the ten stages of faith (*shixin*) are the first reliance; from the first dwelling (*zhuzhu*) to the sixth dwelling is the second reliance; from the seventh dwelling to the ninth dwelling is the third reliance;
and the tenth dwelling is the fourth reliance. All other cases follow this pattern. Regarding the clarification of the first reliance, there are masters who explain it as follows: [text continues].

The position of the younger brother is not so now; the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) pertain generally to the stage of the teacher, for they can act as a support for the world, while they pertain specifically to the stage of the disciple, for they involve the wide proclamation of the Buddha-dharma. To discuss them separately:

the first reliance pertains only to the disciple, the last reliance pertains only to the teacher, and the middle two relyances pertain to both teacher and disciple (and so forth). This chapter is divided into eight sections, the first of which is the heading.

1. Distinguishing Names and Characteristics; 2. Explaining Benefits; 3. Clarifying the Time of Emergence; 4. Discourse on Planting Causes; 5. Judging Offenses and Merits; 6. Exhorting to Offerings; 7.
Discerning the True from the False; 8. Harmonizing the Present and the Past. Regarding the first section, there are three parts:
1. Designating the Chapter and Praising; 2. Enumerating the Number and Praising; 3. Indicating the Characteristics and Praising. As for "Designating the Chapter":

The Buddha again addressed Kāśyapa: "Good son, within this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, there are four kinds of people who can protect the True Dharma, establish the True Dharma, and keep the True Dharma in mind;
they are able to bring great benefit and compassion to the world, serving as a refuge for the world and bringing peace and happiness to devas and humans."
Within the Great Parinirvāṇa, there are four kinds of persons; because all four attain the dharma of nirvāṇa, they are called "persons within nirvāṇa.
If all equally attain the dharma, why is it that the first basis possesses a nature of afflictions? Now, it is clarified that the attainment of the dharma is of many types:
the first basis attains the dharma in a semblance, while the latter three attain the dharma in its reality. When reality and semblance are discussed together, they are all included therein.
In this context of *nirvāṇa*, there is praise for the virtues of these four types of persons in both practicing for themselves and transforming others.

Because they prevent others from being disturbed by external conditions in places where the Buddha-dharma exists, it is said that "they are able to protect. Because they are able to cause [the Dharma] to flourish and manifest in places where the Buddha-dharma does not exist, it is said that "they establish it.
Because they are able to maintain and uphold [the Dharma] in both places—where it exists and where it does not—it is said that "they are mindful. These are the three phrases.
Regarding the virtue of self-cultivation: because it can cause [the Dharma] to flourish wherever the Buddha-dharma exists, it is said to "bring great benefit";

because it enables beings to see and hear [the Dharma] where the Buddha-dharma does not exist, it is said to be "compassionate"; and because it serves as a dual support for both these conditions—where the Dharma exists and where it does not—it is now understood that this phrase praises the virtue of benefiting others.
Second, regarding "from what [do they arise]? and "what are the four?", this enumerates and praises them. What are the four?
There is one who appears in the world who possesses the nature of afflictions; this is called the first, the *srotāpanna*.
The *sakṛdāgāmin* is called the second. The *anāgāmin* is called the third. The *arhat* is [the fourth].

This is called the fourth [category]. These four kinds of persons appear in the world to bring great benefit and compassion to the world, serving as a refuge for the world and bringing peace and happiness to humans and devas.

One who possesses the nature of afflictions is designated as the first; according to the provisional teaching (biejiao), this refers to those in the thirty stages of mind (sishixin), while according to the perfect teaching (yuanjiao), it refers to...

The judgment is that these two stages belong to the position of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Since both sever the common delusions (*sāmānya-kleśa*), one cannot say they "possess afflictions" (*kleśa-vastu*);
however, since the distinct delusions (*viśeṣa-kleśa*) are all suppressed and do not arise—though their nature still persists—it is said they "possess the nature of afflictions.

Next, regarding the designation of the first two fruits as the "second," this is according to the judgment of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-deśanā*): from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the sixth stage. If...

According to one specific path of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), from the first abode (*zhù*) up to the sixth abode, these correspond—according to the common vehicle—to the stages from the Ground of Seeing (*jiàn-dì*) to the Ground of Thinness (*bó-dì*), all of which have not yet abandoned desire.
If one follows the Mahāyāna perspective, even up to the seventh ground there are those who have not yet abandoned the physical body (and so forth).
Regarding the third reliance, if it is based on the doctrinal classification of the teachings, it refers to the eighth and ninth grounds; however, if one relies on the Perfect Teaching...

The distinct judgment of this single path of teaching resides in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). According to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) judgment, one who has attained the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) [is no longer] subject to rebirth in the desire realm;
according to the Mahāyāna judgment, they are at the stage of the seventh *bhūmi*, having become a Non-returner from the three realms, and so forth. The fourth fruit can be understood [in this way].
However, if one were to judge it in detail according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), [it would be as follows], and so forth.

Regarding the third section, "The Threefold Following," what is meant by "going"? This is a demonstration of characteristics and a praise in two parts: first, the demonstration of the characteristics of the four types of persons;

second, a general praise of their virtues. The initial text itself consists of four sections. Regarding the first person, there are three parts: first, the characteristics of the path of subduing; second, the characteristics of cultivation;
third, the characteristics of the stage. First, regarding the path of subduing:
What is meant by "possessing the nature of afflictions"?

Because the afflictions have not yet been eliminated, it is called "possessing" (*samanvāgata*); because the objects [of the afflictions] have already been suppressed but the essence of the delusions remains, it is called "nature" (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, this refers to the path of suppression.
Next, regarding the characteristics of practice:
if there is someone who can uphold the prohibitive precepts and be fully endowed with dignified deportment, establishing the True Dharma;
having heard it from the Buddha, they understand its words and meaning and explain them in detail for others, namely that few desires and many desires are both not the Path.
Having extensively explained these eight awakenings of great persons, he instructs those who have committed offenses to reveal them, repent, and eliminate them;
he also thoroughly understands the secret dharmas practiced through the skillful means of bodhisattvas.
The practice for subduing delusions does not go beyond the practices for oneself and others; the practice for oneself does not go beyond the two trainings of precepts and wisdom;
and transforming others does not go beyond generating good and destroying evil and transgressions. To speak further, these do not go beyond the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real:

skillfully knowing expedient means is provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), and the secret dharma is real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). This can be seen by examining the text. As for the "Eight Great Persons' Awakenings" (*aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavitarkāḥ*):

The *Sutra on the Bequeathed Teaching* states: "Few desires and contentment, detachment, diligence, right mindfulness, right concentration, and right wisdom—these are free from frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Few desires are the path; many desires are not the path... up to: freedom from frivolous proliferation is the path;
frivolous proliferation is not the path," and so forth.
The three positions are established through three successive stages: first, distinguishing the ordinary person from the noble one; second, distinguishing the noble one from the ordinary person;
and finally, distinguishing the cause from the fruit to determine their respective stations.
This is called the "ordinary person" (pṛthagjana) and not the "eighth person" (aṣṭamaka). One who is the eighth person is not called an ordinary person, but is named a bodhisattva.
They are not called Buddhas.

Initially, these are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and not noble ones (*ārya*); as for the Bodhisattvas who are neither Buddhas nor "eighth persons" (*aṣṭamaka*), they are explained by means of the shared stages (*sabhūmi*).

The "eighth person" refers to the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), whereas the initial stage relies on the path of suppression (*vibandhamārga*); therefore, it is not the eighth. Furthermore, one proceeds from the later toward the earlier.
Because the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*) is the eighth, it is said that they are not "eighth persons.

Regarding the second [category], the characteristics based on reliance are also threefold: first, the characteristic of realization; second, the characteristic of practice; and third, the characteristic of position.
As for the second type of person, they are called *srotāpanna* or *sakṛdāgāmin* if they have attained the True Dharma.

Regarding the characteristics of initial realization: if one attains the True Dharma, it means that through the realization of the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), specific delusions are eliminated and the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is manifested.
Because one accords with the Dharma and attains it through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is said that "one attains the Dharma."
To uphold the True Dharma means to hear the Dharma from the Buddha; having heard it as it was taught, one writes it down, upholds it, recites it, and explains it to others.
If, after hearing the Dharma, one does not write it down, receive it, uphold it, or speak it, yet claims that the Buddha permitted the keeping of slaves and impure things—such a thing is impossible.
Next, regarding the aspect of practice, those who uphold the True Dharma arise from the Truth to engage in practice;

for example, even the practices of the Śrāvaka path of cultivation do not fail to include both self-benefit and benefiting others. However, when one realizes the Way and practices, the mind is purely Dharma and contains no non-Dharma.
Therefore, it is impossible for there to be any impure things that the Buddha permitted one to possess. (Thus it is said.)
(Thus it is said).
Third, this is called the minor difficulty of the lower stage.
This is called the second person; such a person has not yet attained the second or third dwelling place, and is thus named a bodhisattva.
Sā has already received the prediction (vyākaraṇa).

The old [translation] states that he had not yet attained the form and formless absorptions (rūpa-ārūpya-samādhi), and furthermore, regarding the four patiences (kṣānti), it was argued that he had only attained suppression and compliance, but had not yet attained non-arising (anutpāda) and cessation (nirvāṇa).
Now it is clarified that if one follows the former case, this should likewise be so; for the former excludes the latter.
This is called the second person; by means of this, those prior who have not yet attained the second or third dwelling places are excluded.
According to the Hīnayāna, the Buddha is first, Śāriputra is second, and Ānanda is third. Here, as in the previous case, those subsequent [to the Buddha] are excluded by the same principle;
thus, the Buddha is first, the fourth reliance (the fourth *niśraya*) is second, and the third reliance is third.
This person has not yet attained such second or third stages of abiding; they are called a Bodhisattva because they are in the causal stage.

Having already received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), they are certain to attain the fruit. Because this person has severed ignorance and perceives the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), once the conditions ripen, they are able to achieve the Way through the eight aspects of manifestation;
therefore, it is said that they have "already received the prediction. None of the three ancient interpretations are acceptable.
Jie Hexi says that later generations receive their names from the first person:
the fourth from the third, the third from the second, and the second from the first; thus, they are named after the first person.

As for why they have not yet attained the dwelling-places of the second and third, Master Guan says that the ordinary and the sage together constitute a single reliance, which is simply the initial reliance.
Regarding the fact that the second and third abodes have not yet been attained, the first two fruits are grouped together as the second basis, based on the *Ekottarika-āgama*.
This is because the first fruit has not yet attained the second, and the second fruit has not yet attained the third;

thus, these two fruits are shown to be alike in their state of non-attainment and identical in their nature as active effort (*prayoga*). This interpretation is easy to understand and differs from other views.

The Master now clarifies that, according to the Complete Teaching (Yuanjiao), since a person relying on the first stage has already severed the pervasive afflictions and is forever separated from the three realms, how could there be a second reliance?
Furthermore, one who has not yet attained a dwelling place in the form or formless realms cannot constitute a second reliance.

According to the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), even at the stage prior to the grounds (diqian), the initial reliance also severs the pervasive afflictions and has already transcended the three realms; therefore, it is improper to designate the form and formless realms as a second reliance.
Thirdly, one should not regard the first fruit as the first dwelling place and the *sakṛdāgāmin* as the second dwelling place;

for the characteristics of a person are also threefold: first, the characteristic of realization (*pratisaṃvid-lakṣaṇa*); second, the characteristic of practice (*caryā-lakṣaṇa*); and third, the characteristic of stage (*avasthā-lakṣaṇa*).
The third person is called an Anāgāmin. An Anāgāmin who slanders the True Dharma—such as by saying that it is permitted to keep slaves, servants, and attendants, or to accept impure things;
or by upholding the scriptures and treatises of external paths;
or by being obstructed by adventitious afflictions and covered by long-standing defilements; or by concealing the true relics of the Tathāgata—is such a person.
Furthermore, it is impossible for one to be afflicted by external diseases or invaded by the four great poisonous snakes while still maintaining the doctrine of a self;
it is only possible if one speaks of non-self. It is impossible to speak of the worldly dharmas as having permanence;
it is only possible if one speaks of the continuity of the Mahāyāna being uninterrupted. It is only possible that the body one receives contains eighty thousand families of worms.
It is impossible for an insect to be forever free from sexual desire, yet it is possible that one does not discharge impurity even in dreams;
it is also impossible for one to feel fear on the day of their death.
The characteristics of the initial realization are here briefly shown as the purification of the three karmas: not slandering the True Dharma is the purity of speech;
being free from adventitious defilements is the purity of mind; and not concealing the *śarīra* (relics) is the purity of body.

While the *dharmakāya* was previously hidden and obscured by bone and flesh, it is now called the *tathāgatagarbha*; now that the *dharmakāya* is manifest, the *śarīra* are no longer concealed. Thus...
This body is pure; not speaking of a self further clarifies purity of speech. Receiving a body free of parasites further clarifies purity of body.
Being without fear at the time of death is precisely purity of mind.
Next, as for the *anāgāmin* (non-returner), what is meant by "departing"? It refers to clarifying the characteristics of practice.
What is meant by the term *anāgāmin* (Non-returner)? It refers to a person who does not return;
they can never again be defiled by the faults and afflictions mentioned above, and thus they do not come and go in cyclic rotation.
This is called "Non-returning. The phrase "as mentioned above" refers to the section following the fourth fascicle, concerning the non-returning from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth.

Not returning to the three realms is the "forward movement" (prasthāna-gati); being able to enter the desire realm without being defiled by the afflictions of the twenty-five states of existence is the "returning movement" (pratiprasrabdhi-gati);
and moving back and forth to benefit sentient beings is "circulation" (parivartana).
The third is called a bodhisattva who, upon departing, is judged by his marks;
having been named a bodhisattva, he has already received the prediction that before long he will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is called the third person.
The fourth basis for characteristics also has three parts: first, the characteristic of realization; second, the characteristic of the two stages; and third, the characteristic of practice.
Although these do not follow the same sequence as the previous [three], their three meanings are identical.
As for the fourth person, they are called an *arhat*; an *arhat* is one who has severed all afflictions and laid down the heavy burden.
Having attained one's own benefit and completed what was to be done:
the first passage states that "severing all afflictions" clarifies the destruction of both the general and specific thieves, thereby explaining the disappearance of their cause;

"casting off the heavy burden" clarifies the loss of its fruit—the cessation of both birth-and-death through segmented succession (*pariccheda*) and birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma*); thus, one has attained one's own benefit.
One who has attained what the Buddha attained and has completed what was to be done, reaching the tenth stage where learning and practice are fully perfected—
this is called the Arhat (Worthy One).
Abiding in the tenth stage is the determination of their rank and the specification of their station.
Abiding in the tenth stage, one attains the wisdom of mastery; following this is the aspect of activity.
Having attained the wisdom of mastery, one is able to manifest all manner of forms and images according to the inclinations of beings, just as they have been adorned.
If one desires to achieve the Buddha-way, one can indeed achieve it; being able to accomplish such immeasurable merit is called being an Arhat.
Having attained sovereign wisdom, one manifests the aspect of self-cultivation; according to what others delight in, one manifests the aspect of transforming others.
Desiring to achieve Buddhahood, one achieves the wisdom of mastery over the fetters.
This is called the praise of the four persons in general for their own practice and their work of transforming others.
These four persons appear in the world to bring great benefit and compassion to the world, serving as a refuge for the world and bringing peace and happiness to humans and devas;
they are the most honored and most supreme among humans and devas, just like the Tathāgata, who is called the "Victorious One Among Men."
As a place of refuge.

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: [The section] from "the second light" (*dvitīya-vidyā*) on relying on benefits, through the external expulsion of Māra and heterodoxy and the internal purification of karmic fetters, up to the marvelous efficacy of merit that benefits the world, is divided into two parts according to the text.
First, the teaching for Śrāvakas to subdue the two... [unsubstantiated fragment].

The teaching for the Bodhisattvas’ descent into the world consists of three parts in the first section: first, the question and answer; second, the proclamation of non-reliance; third, the explanation of non-reliance;
and fourth, the conclusion of the proclamation of non-reliance, as per the text.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I now do not rely upon these four kinds of people.”
Why is this? As stated in the *Ghoṣila-sūtra*, when the Buddha spoke to Ghoṣila, he said:

"If a deva, a Māra, or a Brahmā, desiring to cause destruction, were to transform themselves into the form of a Buddha—complete with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, a halo extending one fathom, a face as perfectly full as the bright full moon, and a tuft of hair between the eyebrows white as a conch shell or snow..."
Regarding these adornments that come toward you, you should examine them to determine whether they are real or false; once you have discerned this, you should subdue them.

Even Māra and others were able to transform themselves into the form of a Buddha, so how much more could they not transform themselves into the four types of bodies, such as those of Arhats, sitting or lying in mid-air with water flowing from their left flanks and fire from their right flanks, or smoke issuing from their bodies?
Their radiance is like a mass of fire.
In the commentary, Ghoṣila is translated as "Beautiful Sound.
For these reasons, no faith arises in my heart toward them, nor can I accept whatever they may say.
Nor should one rely upon them without respectful mindfulness.
The Buddha answered by addressing two points: first, the contemplation of the "thusness" (tathatā) of questions; second, the correct subduing of Māra.
The Buddha said: "Good son, if one conceives doubt regarding what I have taught, they should not accept it even then, let alone [accept] such as this."
For this reason, one should skillfully discern and know what is wholesome and unwholesome, what may be done and what may not be done;
having acted accordingly, one will experience happiness for a long night.
The Buddha is the external condition, while internally there must be faith and wisdom; with wisdom illuminating what is false and wrong, one accepts the True Dharma. Even regarding the Buddha...
One must certainly believe this wisdom, let alone anything else.

The actual subduing of Māra consists of two parts: first, the analogy; second, the application of the analogy. This is further divided into three sections: first, the arrival of Māra; second, the subduing of Māra;
and third, the retreat of Māra.
Good son, it is like a thieving dog that enters a person’s house at night.

The thieving dog is a metaphor for Māra; the house is a metaphor for the Buddha-dharma; entering at night is a metaphor for the decline of the True Dharma; and the disciples giving rise to ignorance is the "night.
As the six-fascicle version says: "thieving dogs."
Next, the maidservants of that household represent the subduing of Māra.
If those maidservants were to become aware [of his presence], they would immediately drive him away and scold him, saying: "Leave quickly!
If you do not leave, we shall take your life!"
Among the three vehicles, the śrāvaka is the most inferior; he is likened to a servant who has had his life cut short, bound by the five fetters.
When the māra acts with deceit and does not practice the Dharma, it is like having one's life severed.
When the three thieves and the dog hear this, the inferior māra retreats.
Upon hearing this, the thief who had stolen the dog immediately departed and did not return.
You should seek out how these lower analogies correspond to the three preceding analogies.
From this day forward, you too should likewise subdue Pāpīyān.
One should say this: "Pāpīyān, you should not now manifest such a form; if you do so intentionally, I shall bind you with the fivefold bonds.
Regarding the fivefold bonds:
the two interpretations are first, the bonds of five corpses, and second, the binding of five locations. The five corpses represent the five kinds of impurity.
By contemplating and subduing the five fetters of the *kāmamāra*, one contemplates and subdues the five gates of the *dṛṣṭimāra*.
This *dṛṣṭimāra* is a thief, while this *kāmamāra* is a dog. When the *māra* hears this, he shall immediately depart; like that thief-dog, he will never return again.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: "This is the second [section] concerning not instructing bodhisattvas to subdue Māra; this chapter contains both questions and answers.
Regarding the questions, there are two parts: first, it clarifies that relying on the Dharma is sufficient in itself."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught to the householder Ghoṣila, one who is able to subdue Māra in this manner may also draw near to Great Parinirvāṇa."
Second, it clarifies what purpose there is in relying on persons.
Why must the Tathāgata state that these four types of persons are the bases for reliance? What these four persons may say is not necessarily trustworthy.
The Buddha’s response consists of three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the formal answer; and third, the praise. Regarding the inquiry, it is as stated in the text:
the Buddha told Kāśyapa, "Good son, what I have spoken is likewise so; it is not otherwise."

Next, the formal response consists of three parts: first, the Dharma; second, the parable; and third, the conclusion that establishes the Dharma. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the proclamation of two topical headings.
"Good son, for those śrāvakas who possess only the fleshly eye, I say they must subdue Māra; this is not for those who train in the Great [Vehicle]."
This is spoken from the perspective of those who ride [the vehicles]. Next, both the small and great [vehicles] are explained together:
although a śrāvaka possesses the divine eye, it is called the "fleshly eye" (māṃsacakṣus); likewise, one who studies the Mahāyāna, though possessing the fleshly eye, [is so designated].
This is therefore called the Buddha-eye. Why is this? This Mahāyāna sūtra is called the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*).
This Buddha-vehicle is the most supreme and most excellent.
Although the śrāvakas possess divine eyes, their fleshly eyes cannot penetrate the ultimate principle; they are ensnared by Māra. Therefore, it is necessary to teach the Bodhisattva path.
Although the flesh exists, the Buddha’s light pervades everywhere without fail; since the realm of Māra is itself the Buddha-realm, he does not provide instruction [to it] (and so forth).
The second analogy is divided into three parts: first, the analogy of the Buddha instructing the śrāvakas; second, the analogy of the Buddha not instructing the bodhisattvas;

third, the analogy of the bodhisattvas instructing the śrāvakas. In the first analogy, there is both opening and closing. The opening analogy has three aspects, namely: the teaching of skillful means.
He teaches the arousal of mindfulness and instructs on the destruction of enemies.
Good son, it is like a person who is brave, robust, and majestic, upon whom those who are timid and weak constantly rely;
that brave man constantly instructs the timid ones, saying: "You should likewise hold the bow and grasp the arrow, and practice the way of the spear for a long time."
The hook, the noose, and the lasso.
In the initial stage of skillful means, it is said that "valiance" is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature, while "timidity" is a metaphor for the śrāvaka.

A śrāvaka person constantly relies upon the Buddha’s four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), which are like a bow; the five roots of goodness (*pañca-kuśalamūla*) are like arrows; and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are like spears. The five... [text fragment]
Bound as if by a lasso, he was further addressed with these words, which constitute the instruction on the three superior recollections.
Furthermore, he was told: "In the midst of combat, even though it may be like treading upon blades, one should not give rise to thoughts of fear."
One should regard others as naturally frail and weak, and accordingly give rise within oneself to a mind of courageous strength.
Not fearing these teachings is [the training in] morality; regarding others [as weak] is [the training in] concentration; and being courageous is [the training in] wisdom.
At times there may be someone who departs from this breaking of the enemy; furthermore, it is said that there are three stages: the arrival of Māra, the subduing of Māra, and the retreat of Māra.

At times there may be someone who lacks courage and bravery yet falsely assumes the appearance of a hero, taking up bows, swords, and various weapons to adorn himself, and coming into the midst of the ranks, shouting with a harsh voice.
Because Māra lacks wisdom, he speaks without courage; he transforms his appearance into the marks and signs of a Buddha to falsely assume the guise of a hero.
With false concentration as his bow and false wisdom as his sword, he uses worldly skills as his weapons.
Amidst the ranks of battle, he proclaims the five truths, the six aggregates, the nineteen elements, and the thirteen bases.
You have rightly subdued these;
you should likewise not give rise to sorrow or fear regarding such persons.
When those of this sort are defeated, it is the Mara who retreats.
If such persons see you and do not feel fear, you should know that they will soon fall apart and perish,
just like those thieving dogs.
Son of good family, this concludes the analogy.
"Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise. He tells all the śrāvakas: 'You should not fear Māra Pāpīyān.
If Māra Pāpīyān should transform himself into the body of a Buddha and come to where you are, you should apply yourself with diligence and make your mind firm so as to subdue him.
Then Māra will immediately become sorrowful and unhappy, and will depart by the way he came.'"
