However, the latter two [sections] correspond, while the first does not. "Firm diligence" corresponds to the three superior forms of mindfulness taught above.

From "Good son" onwards is the second section, the text concerning how the Bodhisattva who is not instructed subdues Māra; it is divided into three parts: first, the failure to instruct him to subdue [Māra];
second, the explanation of why he does not subdue [him]; and third, the illustration by way of analogy.
Good son, it is just as with that strong man who has not learned the Mahāyāna from others;
likewise, upon hearing various profound and secret sūtras, his heart feels joy and he does not give rise to alarm or fear.
For those who have first heard this profound sutra, hearing that the realm of Māra is identical to the realm of the Buddha—for this reason, they are not instructed to subdue him. Why is this?
It is because such persons who practice and study the Mahāyāna have already made offerings to, honored, and prostrated before [the Buddhas] in the past.

Because he has departed from immeasurable tens of billions of Buddhas, even though there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of māras who wish to come and harass him regarding this matter,
he is ultimately not startled or afraid.
Internally riding upon the Mahāyāna and externally relying on the power of the Buddha, the hosts of māras and the multitudes of thieves lose their majesty like fireflies in the presence of the sun.
This light merely explains the reason for his refusal to descend;
the analogy is clear enough to seek out.
Good son, it is like a person who, having obtained the *agada* medicine, has no fear of any venomous snakes or similar threats.
By the power of this medicine, all poisons can likewise be eliminated; this Mahāyāna sūtra is also like this:
by its medicinal power, one need not fear any demons or evil poisons, and it can subdue them so that they do not arise again.

Furthermore, son of good family, regarding the three similes below for the Bodhisattva’s teaching of the Śrāvakas, there are similes and their applications (*uddeśa* and *nirdeśa*), making four parts in total:
first, the Māra who transforms the Śrāvaka; second, the Śrāvaka receiving the transformation; third, the subduing of Māra by means of the Four Reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*);
and fourth, the Śrāvaka returning to his original state and being able to resolve his mind [for enlightenment] once again.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a dragon whose nature is extremely wicked and who, wishing to harm others, may either gaze with its eyes or hiss with its breath.
When Māra employs his supernormal powers to transform himself into a great dragon, he lacks a heart of kindness; this wicked Māra is thus subsumed [under that category].
The transformation of the śrāvakas is like one wishing to harm another's eyes; looking with the gaze is like supernatural power (ṛddhi), while blowing with the breath is like false teaching.
Next, "for this reason" and below refers to the śrāvakas receiving the transformation.
For this reason, all lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, dogs, and hounds give rise to fear; such are these evil beasts.
Upon hearing their voice, seeing their form, or touching their body, none fail to lose their lives.
Those who see their form behold their transformations; those who hear their voice hear their eloquence; those who touch their body are bewildered by their arts;
and those who lose their lives forfeit their roots of goodness.
The third section concerns the excellence of mantras; the following four sections concern subduing Māra by relying on them.

Regarding the excellence of mantras: by the power of these mantras, one is able to cause such evil venomous dragons, garuḍas, and others, as well as wicked elephants, lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, and wolves, to become gentle and compliant, all of whom can then be ridden and controlled.
The "skillful incantation" is precisely the power of the Middle Way Dharma within the Mahāyāna *Nirvāṇa*.
[In the passage] beginning with "These four," it describes how the śrāvakas return to their original state and eventually resolve to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Just as these beasts, upon seeing that skillful incantation, are immediately tamed.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas correspond to the lower part of the analogy; having fully applied the four analogies, he first correlates them with the Śrāvakas receiving transformation.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are likewise thus: upon seeing Māra Pāpīyān, they all give rise to fear.
Next, the transformation of Māra into a śrāvaka is combined;
even though Māra Pāpīyas does not give rise to a mind of fear, he continues to perform demonic deeds.
Third, the practitioner of the Mahāyāna is combined with the four reliances for subduing Māra.
It is the same for those who study the Mahāyāna: seeing that the śrāvakas fear the deeds of Māra and do not give rise to faith or joy in this Mahāyāna,
[the Buddha] first uses skillful means to subdue all Māras, making them well-disciplined and fit to serve as the cause for the vehicle,
and then extensively expounds various sublime dharmas for them.
The four śrāvakas departed together and returned to their original point of departure.
Having seen Māra subdued, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas gave rise to fear;
only then did they develop faith and delight in this unsurpassed, sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna, saying: "From this day forward, we ought not [to remain] within this sublime Dharma."
And thus they create obstacles.
Furthermore, "departing" constitutes the third fetter, while the first three fetters constitute the Śrāvaka.
Furthermore, son of good family, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas give rise to fear toward all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Next, the "Not Teaching Bodhisattvas" seal is formed.
Those who study the Mahāyāna are entirely without fear; they possess such power as this in their cultivation and study of the Mahāyāna.
This third pair of seals binds two meanings.
For these reasons, what has been explained above was intended to subdue the various māras for the sake of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and not for the Mahāyāna.
This is the third section on the praise of the Great Parinirvāṇa; it returns to praising the person and the Dharma of the bodhisattvas, beginning with the present praise.
Regarding the human dharma, this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is indestructible and cannot be subdued; it is most extraordinary and most unique.
If there are those who hear it, and having heard it, believe and accept it, being able to believe that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma—such persons are truly rare.
It is like the udumbara flower.
Next, he praised the people and the Dharma of the future:
"If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are those who hear such a subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna sūtra as this and give rise to a mind of faith and reverence..."
You should know that such persons shall not fall into the evil realms for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas in future ages.

At that time, the Buddha told [the assembly]: "The time has come for the departure of these three and the manifestation of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*). This is the proper time for their application; it would be untimely and useless otherwise.

If the Buddha were still in the world and the True Dharma (*saddharma*) were still flourishing, with virtue fully satisfied and the Path abundant, what need would there be to labor in assisting its propagation?"

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma will decline and weaken; being without physicians or medicine, it must be treated and rescued through the provisional means of the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*).

This is divided into three parts: first, the general teaching by the Buddha at that time; second, the specific questions of Kāśyapa; and third, Kāśyapa’s detailed analysis. Regarding the time of the general teaching: [The text continues with the narrative of the Buddha’s prophecy concerning the future decline of the Dharma and the necessity of relying on the four points.]

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Good son, after my parinirvāṇa, there will be hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sentient beings who will slander and disbelieve this subtle and wondrous sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa."
The period following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—encompassing the eras of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), and the Final Dharma—is the general time frame.
Next, from the passage where Kāśyapa addresses the Buddha onwards, is the specific time of questioning; this consists of both questions and answers. Regarding the questions, there are two types:
first, concerning the duration of the period after the extinction [of the Buddha], and second, concerning the times when the Dharma is not practiced according to the Law.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how long after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa will these sentient beings begin to slander this sutra?
And for how long after the parinirvāṇa will there be those who save the age according to the Dharma?"
"Bhagavān, who among the purely virtuous sentient beings will be able to rescue those who slander the Dharma?
Next, following the Buddha’s command, the Buddha answered these two questions.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "O son of good family, forty years after my parinirvāṇa, in Jambudvīpa..."
After it has been widely practiced and disseminated, it shall then disappear into the earth.

Regarding the "later forty years," this refers to the division of the eighty-year period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) into earlier and later halves; thus, the latter forty years are explained differently in various scriptures:
one says that both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) last for one thousand years each, while another says they last for five hundred years each.
It is said that the True Dharma lasts five hundred years and the Semblance Dharma one thousand; alternatively, it is said to last one hundred or eighty years.
This variation in the duration of the teachings arises because the conditions for them vary in intensity, leading to such divergent explanations regarding their length.

If one considers the first forty years, the Buddha is still near, and those who practice according to the Dharma are numerous; whereas in the latter forty years, although the Buddha is somewhat further removed, there are still those who behold him.
In the *Śāstra*, Upagupta saw a nun of one hundred and twenty years of age who asked about the marks of the Buddha and the deportment of a bhikṣu.
One should know that even forty years hence, there will still be those who have seen the Buddha; this is likely because during the time when the non-Dharma arises later, there will be much slander.
Another interpretation states: of the five hundred years of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), subtracting four hundred and twenty years, [one takes the remainder].
The eighty-year period is divided into two parts: during the first forty years, [the Dharma] was widely practiced and disseminated;

during the latter forty years, it disappeared into the earth. One account says this is not so: one hundred and sixteen years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, a king held a great assembly, and various schools began to formulate their own tenets.
Upagupta was unable to reconcile these differences, at which time the Buddha-dharma gradually declined.
As for this corruption, how could it be limited to four hundred and sixty years before it sinks into the earth?

One should know that during the forty years when Kāśyapa and Ānanda upheld the Dharma, they were no different from the Buddha being present. However, during the subsequent forty years, as the distance from the Sage increased, things already became degenerate and thin.
Later, when Maṇicūḍa Kāśyapa questioned [the Buddha] regarding when the Dharma would sink into the earth after his passing in those final forty years, [the Buddha replied: "It will return."

The Buddha’s response concerning the extinction of the True Dharma: eighty years remain before it is extinguished; forty years ago it emerged again, and after passing this period, it will once more disappear.
This refers precisely to the emergence and disappearance of the Right Path four hundred and twenty years later.

Furthermore, according to another interpretation, if a person who was ten years old attained enlightenment when the Buddha reached thirty years of age since his realization of the Way, then by the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, that person—

At the age of sixty, he beheld the Buddha’s beginning and end, harmonizing the Great and Small Vehicles. Forty years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he upheld the teachings as if the Buddha were still present;
beyond this time, those who had not seen the Buddha’s beginning could no longer rectify the arising of views of permanence and annihilation.
Thus it is said that [the teaching] was hidden from the earth for one hundred and thirty years, during which it did not guide others. "Years" refers to the number of years.

Question: Because those of advanced age and mature faculties are unable to provide correction, their origins are not mentioned. However, regarding the ten-year-old [Śāriputra], it was seen that he first met the Buddha at the same time as Kāśyapa and Ānanda.
Since the Buddha attained the Way on this day, how could this boy have seen its beginning? How then was he able to uphold the Dharma as if the Buddha were still present? Answer:
These two individuals—Kāśyapa being the eldest son [of the Buddha’s lineage] and Ānanda having attained the Buddha’s *bodhi-samādhi*—[were thus capable].
[This section] compares [the Bodhisattva] with other people (as detailed in the text).
Next, from the passage beginning "Furthermore, O son of good family," the response to those who conform to the Dharma and are able to rescue and deliver is divided into two parts:

first, the direct response; second, the praise and exhortation. The direct response is further divided into two: first, the censure of the small vehicle and the praise of the great vehicle; second, the explicit clarification of the means of rescue and deliverance. First... [text continues].
The praise and censure through the analogies and their applications consist of four parts. First is the analogy of greatness:
"Good son, it is like sugarcane, rice, honey, ghee, curd, and clarified butter;
wherever these are found, the people of that land all say, 'This is the foremost of all flavors.'"
Second, it is like something small.
Or again, there may be someone who eats only millet and the seeds of wild grasses, yet this person also says,
"What I eat is the very best."
The three fetters are a censure,
because they are the karmic retribution received by those of meager merit;
the four fetters are a praise.
If one is a person of merit, their ears never hear the names of millet or weeds; what they consume consists only of fine grain, sugarcane, rock honey, and clarified butter (ghṛta).

Thus, within this very praise it is said: "Fine grain" is a metaphor for the permanent; "sugarcane" is a metaphor for bliss; "rock honey" is a metaphor for the self; and "clarified butter" is a metaphor for the pure.
The analogy of pure grain and weeds is like that of impermanence and so forth;
the application of the analogy is as stated in the text.
This subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtra is likewise thus: those of dull faculties and meager merit do not delight in hearing it.
Just as those of meager merit loathe husks, grain, and rock honey, so too do those of the two vehicles loathe this unsurpassed Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra.
There may be sentient beings whose minds delight in hearing and receiving this sūtra; having heard it, they rejoice and do not give rise to slander.
It is like those fortunate people who eat grain with its husks.

Regarding the second point, the two sons of good family, this section clearly elucidates the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) for salvation; first the simile, then the application. The simile has three parts: first, the teaching of the Hīnayāna;
second, the teaching of the Mahāyāna; third, the small [capacities] receiving the Mahāyāna teaching. As for the first part:
Good son, it is like a king who dwells in a remote mountain wilderness, a place of hardship and peril.
Although he possesses sugarcane, grain-husks, and rock honey, because these are difficult to obtain, he hoards them with greed and stinginess, not daring to eat them for fear they might run out;
he eats only millet and weeds.
Those of the Hīnayāna each have their own retinues and territories over which they rule; thus it is said they are "like petty kings.
Their minor practices are biased and crooked, like entering a deep mountain pit of non-action (asaṃskṛta);

thus it is said that although there is sugarcane in an evil place, they are stingy and do not eat it, fearing it will run out—this is "petty transformation" (hīnabhūmikavikurvaṇa). They are exclusively devoted to minor practices, which obstructs [the Great Vehicle].
Although the Great Way possesses great teachings for those who seek it with a mind of practice, its upholding, recitation, and study are likened to being stingy and begrudging what one has acquired;
thus, they are likened to fearing that it might come to an end.
Second, there are kings of different nations who provide relief through the four reliances.
A certain king of another country heard of this and took pity on him; he immediately loaded carts with husks, grain, and sugarcane and sent them to him.

Because he was a king who maintained the Great Dharma, he was called "King Wuche" (Wu-che). Regarding the matter of the "cart-load," it is explained that he was provided with the *Śāstra* (treatises) of the *Sūtra* (scriptures), as well as the *Yoga-śāstra*.

Furthermore, it is said that he transformed [the recipient] through supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to cause the Mahāyāna to be widely proclaimed, which is like being carried by a cart. It is also said:
The wisdom of skillful means brings about understanding; Xinghuang said that propagating the Way through the person is like a carriage carrying [a load].
Here, it is clarified that because one instructs others through great practice, it is described as "carrying in a carriage."
Upon receiving it, the king immediately underwent a great transformation.
Having received it, he then distributed it throughout the entire kingdom for all to eat;
once the people had eaten, they were filled with joy and all spoke thus: "It is because of that king that we have obtained this rare flavor."
Next is the analogy regarding these four types of people.
Good son, these four types of people are likewise so; they are the generals of this unsurpassed Great Dharma.
Among these four types, perhaps there is one person who sees that although immeasurable bodhisattvas in other directions study such a [Dharma],...
If one takes up this sutra— whether copying it oneself or having another copy it— for the sake of profit, for the sake of fame,
for the sake of understanding the Dharma, for the sake of a basis of reliance, or for the purpose of trading it for other scriptures, and thus cannot extensively proclaim it to others,
then one should take this subtle and wondrous sutra and deliver it to that region to give to those bodhisattvas.

Having resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhicitta*) and abiding in bodhi, as soon as this Bodhisattva has obtained this sutra, he extensively expounds it for others, enabling immeasurable multitudes to receive the flavor of such Mahāyāna Dharma.
All of this is the power of this single Bodhisattva; those sutras never heard before are all made available through him, just as the people [benefit] because of the king.
By virtue of power, one obtains rare food.
However, combining the latter two points with the five kinds of faults, the accumulation of wealth out of greed and for profit corresponds to the realm of hell;
seeking fame and reputation corresponds to the realm of hungry ghosts; and using the understanding of the Dharma to increase the ego corresponds to the realm of asuras.
Because it relies upon the conditioned, it is the existence of animals; because it involves the exchange of the conditioned, it is the work of worldly scholars and clever outsiders.
Next, from "Furthermore, good son" onwards, there is a praise and exhortation: first praising the sutra, and subsequently exhorting people.
Furthermore, noble son, you should know that wherever this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is circulated,
that very ground is adamantine (*vajra*).
Just as a king reaching a deep mountain can cause that deep mountain to become level, so too does this sūtra reach crooked views and cause those crooked views to be straightened.
The ground of great directness is like a vajra; it opens up the principle of the Hīnayāna as the principle of the Mahāyāna.
Among these people, there are those who are likewise like a vajra;
if there are any who can hear such a sūtra, they shall not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and all their vows shall be fulfilled just as mine have been.
"What I have proclaimed today, you bhikṣus should well receive and uphold.
If there are sentient beings who are unable to hear such a sūtra as this, you should know that these people are truly to be pitied. Why is this?
Because these people are unable to receive and uphold the profound meaning of such Mahāyāna sūtras."
Those who are human are themselves Vajrasattvas; those who belong to the Hīnayāna are themselves Mahābodhisattvas.
When Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha following the third section of analysis—which consists of questions and answers—Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, during the forty years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, this Mahāyāna scripture shall be great."
After the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* has been widely circulated and propagated throughout Jambudvīpa, how long will it be before it sinks back into the earth?
The intent of the question is: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the sūtra has been hidden for forty years, will it sink forever, or will it emerge once again?
"It will flourish.
The Buddha said, "Good son, if my True Dharma remains for eighty years, during the first forty of those years,
this sutra shall again rain down the great Dharma rain upon Jambudvīpa."

Next, regarding the Buddha’s response, it says that "the remaining eighty years" refers to one interpretation which holds that when only the True Dharma (*saddharma*) remains for eighty years, the [teaching] flourishes during the first forty years and is already extinguished during the latter forty years.

Another explanation states that the True Dharma lasts for fifteen hundred years without being extinguished; within these, it flourishes during the first forty years and is extinguished during the latter forty years.
Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha: "The following is the fourth [section], planting seeds according to depth and shallowness to manifest the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).

For the profound sūtras and wondrous meanings are not easily heard; how much more so when one must expound, analyze, and unravel their subtle nuances, providing guidance and proclaiming them throughout the universe?

This is not something that those who are frivolous can accomplish. Regarding the text, there are two parts. (Note: The character [怡-台+藂] appears to be a rare or variant form; based on context and phonetic likelihood, it is interpreted here as *cong* (叢), meaning "thicket" or "multitude," though its precise usage remains uncertain.)

The question regarding the two [periods] is answered by first addressing the initial inquiry in three parts: first, citing the time of evil; second, seeking out virtuous people; and third, requesting an answer.

Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, at such a time as this—when the True Dharma of these sutras is perishing, when the True Precepts are being destroyed, when unrighteousness increases, and when there are no sentient beings who act according to the Dharma..."

In an age of evil, there are four conditions: the extinction of both right precepts and right teaching; the simultaneous flourishing of wicked people and wicked dharmas. These four conditions must pertain to a time of turmoil during the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
Why? The extinction of the true Dharma is the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); the destruction of the right precepts is the turbidity of life-span (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*);

the increase of what is not the Dharma is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); and the absence of sentient beings who act according to the Dharma is the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). This is that time.
This is the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
Who is able to hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite it so as to master it, and to offer worship, pay respect, transcribe it, and explain it?
There are six phrases regarding the search for a good person: "faith" means receiving; "not forgetting" means upholding; "facing the text" means reading; "reciting from memory" [means reciting].
It is said: reciting and transmitting the text is one way; writing out the meaning of the text is another; and explaining it is yet another—these constitute the five kinds of Dharma masters.
Furthermore, these are the three modes of upholding [the Dharma]: reading and reciting is mental practice; explaining is verbal practice; and writing is physical practice.
In this age of the five turbidities, those who are able to act in accordance with the Dharma through the three karmas—please answer this matter.
We pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings, will analyze and explain this in detail, so that all bodhisattvas, having heard it, may receive and uphold it;
and having upheld it, they shall immediately attain non-retrogression from the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The present response consists of three parts: first, an exaltation of the question; second, the actual answer; and third, an exhortation. The first is as stated in the text:
"At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa, saying: 'Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You are now well able to inquire about such a meaning.'"
"Good son, if there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the river Śītā,
they will then be able to receive, uphold, and not slander such a sūtra in this evil age. Good son,

if there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in a single Gaṅgā River, only then will they be able [to do so]."
In this evil age, one who does not slander this Dharma, who loves and delights in this scripture, yet is unable to analyze and explain it extensively for others— good son,
if there are sentient beings who have generated the bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as the sands of two Ganges Rivers,
only then will they be able, in this evil age, to refrain from slandering this Dharma, and to correctly understand, believe, delight in, receive, uphold, read, and recite it.

Furthermore, they are unable to explain it extensively for others. Only if there are sentient beings who have generated the bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in three Ganges Rivers can they, in this evil age, refrain from slandering this Dharma, and instead receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe its volumes;

yet even when teaching it to others, they do not understand its profound meaning. If there are sentient beings who, in the presence of as many [Tathāgatas] as there are grains of sand in four Ganges...

Only after generating the bodhicitta as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges among all the Tathāgatas can one, in this evil age, refrain from slandering this Dharma and instead receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe its scrolls, explaining to others even a single sixteenth part of its meaning;
yet, even while expounding it, one will not do so in its entirety. If there are sentient beings who, regarding the [teachings of] five Ganges-sands of Buddhas...
Only after generating the bodhicitta toward the Tathāgatas can one, amidst this evil age, refrain from slandering this Dharma, and instead receive,
uphold, read, recite, copy its scrolls, and extensively explain to others the meaning of eight out of sixteen parts. Furthermore,
if there are sentient beings who have generated the bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in six Ganges Rivers, only then can they...
In this degenerate age, one who does not slander this Dharma, but upholds, recites, copies its scrolls, and explains its meaning extensively to others—
specifically twelve-sixteenths of its meaning— and who has previously resolved upon bodhicitta in the presence of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of seven Ganges Rivers,
is then able, in this degenerate age, to uphold, recite, and not slander this Dharma.
If one recites, copies, and extensively explains fourteen-sixteenths of the meaning of this sutra for others,
and if there are sentient beings who have generated the bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers, only then will they be able, amidst this evil world,
to refrain from slandering this Dharma and instead uphold, read, recite, and copy this sutra, as well as encourage others to do the same.
They are able to transcribe it themselves and listen to it, and further exhort others to listen to it, read it, recite it, master it, protect it, and uphold it;
out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world, they make offerings to this sutra and likewise exhort others to make offerings to it,
honoring, respecting, revering, reading, reciting, and prostrating before it in the same manner, fully capable of understanding it to its ultimate extent.
The meaning and flavor are as follows: the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging, ultimately peaceful and blissful; it is extensively taught that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
one thoroughly knows the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata; having made offerings to such Buddhas as these, one establishes this unsurpassed True Dharma and upholds and protects it.
Regarding the nine rivers cited within the formal response, the traditional interpretation states: "If one encounters a single Buddha and makes a single vow, one casts down a single grain of sand;
though one may encounter many Buddhas, if one does not make a vow, no sand is cast down. Though one may resolve to practice, if one does not see a Buddha, no sand is cast down.

Though one may see a single Buddha, even if one resolves to practice many times, only a single grain of sand is cast down; yet though it is a single resolution, if one sees many [Buddhas], [the merit increases]."
The Buddha likewise dropped a single grain of sand; by such a number, he caused one *gaṅgā* to be filled. This constitutes one *gaṅgā*.

As for the difference between the *Hiraṇyavatī* and the *Gaṅgā*: the *Hiraṇyavatī* is located north of Kuśinagara and is relatively small, whereas the *Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā* flows into the eastern ocean and is the greatest among the four great rivers;
therefore, it differs from the *Hiraṇyavatī*. If one proceeds according to the practice, the *Hiraṇyavatī* is merely heard of.
1. Not slandering [the teachings] while constantly adding faith and joy; 2. Constantly adding recitation and chanting;
3. Constantly explaining the shallow meanings; 4. Constantly adding one-sixteenth part; 5. Constantly adding eight-sixteenths; 6. Constantly adding twelve-sixteenths;
7. Constantly adding fourteen-sixteenths; 8. Constantly possessing all sixteen parts. If one always seeks understanding from the perspective of delusions, it will be difficult.
The five [hindrances] are always easy to resolve once understood, whereas the six [defilements] are always more difficult to eliminate because they are deeper and subtler.
This is like how it is easy to reach the rank of Grand Marshal (*Daifu*) but difficult to reach the rank of Prime Minister (*Xiangguo*). Regarding the "sixteenth part" that is difficult to resolve:
for example, in the world, sixteen *liang* make one *jin*. Master Xianhui said that *Xi-lian* (Sīla) represents the stage of a disciple (*śrāvaka*).

The *Heng* (恒) [stages] always correspond to the two pairs of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*), and so forth. Kaishan and Zhicheng state that the first nine *Heng* stages are all the position of the initial reliance;

from the *Xilian* (熙連) to the second *Heng* is the stage of the initial mind’s *śraddhā-bhūmi* (faith-stage); from the third *Heng* to the fifth *Heng* is the middle mind’s *gotra-bhūmi* (lineage-stage);
and from the sixth *Heng* to the eighth *Heng* is the final mind’s *mārga-bhūmi* (path-stage), which is also the ultimate.

It is difficult to understand. If one were to weigh the entirety of the Buddha-dharma as one *jin*, then once the first *āśraya* (basis) has exhausted the Buddha-dharma, what would remain for the second, third, and fourth *āśrayas*?
If one were to weigh only the first *āśraya* as one *jin*, this would merely be the dharma of the first *āśraya* itself;
how could it concern the Buddha-dharma as a whole? Now, it is clarified that from the *Hiraṇyavatī* River to the three *Gaṅgā* Rivers constitutes the first *āśraya*.
One part and eight parts constitute the second basis; ten and twenty-four constitute the third basis; sixteen constitutes the fourth basis.
As the text says: "Possessing complete understanding, one exhausts its flavor" (and so forth).
Third, regarding those who have first resolved their minds [upon enlightenment]: this is an exhortation.

If there are those who have first resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you should know that such persons will, in future ages, certainly be able to establish such a True Dharma and uphold and protect it; therefore, you should not [neglect them] now.
One does not know for what reason those who protect the Dharma in future ages are those who have thus resolved their minds,
yet it is certain that they will be able to uphold the unsurpassed true Dharma in future ages.
The preceding discourse on the nine occasions of invariably encountering a Buddha is profound and far-reaching;

fearing that the sentiments of the times might suppress it, I have further provided guidance and exhortation, merely requiring that one resolve to awaken the mind, for such a person will surely be able to protect, uphold, and establish [the Dharma] in the future.

Good son, there are wicked bhikṣus who, having moved beyond this fifth section on the merit and demerit of slandering those with clear faith, previously [in the section] above the Hiraṇyavatī River, merely possessed faith; now, from the Hiraṇyavatī River onwards, they possess both faith and [the knowledge of] the demerit of slandering and the merit [of praising]. To encourage merit and to obstruct demerit, the text is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the causes and effects of demerit and merit; second, encouraging merit as a conclusion based on the former. Regarding the first part: [The Buddha said: "Good son, if a bhikṣu, having heard that a certain person possesses the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person does not possess the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, or the knowledge and vision of liberation,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who truly possesses these qualities. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has abandoned the five hindrances and attained the four dhyānas, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not abandoned the five hindrances nor attained the four dhyānas,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly abandoned the hindrances and attained the dhyānas. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has realized the Four Noble Truths, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not realized the Four Noble Truths,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly realized the Truths. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the fruit of Stream-enterer, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the fruit of Stream-enterer,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained the fruit. This applies likewise to the fruits of Once-returner, Non-returner, and Arhatship. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the stage of a Pratyekabuddha,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained that stage. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the stage of a Bodhisattva, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the stage of a Bodhisattva,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained that stage. [The Buddha said: "Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the Dharma-eye, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the Dharma-eye,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained the Dharma-eye. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the eye of a Śrāvaka, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the eye of a Śrāvaka,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the eye of a Pratyekabuddha, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the eye of a Pratyekabuddha,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the Buddha-eye, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the Buddha-eye,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. [The Buddha said: "Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the power of a Śrāvaka, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the power of a Śrāvaka,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the power of a Pratyekabuddha, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the power of a Pratyekabuddha,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the power of a Tathāgata, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the power of a Tathāgata,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. [The Buddha said: "Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the unconditioned Dharma, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the unconditioned Dharma,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the path of a Śrāvaka, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the path of a Śrāvaka,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the path of a Pratyekabuddha, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the path of a Pratyekabuddha,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the path of a Bodhisattva, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the path of a Bodhisattva,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. [The Buddha said: "Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has entered the stage of non-retrogression, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not entered the stage of non-retrogression,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly entered it. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the stage of a Buddha, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the stage of a Buddha,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. [The Buddha said: "Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the Dharma-body, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the Dharma-body,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the Sambhogakāya, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the Sambhogakāya,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained it. [The Buddha said: "Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the ten powers, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the ten powers,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained them. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the four fearlessnesses, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the four fearlessnesses,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained them. Furthermore, good son, if a bhikṣu hears that a certain person has attained the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, yet slanders them by saying, 'This person has not attained the eighteen unique qualities,' he commits a grave offense. Why is this? Because he slanders one who has truly attained them. Regarding the first of the four [sections], this clarifies the characteristics of slander:
"Good son, there are wicked bhikṣus who, upon hearing of my parinirvāṇa, do not feel sorrow, but instead think: 'Today the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa;
how joyful! While the Tathāgata was in the world, he obstructed our gains; now that he has entered nirvāṇa, who..."
Furthermore, there will surely be those who obstruct and plunder me; if there were no such obstruction and plunder, I would have regained my original gains and offerings.
Now that the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa, the prohibitions and precepts will all be abandoned.

The saṃghāṭī robes originally received for the sake of the Dharma-methods shall now be discarded and ruined, like banners atop wooden poles. Such people as these will slander and resist [the teaching].
In the Mahāyāna sūtras, it is said that when the Buddha—the teacher and father of all sentient beings—enters nirvana, humans and devas suffer in grief;

even venomous insects harbor benevolence and do not fail to yearn for him with devotion. That wicked people alone say, "His extinction is a joy," is one such evil. [Furthermore,] having few desires...
Those who are content with little, uphold the prohibitive precepts, and are fully endowed with dignified deportment are called the Saṃgha; they have all relinquished the two evils.
The Dharma of the Mahāyāna is the teacher of the worthy and the sages; those who alone resist, oppose, and do not believe in the Triple Gem possess the characteristics of slander.
"Good son, you should now depart and next clarify the marks of faith.

Good son, you should now maintain this mindfulness: if there are sentient beings who have accomplished and perfected immeasurable merit, they will be able to believe in this Mahāyāna sūtra; having believed, they will receive and uphold it. As for other sentient beings..."
If those who delight in the Dharma can extensively explain this sutra,
all the evil karma they have committed throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past will be entirely eradicated upon hearing it.
To personally cultivate the good of the three periods of time and to lead others to extinguish the evil of the two periods of time— each highlighting one aspect—
is what constitutes the characteristic of faith.
From the passage beginning "If there is no faith" up to the end, it explains the retribution for slandering the person [who possesses this faith].
If there are those who do not believe in this sutra, they shall, in their present bodies, be afflicted by immeasurable suffering from disease and be frequently reviled and insulted by the multitude.
After the end of their lives, they will be held in contempt by others; their countenances will be ugly, their livelihoods will be difficult, and they will never have sufficient resources.
Even if they obtain a little, it will be coarse, harsh, and inferior, and throughout their lives they will always dwell in such conditions.

In families that are impoverished and lowly, which revile the True Dharma and hold wrong views—if at the time of death they encounter times of famine and chaos, when weapons rise up in competition and tyrannical sovereigns rule with violence, or if they are oppressed by enemies and vengeful rivals; even though virtuous friends exist, they do not meet them;
and though they seek the necessities of life, they cannot obtain them; and even if they gain a small measure of profit, they constantly suffer from hunger and thirst.
They are regarded and recognized only by the common and base; kings, ministers, and great officials do not even deign to count them among their peers.
Even if they were to hear such a person’s exposition of the Dharma, even if it were the truth itself, they would ultimately never believe or accept it. Such people do not reach a state of excellence;
like a bird with broken wings that cannot fly, these individuals likewise will be unable to reach the higher realms in future lives.
The wholesome realms of humans and devas:

departing while in this present body is the retribution in the present life; departing after the end of life is the retribution in the next life; and departing to dwell constantly in successive births is the retribution in subsequent lives.
Furthermore, compared to the retribution received by one who abandons the four kinds of clear faith,
if there is another person who can believe in such Mahāyāna sūtras as these, then although their physical form may be coarse and ugly,

through the merit of these sūtras they will immediately become upright and handsome; their majestic countenance and physical strength will increase day by day, and they will constantly be honored by humans and devas.
They are delighted to see him, honoring and cherishing him with affection that never wavers. When kings, ministers, and their kinsmen hear what he says, they all revere and believe it.

If any among my śrāvaka disciples wishes to perform a foremost and most marvelous deed, they should widely proclaim such Mahāyāna sūtras as these for the sake of the world. Good son, it is like this: a parable.
Just as the power of mist and dew, though they may wish to remain, does not exceed the rising of the sun, and once the sun has risen, they are extinguished without remainder;
so too, son of good family, all the evil karma of these sentient beings is likewise.
Its power to remain in the world does not exceed the moment they behold the day of the Great Parinirvāṇa. Once that sun has risen, it can completely eliminate all evil karma. Furthermore:
Good son, it is as if there were someone who has left the household life and shaved his hair; although he wears the kāṣāya robe, he has not yet received the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera.
Suppose a householder comes to invite the assembly of monks; even those who have not yet received the precepts go together with the great assembly to accept the invitation.
Although they have not yet received the precepts, they have already entered the ranks of the Saṃgha. Good son, if there are sentient beings who give rise to the aspiration [for enlightenment]...
The initial study of this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra—whether by copying, reciting, or reading it—is likewise so;
although one has not yet fully attained the rank of the ten abodes, one has already entered among the number of those in the ten abodes.
The departure from the physical form one has originally received is the removal of the obstacle of retribution; the departure from this [form] is the removal of the obstacle of karma;
and the departure as when a person leaves the household life is the removal of the obstacle of afflictions. There are many types of analogies established here:

if taken as an analogy for the Great Precepts, it refers to the true understanding of the ten stages (*bhūmi*); if taken as an analogy for the Ten Precepts, it refers to the semblance understanding prior to the stages. This is the intended meaning within the *Cunda-sūtra*.
In this context, the analogy of "non-precepts" begins with an ordinary person who, upon generating the aspiration for enlightenment, immediately attains the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Although they have not yet severed their afflictions, the fruit is spoken of within the cause; that is, while the previous discussion regarding evil persons was based on the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and presented horizontally according to the three types of retribution, the current discussion regarding good persons is presented vertically according to the three obstacles.
These are merely different expressions used interchangeably for stylistic elegance.
Second, from the phrase "There may be some sentient beings" onwards is the exhortation toward merit and the establishment of the basis.
If there are sentient beings— whether they be disciples of the Buddha or not— who, out of greed, fear, or for the sake of gain and sustenance,
hear and receive this sutra even as a single verse, and having heard it do not slander it, you should know that such persons have already drawn near [to the Dharma].
"Anuttarasamyaksambodhi, son of good family, for these reasons I say that these four persons are the refuge of the world.
Son of good family, it is impossible that these four persons would say, regarding what was spoken by the Buddha, 'This was not spoken by the Buddha.
Therefore, I say that these four persons are the refuge of the world."
This text is very broad; it does not distinguish between disciples and non-disciples, nor does it inquire whether the cause is virtuous or evil.

However, anyone who can give rise to the resolve and hear even a single verse is close to the cause of Bodhi. This is because [otherwise] one would be giving rise to the resolve out of greed and fear for gain and offerings, which stems from the three poisons.

How much more so for those who have planted roots of goodness throughout nine *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and possess the merit of the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*)? This means that such a person is able to maintain faith from beginning to end, discerning and warning against slander.
This concerns cause and effect.
"Good son, you should make offerings"—this is the sixth exhortation to make offerings, which is divided into two parts:

first, the exhortation to make offerings; second, the discussion of the meaning. The first part is further divided into two: first, the exhortation to make offerings; second, the question and answer. Regarding the first text:
"Good son, you should make offerings to these four kinds of persons.
Indeed, because the four reliances (catur-apāśraya) provide great benefit and the nine constant causes are profound and difficult to encounter, I exhort you to make offerings."
Next, the question contains two meanings: what constitutes a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), and what constitutes an offering (*pūjā*). [The questioner asks:
"World-Honored One, how should I recognize such a person so as to make an offering to them?
The Buddha’s answer also has two parts: first, the direct response; second, the citation of verses. Regarding the first part:
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "If there are those who establish and uphold the True Dharma, such persons should be entreated and served even at the cost of one's own body and life.
To establish the True Dharma is the mark of a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). [As] the Master of Hexi said: "It means to resolve the mind, maintain the precepts, and uphold the Mahāyāna."

Expounding the teachings for others and protecting the Dharma are characteristics of a field of merit; in the present text, by clarifying only the protection of the Dharma, all other matters are implicitly included.
That one should be willing to sacrifice body and life is a characteristic of making offerings, wherein the heavy supersedes the light.
The next verse is the first citation regarding the teacher:
"As it is said by me in this Mahāyāna sūtra:
'Whether old or young, one who knows the Dharma should be honored, revered, and prostrated to.'"
Just as those who tend the sacrificial fire, such as the Brahmins and others—
according to the two verses cited by the Master—
should honor, revere, and pay homage to one who knows the Dharma, whether they be old or young.
It is also like the various devas serving Śakra;

the two Kāśyapas [present their case]—the following is the exposition of the doctrine, first posing questions and then providing answers. Regarding the questions, there is the reception of the essential meaning, the presentation of doubts, and the request for an answer;
the reception of the essential meaning is as stated in the text.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, making offerings to teachers and elders should indeed be conducted in this manner.
[The following section] sets forth the doubts in three parts: first, three definitive statements; second, three difficulties; and finally, three conclusions.

Now I have a doubt, which I pray you will explain in detail: If there is an elder who upholds the precepts and receives what he has not yet heard from those who are younger, how should this person be treated with respect? If he were to be paid respect, then he would not be called one who upholds the precepts. Conversely, if a youth upholds the precepts and receives [teachings] from an elder who has broken the precepts—how should this person be treated with respect? If he were to be paid respect, then he would not be called one who upholds the precepts. If he were not to be paid respect, then the younger person would be disparaging the elder. the corruption of views, the corruption of precepts, the increase of unrighteousness as the corruption of afflictions, and the concealment of all worthy sages as the corruption of sentient beings. This is the reception [of the teaching].
The accumulation of impurities constitutes the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

For this reason, this consciousness cannot be relied upon.
What is called "consciousness as agent" and "consciousness as experiencer" constitutes a non-harmonized Sangha;

since there is only consciousness acting as the cause of attachment and consciousness receiving the fruit of that attachment—all of which are merely birth and death—there is no eternally abiding, single-essence Sangha.
Third, the detailed explanation based on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); fourth, based on the explicit and the non-explicit.

Regarding the definitive meaning: one who follows the definitive meaning is called "one who knows contentment," for they never falsely manifest a demeanor of purity, nor do they harbor arrogance or haughtiness, nor do they greedily seek gain and offerings;
furthermore, they do not [misinterpret] the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata through skillful means according to the occasion.

To give rise to attachment is called the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). If one can abide in such [teachings], it should be known that this person has already attained abiding in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, it is said that one relies on sutras of definitive meaning and does not rely on those of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
As for those of non-definitive meaning, they are as stated in the sutras: "All is ablaze; all is impermanent; all is suffering."
That "all is empty" and "all is without self" is called the *neyārtha* (provisional meaning). Why?

Because by being unable to understand this meaning, it causes sentient beings to fall into the Avīci Hell. Why is that? Because of their grasping and attachment, they do not fully comprehend the meaning.
Regarding "all is burned," this refers to the Tathāgata’s teaching that even *nirvāṇa* is burned; all is impermanent.
Nirvana is likewise impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self; thus it is called a sutra of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) and is not to be relied upon.

Good son, if there were someone who said: "The Tathāgata, out of compassion for all sentient beings and with full knowledge of the appropriate timing, speaks of the light as heavy and the heavy as light because he knows the time," and if the Tathāgata were to observe...
The Buddha does not permit those disciples whom he knows to have donors providing all their necessities so that they lack for nothing,
to keep slaves, gold, silver, wealth, treasures, or to engage in trade and the sale of impure things. However,
if those disciples have no donors to provide their necessities, or when times are famine-stricken and food and drink are difficult to obtain— [in such cases, he permits it].

In order to establish and uphold the True Dharma, I permit my disciples to accept and possess male and female slaves, gold, silver, carriages, fields, houses, grain, and whatever else is required for trade.
Although I permit the acceptance and possession of such things, they must be given as pure offerings by donors of sincere faith.
These four dharmas are those upon which one should rely, provided there are also the Vinaya and the Abhidharma.
The Sūtras do not contradict these four [points], and one should likewise rely upon them.

If anyone should say that there are times when it is improper and times when it is proper, or that there are those who can protect the Dharma and those who cannot, and that the Tathāgata has permitted all bhikṣus to accept and store such impure things—such words should not be relied upon. This applies whether it concerns the Vinaya, the Abhidharma, or the Sūtras.
In the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*, there is a similar teaching; thus, these three parts [of the rule] should likewise not be relied upon.
If it is said that one may possess eight impure items by virtue of four conditions—namely, first, the absence of a donor;

second, a time of famine; third, the establishment [of a monastery]; and fourth, pure giving—this interpretation is inconsistent. One school asserts that only when these four conditions are fully met does [one obtain permission].
First, it is said that one may possess two [robes], and either one of them may be used at any time; second, it is said that all three [robes] may be possessed individually;

third, it is said that while one may possess each of the first three individually, they must be subject to the ritual of *viśuddha-dāna* (pure giving), for this one act of pure giving cannot be omitted—thus, they must all be possessed through these two conditions.
If it is said that possession is permitted both during the proper season (*kāla*) and the improper season (*akāla*), this is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*); the three parts are as follows.
The Tripiṭaka:
This is the third assembly for those with the fleshly eye.
I have taught these four reliances for the sake of sentient beings with the fleshly eye; it is not for those who possess the wisdom-eye.
Therefore, when I now speak of these four reliances, they are the meaning of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
the meaning of the Tathāgata’s eternal and unchanging wisdom, the definitive meaning that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature,
and the thorough comprehension of all Mahāyāna sūtras.
Sometimes, when the two eyes of the fleshly [perception] and the celestial [wisdom] face each other, they constitute an obstruction between the internal and external;

or when the Dharma-wisdom and the wisdom of insight face each other, this treatise illuminates the distinction between the ultimate and the conventional. Now, as for the facing of the fleshly eye and the wisdom-eye, this treatise elucidates the difference between the ordinary person and the sage.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Fascicle Six.
Translated by the Eastern Sun [at] the Tiantai Monastery, the Śramaṇa Benzhun.
Compiled from the Southern Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Fascicle Six of the Collected Commentaries.

The Ninth Chapter of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra: On the Chapter of Deviant Teachings.
