Huiguan, and Xie Lingyun:
The Chapter on Rectifying Deviation (Volume Six is titled "The Chapter on Distinguishing Deviation and Rectitude").

The "heterodox" (*xié*) refers to Māra; the "orthodox" (*zhèng*) refers to the Sages. There are many kinds of heterodoxy, namely: heterodox evil, heterodox worldly, heterodox partiality, and heterodox gradualism.

"Heterodox evil" refers to the results of the icchantikas, those who slander the Dharma, the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, the ten unwholesome actions, and the four realms of existence.

As the text says: "To permit the keeping of the eight kinds of impure things is to slander the Buddha. To cling to the ninefold canon while claiming that [the Mahayana] does not exist is heterodox evil.

To disparage the Vaipulya [sūtras] is to slander the Dharma; if one intends to engage in sexual misconduct, one should remove the dharma robes, for this constitutes a violation of the four grave offenses—these are termed "perverse evil.
As for "perverse worldly things," this generally refers to the causes and effects, afflictions, karma, the aggregates, and the celestial Māras within the twenty-five states of existence.
A text states: "This body is produced through the union of parents' love and desire; it is a body of craving."
The meaning is as follows: that the afflictions are themselves the body, and that the aggregates (skandhas) are themselves the body; that by means of a tainted form one creates an untainted body;
and that the ascetic practices of the celestial Māra in the past are themselves karma and so forth.

Regarding "perverse and partial," this refers to the views of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas concerning impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and a distorted [notion of] Nirvāṇa. As the text says: "The Tathāgata is impermanent and subject to change."

Is it not the case that the teaching of non-self is precisely that meaning? "Gradualists" refers to those who conceptually differentiate and abandon the two extremes separately in order to seek the Middle Way;
this includes the *samādhi-māra*, the *bodhicitta-māra*, and so forth. As the text says:
"The Tathāgata has no knowledge of the heterodox treatises of the various non-Buddhists, nor does he have knowledge of worldly medicines. There is nothing [he lacks].

Because he knows, he is called the Tathāgata; because he gives rise to neither hatred nor love toward being cut by a blade or smeared with incense, and is able to abide in the middle, he is called the Tathāgata—this is its meaning.

That which is correct is called "holy" (*ārya*). There are many kinds of holy correctness: namely, holding what is correct, being good and correct, being true and correct, and being upright and correct.
These are contrasted with the four perversions to discuss the four corrects and the four perversions. Since these have already emerged...
The text explains that "deviant" is immediately "correct" without waiting for further discussion; these four deviances and four correctnesses correspond to the four *siddhāntas*.

Deviance and evil are particularly grave, and the root of all deviances is the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly). The deviance of worldly convention is established as a designation for those seeking pure transcendence, which is the *pudgala-siddhānta* (the individual).
Deviance that specifically shatters birth-and-death to enter *nirvāṇa* is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic).

It is the governance of that which is gradually reached by the perverse; that which is thus reached is precisely the eternally abiding. From the perspective of the gate of sequential differentiation, this name "perverse" is established;

likewise, the "correct" of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is also such. To cling to the correct as being Māra and the lord of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and to cling to the correctness of the desire realm itself, is the world.
Goodness that is correct is the goodness of the mundane; to accomplish various forms of goodness is to—

Humanity is truly a world-transcending dharma; it is only when one counters and breaks through the mundane that it is called the "correct" sequential Mahāyāna capable of reaching the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
True reality is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and its characteristics regarding the common path of the heterodox and the orthodox are as follows:
the two dharmas and two persons indicated in this sutra refer to the Māra-sutras, the Māra-vinaya, and the upholding of the Māra-sutras and Māra-vinaya.
These are the four māras; this intention is broad, encompassing both the aforementioned errors and the correct [teachings], which are likewise fourfold.

The Buddhist sūtras and vinaya, and the upholding of the Buddhist sūtras and vinaya—these are the four correct [practices]. Since they are named after these four preceding correct practices, this chapter is called the "Chapter on the Erroneous and the Correct.
This chapter answers the previous question by Kāśyapa: "How does one know that the heavenly Māra acts as a leader for the assembly?"
Regarding the obstacles posed by Māra as described by the Tathāgata, how are they to be distinguished and known?

The four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) possess vast merit, and there is a capacity to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. Although these two meanings are mutually supportive, the answer concerning the four reliances clarifies the "vast," while the answer concerning the heterodox and orthodox clarifies "distinction.
Both categories are fully present; however, within the two types of falsehood—those of form and sound—the former category primarily elucidates form.

The "Chapter on Confusion" extensively clarifies the confusion of sounds (and so forth). The text is divided into five sections: first, a brief clarification of the heterodox and the orthodox; second, an extensive clarification of the heterodox and the orthodox;

third, the discussion of the meaning; fourth, the acceptance and understanding; and fifth, the restatement and confirmation. Within the first section, the brief clarification, there is both a question and an answer.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, should one rely upon the four kinds of persons as described above?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, son of good family. One should rely upon them just as I have described. Why is this?"
Because there are four demons (*māra*). What are the four? As stated by the Māra in other sūtras and vinayas that they uphold:
when questioned, they cite the aforementioned four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*); in their answers, they put forth a false Triple Gem.
The Māra is the false Buddha; what he speaks is the false Dharma; those who uphold it are the false Saṃgha. This is as described in the *Śata-śāstra*, where Kāpila claimed himself to be a Buddha.
It is said that because his disciples were thus deluded and confused, they required the four supreme reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, and after the two [sections] on the extensive explanation of the heterodox and the orthodox, there was a question and answer.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, there are four kinds of Māras; if it is by a Māra..."
Regarding what has been taught and what has been taught by the Buddha, how am I to distinguish between them?
Furthermore, among those sentient beings, some follow the conduct of Māra while others comply with the Buddha’s instructions; how are such individuals to be known?
In the question, both the heterodox and orthodox Triple Gems are asked about how they are distinguished, as in the text above.

The previous question, "How does one know that a celestial Māra creates obstacles for the assembly? asks about confusion through form (*rūpa-vikṣepa*). When it says, "Pāpīyān the Tathāgata speaks," how does one distinguish and know this?
This asks about confusion through sound (*śabda-vikṣepa*). Now, the question regarding Māra and what he says follows upon those two preceding questions.
The practitioners of Māra are his followers who return to follow Māra, creating disturbances through both form and sound.
The detailed answer is twofold: first, the answer concerning disturbances of form; second, the answer concerning disturbances of sound.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "Seven hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this Māra Pāpīyas will gradually bring about corruption and disorder."
My True Dharma is like a hunter who puts on the robes of the Dharma; likewise, Māra Pāpīyān also assumes the appearance of a bhikṣu,
a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā, and further transforms himself into the body of a srotāpanna,
even up to the body of an arhat and the physical body of a Buddha— by means of these, Māra [acts].
The physical form subject to outflows (āsrava) becomes the outflow-free body, thereby destroying my True Dharma (saddharma).

Regarding the initial statement that it lasts for seven hundred years: the True Dharma was originally set for one thousand years, but because women were permitted to enter the order, it was reduced by five hundred years.

Thus, at six hundred or seven hundred years, one enters the period of the Semblance Dharma (pratirūpaka-dharma). The Māyā-sūtra states that six hundred years after [the Buddha's passing], Aśvaghoṣa appeared; seven hundred years later...

In the year when Nāgārjuna appeared, Māra was at his height; there were four types of Māras who possessed tainted supernatural powers (*sāsrava-abhijñā*) capable of transforming themselves into the forms of the four reliances (*catuḥ-pratisaraṇa*), the four fruits of the path, and even the physical likeness of a Buddha.

Just as a hunter wears a *kāṣāya* robe on the outside while harboring murderous intent within, so too is Māra: outwardly appearing in the form of a sage while inwardly concealing evil schemes. For the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) does not abide therein.
It does not reside in form; how then can one speak of manifesting an outflow-free (anāsrava) appearance?
For even the noble ones possess outflow-free deportment, which is itself the outflow-free five aggregates (pañca-skandha); thus, Māra studies it.
From this point on, Pāpīyān shall make these assertions; the following two sections clarify the confusion of the sounds and the text into five parts:

first, confusing the Buddha’s body; second, confusing the establishment of the precepts; third, confusing the Buddha’s virtues; fourth, confusing the sūtras and vinaya; fifth, confusing sin and merit.

Regarding the first, confusing the Buddha’s body, there are again four points: first, confusing his birth; second, confusing his conduct; third, confusing his entry into the temple; fourth, confusing his taking of a consort.
Regarding the first passage concerning the consort:
when Māra Pāpīyas destroys the True Dharma, he will speak these words:
"In the past, the Bodhisattva descended from the Tuṣita Heaven and came here to the palace of King Śuddhodana in Kapilavastu, arising through the union of his parents' desire."
It is impossible for one who has been born as a human being to be honored by the great assemblies of devas and humans in all the worlds.

Furthermore, it is said that because he formerly practiced austerities and gave various gifts—his head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdom, city, wife, and children—he has now attained the Way of Buddhahood; for this reason, he is [honored].
Respected by all devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, you should know that any sutra or vinaya that makes such a statement is entirely the teaching of Māra.
Good son, if any sutra or vinaya speaks thus: "The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, has long since attained Buddhahood; it is only now that..."
The manifestation of attaining the Way of the Buddha is for the purpose of delivering all sentient beings;
thus, he manifests having parents and being born through the union of desire, acting in accordance with worldly conventions to make such a display.
One should know that such sutras and vinayas are truly spoken by the Tathāgata, whereas those that follow what is spoken by Māra belong to the retinue of Māra. If one can...
One who accords with what the Buddha has taught is a bodhisattva.
To say that there is actual birth is the teaching of Māra; to say that there is no birth, yet there is birth, is the teaching of the Buddha.
If someone says that it is not to be believed when the Tathāgata was born and took seven steps in each of the ten directions, [they speak falsely].

If this is what Māra says, or if there is another who says that the Tathāgata appeared in the world and walked seven steps in each of the ten directions—know that this is a skillful manifestation of the Tathāgata;
such is called the sūtras and vinaya spoken by the Tathāgata.
Those who comply with what Māra says are the retinue of Māra; those who can comply with what the Buddha says are bodhisattvas.

Next, regarding practice as well, one should apply this same principle; that it is not so [in the current case] clarifies that non-practice is the teaching of Māra, while practice is the teaching of the Buddha.
What is meant by "Māra"? It is that which constantly seeks to conceal the virtues of the Buddha and manifest his faults, which is called "disturbing the Buddha's practice."
If someone should say that after the Bodhisattva was born, the King’s messengers led him to a celestial shrine where all the devas, upon seeing him, descended to pay him homage;
and for this reason he is called "Buddha"—if there is further objection stating that the devas appeared first and the Buddha came later, so how could the devas pay homage to the Buddha?
One should know that such an objection is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

If there is a sutra that says: "When the Buddha went to a deva temple, all these devas—including Maheśvara, Mahābrahmā, and Śakra Devānām Indra—all joined their palms and paid homage at his feet," such sutras and vinayas are spoken by the Buddha;
those that accord with what is spoken by Māra belong to the retinue of Māra, while those that can accord with what is spoken by the Buddha are [the teachings of the Buddha].
This refers to the Bodhisattva.
If there are sūtras or vinayas that state: "When the Bodhisattva was a crown prince, out of desire he sought a wife from the four quarters;
dwelling in the deep palace, he amused himself with the five desires, feeling joy and receiving pleasure"—such sūtras and vinayas were spoken by Pāpīyas.
If there are those who say that a bodhisattva has long since abandoned the mind of desire and the company of wife and children,
not even accepting the exquisite five desires of the Heaven of the Thirty-three as if discarding snot or spittle, let alone human desires;

and that such sutras and vinayas concerning shaving the beard and hair to leave the home life and cultivate the Way were spoken by the Buddha— then for those who follow such demonic sutras and vinayas:
If any among the retinue of this Māra follow the sūtras and vinaya of the Buddha, they are bodhisattvas.
Their entry into the temple and their taking of a consort are all as described in the text.
From the time the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, he departed from that [place] and established the confused precepts as described in the text.
If there are those who say that while the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, he permitted the bhikṣus to accept and keep male and female slaves,
servants, oxen, sheep, elephants, horses, donkeys, mules, chickens, pigs, cats, dogs, gold, silver, lapis lazuli,
pearls, crystal, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, conch shells, jade, copper, iron, cauldrons, pots, and large and small bronze basins;
Regarding necessary items such as plowing fields, planting crops, trading in markets, and accumulating grain—

because the Buddha possesses great compassion and pities sentient beings, he permitted the possession of all such things. If there are those who claim that these sūtras and vinayas were all spoken by Māra,
or who say that the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, the dwelling place of the Nārivu spirits:
At that time, the Tathāgata, on account of the brahmin named Meṇḍhaka and King Prasenajit,
spoke thus: "Monks, you should not accept or keep gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, tridacna shells,
agate, coral, amber, conch shells, jade, male or female slaves, servants, boys or girls, oxen, sheep, elephants, horses, donkeys, mules, or chickens."
Pigs, cats, dogs, and other beasts; copper and iron cauldrons and pots; various sized copper basins; beds, mats, and bedding of diverse colors;

and all necessities for livelihood, namely: houses, plowing fields, planting crops, buying and selling in the markets, cooking with one's own hands, grinding and pounding grain, the arts of healing and incantations, methods for training hawks, observing the stars, and calculating the movements of the heavens.
They falsely practice divination for men and women, interpret dreams, and predict good or bad fortune; they claim whether a child will be male or female, or neither male nor female.
They possess sixty-four arts and eighteen delusive incantations, as well as various crafts and skills.

They may speak of countless worldly secular matters, such as scattering powdered incense, applying unguents, burning incense, making various flower garlands, and the techniques for grooming the hair—all of which involve deceit, falsehood, and flattery.
They are greedily attached to profit without satiety; they delight in bustle, laughter, and idle chatter;
they crave fish and meat; they compound poisons and medicinal oils; they carry precious parasols and leather sandals; they fashion fans, boxes, baskets, and various painted images;
they hoard grains, rice, wheat, barley, beans, and various fruits and gourds; and they associate with kings, princes, and great ministers.

The ministers and the women laughed loudly or remained silent; they gave rise to many doubts regarding all phenomena, spoke much in false words concerning long and short, beautiful and ugly, or good and evil;
they were fondly attached to fine garments and such various impure things, personally praising them with their own eyes before the donors, and moving in and out in an impure manner.
Those who frequent taverns, brothels, or gambling dens—such persons as these I now forbid from remaining among the bhikṣus;
they ought to cease their practice of the Way and return to lay life, like weeds and tares that must be utterly eradicated without remainder.
All such prohibitions established in the sūtras and vinaya are spoken by the Tathāgata. If there are those who follow what is spoken by Māra, [they shall not remain].
Those who belong to the retinue of Māra are those who follow what the Buddha has taught; they are indeed Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the "sixty-four abilities": the Buddha possesses the thirty-two marks, yet the heterodox teachers boastfully claim to rival the Buddha, and thus it is said they possess sixty-four abilities.
Furthermore, the Buddha possesses the thirty-two marks along with his karmic [attainments], whereas the heterodox teachers merely grasp at them.
Because they seek equality [with the Buddha], sixty-four capacities are established.

Third, if it is said that "going" is a confusion regarding the Buddha's virtues, or if it is said that a bodhisattva enters a celestial shrine—such as that of Brahmā—in order to make offerings to the devas; [this refers to such cases].
As for the reasons why [the Bodhisattva] enters the assemblies of Maheśvara, Vedadeva, and Kātyāyanīputra, it is because he desires to subdue all devas and humans;

were it otherwise, such a thing would be impossible. Furthermore, it is not the case that a Bodhisattva cannot enter into the heterodox doctrines of external paths, nor that he is unable to understand their deportment, literature, arts and crafts, servants, or disputes, nor that he is incapable of bringing about reconciliation.
He is revered by men, women, kings, and ministers; yet he does not know how to compound various medicines.
Because he does not know these things, he is called the Tathāgata. If one were to know them, such a person would be among those of false views.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s mind is equal toward enemies and kin; whether someone cuts him with a knife or anoints his body with fragrant incense, he regards these two people without distinction.
One who gives rise to a mind of exaggeration or depreciation can only abide in the middle way; therefore, such a person is called a Tathāgata.

Know that any sutra or vinaya that speaks in this manner is the teaching of Māra. Furthermore, if there is one who says: "The Bodhisattva thus manifests entry into celestial shrines and among those of external paths, leaving the home life to practice the Way;
he manifests knowledge of their dignified deportment and ritual etiquette, and is able to understand all their texts."
In this chapter on arts and crafts, it is shown that in matters of skillful mastery in the schoolhouse, one is able to skillfully reconcile the disputes of servants;
furthermore, among the great assemblies of boys and girls, the ladies of the inner palace, the common people, elders, brahmins, kings,
ministers, and the poor, one is the most honored and supreme, and is also revered by them all.

One who is able to manifest such matters as these, who, though dwelling amidst various views, does not give rise to attachment—just as a lotus flower is unsullied by dust and mire—and who, for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, skillfully employs such various expedient means in accordance with worldly dharmas:
one should know that such sutras and vinayas are indeed spoken by the Tathāgata. If there are those who follow after Māra...
Those who speak thus are the retinue of Māra; those who can accord with what the Buddha has taught are great Bodhisattvas.
Herein it is clarified that the Buddha does not know good from evil nor distinguish between enemy and friend; whether cut by a blade or anointed with perfume, he feels neither joy nor aversion.
This is like saying a person’s eyes do not blink when pricked by a thorn—it is merely a deluded mind confusing virtue with disorder.
Fourth, if someone were to say that the Tathāgata is "mine," this would constitute a subversion of the Sūtras and Vinaya;
first, it subverts the Sūtras and Vinaya in their initial general application, and subsequently, it subverts them regarding the concepts of permanence and impermanence, as the text describes.

If someone were to say, "The Tathāgata has explained for me the sūtras and vinaya, stating that among evil dharmas, the grave and light offenses as well as the sthūlātyaya are all by nature serious; we shall never commit such things within our own vinaya.
Since I have long endured such teachings, how could I, who do not believe you, abandon my own vinaya to follow yours?"
"The Vinaya you possess was spoken by Māra; our Sūtras and Vinaya were established by the Buddha.
The Tathāgata previously taught the ninefold seal of the Dharma (navāṅga-dharmamudrā), and these nine seals have sealed our Sūtras and Vinaya from the beginning.

We have never heard even a single phrase or a single word of the Vaipulya sūtras as spoken by the Tathāgata. Among the immeasurable sūtras and vinayas [taught by him], where is it said that there are Vaipulya sūtras?"
Among such [teachings], we have never heard the names of the ten classes of sūtras. If they did exist, one should know that they were certainly composed by Devadatta;
for Devadatta, being an evil man, created Vaipulya sūtras in order to destroy the True Dharma.
We do not believe in such sūtras as these, for they are spoken by Māra. Why? Because they subvert the characteristics of the Buddha-dharma and create disputes over right and wrong. As it is said:
This statement of yours— that "in my sūtras there is a self, while in your sūtras there is no self," and that in the sūtras and vinayas the Tathāgata has said,
"In the evil age after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be heterodox sūtras and vinayas, namely the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras;
in future ages there shall be such wicked bhikṣus"— and furthermore, my saying that "beyond the ninefold division of the scriptures (navāṅga-buddhavacana) there is [more]," [is what you claim].
Regarding the Vaipulya scriptures, if there is anyone who can thoroughly understand their meaning, one should know that this person correctly understands the sutras and vinaya,
remaining far removed from all impure things and being subtle, wondrous, and pure like the full moon. If someone were to say,

"Although the Tathāgata has expounded the flavor of the meaning of each individual sutra and vinaya as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, these are not found within our own vinaya," [one should know they speak falsely].
If one knows that which is non-existent as if it were existent, why would the Tathāgata not explain this within my Vinaya?
Therefore, I am now unable to accept or uphold it; you should know that such a person incurs an offense. That person further says:
"I shall receive and uphold such sutras and vinayas. Why? Because they will bring about for me contentment, few desires, and the severing [of attachments]."
Those who speak thus because afflictions, wisdom, nirvana, and wholesome dharmas are causes [of one another] are not my disciples.
If there are those who say that the Tathāgata, desiring to deliver sentient beings, preached the Vaipulya sūtras, you should know that such persons are truly my disciples.
If there are those who do not accept the Vaipulya sūtras, you should know that such persons are not my disciples. It is not for their sake [that I have spoken].

To leave the household life for the sake of the Buddha-dharma yet hold such views is to be a disciple of a heterodox teacher with false views. If a scripture or discipline is like this, it was spoken by the Buddha;
if it is not like this, it was spoken by Māra. Those who follow what was spoken by Māra are the retinue of Māra;
those who follow what was spoken by the Buddha are Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, son of good family, if there should be those who say: "The Tathāgata is not accomplished through immeasurable merits;

he is impermanent and subject to change; having attained the dharma of emptiness, he teaches non-self and does not conform to the world"—then such sutras and vinayas are said to be the teachings of Māra.
If someone should say: "The perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, and it is also [characterized by] non-existence..."
It is accomplished through immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* merits; therefore, it is eternally abiding and without change.
Such sūtras and vinayas are spoken by the Buddha. If there are those who follow what is spoken by Māra, they belong to the retinue of Māra;
if there are those who follow what is spoken by the Buddha, they are bodhisattvas.
Fifth, there is another person who says that this passage concerning the confusion of offenses and merits consists of three sections: first, it clarifies the correct;
second, it clarifies the deviant; and third, it again clarifies the correct.
Furthermore, there is another person who says: "There may be a bhikṣu who has not actually committed a pārājika offense, yet everyone claims [he has]."
To commit a *pārājika* offense is like cutting down a *tāla* tree; yet this bhikṣu has actually committed no offense.
Why? Because I have always said that if one commits even one of the four *pārājikas*, it is like splitting a stone that cannot be joined back together.
If he were to claim for himself the attainment of superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), then that would indeed be called committing a *pārājika*. Why? Because [in reality...]
Because one falsely manifests the appearance of attainment when there is nothing to be attained, such a person falls away from the human dharma;

this is called a *pārājika*. That is to say, if there is a bhikṣu who has few desires, is content, maintains pure precepts, and dwells in a secluded place, and a king or a high minister sees this bhikṣu and conceives the thought that he has attained arhatship, they immediately come forward to praise and honor him.
He paid obeisance and further spoke these words: "Such a Great Master, having cast off this body, shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu immediately addressed the king, saying: "I have truly not yet attained the fruits of the śramaṇa path;
Your Majesty, do not claim that I have attained the fruits of the path. I only pray that Your Majesty will not speak of me as one who does not know."

Those who possess the Dharma yet are not content—even those who claim to have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—all remain silent. If I were now to accept this in silence, I would be censured by all the Buddhas.

The practice of contentment is praised by all the Buddhas; therefore, I wish to joyfully cultivate contentment for the rest of my life. The following is a polished translation of the extant portion: "Those who possess the Dharma yet are not content—even those who claim to have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—all remain silent. If I were now to accept this in silence, I would be censured by all the Buddhas.
The practice of contentment is praised by all the Buddhas; therefore, I wish to joyfully cultivate contentment for the rest of my life."

"One who is content knows for himself that he has not yet attained the fruit of the Path. The King said, "I have received [the title] from you; I do not accept it myself now, and for this reason I am called 'Contented'.
At that time, the King replied, "Great Master, you have truly attained the fruit of Arhatship; you are no different from the Buddha.

Then the King issued a proclamation throughout his realm, making it known to all the people both within and without, as well as to those in the inner palace and the queens, so that everyone might know.
Because these are the fruits of the śramaṇa, they cause all who hear them to give rise to reverent faith, to make offerings, and to hold him in high esteem.
Such a bhikṣu is truly one who practices the pure holy life (brahmacarya). By this cause and condition, he causes all people to obtain great merit;
yet, in reality, that bhikṣu has not committed a pārājika offense. Why is this? Because of the person before him...
Because they give rise to a heart of joy and offer praise and offerings, what fault could such a bhikṣu possibly have?
If anyone were to say that this person incurs a transgression, you should know that such a scripture is spoken by Māra.
Furthermore, there may be bhikṣus who preach the Buddha’s secret treasury, the profound sūtras, stating that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature, and because of this nature, [they] sever...
Innumerable billions of afflictions and fetters are immediately transformed into Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, with the sole exception of those who hold to the icchantika view.
If a king or a great minister were to say, "Bhikṣu, will you become a Buddha or not?
Do you possess the Buddha-nature? the bhikṣu would answer: "Within my present body, the Buddha-nature certainly exists; as for whether it is realized or not..."
The King said, "Virtuous One, if he does not become an icchantika, he will certainly attain [enlightenment] without doubt.
The bhikṣu replied, "It is indeed as the King says; although this person claims that he definitely possesses the Buddha-nature, he has likewise not committed a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who, at the very moment of his ordination, thought to himself: "I shall now certainly..."
Such a person will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
although they have not yet realized the fruit of the unsurpassed path, they have already acquired immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable merit.
Suppose someone were to say that this person has committed a pārājika offense—then there would be no bhikṣu who has not committed one. Why is this? Because I, in...
In the past, for eighty billion kalpas, I have always remained free from all impure things;

possessing few desires and being content, I have perfected my dignified deportment and skillfully cultivated the unsurpassed Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, I have personally and with certainty known that my own body possesses the Buddha-nature;
therefore, I have now attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, am named a Buddha, and possess great compassion.
"O Śāriputra, those who cannot comply with such sutras and vinayas spoken by the Buddha are the retinue of Māra;
those who can comply with them are great bodhisattvas."
First, if a bhikṣu knows for himself that he is not an ārya and replies, "I am not an ārya," then there is no offense.
Next, there is another explanation which states that saying "there is no pārājika" is wrong.

Furthermore, there are those who say that there are no four *pārājika* offenses, thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, two *aniyata* dharmas, thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, ninety-one *pāyattika* dharmas, four *pratideśanīya* dharmas, numerous *śaikṣa* dharmas, or the seven methods for settling disputes;
nor are there any *sthūlātyaya* offenses, the five *ānantarya* crimes, or the *icchantika*. [They claim] that if a bhikṣu commits such things as these, he falls to the earth.
As for those in hell, all followers of external paths (tīrthika) should have been reborn in heaven. Why? Because these followers of external paths have no precepts to violate;
it is the Tathāgata who, in order to instill fear in people, has proclaimed these precepts. If one were to say that the Buddha taught:

"O bhikṣus, if you wish to engage in sexual intercourse, you should discard your dharma robes, put on secular clothing, and then engage in sexual intercourse; furthermore, you shall be reborn [in heaven]."
Reflecting on the causes and conditions of lustful desire, one realizes that this is not my fault;

even while the Tathāgata was in the world, there were bhikṣus who practiced lustful desires yet attained right liberation, or were reborn in the heavens after death—such things have occurred throughout antiquity and the present, and are not unique to me.
Whether one violates the four grave offenses or the five precepts, or practices all manner of impure conduct contrary to the monastic discipline, one may still attain [liberation].

One who possesses true liberation may, according to the Tathāgata’s teaching, fall into hell for eight million years—measured by the days, months, and years of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—even for committing a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).
This is merely the Tathāgata manifesting such words to terrify people;
there is no difference in weight between a *pārājika* (defeat) and a *duṣkṛta*. It is the various Vinaya masters who falsely make these claims, saying they are the Buddha’s word.
One should know with certainty that such teachings are not spoken by the Buddha; they are the sūtras and vinaya of Māra.
Third, if it further says: "Within all the precepts, one proceeds toward what is more clear and correct."
Furthermore, if it is said that among the various precepts, should one violate even a minor or subtle rule,
one shall undergo suffering with no limit to its duration— having understood this, one should protect oneself as a tortoise withdraws its six limbs.
If there is a Vinaya master who further says, "There is no karmic retribution whatsoever for any violation of the precepts," such a person should not be associated with.
As the Buddha has taught:
"If one transgresses even a single dharma, this is called false speech. Not seeing the future life, there is no evil one does not commit.
Therefore, one should not associate with such a person. Within my Buddha-dharma, purity is thus; how much more so for one who commits an offense?"
Is it possible that one commits a *sthūlātyaya*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pārājika* offense and yet it is not an offense?
Therefore, one should deeply guard oneself against such matters. If these are not protected, by what other means could they be called "prohibitive precepts"?
In the sūtras, I have also taught that there are offenses ranging from the four *pārājikas* down to even the most subtle *duṣkṛta* (or *āpatti*) transgressions.
One should sternly discipline sentient beings if they do not uphold the prohibitive precepts; for how could they ever perceive the Buddha-nature?
Although all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, it must be through the upholding of the precepts that they subsequently see it.
By seeing the Buddha-nature, they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Among the ninefold canon, the Vaipulya sūtras are absent.
Therefore, it is simply not stated that there is Buddha-nature; though the sutra does not mention it, one should know that it truly exists.
If one speaks thus, one should know that such a person is truly my disciple.
If one transgresses even a single dharma—when the precepts are being recited, if one is first asked whether they are pure, yet does not respond after the third proclamation—then [they have failed].
Regarding the formation of false speech (and so forth): although all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, they must rely upon the observance of the precepts.
This is because Buddha-nature is the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), while the observance of the precepts is the contributing condition (*pratyaya*). (And so forth.)
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: "This third discourse on the principles consists of three sections: first, a discussion on Buddha-nature; second, a discussion on transcending humanity;
and third, a discussion on dreaming and awakening. In the first section, he first asks [as follows]."

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what has been said above—that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature—this has never before been heard within the ninefold canon of scriptures. If it is as you say that they possess it, how is it that one does not commit a pārājika offense?"
The Buddha said, "Good son, as you have said, you have indeed not committed a pārājika offense.
Good son, for example, if someone were to say that the great ocean contains only seven treasures and no eighth, that person would be without fault.
Likewise, if someone were to say that within the ninefold canon there is no Buddha-nature, they too would be without fault. Why is this? Because I..."
Within the great ocean of wisdom of the Mahāyāna, it is said that there is Buddha-nature, which those of the Two Vehicles do not know or see;
therefore, when the Buddhas say it does not exist, there is no fault. Such a realm is known only by the Buddhas and is not within the reach of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Good son, if a person has not heard of the Tathāgata’s profound and secret treasury, how could they...?
One should know that there is the Buddha-nature. What is called the "Secret Treasury"? It refers to the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.
Good son, there are various non-Buddhists who either claim the self is eternal or claim the self is annihilated; the Tathāgata is not like this.
He speaks both of the existence of the self and of the non-existence of the self; this is called the Middle Way. If anyone should say that the Buddha taught the Middle Way...
It is taught that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; because they are shrouded by afflictions, they do not know it and do not see it.
Therefore, one should diligently cultivate skillful means to sever and destroy these afflictions.

If there is anyone who can speak in this way, you should know that such a person does not commit the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*). If one does not speak in this way, then that person is said to have committed a *pārājika* offense.
If there were one among the Mlecchas who said, "I have already attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," why?

Because they possess the Buddha-nature. Since those who possess the Buddha-nature will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, by this cause and condition, it should be known that such a person has now already attained the realization of Bodhi.
This is called committing a *pārājika* offense. Why is this? Although the Buddha-nature exists, because one has not yet cultivated the various skillful means of goodness, it is not yet seen.
Because it is not yet seen, one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Son of good family, for this reason, the Buddha-dharma is profoundly deep and inconceivable.
Next, regarding the response in which the Tathāgata states, "I teach that 'no-self' is called the Middle Way," the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says:
"Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither self nor no-self; both 'self' and 'no-self' are merely provisional designations.
"Self" is a provisional designation, while "no-self" is the reality; that which is neither self nor no-self is precisely the Middle Way.
Next, the second round of question and answer follows the pattern of first questioning and then answering.

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, there was a king who asked: 'How does a bhikṣu fall into the transgression of claiming superhuman states (uttaramanuṣyadharma)?"'"
In the response, first the offenses are clarified, next the non-offenses are clarified, and finally the offenses are clarified again as in the text (as detailed).
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "If there is a bhikṣu who, for the sake of gain and for the sake of food and drink, practices various forms of flattery, deceit, hypocrisy, and fraud, thinking:
'How may I cause the people of the world to truly know me as a genuine mendicant?'"
By these causes and conditions, I have gained great gain, offerings, and reputation.
Because such bhikṣus are largely ignorant and deluded, they constantly think throughout the long night: "I have truly not yet attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
how can I cause the people of the world to say that I have already attained them? Furthermore, how can I cause the upāsakas and upāsikās to all point [to me] as such?"
I speak thus: "The merit of this person is truly that of a noble one. Thinking in this way, he acts solely for the sake of seeking profit and not for the sake of seeking the Dharma;
yet his coming and going, his advancing and halting, are composed and serene; he carries his robes and bowl without losing his dignified demeanor;
he sits alone in a secluded place like an Arhat, causing all people in the world to say of him: "He is just like this."
The Venerable Kāśyapa is skilled in and delights in the foremost diligent practice of austerities and the cultivation of the dharma of tranquility.

For these reasons, I shall gain many followers and disciples; they too shall receive abundant offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites, and many women will revere, remember, and hold him in high esteem. If there be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who act in this manner...
This constitutes a transgression of the superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, desiring to establish the unsurpassed True Dharma, dwells in a secluded place and, though not an arhat, wishes to cause others to say of him:
"He is an arhat; he is a good bhikṣu, a virtuous bhikṣu, a tranquil bhikṣu."
I caused immeasurable people to give rise to faith; by these causes and conditions, I obtained an immeasurable number of bhikṣus as my retinue.
Because of this, I was able to teach precept-breaking bhikṣus and upāsakas, causing them all to uphold the precepts.
By these causes and conditions, I established the True Dharma, glorified the unsurpassed great meaning of the Tathāgata, and revealed the Vaipulya sūtras.
The Mahāyāna Dharma transforms and delivers all immeasurable sentient beings, and it skillfully explains the meaning of the gravity and lightness of the sutras and vinaya taught by the Tathāgata.
It further states: "I too now possess Buddha-nature; there is a sutra titled 'The Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata.
Within this sutra, I shall certainly attain the Way of Buddhahood and be able to exhaust immeasurable billions of afflictions and fetters."
He extensively taught immeasurable upāsakas, saying: "All of you possess the Buddha-nature;
I and you shall all together abide in the stage of the Tathāgata’s path and realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By making such a statement, this person is not said to have fallen into the offense of claiming superhuman qualities (uttaramanuṣya-dharma). This is called...
Bodhisattva,
if it is said that one who commits a *duṣkṛta* offense falls into hell for eight million years by the calculation of days, months,
and years in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to undergo various retributions for their sins, how much more so for one who intentionally commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense within this Mahāyāna?
If there is a bhikṣu who commits a sthūlātyaya, he should not be associated with. What is called a sthūlātyaya offense in the Mahāyāna sūtras?
Suppose a householder constructs a Buddhist temple and uses various flower garlands to make offerings to the Buddha;
if a bhikṣu sees the thread within the flower garland and takes it without asking, this is called a sthūlātyaya, whether he knows [the owner] or not.
It is likewise an offense if one destroys a Buddhist stūpa out of a greedy mind; such a person commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense and should not be associated with.

If a king or a high minister, seeing that a stūpa is dilapidated, wishes to repair it as an act of worship for the *śarīra*, and therein finds precious jewels, he may entrust them to a bhikṣu. Having received them, the bhikṣu may use them as he sees fit.
Such a bhikṣu is called impure and one who frequently engages in strife; a virtuous upāsaka should not associate with, make offerings to, or revere such a bhikṣu.
Such a bhikṣu is said to have no root, to have two roots, or to have indeterminate roots. One with indeterminate roots is as follows:
when desiring a woman, his body immediately becomes that of a woman; when desiring a man, his body immediately becomes that of a man.
Such a bhikṣu is called one with evil roots; he is not called a man, nor is he called a woman;
he is not called a renunciant, nor is he called a householder. Such a bhikṣu should not be approached, served, or honored.

Within the Buddha-dharma, those who possess the qualities of a śramaṇa should give rise to compassion and nurture all sentient beings, even down to the smallest ants, bestowing upon them fearlessness.
Abstaining from drinking intoxicants, even to the point of not smelling their fragrance, is the dharma of a śramaṇa;

not engaging in false speech, even to the point of not thinking of it in one's dreams, is the dharma of a śramaṇa; not giving rise to thoughts of desire, even to the point of likewise doing so in one's dreams, is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
In the third round of questions and answers, there are two parts: first the question, then the answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse in a dream, does this constitute a violation of the precepts?"
The Buddha said, "No. One should conceive thoughts of foulness and impurity toward sensual desire, such that not even a single thought of purity arises;
one should remain far removed from women and the afflictions of craving. If one commits sexual misconduct in a dream, upon waking one should feel remorse.
When a bhikṣu begs for food and receives offerings, he should regard it as if eating the flesh of his own son during a time of famine. If lustful desire should arise, he should swiftly abandon it."
One should know that this Dharma-gate is the sutra and vinaya spoken by the Buddha. If there are those who follow what is spoken by Māra, they are the retinue of Māra;
if one can follow what is spoken by the Buddha, they are called a Bodhisattva.

If someone says that one should constantly stand on one leg, remain silent and say nothing, throw oneself into deep waters or fire, or leap from high cliffs while avoiding no dangers or hardships—[this is not the teaching].
"To consume poison, fast, lie upon ashes and dust, bind one's own hands and feet, kill living beings, employ heterodox paths and incantations,
or for those who are sons of outcasts (*caṇḍāla*), those with no sexual organs, those with double organs, or those with indeterminate organs, or those whose physical faculties are incomplete—

to allow such persons as these to leave the household life and practice the Way is called the teaching of Māra. Furthermore, the Buddha previously permitted the consumption of the five kinds of cow-products."

Furthermore, regarding items such as oil, honey, *kauśeya* silk garments, and leather sandals—apart from these—if anyone were to say that the wearing of *mahāpramga* (large loincloths) is permitted, or that the storage of all kinds of seeds is allowed, or that even grasses and trees possess life, know that if any sutra or vinaya contains such statements, [it is not the word of the Buddha].
After the Buddha had spoken thus, he entered parinirvāṇa. If there are sutras or vinayas that make such assertions, one should know [them to be spurious].
These are the teachings of Māra which I do not accept: standing constantly on one leg;

nor do I accept walking, standing, sitting, or lying down for the sake of the Dharma; nor do I accept consuming poison, fasting, scorching the body with five fires, binding the hands and feet, killing sentient beings, practicing spells and incantations, wearing sandals made of conch shells or ivory, or hoarding seeds and grass.
If there is a scripture or a vinaya that states, "Wood has life," or "Mahālaṅka is attached to life," or if it says, "The World-Honored One spoke thus:

'You should know that such persons belong to the retinue of external paths and are not my disciples,'" or if it says, "I only permit the consumption of the five kinds of cow-products, as well as oil, honey,

and so forth," or "I permit the wearing of leather sandals and *kauśeya* silk garments," or "I have taught that the four great elements possess no life-force"— if such texts exist, [they are not my teaching].
Those who speak thus are said to be speaking the Buddha’s teaching. You should know that those who accord with what the Buddha has taught are truly my disciples;
those who do not accord with what the Buddha has taught are the retinue of Māra.

Those who accord with the Buddha’s sūtras and vinaya—you should know that such persons are great bodhisattvas and good sons. There is a difference between the teachings of Māra and the teachings of the Buddha.
The characteristics of these [dreams] have now been extensively proclaimed and analyzed for you.
There is no offense in dreaming of sexual intercourse, but once awakened, one should repent; if, after awakening, one praises it, one incurs a grave offense.

The meaning in the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Extensive) is also like this (and so forth). *Mahālaṅkā* means "red" in this language; it refers to being clothed in red garments, as mentioned in the following passage.

Regarding the contradiction [in the texts], how is it to be resolved? The explanation states: the subsequent passage speaks of the time before the precepts were established, whereas this passage speaks of the time after the precepts were established.
Furthermore, another explanation holds that there are many types of red: while deep red (such as *kāṇḍa-rakta*) is prohibited, light red (*rakta*) is not prohibited, and so forth.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: "The fourth section following this is the summary of understanding.
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, it is only now that I have come to know the distinguishing characteristics between the words of Māra and the words of the Buddha;
by means of this, I have gained entry into the profound meaning of the Buddha-dharma.'"
Fifth, the conclusion:
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa, saying, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! That you are able to understand and discern in this way is what is called wisdom."
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Fourteen: The Chapter on the Truths (Catuḥsatya-parivarta).
This chapter answers the previous question: "How is it that the Tamer of Men (the Buddha) joyfully proclaims the True Truth? [The old translation states: "Formerly, the Buddha followed..."
The conventional teaching of the finite Four Noble Truths pertains only to within the realms (*dhātu*), where the noble mind is not yet fully realized;
now, by taking the eternally abiding as the object, the infinite Four Noble Truths are taught, which transcend the three realms. Therefore, the Buddha’s mind rejoices.

They are also called the conditioned and unconditioned Four Noble Truths, or the created and uncreated Four Noble Truths. Now, it is asked: do the finite ones transcend the *pariccheda* (segmented existence), or not?
If transformation is immeasurable, it likewise does not transcend transformation; since both do not transcend it, they are equally finite.

How can the contrast between the finite and the immeasurable serve as a basis for joy when both are merely conditions of smallness and greatness? Furthermore, if the finite is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), how can you say that three are conditioned and one is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
If that were so, the meaning of "conditioned" would not be established; if it were non-existent, [the distinction] would be untenable.
If measure (*pramāṇa*) were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), how could there still be the cycle of death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*)? To explain:
it is called "unconditioned" because it is not produced by the body and life-force of the limited分段 (*paricchinna*) realm; it does not mean that the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are absent.

If this were so, it would truly not be unconditioned, and the category of the unconditioned would fail to be established, thereby undermining the concept of the unconditioned through non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Although the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* mentions this name, its teaching is distinct and serves as a separate condition.

One must not employ that [explanation of] the four truths in their immeasurable aspects to interpret the meaning of this sūtra, for the meanings do not correspond. Furthermore, it clarifies the four truths across five periods:
in the first period, they are treated according to phenomena (*dharma*), such as the characteristic of suffering as oppression (and so forth);

from the second period to the fourth period, they are treated according to principle (*li*), such as the realization that the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are empty and non-existent, which is the meaning of suffering.
The meaning is that when one enters contemplation through the understanding of words, names are lost and signs are severed; these four matters do not exist [independently].
Because one relies on the four skillful means, one speaks of the Four Truths. Just as upon seeing the truths one enters the reality, there are no eight patiences or eight knowledges;
rather, patience and knowledge are merely designations based on the single cessation (nirodha). It is for this reason that the four stages [of the path] are not explicitly clarified.
The Buddha-nature and the Buddha-mind do not rejoice in the fifth period, wherein wisdom is taken as the truth. As the text says:
"Because there is no suffering yet there is reality, the Buddha-nature and the Buddha-mind are said to rejoice. Now I ask:

if it is the same as before, then the issues regarding the finite and the infinite have already been refuted as previously stated. If it is neither finite nor infinite, then what truth is it? It would have no distinct name.
Since there is no separate name, there is likewise no separate principle; furthermore, what purpose would there be in using this to explain the present sutra?

Here we clarify that this chapter shares both similarities and differences with the "Chapter on Noble Practices" (*Ārya-caryā-varga*). While the "Noble Practices" chapter fully elucidates the fourfold Four Truths, the present text elucidates only the single reality of the Four Truths.
What are its characteristics? The Buddha-nature and the true mark (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) pervade all places and are able to...
One may only be said to have attained the Truths (*satya*) when one clearly understands the true nature (*lakṣaṇa*) of these four matters;
if one does not understand them, it is inverted and not the Truth. There are explicit texts on this—why cause confusion?

To say that knowing the Tathāgata’s profound realm, his eternally abiding and unchanging subtle-dense Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), is called "Truth" is merely citing the Buddha-fruit as a starting point; in reality, this applies universally.
To fully realize that all the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the animal realm and the hells are the eternally abiding Dharma-body, unchanging—this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
To give rise to true wisdom within impurity and not destroy the True Dharma—this is called the Noble Truth of the Origin [of Suffering].

To recognize the Tathāgatagarbha within cessation—this is called the Noble Truth of Cessation. Clearly recognizing the Three Jewels and attaining correct understanding—[this is the Noble Truth of the Path].

"Deliverance" (niḥsaraṇa) is the name for the Noble Truth of the Path (*mārga-āryasatya*). Although the truth is not a number of four, it is called the "Four Truths" because it is understood by way of these four.

The Tathāgata appeared in the world primarily to teach this; having previously concealed its characteristics, he now reveals them—like applying ointment to a wound or washing away poison—and thus says, "With a joyful heart, I shall speak the True Truth.
Because the title is established from this, it is called the "Chapter on the Four Truths. The text is divided into two parts: first, the elucidation of the Four Truths; second...
Understanding the initial Four Noble Truths constitutes four chapters, each containing six sections; there is only the distinction between those that follow a sequential order and those that do not.

Regarding the six sections of the Truth of Suffering: first, clarifying delusion; second, clarifying the fruit of delusion; third, clarifying understanding; fourth, clarifying the fruit of understanding;
fifth, concluding on understanding; sixth, concluding on delusion. One is precisely four, and four are precisely one; this is inconceivable.
This explanation is clear. First, it clarifies delusion; furthermore, it first directly clarifies suffering and subsequently explains why it is not understood as suffering.
The Buddha further told Kāśyapa: "That which is called 'suffering' is not named the Noble Truth of Suffering. Why?
If what is called suffering were the Noble Truth of Suffering, then all animals and sentient beings in the hells would possess the Noble Truth."

Good son, if there is another person who does not know that the Tathāgata’s profound realm is the eternally abiding and unchanging, subtle, and secret *dharmakāya*, but instead claims it is a body sustained by food and not a *dharmakāya*; or who does not know the Tathāgata’s moral virtue, spiritual power, and majesty—this is called suffering. Why?
Because through such ignorance, they perceive what is Dharma as non-Dharma, and perceive what is non-Dharma as Dharma.
The following passage explains that there are three kinds of suffering: first, that which is suffering but neither a truth nor real; second, that which is suffering and a truth but not real;
and third, that which is neither suffering nor a truth but is real (and so forth).
One should know that such a person will inevitably fall into lower realms; this is the fruit of deluded ignorance.
One should know that such a person will inevitably fall into the evil destinies, transmigrate through birth and death, increase all fetters, and undergo manifold suffering and affliction.
If there is anyone who can know that this [teaching] below is clear understanding,

or if there is anyone who can know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and without change, or even hear the sound of the two characters "eternally abiding" (nitya), [they shall attain liberation].
If [the teaching] passes through the ear even once, this is the fruit of clear understanding.

If it passes through the ear but once, one will immediately be reborn in the heavens; later, at the time of liberation, one will be able to realize and know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change.
Having realized this, one speaks these words: "In the past, I have already heard this meaning."

Now that I have attained liberation, I finally realize and know for certain that because I was ignorant regarding the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), I transmigrated through birth and death in an endless cycle;
it is only from this day forward that I have attained true wisdom.
If one understands in this way, the lower fetters are untied;
if one understands in this way, the true cultivation of suffering is of great benefit;
yet if one does not understand the afflictions of the lower fetters [in this way], [it is not so].
If one does not know this, even though they practice with diligence, it will be of no benefit; this is called "knowing suffering" and is the Noble Truth of Suffering.
If a person cannot cultivate in this manner, it is merely called "suffering" and is not the Noble Truth of Suffering.
Next is the Chapter on Origination (*Samudaya-varga*), which also consists of six sections in the same order as before. Herein, the first clarifies delusion.

Regarding the Truths of Suffering and Origination: within the true Dharma, they fail to give rise to true knowledge and instead accept impure things—namely, slaves and servants—and are able to use unrighteous speech to claim these are the True Dharma.
They destroy the True Dharma and do not allow it to abide for long.
By means of this ignorance, the subsequent delusive effects are clarified.

Because of these causes and conditions, one does not know the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because of this lack of knowledge, one revolves in birth and death, undergoes much suffering and affliction, and fails to attain rebirth in heaven or right liberation.
If there is one with profound wisdom who possesses inferior clear understanding,
or if there is one with profound wisdom who does not destroy the true Dharma,
by these causes and conditions, they will attain the fruit of inferior clear understanding.
By these causes and conditions, one attains rebirth in the heavens and right liberation. However,

if there are those who do not understand the truth of the origin of suffering and instead claim that the True Dharma has no permanence and is entirely subject to extinction, they will, by these causes and conditions,
wander through birth and death for immeasurable eons, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
Furthermore, by reiterating past delusion, it negates what is false to reveal what is true.
If one can know the binding and its liberation below,
and if one can know that phenomena are eternally abiding and unchanging, this is called "knowing the origin" and is termed the Noble Truth of the Origin.

If a person is unable to subdue the fetters and afflictions, or if a person is unable to practice in this manner, this is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering rather than its non-origination.
Next, in the chapter on the truth of cessation, there are likewise six sections, though the sequence differs slightly; first, the afflictions are explained.
Regarding the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering: if one extensively practices and studies the dharma of emptiness, this is not wholesome. Why?
Because it extinguishes all dharmas and destroys the Tathāgata’s true treasury of the Dharma; to practice and study in such a manner is called "cultivating emptiness."

Regarding the statement that those who cultivate emptiness excessively are of two kinds: first, the followers of the Two Vehicles who sink into emptiness; second, the non-Buddhists who negate existence.
This refers to the excessive cultivation of emptiness.
Next, the cultivation of the cessation of suffering refers to clear understanding.
Those who cultivate the cessation of suffering act in opposition to all non-Buddhists.
If it were said that the cultivation of emptiness constitutes the Truth of Cessation, then all non-Buddhists also cultivate the dharma of emptiness and should likewise possess the Truth of Cessation.
If there are those who say that although the *tathāgatagarbha* is invisible, one may enter [the path] once all afflictions have been extinguished, provided that such a mind is generated;
Through the causal conditions of a single thought-moment, one attains mastery over all phenomena.
Furthermore, it should be said that "contradicting the Śrāvakas" and "speaking specifically to the non-Buddhists" have two meanings: first, as previously stated, the Śrāvakas were rebuked;
second, the Śrāvakas who deviate from the truth are themselves non-Buddhists.
If there are those who cultivate the fruits of inferior knowledge and delusion,
or those who cultivate the Tathāgata’s secret store as being selfless, empty, and quiescent—
such persons will wander through birth and death for immeasurable eons, undergoing suffering.

If there are those who do not produce inferior understanding of the fruit, and if there are those who do not practice in this way, yet they are able to swiftly eliminate their afflictions—why is this?
It is because they know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata; this is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.
If one can thus loosen the lower fetters and if one can thus cultivate cessation, such a person is my disciple.
If there are those who cannot loosen the fetters and afflictions...
If there are those who cannot practice in this way, it is called "cultivating emptiness" rather than "extinguishing the Noble Truths.

The chapter on the Truth of the Path also consists of six sections, following the same sequence as before; however, the final conclusion differs slightly from the beginning, which first clarifies the delusions (*kleśa*).
The Noble Truth of the Path refers to the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, as well as Right Liberation.

There are sentient beings with perverted minds who claim that the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, and Right Liberation do not exist; they regard the cycle of birth and death as being like an illusion or a magical transformation, and they cultivate such a view.
First, that which is deluded is presented; next, the delusion itself is correctly elucidated.
With these causes and conditions, the following explains the fruit of delusion:
by means of these causes and conditions, one revolves through the three realms of existence and undergoes great suffering for a long time.
If one can give rise to the mind and attain the lower level of clear understanding,
and if one can give rise to the mind and perceive that the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Sangha are eternally abiding and unchanging, liberation is likewise so.
By means of the fruit of this single thought of lower clear understanding, one attains it.
Riding upon this single thought, one attains the sovereign fruits and rewards of immeasurable eons according to one's wish. Why is this?
Because in the past, due to the four inversions, I took what is not the Dharma to be the Dharma and underwent the retribution of immeasurable evil karma.
Now, by extinguishing such views, I have attained the perfect enlightenment of a Buddha; this is called the Noble Truth of the Path.
If someone says that the Three Jewels are impermanent, they are bound below by delusion.
If someone says that the Three Jewels are impermanent and cultivates this view, they are practicing what is false and not the Noble Truth of the Path.
If one cultivates this Dharma, the lower fetters are untied.
If one cultivates this Dharma as that which is eternally abiding, such a person is my disciple who truly sees and practices the Four Noble Truths;
this is called the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding the statement that the "actual fetters" are extinguished through the Path, concerning the Four Truths: since the Path and Cessation follow the [other] four truths, they should be placed as the fourth.

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, it is only now that I have come to know how to cultivate the profound Four Noble Truths. This is the second section on comprehension, wherein Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addresses the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have only now begun to understand the cultivation of the extremely profound Four Noble Truths."
The Dharma.
Chapter Eleven: The Four Perversions of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Chapter on the Four Perversions.
"Upside-down" refers to delusion. As it was said above, when a person is intoxicated, they become dazed and confused, and even the sun and moon appear to revolve;
how much more so does this manifest the delusions and karmic actions? These delusions are not fixed in number, occurring as one, two, three, four, eight, or even many.

The first is simply ignorance (*avidyā*), which is a false and empty snare that ensnares oneself. The second is the attachment of views and perceptions, which leads to injury and ruin. The third is... [text fragment ends]
The deluded mind is an inversion of mind; the crazed and impetuous are inversions of thought; and the discriminative views are inversions of view—these constitute the four [inversions].
The four—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—are false arts devoid of reality. The eight—impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity—are like tiles and pebbles, not the truth.

As for the multitude [of phenomena], they are merely nirvana and buddha-nature, which are ultimately pure, neither inversions nor truths; it is only from the causes and conditions of delusion and awakening that one speaks of inversions.

When the Buddhas first appeared in the world, they taught the Dharma to destroy perverted views; yet when their bequeathed teachings remained in the world and the distance from the Sage grew great, people clung to the literal words while losing the intended meaning.
Not understanding that skillful means were like medicine, the medicine turned into poison, and they immediately gave rise to the four perversions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

When the Buddha first appeared in the world, he administered the medicine of impermanence to pour out these perversions; once the illness was gone, the medicine remained, yet they clung to it as being the ultimate truth.

When sentient beings are deluded by the Buddha’s skillful means and give rise to views of impermanence and so forth as being the Buddha, this is an affliction; one should apply views of permanence and so forth to treat that illness.
If, in a future age at the end of the Dharma, views of permanence and so forth become an affliction, it will be transmitted to a subsequent Buddha who alone will be able to treat it.

These alternating perspectives throughout the past and future are all termed the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*). If one treats the afflictions of permanence and so forth, it is as in the ancient teachings; if one treats the afflictions of impermanence and so forth, it is as [in the later teachings].
In this "Chapter on Sorrowful Lamentation," only the illness of delusion is clarified. If one understands the illness, one can immediately apply the remedy.

Since the departure from perversion and the absence of [false] truths should be explained separately, the four perversions (*catur-viparyāsa*) are clarified, and the eight perversions (*aṣṭa-viparyāsa*) are also elucidated.
The scribe of the scripture has abbreviated by combining them into four; here, following that combined title, they are presented in order to correspond with the Four Noble Truths.
Because they are mutually established, the three aspects are discussed in proximity. The teachings of Māra and the teachings of the Buddha are discussed in general terms;

the four truths are distinguished to clarify right understanding, and the four inversions are distinguished to clarify erroneous delusion. If one understands only the truths while remaining inverted, it is like a person with partial vision who enters a grove and perceives only a tree stump;
such a person does not possess complete knowledge and is therefore not called one who has correctly and fully accomplished the wholesome.

To perform wholesome karma is to simultaneously resolve both the heterodox and the orthodox, as well as the inverted and the true truths; thus, one universally penetrates them and fully accomplishes what is correct and wholesome.
The agent who is able to perform such wholesome karma is the *tathāgatagarbha*. These stages are sequentially established and combined to form the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*).

Because their meaning is thus convenient, they are called the "Chapter on the Four Inversions. The text is divided into two parts: first, the clarification of the four inversions; second, the summary and understanding thereof. First, regarding the former:
The four inversions constitute four chapters. The first chapter is divided into three parts: first, identifying the realm of suffering; second, identifying the essence of suffering;

and third, the conclusion. The Buddha again addressed Kāśyapa, saying: "As for the four inversions, to give rise to the perception of suffering within that which is not suffering is called 'perversion.'"
This is a perversion.
To regard that which is not suffering as suffering is called the Tathāgata’s conception of suffering; it means that all Tathāgatas are impermanent and subject to change.
If one says that the Tathāgata is impermanent, it is called a great sinful suffering. If one says that the Tathāgata has abandoned this body of suffering and entered [nirvāṇa]...
To regard nirvāṇa as being like the extinction of a fire when the fuel is exhausted—this is called perceiving what is not suffering as suffering; this is called a perversion.
If I were to say that the Tathāgata is permanent, that would be the view of a self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*). Because of the view of a self, there are immeasurable faults.
Therefore, one should say that the Tathāgata is impermanent. If one speaks in this way, I shall find joy; the Tathāgata is impermanent.
That which is thus [regarded] is suffering. If it is suffering, how can pleasure arise? Because one conceives the notion of pleasure within suffering, it is called a perversion;
to conceive the notion of suffering within pleasure is also called a perversion. That which is pleasure is the Tathāgata, and that which is suffering is the impermanence of the Tathāgata.
If one says that the Tathāgata is impermanent, this is called conceiving the notion of suffering within pleasure.
The Tathāgata’s eternal abiding is called bliss. If I were to say that the Tathāgata is permanent, how could he enter into nirvāṇa?
If one says that the Tathāgata is not suffering, why would he relinquish his body and undergo extinction?
To conceive the notion of suffering within what is bliss is called a perversion.

To regard that which is not suffering within the fruit of Buddhahood as suffering is itself a delusion; it would entail the retribution of suffering, yet they claim this is liberation—this is to conceive the notion of pleasure within suffering.

Regarding impermanence and change, they say that the Buddha undergoes the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) when he relinquishes his body and enters parinirvāṇa, and that he undergoes the suffering of decay (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
To claim that the Tathāgata is permanent is an inversion; to claim that he is impermanent is [an inversion].
Listen, if I were to say that perceiving the impermanent as permanent is precisely the inverted mind that takes pleasure in what is suffering (and so forth),
this is called the first inversion. Regarding the second inversion—
the perception of the impermanent as permanent— I have here presented both perceptions within the context of the object, while specifically explaining only one within the essence [of the inversion].

Having already explained the above, I shall not trouble the text with further elaboration; the perversion of the object has been set forth, and the nature of the perversion will be clarified and concluded later.
To perceive the impermanent as permanent and the permanent as impermanent is called a perversion (*viparyāsa*).
That which is impermanent is called not cultivating emptiness; because one does not cultivate emptiness, one's lifespan is short.
If anyone should say that by not cultivating emptiness and quiescence one obtains eternal life, this is called a perversion.
What is called "non-cultivation" refers precisely to the non-cultivation of the wisdom of *prajñā* and emptiness;
this is termed the second inversion.
The latter two inversions may be sought out [by the reader].
To perceive non-self as self, or self as non-self, is called a perversion.
People of the world also say there is a self, and within the Buddha-dharma it is also said that there is a self.
Although people of the world speak of a self, they lack the Buddha-nature; this is what is meant by giving rise to the notion of self within that which is non-self.
This is called a perversion of the Buddha-dharma: to say that the existence of a self is itself the Buddha-nature is what worldly people call the "conception of non-self within a self.
If one says that the Buddha-dharma definitely asserts there is no self, and therefore the Tathāgata commands his disciples to practice the cultivation of non-self, this is called a perversion.
This is called the third inversion.
To perceive the pure as impure and the impure as pure is called an inversion.
That which is pure is the Tathāgata, who is eternally abiding, whose body is not composed of mixed food, whose body is not of afflictions, and whose body is not of flesh.

It is not that this body is bound by sinews and bones; if one were to say that the Tathāgata is impermanent, a body sustained by mixed food, even down to being a body bound by sinews and bones, or that the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and liberation are subject to extinction—this is called perversion.
To perceive the impure as pure is called perversion. If one were to say, "Within this body of mine, there is not a single dharma [that is truly existent]," [this is not perversion].

To say that by means of this impurity one will surely enter the state of purity through the concentration on impurity—as the Tathāgata has spoken such words regarding the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity—is a false statement; it is called a perversion.
This is called the fourth inversion.
Regarding the second part, the understanding and realization, there are two sections: first, the realization; second, the description of delusion.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, from this day forward, I have finally attained right view."
"World-Honored One, prior to this, we all considered ourselves people of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
To speak analytically, one who denies cause and effect is called a person of wrong view;
yet, Kāśyapa, for a long time you have been characterized by a general perversion that encompasses everything, and thus you still possess [wrong view]... (and so forth).
