*The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Chapter Twelve: "The Nature of the Tathāgata" (Scroll Eight).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty;
re-edited by the Śramaṇas Huiyan and Huiguan,
and Xie Lingyun of the Jin Dynasty.

Regarding the title of this chapter, "The Nature of the Tathāgata": the use of the term "Tathāgata" rather than "Buddha" accords with the three periods of time; for all Buddhas of the three periods are initially titled "Tathāgata.
Furthermore, by citing the beginning to indicate what follows, it shows that the name is no different [from the Buddha], thereby refuting various heterodox views.
Furthermore, because the Tathāgata is the Buddha and the Buddha is the Tathāgata, it is said that the "Tathāgata-nature" chapter consists of the four *siddhāntas* (and so forth).
Moreover, "Tathāgata" is the supreme designation for the ultimate fruit (*phala*), while "nature" (*prakṛti*) is the fundamental name for the ultimate principle (*tattva*).
It is not only the ultimate fruit that is called "Tathāgata"; the original nature of sentient beings is also called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is modeled after the fruit.

Although "nature" (*prakṛti*) is conceptually modeled upon the cause, even though both cause and fruit are listed, the intent lies in the cause; therefore it is called the "Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature.
Furthermore, because the fundamental nature of the fruit is hidden and difficult to discern, the manifest is cited to indicate the hidden; thus it is called the "Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature.

Moreover, the principle of nature contains and encompasses all various natures—good and evil, as well as the three vehicles—and by citing the superior while setting aside the inferior, [it is so named].
Regarding the "Chapter on the Nature of the Tathāgata": furthermore, the name "Tathāgata" applies universally to all sentient beings who possess a mind, as they are all future Tathāgatas.
The four reliances (*catvāraḥ pratisaraṇāḥ*) and the bodhisattvas are likewise called "Tathāgata," just as the Buddhas of the ten directions are all equally termed "Tathāgata.

Within a single Buddha, there are the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the response body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*), all of which are termed "Tathāgata. In this present text, however, it specifically elucidates the *tathāgatagarbha*.
In these Tathāgatas, the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) all possess a self; because they are identical to this self, they are called "Suchness" (*tathatā*).

Because they manifest this Suchness to people, they are called "Come" (*āgata*); being eternally indestructible, it is termed their "nature" (*prakṛti*). Based on this, the name is established as the "Chapter on the Nature of the Tathāgata.
One should know that this Tathāgatagarbha is precisely the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). [This concludes] the masters' explanation of the meaning of "garbha" (storehouse).
Various masters of the treatises have stated that because the fruit of Buddhahood does not yet exist at the present moment but will exist in the future, it is called a "treasury" (*garbha*).
Others have stated that the Buddha-nature is the sentient being’s mind and consciousness, and that this mind and consciousness itself can avoid suffering and seek happiness;

thus, they claim that the mind and consciousness constitute the meaning of the six dharmas as Buddha-nature. All such views are incorrect, for this chapter [demonstrates] that the Tathāgata’s self-nature is...
The mind-essence (*cittatman*) is not [manifested] by means of the six dharmas; yet, while the Tathāgatagarbha remains hidden, the mind-essence and the six dharmas are all manifest.

Furthermore, the Tathāgatagarbha is eternal, whereas the mind-essence and the six dharmas are subject to change and impermanent; they have no relation whatsoever to the nature of the Tathāgata. Now, none of these are employed.
The followers of the *Dì* (Earth) school claim that because delusion obscures the principle, it is called "garbha" (storehouse). Is this interpretation correct?
However, I privately maintain that it is not that there is no single aspect [of truth], but rather that it does not accord with the title of this chapter.
For that [other view] treats delusion and principle as distinct, asserting that delusion can obscure principle; yet according to the sutra, within all dharmas there is entirely the nature of bliss.
How could a delusion characterized by "no-nature" obscure a nature that is itself "free from delusion"? As this would fail to capture the intent of the sutra, I do not adopt it.
I say that not only is the nature of delusion identical [to nirvana], but what is there that is not subsumed within it?
What dharma is not present in nirvana? All sentient beings are the very mark of nirvana; all lands are the very mark of nirvana (and so forth).
Furthermore, some scholars of the treatise say that the future fruit constitutes its nature; others say that the six external dharmas constitute its nature. This refers to the latter.
The people of the interior say that delusion and obscuration reside in the *ālayavijñāna*; this too is an internal [view]. Xinghuang says it is neither internal nor external.

Those who exclusively rely on the "correct nature-ground" (*zhengxingdi*), those who exclusively rely on the "inherently existing" (*benyou*) theory, and those who exclusively rely on the "conditions and rewards" (*yuanliao*), as well as those who rely on the future fruit, the fruit-nature, and the fruit-of-fruit-nature—all are rebuked by the Sūtra like blind men touching an elephant, failing to grasp the profound intent. Now...
Because it clarifies the equality and purity of the four propositions and is free from contention, it is called "Tathā" (Thus);
because it skillfully manifests to sentient beings through the four *siddhāntas*, it is called "Āgata" (Come); and because it is eternal and unchanging, it is called "Gotra" (Nature).

How could the *tathāgatagarbha* consist of only a single dharma? Furthermore, as for those who cling to the view that the *tathāgatagarbha* must necessarily possess these specific meanings—that is not so.
The Buddha-nature is neither existent nor non-existent, neither both existent and non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent;

how then can it be said to be exclusively existent? Although it is not any of these four [extremes], when there are causes and conditions, it is explained through the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold teachings) from a single perspective; therefore, regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*, one cannot say it does not exist.
By means of existence, one receives those who are nihilistic; by means of existence, one refutes those who hold to eternalism.
When there is an awakening that causes one to realize the Buddha-nature, the Buddha-nature does not consist of three gates; it is likewise with this.

Why then do you cling to its existence and thereby harm the three gates? It is like a person asking about a bridge—what benefit is there in such dispute? Now, in clarifying the Buddha-nature, the intent is as follows:
if one grasps this meaning, then within the fundamental nature itself, the ultimate fruit is both hidden and manifest, and both internal and external.

Furthermore, it is as described in the sutras: "Within the house there is a treasure of gold, its size unknown; one who is skillfully able to excavate it and whom people revere and look up to—this is precisely the meaning. Question:
Regarding the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha* (the nature of the treasury), how are the three [aspects] the same or different? Answer: They are simply one single meaning.
If one wishes to distinguish them, the principle and delusion are discussed together and termed the "treasury" (*garbha*). If delusion is not discussed at all, it is called the "nature" (*prakṛti*).
The principle that cannot be altered is called "nature" (svabhāva), and so forth. There are five similes given by the Teacher regarding the arising [of this nature]. First, he asks:

"In the twenty-five states of existence (pañcaviṃśati-bhava), does the self (ātman) exist? The Buddha answers with the simile of the poor woman’s hidden treasure to clarify that the self exists, yet it is concealed and not manifest.
If this is so, why was it not explained earlier? The Buddha then provides the simile of the poison-smeared [finger] because of the chronic illness [of sentient beings].

If one has not yet ceased [the flow], one must not wash the breasts; these two ailments—whether manifest or hidden—apply to sentient beings when discussed in terms of their physical condition, and to the Buddha’s teaching when discussed in terms of practice.
If that is so, why is it that among sentient beings there are distinctions between the six realms, with such vast differences in their ascent or descent?
The Buddha raised the example of losing a pearl during a fight, which led to unequal feelings of sorrow and joy. If that is so, for what reason did they fight? The Buddha [replied].

To cite sweet medicine as being truly present while remaining in the mountains, yet resulting in salty and sour flavors from a lack of virtue—if this were so, then since the true and the obscure are immutable, who could possibly harm them?

If they cannot be harmed, then there is no offense of killing. Just as the Buddha raised a sharp pickaxe that could pierce stone and sand but could not damage a diamond, so too the Buddha cannot be harmed; yet the nature of the offense of rebellion arises from the intent of the mind.
It is not that one incurs sin by disparaging the *skandhas*, yet a single response can resolve this. Why, then, are there so many successive [explanations]?

It is solely because the Buddha-nature is difficult to clarify; thus, ten thousand axes are needed to fell the tree. The arising of these five similes is due to the skillful thought of that [author], and for this reason they are preserved here (and so forth).
Now, this chapter answers the two preceding questions. First, it answers the question: "How does one perform wholesome karma?"

Next, I respond to the objection that it is difficult to perceive the nature (*dharmatā*). These two aspects are mutually established: it is precisely through wholesome karma (*kuśala-karman*) that one can perceive the nature, and the nature is manifested through wholesome karma.
Karma begins and the nature concludes; based on this final point, we shall discuss the person who understands the meaning of wholesome karma.

One who is provisionally named a "practitioner" is able to govern both good and evil. By governing the good, one refines the mind and spirit, thereby attaining perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
A proponent of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* asks: "If there is a provisional person (*pudgala*) within the cycle of birth and death, is this person the Buddha-nature?
The opponent replies: "That cannot be the Buddha-nature; likewise, it also cannot be the self (*ātman*). Since there is no self, who is it that directs wholesome karma?

Furthermore, you clarify that the provisional person is non-autonomous, whereas the self is autonomous; these two matters are mutually contradictory. [This is the objection of] the Earth-people (*Bhūmika*).

It clarifies that the substance of the dharma-realm possesses both good and evil functions; substance and function are fully present even within delusive afflictions, like gold covered by soil, incapable of being destroyed.
If delusive afflictions were thus [absolutely non-existent], these functions would be useless; how then could they perform karma?
Now, to clarify this meaning: as the sutra says, "The golden treasury cannot be seen"—at such a time, one is unable to perform wholesome karma.
Once the hidden treasure has been excavated, what need is there for the cultivation of wholesome karma? The activities of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) are not wholesome karma.
It is through the skillful means of another person that the son is shown the golden treasure in his house; digging it up is precisely the meaning of performing wholesome karma.
If one considers this in terms of six stages: in the first stage it is impossible [to find it], in the final stage it is unnecessary, and it is during the four intermediate stages that it occurs.

Regarding the stage of performing activity (*karmakāraṇa-avasthā*), if one considers it in terms of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): that which is hidden cannot manifest; that which is not required is also hidden; and that which is both hidden and manifest is precisely what performs the activity.
In response to this, regarding virtuous action (*kuśalakarma*), there are two parts: first, clarifying that Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) acts as the condition (*pratyaya*) for virtuous action;

second, clarifying that Buddha-nature actually gives rise to virtuous action. Regarding the first—acting as the condition for virtuous action—there are again two parts: first, clarifying the conditions for the action; second...
In the initial section on conditions within this treatise, there is further dialogue.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the twenty-five states of existence, is it not the case that there is a self?
The Buddha asked: "Is this [self] produced from the four inversions? Although all worldly beings speak of a 'self,' it is not called Buddha-nature."

The transcendental true self is called the Buddha-nature; therefore, he raises the question: "Regarding the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), if there were definitely a self, then they would not be 'existences' (*bhava*);
if there were definitely no self, who would perform wholesome deeds? Thus, one asks: do these twenty-five existences possess a self?"

The Buddha answered with two analogies. The first analogy clarifies that what is originally present cannot be seen; the second analogy explains that it cannot be described immediately, thereby resolving doubts.

Within the first analogy, there are two parts: the teaching (dharma) and the application of the analogy (upamāna). Regarding the first part, there are two points: the original existence and the two ways in which it is invisible.
The Buddha said: "Good son, 'I' is the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*; that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is the meaning of 'I.
This meaning of 'I' has, from the very beginning, been constantly shrouded by immeasurable afflictions; therefore, sentient beings..."
It cannot be seen. However, the Buddha-nature is neither original nor future; it is spoken of as such for the sake of conditions.

Next, the analogies in the text are divided into four parts: first, an analogy for the original nature; second, an analogy for its being invisible; third, an analogy for the response of conditions; fourth...
This is an illustration through analogy.
Good son, it is like a poor woman who has within her house a vast store of genuine gold.

The meaning of the first passage is as follows: she is called "poor" because of the deficiency of the conditions for awakening (pratyaya), and she is called a "woman" because she possesses the capacity to give birth [to the Buddha-nature].
Because it relies upon the five aggregates, it is called a "house"; because it possesses the true Buddha-nature, it is called "gold"; because this nature encompasses all, it is called a "treasury";
and because this nature is vast and extensive, it is called "abundant.
Yet, among the family members, both great and small, there is no one who knows of its existence.

Next, regarding those among family members who do not understand—according to the old interpretation, those who have attained the four fruits of sagehood are "great," while ordinary beings within the three realms are "small"—none of these understand the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
Some say that only Bodhisattvas are "great" and only Śrāvakas are "small," yet they too do not understand.
Here, it is clarified that humans and devas are "small," while the two vehicles that analyze emptiness are "great. Furthermore, [the latter] analyzes...

They do not understand that taking the emptiness of the two vehicles as the small body of emptiness and the two vehicles as the great is [the perspective of] "mere emptiness" for śrāvakas as small and "mere emptiness" for bodhisattvas as great;
nor do they understand that "mere emptiness" for bodhisattvas is small while "bodhisattvas emerging from the conventional" is great.
At another time, there was a different person who came, serving as an analogy for the conditions that evoke a response.
At that time, a man skilled in expedient means spoke to a poor woman, saying, "I will now hire you;
you may weed and clear away the filth for me. The woman replied, "I cannot do so now; however, if you can show me where my son’s store of gold is hidden..."
Thereupon, he should quickly provide this person with such an answer. The man says, "I know the skillful means.
The woman speaks again, saying, "Even my own family members, both great and small, do not know [this]; how much less could you possibly know it?
The man replies, "I am now truly able [to do so]. The woman speaks again, saying, "I also wish to see it; please show it to me."
Within this, the question-and-answer section first employs the "lesser path" to accommodate him; thus it says he "weeds out the weeds and filth.
Because the conditions were unwilling to accept [the teaching], it says he "could not. When the conditions for showing him the gold arose, it was due to the power of transformation;
because he wished to precede others, I likewise desired to see him—this constitutes the latter part.
Fourth, the person immediately goes forth to proclaim it.

That person then digs up a hidden treasure of gold within that house; when the woman sees this, her heart is filled with joy, she conceives a sense of wonder, and she comes to revere and look up to that person.
The three combined analogies have two parts: first, the analogy; second, the application, which can be seen [as follows].
"Good son, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
All sentient beings are unable to perceive it, just as that poor man did not know of the treasure store. Good son, I..."
Now, for the sake of all sentient beings, the Buddha-nature that exists within them has been universally revealed;

though it is obscured by various afflictions, it is like a poor man who possesses a treasury of genuine gold yet cannot see it. Today, the Tathāgata has universally shown to all sentient beings the treasure-store of awakening, which is called the Buddha-nature.
When all sentient beings have seen this matter, their hearts give rise to joy, and they take refuge [in the Buddha].
To look up to the Tathāgata’s skillful means is precisely the Tathāgata; the poor woman is precisely all immeasurable sentient beings;
and the treasury of true gold is precisely the Buddha-nature.
The second analogy consists of two parts: first the analogy and then the application. The initial analogy is divided into four sections: first, clarifying the arising of the illness of the self;
second, prescribing the medicine of non-self; third, the cessation of the illness of the false self; and fourth, the emergence of the teaching on the true self.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a woman who gives birth to a child, and that infant falls ill.

Her heart is filled with sorrow as she laments for him. This analogy is explicit, while the previous one was implicit. Regarding the former interpretation, there were four masters who explained the woman and the physician:

the first said the woman represents the *dharmakāya* and the physician represents the *nirmāṇakāya*; the second said the woman represents true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) and the physician represents... [the remainder of the text follows].

Third, the daughter represents expedient wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*), while the physician represents the subsequent Buddha. Fourth, the daughter represents the Buddha’s wisdom, and the physician represents the conditions of the faculties (*indriya-pratyaya*).

In the preceding passage, the impoverished woman represented the bodies of sentient beings; since this woman is not described as poor, she serves as an analogy for the Buddha’s wisdom, which should be superior [to the previous].
The single son born represents sentient beings who, having received the teaching, give rise to understanding; however, because that understanding was slight...
Therefore, it is said that because an infant is attached to what is false and constant, they contract illness.

Next, the passage beginning with "Then this woman was filled with grief and distress" provides a parable for the medicine of non-self, which consists of three parts: first, the Buddha’s wisdom observing the capacities of beings;
second, providing transformation according to those observed capacities; and third, severing the false self. Regarding the first section:
This woman, distressed by grief, seeks a skilled physician.
Because expedient wisdom gives rise to compassion, it is said she is "distressed"; because she seeks a recipient who lacks the sense of self (*anātman*), it is said she "seeks a physician.
Once the skilled physician arrives, he immediately finds the recipient and bestows his transformative teaching.
Once the skilled physician has arrived, he combines three kinds of medicine—clarified butter, milk, and honey—and gives them to him to drink.
These three medicines are an analogy for the three contemplations on impermanence.
The three causes [of the teaching] are the instruction given to the woman to sever the false notion of self.
He then told the woman, "Once your son has taken the medicine, do not give him your breast milk; you must wait until the medicine has been digested before giving it to him.
At that time, the woman immediately applied a bitter substance to her breasts and said to her son, "My breasts have been smeared with poison;
they must not be touched again."
In this context, milk is a metaphor for the true self (*ātman*), because it is not the [conventional] self. Thus, it is said that one must not add a bitter taste to the milk;
this is a metaphor for covering the true self with the notion of non-self (*anātman*).

Just as bitterness and sweetness are contrary in their nature, why is there milk again among the three previously combined medicines? This, too, is because the bitter taste of non-self is contrary to the permanent [nature].

Third, when the child’s thirst and exhaustion subside—this is a metaphor for the cessation of my affliction by wrong views—the child, desiring to obtain his mother’s milk, smells the poisonous odor of the milk and immediately abandons it from afar; he only returns once that medicine has been digested.

First, the cessation of the disease-breath is clarified; next, the elimination of the medicine is clarified because it is the dependent origination of the true self. Therefore, it is said that "thirst" refers to the contradiction between self and non-self;

it is said that "poisonous vapor" refers to the treatment of the heterodox by means of non-self; and it is said that "the medicine is eliminated" because once the heterodox is extinguished, the medicine itself ceases.
The four stages of the mother washing her breast illustrate the arising of the teaching of the True Self: first, she speaks to him; second, it goes against his expectations;
third, she speaks again; and fourth, he accepts and practices it.
This can be seen as being like a mother who washes her breast, calls her child, and gives it to him.
At that time, although the child was hungry and thirsty, he did not come because he had previously smelled the odor of poison.

His mother spoke to him again, saying: "I applied poison to your medicine so that you would take it; now that the medicine has been digested and I have finished washing it away, you may come and drink milk; there is no harm."
Having heard this, the child gradually returned to drinking.
The Tathāgata is likewise; this is the application of the analogy.
Good son, the Tathāgata is also like this: in order to deliver all beings, he teaches all sentient beings to cultivate the dharma of non-self.
Having cultivated this, one eternally severs the notion of self and enters nirvana;

yet, for the sake of eliminating all false views in the world, one manifests that which transcends the world, and further demonstrates that the worldly conception of a self is empty and false rather than real, thereby cultivating the pure body of the dharma of non-self.
It is like a woman who, for the sake of her child, coats her breast with a bitter flavor.
The Tathāgata is likewise; for the sake of cultivating emptiness, he declares that all phenomena are entirely without self.
Just as that woman, having thoroughly washed her breasts, calls to her child to make him drink again, so too do I now speak of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Therefore, monks, you should not give rise to fear, just as that young child, upon hearing his mother’s call.
Gradually returning to drink milk, the bhikṣu is likewise; he should distinguish for himself that the Tathāgata-garbha must necessarily exist.
It is simply that two medicines are combined, but two diseases are not. The original intention was to doubt whether there is a self or no-self;

thus, combining the medicine to treat the disease is secondary, and therefore the two are not combined. The expression of lamentation is also like this. Question: Why is it called the "Tathāgata-garbha" (the hidden name)?
Question: "If I am the Buddha-nature, do all sentient beings possess my nature? Answer:

All sentient beings possess this nature, yet they are not yet Buddhas; therefore, while there is 'I' (ātman), it is not yet the virtue of 'I'. Why? Because the person is particular while the Dharma is universal.
Because the Dharma is universal, there is nature and there is 'I'; because the person is particular, one is not yet a Buddha and does not yet possess that virtue. Question: What is this Dharma?

Regarding the statement "human phenomena (dharma) have never existed since of old," one asks: "If human phenomena do not exist, whose phenomena are they? The explanation states: "Phenomena belong to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)," and so forth.

From the passage "Kāśyapa said to the Buddha" onwards is the second section on the discussion of principles through questions and answers. The initial questioner previously clarified that there are twenty-five realms of existence (*bhava*) and that there is a self (*ātman*);
now, he challenges this meaning by first asserting in general that [the self] does not exist.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in truth there is no self.

Why, following this, does the text below separately formulate twelve difficulties which are then combined into four meanings? The first four difficulties concern the fruit; the next two concerns the cause;
the following three and four difficulties again concern the fruit; and the final two difficulties concern the locus [of the self]. Thus, the first consists of two parts."
"Paired" refers to the observable distinctions between birth and death, and between victory and defeat.
Why is this so? When an infant is born, there is no cognitive awareness. If a self (ātman) existed, then on the very day of birth, it should immediately possess cognition.
For this reason, one knows with certainty that there is no self. If a self were definitively existent, then after having taken birth, [it should remain so]...
There is no end or cessation.
If all beings possessed this Buddha-nature as something eternally abiding, there should be no characteristic of destruction;
if there were no characteristic of destruction, how could there be distinctions such as Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Caṇḍālas, animals, and so forth?
Furthermore, we now observe that karmic conditions vary in their manifold forms and the various realms of existence differ from one another;

if a permanent self truly existed, all sentient beings would be without distinction in their capacities for excellence or inferiority. For this reason, it is certain that Buddha-nature is not an eternal dharma.
Next, regarding the objection: it can be seen that the ten evil deeds and so forth refer to evil causes, while intoxication with liquor refers to evil conditions.
If you say that Buddha-nature is definitively permanent, for what reason do you further speak of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, and harsh speech?
False speech, frivolous talk, greed, anger, and wrong views:
if my nature were permanent, why would I become dazed, intoxicated, and deluded after drinking alcohol?

Regarding the three points concerning the results and the four difficulties: the first is based on the result of suffering; the second is based on the conditions for suffering; and the third is based on forgetfulness.
Fourth, based on mindfulness:

if my nature were permanent, I who am blind by nature should be able to see forms; I who am deaf should be able to hear sounds; I who am mute should be able to speak; and I who am crippled or lame should be able to walk.
Furthermore, if my nature were permanent, I should not have to avoid fire-pits, great waters, poisons, swords, blades, wicked people, or predatory beasts.
If the self were permanent, one should not forget the things experienced in the past;
yet if there is no forgetting, for what reason would one ask, "Where did I previously see this person?
If the self were permanent, there should be no aging, youth, flourishing, or decline, nor any recollection of past events.
The four points of censure present two difficulties: first, in what specific place does [the self] reside? Second, does it pervade the entire body?
If the self were permanent, where would it abide? Would it exist within the various colors of mucus, saliva, blue, yellow, red, or white?
If the self were permanent, it should pervade the entire body like sesame oil, with no empty space between; thus, when the body is severed, the self should also be severed.
Alternatively, one may formulate six pairs to constitute twelve difficulties, or one may use ten difficulties to challenge the two currently employed difficulties.
Regarding the "Difficulties concerning the Locus" (and so forth):
Second, the Buddha’s response below answers [the objections]. It returns to address the twelve difficulties;

first, it offers two similes in response to seeking the present utility, and subsequently, it uses the simile of the sharp hoe to respond to seeking the locus. As for what is called "present utility," the difficulty is that if the True Self were permanent, it should...

Regarding the difficulty of distinguishing between arising and ceasing, sequence and differentiation, or victory and defeat, the Buddha’s intended meaning was that although a true self (*ātman*) truly exists, it cannot be perceived because it is shrouded by hatred and delusion;
thus, there is "ending and perishing" and "ascending and sinking. The former analogy refers to gaining and then losing, while the latter analogy refers to losing and then gaining.
Since ordinary beings have not yet attained this sublime understanding, how can they suddenly claim to have lost it? This is the natural order of principle (*dharmatā*).

Because what was to be obtained was not obtained, it is said that one obtains and yet loses; there is no distinct obtaining, for one regains what was lost, and there is no distinct losing, for one loses again what was obtained. Thus, there is no obtaining of what was obtained, and likewise no losing of what was lost (and so forth). Regarding the first two analogies, the first analogy consists of three points—namely, the analogy, the application, and the conclusion—which together constitute four parts: first, original existence; second, [the state of] non-obtaining; third, the obtaining of what was previously lost; and fourth, the losing of what was previously obtained. Thus, there is no obtaining of what was obtained, and likewise no losing of what was lost. (And so forth. 1. Nature and Principle; 2. Encountering conditions and giving rise to delusion; 3. The faculties and conditions summoning one another; 4. The Sage responding to destroy delusion.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "Good son, it is like a royal family that has a great strongman, upon whose brow there is a diamond jewel."
In the initial passage, "the royal family" refers to the domain governed by the Buddha.

"Wrestlers" (*malla*) is a metaphor for sentient beings who possess the capacity to subdue Māra and restrain external adversaries; thus they are called wrestlers. "Between the eyebrows" signifies the Middle Way.
"Vajra-jewel" may refer to principle (*li*), or to understanding (*jie*), or to the perfection of both principle and understanding; it is pure and indestructible, like gold.
The Diamond-like Samādhi.

Next, regarding those who are other than the *ṛṣabha* (powerful ones), there are two aspects to their encountering conditions and giving rise to delusion while losing the fundamental principle: first, the arising of delusion;
second, the loss of the principle.
When competing in wrestling with other strongmen, those strongmen strike him with their heads.
Regarding the first phrase, "other strongmen" refers to the celestial Māras, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), and all evil associates (*pāpa-mitra*), and so forth.

"Competing in wrestling" means that the views of nihilism (*uccheda*) and eternalism (*śāśvata*) deviate from correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), whereas correct contemplation destroys nihilism and eternalism; therefore, it is called "wrestling."
When one touches it with the head, one realizes through the body-sense that the Middle Way has been understood.
Next, the pearl above the forehead descends; its radiance fades and it loses its proper state.
The pearl above the forehead then sinks into the skin, and one is entirely unaware of where the pearl now resides.
They do not dwell within a body of the false views of annihilationism or eternalism.
Third, where there is a wound in that place, it is the karmic condition for experiencing suffering.
When a wound is present in that place and one seeks a skilled physician to treat it oneself, there happens to be a wise physician who is well-versed in prescriptions and medicines.
He immediately realized that this wound was caused by a jewel having entered his body, and that once the jewel had penetrated the skin, it remained lodged there.
Second, seeing the injury, he correctly understood it to be a wound. (The old translation states that experiencing the bitter fruits of birth and death is the wound.

He then summoned a skilled physician to call upon the Buddha; at that time, there was a brilliant physician—namely, the noble one whose wisdom is penetrating—who knew that losing the correct principle invites suffering.
The phrase "he then stops" clarifies whether there is loss or no loss.
Fourth, at this time, the skilled physician expounds the Dharma to destroy delusions; this further has two parts: first, an analogy for partial teaching, and second, an analogy for complete teaching.
First, regarding the partial teaching:
At that time, the skilled physician immediately asked the strongman, "Where is the jewel upon your forehead?
Startled, the strongman replied, "Great Master, King of Physicians, has the jewel on my forehead not gone? Where is it now?
Is it not a magical illusion? I am filled with grief and weep."
The "no-self" (anātman) examination of error is like the parable of the strong man who, upon searching for a pearl, answers with alarm;

this illustrates receiving the teaching and practicing the contemplation of no-self, whereby one attains liberation from delusion—hence the phrase "answering with alarm. To wonder, "Is this not an illusion? is the contemplation of no-self; to ask, "Where is it?
is the contemplation of impermanence (anitya); and to grieve and weep is the contemplation of suffering (duḥkha). This is explained as being partial.
The Teaching.

Next, at this time, the parable of the skilled physician is explained for the sake of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which is also divided into four parts: first, the teaching; second, not receiving it;
third, repeated teaching; and fourth, immediate reception. This parable explains the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*); that it is "not received" refers to the initial failure to accept it.
At that time, the skilled physician consoled the strongman, saying: "You should not give rise to great sorrow and suffering now.

When you were fighting, a precious jewel entered your body; it is currently within your skin, yet its reflection appears on the outside. Because the poison of anger was so intense while you were fighting, the jewel sank into your body, and thus you did not perceive it yourself."

Regarding the phrase "within the skin" in the initial passage, it refers to what is hidden within the [extreme views of] annihilationism and eternalism. Regarding "manifesting externally," the former tradition says this refers to future fruits;

Xuanhuang said it refers to the Buddha’s wisdom silently illuminating. Now we clarify that the nature and principle are empty and pervasive, reaching all places—this is what is meant by "manifesting externally."
Next, at that time, the Malla said: "These sentient beings do not accept it.
At that time, the Malla did not believe the physician’s words: 'If the pus and blood are inside the skin, by what cause would they not emerge?
If they are inside the sinews, they should not be visible. Why now do you deceive me? "
The old interpretation states that "skin" (*pí*) represents the present and "sinews" (*jīn*) represent the future. [It asks:
If it is in the present, why does one not break through delusions and emerge? If it is in the future, it should not be visible. Xinghuang said: "Light delusions are called 'skin';
heavy delusions are called 'sinews'."
The physician of the three times takes up a mirror; this is the Tathāgata’s repeated teaching.
The physician takes up the mirror to reflect his face, and the pearl appears clearly within it.
The mirror is a metaphor for the circular sūtra; reflecting the face of the faithful mind, the patterns of the principle become manifest and the truths of faith are clearly revealed.
Upon seeing this, the four strongmen immediately believed and accepted it.
Having seen it, their hearts were filled with wonder and they conceived a sense of its extraordinariness.
Next, from the words "Good son" onwards, the analogy is applied; however, only three points are matched and not the first, while the second is met.
This gives rise to delusion.

Good son, all sentient beings are likewise thus: because they cannot draw near to spiritual friends, although they possess the Buddha-nature, they are unable to see it, being shrouded and obscured by greed, lust, anger, and ignorance.
For example, there are two [factors] within the intermediate state, but now they are joined together to give rise to delusion, like two wrestlers joining to grapple.
Consequently, one falls into hell; this corresponds to the third [point], which describes how suffering is summoned and experienced.
Therefore, one falls into the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, caṇḍālas, kṣatriyas, and brahmins.
Born into various such families as those of the śūdras and others, due to the manifold karmic conditions arising from the mind,
although they have received human bodies, they are deaf, blind, mute, crippled, hunchbacked, or lame; they undergo various retributions within the twenty-five states of existence,
and with their minds shrouded by greed, lust, anger, and ignorance, they do not know the Buddha-nature.
Within this, the preceding ten difficulties are answered collectively.
Regarding the third point, "like those wrestlers," the first part corresponds to the fourth [difficulty], that the Noble Ones should preach the Dharma;

the initial portion corresponds to the prior [point] regarding the Buddha’s teaching on sentient beings practicing the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*). Now, however, it corresponds only to the latter intent. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the practice of the contemplation.
The latter clarifies ignorance.
It is like that strongman who had a precious jewel on his person but claimed it was lost;

sentient beings are just the same, for because they do not know how to draw near to spiritual friends, they fail to recognize the Tathāgata’s subtle and secret treasure-store and instead practice the cultivation of non-self.
The passage within [the text] cites an analogy to provide the formal application.
For example, although non-sages speak of a self, they do not know the true nature of the self; my disciples are likewise thus:
because they do not know how to draw near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they practice and study non-self, yet they still do not know it.
If one does not even know the true nature of selflessness within the state of non-self, how much less could one know the true nature of a self?
For example, those who are not noble, though they contemplate non-self, cannot understand it. Why is this? If one understands the true self, only then can one recognize non-self;
since they do not understand the self, their non-self is not established. [This first restates the analogy, followed by the subsequent explanation.]
This is the correspondence.
Next, from "The Tathāgata thus" onwards, the preceding analogies are combined for the sake of explaining the Perfect [Teaching]. Of the four [analogies], only the latter two are corresponded;
here, first, the third analogy is corresponded as the Tathāgata speaks again.
Good son, when the Tathāgata thus says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, it is like a skilled physician showing a powerful man a vajra-jewel.

This passage from "all these sentient beings" down to "the fourth [stage] of faith and acceptance" corresponds to the subsequent illustration; it is the primary correspondence within the section of the analogy where the application of the example is precisely matched to the meaning.
First, it clarifies that when one is possessed of delusions, there is no faith;
these sentient beings are shrouded by immeasurable billions of afflictions and the like, and thus do not recognize their Buddha-nature.
Subsequently, it clarifies that when delusions are removed, there is faith and acceptance.
When the afflictions are exhausted, at that time one attains clear realization and understanding,
just as that strongman sees his precious jewel in a clean mirror.
This is the third verse of praise for the inconceivable.
"Good son, the Tathāgata’s secret treasury (*tathāgatagarbha*) is thus immeasurable and inconceivable.

Furthermore, good son, the analogy of the sweet licorice from the Snowy Mountains—formerly called 'assisting in answering the previous question'—Master Guan says it is an analogy for losing and then regaining.
It consists of four parts: first, the loss; second, the recovery; third, [the analogy]; and fourth, the application of the analogy."

Reiterating the loss of the four [aspects] and attaining the first of the four clarities; within the section on the loss of the middle two, there are first the rational nature and second the analysis of the loss.
Regarding the first passage: Furthermore, good son, it is like a mountain of snow where there is a single-flavored medicinal herb called "Taste of Joy," whose flavor is extremely sweet.
The Snowy Mountains are a metaphor for the bodies of sentient beings; the single-flavored medicine is a metaphor for the Middle Way and non-duality, hence it is called "one flavor.

Because this principle can eliminate inverted delusions, it is called "medicine," and its flavor is termed "joyful. That its flavor is "extremely sweet" means that the teaching and the principle accord with one another;
this is the sweetness of the principle within the joy of the teaching.
Being beneath deep thickets, no one can see them.
This "being beneath deep thickets" clarifies that they lose the principle because it is shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*);
for afflictions are profound and dense, and with perverted delusions intermingling, they cause one not to see.
Next, there is one who perceives by scent; this is the second [category] clarifying attainment. This further divides into two: first, partial attainment, and second, complete attainment.
There is a person who, upon smelling a fragrance, immediately knows that such a medicinal herb must exist at that location.
Regarding the first section, it is said that "those who smell the fragrance" refers to: first, those who, based on the sutras, know through faith, and thus are said to "smell the fragrance";
second, because the vision of Bodhisattvas in the Ten Abodes is not yet clear, they are said to "smell the fragrance."
The second section clarifies the attainment of perfection regarding the past.
In a past life, there was a wheel-turning monarch who, for the sake of this medicine, constructed wooden conduits in various places throughout the Snowy Mountains to collect it.
When the medicine ripened, it flowed from the earth and gathered within those wooden conduits.
Its flavor is authentic and true.
This refers to the former Buddhas who, having already realized this principle, fashioned wooden tubes;

this is a metaphor for the teaching that explains the "enabling cause" (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*) of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), for it is by means of the cause that one receives the fruit. Therefore, it is said that the medicine is "connected" wherever one may be; this refers to past lives.

The phrase "the causes for generating and cultivating the ten stages flow forth from the stages and collect within wooden tubes" means that because the clarifying cause (了因) accords with the fruit and achieves the correct [realization], it is said to "flow forth.
The passage beginning with "Once the three kings have passed away" below further clarifies the loss.
After the king had passed away, that medicine later became sour, salty, sweet, bitter, pungent, or bland;
thus, though it was of one single flavor, it manifested various differences according to where it flowed.
The true essence of this medicine remained on the mountain like the full moon, yet ordinary people of meager merit, despite digging and laboring with great effort, were unable to obtain it.
This refers to when the previous Buddha passed into extinction and sentient beings became heedless, giving rise to various afflictions and thereby losing [the medicine].

The six flavors represent the fundamental flavors of the six realms; the true flavor originally arose from them, yet after delusion set in, they flowed into the six realms, becoming either sour or salty.

That the true flavor of this medicine remains on the mountain is a metaphor for the true nature within the bodies of sentient beings, which does not differ [from its original state], even as it follows along with the six [realms].
Therefore, O followers of the Way, there is a distinction from ordinary people of meager merit who fail despite their exertion.

This is like those with attached minds who seek the True Principle through asceticism, meditation, and wisdom, yet cannot find it; it is also like various forms of digging and excavating in a futile attempt to discover the nature of reality, which remain entirely unrelated to it.
Furthermore, there are noble kings who obtain it through successive generations;
moreover, when a noble king appears in the world, by virtue of his meritorious causes and conditions, he immediately obtains this medicinal essence of true nature.
This is precisely the present Buddha who again realizes this principle.
"Good son" marks the second section, which applies the analogy; it only applies the two losses and does not apply the two gains.
This first application concerns the loss despite the existence of the principle.
Good son, the flavor of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury is likewise; though it is covered by the thickets of all afflictions, sentient beings obscured by ignorance cannot perceive it.
This single flavor is, for example, like the Buddha-nature.
What was previously described as being "beneath deep thickets" is now correlated with being "covered by the thicket of afflictions.
What was previously illustrated by the analogy of "no one seeing [the person]" is now correlated with "sentient beings, due to ignorance, not seeing [it]."
By means of the afflictions, it joins with the third layer to clarify the loss.

Because of the afflictions, various flavors emerge, namely: hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, devas, humans, males, females, those who are neither male nor female, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras.
This refers to either the sour or the salty, which directly answers the previous question regarding the distinctions between victory and defeat.
From "The Buddha-nature is valiant and fierce" onwards is the second response to the latter two of the twelve previous challenges concerning the location where [the Buddha-nature] is sought.

Previously there were specific and general challenges; now, the general question is being answered directly. Although it is discussed in terms of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), existence [of the Buddha-nature] is affirmed.
This nature may destroy the body, but the nature itself cannot be destroyed. The body is the dwelling place of this nature; the nature within the body is precisely the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Within the nature, there is no body that is not Buddha-nature. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the formal exposition, and second, the discussion of meaning.
The formal exposition has three sections: first, restating what is indestructible; second, extensive analysis; and third, a summary conclusion.
The Buddha-nature is heroic and fierce, and thus difficult to destroy.
For this reason, there is no one who can kill it; if there were one who could kill it, then the Buddha-nature would be severed.
Such a Buddha-nature can never be severed. It is impossible for the nature to be severed. That which is my own nature is precisely the Tathāgata.
Such is the secret treasury; this secret treasury cannot be destroyed or incinerated by anyone.
Although it is indestructible, it cannot be seen; only when one attains the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* will one realize and know it.
For this reason, there is no one who can kill.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: [The following two points concern the discussion of doctrine, consisting of questions and answers.
The questioner, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if there is no killer, then there should be no unwholesome [action]."
Regarding this karma:
previously it was stated that because the Buddha-nature is heroic, fierce, and indestructible, there should be no sin of killing.

Next, the Buddha’s answer consists of two parts: first the teaching (*dharma*), then the analogy (*upamā*). The initial teaching has four sections; the first states that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) can be killed.

Therefore, it constitutes an evil deed. The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "In truth, there is such a thing as killing. Why is this so, son of good family? Because the Buddha-nature of sentient beings dwells within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If one destroys the five aggregates, it is called 'killing. If there is killing, one will immediately fall into the evil realms."

Regarding the statement "dwelling within the five aggregates," some take six dharmas to constitute the Buddha-nature; however, if one does not understand this text, those six dharmas are nothing other than the five aggregates.
How could the five aggregates dwell within the five aggregates? Sentient beings would likewise have to dwell within sentient beings.
If one takes the mind and spirit to be the Buddha-nature, since the mind consists of four aggregates, then the mind and spirit [would be the Buddha-nature].

If you maintain that the future fruition (*āyati-phala*) is the Buddha-nature, then because this future fruition is continuous with sentient beings, it must be said to abide within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If there is such a future fruition, yet it is not [identical to] the future fruition, or if there is no future fruition, to what would it be continuous?
The people of the earth take the *ālayavijñāna* to be the Buddha-nature; [they claim] it is merely covered by afflictions. To explain this, it is simply as follows:
If sentient beings possessed Buddhahood at the very moment of birth, they should have been aware of it immediately; this point will now be explained by means of the following passage.
Buddhahood is not identical to the six dharmas, yet it is not separate from them. Because it is not identical, it does not accord with the interpretations of other masters;
because it is not separate, it is said to abide within the five aggregates. However, speaking in terms of ultimate reality, how could Buddhahood possibly possess [such attributes]?

To say that "abiding" and "non-abiding" are specifically taught as distinct conditions is merely a provisional explanation. If one were to dogmatically cling to this, it would obstruct the preceding and following texts;

for if [the nature] is ultimately pure, how could there be internal or external, or past, future, and present abiding and non-abiding? I privately maintain that this teaching represents the ultimate conclusion.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "within the five aggregates," this refers to the possibility of possessing this nature in relation to the five aggregates, not in relation to grass.
Master Mu says: Those who offer this explanation still harbor expedient means.
Next, he resolves doubts by means of the causes and conditions of karma, stating that through the causes and conditions of karma there exist the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and caṇḍālas.
Whether male, female, or neither male nor female, beings transmigrate through birth and death according to the distinct characteristics of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
A doubt may arise, asking: "If one must fall into hell solely for the act of killing, how can there also be twenty-five states of existence?
To resolve this, it is now explained that the differences among the various realms of rebirth (*gati*) result from the diversity of karmic conditions.
Third, regarding "non-noble persons," this excludes the various heterodox practitioners below.
These non-noble persons recklessly conceptualize the self through various marks of size, such as being like a weed seed, or like rice, beans, or even the thumb;
thus they give rise to all manner of false recollections and deluded conceptual marks that possess no reality.
One considers oneself to have attained the state of a sage and reckons that one is not like others.
Fourth, regarding the supramundane mark of self, the following clarifies the correct mark of self.
The supramundane mark of self is called Buddha-nature; to reckon the self in this way is called the most excellent.
Second, furthermore, "Good son" and below is the analogy, which also has two parts: first the analogy, then the application. The initial analogy is divided into two:
first, an analogy for the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as being subject to destruction; second, an analogy for the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) as being indestructible.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a person who, being skilled in locating hidden treasures, takes a sharp mattock and digs straight down into the earth;
he passes through bedrock, sand, and gravel without any difficulty.
In the first analogy, "skillfully knowing the hidden treasure" (nidhi) is a metaphor for the one capable of killing; the sharp pickaxe is a metaphor for the instrument of killing;
and the frequent killing upon bedrock, sandy soil, and salt flats is likewise a metaphor.
Next, the passage from "only reaching the diamond" (*vajra*) downward serves as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), which cannot be destroyed; this may be clearly seen.
Only when it reaches the vajra can it not be pierced; for that which is a vajra cannot be destroyed by any sword or axe.
Next, among compounded things, only the vajra is indestructible.
Son of good family, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this; it cannot be overcome by any disputants, nor by Māra Pāpīyān, nor by—
The characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which cannot be destroyed by any gods or humans, are characterized by arising and conditioned activity;
such characteristics are like stone or sand, which can be pierced and broken. The Buddha-nature and the true self (*ātman*) are like a diamond (*vajra*), which cannot be destroyed.
For this reason, to destroy the five aggregates is called "killing. Good son, you must certainly know that this is the Dharma of the Buddha.
Thus it is inconceivable.
From the passage "From the Mahāvaipulya Sūtras, O son of good family" onwards is the second chapter, which correctly elucidates that the Buddha-nature can give rise to wholesome karma.
This section consists of two parts: first, the exposition on performing wholesome karma; second, the discussion of the meaning. Regarding the first part:
Good son, the Vaipulya sutras are like ambrosia and yet like poison.
Some say that the Buddha-nature can give rise to the arising of the right path and the wholesome karma one performs;

now, observing the previous analogy, the Buddha-nature serves merely as a condition for wholesome karma. Now, the present text clarifies that by means of the teaching on the Buddha-nature, one performs both good and evil.
Because of [the nature of] karma, he uses analogies to illustrate it.

From the point where Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha—following the initial pair of questions regarding the sweet and the poisonous as in the text—Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata say that the Vaipulya sūtras are like ambrosia?"
It is also like a toxic medicine.
Next, the Buddha’s response consists of three parts: first, clarifying the two types of people—the ignorant and the wise; second, clarifying the single essence of the Triple Gem;

and third, clarifying how the Middle Way, the perfect contemplation, and the wondrous understanding arise in succession, whereby through wisdom one is not deluded and, by means of the teaching, recognizes the single essence of the Three.
The accomplishment of the wondrous contemplation of the jewels enables the performance of wholesome karma, whereas the fool acts contrary to this and fails to accomplish wholesome karma.
First, regarding the distinction between the foolish and the wise, the Buddha further inquires:
"Son of good family, do you now wish to know the true meaning of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury?"
Next, Kāśyapa replied. Kāśyapa said:
"I now truly wish to understand the meaning of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury. The Buddha explained this for him;
within that explanation, there are first seven and a half verses, and of these, the first four and a half lines present a dual [teaching].
In distinguishing between the ignorant and the wise, the next three lines specifically clarify the wise person. The first section consists of two analogies and two applications;

the first line is analogous to those who equally consume ambrosia, yet some die while others live. The subsequent half-verse is analogous to those who equally consume poison, yet some die while others survive.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Some may consume the nectar of immortality, yet harm their lives and die young; Others may likewise consume the nectar of immortality, and their lifespan shall endure for long."
Some survive by taking poison, while others die because of it.

Regarding this, there have been three ancient interpretations: first, that both equally received the Mahāyāna, yet one attained realization while the other failed; second, that both equally received the Hīnayāna, yet one attained realization while the other failed;
third, that it concerns the relationship between teacher and disciple, where the teacher preached the Mahāyāna doctrine of non-attainment, while the disciple...
Those who understand it attain longevity; those who are deluded meet an early end.

The teachers of the Lesser Vehicle speak of a teaching that involves "attainment," yet their disciples regard great understanding as life and adherence to the Lesser Teaching as death. These three are merely one Mahāyāna sūtra:
for those who have attained it, it is called nectar (*amṛta*); for those who have lost it, it is called poison. Furthermore, it is simply one [teaching].
Amṛta (the nectar of immortality) is said to be that which practitioners receive; it has both gain and loss, and is spoken of as being merely a single poisonous drug.
For all who receive it, there is birth and death, which mutually condition one another. Now, regarding those who encounter its loss, both are termed amṛta and poison:
cherishing and clinging to defilements is called amṛta, while harming, fragmenting, and destroying [those defilements] is called poison.

Therefore, it is called "poisonous medicine"; to those who obtain it, it is equally called "ambrosia" and also called "poisonous medicine. Because it enters into principle and gives rise to goodness, it is called "ambrosia";
because it reveals the essence and destroys evil, it is called "poisonous medicine. Possessing these two meanings, it is named the "Teaching of Wholesome Karma."
The nectar of unimpeded wisdom is what is called the Mahāyāna scripture.
Yet such a Mahāyāna scripture is also called a "mixed poison. It is like ghee, clarified butter, and various rock honeys:
when digested, they act as medicine; when not digested, they act as poison. The Vaipulya scriptures are likewise.
For the wise, it is nectar; for the ignorant who do not know the Buddha-nature, taking it results in poison.
At the end of each passage, there is a corresponding analogy which can be seen by seeking them out. For example, it is like a leper who takes aconite:

when his illness subsides, he must take an antidote to awaken from its effects. Likewise, one who studies impermanence, suffering, and emptiness to sever delusions realizes that this is the Great Expedient Means.
Entering the Mahāyāna:
from the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas down to those of limited wisdom,
for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the Mahāyāna is like nectar among all flavors.
Milk is the most supreme; likewise for those who exert themselves with diligence, relying upon the Mahāyāna, they attain nirvāṇa.
They become elephant-kings among men; sentient beings who know the Buddha-nature, such as Kāśyapa and others, partake of the unsurpassed flavor of ambrosia—neither born nor dying.
All of these are distinguished according to persons: first according to the two vehicles, next according to bodhisattvas, and finally according to sentient beings.

This appears to be done in relation to the three truths: when a bodhisattva cultivates wholesome karma, they do so by taking the Middle as their increase; when a follower of the two vehicles cultivates wholesome karma, they do so by taking the Middle within emptiness;
and when a sentient being cultivates wholesome karma, they do so by taking the Middle within the conventional. Therefore, the intention of these three types of persons is presented here.
Or it may be here. From Kāśyapa:
"You should now proceed to the second [section], which clarifies the single essence of the Three Jewels.

However, in the initial teaching, by negating what is false to reveal what is true, the distinct essences of the Three Jewels were established to clarify the return to the orthodox; this meaning is easy to understand. [This was] previously [discussed in the] *Dīrgha-āgama*."
The middle section clarifies the protection of the Dharma by taking refuge in all Buddhas; once this has been accomplished, one becomes the Three Jewels as a single entity.
It is not permitted to take refuge separately in individual entities, for those who do so lack the full precepts.

The present text exhorts one to take refuge in one’s own body, which shall become the Three Jewels as a single entity, thereby manifesting the accomplishment of wholesome karma within one's own being and avoiding the bonds of Māra, each according to its respective basis.
The text consists of three parts: first, an exhortation; second, a discussion of the principles; and third, an acknowledgment of understanding.

Regarding the initial section, it says "skillfully discerning," which exhorts one to discern the single essence of the Triple Gem within one's own person. First comes the exhortation, followed by the explanation; the former is as stated in the text.
Kāśyapa, you should now skillfully distinguish the Three Refuges; such is the nature of the Three Refuges, which is precisely my own nature.
Furthermore, if one can contemplate this with true insight—this is the exhortation of Śākya[muni].
If one can observe with true discernment that within the nature of the self there exists the Buddha-nature, it should be known that such a person has entered the Secret Treasury.
Knowing both "self" and "what belongs to the self," such a person has already transcended the world and realized the nature of the Triple Gem of the Buddha-dharma.
They are the unsurpassed, foremost Honored One, just as I have declared in this verse.
The meaning of its nature is such that one who enters the secret treasury realizes the principle of the nectar of goodness; this is the meaning of being one who has already transcended the world.
This is the meaning of destroying the poisonous medicine of evil. That both [meanings] are attained is precisely what this clear text reveals, and through it, one knows me.

That which is the Buddha Jewel is "that which belongs to me," while the Dharma and Sangha Jewels are the two [remaining] jewels; though they have no distinct essence, they are explained as three from a functional perspective.
Furthermore, the Buddha is awakening, the Dharma is non-awakening, and the Sangha is harmony; these three meanings are taught within the single Buddha-nature.

2. At that time, Kāśyapa [descends]. The discussion of the doctrine consists of two rounds of question and answer: first, neither accepting [the teaching]; later, both taking refuge in the Buddha, yet both being refused.
The first inquiry consists of ten verses divided into four parts: the first one and a half lines proclaim ignorance; the next two lines inquire about the former distinct entity;
the next three and a half lines inquire about the present single entity; and the final two lines [conclude].
Having posed the question and requested an answer, he first stated in general that he did not know.
At that time, Kāśyapa spoke again in verse:
"I now do not know at all The place for taking refuge in the Triple Gem."
How shall one take refuge? In the unsurpassed and fearless. Not knowing the locus of the Three Jewels, how does one practice non-self?

Next, regarding "unsurpassed," this specifically refers to not knowing where to take refuge in the Buddha; regarding "fearless," it refers to not knowing where to take refuge in the Saṅgha. How does one practice [this]?
Those who lack the realization of selflessness do not know how to take refuge in the Dharma.

Next, regarding the two verses on "how to take refuge in the Buddha," the former half-verse asks about the distinct entities of the three [jewels] from the past; this [specific] half-verse asks about the Jewel of the Buddha.
How does one who takes refuge in the Buddha obtain consolation?
As for obtaining consolation, it is as explained in the four preceding signs.
Next, one verse asks about the Dharma.
What is the refuge in the Dharma? I pray that you will explain this to me. How does one attain mastery?
How does one lack mastery?
Thus he questioned the Saṃgha regarding the three-and-a-half practices.
What is taking refuge in the Saṃgha? Regarding "attaining unsurpassed benefit":
as previously mentioned, when Mahāprajāpatī took refuge in the Saṃgha, she attained the merit of the Buddha-dharma;
because the Saṃgha consists of those who transmit the Dharma, it is said that one attains unsurpassed benefit.
Third: How is it that one speaks of reality? [The following] four lines and a half pose the question. Within this single essence, there are further four parts;
first, one line and a half explain it through the Dharma:
"How is it that one speaks of reality? If one does not attain the path to Buddhahood in the future, yet in the future..."
How can one take refuge in the Three Jewels? I have no prior knowledge of this. One should practice in sequence according to the future;
if [the goal] is not accomplished, it will already be hidden within one's own person. If it is accomplished in the future, one will be able to obtain refuge.
If it were not accomplished, how could it be a basis for reliance? It is not as you say—that one relies on a separate entity in sequence without prior knowledge.
The Knower has no prior appointment; self-illumination proceeds sequentially according to others.
Next, how is it that one who is not yet pregnant conceives the thought of having given birth? This is a metaphorical explanation.
How is it that one who is not yet pregnant conceives the thought of having given birth? If [the child] were necessarily within the womb...

This is what is meant by "having a son. If the son is within the womb, he will certainly be born before long; this is the meaning of "having a son. The analogy of "conceiving a child" refers to understanding;
one who conceives a child will surely [carry it] for ten months. The ten months are an analogy for the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); if there is one who understands, they are the ten [stages].
If the earth were filled [with those who practice], one could attain Buddhahood; yet if there is no understanding, even ten thousand moons of self-effort will not lead to Buddhahood.
The third point—that the karma of sentient beings is likewise—is a single phrase that unifies the analogy.
The karma of sentient beings is likewise.
[The Buddha] refutes the claim that the Buddha’s teaching is not definitive with the following verse:
"As the Buddha has taught, the foolish cannot understand; because they do not understand..."
The prison of saṃsāra and birth-and-death causes one to return either to the present or to the future, thereby leading the ignorant to wander in saṃsāra and fall into suffering.

Regarding the four provisional names, the second section consists of a concluding question and request for an answer; the first line clarifies the conclusion of the request by stating, "I do not know."
The next line clarifies the request for an answer because the Buddha knows [the truth]:
"O you who are nominally called an upāsaka, yet do not know the true meaning— I pray that you will explain it in detail to sever the net of my doubts."
The Tathāgata’s great wisdom— Please deign to analyze it out of compassion. I pray that you will speak of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.
Kāśyapa, you should know: hereafter, the Buddha answers the four questions in reverse order; this is the first.
The practice, the permission, the severing of doubt, and the response to the request are as stated in the text:
"Kāśyapa, you should know: I shall now for your sake Thoroughly open the subtle and secret treasury, So that your doubts may be severed."
The next verse answers the question regarding their single essence:
Now listen with a sincere mind: Among all bodhisattvas, you shall share the same name as the seventh Buddha.
The previous citation concerning pregnancy was posed as a question based on the "completed cause" (niṣpatti-hetu);

the Buddha answered with the "middle way" (madhyamā-pratītyasamutpāda) as the "correct cause" (samyak-hetu), clarifying that since bodhisattvas are no different from Buddhas, how can it be said that they lack the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the womb (*garbha*), and thus cannot be taken as objects of refuge?

Regarding those who say that bodhisattvas [cannot be relied upon], there have traditionally been three interpretations: first, that the character "and" (*ca*) means "you and the various bodhisattvas."
This is equivalent to the verse concerning the seventh Buddha. Regarding the textual discrepancies: first, "不安" (anbān) should be changed to "於" (yú); second, "及" (jí) should be changed to "及" (jí);
third, there is no need to change "明" (míng). All Bodhisattvas are identical to this Buddha. As for the "Worthy Kalpa" (Bhadrakalpa), it is the fourth [kalpa] when counting from the seven Buddhas;
thus, he is the seventh Buddha. "Buddha" (Fó) carries the meaning of "awakening" (jué): one who can awaken to the Buddha-nature is identical in meaning to a Buddha (and so forth).
The next three lines respond to the question regarding their distinct natures:
One who takes refuge in the Buddha is truly called an upāsaka; He shall never again take refuge in other celestial deities.
One who takes refuge in the Dharma Is then free from all killing and harming.
Those who take refuge in the Noble Saṅgha do not seek it among non-Buddhists;

rather, they turn from error toward the Right Path and must therefore take refuge. As for those who are "wrongful," they take the heavenly deities as their Buddha-jewel and the sacrificial mantras that kill sheep as their Dharma-jewel, saying:
"It is Vasu who kills you so that you may be born in heaven"—this is their Dharma-jewel; and the person who performs the killing is [their Saṅgha].
This Sangha Jewel reverses these three perversions and returns them to the three correct [jewels]. Question: Previously, you used the three correct [jewels] to reverse the three perversions;
why not use "correct self" to reverse "perverse self," or use "non-self" to reverse "perverse self"?

If one uses "non-self" to reverse "perverse self," why not use "non-three-jewels" to reverse "perverse three-jewels"? Answer: The methods of counteractive treatment (*pratipakṣa*) are briefly of two kinds: first...
Regarding the establishment of the gate of existence (*bhava-mukha*) as an antidote, there are two functions: correcting the right and refuting the wrong;

regarding the establishment of the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*) as an antidote, one uses non-self (*anātman*) to refute false self. Each has its own utility. The Three Jewels are the objective realm to which one turns for reliance, so it is appropriate to employ the gate of existence.
False self is an internal delusion, so it is appropriate to use the gate of non-substantiality (emptiness) [to refute it] (and so forth).
The second half of this verse, "Thus taking refuge in the Triple Gem, one attains fearlessness," responds to the previous statement regarding not knowing.
Since it is said here that by being able to know, one attains fearlessness, it should not be [the case that] one does not know.

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha with the second question and answer. The intent of the initial question is that he wishes to take refuge in all three types of Triple Gem, as they are all taught by the Buddha;
what, then, is to be accepted and what is to be rejected? The first line intends to rely on the former [distinction of] separate entities.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "I too take refuge in the Triple Gem;
this is called the true path, the realm of all Buddhas.
Since 'distinct' (bie) is the opposite of 'deviant' (xie), it is therefore the true path."
Next, the two lines concerning the time when one relies on one's own hidden nature as a single entity:
The three jewels possess the characteristic of equality; They always possess the nature of great wisdom.
My own nature and the Buddha-nature are non-dual and without distinction; This path is praised by the Buddhas, The place where right progress comes to rest.
He is also named the Perfectly All-Knowing One; therefore, he is praised by the Buddha.
The final verse states: When wishing to manifest through dependence on others, my own essence is one with that.
I too shall follow the unsurpassed path praised by the Sugata; this is the supreme nectar.

Because all that exists and all that does not exist have already transcended birth and death and attained perfect enlightenment, it is said that "all that exists and all that does not exist" [are realized]. Furthermore, this is interpreted as:
having manifested the attainment of Buddhahood, there is neither existence nor non-existence within the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).

Second, at that time, the Buddha spoke [the following] as his response. The Buddha wishes to further analyze this in three parts: first, regarding the distinct entities of the past, there is reliance or non-reliance on the text; second, manifesting the single entity of the present, there is reliance or non-reliance; third, the single entity of the hidden state is precisely what is being exhorted, and one must invariably rely upon it.
