Their physical form is fifty *yojana* in length and breadth; the lunar orb is forty-nine *yojana*, and even the smallest stars are no less than three *yojana* (equivalent to one hundred and twenty *li* square).
The solar city is composed of two jewels, two parts of which are fire.
The moon is composed of two precious substances: two parts of refined gold-essence and two parts of refined crystal-essence.
The stars are composed of a single precious substance, namely crystal. They encircle Mount Sumeru and illuminate the four continents.

The *Loutan jing* (Kāṣṭhamañjarī-sūtra), chapter five, states: "At the beginning of the kalpa, before the three luminaries existed, the power of the merit of sentient beings caused turbulent winds to blow."
The two treasures of fire-essence gold and [fire-essence] silver form the sevenfold city-walls of the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva);
it is two thousand li from east to west, and likewise in height and breadth from south to north, with a circumference of eight thousand [li].

Furthermore, when turbulent winds blow, the two treasures of lapis lazuli and white silver form the city of the Moon Deity (Candradeva), which has sevenfold walls; it is one thousand [li] from east to west.
It is nine hundred and sixty *li* from north to south, and its elevation and depression are likewise; its circumference is seven thousand eight hundred and forty *li*.
Furthermore, turbulent winds blow upon the crystal [surface], forming stars where the Heavenly Son resides.

These are all sustained by great winds, moving like floating clouds, turning to the right. The largest have a circumference of seven hundred and twenty *li*, while those of medium size are four hundred.
The [diameter] is one hundred and eighty *li*; at its smallest, it is one hundred and twenty *li*. The moon wanes due to three factors: first, because it moves with its horns;
second, because the appearance and dress of the attendant deities become like the color of lapis lazuli as they stand before the moon; and third, because the sun’s sixty rays illuminate it.

Furthermore, it waxes due to three factors: first, because the moon moves in its proper course; second, [because of the aforementioned reasons for waxing]; and third, [because of the aforementioned reasons for waxing].
On the fifteenth day, because the ministers do not stand before him in the main hall, three days are added;
the sixty rays he emits are all received by the moon. Therefore, it is increased to fullness. As for the direct answer to this chapter:
how is it that the sun, the moon, Venus, and Jupiter—having already fully answered regarding these three luminaries—are used as metaphors for the names [of the Buddhas], as was previously explained?

Regarding the first point concerning "Discrimination" (*vibhaṅga*): the moon is situated within [the text], and thus the chapter titles are inscribed from within it. Furthermore, the moon undergoes waning and waxing, which serves as a metaphor for concealment and manifestation, making them easy to perceive.
Moreover, the moon is used as a metaphor for the text because it is both abundant and easily accessible;

thus, it is employed to title the chapters. It has been said since ancient times that when the sun rises the following day, all dew is removed. The ten lines and six characters belong to the Bodhisattva Chapter; this was established when the scripture was translated.
Regarding the phrase "not an error," it is not that there is no error; rather, it is a passage praising the power and function of the sutra.

Regarding the uncertainty of Xinghuang (興皇), some attribute it to the preceding section while others attribute it to the subsequent section. Master Guan (觀師) says it belongs to the preceding section. Now, we divide it into two parts:

first, answering the questions, and second, concluding with praise for the sutra. Initially, based on the three lights, it is divided into three segments to answer the three questions, starting with the moon.
Regarding the six points—1. appearance and disappearance, 2. waning and waxing, 3. large and small, 4. good and evil, 5. long and short, and 6.
joy and weariness—the first clarifies appearance and disappearance; therein, as in the text, there is first an analogy followed by an application.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "It is as if there were a person who, seeing the moon not appearing, would say that the moon has set and form the notion that it has vanished;
yet the nature of this moon truly has no setting. When it appears again in another direction, the sentient beings there will say that the moon has risen;
yet the nature of this moon truly has no rising. Why is this? Because it is obscured by Mount Sumeru, it does not appear."
The moon’s nature is eternally born without appearing or disappearing.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise:
when he appears in a trichiliocosm or manifests in Jambudvīpa, sentient beings all say that he was born in Jambudvīpa or that he manifested in Jambudvīpa, claiming he has parents.
The nature of the Tathāgata manifested as entering parinirvāṇa is in truth without parinirvāṇa, yet all sentient beings say that the Tathāgata has truly entered parinirvāṇa.
Good son, it is like the setting of the moon; the nature of the Tathāgata is in truth without birth or extinction, yet for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he manifests birth and extinction.
"Good son, regarding the waxing and waning of the moon following this full moon, first there is the analogy and then the application.
Good son, just as this full moon appears half-full in other directions while appearing half-full here, it appears full in other directions;
so too, when the people of Jambudvīpa see the beginning of the moon, they all think it has arisen on the first day, yet when they see the moon at its fullness, they think—"
On the fifteenth day, one forms the perception that it is full; yet the nature of this moon is actually devoid of waning or waxing, and its apparent increase and decrease are caused by Mount Sumeru.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"From the sixteenth day onwards, the black-clad attendants [of the moon] begin to ascend by one *liang* each day."

When [the moon] serves [the sun] for thirty days, the ministers all ascend together; thus it gradually wanes. From the first day of the month, the ministers gradually descend until the fifteenth day, when the ministers all descend;
thus it gradually waxes. Second, it is said that on each day the Son of Heaven (the Sun) emits sixty kinds of light which eclipse the moon, causing it to wane;
however, when the Moon’s Son of Heaven resides in his central palace, the light faces him directly.
Therefore, O Sun God, three clouds become full: from the first day of the month until the fifteenth, the silver surface appears while the lapis lazuli surface is entirely hidden;
from the sixteenth until the thirtieth, the lapis lazuli surface appears while the silver surface is entirely hidden. This is because Mount Sumeru is blown by the five winds.
There are five winds that operate spontaneously: first, the sustaining wind; second, the abiding wind; third, the moving wind;
fourth, the turning wind; and fifth, the circulating wind. Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise. Within Jambudvīpa, he may manifest his initial birth or demonstrate his parinirvāṇa.
When he manifests his initial birth, he is like the new moon; all say he is but a newborn infant. Yet, as soon as he is born, he walks seven steps.
Second, he may manifest as entering a school on the second or third day of the moon; he may manifest leaving home like the moon on the eighth day;
he may emit the subtle light of great wisdom capable of destroying the demonic hosts of immeasurable sentient beings like the full moon on the fifteenth day;
or he may further manifest the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Adorning oneself and manifesting parinirvāṇa is like an eclipse of the moon;

thus, the perceptions of sentient beings differ—some see a half-moon, some see a full moon, and some see an eclipsed moon. Yet the nature of this moon is truly without increase or decrease, and that which eclipses it is always a full moon.
The body of the Tathāgata is likewise so; therefore, it is called "constant."
The abiding [of the sun and moon] is unchanging.
What the world calls "an eclipse once every six months" is recorded in the scriptures as resulting from their orbital conjunction;
after a cycle of six months, the yin and yang forces interact, hence this eclipse occurs. The Sūtras state that it is caused by the Asuras.
Third, furthermore, it is like the full moon. [The text] first provides the simile and then applies it to the meaning.

Furthermore, son of good family, it is like the full moon which appears everywhere—in every city, town, village, mountain, marsh, and body of water, whether in wells, ponds, or any other water-vessels—it is seen by all the multitudes.
Whether traveling for a hundred *yojanas* or a hundred thousand *yojanas*, one sees the moon constantly following them. Foolish ordinary people give rise to false conceptualizations, thinking:
"I previously saw this moon in cities and houses; now I see it again here in this empty marsh.
Is this the same moon as before, or is it different from the original? Each forms such thoughts regarding the size of the moon’s form, some saying it is like [the size of a city], and so forth.
From the opening of the cauldron, some say it is like a chariot wheel, while others say it is forty-nine *yojanas* in size;
all see the light of the moon, yet some see it as perfectly round, like a golden platter. Such is the nature of the moon, yet various sentient beings each perceive it as having different forms.
In the initial analogy, it says "the mouth of the *chou*"; those in the region west of the Pass call a cauldron a *chou*, while those east of the Pass call a *chou* a cauldron.

Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise; appearing in the world, there may be humans or devas who think, "The Tathāgata now dwells before me," and even animals likewise give rise to this thought: "The Tathāgata now [dwells before me]."
In my former abodes, there were those who were deaf or mute, yet they also saw the Tathāgata;
among the various classes of sentient beings whose languages and sounds differ, all believed that the Tathāgata spoke entirely in their own tongue, and each conceived the thought:
"He is receiving offerings in my own home. Furthermore, some sentient beings saw the body of the Tathāgata as vast and immeasurable, while others saw it as minute. Or...
Some see the Buddha in the form of a śrāvaka, while others see him in the form of a pratyekabuddha;

furthermore, various non-Buddhists each think to themselves, "The Tathāgata has now gone forth to study the Way within my own teaching. There are also sentient beings who think, "The Tathāgata has appeared in this world solely for my sake.

The true nature of the Tathāgata is like this: [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a larger passage concerning the diverse perceptions of the Buddha by various classes of beings.*
Just as that moon is the Dharma-body, the unarisen body, and the body of skillful means that accords with the world,
manifesting immeasurable original karmic causes and conditions and appearing to be born in every place— just like that moon— for this reason,
the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and without change.
Fourth, furthermore, regarding Rāhu’s departure, this section clarifies good and evil and explains the text of the established precepts in three parts: first, prohibitions;
second, the gravity [of offenses]; and third, the Tathāgata’s instructions on the precepts. Each of these contains both analogies and their applications.
Furthermore, good son, it is like the asura king Rāhu who, when he covers the moon with his hand, people of the world all say that there is an eclipse of the moon.
Yet the asura king cannot actually eclipse it;

it is because the asura obstructs its light that the moon appears full and without any loss, but because of the obstruction by his hand, it does not appear. If he withdraws his hand, [it becomes visible again].

At that time, all the people in the world said that the moon had been reborn; they all remarked that this moon had endured much suffering and affliction, such that even a hundred thousand asura kings could not distress it.

The Tathāgata is likewise; he manifests the existence of sentient beings who, toward the Tathāgata, give rise to harsh and evil thoughts, shed the blood of a Buddha, commit the five heinous crimes, and even become icchantikas.
For the sake of all sentient beings in future ages, he thus manifests such things as the destruction of the Saṃgha, the severing of the Dharma, and the creation of obstacles;
even if there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of Māras, they could not invade or overcome him.
Why is it that the body of the Tathāgata sheds blood? Because the body of the Tathāgata possesses no flesh, blood, sinews, veins, marrow, or bone.
In reality, the Tathāgata truly has no affliction or destruction; yet all sentient beings say that the Dharma and the Saṅgha are destroyed and that the Tathāgata has passed into extinction.
However, the nature of the Tathāgata is truly immutable and indestructible; he merely manifests such appearances in accordance with the ways of the world.

Furthermore, good son, it is like two people fighting; if they wound each other with knives or staves, causing blood to flow even unto death, yet no thought of killing arises, such karmic characteristics are light and not heavy.
Since he originally had no intent to kill regarding the Tathāgata, even though he drew the Tathāgata’s blood, this karma was likewise light and not heavy;
in this way, the Tathāgata manifests the retribution of karma in future ages in order to transform sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is just as when a skilled physician diligently instructs his son in the fundamental principles of medical science:
"This is a root medicine; this is a flavor medicine; this is a color medicine. He teaches him their various characteristics, saying, "You must understand them well.

The son respectfully follows his father's instructions and practices with diligence until he thoroughly understands all medicines and becomes a physician. Later, when that physician’s life comes to an end...

At last, the son, crying out in longing and mourning, spoke these words: "Father, you originally taught me that the root medicine is such, the stem medicine is such, the flower medicine is such, and their colors and characteristics are such."
The Tathāgata is likewise; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he manifests the establishment of the precepts. You should receive and uphold them in this manner and not transgress them.
[He speaks thus] because those who commit the five heinous crimes, slander the true Dharma, or are icchantikas will arise in future ages;
therefore, he manifests this so that monks after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa may know: "This is a sūtra."
The profound meaning herein concerns the characteristics of the gravity of the precepts; this is the analytical exposition of Dharma-terms according to the Abhidharma, like the son of a physician.
Furthermore, there are five further instances: as when a person sees the moon moving, they perceive its brightness and its dimensions; here too, there is both a simile and its application.

Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a person who, having seen the moon while eating but once every six months, sees an eclipse of the moon in the space of a mere moment upon ascending to the heavens.
Why is this? Because the days are long in those heavens, whereas they are short in the human realm.
In the parable, the fact that the various devas see an eclipse for only a brief moment refers to the Four Heavenly Kings seeing this moon together;
as for the Trāyastriṃśa devas, the radiance of their own bodies makes the sun and moon unnecessary.
Good son, the Tathāgata is also like this: gods and humans all say that the Tathāgata’s lifespan is short, just as those devas [perceive the moon].
In the brief interval between moments, the Tathāgata repeatedly manifested lunar eclipses;

furthermore, within a mere instant, he displayed hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of parinirvāṇas, severing the māras of affliction, the māra of the aggregates, and the māra of death. Therefore, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial māras all knew that the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa.
Yet again, he manifested immeasurable hundreds of thousands of karmic causes and conditions from previous lives.
Because he conforms to the various natures of the world, he manifests such immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable [qualities];
therefore, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Sixth, "like the bright moon" and so forth: this first analogy illustrates the joy of clarity, followed by the application to the doctrine.
Furthermore, good son, it is like the bright moon, which all sentient beings delight in beholding; therefore, the moon is called "Delightful to Behold.
However, if sentient beings possess greed, anger, and ignorance, they cannot be called "Delightful to Behold."
The text states: "If sentient beings possess greed, hatred, and delusion, they cannot be called those who delight in seeing [the moon].
Is it that these sentient beings do not delight in seeing the moon, or is it that the moon does not delight in being seen? The commentary explains that there are two meanings:
first, it is simply because sentient beings, due to the three poisons, do not delight in seeing the moon; second, it means the moon is named "not delighting in being seen."
Just as a thief might call his own moon "unpleasant to behold," so it is with the Tathāgata:
his nature is purely good, pure, and stainless, and he is most appropriately called "delightful to behold.
While sentient beings who delight in the Dharma gaze upon him without weariness, those who harbor malice do not rejoice in beholding him; for this reason [he is so named].
Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata is like the bright moon.
Furthermore, it is like the rising sun; this is the second instance where the sun is cited. First the analogy is given, followed by the application.
Furthermore, son of good family, when the sun rises, there are three distinct seasons: namely, spring, summer, and winter. In winter, the sun...
In the spring days are short; in the summer days are at their longest.
Regarding the difference in the three seasons: since the Buddha-dharma has no autumn, it speaks of "three seasons. Second, it is said that the Buddha-dharma does have autumn;
the Sūtra says that plowing in autumn is supreme, and it also says that what passes summer is called autumn, with autumn rains falling continuously. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
The three periods originally encompassed the full four seasons; the Vinaya specifies three periods to exclude those who dwell as thieves (caura-vāsika).
The present mention of "three periods" does not exclude those who dwell as thieves, for spring and autumn are treated together and not divided into two.
The application of these analogies has two parts: first, the application to the Tathāgata’s lifespan, and second, the application to the scriptural teachings;
these may be sought [in the text]. The Tathāgata is likewise: within this trichiliocosm, for those of short life and for the śrāvakas, he manifests a short lifespan.
Having seen this, they all say that the Tathāgata’s lifespan is brief, like a winter day.
For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he manifests a medium lifespan, whether reaching one kalpa or falling short of one kalpa; it is like the spring sun.
Only a Buddha beholds a Buddha, for his lifespan is immeasurable, like the summer sun.
"Good son, the profound and secret teachings of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna spoken by the Tathāgata manifest in the world and rain down the great Dharma-rain.

In future ages, if there are those who can protect and uphold this scripture, elucidate and analyze it, and benefit sentient beings, you should know that such individuals are true Bodhisattvas. It is like when sweet rain falls during the height of summer."
When śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas hear the subtle and secret teaching of the Buddha-Tathāgata, it is like encountering much suffering from the cold during winter.
When bodhisattvas hear such subtle and secret instructions, they understand that the Tathāgata’s permanent nature is without change;
it is like the sprouting and blossoming of buds in springtime, yet the nature of the Tathāgata truly has no increase or decrease.
To manifest such things for the sake of the world is precisely the true *dharmatā* of all Buddhas.
Regarding the phrase "just as the various stars," this third section citing the analogy of stars consists of three parts: first, citing the various stars; second, citing the darkness;
and third, citing the brilliant star (Venus). In each case, the analogy is presented first, followed by the application (*yoga*). The first two [analogies] may be understood from the preceding text.
Furthermore, good son, it is like the various stars which do not appear during the day; yet everyone says that the stars have vanished during the day, when in fact they have not vanished.
The reason they do not appear is because they are eclipsed by the light of the sun.
The Tathāgata is likewise; śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to see him, just as worldly people cannot see the stars during the day.

Furthermore, good son, it is like this: when the sky is dark and the sun and moon do not appear, foolish people say that the sun and moon have perished and vanished, yet in reality, the sun and moon have never perished or vanished.
When the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is extinguished and the Three Jewels appear to vanish, it is likewise so; they do not perish eternally.
Therefore, one should know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and without change. Why is this?
Because the true nature of the Three Jewels cannot be defiled by any impurities.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a comet appearing at night during the dark fortnight; its brilliance blazes fiercely as it gradually emerges and then vanishes.
When sentient beings see it, they conceive the thought that it is an omen of misfortune.
Regarding the "dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) mentioned in the third analogy, the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states that from the sixteenth day to the thirtieth day is called the dark fortnight.
The six-fascicle version says it is the constellation *Jiǔdòu* (箕斗); Emperor Liang translated this as the "Constellation of Evil Signs.
It is also pronounced with the sounds *suì* or *shù*; its shape is like a broom, and people of the world sometimes call it *diāo*.
They call it "ma" because it performs the miracle of removing the old to manifest the new; this is just as when a Pratyekabuddha appears in a world without a Buddha.
All Pratyekabuddhas are likewise born in worlds without a Buddha, and when sentient beings see them, they all claim them to be the Tathāgata.

Although there arises the thought of sorrow and grief regarding his true parinirvāṇa, the body of the Tathāgata does not truly perish or vanish; it is like the sun and moon, which have no such perishing or vanishing.
Furthermore, son of good family, for example, when the sun rises—[this concludes the second section, praising the preceding analogy, which is divided into three parts].
First is the praise, second is the exhortation to believe, and third is the concluding praise; this further consists of two parts: first, the exhortation to eliminate evil.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like the rising of the sun which completely dispels all mists;
this subtle and wonderful Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also like this, appearing in the world so that if there are sentient beings who hear it even once, they will be able to eliminate [all afflictions].
It extinguishes all evil karma and the offenses of the *ānantarya* crimes.
Next, it praises the profundity of its meaning:
this Great Nirvāṇa is an inconceivable and profound realm that excellently expounds the subtle and secret nature of the Tathāgata.
For this reason, the following section encourages faith in two parts: first, encouraging faith; second, encouraging study.

For these reasons, all sons and daughters of good family should conceive the thought that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging, that the True Dharma is never interrupted, and that the Jewel of the Sangha never perishes.
Therefore, one should extensively cultivate skillful means and diligently study this scripture; such a person shall before long attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The concluding praise is as stated in the text.
Therefore, this sutra is named "Accomplished by Immeasurable Merit" and is also named "Inexhaustible Bodhi.
Because it is inexhaustible, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa. Because it possesses excellent light, it is like the summer sun;
because its body is boundless, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Now, by means of these three passages, the analogy of the three luminaries is employed: the first praises the teaching and practice through the analogy of the sun, concluding with the sun;
the second praises the eternal teaching, concluding with the moon; and the third praises the eternal practice, concluding with the stars.
The Sixteenth Chapter of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra:
The Bodhisattva Chapter.

Regarding the sequence of this chapter: there are thirteen or fifteen questions above [in the preceding chapters] concerning the Buddha’s deeds; these [questions] are now posed, and the Buddha provides the answers.
Having concluded [the previous section], from this chapter onward there are nineteen questions concerning the Bodhisattva, to which the Buddha provides answers.
Some masters say that this chapter answers questions twelve through seventeen; however, it is now clarified that it answers question twelve.

Since it is not possible to list all the questions in their entirety, the title is taken from the beginning; thus, it is called "The Explanation of the Bodhisattva. Briefly stated, the meaning of "Bodhisattva" is as follows:

Regarding the four stages: first, the Bodhisattva of the Tripitaka, from the time they see Śākyamuni Buddha and make offerings through the three things, is called "the initial arousal of the mind" (*prathamacittotpāda*);
practicing the marks for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred kalpas is called "the middle mind"; sitting at the Bodhi tree is called "the final mind.

Second, the Bodhisattva of the Two Vehicles, from the beginning, has a hollow faith that all phenomena are illusory transformations; they have not yet been moistened by the water of principle. This is called [the initial stage].
In the stage of Dry Wisdom, the earth is dried up and the spirits are subdued by the application of water; severing the views and afflictions is called the "Middle Mind.
Playing with supernormal powers and purifying Buddha-lands while still having residual habits—like thin smoke or slight obstructions—is called the "Later Mind. These are the three distinctions.
Furthermore, for Bodhisattvas, the Ten Faiths and the Thirty Minds constitute the Initial Mind; the Ten Grounds constitute the Middle Mind; and Equal Enlightenment constitutes the Later Mind.
Regarding these three types of Bodhisattvas who encompass the Dharma: they do not exhaustively encompass all sentient beings in their retreat;

they advance to encompass those of the Buddha-nature; and there are the fourfold perfect Bodhisattvas. The first refers to Bodhisattvas of the principle-nature (*li-xing*), nominal, contemplative-practice, semblance, partial-truth, and ultimate Bodhisattvas.
Beginning with the principle-nature which pervades all sentient beings, it culminates in wondrous enlightenment (*myō-kaku*).
All are named *bodhisattvas*. This is why Kāśyapa asked, "How can one who has not yet resolved to attain enlightenment be called a *bodhisattva*?
Thus we know that he did not ask about the first three types of *bodhisattvas*, but specifically asked about the *bodhisattva* of the Perfect [Teaching];

he did not ask about the five stages, but specifically asked about the rational nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, they receive their name based on what was asked; they are precisely *bodhisattvas* of the rational nature.
Regarding the heading, as answered by the Tathāgata in the "Correct Answer": the rational nature (*dharmatā*) is termed a "bodhisattva" even before the arousal of the aspiration (*cittotpāda*).

This rational nature serves as the cause, while the light of the teaching on *nirvāṇa* serves as the condition. Through this process, one turns from slander toward faith, thereby becoming a "bodhisattva by name.
This "name" constitutes the bodhisattva who has aroused the aspiration; the "rational nature" constitutes the one who has not yet aroused the aspiration. This concludes the question and answer.
The meaning of this is clearly manifest in the text; why would Ananda compose a further commentary? How could it possibly grasp the core essence of the sutra?

It is for this reason that the title is given as the "Bodhisattva Chapter. However, Master Ming of Hexi explained that this chapter answers four questions which, though distinct, share a single underlying intent:

those who have not yet resolved their minds to attain enlightenment do so by virtue of this sutra, thereby attaining the vision of Buddha-nature; and because they see Buddha-nature, they dwell among the masses without fear.
Even unto the realization of the Buddha-nature, it is like a physician treating an illness who does not perspire for the sake of the disease;
now, to clarify the perfect intent of the sutra, there is nothing it does not penetrate—how could it merely answer four questions?

Even unto the realization of the nature, it can act as a boatman to enable liberation from the old skin, like the *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree) of the heavens; through the power of the Buddha-nature, there is nothing it cannot accomplish.
The entire body is permeated, yet it is sparse in its eyebrows and eyes. Now, responding to the twelve questions, there are two parts: first, self-cultivation; second, benefiting others.
Within the section on self-cultivation, there are again two parts: first, responding to the generation of goodness; second, responding to the extinction of evil.

Within the response regarding the generation of goodness, there are three sections: first, citing the analogy to praise the sutra while incidentally answering the previous question; second, the formal answer to the question; and third, the initial praise of the sutra.
The secondary responses consist of two parts: [the first] response and [the second] analysis.
Furthermore, son of good family, just as the light of the sun and moon is the foremost among all lights and cannot be equaled by any other light, so too is the light of the Great Nirvāṇa;
it is the most preeminent among the lights of the sūtras and samādhis.
The radiance of all samādhis found in the various sūtras cannot reach it. Why? Because the light of the Great Nirvāṇa can enter the pores of all sentient beings.
Although sentient beings may lack the mind of bodhi, it can act as the causal condition for their bodhi;
therefore, it is further named Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Xinghuang said: "By the power of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it causes those who have not yet resolved their minds to resolve them;

furthermore, it compels them to resolve their minds, as in the case of the rākṣasa in a dream—this is precisely its meaning. If this were so, then it would be through internal causes and external conditions that one attains the resolution of mind;
only upon resolving the mind is one called a bodhisattva, whereas one who has not yet resolved the mind does not receive the name 'bodhisattva. Furthermore...

Jiū said: "Previously, I had heard this in the sutras but forgot its meaning; now, having been graced by the radiance of your voice, it has entered my being in secret, and I am finally able to give rise to the bodhicitta.
Before giving rise to this mind, I was already a bodhisattva, so there is no need for this interpretation.

Why? Because even during the period of forgetting, I had already previously given rise to the mind. If I had not previously given rise to it, how could it be called 'forgetting in the interim'? Since I had already given rise to it before."
Since they have already resolved their minds [for enlightenment], what is meant by "not yet having resolved"? This refers to the "Nirvāṇa-light Bodhisattva. There are two interpretations:
first, it is said that when the Buddha emits light from his body which enters the pores of that [Bodhisattva], the Buddha then enters nirvāṇa; this is called "nirvāṇa-light.

Second, it is said that because the teaching of nirvāṇa clarifies the principle with distinctness, it is metaphorically likened to light; however, for icchantikas who lack wholesome roots, this light does not enter.

Because their minds are burdened by the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes, and because their roots of goodness are meager, it is said that the light from the pores is used as a metaphor for the teaching;
"pores" here is a metaphor for faith. The term *sūtra* refers to the *Sūtrapiṭaka*. By citing the Three Piṭakas to highlight their inferiority, [the text] manifests the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* as superior.
Furthermore, this present sutra is more suited to the capacities of its audience than other sūtras, and is thus superior to them.

In the second section on critical analysis, there is first a question and then an answer. Within the question, there is first an acknowledgment of the profound purport, followed by an expression of veneration for its excellence, and finally the formulation of an objection.
First, regarding the acknowledgment of the purport:
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, the light of the Great Nirvāṇa enters into one..."
Regarding those sentient beings within the pores of all beings who, though lacking the bodhicitta, can act as the cause for awakening:
first, the praise for the arising of goodness refers to the preceding section; next, the praise for the destruction of evil refers to what precedes this chapter.
At the end of this chapter,
it next looks up to what is not as stated in the text;
however, this interpretation is incorrect.

There are three subsequent difficulties: first, the difficulty regarding the observance and violation [of precepts]; second, the difficulty regarding the unequal distribution of rewards for good and punishments for evil;

third, the difficulty regarding the disparity between what is difficult and what is easy. As for the first, why is this so? Because it involves the difficulty of the observance and violation [of precepts].
For what reason, World-Honored One, would those who have committed the four grave prohibitions, those who have committed the five heinous crimes, and the icchantikas—
whose bodies are entered by light to serve as the cause for bodhi— be no different from those who maintain pure precepts and cultivate all manner of wholesome virtues?

"If light enters every pore, what difference is there between those who can resolve to attain enlightenment, those who uphold the precepts, those who violate the precepts, and those who cultivate goodness or commit evil? (and so forth).
Next, why did the Tathāgata teach the meaning of the four reliances? This is the objection regarding inequality.
If there were no distinctions, for what reason would the Tathāgata have taught the four reliances?

The four reliances are intended for the transcendental purpose of bestowing rewards and meting out punishments; if one generates the resolve for enlightenment through the light [of the Buddha], what need would there be for rewards and punishments?
Third, as the Buddha said below, this is the "difficulty within ease.

World-Honored One, furthermore, as the Buddha said: "If there are sentient beings who hear the single sutra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa even once with their ears, they shall then be able to sever all afflictions.
How is it, Tathāgata, that you previously stated that some people have resolved upon bodhicitta in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?
If one hears the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* with a focused mind yet does not understand its meaning, and if one does not understand the meaning, how can one sever all afflictions (*kleśas*)?
Previously it was said that Qi Lian Sanheng still did not understand the meaning; this constitutes a difficulty. Now you say that merely hearing the sutra [is sufficient].
To eliminate afflictions is precisely what is easy; yet, if one does not understand the meaning, how can one eliminate delusion? Using this difficulty to challenge that ease, we now clarify:

Kāśyapa uses the distinct (vyatireka) to challenge the perfect (pariniṣpanna). If we proceed from the distinct to clarify the meaning, then the distinctions between upholding and violating, ascending and sinking, and reward and punishment are inherently different—how could they be equal?
If we discuss them from the perspective of the perfect, all are immediately the Buddha-nature; for what reason would they not be equal?
Speaking specifically of "accumulating goodness," it refers to the provisional understanding (*vyākhyāna*); speaking of "attaining the perfect," it takes the principle itself as the understanding.
Therefore, the Buddha’s response, "A great matter, O Great Virtuous One," precisely conveys the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching].
Second, regarding the Buddha’s words in his reply, there are two parts: first, the direct answer; second, the explanatory answer. Within the initial direct answer, there are two further points.
First, the exclusion and inclusion are clarified; second, the formal response is given. Regarding the first [of these two], there is the initial exclusion of the icchantikas.
The Buddha said: "Good son, with the exception of the one icchantika.
Next, it is clarified that all others are capable of generating the aspiration for enlightenment.
Furthermore, all other sentient beings who, having heard this sutra, are able to produce the sound and light of the Dharma that serves as the causal condition for bodhi,
and into whose pores it enters, will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi with a settled mind.
Why is this? If there are those who can make offerings to and revere immeasurable Buddhas, they shall then be able to hear the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra;
persons of meager merit cannot hear it. Why is this so?
Only those of great virtue can hear such a momentous matter; ordinary people of inferior capacity cannot hear it.
However, the generation of the bodhicitta is not a matter of mere expediency; it is a matter of great merit and a great undertaking.
Regarding the second explanation of the answer:
what constitutes "great"? It refers to the profound and secret treasury of all Buddhas, the tathāgatagarbha. For this reason, [it is called great].
This is called the "Great Matter.
This Great Matter of great merit is the secret treasury of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature. This does not exclude the icchantika;

for while the icchantika might indeed not [possess it], the secret treasury of the Buddha-nature desires to clarify that names and so forth are equal to those of the bodhisattvas. Thus, by excluding the icchantika, it is made universally applicable.
To clarify the rational nature (*li-xing*) of the Bodhisattva by taking up what remains [of the teaching], it is said that the "secret treasury" is the Tathāgata-nature.
If one does not possess the meaning of the "perfect and distinct" (yuan-bie) within a single school, how can one interpret the Sūtra? (etc.)
From the point where Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha downward, this is the second part: the direct answer to the question, which consists of two sections—a question and an answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how can those who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta obtain the causes for bodhi?"

The initial inquiry precisely serves to elevate [the discussion] and request this [teaching]. This [elevation] has both distant and proximate aspects: the distant refers to elevating the twelve questions of the opening verse;
the proximate refers to elevating the discourse at the beginning of the chapter.

From "The Buddha said" onwards, the response is further divided into two parts: first, the direct response; second, the exclusion of icchantikas. The direct response is further divided into two parts.
First, the dream resulting from the sutra, followed by the praise of the sutra.

The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "If there are those who, upon hearing this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, say, 'I have no need to resolve for bodhicitta,' and thus slander the True Dharma, such persons will immediately see the image of a rākṣasa in their dreams, and in their hearts they will be struck with terror of the rākṣasa."
He spoke these words: "O son of good family, if you do not now resolve to attain bodhicitta, I shall take your life!

Terrified by this, the person awakens and immediately resolves to attain bodhicitta. When that person’s life comes to an end, whether they are reborn in the three miserable realms or among humans and devas, they will continue to remember the mind of bodhicitta. You should know that such a person is a great Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

"Sāya. Regarding the initial dream caused by the sutra, this is the answer concerning the four stages of the bodhisattvas; setting aside the first and last, only the middle four are answered. Why is this?
Because the question concerned the causes of bodhi, the answer directly addressed that question by briefly citing these four points, which were then heard.
Nirvana is the name for a Bodhisattva who, upon seeing a rākṣasa in a dream and awakening, immediately resolves to attain enlightenment;

such is the Bodhisattva of contemplative practice (観行菩薩), who does not fall into the three evil realms. One who continues to resolve [to attain enlightenment] among humans and devas is the Bodhisattva of semblance (相似菩薩).
A Great Bodhisattva (大菩薩) is one who possesses partial true clarity (分眞明); the explanation of this is as follows (云云).
Next, one may praise that the sutra is intelligible.
For this reason, through the majestic spiritual power of the Great Nirvana, it can cause those who have not yet resolved upon Bodhicitta to create the causes for Bodhi.
Good son, this is called the causal condition for a bodhisattva’s resolution of mind; it is not without causal conditions.
For this reason, the sublime scriptures of the Mahāyāna are truly spoken by the Buddha.

Second, from the words "Good son" onwards, the passage that employs ten similes to distinguish the icchantikas is divided into four parts: first, one simile that distinguishes both [types of icchantikas];
second, one simile that distinguishes them individually; third, three similes that distinguish them again as a pair; and fourth, four similes that distinguish them again individually. First...
For example, because it excludes the icchantikas and extracts their roots of goodness, it is said that both are excluded.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like when great clouds and rain arise in the sky and pour down upon the great earth;
though they do not abide in withered trees, stones, mountains, high plateaus, or mounds, they flow into the lower fields, filling the reservoirs and ponds, thereby bringing benefit to all.
It is likewise with this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, which measures out for all sentient beings a great rain of Dharma that universally moistens them;
yet it is impossible for a single icchantika to give rise to the bodhicitta.
Space is a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*; clouds are a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya*; thunder and rain are metaphors for the preaching of the Dharma by the *nirmāṇakāya*;

the great earth, low-lying fields, ponds, and reservoirs are metaphors for the bodhisattvas of the four stages; and withered trees, rocks, mountains, high plateaus, and mounds are metaphors for those of *icchantika* nature who do not receive the Buddha's teaching.
The next analogy specifically excludes the icchantikas; therefore, it is called "distinct.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a scorched seed: even if it encounters sweet rain for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, it will never sprout.
It is impossible for a sprout to grow from it. The icchantikas are just like this: although they hear the Tathāgata’s...
This subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa can never cause the sprout of the bodhicitta to emerge;

if it were possible for such a person to produce it, it would be impossible. Why is this? Because such a person has severed all roots of goodness, just as a scorched seed cannot again produce the root or sprout of a Bodhi tree.
Among the three or four similes, the first may be understood.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a bright jewel placed in turbid water;
by the majestic power of the jewel, the water immediately becomes clear, yet if it is thrown into mud, it cannot make it clear. This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also like this.
Setting aside other sentient beings, even the five crimes of immediate retribution and the four grave prohibitions—though they are like turbid water—can still be clarified.
However, if one arouses the bodhicitta and casts it into the mire of an icchantika, it cannot be made clear even after hundreds of thousands of myriads of years.
Why is this? It is because an icchantika has extinguished all roots of goodness and is therefore not a fit vessel.
Even if such a person were to listen to and receive this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, they would ultimately be unable to give rise to the bodhicitta;
why is this? Because they lack a virtuous mind.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a medicinal tree named King of Medicines (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*), which is the most preeminent among all medicines.
Whether mixed with milk, curd, honey, ghee, water, or syrup;

whether as a powder, a pill, or used to anoint wounds, fumigate the body, or apply to the eyes—whether seen or smelled—it can eliminate all the diseases of sentient beings. Such is this medicinal tree.
It does not form such thoughts as: "If all sentient beings take my roots, they should not take my leaves; if they take my leaves, they should not take my roots;
if they take my trunk, they should not take my bark; if they take my bark, they should not take my trunk.
Although this tree does not give rise to such thoughts, it is nevertheless able to eliminate all suffering of illness. Good son, it is like this.

The subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is likewise able to eliminate all evil karma of sentient beings, including the four pārājika offenses and the five ānantarya crimes, whether internal or external.

As for all evils and those who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta, by means of this sūtra they shall be able to give rise to the bodhicitta. Why is this? Because this wondrous sūtra is [the foremost] among all sūtras.
The King of Medicines is like that medicinal tree, the sovereign among all medicines.

Whether one practices this *Mahāparinirvāṇa* or does not practice it, if they hear the name of this sutra and, having heard it, develop reverent faith, all their heavy illnesses of affliction will be entirely eliminated;
yet, it alone cannot cause those who are icchantikas to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Anuttarasamyaksambodhi is like that wondrous medicine; although it can cure various kinds of grave illnesses, it cannot treat those who are destined to die.
In the second analogy, regarding the "king of medicinal trees" combined with the six substances including milk and curd, the old [translation] says: "According to the sūtra, it is made thus."

The contemplation of the six aspects is as follows: the "powder" (*cūrṇa*) is likened to prose exposition (*gadya*); the "pill" (*guḍika*) is likened to verse (*śloka*); the "ointment for a wound" (*vraṇalepana*) is likened to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*);

the "incense" (*dhūpa*) is likened to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*); the "ointment for the eyes" (*cakṣur-añjana*) is likened to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*); "seeing" is likened to reading; "smelling" is likened to reciting;

the "root" is likened to the literal teaching (*nītārtha*); the "leaf" is likened to the illustrative teaching (*neyārtha*); "taking the body" is likened to the flavor of the principle (*artha-rasa*); and "taking the bark" is likened to the words and letters (*vyañjana*). (And so forth.)
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a person with a hand wound who, upon grasping poisonous medicine, has the poison enter through it;
if there were no wound, the poison would not enter. It is the same for those of the icchantika class:
they lack the cause for bodhi, just as poison cannot enter where there is no wound. What is called the "wound" is precisely the causal condition for unsurpassed bodhi; the "poison" is...
This supreme, wondrous medicine is entirely ineffective for those who have no sores, namely the icchantikas.

Furthermore, good son, it is like the vajra, which nothing can destroy, yet is able to shatter all other things—except for tortoise shells and the horns of white rams. This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also like this.
These are all able to establish immeasurable sentient beings securely upon the path to Bodhi; however, they alone cannot cause those of the icchantika class to establish the causes for Bodhi.
Furthermore, good son, it is like the horse-tooth grass, the śākhī tree, and the nyagrodha tree, which, though their branches are severed...
The stem continues to grow as before; it is not like the *tāla* tree, which, once severed, does not sprout again. All these sentient beings are likewise:
even if they have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five *ānantarya* sins, they are still able to produce the causes and conditions for Bodhi upon hearing this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The *icchantikas*, however, are not like this; though they may hear and receive this wondrous sūtra, [they cannot produce such roots].
Though they possess the scriptures, they cannot produce the causes for the path to Bodhi.
Furthermore, son of good family, just as the *khadira* and *candana* trees do not grow again once cut down, so it is with those of the icchantika class;
although they may hear this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they are unable to give rise to Bodhi.
The causal condition.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a great rain that ultimately does not abide in empty space;
this subtle and wondrous sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa is also like this, universally raining down the rain of Dharma, yet it cannot abide within those of icchantika nature.
The body of this icchantika is dense and compact throughout, like a vajra, not admitting any external object.
Kaishan [Daosheng] uses only nine metaphors and does not adopt the final vajra metaphor;
however, in the sixth metaphor prior to it, he mentions "the horn of a white sheep," while the *Śāstra* (Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra) says "the horn of a goat" (*yaksṛṅga*) [and so forth].

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: "The second section within this chapter consists of two parts: first, the response concerning those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), which explains the meaning of generating wholesome qualities;

next, the response to the three questions, which explains the meaning of extinguishing unwholesome states. Generating wholesome qualities and extinguishing unwholesome states constitute the essential path to Bodhi and the proximate cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Because Kāśyapa sought to open the eyes of future generations, he posed these questions; now, we shall proceed with the section on extinguishing unwholesome states."

The three questions immediately extinguish the three obstructions. The first answer—“How does one attain fearlessness amidst the great assembly?”—extinguishes the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*).
The second answer—“How does one remain unstained by the turbid world, like a lotus flower?”—extinguishes the obstruction of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
The third answer—“How does one abide amidst afflictions (*kleśa*) without being defiled by them?”—extinguishes the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Now, these are cited:

The three verses answer the first question: the first two verses clarify the eradication of karmic obstructions through repentance (*pratikramana*), while the final verse clarifies the eradication of karmic obstructions through the protection of the Dharma (*dharmarakṣā*).
This latter refers to reforming evil, cultivating merit, and compensating for past faults.

Generally speaking, there are ten meanings to repentance—namely, ten points each for the "contrary" and the "concordant"—as detailed in separate records; repentance and protection constitute two of these. Within the section on repentance, there are two [subdivisions].
The first verse raises what is incorrect, while the subsequent verses clarify what is correct. The first section clarifies repentance by way of evil;
it should be understood that the initial verse poses the question, and the following verses provide the answer through explanation.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has spoken in these verses..."
"Not seeing what is good, one does not practice it; seeing only evil as something to be done—this state is terrifying, like a perilous and evil path.
"What is the meaning of that which was spoken by the World-Honored One?
The Buddha said, "Good son, 'not seeing' means not seeing the Buddha-nature. 'Good' refers to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

That which is not to be done for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* refers to being unable to draw near to virtuous friends and seeing only those who perceive neither cause nor effect—the "evil ones" who slander the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.
That which is to be done refers to the icchantikas who claim that the Vaipulya does not exist; for this reason, the class of icchantikas has no mind to incline toward pure goodness.
What are the wholesome dharmas? They are called nirvāṇa. Those who proceed toward nirvāṇa are those capable of practicing noble and wholesome conduct;
however, icchantikas lack noble and wholesome conduct, and therefore they cannot proceed toward nirvāṇa.
That which is fearsome is the slandering of the true Dharma. Who should be afraid? It is the wise. Why? Because they slander the Dharma.
Because they lack a virtuous mind and skillful means, "perilous and evil paths" refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Second, the passage beginning with "Kāśyapa spoke again" explains repentance by way of the wholesome; it also first presents a verse as a question.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "As the Buddha has taught, how does one see what is to be done? How does one attain wholesome dharmas?
Where is there no fear, like a king on a level and smooth road? What is the meaning of this?"
Next, the explanation of the verse as a response consists of three successive expositions.
The Buddha said: "Good son, regarding what has been done, one confesses all evils;
from the very limit of saṃsāra, one confesses all evils committed, reaching the place where there is no further going. For this reason, there is fearlessness in this state, just as with a person..."
On the royal highway where the King travels, all thieves flee; likewise, by thus confessing, all evils are extinguished without remainder.
In the first stage, one sees what has been done as it occurs at the limit of present birth-and-death; this is the past reaching the place of non-arrival.
The future [section] universally expiates the karmic obstacles of the three periods of time.
The next section cites those who do not see what they have done, namely the icchantikas.
Furthermore, "not seeing what one has done" refers to the various evils committed by icchantikas which they themselves do not perceive.
Because of their prideful minds, icchantikas commit many evils and feel no fear whatsoever regarding these matters;
for this reason, they do not attain nirvana. It is like a monkey grasping at the moon in the water.
Good son, even if all immeasurable sentient beings were to simultaneously achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, [the icchantika would still not attain it].
These Tathāgatas likewise do not see that those icchantikas will attain bodhi; for this reason, it is said they "do not see what is done.
Furthermore, they do not see who does it—namely, they do not see the deeds performed by the Tathāgata.
Although the Buddha has taught for the sake of sentient beings that there is buddha-nature, the classes of icchantikas, wandering through birth and death, are unable to know it.
Because of this meaning, it is called "not seeing" what the Tathāgata has performed.
Furthermore, an icchantika sees the Tathāgata’s ultimate parinirvāṇa as true impermanence, like the extinguishing of a lamp when both the wick and the oil are exhausted. Why is this?
Because that person’s evil karma has not been diminished or extinguished.
Furthermore, whatever wholesome karma a bodhisattva performs, this is what is being raised here.
When a bodhisattva dedicates the wholesome karma they have performed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
even though the icchantikas may revile, destroy, and disbelieve it, the bodhisattvas nevertheless continue to bestow it.
If one wishes to accomplish the unsurpassed path together [with others], why is this so? Because such is the nature of the Buddhas' Dharma.

Regarding the second point—that those who commit evil do not immediately receive retribution in the lower realms—the third verse explains that this is the protection of the Dharma. Through the power of protecting the Dharma, one can extinguish karmic obstacles;
furthermore, it brings about long life and indestructible retinues. Thus, the verse is first presented and then explained.
Committing evil does not yield immediate retribution, Just as milk does not instantly become curd;
Like fire covered by ashes, the fool lightly treads upon it.
This verse has four intended meanings: first, citing what is wrong; second, clarifying what is right; third, again citing what is wrong; and fourth, praising the sutra.
Those who are icchantikas are called "blind"; therefore, they do not see the path of the arhat.
Just as an arhat does not travel the perilous and evil paths of saṃsāra, because the icchantikas are blind, they slander the Vaipulya sūtras and are unwilling to practice them.
Just as an arhat diligently cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, it is likewise with the icchantika factions who do not cultivate the Vaipulya sūtras.
If someone should say: "I now do not believe the Śrāvaka sūtras, but I believe in, accept, read, recite, and explain the Mahāyāna;

therefore, I am now a bodhisattva. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and because of this Buddha-nature, within the bodies of sentient beings there exist the ten powers, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics. This is what I have taught.
"It is no different from what the Buddha has taught: you and I have now together shattered immeasurable evil afflictions, just as one breaks a water jar;
because these fetters are broken, one is able to see *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Although such a person may speak in this way, their heart does not truly believe that there is the *tathāgatagarbha*; for the sake of gain and offerings, they merely follow the words."

One who speaks such words is called an evil person. Such an evil person does not receive the fruit [of their actions] immediately, just as milk becomes curd. First, he raises the objection; the Master of Hexi (Heshi) says that in India, when milk is kept warm for a short time, it naturally turns into curd. *Textual Note:* This passage concerns the process of karmic retribution and the analogy of milk turning into curd.

The "Master of Hexi" refers to Sengrui (僧叡), a prominent disciple of Kumārajīva. The commentary explains that while the ripening of karma is not instantaneous, the analogy of milk turning into curd illustrates how certain conditions can cause a transformation to occur relatively quickly. The phrase "初舉非" indicates the initial presentation of a counter-argument or a point of contention regarding the timing of karmic fruition.
The fact that evil does not receive its retribution immediately is unlike milk turning into curd at once;
thus, the character "not" (不) need not be added again, as it has already been placed above to govern what follows.
Next, for example, like a king’s messenger—this clarifies that one who correctly protects the Dharma extinguishes karmic obstructions; first the simile, then the application.

For instance, a king’s messenger who is skilled in discourse and adept in expedient means, having been entrusted with a command to another country, would rather lose his own life than ever conceal the words and teachings spoken by the king.

The king is like the Buddha; the messenger is like the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*); skillful discourse is like internal wisdom; being adept in expedient means (*upāya*) is like the external ability to preach the Dharma;
having true knowledge dwelling within one's breast is like the merit of preaching for the sake of outward transformation. A person such as this can protect the Dharma and benefit others;

upon receiving the command, they immediately transmit the Buddha’s intent and enter other lands. Even amidst the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), would they ever begrudge the loss of their own body or life?
The analogy is clear: those who conceal the teaching value their own bodies over the Dharma, whereas those who die for the sake of propagating the Dharma value the Dharma over their bodies.
The wise are likewise; among ordinary people, they do not spare their own lives, but resolutely proclaim the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
The Tathāgata’s secret treasury states that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Third, there are three types of icchantikas; having previously raised this point, he now reiterates it to clarify what was not fully expressed in the preceding verse.
Good son, there is an icchantika who assumes the appearance of an arhat and dwells in a secluded place.
When ordinary people see him, they all say, "This is a true arhat; this is a great bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Yet such evil bhikṣus who are icchantikas dwell in araṇya hermitages while destroying the dharma of araṇya.
Seeing others obtain benefit, they give rise to envy in their hearts and speak thus: "All the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras are spoken by the Māra Pāpīyān;
they also claim that the Tathāgata is an impermanent phenomenon, destroy the True Dharma, and bring about the schism of the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, they say: "What is spoken by Pāpīyān is not well-spoken or in accordance with the truth," and they proclaim this.
Regarding the dharma of evil: when a person commits an evil deed, they do not receive the retribution immediately, just as milk does not turn into curd at once. It is like ashes covering a fire;
the foolish tread upon it lightly. Such a person is called an icchantika.

Fourth, one should know that the following section praises the sutra: first, it praises the eradication of evil as being like a lotus; second, it praises the cultivation of goodness, both of which are clearly visible.
Therefore, one should know that this subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna Vaipulya scripture is certainly pure, like a mani jewel.
If it is cast into turbid water, the water immediately becomes clear; the Mahāyāna sūtras are likewise so.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a lotus flower which, when touched by the sun’s rays, does not fail to bloom;
all sentient beings are likewise so—if they obtain the sight or hearing of the sun of the Great Nirvāṇa, those who have not yet resolved their minds will all resolve them.
The mind is the cause of bodhi; therefore, I say that wherever the light of the Great Nirvāṇa enters a pore, it will certainly become a wondrous cause.
Although those icchantikas possess the Buddha-nature, they are entangled by immeasurable defilements of sin and cannot escape, like a silkworm within its cocoon.
Due to these karmic conditions, they are unable to give rise to the wondrous cause of bodhi and continue to transmigrate through birth and death.
Death has no end.
Furthermore, son of good family, as with the *utpala* lotus—this is the third chapter, answering the question raised above:
"How does one dwell in a turbid world without being defiled, like a lotus? This text consists of two parts; first, the analogy of the flower is presented.
The direct answer is followed by the analogy of the wind to assist the response:
"Furthermore, son of good family, just as the utpala, padma, kumuda,
and puṇḍarīka lotuses grow from within the mud yet are not defiled by that mud, so too it is with sentient beings who cultivate the Great [Vehicle]."
The subtle and wondrous sūtra of nirvāṇa is also like this: although afflictions exist, it is ultimately never defiled by them.
Why is this? Because it possesses the power of knowing the nature and characteristics of the Tathāgata.
Regarding this explanation of the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), why is it said that "flowers grow from mud"?

It is because afflictions (*kleśa*) are able to produce retribution, just as flowers arise from mud through their mutual conditions; thus, one may seek the primary intent regarding afflictions within the context of retribution.
Good son, it is like a country where there is a wind of great coolness; when it touches the pores of sentient beings' bodies, it can eliminate all the afflictions of stifling heat.
This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is also like this:
it enters universally into the pores of all sentient beings to act as a subtle and wondrous cause and condition for bodhi, with the sole exception of the icchantikas.
For this reason, because they are not vessels for the Dharma.
Furthermore, for example, it is like a skilled physician. This refers to the fourth response to the question: "In what state can afflictions not defile one?
This answers the inquiry regarding the cessation of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). There are fourteen analogies in total; the first twelve analogies illustrate [this point].

Regarding the two analogies used for the sequence of the teachings explained, they illustrate the person who speaks them. In the first analogy within the teaching, the initial analogy illustrates the former Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings.
First the analogy, then the application.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a skilled physician who understands eight kinds of medicines to eliminate all diseases, yet alone cannot [cure]...
Excluding the *asāṭha* disease:

the first analogy refers to the ancient teaching of the eight types of analogies for the Eightfold Noble Path; furthermore, it is said that the five gates of impermanence, impurity, and so forth, along with the causal conditions of compassion and the contemplation of impurity, constitute these eight types.
Regarding *asāṭha*, there is no definitive translation; the term literally means "that which cannot be [described or grasped]."
It cures all afflictions such as greed, anger, and delusion, and can extract the poisonous thorns and arrows of the defilements;
likewise, it applies to all sūtras, dhyānas, and samādhis, yet it cannot cure those who have committed the four grave prohibitions.
Regarding the five crimes of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), the analogy of the skilled physician can now be understood through this teaching.
Furthermore, noble son, there is a skilled physician who surpasses the eight branches of medical science and is able to eliminate all the sickness and suffering of sentient beings. Only...
This Great Nirvana Mahayana Sutra is also like this:
it can eliminate all the afflictions of sentient beings and cause them to abide in the pure and wondrous causes of the Tathagata.
It enables those who have not yet resolved to attain the resolve, with the sole exception of those icchantikas who are destined for certain death.
The third is as stated in the text.

Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a skilled physician who, by means of wondrous medicines, can cure those with cataracts so that they may see the sun, the moon, the stars, all luminous forms, and every variety of color; yet he alone cannot cure one who is blind from birth. This is the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is likewise: it can open the eye of wisdom for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, causing them to abide securely in the immeasurable and boundless Mahāyāna sūtras;

even those who have not yet resolved their minds, or who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution, it can cause all of them to give rise to the bodhicitta—excepting only those born blind, the icchantikas.

The four successive analogies together clarify the generation of good and the cessation of evil, which are divided into three parts: first, the formal presentation of the analogies; second, further questions and answers for analytical clarification;
and third, the restatement of the analogies, beginning with the first analogy followed by its application.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a skilled physician who is well-versed in the eight branches of medicine.

To treat all the suffering of the illnesses of sentient beings, he provides various prescriptions and medicines according to each specific ailment—namely, emetics, purgatives, ointments for the body, nasal drops, fumigations, washes, pills, or powders—and yet a poor and ignorant person is unwilling to take them. The skilled physician feels compassion for him.
He will then take that person back to their home and force them to take it; by the power of the medicine, their ailment shall be removed.

If a woman in childbirth has a *jaṭhara* (fetal membrane) that does not emerge, if she takes this medicine, the *jaṭhara* will immediately come out, and she will also cause the infant to be peaceful, healthy, and free from suffering.

The ancient interpretation explains that "spitting out" (tǔ) refers to repentance for the present; "confessing" (chàn) refers to repentance for the past. Bringing forth wholesome states and extinguishing evil is likened to "anointing the body.

Maintaining the precepts to extinguish evil is likened to "pouring [medicine] into the nose. Seeking the principle is likened to "incensing. Receiving and upholding the words and phrases is likened to "washing.

Upholding the verses is likened to "pills," and upholding the long prose is likened to "powder. Master Xinghuang divided these eight lines, with the first four serving as metaphors for the impermanence of the past.
Vomiting is a metaphor for suffering; passing downward is a metaphor for impermanence; smearing the body is a metaphor for non-self; impurity is a metaphor for the nasal wash.

The latter four lines are metaphors for the present teaching: the constant virtue is like incense, the pure virtue is like bathing, the blissful virtue is like medicinal pills, and the self-virtue is like scattering [powder].
If the poor and ignorant do not take the medicine, the physician will return home. The ancient interpretation states: sentient beings are inverted and loathe the teaching.

Because they have received [the teaching], it is said that those who were unwilling to submit and were about to return home were shown the retributive suffering of the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*) as the dwelling place of their transgressions.
Master Xuanguang said: "One version states that because they did not accept it the first time, he explained it again. Here, it is clarified that compassion is the abode of the sages;
because he preached with a compassionate heart, it is said that he was "about to lead them back. Regarding the woman in childbirth, the old interpretation says "woman" is used as a metaphor.
"Jenshālou" (生善闍樓) means "child's garment. The child is a metaphor for the constant; the garment is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*).

Afflictions are difficult to eliminate, hence they are likened to clothing that cannot be discarded. Master Xinghuang said: "The woman is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva; giving birth is a metaphor for correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*);
the garments are a metaphor for the two teachings of the eternal and the impermanent. Now, a child is wrapped in clothes; if the child emerges, the clothes must also be removed. If not...

That which was intended as an expedient departure instead becomes a great affliction; whether through the teachings on the permanent or the impermanent, the *Abhiniṣkramaṇa-sūtra*, the *Jātaka*, or the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, if the understanding derived from these teachings is established, those teachings themselves must be relinquished.
If they are not relinquished, they will repeatedly become a source of illness.
The two similes combined below can be seen as follows:

this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise; wherever it goes, if it reaches a house, it can eliminate the immeasurable afflictions of sentient beings, including those who have committed the four grave prohibitions, the five crimes of immediate retribution, or those who have not yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment.
He causes all to resolve their minds toward enlightenment, with the sole exception of those possessed by the icchantika.
Furthermore, within the subsequent analysis, one may observe that it first poses a question and then provides the Buddha’s answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the transgression of the four grave prohibitions and the five acts of immediate retribution is called the most extreme gravity."
Evil is like the cutting off of the head of a tāla tree, from which nothing further grows;
how can such persons, who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta, act as a cause for bodhi?

The Buddha said, "Good son, if these sentient beings, even in their dreams, dream that they have fallen into hell and are undergoing various sufferings and afflictions, they immediately give rise to a mind of repentance, thinking:
'Alas! We have brought this sin upon ourselves.
If we can now escape from this transgression, we shall certainly resolve to attain bodhicitta. What I see now is the most extreme evil; from this, I awaken."
Having realized this, one immediately understands that the True Dharma yields great fruit and reward.
Thirdly, as with that infant, the analogy is raised again to clarify the preceding meaning:
just as that infant gradually grows up and constantly thinks, "This physician is most excellent and well-versed in prescriptions and medicines."
When I was originally in the womb, my mother took medicine; because she took this medicine, her body attained peace and stability, and by these causes and conditions, my life was preserved.
How extraordinary! My mother underwent great suffering and distress for ten full months while carrying me in her embrace.
After I was born, she pushed aside the dry and removed the wet, clearing away impurities such as excrement and urine, and nourished me with her breast milk until I grew.
Because he protects my body for this reason, I shall repay his kindness by providing him with material support, attending to him, and serving him in accordance with his needs.
As right contemplation gradually increases—just as an infant grows up first relying on instruction to develop understanding—it is said that he is the most excellent physician;
and because illnesses differ, it is said that he is well-versed in [treating] all sentient beings. When they have not yet heard the sutras, he constantly dwells [in their midst].

Because of ignorance, it is said: "I was originally in the womb with my mother’s medicine. Here, the mother is a metaphor for the scriptural teachings, and the medicine is a metaphor for the characteristics of permanence and impermanence that cure illness.
Because understanding arises, it is said: "Peaceful and secure. Once the deluded mind has been resolved, one returns to praise the teaching, saying:
"How marvelous! Regarding the "ten months," there are two interpretations: first, being shrouded by the ten fetters (*daśa-āsrava*); second, [the ten stages of fetal development].
"Completing the practices of the ten stages and pushing aside the dry while removing the damp": the old commentary explains "dry" as pride (*māna*) and "damp" as craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Xinghuang says that the two vehicles are like the dry and ordinary beings are like the damp. "Removing impurities": the old commentary explains this as removing ignorance (*avidyā*).
Xinghuang says it means removing the inversions of permanence and annihilation (*śāśvata-uccheda*). Because one can accommodate the Middle Way, it is said that "one nourishes the body."
The meaning of the subsequent lines regarding the commission of the four grave offenses may be sought through investigation.

Even for one who has committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), at the time of death, if they bring to mind this Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*,
although they may fall into the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, devas, or humans, this very sūtra shall still serve them.
It acts as the cause for attaining bodhi, with the exception of those who are icchantikas.
Furthermore, it is like a skilled physician; this is the fifth analogy.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a skilled physician and the son of a skilled physician whose knowledge is profound and transcends all others.

A physician who is skilled in the unsurpassed incantations and arts for removing poison—whether from malignant venomous snakes, nāgas, or vipers—uses various incantations to make medicinal herbs efficacious.
He applies these potent medicines to his leather sandals; when he steps upon venomous insects with these sandals, their poison is neutralized.
There is only one exception: a poison called the "Great Nāga," which is the Mahāyāna scripture, the Great Nirvāṇa.

The Sūtra is also like this: if there are sentient beings who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution, it can completely eliminate them all and cause them to abide in Bodhi.

Just as medicinal leather shoes can neutralize various poisons, this Great Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra of the Mahāyāna is a divine medicinal drug that enables those who have not yet resolved their minds to do so, and establishes them in the path of unsurpassed Bodhi.
Therefore, all sentient beings are caused to dwell in peace and happiness, with the sole exception of the great dragons, the icchantikas.
Regarding the different interpretations: one says that the physician represents the Buddha, the son represents the bodhisattva, and the medicine represents the scriptural teachings.
