Another says that the physician generally represents this teaching, the son represents the upholding of precepts and the extinction of transgressions, and the snake represents those who slander the Dharma; the snake resembles a dragon.

Slandering [the Dharma] is likened to an icchantika; dragons are likened to the five heinous crimes; vipers are likened to the four grave offenses; excellent medicine is likened to the principle (li); ointment for sandals is likened to the teaching (jiao);
and contact with poison is likened to the mind that slanders the Dharma. Furthermore, it is said that sandals are base objects, which serve as a metaphor for the unwholesome mind;
when the unwholesome is tamed, it can destroy evil poisons.
For example, it is like a person who coats a drum with poison; this is the sixth simile.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a person who takes fresh poisonous medicine and smears it upon a large drum, striking it among a great multitude to produce a sound.
Although they have no intention for anyone to hear it, all who hear it die, with the sole exception of one person who does not meet an untimely death.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, a Mahāyāna scripture, is likewise thus:
wherever sentient beings who engage in conditioned formations hear its sound, all their greed, hatred, and delusion are completely extinguished.
Although they may have no conscious thought regarding it, by the power of the causes and conditions of this *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, they are able to extinguish the afflictions and the fetters.

Even those who have themselves committed the four grave prohibitions or the five acts of immediate retribution, upon hearing this sutra, will likewise create the causal conditions for unexcelled bodhi;
they will gradually sever their afflictions, eliminate untimely death, and exclude only those of the icchantika class.
The person is like the Buddha; the poisonous medicine is like the present teaching; the drum is like the past teaching. It is further said that the person is like this sutra:
although one may have no desire to hear it, those who encounter it and hear it will certainly be able to sever their afflictions.
The seventh simile is as follows:
"For example, O son of good family, it is like the dark of night, when all activities and undertakings come to a halt;
whatever remains unfinished must wait for the light of the sun. Likewise, those who study the Mahāyāna, though they cultivate the sūtras and all various samādhis, must wait for the Great [Vehicle]."

Only when one rides upon the sun of the Great Parinirvāṇa and hears this subtle and secret teaching of the Tathāgata shall one then proceed to cultivate the karma of Bodhi and dwell securely in the True Dharma.
The former teaching was like the night; the present teaching is like the light of day.
This is the eighth simile:
just as when the heavens send down rain, it moistens, benefits, and causes all seeds to grow and ripen into fruit, thereby eliminating famine and allowing for great abundance and joy;
so too is the immeasurable Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, which likewise has the power to eliminate [all suffering].
These eight kinds of fever-like afflictions transcend the world; like those fruits, they provide great benefit and peace for all,
enabling sentient beings to perceive the Tathāgata-nature, just as the eight thousand śrāvakas in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* received their predictions and attained the great fruit.
Regarding the "eighty": first, some explain that it should be read as "eight thousand," just as in the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta*, where eight thousand receive their prediction;

this is an error made by the one who produced the translation. Second, foreign editions contain the text stating that eighty people received the prediction, which was not included in this version, and thus it is absent here.
Third, others say these are not numbers of persons, but rather refer to various elders.
The Śrāvakas were already advanced in years when they finally attained faith and understanding through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The latter two interpretations cannot be accepted:
if one definitively takes eighty years as the number, the count is too narrow and fails to encompass all those who received their predictions;

if one definitively takes it to be exactly that many years, why must everyone be identical, given that there are both those who exceeded and those who fell short of this duration? Therefore, these [interpretations] cannot be used.
"Harvesting in autumn and storing in winter" is the ninth analogy.
Just as there is nothing further to be done after harvesting in autumn and storing in winter, those who are icchantikas likewise perform no cultivation or activity regarding wholesome dharmas.
Although this is not a direct analogy, it must rely upon the teaching because [the Dharma] is obtained through the teaching and preserved therein.
Hearing that another’s son has been seized by a non-human spirit is the tenth analogy.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a skilled physician who, hearing that another’s son has been possessed by a non-human spirit, immediately [applies] a marvelous...
I shall also dispatch a messenger with these medicines, commanding the messenger to say: "You must take these medicines and give them quickly to that person.
If that person encounters any malevolent spirits or ghosts, they shall all depart by the power of these medicines. If you are delayed, I shall go there myself;
I will never allow that person to die an unjust or violent death. If that sick person is able to see this messenger and my majestic presence..."
Virtue removes all suffering and attains peaceful bliss; this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise so.

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as followers of other paths, are able to receive and uphold such a sūtra, reciting it until they have mastered it, and further analyze and explain it extensively for others, or write it out themselves—
If one causes others to transcribe these [teachings], all such acts become causes and conditions for Bodhi.

Even if one has committed the four grave prohibitions or the five heinous crimes, or is possessed by heterodox ghosts, poisons, or evils—upon hearing this sutra, all such evils shall be completely extinguished.
Just as when one sees a skilled physician, malevolent ghosts depart from afar; know that such a person is a true Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
For what reason? Because they have briefly heard this Great Parinirvāṇa and have likewise given rise to the thought that the Tathāgata is eternal.
If even those who have merely heard it briefly obtain such [benefits], how much more so for those who copy, receive, uphold, read, and recite it!
With the exception of the icchantikas, all others are indeed Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
The physician is like this sutra; the messenger is like its propagator. Furthermore, it is said that these words and phrases for extinguishing sins and generating merit are "the children of others.

Those who previously were sons of the Buddha, yet give rise to rebellion and grave offenses, immediately become "children of others" and are possessed by non-human beings—this is like being seduced from without.
When you say, "If you delay, I shall go myself," this refers to the propagator of the sutra who does not succeed in converting them.
If one relies on the Buddha to transform oneself, it will be slow; this is because the capacity [of the practitioner] is mismatched with the means.
If one can reach the principle itself, then one goes by oneself. The deaf person is the eleventh analogy.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a deaf person who does not hear sounds; the icchantikas are just the same.
Although they wish to hear this sublime sūtra, they are unable to hear it. Why is this? Because they lack the necessary causes and conditions.
For example, the skilled physician is the twelfth simile.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is as if there were a skilled physician who has mastered all medical treatises without exception and is also widely learned in immeasurable incantations;
when this physician sees the king, he says to him: "Great King, you will surely die."
The king replied to him, "How can you say that I have a fatal illness when you do not see what is within my belly?
The physician spoke again, "If you do not believe me, you should take a purgative; once it has been expelled, Your Majesty may examine it for yourself.
The king refused to take it. At that time, the skilled physician used the power of incantations to cause sores to break out all over the king's private parts.
The blisters were further accompanied by an ailment, and worms and blood issued forth together. When the King saw this, he was struck with great terror and praised the excellent physician, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! That which you previously reported to me, I did not accept; only now do I realize that you have brought great benefit to this body of mine.
He honored that physician as if he were his own father or mother. This is the Mahāyāna scripture, the Great Nirvāṇa.
The sutra is also like this: toward all sentient beings, whether they have desire or are free from desire, it is able to cause their afflictions to crumble and fall away.
These sentient beings shall even see this sutra in their dreams and pay it respectful homage, just as a great king pays respect to a skilled physician.
This great physician knows that those who are certain to die will ultimately not be treated; this is the Mahāyāna.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is also like this: it ultimately cannot cure those who are icchantikas.
The king is like sentient beings who have committed crimes; the fatal illness is like those certain to enter the evil realms;
the king’s lack of faith is like not receiving this teaching; not seeing within the belly is like not seeing the future; and administering medicine is like repentance.
In the past, King Ajātaśatru was unwilling to submit, just as sentient beings are unwilling to repent. By the power of the mantra, sores were caused to grow in his private parts;
this is analogous to how the power of the sutra causes one to see oneself falling into hell in a dream (and so forth).
Furthermore, good son, there are two analogies below; this is the second discourse on the person who teaches the Dharma. The text consists of two parts:
first, an analogy for the former Teacher, and second, an analogy for the present Teacher.

Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a skilled physician who thoroughly understands the eight branches of medicine and is able to cure all diseases, yet cannot cure those who are destined to die. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this:
they can save and heal all those with transgressions, yet they cannot cure those destined to die—the icchantikas. Furthermore, son of good family...
"Son, it is like a skilled physician who thoroughly understands the eightfold subtle medical arts and is further extensively proficient in those beyond the eight.

Having first taught his son what he himself knows—causing him to recognize medicinal herbs of both water and land, as well as those of the mountains and valleys—he gradually teaches him these eight matters.
After that, he further teaches him other supreme and wondrous arts. Thus it is with the Tathāgata."

The Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was likewise in this regard: he first instructed his sons, the bhikṣus, in the skillful means for eliminating all afflictions and training in the perception of the impurity and non-solidity of the body.
In this analogy, "water" refers to the suffering experienced by the body, like bubbles upon water;
"land" refers to the body's lack of solidity, like a plantain tree; and "mountains and valleys" refer to the body’s hollow and empty nature.
This is like cultivating the perception of non-self amidst the afflictions; for this reason, the body is called "non-self.

In this same way, the Tathāgata gradually teaches his disciples the ninefold scriptures (navāṅga-dharma) so that they may thoroughly master them, and only thereafter does he teach the Tathāgata’s secret treasury (tathāgatagarbha).
Because they are his children, he declares that the Tathāgata is eternal. It is in this manner that the Tathāgata proclaims the Mahāyāna.

This Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra serves as the causal condition for Bodhi for all sentient beings—both those who have already resolved their minds toward enlightenment and those who have not—excepting only the icchantikas.
Such a son of good family, this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and unprecedented;
you should know that it is the supreme, unsurpassed physician and most honored one.
This is the king among all the most excellent sūtras.
The preceding twelve similes are likewise so: the first simile illustrates the former teaching, while the subsequent eleven similes illustrate the present teaching.

Regarding the "eight arts" mentioned in the former teaching at the beginning, it is here said to be "beyond eight. Furthermore, in the lower section of the text, the synthesis of the similes is entirely based upon this.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas combine these [teachings] so that one may thereby know the teachers of both the present and the past.
This corresponds to the fifth response within the "Chapter on the Great Ship Departing," which answers the question: "How does one become a captain in the great ocean of birth and death?
While the previous response concerned the removal of hindrances through merely liberating oneself, the current response concerns the captain’s ability to liberate others.
In the previous causal stage, he relied upon the sūtra to attain the power of self-practice; now, at this resultant stage, he relies upon the sūtra to possess the power of transforming others.
Previously, it was the power of the Dharma-body Sugata; now, it is the power of the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) that comes to meet [beings].
The text presents four analogies: the first two are the direct answers, while the latter two are praises of the sūtra as an auxiliary answer.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a great ship that travels from this shore of the ocean to the other shore, and from that shore returns again to this shore.
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, is also like this: riding upon the precious ship of the Great Vehicle of Mahāparinirvāṇa, he circulates back and forth, delivering sentient beings;
wherever there are those who should be delivered, he causes them all to attain [liberation].
Because one perceives the body of the Tathāgata through this principle, the Tathāgata is called the Unsurpassed Captain.
For example, where there is a ship, there is a captain; and where there is a captain, there are sentient beings who are ferried across the great ocean.
The Tathāgata’s constant abiding in the transformation and deliverance of sentient beings is likewise so.
Regarding the first [analogy], the boat is explained but the boatman is not; subsequently, both the boatman and those to be ferried across are fully explained.
The boat represents *nirvāṇa*, the boatman is the Master of Transformation, and those to be ferried across are the recipients of transformation.
The two analogies of the wind and the wind-king both praise the scriptural teachings as stated in the text.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a person who, aboard a ship in the great ocean, wishes to cross over;
if he obtains a favorable wind, he can traverse immeasurable yojanas in a mere moment, but if he does not obtain one, even after a long time...
Dwelling there for immeasurable eons without leaving their original place, these sentient beings may at times have their boat wrecked and sink into the water, perishing;
thus it is with those in the great ocean of birth and death of ignorance.

If they encounter the fierce and sharp wind of the Great Parinirvāṇa, they will be able to swiftly reach the shore of the Unsurpassed Way; if they do not encounter it, they shall continue to drift for a long time.
They undergo immeasurable births and deaths, and at times, being destroyed, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a person who, not encountering a favorable wind, remains long in the great ocean and thinks to himself, "We shall surely die here.
While he is thinking thus, he suddenly encounters a sharp wind that carries him across in accordance with his course.
The ocean again spoke these words: "How marvelous is this wind! It is unprecedented, for it has enabled us to pass safely through the perils of the great ocean.
In the same way, sentient beings have long dwelt within the great ocean of birth and death, mired in ignorance, suffering, and exhaustion;
had they not encountered such a wind of the Great Parinirvāṇa, they would surely have conceived the thought that they were destined to fall to the earth."

When these sentient beings—those in the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts—were thus reflecting, they suddenly encountered the wind of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, which blew favorably toward them, causing them to enter into *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Only then did they realize the truth, conceive a sense of wonder, and exclaim, "How wonderful! From time immemorial, we have never before seen or heard of such a Tathāgata."
Only then will one give rise to pure faith in this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, which is the subtle and secret treasury.
Furthermore, regarding the question of how to abandon birth and death—as a snake sheds its old skin—the answer is provided by means of the analogy of the snake.
In this context, the analogy of the snake is again raised as the response; the text contains two similes.
The preceding parable of the snake was the direct answer; the subsequent analogy of the goldsmith was the supporting answer.
Furthermore, son of good family, if a snake sheds its skin, is it considered dead and extinguished? "No, World-Honored One. "Son of good family, the Tathāgata is likewise.
Through skillful means he manifests the discarding of his poisonous body; can it therefore be said that the Tathāgata is impermanent and subject to extinction?"
"No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata, through skillful means, relinquishes his body here in Jambudvīpa just as that venomous snake sheds its old skin;
for this reason, the Tathāgata is said to be eternally abiding."
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a goldsmith who, having obtained fine, genuine gold, fashions various vessels as he pleases;
so too is the Tathāgata, who is able to manifest various bodies of form within the twenty-five states of existence in order to transform sentient beings and uproot them from birth and death.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is named "Boundless Body" (Anantakāya), even though he manifests various forms.
All bodies are also called eternally abiding and without change.

The analogy of the snake illustrates that it should depart from one place; the analogy of the goldsmith illustrates that it should come to various places and depart from various places (and so forth).

Furthermore, as with the mango tree (*āmra*) mentioned in the seventh response of this chapter—asking how one contemplates the Three Jewels as being like the celestial *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree)—the human tree is now cited here in response.

Just as the celestial tree manifests flowers, fruits, height, and so forth entirely according to the desires of the devas, so too does the Buddha appear according to the suitability of conditions: he appears born in a royal palace for some, while for others he appears in parinirvāṇa.

The Twin Trees (and so forth). Regarding the three stages of flourishing and withering of humans and trees, which differ from one another, taking them as a metaphor, it should likewise be understood that there is no fixed [duration].
This is divided into five sections: first, clarifying that the Buddha’s body has three differences; second, clarifying the Tathāgata’s esoteric speech; third, discussing prosperity and decline;
fourth, exhorting one to establish the vow of a man of great purpose; and fifth, discussing arising and passing away. The first three [sections] concern the Three Jewels and the Buddha’s body.
This is the secret language of the Buddha-jewel; this is the flourishing and decline of the Dharma-jewel; this is the Saṃgha-jewel. Regarding these Three Jewels, there are two types:

those that are one essence and those that have distinct essences. Generally, they are distinguished by the person who has attained the fruit; as for distinct essences, they are distinguished by both cause and fruit. The Buddha is a person of the fruit, while the Saṃgha consists of persons in the state of cause.
Since it is stated here that the Saṃgha undergoes flourishing and decline, it refers to the distinct essence. First, regarding the analogy of the Buddha’s body, there are three parts. First:
The subsequent three sections on understanding may be sought accordingly.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like the *āmra* tree and the *jambu* tree, which undergo three transformations in one year:
at times they produce flowers, their radiance and colors flourishing; at times they produce leaves, growing lush and verdant; and at times they wither and fall, appearing as if dead.
"What do you think, son of good family? Does this tree truly wither and die? "No, World-Honored One.
"Son of good family, the Tathāgata is likewise. Within the triple world, he manifests three kinds of bodies:
sometimes appearing newly born, sometimes appearing grown to maturity, and sometimes appearing in parinirvāṇa; yet the body of the Tathāgata is in truth not impermanent."
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa praised him, saying: "Excellent! It is truly as the Holy One has said: the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and undergoes no change.
Next, "Good son, the secret words of the Tathāgata... and below, the section clarifying the Dharma Jewel consists of four parts: the analogy, the application, the conclusion, and the summary.
Good son, the secret words of the Tathāgata are extremely profound and difficult to understand.
For example, it is like a great king who addresses his ministers, saying, "Bring the *saindhava*! Bring the *saindhava*! This single name refers to four actual things:
first, salt; second, a vessel; third, water; and fourth, a horse. Thus, these four distinct objects share a single name.
A wise minister who understands these names well will, when the king is washing and asks for *saindhava*, immediately offer water;

when the king is eating and asks for *saindhava*, he will immediately offer salt; when the king has finished eating and wishes to drink a beverage and asks for *saindhava*, he will immediately offer a vessel;
and when the king wishes to go on a journey and asks for *saindhava*, he will immediately offer a horse.
In this way, the wise minister well understands the four kinds of secret speech of the Great King.
Regarding "ornamented secret speech," it is a general name for *nirvāṇa* and cannot be translated individually;

just as the four marks of impermanence emerge from the Mahāyāna, within a single mark of impermanence all four meanings are complete, each having its own specific intent. "Suffering" is intended to subvert the notion of pleasure.

Even up to the statement that "emptiness is for the purpose of destroying [the view of] existence," the wise should understand such esoteric language (*sandhyābhāṣa*) in this way; the Mahāyāna is also like this.
Although it speaks of "one" and "permanent," each has its own intended meaning (and so forth). Now, regarding the discussion of esoteric language based on a single instance:

the Buddha spoke only of "one," yet it possesses four types of meanings. For example, when he speaks of the term "existence" (*asti*), it simultaneously encompasses non-existence (*nāsti*), both existence and non-existence (*astināsti*), and neither existence nor non-existence (*naivāstināsti*).
If one understands "existence" merely as existence rather than as non-existence, they are not called a wise minister; this accords with the meaning of the Four Teachings.

When the Buddha speaks of arising-and-ceasing as being non-arising-and-non-ceasing, as being both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing, and as being neither arising-and-ceasing nor non-arising-and-non-ceasing—if one interprets this solely according to the arising-and-ceasing of the Tripitaka Teaching, one is not a wise minister. This principle also accords with...
The meanings of the four gates range from the gate of existence to the gate of neither existence nor non-existence (and so forth).
The six fascicle [version] differs from this in three respects: [the first two are] a sword and a basin for washing (and so forth).
In the three analogies, first the impermanent is applied and subsequently the permanent is applied.
It is the same with this Mahāyāna sūtra; there are four kinds of impermanence that the Mahāyāna wise minister should know well.
If a Buddha appears in the world and speaks for the sake of sentient beings regarding the *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata, the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata.
For those who conceive of permanence, he speaks of the characteristic of impermanence, desiring to cause the bhikṣus to cultivate the perception of impermanence;

or again, he may say that the True Dharma is about to perish—a wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the characteristic of suffering for those who conceive of pleasure, desiring to cause the bhikṣus to extensively cultivate the perception of suffering;
or again, he may say, "I am now afflicted by illness, and the Saṃgha is being disrupted."
Wise minister, you should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the mark of non-self for those who conceive of a self, wishing to cause the bhikṣus to cultivate the perception of non-self;
or again, when he speaks of what is called emptiness, wise minister, you should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of right liberation—
the absence of the twenty-five states of existence— wishing to cause the bhikṣus to practice and learn emptiness.
Regarding the characteristics: the first section fully combines the four types of impermanence with the four kinds of speech.
For this reason, "this is right liberation" is cited as the teaching on permanence to serve as a point of conjunction.
For this reason, this right liberation is called "emptiness" and is also called "immovability.
Immovability means that within liberation there is no suffering; therefore, immovability is right liberation.
It is called "signlessness," meaning that it is signless because it is devoid of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and so forth; thus, signlessness is right liberation.
That which is eternally unchanging is liberation; within liberation there is no impermanence, feverish affliction, or transformation.
Therefore, liberation is called eternal, unchanging, and cool. Furthermore, it may be said that all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*.
O wise minister, you should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the eternal Dharma, wishing to cause the bhikṣus to cultivate the eternal Dharma.
There are also four aspects, yet they do not correspond to the previous ones: first, clarifying immovability; second, clarifying signlessness; third, clarifying permanence and unchangingness;
and fourth, clarifying the Buddha-nature. Although there are these four kinds, they are but a single nirvāṇa, just as the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are but the single term *siddhārtha*.
The fourth point, the concluding summary by the bhikṣus, may be sought therein:
"If these bhikṣus can thus follow and practice this teaching, you should know that such persons are my true disciples,
who well understand the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata, just as the wise ministers of a great king well understand the king’s intentions."
"Noble son, if even a great king possesses such a method of secret speech, how much more so must it be for the Tathāgata?
Noble son, for this reason, the subtle and secret teaching of the Tathāgata is difficult to understand;
only those who possess wisdom can comprehend my profound Buddha-dharma, for it is not something that can be grasped by ordinary worldly beings."
This is faith.

Thirdly, as with the *palaśa* tree, the signs of decline for the two jewels are clearly explained in pairs. First, it clarifies that when the sutras lack majestic virtue, this is the decline of the Dharma;
second, when bhikṣus give rise to transgressions, this is the decline of the Saṃgha; third, there is a profound admonition regarding the propagation [of the teachings].
The Sūtra clarifies both [jewels] together in its opening passage, first providing a simile and subsequently applying it to the meaning.
Furthermore, son of good family, just as when the *pāṭala*, *karṇikāra*, and *aśoka* trees encounter a severe drought,
they do not produce flowers or fruit, and all other things produced on land or in water likewise wither away and cease to exist.
Just as moisture cannot increase the potency of all medicinal herbs, which then lose their power, so too, son of good family, is it with this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
After my parinirvāṇa, there will be sentient beings who are unable to show it respect and who possess no majestic virtue. Why is this? Because these sentient beings do not know.
Because it is the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata. Why is this? It is because these sentient beings have meager merit.
Now, if a medicinal tree encounters rain, it is fully capable of curing diseases; yet if it encounters a severe drought, the tree will die and lack the power [to heal]. The True Dharma is likewise:
when it encounters excellent disciples who propagate and proclaim this Dharma, it can destroy perversions; but when it encounters wicked bhikṣus, [the Dharma]... [is lost].
It will immediately decline and perish.
Furthermore, when the True Dharma of the Tathāgata departs, the faults arising from this bhikṣu are the decline of the Saṃgha.
Moreover, son of good family, when the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is about to be extinguished, at that time there will be many bhikṣus who practice evil.
I do not know the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata; being indolent and lazy, I am unable to read, recite, proclaim, or analyze the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
It is like a foolish thief who discards genuine jewels to carry away grass and wood.
Because I do not understand the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata, I am indolent and lack diligence regarding this sutra. Alas! This shall become a great peril for those in the future.
The world is most terrifying; how bitter it is that sentient beings do not diligently listen to and receive this Mahāyāna scripture, the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra!
Only the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to grasp the true meaning within this sūtra, rather than clinging to the literal words;
they accord with it without opposition and preach it for the sake of sentient beings.
In the final age, evil people will be indolent and commit transgressions, causing the Sangha to decline and fall into corruption.

The third point, like the analogy of tending cattle below, is a profound admonition for those who propagate the sutras to protect and uphold them well; it shows how faults arise from human beings, leading to the destruction of the Dharma and the Sangha.
First comes the analogy, followed by its application.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a cowherd woman who, desiring to sell milk and seeking great profit, adds two parts of water and sells it to another cowherd woman.
Having received it, that woman again adds two parts and sells it to a woman living near the city.
Having received it, that woman again adds two parts and sells it to a woman within the city.
After the woman had obtained it, she added two more parts and went to the market to sell it.

At that time, there was a man who, having taken a wife for his son, was in urgent need of high-quality milk to provide for his guests. He went to the market wishing to buy some, but the seller demanded a high price.
The man said, "This milk contains much water; it is not truly worth this value. Today I am hosting guests."
"Guest, for this reason you should take it; having taken it, bring it home and boil it to make gruel.

Although it will no longer have the flavor of milk, even without that milk-flavor, it will still be a thousand times superior among bitter flavors. Why is this? Because the flavor of milk is the foremost among all flavors."
Regarding the analogy: the traditional explanation states that originally there was one *dǒu* of milk. First, adding two parts means adding two *dǒu* of water to make three *dǒu*.
Then, adding six *dǒu* makes nine *dǒu*. Next, adding eighteen *dǒu* makes twenty-seven *dǒu*.
Finally, adding two parts makes eight *hú* and one *dǒu*. Furthermore, there is another interpretation which says this should not be understood in that way; it began with one original *dǒu*.
Adding two parts makes three; adding two more makes five. Again, from two it becomes seven; adding two more makes nine. This analogy comprises seven phrases.
The first four instances of adding water represent the successive additions to the translation; the latter part is the primary analogy for the person who propagates the Dharma.
The cowherd woman represents the one who disseminates the sutra; her feminine nature being deceitful and crooked represents the devious character of the person who disseminates the sutra.
Because those who are able to abandon their attachments for the sake of the Dharma yet seek profit through much flattery, they are compared to cowherds.
Regarding the first addition of two parts: first, a brief excerpt of this sutra; second, the "Many Parts" (Mahāvaipulya).

Regarding the second addition of two parts: first, the removal of profound and subtle words; second, the insertion of worldly phrases. Regarding the third addition of two parts: first, the copying of what was previously attached.

Regarding the phrase "the latter two citations are placed after, and the former fourth is added with two divisions," it means they are placed before and after, and in the middle, both before and after.
There are those who interpret the addition of two divisions to the fourth [section] as follows: first, that which is prohibited is opened; second, that which is opened is prohibited.
At this time, there will be various evils, which corresponds to the third addition of two divisions. These are all evil persons.

Although one may recite and chant [the scriptures], this corresponds to the fourth stage; adding two parts to it corresponds to the fifth, which is likened to a student seeking the Dharma—like a son, taking a wife, or hosting guests.
The traditional interpretation states that "son" represents constant understanding, "wife" represents the constant realm, and the rest—the knowledge and vision—represent the guests.
Furthermore, "son" represents the Middle Way’s ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), while "wife" represents the succession between teacher and disciple throughout the generations.
A person taking a wife in the future so that the lineage is not cut off is like desiring that transformation be continuous;

a teacher bestowing instruction upon a disciple who urgently requires this "milk" is like a seeker of the Dharma quickly requesting one who possesses understanding; guests are like skillful means used to reach the marketplace;
wishing to buy is like arriving at the lecture hall to seek the Dharma; and the seller of milk is the sixth [chapter] on the propagation of the sutra.
Such people mostly seek profit and sustenance. Seventh, these "speakers" are those who listen to the Dharma; they are skilled at discerning the depth or shallowness [of the teaching].
Those who encounter my "guests" in haste are likened to listeners who say, "I have no place to listen, so I have come here to take this [teaching] back home.
This is likened to having finished listening and then practicing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), yet finding it entirely without basis. Even so, it is still a thousand times superior. Although—
Though it lacks profound intent, it is still Mahāyāna; compared to the Hīnayāna scriptures, it is several times superior.
The passage beginning with "The two good sons" below fully corresponds to the seven points mentioned above.
"Good sons, after my parinirvāṇa, when eighty years remain before the True Dharma has perished, at that time this sutra..."
At that time, this [sūtra] shall be widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa. There will then be certain evil bhikṣus who will abridge this sūtra, dividing it into many parts;
they will destroy the color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor of the True Dharma.
Although these evil persons may recite such scriptures, they will eliminate the profound and secret essential meanings of the Tathāgata and substitute them with worldly ornaments and embellishments.

In the *Yìzhīyǔchāo*, those mentioned at the beginning are placed at the end, and those mentioned at the end are placed at the beginning; those mentioned at the beginning and end are placed in the middle, and those mentioned in the middle are placed at the beginning and end.

One should know that such evil bhikṣus are companions of Māra who accept and store all kinds of impure things, yet claim, "The Tathāgata has permitted me to store them all," just as a cowherd's daughter adds excessive water to milk. So too are these evil bhikṣus.

Furthermore, by thus intermingling worldly speech and corrupting the determination of this sutra, they cause many sentient beings to be unable to correctly explain, correctly transcribe, or correctly grasp it, nor to honor, praise, make offerings to, or revere it.

For the sake of gain and support, these evil bhikṣus are unable to widely proclaim and disseminate this sutra; that which is disseminated is so slight as to be hardly worth mentioning, like those poor cowherds.
When a destitute woman sells her milk from hand to hand until it is made into gruel, it loses its milky flavor; the Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is also like this.
As it is transmitted through various stages, it becomes thin and diluted and lacks its original flavor. Although it lacks that flavor, it still surpasses other sūtras by more than a thousandfold.
Just as the taste of milk is a thousand times superior to the taste of all bitter flavors, how much more so is this sūtra!

For this reason, among the Śrāvaka sūtras, this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is the most preeminent, just as cow’s milk is the most excellent among all flavors; for this meaning, it is called the "Great Nirvāṇa."

The Great Master of Tiantai explained: "The cowherd girl is a metaphor for the Buddha; the fresh milk is a metaphor for the Dharma of Nirvana. When the Buddha wishes to preach this Dharma, the Dharma itself is inexpressible;
its expression must necessarily rely upon the truths, namely the Two Truths. Therefore, it is said that two parts of water are added [to the milk].

The remaining cowherd girls are metaphors for the Bodhisattvas who compose treatises to interpret the sutras; because the sutras are difficult to understand, they further compose [explanations] for them."
The *Upadeśa* (Exegesis) expounds the teaching of the two truths; this corresponds to the second analogy of the woman near the city adding water.
The masters of the great treatises, finding the arguments difficult to resolve, further compose commentaries (*arthavyākhyā*) to explain this treatise;

this corresponds to the third analogy of the woman in the city dividing the water into two portions. Those who receive the teachings, finding the commentaries difficult to understand, further compose sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*).

This explanation clarifies the fourth section of the *Jiǎshuǐ jīng* (Sūtra on Adding Water), which divides the text into two parts. First, regarding the "adding water" for the bhikṣus of the degenerate age:

the sūtra’s abbreviated version combines many sections into one. Second, regarding the "adding water" according to the Tathāgata: it does not take the Tathāgata as the primary condition for preaching the Dharma, but rather takes the "condition of delight" as the basis;

this abbreviated version distinguishes [the teaching] by means of the Two Truths. The Buddha provides the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) that is to be received, while the wise provide the "subject-condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*) that is able to receive it.
The synthesis does not contradict the sutra; this second addition of water [is] called "the hidden and secret language. This appears to be a treatise explaining the sutra.

Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "Moreover, good son" (the fourth section), the exhortation to establish the resolve of a great man is divided into two parts: first, the exhortation, and second, the acceptance.

The first explanation also has two parts: first, the disparagement of the female body; second, the definitive determination regarding the male body. First, the reproach and disparagement is as stated in the text.
Furthermore, son of good family, there is no son of good family or daughter of good family who does not seek a male body.
Why is this? Because all women are abodes where manifold evils reside. Furthermore, son of good family...
My son, it is like mosquitoes and gnats; water cannot moisten this great earth. It is the same with women: their desire is difficult to satisfy.
For example, if the entire great earth were made into pellets the size of mustard seeds, even if all such men were to engage in sexual acts with a single woman, they would still not satisfy her.
This would remain true even if the number of men were as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Even if sand were to engage in sexual acts with a single woman, it would likewise never suffice. Good son, it is like the great ocean:
though all the rains from heaven and the myriad rivers and streams flow into it, that great ocean is never filled.
The nature of women is just like this; even if every man in existence were to become a lover of a single woman, [it would still not be enough].
They engage together in acts of desire, yet they remain unsatisfied. Furthermore, son of good family, it is like the *aśoka*, *pāṭala*, and *karṇikāra* trees when their spring flowers bloom;
swarms of bees gather to take their color, fragrance, and subtle flavors, never knowing satiety.
A woman’s desire for a man is likewise insatiable. Son of good family, by this principle...
Therefore, all sons and daughters of good family who hear this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra should always censure the characteristics of women and seek the state of a man.
Why is this? It is because it serves as a definitive judgment at the lower level.
Why is this? Because this Mahāyāna scripture contains the characteristics of a *puruṣa*, namely the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
If a person does not know this Buddha-nature, they lack the male characteristic. Why is that? Because they are unable to know for themselves that they possess the Buddha-nature. If...
Those who cannot know the Buddha-nature, I call them women; those who can know for themselves that they possess the Buddha-nature, I call them great men.
If there are women who can know that their own bodies definitely possess the Buddha-nature, you should know that these individuals are truly men.
Good son, this is a Mahāyāna scripture, the Great Nirvāṇa.
The *Pǎn jīng* (Brahmajāla-sūtra) is an accumulation of immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable merit. Why is this?

Because it expounds the secret treasury of the Tathāgata. Therefore, good sons and good daughters, if you wish to quickly know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata, you should diligently cultivate this sūtra through skillful means.
The Sūtra judges this by presenting two phrases; if explained in detail, there should be four phrases (and so forth).
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is so, it is so, just as the Buddha has taught.

I now possess the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*), for I have attained entry into the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata. It is only today that the Tathāgata has awakened me to my cause."
"This is precisely what constitutes definitive penetration of the Buddha’s words: 'Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have now spoken thus in accordance with worldly conventions. Kāśyapa spoke again: 'I do not follow worldly conventions.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa: 'Excellent, excellent! That unsurpassed flavor of the Dharma which you now know is exceedingly profound and difficult to comprehend.'"
And yet you are able to know it, just as a bee gathers nectar; you are likewise so.
Furthermore, regarding the fifth section on the arising and ceasing of the Great Dharma, there are two parts: first, the signs of cessation, and second, a dual exposition of arising and ceasing.
In the initial passage, there is first the analogy and then the application.
Furthermore, son of good family, just as the moisture from a mosquito's wing cannot saturate this great earth, so too shall it be when this sutra circulates in future ages.
Just as that mosquito's moisture [is insufficient], when the True Dharma is about to perish, this sutra will first vanish from this land;
you should know that this is the sign of the decline of the True Dharma.
In this evil age, evil people are many while those who widely proclaim [the Dharma] are few; it is like a small pool of water from a mosquito’s wing that cannot save one from a drought.
Next, when summer passes, it is called autumn; the pair of discernment [of arising and ceasing] begins to subside.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like the first month after summer has passed, which is called autumn; the autumn rains fall continuously, and this Great Vehicle is likewise.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is likewise so: for the sake of the bodhisattvas of the southern regions, it shall be widely disseminated and the rain of Dharma shall pour down, filling those lands.
When the True Dharma is about to perish, it shall reach Kaśmīra and remain there complete and without deficiency before sinking into the earth.
Whether there be those who believe or those who do not, such is the nature of this Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra.
The Dharma-taste of the Ambrosia, which governs all, shall entirely sink into the earth; once this sutra has vanished, all other Mahāyāna scriptures will likewise perish and disappear.

When those who are like elephant-kings among men and the various bodhisattvas obtain this sutra complete and without deficiency, they should know that the unsurpassed True Dharma of the Tathāgata will not long remain before it is extinguished.
"Disappearing like the earth, flourishing like the autumn rain" (and so forth).

From the passage "At that time, Mañjuśrī descended" onwards is the eighth response within this chapter to the prior question regarding whether the three vehicles possess no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

This section is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the verses' intent while simultaneously dispelling the preceding questions; second, Kāśyapa’s formal discussion as the direct answer to the prior inquiry.
The first section is divided into five parts: (1) Mañjuśrī raises Cunda’s doubt; (2) the Tathāgata grants permission to speak;
(3) Mañjuśrī puts forth his inquiry; (4) the Tathāgata provides the explanation; and (5) Mañjuśrī receives the teaching with understanding.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, Cunda still harbors doubts;
we only pray that the Tathāgata will explain them further for him, so that they may be severed."
However, this was an answer to a question; why then do you suddenly raise a doubt? Since the doubt is not yet resolved, why further cause another to raise it?

The interpretation from Hexi says: Mañjuśrī is a great bodhisattva who wanders freely, acting as the shadow and echo of Śākyamuni and serving as the presiding elder among the assembly who constantly inspires others.
This is why he raises the doubt on their behalf. Second, it is said that the Sage has no "self" or "other," and acts solely for the benefit [of others].
This being so, how much more so for two people acting as friends; what harm is there in [the Buddha] transmitting [this teaching]? Why did Cunda give rise to doubt?
Previously he posed five difficulties, and in the Buddha’s response therein, it was not seen that the Buddha-nature is non-eternal, nor that seeing the Buddha-nature constitutes permanence.
After the Tathāgata had accepted the food and entered the Vajra-samādhi, once that food was digested, he then saw the Buddha-nature and attained the three [bodies].
If awakening were such a permanence, then that which was originally non-existent now exists, and having existed, returns to non-existence; this would be impermanence.
One should know that the Tathāgata does not attain such permanence. For what reason, then, did he further speak [of it]?
This is also an answer to Kāśyapa’s question regarding how there can be distinctions among the three vehicles if they lack intrinsic nature. Now, this verse is cited to clarify these distinctions.
The absence of distinction allows for a comprehensive response to the questions. Kāśyapa’s inquiry is fundamentally consistent with the underlying principle:

if those of the three vehicles possess the same single vehicle nature (*ekayāna-gotra*), how can there be three differences? If those of the three vehicles do not yet at all possess the nature of the single vehicle, how can it be said that they have it?
By citing this verse as a response, all doubts regarding difference and non-difference are resolved.
This is sent to all as a simultaneous response to their intentions. However, when Cunda discussed with the Buddha, he had not yet seen the nature [of reality];

seeing the impermanent as impermanent and the permanent as permanent, there were three levels of capacity for understanding. Those of superior capacity had already attained awakening during the "Chapter on Sighing" (*Saṃvega-parivarta*);
those of middling capacity attained it during the "Questions of Kāśyapa. As for those of inferior capacity who have not yet attained understanding, Mañjuśrī now acts further on their behalf.
Teng raised a doubt.
The Buddha said, "Good son, what is this doubting mind? You should speak of it, and I shall eliminate and sever it for you.
Mañjuśrī replied, "Cunda’s mind doubts that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, because he has attained the power of seeing and knowing the Buddha-nature."
Therefore, if the Buddha-nature were eternal upon being seen, it must have been impermanent before it was seen.
If it were originally impermanent, it should remain so afterward. Why? Because worldly objects that did not exist and now exist, or that existed and then ceased to exist, are all impermanent.
For this reason, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas—
There is no distinction.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

What existed originally is now non-existent; What was non-existent originally is now existent. That there could be such a thing as a phenomenon existing throughout the three periods of time— This is impossible.
"Good son, for this reason, there is both difference and non-difference among the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
This single verse appears four times: once here [in this section], twice in the *Brahmacarya* chapter, and three times in the twenty-fifth [chapter]."

The fourth section [of the twenty-sixth chapter] has the same general purport as the previous one, yet differs in its treatment of conditions; herein it explains the meaning of "difference within non-difference.
Within the section on the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya), it explains the meaning of "attaining non-attainment.

The twenty-fifth [section] explains the meaning of the Middle Way—wherein existence is neither determinate existence nor indeterminate existence, and non-existence is neither determinate non-existence nor indeterminate non-existence. The twenty-sixth is for the purpose of explaining refutation.
The clarification that "determined nature" (niyati) means "the absence of nature" (niḥsvabhāva)—these four points of exposition—are also for the sake of those with the three lower faculties.
The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* say: "The diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*) is not yet permanent; it is the subsequent mind that is permanent. Regarding permanence and impermanence:

if it were originally existent but now non-existent, or if it were originally non-existent but now existent—this interpretation is precisely what Cunda doubted and has no bearing on the meaning of the verse.
Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that "originally existing" refers to the original existence of afflictions (kleśa), which existed in the past but are now absent;

and "now non-existent" refers to the present absence of prajñā, which was [present] in the past—both of these refer to the Vajra-mind (*vajracitta*) as being originally existent in the former state and non-existent in the latter.

As for the statement, "There is no such place where a dharma exists throughout the three periods of time," this is based on the fact that after the attainment of the Vajra[-mind], one abides eternally in the fruit of Buddhahood, and is not subject to the three [periods].
Because they are subsumed within the [three] periods of time, it is said that such a thing is impossible (*asthānam etat*).

Furthermore, since the first half is no different from what preceded, and because it is stated that persons of the three vehicles equally enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, it is said that for a phenomenon to exist across the three periods of time is impossible.

Another interpretation is that while afflictions (*kleśa*) originally existed but now do not, these are not subsumed within the three periods of time; whereas *nirvāṇa* did not originally exist but now does.
Nirvāṇa is likewise not subsumed within the world; although the various masters have offered numerous interpretations, none of them dispel Cunda’s doubt.

For if your original state was already impermanent, then it is now also impermanent. If your original state had not yet attained permanence and you only now attain it, or if what was originally non-existent now exists and is subsumed within the three periods of time, then the difficulty of the doubt remains exactly as it was.
How does this relate to the meaning of the verse? The followers of the *Dì* school say that it is "permanent."

The Dharma is not something newly acquired; its original essence and function have been complete from the beginning. It is merely covered by delusive afflictions and only becomes manifest at a later time.
If this were so, then having first been hidden and later being revealed, it should also become hidden again after being revealed.

Since it does not become hidden once revealed, it should likewise remain hidden and never be revealed (and so forth). The Tripiṭaka Master said: "Birth and death are beginningless, yet they have an end."

Nirvana has a beginning but no end; because it is attained for the first time at this present moment, it is said to have a beginning; because once attained it is forever established, it is said to have no end.
Those who offer this interpretation are still the same as the people of the [Mahāyāna] Grounds (bhūmi). Even those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) may likewise say this:
that while delusions are extinguished and the Path remains, what was originally non-existent now exists, and thus all is impermanent. Those who speak in this manner follow the traditional [exegesis].

One cannot avoid the objection raised by Cunda. Emperor Huang said: "The meaning of Kāśyapa’s objection is that since the three vehicles each attain nirvāṇa, how can they share the same Buddha-nature?
If they share the same Buddha-nature, they should also share the same Buddha-vehicle. The Buddha replied: "The three vehicles are in fact only one Buddha-nature.
What was formerly one has become three; now, these three are simply one. How could the three vehicles [be separate]?"
That which previously lacked intrinsic nature now exists; this is merely distinguished according to the differences in conditions.

To discern that what was previously unawakened is "originally present but now absent," while what is now first awakened is "originally absent but now present"—this is, for example, like the Lamp-King and Prabhūtaratna of the past, who were originally present but are now absent, and Maitreya of the future, who is originally absent but will be present.
This also refers to the present, the past, and the future; this is the meaning of the first half [of the verse].

As for the discussion on Buddha-nature, what concern does it have with existence or non-existence, or with the "present basis"? This is the meaning of the second half. Furthermore, he critiques other interpretations, saying:
"If there are three that can be three, then distinctions are established; if there is one that can be one, then no distinction is established. If there is distinction, then [the truth] is lost."
If there were no difference, then one would lose the distinction between differences; if one opens the One to become three, then one loses the One;

if one unifies the three to become the One, then one loses the three. Now it is clarified that this is not so: the three of the past are still the One of the present, and the One of the present is still the three of the past.

To open the three does not cause one to lose the One, and to unify them does not cause one to lose the three. This is precisely difference, which is precisely non-difference; non-difference is precisely...
If one grasps this meaning, [one sees that] it is impossible for a dharma existing in the three periods of time to exist now having not existed before;
one should likewise state that it is possible for a dharma existing in the three periods of time to exist now having not existed before. Regarding the realm of impermanence, wisdom is not its object;
regarding cause and effect, they are not [mutually] cause and effect—examples such as these are all like this. Furthermore, it is said that "existing from the beginning" simply means "existing."
"Present non-existence" is simply that it was originally non-existent; "present non-non-existence" is simply that it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Furthermore, it is said that the first half [of the verse] refers to existence and the second half refers to non-existence, yet there is no such place where this is so;
thus, "neither existent nor non-existent" follows the same principle as "originally non-existent, now existent," and so forth. However, Xinghuang [Huijiao] took the single Buddha-nature as...
The first part explains that what originally existed is now understood as being non-existent; the second part explains that the Buddha-nature is neither of the present nor of the original [state].
This points to the meaning of "difference and non-difference. This [previous interpretation] divides the text into two distinct streams whose meanings are unrelated;
however, this is not the case here. It relies solely on a single phrase: difference is precisely non-difference, and non-difference is precisely difference. Thus, the Single Truth is...
Because there are three truths, it is said that originally there are three truths; because these three truths are in fact one truth, it is said that now they do not exist.

Since the three and the one are neither identical nor different, it is said that for any dharma to exist throughout the three periods of time is impossible. Thus, turning back upon each other, they cannot be separated;
this is precisely the difference that is non-different, and the non-difference that is difference. It is neither difference nor non-difference. This is then—

The resolution of Kāśyapa’s difficulties is so thorough that not a trace remains; this is impermanence itself, which is precisely permanence, and permanence itself, which is impermanence—neither permanent nor impermanent.
Thus the clouds of Cunda’s doubts are dispersed and the ice melts; the realization of wisdom is likewise.

To realize that one is three names is to see their original existence; to realize that three are one name is to see their present non-existence. Realizing that one and three are neither one nor three is the ultimate awakening.
To say that such a thing is impossible—what difficulty is there in this? What doubt remains undispelled, what delusion remains unremoved?
Thus, that which is "originally existent" means that one exists and all exist; this is the world (*loka*). That which is "now non-existent" means that one does not exist and all do not exist;
this is the remedy (*pratipakṣa*). Combining this existence and non-existence, where all both exists and does not exist, constitutes the three periods of time for human beings.
That there exists a dharma which is non-existent is impossible; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Now, this single *siddhi* (accomplishment) fully possesses the four *siddhis*.

It dispels difficulties and resolves doubts. I privately maintain that if both the doubts and difficulties of two people are dispelled and resolved, then the capacities of all beings are harmoniously integrated and fully accord with what is originally possessed—this is the "existence-phrase" and the "existence-gate.
That it is currently non-existent is the "non-existence-phrase" and the "non-existence-gate," the sound [of the teaching].

Hearing that there is both distinction and non-distinction among Pratyekabuddhas—that is, the phrase "both existent and non-existent" and the gate of "both existent and non-existent"—one realizes that for phenomena to exist throughout the three periods of time is impossible; this is the phrase "neither existent nor non-existent" and the gate of "neither existent nor non-existent.
The identity of these four aspects serves to dispel difficulties and resolve doubts. Regarding the Master’s three interpretations, the first states as follows:
The first three phrases eliminate what is not the case by negating both existence and non-existence; the final phrase concludes that such a thing is impossible.
Second, if it were originally existent, then this existence could not be made non-existent; if it were originally non-existent, then this non-existence could not be made existent.
Since this existence does not exist, it is not existent; since this non-existence is not non-existent, it is not non-existent. Thus, it is neither existent nor non-existent.

It is not that they do not exist; thus it is said that the three periods of time do not encompass the three [vehicles]. The first half [of the verse] is non-differentiation within differentiation, while the second half is differentiation within non-differentiation.
This is explained in two ways: first, from the perspective of the essence itself (*tattva*), and second, from the perspective of conditions (*pratyaya*).

From the perspective of the essence itself—that is, the fundamental state of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)—there is no differentiation. However, with respect to conditions, there are the distinctions of the three vehicles.
Regarding the differences in interpretation: furthermore, the explanation that "what existed originally is now non-existent" means that this present non-existence is the original [state];

since this original state is not the present, it is the original state that is not the present. The explanation that "what was originally non-existent is now existent" means that this present existence is the absence of the original;

since this present is not the original, it is the present that is not the original. Therefore, these are not subsumed within the categories of the world (*loka*). Is the general meaning of this interpretation not evident?
He further elaborated on this (as detailed above).
Mañjuśrī praised him, saying: "Excellent! It is truly as the Holy One has said.
Only now do I understand that the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas are both distinct and non-distinct."
The second section, "Kāśyapa’s Reply," which directly answers the preceding question, is further divided into four parts: first, a discussion on the absence of distinction;

second, a discussion on the presence of distinction; third, a summary of both meanings; and fourth, a re-discussion of the presence of distinction. Regarding the first, there is a question and answer, as found in the text.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, there is no difference in the nature of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
We only pray that the Tathāgata will analyze and explain this extensively for the benefit and peace of all sentient beings."

The answer provides two analogies: the first illustrates hearing the sutra and believing in its vision; the second illustrates clear and manifest realization. Within the first analogy, there are two parts:

first, the analogy itself, and second, the application of the analogy (the *yōgi*). Within the application of the analogy, there are three sections: first, the analogy of sentient beings all equally possessing Buddha-nature;
second, the analogy of giving rise to doubt; and third, the analogy of attaining understanding and enlightenment.
The Buddha said, "Good son, listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain this for you.
Good son, it is like a householder who keeps many milch cows of various colors. He constantly employs a man to guard and nourish them.
At one time, for the sake of a sacrificial offering, this man milks all the cows into a single vessel and sees that the milk from all the cows is uniformly white."
The elder has two interpretations: first, it is said that he is an analogy for the Buddha; second, it is said that he is an analogy for sentient beings.

The various oxen represent the different states of the six realms of existence; their diverse colors represent the myriad distinct species within those six realms. The single person who guards them represents one who possesses faith.
Furthermore, it is said that he represents a Bodhisattva propagating the sutras, causing others to be transformed and taught as a form of sacrificial offering.

Those who propagate the sutra are able to repay the Buddha’s kindness by exhausting their sincerity in this single vessel; they contemplate all sentient beings as sharing the nature of the Middle Way.
That the color is white is a metaphor for the purity of the fundamental nature.
Upon hearing this, they were immediately struck with wonder and doubt.
They marveled at how the colors of the cows were each different, yet why was the milk all of one color?
One person gave rise to a doubt and questioned Kāśyapa: "Since sentient beings are distinct, how can their Buddha-nature be one?"
Third is the person’s contemplation of the lower analogy for understanding and realization.
This person contemplates and knows that all of this is due to the causes and conditions of the karmic retribution of sentient beings, which causes the color of the milk to become uniform.
The karmic retribution of sentient beings causes the color of the milk to become uniform; this is known as the nature of the true cause of sentient beings, which is precisely the One Middle Way.
Next, in the reconciliation of the parable, it again reconciles the three points mentioned above: first, it reconciles the single Buddha-nature.
Good son, it is the same for the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; they share the same Buddha-nature, just like that milk. Why is this?
Because they equally exhaust all outflows (āsrava).
Next, the various classes of sentient beings together give rise to doubt.
Yet sentient beings say that there are distinctions between Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas;
how is it that there is no difference among the three vehicles, given that there are Śrāvakas and ordinary persons who harbor doubts about them?
After a long time, these sentient beings will eventually attain understanding and realization.
These sentient beings will, after a long time, spontaneously understand that all three vehicles share the same Buddha-nature,
just as that person understood the nature of milk through the causal conditions of karma.
Next, as in the analogy of the gold ore, the illustration of realization and vision follows the same pattern: first the illustration, then the application.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like gold ore which, after being refined to remove impurities and subsequently melted down to become pure gold, becomes of immeasurable value.
Good son, it is the same for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; they all achieve the accomplishment of the same Buddha-nature.
Why is this? Because they eliminate afflictions, just as that gold ore eliminates all dross and impurities.
For this reason, all sentient beings possess the same Buddha-nature without distinction, because they first hear the Tathāgata’s secret treasury and subsequently achieve it.
At that time, the Buddha spontaneously understood it to be like that elder’s knowledge of milk having a single characteristic. Why?
Because he had severed immeasurable billions of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Kāśyapa then spoke, initiating the second section which clarifies the distinctions through two rounds of question and answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, what difference is there between a Buddha and sentient beings?

To speak in such a way is fraught with many errors. If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, for what causes and conditions do Śāriputra and others enter parinirvāṇa through a lesser nirvāṇa, and why do pratyekabuddhas [do so]?"
If such individuals attain parinirvāṇa within [the realm of] nirvana, while bodhisattvas attain parinirvāṇa in great parinirvāṇa,
and if these people share the same buddha-nature, why do they not likewise attain parinirvāṇa in the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata?
Regarding the initial question that the three vehicles share the same Buddha-nature, they should likewise share the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding nirvāṇa;
it should not be a state of extinction like ashes that causes the three to remain distinct. A text states that they do not attain the same nirvāṇa as the Tathāgata, yet they enter parinirvāṇa.
Another text states that they do not attain the same nirvāṇa as the Tathāgata, yet they do not enter parinirvāṇa. Both of these cases can be considered identical in their entry into parinirvāṇa.
"Those who realize the same eternal and non-extinguishing state—how could that which is eternally abiding and unchanging ever be 'entered' as a realization?
Good son, the *nirvāṇa* attained by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is not the same as that attained by the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
For this reason, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is called 'the existence of goodness. Even if there were no Buddhas in the world, it would not be that the two vehicles do not attain it."
Second, regarding *nirvāṇa*:

Next, the Buddha’s intended meaning in answering was that for those who are indolent, he taught that there are three vehicles which are in reality identical to the single, universal *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata.
If there were no Buddhas in the world, these would be merely provisional expressions; in reality, however, it is not so. Therefore, in truth, there are not two [vehicles].
If the Buddha does not appear in the world while they ride upon *nirvāṇa*, there are two vehicles that attain two types of *nirvāṇa*;
if the Buddha does appear in the world, they all equally attain the single *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata.
The second round of question and answer is as in the text.
Kāśyapa spoke again, "What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, "Only once in immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas does a single Buddha appear in the world to reveal the Three Vehicles.
Son of good family, regarding what you have said—that there is no difference between Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles—I have previously [stated]..."
In this Great Nirvana, which is the secret treasury of the Tathāgata, its meaning is thus explained:
the Arhats possess no goodness. Why is this? Because all Arhats shall eventually attain this Great Nirvana.
For this reason, the Mahāparinirvāṇa possesses ultimate bliss; therefore, it is named the Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Under the third pair of points following Kāśyapa’s words, two meanings are summarized.
Kāśyapa said: "As the Buddha has taught, I now for the first time understand the meaning of distinction and the meaning of non-distinction.
Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas shall in a future age all return to the Great Parinirvāṇa."
Nirvāṇa is like the many rivers that flow back to the great ocean;
therefore, those who are Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are all said to be eternal and not impermanent. For this reason, there is both distinction and non-distinction.
Kāśyapa asked: "What is the distinction of natures? Thus, the fourth section on the distinctions of the treatise has three parts.
Kāśyapa asked: "What is the distinction of natures?
The Buddha said: "Good son, śrāvakas are like milk; pratyekabuddhas are like curd; and bodhisattvas are like raw and cooked [milk products]."
The ghee of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is like the finest cream (*sarpis*); for this reason, within the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, four types of nature are taught with their distinctions.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "What are the characteristics of the nature of all sentient beings?"
The Buddha said, "Good son, it is like the milk and blood of a newborn calf that have not yet been distinguished; the nature of ordinary beings, mixed with various afflictions, is also like this.
In the first two questions and answers, although the Buddha remained without making distinctions, he nevertheless provided a differentiated response.
Regarding the meaning of the third Kāśyapa’s subsequent inquiry: Kāśyapa spoke again,
saying that in the city of Kuśinagara there was a *caṇḍāla* named Nandika, whom the Buddha had prophesied would,

by virtue of a single arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), swiftly attain the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) among the lineage of a thousand Buddhas in this world-system.
For what reason did the Tathāgata not grant the prediction that the Venerable Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others would swiftly attain the Buddha-way?
Since it is said that the *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) of the śrāvakas is superior, why do ordinary persons suddenly receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood before them?
The meaning of the Buddha’s reply is as follows:
The Buddha said, "Good son, there may be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas who make a vow, saying:

'I shall protect and uphold the True Dharma for a long time, and only thereafter shall I attain the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood. Because they have made such a vow for speed, they attain it quickly."
Furthermore, good son, it is like a merchant who possesses a priceless jewel and goes to the market to sell it.
When a foolish person sees it, they do not recognize it and laugh at the owner of the jewel, saying, "This jewel of mine is worth countless riches.
Upon hearing this, [the merchant] laughs again, and they each say to one another, "This is no true jewel; it is merely a crystal. Good son, [it is the same for] the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas...

Awakening is also like this: if one hears that a prediction of enlightenment will be swiftly granted, one may become indolent, laughing it off with contempt and treating it with disdain—just like that fool who did not recognize genuine treasure.
In future ages, there will be bhikṣus who are unable to diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas;
impoverished, distressed, and oppressed by hunger and thirst, they will, because of this, nurture their bodies and minds as householders while remaining light in their resolve.

Those who are restless, of wrong livelihood, and deceitful—if they hear the Tathāgata bestow a prediction of swift enlightenment upon the śrāvakas—they will laugh loudly, treat it with contempt, and disparage it.
You should know that such persons are those who have broken the precepts yet claim for themselves superhuman attainments;
for this reason, because they have made a vow for speed, they are granted a swift prediction, whereas those who protect the True Dharma are granted a distant one.
Record.
It is not on account of their Buddha-nature that those who previously made vows for swift Buddhahood are immediately granted a prediction (vyākaraṇa).
From the passage beginning with "Kāśyapa again said" below, this is the ninth response within this chapter to the question: "How is it that the various bodhisattvas..."
Having obtained the assembly that cannot be divided, Kāśyapa again restated his question as a request.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha once more, saying: "World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva obtain an undivided retinue?"
Next, in the Buddha’s response, he again answers by means of the protection of the Dharma.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "If bodhisattvas apply themselves with diligent vigor, desiring to protect the true Dharma, then for this reason the retinue they obtain shall be indestructible."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: "For what reason does this chapter provide the tenth answer to the question:
'How does one act as eyes and a guide for those born blind?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions do sentient beings obtain these lips and mouth?'"
"Dry and parched.
First, "the lips and mouth become dry and parched" refers to the meaning of being born blind.
In the Buddha’s response, he first answers regarding the loss of taste in the mouth, and subsequently answers regarding being born blind.

The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "If there are those who do not recognize that the Three Jewels are eternally present, by reason of this they will have parched lips and mouths, just as one whose sense of taste is impaired cannot distinguish between the six flavors—sweet, bitter, pungent, sour, salty, and bland.
All such sentient beings are foolish and ignorant; because they do not recognize that the Three Jewels are eternal dharmas, they are said to have parched lips and mouths."
The initial statement regarding "a distaste for flavors" means that one does not know the flavor of the Three Jewels' eternal abiding; this is called a distaste for flavors.
Such a person is like one born blind. If one calculates that things must definitely exist and searches for them, they are not to be found.
From the passage beginning "Furthermore, good son," the answer regarding those born blind is given.
Furthermore, good son, if there are sentient beings who do not know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, you should know that such persons are like those born blind;
