yet if they know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, such persons, although possessing fleshly [eyes], [are not so].

I say that such as these are called those with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Furthermore, son of good family, if there are those who know that the Tathāgata is eternal, you should know that these people have long since practiced such sūtras; I say that these also are called those with the divine eye.
Although they possess the divine eye, they are unable to know that the Tathāgata is eternal; I say that such as these are called... [those with the physical eye].
The fleshly eye belongs to humans; it is such that they do not even recognize their own hands, feet, limbs, or joints, nor can they cause others to recognize them.
For this reason, it is called the "fleshly eye."
Because they are blind, they do not recognize; those who do not recognize their hands and feet do not recognize the Buddha-nature within their own bodies.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata constantly provides the following answer as the eleventh response to the question posed above:
"How is the many-headed one shown?"
Furthermore, good son, the Tathāgata constantly acts as the father and mother for all sentient beings. Why is this?
Because among the various forms and classes of all sentient beings—whether they have two legs, four legs, many legs, or no legs—the Buddha preaches the Dharma to them with a single voice;
each of those different classes understands it according to their own kind, and they all exclaim: "The Tathāgata now..."
The Sun preaches the Dharma for me; for this reason, he is called "Father and Mother.
The Buddha replied: "The Tathāgata manifests various bodies, which is like having many heads; he expounds various Dharmas, which is like having many tongues" (and so forth).
Furthermore, from the passage "Just as when a person gives birth to a child" onwards, this section provides the twelfth response to the question posed above:
"How does a speaker of the Dharma increase [in virtue] like the waxing moon?

Furthermore, son of good family, it is like when a person gives birth to a child who is sixteen months old; although their speech is not yet intelligible, [the child already possesses the potential for expression].
Once [the child] has mastered it, those parents, wishing to teach him speech, first imitate his own sounds and gradually instruct him.
Would the speech of those parents not be correct? "Indeed it would, World-Honored One. "Good son, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this:
they preach the Dharma by following the various sounds of sentient beings, so that they may cause them to dwell securely in the True Dharma of the Buddha."
“Does it not follow that the Tathāgata manifests various forms according to what is to be seen, and likewise employs their respective languages? Is this not so?
“It is so, World-Honored One. “Why is this? “Because that which the Tathāgata speaks is like the lion’s roar;
in accordance with the various sounds of the world, he proclaims the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.”
The previous question regarding the moon was posed to the Buddha; now, the answer is given concerning the birth of a child, stating that there is growth throughout.
Regarding the "sixteen months," there are two interpretations: first, ten periods of six months, which constitutes five years;
second, beginning from the passage of sixteen months, which implies that four additional months have elapsed. This is evident in the text.

The Questions of the Entire Assembly Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty Fascicle Ten of the Commentary on the Southern Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Seventeen:
The Questions of the Entire Assembly (Fascicle Ten) Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Revised by the Jin dynasty śramaṇas Huìyán,
Huìguān, and Xiè Língyùn:
The Chapter on Questions from the Great Assembly.

The sixth fascicle is titled "Chapter on Rejoicing" (*Anumodanā-parivarta*) in the current edition, while the ancient manuscript (*guben*) titles it "Chapter on Verses of Sorrow, Grief, and Lamentation" (*Udvega-śoka-parideva-gāthā-parivarta*).
Regarding the content: the current edition takes the passage where Kāśyapa sees Cunda and [realizes] the cultivation and completion of the bodhisattva path as the basis for the title "Rejoicing.

The ancient manuscript takes the passage where the Buddha accepts Cunda’s offering and immediately enters *nirvāṇa* as the basis for the title "Verses of Sorrow, Grief, and Lamentation. Now, based on which meaning is the chapter title determined? There are two [possibilities].
In explaining the text: there is actually no mention of the assembly posing questions, nor any account of the assembly questioning the Buddha;
rather, it is simply that the manifested Buddha accepted the offerings of the assembly and became the object of their inquiry. Second, [the assembly thought]:
"Today the Tathāgata has accepted our offerings and shall enter parinirvāṇa; whom else among us should we now offer to?"
This is the section where the great assembly further offers mutual greetings. The Master Guān says that Kāśyapa’s initial inquiry was made for the sake of the great assembly;

since the Buddha is the object of the question and the inquiry itself is the means, the intent lies in this chapter. It is from this that it derives its name, and thus it is called the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly.
Now, regarding the text, the actual words of the questions are not recorded therein; rather, the questions are revealed by the answers. Above, the permanence [of the Tathāgata] has been clarified.

Abiding without change, he now manifests the appearance of entering *nirvāṇa*. This appearance seems contrary to what is taught; thus, the assembly asks about this meaning, and the Buddha answers in verse:
"Ultimately and eternally abiding, he does not enter *nirvāṇa*. Because the answer reveals the question, it is called the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly.
The text is divided into two parts: first, answering the questions in sequence; second, the joyful acceptance and understanding [of the teaching]. Regarding the first, the masters of Hexi say:

This chapter answers seven questions in four sections: the first section answers the question regarding the manifestation of *nirvāṇa*, while also answering the question regarding the manifestation of the paths of humans, devas, and māras;
following the recitation of the verses, the second section answers the question regarding the knowledge of the *dharmatā*;

the third section, through the explanation of the remaining verses, directly answers the question regarding the teaching of the secret [meaning], while also answering the questions regarding the removal of illness and the proximity to the unsurpassed path.
Fourth, what further is meant by the "meaning of no remainder"? The answer is that, regarding the ultimate inquiry, it is divided into two parts from the outset:

first, the great assembly offers worship; second, the Tathāgata accepts the offering. Furthermore, there are two sections: first, the causal origination (*nidāna*); second, the presentation of the offering. The causal origination consists of five parts:

first, the emission of light; second, the desire to present the offering; third, the obstruction by humans and devas; fourth, the repeated emission of light; fifth, the presentation [of the offering].
Offering. At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from his face various colored rays of light— blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and purple—
which illuminated the body of Cunda.

Having encountered [the Buddha], Cunda, together with his retinue, took various delicacies and hurried to where the Buddha was, wishing to present them as the final offering to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus;
he brought these to the Buddha’s presence, carrying a full array of diverse vessels, complete and abundant.
At that time, there were devas of great majesty and power who blocked his path, surrounding him on all sides, and said to Cunda:
"Stop, Cunda! Do not yet present this offering.
At that moment, the Tathāgata again emitted immeasurable and boundless rays of various kinds of light.

When the great assembly of devas encountered this light, they immediately permitted Cunda to proceed to the Buddha’s presence to present his offerings, using this as their response to those who had inquired about the manifestation of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding this, the Master of Hexi explained that there are three kinds of manifestations of *nirvāṇa*:
first, manifestation through verbal expression; second, manifestation through supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*); and third, manifestation through actual events.
The "matter" refers to the fragrant wood, ghee, and oil used for his final meal; the "supernatural power" refers to the emission of light and the manifestation of auspicious omens;

and the "discourse" refers to his address to Cunda, saying, "If you wish for me to remain long in the world, you should promptly present this final offering," which directly answers the intent of the question.
At that time, the "Heavenly Beings" section below constitutes the second offering, which is further divided into two parts: first, the offering by the great assembly; second, the offering by Cunda.
The first part, the offering by the great assembly, is further divided into two sections: the first is the offering by the great assembly itself.
At that time, the devas and all sentient beings each brought their own offerings for the fast-food observance before the Buddha;
kneeling long upon the ground, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "We only pray that the Tathāgata will permit the bhikṣus to accept these offerings."
Two bhikṣus carried the robes and bowls;
at that time, because the bhikṣus knew it was the proper hour, they held their robes and bowls with single-minded composure.
Next, Cunda prepared offerings for the fourfold assembly.
At that time, Cunda prepared various lion thrones made of precious gems for the Buddha and the Sangha, hanging silk banners,
canopies, incense, flowers, and necklaces;
he performed two transformations of the ground.
At that time, the great trichiliocosm was adorned with such subtle and wondrous beauty as the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[He] made three requests out of grief.
Then, Cunda stood before the Buddha, filled with sorrow and despondency, and addressed the Buddha once more, saying: "I only pray that the Tathāgata..."
As if out of compassion, he remained for one kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa. The Buddha said to Cunda:
"If you wish for me to remain long in the world, you should quickly offer this final, complete perfection of dāna."
Fourth, the praise:
At that time, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, devas, humans, and various other beings, with one voice and in unison, proclaimed these words:
"How marvelous! Cunda has accomplished such great merit and virtue that he is able to cause the Tathāgata to accept his final, unsurpassed offering."
"The offerings prepared by us, who possess no merit, would then be in vain.
At that time, the World-Honored One descended; this was the second Tathāgata receiving offerings, followed by four others, each receiving the offerings of the great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to satisfy the aspirations of all the assembly, manifested from each and every pore of his own body immeasurable Buddhas;
each of these Buddhas had their own immeasurable community of bhikṣus.
All these World-Honored Ones and their immeasurable retinues were fully manifested, receiving offerings.
Second, accepting Cunda’s offering: at that time,
Śākyamuni Tathāgata personally accepted the food prepared and offered by Cunda— namely, the mature grain and husked rice from the kingdom of Mahāsthāna,
amounting to eight *droṇas*— and through the Buddha’s supernatural power, it became sufficient for all.
At that time, when the entire great assembly saw this event, their hearts were filled with joy and they leaped for joy immeasurably;
all the great multitude was likewise so.
The three assemblies gave rise to the thought that the vast and the minute could contain one another.
At that time, the great assembly, receiving the Buddha’s holy intent, each formed this thought: "The Tathāgata has now accepted our offerings;
before long he will surely enter parinirvāṇa. Having formed this thought, their hearts were filled with both sorrow and joy.
At that moment, although the ground of the grove was narrow and small, by the Buddha's spiritual power, even at the tip of a needle there were immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
When he and his retinue sat down to eat, there was no difference in the food they consumed.
The four great assemblies sighed with grief;
at that time, the devas, humans, asuras, and others wept and lamented, saying: "Today, the Tathāgata..."
"Having received our final offering, and having accepted this offering, he shall enter parinirvāṇa. To whom shall we offer further offerings?
We are now forever separated from the Unsurpassed Tamer; we are blind and without eyes."
Regarding the reason for answering both [the question on the Buddha-body] and the question concerning the realms of humans, devas, and māras:

Hexi (Daorong) says that because the world is adorned and purified, the transformation Buddhas emerge from every pore, and Cunda’s meager offering universally suffices for the great assembly—all such extraordinary and rare great matters enable those present at the gathering to perceive them clearly;
therefore, this constitutes an answer that simultaneously addresses the question concerning the realms of humans, devas, and māras.

At that time, the World-Honored One—herein begins the second chapter, answering the question regarding the knowledge of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the experience of the joy of the Dharma.

This section has two parts: first, the direct answer to the question; second, the reception of the auspicious sign and the conclusion. Within the first part (the direct answer), there are two further divisions:

first, the answer to the question regarding the knowledge of the nature of phenomena; second, the answer regarding the experience of the joy of the Dharma. Within the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the correct understanding of the nature of phenomena as presented in the verses; [second, the prose commentary].
Following the nature [of the teaching], the prose section praises and censures points of gain and loss. It begins with twenty-one verses divided into three parts:

first, four lines that cease lamentation and exhort the listeners; second, thirteen lines that correctly discern the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); and third, four lines that conclude by exhorting to practice.
The first four lines are as explained in the text.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to comfort the entire great assembly, spoke these verses:
"Do not lament, O you all; such is the natural law of all Buddhas.
I have entered parinirvāṇa for immeasurable kalpas, Constantly experiencing the most supreme bliss, Forever dwelling in a state of peace and security."
Listen now with a sincere heart; I shall speak of Nirvāṇa. Having abandoned the perception of food, I am forever free from the affliction of hunger and thirst.
Now, for your sakes, I shall speak in accordance with your aspirations, so that all beings may attain peace and happiness. Upon hearing this, you should practice accordingly.

The "Dharmatā-nitya-sthiti" (The Permanence of the Dharma-nature) section consists of thirteen verses. Of these, the first twelve are divided into six pairs, each pair corresponding to one another to reveal the principle of the dharma-nature;

the final verse serves as a summary that brings both cessation and compassion to a conclusion. Thus, although there are precisely twelve verses [in the main body], [the section concludes with] the latter...
The text states that the "thirteen verses" include the summary verse as well:
"Even if a crow and an owl Were to perch together upon the same tree, Only when they are like close brothers Will there be eternal nirvāṇa. The Tathāgata regards all beings Just as he does Rāhula."
Always honored by sentient beings, how can you enter parinirvāṇa forever?
Regarding the first bird among the initial pair mentioned in the first section: as for the "crow and the owl," these two birds may dwell together;
however, the crow and the *yù* (sparrow-hawk/owlet) cannot dwell together. The *yù* is the *qūyù*, which is simply the *xiū* (owl). This bird and—
An owl and a crow cannot dwell together;
next, one may see a pair [of opposites].
Even if a snake, a rat, and a wildcat were to share a single burrow, they might love one another like brothers.
Then you shall enter eternal nirvana; the Tathāgata regards all beings as he does Rāhula.
Always the honored one among sentient beings, how could you enter eternal nirvana?
Even if the seven-leaf flower were to turn into the fragrance of the vārṣika, and the kālīya into the tinduka.
Then you shall enter eternal nirvāṇa; the Tathāgata regards all beings as he does Rāhula.
How can you abandon compassion and enter eternal nirvāṇa?
Regarding the third pair [of verses]: from the seven-leaf tree to the stinking pāṭala, the extremely fragrant, the kālaka poison-tree, and the tinduka.
Sweet fruit.
The remaining three pairs may be seen [in the same way].
Even if an icchantika were to manifest the attainment of the Buddha-way in this very body, they would dwell forever in the supreme bliss.
Then you enter nirvana; the Tathāgata regards all beings as he does Rāhula.
How can you abandon compassion and enter nirvana forever?
Even if all sentient beings were to attain the Way of the Buddha at once and be far removed from all faults and afflictions, [you would still not depart].
When you thus enter nirvana, the Tathāgata views all beings as he does Rāhula;
how can you abandon compassion and enter forever into nirvana?
Even if mosquitoes and gnats were to soak and destroy the great earth, filling the rivers, valleys, and oceans [with their blood], [you would still not depart].
When he thus enters nirvana, look upon all beings with a heart of compassion;
as one who was always honored by sentient beings like Rāhula, how could he enter final nirvana?
For this reason, you all should take deep delight in the True Dharma and should not give rise to grief or distress.
Wailing and weeping as if wishing to rectify one's own conduct, one should cultivate the permanence of the Tathāgata;
one should contemplate that such dharmas exist eternally, unchanging and immutable, and further give rise to this thought: "The Three Jewels are all permanently abiding."
This shall bring about great protection, Like a spell that makes a withered tree bear fruit. This is called the Triple Gem;
the fourfold assembly should listen well. Having heard it, they should rejoice and immediately resolve upon Bodhicitta.
If one can reckon the Triple Gem as eternally abiding and identical to the ultimate truth, This is indeed the state of all Buddhas.

Regarding the statement in the *Exhortation to Practice* (*Xiuxing juan*) that "the Three Jewels are identical to the True Reality" (*tathatā*), Kaishan says: "The Buddha-fruit is darkly merged with the True;
since the True is eternally transcendent, the fruit is also eternally transcendent. Zhuangyan says: "The Buddha-fruit emerges from the True, yet it is not subsumed by the True."

Because the eternally wondrous and transcendent is identical to the Real, it is therefore identical to the True Truth (*satyadharma*). Regarding this, the two masters [Zhiyi and Zhanran] still provided an interpretation of "partial truth" (*pradeśasatya*), stating:
"If the fruit emerges outside of the Real and yet is identical to the Real, how can it emerge if it is already identical? If it has emerged, how can it be identical?

Now I clarify that the Buddha and the Sangha are the Human Truth (*pudgalasatya*), which is precisely the Middle Way. The Dharma of the Middle Way is the Dharma, and the Human is the Human. It is precisely the Human.
Because of the Dharma, it is said that the Triple Gem is identical to the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding the praise and censure of gain and loss in the prose following the verse:
if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who are able to [uphold] the supreme vow of the Tathāgata...
One who makes such a vow should know that this person is free from delusion and worthy of receiving offerings;

by the power of this vow and the karmic fruit of its merit, they shall be most supreme in the world, like an Arhat. If there is anyone who cannot thus contemplate and realize that the Triple Gem is eternal, they are a Caṇḍāla.
If there is anyone who can know that the Three Dharmas are eternally abiding, they are the cause of the true Dharma.
Because it is free from suffering and endowed with peace and bliss, there is no one who can cause harm or create obstacles.
Using this text as an adornment, he answers and shows that the path of humans and devas is distinct from the path of Māra.

As for the question regarding the *caṇḍāla* being the path of Māra and the *arhat* being the path of humans and devas, the Master does not accept this interpretation; for an *arhat* is neither a human nor a *caṇḍāla*.
Luo Feimo, this merely summarizes the preceding points regarding gain and loss:

to know that the Three Jewels are always worthy of receiving offerings is called "gain," as in the case of one named Arhat; to fail to know they are constant and thereby harm the Dharma-body is called "loss," as in the case of one named Caṇḍāla.
Next, at that time, the great assembly of humans and devas departed; this section answers questions regarding the causes for receiving the joy of the Dharma and consists of two parts:
first, receiving the joy of the Dharma, and second, presenting offerings.
At that time, the great assembly of humans, devas, and asuras, having heard this Dharma, felt joy in their hearts and leaped for gladness.
His mind is immeasurable, well-tamed, and skillfully extinguishes all hindrances; his mind is free from high or low, his majestic virtue is pure, and his countenance is serene and joyful.
Knowing that the Buddha is eternally present, they therefore arrange various celestial offerings, scattering diverse flowers, powdered incense, and ointments, and sounding heavenly music.
To make offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha spoke [the following], which constitutes the second section on the reception of auspicious signs and their formal conclusion, divided into two parts:

first, the command for Kāśyapa to receive [the teachings], and next, the command for Cunda to receive them. In the preceding passage concerning Kāśyapa, it says: "Furthermore, seeing the great assembly, he spoke thirteen verses."

First interpretation: It is said that the Buddha and the great assembly each spoke thirteen verses; this text represents the Buddha’s speech, while the verses of the great assembly are not spoken by them, as they do not come [to the assembly].

Second interpretation: Furthermore, it is seen that the "great assembly" belongs to the preceding phrase, while the recitation of the thirteen verses belongs to the Buddha and is not spoken by the great assembly.
Regarding the passage concerning the command for Kāśyapa to lead [the assembly], the text is divided into four parts: first, the command.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, saying: "Good son, do you see these rare and marvelous events?
[Kāśyapa] replied twice.
Kāśyapa answered: "I have seen them, World-Honored One; I have seen the Tathāgatas, who are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable."
He received the offerings of food presented by the great assembly of humans and devas;

he also saw that the places where the Buddhas sat—whose bodies were adorned with great majesty—were like the point of a needle, yet they were surrounded by a vast multitude without obstructing one another.
Furthermore, he saw the great assembly all resolve their vows and recite thirteen verses, and he also knew the thoughts in each member's mind, saying: "The Tathāgata now..."
He alone receives my offerings;
yet he thrice defers the merit to the Buddha.
Even if the food and drink offered by Cunda were ground into fine dust, with each particle representing a Buddha, they would still not suffice for all.
Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, all the great assemblies were fully satisfied.
Only Bodhisattvas can understand this;
indeed, only Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince can understand the rare [qualities] of the Tathāgata.

There was a matter that all were to hear: this was entirely a skillful manifestation by the Tathāgata. The great assembly of śrāvakas, as well as the asuras and others, all knew that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma.
Next, he commanded Cunda; likewise, there were four such commands.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cunda, saying: "Is what you have now seen not a rare and extraordinary marvel?
Cunda replied twice:
"It is so, World-Honored One. What I have previously seen of immeasurable Buddhas possessed the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics."
Adorned with his body, he is now seen entirely as a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva of immense stature and incomparable countenance;
seeing only the Buddha-body, he is like a medicinal tree surrounded by all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
The Buddha bound this seal three times.
The Buddha said to Cunda: "Those immeasurable Buddhas whom you previously saw were all my own emanations, created for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings and causing them to rejoice;
such is the practice to be undertaken by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas."
Inconceivable and capable of performing the immeasurable deeds of all Buddhas, Cunda, you have now fully accomplished the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
you have attained the ten stages of a bodhisattva and have completely fulfilled their conduct.
The four Kāśyapas rejoiced.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is so, it is so, just as the Buddha has taught.
I too rejoice in the bodhisattva practices cultivated by Cunda. Now, the Tathāgata desires to act for the sake of immeasurable multitudes in the future."
Because it gives birth to the Great Illumination, the World-Honored One speaks this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
This constitutes the third chapter of all the sūtras, which answers the previous question, "How does one expound the secrets for the sake of sentient beings?
and simultaneously answers the question regarding how to distance oneself from all illnesses and draw near to the Unsurpassed Way. However—
There are further verses which represent the Tathāgata’s provisional teachings given according to circumstances, rather than the ultimate meaning that reveals the principle of equality.
To now expound these concealed meanings so that what was secret is made manifest is precisely to answer the question posed above;

furthermore, within the text, the explanation of how the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, and the slandering of the Dharma—along with the three types of "sick persons"—are extinguished and their ailments cured is an incidental inclusion.

Answer: One becomes free from all illnesses through the cessation of illness and the extinction of transgressions, thereby drawing near to the Unsurpassed Way. This simultaneously answers the two questions;
the intent lies in this passage, which is divided into two parts: first, a brief question-and-answer, and second, an extensive presentation of seven verses.
"Blessed One, do all the sūtras spoken by you have a meaning that is incomplete or a meaning that is complete?
Son of good family, what I have taught has both a meaning that is incomplete and a meaning that is complete."
At the beginning of the first section, there is a brief presentation of questions concerning the *saśeṣa* (with remainder) and *niḥśeṣa* (without remainder);
next, there is a brief response stating that the *saśeṣa* is not fully understood and is esoteric, while the *niḥśeṣa* is fully understood and is manifest (and so forth).
Next, Cunda’s address below consists of an extensive presentation of seven verses of question and answer, which form seven chapters.
These seven chapters are either raised by Cunda, or raised by Mañjuśrī, or spoken by the Buddha himself (and so forth).
The first chapter is Cunda’s inquiry, which contains six sections: 1. Distinguishing icchantikas; 2. Grasping; 3. Sinners; 4. Explaining grasping.

The fifth section, the conclusion of the verses, consists of six parts: first, the general introduction; second, the explanation of the meaning; third, the fourfold interpretation to clarify the meaning; fourth, the fivefold summary of the verses; fifth, the conditions for the arising [of the path]; and sixth, the initial clarification regarding icchantikas, which contains four rounds of questions and answers.
Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught..."
Giving away all that one possesses—this alone is worthy of praise and cannot be disparaged.
World-Honored One, what is the meaning of this? What is the difference between observing the precepts and violating them?
First, he raises a verse to request an explanation, saying: "How is it that all acts of giving are worthy of praise?
How can giving, as well as the observance of precepts, be praised? And how can breaking the precepts and stinginess be praised?"
The Buddha said, "With the exception of one person, all other forms of giving may be praised.
This refers to the exclusion of the icchantika in the Buddha's response;
the second and third rounds of question and answer can be understood accordingly.
Cunda asked, "In what sense do you say 'with the exception of one person'?
The Buddha replied, "It refers to those who break the precepts as described in this sutra.
Cunda spoke again, "I am not yet weary; I only pray that you will explain it to me."
The Buddha told Cunda: "Those who break the precepts are called icchantikas;
all other acts of giving, wherever they may be, are worthy of praise and will yield great rewards.
This was the fourth question: "What is meant by the term 'icchantika'?"
Cunda asked again, "What is the meaning of 'icchantika'?
Next, in the Buddha’s response, there are three sections.
The Buddha told Cunda: "If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who give rise to coarse..."
Those who slander the True Dharma with evil words, commit such grave karma, never repent or reform, and possess no sense of shame or remorse—
such persons are said to be heading toward the path of the icchantika.

The first section provides a general explanation that disciples of the four assemblies who slander the Dharma and commit grave offenses reach a point of no return despite not being identical [to icchantikas],
yet they nonetheless tend toward the path of the icchantika.
The second section specifically points to the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes.
If one commits the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes, and knowing for certain that they have committed such serious matters,
feels no fear, shame, or remorse from the outset, refuses to disclose them, lacks any intention to protect or cherish the Buddha’s True Dharma forever,
and instead disparages and degrades it with many faults and transgressions— such persons are also said to be heading toward the path of an icchantika.
The third type of person is one who says that the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha do not exist, and who denies cause and effect.
Furthermore, those who say that the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha do not exist—such individuals as these are also said to be heading toward the path of the icchantika.
With the exception of such icchantikas, all others are to be praised for their giving.
Except for the three [grave] offenses, all other acts of giving may be praised.

At that time, Cunda again addressed [the Buddha with the following questions and answers]. Taking the three types of offenders—namely, those who commit the four grave offenses (*ānantarya*)—there are five points herein:
first, the initial question and answer briefly sets forth the three characteristics; next, it extensively clarifies the four grave offenses and the fifth, the slandering of the Dharma.
The preceding section explains the extinction [of offenses]; hereafter, the causes and conditions for slandering [the Dharma] are clarified separately. First, a brief summary follows the text:
At that time, Cunda again addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'breaking the precepts' as you have spoken? The Buddha told Cunda:
"If one commits the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*) or the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), or slanders the True Dharma—such persons are called [those who break the precepts]."
Regarding the breaking of precepts:
next, within the extensive section, there is first a question.
Cunda further asked: "Can one who has thus broken the precepts be rescued?"

Next, the meaning of the response is divided into three parts: first, clarifying the extinction of unwholesome dharmas; second, explaining the extinction of unwholesome dharmas; and third, correctly clarifying the extinction of evil.
Regarding the first, the extinction of unwholesome dharmas:

the Buddha told Cunda that because there are causes and conditions, one may be rescued and delivered; even if one has donned the dharma robes, if one has not yet abandoned [evil] and distanced oneself from it, [one cannot be saved].
With a mind constantly filled with shame, remorse, and trepidation, he reproaches himself, saying: "Alas! Why have I committed such a grave offense?
How strange it is that I have created such karma of suffering! Deeply repenting and reforming himself, he gives rise to a mind that protects the Dharma, desiring to establish the True Dharma.
He thinks: "If there are those who protect the Dharma, I shall make offerings to them; if there are those who read and recite the Mahāyāna scriptures, I shall consult them."
Once one has mastered the practice of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting [the teachings], one should further analyze and explain them extensively for others;
I say that such a person is not called one who has broken the precepts.
Hexi said there are six subtle medicines: first, generating the bodhicitta; second, feeling shame and remorse for transgressions; third, maintaining...

There are four ways to protect the True Dharma: first, respectfully protecting those who uphold the Dharma; second, discerning the characteristics of transgressions; third, receiving and upholding Mahāyāna sūtras and explaining them;
fourth, [the following six conditions, which are largely the same as the previous set but with slight differences]: first, wearing the dharma-robe; second, feeling shame and remorse;

third, generating the mind that protects the Dharma; fourth, making offerings to those who protect the Dharma; fifth, personally upholding, receiving, reading, and reciting [the scriptures]; sixth, [the sixth condition].

Regarding the statement by He Xi that "arousing the mind and reaching the transgression can also be reconciled with this," the subsequent section beginning with "For what reason" explains its meaning through an analogy, its application, and a conclusion.
For what reason? Good son, it is like the rising of the sun, which is able to dispel all dust, obscurations, and darkness.
This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra appearing in the world is just the same;
it is able to eliminate the manifold transgressions committed by sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Therefore, this sutra states that protecting the true Dharma yields great rewards and rescues those who have violated the precepts.
Third, if there are those who slander it, this clearly explains the extinction of evil:
if anyone slanders this true Dharma, they are able to reform themselves, repent, and return to the Dharma, reflecting upon their own actions.
All unwholesome states are like a person harming themselves, giving rise to terror, alarm, and shame;
apart from this True Dharma, there is no other protection. Therefore, one should return to and take refuge in the True Dharma.

If one can thus take refuge as taught and practice generosity, such a person will obtain immeasurable merit and is called one who should receive offerings in the world. If, however, one commits the aforementioned transgressions...

If, after one month or even fifteen days, one does not give rise to the mind of taking refuge and confessing the transgressions of evil karma, the fruit and retribution for giving to such a person will be very meager;
it is the same for those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).

However, if they can give rise to a mind of repentance and inwardly harbor shame and remorse, thinking, "The unwholesome karma I have now committed is a source of great suffering; I shall establish [myself in virtue]," [then the merit is great].
To uphold the True Dharma is not termed a grave offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya). If one gives to such a person, the merit obtained is immeasurable;

whereas if, after committing a grave offense of immediate retribution, one fails to give rise to a mind of refuge and protection for the Dharma, the merit of giving to such a person is insufficient to mention.
One should be fully equipped as previously described; however, the current text is abbreviated, stating directly that one returns to the True Dharma.

By mentioning both what is right and what is wrong, it clarifies that those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) can still extinguish them. This indicates that even those who commit the five heinous crimes may achieve purification; thus, by mentioning both the right and the wrong, the three offenses herein are all shown to be extinguishable.
This simultaneously answers the question regarding distancing oneself from all illnesses. Since one has attained the extinction of sins, one immediately attains proximity [to the goal].
Regarding the unsurpassed path:

furthermore, concerning the third section on the explanation of those who have committed grave offenses— the taking up of the minds of those who have committed the three types of offenses— there are both the principle and the analogy combined.
Furthermore, son of good family, as for those who have committed grave offenses, listen attentively now as I shall explain this to you in detail and distinguish its meaning:
you should give rise to this thought—that the True Dharma is the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata;
therefore, I must protect, uphold, and establish it. One who bestows [this teaching] upon such a person shall obtain a superior karmic reward.

This is illustrated by four analogies: first, the non-arising of understanding; second, the arising of understanding; third, the protection of the Dharma; and fourth, the attainment of the fruit of retribution.
The first analogy concerns the time of committing offenses and breaking the precepts.
Good son, it is like a woman who is pregnant and about to give birth, who encounters national famine and chaos and travels far to another land. The woman—
For example, a bodhisattva of shallow practice who has developed an understanding of the meaning is like a woman who is pregnant; though she harbors the embryo, the understanding has not yet emerged.

This is likened to encountering national famine and chaos, because for those in the assembly who have broken the precepts, the path of maintaining them is severed. Thus it is said that they travel far to another land, where they next reside in a celestial temple;
this represents the generation of understanding.
Just as one who has given birth in a foreign land, upon hearing that their native country is peaceful and prosperous, takes their child and desires to return to their homeland;
so too, the "foreign land" is a metaphor for this sutra, while the "native country" is a metaphor for the merit of hearing and upholding the precepts, based on which one gives rise to understanding.
He attains the fruit of retribution.
The analogy of three paths crossing the Ganges represents the protection of the Dharma.
As he travels along the path by the waters of the Ganges, which are long, turbulent, and swift, and being unable to carry his child across, he thinks to himself:
"I would rather perish with you in one place than abandon you to save myself alone. Having formed this thought, he sank together with his son.

The various heterodox groups that cling to eternalism and nihilism are like the Ganges; their fallacious arguments and sycophancy are like the violent, rushing waters of the river—it is better to lose one's reward [of life] than to follow them.
Because her life-force did not abandon its resolve, it is said that she was not saved alone.
After the end of her life, she obtained the fruit of retribution and was born in heaven.
Following the end of her life, she was immediately reborn in the heavens; out of compassionate thoughts for her son, she desired to enable him to attain liberation—this was that woman.
One whose nature is inherently depraved may, by reason of loving their child, attain birth among the devas.

the darkness symbolizes that the manifested trace is impermanent.
For this reason, you should not harbor great sorrow and affliction in your heart.
At that time, the great assembly—this concludes the third section on the Great Assembly’s Offering and Arousing of the Resolve, which further consists of three parts: first, the offering;
second, the arousing of the resolve; and third, the advancement of the stage (which may be observed).
At that time, the great assembly made offerings to the Tathāgata with various kinds of objects.
Having made offerings to the Buddha, they immediately resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
At that time, the World-Honored One [proceeds with] the second part: the Tathāgata’s conclusion, which further consists of three sections: first, the bestowal of prophecy; second, the entrustment;
and third, the manifestation of illness. (The old translation states that from the section on entrustment onwards it constitutes the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness," but this is not the case here;
the manifestation of illness serves to conclude the preceding [sections], and its placement here is not problematic.)
At that time, the World-Honored One conferred the prediction of enlightenment upon Mañjuśrī, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, and Cunda.
Having bestowed these predictions, he spoke these words: "Good sons, cultivate your own minds and be careful not to be negligent.
I now suffer from a back ailment; my entire body is in pain. I wish now to lie down, just as a small child or an ordinary person does."

Regarding the patient suffering from back pain: according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in the past, when the Deer King was about to die, he waited for a later lame rabbit, enduring death for its sake;
now, the Buddha suffers back pain for the sake of Subhadra.
Mañjuśrī, you and the others should extensively expound the Great Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
Now, I entrust this Dharma to you, and it shall be further entrusted to Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and the others, until this True Dharma is thus transmitted.
At that time, having spoken these words, the Tathāgata, desiring to subdue all sentient beings,
manifested illness and lay on his right side like a sick person.
*Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle Six.
Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Seven, composed by Dharma Master Jing; revised by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhànrán.
The Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Eighteen: Manifesting Illness.
Chapter 18: Manifesting Illness, titled "The Eighteen Adornments," is the second cycle.
Emperor Wu of Liang praised this as being superior to the later response of Kaishan, which sought to transcend all illness, and the earlier response of Xinghuang, which maintained both.
Although the former has already provided its answer, what prevents it from further explaining? Although the latter provides a further explanation, what prevents it from answering the former?
Regarding the Master’s two perspectives: looking forward constitutes the conclusion of the previous response, while looking backward constitutes the arising of the five practices.

Although these two perspectives exist—with the former being lateral and the latter being primary—neither is the case here. From this chapter onward, this is the third [section], the practice of Nirvana.
Its text is twofold: first, it clarifies the cultivation of the five practices; second, it clarifies the realization of the ten [perfections].

The first section of this chapter on virtue consists of five parts: 1) the practice of illness, 2) the practice of the sages, 3) the Brahma-practice, 4) the celestial practice, and 5) the infant-like practice.
Now, the first practice is explained; because the title of the chapter is derived from this, it is called the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" (*Vyādhi-saṃdarśana-parivarta*).

However, while the chapter title speaks of manifesting illness, the text itself describes being free from illness. How is this to be understood? It is because at the end of the preceding chapter, the bestowal of prophecies and the entrustment of the teaching have already been concluded.
He then said, "I now have a backache; my entire body aches like that of a small child or one who is chronically ill.

For this reason, the chapter is titled "Manifesting Illness" (*Vyādhi-saṃdarśana-parivarta*). Because he manifested this illness, there arose three instances of refusal and three instances of entreaty, clarifying that the Tathāgata was not ill.
According to the text, this consists of four parts: first, the refusal and entreaty; second, the manifestation of the signs of illness; third, the great assembly... [text continues].
The offering to the Four [Buddhas] extensively clarifies the beginning of freedom from illness. First, there are three instances of deferring and three instances of requesting:

one request for the preaching of the Dharma, two requests to cease harmful pride, and three dual requests for two matters. Regarding the three deferrals: the first deferral concerns one's own practice, the second concerns transforming others, and the third concerns realizing the fruit.
These three pairs alternate, each beginning with a deferral followed by a request, thus forming three sections; when expanded, they become six.

In the first part of the sixth chapter, the argument is advanced from the perspective of his own practice: since the Buddha has fully perfected all myriad practices and eliminated all suffering, how could he possibly have illness?

Next, the argument is advanced from the perspective of transforming others: having completed his own practice and perfected his merit in transforming others, he is able to sever the diseases of the three poisons in sentient beings;
how could he possibly have illness? Third, the argument is advanced from the perspective of the realization of the fruit: the Buddha’s ground is complete and his omniscience is perfect.
The present state is profoundly tranquil and eternally abiding; how could there be illness? To investigate this, the text on one's own practice is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the absence of causes for illness; second, clarifying the presence or absence of causes for illness.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has already been freed from all suffering and affliction of illness."
"Except for those who are free from fear, World-Honored One, all sentient beings have four poisonous arrows which constitute the causes of illness.
What are these four? They are greed, hatred, delusion, and pride.
When there is a cause of illness, then illness arises—namely, chills and fevers, lung disease, shortness of breath, vomiting, skin eruptions, mental agitation and confusion, diarrhea, and hiccups."

Drooling from the throat, dysuria, pain in the eyes and ears, distension of the abdomen and back, insanity, emaciation, and possession by malevolent spirits—such various diseases of body and mind as these no longer exist at all for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
For what reason does the Tathāgata today look upon Mañjuśrī and speak these words: "I now have a backache; you should [attend to me]"?
He preached the Dharma for the great assembly.

He specifically mentions the four parts because they encompass both the views and the afflictions; whereas the five views and doubt are specifically categorized under the vision of the truths (*darśana-mārga*).
As for the causes and conditions, the Buddha certainly possesses none of these.
There are two causes and conditions for pushing down the presence or absence of illness.
There are two causes and conditions by which there is no suffering of illness; what are these two? First, to have compassion for all sentient beings;
second, to provide the sick with medicine. In the past, throughout immeasurable tens of billions of kalpas, the Tathāgata...
While practicing the bodhisattva path, you have always employed kind speech to benefit sentient beings and never allowed them to suffer;
you have bestowed various medicines upon those who were ill. For what reason do you now say that you yourself are sick?

Compassion is the internal giving, while bestowing gifts is the external relinquishing. Saving from within and aiding from without to eliminate all suffering and affliction is the cause of being free from illness;
this has been concluded above.

Next, from the passage "World-Honored One, people of the world have illnesses" onwards is the text requesting the teaching of the Dharma, which consists of four parts: first, the request for instruction regarding the disciples.
The second [request] is to please expound upon the Mahāyāna; the third is to request instruction on non-retrogression, which is the cultivation of good;

the fourth is to request the subduing of evil persons, which is the eradication of evil. These are evident in the text, and they likewise correspond to the four *siddhārtha* (purposes) of the Buddha’s teaching.
"World-Honored One, when people in the world are ill, they may sit or lie down, finding no peace in their place,
and they may even request food and drink while instructing their families to manage their household affairs and industries. Why does the Tathāgata lie in silence without teaching his disciples,
the śrāvakas, the perfection of morality (śīlapāramitā), the various dhyānas, liberations (vimokṣa), samāpattis, and the practice of right exertion (samyakpradhāna)?"
For what reason do you not speak such profound Mahāyāna sūtras?
For what reason do you not employ immeasurable skillful means to instruct Mahākāśyapa, the elephant-king among men, and other great beings,
so as to cause them not to regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"Why do you not discipline those wicked bhikṣus who accept and store all kinds of impure things? The World-Honored One is truly not ill;
why do you lie silently on your right side?"

Next, the passage beginning with "The various bodhisattvas, etc. is the section that dedicates the merit to transforming others. It is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the transformation of others to eliminate the three obstacles;

second, clarifying the transformation of others along with the making of vows. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the presentation of the three obstacles; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. The initial presentation is as follows.
Whatever roots of goodness the bodhisattvas obtain from providing medicine and medical care to the sick,

they bestow all upon sentient beings and collectively dedicate them toward omniscience (sarvākārajñatā), in order to eliminate the afflictive obstructions, karmic obstructions, and retributive obstructions of sentient beings.
Next, in the explanation, there are again three parts. First, regarding the explanation of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*):

the afflictive hindrance consists of greed, hatred, delusion, anger, the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), distress, envy, stinginess, guile, flattery, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), self-pride (*asmimāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
Pride, arrogance, negligence, haughtiness, resentment, litigation, wrong livelihood, flattery, hypocrisy, feigning extraordinary signs to seek profit through profit,
evil seeking, excessive seeking, lack of reverence, failure to follow instruction, associating with evil friends, insatiable greed for gain,
being bound by fetters difficult to untie, desire for what is evil, craving for what is evil, the view of a self-body, and the view of existence.
Furthermore, having views of non-existence; yawning, drowsiness, and lethargy; lack of joy; craving for food and drink; a mind that is dull and clouded;
mental engagement with diverse signs and unwholesome reflection; abundance of evil in body and speech; delighting in much talk; dullness of the faculties; speaking much that is false;
and being constantly shrouded by thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harm—these are called afflictions (*kleśa*).
Obstructions.

A fourfold analysis [of these] distinguishes between those that are beneficial but not deep, those that are both deep and beneficial, those that are deep but not beneficial, and those that are neither deep nor beneficial.

Those that arise repeatedly and obstruct the cultivation of the path are called afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Those that are deep but not beneficial, or neither deep nor beneficial, do not arise repeatedly; although they are... [they are not afflictive obstructions].

While they are afflictions (*kleśa*), they are not specifically termed "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*); in general discourse, all four categories of the fourfold classification are afflictions, but this is because of such specific distinctions.
Regarding the seven types of pride (*māna*), as the text states, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* establishes eight by including "great pride" (*abhimāna*).

However, this text is concise. According to Hexi, there are nine types of pride: namely, small, medium, and great; and medium, medium, and great. This is because the single category of "small, medium, and great" pride is divided into two: the self-pride [of small, medium, and great] and [the pride of others].

Relying on the fact that one’s own understanding is superior to that of others who are small and foolish, one is constantly arrogant toward those who are inferior; this is *māna* (pride). Regarding those who are equal, to think "I am equal to them" is also *māna*.
To think "I am superior to them" is *atimāna* (excessive pride). To think that one’s own wisdom and understanding surpass all people and that no one can equal it is *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride).
To think that those who are equal are actually inferior is *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am"). To think that those who are mostly inferior are actually equal is *abhimāna* (conceit).

To say "I am slightly inferior" when one is actually vastly different is the conceit of self-importance (*māna*); to view the five aggregates as the self and to be attached to what belongs to the self is the conceit based on error (*mithyāmāna*);
and to consider oneself to possess accomplishments when one actually has none is [the conceit of overestimation].
Regarding "karmic obstacles" (*karmāvaraṇa*): they are the grave and evil diseases of the five *ānantarya* sins. Next, to explain "karmic obstacles":
there are four definitive types of karma that can obstruct the first fruit; the karmic obstacles of the desire realm definitively obstruct the third fruit;
and the karmic obstacles of the form and formless realms definitively obstruct the fourth fruit. Among these, [it refers to] the grave and evil...
Illness is indeed an obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*); how then can it be explained as an obstacle of karma? There are two traditional interpretations:

first, that illness resulting from grave evil is truly an obstacle of retribution, yet it is explained as an obstacle of karma because the effect is described by means of its cause; second, that the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*) are like a malignant illness, and this [illness] is used as a metaphor for them.
Regarding the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*): being born in the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts; slandering the True Dharma;

and being an icchantika—these are called the obstacle of retribution. Three explanations of the obstacle of retribution state: "How does slandering the Dharma and being an icchantika relate to the obstacle of retribution? There are also two interpretations: first, [it refers to] being born...
In the case of the icchantikas who slander the Dharma, is it not true that they possess both [types of obstacles]? Second, it is said that evil persons possess two:
first, evil karma, and second, the retribution for evil. Thus, the sparrow’s desire and the snake’s anger are both results of prior karma.
These three obstructions are called the great diseases; yet when Bodhisattvas cultivate bodhi over immeasurable eons, providing all medicines for the sick, they constantly make this vow:
"May all sentient beings forever sever these three obstructions, which are like grave illnesses."
Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates awakening, he provides medicine to all who are ill and constantly makes this vow:
"May all sentient beings forever sever all illnesses and attain the adamantine body of a Tathāgata;
may all immeasurable sentient beings become sovereigns of wondrous medicine and eliminate all evil and heavy [karmic] burdens."
I pray that all sentient beings may obtain the *agada* medicine; by the power of this medicine, they may eliminate all immeasurable and evil poisons.

Furthermore, I pray that sentient beings shall never retreat from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, swiftly attaining the supreme Buddha-medicine to eliminate all poisonous arrows of affliction (*kleśa*). Moreover, I pray that sentient beings...
Diligently cultivating vigor, they achieve the Tathāgata’s adamantine mind and act as subtle medicines to treat all illnesses, ensuring that no one gives rise to thoughts of contention or dispute.
They also vow that sentient beings shall become great medicinal trees to cure all manner of evil and grave diseases;
furthermore, they vow that sentient beings shall extract the poisonous arrows [of affliction] and attain the unsurpassed radiance of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, he made this vow: "May all sentient beings enter the Tathāgata’s great medicinal and profound Dharma-treasury of wisdom.

World-Honored One, since the Bodhisattva has thus made such vows throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, causing all sentient beings to be entirely free from illness, for what reason does the Tathāgata now proclaim that he is ill?
Furthermore, the section beginning with "Moreover, World-Honored One" consists of two parts: first, the text requesting the removal of the evil pride of fools;
second, [the request] beginning with "Moreover, World-Honored One, there are those who are ill and cannot sit or rise, look up or down, move forward or back, or consume food and drink."
Just as one who cannot swallow even water-gruel is likewise unable to instruct his sons or manage the affairs of the household,
so too at that time did the parents, wife, children, brothers, kinsmen, and acquaintances all conceive the thought that this man was surely dead; they said, "The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata,
is likewise today lying on his right side, saying nothing at all to anyone in this Jambudvīpa."

Foolish people should not entertain such thoughts as that the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, will certainly enter parinirvāṇa, giving rise to the notion that his birth and death have been exhausted;
for the nature of the Tathāgata does not ultimately enter parinirvāṇa. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and immutable.
For these reasons, one should not say, "I now suffer from back pain."
Seeing the Buddha manifest illness, he conceived the thought that he would surely die;
later, he was asked to cease his pride as a non-Buddhist.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, there are those in the world who are ill, their bodies emaciated and weakened, lying prostrate or on their sides upon beds and mats.
At that time, the people in the assembly will give rise to feelings of contempt and loathing, conceiving the thought that the Tathāgata is surely about to die;
they will likewise think that he is now being treated with such slight by the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths, giving rise to the notion of his impermanence.
Those non-Buddhists will say: "He is not like us, for we [rely on] the principles of the primal nature (ātman), the person (puruṣa), the Lord (īśvara), time (kāla), or atoms (paramāṇu)."
Yet you, Śramaṇa Gautama, claim to be eternally abiding and subject to no change; yet you are carried away by impermanence and are subject to the law of transformation.
For this reason, World-Honored One, you should not today remain silent while lying on your right side.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover, World-Honored One" below is an inference [of the Buddha's state], proving that his physical strength is fully perfected; how could he possibly have illness?
Moreover, there are two parts: first, it clarifies his physical strength, and next, it clarifies his wisdom-power.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, there are those among the world who are ill, whose four great elements are increased or diminished and thus lack mutual harmony;

they become emaciated and utterly exhausted, such that they cannot sit, rise, or lie down as they wish, but must remain upon their beds and mats. The Tathāgata’s four great elements are never disharmonious;
his physical strength is complete and he suffers no emaciation or decline. World-Honored One, the strength of ten young oxen does not equal that of one large bull.
The strength of ten great oxen is not equal to the strength of one blue ox; the strength of ten blue oxen is not equal to the strength of one ordinary elephant;
the strength of ten ordinary elephants is not equal to the strength of one wild elephant; the strength of ten wild elephants is not equal to the strength of one two-tusked elephant;

the strength of twelve two-tusked elephants is not equal to the strength of one four-tusked elephant; the strength of fourteen four-tusked elephants is not equal to... [the strength of one six-tusked elephant].
The strength of ten white elephants of the Snowy Mountains is not equal to the strength of one fragrant elephant;

the strength of ten fragrant elephants is not equal to the strength of one blue elephant; the strength of ten blue elephants is not equal to the strength of one yellow elephant; the strength of ten yellow elephants is not equal to the strength of one red elephant;
the strength of ten red elephants is not equal to the strength of one white elephant. Ten [white elephants]... [is not equal to the strength of one... white elephant.
The strength of a white elephant is not equal to that of one mountain-elephant; the strength of ten mountain-elephants is not equal to that of one utpala-elephant;
the strength of ten utpala-elephants is not equal to that of one kumuda-elephant; the strength of ten kumuda-elephants is not equal to that of one puṇḍarīka-elephant;
and the strength of ten puṇḍarīka-elephants is not equal to that of a single human being.

The strength of ten ordinary strongmen is not equal to the strength of one *pāṭaliputra* strongman; the strength of ten *pāṭaliputra* strongmen is not equal to the strength of one eight-armed Nārāyaṇa;
the strength of ten Nārāyaṇas is not equal to the strength of a single joint of a Bodhisattva at the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
In the body of an ordinary person, the joints do not reach one another, whereas in the joints of a human strongman, the heads of the joints touch one another.
In the body of Pāṭaliputra, the joints of the limbs are joined together; in the body of Nārāyaṇa, the heads of the joints are hooked together;
in the bodies of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, the bones of the joints are intertwined like coiled dragons. For this reason, the power of the Bodhisattva is the greatest.
In the initial section on physical strength, various types of elephants such as the *utpala* and others are extensively cited for comparison. Regarding these elephants:
their color is blue, while the *puṇḍarīka* is red; secondly, it is said that when these elephants walk, there are flowers beneath their feet like the *utpala*, and they are thus named after them.
The "White Elephant Walking upon Lotus Flowers" mentioned by Daṇḍin is precisely the evidence for this. Furthermore, it is said:
Because *utpala* flowers grow upon its fangs when thunder roars, it is named accordingly; other instances may be inferred by this analogy.
*Bhṛṅgīti* is translated as "Firm" (*kang-ku*), and *Nārāyaṇa* is translated as "Vajra" (*jin-gang*).
When the world is formed, from the adamantine foundation up to the seat of adamant upon which the Bodhisattva sits beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment,
as soon as he has taken his seat, his mind immediately attains the ten powers.
Regarding the three [points] below, "The Tathāgata now... and so forth, these constitute a dual request for the preaching of the Dharma and the cessation of evil;
first, there is a brief formal request. "The Tathāgata now should not be like that infant child; for an infant child is foolish, lacks wisdom, and is incapable of speaking.
For this reason, he may lie down or turn over at will without anyone censuring him. The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, [should not be like this]."
A great dragon of vast wisdom who illuminates all beings, possessing great majesty and power, accomplished in supernatural faculties,
an unsurpassed seer who has forever severed the net of doubt and extracted the poisoned arrow; one whose composure in advancing and retreating is serene and whose deportment is perfect,
having attained fearlessness— for what reason does he now lie on his right side, causing all devas and humans to grieve, lament, and suffer?

The subsequent verses provide a detailed request; there are seven lines in total. The first three lines constitute the formal request, the next three lines explain the request, and the final line concludes the request.
Within the initial formal request, there are two parts: the first line requests the commencement of the teaching, and the following two lines request the removal of evil pride.
At that time, Kāśyapa spoke these verses before the Buddha: "O Gautama of great and holy virtue, please arise and expound the wondrous Dharma.
You should not remain like a child; it is not fitting for one who is ill to lie upon a bed and bedding.
[Note: Regarding the initial statement that Kāśyapa was a disciple of the Buddha, why does he here address the Buddha as "Gautama," as if he were an outsider?]
Tanyue says: Generally, when one refers to Gautama, there is always a distinction intended. For instance, whether people call out "Zhang" or "Wang" in anger or in joy, they do so;
how much more so when merely saying "Gautama"—how could this holy virtue be the same as the arrogant calling of non-Buddhists?
The Tamer of Gods and Humans lies reclining between the twin trees;

When those of inferior wisdom and commoners see this, they say he must surely enter parinirvāṇa. Not knowing the Vaipulya scriptures, nor the profound conduct of the Buddha, They do not perceive the subtle and secret treasury, like the blind who do not see the path.
Next, the explanation of the request has two parts; first, one verse explains the cessation of evil:
"Only the various Bodhisattvas, such as Mañjuśrī and others, can understand this profound [teaching], just like a skilled archer."
The next two lines explain the teaching:
The World-Honored Ones of the three periods of time take great compassion as their root.
Where, then, is such great compassion now? If there were no great compassion, one would not be called a Buddha.
If the Buddha were necessarily to enter parinirvāṇa, he would not be called "Eternal.
[The subsequent verses of the petition may be understood accordingly.
We pray only that the Unsurpassed Honored One will compassionately accept our request and bring benefit to all sentient beings.
Subduing All Non-Buddhists:
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, [manifests] the second section, "The Buddha’s Demonstration of the Sign of Freedom from Illness. This text consists of three parts:
first, the benefit of the light; second, the benefit of the lotus; and third, the benefit of the transformation Buddhas. Within these three meanings, there is...

Regarding the matter of phenomena and principle: the appearance of illness is emaciated and withered, while the appearance of health is radiant and joyful; now, the emission of brilliant light signifies the absence of illness.
The lotus flower is an auspicious omen, not a sign of illness. As for the emanated Buddha, it is created by the Tathāgata;
if it were a sick person, it would be incapable of such deeds, yet since it performs these deeds, it is not a sign of illness. This manifests the underlying principle through the light.
The flowers emerging from the body represent the Dharmakāya; their ability to contain fruit represents the Buddha of Liberation; and the [flowers] representing awakening-wisdom represent Prajñā.
Since these three virtues are fully possessed, how could there be illness? Each of the three chapters has two parts: first, the radiance, and second, the benefits.

At that time, the World-Honored One, his heart permeated by great compassion, knowing the various thoughts of all sentient beings and wishing to accord with them for their ultimate benefit, rose from his reclining position and sat cross-legged. His countenance was serene and joyful like a mass of molten gold;
his face was dignified and majestic like the full moon; his form was pure and free from all defilement, as he emitted a great radiance.

Pervading all of space, its light was exceedingly magnificent, surpassing that of a hundred thousand suns as it shone upon the Buddha-worlds of the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

Within the initial light, it says: "Those whose hearts are suffused with great compassion (mahākaruṇā)"—how could the virtues of the Buddha be merely great compassion? As stated in the preceding passage: "The virtues of the Buddha are immeasurable."
The request was made: "The great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time is the very foundation;
where is such compassion now? To answer this request, it is said that 'great compassion permeates his mind. Previously, when he emitted light, it was not stated to exceed a hundred thousand suns;
this was specifically because he manifested illness, which cannot manifest light. Here, the light emitted by great compassion permeating his body shatters all doubts."
The following clarifies the benefits for sentient beings through the gift of wisdom:

By means of the great torch of wisdom, they cause all sentient beings to extinguish the darkness of ignorance and establish hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sentient beings in the non-retrogressive resolve for bodhi.
2. At that time, the World-Honored One was free from doubt and anxiety; this section on the benefits of the lotus is also divided into two parts.
First, the identification of the lotus:
at that time, the World-Honored One was free from doubt and anxiety, like a lion king, possessing the thirty-two marks of a great man.
His body was adorned with the eighty minor marks of excellence; from every single pore upon his body there emerged a lotus flower.
These flowers were exquisite, each possessing a thousand petals of pure, true golden color, with stems of lapis lazuli, filaments of diamond, and calyxes of ruby.
They were perfectly round in shape, like chariot wheels; such were these lotus flowers.
Each emitted various multicolored rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and crystal-colored.
Next, these rays of light descended to provide benefit.
These rays of light all reached everywhere throughout the Avīci Hell, the Saṃjīva Hell, and the Kālasūtra Hell.
The Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci hells—within these eight hells, sentient beings are constantly tormented by various sufferings, namely:
being burned, boiled, roasted by fire, hacked, pierced, sliced, and flayed. Upon encountering this light, all such sufferings are extinguished without remainder, and they find peace.
Secluded in coolness and bliss beyond measure, within this radiance he proclaimed the secret treasury of the Tathāgata, saying:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Upon hearing this, sentient beings immediately passed away and were reborn among humans and devas, or even in the eight cold hells, namely:
the Avīci hell, the Atata hell, the Hahava hell... [and so forth].
In the Raurava hell, the Arbuda hell, the Utpala hell, the Padma hell,
the Kumuda hell, and the Puṇḍarīka hell, sentient beings are constantly tormented by the suffering of cold—
namely, having their bodies split open, shattered, and torn apart, and harming one another; yet, upon encountering this light, all such [sufferings] cease.
When suffering is also extinguished without remainder, one immediately attains harmony, warmth, and physical comfort.
Within this light, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata is also proclaimed, stating that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Upon hearing this, those beings immediately pass away and are reborn among humans or devas. At that time, throughout this Jambudvīpa and all other worlds, upon every ground...
The hells were all entirely empty and void, with no beings remaining to undergo punishment, except for those icchantikas and hungry ghosts who were oppressed by hunger and thirst;
with their bodies bound by their own hair, they had not heard the name of even water or broth for hundreds of thousands of years.

Upon encountering this light, their hunger and thirst were immediately stilled. Within this light, it was also proclaimed that the Tathāgata possesses a subtle, secret, and hidden treasury, and that he speaks to all sentient beings.

All living beings possess the Buddha-nature; having heard this, sentient beings immediately pass away and are reborn among devas and humans, causing the realm of hungry ghosts to become entirely empty.

With the exception of those who slander the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, the sentient beings of the animal realm—who previously killed one another and preyed upon each other—have their hearts of anger completely extinguished upon encountering this light. Within this radiance, it is also preached as follows:
This is the treasury of secrets, which states that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Upon hearing this, those beings immediately pass away and are reborn among humans or devas;
at that time, even animals will cease to exist, with the sole exception of those who slander the True Dharma.
Wherever there is an abundance of flowers, it pervades the three miserable realms; that they appear so profusely clearly signifies liberation. Regarding the eight cold hells:
the first four derive from sound, while the latter four derive from form. When a sinner first enters and sees this flower pond, they give rise to craving and immediately go toward it;
thus they receive their name. Alternatively, it is said that these are merely the forms of the hell itself, appearing like the four types of flowers when split open.
The character "zi" (字) should be read as "pīliè" (劈裂; pǔjì fǎn).
Thirdly, the transformation Buddhas who benefit [beings] beneath each individual flower also constitute two [aspects], as previously explained (*etc.*).
Upon each of these flowers sits a Buddha, with a halo extending one fathom, his golden body radiant, subtle, and most exquisite in its majesty;
incomparably supreme, his form is adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs.
Among these World-Honored Ones, some are seated, some are walking, some are reclining, some are standing, and some are emitting the sound of thunder.
Some pour down torrential rain, some discharge flashes of lightning, some fan great winds, or emit smoke and flames from their bodies like a mass of fire;
some manifest various mountains of the seven treasures, ponds, springs, rivers, forests, and trees;
or again, they manifest lands of the seven treasures, cities, towns, villages, palaces, and dwellings; or again, they manifest elephants, horses, lions, and tigers.
He may manifest as wolves, peacocks, phoenixes, or various other birds;
or he may manifest so that all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa see the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; or he may manifest the six heavens of the desire realm.

Furthermore, there are World-Honored Ones who speak of the many faults and afflictions of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; or there are those who speak of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; or again, there are others...
Some speak of the causes and conditions of all phenomena; others say that all karma and afflictions are born of causes and conditions;
others speak of self and non-self; others speak of the two dharmas of suffering and pleasure; others speak of the eternal and the impermanent, and so forth;
others speak of the pure and the impure; and furthermore, there are those for whom the World-Honored One has expounded the teachings for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
There are those who speak of the practice of the six pāramitās; or again, there are those who speak of the merits attained by the great bodhisattvas;
or again, there are those who speak of the merits attained by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; or again, there are those who speak of the merits attained by the śrāvakas;
or again, there are those who speak of conforming to the One Vehicle (ekayāna); or again, there are those who speak of attaining the Way through the Three Vehicles; or there are those in the world...
The Honored One emits water from his left side and fire from his right side;
or he manifests his initial birth, his renunciation, his sitting beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment, his turning of the wondrous Wheel of Dharma, and his entry into Nirvana.

Or there are World-Honored Ones who let out a lion’s roar, causing those within this assembly to attain the first fruit, the second fruit, the third fruit, or even the fourth fruit; or again, there are others.
