He spoke of the immeasurable causes and conditions for transcending birth and death.
At that time, all sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa who encountered this light had their blindness cured so they could see forms,
their deafness cured so they could hear sounds, the mute were able to speak, the lame were able to walk, the poor obtained wealth, and the stingy became capable of giving.

Those who harbor anger shall develop a mind of loving-kindness; those who lack faith shall gain faith. In such a world, there is not a single sentient being who practices unwholesome dharmas, with the sole exception of the icchantikas.
At that time, all the devas and nāgas—this refers to the third great assembly’s offering and exhortation—the intent of which is as follows:
The one previously mentioned, who was lying ill and feared he might enter nirvana immediately, now sees these signs of light and knows that [the Buddha] has not yet entered extinction;
for this reason, he requests the Dharma, first making offerings and then making his request.
At that time, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras...
The mahoragas, rākṣasas, kinnaras, ugradhanvas, apasmāras, humans, non-humans, and others all raised their voices in unison, crying out these words:
"Excellent, excellent! O Unsurpassed World-Honored One, you bring benefit to many!
Having spoken these words, they leaped for joy and rejoiced; some sang, some danced, and some moved their bodies as they scattered various kinds of flowers.
The Buddha and the Sangha are like the celestial flowers: the utpala, kumuda, padma,
puṇḍarīka, māndārava, mahāmāndārava, mañjūṣaka, mahāmañjūṣaka, saṃtāna, mahāsaṃtāna, rocanā, and mahārocanā.
They scattered various flowers— namely, *puṣpa*, *mahāpuṣpa*, *manojñapuṣpa*, *mahāmanojñapuṣpa*, *priyadarśanapuṣpa*, *mahāpriyadarśanapuṣpa*, *abhirūpapuṣpa*,
and *paramābhirūpapuṣpa*— as well as various fragrances, such as agallochum, *tagara*, sandalwood,
*kunkuma*, blended incenses, and coastal resin incense. They further offered celestial jeweled banners and pennants.
Indeed, the various celestial musicians offered instruments such as the *kṣīra*, flute, reed pipe, lute, harp, and drum to make offerings to the Buddha.
Regarding the first passage, it states: *khandha*—the Hexi [translation] says this is a "one-shouldered ghost" who causes pain in the shoulder;
*ummadā* is a ghost that can cause intoxication; *apasmāra* is a ghost that causes madness.

Regarding the second [section], the verses that follow are the *adhyeṣaṇā* (exhortation). These fifteen lines, together with a short prose passage, are divided into two parts: first, fourteen lines of the actual exhortation;
second, one line and the subsequent prose passage where the sūtra-narrator recounts the events. The first part has three sections: first, two lines indicating the exhortation;
second, ten lines explaining the exhortation; third, two lines concluding the exhortation. The first [section] is as stated in the text.
And he spoke these verses:

I now bow my head in homage to the Greatly Diligent One, The Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One, the Honored One among bipeds, Whom the multitudes of devas and humans do not know; Only Gautama is able to comprehend him.
Next, the ten lines constitute the first of five sections on the initial vow; thus he entreats:
"World-Honored One, for my sake in the past, You practiced asceticism through immeasurable kalpas.
How could you now suddenly abandon your original vow, And pass away into parinirvāṇa?"
Next, because they fall into evil states, I entreat you:
all sentient beings are unable to see the secret treasury of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
for this reason, it is difficult for them to escape, as they cycle through birth and death and fall into the evil paths.
Because those of inferior and ignorant minds do not understand, they request [this teaching].
As the Buddha has said: "All Arhats shall surely attain Nirvana.
Yet, regarding such a profoundly deep sphere of the Buddha's activity, who among ordinary people of inferior and ignorant minds could know it?
I entreat you because you bestow the Dharma of ambrosia.
You bestow the ambrosial Dharma upon all sentient beings in order to sever their various afflictions;
if one has partaken of this ambrosia, one will no longer undergo birth, aging, sickness, or death.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has been invited for the purpose of healing; he employs his treatment to cure hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sentient beings,
causing all their various grave illnesses to be completely extinguished without remainder.
Next, perform the ritual of invitation as prescribed in the text:
The World-Honored One has long since abandoned the suffering of illness; Thus he is named the Seventh Buddha.
I pray that today you will rain down the rain of Dharma, To moisten and nourish the seeds of our merit.
Second, from "the great assembly" onwards, the narrator of the sutra describes the events in two parts: first, having made their request, they remained silent;
then, after the great assembly—including humans and devas—had thus requested and remained in silence, the sound of the subsequent request reached [the Buddha].
When these verses were spoken, all the Buddhas within the lotus pedestals—from Jambudvīpa throughout as far as the Śuddhāvāsa heavens—all heard them.

As for those who reach the Śuddhāvāsa, it is because at the Peak of Form (Rūpāvacara) there are physical forms and auditory consciousness; it is not so in the Formless Realm (Arūpyadhātu), and therefore [the sound] does not reach there.

In that *Nidāna-parivarta*, it says: "The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)... and so forth; by analogy with the Worldly Gods (*laukika-deva*), the Heaven of Birth (*upapatti-deva*), and the Heaven of Purity (*śuddhāvāsa-deva*), one should say:
"born in the Pure Abodes," "untainted Pure Abodes," and "the ultimate Pure Abodes," and so forth.

At that time, the Buddha told [the assembly] the fourth section of the lower grade, which extensively explains freedom from illness. This is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying that the Tathāgata is free from illness;

second, contrasting this with the practice of illness. The first part is further divided into three sections: first, clarifying freedom from illness; second, citing past instances as proof for the present;
third, explaining that manifesting illness is a skillful means and esoteric teaching.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have already perfected such profound and subtle wisdom, remaining unshakable by any demons or non-Buddhists.
Son of good family, you have already established yourself securely, remaining unmoved by any winds of evil."
"Son, you have already accomplished the eloquence of joyful speech; you have previously made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Therefore, you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, about such a meaning."
This first section praises Kāśyapa; as he was the foremost among those who requested [the teaching], he is thus praised.

"Excellent" is the general praise, while the four lines that follow are the specific praise. This praise concerns both attainment and renunciation: renouncing external adverse conditions and internal unwholesome causes, one attains internal wholesome causes and external wholesome conditions.
"Second, 'Good sons, in the past... and so forth, clarifies that I have long been free from this illness.

Good sons, in the past, across immeasurable, boundless billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, I have already removed the root of illness and am forever free from reclining or lying down. Kāśyapa, immeasurable asankhyeya kalpas ago, there appeared a Buddha in the world."
At that time, the World-Honored One— the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-sampanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha— preached for the sake of the śrāvakas this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
revealing, analyzing, and elucidating its meaning; at that time, I was also among them.
If a Buddha acts as a śrāvaka and upholds such a Mahāparinirvāṇa sūtra as this— reading, reciting, mastering it, copying the scrolls,
and extensively revealing, analyzing, and explaining its meaning to others—
and dedicates these roots of goodness toward anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, then, son of good family, from that time forth, I have never again experienced evil afflictions.
Due to the karmic conditions of affliction, one falls into the evil realms, slanders the True Dharma, becomes an icchantika, receives the body of a eunuch, or possesses no genitals or dual genitals;
one commits treason against one’s parents, kills an arhat, destroys stupas, disrupts the Sangha, sheds the blood of a Buddha, or violates the four grave prohibitions.
From that time forward, my body and mind have been peaceful and secure, free from all suffering and affliction. Kāśyapa, I am now truly...
There are no diseases whatsoever. Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have long since distanced themselves from all illness.
Kāśyapa, these sentient beings do not understand the esoteric language of the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, and thus they claim that the Tathāgata truly has an illness.
"Those of the past, immeasurable in number" refers to citing the past to substantiate the present.
Regarding the three points beginning with "As the Tathāgata spoke," the subsequent manifestation of illness is a skillful, esoteric teaching;
in total there are twelve such matters of esoteric teaching, of which the first eleven cite analogous cases.
Kāśyapa, as it is said that the Tathāgata is a lion among men, yet the Tathāgata is truly not a lion—such words are the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa, as it is said that the Tathāgata is a great dragon among men, I have already abandoned such karma throughout immeasurable eons. Kāśyapa, as it is said that the Tathāgata is a human being...
I am not a deva; I am truly neither a human nor a deva, nor am I a ghost (preta), a gandharva, an asura, a garuḍa, a kiṃnara, or a mahoraga.
I am not a self (ātman), not a life-principle (jīva), not a nourisher (poṣa), not a person (pudgala), not a man (manuja), nor a human being (mānava).
I am not an agent, nor a non-agent; I am not one who experiences, nor one who does not experience; I am not a World-Honored One (Bhagavat), nor a śrāvaka, nor a teacher.
It is not that such statements as these are not all the Tathāgata’s secret teachings.
Kāśyapa, when it is said that the Tathāgata is like the great ocean or King Sumeru, one should know that this statement is also the Tathāgata’s secret teaching;
for the Tathāgata is in truth not salty and is not like a mountain of stone. Kāśyapa, when it is said that the Tathāgata is like...
"Kāśyapa, when it is said, 'I am a *puṇḍarīka*,' yet I am in truth not a *puṇḍarīka*, such words are the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.

Kāśyapa, when it is said that the Tathāgata is like parents, yet the Tathāgata is in truth not parents, such words are also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata. Kāśyapa, when it is said that the Tathāgata is..."
“Kāśyapa, when it is said that the Tathāgata is a great captain, the Tathāgata is in fact not a captain;
such words are also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata. Kāśyapa, when it is said that the Tathāgata is like a merchant leader, the Tathāgata is in fact not a merchant leader;
such words are also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata. Kāśyapa, when it is said that the Tathāgata is able...”
"Kāśyapa, when it is said that 'the Tathāgata subdues Māra,' the Tathāgata has no evil intent to cause others to submit;
such words are all the secret teachings of the Tathāgata. Kāśyapa, when it is said that 'the Tathāgata can treat abscesses,' I am in truth not a physician who treats abscesses;
such words are also the secret teachings of the Tathāgata. Kāśyapa... [as before].
I have previously said that if a son of good family or a daughter of good family is well able to cultivate and purify the actions of body,
speech, and mind, then at the time of death, even though their kinsmen may take their remains— whether by cremating them with fire, casting them into great waters,
or abandoning them among the graves where foxes, wolves, birds, and beasts compete to devour them— their mind, consciousness, and intellect will immediately be reborn in a good realm.
This mental dharma truly has no coming or going, nor does it go anywhere; it is simply a continuity of similar states before and after, with no difference in appearance.
Such words as these are the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
The last matter should have been free from illness.
Kāśyapa, my current statement regarding illness is likewise so; it is also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, in his final charge, he entrusted Mañjuśrī, saying: "I now suffer from back pain; you all should preach the Dharma for the fourfold assembly. Kāśyapa.
The Tathāgata, the Truly Enlightened One, is in fact free from illness; he does not lie on his right side, nor does he enter final nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa, this Great Nirvāṇa is the profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of all Buddhas.
Such meditative concentration is not the domain of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Kāśyapa, as to what you asked above—why the Tathāgata leans and lies down without rising—the answer is as follows.
He does not seek food or drink, nor does he instruct his family to cultivate their livelihoods;
Kāśyapa, the nature of space likewise has no sitting or rising, no seeking of food or drink, and no instruction to family members to cultivate their livelihoods.

It is without coming or going, birth or death, old age or vigor, appearance or disappearance, injury or liberation, and neither bondage nor release. It speaks neither of itself nor of others, nor does it...
Being liberated oneself and not liberating others is neither peace nor health, O son of good family;
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are likewise like space—how could they possibly have any suffering from illness?
Kāśyapa, in the world there are three types of people; this is the second [category] cited: those who have illness contrasted with those who are without illness.

Such persons may indeed have illness, but the Buddha is not like this—how could he possibly have illness? Furthermore, there are two [parts]: first, clarifying the three types of sick people; second, clarifying the five types of sick people.
Among these, the three types of sick people differ from the previous three types of people. As for the previous three types of people: [text continues].
The first three individuals do not differ; they differ in their transgressions. The first are those who commit the three types of offenses;

next are those of the Two Vehicles on the Lesser Path; and third are the Bodhisattvas who have heard the sutra. Regarding the first [category], there are the dharma, the parable, and the synthesis; for the latter two, both the parables and the syntheses are present.
Kāśyapa, in this world there are three types of illnesses that are difficult to cure: first, slandering the Mahāyāna; second, committing the five heinous crimes;
and third, being an icchantika. These three illnesses are the most grave in the world and cannot be cured by either śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Good son, it is like a disease that is inevitably fatal and beyond cure:

if there is a caregiver who provides medicine as desired, or if there is no caregiver and no medicine as desired, such a disease is certainly incurable; you should know that this person will surely die without doubt.

These three kinds of people are likewise so: whether they are śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas, and whether they preach the Dharma or do not preach it, they are unable to cause them to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa, it is like a sick person: if they have a caregiver and medicine according to their needs, they can be cured;
yet without these three, they cannot be cured.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are also like this: having heard the Dharma from Buddhas and bodhisattvas, they are immediately able to generate [the aspiration for enlightenment].
“Kāśyapa, the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi cannot be generated without hearing the Dharma.
It is like a sick person: whether they have a caregiver who provides medicine as desired, or they lack a caregiver who provides medicine as desired, both can be cured.”
There is a certain kind of person who is likewise: they may encounter a śrāvaka or not encounter a śrāvaka; they may encounter a pratyekabuddha or not encounter a pratyekabuddha;
they may encounter a bodhisattva or not encounter a bodhisattva; they may encounter a Tathāgata or not encounter a Tathāgata;
they may hear the Dharma or not hear the Dharma, yet they will naturally achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
It is said that there may be someone who, whether for their own sake, for the sake of others,
out of fear, for the sake of gain, out of flattery, or to deceive others, writes down this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, receives it, upholds it, reads it, recites it,
makes offerings to it, honors it, and explains it to others.
The third person is described as one who, for the sake of flattery and gain, deceives others by upholding this scripture; this differs significantly from the previous case.
It is better not to receive, uphold, or use it than to do so while violating the precepts and reciting it—this is the intended meaning of "giving and taking.

First, three types of incurable patients are listed; these are the three cases where [the use of the scripture] is permitted for those who are incurable, whereas for those who are curable, it is not yet permitted.

Regarding the "differences," these refer to the six matters such as fear and gain which were previously set forth; when combined with the thirty types concerning the five Dharma-preachers, they total thirty-six.
Furthermore, five types of illnesses are subsequently added, bringing the total for all individuals to thirty-eight types (and so forth).
Kāśyapa, there are five types of persons who, though currently at a lower level, will eventually attain the higher state. Second, regarding the sick person:
Kāśyapa, there are five types of persons within this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa scripture who possess a "sickness" in their practice;
they are not yet Tathāgatas. What are these five? First, one who has severed the three fetters and attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, who does not fall into the realms of hell or animals.

Having been born seven times among hungry ghosts, humans, and devas, they will forever sever all suffering and enter nirvāṇa. Kāśyapa, this is called the first type of person who dwells in the realm of illness;
such a person, after eighty thousand kalpas have passed in the future, shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa, as for the second type of person: they have severed the three fetters and attenuated greed, hatred, and delusion, and have attained [the fruit of] stream-entry.
The fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin involves returning once more to sever all suffering and enter into nirvāṇa;
Kāśyapa, this is called the second stage of practice involving illness. Such a person will, after sixty thousand kalpas in the future, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa, as for the third person: having severed the fetters and the lower fetters, they attain the state of an Anāgāmin.
If one does not return to this world again, eternally severing all suffering and entering nirvana, this is called the third stage of practice involving illness.
Such a person, after the passing of forty thousand kalpas in the future, shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa, as for the fourth person, they eternally sever greed, hatred, and delusion, and attain arhatship.

When the fruits of affliction have been extinguished without remainder and one enters nirvana—yet this is not the solitary practice of a qilin—this is called the fourth person who possesses the conduct of illness;
such a person shall, after twenty thousand kalpas, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa, as for the fifth person, they have eternally severed greed, anger, and delusion, and have attained...
The path of the Pratyekabuddha, entering nirvana with no further afflictions remaining, is truly the solitary conduct of a qilin;

this is called the fifth type of person who possesses the practice of illness. Such a person, after ten thousand kalpas have passed in the future, shall attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Kāśyapa, this is called the fifth type of person who possesses the practice of illness.
The state [of illness] is not the Tathāgata.
Since it is said that one may recover if conditions are encountered, dying without encountering such conditions constitutes the fourth fruit, the Pratyekabuddha;

these individuals practice while carrying illness, and thus it is said they have a "state of practicing with illness. By analogy, a Bodhisattva on the causal stage should also be understood in this way.

Such a person may be said to have illness; when the Buddha has severed all delusions, he is no longer subject to illness. One who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) has severed the three fetters:

self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). For one who undergoes seven more rebirths among humans and devas, the number is already brief; if expanded, it is fourteen or twenty-eight.
This text states that [one attains] Bodhi after eighty thousand *kalpas*, while the following text states that one generates the mind for Bodhi after eighty thousand *kalpas*. It is necessary...
Commentary on the Exposition: Regarding the three fruits, the abandonment of the five lower fetters refers to the afflictions of the desire realm;

these are further categorized as five lower-fettering factors by adding greed, hatred, self-view, doubt, and attachment to precepts (and so forth). Arhats may appear either during the time of a Buddha or in a world where no Buddha exists;
thus, they do not represent a singular path of practice. Pratyekabuddhas, however, invariably appear only in worlds where no Buddha exists.
Named "The Practice of Solitude.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle Ten.
Translated by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Benzhun during the Dayong era. Sectioned and compiled.
Collected Commentary on the Southern Version of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Ten;
Collected Commentary on the Southern Version of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Eleven.
The Nineteenth Chapter of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra: The Holy Conduct (Āryacaryā). (Scroll Eleven)
Translated during the Northern Liang dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master from India, Dharmakṣema;
re-edited by the Śramaṇas Huiyan, Huiguan,
and Xie Lingyun of the Jin dynasty.
The "Chapter on Noble Conduct" (Ārya-caryā-varga), Part One:
An Exposition of the Sequence of Names and Branches. Regarding the sequence of what is taught and what is not taught:

the Master of Hexi explains that the preceding section, through the gates of the brief and the extensive, teaches the fruit of *nirvāṇa* via the five types of noble conduct (*pañca-ārya-caryā*), and the cause for cultivating *nirvāṇa* via the ten clusters of virtues (*daśa-guṇa-rāśi*), thereby exhorting one to practice these causes. The "Old" [commentary] states: "The sequence of what is taught and what is not taught... [as above].

Regarding the statement that "the five practices distinguish the cause and the ten virtues clarify the fruit," Kaishan claims that the five practices clarify the practice of existence while the ten virtues clarify the practice of emptiness;

however, both interpretations are incorrect. Hexi [Master Senglang] maintains that the text follows the sequence of first contemplating the fruit and then practicing the cause, and thus these meanings do not contradict one another.
Why is this? It is because the preceding section clarifies the fruit of perfect culmination, whereas the five practices herein constitute the causal steps leading toward it.
If "round" (perfect) is not of the same category [as the other causes], the meaning is not tenable.
If the five practices (*pañca-caryā*) are the cause, one should not say they are "the conduct of the Buddha," and thus name them "Noble Conduct" (*ārya-caryā*).

If the ten virtues are the fruit, then again one should not say that a bodhisattva, by practicing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, obtains these ten matters of merit. Furthermore, the five practices are not the perfect cause, and the ten virtues are not...
To claim that the ultimate fruit is not achieved through the sequential opening of the five practices of the Good (Kai-zen) is likewise incorrect.

The Holy Practice (Ārya-caryā) is the path of opening the Dharma of emptiness; the Brahma Practice (Brahma-caryā) is the cultivation of the eleven kinds of emptiness while abiding in the stage of equality; the Celestial Practice (Devatā-caryā) is the principle of the ultimate truth (paramārtha);
and the Infant Practice (Śiśu-caryā) and the Illness Practice (Vyādhi-caryā) are the esoteric words of the Tathāgata—how could they be treated as partial?
To claim that the ten virtues are the meaning of emptiness based on one's own conduct and principles is also incorrect. "Ten" is a numerical dharma;
what was previously unattainable, unheard of, and unknown, has now been heard and known. By hearing even a single phrase or half-phrase, one perceives a small measure of Buddha-nature.
Why then do you selectively rely on them as being merely the practice of emptiness? Now, to clarify the sequence, as stated above:
Having extensively explained the discourse on eating and non-eating regarding the Great Parinirvāṇa, the discussion on giving is now concluded.

Now, by means of illness, the state of non-illness is taught. There are three kinds of illness: first, that which is incurable; second, that which must be treated; and third, that which requires no treatment.

That which is incurable and that which requires no treatment both do not require a remedy; only that which requires it is treated by a remedy. Furthermore, this treatment is twofold: first, sequential; second, [simultaneous].

Taking this method without following a sequential order is called "cultivation. Because one cultivates, there is realization. Realization consists of ten merits. These merits are freedom from illness;
because one is free from illness, the physical body manifests. When the body manifests, one perceives the nature. Because one perceives the nature, its function pervades the Dharma-realm.
This function subsumes the wicked and the heterodox. Having finished subsuming the wicked and the heterodox, one entrusts [the teaching] and performs self-immolation, distributing the relics.
If we take this meaning, the sequence is well established. To explain the names in order, the text states:
"Because it is that which is practiced by the noble ones—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—it is called 'Noble Conduct' (*ārya-caryā*). This encompasses two meanings:

that which is practiced by Bodhisattvas is "gradual conduct," while that which is practiced by Buddhas is "non-gradual. Furthermore, there is yet another form of conduct, which is that of the Tathāgata.
The general explanation of the "Noble Practices" (*ārya-caryā*) has not yet clarified their specific meaning; this shall now be explained individually. Why is this?

That which is called "noble" refers to the correct practices of Bodhisattvas, which are shallow at first and deep thereafter. [In contrast,] the True does not know the Conventional, and the Conventional does not know the Middle;

being partial rather than correct, they are merely designated collectively as "noble practices" and do not constitute a distinct meaning. Furthermore, if there is one practice that is the practice of the Tathāgata, [that alone constitutes the noble practice].
Because one practice encompasses all practices and one wisdom encompasses all wisdom, it is known that "perfect practice" is termed "correct" and "holy.
Therefore, the preceding passage states: "This Mahāyāna sūtra is called the Buddha-vehicle;

such a person of the most excellent and supreme perfect faculties practices the Buddha-vehicle and cultivates the Tathāgata’s practices. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The sons of the Buddha walk the path."

The statement that "one will attain perfect enlightenment in a future life" refers precisely to this meaning. Although the scriptural text allows for two interpretations—a general one and a specific one—most people follow the general interpretation and fail to distinguish the specific intention.
Here, we follow the specific interpretation. It is called "Noble Conduct" (*ārya-caryā*). Regarding "Brahma-conduct" (*brahma-caryā*): "Brahma" means purity.

Though one engages with existence and shares in the defilements, the defilements cannot stain one; thus, the name is established based on this functional capacity. This is "Heavenly Conduct" (*deva-caryā*).
The "Infant Practitioner" (bāla-yogin) is named according to the principle of the Truths; the "Sick Practitioner" (glāna-yogin) is named according to a metaphor;

the "Tathāgata Practitioner" (tathāgata-yogin) is named according to that which is to be remedied; and the "Perfect Person Practitioner" (paripūrṇa-pudgala-yogin) is named according to the fully realized individual. The general designation "Practitioner" (yogin) refers to one who does not abide in names or practices.

Because they personally realize non-attachment and cause others to abide in non-abiding, they are called "Practitioners. The listing of the five types of practitioners is as follows: 1. The Infant Practitioner. 2. The Sick Practitioner. 3. The Tathāgata Practitioner. 4. The Perfect Person Practitioner. 5. The General Designation of Practitioner. [End of Section One]
Regarding the practice, the "Noble Practice" (ārya-caryā) is at the beginning; because it is established from the outset, it is called the "Chapter on Noble Practice.

As for the relationship between the branches and the root, some say that illness is the root and that the four [types of illness] are derived from illness—this interpretation is incorrect. They see illness as the practice, yet its text appears earlier [in the sequence], yet they claim it is the root.
This is merely following the order of the text; what does it have to do with investigating the meaning? For what reason? Because the illnesses are identical.
The other evils are merely branches and leaves; how can one take these branches and leaves as the root?
The text states that when a bodhisattva dwells in the Great Parinirvāṇa and single-mindedly cultivates the five kinds of practices, then Nirvāṇa is the root.

That which is called Nirvāṇa is precisely the Celestial Practice (*devacara*); cultivating it for oneself by relying on Nirvāṇa is called the Holy Practice (*āryacaryā*); and relying on Nirvāṇa... [the text continues].
Transforming others through skillful means is called the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*); manifesting the principle of *nirvāṇa* and advancing according to that principle is called the Deva-conduct;

transforming beings through the principle and harmonizing with them is called the Infant-conduct; and harmonizing with evil is called the Sickness-conduct. Is it not because the Deva-conduct is the foundation?
Yet, some abandon the foundation to follow the branches, claiming that all five conducts are fundamentally sickness-conduct, citing a text that says: "This is..."
Regarding the statement that among the five types of persons there are those who practice illness while only the Buddha is without illness, this interpretation is incorrect.

These five persons practice the noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*) in order to cure their own illnesses; how could they be said to "practice illness"? Only the Buddha, being without illness, is able to perform the practice of illness.
If one considers the sequence of the five practices from shallow to deep, the practice of illness would occupy the final position; however, if one discusses them as a single practice...

That is to say, regarding the five practices (*pañca-caryā*): the practice of illness is fully present within the five practices. Kāśyapa, inferring from the Buddha’s cause, his being free from illness is the holy practice (*ārya-caryā*);
inferring from the result, his being free from illness is the celestial practice (*divya-caryā*); great compassion permeating his heart is the Brahma practice (*brahma-caryā*);
being like that young child is the infant practice (*bāla-caryā*); and constantly having an ailment is the practice of illness (*vyādhi-caryā*). One.
That is to say, possessing all five names constitutes "perfect practice" (*paripūrṇa-caryā*), which is the practice of the Tathāgata; the remaining four practices are likewise so.

If one were to distinguish between the general and the specific, the practice of the devas would be considered general while the other practices would be specific. Although this explanation may be offered, it cannot be taken as absolute (and so forth).
Some masters claim that the five practices are the cause and the one practice is the fruit; is this not the case?
Yet, since both are equally termed "practices" (*caryā*), why is there a partial judgment?

Some masters say that five practices are distinct while one practice is general, and that within the "one, five, and five," there is a distinction between being bundled and dispersed. This is the nature of their principle; however, the practices themselves are not so.
The realm of the Buddhas is not something known by Śrāvakas or Bodhisattvas; the superior can bundle or disperse [the inferior], but the inferior cannot contract or expand [the superior].
Regarding the above (and so forth): in this chapter, five types of practice (*caryā*) are enumerated; three are explained while two are not. Why is this?
Because the "Heavenly Practice" (*deva-caryā*) is the foundation of all practices and the root of all sages; its significance is thus evident, and it is therefore indicated from afar.

[The author] privately maintains that within the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, from beginning to end, the matters of the Bodhisattvas—whether partial or universal, phenomenal or noumenal, as well as their practices, vows, causes, and fruits—are fully established.

It is impossible to prepare for all at once; therefore, it is better to point to the sūtras to instruct. By following these pointers, one seeks out the extensive texts, which do not exceed a single principle.
Because these are the practices of the stages from the First Abode upward, they are called "celestial practices" (*devacaryā*).

Because the practice itself is celestial, they are called "celestial practices. Because they are practiced as the conduct of the heavens, they are called "celestial practices. Because one advances by means of celestial practices, they are called "heavenly."
The practice of traveling far points toward heaven, and is thus called "heavenly practice" (*deva-caryā*). There are both general and specific aspects; reflect upon this and it will become clear.

Regarding the practice of illness (*vyādhi-caryā*), it has already been manifested previously, and the practice of the Way (*mārga-caryā*) will manifest itself later; therefore, these two are not mentioned, but only the three are taught. [The author] says privately:

"Since the two are not mentioned, it still constitutes the manifestation of the present category. If that were so, one should say that the illness [category] lacks the function of concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent. No.
The characteristics of illness were previously explained; [the Buddha] constantly fulfilled Kāśyapa’s request to explain the causes and effects of practice.

Following this, it is not otherwise, for it says: "He explains four, but does not explain one. Taking the text as it stands, there are three parts: first, the dual presentation of the five practices; second, the dual explanation of the five practices;
and third, the single conclusion regarding the five practices. Within the presentation of the sequence of practices, there are four sections; first, the presentation of the persons.
It refers to the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kāśyapa:
"Good son, there are two designations for the dharmas that serve as objects of focus, namely, the Great Parinirvāṇa."
In this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one should single-mindedly contemplate five kinds of practices.
To list their names in order, these five practices are as follows:
first, the noble practice (ārya-caryā); second, the Brahma practice (brahma-caryā); third, the celestial practice (deva-caryā); fourth, the infant practice (bāla-caryā).
The fifth practice is the practice of illness.
There are four exhortations to treat it: namely, that it is cured if treated and not cured if left untreated; therefore, one exhorts [others] to treat it.
Good son, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should constantly cultivate these five kinds of practices.
The headings for the three non-sequential practices are as follows: first, the heading for the names of the practices, which states: "Furthermore, there is one practice;
furthermore, there is another practice.
Second, the heading for the non-sequential person, which refers to the Tathāgata.
This is the practice of the Tathāgata;
because the causal practice of the Tathāgata is itself the person who practices it.
The third is the designation of the non-sequential Dharma, namely, the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
This refers to the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
The Mahāyāna is the perfect cause, and Nirvāṇa is the perfect fruit; because the fruit is fully present within the cause without deficiency, this constitutes "one practice as all practices.
As for not offering an exhortation: such a person will certainly recover, and therefore no exhortation is needed. Question: [Why is this so?]

Regarding the statement that both [types of] practice take *nirvāṇa* as their object, what is the meaning? The answer is: although they equally take *nirvāṇa* as their object, there is a difference in how the practices are established.
One takes *nirvāṇa* as the object and establishes the practices sequentially, proceeding from the shallow to the deep.

The other takes *nirvāṇa* as the object and regards *nirvāṇa* itself as the practice; in each and every practice, there is nothing that is not *nirvāṇa*, yet there is a distinction between the partial and the perfect. Regarding the others... [text ends].
Seeing this, many have fallen into error and confusion by propounding theories of the convergence and divergence of cause and effect.
From the passage beginning "Kāśyapa, how does a bodhisattva... onwards, the second section—the dual explanation of the text—is divided into three parts:
first, the noble and the Brahma-conduct; second, the sequential and non-sequential practices; and third, the praise of the sūtra. Within the first [section], there are five sub-parts.

In the first part of the middle section, the noble practices (*ārya-caryā*) are explained in three parts: (1) a dual explanation of the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla-caryā*); (2) a dual explanation of the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi-caryā*); and (3) a dual explanation of the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*).

The first explanation of the practice of ethical discipline is divided into three parts: (a) a dual explanation of the practice of ethical discipline; (b) a dual explanation of the fruit of ethical discipline; and (c) a dual explanation of the names of the practices.
Within the first explanation of the practice of ethical discipline, there are two sections: first, an explanation of the sequential order; second, an explanation of the non-sequential order.
First, the sequential explanation of the precepts of conduct is divided into two parts: first, establishing the mind; second, establishing the practice.

Establishing the mind is further divided into two: first, encountering conditions related to persons; second, encountering conditions related to the Dharma. Regarding the first, conditions related to persons:
Kāśyapa, what is the noble practice cultivated by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra from either a śrāvaka or a Tathāgata, and having heard it, gives rise to faith, and having given rise to faith, should reflect in this way:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the unsurpassed path, the Great True Dharma, and the Great Assembly."
Right Practice:
If one encounters a nurse through the Śrāvakas, or encounters a skilled physician through the Tathāgata;

if one hears of the Great Nirvāṇa as encountering excellent medicine, and having heard it, gives rise to faith, resolves the mind with joy and revulsion, and seeks the unsurpassed path—this is right practice.
Prajñāpāramitā is the Great True Dharma; the correct practice of this Dharma-body is liberation. The Buddhas are the Buddha-jewel; the Unsurpassed Way is the Dharma-jewel;
and the Great Assembly is the Sangha-jewel. Within this context, it is not that there are no conditions consisting of dharmas;
rather, the name is established based on the predominant factor. When one encounters the condition of a person, the mind is immediately established.
Next, regarding the object of the Dharma: furthermore,
there are Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras which I shall now, for the sake of loving and desiring the Mahāyāna sūtras,
renounce— namely, my beloved wife, children, kinsmen, dwelling, house, gold, silver, precious jewels, and exquisite necklaces.

With perfumes, flowers, music, male and female servants, attendants, men and women, large and small elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, sheep, chickens, dogs, pigs, and other such creatures, they further reflect:
"Living at home is confining, like a prison, from which all afflictions arise;
leaving the home life is open and spacious, like empty space, through which all wholesome dharmas increase."

"If I remain a householder, I shall not be able to practice the pure conduct of the Brahma-faring to the end of my life; therefore, I must now shave off my hair and beard, leave the home life, and study the Way.
Furthermore, he thought: "I must certainly leave the home life now to cultivate and study the path of unsurpassed, right, and true Bodhi.
When the Bodhisattva thus desired to leave the home life, Māra Pāpīyān was filled with great anguish and distress.
To say that this bodhisattva will further engage in a great war with me, noble son—
how could such a bodhisattva ever again wage war against others?
Furthermore, there is the Vaipulya, from which one hears of the three virtues, the Three Jewels, and so forth, within the sutra scrolls.
Delighting in craving and seeking is the arousal of joy; abandoning what is loved is the arousal of aversion. When one attains the Dharma as a condition, one is able to establish the mind;
this is what can be remedied. Once these causes and conditions are encountered, joy and aversion become distinct, causing Māra to feel distress and anxiety.
From this point, the Bodhisattva immediately proceeds to the monastic quarters; this second section on the formal procedure for standing consists of two parts:

first, receiving the precepts, and second, upholding the precepts. The text for receiving the precepts is divided into two: first, approaching the teacher, and second, receiving [the precepts] according to the text.

At that time, the bodhisattva goes to the monastery; if he sees the Tathāgata or the disciples of the Buddha, who are fully endowed with dignified deportment, whose sense faculties are tranquil, and whose minds are gentle, pure, and extinguished in peace.
He immediately went to that place and sought to leave the household life, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the three dharma robes.
Since he had already left the household life, this is the second section on upholding the precepts; it consists of two parts, namely the Dharma and the simile.
Having already left the household life, he upholds the prohibitive precepts with his majestic deportment unimpaired; his movements are composed and serene, and he commits no transgressions.
Even regarding minor offenses, he gives rise to a sense of dread, guarding the precepts with a mind as firm as a diamond.
This analogy has two parts: first the illustration, then the application.
Good son, it is as if there were a person carrying a life-preserving float, wishing to cross the great ocean.
At that time, a rākṣasa in the sea immediately begged this person for the float. Having heard this, the person thought to himself: "I..."
Now, if he were to give it, he would certainly perish; so he answered the rākṣasa, "Rākṣasa, you may kill me, but you shall not obtain my life-preserving bag.
The rākṣasa spoke again, "If you cannot give it to me in its entirety, then give half of it to me. The man still refused to give it.
The rākṣasa spoke again, "If you cannot give half to me, I pray that you will at least give me a third."
The person was unwilling to give even a portion the size of a fingernail. The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you are unable to do so, grant me something the size of a hand. The person was still unwilling. The rākṣasa spoke again:

"If you now cannot give me even as much as a hand, and I am currently tormented by hunger, poverty, and manifold sufferings, you must surely relieve me with at least something the size of a mote of dust. The person spoke again: "You..."
"What you now seek is indeed not much; however, I am only just now about to cross the sea, and I do not know whether the path ahead is near or far.
If I give it to you, my strength will gradually fail, and how could I possibly overcome the perils of the great ocean?
Should I sink and die midway, [what would become of you]?"
The first analogy consists of five parts, namely: the four *pārājika* offenses, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the *sthūlātyaya*, the *pāyattika*, and the *duṣkṛta*.

Noble son, it is likewise with the bodhisattva’s observance of the prohibitive precepts. Just as that person crossing the water guards and cherishes his life-preserving float, so too does the bodhisattva guard and protect the precepts.
While he is thus guarding them, afflictions and various evil *rākṣasas* constantly speak to the bodhisattva.

He says: "You should believe me; I will never deceive you. Merely by breaking the four grave prohibitions while guarding the remaining precepts, through these causes and conditions, I shall bring you peace and security so that you may enter nirvana. At that time, the bodhisattva should speak thus:
"I would rather uphold such prohibitory precepts and fall into the Avīci Hell than violate them and be born in the heavens with afflictions."
The rākṣasa spoke again, saying: "If you cannot break the four pārājika precepts, you may break the saṃghāvaśeṣa;
by this means, you will find peace and enter nirvāṇa. The bodhisattva should likewise not follow these words. The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot commit the saṃghāvaśeṣa, you may intentionally commit a sthūlātyaya offense; by this means..."
The Bodhisattva, at that time, did not comply with the rākṣasa when he said, "By this cause and condition, you shall attain peace and enter nirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva likewise did not comply with the rākṣasa when he further said, "If you cannot commit a sthūlātyaya offense, you may commit a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense;
by this cause and condition, you shall attain peace and enter nirvāṇa. The Bodhisattva likewise did not comply with the rākṣasa when he further said, "If you do not..."
"One who is able to commit an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* may break a *pāyattika* rule; by this cause and condition, you shall attain peace and enter *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva likewise did not follow the rākṣasa. The rākṣasa spoke again:
'If you cannot commit a *pāyattika* offense, you might as well violate a *duṣkṛta* precept; by this cause and condition, you may obtain security and enter [peace]. "
Regarding nirvāṇa, at that time the bodhisattva thinks to himself:
"If I were now to commit a *duṣkṛta* offense and fail to confess it, I would be unable to cross to the other shore of birth and death to attain nirvāṇa.
Thus, regarding even these minor precepts, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains them with a firm resolve as steadfast as a vajra. The bodhisattva-mahāsattva...
The Bodhisattva maintains the four grave prohibitions (*catur-śrāmaṇera-śikṣāpada*) and the *duṣkṛta* offenses with equal firmness and reverence, without distinction.
Including the text, there are six [sections]; the third part consists of thirty-nine and ten [items], which are opened into two when combined (and so forth).

Alternatively, it may be that the two [categories] are opened for the sake of the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* involving an overnight stay and the *pāyattika* requiring confession before another (*pratideśanīya*). Regarding the *rākṣasa*, there are two interpretations. One...

The first "cloud" is a metaphor for external evil associates; the second "cloud" is a metaphor for the internal inverted mind. This is as fully explained in the fourth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, within the section on the purity of upholding the precepts.

From the passage beginning with "If a bodhisattva can... onwards, the second part clarifies the non-sequential precepts, which is divided into four sections: first, possessing both the branches and the root.
Second, possessing both fact and principle; third, possessing both light and heavy [offenses]; fourth, possessing the vow.
If a bodhisattva can thus firmly maintain [the precepts], they will be fully endowed with the fivefold set of precepts, namely:
the bodhisattva’s fundamental precept of pure karma, the preceding and following auxiliary precepts of purity, and the absence of unwholesome thoughts.
The precept of awakening that is pure, the precept of maintaining right mindfulness that is pure, and the precept of dedicating toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The initial root is the nature-offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); those preceding and following it are the preparatory and subsequent offenses.

The two [precepts] belonging to the *saṃvara-śīla*—the non-arising of various evil thoughts, which is the *samādhi-sahaja-śīla* that guards the mental ground—and the *saddharma-parigraha-viśuddha-śīla*, which is the *mārga-sahaja-śīla*:
these two belong to the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*. Dedication toward the Mahāyāna constitutes the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla*.
Taking the gravity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-gaurava*) as the foundation, all other precepts flow forth from it.
Next, following Kāśyapa, there are again two kinds of precepts; setting aside these, there are the precepts that fully embody both principle and practice.
Kāśyapa, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva further has two kinds of precepts: first, the precepts received through worldly instruction;
second, the precepts attained through the True Dharma. If a Bodhisattva attains the precepts of the True Dharma, they will never commit evil even while receiving the worldly precepts.
This is obtained only after the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
The preceding branches and roots all belong to the category of ritual matters (*vastu*). Ordinary persons who can practice the precepts of the True Dharma act in accordance with principle;
noble ones are able to maintain them.
Repeating this three times, there are two kinds of precepts: those that possess gravity and those that are light.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are two kinds of precepts: first, the precepts of natural gravity; second, the precepts for avoiding worldly reproach.
The precepts of natural gravity refer to the four prohibitions. The precepts for avoiding worldly reproach refer to not engaging in frivolous trade.
He deceives others by using small measures; he seizes the property of others through the influence of others; with a harmful mind, he binds and destroys successful enterprises.
Furthermore, although he is wealthy, he sleeps [negligently]; he does not cultivate fields or houses for his livelihood, nor does he maintain shops.
He does not keep elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, sheep, camels, donkeys, chickens, dogs, monkeys, peacocks, parrots, *saṃjīva* birds, or *kroñca* cranes, nor does he keep jackals.
Wolves, tigers, leopards, wildcats, lynxes, pigs, boars, and other malevolent beasts; boys and girls, men and women, slaves and servants;
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, tridacna shells, agate, coral, jade, white jade, conch shells, and various treasures;
red copper, tin, brass, basins and vessels, woolen rugs, carpets, and garments of fine hair—these constitute the first [category].
He processed all grains—rice, wheat, barley, beans, millet, sorghum, paddy, and hemp—into raw and cooked foods, yet he always observed the practice of eating only one meal and never ate a second.
Whether begging for food or receiving meals within the Sangha, he always knew moderation and contentment;
he did not accept special invitations, nor did he eat meat, drink alcohol, or consume the five pungent herbs or strong-smelling vegetables. For this reason, his body was free from any foul odor.
He was constantly revered, honored, respected, and praised by all the devas and all people of the world;

he ate only to satisfy his needs and never accepted food in excess. The robes he received were just sufficient to cover his body, and whether moving or staying still, he was always accompanied by his three robes and alms bowl, never parting from them like a bird with its two wings.
He did not store roots, stalks, joints, or seeds.
He shall not maintain storehouses for gold or silver, nor for food, drink, kitchens, clothing, or ornaments;
he shall not sit or lie upon high, wide, or large beds, nor upon ivory or golden beds, nor upon those woven with various colors.
He shall not keep any fine or soft mats, nor sit upon any elephant-rugs or horse-rugs, nor use fine, soft, or exquisite garments as coverings for his bed.
When lying down to rest on his bed, he does not place two pillows; nor does he accept or keep fine red pillows, but only uses wooden pillows with spring-mechanisms.

He never watches elephant fights, horse fights, chariot fights, or battles between soldiers; nor does he watch fights between men or women, oxen, sheep, chickens, pheasants, parrots, and the like, nor does he intentionally go to see them.
He also does not intentionally listen to the blowing of conch shells or the beating of drums in military arrays.

The sounds of horns, lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, *konghou* lutes, singing, shouting, and various forms of music— except for those offered in worship of the Buddha— he does not observe or engage in any games or amusements,
such as *chupu*, *weiqi*, *bolasexi*, lion fights, elephant fights, *tanqi*, *liubuo*, *baiqu*, stone-throwing, *touhu*, *qian dao*, or *badao xingcheng*.
He never practices physiognomy or divination of the hands, feet, face, or countenance.
One does not use one's fingernails, mirrors, milfoil stalks, willow branches, alms bowls, or skulls to perform divination;

nor does one gaze upward at the void or the stars and constellations. One does not engage in coming and going on errands for royal households, nor does one speak of this person to that person or that person to this person.
One never lives by flattery or wrong livelihood, nor does one proclaim the thefts of kings or ministers.
"O son of good family, matters such as bandits, strife, food and drink, lands, famine, fear, abundance, joy, peace, and security—
these are called the precepts for pacifying worldly reproach of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. O son of good family,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva firmly upholds these prohibitive precepts, they are no different from the fundamental precepts of natural gravity."

The principles of the aforementioned matters are all termed "heavy" (*guru*); removing them to avoid worldly censure is termed "light" (*laghu*). A Bodhisattva maintains these equally without distinction.
Regarding the term *ḍi-tsa*, the old [translation] says it is pronounced as *jie* (接) and refers to a type of fruit such as the *bō-lí* (博梨) or persimmon.

Master Guān says it is pronounced as *dì* (蔕), referring to the peduncle. Furthermore, this is the name of Hán Guǎngchéng Hóu; moreover, the *Lǐjì* (Book of Rites) states: "For a scholar-official (*shì*), one breaks... [the fruit].
Regarding the phrase "the value of a melon's stem is merely to remove the stem," the intent clarifies that the various sons may not possess it.
As for the "yellow wooden pillow," there are two interpretations: one says its interior is hollow like the skin of a drum; the other says the wood has a pattern resembling yellow flowers.
Regarding the *pārasaka* (or *pārasīka*), Emperor Wu of Liang said it was a form of *shuanglu* (backgammon). This originated from a practice of the recent past.
This is the completion of the practice of the eight paths within the "clamping" [of the senses], which constitutes the game of *se* (obstruction).
From the fourth section, "The Good Son Bodhisattva’s Vow," downward, this is the possession of vows. Restraining the mind is the vow; making a formal commitment is the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
These two constitute the text of the vow: first, the vow for oneself, and second, the vow for others. Regarding the initial self-vow, there are twelve items, the first of which is...
"I vow that within myself I shall never give rise to a mind that breaks the precepts.
Good son, once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has received and upheld these various prohibitive precepts, he makes this aspiration:
"I would rather cast this body into a deep pit of blazing, fierce fire than ever violate the precepts of the past or the future."
Now, regarding the prohibitive precepts established by the Buddhas of the present: one should not engage in impure conduct with women of the kṣatriya, brāhmaṇa, or householder castes.
Furthermore, there are six vows concerning the non-acceptance of external offerings.
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes this vow:
"I would rather have my body wrapped all over with glowing iron than ever dare to receive the robes of a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts.
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes this vow: "I would rather swallow glowing iron balls with this mouth..."
I shall never, out of a mouth that has violated the precepts, consume the food and drink of a faithful donor.

Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes this vow: "I would rather lie upon this body on a great, glowing-hot iron surface than ever, with a body that has broken the precepts, accept the beds, couches, and bedding of a faithful donor. Furthermore, son of good family...

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva makes this vow: "I would rather let this body receive three hundred spears than ever dare to accept the medicine and medical care from a faithful donor with a body that has violated the precepts. Furthermore, son of good family, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
"I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of boiling iron than ever dare to [accept such things with a broken body]..."
Regarding the precepts, one receives with a faithful heart the rooms, houses, and dwellings of donors. Furthermore, good son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes this vow:

"I would rather have this body of mine, from head to foot, shattered by an iron mallet until it is like fine dust, than receive the respectful salutations and honors of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, or householders while violating the precepts."
Homage.
Throughout the three realms of existence, I vow never to be broken by internal faculties or external objects.
Furthermore, son of good family, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva makes this further vow: "I would rather have my eyes gouged out with hot iron..."
He does not look at the beautiful forms of others with a defiled mind. Furthermore, son of good family, the bodhisattva mahāsattva makes this vow:
"I would rather have iron awls pierce my ears all over than listen to pleasant sounds with a defiled mind."
Furthermore, good son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes this vow:
"I would rather have my nose cut off with a sharp blade than, with a defiled mind, greedily smell various fragrances. Furthermore, good son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes this vow:
"I would rather have my tongue slit with a sharp blade than, with a defiled mind, greedily crave delicious flavors."
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes this vow:
"I would rather have my body split asunder with a sharp axe than, with a defiled mind, become greedily attached to various tactile sensations. Why is this?

Because by such causes and conditions, it causes the practitioner to fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts. Kāśyapa, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s protection and upholding.
Regarding the precepts:
from the moment a bodhisattva upholds them, they vow to share them with others.
Having upheld such precepts, the bodhisattva mahāsattva bestows them all upon the entire multitude of beings.
By these causes and conditions, I vow that all sentient beings shall protect and uphold the prohibitive precepts, attaining the pure precepts, the virtuous precepts, the unimpaired precepts,
the indivisible precepts, the Mahāyāna precepts, the non-retrogressive precepts, the conforming precepts, the ultimate precepts,
and fully accomplishing the precepts of the pāramitās.

There are ten kinds of textual [explanations]. One kind of protection and maintenance applies universally to both the pure precepts (*śīla*) and the precepts for gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-śīla*).

The "gathering of wholesome dharmas" is subsumed under both the "non-deficient" and "non-fractured" [precepts], while the "restraint of prohibitions" is subsumed under the "limit of avoiding transgressions.
The latter five [categories] take up the vast application and lack of deficiency; all are subsumed under the "gathering of sentient beings. Regarding "non-retrogression," it refers to alcohol.
Furthermore, the royal palace does not allow for the decline of the precepts; those who accord with this are in harmony with principle. That which is ultimate is all-encompassing and complete.
As for the *pāramitās*, they exhaust both this shore and that. When the single mind of upholding the precepts is fully perfected, it encompasses all precepts;
this is called "one precept as all precepts. Since the precepts are subsumed within the Dharma-realm, all phenomena are thereby gathered into the perfect precepts.
[This is] practice.

Next, following "The Bodhisattva’s Cultivation," the second pair clarifies the fruits of the precepts: if one discusses the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it should summon a retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*), which is the proximate result of attaining superior rewards among humans and devas;
if one discusses the formative cause (*abhyāsa-hetu*), it summons a formative fruit (*abhyāsa-phala*), which is the remote result of [attaining] permanence.
Regarding the statement that "abiding in the Dharma-body is neither near nor far now, taking the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) as the fruit," there have been three traditional interpretations:
1. One says that among the ten grounds, the eighth is the Immovable Ground. 2. Another says that the accomplishment of true understanding on the first ground is called the Immovable Ground.
3. A third says that according to the *Bhūmi-sūtra*, this refers to the precepts (*śīla*) which are assigned to the second ground; thus, it is here termed "immovable."
This refers to the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*). Now it is clarified that this is not so; previously, both sequential and non-sequential practices were explained together as analyzed above.

Now, their fruit is discussed collectively: one must necessarily attain the path of realization (*abhisamaya-mārga*). As for the "same place" mentioned regarding the path of realization, this refers to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
If one speaks of the fruit solely in terms of the three trainings (*triśikṣā*) according to the sequential order, then entering into principle is called "abiding" (*vihāra*).
"Abiding" means immovability; the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) are the fruit of morality (*śīla*). "Abiding gives rise to merit," which is called the practice of practice (*caryā-caryā*);

"practice" takes mastery as its meaning. The Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*) are the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The Ground that can give rise to and carry the Ground of Fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) is the fruit of wisdom (*prajñā*).
This is the intended meaning of this sequence. If one considers the fruit of morality in terms of perfect clarity (*pariśuddha*), it is the First Abiding. Such is the meaning of the text.
It should be understood that this section on "Single" and "Appropriate" serves to distinguish and clarify that the stage of realizing the Path belongs to the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).

By clearly explaining the fruit of the precepts through these two meanings, the significance will become self-evident within the subsequent commentary. The explanatory text is divided into four parts: the heading, the analogy, the explanation, and the conclusion.
The first, the heading, is as stated in the text.
Good son, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such pure precepts, he immediately dwells in the first stage, the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
Why is it called the Immovable Ground? When a bodhisattva dwells within this Immovable Ground, he is immovable, does not fall, does not regress, and does not scatter.
Good son, it is as if Mount Sumeru cannot be moved, caused to fall, made to retreat, or dispersed by the violent Vairambha wind.
Regarding the phrase "immovable" and so forth in the subsequent analogy: because it is eternal, it is immovable; because it is blissful, it does not fall;

because it is the self, it does not retreat; because it is pure, it is not dispersed (and so forth). Question: The *Śāstra* states that one is unmoved by the eight winds, yet the Vairambha wind arrives. How is this?
"Shattered like withered grass—what does this mean? Now, taking the *Anabhisamskāra-śāstra* as the standard, we take the end of the kalpa.
Within the three sections of the commentary by the three Bodhisattvas below, the first section concerns the Three Truths."
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in this stage, they likewise remain unmoved by forms, sounds, odors, or tastes;
they do not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; they do not regress to the levels of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
and they are not scattered by the perverse winds of heterodox views, nor do they engage in wrong livelihoods.

If one speaks of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, these are the good fruits within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). If one speaks of the hells and so forth, these are the evil fruits within conventional truth.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are persons within ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Those who hold divergent views due to the "evil winds" of heterodoxy are phenomena within ultimate truth.
Neither birth-and-death with its good and evil, nor nirvāṇa, nor persons or dharmas, can move it.
Falling into non-retrogression and non-dispersal clearly reveals the ground of the fruit of the Middle Way precepts: permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Next, the three bodies are revealed by way of the three obstacles.
Furthermore, good son, "immovable" means not being moved by greed, anger, or delusion, and not falling [into them].
"Those who do not fall into the four grave offenses, nor regress— that is, do not retreat from the precepts and return home— and are not dispersed— that is,
are not destroyed by those who oppose the Mahāyāna sūtras."

The three poisons are the affliction-obstruction; the four grave slanders of the Dharma are the karma-obstruction; and the regression from the precepts and returning home are the retribution-obstruction.

When the retribution-obstruction is removed, the dharma-body manifests; when the karma-obstruction is removed, the response-body manifests; and when the affliction-obstruction is removed, the enjoyment-body manifests.
Upon reaching the first stage (bhūmi), these three bodies appear and all three obstructions are eliminated.
The third section concerns the four virtues.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise not shaken by the various demons of affliction (*kleśa-māra*), nor does he fall under the power of the demon of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), even until he sits at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree;
although the celestial demon (*deva-māra*) may be present, [he remains unshaken].
It enables one to never retreat from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor to be scattered by the Māra of Death.
Being unmoved by the Māra of Afflictions is the quality of purity; not falling under the power of the Māra of the Aggregates (*skandha-māra*) is the quality of bliss.
Being withdrawn from by the celestial Māras signifies my virtue; not being dispersed by the Māra of death signifies my permanence.
Possessing permanence, bliss, self, and purity in the first stage constitutes the fruit of the precepts, which is expedient regarding two meanings.
"Good sons, from here below is the section on the holy practice (*ārya-caryā*) that establishes the precepts.
Good sons, this is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the holy practice.
Good sons, as for what is called 'holy practice,' from here below is the third pair of explanations regarding the meaning of the name 'holy practice.'"
This consists of three parts: first, the general indication; second, the detailed explanation; and third, the conclusion.
Regarding the question, "Good son, what is called the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*)?", the explanation is divided into three sections:
first, by citing two types of individuals—the partial and the perfect—the dual explanation is made manifest.
It is called "Noble Practice" (*ārya-caryā*) because it is the practice of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; thus, it is named Noble Practice.
Second, by specifically citing the two dharmas of concentration and wisdom, one establishes [the excellence of] morality.
For what reason are such beings as Buddhas and Bodhisattvas called "noble ones"? Because such persons possess noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
Because they constantly contemplate that the nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent, for this reason they are called "Noble Ones" (ārya);
because they possess noble precepts, they are called "Noble Ones"; and because they possess noble concentration and wisdom, they are called "Noble Ones."
Third, summarizing the explanation of the noble ones (*ārya*) by means of the seven treasures and the seven factors of enlightenment:
there are seven noble treasures, namely faith, precepts, shame, dread of blame, extensive learning, wisdom, and relinquishment;
for this reason they are called noble ones. Furthermore, because they possess the seven factors of enlightenment, they are called noble ones.
The noble ones practice the noble Dharma, and because the noble Dharma brings about the noble ones, it is called "noble conduct" (ārya-caryā).

If those who have realized the Path are identical [in nature], one should explain the name "noble conduct" by means of the precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the first stage, as well as the seven riches and the seven factors of enlightenment.
The third section is as in the text.
For these reasons, it is further called "Noble Practice" (*ārya-caryā*).

Furthermore, son of good family, the second part, the "Exposition on the Noble Practice of Concentration," is divided into two sections: first, the exposition on sequential concentration (*anupūrva-samādhi*).
Second, the explanation of Perfect Concentration (*pariniṣpanna-samādhi*). The first section has two parts: first, explaining the practice; second, explaining the fruit.

Kaishan’s commentary explains that the practice of concentration consists of performing the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), and all other masters follow him. This interpretation is incorrect, as it contains two errors: it contradicts the sutra and it obstructs the meaning. Regarding the contradiction with the sutra:
the text states, "Having performed this contemplation, one attains the four foundations of mindfulness; having attained the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so forth].

If one abides in the Stage of Patience (kṣānti-bhūmi) and practices the holy conduct of meditative concentration (samādhi-caryā), then the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) should also follow in succession as one enters the Stage of Patience.
If one has not yet attained this Stage of Patience, how could one possess these four foundations of mindfulness? Regarding the point of contradiction:

here it clarifies that the practice of concentration employs the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness; below, it clarifies that the practice of wisdom should employ the eight concentrations (aṣṭau samādhayaḥ).
"The practice of precepts is itself the practice of concentration; this error is no small matter" (and so forth).

Within this context, the sixteen special stages (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), the nine meditations on the repulsive (*nava saṃjñāḥ*), and other such dharma-gates are opened.

Since these are not the fundamental [attainments] but all possess contemplative wisdom capable of knowing impermanence and non-self—and because "self" is the root of all evils—they are explained specifically here. The various masters have seen that there is no [fault in] doing so.
My observation is that what is called "application of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna) is actually not [merely] application of mindfulness; the initial section is divided into two parts:

first, the "special qualities" (viśeṣa), and second, the "reversals" (pratikūla-vimokṣa). Within the first, the special qualities, there are two further divisions: first, the explanation of cultivation, and second, the explanation of realization.
Furthermore, son of good family, the noble practitioner, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, contemplates this body from head to foot.
First, regarding "cultivation," he contemplates this body from head to foot.

Next, regarding "realization," there are two parts: first, the characteristics of realization itself; second, from "the bodhisattva" onwards, it clarifies that this realized dharma arises simultaneously with understanding.
Within this [body], there are only hair, body hair, nails, teeth, impurities, filth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, and liver.

The liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, and the two organs of the raw and cooked; the large and small excretions, nasal mucus, saliva, tears, fat, grease, brain, membranes, marrow, blood, pus, the brain-crust, and all the vessels.
The initial text states that within it there are only thirty-six items—hair, body hair, nails, and teeth—which proves this [body] to be particularly superior.
"Open the storehouse of the body to fully observe that within, without, and in between, there are twelve [parts] each, totaling thirty-six (and so forth).
The brain is above; the marrow is here. Taken together from top to bottom, both the Hexi and the Jāṭila schools say these are peach kernels.
Within the brain there is bone like the kernels of peaches and plums; Bian Que’s medical formulas state this is so."
The place where the three hairs are located is called the *gāi* (the calf); within it is the *gāi*.

Next, from the Bodhisattva’s single-minded mindfulness, as he departs from this *viśeṣa-samādhi* (special victory concentration), [wisdom] arises together with liberation, and he does not give rise to attachment to its flavor.
When the bodhisattva thus contemplates with single-minded attention, he reflects: "Who is this that is 'I'? To whom does 'I' belong?
Where does it abide? And who belongs to me? He further considers: "Is the bone 'I', or is 'I' apart from the bone?"
In this passage, the text is abbreviated, merely inferring non-self; a complete exposition must include suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and impermanence (*anitya*).
Second, from the removal of skin and flesh onwards, the text concerning the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) is divided into two parts: first, explaining cultivation;
second, explaining realization.
At that time, the Bodhisattva removes the skin and flesh.
What was initially called "cultivation" refers to the removal of the skin and flesh, which is precisely the characteristic of cultivation.

Next, the contemplation of white bones alone constitutes the characteristic of realization; this characteristic of realization also has two parts, the first of which is precisely the characteristic of realization itself.
One contemplates only white bones.
Next, one further forms this thought: "The understanding of the signs of lower realization is devoid of any relish or attachment.
Immediately, one succeeds in severing all desire for form and further increases that realization.
Again, he forms this thought: "The colors and appearances of these bones are different—namely, blue, yellow, white, and pigeon-colored.
Such skeletal appearances are likewise not the self. Why is this? Because the self is neither blue, nor yellow, nor white, nor pigeon-colored.
When the Bodhisattva fixes his mind and contemplates in this way, he immediately succeeds in severing all desire for form. Again, he forms this thought: "Just as..."
These bones arise from causes and conditions: depending on the foot bone, they support the ankle bone;
depending on the ankle bone, they support the shin bone; depending on the shin bone, they support the knee bone; depending on the knee bone, they support the thigh bone;
depending on the thigh bone, they support the hip bone; depending on the hip bone, they support the waist bone; depending on the waist bone...
It supports the backbone; relying on the backbone, it supports the ribs. Again, relying on the backbone, it supports upward to the cervical vertebrae;
relying on the cervical vertebrae, it supports the jawbone; relying on the jawbone, it supports the teeth. Above, there is the skull;
again, relying on the cervical vertebrae, it supports the clavicle; relying on the clavicle, it supports the humerus; relying on the humerus, it [supports]...

The radius bone supports the ulna bone; depending on the ulna bone, it supports the carpal bones; depending on the carpal bones, they support the metacarpal bones; and depending on the metacarpal bones, they support the phalanges.
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates in this way, all the bones of the body become entirely separated. Having attained this contemplation, he immediately abandons the three desires:
first, the desire for physical form; second, the desire for graceful gestures; and third, the desire for subtle touch. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
