When the Bodhisattva contemplates blue bones, he sees this great earth—in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—all as entirely blue in appearance, just like the color blue.
His contemplation of yellow, white, and pigeon-colored [bones] is likewise.

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva performs this contemplation, light in the colors of blue, yellow, red, white, and pigeon emerges from between his eyebrows. At that time, the Bodhisattva, one by one...
Within those various radiances, they saw images of Buddhas; having seen them, they immediately asked:
"How is it that such a body—composed through the combination of impure causes and conditions—is able to sit, rise, walk, stand, bend, stretch, look up or down, blink, breathe, weep, or laugh?
There is no master here; who causes it to act thus? Having asked this, [they beheld] the Buddhas within the radiances.
Suddenly it vanished, and he again thought: "Perhaps because consciousness is the self, the Buddhas have not taught it to me.
He further observed that this consciousness arises and ceases in succession, like a flowing stream, and thus it too is not the self. Again he thought:
"If consciousness is not the self, perhaps the out-breath and in-breath might be the self. Again he thought: "These out-breaths and in-breaths..."
That which is the nature of wind is indeed the nature of wind, yet this nature of wind is among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Among these four great elements, which one is the self?
The nature of earth is not the self; the natures of water, fire, and wind are likewise not the self. Furthermore, he reflects: "In this body, there is no self whatsoever;
it is only through the causal conjunction of mind and wind that various activities and functions are manifested."
For example, it is like that which is produced by the power of spells or by illusion, and like a lute that produces sound according to one's will.
Therefore, this body is likewise impure, a composite formed through the conjunction of various causes and conditions; where, then, could desire arise?
And if it is reviled, where could anger arise? Such as this body of mine, composed of thirty-six elements.
In this impure and foul-smelling body, where could there be one who receives abuse? If you hear such abuse, you should immediately reflect:

"By what sound am I being abused? Since each individual sound cannot abuse me, and many sounds together are likewise incapable, for this reason one should not give rise to anger. If another comes to strike you, you should likewise reflect.
Regarding such striking, from what does it arise? He further reflects: "It is named 'striking' because of the hand, the sword, the staff, and my own body.
For what reason do I now pointlessly direct anger toward another? It is my own body that has invited this fault.
Because I have received this body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it is like this: just as there is a hit by an arrow because of a target, so too is it with my body."
If one possesses a body, there will be blows; if I do not maintain forbearance, my mind will become distracted. If the mind is distracted, right mindfulness will be lost.

If right mindfulness is lost, one cannot discern the meaning of what is wholesome and what is unwholesome. If one cannot discern the meaning of what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, one will practice unwholesome dharmas.
Due to the causal conditions of these unwholesome dharmas, one will fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
The subsequent four stages further state, "one again forms this thought," which merely refers to the arising of contemplation based on further conditions.

The initial mention of "removing the three desires" is likewise a sign of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). This resembles the realization of the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), yet the textual description of their cultivation is not seen here.
It is possible that one cultivates the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and thereby realizes the nine perceptions; there is indeed such a principle. Next, when observing the blue bones, one sees them...
When this great earth appears as if receding, it is like the sign of cultivation during the contemplation of the "superior place" (*abhibhvāyatana*) while observing blue bones;
that this great earth recedes is the sign of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). When the Bodhisattva performs this contemplation, it is also the sign of cultivating the "liberations" (*vimokṣa*).

Furthermore, when blue, yellow, and other colored lights emerge from between his eyebrows, this is the sign of realization. Having seen this, he immediately asks about the conditions for realizing the receding.

Regarding internal contemplation (*adhyātma-vipaśyanā*) and external contemplation (*bahirdhā-vipaśyanā*): if one is reviled, to investigate "who is it that receives the abuse? constitutes internal contemplation;

if, upon hearing the abuse, one departs from it, this is external contemplation. If one does not depart from it due to a lack of forbearance, this constitutes the cultivation of wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*).
Thus, by skillfully recognizing obstacles and nurturing the concentrated mind (*samādhi-citta*), the causes of unwholesome dharmas do not arise, and consequently, there will be no hell.
This is the fruit.
From the time the Bodhisattva attained this, it was the second clarification of the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Herein, because those who are liberated through both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) cultivate both concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*) in tandem, it is said that after performing this contemplation, one attains the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); for the foundations of mindfulness are capable of...
The passage concerning severing the fetters and entering the stages, specifically the Stage of Patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), contains both a heading and an explanation. It states:

"When the Bodhisattva has performed this contemplation, he attains the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). Having attained the four foundations of mindfulness, he then abides within the Stage of Patience."
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this stage, they are able to endure greed, hatred, and delusion;

they are also able to endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and lice, as well as violent winds, harsh touch, various epidemics, abusive speech, insults, beatings, and corporal punishment.
They can endure all such physical and mental sufferings; for this reason, it is called "dwelling in endurance" (kṣānti).
Regarding the Grounds:
formerly it was said that the fifth ground, where the dhyāna-pāramitā is perfected, is the Kṣānti-bhūmi (Ground of Forbearance). Now it is clarified that this is not so.

If one discusses the fruits of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) according to the distinct and perfect [teachings] individually, it is as previously explained. If one discusses them by combining the distinct and the perfect, it is still... [as follows].

From the first stage, enduring desire up to hunger and thirst is the endurance of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*); enduring gadflies and mosquitoes up to flogging and whipping is the endurance of beings (*sattvakṣānti*).
These constitute the summary of physical and mental suffering.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: [This concludes] the second section, which clarifies the practice of perfect concentration; others say it is a detailed analysis concerning the violation of precepts.
Regarding the fact that this is taught after the section on ethical discipline (*śīla*), there are three interpretations: first, it is said that the compiler of the sūtra made an error;

second, it is intended to harmonize the two stages so they do not differ in essence—the former being called "Immovable" (*acala*) and this being called "Endurance" (*kṣānti*), which are but one and the same stage;

third, it is held that while one may simply maintain ethical discipline, one has not yet been able to perceive the [appropriate] opportunity (*nimitta*) and thus cannot perform the act of killing, whereas here one is certainly able to perceive it.
The claim that the capacity [of this stage] can lead to the violation of precepts is incorrect; here, the intent is precisely to clarify the perfect concentration (*pariniṣpanna-samādhi*). Question:
This text states that one may break the precepts before entering the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*); how then can it be said that this is perfect concentration? Answer:

If it were not perfect precept (*pariniṣpanna-śīla*), how could one simultaneously violate and maintain them? Since one possesses such mastery over both maintaining and violating, it is by analogy [classified as perfect].
It is the same with meditative concentration (*samādhi*): it is tranquil even within distraction, and one practices killing while remaining in perfect concentration (*pariniṣpanna-samādhi*).

Since the precepts can be understood as being both precepts and concentration, there is no need for further elaboration; therefore, this is designated as the practice of perfect concentration. Question:

Having previously clarified perfect precepts and then explained the fruit of the precepts, why is it that the fruit of concentration is now clarified only after [the discussion of] perfect [precepts]? Answer: [Because the sequence follows the stages of cultivation.]

What is "fixed" (determined)? The answer is that the lack of fixed sequence between preceding and following [sections] more clearly manifests the perfect determination. The text consists of three rounds of question and answer:
the first is brief, the second is extensive, and the third is Mañjuśrī’s narration of the events.

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva has not yet attained the stage of immovability (akampya-bhūmi) and is maintaining pure precepts, could there be any causes or conditions by which they might break those precepts?”
"Good son, because there are causes and conditions, a bodhisattva who has not yet attained the Immovable Bhūmi may break the precepts.
Kāśyapa said, "Indeed, World-Honored One; what are these?"

The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "If there is a bodhisattva who knows that by means of the causes and conditions of breaking the precepts, they can cause others to receive, uphold, and cherish the Mahāyāna sūtras;

and can further cause them to read, recite, master them thoroughly, copy the scrolls, and explain them extensively to others, so that they do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—it is for such reasons as these."
When a bodhisattva has broken the precepts, they should at that time form this thought:

"I would rather fall into the Avīci Hell for one kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, to undergo this retribution for my transgression, so as to ensure that this person does not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Kāśyapa, it is for this reason that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva may break the pure precepts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if there is a bodhisattva who takes such a person under their care and protection,
causing them not to retreat from the mind of enlightenment, it is impossible for that person to be one who has violated the precepts or to fall into the Avīci Hell."
When the facts contradict the principle and it ought not to result in an evil retribution, the Buddha answered as written in the text.
At that time, the Buddha praised Mañjuśrī, saying, "Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said. I recall in the distant past..."
In Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Śāntamati who cherished and revered the Mahāyāna sūtras;
his mind was purely virtuous and free from coarseness, malice, envy, or stinginess.

His mouth constantly uttered words of affection and goodness, and his body constantly protected the poor and the solitary through generosity and diligence, never ceasing for a moment. At that time, no Buddha was present in the world.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, at that time I delighted in the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras;
for twelve years I served the brahmins, providing them with all their necessities. When the twelve years were complete and I had finished bestowing peace upon them, I spoke these words:
"Teachers, you should now resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. The brahmins said, "Great..."
"O Great King, the nature of Bodhi is non-existent, and the Mahāyāna sūtras are likewise so.
O Great King, why then do you wish to cause people to become like empty space? Good son, at that time my heart held the Mahāyāna in high esteem;
when I heard the brahmin revile the Vaipulya sūtras, having heard it, I immediately cut off his life-faculty. Good son, because of this..."
For this reason, from that time forward, sons of good family who do not fall into hell and who protect and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras possess such immeasurable power as this.

Furthermore, there is also the practice of the noble ones (*ārya-caryā*), which is the third [topic]: clear wisdom (*vidyā-jñāna*). This consists of two parts: first, the practice of clear wisdom; second, the fruit of clear wisdom.

Regarding the practice of clear wisdom, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the practice of clear wisdom; second, the explanation of the name of the practice of clear wisdom. First, regarding the explanation of the practice of clear wisdom, there are again two parts:
first, the explanation of sequential clear wisdom (*anupūrva-vidyā*); second, the explanation of perfect clear wisdom (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*). [This is] sequential clear wisdom.
Regarding the three [types of wisdom]: first, the wisdom that explains the Four Noble Truths; second, the wisdom that explains the Two Truths; and third, the wisdom that explains the Single Reality.
Others say this refers to the principle of opening and closing: within ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), it is taught as a single truth;
next, one is opened into two; then, two are opened into four; furthermore, four can be opened into sixteen, and so on up to the infinite. If they are closed together...
The immeasurables are sixteen; combining these sixteen makes four, which further combine into two and one, finally entering emptiness.

Now, although these are explained through the methods of binding, scattering, opening, and closing, their names and meanings differ, and they vary according to the conditions they face, bearing significant relevance.

Here, for the time being, we speak in contrast to the three baskets (Tripitaka): the wisdom of the Four Truths faces conventional conditions; the wisdom of the Two Truths faces the common [Mahayana] conditions; and the wisdom of the Distinct [Vehicle] faces specific conditions.
It is said that the wisdom of the single ultimate truth (ekasatyajñāna), in relation to its objects, also establishes the meaning of the sequential [Four Truths] (*yathākrama-artha*) (and so forth).
Formerly, some took the objects as the Four Truths, while others took the wisdom as the Four Truths. Whether it be suffering, origin, cessation, or the path, all are objects;

in relation to these objects, one speaks of wisdom. Wisdom itself is the Truth. The object is that which can give rise to wisdom, causing wisdom to be non-existent [in terms of independent self-nature]; wisdom is that which can... [give rise to] the object.

The illumination of objects and the cognition of objects are fundamentally without objects; because wisdom and its object are established in mutual dependence, it is said that the Four Noble Truths arise.

Master Xinghuang said: "What are called the Noble Truths are simply Buddha-nature and Nirvana. They are neither object nor wisdom, neither outflowing nor non-outflowing, neither cause nor fruit, and neither mundane nor supramundane;
therefore they are named the Noble Truths. If one relies on the various masters, each adheres to a single view and interpretation.
The text does not accord with the meaning of the Four Noble Truths; it primarily offers a single-directional interpretation. Now, this text enumerates three types of the Four Noble Truths:
if one says that "suffering" refers to the characteristic of oppression, this constitutes the Four Noble Truths of conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*).

If one says that by understanding suffering there is no suffering, but rather the presence of True Truth (*satya*), this constitutes the Four Noble Truths of non-arising (*anutpāda*). If one proceeds from the perspective that suffering possesses immeasurable characteristics...
As for "departing," it refers to the immeasurable Four Noble Truths; these three types of the Four Truths are all the objects of contemplation for Bodhisattvas.

Those who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa possess the wisdom of the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) Four Truths. When discussing both the subject and object of cognition together, there are fully four types.

Regarding the first [the Unconditioned], there are three: first, the brief; second, the extensive; and third, the conclusion. Furthermore, regarding the brief: [The text continues with the specific details of the brief, extensive, and concluding sections.]

Sixth: First, the enumeration; second, the explanation of names; third, the explanation of functions; fourth, the explanation of essence; fifth, the explanation of the establishment [of the categories];
sixth, a further expansion on the essence. The first is as in the text.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there are also the noble practices, namely the Four Noble Truths: suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

Kāśyapa, "suffering" (duḥkha) has the characteristic of oppression; "origination" (samudaya) has the characteristic of being able to produce and grow [suffering]; "cessation" (nirodha) has the characteristic of quiescence; and the "path" (mārga) has the characteristic of the Great Vehicle.
Next, regarding the explanation of the names: it is explained as "suffering" by way of oppression, because the body is the root of suffering and is the locus where all sufferings accumulate.
Oppression is the accumulation [of suffering]; "able to grow" refers only to the cause that can produce the fruit; "extinction" is the characteristic of quiescence, the exhaustion of birth and death.

The Path is called the Mahāyāna because it carries one from the cause toward the fruit. If one were to claim that the Four Truths are the meaning of the Tripiṭaka, how could one say that the Path is the characteristic of the Mahāyāna?
If, for a moment, one were to correlate this with the Tripiṭaka, then the Bodhi of the Tripiṭaka—
Because the path of the bodhisattva is supreme, it is also called the Mahāyāna.
Third, regarding the explanation of its function:

furthermore, son of good family, "suffering" (duḥkha) has the characteristic of manifestation; "origination" (samudaya) has the characteristic of transformation; "cessation" (nirodha) has the characteristic of removal; and the "path" (mārga) is that which is able to...
Eliminating characteristics.

As for "suffering," the manifestation of its characteristics clarifies its function; suffering is the fruit of retribution, and the manifestation of this fruit of retribution reveals that accumulation (*saṃudaya*) is the characteristic of the cause.

Because the characteristic of the cause is subtle and hidden, it is called the "transformative characteristic" (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*). Some people say that seeing attachment is seeing the subtle; from the subtle, one arrives at [the truth].
"Attachment" refers to the characteristic of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*). Those in the world who suffer do so based on present phenomena and do not require a continuous succession;

therefore, it is called the "characteristic of manifestation" (*saṃdarśana-lakṣaṇa*). "Accumulation" (*samudaya*) is the functional power of karma, which necessarily involves the transformation of two moments of mind; therefore, it is called the "characteristic of transformation. "Cessation" (*nirodha*) is the characteristic of removal.
To remove that which is to be removed is precisely to remove suffering and its accumulation; the Path (*mārga*) is that which can remove them.
Furthermore, regarding the three characteristics of suffering, the following four sections explain their essence.

Furthermore, son of good family, suffering has three characteristics: the characteristic of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the characteristic of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), and the characteristic of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).

Origination consists of the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*). Cessation is the cessation of these twenty-five states of existence. The Path is the cultivation of morality, concentration, and wisdom.
Regarding "accumulation" (*samudaya*) as the twenty-five states of existence: some teachers say that the uninterrupted continuity of habitual practice is called accumulation;

other commentators say that "gathering and bringing forth" is accumulation. This accumulation can habitually continue the twenty-five states of existence and can bring forth the fruits of those twenty-five states of existence.
Furthermore, there is the establishment of the five sciences regarding the lower category of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, noble son, contaminated phenomena are of two kinds: those with cause and those with fruit. Uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava*) are also of two kinds:
those with cause and those with fruit. That which is the fruit of the contaminated is termed "suffering" (*duḥkha*); that which is the cause of the contaminated is...
That which is called the accumulation of outflow-free results is termed "Cessation," and that which is called the cause of outflow-free results is termed the "Path.
These Four Noble Truths are established based on the two sets of causes and results: those with outflows and those without outflows.
Furthermore, the eight aspects below the six further clarify that the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths are themselves the extensive essence.

Furthermore, son of good family, the eight aspects are called suffering: namely, the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging. These are able to give rise to such eight [aspects of] suffering.
That which is the dharma of suffering is called the origin; the absence of such a locus of the eight sufferings is called cessation;
and the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion are called the path.

Regarding the statement that the Ten Powers (*daśabala*) and so forth constitute the Path (*mārga*), the *Zhuangyan* (Adornment) commentary states: "The Ground of Fruition (*phalabhūmi*) is not the Path; rather, the Path is the cause.

Yet, while speaking of the 'Ten Powers,' these are differentiated within the causal stage as the cultivation of the Ten Powers and the Fearlessnesses. Kai-shan says: "The Path permeates both cause and fruition.

On the Ground of Fruition, Bodhi is taken as the Path and Nirvana as Cessation (*nirodha*). There is no distinct essence [between them], yet they are explained as two from the perspective of conventional designation."
From the departure of the good man, this second section extensively explains the Four Noble Truths, which constitutes four chapters. Regarding the Truth of Suffering, there are three parts:

first, a brief exposition of the eight sufferings; second, an extensive exposition of the eight sufferings; and third, a comprehensive reconciliation. First, as for the brief exposition, the eight sufferings are treated as eight separate chapters.
Good son, birth has five characteristics of emergence: first, initial emergence; second, reaching the end; third, growth;
fourth, emergence from the womb; and fifth, birth by species.

"Initial emergence" refers to the first reliance upon the *vijñāna*-stage (*vijñānāṅga*), wherein only the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) exists and the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are not yet complete;

this extends from the initial entry into the womb until the end of the period. "Until the end" means reaching the conclusion of one lifetime. "Growth" refers to the development through the six stages of the embryo (*kalala*, etc.).
"Emergence from the womb" refers to the time of birth. "Species" refers to the subsequent differentiation and increase of teeth, hair, and body hair after emerging from the womb.
"Long, what is aging? There are two kinds of aging: first, moment-to-moment aging; second, aging throughout one's entire life. Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, aging as growth; second, aging as decay. This is called 'aging.'"
Regarding "destruction," there are two interpretations: first, that at the time of old age, the signs of vigor are destroyed as senility and illness increase;
second, that from birth until maturity is growth, while from maturity until old age is destruction.
What is meant by "sickness"? Sickness refers to the four great poisonous serpents [the four elements] being mutually disharmonious.
Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, physical sickness; second, mental sickness. Physical sickness has five types: first, caused by water; second, caused by wind; third, caused by heat;
fourth, miscellaneous illnesses; and fifth, adventitious illnesses. Adventitious illnesses have four types: the first is overexertion beyond one's capacity.
Second, falling through forgetfulness or error; third, being struck by blades, staves, tiles, or stones;
fourth, being possessed by malevolent spirits. Mental illness also has four types: first, agitation; second, terror; third, sorrow; and fourth, delusion.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are three kinds of physical and mental illnesses. What are these three? First, those resulting from karmic retribution;
second, those arising from not being able to avoid adverse conditions; and third, those produced by the shifting of the seasons. Such are the causes and conditions.

Regarding the names of these causal factors for the classification of illness, there are diseases such as wind-disorder (*vāta*), and so forth. As for their names, they include heart-stupor (*citta-mūrchana*) and lung-disease (*pitta*).
Bloating, upward movement of qi, hiccups, a startled mind, and diarrhea—those who undergo such conditions experience headaches, eye pain, and pain in the hands, feet, and other limbs;
these are called illnesses.
Although the suffering of illness should consist of all four great elements (*mahābhūta*), only three are mentioned because the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*) is not as mobile as wind and fire;
therefore, it is omitted. Miscellaneous illnesses and adventitious illnesses already include the earth element.
What is meant by "death"? Death is the relinquishing of the body one has received; this relinquishing of the body is also of two kinds:

first, death through the exhaustion of the life-span; second, death due to external conditions. Death through the exhaustion of the life-span is also of three kinds: first, the exhaustion of the life-span but not the exhaustion of merit;
second, the exhaustion of merit but not the exhaustion of the life-span; third, the exhaustion of both merit and the life-span. As for death due to external conditions:
There are also three kinds: first, death by self-harm through improper means; second, death brought about by others through improper means; and third, death resulting from both.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of death: first, death through negligence; second, death through breaking the precepts; and third, death through the destruction of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
What is meant by death through negligence? It refers to one who slanders the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā.
What is called death through negligence? That which is called death through breaking the precepts refers to violating the prohibitions established by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
this is called death through breaking the precepts. What is called death through the destruction of the life-faculty?
The discarding of the five aggregates (skandhas) and the body is called death through the destruction of the life-faculty. Thus, it is said that death is a great suffering.
Regarding the deceased, there are three propositions concerning merit and life-span (*puṇya* and *āyus*). First, it is said that one merely loses wealth while life itself remains;
this is the exhaustion of merit while wealth remains, yet life is lost. Second, both are exhausted; these can be understood [as they stand].

As for the first proposition, it does not constitute the meaning of death. (And so forth. Hexi says: "Life-span should originally last a thousand years, but one obtains only a hundred years because merit is exhausted."
Since life also perishes along with it, one says that "merit is exhausted" rather than "life is exhausted," or "life is exhausted" rather than "merit is exhausted.

This means that although the original karma of merit was extensive and should still not yet be exhausted, because life has ended and can no longer be maintained, one says "life is exhausted" rather than "merit is exhausted.
It is understandable that both may be exhausted simultaneously. Personally, I maintain that there are two reasons why their mutual exhaustion differs: first, due to transgression...

Regarding the two causes, there are mutual distinctions between the two: [the first] involves the expenditure of wealth and the infliction of harm to bring about merit, whereas [the second] involves the mutual destruction of life in the present.
This is different from the case where one’s life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is severed due to negligence and the breaking of precepts; the latter is the opposite, termed "non-negligence.

One who maintains the precepts while giving up their life is simply said to have "destroyed life. Furthermore, another interpretation states that this is not merely giving up life, but rather the immediate commission of a transgression which is itself termed [the destruction of life].

A corpse possesses no further roots of goodness or life-force of wisdom; slandering the Dharma and promoting heresy is called negligence, while violating the four grave prohibitions is called breaking the precepts.
What is meant by the suffering of separation from the beloved? It is the destruction and dispersal of those things one holds dear.
There are also two kinds of suffering from destruction and separation: first, the destruction of the five aggregates among human beings; second, the destruction of the five aggregates among devas.
Thus, the various types of five aggregates experienced by humans and devas, when analyzed and calculated, are of immeasurable kinds;
this is called the suffering of separation from what is loved.
What is called the suffering of association with the disliked? It is the gathering together with those one does not love;
this gathering with the disliked is also of three kinds, namely: the three realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
When these three destinies are analyzed and calculated, they comprise immeasurable varieties. This is what is called the suffering of association with the disliked.
What is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks? The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks also has two aspects:
first, being unable to obtain that which one hopes for; second, exerting great effort yet failing to obtain the fruit of one's labor.
This is termed the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

What is called the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging? The suffering of the five aggregates of clinging consists of the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; therefore, it is called the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.

Regarding the five, six, seven, and eight [sufferings] as stated in the text: among the eight sufferings, the first seven have distinct entities, while the last one subsumes the seven and has no separate entity of its own.
Now, according to the scriptural text, the "intense flourishing of the five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha-upacaya*) constitutes their distinct entity;

the intense flourishing of the "wholesome or unwholesome aggregates" is itself the essence of suffering, whereas the intense flourishing of the "provisional aggregates" is not the essence of suffering (and so forth).
Next, following the "Root of Kāśyapa’s Birth," the second section extensively explains the eight sufferings, which is divided into eight parts.
First, the suffering of birth is treated in three sections: (1) clarifying that birth is the root of suffering; (2) clarifying the mutual relationship between birth and death;
and (3) clarifying the many afflictions of birth.
Kāśyapa, the roots of birth consist of these seven kinds of suffering, from the suffering of old age up to the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Kāśyapa, as for those who are decrepit, this does not apply to all; among Buddhas and devas it is invariably absent, while among humans it is indefinite—sometimes present and sometimes absent.
Kāśyapa, within the three realms, there is no one who receives a body who is not subject to birth and old age.
It must therefore be that birth is the root of all [suffering].

First, it is clarified that the suffering of birth is the root of the seven types of suffering; furthermore, by singling out one type of suffering from among the six, birth is likewise established as the root.
Regarding the second section on the relationship between birth and death among worldly beings, within the exposition of the Dharma with its analogies, there are two parts;
first, it clarifies the attachment of ordinary persons.
Kāśyapa, the minds of worldly beings are inverted and obscured; they are attached to the characteristic of birth and feel weary of old age and death.
Next, the bodhisattva’s revulsion is explained. It is not so for the bodhisattva;
having observed the faults of birth from the very beginning, he perceives them as such.

Within the analogy, there are two parts: first the analogy, then the application. Within the first analogy, there are two further points: first, the analogy of practicing revulsion, and second, the analogy of practicing craving.
The first section of the analogy is divided into four parts: first, birth is to be rejoiced in; second, death is to be loathed; third, the interrelation of birth and death;
and fourth, the explanation of how Bodhisattvas relinquish both.
Kāśyapa, it is as if there were a woman who entered another’s house; this woman was upright, her countenance beautiful, and she was adorned with fine...
Her body was adorned with necklaces and ornaments; when the host saw her, he immediately asked, "What is your name, and to whom do you belong?
The woman replied, "I am the goddess Guṇamahādevī. The host asked, "Wherever you go, what do you do?
The goddess replied, "Wherever I go, I can provide all kinds of gold and silver."
Upon hearing that there were lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, coral, amber, tridacna shells, and agate, as well as elephants, horses, carriages, and male and female slaves,
the master was filled with joy and immeasurable exultation. "By virtue of my own merit, you have come to my home," he thought,
and he immediately burned incense, scattered flowers, and made offerings with reverence and prostrations.

The initial exchange consists of six points; in reality, there is no one asking or answering questions, but rather the arising of objects and the Bodhisattva’s contemplative wisdom mutually investigate each other, provisionally assuming the roles of guest and host.
"Women" is a metaphor for the fruit of arising, which deceives ordinary people and causes them to give rise to defiled attachment—this is likened to women.
Because the Bodhisattva’s wisdom contemplates the initial emergence of arising, it is said that she enters the house, beautiful and graceful.

Lai (Li) represents the joy and delight in things; the place where those who wear necklaces (*kaṇṭhābharaṇa*) produce fruit is a site of abundant splendor. The "master" is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva;
the "woman" who is examined and questioned is a metaphor for the production of fruit in response to wisdom (*jñāna*).
Next, outside the gate, he again beheld the second illumination on the loathsomeness of death.
Furthermore, outside the gate, he saw another woman whose form was hideous, her clothes tattered and filthy with much grime and grease, her skin cracked and her complexion as pale as mugwort.
Having seen her, he asked: "What is your name, and to whom do you belong?"
The woman replied, "My name is Kṛṣṇā. He asked again, "For what reason are you named Kṛṣṇā?
The woman replied, "Wherever I go, all the wealth and treasures in that household are made to perish and decline.
Upon hearing this, the master immediately took up a sharp knife and said, "If you do not leave, I shall take your life! The woman replied:
"You are extremely foolish and devoid of wisdom.
Since there are six deaths that follow after birth, it is said that 'dying outside the gate' is a fruit that deceives people; it is likened to a woman who is ugly.
Because the state of death destroys the fruit, causing all things to become base and evil, and because birth and death are mutually contradictory, it is so called."

Because the blood and qi have been completely exhausted by the cracking [of the skin], it is said that the moxa has turned white. Regarding the "Master holding the knife," there are two interpretations.
Yecheng says: "Diligence and intense aversion are likened to holding a knife. Zhaoti says: "Take wisdom as the knife;
if death does not depart, cultivate wisdom and severance."
Third, regarding the questioner’s inquiry on the mutual connection between this life and the next:
the hostess asked, "For what reason do you call me a foolish woman lacking wisdom? She replied, "The one in your household is my elder sister;
I am always with her in every movement and stay. If you drive me away, you must also drive her away."
The master returned inside and asked about the goddess Puṇyavatī. A woman appeared outside and said, "I am your younger sister;
is this truly so? Puṇyavatī replied, "Truly, she is my sister. I and this sister always travel and dwell together, never parting from one another.
Wherever we reside, I always bring about what is good, while she always brings about what is evil; I produce benefit, while she produces ruin."
If you love me, you should also love her; if you see and respect me, you should also respect her.
She was my elder sister before birth and my younger sister after death; since we were never separated, it is said that we returned together.
As for the questioner who asked about returning to heaven, the Bodhisattva examined birth and knew it is coexistent with death.
The host immediately spoke, clarifying the fourth section on the Bodhisattva’s simultaneous relinquishment, which is divided into three parts: first, simultaneous relinquishment.
The host said: "If there are such matters of good or evil, I shall not accept them at all; you may each depart as you please."
The two went together.
At that time, the two girls took each other back to their dwelling place;
the older translation says "Golden Heart" (Jinxin), and since she had already returned, it states "returned to her dwelling place."
Third, the Bodhisattvas rejoice.
At that time, the host, seeing them depart, felt immeasurable joy and exultation in his heart.
At this point, the two daughters descend; second, for the sake of illustrating greed, there are four sections in the cycle of coming and going, the first of which clarifies their being together.
They went toward an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
At that time, the two women again followed one another to a poor household;
it is called a "poor household" because the ordinary person lacked merit.
The poor man, seeing this,
felt joy arise in his heart and invited them, saying, "From this day forward, I pray that you two will dwell constantly in my home."
Under the third point of Śrīdevī’s speech, she examines and rebukes the ordinary mind regarding its objects of perception.
Śrīdevī said: "We were previously driven away by others; for what reason do you now both request that we remain?"
The poor man replied: "In the fourth stage, the ordinary mind responds to its objects.
The poor man replied: 'If you now think of me, and I, for your sake, shall in turn show respect to him, then let us both invite him to stay in my house.'"
Since the arising of joy is precisely what leads to the acceptance of death, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva first provides a simile below to illustrate the bodhisattva’s weariness with existence.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise thus: he does not wish to be born in the heavens, for birth is inevitably followed by old age.
Because they are subject to old age, sickness, and death, these [beings] are both abandoned [by the wise], and there is never any intention to accept them.
Subsequently, they conjoin with the craving of ordinary people.
Because foolish ordinary people do not know the faults and afflictions of old age, sickness, death, and so forth, they greedily grasp at the two phenomena of birth and death.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, regarding the third section on the faults of birth among the lower castes of the Brahmins, there are five similes in total;
the first simile concerns shallow goodness and has four parts.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a young, childish Brahmin boy who, driven by hunger, sees human excrement in a pit.
There was an *āmra* fruit, which he immediately took.
The Brahmin of pure conduct is like a bodhisattva who first wishes to cultivate the path of ultimate purity through *prajñā*.

The young child whose understanding and practice are shallow and weak is like one oppressed by hunger; those oppressed by the sufferings of the three miserable realms are like the fruit within the filth. Suffering is impermanence.
Among these, there is the fruit of rebirth in heaven.
A wise person, observing the two lower types of deep practitioners, censures them.
Having perceived this with wisdom and insight, he reproaches them, saying: "O Brahmin, your lineage is pure; for what reason have you taken this?"
"Those foul fruits from within the dung.
Having heard this, the youth lowered his three shallow vessels and felt ashamed.
Having heard this, the youth was abashed with shame and immediately replied, "I truly do not eat them; it is for the sake of washing them clean."
He then abandons them.
It is said that he abandons them because he does not crave celestial pleasures, desiring instead to cultivate the Path therein.
Regarding the words "The Wise One speaks," this refers to the exhortation by the four bodhisattvas below to abandon [them].
The wise man says to you: "You are greatly deluded; if you discard it now, you should not have taken it in the first place.
Good son, the lower analogy applies only to the latter two cases and not to the former two.
Good son, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: regarding this birth, he neither accepts nor rejects it, just as that wise man rebuked the boy.
Ordinary people delight in birth and loathe death, just as that boy took the fruit and then threw it away.
Furthermore, the following is the second simile.
Moreover, Kāśyapa, it is as if there were a person at a crossroads with a vessel filled to the brim with food, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor, which he wished to sell.
Then, another person came from afar, hungry, parched, and exhausted, and saw that the food was perfect in color, fragrance, and flavor.
He pointed and asked, "What is this food? The host replied, "This is superior food, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor.
If one eats this food, one gains beauty and strength, can eliminate hunger and thirst, and is able to see the various devas;
it has only one drawback, which is that at the end of one's life [one must die]. Having heard this, the man immediately thought: "I have no need now for beauty, strength, or seeing the devas."
Nor does he intend to die immediately upon saying this: "If you should pass away after eating this food, why are you selling it here now?
The owner of the food replies: "A wise person would never consent to buy this;
only a fool, unaware of this matter, would greedily eat it by paying me a high price. Good son, such is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
It is likewise so that they do not wish to be born in the heavens to obtain celestial form or power, nor do they seek to behold the devas.

Why is this? Because they cannot escape the various sufferings and afflictions. Ordinary people, being foolish and deluded, greedily accept whatever place of birth they encounter, for they do not perceive old age, sickness, and death.
There is a person who represents the Buddha; the crossroads represent the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*); the initial vessel for receiving a body represents the scriptural teachings;
the abundant food represents the Buddha’s preaching of the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths to invite the fruits of the human and celestial realms;

"selling" by means of this refers to transforming beings who have come from afar, representing those coming from the evil realms; being "hungry, emaciated, and exhausted" represents the weight of suffering; and "asking questions" represents [the seekers].
"Is this truly so? The Master replied, "It is like the Buddha's answer: there is but one poison;
none can escape impermanence, for they shall die and perish. He further inquired again, "If all is impermanent, why does the Tathāgata cause people to cultivate it?
Therefore he asked, "Why do you sell it? The Buddha replied once more, "Profound wisdom causes one to abandon the foolish and shallow commoners."
Now, the first instance of receiving [him] can be seen in the two analogies concerning the third and fourth [cases].
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a poisonous tree whose roots can kill a person, as can its branches, trunk, stem, joints, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruit.
He is also able to kill the five aggregates experienced in all places of rebirth within the twenty-five states of existence;
it is likewise for all such things that he can kill.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like excrement and filth: whether small or large, both are equally foul-smelling. The birth of a son of good family is also like this. Even if...
Those who undergo eighty thousand [years], down to those of ten years, all likewise experience suffering.
This is like a steep precipice; this is the fifth analogy for the fruit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is as if on a steep precipice there is grass covering it, and on the edge of that other shore there is much nectar (*amṛta*).
If there were someone who ate it, they would live for a thousand years, forever free from all illnesses and dwelling in peace and happiness.

Yet, because ordinary, foolish people crave its flavor, they do not realize that beneath it lies a vast, deep pit; they step forward to seize it, unaware that their feet will slip and they will fall into the pit and die.
When the wise person knows this, they abandon it and depart far away. Good son, so it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
It is likewise so; one would not even desire to accept the exquisite food of the heavens, much less that of ordinary people in the human realm.
How much more so for one who must swallow iron balls in hell—how could such a person fail to refuse the exquisite delicacies of humans and devas?
Kāśyapa, by means of these analogies and countless other boundless parables, you should know that this birth is truly [suffering].
Mahākāśyapa, this is called a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra contemplating the suffering of birth.
The grass covering above is a metaphor for the provisional designation of a "self" and its continuity within saṃsāra; the frequent consumption of ambrosia is a metaphor for false pleasure;
the deep pit is a metaphor for the three miserable realms; and the tripping of the foot is a metaphor for the severance of the life-faculty.

The second contemplation on old age and the third contemplation on illness are both understandable from their respective texts. However, while birth must necessarily precede death, illness does not necessarily follow old age.
In this present text, old age is mentioned first and illness second because when one is young and ill, there is still hope for recovery;
whereas when one is old and illness hastens death, it is as swift as a collapsing mountain being further dismantled. Therefore, illness is clarified as occurring after old age.
Sickness.
Kāśyapa, how does a bodhisattva contemplate the suffering of old age within this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra?
Old age can cause one to become perverse and rebellious, it can cause upward-heaving breaths, and it can destroy valor, strength, mindfulness, perseverance, the vigor of youth, and arrogance.
Arrogance, complacency, self-indulgence, the ability to cause backaches [in others], indolence, and laziness lead one to be despised by others.
Kāśyapa, it is like a pond filled with lotus flowers, blooming and radiant, most lovely to behold; yet when heaven sends down hail, they are all destroyed.
Son of good family, old age is likewise; it can utterly destroy youthful vigor and beautiful complexion.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a king who has a wise minister well-versed in the art of war.
When a hostile king resists and acts in defiance, the king dispatches this minister to campaign against him; he immediately captures the enemy and brings him before the king.
Old age is also like this: it seizes one’s youthful vigor and delivers it over to the King of Death. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a broken axle that can no longer function.
Furthermore, old age is likewise useless; it is of no further use.

Moreover, Kāśyapa, it is like a wealthy household that possesses much wealth and treasure—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, tridacna shell, and agate—if hostile bandits were to enter that house, they would immediately plunder and seize everything until it was completely emptied.
Son of good family, the prime of youth and its fine complexion are also like this.
Thus, one is constantly plundered by the thief of old age. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a poor man who covets exquisite food and fine, soft garments;
though he longs for them, he cannot obtain them. Son of good family, old age is also like this:
although there is a greedy mind that desires to enjoy wealth and pleasure, indulging in the five sensual desires, one cannot obtain them. Furthermore...
Its leaves are like those of a land tortoise, yet its heart constantly longs for water. Good son, human beings are also like this:
once they have been withered by old age, their hearts constantly recall the pleasures of the five desires experienced in their youth.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is just as when the lotuses of the autumn moon are all objects of delight for everyone, yet they eventually wither and turn yellow.
Just as that which people loathe and despise, so too is it with a virtuous man in the full prime of his youth and vigor—he is beloved by all;
yet when old age arrives, he is likewise loathed and despised by the multitude. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like sugarcane:
once it has been pressed, the dregs have no more flavor. So too is it with the full prime of youth and vigor: once it has been crushed by old age, it is devoid of essence.
There are three kinds of flavors: first, the flavor of renunciation; second, the flavor of recitation and study; and third, the flavor of seated meditation.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like the full moon at night, which possesses abundant radiance, whereas during the day it is not so. Good son, people are also like this: in their youth they are upright and dignified, with magnificent features;
in old age they become frail and decrepit, their physical form and spirit withered and exhausted. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like...
There was a king who always governed his kingdom and ruled his people with the True Dharma; he was upright and sincere without crookedness, compassionate and fond of giving.
At one time, he was destroyed by a hostile nation and, wandering in exile, fled far away to another land. When the people of that other land saw him, they felt pity for him and all spoke thus:
"Great King, in the past you governed the kingdom with the True Dharma and did not wrong the myriad people; how is it that [you have come to this]?"
Once one has wandered into this state of exile, O son of good family, a person is likewise so;
having been utterly ruined by sorrow and old age, they constantly praise the deeds performed during their youth. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a lamp wick that relies solely upon oil;
once the oil is exhausted, its power will not endure for long. Son of good family, a person is likewise so, relying solely upon the "oil" of youth.
Once the rich fat has been exhausted, how can the wick of old age remain for long?
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a dried-up river that cannot benefit humans, non-humans, birds, or beasts;
son of good family, a person is likewise dried up by old age and cannot benefit from any of their activities. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like the edge of a riverbank...
Just as a tree on a precipice will surely fall when it encounters a violent wind, so too, son of good family, is a person at the perilous brink of old age;
once the wind of death arrives, there is no power to remain.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, just as a broken axle cannot bear a heavy load, so too, son of good family, is one who has grown old unable to inquire about or receive any wholesome dharmas. Furthermore...
"Kāśyapa, it is like an infant who is despised by others; good son, old age is likewise always despised and reviled by all.
Kāśyapa, through these and other immeasurable and boundless parables, you should know that this old age is truly a great suffering.
Kāśyapa, this is called a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra."
Regarding the contemplation of the suffering of old age:
Kāśyapa, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra contemplate the suffering of illness?
That which is called "illness" can destroy all matters of peace and happiness, just as a rain of hailstones damages and destroys grain.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a person who harbors resentment, constantly dwelling in sorrow and filled with fear.
Good son, all sentient beings are likewise; they are always afraid of the suffering of illness and their hearts are burdened with grief.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is as if there were a man of handsome appearance whom the wife of a king loved with desire, and she sent a messenger to summon him by force.
When he engaged in sexual intercourse with her, the king captured him, gouged out one eye, cut off one ear, and severed his hands and feet.
At that time, this man’s appearance was transformed and altered; he was loathed and despised by others. Good son, people are also like this:
though they were previously handsome and possessed of complete eyes and ears, once they are beset and oppressed by the suffering of illness, they become objects of contempt for all people.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, that which is loathed and despised is like the plantain, the bamboo, the reed, and the mule, which die as soon as they bear fruit.

Good son, human beings are also like this: they die when they fall ill. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like the wheel-turning king (cakravartin) and his minister of war, who always lead the way while the king follows behind;
it is also like the fish-king, the ant-king, the conch-king, and the ox-king.
When the merchant leader walked ahead, all these crowds followed him, none abandoning him;
noble son, the death of a wheel-turning king is likewise thus, constantly followed by the minister of illness, never parting from him.
Fish, ants, conches, oxen, merchant leaders, and sick kings are likewise always pursued by the hosts of death. Kāśyapa, this is the illness.
The causal conditions are as follows: so-called suffering, affliction, grief, lamentation, and mental and physical unease; being oppressed and harmed by enemies and thieves;
the destruction of the life-preserving float and the dismantling of the bridge; the ability to plunder the very root of right livelihood;
the ability to destroy vigor, beauty, power, and well-being; the abandonment of shame and remorse; and the ability to cause the body and mind to burn with anguish.
With these and other immeasurable and boundless parables, one should know that the suffering of illness is a great suffering.
Kāśyapa, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra of the Great Vehicle contemplating the suffering of illness.
In the commentary on the suffering of illness, it is stated that "body and mind are at peace"; there are two interpretations of this. First, some say that peace itself is the illness.

For example, the story of Daishu and Shōshu, father and son, who were separated for ten years and upon meeting again by day, celebrated their reunion, only to die that very night; such "peace" is indeed illness.

The fourth contemplation on the suffering of death also has two parts: first, the actual contemplation of death; second, the lamentation following the death, beginning with "Now, as for those who die...
Regarding the first section, Kāśyapa asked: "How does a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra contemplate the suffering of death? It is as follows:
Because death can burn and destroy, Kāśyapa, it is like the fire calamity that arises and can burn everything except for the second dhyāna, because its power does not reach there.
Son of good family, the fire of death is also like this: it can burn everything except for the Bodhisattva abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, because its force cannot reach him.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like the water calamity that arises...
All are swept away, except for those who have attained the power of the third dhyāna, as it does not reach them. Good son, the water of death is likewise;
it sweeps away all, except for Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, when the calamity of wind arises, it can blow away and utterly destroy everything, except for those who have attained the power of the fourth dhyāna, as it does not reach them. Good son...
The death of a son is like the wind; it can blow out and extinguish everything that exists, with the sole exception of a Bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions is it that in the fourth dhyāna the wind cannot blow, water cannot sweep away, and fire cannot burn? The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "Good man..."

Son, because all internal and external defects are entirely absent in that fourth dhyāna, noble son, the defect of the first dhyāna is that internally there is vitarka and vicāra, and externally there is the calamity of fire;
the defect of the second dhyāna is that internally there is prīti, and externally there is the calamity of water;
the defect of the third dhyāna is that internally there is āśvāsa-praśvāsa (inhalation and exhalation), and externally there is the calamity of wind. Noble son, as for that fourth dhyāna, internally—
Because all external calamities and afflictions are entirely absent, no disasters can reach them. Good son, it is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
dwelling securely in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, all internal and external calamities and afflictions are completely exhausted;
therefore, the King of Death cannot reach him. Furthermore, good son, it is like the garuḍa bird.
It can devour and digest all kinds of treasures, such as dragons, fish, gold, and silver, except for the vajra, which it cannot digest.

Good son, the dead garuḍa is also like this: it can devour and digest all sentient beings, yet it alone cannot digest a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa. Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
For example, all the grasses and trees on a riverbank are swept away by a sudden surge of floodwaters and flow into the great ocean;
only the willows are spared because they are supple. Son of good family, it is the same for all sentient beings:
they are all carried along into the sea of death, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Next, Kāśyapa, just as Nārāyaṇa is able to subdue all other wrestlers except for the great wind, because it is unimpeded;

so too, son of good family, the deceased Nārāyaṇa is likewise able to subdue all sentient beings, except for Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa. Why is this? Because [they] are unimpeded.

Because they are unimpeded. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a person who, amidst enemies and those he hates, feigns intimacy and pursues them constantly, like a shadow following a form, seeking an opportunity to kill them.
Because that enemy is cautious, firm, and well-prepared, this person is unable to kill him. Son of good family, the death of an enemy is also like this; it is constant.
When a being seeks to kill another, they are unable to do so against a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who abides in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Why is this? It is because such a Bodhisattva is never heedless.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a sudden, violent rain of vajra that utterly destroys medicinal herbs, trees, forests, mountains, earth, sand, shards, stones, and gold.
"O son of good family, just as all things made of silver or lapis lazuli cannot destroy the supreme jewel of diamond, so too is it with the rain of death;
it can destroy all sentient beings, except for the Diamond Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, just as the golden-winged bird is able to devour all dragons..."
Only those sons of good family who have received the Three Refuges cannot be devoured; the death of a golden-winged garuḍa is likewise:
it can devour all immeasurable sentient beings, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas dwelling in the three concentrations. What are the three concentrations?
They are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, when the Māra-viper bites anyone, even if there is an efficacious incantation, [it cannot save them].
Even the most excellent and superior medicines can do nothing for such a case; only the *Agada* star-mantra can cause it to be healed.
Son of good family, being bitten by the venom of death is likewise beyond the power of all medical prescriptions;
only the Great Nirvāṇa mantra of the Bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna can remove it. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a person who has been punished by a king.
If one who is angry with another person can be released by offering gentle, kind words or by presenting wealth and treasures, then one might escape;
however, O son of good family, it is not so with the King of Death. Even if one offers gentle words, money, and precious jewels, one cannot escape.
What constitutes the suffering of death? If the breath has not yet ceased, it is due to birth and not death;
if the breath has already ceased and there is no further sensation, it is the experience of hell, which pertains to a future body and is not related to the suffering of death.

This matter is difficult to know, just as when one asks whether "extinction" occurs at the time it has not yet been extinguished or at the time it has already been extinguished—it is difficult to determine definitively from either perspective.

"It is like that which exists originally but is now absent, or was originally absent but now exists" (and so forth). Now, we simply take the state where [life] is about to cease but has not yet ceased as being the "suffering of death.
To discuss this in depth, although Bodhisattvas have not yet completely escaped death, it is said that "except for those Bodhisattvas who abide in *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding these three interpretations: the first identifies the Buddha as a Bodhisattva; the second refers to a Bodhisattva of the Golden Mind (*suvarṇacitta*) who is one step removed [from Buddhahood].

Regarding the three clouds of attaining Buddhahood: although a Bodhisattva of the first stage has not yet escaped birth and death, they seek Nirvana with such resolve that they are not disturbed by birth and death.
Now it is clarified that this initial understanding refers to a Bodhisattva who corresponds [to the teaching]; this does not accord with the sutra.

Next, regarding the single turning of the golden mind—this is precisely death; for what reason is it eliminated? As for the subsequent understanding, although the Bodhisattva is not disturbed by death...
Though in chaos, one does not escape death; for what reason is it said that death is eliminated?

That which is "eliminated" refers to the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), for whom afflictions are themselves bodhi and birth-and-death are themselves nirvana, such that they can no longer be extinguished. Birth-and-death is neither birth-and-death nor is it nirvana;
since even birth-and-death cannot bring about birth-and-death, how could [anything else] bring about birth-and-death? It is like non-birth-and-death.
This Bodhisattva is thus protected and not harmed by birth-and-death. As the text says:
"Just as a vajra-rain can shatter all things, yet this rain itself cannot be shattered by a vajra;

if it could not shatter [the other], its utility would not be established, and if it were itself shattered, its quality of solidity would not be established" (and so forth). Death harms all things like a vajra-rain.
Only the Bodhisattva is not harmed by it; the subsequent metaphor of the vajra should be understood as follows:
while ordinary vajras may be shattered and scattered, they cannot harm a massive, immovable vajra mountain; likewise, the Bodhisattva is not killed by death. Regarding the *māra* serpent:
the Master of Hexi (Hexi Shi) says it is a black snake whose venom kills a person upon merely touching their clothes, and others who touch those clothes also die.
As for the Kṛttikā asterism, this asterism appears in the eighth month; if anyone obtains the mantra of this asterism, they can eliminate its poison.
Next, regarding the deceased, there are ten phrases below that express grief and pain most poignantly; if separated, they immediately form two [sections].
Ten phrases.
Good son, as for death: it is like being in a perilous place where there are no provisions; the destination is far distant and one has no companion;
one travels day and night without knowing its limits; it is deep, dark, and gloomy, with no lamp-light, and one enters into nothingness.
Though it has gates and a location, and although there is no specific site of pain where it can be treated, it cannot be stopped when it approaches;
once it arrives, one cannot escape it. It causes no physical injury, yet those who see it are filled with grief and distress. It is not an ugly form, yet it strikes terror into people.
Lying upon the body, it cannot be perceived. Kāśyapa, by means of these and other countless, boundless parables, [he explained this].
One should know that birth and death are truly great suffering. Kāśyapa, this is called a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra of the Mahāyāna contemplating the suffering of death.
In places of peril and difficulty, illness is the heaviest suffering; those who lack provisions are said to be destitute of wholesome dharmas.
Situated in a remote and distant place, its path is endless; being without companions, the solitary soul departs alone with no one following.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, it never rests; moving constantly through day and night, there is neither front nor back, and thus it is boundless.
Like a pit ten thousand fathoms deep, it is said to be profound; because of internal darkness, it does not illuminate the external.
Therefore, there is no lamp-light; death is a path of exhaustion where all roads and ground are blocked, hence it is said that one enters through no gate.
It is also said that death does not enter through the six sense-faculties, hence there are no gates. Since there must be a place from which one comes, it is said that there is a location.
At that time, one is dazed and bewildered, hence it is said that although there is no place of pain, a skilled physician stands with hands folded in reverence.
Because it is brought about by one's own hands, it is said that it cannot be cured; because it cannot be restrained even by sages and saints, it is said that there is no stopping it as it approaches;
because upon arrival one finds no release, it is said that death is solemn and grave; because it is not a physical injury or execution, it is said that nothing can destroy it;

because friends and kin weep in sorrow, it is said that those who see it are afflicted with grief; and because it is not something to be devoured by tigers, wolves, birds, or beasts, [it is said that it cannot be consumed].
It is said that there is no one who does not fear death; therefore, it is said that this causes terror in people.

Because it follows immediately after the aggregate-body (*skandha-kāya*), it is said to be spread around the body. Because its quality—whether good or evil—cannot be measured, it is said that one is unaware of it oneself.
According to this meaning, the cessation of life within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) constitutes the suffering of death.
Fifth is the contemplation on the suffering of separation from what is loved.
Kāśyapa, how does a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra contemplate the suffering of separation from what is loved?
It is as has been said: the suffering of separation from what is loved can serve as the root of all sufferings.
From craving arises sorrow; from craving arises fear. If one is free from craving, what sorrow or fear could there be?

Because of the conditions of craving, sorrow and suffering arise; because of sorrow and suffering, they cause sentient beings to experience aging and decay, and the suffering of separation from what is loved—namely, death.
Noble son, through such separation, various subtle [sufferings] can arise.
I shall now analyze and reveal these various sufferings for you, O son of good family.
In the past, when the human lifespan was immeasurable, there was a king named Supratiṣṭhita.

During that time, he served as a crown prince for eighty-four thousand years, and he reigned as king for another eighty-four thousand years. At that time, a fleshy tumor grew upon the crown of the king’s head.
That blister was as soft as *tūla* cotton and as fine as *karpāsa* silk; it grew gradually without causing any distress.
When the ten months were fully completed, the blister burst open, and a boy was born. His form was upright and extraordinary, with few equals;
his features were distinct, making him the foremost among men. King Pitṛpati rejoiced and named him Mūrdhaja (Crown-Born). At that time, King Supratiṣṭhita...
He immediately entrusted the affairs of state to Mūrdhaja, abandoned his palace, wife, children, and retinue, and entered the mountains to practice the Way for a full eighty-four thousand years.
At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, Mūrdhaja was atop a high tower, having bathed and observed the fast;
then, from the eastern direction, there appeared a precious golden wheel, complete with a thousand spokes, hub, and rim, which did not depend [on human effort].
The artisan appeared spontaneously, having arrived to attend to him. King Māndhātṛ then thought to himself:

"In the past, I heard a seer with five supernormal powers say that if a Kṣatriya king, on the fifteenth day, stands upon a high tower, bathes, and observes the fast, there shall appear a golden wheel with a thousand spokes, complete with hub and rim, not fashioned by any artisan."
One should know that the one who has come to respond through such accomplishment shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
Furthermore, he thought: "I shall now test it. He then supported the precious wheel with his left hand, held a censer in his right hand, placed his right knee upon the ground, and made this vow:
"If this golden wheel-treasure is truly not false, it should proceed as in the past for a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
When the Dharma-practice of the noble king had made this vow, the precious golden wheel ascended into the void, pervaded the ten directions, and then returned to rest upon the left hand of Mūrdhaja.
At that time, Mūrdhaja’s heart was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation, and he spoke these words:
"I shall now certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King. Not long thereafter, there appeared again...
The Elephant Treasure was of majestic and upright appearance, like a white lotus, with its seven limbs touching the ground. Having seen it emerge from his crown, he further thought:

"In the past, I heard a seer possessing the five supernatural powers say that if a Wheel-Turning King, on the fifteenth day, stands upon a high tower, bathes, and observes the fast, and if there is an Elephant Treasure of majestic and upright appearance like a white lotus with its seven limbs..."
One who comes supporting himself upon the earth should know that this king is indeed a holy sovereign. He further thought, "I shall now put him to the test.
He then held up an incense burner, placed his right knee upon the ground, and made this vow:
"O White Elephant Treasure, if this is truly not false, you should act according to the path and dharma practiced by the past Wheel-Turning Holy Kings. Having made this vow, it was then white.
The elephant-treasure traveled from dawn until dusk, circling the eight directions as far as the limits of the great ocean, before returning to its original place.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja was filled with immense joy and leaped for boundless delight, exclaiming: "I am now certainly a Wheel-Turning Sage-King.
Not long thereafter, the horse-treasure appeared; it was a deep azure color with a golden mane and tail, and King Mūrdhaja [mounted] it.

Having seen this, he further thought: "In the past, I heard a rishi possessing the five supernatural powers say that if a Wheel-Turning King, on the fifteenth day, stands upon a high tower after bathing and observing the fast, and if there is a horse-treasure of deep blue-black color with a golden mane and tail that comes to serve him, it should be known that this king is indeed a Holy Emperor. He then thought again: "Now, I..."
Upon testing it, one should take hold of the incense burner, place the right knee upon the ground, and make this vow:
"If this dark-blue horse treasure is truly not false, it should follow the path and dharma traversed by the past wheel-turning sage-kings.

Having made this vow, the dark-blue horse treasure, from morning until evening, circles through the eight directions as far as the limits of the great ocean, and then returns to its original place. At that time...
Māndhātṛ’s heart was filled with immeasurable great joy and exultation, and he spoke these words: "I am now certainly a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
Not long thereafter, there appeared the Woman-Jewel (strī-ratna), whose physical form was upright, exquisite, and unsurpassed;
she was neither tall nor short, neither too pale nor too dark, and from every pore of her body issued the fragrance of sandalwood, while her breath was as pure and fragrant as blue lotus.
Padmā’s eyes could see for a distance of one *yojana*; her hearing and sense of smell were likewise so.
Her tongue was vast and broad, capable of covering her face; its color was fine and thin like a leaf of red copper.

Her mental consciousness was sharp and wise, possessing great insight, and she always spoke gentle words to all sentient beings. When this woman touched the king’s robe with her hand, he immediately knew [her thoughts].
The king’s body was at ease, and he also knew the object of the king’s mental focus. At that time, King Mūrdhaja again thought to himself:
"If there were a woman who could know the king's mind, she would be the Woman-Jewel (strī-ratna).
Not long thereafter, within the royal palace, there spontaneously appeared a precious maṇi jewel made of pure blue lapis lazuli, as large as a chariot wheel, which was capable of—

In the darkness, it illuminates for one *yojana*; if the heavens send down rain with drops as thick as axle-shafts, the power of this jewel can act as a great canopy, covering one *yojana* and blocking this heavy rain so that it does not fall through. At that time, King Mūrdhaja again thought:
"If a Wheel-turning King possesses such a precious jewel, he must surely be a holy sovereign; before long, there will be a master [of this realm]."
The ministers of the treasury emerged spontaneously, possessing abundant wealth and immeasurable riches; their storehouses were overflowing and lacked for nothing.
By the power of his retributive eye-faculty, he was able to see clearly all hidden treasures within the earth, and whatever the king thought of, they could provide it.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja wished to test him further, so they set out together by boat and entered [the sea].
The Great Ocean addressed the Minister of Treasures, saying, "I now desire to obtain a treasury of rare and extraordinary jewels.
Having heard this, the minister immediately stirred the waters of the great ocean with both hands; at that moment, ten jewel treasuries emerged from the tips of his ten fingers.
He presented them to the Holy King and said to him, "O Great King, you may use these as you please. As for those remaining, they shall be cast back into the great ocean. At that time...
Māndhātṛ’s heart was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation, and he further thought to himself: "I am now certainly a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
Not long thereafter, a minister of the military appeared spontaneously, one who was brave, fierce, and strategic, possessing the foremost counsel and skill in the four types of troops.
If they were fit for battle, he presented them to the Sage King; if they were unfit, he withdrew them.
It causes those who have not yet been subdued to be subdued, and it has the power to protect those already subdued.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja thought again: "If a Wheel-Turning King possesses such a military treasure, one should know for certain that he is a Wheel-Turning Holy King.
Then, the Wheel-Turning Holy Emperor Mūrdhaja addressed his ministers: "You should all know this Jambudvīpa..."
"Jambudvīpa is peaceful, secure, and prosperous; I have now already attained the seven treasures and am fully endowed with a thousand sons.
What more remains for me to do? The ministers replied, "Indeed, Great King! Pūrvavideha has not yet submitted to your virtue. Your Majesty should now go there.
