At that time, the Holy King, together with the seven treasures and his entire retinue, flew through the air and proceeded to Pūrvavideha.
"Videha! The people of that land have joyfully submitted to my rule. He further addressed his great ministers:
"Jambudvīpa and Pūrvavideha are peaceful, prosperous, and flourishing; their inhabitants have all come to submit to me. I am endowed with the seven treasures and possess a full thousand sons.
What more remains to be done? The ministers replied, "Yes, indeed, Great King. However, Aparagoyānī has not yet [submitted]."
At that time, the Holy King returned to virtue and, together with his seven treasures and entire retinue, flew through the air to Aparagoyānī.
Once he arrived there, the people of that land likewise submitted and took refuge in him. He then addressed his ministers:
"In Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, and this Aparagoyānī, all are now peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, and their populations are flourishing."
"Having brought the seven treasures under his sway and being endowed with a full thousand sons, what further remains for him to do?
The ministers replied, "Indeed, Great King, Uttarakuru in the north has not yet been converted.
At that time, the Holy King, together with the seven treasures and his entire retinue, flew through the air and went to Uttarakuru. Once he arrived there, the people of that land rejoiced.
King Guide (Guide) again addressed his ministers: "The four continents are peaceful, prosperous, and joyful; the population is flourishing and has all turned to me for refuge.
The seven treasures are perfected and I am endowed with a thousand sons. What more remains to be done? The ministers replied:
"Indeed, O Holy King, the lifespan in the Heaven of the Thirty-three is exceedingly long, and they dwell in peace and happiness. The bodies of those gods are upright and majestic."
The palace, couches, and bedding where the Peerless One resides are all made of the seven treasures. Relying on his celestial merit, he has not yet come to submit;

you should now go to subdue him and bring him under control. At that time, the Holy King, together with the seven treasures and his entire retinue, soared through the void up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
There he saw a tree, its color a vibrant green-blue, and the Holy King—
Having seen it, he immediately asked the minister, "What color is this? The minister replied, "This is the Pārijātaka tree;
during the three months of summer, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven constantly enjoy themselves and take pleasure beneath it.
He then saw another white color, like a white cloud, and asked the minister again, "What color is that? The minister replied, "That is the Sudharmā hall."
In the Dharma Hall, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven constantly gather to discuss matters concerning humans and devas.

Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra, Lord of the Gods, knowing that King Mūrdhaja had already arrived outside, went out to meet him. Having seen him, he took his hand and ascended the Sudharmā Hall, where they sat together sharing a seat.
At that time, the physical forms and appearances of the two kings were indistinguishable from one another; there was only...
The difference between them is merely in their blinking. At that time, the Holy King immediately gave rise to this thought:

"I should now rather depose him from his royal position and take up residence therein as the Heavenly King. O unwholesome man, at that time Śakra-devānām-indra received, upheld, read, and recited the Mahāyāna sūtras;
he revealed, analyzed, and expounded them for others, yet he had not yet fully mastered their profound meanings.
Because of the power of having extensively read, recited, received, upheld, analyzed, and explained this for others, this son of good family possesses great majesty and virtue.
However, once King Mūrdhagata conceived an evil thought toward Śakra, he immediately fell back to Jambudvīpa;
separated from those dear to him among gods and humans, he experienced great suffering and affliction, and further encountered a malignant disease.
Even at the time of his death, Śakra was that Cakravartin King Kāśyapa Buddha, and I myself was that very person.
Son of good family, you should know that such suffering of separation from the beloved is extremely great.
Son of good family, if even a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva remembers such sufferings of separation from the beloved from the past, how much more so for a Bodhisattva who dwells [in this state]?
In the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one should not fail to contemplate the suffering of separation from loved ones in the present life.

That which arises from the condition of separation is itself the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). If one speaks of the result within the cause of the suffering of change, it refers to the sensation of pleasure as its essence;
now, it is likewise here, where "affectionate love" is pointed out as the suffering of separation, and the text clarifies its relinquishment.
When one's beloved body ends its life, it constitutes the suffering of death;

since that has already occurred in a previous existence, the present taking away of what was beloved—the body, beloved relatives, and the environment of dependent retribution—is the suffering of separation from the beloved (*priyaviprayoga-duḥkha*). The Commentary explains:
"It is easy to separate from others, but difficult to separate from one's own kin; it is easy to separate from one's kin, but difficult to separate from one's parents."

It is easy to detach from one's own body, but difficult to detach from one's own mind; it is easy to detach from one's own thoughts, but difficult for one born from the crown of the head (Mūrdhaja) to do so.
Mūrdhaja was born of moisture; according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, a human being standing beside a celestial being is like a beggar standing beside a king.

How can it be said that the two kings are similar? Indeed, Mūrdhaja attained his status as a celestial through his merit (*puṇya*); if he were one who possessed actual retribution (*vipāka*), this would not be the case.
Furthermore, because the lifespan of the Heavenly Kings is long, their blinking is infrequent; because the lifespan of human kings is short, their blinking is frequent.

As for the gold wheel being exceedingly heavy such that others cannot lift it, the King makes it light through the power of his virtue when it ought to be heavy. Regarding the term *māo-wei* (髦尾): ancient readers read this as *meng-wei* (蒙尾), but this is not so.
For the "short" version, the character is simply written as *mao* (毛); for the "long" version, the radical *biao* (髟) is added below, as in the case of *hu-duo* (呼多).
"Ji-ren" (技人) refers to a "mao-shi" (髦士), meaning one who takes excellence as their virtue; Liu Xiaobiao praised Ren Fang as a "mao-jie" (髦傑) within the realm, referring to this very character.
Formerly, the pearls of King Wei illuminated twelve chariots; how much more so the pearl of King Mūrdhaja—would it not illuminate one *yojana*?
This means it was as large as a chariot hub. Furthermore, a sutra says: "That which is within the sash [is there]."
The power of virtue does not depend on the magnitude [of the person]. A "Jewel Woman" (*ratnabhāryā*) is one who can give birth to a thousand sons;
thus she is named a Jewel Woman. The *Faxian zhuan* (Record of Faxian) states that the Queen gave birth to flesh shaped like melons, with a thousand segments, each segment being a son.
However, the *Śāstra* (Treatise) states that Gopī was a Jewel Woman who was barren. Since these two accounts differ, how are they to be reconciled? Each of these...
[This is] what is highly esteemed at that time (and so forth).
Sixth is the contemplation of the suffering of association with the hated and disliked.
Good son, how does a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra contemplate the suffering of association with the hated and disliked?

Good son, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that within the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas, there is everywhere such suffering from association with the hated and disliked (*dveṣa-saṃyoga-duḥkha*).
It is, for example, like a person who regards being imprisoned, confined, and bound by shackles, fetters, and manacles as great suffering;
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise contemplates all things within the five destinies in this same way.
To undergo rebirth is entirely the great suffering of being joined with those one hates.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a person who, constantly fearing an enemy, shackles, and fetters, abandons his parents, wife, children, kinsmen, treasures, and property to flee far away.
Son of good family, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this, fearing and terrified of the cycle of birth and death.
Kāśyapa, when one has sufficiently practiced the six pāramitās and entered into nirvāṇa,
this is called a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa and contemplating the suffering of encountering those one hates.

Since that which arises from the conjunction of conditions is itself suffering— because when external objects press upon the mind, the mind experiences those objects as pressing, leading to distress and affliction—
it is called the suffering of association with the loathed. Seventh,
one contemplates the suffering of not obtaining what is sought.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa contemplate the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks?
'Seeking' refers to all that is sought; there are two kinds of such seeking: first, seeking wholesome dharmas; second, seeking unwholesome dharmas.
Not yet having obtained wholesome dharmas is suffering, and not yet having abandoned unwholesome dharmas is suffering."

Furthermore, regarding the previously mentioned separation from what is loved and meeting with what is hated: when one seeks to meet with the loved but instead encounters separation, or seeks to be free from the hated but instead encounters union—such failure to fulfill these two desires constitutes the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
The eighth [section] concludes that the aforementioned seven types of suffering are, in fact, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
This is a brief explanation of the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging; Kāśyapa, this is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
As previously explained, it certainly possesses a distinct ontological substance (etc.).
At that time, Kāśyapa’s third assembly [begins]. Regarding the reconciliation of the Truth of Suffering:

previously, the Āgamas and other sūtras all stated that among the three types of sensation there is the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*); now it is said that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are entirely suffering and possess no quality of pleasure.

Since the meanings of the earlier and later periods diverge, Kaishan (Kaisan) divided this into four chapters consisting of four rounds of questions and answers, while Guanshi (Guanshi) divided it into two. Hereafter...
The third section, "The Threefold Sub-section," merely serves to raise objections; it first poses questions and then provides answers. Regarding the initial questioning, there are three parts:
(1) a general negation, (2) the formulation of five difficulties, and (3) the conclusion. First is the "Accepting the Intent and Looking Up in Negation."

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as for what the Buddha has taught—that the five aggregates of clinging are suffering—this meaning is not so. Why is this?
[The following raises an objection: First, the first and fourth questions are identical in their basis on the conditions of pleasure; second..."

Question: Regarding the distinct basis on the essence of pleasure (*sukha-svabhāva*)—wherein the third and fifth questions likewise take pleasure as their basis—the first question takes pleasure as its condition (*pratyaya*).
For what reason? As the Buddha formerly told Śreṇika: "If form (*rūpa*) were suffering (*duḥkha*), no sentient beings would [seek it]."
One should seek form; if there were seeking, it would not be called suffering.
In the past, the Buddha told Śreṇika in the Āgama: "If form were definitively suffering, one could not seek form;
if form were definitively pleasure, one should not loathe form. But since now there is only difficulty and no pleasure, one should not seek form—if one seeks it..."
One should know that red and yellow [perceptions] involve pleasure; for what reason do you now say entirely that there is no pleasure?
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus, there are three kinds of feeling: the feeling of suffering, the feeling of pleasure, and the feeling of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Furthermore, as the Buddha previously taught the bhikṣus, if a person is able to practice wholesome dharmas, they will experience the feeling of pleasure.
Furthermore, as the Buddha taught, among the wholesome paths, one experiences pleasure through the six contacts: seeing beautiful forms with the eye is pleasure;

it is likewise for hearing pleasant sounds with the ear, smelling pleasant odors with the nose, tasting pleasant flavors with the tongue, touching pleasant objects with the body, and cognizing pleasant mental phenomena with the mind.
Now, we shall fully enumerate the six sense organs in relation to the six sense objects as conditions for pleasure.
As stated in the verse spoken by the Buddha below, this is the fifth section concerning the causes of pleasure.

This shares the same framework as the third section in citing the causes of pleasure, yet it differs in that the previous section cited "wholesomeness" (*kuśala*) as the cause of pleasure, referring only to mundane wholesomeness; here, however, we provide a complete enumeration.
The mundane virtues of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas are called the causes of happiness. Regarding these five verses, they are divided into four sections;
the first two verses clarify that the virtues of Śrāvakas are the causes of happiness.
As the Buddha spoke in verse: "To maintain the precepts is happiness, For the body does not undergo manifold sufferings."
Sleeping, one finds peace; waking, the mind is joyful.
If, while receiving food and clothing, one recites and practices while walking, And dwells alone in the mountain forests— Such is the supreme bliss.
The next verse clarifies that for a bodhisattva, goodness serves as the cause of bliss.
If one can constantly cultivate loving-kindness toward sentient beings day and night, one will thereby attain perpetual happiness because of not causing affliction to others.
(This third verse concludes the section on the Hīnayāna.)
The joy of few desires and contentment, the joy of extensive learning and discernment,
and the joy of the unattached Arhat—
this verse, consisting of four lines, reiterates the Mahāyāna.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva ultimately reaches the other shore; having accomplished all that was to be done, this is called the "Supreme Joy.
This refers to the Bodhisattva’s ultimate state, which is not identical to that of a Buddha; it is an ultimate state that is nevertheless partial.
World-Honored One, as in various sūtras it is not the case that the three lower fetters [are abandoned],
and as the meaning of the characteristic of pleasure (*sukha-lakṣaṇa*) taught in those sūtras is thus,
how should what the Buddha now says correspond to this meaning?
The various sūtras refer to the former teachings, as the Buddha now speaks of them; thus, he points to this teaching that there is no pleasure, only suffering.
From "The Buddha told Kāśyapa" onwards is the second part, the Tathāgata’s response, which is divided into two sections: first, praising the question asked.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, “Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have skillfully questioned the Tathāgata regarding this matter.
Next, son of good family, [the Buddha] provides the correct answer for all the assembly, which is further divided into two parts: first, the general answer; second, the specific answer.
Within the general answer, there are two sections: first, the response; second, the discussion. Regarding the first section:
"Good son, all sentient beings perversely conceive the notion of pleasure within the midst of lower suffering;
therefore, the characteristics of suffering I have now described are no different from those of the past.
Formerly, following the intentions of others, they took lower suffering to be pleasure; now, following my own intention, I declare that everything is suffering."

Kāśyapa raised five difficult questions one after another, and the World-Honored One answered these five difficulties with profound resolution; thus, the two teachings of the past and present do not contradict each other.
It is certainly not that this is a matter of mistaken sentiment or arbitrary imagination giving rise to false notions of pleasure.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, initiating the second section of the discourse: a counter-objection to the Buddha’s explanation regarding the meaning of the alleviation of suffering.

This section is further divided into two parts: first, the formal objection; second, the acceptance and understanding [of the teaching]. Regarding the first part, there are three sub-sections: 1) an objection based on a mistaken understanding;
2) an objection based on a reversal [of the truth]; and 3) an objection based on factual evidence. As for the objection based on a mistaken understanding:
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As the Buddha has taught, those who conceive the notion of pleasure within inferior suffering—namely, the suffering of inferior birth, inferior aging, inferior illness, inferior death, inferior separation from the beloved, inferior failure to obtain what is sought, inferior association with the hated, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging—would also [experience] pleasure, World-Honored One. Inferior birth refers to the three evil realms."
Regarding birth within the realms of existence: that which is called "inferior" refers to birth among humans, while that which is called "superior" refers to birth in the heavens.
The Buddha’s intention was to consider the light as inferior suffering and the heavy as inferior suffering; thus, his understanding became erroneous when faced with the challenge.

Kāśyapa enumerated the eight types of suffering and categorized them all into three grades: those experienced in the three miserable destinies, those among humans, and those in the heavens. If [the Buddha] had considered the heavens as inferior...
If suffering contained pleasure, there should be the perception of pleasure within the three miserable realms.
Furthermore, if someone were to ask the following difficult question:
"If one perceives suffering in what is actually pleasure, and [perceives] pleasure in what is actually neutral..."

If one gives rise to the perception of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure regarding superior pleasure, yet gives rise to the perception of pleasure within that [superior] pleasure, how should this be answered?
If the perception of pleasure arises toward inferior suffering, then it would likewise follow that the perception of suffering should arise toward inferior pleasure.

What is meant by "inferior pleasure"? For the time being, let us take the joy of the beauty and grace of worldly singers and dancers as superior pleasure, while [the pleasure of] the body as inferior pleasure.
Regarding this, one should cultivate the perception of suffering toward what is pleasant below; this is done by applying these erroneous experiences to their errors collectively.

World-Honored One, if one were to give rise to the perception of pleasure within lower suffering, it would be difficult to find anyone who, when facing a thousand punishments, would feel pleasure at the very first stroke.
If a pleasant perception has not already arisen at the time of descending, how can it be said that a pleasant perception arises within the suffering of the descent?
Would a person undergoing a thousand lashes of punishment experience pleasure upon receiving the first lash?
The Buddha told [Kāśyapa] in response to the latter part of the question, which is twofold: first, a preliminary inquiry, and second, the formal answer.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa: "It is so, it is so, just as you have said.
However, the meaning of that third 'single punishment' clarifies that one actually gives rise to the perception of pleasure within lower suffering; if one were to..."
To be exempt from many punishments while willingly accepting even one is also considered a source of joy.
Following this principle, the formal answer below is given.
For this reason, there is no perception of pleasure; why is this? It is just as that person who is about to receive a thousand punishments [yet accepts one].
One who attains liberation immediately upon hearing [the teaching] gives rise to the notion of pleasure at that time;
therefore, one should know that they falsely give rise to the notion of pleasure within what is actually devoid of pleasure.
I have merely answered their third point; when the difficulty based on the facts is raised, the previous error and the inverted objection naturally fall away of their own accord.

It is not as you say; that which is below is heavy suffering and that which is below is light suffering—why do you misinterpret this? Therefore, [the opponent] does not answer, yet this is also incorrect.

Because one perceives suffering even when there is pleasure below, there is no need to answer [that objection]. The correct response to the third point is that one ought to receive a thousand punishments.

When one first attains [even] a single moment of pleasure and immediately hears of being released, is that not a case where the perception of pleasure arises from what is actually lower-level suffering?

It is like a person condemned to execution who, upon hearing that they have been released from one hundred lashes, conceives a notion of pleasure even amidst those lower forms of suffering (and so forth).
The subsequent section first summarizes the understanding and then provides the detailed exposition.

Kāśyapa said: "World-Honored One, that person does not give rise to a perception of pleasure because of a single blow; rather, they give rise to a perception of pleasure because they have attained liberation.
Alternatively, it may be said that this passage constitutes a single objection, stating that this person does not give rise to a perception of pleasure regarding a single punishment.
It is merely that one conceives the notion of pleasure regarding liberation; this is an understanding attained through mastery and is not called difficult.
Kāśyapa, for this reason, when I previously spoke to Śreṇika Bimbisāra’s son, Śramaṇa-māna, I said that the pleasure within the five aggregates is truly not false.
The Buddha stated that what is real is not false; this is a teaching according to conventional sentiment. What was previously called "the existence of pleasure" was said according to sentiment;
what is now called "non-existence" is so according to the principle of reality (*yukti*).
Kāśyapa, there are three feelings and three sufferings. [This concludes] the second section, which specifically answers the five difficulties; it consists of only three textual passages.
The first response answers the second question regarding the nature of pleasure; the second response answers the two questions regarding the third and fifth causes of pleasure;

and the third response answers the first and fourth questions regarding the conditions for pleasure. Within this initial response answering the second question on the nature of pleasure, there are three parts:
first, citing two teachings; second, identifying the three types of sensation; and third, concluding with the refutation of [false] views.
In truth, these were initially presented as two teachings.
Kāśyapa, there are three feelings and three sufferings. As for the three feelings, they are the feeling of pleasure, the feeling of pain, and the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

As for the three sufferings, they are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
First, the teaching on the three types of sensation; second, the teaching on the three types of suffering, which can be seen [in the text].
"Good son, regarding the three sensations below the section on painful sensation":

good son, what is called painful sensation consists of the three sufferings—namely, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). The other two [sensations] are likewise [included].

Regarding the "experiencer," this refers to the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). However, the former teachings also indicate three types of sensation: they point to the sensation of pain as the "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the sensation of pleasure as the "suffering of change," and the sensation of equanimity as the "suffering of conditioned existence.
This is the teaching of the Hīnayāna; its meaning is not ultimate, as it merely points to these individually.

Regarding the person’s application of this ultimate teaching, it further clarifies that the initial sensation of suffering possesses all three types of suffering. As for "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*):
when the mind takes an object of suffering as its condition, the object of suffering oppresses the mind; because the mind and the object are raised together, it is called the suffering of suffering.

Pleasure does not endure long; it remains only for a brief moment. Once the conditions for pleasure have ceased, it becomes the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), being invaded by impermanence.

That is to say, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) applies to the remaining two feelings, while each of the other two [feelings] possesses two sufferings—or as some say, one suffering each. Therefore, the text states "two.

However, this interpretation is incorrect. Since the previous section applied both [suffering of change and suffering of conditioned existence] in tandem, why would it now apply the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) alone to pleasant feeling and the suffering of conditioned existence alone to neutral feeling?
Thus, we know that a single feeling possesses both sufferings; pleasant feeling likewise possesses both the suffering of change and the suffering of conditioned existence.

Painful feeling (*duḥkhā-vedanā*) and neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) also possess both types of suffering: the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). Since the entire body of pleasure is subject to disintegration, it is the suffering of change;

furthermore, because it is assailed by impermanence, it also possesses the suffering of conditioned existence. Neutral feeling likewise has two aspects: because one must inevitably part from it when it changes, it is the suffering of change;
yet, because it cannot escape impermanence, it is the suffering of conditioned existence. However, these two types of suffering do not require the pressure of external objects.
Therefore, there is no suffering of suffering.
Good son, for these reasons, the third section below—concerning the falsity and reality of the bonds—is further divided into two parts: first, the bond of previously asserting that pleasure is false.
"Good son, for this reason, although there is indeed the sensation of pleasure within the cycle of birth and death,
because the natures of suffering and pleasure are inseparable, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva says that 'all is suffering.'"
It is not that there is truly pleasure; it is said that ordinary beings speak of pleasure while Bodhisattvas do not, for all is suffering.

Although the text states that within birth and death (*saṃsāra*) there is truly the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), and later states that within birth and death there is truly no pleasure at all, these are both merely false conceptualizations according to worldly sentiment.
The Tripitaka Master of Liang held that the existence or non-existence of pleasure within birth and death is likewise [a matter of such conceptualization].
The arguments for dispute are as previously stated (etc.).
Noble son, within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the two lower fetters (*saṃyojana*) should now be understood as truly suffering.
Noble son, within the cycle of birth and death there is truly no happiness; it is only that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, in accordance with worldly convention, [provisionally] speak of it as such.
It is said that there is pleasure.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, providing the second response to the third and fifth of the preceding objections based on causes.
This section consists of two parts; herein, Kāśyapa restates his question in order to seek an answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak in accordance with worldly convention, it is false and not as the Buddha has taught.
Those who practice goodness receive the retribution of happiness;

those who maintain the precepts and meditative concentration experience the bliss of the body and do not undergo suffering, until all that is to be done is accomplished—this is the supreme bliss. Such is the pleasant sensation described in these various sutras."

If falsehood were not thus, why would the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—who have long cultivated the path to enlightenment for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas and are already free from false speech—now make such a statement? What is its meaning?

Some may claim that this is a separate and new question, but that is not the case; rather, it is a restatement of the previous inquiry regarding mundane and supramundane virtues from the verse, merely elaborating upon its phrasing rather than constituting a different question.
The Buddha said: "Good son, the verses on experiencing various forms of bliss as previously explained are the very root of the path to bodhi;
they are also able to nurture anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, these characteristics of bliss were first taught in the sūtras."

The meaning of the Buddha’s reply is this: when I say that one who is well-capable of inducing happiness will ultimately attain the bliss of Bodhi, I am not speaking of the happiness found within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

My initial statement that the root of Bodhi is the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*) for the fruit of Buddhahood, and my subsequent statement that nurturing Bodhi constitutes the completing cause (*pariniṣpādaka-hetu*) for the fruit of Buddhahood, mean that it was previously said that there could never be a generative cause [for Buddhahood]. Now...
That is to say, there are causes and conditions by which it may also be so explained.
Good son, for example, in the world—[this refers to] the third answer to the first [question], and the fourth is based on the inquiry regarding the conditions for happiness.

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the direct answer; second, citing the understanding and delusion to conclude the direct answer. Again, there are two parts: first, clarifying that [the teaching] serves as a condition for happiness.
The subsequent clarification is that because the conditions for suffering are not fixed,
there is no pleasure. Good son, it is like the worldly necessities of life which can serve as causes for pleasure and are therefore called "pleasure"—
namely, female beauty, indulgence in wine, choice delicacies and sweet flavors, obtaining water when thirsty, encountering fire when cold, and clothing.
Wearing necklaces and ornaments; possessing elephants, horses, chariots, and carriages; having male and female slaves and servants; gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, and pearls;
and storehouses filled with grain and rice—such things as these, which are required by the world and can serve as causes for pleasure, are called "pleasure."
Good son, such things as these can also give rise to the causes of suffering. From women arise the suffering of men, grief, sorrow, lamentation, and even the loss of life.
Due to the sweet taste of wine, and even because of granaries and treasuries, they can cause people great distress and affliction.
For this reason, all things are suffering; there is no characteristic of pleasure.
The various precious treasures and such that appear later are all entirely suffering; to cite but one instance:
initially, possessing many treasures was thought to be pleasure, yet losing one's life for their sake is likewise extreme suffering.

Good son, the second section below, titled "Raising the Misunderstanding and Clarifying the Understanding," is further divided into three parts. First, it summarizes the Bodhisattva’s understanding of suffering:
"Good son, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, regarding these eight sufferings, understands suffering as being without suffering."
Next, because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand this, I have taught it according to their dispositions.
Good son, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others do not know the cause of bliss;
therefore, for such people, I have spoken of the characteristic of bliss within the midst of inferior suffering.
This is the third instance of the Bodhisattva’s summary.
Only those Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa are able to know what is the cause of suffering and what is the cause of happiness.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Eleven.
Compiled by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Benjun of Nittō.
Combined Commentary on the Southern Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, Fascicle Eleven.
Combined Commentary on the Southern Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, Fascicle Twelve.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter on the Holy Conduct (Scroll 12).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty;
revised by the Śramaṇas Huìyán and Huìguān of the Jìn Dynasty.

Xie Lingyun: Revising the Section on the Noble Practice, from the middle of the scroll, extensively clarifying the text on the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) in three parts: first, elucidating the Truth of Origination; second, harmonizing and integrating it; third, analyzing and examining it.

The first section has three parts: (1) stating the title, (2) explaining the essence, and (3) clarifying what is correct and incorrect. First, stating the title: [the text] first restates the topical outline:
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa contemplate?"
The Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Good son, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates this Truth of Origination as the causal condition for the aggregates (*skandha*).
Next, it is explained that because the cause of origination is able to produce the fruit of the aggregates, it is said to be the causal condition for the aggregates.
Regarding what is called "origination" (*samudaya*), there are two explanations below concerning its essence. The teachings of the past identified karma and afflictions as origination;

however, within afflictions, the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully present. Now, we speak only of afflictions and do not explicitly mention karma, because karma is fundamentally rooted in affliction.
Afflictions moisten karma, and among these afflictions, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is specifically emphasized. Craving is the delusion that binds one to the realms of existence and it moistens karma.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra on Birth and Death* states: "There is no karma and no afflictions; the Truth of Suffering has no abiding place;

ignorance has no activity; one practices the equality of the world. Furthermore, that the twelve links of dependent origination are neither arising nor ceasing constitutes equality, which is called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
If the twelve links of dependent origination were subject to arising and ceasing, they would be the [phenomenon of] origination and not the Truth. Within this [teaching], there is...
The seventh section clarifies that the cause for the arising of the fruit is the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). When these are fully accomplished, there is craving;
one craves this existence, which is the body of the aggregate of craving.
What is called "accumulation" (*samudaya*) refers to craving for existence once again.
Next, craving is of two kinds; the following clarifies these two types of craving.
Craving is twofold: first, craving for one's own body; second, craving for what is required.
One's own body is the "I," and what is required is the "mine."
There are two kinds of craving regarding what has already been obtained;

furthermore, there are two kinds regarding what has not yet been obtained: first, binding the mind to the five objects of desire and seeking them with single-minded focus; second, having already obtained them, being able to endure and remaining single-mindedly attached to them.
The fourth consists of craving for the three realms.
Furthermore, there are three kinds: craving for the realm of desire (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*), craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*), and craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-tṛṣṇā*).
The fifth consists of three kinds.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of craving: craving as the causal condition of karma, craving as the causal condition of afflictions, and craving as the causal condition of suffering.

Regarding craving as the causal condition of karma: because it takes retribution as its cause, it brings about these fruits of suffering, just as pigeons and sparrows, being full of desire, first encounter their [karmic] results.
Next, regarding craving as the causal condition of afflictions: because it takes habitual practice as its cause, the arising of craving can be observed.
Next, regarding the causal condition of suffering: out of a desire to escape heavy suffering, one develops craving for light suffering. It is like fearing the pain of death;
when a disease is treated so that it may be cured, even though the acupuncture and moxibustion are actually painful, one nevertheless develops craving for them because they lead to recovery.
Furthermore, there are four types of craving, which correspond to four matters.
For one who has left the household life, there are four kinds of craving; what are these four? They are: clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for bathing.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of craving, which are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Moreover, there are five kinds of attachment to the five aggregates; according to whatever is required, one experiences all manner of craving, attachment, discrimination, and calculation, which are immeasurable and boundless.
"Good son, there are two kinds of craving. This marks the third section, clarifying what is right and what is wrong.
"Good son, there are two kinds of craving: first, wholesome craving; second, unwholesome craving."
If it is unwholesome craving, it is the origin; if it is wholesome craving, it is not the origin.
Within this, there are three further stages of analysis. First, one distinguishes between the noble ones and ordinary beings:
unwholesome craving refers to the seeking of ordinary, foolish people, while wholesome craving refers to the seeking of all bodhisattvas.
Next, the Bodhisattva is distinguished from those of the Two Vehicles.
Regarding "affection for wholesome dharmas," there are two types:
seeking the Two Vehicles is called unwholesome seeking, while seeking the Great Vehicle is called wholesome seeking.
The three truths are distinguished from what is not the truth.
Good son, the craving of ordinary people is called "accumulation" (samudaya) but is not called "truth" (satya);
the craving of Bodhisattvas is called "true truth" but is not called "accumulation. Why is this? It is because they accept birth for the sake of delivering sentient beings, and not [out of craving].
Because of craving, one undergoes birth.
Therefore it is said that for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), craving is called "origination" (*samudaya*) and not called "truth" (*satya*);

whereas for Bodhisattvas, craving is called "true truth" (*bhūta-satya*) and not called "origination. That which is called "true truth" and not "origination" for Bodhisattvas is taken [in this sense].
Because it is understood through wisdom, it is called a "truth" (*satya*); ordinary people do not perceive it thus, and therefore it is merely called "origination" (*samudaya*).

If one applies this same principle, then the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) would also not be a truth; yet if viewed from the perspective of comprehension, it can be termed a truth. Furthermore, if it follows worldly sentiment, it is designated as "conventional. Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
[The following is] the second reconciliation of previous teachings—previously it was stated that karma and afflictions constitute origination; why then is it now said [that craving alone does so]?

Regarding the statement that craving is the cause of suffering, [the author] first poses a question and then provides an answer. In the question, he first cites four sūtras and subsequently presents the formal objection.

The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has stated in other sūtras for the sake of all sentient beings that karma is the causal condition, or that pride is the cause, or that the six contacts are the cause, or that ignorance is the fifth [cause].”
The five aggregates flourish and act as causes and conditions.
As stated in the initial citation from the Sūtra, the "six contacts" refer to the six consciousnesses taking up objects and thereby producing contact;

this is also the condition for the accumulation of this consciousness-mind, which brings about results in future lives, just as the four stations of consciousness serve as the basis for the five flourishing aggregates.
Now, for what reason does he conclude the objection below?
For what reason is it said that among the Four Noble Truths, craving alone is the cause of the five aggregates?
In the Buddha’s response, there are again two parts: first, praising his question; second, providing the actual answer. The first is as in the text.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
In the subsequent formal response, the meaning is that the former teaching and the present teaching do not contradict one another;

therefore, it is said today that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the root of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*). Regarding the present teaching, there are two parts: first, clarifying that craving is the fundamental root; second, clarifying craving [itself].
Furthermore, there are two roots of these faults: first, the explanation by way of dharma, and second, the explanation by way of analogy.
Son of good family, as for the various causes and conditions you have mentioned, they are not non-causes; rather, it is the five aggregates that must depend upon craving [as their cause].
Good son, it is like a great king who, when he goes out on a tour of inspection, is followed by his ministers and retinue;
craving is also like this, for wherever craving moves, these various fetters likewise follow. It is like a greasy garment upon which dust settles;
wherever it settles, it remains there. Craving is also like this: wherever there is an object of craving, the fetters of karma also abide. Furthermore...
Next, noble son, it is like this: for example, just as moist ground can produce sprouts, so too does craving (*tṛṣṇā*) produce the sprouts of all karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).
There are three similes—namely, the great king, the oily garment, and the moist ground—all of which are as stated in the text.
Good son, this second section clarifies the faults and afflictions of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). It is further divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the nine topical headings;
second, the detailed explanation of each one.
Good son, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, he deeply contemplates this craving.
There are nine kinds in total: first, like one who is reproached for having a surplus; second, like a rākṣasī wife;
third, like a beautiful flower stalk with a venomous snake within; fourth, like unwholesome food that one forces oneself to eat despite it being unsuitable to one's nature;
fifth, like a courtesan; sixth, like the seed of a *mālūka* gourd; seventh, like a malignant tumor within a sore; eighth, like a violent wind; and ninth, like a comet.
In the explanation, there are nine chapters; within each chapter, the analogies are further divided and combined:
the first serves as an analogy for the two vehicles, while the subsequent eight serve as analogies for ordinary beings. Regarding the initial passage:
What is meant by "being like one who has been accused of having remaining debt"? Good son, it is, for example, like a poor man who owes another money;
although he has nearly finished repaying it, because a small portion remains unpaid, he is still bound in prison and cannot escape.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are likewise; because they still possess the residual traces of the habit-energy of craving, they are unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son, this is called "the reprimand for having a remainder."
The two vehicles have not yet severed their residual habits (*vāsanā*), like a debt for which the assets have not yet been fully repaid.
The lower eight [stages] are for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); this can be seen by consulting the text.
"Good son, how is it like having a rākṣasī as a wife? Good son, it is, for example, as if a person were to obtain a rākṣasī...
The woman took her as a wife; this rākṣasī would devour every son born to her as soon as he was born.
Once her sons were all consumed, she then devoured her husband.
Noble son, the love for a rākṣasī woman is just like this: it consumes the roots of goodness produced by sentient beings, following after them until nothing remains.

Having been born, they consume their own virtuous offspring until none remain; they then further devour sentient beings, causing them to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts—except for Bodhisattvas.
They are called like rākṣasī women.

Good son, how is it like a poisonous snake entwining the stem of a beautiful flower? It is like a person who, by nature being fond of flowers, fails to see the danger posed by the poisonous snake on the flower's stem;
he immediately reaches out and grasps it, and once grasped, he is bitten by the snake, and having been bitten, his life comes to an end.
All ordinary beings are likewise thus: they crave the flowers of the five desires and fail to see the peril of these poisonous snakes of attachment;
they then seize them and are immediately stung by the venomous snake of craving, so that at the end of their lives they fall into the three evil realms—except for Bodhisattvas.
This is called "a wondrous flower-stalk entwined by a poisonous snake."
"Good son, what is it that is like being forced to eat food that one finds unwholesome? It is, for example, as when a person is forced to eat food that they find unwholesome;
having eaten it, their belly aches, they suffer from diarrhea, and they die."
Sentient beings in these five realms of existence greedily consume and are strongly attached to such food of craving;
by this cause and condition, they fall into the three evil paths—with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas. This is called "forcibly consuming that which is unwholesome."
Good son, how is it like a courtesan? For example, suppose a foolish man has an affair with a courtesan;
that courtesan skillfully employs various forms of flattery and pretends to be intimate, yet she completely robs him of all his wealth.
Once his wealth is exhausted, she then drives him away.
The lustful woman is likewise so: the foolish and ignorant man who engages in intimacy with her finds that this lustful woman robs him of all his wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).
Once his wholesome dharmas are exhausted, she drives him away and causes him to fall into the three evil realms (*durgati*), with the sole exception of a Bodhisattva.
This is what is meant by being "like a lustful woman."
"Good son, how is it like the seed of the *mālūka*?
For example, if a bird has eaten a *mālūka* seed and it falls to the ground with its excrement, or if it is carried by the wind to the foot of a tree, it will immediately sprout and grow.
It then entwines and binds the *nyagrodha* tree, preventing it from growing further until it eventually withers and dies."
The *āmalaka* fruit is likewise: it entangles and binds all the wholesome dharmas of ordinary persons, preventing them from increasing and causing them instead to wither and perish.
Once they have withered and perished, after the end of life, one falls into the three evil realms—except for Bodhisattvas.
This is called being "like the *āmalaka* fruit."
Good son, what is meant by "like a tumor within a sore"? It is like a person who develops a tumor within a chronic sore;

that person must diligently apply themselves to treat it and not give rise to a mind of abandonment. If they give rise to a mind of abandonment, the tumor will increase, and maggots and abscesses will further arise.
Due to these causes and conditions, they will then meet their end.
The sores and wounds of the five aggregates of ordinary, foolish people are likewise thus: they cherish them within, yet these become malignant growths (*adhimāṃsa*).

One should diligently apply the mind to treat these growths of craving; if they are not treated, at the end of life one will immediately fall into the three evil realms, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas.
This is what is called "a malignant growth within a wound."
Good son, how is it like a violent wind? Just as a violent wind can topple mountains, level peaks, and uproot deep roots, so too is the violent wind of craving and desire;
it gives rise to evil thoughts toward one’s parents and can uproot great wisdom.
Śāriputra and others possess the root of unsurpassed, profound, and firm bodhi; with the exception of bodhisattvas, they are called "like a violent wind.
Good son, why are they "like a comet"? For example, when a comet appears in the world, all the people of the world...
Famine, illness, emaciation, and various afflictions—
this comet of craving is likewise able to sever all seeds of the roots of goodness, leaving ordinary persons destitute and famished,
giving rise to the disease of afflictions, causing them to transmigrate through birth and death, and endure manifold sufferings; this is true for all except for Bodhisattvas.
This is called the "Comet-like" [Chapter], wherein a son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa,
contemplates these nine kinds of the fetter of craving.
Next, for this reason, the third section—the detailed analysis of the causes and effects of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) within the world—is concluded.

Regarding the four truths (*catuḥsatya*), the preceding [section] establishes the arising of conditioned suffering and its origin, while the subsequent [section] concerns the non-arising of the four truths.
To "forget the former" is to forget saṃsāra; to "forget the latter" is to forget nirvāṇa. This section analyzes these aspects of arising and ceasing within the text.
Jian immediately commanded that the second, third, and fourth [sections] all clarify the reason why. What is the reason? If one perceives suffering as existing, then suffering arises;
if suffering arises, then suffering ceases. Once it is understood that suffering is non-existent, suffering does not arise;
since suffering does not arise, it does not cease. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form is separate from emptiness."
The extinction of the nature of form and emptiness is itself empty; within this emptiness, there is neither arising nor ceasing. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"To penetrate the five aggregates of clinging as empty and non-arising—this is the meaning of suffering. If one can understand it thus, then although suffering exists, there is no [substantial] suffering, and therein lies the True Dharma (*satya*).
Since the origin (*samudaya*) arises from suffering, if one understands that suffering is without [substantial] suffering, how could there still be an origin? Thus, one understands the origin.

The absence of origination is itself the ultimate truth; because suffering and its origination have ceased, it is called the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Since suffering and its origination do not exist, how could there be the truth of cessation?
Cessation was originally non-existent, and now there is no cessation; this is the understanding of cessation as non-cessation.

While the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) treats suffering and its origination, since that which is treated does not exist, there is also nothing that can treat; therefore, the path is understood as non-dual.

If the Path and non-Path both exist yet possess the True Dharma, and one relies upon this intermediate state to exclude that which is "non-arising," it clarifies that there is no arising in either of the two extremes.
Since worldly causes and effects do not arise, supramundane causes and effects likewise do not arise;

thus, the Four Noble Truths do not exist. One understands that while worldly suffering and its origin appear to exist, they are in fact without suffering or origin; likewise, one understands that the supramundane Path and Cessation appear to exist, yet they are without Path or Cessation.
The Path and Cessation are precisely non-arising; the intent of the Four Truths is immeasurable, yet I shall speak of it briefly.

If one wishes to extract the third category specifically: the understanding that suffering is without suffering yet possesses reality involves two further meanings regarding this reality—sequential reality and non-sequential reality.
Sequential reality refers precisely to the immeasurable Four Truths.
In truth, that which is not sequential is the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) Four Noble Truths. Returning to the analysis of the Four Noble Truths, they are divided into four chapters;
first, the Truth of Suffering is analyzed. "Good son, for this reason, all ordinary worldlings have suffering but no Truth, whereas Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas [have both]."

Suffering exists as the Truth of Suffering, yet it lacks ultimate reality; because Bodhisattvas and others understand that suffering is without suffering, there is thus no suffering, and there is the True Truth.
There are two versions of this text: according to the old version, it says that ordinary persons, together with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, all...

Regarding the statement that there is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): according to a newly established version of the text, within the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), a distinction is made between ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Ordinary beings possess suffering but lack the Truth; those of the Two Vehicles, however, possess both suffering and the Truth. This represents a process of granting and withholding [the Truth] with respect to the Two Vehicles.
The old interpretation states that suffering is the object (*viṣaya*) and the Truth is the wisdom (*jñāna*); ordinary beings lack this wisdom and thus possess only [suffering].

As for why objects of perception are exclusively suffering and lack a [separate] truth: because those of the Two Vehicles possess a limited degree of knowledge, they perceive suffering and possess a truth regarding it;

however, for those who lack true realization, they cannot contemplate suffering or understand suffering as being without suffering, and thus it is not the ultimate truth. The same principle applies by analogy to the Truth of Origination.
Ordinary worldlings possess the accumulation [of suffering] but not the truth of accumulation; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess both the accumulation and the truth of accumulation;
whereas Bodhisattvas understand that accumulation is without accumulation, and therefore, while there is no accumulation, there is the true truth.
The extinction of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not the true [extinction]; the extinction of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the true truth.
The path of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not the true [path]; the path of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the true truth.
Regarding the two truths of the Path and Cessation, ordinary beings are not discussed;

rather, it is only for the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and for Bodhisattvas that there is a distinction between the true and the false regarding these two truths. This is because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are unable to perceive the truth of cessation as non-truth, and thus [for them] it is not true, whereas Bodhisattvas are able to know it, and thus it is truly real.
From the section on "Good Sons" downward, the third part extensively clarifies the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

Although the Truths of Cessation and the Path (*mārga*) were previously situated between those of Arising and Cessation, they have been briefly analyzed; since the Paths of Arising and Cessation have not yet been fully explained, they are now further elucidated.
The three [truths] beginning with Non-arising will be explained in detail later. Next, the text explaining the Truth of Cessation is divided into three parts: first, two chapters are announced.
Next, regarding the explanation of the three fetters:
Good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa perceive cessation and perceive the truth of cessation?

Regarding the two gates of "proclaiming the vision of cessation" and "the vision of the truth of cessation": if one sees cessation, it is the gate of the chapter on abandonment; if one sees the truth of cessation, it is the gate of the chapter on detachment.
For those of the Two Vehicles, who extinguish the body and eliminate wisdom, there are only these two matters of abandonment and detachment;
however, for Bodhisattvas, there are matters such as the perfection of wisdom and virtue (and so forth).

The second [point], namely "the severance of all afflictions" (*sarvakleśaprahāṇa*), is the explanation of the first eight characters; it explains the gate of seeing cessation (*nirodhadarśanamukha*).
"The severance of all afflictions" means that this severance of delusions is characterized by the absence of anything [substantial] to be severed.
If the afflictions are eliminated, this explains the section on the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (*nirodha-satya*) in two parts: first, its function, and second, its essence.
When afflictions are severed, it is called "eternal cessation" (*nitya-nirodha*); when the fire of afflictions is extinguished, it is called "quiescence" (*śānti*).

Because afflictions have ceased, one attains the experience of bliss; because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas seek out its causes and conditions, it is called "purity" (*śubha*), as there is no further rebirth.
Because it transcends the twenty-five states of existence, it is called "transcending the world" (*lokottara*); because it transcends the world, it is called "Self.

Regarding the initial application, there are five phrases in total; the first four phrases constitute the four virtues (or, as some say, the five virtues), but for now we shall treat them as the four virtues from the perspective of their functional application.
Second, "always [remaining] within form and sound" refers to ultimate quiescence (*atyanta-śānti*), which is discussed here in terms of its essential nature (*tattva*).
Because it does not grasp at the characteristics (*nimitta*) of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and so forth— whether male or female, arising, abiding, or ceasing,
or whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— it is called the ultimate truth of ultimate quiescence.
Third, the conclusion for the bodhisattva son of good family is as in the text:
"Son of good family, in this way the bodhisattva dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa and contemplates the noble truth of cessation."
Good son, how is it that the fourth section below, which extensively explains the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), is divided into two parts? First, the explanation of the Truth of the Path;
second, the reconciliation [of its meaning]. The first part is further divided into three: first, the topical outline (*uddāna*); second, the explanation; third, the conclusion.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa contemplate the noble truth of the path?
In the explanation, first there is a simile, followed by its application."
Good son, it is like being able to see coarse and fine objects in the dark by means of a lamp.
In the initial analogy, "by means of a lamp" is a metaphor for the Eightfold Path.

Just as a lamp illuminates objects—whether they be the permanent or the impermanent, and so forth—which differ yet ultimately constitute a single path, the path is taught differently according to conditions.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, by means of the eightfold noble path, they perceive all dharmas as follows:

namely, the permanent and the impermanent, the conditioned and the unconditioned, sentient beings and non-sentient beings, things and non-things, suffering and pleasure, self and non-self, purity and impurity, afflictions and non-afflictions, karma and non-karma, and reality.
One knows that which is unreal as non-vehicle, knowledge as non-knowledge, substance (*dravya*) as non-substance, quality (*guṇa*) as non-quality,
view as non-view, form as non-form, the path as non-path, and liberation as non-liberation.
Next, regarding the analogy within the text, it says that *dravya* (陀羅驃) is translated by those from Hexi as "that which is real" (*zhēnshí*).

*Dharma* (諦) refers to the adornment of merits such as necklaces and so forth. The older translations rendered these as "primary truth" (*zhǔdì*) and "dependent truth" (*yīdì*), but this is incorrect;
*dravya* is not the ultimate truth, and *guṇa* (求那) is not the conventional truth.
"Noble son, in this way the bodhisattva dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, contemplating the Noble Truth of the Path.

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: [This concludes] the second assembly, which reconciles the various different teachings previously given by the Buddha and now asserts that there are only the Eightfold Path.
Thus, the text for this reconciliation is divided into two parts: first the question, then the answer. Within the question, there are two sections: first the question, then the objection."

The initial inquiry consists of three parts: first, stating that they are not associated; second, explaining why they are not associated; third, concluding that they are not associated. The first is as in the text.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if the Eightfold Noble Path is the meaning of the Noble Truth of the Path, it is not associated [with the other truths]."
[The response is] "It should be so. Next, regarding the explanation beginning with "Why is this?
[it means]: Why is it that the Tathāgata sometimes says that faith is the path capable of crossing over all outflows (*āsrava*), and at other times speaks of the path?
Heedlessness is [the opposite of] that by which the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, through heedfulness, attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
it is also a factor for the Bodhisattva’s path to enlightenment. At times, it is said that diligence is the path, as when [the Buddha] told Ānanda:
"If there is anyone who can diligently cultivate diligence, they will achieve the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Regarding Bodhi, it is sometimes said that if one contemplates the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) and applies the mind with diligent cultivation of this mindfulness of the body, one will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At other times, it is said that right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) is the path, as it was told to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa: "That which is right concentration is truly the path; it is not otherwise."

That which is not fixed concentration is the Path; only when one enters meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samādhi*) can one contemplate the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), for it is not possible to contemplate them without entering absorption. Some speak of a single dharma:

if a person cultivates it, they can purify sentient beings, eliminate all sorrow and affliction, and attain the True Dharma—namely, the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). Or again, it is said:
To speak of cultivating the perception of impermanence is called the Path; as it was told to the bhikṣus:
"One who is able to cultivate the perception of impermanence extensively can attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Or, it is said that by sitting alone in contemplation in a solitary and tranquil araṇya, one can quickly achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. At other times, it is said:
To preach the Dharma for others is called the Path; if one hears the Dharma, the net of doubt is immediately severed.
Once the net of doubt is severed, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. At other times, it is said that upholding the precepts is the Path, as when [the Buddha] told Ānanda:
"If there is one who diligently cultivates and maintains the prohibitive precepts, such a person will cross over the great suffering of birth and death."
At times he says that associating with virtuous friends is called the Path, as when he told Ānanda:
"If one associates with spiritual friends, then one possesses pure precepts; if there are sentient beings who can associate with me, they will give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At other times he says that cultivating loving-kindness is the Path, and that one should practice and study it.
One who possesses loving-kindness (*maitrī*) severs all afflictions (*kleśa*) and attains the state of immovability.

At times, it is said that wisdom (*prajñā*) is the path, as when the Buddha formerly spoke to the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī: "Sister, just as the śrāvakas, by means of the sword of wisdom, are able to sever the floods (*ogha*), the outflows (*āsrava*), and the afflictions.
At other times, the Tathāgata says that giving (*dāna*) is the path, as the Buddha did in the past.
"Great King Prasenajit, you should know that because I practiced the giving of wisdom extensively in the past,
by these causes and conditions, I have today attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
In fourteen sutras, most of which are teachings from the Āgamas and other sources, the paths ranging from faith to generosity are explained differently.

Next, regarding the World-Honored One’s [teaching] on the Eightfold Noble Path, there are three further difficulties: first, using the present to challenge the past; second, using the past to challenge the present;
and third, concluding with the refutation of errors.
World-Honored One, if the Eightfold Noble Path is the Truth of the Path, would not such sūtras as these be false?
Regarding the first point: if it was so in the past, it is not so now;
if those various sūtras are not false, for what reason do they not state therein that the Eightfold Path is the Noble Truth of the Path?
2. "If this were the case now, why did you not say so in the past?
(and so forth). 3. The conclusion is as in the text.
If he had not said [this], one would ask: "Why was the Tathāgata mistaken in the past? I know for certain that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas..."
Having long been free from error, the Buddha replied in two parts; first, he praised the question:
"At that time, the World-Honored One commended Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, saying: 'Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You now wish to know.'"
Because the secret meanings contained within the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna sūtras of the Bodhisattvas are profound, he asks this question.
"Good son, go" is the direct answer, which further consists of two parts: the teaching (dharma) and the analogy (upamā).
Good son, all such sūtras as these are entirely included within the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya). Good son, as I have previously stated, if there is...
To have faith in this way is the root of faith; it is that which can assist the path to Bodhi.

Therefore, what I have said is without error. Good son, the Tathāgata, well-knowing immeasurable skillful means and wishing to transform sentient beings, thus preaches the Dharma in these various ways.
Regarding the intent behind the "Teaching of the Dharma" (Dharmaparyāya): because the capacities [of sentient beings] differ, the teachings are diverse;
yet because the assemblies are unified, the principle is the same. This is illustrated by six analogies, beginning with the analogy of the skilled physician.

First, the skilled physician; second, drinking water; third, the goldsmith; fourth, kindling fire; fifth, consciousness; sixth, form. Each consists first of the analogy and then of the application. First, the skilled physician:
This can be illustrated by an analogy.
Good son, it is like a skilled physician who recognizes the various sources of diseases in sentient beings and prepares medicine according to each specific ailment.
While he prescribes certain dietary restrictions for the medicine, water alone is not included among those prohibitions; thus, one may take ginger with water, or...
With licorice water, or fine-rooted pepper water, or black rock-honey water, or *āmalaka* water,
or *nīpāra* water, or *pāṭhā* water; or by drinking cold water, or drinking hot water,
or grape water, or pomegranate water— O son of good family, such a skilled physician well understands the various medicines for the ailments of sentient beings.
Although there are many prohibitions regarding water, they are not included in this category.
In Hexi, water is called *nipāla*; boiled *harītakī* is called *pāñjula*.
They boil tree leaves to make a decoction, naming it after the tree itself.

The Tathāgata is likewise; skillfully knowing expedient means, he analyzes and extensively explains various names and characteristics within the single characteristic of phenomena according to the various sentient beings.

Those sentient beings receive what is taught according to their capacities, and having received it, they practice and cultivate it until their afflictions are eliminated—just as that patient’s ailment is cured by following the instructions of a skilled physician.
Furthermore, good son, suppose there is a person who is well-versed in many languages and is in a great assembly.
This assembly is oppressed by heat and thirst, and they all cry out in unison, "I want water! I want water!
At that moment, this person takes cool, clear water and, according to their respective kinds, speaks of it as "this is water," or says "pānīya," or says "udaka."
They may call it *dhṛti*, or *sāri-laya*, or *pali*, or *payas*,
or *amṛta*, or "cow's milk"— using such immeasurable names for water, he speaks to the great assembly.
Next, regarding the waters: the water of Pāṇi in Kaśmīra is named Utpala;
the water of Eastern India is named *Uddhara* (some versions of the sūtra text read *Uddhṛta*, though this remains unsettled), which is traditionally transmitted as *Utpala*;
the water of Central India is named Śālilā; and the water of Śabdavidyā is named Pāyasa-yauvana.
Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise; by means of a single noble path, he expounds it in various ways for the sake of the śrāvakas, ranging from the faculty of faith up to the eightfold noble path.
This is the analogy of the three goldsmiths.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a goldsmith who, using a single kind of gold, fashions at will various kinds of ornaments—
namely, necklaces, chains, rings, bracelets, hairpins, earrings, celestial crowns, armlets, and seals.
Although there are such diverse differences among them, they do not depart from gold.
Good son, the Tathāgata is also like this: with the single Buddha-way, he teaches according to the various distinctions of sentient beings.
He may teach one kind, namely that all Buddhas have a single way which is non-dual; he may further teach two kinds, namely concentration and wisdom;
he may further teach three kinds, namely view, insight, and knowledge; and he may further teach four kinds, namely the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
The path of no-more-learning and the Buddha-path are further explained as being of five kinds, namely:

the path of practice through faith, the path of practice through Dharma, the path of liberation through faith, the path of vision-attainment, the path of bodily realization, and the path of the sixfold supernormal powers. They are further explained as being of six kinds, namely:

the path of the stream-enterer, the path of the once-returner, the path of the non-returner, the path of the arhat, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha. They are further explained as being of seven kinds.
These are the factors of enlightenment known as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

Furthermore, eight kinds are taught, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Furthermore, nine kinds are taught, namely: the Eightfold Path together with faith.
It is taught in ten ways, namely the ten powers; furthermore, it is taught in eleven ways, namely the ten powers plus great loving-kindness;
furthermore, it is taught in twelve ways, namely the ten powers, great loving-kindness, and great compassion;

furthermore, it is taught in thirteen ways, namely the ten powers, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*; furthermore, it is taught in sixteen ways, namely the ten powers, great loving-kindness, and [great compassion...]

The *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*, the Buddha-recollection samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), and the three correct foundations of mindfulness (*samyak-smṛtyupasthāna*) attained by the Buddha—these are further explained as the twentyfold path, namely:

the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the Buddha-recollection samādhi, and the three correct foundations of mindfulness.
Good son, these paths are of one essence; it was for the sake of sentient beings that the Tathāgata in the past made various distinctions.

The combined text states: Some speak of five types, namely those who practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita*) and so forth. Those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭi-prāpta*) belong to the path of seeing the truths (*darśana-mārga*), which consists of both the practice through faith and the practice through the Dharma (*dharma-carita*).
Those who have attained liberation through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) are also called "those who have attained vision" (*dṛṣṭi-labdha*);

these two belong to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). These four persons are divided into sharp and dull faculties within their respective paths; the practitioner through faith (*śraddhā-carita*) is situated in the path of seeing.

When one enters the path of seeing the truths with dull faculties through reflection, it results in the practice of dull dharma through faith-understanding (*śraddhādhimukta*); this may be known generally in this way. Through repeated cultivation, one becomes sharp;

without cultivation, one remains dull—thus they fluctuate and are not fixed. Some people say that fifteen moments of mind constitute the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), while from the sixteenth moment onward is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The masters of the treatises do not hold this view; rather, all sixteen moments are [the path of seeing].

The masters of the *Dṛṣṭimārga-śāstra* distinguish between the sharp and the dull faculties within the five *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness). One enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) without such distinction of sharpness or dullness;
it is like a boat on level water that may move slowly or quickly, yet once it catches the wind and follows the current, there is no longer any distinction between sharp and dull.
The remaining three [foundations of mindfulness] can be understood by analogy with this.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a single fire that, depending on what it burns, receives various names—
namely, wood-fire, grass-fire, chaff-fire, bran-fire, cow-dung-fire, or horse-dung-fire.
Good son, the Buddha-way is also like this: it is one and without duality, yet for the sake of sentient beings, it is differentiated in various ways.

Furthermore, good son, it is like a single consciousness that is explained as sixfold; when it reaches the eye, it is called eye-consciousness, and so on up to mental consciousness—it is just the same.
Good son, the Way is also like this: it is one and without duality, yet the Tathāgata makes various distinctions for the sake of transforming all sentient beings.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a single form: that which is seen by the eye is called "form," while that which is heard by the ear is [called "sound"].
That which is heard is called sound; that which is smelled by the nose is called fragrance; that which is tasted by the tongue is called flavor;
and that which is felt by the body is called touch.
Good son, the Path is likewise thus: it is one and without duality. Yet, because the Tathāgata desires to transform sentient beings, he makes various distinctions.
Good son, for this reason, that which enters the factors of the noble path is called the Noble Truth of the Path.
"Good son, this is the third summary concerning the Four Noble Truths.
Good son, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught these Four Noble Truths in their proper sequence;
by means of these causes and conditions, immeasurable sentient beings have attained deliverance from birth and death."

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha. [This concludes] the third section, which clarifies the wisdom of the immeasurable Four Noble Truths. The text is divided into three parts: first, it clarifies the immeasurable and the immeasurable;

second, it summarizes them as the four immeasurable wisdoms; third, it summarizes them as the two immeasurables. Regarding this, the "Huiwen" (Commentary on Meaning) states that this passage reconciles the Four Noble Truths;
