the "Kaishan" (Good Opening) school maintains that it concerns whether the inclusion of phenomena is exhaustive or not. Now, I maintain that this is precisely the [immeasurable].
The initial passage of the Chapter on Measurable and Immeasurable Wisdom, consisting of a dialogue, begins as follows:

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, once in the past, when the Buddha was staying by the Ājīvikas’ Grove on the bank of the Hiraṇyavatī River, the Tathāgata took a few tree leaves and said to the bhikṣus:
‘Are the leaves held in my hand now more numerous, or [are those in the forest] more so?’”

"O Bhikṣus, as for the grasses, trees, and leaves upon the earth, many of you say: 'World-Honored One, the grasses, trees, and leaves upon the earth are so numerous that they cannot be measured or calculated;
what the Tathāgata has grasped is but a small fraction, not worth mentioning.
O Bhikṣus, all dharmas realized by me are like the grasses and trees growing from the great earth; those which I have proclaimed for the sake of all sentient beings [are likewise vast]."
"O Bhagavān, it is like the leaves in one's hand. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:

"Regarding the immeasurable dharmas realized by the Tathāgata, if they were included within the Four Noble Truths, they would have already been taught; if they were not so included, there ought to be five truths."
In the question, first the past events are cited. The metaphor of the grasses and trees of the great earth represents the immeasurable;
the small amount held in immeasurable hands represents that which is conditioned and non-arising. One should know that what was previously mentioned is little, while what was not mentioned is much.

Such a vast quantity is fully encompassed by the Four Truths, yet it is not fully encompassed by the Four Means of Attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). If it were fully encompassed, one should not say it is "much"; if it were not fully encompassed, [the means would be insufficient].
There ought to be a fifth truth.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! Your question now will bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
Son of good family, all such dharmas are already fully subsumed within the Four Noble Truths."
Regarding the Truths (*satya*), the Buddha’s answer is both inclusive and non-inclusive. If one speaks of inclusion by way of the common name "Four Truths," it is exhaustive;

however, regarding the inclusion of their specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) through detailed analysis, he ultimately does not state that they are exhaustive. Because the names are identical while the meanings differ, there is both exhaustiveness and non-exhaustiveness.
The present Buddha answered them exhaustively; by collecting them under these names, they are all fully encompassed.

Kāśyapa spoke again, saying that beyond the second immeasurable, there are immeasurably many [others], which constitute the four immeasurables of wisdom. In the text, there is a question and answer regarding this.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying: "If such dharmas as these are contained within the Four Noble Truths, for what reason does the Tathāgata declare that he has not taught them?
In the answer, there are two parts:
first, showing the faculties and distinguishing the wisdom; second, correctly explaining the characteristics of the truths. Regarding the first part:
The Buddha said, "Good son, although one may enter therein, it is still not called 'expounding. Why is this?
Good son, there are two kinds of knowledge regarding the Noble Truths: the first is middling, and the second is superior. The middling belongs to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
the superior belongs to all Buddhas and bodhisattvas."
Regarding the wisdom of the truths (*satya-jñāna*) as fully discussed, there should be three grades. The lowest grade is that of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), who are not worth discussing;

therefore, it is not mentioned. Only the middle and superior grades are cited. Among the four types of persons, these are judged as middle and superior. If one were to judge them according to the dharmas, one should point to the fourfold Four Noble Truths to distinguish the middle and superior.
As previously stated, there is the "with-outflow" (*sa-niṣyanda*) and the "unborn" (*anutpāda*); [the latter] is immeasurable now.

One must distinguish that "the immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) does not refer to something that emerges separately outside the Four Noble Truths; rather, it refers to the different classifications within the Four Noble Truths themselves.
As the text says: "When analyzed and calculated, there are immeasurable kinds.

To discuss this exhaustively, one should consider how the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) differ in their specific types across all levels—from the hells up to Buddhahood—among both ordinary beings and sages, within each and every aggregate.
Furthermore, if one were to further analyze the immeasurable realms and entrances, how could these be known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas?
Moreover, from the hells up to the Buddha, the activities of practice differ;
if one were to analyze and calculate each and every activity, there are immeasurable kinds, which are likewise not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—this is what is meant by "immeasurable."
Furthermore, regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), from the hells up to the Buddha, by means of which body and by what Dharma should one teach so that they may practice and learn?
One must analyze and calculate each individual body and phenomenon, taking immeasurable Dharma-gates as their retinue;
this is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and is thus called the immeasurable Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Furthermore, from the hells...
As for the time when the Buddha attains liberation, the causes and conditions differ;
furthermore, each individual liberation has immeasurable distinctions and classifications of liberation, numbering countless kinds, which are not known even by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Thus, there are immeasurable truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Since these four objects are distinct, both that which is produced and that which is non-arising are not two.
Regarding the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths as they are understood by the wisdom within the vehicles, their names and designations differ;
they are like the great earth, which has a single name yet is called "immeasurable," its characteristics being vast and profound. Now, I shall briefly explain them.

Regarding the formal explanation, the Four Noble Truths constitute the four [sections]. Within the first, the Truth of Suffering, the scriptural text briefly indicates the characteristics of suffering by means of the three categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), and further clarifies the aggregates. First, as for the aggregates:
"Good son, knowing that the aggregates (skandhas) are suffering is called middle-grade wisdom.
To discern that the aggregates possess immeasurable characteristics and that all of them are suffering—something which is not known by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—is called superior wisdom.
Good son, such meanings as these I did not fully explain in that sūtra."
The text states: "To know that the aggregates (skandhas) are suffering is called middle wisdom; to discern that the aggregates possess immeasurable characteristics is called superior wisdom.
As for the discernment of the aggregates of the six realms of existence, this refers to the wholesome [states] of humans and devas.
Furthermore, worldly wholesome states such as those of humans and devas are obscured by the three miserable realms; untainted wholesome states are obscured by the various realms of saṃsāra.
For those of the two vehicles who possess the aggregates (skandhas), their equal virtues are obscured; because the four immeasurables are obscured, they cannot transform and deliver sentient beings;
because the four virtues are obscured, they cannot reach the place of treasure. The aggregates of a bodhisattva obscure [the realization of] birth.
Death and nirvāṇa are the canopies; birth and death are the canopy for the Great Compassion that uproots suffering, while nirvāṇa is the canopy for the Great Loving-kindness that bestows happiness.

The Buddha’s *skandhas* (aggregates) are the canopy that covers both phenomena and principle within the Dharma-realm: phenomena are covered by the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) which universally responds to all capacities and faculties, while principle is covered by the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) which pervades all places.

Furthermore, the *skandhas* of suffering within the six realms and those of the two vehicles— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation above reflects the full scope of the preceding segment.]
To discriminate that the aggregates (skandhas) are pleasure, the aggregates are duality, and the aggregates are non-duality—how could such discrimination be known by those of the Two Vehicles?
Good son, one who knows the various sense bases (āyatana) calls them "gates" and also calls them "suffering"; this is called the portion of middle wisdom.
The various entrances have immeasurable characteristics, all of which are suffering;
these are not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and are thus called "supreme wisdom. Such meanings as these I did not explain in that sūtra.
Next, knowing that the sense bases (*āyatana*) are the gateways is called middle-level wisdom; discerning that these sense bases possess immeasurable characteristics is called superior wisdom.
How does one discern the six realms and the six sense bases? This is called the "gate of entry" and is also called the "convergence of entry.

From the convergence of the eye-faculty with visual objects into conditioned phenomena, up to the convergence of the mind-faculty with mental objects into conditioned phenomena, [this applies] even to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
As for "entering," it is entering impermanence and non-self; one enters by means of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
When a Bodhisattva enters, they enter through the sense-faculty of the eye into the assembly of giving and enter the *dāna-pāramitā*; this applies likewise up to the mind.

When they enter through the sense-faculty of the eye, they enter the gates of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom, and enter the assemblies of all the *pāramitās*; this applies likewise up to the mind. This is the entry of all Buddhas.

The Buddha-eye enters the Gate of Universal Access; it enters all dharma-realms through the dharma-realms of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, responding through resonance to enter the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge); this applies likewise even to the mental faculty.

In various sutras, it is clarified that the six sense faculties are the gate of tranquility and the gate of equality—this principle is manifold (*etc.*). Furthermore, these are the entries into the six realms of existence.

The entrance through the gate of suffering is the entrance of the two vehicles; the entrance through the gate that is not suffering is the entrance of the bodhisattvas; the entrance through the gate that is both pleasant and painful is the entrance of the Buddhas;
and the entrance through the gate that is neither painful nor pleasant is [the entrance of] the Buddhas.

"Good son, one who knows the various elements (dhātu) is said to possess 'discrimination' (vibhāga), and is also said to possess 'nature' (prakṛti), and is also said to possess 'suffering' (duḥkha). This is called middling wisdom.
To discern that the various elements have immeasurable characteristics and that they are all entirely suffering—something not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—is called superior wisdom.
Good son, regarding such meanings as these, I have also [not] [expounded them] in that sūtra."
To explain this:
thirdly, knowing the nature of the divisions of the elements (*dhātu*) is called middle wisdom; discerning that the various elements possess immeasurable characteristics is called superior wisdom.
How does one discern the nature and divisions of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) within the six realms? It perceives only visible forms (*rūpa*).

The nature and constituents of the spheres of sound and form are perceived only by the eye and not by the ear, and so on up to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*), which can only be known and not seen by the sphere of mind (*manodhātu*).
The nature and constituents of the sphere of mental objects are perceived only by the mind and not by the ear or eye.
For those of the two vehicles, the nature and constituents of the eye-sphere are merely impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One may not constantly delight in [the sensory realms] up to and including the nature and constituents of the mind-realm (*manodhātu*). It is likewise for the Bodhisattva-realm:

the nature and constituents of the Bodhisattva’s eye-realm (*cakṣurdhātu*) see only the emptiness of forms, yet cannot immediately realize the simultaneous identity of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;

it is likewise for the nature and constituents of the mind-realm, which can only realize emptiness but cannot immediately realize the simultaneous identity of the provisional and the middle. Thus it is for all.

Regarding the Buddha-realm: the eye is the Dharma-realm; the nature of the Dharma-nature is such that it can see forms, hear sounds, smell fragrances, distinguish flavors, feel tangibles, and know phenomena.
It is emptiness, it is the provisional, and it is the Middle—inconceivable, and fully endowed with all immeasurable Buddha-dharmas.
This applies even to the mind in the same way. Furthermore, the six realms take suffering as their realm. Second.
The Bodhisattva takes that which is neither suffering nor pleasure as his realm, while the Buddha takes that which is neither pleasure nor pain as his realm.
Furthermore, knowing that the characteristic of the disintegration of form is called "middling wisdom" constitutes the lower grade of the extensive exposition on the aggregates (*skandha*).
"Good son, knowing that the characteristic of form is its disintegration is called middle wisdom;
discerning that all forms possess immeasurable characteristics of disintegration, and that these are entirely suffering—something unknown to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—is called superior wisdom.
Such meanings as these were not even mentioned by me in that sūtra."
The text states: To discern the infinite marks of disintegration in all forms is called superior wisdom. The forms of the six realms disintegrate their goodness;
the forms of the two vehicles disintegrate both cause and fruit; the forms of Bodhisattvas disintegrate existence and non-existence.

As for the forms of the Buddhas, they disintegrate the aforementioned disintegrations, yet this disintegration is itself the Dharma-realm—neither disintegration nor non-disintegration; it is entirely the Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding the realms: for those in the six paths of existence, it is the suffering of the destruction of form; for the two vehicles, it is the suffering of the destruction of form; for Bodhisattvas, it is the dual [suffering] of the destruction of form;
and for Buddhas, it is the dual non-[suffering] of the destruction of form (and so forth).

Good son, to know the characteristics of the perception of sensation is called middle-level wisdom; to discern that there are immeasurable characteristics of perception within all sensations is [supreme wisdom].
That which is not known by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is called superior wisdom.
Noble son, such meanings as these I did not even mention in that sūtra.
Furthermore, knowing that sensation is the characteristic of perception is called middling wisdom; discerning that sensation has immeasurable characteristics is... [called superior wisdom].

The "superior wisdom" refers to the experiences of the six realms of existence: experiences that are contrary, favorable, or neither contrary nor favorable. Toward the contrary, one gives rise to the perception of aversion; toward the favorable, the perception of craving;

and toward that which is neither contrary nor favorable, the perception of delusion. As for the experiences of those of the Two Vehicles, within these three types of perceptions, each gives rise to the fivefold Dharma-body.
For a *srotāpanna*, the first realization is the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). (Thus it is said.)

It is said: When a Bodhisattva receives, they receive the Buddha-dharma and receive sentient beings; when receiving the Buddha-dharma, they awaken to the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the various pāramitās;
when receiving sentient beings, they awaken to the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.
Those who receive the Buddhas awaken themselves and awaken others; this awakening is neither awakening nor non-awakening, neither not awakening nor not non-awakening.
To realize that all is the Dharma-realm:
O son of good family, to know that the grasping of signs through conceptualization is called middle wisdom;

to discern that this conceptualization involves immeasurable grasping of signs which is not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas is called superior wisdom. Such meanings as these were [taught] by me in that sūtra.
Nor does he speak of them.
Furthermore, knowing that the grasping of signs within perception is called middling wisdom, while the discernment that there is the grasping of immeasurable signs is called superior wisdom;
and that the grasping within the six realms of existence consists only of grasping at the person, the self, sentient beings, life-span, and the two [realms] of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
Riding upon this, one takes up impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; one takes up nirvana.
The taking of a bodhisattva does not take up the two extremes, but takes up only the Middle Way. As for the taking of a Tathāgata, taking is itself non-taking;
it is neither taking nor non-taking—all is the Dharma-realm.
"Good son, knowing that the characteristic of conditioned activity is called middling wisdom;
discerning that the characteristic of immeasurable activity is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas is called superior wisdom.
Good son, meanings such as these I did not even mention in that sūtra."
Furthermore, knowing the characteristic of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*) is called middle wisdom; discerning that activity has immeasurable characteristics of formation is called superior wisdom.
The activities of the six realms can produce the twenty-five existences; the practices of the two vehicles can produce *nirvāṇa*;
and the practices of Bodhisattvas produce the various *pāramitās* and the practices of all Buddhas—this is "acting while not acting."
The dharma-realm is neither created nor uncreated.
Son of good family, to discern the characteristics of consciousness is called middle wisdom;
to discern that consciousness is immeasurable and its characteristics are not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas is called superior wisdom. Son of good family, such meanings as these I—
That sutra also does not speak of it.
Furthermore, the discernment of consciousness is called middling wisdom; the discernment of the immeasurable characteristics of consciousness is called superior wisdom.
The six realms of existence are distinguished by taking this and rejecting that, drinking bitterness and consuming poison; the two vehicles distinguish them [in this way].
The Bodhisattva who detests birth-and-death and sinks into nirvana discriminates within the assembly of Buddhas of the "Detachment from Extremes" chapter;
the sūtra text concerning the discrimination of that which is neither extreme nor middle concludes with the Truth of Suffering.
"Good son, knowing that the causal conditions of craving can give rise to the five aggregates is called middling wisdom. When a single person gives rise to craving...

The immeasurable [nature of] such cravings as arise in all sentient beings, which cannot be known by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas but can be known [only by the Buddha], is called supreme wisdom; such meanings as these were not even mentioned by me in that sūtra.
Second, knowing that the causal conditions of craving can give rise to the various aggregates (skandhas) is called middle wisdom; knowing all cravings is called superior wisdom.
The craving of the six realms of existence is the causal condition for the subsequent aggregates; the craving of the two vehicles is the causal condition for the five parts [of the personality];

the craving of Bodhisattvas is the causal condition for the unequaled form (rūpa) up to the unequaled consciousness (vijñāna); and the craving of the Buddhas is the causal condition for the Buddhas themselves.
This love is the causal condition for liberation from form up to liberation from consciousness.
Good son, knowing the extinction of afflictions is called middle wisdom;
the discrimination of afflictions is incalculable, and their extinction is likewise incalculable—this is not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and is thus called superior wisdom. As it is said:
I have not explained these meanings in that sūtra either.
To know the cessation of afflictions is called middle wisdom; to know that the cessation of afflictions is immeasurable, and that this cessation is likewise immeasurable, is called superior wisdom.
Even ordinary beings in the six realms of existence can attain cessation with distinctions.

Having returned, one gives rise to the extinction of the two vehicles—the extinction of ash and severance which does not arise; one brings about the self-extinction of a bodhisattva and causes others to extinguish as well.
The extinction of all Buddhas is the extinction of all extinctions, which is precisely the Dharma-realm.
"Good son, knowing these characteristics of the path as being able to abandon afflictions is called middle wisdom.

To discern that the characteristics of the path are immeasurable and boundless, and that the afflictions abandoned are likewise immeasurable and boundless—such that this is not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—is called superior wisdom. I did not explain such meanings in that sūtra."
The four paths that abandon afflictions are called middle wisdom; the immeasurable and boundless paths capable of abandoning them are called superior wisdom.
The path of the six realms abandons evil for the sake of good and abandons good for the sake of evil;

the path of the two vehicles abandons outflows for the sake of the outflow-free; the path of the bodhisattvas abandons extremes for the sake of the middle; and the path of the Buddhas is without [extremes].
There is no arrival through detachment. Why? Because all dharmas are themselves the Buddha-way. One who perceives movement practices the factors of the path;
one who perceives non-movement practices the factors of the path; one who perceives both movement and non-movement practices the factors of the path;
and one who perceives neither movement nor non-movement practices the factors of the path (and so forth). This concludes the detailed analysis of the immeasurable Four Noble Truths.
To know the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is called middle wisdom. This constitutes the third section. Regarding the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), they are reduced to two.
Furthermore, first the two truths are clarified, and subsequently the wisdom of the two truths is clarified; the initial passage refers precisely to the two truths.
"Noble son, one who knows the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is said to possess middle-level wisdom.
To discern that the conventional truth is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable—something unknown to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—is called supreme wisdom.
Such meanings as these I have not even mentioned in that sūtra. Noble son, [one who knows] that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent and that all dharmas are without self..."
Nirvāṇa and quiescence are the ultimate truth; this is called middle-level wisdom.
To know that the ultimate truth is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable—such that it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—is called superior wisdom.
Such meanings as these I have also not explained in that sūtra.
In this text, directly knowing the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is middle wisdom; discerning that the conventional truth is immeasurable and boundless is superior wisdom.

Directly knowing the three seals of the Dharma (*tri-dharma-mudrā*) is middle wisdom; knowing that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable is superior wisdom.
Worldly people speak only of the ultimate truth, the true reality, and *nirvāṇa*.
One may only attain the One; there cannot be two, much less an infinite number. Now, the text clarifies that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is beyond measure and calculation;
how could it be merely of one kind? What is here termed the "eternal *nirvāṇa* and other true truths" differs from the Sāṃkhya school.
The Sāṃkhya speaks of four truths and sixteen principles (*tattva*), asserting that by perceiving all of them, one realizes the truth and attains sainthood. However, this is not the case here.

The proponents of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-vādin) maintain that only the doctrine of non-self (anātman) applies to both the ultimate and conventional levels, while all else pertains only to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

Nevertheless, they follow one another in asserting that these [other doctrines] are "true. This is because [they hold that] impermanence exhausts the perversion of permanence, and suffering and its origin conform to their respective characteristics as being "true.
As it is said in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "That which is neither born nor extinguished is the meaning of impermanence; exhaustion is [the meaning of suffering]."
The true nature (*dharmatā*) is entirely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and it is also these three seals of the Dharma (*dharma-mudrā*).
At that time, Mañjuśrī descends [to explain] the second point, clarifying the wisdom of the two truths (*satyadvaya*). First, he presents the six types of two-truth theories from previous exegesis:

(1) existence and emptiness; (2) the unreal and the real; (3) worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*) and what is widely disseminated; (4) also called "according to phenomena" (*suvastuka*); (5) continuity; and (6) ... [the sixth].
The six causes arising through mutual dependence refer to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dapin); the flow of the empty and the real refers to the *Abhidharma*;

and the causal arising through the continuity of mutual dependence refers to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. Furthermore, there is another interpretation regarding the identity of meaning despite the difference in names:

first, ordinary person versus sage; second, the unreal versus the real; third, the empty versus the existent; fourth, the provisional versus the real; fifth, phenomena versus principle; and sixth, the proximate versus the remote. The ancient commentary states that "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*) is...
The floating and empty is called "true" [only] because it is real; the world is subject to change and decay, whereas the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is without fault.
The conventional depends on the non-conventional, and that which is not conventional is called "true. The true depends on the non-true, and that which is not true is called "conventional.

Thus, the mutual dependence of the empty and the real gives rise to the names "true" and "conventional. Another asks: "The true is truly real and can be called a 'truth' (satya); the conventional is floating and empty—why is it also called a truth?"
Regarding the interpretation of *di* (truth/reality): "To examine" means to scrutinize whether something is substantial or empty. If this is so, there are two explanations for the meaning of *di*:

the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) is explained by "emptiness," while the ultimate (*paramārtha*) is explained by "substantiality. Xinghuang says: "Truth is never dual; it is dual only in terms of conditions.
The conventional is real for ordinary people, and the ultimate is real for sages; both use 'reality' to explain *di*, rather than using 'emptiness.'"

Now, if that which is true for the noble is real for the noble, and they possess an illuminating wisdom of the true that can be called "truth," then how can that which is real for the ordinary person be called "truth" when they lack an illuminating wisdom of the conventional?
If that which is real for the ordinary person regarding the conventional could be called "conventional truth" despite their lack of an illuminating wisdom of the conventional,
then [by parity of reasoning], the ordinary person would also possess an illuminating wisdom of the true regarding the true.
If the real must also be called the "True Truth" (*satya*), then for one who lacks knowledge of the real, how could it not be called the True Truth?

Furthermore, if one lacks knowledge of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), how can it be called the Conventional Truth? Moreover, if the noble ones regard the real as true and thus call it a "truth," why would they not regard the conventional as true and likewise call it a "truth"?
This would imply that the noble ones lack expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Now...

Regarding the term "truth" (*satya*): it refers to that which is examined and verified as real. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states that the Four Noble Truths are bodhi because they are not false or deceptive;
thus, they are examined and verified as real. There is verification according to conventional sentiment, verification according to wisdom, and verification according to both sentiment and wisdom.

Therefore, whether in relation to ordinary beings or noble ones, and whether in terms of the ultimate or the conventional, they may all be called "truths. To illustrate this with a single example: regarding a single form, an ordinary person says—
There are noble sages who hold that existence and non-existence are likewise like one day’s difference between being intoxicated and sober;

for them, there is the distinction between shifting and non-shifting, and the same applies to the meaning of the Single Truth and the Two Truths. The old interpretation held that the Two Truths are of one essence and not different. Longguang said: "Since they are called 'Two Truths,' how could they possibly be of one essence?
The Two Truths possess two distinct essences, yet both equally take provisional dharmas as their objects; the conventional truth is [the perception of] the world."
The principle of the absence of marks (*animitta*) constitutes the true essence (*tattva*). Although there are two essences, their ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) is identical:
the conventional is identical to the nameless and markless, and the true absence of names and marks does not obstruct names and marks. Furthermore, it is said that the two truths are one essence;
because emptiness is the fundamental principle, the true is taken as the essence and the conventional as its function. Or it is said that the true is derived from the conventional.
To claim that the Middle Way is the substance for both [truths] as their function—this is what Kaishan says—but these interpretations are all incorrect.
If the two truths had two distinct substances, then the mundane would lack the ultimate, and the ultimate would lack the mundane;
they would merely be non-identical and could not possess mutual identity. If they were of one substance, there would be only one truth, and thus no second.

If the two truths take the Middle Way as their essence, then while the grasping of characteristics obstructs the Real (paramārtha-satya) and ignorance obstructs the Conventional (saṃvṛti-satya), what further thing would obstruct the Middle?
If the wisdom regarding the two truths cannot perceive the Middle, how can it constitute its essence?

If the two truths have two distinct essences and these two essences are each different, one need not discuss their mutual identity. If the two truths are a single essence, then they would be merely a single truth; with whom [or what] would there be a second?
The *Renwang Banruo* (Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) states that the two truths are not mutually identical, "just like the two horns of an ox.

However, the *Dapin* (Large Version of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) asserts that "form is emptiness," and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* explains that the thorough penetration of the five aggregates of clinging as empty means that there is nothing that arises;

this is the meaning of suffering. Furthermore, within this very sūtra, it is repeatedly stated that the two truths are mutually identical. Formerly, it was said that the four truths were combined into two truths.
Some say that suffering, its origin, and the world are conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the path and cessation are supramundane and constitute ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Others say that three of the truths are conventional truth, and only cessation is ultimate truth. Still others say that all four truths are conventional truth because they clarify cause and effect;
rather, the signless cause and effect is ultimate truth. Others say that the four truths themselves are conventional truth...

The mundane truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The text states: "By understanding that suffering is without suffering, there is the ultimate truth; the same applies to the remaining three [truths].
Now it is clarified that not only do the four truths differ in their expansion and contraction, but even regarding the expansion and contraction of the two truths, they are not uniform;
this will be explained later. According to the text, there are two rounds of question and answer; the first question is divided into three parts, the first of which is a direct inquiry.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) which you have taught, what is their meaning?
Furthermore, World-Honored One, do these two truths possess mutually exclusive characteristics?"
"World-Honored One, does the conventional truth exist within the ultimate truth? Does the ultimate truth exist within the conventional truth?
If it is as you say that they both exist, then there would be two truths;

if it is as you say that they do not exist, then is it not the case that the Tathāgata has spoken falsely? Thus he raised a twofold objection. If they existed, they would constitute two truths; if they did not exist, would it not imply that the Tathāgata’s teaching was deceptive?
Regarding the meaning within this difficulty: if one says they exist, this refers to the "one truth," because the ultimate and the conventional are mutually identical;
since the ultimate contains the conventional and the conventional contains the ultimate, the two truths are not distinct, and thus one speaks of them as being one.

If, on the other hand, one says they do not exist, this is a false view. To speak in terms of reality, to maintain that things are definitively existent or definitively non-existent, definitively identical or definitively different—all such positions are false.

Those who produce various sūtras present their texts in mutual contrast; if one were to insist on the existence or non-existence [of these], it would result in the false doctrines of nihilism or eternalism.
"Good son," below, the Tathāgata answers directly.
"Good son, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
These two truths are mutually identical; they are neither interrupted nor eternal, and are certainly not false.
This concludes the second round of questions and answers from the World-Honored One.
World-Honored One, if that were so, there would be no two truths.
The intention of the initial question is that it would revert to becoming a single truth; therefore, it is said that there would be no two truths.
Just as if length exists within shortness, length is lost, and if the ultimate exists within the conventional, the ultimate is lost; thus, only a single truth remains.
The Buddha replied that there are two [truths]. First, he briefly clarifies the general meaning:
The Buddha said, "Good son, there are skillful means that accord with sentient beings, whereby I speak of two truths.
In reality, the Middle Way has but a single essence; it is only for the sake of conditions and through skillful means that I speak of two."
If one follows conventional discourse, the second [section] provides a detailed exposition consisting of eight categories: (1) mundane and supramundane; (2) named and nameless; (3) real and unreal;
(4) determinate and indeterminate; (5) dharmas and non-dharmas; (6) combustible and non-combustible; (7) suffering and non-suffering;
(8) that which is conjoined with others. This also constitutes six types of the two truths (*satyadvaya*). If one speaks of emptiness and existence, or the false and the real:

The claim that both truths (the conventional and the ultimate) equally possess both the illusory and the real aspects—such that these two principles stand in firm opposition—is not the intended meaning of the sutra.
The current text states: "In accordance with sentient beings, it is taught that there are two truths. This is like telling a person who is intoxicated that the sun is moving;

one should employ this principle to interpret the scriptural passage. One master says: "The seven kinds [of consciousness] are unified, yet they are spoken of as different according to conditions. Another master says: [The same].

Regarding the statement that there are seven distinct types, the wise masters of the present day maintain that although the names of these two truths differ in seven ways, their underlying meaning can be harmonized:
(1) arising and ceasing; (2) non-arising; (3) the conventional alone and the compounded ultimate; (4) the conventional alone and the single middle way;

(5) the compounded conventional and the single middle way; (6) the compounded conventional and the compounded middle way; and (7) the perfect two truths. This is according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The terminology and characteristics in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) differ slightly, yet their underlying meaning must be the same; readers should understand this. Within each of these categories, there are further three types:

those that follow sentiment (*suíqíng*), those that follow wisdom (*suìzhì*), and those that follow both sentiment and wisdom (*suíqíngzhì*). Now, I wish to explain this passage by means of those seven types of the two truths (*dīngshí*).
Since the Buddha’s intent is difficult to fathom, I shall first present the views of one master regarding the eight different [interpretations]. That is:
Regarding the first of the eight points, which establishes the two truths by distinguishing between the mundane and supramundane persons, this applies generally to the following seven.
"Good son, if one follows verbal expression, there are two kinds: first, mundane dharmas; second, supramundane dharmas."

Good son, that which is known by those who have transcended the world is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), while that which is known by worldly people is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

Each of these two truths possesses this significance: the manifold conceptualizations of worldly sentiment are bound together as the conventional truth, whereas the manifold [realizations] of noble wisdom [constitute the ultimate truth].
To know that which is bound together as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is to distinguish the two truths according to conventional sentiment and wisdom.
Next, "O son of good family, the aggregation of the five aggregates" is a distinction made regarding whether names exist or do not exist.
"O son of good family, the aggregation of the five aggregates is called 'so-and-so'"; this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who follow whatever they are so designated.

To understand that within the aggregates there is no such thing as a personal name, and that apart from the aggregates there is likewise no such thing as a personal name—this is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
To be able to know the person who transcends the world according to its true nature and characteristics is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

To grasp the aggregates (skandhas) is called "birth," which is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). To know the nature of the aggregates as being apart from the aggregates—that nature is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
This is established based on the four truths with activity (sābhisaṃskāra-catur-āryasatya).
Third, furthermore, son of good family, there may be dharmas that have both a name and a reality.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are some dharmas that possess both name and reality, and there are other dharmas that possess a name but lack reality.
Son of good family, that which possesses a name but lacks reality is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya); that which possesses both name and reality is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
He said: "In the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), names exist and these names summon their corresponding entities;
in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there are only names without reality. The present text reverses this: here, there are only empty names without reality.
That which is neither arising nor ceasing and accords with the characteristics of dharmas is the ultimate truth. Because it cannot be that form is itself emptiness, there are names but no reality."
Because one can realize that form is itself emptiness, there is the existence of real names; this is established based on the Four Truths of Non-arising.
Furthermore, "Good sons, sentient beings, life-span, and so forth are like a whirling firebrand"—this discusses the Two Truths by means of the simple conventional and the compound ultimate.
Good son, as I perceive the lifespan, knowledge, vision, nourishment, husband, agent, and experiencer of sentient beings—

as well as the mirage, the city of the Gandharvas, the hair of a tortoise, the horns of a rabbit, and the wheel of a whirling firebrand— the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Provisional names, illusions, mirages, and fire-wheels exist only as names but lack actual substance; they are called "worldly truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*) because they conform to worldly convention.
When "truth" is combined with the "middle," they together constitute "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).

If one were to take "truth" alone as the first principle, one could not say that suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are the first principle; rather, it is by referring to all four truths together that they are identified as the ultimate.
In this context, it is explained that within the immeasurable Four Noble Truths, whether they are the ultimate (*tattva*) or the middle, they are collectively the First Noble Truth;
as the preceding text states, the First Noble Truth is immeasurable, boundless, and ineffable.
"Good son, there are five worldly dharmas. These five are established here to clarify the two truths by means of the simple conventional and the simple ultimate.
Good son, what are the five worldly dharmas? First, the world of names; second, the world of phrases; third, the world of bonds; fourth, the world of dharmas;
and fifth, the world of attachment. Good son, what is the world of names? It refers to male, female, jar, and clothing."

Vehicles, houses, and such things as these are called the world of names (*nāma-loka*). What is the world of phrases (*pada-loka*)? Verses consisting of four lines, and such verses as these, are called the world of phrases.
What is the world of bonds (*bandhana-loka*)? Folding, joining, tying, binding, and clasping the hands—these are called the world of bonds.
What is the world of phenomena (*dharma-loka*)? It is like striking a gong to assemble the monastics, beating a drum to prepare the army of precepts, or blowing a conch shell to give notice.

This is called attachment to the world. What is meant by "attachment to the world"? It is like a person looking from afar who, seeing someone wearing dyed robes, forms a perception and becomes attached, thinking, "This is a śramaṇa, not a brāhmaṇa.
Or, seeing someone with a cord tied and worn across their body, they immediately form the thought, "This is a brāhmaṇa, not a śramaṇa.
This is called attachment to the world, son of good family; it is thus.

"Noble son, these are called the five worldly dharmas. If there are sentient beings who, regarding these five worldly dharmas, possess no inverted views and know them as they truly are, this is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)."
Above, the five analogies of the hot, blazing wheel of fire were used to illustrate the "person-self" (pudgala-ātman) as conventional truth;

now, the five dharmas are taken as conventional truth. The five dharmas are like the blazing wheel, and the blazing wheel is an analogy for the dharmas; these are raised reciprocally as being equally mere mundane conventions.
When the mind is free from inversion and knows them as they truly are, one directly points to the Middle Way as suchness (tathatā).

In truth, this illumination [teaches] that conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*) is non-arising and so forth; taking suffering and its origin as the conventional, it points downward to the single ultimate truth as the real.
Good sons, whether by burning or by cutting—this refers to the conventional of the double and the single, thereby clarifying the two truths.
Furthermore, son of good family, if there is burning, cutting, death, or destruction, this is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
that which is without burning, without cutting, without death, and without destruction is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"Whether burning or dying" clarifies the beginning and end of the nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*); "whether cutting or destroying" clarifies the beginning and end of the analysis of phenomena.
Thus, these two beginnings exist and their two ends are non-existent; this union of existence and non-existence constitutes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is a "double conventional.
To single out the Middle Way—which is neither existent nor non-existent—is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, the absence of burning and cutting is the first [truth].
In the *Yimíng shàngwǔ*, it is held that the true and the conventional regarding non-arising are both termed "conventional," while the single ultimate truth below is taken as "true.
[The passage] from "7.
Good son" to "8. the existence or non-existence of suffering" explains the two truths by means of the complex conventional and the complex middle.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are eight characteristics of suffering which are called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*):

the absence of birth, the absence of aging, the absence of illness, the absence of death, the absence of separation from the beloved, the absence of meeting with the hated, the absence of not obtaining what one seeks, and the absence of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
These are called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding the "redundant conventional" mentioned previously: the "redundant middle" does not merely refer to principle as identical to phenomena;

rather, because the Dharma-realm of principle is perfectly complete, it is called the "redundant middle. This combines the preceding "conditioned" and "unborn" aspects—both true and conventional—and designates them all as "conventional.
It points to the "one reality that is inconceivable" below as the "True Truth. Although this is not explicitly stated in the text, such is the meaning.
The preceding section has established that this instance still pertains to the two truths of the single mundane and the double intermediate.
Furthermore, from "Good son" onwards, the text first provides analogies and subsequently offers their applications to clarify the perfect two truths.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a single person who possesses many capacities: when he runs, he is called a runner; when he harvests crops, he is called a reaper;
when he prepares food and drink, he is called a cook; when he works with timber, he is called a carpenter;
and when he smelts gold and silver, he is called a goldsmith. In this way, a single person has many names.
Regarding characters:
the Dharma is also like this; in reality it is one, yet it has many names. That which arises based on the union of father and mother is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
that which arises from the union of the twelve links of dependent origination is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

The mutual identity of the ultimate and the conventional is entirely inconceivable. For example, when parents unite to produce a single child, this can serve as an analogy for the perfect conventional:
the convergence of the three paths within the twelve links of dependent origination is itself the three virtues, which manifest the ultimate truth of the perfect reality.
This is what is called the inconceivability of the two truths; all dualities of the two truths are likewise so.

Entering into this, the skillful means of conventional discourse explain the two truths as being immeasurable and boundless; why then should it be surprising that they are summarized into seven types?
To be able to know them thus is the noble practice of wisdom (*jñāna-caryā*). Since ancient times, all have been deluded regarding these two truths.
Now, by employing the Master Tiantai’s doctrine of the sevenfold two truths to explain the eightfold meanings, their characteristics will become clear.
The Arhats follow the noble wisdom.
In the third section below, Mañjuśrī clarifies the noble practice of the wisdom of the single ultimate truth (*ekasatyatattva*).
Why does he not proceed from four to three, but instead leap directly to two? It is not that there is no [logical sequence].
Regarding the three truths, this text groups four into two; however, as for their meaning, it groups four into three.

Since the latter is slightly less convenient, it does not speak of "three. This interpretation differs from the following question, which cites the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*—stating that the single truth of the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha-satya*) is the true ground—to argue that the fruit of Buddhahood is eternally abiding and constitutes a single, real truth.
Master Shi says that "removing delusion to reveal the *ālayavijñāna*" means establishing the provisional teacher within the ultimate truth (*satya*).

Master Xinghuang says that "removing permanence and annihilation to reveal the Middle Way" constitutes the single ultimate truth. Master Xinghuang does not accept [the distinction between] the basis and that which is based upon it within the fruit of Buddhahood.
Is this single reality identical to or different from delusive afflictions and the *ālaya*? If they were identical, then since delusive afflictions are removed, the *ālaya* would also be removed.

If one falsely claims that there is reality based on a conceptual dependence on difference, how could this be the single reality? To speak of a "middle" in opposition to the "extremes" is itself still an extreme;
it is not the single reality. Since all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent and ultimately pure, truly having nothing at all, when has there ever been anything real or unreal?
"Truth" and "untruth" are merely provisional designations established through conditions and skillful means.
The verbal teachings rely on the text precisely because the single path of purity constitutes the one true reality (*eka-satya*); for this is the correct and true Dharma. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says:
"The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is far removed [from conceptualization]. Therefore, it is clarified here that if something is not that [nature], it is not this; it is not the one true reality.

However, if one follows conditions to provide diverse explanations while grasping the intended meaning, there is no fault. The text clearly reveals the one true reality, which is exceedingly self-evident. As for the passage:

The text is divided into two parts: first, the statement of the thesis, and second, the discussion of the meaning. In the first part, regarding the statement of the thesis, there is a question and an answer.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of that which you call 'the truth of reality' (satya)?"
In the response, there are eight noble sons (*kulaputra*). The first two together establish the initial meaning, which thus consists of seven distinct points.
First, regarding the object:
the Buddha said, "Noble son, that which is called 'the ultimate truth' (*satya*) is named the True Dharma (*saddharma*). Noble son, if a dharma is not true..."
It is not called the ultimate truth (*bhūtārtha-satya*).
Second, with respect to the mind:
"Good son, the ultimate truth is that which is non-erroneous; that which is non-erroneous is what is called the ultimate truth."
Third, regarding verbal expression, I personally maintain that it may also be understood in terms of conduct.
Son of good family, true reality (satya) is devoid of falsehood; if there were falsehood, it would not be called true reality.
Fourth, according to persons:
O son of good family, that which is the ultimate truth is called the Mahāyāna; that which is not the Mahāyāna is not called the ultimate truth.
Fifth, according to the teachings.
Good son, that which is the ultimate truth (satya) is spoken by the Buddha and not spoken by Māra;
if it were spoken by Māra and not by the Buddha, it would not be called the ultimate truth.
Sixth, [this is] in terms of the essence of the cause.
Good son, as for true reality (*satya*), it is the single path of purity, which is non-dual.
Seventh, regarding the essence of the fruit:
good son, that which possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity is what is called the meaning of true reality.

Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha. This is the second section, "The Discussion of Principles," which consists of seven chapters. The first chapter concerns the discussion of principles regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*), consisting of questions and answers.
In the question, the inquiry is first acknowledged:
Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, if that which is true is taken as the True Truth (*satya*)," and so forth. Regarding this "true reality" (*tattva*):...
If the Dharma is the Tathāgata, space, and Buddha-nature, then there would be no distinction between the Tathāgata,
space, and Buddha-nature. At first glance,
this seems to ask what the difference is among these three— Tathāgata, space, and Buddha-nature— but the answer follows below.
The intention [of this question] is precisely to ask what the difference is between these three kinds and the single ultimate truth (*ekābhisaṃbodhi-satya*).

The Buddha’s answer has three parts: first, the presentation of the two headings; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Regarding the first, the presentation of the headings, there are two sections:
first, the presentation of the former Four Truths; second, the presentation of the present Single Ultimate Truth. Master Xinghuang names the first the "heading of Reality and Cessation."
Next is the chapter on the "Extinction of Reality," which takes the teaching as reality and the extinction of grasping at principles as the extinction of reality.

Furthermore, that which is real within the teachings of the Four Noble Truths is itself the Truth of Reality; since both space and Buddha-nature are the reality of principle, they constitute the reality of the Truths, and are therefore called "Truths.
Now, this initial proclamation concerns the former Four Noble Truths.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “There is suffering, which is a truth and a reality; there is origination, which is a truth and a reality;
there is cessation, which is a truth and a reality; and there is the path, which is a truth and a reality.”
Each [of these] has three phrases: suffering is the objective realm of suffering (*duḥkha-viṣaya-satya*); the teaching on suffering is the instruction on suffering (*duḥkha-deśanā-satya*);

and the wisdom of suffering is the actual principle of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya-tattva*). These are non-dual and thus constitute reality. Furthermore, it is said that by excluding the phrase "suffering," the remaining two may also be judged as reality;
or, one may simply take "reality" alone and exclude the other two phrases, using only reality itself as the truth.
Next, following the section "The Tathāgata is not suffering," is the second recitation: the chapter on the single reality.
"Good son, the Tathāgata is neither suffering nor a truth, yet he is real; empty space is neither suffering nor a truth, yet it is real;
the Buddha-nature is neither suffering nor a truth, yet it is real."
All three types are real; that which is not suffering is neither an object (*viṣaya*) nor a truth (*satya*), and is not a teaching.
That which is real is principle (*tattva*); the latter three truths are likewise so. The Tathāgata, space, and the Buddha-nature are also like this:
when manifest, they are called the Tathāgata; when hidden, they are called the Buddha-nature. Space takes both the hidden and the manifest as non-dual.

Regarding what is called "suffering," the second section below provides an explanation of two chapter-headings. This is based solely on the Four Noble Truths, which are divided into four distinct parts.
Within each truth, there is first an explanation of the "real truth" (*satya*), which refers to the reality within the former Four Noble Truths;
next, there is an explanation of the "truth of reality," both of which follow the text as written.
Mañjuśrī, that which you call suffering is characterized by impermanence and is subject to cessation; this is the conventional truth.
The nature of the Tathāgata is neither suffering nor impermanent, nor is it subject to cessation; therefore, it is the ultimate reality.
It is the same with the *ākāśa* (space) and the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, son of good family, that which is called "origination" (samudaya) is that which causes the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) to combine and arise;
it is also called suffering (duḥkha), and it is also called impermanent (anitya). It is a characteristic that can be abandoned, and this is called the True Truth (satya).
Good son, the Tathāgata is not of the nature of an aggregate, nor is he the cause of the aggregates, nor is he a characteristic that can be severed;
therefore, he is real. Space and the Buddha-nature are also like this.

Good son, that which is called "extinction" refers to the extinction of afflictions. Furthermore, what is attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles is termed impermanent, whereas that attained by the Buddhas is termed permanent;
it is also called the "realized Dharma," and this constitutes the ultimate truth.
"Good son, the nature of the Tathāgata is not called 'extinguished,' yet it can extinguish afflictions;
it is neither eternal nor impermanent, and is not termed a 'realized dharma' because it is eternally abiding and unchanging. Therefore, it is real. The same is true for space and the Buddha-nature."
"Good son, the Path is that which can sever afflictions; it is both eternal and impermanent, a dharma that can be cultivated, and this is the ultimate truth.
The Tathāgata, however, is not the Path; he cannot sever afflictions, he is neither eternal nor impermanent, he is not a dharma that can be cultivated, and he is eternally abiding and unchanging."
Therefore, it is real; the emptiness of space and the Buddha-nature are also like this.
Furthermore, that which is called "true reality" is the Tathāgata. This concludes the third section, which is divided into two parts:
first, it establishes that the three dharmas are identical with true reality and have no separate essence.
Furthermore, son of good family, that which is called "reality" (bhūta) is the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata is reality. Reality is space (ākāśa); space is reality.
Reality is the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu); the Buddha-nature is reality.
Next, following the passage "There is suffering and there is the cause of suffering," the text further concludes the points of correctness and error in two parts.

First, it concludes that the three dharmas are distinct from the Four Noble Truths; therefore, they are truths. Next, it concludes that the three dharmas are distinct from conditioned and out-flowing phenomena;
therefore, they are real.
Mañjuśrī, there is suffering, there is the cause of suffering, there is the cessation of suffering, and there is the remedy for suffering;
yet for the Tathāgata, these do not exist, nor even does the "remedy" exist. Therefore, it is called "reality" (satya) and not "truth" (satya). Space and the Buddha-nature are also like this.

That which is suffering is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and tainted (*sāsrava*), and is devoid of bliss; the Tathāgata is neither conditioned nor tainted, being profoundly tranquil and blissful—this is the reality (*satya*), not merely a conventional truth (*satya*).

What is called "there is suffering" refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); the cause of suffering is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); the cessation of suffering is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); and the path in opposition to suffering is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

Question: The Truth of the Path is neither false nor real, yet it is called "real. Should that which is neither false nor real also be called a "Truth" (*satya*)? Answer: It is as you have asked. Question: If the two truths are equal, why do the followers of the Two Vehicles call them "truths" (*satya*), while the Tathāgata calls them "reality" (*bhūta*)? Answer: This distinction arises from the difference between granting and withholding. The followers of the Two Vehicles thoroughly know this as suffering; furthermore, they understand that suffering is without suffering. It is granted to them. However, the Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself non-suffering, and he does not grant it [as suffering]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is empty and without self, and they do not grant it [as having a self]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself non-self, and he does not grant it [as having a self]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is quiescent and extinguished, and they do not grant it [as being something further to be attained]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself quiescence and extinction, and he does not grant it [as something further]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is unarisen and unceasing, and they do not grant it [as arising or ceasing]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself non-arising and non-ceasing, and he does not grant it [as arising or ceasing]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is unborn and undying, and they do not grant it [as being born or dying]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself non-birth and non-death, and he does not grant it [as being born or dying]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally tranquil and fundamentally extinguished, and they do not grant it [as something else]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original tranquility and fundamental extinction, and he does not grant it [as something else]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-existent and fundamentally non-existent, and they do not grant it [as existing]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-existence and fundamental non-existence, and he does not grant it [as existing]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally empty and fundamentally empty, and they do not grant it [as being otherwise]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original emptiness and fundamental emptiness, and he does not grant it [as being otherwise]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally signless and fundamentally signless, and they do not grant it [as having signs]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original signlessness and fundamental signlessness, and he does not grant it [as having signs]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally wishless and fundamentally wishless, and they do not grant it [as being wished for]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original wishlessness and fundamental wishlessness, and he does not grant it [as being wished for]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-dual and fundamentally non-dual, and they do not grant it [as dual]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-duality and fundamental non-duality, and he does not grant it [as dual]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-conceptual and fundamentally non-conceptual, and they do not grant it [as conceptual]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-conceptuality and fundamental non-conceptuality, and he does not grant it [as conceptual]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-attainment and fundamentally non-attainment, and they do not grant it [as attainable]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-attainment and fundamental non-attainment, and he does not grant it [as attainable]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-differentiation and fundamentally non-differentiation, and they do not grant it [as differentiated]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-differentiation and fundamental non-differentiation, and he does not grant it [as differentiated]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-distinction and fundamentally non-distinction, and they do not grant it [as distinct]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-distinction and fundamental non-distinction, and he does not grant it [as distinct]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-discrimination and fundamentally non-discrimination, and they do not grant it [as discriminated]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-discrimination and fundamental non-discrimination, and he does not grant it [as discriminated]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-attachment and fundamentally non-attachment, and they do not grant it [as an object of attachment]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-attachment and fundamental non-attachment, and he does not grant it [as an object of attachment]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-grasping and fundamentally non-grasping, and they do not grant it [as graspable]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-grasping and fundamental non-grasping, and he does not grant it [as graspable]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-clinging and fundamentally non-clinging, and they do not grant it [as clung to]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-clinging and fundamental non-clinging, and he does not grant it [as clung to]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-entrustment and fundamentally non-entrustment, and they do not grant it [as entrustable]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-entrustment and fundamental non-entrustment, and he does not grant it [as entrustable]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-abiding and fundamentally non-abiding, and they do not grant it [as abidable]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-abiding and fundamental non-abiding, and he does not grant it [as abidable]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-reliance and fundamentally non-reliance, and they do not grant it [as reliant]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-reliance and fundamental non-reliance, and he does not grant it [as reliant]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-coming and fundamentally non-coming, and they do not grant it [as coming]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-coming and fundamental non-coming, and he does not grant it [as coming]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-going and fundamentally non-going, and they do not grant it [as going]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-going and fundamental non-going, and he does not grant it [as going]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-arising and fundamentally non-arising, and they do not grant it [as arising]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-arising and fundamental non-arising, and he does not grant it [as arising]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-ceasing and fundamentally non-ceasing, and they do not grant it [as ceasing]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-ceasing and fundamental non-ceasing, and he does not grant it [as ceasing]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-birth and fundamentally non-birth, and they do not grant it [as being born]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-birth and fundamental non-birth, and he does not grant it [as being born]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-death and fundamentally non-death, and they do not grant it [as dying]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-death and fundamental non-death, and he does not grant it [as dying]. Therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, the Two Vehicles know that suffering is originally non-existence and fundamentally non-existence, and they do not grant it [as existing]. The Tathāgata knows that suffering is itself original non-ex
Because the term "truth" (諦) has not yet exhausted the reality of the principle, its actual substance is negated.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the Buddha [taught] below... This explains the second section, the Chapter on Relying on the Mind, which first poses a question and then provides an answer.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, that which is non-perverted is called the True Truth (*satya*).
If this is so, then among the Four Truths, would there not be four perversions?
If such were the case, how can you say that being free from perversion is called the True Truth, while all perversions are not called true?"
The intent of the initial question is as follows: If the truths encompass the inversions, then how can one say that they are "non-inverted" and thus real?
If they do not encompass them, this contradicts the previous statement that the categories of phenomena are exhaustively subsumed. Considering both possibilities, there are faults in either case.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, “All inversions enter into the Truth of Suffering.

Just as sentient beings who possess an inverted mind are said to be ‘inverted,’ good son, it is like a person who does not accept the instructions of their parents or elders, or who, though having accepted them, cannot practice in accordance with them; such people are called ‘inverted. It is thus.”
That which is inverted is not non-suffering; it is indeed suffering.

However, while the text below clearly explains that this is subsumed under both the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origination, the present passage explains it solely as the Truth of Suffering, doing so specifically from the perspective of the fruit reaping the reward of its cause.
The third question and answer explains the section on verbal designations.
Mañjuśrī said: "If that which the Buddha has spoken is not false, then it is the ultimate truth (*satyadharma*).
If this is so, one should know that what is false is not the ultimate truth."
The Buddha said, "Good son, all that is false and deceptive enters into the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

For example, if there are sentient beings who deceive others, by reason of these causes and conditions they fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. Such phenomena as these are called 'falsehood.
This falsehood is not something other than suffering; it is itself suffering. [Thus spoke] the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Because the Honored One remains far removed from and does not engage in [falsehood], it is called "illusory. Since such illusions are severed and eliminated by the Buddhas and the followers of the Two Vehicles, they are therefore called the "Truth of Reality" (satya).

Among these, two matters can be seen; my personal opinion is that, according to the Buddha’s response, since it concerns the severing of afflictions, it should be understood as referring to [the Truth of Cessation].
[The Buddha] proceeded.
Mañjuśrī said: "As the Buddha has taught, [this is the fourth section], asking about persons.
Mañjuśrī said: "If, as the Buddha has taught, the Mahāyāna is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), then it should be known that the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas..."
The vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas is likewise unreal.
[The question was: "Are the teachings of the two vehicles real or unreal?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī, those two vehicles are both real and unreal. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have severed all..."
Afflictions are termed "real" [in the sense of being existent], while that which is impermanent, non-abiding, and subject to change is termed "unreal.

The Buddha did not definitively judge the real and the unreal; rather, from the perspective of the abandonment of afflictions, that which is "real" carries the meaning of being non-permanent, and thus it is "unreal" in its ultimate sense.
In the section following "Mañjuśrī’s discourse on Māra," the fifth point raises an objection based on the teaching.
Mañjuśrī said: "If what the Buddha has spoken is called 'real,' then one should know that what Māra speaks is unreal.
World-Honored One, is that which Māra speaks subsumed within the Noble Truths?"
"Are the words spoken by Māra subsumed within the Noble Truths?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī, the words spoken by Māra are subsumed within the two truths—namely, suffering and its origin.
All such things are neither Dharma nor Vinaya; they cannot bring benefit to people, and even if proclaimed all day long, they are of no avail."

If someone views suffering as something to be abandoned, the origin as something to be severed, cessation as something to be realized, and the path as something to be cultivated, this is called delusion; such delusion is termed the teaching of Māra.

The Buddha’s intended meaning in answering was that among the Four Noble Truths, these [views] are subsumed within the truths of Suffering and its Origin. [He then addressed] the twenty-five or twenty-six [categories of] external paths.
To which of the Truths do these [categories] belong? Furthermore, among the Four Truths taught by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), how many of those Truths are subverted?
Here it is clarified that they subvert only Suffering and its Origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), but do not subvert the Path and Cessation (*mārga* and *nirodha*). Why is this?

They claim that Primordial Darkness (*avyakta*) gives rise to Intellect (*buddhi*), and subsequently the five gross elements and the five subtle elements give rise to Intellect; thus, they subvert the Buddha’s Truth of Origin by asserting that Intellect is the cause. They also subvert [the Truth of Suffering] by asserting that the subtle elements are the effect.

The twenty-five or twenty-six aspects of the Buddha’s Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) are subsumed within the two truths of the Buddha’s Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Mañjuśrī said: "As the Buddha [taught] below... This is the sixth section, explaining the chapter on the essence of causes.
Mañjuśrī said: "As the Buddha has taught that there is one path of purity and no second, so too do the various non-Buddhists say:
'I have one path of purity and no second. If this one path were the ultimate truth, what difference would there be between it and those non-Buddhists?
If there is no difference, you should not speak of 'one path of purity.'"
Mañjuśrī said: "If 'the single path of purity' is the true reality as taught by the Buddha, then non-Buddhists also speak of 'the single path of purity';
it should therefore also be the true reality."
The Buddha said, "Good son, among the various non-Buddhists, there is the truth of suffering and its origin, but they lack the truths of cessation and the path.

They conceive the notion of cessation regarding that which is not cessation; they conceive the notion of the path regarding that which is not the path; they conceive the notion of the fruit regarding that which is not the fruit;
and they conceive the notion of the cause regarding that which is not the cause. For this reason, they do not possess even a single path that is pure."
2. The Buddha’s response clarifies that non-Buddhists possess only suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), yet lack the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*).

Those who conceive the notion of cessation within what is not cessation falsely reckon non-perception (*asaṃjñi*) to be *nirvāṇa*. Those with the notion of a path where there is no path reckon the [practice of] chickens... [and so forth].
