To regard dog-precepts as the Way while harboring the notion that they are the fruit when they are not the fruit, or to calculate that the nature of the world’s minute particles is the fruit of all things when it is not the cause, or to calculate that the nature of the world’s minute particles is the cause of all things when it is not the cause—this is what was previously called "not destroying the Way. Now, you ask:
"If one calculates what is not the [true] thought, are not the precepts of chickens and dogs, etc., indeed a destruction? The answer is: This arises from...
Regarding the horizontal calculation and the horizontal destruction, the path of cessation does not apply to the former; that [text] clarifies the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).

Within the direct statement that "the primordial darkness (*prakṛti*) gives rise to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other six principles," it mentions only the principle of the Lord (*prabhu-tattva*) and the principle of dependence (*āśraya-tattva*).

Where, then, is it said that there is a calculation of "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*) and the "dog-vow" (*śvavratika*)? Therefore, one knows that the two principles are not destroyed by the path of cessation. Furthermore, it is asked: Do non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) possess suffering?
Regarding the Truths (*satya*), why was it previously stated that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess suffering but not the Truth? The answer was given directly:
they possess the objective realm of suffering, which constitutes the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), but this does not refer to the wisdom of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
Mañjuśrī says, "As the Buddha has taught... and below, he explains the seventh chapter, "The Section on the Essential Nature of the Fruit," first by posing a question and then [proceeding].
The answer to the question consists of three parts: first, the proclamation that the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) possess four virtues; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
This is the initial proclamation, as stated in the text. Mañjuśrī said: "As the Buddha has taught, there is permanence, there is self, there is bliss, and there is purity; this is the true meaning."
These various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) must possess a real truth that does not exist within the Buddha-dharma.
Why is this? The following explanation contains twenty-four successive sections (*paryāya*). The calculation of the existence of permanence, bliss, self, and purity constitutes four distinct parts:

first, eight successive sections calculate the existence of permanence; second, five successive sections calculate the existence of bliss; third, three [successive sections calculate the existence of self]; and fourth... [three successive sections calculate the existence of purity].

Furthermore, there is the reckoning of the four sets of eight as pure; furthermore, there is the reckoning of a self, which consists of the first eight [of those]; furthermore, there is the reckoning of permanence.
As for the text appearing at the beginning, it is because [the view] generally takes both cause and effect [as its basis] that one knows there is permanence.
Why is this? For the various non-Buddhists also claim that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are eternal. How so? Because they are eternal;

for the retributions of karma—whether agreeable or disagreeable—are never lost. That which is agreeable is called the retribution of the ten wholesome actions, and that which is disagreeable is the retribution of the ten unwholesome actions.
If one were to say that all conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent, then as for the agent who performs karma...
Since this has already ceased, who would then experience the retribution for it? For this reason, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permanent.
Second, because one must inevitably obtain an evil fruit for the cause of killing, they are permanent.
"World-Honored One, because of the causes and conditions of killing, it is called 'constant.

If you say that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent, then both the killer and the victim are impermanent. If they are impermanent, who would undergo the retribution for sins in hell?
If you say that there definitely exists the experience of retribution in hell, then one should know that conditioned phenomena are in reality not impermanent."
Third, it is permanent because it is based on the ability to maintain focused mindfulness.
The World-Honored One binds his mind in focused mindfulness, which is also called "permanent"; that which he has contemplated over ten years, even up to a hundred years, is never forgotten.
Therefore, it is permanent. If it were impermanent, who would remember and who would contemplate the things originally perceived?
For these reasons, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are not impermanent.
Fourth, regarding the recollection based on mental conceptualization:
the World-Honored One states that all such conceptualizations are also called "permanent. For example, suppose a person previously saw the hands, feet, head, and neck of another.
Regarding the characteristic of equality: if one sees it at a later time, one recognizes it again; if it were impermanent, its original characteristic would have ceased.
Fifth, the cultivation:
whatever actions the World-Honored One performs are the result of long-term cultivation; whether starting from the beginning, or after three years, or...
After five years, because one has come to know them well, they are called "constant.
Sixth, the enumeration of numbers:
according to the World-Honored One’s method of calculation, one proceeds from one to two, from two to three, and so on up to hundreds and thousands; if there were none—
If that which is eternal were initially one, it ought to perish when that one perishes; if it perished, who would then reach the state of two?
Thus, that which is eternally one can never become two. Because the one does not perish, it can reach the state of two, and so on up to a hundred thousand; therefore, it is eternal.
Seventh, based on recitation and study:
the World-Honored One, according to the rules for recitation and study, would recite one Āgama, then two Āgamas, and even up to three or four Āgamas;
yet regarding that which is to be recited as impermanent, it never exceeded four. It was through these causes and conditions for the increase of recitation and study [that this occurred].
Therefore, they are called "permanent.
The eight points regarding their formal characteristics are all as stated in the text.
The World-Honored One [compares] a jar, clothing, a carriage, a person bearing a debt, the form of the great earth, mountains, rivers, trees, forests, medicinal herbs, and wood.
"World-Honored One, it is likewise with all sentient beings, such as grasses and leaves, whose healing of illnesses is entirely eternal.
All non-Buddhists also say this: 'All conditioned phenomena are eternal. If they are eternal, then they must be the ultimate truth."
Next, there are five further considerations regarding pleasure (*sukha*). First, according to cause and effect:
the World-Honored One [responded to] various non-Buddhists who again asked, "Is there pleasure? How is this known? [The answer is: because the experiencer certainly obtains desirable retribution.
Thus, the World-Honored One stated that whoever experiences pleasure will certainly obtain it—namely, the Great Brahmā King, Mahābrahmā, and so forth.
In the heavens, Śakra Devānām Indra, Viṣṇu, and all humans and devas, for this reason, there is necessarily happiness. Second,
it is based on the existence of seeking.
World-Honored One, there are other heterodox teachers who further claim that pleasure exists because it causes sentient beings to give rise to longing;
thus, the hungry seek food, the thirsty seek drink, the cold seek warmth, the hot seek coolness, the exhausted seek rest, the sick seek recovery, and those with desire seek forms.
If pleasure did not exist, for what reason would they seek these things? Since they do seek them, we know [that pleasure exists].
There is happiness.

Thirdly, based on the causes of happiness, the World-Honored One [taught that] there are various non-Buddhists who further say: "Giving can obtain happiness; those in the world who enjoy practicing generosity..."
Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, out of poverty and hardship, provide various kinds of gifts— such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, elephants, horses,
carriages, powdered incense, ointments, various flowers, dwellings, and lamps— for me.
Because they receive such agreeable rewards in future lives, one should know for certain that happiness exists.
Fourth, based on the condition of pleasure:
The World-Honored One has said that there are certain non-Buddhists who further claim that because of causes and conditions one should know that pleasure exists;

that is to say, that which experiences pleasure exists because of causes and conditions, and is therefore called "pleasurable contact. If pleasure did not exist, how could there be such causes and conditions?
If there were no rabbit horns, they would have no causes and conditions; since there are causes and conditions for pleasure, one knows that pleasure exists.
This is based on the three grades.

World-Honored One, there are certain heterodox teachers who further say: "Because there are superior, middling, and inferior [grades], one should know that pleasure exists, namely, the inferior feeling."

Regarding pleasure: those who experience pleasure among Śakra-devānām-indra [experience it] at the middle level; those who experience pleasure as the Great Brahmā King [experience it] at the upper level; and those who experience pleasure as Maheśvara [experience it] at the highest level.
Because there are such distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, one should know that pleasure exists.
Third, furthermore, there are three ways of reckoning that purity exists: first, based on the cause of purity.
World-Honored One, various non-Buddhists further claim that purity exists. Why is this? If purity did not exist, desire would not arise;
since desire does arise, one should know that purity exists.
Second, based on pure conditions,
it is further stated: gold, silver, precious jewels, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva,
agate, coral, pearls, jade, conch shells, flowing springs, bathing pools, food and drink, clothing, flowers, incense powder, ointments, lamps, and candles.
The clarity regarding such things as these is that they are all pure dharmas.
Third, it relies on the pure vessel.
Furthermore, there is purity in what are called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); these are the pure vessels that contain all pure things, namely, humans and devas.
The various sages, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas name it "purity" based on this meaning.
Furthermore, the fourth and eighth [points] involve calculating the existence of a self based on the act of creation.
World-Honored One, there are other heterodox teachers who further claim that there is a self because it perceives and is capable of acting.
For example, if a person enters a potter’s house, even if they do not see the potter’s body, by seeing the wheel and the cord, they know for certain that the house must belong to a potter.
I am also like this: having seen forms with my eyes, I know for certain that there must be a self; if there were no [self], [this would not be so].
As for "I," who is it that can see forms or hear sounds, and so on, up to touching dharmas?
It is likewise thus. Second, according to characteristics:
furthermore, how is it known that there is a self? It is known by means of its causal characteristics. What are these characteristics? They are breathing, looking, and blinking.
The lifespan, the active mind, the experience of various sufferings and pleasures, and the dharmas such as craving and anger—all these are the mark of a self;
therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
Third, based on distinct flavors.
Furthermore, there is a self because it is capable of discriminating flavors; when a person eats fruit, they perceive it and thereby know its taste.
Therefore, one should know that there must necessarily be a self.
Fourth, [the argument] based on the performance of action.
Furthermore, how is it known that there is a self? Because one grasps at the performance of actions: one grasps a sickle and is able to reap;
one grasps an axe and is able to cut; one grasps a jar and contains water; one grasps a chariot and is able to drive it. In such matters as these, the grasping at a self is able to act.
Therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
Fifth, based on the seeking of milk:
Furthermore, how is it known that there is a self? At the very moment of birth, one desires to be nursed because of the influence of past habitual tendencies;
by this, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
Sixth, based on names and designations.
Furthermore, how is it known that there is a self? Because it is for the sake of benefiting other sentient beings through combination.
For example, such things as jars, clothing, vehicles, fields, houses, mountains, forests, trees, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep—if these are combined [they serve a purpose].
In this way, there is benefit; the five internal aggregates are likewise so. Because the various faculties, such as the eye, are in combination, they benefit the self.
Therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
Seventh, based on the existence of negation (*pratiṣedha*).
Furthermore, how is it known that there is a self? Because there are phenomena that are negated. For example, because an object exists, there is the obstruction of that object;
if it did not exist, there would be no obstruction. Since there is negation, one knows that there is a self. Therefore, it should be understood.
There must certainly be a self.
Eighth, based on the category of companions:

furthermore, how is it known that there is a self? Because of the distinction between companions and non-companions; for one who is a relative and one who is not a relative cannot be companions [without a self].
The True Dharma and the false Dharma are not companions; wisdom and non-wisdom are not companions;

the śramaṇa and the non-śramaṇa, the brāhmaṇa and the non-brāhmaṇa, the son and the non-son, day and the non-day, night and the non-night, and "I" and the non-I—such dharmas as these are either companions or non-companions. Therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
The third section, "The World-Honored One [addresses] the various non-Buddhists," concludes that the non-Buddhists must possess a true reality (*satya*).
The World-Honored One [says]: "The various non-Buddhists speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; one should know that there must certainly be permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
For this reason, the World-Honored One [allows that] the various non-Buddhists may also say, "I possess the True Reality."

The Buddha’s words and the subsequent responses of the two Tathāgatas are divided into three parts: first, the brief exposition; second, the detailed exposition; and third, the conclusion. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, the negation, and second, the explanation. Regarding the first, it is as stated in the text:
The Buddha said, "Good son, if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who maintain that there is permanence, pleasure, purity, and a self..."
Such a person is neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
Next, for what reason does the following passage explain why they are not?
For what reason? Because they are deluded regarding birth and death and have departed from the Great Guide, the One of All-Knowledge; thus [are] the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Because the Brahmins and others have sunk into various desires and their wholesome dharmas have been weakened;

because these non-Buddhists are bound in the prison of greed, hatred, and delusion, and endure and delight therein; because although these non-Buddhists know that the fruits of karma are self-inflicted and self-received, they are still unable to distance themselves from unwholesome dharmas;
and because these non-Buddhists do not possess the true Dharma or right livelihood.
Why is this? It is because they lack the fire of wisdom, which cannot consume [their defilements].

Although these non-Buddhists desire to crave and cling to the five exquisite sensual pleasures, they are impoverished by the absence of wholesome dharmas and do not apply themselves diligently to cultivation.
Although these non-Buddhists desire to reach true liberation, their feet of ethical discipline are not perfected. Although these non-Buddhists desire to seek happiness...

Because they are unable to seek the causes and conditions for happiness, although these non-Buddhists loathe all forms of suffering, their conduct is nonetheless unable to distance them from the causes and conditions of suffering.
Although these non-Buddhists are entwined by the four great poisonous snakes, they still act with negligence and fail to exercise caution; these non-Buddhists are shrouded by ignorance.
Far removed from virtuous friends, they take pleasure in remaining within the triple world—a great, blazing fire of impermanence—from which they cannot escape.
These non-Buddhists encounter the incurable diseases of the various afflictions, yet they do not seek the Great Wisdom Physician.
As these non-Buddhists are about to traverse the boundless, perilous, and distant paths of the future, they remain unaware of [the way].

They adorn themselves with the provisions of wholesome dharmas; yet these non-Buddhists are constantly harmed by the calamitous poison of lustful desire, and instead embrace the frost-like poison of the five sensual pleasures.
These non-Buddhists have a blazing intensity of hatred, yet they further draw near to evil friends.
These non-Buddhists are perpetually shrouded by ignorance, yet they continue to pursue it.
These wicked dharmas are such that all non-Buddhists are constantly deceived and deluded by false views, yet they instead conceive thoughts of intimacy and affection toward them;
these non-Buddhists long for sweet fruits to eat, yet they plant bitter seeds;
these non-Buddhists already dwell within the dark chamber of afflictions, yet they instead distance themselves from the brilliant light of the great torch of wisdom—such are these non-Buddhists.
Afflicted by the thirst of the afflictions (*kleśa*), they further drink the salty water of sensual desires (*kāma*).

These followers of external paths (*tīrthika*) are adrift and submerged in the boundless great river of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and they have furthermore distanced themselves from the unsurpassed boatman.

These followers of external paths are deluded by various inversions, claiming that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permanent; yet it is impossible for conditioned phenomena to be permanent.
