Greatly astonished and amazed, they gathered together and, addressing one another, spoke these verses: Pointing each other out, [they said]:
"In the pure Snowy Mountains dwells the Lord who is tranquil and free from desire, the King adorned with merit.
He has already abandoned greed, hatred, and pride; he has forever severed flattery, folly, and delusion."
His mouth has never uttered coarse or harsh speech.
At that time, there was a devaputra in the assembly named Nandika who spoke this verse:
If such a person who has abandoned desire, who is pure and diligent in effort,
were to seek Śakra or the various devas— if this seeker of the Way were to practice various austerities—
it would mean that this person has many desires and seeks the seat where Śakra dwells.
At that time, there was another celestial being, a rishi-son, who spoke this verse to Śakra:
"O Lord of Devas, Kauśika, you should not give rise to such anxiety. Why must those who practice asceticism among the outsiders seek the station of Indra?"
Having spoken these verses, he further said: "Kauśika, there are great beings in the world who, for the sake of sentient beings, do not covet their own bodies.
Desiring to benefit all sentient beings, they practice various kinds of immeasurable asceticism.
Because such persons perceive the faults within birth and death, even if they were to see precious jewels filling this entire earth—"
Just as one views mountains, great oceans, mucus, or spittle without giving rise to greedy attachment, so too does this Great Being renounce wealth and treasures,
beloved wives and children, head, eyes, marrow, brain, hands, feet, limbs, and joints, as well as his dwelling, elephants, horses, carriages,
and male and female servants; he does not even aspire to birth in the heavens, but only wishes that all beings may experience happiness.
"As I understand it, such a Great Being is pure and undefiled, with all fetters forever exhausted,
desiring only to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śakra-devānām-indra further said, "If it is as you say, then such a person has indeed grasped all."
O Great Sage, if there were such a Buddha-tree in this world, it would be able to eliminate the poisonous snakes of affliction for all Brahmās, worldlings, and asuras.
If any sentient beings dwell within the cool shade of this Buddha-tree, the various poisons of their afflictions will all be extinguished.
O Great Sage, if such a person should appear in a future age...
"We shall all become Sugatas and extinguish immeasurable, blazing afflictions"—such a reality is indeed difficult to believe.

Why is this? Because immeasurable sentient beings who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* will, upon encountering even a slight minor condition, immediately waver from that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Just as the moon in water moves when the water moves, so too is the bodhicitta: difficult to generate but easy to destroy.
Great Seer, it is like many people who, having firmly armed themselves with various shields and weapons, desire to advance and subdue an enemy;
yet when confronted by the terror of battle, they immediately retreat and scatter. So too is it for immeasurable sentient beings.

In this way, those who have resolved upon bodhicitta and firmly adorned themselves with its armor may, upon seeing the faults of birth and death, give rise to fear and subsequently retreat and disperse.
Great Seer, I see that after such immeasurable sentient beings have resolved their minds, they all undergo fluctuation and regression.
Therefore, although I now see this person who exclusively practices asceticism—free from affliction and feverish distress, and abiding in the restraints of the Path—I [do not regard him as firm].

"His conduct is pure, yet I have not yet gained faith in him. I must now go there myself to test him and know for certain whether he is truly capable of bearing the great heavy burden of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Great Seer, it is like a chariot that has two wheels and thus has the utility of carrying a load, or a bird that has two wings and is capable of flight; such is his asceticism."
It is likewise with this person: although I see that they strictly uphold the prohibitive precepts, I do not yet know whether this person possesses profound wisdom.
If they possess profound wisdom, you should know that they will be capable of bearing the heavy burden of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Great Seer, it is like a fish-mother who has many offspring in her womb, yet those that reach full maturity are few.
Just as the *āmra* tree has many flowers but few fruits, so too do sentient beings give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment in immeasurable numbers,
yet those who achieve it are so few as to be scarcely worth mentioning.
The "two wheels" refer to merit and wisdom.
"Great Seer, I shall go down with you"—this is the third trial. Great Seer, I shall go with you to test you;
Great Seer, it is like true gold that has been tested by three methods: burning, cutting, and rubbing.
Thus one knows that the "true" refers to the tests of burning, grinding, and polishing.
Next, regarding the three combined tests: first, the test of whether one possesses wisdom or not by reciting half a verse;
if one understands the meaning of the text, though it is not yet complete, one possesses wisdom; if one does not understand, one lacks wisdom. Second, the test by displaying a terrifying form.
Regarding fear and fearlessness: if the mind is firm and resolute, fear does not arise; if it is wavering and weak, fear arises.
Third, he sought his body three times to test whether he could renounce it or not (and so forth).
When he was thus testing his ascetic practices, Śakra-devānām-indra transformed his own body into the form of a rākṣasa, most terrifying to behold.
He descended to the Snowy Mountains and stood not far away. At that time, the rākṣasa’s mind was devoid of fear;
he was courageous and difficult to withstand, possessing eloquence in proper sequence, and his voice was clear and elegant as he proclaimed [the Bodhisattva’s] transgressions.
Regarding the half-verse spoken by the Buddha:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; this is the law of arising and ceasing.
This half-verse speaks only of one side—impermanence—and does not speak of the side of permanence; therefore, it is called a "half-verse" concerning the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Why are only arising (*utpāda*) and ceasing (*nirodha*) explained among the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*), while abiding (*sthiti*) is not mentioned? One interpretation is that because the four-line verse is concise, it is therefore abbreviated.
Question: If it is abbreviated, why are the other characters not abbreviated as well? Answer: There is further meaning here.

The characteristic of abiding does not manifest the transition and passing away of phenomena; it merely clarifies the beginning and end, so the middle portion is appropriately omitted. Question: How do the three characteristics flow and change?
If there were a "dwelling of dwelling," that would mean permanence, which would imply no change; furthermore, it would differ from impermanence. To this, he replied:

"This is the dwelling of impermanence. Since the three marks [of existence] are themselves impermanent, yet there is a "dwelling of impermanence," there should likewise be a "permanence of non-dwelling" (and so forth).
Having spoken this half-verse, he stood before him; his manifested form was most terrifying, and he gazed about, looking in all four directions.

When that ascetic heard this half-verse, his heart was filled with joy, just as a merchant traveling at night through a perilous wilderness who has lost his companions might feel when, in his terror, he searches for them and suddenly encounters his fellow travelers, and his heart is filled with joy.
He experienced immeasurable joy and exultation, like a long-suffering patient who finally encounters a skilled physician, finds excellent medicine, and subsequently recovers;
like a person drowning in the sea who suddenly encounters a ship; like a parched and weary man who meets with clear, cool water; like one pursued by enemies who suddenly escapes them;
like a man long imprisoned who finally hears he has been released; and like a farmer who meets with rain during a scorching drought.
"Rain is also like a traveler who has returned home; when his family sees him, they give rise to great joy.
Son of good family, at that time, upon hearing this half-verse, my heart’s joy was likewise the same.
I immediately rose from my seat, lifted my hair with my hand, looked toward the four quarters, and spoke these words: 'From whom was this verse I have just heard spoken?'"
At that time, looking in the four directions, he saw no other person but only the rākṣasa, who spoke these words:
"Who has opened such a gate of liberation? Who can thunder forth the voice of all Buddhas? Who, while others sleep in the slumber of birth and death, has alone awakened and proclaimed these words?
Who is able to guide and lead the sentient beings who are famished within this cycle of birth and death?"
"The flavor of the unsurpassed path—how many immeasurable sentient beings are sinking in the ocean of birth and death? Who can act as a great shipmaster therein?
These sentient beings are constantly entangled by the grave illness of afflictions; who can act as a skilled physician therein?
When he spoke these half-verses, they awakened my mind, just as the crescent moon gradually opens a lotus flower. "O Son of Good Family, I..."
At that time, seeing nothing else, he saw only the rākṣasa and thought to himself: "Is it this rākṣasa who has spoken these verses?
Again, doubt arose: "Or perhaps it was not his speech. For what reason? This man's appearance is most terrifying;
yet if anyone were to hear these lines of verse, all their fears and ugliness would be immediately removed—how could such a thing be?"
That person’s appearance was such that they were able to recite this verse:
"A lotus cannot grow from within fire, nor can cool water be produced from the rays of the sun. Good son, at that time I further thought to myself:
"I am currently without wisdom, yet perhaps this rākṣasa has been able to see the Buddhas of the past and heard this half-verse from those Buddhas."
The verse says: "I shall now question him. He immediately went forward to where the rākṣasa was and spoke these words: "Excellent, Great Being!
Where did you obtain this half-verse spoken by the one who was formerly free from fear?
Great Being, where did you obtain such a half-jewel of a wish-fulfilling gem? Great Being, the meaning of this half-verse is indeed [superior]..."
This is the true path of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.
All the infinite sentient beings in the world are perpetually shrouded by the net of various views;
throughout their lives, amidst these externalist teachings, they never once hear such meanings of emptiness as are expounded by the Ten-Powered Heroes who have transcended the world.
The text states: "Regarding the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as explained, this verse clarifies impermanence (*anitya*).

How can it be that which is empty? The traditional interpretation holds that impermanence is not yet emptiness; rather, it is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) for emptiness, and only subsequently does one attain emptiness.

This interpretation is incorrect; impermanence itself is simply another name for emptiness. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: 'Impermanence is the characteristic of movement, and the characteristic of movement is the characteristic of emptiness.'"
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that "neither arising nor ceasing" is the meaning of impermanence; now, "impermanence" likewise has the meaning of "neither arising nor ceasing.
"Good son, after I had asked this, he replied to me: 'Great Brāhmaṇa, you should not ask such a question.'"
"I am a *ṛṣi*. Why is this? It has already been many days since I last ate; though I have searched everywhere, I have been unable to find anything.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, my mind is disordered and I speak erroneously; this is not what my original mind knows.
I now possess the power to fly through the void to Uttarakuru, and even to the heavens, searching for food everywhere, yet [I have found none]."
"Because I was able to obtain this, I say these words: 'Good son, at that time I again spoke to the rākṣasa, saying:
"Great Being, if you can finish reciting these verses for me, I shall become your disciple for as long as I live.
Great Being, what you have spoken—both the names and their meanings—are neither exhausted nor finished. For what reason do you not wish to speak further?'"
"Indeed, while material gifts are subject to exhaustion, the causes and conditions for the gift of Dharma are inexhaustible. Since the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible, it brings benefit to many.
Having now heard this half-verse of the Dharma, my mind is filled with wonder and doubt; you should fortunately dispel them for me.
"Once you have finished speaking this verse, I shall be your disciple for the rest of my life," the Rākṣasa replied.
He said, "Your wisdom is excessive; you worry only for yourself and do not consider me at all.
I am currently being tormented by the suffering of hunger and truly cannot speak. I then asked him, "What is it that you eat? The rākṣasa replied, "You need not ask me this;
if I were to tell you, it would cause many to be terrified. I spoke again, saying, "In this place, you are alone..."
"In this place there is no one else—neither person nor non-person—I have no fear of you. For what reason do you not speak? The rākṣasa replied:
"That which I eat is only the warm flesh of humans; that which I drink is only the hot blood of humans. Because my merit is meager, I subsist solely on this food.
Though I have searched everywhere, I am exhausted and unable to find it. Although there are many people in the world, they all possess merit and are further protected by various [deities]."
"Protected as I am by the gods, I lack the power to kill this noble son. I spoke further, saying:
'You need only recite this half-verse in its entirety; once I have heard the verse, I shall offer up this very body as a gift to serve you, Great Being.
Even if my life should end here, there would be no further use for such a body, which would otherwise become food for tigers, wolves, owls, and hawks.'"
"You are merely food for vultures and eagles, and you shall not obtain even a hair’s breadth of merit.
Now, seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you abandon this non-firm body to exchange it for a firm one. The rākṣasa replied, "Who would believe such words of yours?
To the extent of eight syllables, you have cast away your beloved body. Good son, I am indeed..."
He replied: "You are truly without wisdom. It is like a person who, by giving away an earthen vessel to another, obtains a vessel of the seven precious jewels;
I am likewise, having relinquished this non-durable body, shall obtain a vajra-body. As for your question, 'Who would believe this?', I now have witnesses:
Mahābrahmā, Śakra-devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings can testify to this matter, as they possess the divine eye."
The various bodhisattvas who, desiring to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, practice the Mahāyāna and are endowed with the six perfections, are likewise able to realize this;

furthermore, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions who benefit sentient beings are also able to witness that I have sacrificed my body and life for the sake of these eight characters.
The rākṣasa spoke again: "If you are thus able to sacrifice your body..."
"Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall now recite for you the remaining half-verse. Good son, at that time, having heard these words, my heart was filled with joy.
I immediately removed the deerskin I was wearing and spread it out as a Dharma-seat for this rākṣasa, saying:
'Venerable sir, please sit upon this seat. I then stood before him with palms joined and knelt down on my right knee."
He spoke these words: "I only pray that the Upādhyāya will kindly recite the remaining half-verse for me so that it may be complete.
The Rākṣasa then spoke:
"Birth and death have ceased; Nirvāṇa is bliss."
At that time, having spoken these verses, the rākṣasa further said: "O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, you have now heard the complete meaning of these verses;
your aspirations shall be entirely fulfilled. If you truly desire to benefit all sentient beings, then give me your body at this time.
Good son, at that moment I contemplated this matter deeply, and then, in various places..."
Whether upon a stone, a wall, a tree, or a path, I inscribed this verse.
Fearing that my body might be exposed after death, I immediately tied up the garments I was wearing and climbed a tall tree. At that time, the tree deity asked me again, "Excellent, O benevolent one!
What do you intend to do? "O Son of Good Family," I replied at that time, "I wish to relinquish my body."
The tree deity replied with a verse, saying: "What benefit does such a verse provide? I then answered:
"These verses were spoken by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; they open the path of the Dharma of emptiness.
For the sake of this Dharma, I would sacrifice my body and life, not for profit, fame, wealth, or the four [rewards] of a Cakravartin King."
The Great Heavenly King Śakra-devānām-indra and the Great Brahmā Heavenly King—among gods and humans, they delight in benefiting all sentient beings—and for this purpose, they relinquish this body.
Good son, when I relinquish my body, I further make this vow:
"May all those who are stingy and possessive come to witness me relinquishing this body; may even those who give but a little [gift] abandon their pride."
I also caused those who were on high to see me cast away this body and life for the sake of a single verse, as if discarding grass or wood.
When I had spoken these words, I immediately released my body and threw myself down from the tree.
Before I had even reached the ground, various sounds issued forth from the void, reaching as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven. At that time, the rākṣasa returned to his original form.
Śakra immediately caught my body in mid-air and placed me upon level ground.
Then Śakra-devānām-indra, along with the devas and humans and the Great Brahmā King, bowed their heads at my feet and praised me, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You are truly a bodhisattva who can bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings within the dark ignorance."
In this midst, I have kindled the great torch of the Dharma; because I cherish the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata, I have troubled you.
I only pray that you will grant me absolution for my transgressions. You shall certainly achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the future;
I pray that you will grant me deliverance. At that time, Śakra-devendra and the assembly of devas prostrated themselves before me.
Pāda then took his leave and suddenly vanished. "Good son, in the past, for the sake of a half-gāthā, I cast away this body;
by this cause and condition, I was able to transcend twelve kalpas and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before Maitreya. Good son, I have thus obtained such immeasurable merit."
All virtues arise from making offerings to the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.
As for the statement that "nirvāṇa is bliss," the essence of nirvāṇa is neither arising nor ceasing;

yet, since it is now said that "nirvāṇa is bliss," does this mean that arising and ceasing constitute bliss—wherein one arises and then ceases, taking that arising as bliss? The answer is: it depends on the path one follows.
This is an analogy; where there is no responsibility, the analogy does not apply. Regarding the characteristics of arising and the characteristics of cessation:
correctly grasping the removal of arising and the removal of cessation is the bliss of *nirvāṇa*. Since this is the characteristic of non-arising, it is therefore not analogous [to ordinary birth].

As for "transcending twelve *kalpas*," various scriptures such as the *Udānavarga* and the *Buddhapiṭaka* all state that nine *kalpas* are transcended, or they speak of the faculties (*indriya*) and conditions (*pratyaya*).
It is not that the Buddha speaks with increase or decrease for different [capacities].
Next, "Good son, you now are also like this," and so forth, which serves as proof for the present [context] (etc.).
"Good son, you now are also like this; having given rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you have already [attained it]."

A good man who surpasses all bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of immeasurable and boundless Ganges Rivers is called a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa and practicing the noble conduct.

The Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Twenty: The First Part of the Brahma-Carya Chapter (Volume Fourteen).
Translated during the Northern Liang dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master from India, Dharmakṣema;
re-edited by the Śramaṇas Huìyán and Huìguān,
and Xiè Língyùn of the Jin dynasty.

Regarding the Chapter on the Holy Life (*Brahmacarya-varga*), various masters maintain that the holy life has the four immeasurable minds as its essence, while the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*) has the three categories as its essence. As a cited sutra states:
"The teaching of the four immeasurables is called the path of the Brahma-heaven; it is termed 'turning the Brahma-wheel. The teaching of the Four Truths is the ultimate heaven (*paramārtha-deva*)."

The Way is called the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma. Furthermore, the Master says that wisdom (*prajñā*), concentration (*samādhi*), and precepts (*śīla*) constitute the essence of the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*).

The seven types of wholesome knowledge are all "knowing," which is precisely wisdom; the four mental states are the twelve gates of dhyāna, which is concentration; and the subsequent clarification of the gains and losses of upholding the precepts is the precepts.
If this is so, how does it differ from the Holy Conduct (*ārya-caryā*)? The difference is that "Brahma" refers to transforming others, whereas "Holy" refers to oneself.

In this regard, when one practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*) oneself, wisdom (*prajñā*) constitutes the correct [path], and it is perfected by means of morality (*śīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*);

when practicing the holy life as a brahmin, morality constitutes the correct [path], and it is perfected by means of wisdom and concentration. This holy life practiced by the noble ones (*ārya*) is the pure path that leads to both ordinary beings and the noble ones.

For the noble ones, morality comes first and wisdom follows; for the brahmins, wisdom comes first and morality follows. This is the distinction between the brahmin and the noble one. Furthermore, the Master says that these are cause and effect.

Regarding the essence of the *brahmacarya* (holy life): the term "Brahman" signifies purity; because it is the cause for *nirvāṇa* and can lead to the attainment of *nirvāṇa*, it is taken as the essence of the holy life.

However, these interpretations based on cause and effect are both incorrect. If its essence consists of the four [heavenly] minds, then this is merely the path of the Brahma-heavens and not Great *Nirvāṇa*.
If its essence consists of the three grades [of practice], although they differ from the noble practices (*āryacaryā*), they do not transcend the two vehicles and are thus not Great *Nirvāṇa*.
If that which has cause and effect as its essence still retains cause and effect, how can it be called "pure"? It is not the Great Nirvana.
If it is not the Great Nirvana, then for whom is this "Brahmacarya" (holy life)? Since neither the name nor the meaning can be apprehended, neither is accepted here.
Now, when we speak of "Brahma," it signifies purity. There are three meanings of purity: namely, pure-purity, impure-purity, and neither-pure-nor-impure-purity.

What is meant by "pure purity"? It refers to the seven wholesome factors, the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), the three categories, the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), and other such dharmas;

all these are the supramundane path of purity leading to *nirvāṇa*. Now, regarding the text which states that the "purity of the complete purification of the holy life" (*brahmacarya-pariśuddhi*) is the source of all virtues, one should say it is loving-kindness (*maitrī*). This is called "pure purity. Why is this so?

I say that this purity of purity is the immeasurable gateway of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). It is what is called: the supernormal powers; taming elephants; taming the insane; healing the eyes; healing sores;
wandering through the world with loving-kindness; entering the cauldrons and furnaces of hell with compassion;

and the power of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) manifesting everywhere so that all that is impure may become pure. This is called "the purification of the impure. What is "neither-purity-nor-impurity"? It is neither... nor... [purification].
The impure and the pure refer to the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, which is neither cause nor effect, neither self nor other, neither defiled nor pure;
it is ultimately pure, and this is precisely the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity. The text says:
"If compassion exists or does not exist, it is 'is' or 'is not'; this is the compassion of the śrāvakas. If compassion exists or does not exist, it is neither existent nor non-existent."
Such compassion is the Tathāgata’s compassion. This Tathāgata’s compassion is neither pure nor impure, yet it is not the case that it is not pure.
If these three types of compassion were separate from one another—whether vertically or horizontally—they would be neither wondrous nor pure.
Rather, they are three in one and one in three; being inconceivable, it is called the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*), which derives its name from these three.

The chapter titled "On the Holy Life" (*Brahmacarya-varga*) consists of two parts: first, the exposition of the holy life; second, the praise of the sutra. The initial section on the holy life is divided into three:

first, the seven wholesome qualities; second, the four mental states; third, the observance of the precepts. Within the first section on the seven wholesome qualities, there are two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation.
"Good son, what is the brahmacarya of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
This section consists of three parts: the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion.
"Good son, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa and abides in the seven wholesome dharmas."
What are the seven ways of attaining the complete holy life (*brahmacarya*)? First, knowing the Dharma; second, knowing the meaning; third, knowing the time;
fourth, knowing contentment; fifth, knowing oneself; sixth, knowing the assembly; and seventh, knowing the distinctions of rank.

Regarding the headings: the headings consist of the topical chapters, the chanting of numbers, and the listing of names. Among these seven types of goodness, the first three pertain to both oneself and others;

the next two are dedicated solely to one's own practice; and the final two are for transforming others. To speak in terms of the primary and secondary aspects: the primary aspect is transforming others, while the secondary aspect is one's own practice.

In the commentary, there are two parts: first, an explanation of the seven distinct virtues; second, an explanation of the seven perfect virtues. Within the section on the seven distinct virtues, there are seven chapters.
The first explains "knowing the Dharma. Here, "Dharma" refers generally to both self and others; because one knows the Dharma, one is able to practice it oneself and transform others.
This chapter also follows the structure of introduction, explanation, and conclusion. First, the introduction is as stated in the text.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know the Dharma?
Next, regarding the explanation, there are two parts: first, the enumeration, and second, the detailed exposition.
"Good son, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the twelve divisions of the scriptures, namely: the sūtra, the geya..."
The Gāthās, Udānas, Nidānas, Avadānas, Itivṛttakas,
Jātakas, Vaipulyas, Adbhutadharmas, and Upadeśas received their predictions at night.
In the explanation, the twelve divisions of the scriptures are divided into twelve sections. Regarding the first, it says:
"O son of good family, what is called a *sūtra*? From 'Thus have I heard' up to 'rejoicing and practicing accordingly'—all such as these are called *sūtras*."
The old [tradition] says there is no translation [for *geya*], explaining it through five meanings; some say that *sūtra* is used here as a substitute for it;
others say that *sūtra* is the direct translation. The Kai-shan school says it is merely general and has no distinction;
Zang-yang says there is a distinction, namely that it refers to verses (*gāthā*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Geya is verses that praise the *sūtra*."
What is called the Geyya Sūtra? The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In the past, I and you were foolish and lacked wisdom; we could not see the Four Noble Truths as they truly are.
For this reason, we have wandered through saṃsāra for a long time, dwelling in birth and death and sinking into the great ocean of suffering.

What are the four? They are suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path [to the cessation of suffering]. This was as the Buddha formerly taught in the sūtras for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there were again sentient beings of sharp faculties who, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling later than others.
They immediately asked those people, "What did the Tathāgata say just now? When the Buddha knew their thoughts, he spoke in verse based on the original sutra:
In the past, I and you all did not perceive the Four Noble Truths;
therefore, we have long wandered through the great ocean of suffering in saṃsāra. If one can perceive the Four Truths, then one shall sever birth and death.
Once birth and death are exhausted, one will no longer undergo further existence. This is called *geya*.
Regarding *geya*, it should be fully termed *lūka-geya*; *geya* is translated as "verse" (*jù*) or "stanza" (*sòng*).

Kaishan says it means "equal verses" (*děngjù*), Zhuangyan says "equal stanzas" (*děngsòng*), and Guangzhai says "repeated stanzas" (*chóngsòng*. It refers to stanzas that repeat the prose [of the sūtra].)
What is called a *vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (sūtra of prophecy)? It refers to sūtras and vinayas such as when the Tathāgata, while speaking, bestows a prophecy upon devas and humans, saying:
"Ānanda, in the future there shall be a king named Śaṅkha;
in that world he shall attain the path of Buddhahood, and his name shall be Maitreya. This is called a *vyākaraṇa*.
The term *vyākaraṇa* (Sanskrit) is translated as "Prediction" (*jìshòu*) in Chinese; the *Śāstra* explains it as the "Scripture that Explains Meaning.
This refers to the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) for the six destinies, the three vehicles, and so forth.
What is called *gāthā-sūtra*? It refers to all other discourses, excluding the *sūtras* and the various codes of discipline (*vinaya*). There are four [types] of such discourses.
The verse of a single line is as follows:
"Commit no evil; practice all that is good; purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
This is called a gāthā.
Regarding the *Gāthā-sūtra*, it is called "Verses of Unequal Phrasing" (1), "Verses of Unequal Stanzas" (2), or "Direct Verses" (3)—that is, *udāna* verses.
As for the phrase "excluding the *sūtras*," this means excluding those verses that are attached to prose (*gadya*) explaining specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and the various *vinayas*," this means that when such verses are found within the *vinaya*, one knows there was previously prose; where no prose exists, [the verse does not appear].
The "Prakaraṇa" (Discourse on Specific Topics) is that which is independent.

What is called the "Udāna" (Inspired Utterance)? It is as when the Buddha entered meditative concentration in the afternoon and extensively expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the assembly of devas;
at that time, the bhikṣus each had this thought: "What is the Tathāgata doing now?"
At dawn, the Tathāgata arose from meditative concentration; though no one asked him, by means of his knowledge of the minds of others, he spoke of his own accord:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the lifespans of all devas are extremely long. Bhikṣus, it is well that you act for the sake of others rather than seeking your own benefit;
it is well that you have few desires; it is well that you are content; it is well that you are tranquil. Such are the sūtras.
That which is spoken spontaneously without being questioned is called an *udāna*.
The *Udānavarga-śāstra* states: "The prose sūtras that lack verses are called 'unquestioned spontaneous utterances' (*udāna*).
This verse appears in the *Dharmapada*.
What is called the *Nidāna-sūtra*? It refers to the fundamental causes and conditions upon which the verses of various sūtras are based, explained for the sake of others.
For example, there was once a man in Śrāvastī who caught birds with a net; having captured them, he confined them in a cage, providing them with water and grain, and then released them again.
The World-Honored One, knowing the beginning and end of this causal sequence, spoke these verses.
Do not despise small evils, thinking they will bring no calamity; though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel.
This is called the Nidāna.
The Nidāna-śāstra states that the sequential order of beginning and end is the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* (Sūtra on Dependent Origination).
What is called an *avadāna* sūtra? The parables taught within the Vinaya are termed *avadānas*.
The *Avadāna-śataka* states that these are precisely the *Avaivartika-avadāna-sūtra* (the Sūtra of Parables).
What is called an *ityuktaka* sūtra? As the Buddha has said: "Bhikṣus, you should know that what I have taught since my appearance in the world is called the *Dhātusūtra*;
at the time of the appearance of Krakucchanda Buddha, it was called the 'Ambrosial Drum';
at the time of Kanakamuni Buddha, it was called the 'Mirror of Dharma'; and at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, it was called the 'Analysis'."
"Emptiness" is called *itītakā*.
According to the *Itītakā-śāstra*, "one bamboo *itītakā*" is translated by Kai-xian as "words such as these" (*itī-vākya*) and by Zhuang-yang as "original matter" (*nidāna*).
As for what I have called the "Sūtra on Elements" (*dhātu-sūtra*), each has its own distinct classification of elements.
To clarify that each [sūtra] has its own specific seal, it is called "Thus Spoken" (*evam-vāda*).
What is termed a *jātaka-sūtra*? It is as when the Blessed One, in his former life as a bodhisattva, practiced various ascetic austerities, saying:
"O bhikṣus, you should know that in the past I was a deer, a bear, a roe deer, a rabbit, and a wild goose."
The various bodies received by those such as the Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*), the Wheel-turning Kings, nāgas, and garuḍas while practicing the bodhisattva path—these are called *jātaka*.
Regarding the *Jātaka-śāstra*, it states that the "Birth Stories" (*jātaka*) and the "Past Deeds" (*itivṛttaka*) are not different; thus, they are combined into the ninth category.
The eighth [section], Jātakas, refers to those stories that provide alternative explanations; the ninth is called Itivṛttaka (Past Events), and the tenth is called Jātaka (Birth Stories).
What is meant by the Vaipulya Sūtras? These are the Mahāyāna Vaipulya scriptures whose meaning is vast.
It is like space; this is called Vaipulya. Regarding "Vaipulya," the treatise states it means "extensive" (*vipula*).
In this sutra, "fangguang" (方廣) is used, which is also transliterated as *vaipulya*. It is "directly extensive" (*zhiguang*);
"fangguang" is the name used within the Śrāvaka vehicle, while "vaipulya" is the name used within the Mahāyāna.

What are called the Adbhuta-dharma Sūtras? They are such as when that Bodhisattva, at the time of his first birth, walked seven steps without anyone supporting him and emitted a great light that illuminated the ten directions;
or like the monkey who, with his hands, held up a vessel of honey to offer to the Tathāgata;
or like the white-topped dog who listened to the Dharma beside the Buddha; or like Māra Pāpīyas who transformed himself into a blue ox.
When he walked among the clay alms bowls, causing them to strike against one another without sustaining any damage;

and when, like the Buddha at his birth entering a celestial temple, he caused the divine images there to rise and prostrate themselves in reverence—scriptures such as these are called "Marvelous" (Adbhuta).
The *Adbhutadharma* (Marvels) refers to that which is unprecedented.

What is called the *Upadeśa-sūtra*? It refers to those sūtras spoken by the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, for which commentaries have been composed to analyze and explain them in detail, distinguishing their characteristics; these are called *Upadeśa*.

Upadeśa refers to the exposition of meaning; it is also called the Great Teaching (Mahā-upadeśa) and the Explanation of Meaning. Within the Mahāyāna tradition, the term "Explanation of Meaning" was dropped.
Prior to Guangzhai, the term *vyākaraṇa* was translated as "Explanation of Meaning," referring to the explanation of the meaning of receiving predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). (And so forth.)
If a bodhisattva can thus understand the twelve divisions of the scriptures, this is called "knowing the Dharma. This concludes the third section.
Next, the meaning of "knowing" is explained.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the meaning? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva extensively understands the meaning of all letters and languages, this is called "knowing the meaning."
One should know that the principles elucidated by the twelve divisions of the scriptures are now being clarified;

this interpretation is extremely concise, yet it should be understood as the interpretation of the meaning of emptiness and equality throughout the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Furthermore, one interprets immeasurable meanings within a single phrase, and interprets the meaning of ultimate purity.
If these three meanings are interpreted, the force of their significance will be complete.
Third is knowing the proper time.

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the proper time? A son of good family, a bodhisattva, skillfully knows that at such a time it is appropriate to cultivate tranquility, at such a time it is appropriate to cultivate diligence, and at such a time it is appropriate to cultivate equanimity and concentration.
To serve and make offerings to the Buddha at the appropriate time, to serve and make offerings to the teacher at the appropriate time,
and to cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom at the appropriate time—
this is called knowing the proper time.
During such times, practicing generosity at will is for the purpose of transforming others; the remaining phrases are mostly for one's own practice.
Regarding the four explanations of contentment, the latter two virtues are for one's own practice.

What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contentment? Good son, for a bodhisattva, contentment refers to food, drink, clothing, medicine, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent; this is called contentment.
Fifth, regarding self-knowledge:
Good son, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know himself? A bodhisattva knows himself:
"I possess such faith, such ethical discipline, such extensive learning, such renunciation, such wisdom, and such [understanding of] past and future lives."
To possess right mindfulness, to practice such wholesome conduct, and to ask and answer in such a manner is called self-knowledge.
One should examine the wholesome and unwholesome with earnest scrutiny, just as the Master Zeng said: "I daily examine myself three times."
Sixth: How does one know the assemblies? Both of the following two virtues belong to benefiting others. Regarding "knowing the assemblies":

how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the assemblies? A son of good family, a bodhisattva knows that such groups as these—the assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of brāhmaṇas, the assembly of householders, and the assembly of śramaṇas—are assemblies; he should practice in this manner toward these assemblies.
To come in such a manner, to sit and rise in such a manner, to preach the Dharma in such a manner, and to engage in question and answer in such a manner—this is called "knowing the assembly.
One should fully understand that within the texts concerning the assemblies of the ten dharma realms, humans and those of the two vehicles are briefly mentioned;

regarding each of these assemblies, one performs transformations through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind. However, here only body and speech are briefly mentioned, for when transforming others, the use of body and speech is predominant, while the use of the mind is slight.
Therefore, this is summarized.
Seventh, knowing the honorable and the humble:
Good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know the honorable and the humble among people? Good son, there are two kinds of people.

There are two kinds of people: the first is those with faith, and the second is those without faith. A bodhisattva should know that those with faith are virtuous, while those without faith are not called virtuous.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of faith: the first is constantly going to monasteries, and the second is not going.
A bodhisattva should know that those who go are virtuous, while those who do not go are not called virtuous. Regarding those who go to monasteries, furthermore—
There are two kinds: first, prostration; second, non-prostration. A bodhisattva should know that prostration is wholesome, while non-prostration is not called wholesome.
Furthermore, regarding those who prostrate, there are again two kinds: first, listening to the Dharma; second, not listening to the Dharma.
A bodhisattva should know that listening to the Dharma is wholesome, while not listening to the Dharma is not called wholesome. Regarding those [who listen]...
There are two kinds of listeners of the Dharma: first, those who listen with a single-minded heart; second, those who do not listen with a single-minded heart.

A bodhisattva should know that one who listens with a single-minded heart is called "virtuous," whereas one who does not listen with a single-minded heart is not called "virtuous. Furthermore, there are two kinds of listening to the Dharma with a single-minded heart:
first, reflecting upon the meaning; second, not reflecting upon the meaning. A bodhisattva should know that one who reflects upon the meaning is virtuous.

One who contemplates the meaning is not yet called "virtuous. Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who contemplate the meaning: first, those who act according to what they have taught; second, those who do not act according to what they have taught.
One who acts according to what they have taught is indeed virtuous; one who does not act according to what they have taught is not called virtuous.
Moreover, there are two kinds of those who act according to what they have taught: first, those who seek the state of a śrāvaka and are unable to bring benefit, peace, and prosperity to all beings.

Regarding the second [type of dedication], for the sake of sentient beings suffering in affliction, the Bodhisattva should dedicate [merit] toward the unsurpassed Mahāyāna to benefit many people and cause them to attain peace and happiness.
A Bodhisattva should know that that which benefits many people and enables them to attain peace and happiness is the most supreme and most virtuous.
One should fully understand the hierarchy of the ten realms; the text is also concise. Not believing [in the Dharma] is the icchantika, which is the realm of hell—this is the most base.
Not going to the monastic quarters and having no meritorious deeds is the realm of hungry ghosts.
Not prostrating is arrogance, which is the realm of animals. Not listening to the Dharma and not receiving its instruction, being sycophantic, crooked, and obstinate, is the realm of asuras.

The *asura* realm does not listen with a sincere heart, and their wholesome roots are scattered and not focused; this is the human realm. Those who do not contemplate the meaning cannot contemplate the meaning even if they listen with a sincere heart;

this is the realm of the devas. They are unable to practice, possessing only the wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) but lacking the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
These two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are of shallow and inferior expedient means, all of which are base; they seek only—
The Hinayana lacks great aspiration; even if one has awakened to the truth, this is still considered base. If one seeks the Mahayana, this is then considered noble.
Viewed in successive stages, up to the Perfect and Distinctive [teachings], these constitute the realms of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
thus, at every stage, they alternate between being noble and base.
Good son, "going" refers to the second [aspect], the perfect illumination of the seven kinds of goodness. To cite two analogies:

the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) is an analogy for the perfection of producing goodness, and the nectar of immortality (amṛta) is an analogy for the perfection of extinguishing evil. Because one goodness encompasses all goodness such that no goodness is lacking, and one extinction encompasses all extinction such that no evil is not removed, these two analogies are presented;
first the analogy is given, and then the application to the meaning (the *upanaya*) may be seen.
Good son, just as among all jewels the wish-fulfilling gem is the most excellent and sublime, and just as among all flavors ambrosia is the supreme,
so it is with the following analogy.
Thus, this Bodhisattva is the most excellent and supreme among humans and devas, beyond all analogy.
As for how he is the most honored and most eminent among humans and devas, if one were to understand "humans and devas" merely as worldly humans and devas, it would not be appropriate;
rather, it should be understood according to the present text as being most honored and supreme among the humans and devas who are noble sages (*ārya*).
"Good son, this is called the third summary.
Good son, this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abiding in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra;
having abided in these seven wholesome dharmas, the Bodhisattva becomes fully endowed with pure conduct."
Being able to possess the seven virtues constitutes one category within the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*).

Second, the explanation of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) is also called the four equalities and immeasurables. This is so named because they are "immeasurable" with respect to their objects;
while the preceding objects are not singular, they are thus called immeasurable. Although the objects are many, my own mind remains of a single character.
Therefore, it is called "Equal Pervasion" (*samanta-vyāpti*); as for its verbal object, it is also called "Equal Mind" (*samacitta*) and "Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*), and so forth.

The text is divided into two parts: first, the clarification of the four minds; second, the clarification of the fruits of these minds. Regarding the initial analysis of the four minds, there are two sections:

first, the clarification of the sequential order; second, the clarification of the perfect order. Regarding the sequential order, there are three further divisions: first, a brief indication; second, a discussion of the meaning; third, the acceptance and understanding [of the teaching].
The initial heading is as in the text.
Furthermore, son of good family, there is another holy life (*brahmacarya*), namely: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Following the passage beginning with "Kāśyapa," the discussion of the meaning proceeds with a question followed by an answer. The question raises five difficulties; the first difficulty concerns the four mental states (*citta*) that should...

The three [instances of] two-fold difficulties and the four minds correspond to one; the three-fold difficulties and the four minds correspond to three; the four-fold difficulties and the four minds correspond to two;

and the five-fold difficulties and the four minds correspond to one. Taken together, these also constitute three difficulties: the first and third [sets of] four-fold difficulties cause [the result] to be three;
the second and fifth [sets of] four-fold difficulties cause it to be one; and the fourth single difficulty [causes it to be one].
Regarding the four difficulties, let us first divide them into five based on the scriptural text.

The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if the extensive cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever hatred, and the cultivation of compassion (*karuṇā*) likewise severs hatred, why do you speak of the 'four immeasurables' (*catur-apramāṇa*)? If we were to infer the meaning from this, there ought to be [only two]."
Third:
First, because two minds are not different in their capacity to counteract hatred, they should be the same single factor of joy;
and because equanimity can eliminate delusion, there should be only three [immeasurables] rather than four.
Loving-kindness has three objects. [The following section] is the second [part], which is identical in having two difficulties that would cause it to be only one.
The World-Honored One’s loving-kindness has three objects: first, sentient beings; second, dharmas; third, the objectless.
Compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are likewise so. If this principle were followed, there should be only one [type of mind] and not four, because sentient beings [are the same].

Regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*): to take the five aggregates as the object and wish for them to possess happiness is called "compassion focused on sentient beings" (*sattvālambana-maitrī*).

To take as the object the various necessities required by sentient beings and bestow them upon them is called "compassion focused on phenomena" (*dharmālambana-maitrī*). "Objectless compassion" (*anālambana-maitrī*) takes the Tathāgata as its object;
this is called objectless compassion. Furthermore, such compassion mostly takes impoverished sentient beings as its object, whereas the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, is eternally free from poverty.
Experiencing the foremost bliss to the ultimate degree, if one takes sentient beings as the object, then one does not take the Buddha-dharma as the object; it is likewise so.
For this reason, that which takes the Tathāgata as its object is called "objectless" (anālambana).

First, the three conditions are proclaimed, followed by the explanation of the three minds. Although the depth of these three conditions constitutes a single meaning, they differ in terms of their objects;

yet, while the objects may vary, there is no distinction in the mind that conditions them. For example, when one conditions upon poverty, this is the "conditioning upon sentient beings" (*sattvālambana*);

knowing that this poor person requires food and clothing is the "conditioning upon phenomena" (*dharmālambana*); and if one knows that sentient beings must know the Tathāgata who experiences supreme bliss, this is the "conditioning upon the non-referential" (*anālambana*).
Thus, that which has nothing required is itself without conditions; since the object-condition and the subjective condition are one, there should not be four types. Therefore, it is simply one type.

That which takes the five aggregates as its object is called "conditioned by sentient beings," for the five aggregates arise from what is required and one bestows gifts upon them—this is called "conditioned by dharmas.
If one takes the Tathāgata as the object, he requires no such things, and thus it is "unconditioned" (anālambana).
This is intended to clarify that because the mind that takes an object as its condition is all-pervasive, it can even take the Buddha as its superior object, let alone other objects.
This concludes the third section, which raises difficulties regarding the three types of objects of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The objects of the World-Honored One’s compassion are all sentient beings, regarding them as he would his own parents, wife, children, or kinsmen;

for this reason, it is called "compassion directed toward sentient beings" (*sattvālambana*). As for "compassion directed toward phenomena" (*dharmālambana*), one does not perceive parents, wife, children, or kinsmen, but perceives that all phenomena arise from conditions;
this is called "compassion directed toward phenomena. "Compassion without an object" (*anālambana*) does not dwell upon the characteristics of phenomena nor the characteristics of sentient beings.
This is called "objectless" [compassion, joy, and equanimity]; the same applies to these as well. Therefore, there should be three and not four.

The realm of sentient beings is shallow, while the emptiness of dharmas is deep; objectlessness is the negation of both, and is therefore extremely deep. Since there are already three objects, how could there be four? There should only be three.
The proponents of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* say that "conditioned origination" is the object of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
To say that "dharmas are empty of dharmas" and that "the Tathāgata is the emptiness of equality" misses the meaning of the text.
The text states that one takes sentient beings as objects—namely parents, wives, and children—and vows to grant them happiness; when, then, would these be called empty?
There are two types of persons; this is the fourth objection.
World-Honored One, there are two types of persons: first, those whose conduct is dominated by views (*dṛṣṭicarita*), and second, those whose conduct is dominated by craving (*tṛṣṇācarita*).

Those whose conduct is dominated by views cultivate compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) extensively, while those whose conduct is dominated by craving cultivate joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) extensively. Therefore, there should be only two [immeasurables], not four.
There are two types of practitioners: those of sharp faculties who follow views, and those of dull faculties who follow craving. Among these, those of sharp faculties tend toward anger;

because they do not understand even after ten repetitions of the teaching intended for the dull-witted, they give rise to anger. For this reason, one must cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) in order to abandon the mind of anger.
Furthermore, those of dull faculties who follow views constantly harbor jealousy; therefore, one causes them to practice sympathetic joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
[The Buddha] removed [the fault of] jealousy. If that were so, there would only be two [immeasurables], and it should not be four.
Now, in the fifth section, he raises an objection regarding the combination of names:
"World-Honored One, as for 'immeasurable' (apramāṇa), it is called 'boundless' (ananta); because no limit can be found, it is called immeasurable. If it does not exist...
If they were [limited] measures, they ought to be one and not four; if one speaks of four, how can they be "immeasurable"?
Therefore, they ought to be one and not four.
Since you have already spoken of them as immeasurable, how could they be merely four? If they are only four, they should not be immeasurable; if they are immeasurable, [they cannot be four].
This [subject] should be considered as one alone. Next, the Tathāgata’s response is twofold:
first, he refutes the attachment to a fixed number of four; second, he answers the objection regarding the absence of four. The first part contains three sections:
(1) clarifying that the breadth or brevity of the teaching is not fixed; (2) clarifying that it is not fixed by contradicting the conventional norm; and (3) [the third section].
Since delusions are not fixed, why must there necessarily be four? First, the answer is given by way of the indeterminacy of the twelve links of dependent origination.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "Good son, the essential teachings proclaimed by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas for the sake of sentient beings..."
It is said that the secret is difficult to comprehend; yet for the sake of sentient beings, one may explain it through a single causal condition, such as when it is asked:

"What is the single causal condition? and it is replied: "It is all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), O son of good family. Or one may explain it through two kinds of causes and effects; or one may explain it through three kinds:

afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*); or one may explain it through four kinds: ignorance (*avidyā*), formative forces (*saṃskāra*), birth (*jāti*), and [aging and death].
Old age and death are sometimes explained as fivefold, namely: feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*), and birth (*jāti*);

or as sixfold, referring to the causes and effects of the three periods of time; or as sevenfold, namely: consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*);
or as eightfold, excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and birth-and-old-age-death (*jātijarāmaraṇa*), consisting of the remaining eight factors; or as ninefold, like a city.
In the sūtras, with the exception of ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), nine matters are mentioned;
or, as in the case of the teaching for Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputra, eleven are mentioned with the single factor of birth (*jāti*) excluded.

At other times, the twelve links of dependent origination are explained in their entirety, as when they were fully taught to Kāśyapa and others in Rājagṛha, beginning from ignorance up to birth, old age, sickness, and death. These are wholesome (*kuśala*).
Just as a man, for the sake of sentient beings, makes various distinctions based on a single causal condition, so too are the immeasurable mental dharmas.
Son of good family, for this reason, you should not give rise to doubt regarding the profound and secret sphere of activity of the Tathāgatas.
Sometimes there are eleven [causes], down to two or one; these causal conditions are established according to the capacity of beings for their benefit and cannot be fixed.

Regarding the exception of those who have produced even a single wholesome dharma, the Master of Hexi said: "Saccaka Nigaṇṭha was clever and possessed a copper-plated belly; he came before the Buddha wearing a crown of fire upon his head.
His mind was haughty and aloof, so he would not listen to the Buddha’s Dharma. Only when Guhyapada (Mijue) brandished his mace to threaten him did he finally listen to the Dharma."
His father was a Brahmin and his mother was a Nirgrantha; both had left the household life together to follow what is not the Dharma.

Because he was born of such parents, this alone was a source of shame for him, while he felt no dread toward anything else. Out of compassion and protection for him, the Buddha set aside one teaching and taught only eleven [dharmas].
Furthermore, because Kāśyapa possessed sharp faculties as a pratyekabuddha and was free from hesitation, the Buddha explained everything in full.
12. "Good son,
regarding the Tathāgata’s skillful means, the second reversal of the extraordinary is called the indeterminacy of the secret of speech."
"Good son, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great skillful means: he speaks of the impermanent as permanent and the permanent as impermanent;
he speaks of suffering as happiness and happiness as suffering; he speaks of the impure as pure and the pure as impure; he speaks of non-self as self and self as non-self;
he speaks of what is not a sentient being as a sentient being and what is a real sentient being as not a sentient being."

To speak of things as things, and to speak of non-things as non-things; to speak of the unreal as real, and to speak of the real as unreal; to speak of what is not an object as an object, and to speak of an object as not an object;
to speak of that which is not birth as birth, and to speak of birth as not birth—and so on, up to speaking of ignorance as clarity, and speaking of clarity as ignorance;
speaking of form as non-form, and speaking of non-form as form; speaking of the Path as the Path, and speaking of the Path as not the Path, O son of good family.
The Tathāgata employs these immeasurable skillful means to discipline sentient beings; how could this be false?

The Buddha truly possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity, yet he also speaks of impermanence and impurity; birth-and-death is indeed impermanent and impure, yet he also speaks of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Good son, there are some sentient beings who have descended into the third stage of subduing afflictions, which is called "uncertainty regarding the body's secrecy.

Good son, there are some sentient beings who crave wealth and goods; for such people, I personally manifest my own body as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and, for immeasurable years, provide them with all manner of necessities according to their needs, and only thereafter do I teach and transform them.

When I am established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, if there are sentient beings who are attached to the five desires, I shall fulfill their wishes by providing them with exquisite five-desire objects for immeasurable years;

thereafter, I will exhort and transform them, causing them to be established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If there are sentient beings who are prosperous, powerful, and self-important, I shall [act] toward them...
For immeasurable ages, I served as a servant, running errands and attending to others until I had won their hearts;
having done so, I further exhorted and transformed them, causing them to dwell securely in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If there were sentient beings who were perverse and self-willed, requiring reprimand and admonition, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years I taught, rebuked, and used parables to bring their minds [to maturity].
Once they have become disciplined and compliant, he further exhorts them to dwell securely in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"O son of good family, since the Tathāgata has, over immeasurable eons, used such various skillful means to cause all sentient beings to dwell in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, could this possibly be false? Although the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, abide..."
Unstained by any evils, just like a lotus—noble son, you should understand the meaning of the four immeasurables in this way:

acting as a wheel-turning monarch and bestowing wealth is equanimity; giving the pleasures of the five senses is sympathetic joy; and serving as a servant, running errands, and attending to others is loving-kindness.
This loving reproach and admonition is compassion.

Good son, this is the second answer to the question regarding the four absences within the section on the "immeasurables. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the general, and second, the specific.

Within the general part, there are again two: first, the presentation of two matters, and second, the general negation of the previous question. Regarding the presentation of the two matters mentioned previously: [the text] previously presented...
Next, the difference in function is clarified following the difference in essence. First, regarding the difference in essence:
"Good son, the essential nature of these immeasurable minds has four aspects; if one practices them, one will be born in the realm of Mahābrahmā."

The fruits obtained differ: loving-kindness attains the Sphere of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*), compassion attains the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), sympathetic joy attains the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and equanimity attains the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);
because these spheres are distinct, the remedies for the afflictions differ accordingly.
Thus, the first part has been explained; next, the second part clarifies the differences in their functions.
Good son, such immeasurable categories of companions are fourfold; therefore, they are called the "Four. One who cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever covetous desire;
one who cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*) can sever ill will; one who cultivates sympathetic joy (*muditā*) can sever discontent;
and one who cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*) can sever both covetous desire and ill will in sentient beings.

To greedily seize from others is greed; to compassionately give to others is generosity. To cause others suffering is hatred; to compassionately uproot others' suffering is compassion. To envy others' happiness is jealousy;
to joyfully bestow happiness upon others is sympathetic joy. Delusion increases attachment and aversion; equanimity eliminates both attachment and aversion.
For this reason, the following two lines summarize the preceding negations.
Good son, for this reason they are named "four" rather than "one, two, or three.
"Not one" means not the second or the fifth; "not two" means not the fourth; "not three" means not the third.
First, the third [section].
As you have stated, the second part below provides separate answers to the five questions, which constitute five chapters.
This first [chapter] answers the first difficulty regarding the treatment of afflictions, asserting that there are only three [remedies] and not four.
"Good son, as you have said, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever anger, and compassion (*karuṇā*) is likewise; thus one should speak of three [immeasurables].
You should not now raise such an objection. Why? Good son, there are two kinds of malice: first, that which can take life; second, that which can lash and beat.
Cultivating loving-kindness can sever the former—taking life—and cultivating compassion can eliminate the latter—beating."
Good son, for this reason, are there not four? Furthermore, there are two kinds of anger: first, anger toward sentient beings; second, anger toward non-sentient things.
One who cultivates the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) abandons anger toward sentient beings, while one who cultivates the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) abandons anger toward non-sentient things.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of anger: first, that which has a cause and condition; second, that which lacks a cause and condition. One who cultivates the mind of loving-kindness...
One who cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*) severs that which has causes and conditions; one who cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) severs that which lacks causes and conditions.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of hatred: first, that which has been accumulated over a long time in the past; second, that which is being accumulated for the first time in the present.

One who cultivates loving-kindness can sever the former, while one who cultivates compassion severs the latter. Furthermore, there are two kinds of hatred: first, hatred directed toward noble beings (*ārya*).

Regarding the two types of hatred in persons: ordinary beings who cultivate the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) sever hatred, and noble ones (*ārya*) who cultivate the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) sever hatred.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of hatred: first, the superior; second, the middling. One cultivates loving-kindness to sever the superior and cultivates compassion to sever the middling.
Son of good family, for this reason they are called four; how can you raise the objection that there should be three and not four?

Now, although anger is treated identically in both cases, there are degrees of lightness and heaviness; therefore, four [categories] are established, and six [factors] are further added, as explained in the text.
Thus, Kāśyapa, this is the second response to the objection regarding the identity of the object (*samanālambana*).
Therefore, Kāśyapa, these immeasurable minds are distinguished as four by way of their corresponding categories.
Since the remedies for the afflictions differ, there are four categories; how can they be made identical? [The opponent asks: "There are only three conditions, so why are they combined into one?
Furthermore, by means of the vessel's inferiority, he answers the third objection regarding the difficulty of the degrees of depth, showing that there must be three.

Furthermore, because they serve as vessels, they should be called the "four vessels. If there were loving-kindness (*maitrī*), then compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) could not exist;
for this reason, the four [immeasurables] should not be diminished.

Now, it is clarified that there are four according to their functions; how could they be reduced to three based on their sequential practice? Or, it may be said that the "vessel" refers to the object (*viṣaya*).
By distinguishing according to practice, the fourth [question] regarding the difficulty of the sharpness or dullness of individuals is answered.

Son of good family, because they are distinguished by practice, there should be four; for when one practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*), if there is no compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*), there are therefore four.

To clarify that although there are two persons, there are four modes of conduct and they cannot be considered as two, [the text] provides the answer to the fifth difficulty regarding names based on their immeasurability. This consists of two parts: first, the listing of the four topical headings;
second, the detailed explanation.
Good son, because they are immeasurable, they are also called the "four. Regarding these immeasurables, there are four kinds:
there is an immeasurable mind that has an object but is not sovereign; there is an immeasurable mind that is sovereign but does not have an object;
there is an immeasurable mind that both has an object and is sovereign; and there is an immeasurable mind that neither has an object nor is sovereign.
What is that which is immeasurable and has an object, yet is not a sovereign object? It refers to the inability to attain sovereign samādhi regarding immeasurable and boundless sentient beings;
even if attained, it is not fixed, being sometimes gained and sometimes lost. What is that which is immeasurable and sovereign, yet not an object?
It is like [the love for] parents, brothers, sisters, and so forth, desiring to bring them peace and happiness; this is not an immeasurable object. What is that which is immeasurable...?
"Measure, object, and mastery" refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. What is immeasurable, non-objective, and non-mastery?
It is that which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot extensively take as an object—immeasurable sentient beings—and for which they lack mastery.
Good son, for this reason, the four immeasurables are not known by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; rather, they are the domain of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.

"O son of good family, regarding these four matters that come within their sphere of experience, although the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are said to possess them in 'immeasurable' amounts, this is not sufficient to be called 'immeasurable';
it is only for the Buddhas and bodhisattvas that they can truly be called 'immeasurable and immeasurable.'"
To clarify that even "immeasurability" (apramāṇa) still possesses four categories, what prevents there being four kinds of immeasurability?
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha; this third section on understanding the teaching is as in the text.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, it is so, it is so; it is truly as the Holy One has spoken. All Buddhas, Tathāgatas...”
The realms that arise are not within the reach of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

World-Honored One, are there any Bodhisattvas who, bypassing the second stage of illumination without following the sequential order, immediately perfect the four [immeasurable] minds? Furthermore, there are two parts:

first, a preliminary analysis of "small" compassion; second, the manifestation of "great" compassion. Regarding this distinction between the small and the great, even the small is not small and cannot be so categorized.
Ordinary persons are considered "small" and the two vehicles are considered "great," while the two vehicles are considered "small" and Bodhisattvas are considered "great.
Why is this? Because both ordinary persons and those of the two vehicles do not abide in Great Nirvāṇa;

therefore, compassion that follows a sequential order is now considered "small," whereas compassion that does not follow a sequential order is considered "great," for both of these abide in Great Nirvāṇa. Some, based on [what appears to be] similarity...

To claim that the small is true while the large is not, or vice versa, is also incorrect; for when they appear in sequence, both are similar to the true [nature] yet are small, and when they do not appear in sequence, both are similar to the true [nature] yet are large.
Thus, there are two sets of questions and answers to distinguish between the small and the large.
"Bhagavān, is it possible that there are bodhisattvas dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa who possess a mind of compassion, yet it is not the mind of great kindness and great compassion?
The first question was: "Are there bodhisattvas dwelling in Mahāparinirvāṇa who possess a mind of compassion, yet it is not the mind of great kindness?"
This is the correct sequence of questions regarding the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Next, the Buddha’s response consists of three parts: first, the proclamation; second, the two interpretations; third, the three conclusions. Regarding the initial proclamation, it is as stated in the text.
The Buddha said: "It exists."
Next, in explaining the "existence within," there are two parts: first, delineating the objects; second, clarifying the contemplation.
Good son, if a bodhisattva makes a threefold distinction among sentient beings—first, those who are dear; second, those who are hostile;
and third, those who are neutral—and further divides those who are dear into three grades, namely superior, middling, and inferior; and likewise for those who are hostile...
Hatred is likewise.

Regarding the initial objects, there are nine grades: among enemies, friends, and neutral persons, there are three grades each; or it is said that neutral persons constitute only one grade, making seven in total.
As for neutral persons—those who are neither enemies nor friends toward me—it is not necessary to divide them into three; at first glance, this is indeed the case.
In this context, because there are distinctions among people such as the ignorant and the wise, the noble and the lowly, they can be divided into three groups, which further constitute nine objects;
thus, there are nine types of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Next, from "Furthermore, these bodhisattvas... onwards, the text correctly clarifies the cultivation of the contemplation.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva bestows supreme happiness upon those who are superior relatives; likewise, he bestows it equally upon those who are middling or inferior relatives.
Toward those who are superior enemies, he bestows a small measure of happiness; toward those who are middling enemies, he bestows a middling measure of happiness;
and toward those who are inferior enemies, he bestows supreme happiness. In this way, the bodhisattva increasingly cultivates and practices [this] with respect to the superior [category].

When one who is treated with middling happiness by an enemy gives superior happiness to that middling or inferior enemy, and further cultivates this practice so as to give superior happiness to those of superior,

middling, and inferior status; and when one who is treated with superior happiness by a superior enemy attains at that time what is called the accomplishment of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*),
then one possesses a mind of equanimity toward both one's parents and one's superior enemies, without distinction.
Regarding the distinctions:

if one has not yet practiced at all, one merely intends to bestow the three kinds of happiness upon the three types of relatives, and neither suffering nor happiness upon the three types of enemies and the three types of neutral persons;
or, if one first practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one bestows the three grades of happiness upon the three types of relatives.

The neutral person gives the third grade of happiness to the three types of enemies: the superior enemy receives the lower grade of happiness, the middling enemy receives the middle grade, and the inferior enemy receives the upper grade.
During the second stage of cultivation, the superior enemy receives the middle grade of happiness, while both the middling and inferior enemies receive the upper grade.
During the third stage of cultivation, all three enemies together receive the upper grade of happiness; this is still not yet the level of a friend.
When practicing the fourth [stage], one gives the medium person’s lower pleasure to the three enemies;
when practicing the fifth, one gives the medium person’s medium pleasure to the three enemies; when practicing the sixth, one gives the medium person’s superior pleasure to the three enemies;
and when practicing the seventh, one gives the lower pleasure of the three relatives to the three enemies.

In the eighth stage of cultivation, one bestows the happiness of the three types of friends upon the three types of enemies; in the ninth stage of cultivation, one bestows the superior happiness of the three types of friends upon the three types of enemies.
This is called "bestowing superior happiness upon superior enemies," at which time the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is said to be accomplished.

Furthermore, when directly taking two grades of happiness and applying them to the nine types of objects, at the initial moment of entering the contemplation, [one begins with] the three types of friends.
In the second period, one gives the highest pleasure to close relatives and the middle pleasure to distant relatives; in the third period, one gives the highest pleasure to distant relatives;
in the fourth period, one gives the lowest pleasure to both close and distant relatives; in the fifth period, one gives the middle pleasure to both close and distant relatives;
in the sixth period, one gives the highest pleasure to both close and distant relatives; and in the seventh period, one gives [the same] to superior enemies.
