In the eighth stage, one bestows superior happiness upon those who were previously inferior enemies; in the ninth stage, one bestows middling happiness upon those who were previously middling enemies;

and in the tenth stage, one bestows superior happiness upon those who were previously superior enemies—this is called the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Alternatively, according to the present text, there are briefly four stages of entering meditative observation:

in the first stage, one bestows superior happiness upon the three types of relatives, treating these three collectively as one stage, while separately distinguishing the three types of enemies as three stages.
Furthermore, although the Bodhisattva’s clear cultivation of contemplation actually consists of nine grades of distinct practice, the present text explains only three grades.
"Good son, this is called attaining loving-kindness. This concludes the third section on the existence [of loving-kindness].
“Good son, this is called attaining loving-kindness, but not great loving-kindness.
World-Honored One, for what reason did you repeat this second round, first asking and then answering?
World-Honored One, for what reason is it that although a bodhisattva attains such loving-kindness, they still cannot be said to have attained great loving-kindness?”
The answer consists of three parts: first, stating the objection; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Regarding the first part, the statement:
"Good son, because it constitutes an objection, it is not called great compassion.
Next, from "Why is this? onwards is the explanation, beginning with the principle (*dharma*).
Why is this? Because throughout immeasurable kalpas in the distant past, they have accumulated many afflictions and have not cultivated wholesome dharmas;
therefore, they are unable to subdue their minds within a single day.
Next is the analogy:
"Good son, it is like a dried pea; a awl can never pierce it. The hardness of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) is likewise:
even if one binds the mind for a single day and night so that it does not scatter, it is difficult to subdue. It is also like a domestic dog."
Fearing others, like a deer in the mountains, forests, or wilds that runs in terror upon seeing a person, it is difficult to remove through anger, like a dog guarding a house;
yet its compassionate mind is easily lost, like that wild deer. For this reason, this mind must be disciplined when separated from [its objects];
for this meaning, it is not called "Great Compassion. Furthermore, son of good family, it is like writing on stone—the inscription remains forever—while writing on water perishes quickly.
Its momentum does not endure long and its anger is difficult to remove; it is like a drawing on stone. Good roots perish easily, just as a drawing in water.
For this reason, this mind is difficult to subdue. It is like a mass of fire whose brilliance lasts for a long time, whereas the light of lightning cannot remain even for a moment.
Anger is like a mass of fire, while loving-kindness is like the light of lightning; therefore, this mind is difficult to subdue.

In total, four analogies are presented: when delusion is strong and compassion is weak, it cannot be called "Great"; only when delusion and compassion are perfected can it be termed "Great Compassion.
Based on this principle, the third section concludes below.
For this reason, it is not called "Great Compassion" (*mahāmaitrī*).
Good son, when a bodhisattva dwells in the first stage (*bhūmi*), these four minds—which manifest the clarity and perfection of the second [stage]—are then truly Great Compassion.

This text is divided into two parts: first, the elucidation of Great Compassion; second, the elucidation of the empty and the real. Within the first section on Great Compassion, there are three further divisions.

First, the explicit explanation of great compassion; second, the explanation of its combined application; third, the explanation of its wholesome root. Regarding the first, the explicit explanation of great compassion, there are three parts:
the statement, the explanation, and the conclusion. First, the statement is as in the text:
"Good son, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the first stage, it is called 'Great Compassion'."
Why is this? Good son, those who are most extremely evil are called icchantikas.
When a bodhisattva dwelling in the first stage cultivates great compassion, his mind makes no distinction regarding icchantikas; because he perceives no fault in them, he does not give rise to anger.
Next, regarding the meaning of the commentary: previously, one bestowed supreme happiness upon those who were supreme enemies, but this had not yet been done for icchantikas.

Now, this perfect compassion takes icchantikas as its object; because it perceives only the true reality (*dharmatā*) and does not see their faults, anger does not arise—this alone constitutes great compassion.
The three fetters are as stated in the text.
For this reason, it is called "Great Loving-kindness" (*mahāmaitrī*).
Son of Good Family, for the sake of all sentient beings, the following is the second [section] clarifying loving-kindness as being employed concurrently.

Good son, to eliminate what is unbeneficial for all sentient beings is called great loving-kindness (*maitrī*); to desire to bestow immeasurable benefit and happiness upon sentient beings is called great compassion (*karuṇā*);
to give rise to a heart of joy toward all sentient beings is called great sympathetic joy (*muditā*);

and to have nothing to protect or guard is called great equanimity (*upekṣā*). If one does not perceive the marks of self or phenomena, and sees all phenomena as equal, this is [the realization of] the Dharma.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the state of non-duality; it is called "great equanimity" because one relinquishes one's own happiness to bestow it upon others.

If loving-kindness (*maitrī*) were merely to grant happiness and compassion (*karuṇā*) were solely to extract suffering, they would not function in tandem. Here, however, it is clarified that loving-kindness also extracts suffering and compassion also grants happiness;
within equanimity, too, there are these two aspects, as the text explains.

Only the four immeasurable minds [are the basis]; third, it clarifies that the roots of goodness serve as the foundation for the three [categories]. First, they serve as the foundation for the six perfections.
"Good son, only the four immeasurable minds can cause a bodhisattva to increase and fulfill the six pāramitās;
other practices do not necessarily have this capacity."
Next is the foundation for generating the mind [of enlightenment].

Good son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva first attains the four worldly immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*), and only thereafter generates the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is through this sequence that one subsequently attains the supramundane.
Third, the basis of intrinsic characteristics.
Good son, because one attains supramundane immeasurability by means of mundane immeasurability, it is for this reason called "Great Immeasurability.

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: [This concludes the second section, clarifying the distinction between the empty and the real; the following explains that which is called "real," namely, the contemplation, which also begins with a question.]

Next, the response to the questions consists of three parts: first, the refutation of the objection; second, the concession of the objection; and third, the prevention of the objection. Regarding the first, the refutation of the objection, there are two further sections:
first, the method (dharma), and second, the analogy. First, as for the method:
the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, apart from that which is without benefit and that which brings benefit and joy, there is truly nothing [else to be found]."
To engage in such reflection is merely a hollow contemplation that possesses no real benefit.

Although one clearly intends to uproot suffering, in reality one has not uprooted it; all such claims are empty words. Although one intends to bestow happiness, in reality one does not obtain happiness;
this is but a provisional designation.
Next, an analogy is raised to clarify this:
"World-Honored One, it is as if a bhikṣu, when contemplating impurity, perceives the clothes he wears as being entirely skin, though they are not actually skin;
he perceives what is fit to be eaten as being entirely worms, though they are not actually worms; and he contemplates delicious, fine soup as being foul."
One contemplates broth as being excrement, yet it is not actually excrement; one contemplates the curd one eats as being like marrow and brain, yet it is not actually brain;
one contemplates the fine powder of bones as being like bran, yet it is not actually bran. The four immeasurable minds are likewise thus:
they cannot truly benefit sentient beings or cause them to attain happiness; though one speaks with the mouth of granting happiness to sentient beings, in reality...
Is it not false to hold such a view?
It is like a bhikṣu who practices a conceptual visualization, perceiving soup as foul when it is actually not foul;
though he speaks of obtaining pleasure, he truly does not obtain pleasure.
If the Blessed One is not deceptive— this begins the second section, the hypothetical objection:
if the Blessed One truly bestows happiness, why is it that all those sentient beings do not experience happiness through the majestic power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
Even if there were actual benefit, why is it that one does not perceive peace and happiness?
If they truly bestow happiness, then since the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are immeasurable and boundless, why do we not see them bestowing happiness upon sentient beings?
Third, the refutation of the objection regarding the reality [of suffering]:
If it were truly the case that one cannot attain happiness, then as the Buddha said:

"I recall that in the past, while practicing only the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*) throughout this kalpa, during seven cycles of the world’s formation and destruction, I did not return to this world; when the world was forming, I was born among the Brahmā gods."

When the world was being destroyed, I was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; when it was being formed, I was born in the Brahma Heaven, possessing power, majesty, and sovereignty such that none could overcome me.
Among a thousand Brahmas, I was the most excellent and supreme, known as Mahābrahmā. Furthermore, there were sentient beings who all conceived the highest regard for me.
Thirty-six times I served as Śakra Devānām Indra, the king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years.
One becomes a Wheel-Turning King only by cultivating a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), thereby attaining such fruits of retribution among humans and devas;
if this were not true, how could it correspond to this principle?
If the Buddha were to answer that this is empty and unreal, then the Tathāgata himself would likewise have become a Brahmā only through practicing loving-kindness in the past.

Since the Lord is the most excellent and supreme, how could he obtain anything that is without benefit? Therefore, it is refuted by stating that he cannot obtain what is without benefit; thus, it is called a "refutation by way of negation" (*pratiṣedha-vighāta*).

Next, from the words "Good son," the Buddha answers the three preceding objections: first, he answers the refutation by way of negation; second, he answers the objection of deprivation (*apahāra-vighāta*).
The third response, which addresses the objection, consists of two parts: first, the initial response refuting the objection by praising its refutation.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You are truly courageous and fearless."
Next, in the formal response, four verses are divided into three parts; the first verse clarifies great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*).
It was spoken as a verse for Kāśyapa:
If, toward even a single sentient being, One does not give rise to a mind of anger, But vows to bestow happiness upon them—
This is called the first practice of benevolence and compassion;
when one gives rise to a heart of pity toward all sentient beings, this is called the noble lineage.
The merit obtained is immeasurable;
this is compared in three or two lines.
Even if seers possessing the five supernormal powers were to completely fill this great earth, there would still be a Great Lord of Sovereignty.
To offer whatever brings peace— elephants, horses, and various other things—
the fruit of the merit obtained does not equal even one-sixteenth part of the practice of a single moment of loving-kindness;
the merit of truly being able to grant happiness is immeasurable.
Good son, regarding the cultivation of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), there are two responses to the challenge of refutation. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, proclaiming the truth.
Good son, as for one who cultivates loving-kindness, it is truly not a false conceptualization; it is indeed reality.
If it is the loving-kindness of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, it is called false; the loving-kindness of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is real and not empty.
Therefore, by citing the compassion of the śrāvakas as being merely conceptual, it is shown that that of the bodhisattvas is real.
How is this known? The second section extensively clarifies its reality, which consists of five parts: (1) reality in its ability to transform the objective sphere;
(2) reality in its ability to counteract afflictions; (3) reality in its being the root of virtue; (4) reality in its pervading all phenomena; and (5) reality in its being inconceivable.
The discussion is initially divided into three parts: first, the proclamation; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
The first is as stated in the text. How is this known?
Good son, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such Great Nirvāṇa, he perceives earth as gold.
One contemplates gold as the earth-element and produces the appearance of water; one contemplates water as the earth-element, water as the fire-element, and fire as the water-element;
one contemplates earth as the wind-element and wind as the earth-element. These are accomplished at will and are without falsehood.
One contemplates real sentient beings as non-sentient beings, and contemplates non-sentient beings as real sentient beings; all are accomplished at will and are without falsehood.
The meaning of the commentary is explained as follows: there are two aspects to this. First, it can truly transform the object; second, it can merely cause it to be seen [as something else].
If gold were transformed into earth, that would be a true transformation. If sentient beings were made into non-sentient beings, that would merely be a matter of causing them to be seen [as such].
One master says: "The sutra speaks of 'being able to accomplish'—how can there be two interpretations? A Bodhisattva is not merely able to transform gold."

Earth is also transformed; sentient beings are likewise transformed into non-sentient beings. That which is non-sentient—namely grasses and trees—is transformed from being non-sentient into sentient beings.
If one says that sentient beings are originally empty, illusory, and non-existent, one should know that among sentient beings there are those who are non-sentient.
If one says that all dharmas possess a nature of peace and bliss, they are not [ordinary] sentient beings.
Birth is also [the case for] sentient beings; whether the animate and the inanimate possess nature or lack nature can be understood by this analogy. [The author] privately asks:

If sentient beings and non-sentient beings were truly able to transform into one another—sentient beings becoming inanimate and inanimate beings becoming sentient—this principle would be difficult to believe.
If they do not truly transform, then the power of the Sage is applied in vain. In sum, it is merely all... [text ends].
Since the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas themselves abide in the non-duality of the primary and the secondary, yet manifest as two while remaining non-dual, they enable sentient beings to do likewise.
This constitutes a perpetual transformation;

even if it were but a temporary transformation, such a principle would not be impossible, and those who undergo this transformation would not fail to realize it themselves—let alone when compassion is itself the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata is himself compassion, and compassion is itself Buddha-nature.
The Buddha-nature is precisely all dharmas; I entreat future virtuous ones to contemplate this, to contemplate it deeply.
Good son, you should know that the four immeasurable minds of a bodhisattva are genuine contemplation and are not unreal.
Furthermore, son of good family, the second section below explains that true [wisdom] can indeed treat the afflictions; it is further divided into three parts:
the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. Furthermore, son of good family, what is called "true reflection"? It is that which is able to sever all afflictions.
Good son, one who cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever covetous desire; one who cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*) can sever malice;
one who cultivates sympathetic joy (*muditā*) can sever discontent; and one who cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*) can sever both covetousness and malice, as well as the perception of sentient beings.
For this reason, it is called "true contemplation.
The former [tradition] held that the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) are merely qualities of blissful tranquility that suppress [afflictions] but do not constitute ultimate abandonment;
here, however, the four immeasurables are themselves *prajñā* (wisdom), which is precisely what effects such abandonment.
Furthermore, son of good family, regarding the four immeasurables, the third section clarifies that they are truly the root of goodness.

This is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying that they can serve as the root of goodness for the Mahāyāna; second, clarifying that they can serve as the root of goodness for the three vehicles. The first of these is also divided into two:
first, clarifying that they universally constitute the root of all goodness; second, clarifying that they can serve as the foundation for giving. The initial passage is readily understandable.
Furthermore, son of good family, the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva can serve as the root of all wholesome roots.

Son of good family, the latter two [immeasurables] specifically clarify their role as the foundation for giving; furthermore, there are five aspects, the first of which is right giving (*samyak-dāna*).
1. The two fundamental [realities] are signless; 2. to perceive signs is a failure; 3. realizing that the one mind is identical to the four minds;
4. extensively formulating vows.
Good son, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not perceive impoverished sentient beings, they will have no basis for generating loving-kindness.
If one does not give rise to loving-kindness, one cannot arouse the mind of wise generosity;

through the causes and conditions of such giving, one enables all sentient beings to obtain peace and happiness—namely, food and drink, vehicles, clothing, flowers and incense, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
First, the exposition of the basis of giving presents eight matters as the foundation for the eight matters that follow.

Regarding such giving, the second section clarifies signlessness (*animitta*) for the sake of attainment. This consists of three parts: first, the general; second, the specific; and third, the conclusion.
The initial general section is as stated in the text.
When giving in this manner, the mind is free from bondage and does not give rise to greedy attachment;
it is resolutely dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the mind has no point of reliance, delusive thoughts are forever severed, and one is not moved by fear, fame, or gain.
One does not seek the pleasures experienced by humans or devas; one does not give rise to arrogance; one does not hope for a reciprocal reward;

one does not practice giving for the sake of deceiving others; and one does not seek wealth or status. Whenever practicing giving, one does not regard the recipient as either observing or violating the precepts, nor as a field or a non-field;
one does not regard them as a kinsman or a non-kinsman; and when giving, one does not regard them as a worthy vessel or an unworthy vessel.
They do not select specific days or times; they do not calculate what is possible or impossible, nor do they reckon with famine or abundance, suffering or joy.
They do not perceive cause and effect, nor do they distinguish between "this is a sentient being" and "this is not a sentient being," or between "this is merit" and "this is not merit."
Next, in the specific discussion, it says that "not seeing cause and effect" means that giving is the cause and obtaining retribution is the effect;
if one were to think that obtaining the fruit is eternal or that not obtaining it is annihilation, the Bodhisattva does not practice such giving.
Third, the concluding summary below follows the text:
although one does not perceive the giver, the recipient, or the material gift, and even does not perceive the cessation [of defilements] or their karmic fruition,
one constantly practices giving without interruption.
Good son, if a bodhisattva sees those below the third level who possess signs of existence as a fault, there are three dharmas;
the analogy and its application to the text are as written.
Good son, if a bodhisattva sees those who uphold the precepts or violate them, and so forth, up to their karmic retribution, yet are ultimately unable to practice giving—if...
If one does not practice giving, then the dānapāramitā will not be fulfilled;
if the dānapāramitā is not fulfilled, then one cannot achieve anuttarasamyaksambodhi.
Good son, it is like a person whose body has been struck by a poisoned arrow.
His kinsmen, wishing to bring him peace and remove the poison, summon a skilled physician to extract the arrow. That person then says, "Wait a moment; do not touch me!
I must first observe from which direction this poisoned arrow came and by whom I was shot—whether by a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa..."
The Brahmins, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras further reflected: "What kind of wood is this—is it bamboo, or willow?
As for its iron point, from what forge does it originate—is it hard or soft? As for its feathers, to which bird do they belong—is it a crow, a hawk, or a vulture?
And as for all these poisons, did they arise through intentional creation, or are they natural? Are they the poison of humans or of venomous snakes?"
"Is it poison? Thus, this deluded person, being ultimately unable to know [the truth], immediately meets his end.

The "man in the middle" is a metaphor for a bodhisattva of shallow practice; the "arrow" is a metaphor for the arising of stinginess; the "invitation of a physician by his kinsmen" is a metaphor for spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) exhorting him to give, saying, "Wait a moment";

"not consenting to give at that time" is a metaphor for not practicing immediate giving; and "I shall observe" is a metaphor for grasping at signs and engaging in conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
The poisoned arrow who shot it is a metaphor for discriminating regarding the field of merit—whether one upholds or violates [the precepts].

The arrow shafts of bamboo and willow are metaphors for discriminating regarding the objects of giving—what things may be relinquished and what things may not. "The poison" is a metaphor for the person who clings to their giving;
having failed to understand the nature of giving, they pass away. Because they did not properly practice giving and were obscured by stinginess, their roots of goodness are severed.
Root Life.
This is analogous to the preceding text.
Good son, it is the same for a bodhisattva: when practicing generosity, if they discriminate between recipients based on whether they uphold the precepts or violate them, then...
When the fruit of retribution is reached, one will ultimately be unable to give; if one cannot give, then the dānapāramitā is not fulfilled;
and if the dānapāramitā is not fulfilled, then one cannot achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, good son, the fourth section below, "The Single Mind," reveals the characteristics of perfect compassion.
Furthermore, good son, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices giving, he regards all sentient beings with a mind of equanimity and compassion, as if they were his own children.
Moreover, when practicing giving, he gives rise to a heart of pity and sympathy toward all sentient beings, just as...
When parents care for their sick child while practicing generosity, their hearts rejoice just as parents do when they see their child’s illness cured;
after having given, their hearts are set at ease, just as parents feel when they see their child grown up and able to support themselves.

When practicing the giving of the clear-knowledge and conduct (*vidyā-caryā*), one possesses the four immeasurables: at the time of giving, one generates loving-kindness (*maitrī*); at the time of giving, one arouses compassion (*karuṇā*);
at the time of giving, the mind is joyful (*muditā*); and having given, one abides in equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Within this state of loving-kindness, the Bodhisattva makes five successive broad vows; these consist of eight layers in total, the first of which is explained as follows:
Regarding the giving of food up to the offering of lamps, the first three cases are as stated in the text.
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives food from a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they constantly make this vow:
"May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings; by this cause and condition, may all sentient beings attain greatness."
May all beings obtain the food of wisdom through diligent progress and dedicate it to the unsurpassed Great Vehicle;
may they seek not the food of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. May all beings obtain the food of Dharma-joy and seek not the food of craving.
May all beings fully attain the food of the Prajñāpāramitā, being completely filled with it, and may they grasp it with unimpeded and superior resolve.
"By these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings understand and penetrate the mark of emptiness and attain an unobstructed body like space.
May all sentient beings always be recipients [of offerings], taking pity on all and serving as fields of merit for the multitude.
Son of good family, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, they should firmly make such vows as these whenever they give food."
Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives beverages with a mind of loving-kindness, he constantly makes this vow:
"May all that I now give be shared together with all sentient beings;
by these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings enter the river of the Mahāyāna, drink the water of the eight flavors, swiftly tread the path of unsurpassed bodhi, and depart from..."
May the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, who have exhausted their thirsting yearning for the unsurpassed Buddha-vehicle,
sever the thirst of afflictions and thirst for the flavor of the Dharma; may they leave behind the craving for birth and death, delight in the Mahāyāna and the Great Parinirvāṇa,
be fully endowed with the Dharmakāya, attain all samādhis, enter the great ocean of profound wisdom, and may all sentient beings obtain the nectar-flavor of Bodhi.
May all sentient beings be fully endowed with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of such flavors of the supramundane, desireless tranquility.
Having attained these flavors of the Dharma, may they perceive the Buddha-nature; having perceived the Buddha-nature, may they be able to rain down the rain of the Dharma;
and having rained down the rain of the Dharma, may the Buddha-nature pervade everywhere like space, further enabling immeasurable other sentient beings to attain it as well.
The flavor of the Dharma refers to that of the Mahāyāna, which is not the flavor of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
May all sentient beings obtain this single sweet flavor, free from the six kinds of differentiated flavors.

May all sentient beings seek only the flavor of the Dharma—the flavor practiced within the unobstructed Buddha-dharmas—and not seek any other flavors. Good son, regarding the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s [practice] of loving-kindness...
When giving the gift of drink with a mind of compassion, one should firmly make such vows as these.
Furthermore, son of good family, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives vehicles from a mind of loving-kindness, they should always make this vow:
"May all that I now give be shared in common with all sentient beings; by means of these causes and conditions, may I cause them all universally..."
Sentient beings are born into the Great Vehicle, abide in the Great Vehicle, do not regress from the vehicle, do not waver from the vehicle, possess the vehicle of the diamond throne,
do not seek the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, are oriented toward the Buddha-vehicle, possess a vehicle that cannot be overcome,

a vehicle free from weakness or exhaustion, a vehicle that does not fall back or sink, the unsurpassed vehicle, the vehicle of the ten powers, the vehicle of great merit, and the unprecedented vehicle.
"Rare is this vehicle, difficult to obtain is this vehicle, boundless is this vehicle; it is the knowledge of all vehicles.
Son of good family, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a carriage from a heart of loving-kindness, they should always firmly make such a vow."
Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives clothing from a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he constantly makes this vow:

"May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings; by these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings obtain the garment of shame and modesty (*hrī-apatrāpya*) to cover their bodies within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), tearing away the garments of false views, such that their clothing remains one foot [one *vitasti*] away from their bodies."
With six inches [of growth], one attains a golden body; all sensations it receives are soft and unimpeded, its radiance and color are lustrous, and its skin is fine and supple.
It possesses immeasurable constant light and is free from form.
May all sentient beings universally attain this formless body, transcend all forms, and enter the formless Great Parinirvāṇa. Good son, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
When a Bodhisattva gives clothing, they should make a firm vow in this manner.

Regarding the fourth gift of clothing, "at a distance of one chi and six cun from the body": first, according to the principle, it means tearing the garment of all views to eliminate the sixteen types of false knowledge and views;
second, according to the literal fact, it means four cun on each side, which constitutes one chi and six cun.

Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices loving-kindness by giving flowers, incense, ointments, powders, and various blended perfumes, they constantly make this vow: "May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings;
by these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings attain the Buddha-flower Samādhi and the seven factors of enlightenment."
May a wondrous garland be bound upon their heads and crowns; may all sentient beings have forms like the full moon, and whatever colors they behold, may these be most subtle and supreme.
May all sentient beings become of a single appearance, adorned with the hundred blessings. May all sentient beings, according to their wishes, perceive pleasing forms.
May all sentient beings constantly encounter virtuous friends, obtain unimpeded fragrances, and be free from all [defilements].
May all sentient beings be endowed with the unsurpassed, precious jewels of all roots of goodness;
may all sentient beings look upon one another with harmony and joy, free from sorrow and suffering, and fully equipped with all virtues so that they do not harbor anxiety for one another;

may all sentient beings be replete with the fragrance of the precepts; may all sentient beings uphold the unobstructed precepts, their fragrant scent pervading and filling the ten directions. May all...
May all sentient beings attain the firm precepts, the precepts free from regret, and the precepts of omniscience;

may they be entirely free from all broken precepts and fully attain the precept of non-precept, the unprecedented precept, the teacherless precept, the unconditioned precept, the stainless precept, the undefiled precept, the ultimate precept, the precept of finality, and the precept of equality;
and may they apply these to both good and evil alike, being without hatred or attachment, and wish for all sentient beings [to attain this].

May all sentient beings fully attain the unsurpassed precepts—the Mahāyāna precepts, not the precepts of the Hīnayāna—and may they be endowed with the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) just as it was accomplished by all the Buddhas.
May all sentient beings be thoroughly cultivated by generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. May all sentient beings achieve complete accomplishment.
The subtle and wondrous lotus of the Great Parinirvāṇa has its fragrance filling the ten directions.
I vow that all sentient beings shall purely partake of the supreme fragrant food of the Mahāyāna Great Parinirvāṇa;
just as bees gather from flowers taking only the scent and flavor, may all sentient beings fully achieve bodies perfumed by immeasurable merit. Good son, Bodhisattva...
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva offers flowers and incense from a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they should always firmly make such a vow.
Regarding the fifth offering of flowers and incense, it says: "That which is 'without precepts' is the precept of no-precepts;

it is not a matter of not receiving [the precepts], nor is it the non-attainment of having received them. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "The precept like space, the precept that has nothing upon which to rely. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* says: [The same].
It is said that there is no abiding in the precepts because one does not abide in the view of the precepts; therefore, it is called "unconditioned" (*avijñapti*) morality.

This unconditioned morality is neither form nor mind; it is the morality of this [precept] which does not create the cycle of birth and death or nirvana. The remaining three [precepts] are as explained in the text.
Furthermore, son of good family, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives beds and mats from a heart of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he constantly makes this vow:
"May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings;
by these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings obtain the beds upon which the God among Gods lies, obtain great wisdom, sit in the station of the four dhyānas, and lie down therein."
May Bodhisattvas never lie upon the beds of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
may all sentient beings obtain peaceful and blissful rest, leaving behind the bed of birth and death to achieve the lion’s reclining bed of Great Nirvāṇa.
May all sentient beings, having sat upon this bed, further manifest supernatural powers and the lion’s playful sport for the sake of other immeasurable sentient beings. May they... [all] attain this.
May all sentient beings dwell within this great palace of the Mahāyāna and expound the Buddha-nature for the sake of all beings.
May all sentient beings sit upon the unsurpassed couch and not be overcome by worldly dharmas.
May all sentient beings obtain the couch of patience and be free from the famine and hunger of birth and death. May all sentient beings obtain the couch of fearlessness and forever be liberated.
May all sentient beings obtain the bed of purity, being free from the enemy-thieves of all afflictions; may they single-mindedly seek the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
May all sentient beings obtain the bed of wholesome dharmas, always being protected by virtuous friends.
May all sentient beings obtain the bed of lying on the right side, relying upon and following the practices performed by all Buddhas, O noble son, Bodhisattva.
When a Mahāsattva gives beds and seats from a heart of loving-kindness, he should firmly make such a vow.
Furthermore, son of good family, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives houses and dwellings from a heart of loving-kindness, he constantly makes this wish:
"May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings; by means of these causes and conditions, may [all beings]..."

May all sentient beings dwell in the mansion of the Mahāyāna, practicing the conduct of spiritual friends, the practice of great compassion, the practice of the six *pāramitās*, the practice of great perfect enlightenment, and the path practiced by all bodhisattvas—a path that is boundless, vast, and like space.
May they vow that all sentient beings may attain right mindfulness and remain far removed from evil thoughts; may all sentient beings...
May they attain abiding in permanence, bliss, self, and purity, forever free from the four inversions; may all sentient beings fully receive and uphold the supramundane syllables;
may all sentient beings surely become supreme vessels for all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*);
may all sentient beings enter the nectar-like Dharma-abode; and may all sentient beings, throughout their initial, middle, and final moments of mind, always enter the Mahāyāna Nirvāṇa.
May all sentient beings, like the house of [the donor's] name, always dwell in the palaces inhabited by Bodhisattvas in future worlds.
Good son, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives a house from a heart of loving-kindness, they should always firmly make such a vow.
Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives lamps from a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they constantly make this vow:
"May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings;
by these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings possess immeasurable radiance and dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma. May all sentient beings always obtain illumination. May all...
May all sentient beings attain a subtle radiance of form that is foremost in brilliance. May all sentient beings have pure eyes, free from all veils and nets of affliction.

May all sentient beings obtain the great torch of wisdom, skillfully understanding the marks of non-self, the absence of a sentient being, the absence of a person, and the absence of a life-principle.
May all sentient beings behold the pure Buddha-nature, which is like empty space. May all...
May the fleshly eyes of sentient beings be purified so that they clearly see the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
May all sentient beings obtain the Buddha’s radiance to universally illumine the ten directions. May all sentient beings obtain unobstructed clarity and fully perceive the pure Buddha-nature.
May all sentient beings obtain the light of great wisdom to shatter all darkness, including that of the icchantikas. May all...
May all sentient beings attain immeasurable light that universally illumines the worlds of immeasurable Buddhas;

may they kindle the lamp of the Mahāyāna and abandon the torches of the two vehicles. May the light attained by all sentient beings extinguish the darkness of ignorance, surpassing the brilliance of a thousand suns.
May all sentient beings obtain the radiance of the fire-jewel, which completely extinguishes all [darkness] within the trichiliocosm.
In the midst of darkness, may all sentient beings be endowed with the five eyes and awaken to the characteristics of all phenomena, attaining untaught enlightenment.

May all sentient beings be free from views and ignorance. May all sentient beings fully attain the subtle and wondrous light of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, which reveals and awakens sentient beings to their true Buddha-nature. Good son, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in loving-kindness...
When offering lamps within the mind, one should always firmly make such a vow:

"O Son of Good Family, all Śrāvakas [are based upon] the second [vehicle], which is the root of the three vehicles; furthermore, regarding the three [vehicles]: first, the three vehicles are clarified;
next, all dharmas [are clarified]; third, this chapter concludes by using compassion to encompass all dharmas, such that there is no dharma that is not [so encompassed]."
The meaning of non-partial and perfect compassion becomes even more evident;
furthermore, the root of goodness is precisely altruism, and within altruism, compassion is supreme. The initial passage refers to the three vehicles.
Good son, all the roots of goodness belonging to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all Tathāgatas have compassion as their root.
This concludes the second section, in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enumerates all dharmas individually.
Good son, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they are able to give rise to such immeasurable roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*),

namely: the impurity of inhalation and exhalation, impermanence and arising-and-ceasing, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*), the three contemplations,

the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the contemplation of impermanence and so forth, the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*), the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), and the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

The Path, the cultivation of the Path, the right efforts (*samyak-pradhāna*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhi-pāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the eightfold path, the four dhyānas,

the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇā*),

the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), the knowledge of the beginningless limit of existence (*pūrvāntajñāna*), the knowledge of the śrāvakas, the knowledge of the pratyekabuddhas, and the knowledge of the bodhisattvas.
Sajñā-buddhajñāna, son of good family, for such dharmas as these, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the root.

Impurity (*aśubhā*) and mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*) are the two gates of ambrosia (*amṛtadvāra*). Regarding the seven expedient means (*saptopāya*), the masters of calculation say:

first, impurity; second, specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); third, general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); fourth, warmth (*uṣmagata*); fifth, the summit (*mūrdhan*); sixth, patience (*kṣānti*); and seventh, the supreme worldly dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
The Master of Treatises says: first, the suffering of form; second, the origin of form; third, the cessation of form; fourth, the path regarding form; fifth, the fault of form;

sixth, the gratification of form; seventh, the escape from form. As for the three objects of contemplation, they refer to suffering, impermanence, and non-self—these being the designations of the Hīnayāna.

In the Mahāyāna, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, taking suffering, karma, and afflictions as the three objects of contemplation. Furthermore, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (The Jewel Garland)... [text continues].

The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* clarifies the three contemplations: the contemplation of the two truths, the contemplation of equality, and the contemplation of the supreme meaning of the Middle Way (and so forth).

Regarding "non-contention," there are three interpretations: first, that non-contention arises because the mind of loving-kindness is perfected; second, that non-contention arises because the realization of emptiness is clear;

and third, that non-contention with all things arises through the awakening-illumination of the mind in accordance with reality. Regarding "knowledge of the original limit" (*mūlānta-jñāna*), there are two interpretations.
First, because the realization of emptiness is the primordial limit (*pūrvānta*), Ājñātakauṇḍinya is named "He Who Has Realized the Primordial Limit.
Second, by means of the knowledge of limits, taking mastery over the extension and brevity [of time] as the knowledge of the primordial limit.
Based on this meaning, the third section below provides a summary:
"Good son, for this reason, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is real and not false. If someone asks, 'Who is the root of all wholesome dharmas?
one should say it is loving-kindness. For this reason, it is real and not false."
"Good son, those who are able to perform good deeds"—this is the fourth reality, pervasiveness (*vyāpti*). This means that all virtues are also pervasive throughout all wholesome dharmas.

Herein, the manifestation of the perfect and compassionate transformation is further clarified in two parts: first, clarifying that it is identical to the various virtues of the Mahāyāna in fifteen phrases;
second, clarifying that it is identical to the various virtues of the Hīnayāna in sixteen phrases.
Noble son, one who is able to perform what is wholesome is called one of true reflection; one of true reflection is precisely what is called compassion (*maitrī*);
compassion is the Tathāgata; compassion is the Mahāyāna; the Mahāyāna is compassion; compassion is the Tathāgata. Noble son, compassion is the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*);
the path to enlightenment is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is compassion. Noble son, compassion is Great Brahmā (*mahābrahman*).
Mahābrahmā is precisely loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and loving-kindness is precisely the Tathāgata. Good son, loving-kindness is able to act as father and mother for all sentient beings;
father and mother are precisely loving-kindness, and loving-kindness is precisely the Tathāgata.
Good son, loving-kindness is the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas; that inconceivable realm of the Buddhas is precisely loving-kindness. You should know this.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the Tathāgata, O son of good family; loving-kindness is the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) of sentient beings.
Because this Buddha-nature has long been shrouded and obscured by afflictions (*kleśa*), it causes sentient beings not to perceive the Buddha-nature.
Loving-kindness is itself the Tathāgata. Son of good family, loving-kindness is the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*); the Great Emptiness is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.
Good son, compassion is space, and space is compassion; compassion is the Tathāgata.
Good son, compassion is permanence, and permanence is the Dharma; the Dharma is the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is compassion; compassion is the Tathāgata.
Good son, compassion is bliss, and bliss is the Dharma; the Dharma is the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is compassion; compassion is the Tathāgata.
Come, son of good family! Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is purity; purity is the Dharma; the Dharma is the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Tathāgata. Son of good family, loving-kindness is myself; I am the Dharma; the Dharma is the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Tathāgata. Son of good family, loving-kindness is the nectar (*amṛta*); the nectar is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is...
Buddha-nature is the Buddha; the Dharma is the Sangha; the Sangha is compassion; and compassion is the Tathāgata.
Good son, compassion is the unsurpassed path of all Bodhisattvas; the path is compassion, and compassion is the Tathāgata.
Good son, compassion is the immeasurable realm of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; that immeasurable realm is [compassion].
This is precisely loving-kindness (*maitrī*). One should know that this loving-kindness is itself the Tathāgata.
In the first fifteen sentences, each phrase concludes by identifying it as the loving-kindness of the Tathāgata.
From the point "If loving-kindness were impermanent" onwards, this is the second section, which universally encompasses the wholesome dharmas of the Hīnayāna.
"Good son, if compassion is impermanent, then impermanence is itself compassion; you should know that such compassion is the compassion of a śrāvaka.
Good son, if compassion is suffering, then suffering is itself compassion; you should know that such compassion is the compassion of a śrāvaka.
Good son, if compassion is impure, then impurity is itself compassion; you should know that such compassion is the compassion of a śrāvaka. Good son.

If loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is without self (*anātman*), then that which is without self is loving-kindness; one should know that such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of a *śrāvaka*, O virtuous son.

If loving-kindness is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then that which is conceptual construction is loving-kindness; one should know that such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of a *śrāvaka*, O virtuous son.

If loving-kindness is not named the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), then it is not the giving of giving; one should know that such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of a *śrāvaka*, and so forth.
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this. Good son, if compassion cannot benefit sentient beings, such compassion is the compassion of a śrāvaka.
Good son, if compassion does not enter the Way of the Single Characteristic, you should know that such compassion is the compassion of a śrāvaka.
Good son, if compassion cannot awaken to and comprehend all dharmas, you should know...
This is the compassion of the śrāvaka; good son, this is the compassion of the śrāvaka. If one cannot perceive the Tathāgata-nature, know that this compassion is the compassion of the śrāvaka;
good son, this is the compassion of the śrāvaka. If one perceives all phenomena as having substantial existence, know that this compassion is the compassion of the śrāvaka;
good son, this is the compassion of the śrāvaka. If it is tainted (*sāsrava*), compassionate love that is tainted is the compassion of the śrāvaka.
Good man, if compassion is conditioned, it is the compassion of a śrāvaka.
Good man, if compassion cannot abide in the first stage and is not the compassion of the first stage, you should know that this is the compassion of a śrāvaka.
Good man, if compassion cannot attain the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of a Buddha, you should know that this compassion is the compassion of a śrāvaka.
Good son, if one is able to attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya through this loving-kindness, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvaka.
Furthermore, in each of the sixteen phrases, at the conclusion of every phrase, it is concluded that this is the loving-kindness of the śrāvaka.

Good son, regarding the presence or absence of compassion, the fifth section clarifies that reality is truly inconceivable. Furthermore, there are four parts: first, praising the essence of great compassion;
second, praising those who practice compassion; third, praising the teaching that explains compassion, namely the Great Nirvāṇa;
and fourth, praising the master who expounds compassion. First, the praise of the essence of compassion.
Good son, if compassion is neither existent nor non-existent, neither being nor not being, such compassion cannot be conceived by śrāvakas,
pratyekabuddhas, or others. Good son, if compassion is inconceivable, the Dharma is inconceivable,
the Buddha-nature is inconceivable, and the Tathāgata is likewise inconceivable.

There have been three traditional interpretations: first, it is said that for sentient beings there is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), for dharmas there is the object-condition, and for the non-object-condition (*anālambana-pratyaya*) there is neither existence nor non-existence;

second, it is said that from the first to the third bhūmi it is "non-existent" because the mind of emptiness predominates, while from the fourth to the seventh bhūmi it is "existent" because the mind of form predominates, and from the eighth to the tenth bhūmi it is both existent and non-existent because one contemplates them simultaneously; third, [it is said that]... (the text continues).

Regarding the claim that "neither existent nor non-existent" refers to the same principle: it is said to be "existent" because the wondrous existence of the Buddha-fruit is based upon it; it is "non-existent" because the realm of birth-and-death is based upon it;

and it is "neither existent nor non-existent" because the profound truth is based upon it. Now, this [position] is incorrect. If it relies on the dharmas of the five aggregates, how can it be non-existent?
If it were non-existent, it would immediately enter into the Truth (tattva). Since it does not enter into the Truth, how can it be non-existent?
Furthermore, if it were non-existent, how would it differ from the absence of an object of cognition? Moreover, from the first stage to the third stage, could it be exclusively empty?

And if it were neither existent nor non-existent, would that necessarily be the Buddha-stage? The present passage praises those who practice loving-kindness; indeed, all who practice loving-kindness possess this "double negation" (*ubhayānta-vinirmukta*), and it is not restricted solely to the Buddhas.
This is precisely what clarifies the intended meaning within the context of the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*). If one takes purity as the object of cognition...

Purity is non-existence when conditioned by impurity; purity is existence when conditioned by that which is neither pure nor impure; and that which is neither pure nor impure is neither existent nor non-existent.

These are not simultaneous, nor are they distinct. Furthermore, regarding the three truths: because it conditions the Truth of Reality (*tattva-satya*), it is non-existent; because it conditions the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is existent;

and because it conditions the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), it is neither existent nor non-existent. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions are themselves emptiness."
Question: If "provisionality" (jia) has the meaning of the Middle Way, why are the four alternatives (catuskoṭi) described as conceptual proliferation (prapañca)? Answer:
The four alternatives regarding a fixed nature (svabhāva) are indeed conceptual proliferation; however, the four alternatives as mere designations (prajñapti) are not conceptual proliferation.
The Bodhisattva abides in the second lower stage, praising those who practice loving-kindness.
Good son, although the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa cultivates such loving-kindness,
even while in the midst of sleep he does not truly sleep, because he exerts himself with diligent vigor and remains constantly awake.

Furthermore, because there is no sleep, there is no awakening; thus, even though the devas protect one during sleep, there is no one who protects, for since one does not commit evil, one has no bad dreams while sleeping.

Being free from unwholesomeness and having abandoned sleep, even after the end of life, although one is born in the Brahma Heaven, there is no place of birth, for one has attained mastery. Good son, one who cultivates loving-kindness is able to...
One attains the accomplishment of such immeasurable and boundless merits.
This is the third section of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which extols the teaching of compassion.
Noble son, this subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* can also accomplish such immeasurable and boundless [merits].
Regarding the merit of the extremes:
this fourth section below praises the Lord of Loving-kindness.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have likewise attained and accomplished such immeasurable and boundless merit.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha with this third response, which follows up on the second hypothetical objection raised previously;
since compassion, if it were real, ought to bring benefit, he restates the question and requests an answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all the contemplations of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are entirely real, whereas those of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not.
For what reason do all sentient beings not equally receive happiness through the majestic power of the Bodhisattvas?
If sentient beings truly do not obtain happiness, one should know that this is because of what the Bodhisattvas have cultivated."
If a compassionate mind is of no benefit, then one faces the difficulty of being unable to advance or retreat; it is difficult to truly practice compassion.

If a Buddha were to truly practice [compassion], why would sentient beings not receive the benefit of that compassion? If compassion cannot bestow benefit upon sentient beings, then what is the use of compassion?

[This would be] useless. The answer further has three parts: first, clarifying that there is indeed benefit; second, citing examples to provide proof; third, concluding with praise for its inconceivability.
The first part also has three sections: first, proclaiming that there is benefit; next, from "Good son" onwards, explaining the benefit; third, from "For this reason" onwards...
The initial summary of the benefits is as in the text.
The Buddha said: "Good son, the compassion of a bodhisattva is not without benefit.
Next, the benefits are explained.
Good son, there are sentient beings who must necessarily undergo suffering and those who do not.
If there are sentient beings who must necessarily undergo suffering—such as the icchantikas—the bodhisattva’s compassion is of no benefit to them.
However, if the suffering they undergo is not predetermined, the bodhisattva’s compassion is beneficial, causing those sentient beings to experience complete happiness and well-being.
Good son, it is like a person who, seeing from afar a lion, tiger, leopard, jackal, wolf, rākṣasa, or ghost, naturally gives rise to fear;
or one walking at night who, seeing a pillar, likewise gives rise to fear.
Good son, in this same way, when sentient beings see one who practices loving-kindness, they naturally experience happiness.
If determinate karma does not shift, one will not obtain benefit; if it is indeterminate karma, then one obtains benefit.

Even if it is determinate karma, for one who cultivates goodness, it becomes indeterminate again. For example, if one’s lifespan is fixed at eighty years and cannot be shifted, yet through the power of compassion one avoids untimely death in the interim—how can this be determinate karma?
It is like the initial arousal of the intent to kill, which gives rise to heavy poison.
When one commits an act of killing, if at the time of the act or after the killing a sense of exhilaration and a mind of malice arise together, this karma becomes fixed;

thus, it cannot bestow happiness. If the karma were not fixed, compassion (*maitrī*) would be able to bestow happiness. Question: Since the karma itself is not fixed, it should naturally result in happiness;

why then is it necessary for compassion to bestow it? Answer: Although the karma is not fixed, it may sometimes turn into a fixed state. If one receives the benefit of compassion, [the karma] may be transformed.
The fact that heavy objects cause tigers, leopards, and the like to naturally feel fear is a metaphor for how people feel joy upon seeing one who practices loving-kindness.
Noble son, for this reason, when a bodhisattva cultivates loving-kindness, it is a genuine contemplation and is not without benefit.
"Good son, I say that this loving-kindness has immeasurable doors; this is the second instance cited as proof.
Good son, I say that this loving-kindness has immeasurable doors, namely the supernormal powers (abhijñā).
Good son, for example, when Devadatta instructed Ajātaśatru to harm the Tathāgata, at that time I entered the great city of Rājagṛha in due order."
Bhikṣu, King Ajātaśatru immediately released the mad and intoxicated elephant Dhana-pāla, intending to harm me and my disciples.
At that time, the elephant trampled and killed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings; after these beings had died, there was much blood and stench.
Having smelled this, the elephant became even more crazed and intoxicated than before, and seeing my attendants clad in red garments, he cried out:
Seeing this blood, my disciples who had not yet abandoned desire fled in all directions, with the sole exception of Ānanda.
At that time, all the people in the city of Rājagṛha simultaneously raised their voices in wailing and weeping, saying:
"How strange! Today the Tathāgata has passed away; how can the Perfectly Awakened One suddenly be destroyed?"
At that time, Devadatta’s heart was filled with joy, thinking: "It is most excellent that the Śramaṇa Gautama has passed away;
from this day forward, he will truly no longer appear. How wonderful! This plan of mine has been fulfilled as I wished.

O son of good family, at that time, desiring to subdue the elephant Dhanapāla, I immediately entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and extended my hand to show it to him; thus, the five fingers appeared.
When the elephant saw the five lions, its heart was struck with terror; it voided both excrement and urine and threw its entire body to the ground to pay homage at my feet.

Good son, at that time, there were truly no lions upon my fingers; rather, it was through the power of the roots of goodness cultivated by my practice of loving-kindness that I caused him to be tamed.

In general, eight matters are set forth through the compassionate exercise of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to teach sentient beings. Regarding the first matter, the text states: "As for what is called 'this blood,' there are three interpretations. First, this refers to the period twelve years prior [to the establishment of the Vinaya], when the dyeing of robes in altered colors (*kāṣāya*) had not yet been prescribed; thus, they wore exclusively red. Second, it refers to the differences among the five schools: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) mentions three types of mixed dots on a single robe, while the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* [mention different methods]. Third, it refers to the various ways of mixing colors according to the specific circumstances of the time. These are the three interpretations. Furthermore, regarding the second matter, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with local customs. This means that because the color of the *kaṣāya* was not yet fixed, one should wear it in accordance with the local customs of the region where one resides. Third, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the country. This means that if one travels to another land, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that country. Fourth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the village. This means that if one enters a village, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that village. Fifth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the household. This means that if one enters a household, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that household. Sixth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the monastery. This means that if one stays within a monastery, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that monastery. Seventh, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the assembly. This means that if one attends an assembly, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that assembly. Eighth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the occasion. This means that if one encounters a specific occasion, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that occasion. These are the eight matters. Furthermore, regarding the third matter, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the region. This means that if one travels to a different region, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that region. Fourth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the country. This means that if one travels to a different country, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that country. Fifth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the village. This means that if one enters a village, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that village. Sixth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the household. This means that if one enters a household, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that household. Seventh, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the monastery. This means that if one stays within a monastery, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that monastery. Eighth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the assembly. This means that if one attends an assembly, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that assembly. Ninth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the occasion. This means that if one encounters a specific occasion, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that occasion. Tenth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the region. This means that if one travels to a different region, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that region. Eleventh, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the country. This means that if one travels to a different country, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that country. Twelfth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the village. This means that if one enters a village, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that village. Thirteenth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the household. This means that if one enters a household, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that household. Fourteenth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the monastery. This means that if one stays within a monastery, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that monastery. Fifteenth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the assembly. This means that if one attends an assembly, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that assembly. Sixteenth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the occasion. This means that if one encounters a specific occasion, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that occasion. Seventeenth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the region. This means that if one travels to a different region, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that region. Eighteenth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the country. This means that if one travels to a different country, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that country. Nineteenth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the village. This means that if one enters a village, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that village. Twentieth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the household. This means that if one enters a household, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that household. Twenty-first, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the monastery. This means that if one stays within a monastery, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that monastery. Twenty-second, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the assembly. This means that if one attends an assembly, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that assembly. Twenty-third, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of the occasion. This means that if one encounters a specific occasion, one should wear the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the local customs of that occasion. Twenty-fourth, the text says: "The Buddha permitted the wearing of the *kaṣāya* in accordance with the
The three follow into one: namely, blue, mud-color (mṛdā-varṇa), and maulana; and maulana is the color red.
Regarding these three colors for robes, a single robe may be marked with these three colors in spots the size of soybeans.
Although the disciples all wear robes marked in this way, even though the spots are small, they still appear red when viewed from afar.
Next, five matters may be seen.

Furthermore, son of good family, when I was about to enter parinirvāṇa and first set out toward the city of Kuśinagara, there were five hundred strongmen on the road who were leveling, clearing, and sprinkling it. Among them was a stone that they all wished to lift and move.
When they were unable [to move it], I felt compassion and immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness.

Those strongmen then saw me lift this great stone with my big toe and cast it into the air; I caught it again with my hand, placed it upon my right palm, blew upon it to reduce it to fine dust, and then reassembled it.
Thus, I caused the arrogant minds of those strongmen to subside and briefly explained the various [vehicles] to them.
One must cause all beings to simultaneously resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Good son, at that time the Tathāgata did not actually lift this great stone into the air with his finger and place it upon his right palm; rather, he blew upon it to shatter it into fine dust, which then recombined as it was before.
Good son, you should know that this was due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness (*maitrī-kuśala-mūla-bala*).
When the Mallas saw these things, [they were amazed].
Furthermore, son of good family, in this southern region of India there is a great city named Śobhāvatī.
In that city there was an elder named Rudrāyaṇa, who was a leader of the multitude and had already served under immeasurable Buddhas in the past.
"O son of good family, regarding the roots of goodness planted therein:
in that great city, all the people believed in and followed false paths, serving the Nirgranthas.
At that time, wishing to deliver that elder, I traveled from Rājagṛha to that city—a distance of sixty-five *yojanas*—walking on foot with the great assembly, desiring to transform them."
For the sake of delivering those people, when the Nirgranthas heard that I intended to go to that city, they immediately thought:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama arrives here, these people will surely abandon us and no longer provide for us; how shall we, now impoverished and distressed, continue to survive?
Thereupon, the various Nirgrantha followers dispersed and informed the people of that city: "The śramaṇa Gautama..."
"Today Gautama wishes to come here; however, these śramaṇas abandon their parents to roam about in all directions.

Wherever they go, they cause the five grains to fail to ripen in that land, leading to widespread famine and death among the people, with those who are sickly and emaciated following one after another, beyond all means of rescue or relief.
Gautama is a rogue who leads only evil rākṣasas and spirits as his attendants."
Having approached one who is fatherless, motherless, solitary, and destitute to seek instruction and become his disciple, he was taught only that which concerns empty space;

wherever he went, there was no peace or happiness. Upon hearing this, the man immediately became filled with fear, prostrated himself at the feet of the Nirgrantha-putra, and said: "O Great Master, what should we do now?"
The Nirgrantha replied, "The Śramaṇa Gautama is by nature fond of groves, flowing springs, and clear waters;

whatever such things exist outside [the city], you should destroy them. You may all go out together from the city to cut down the forest trees so that none remain, and fill the flowing springs, wells, and ponds with foul filth.
Firmly close the city gates, and each of you, being well-armed, shall defend the walls."
"Guard yourselves with diligence and hold your own; let no one who comes forward gain entrance.
If they do not advance, you shall remain in safety, and we too shall employ various stratagems to cause that Gautama to turn back along the way.
When those people heard these words, they respectfully put them into practice: they cut down trees, defiled the waters, and prepared their vessels.
Armed with firm self-protection, O son of good family, at that time when I arrived at that city, I saw no trees or groves at all;
I saw only people guarding their walls with various adorned weapons.
Having seen this, I immediately gave rise to compassion and a mind of loving-kindness toward them; all the trees grew back as they were before and continued to flourish further.
The remaining trees were beyond measure or calculation; its rivers, ponds, wells, and springs were filled with pure water like blue lapis lazuli.

Various kinds of flowers grew there, completely covering the surface. Its city walls were transformed into walls of deep-blue lapis lazuli, through which the people within could see me and the great assembly clearly.
The gates opened of their own accord, and none could restrain them.
The weapons with which they were armed were transformed into various flowers; the elder Lu-zhi was their leader, and together with his people, he followed me to where I was.
I immediately preached various essential teachings for them, causing all those people to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Good son, at that time...
At that time, I did not actually manifest various kinds of trees, pure flowing waters filling the rivers and ponds,
nor transform their original city into deep-blue lapis lazuli so that the people could see my body through it, open the city gates, and turn their weapons into flowers. Good son,
you should know that all these things were made possible by the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which enabled those people to see such phenomena.
Furthermore, son of good family, there was a Brahmin woman in the city of Śrāvastī named Vāsiṣṭhī who had an only son whom she loved exceedingly.
When he fell ill and passed away, the woman was so consumed by grief that her mind became deranged and she lost her senses.
She wandered naked and shameless through the crossroads, wailing until her voice failed, crying out: "Son! Son! Where are you?"
She traveled through cities and towns without ceasing; yet this woman had already planted many roots of virtue under previous Buddhas.
Son of good family, I then gave rise to a heart of compassion for this woman. At that moment, the woman was able to see me and conceived the thought that I was her son;
she regained her original mind and embraced my body as one would a beloved child. I then spoke to her:
“Attendant Ānanda, you may take this robe and give it to this woman. Once the robe had been given, he then expounded for her various essential points of the Dharma.
Upon hearing the Dharma, the woman was filled with joy and exultation, and she resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Good son, at that time, I was truly not her son, nor was she my mother; furthermore, there was no [such relationship].”
"Good son, you should know that it was all through the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness that caused that woman to see such things.
Furthermore, good son, in the city of Vārāṇasī there was an upāsikā named Mahāśraddhā."
Having planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas of the past, this upāsikā invited the Saṃgha for the ninety-day summer retreat and offered them medicine.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu among the assembly who was afflicted with a grave illness;
a skilled physician examined him and declared that he required meat as medicine. If he could obtain meat, his illness would be cured; if he could not obtain meat, [it would not].
When the physician announced that the life could not be preserved, the upāsikā immediately took gold and went throughout the marketplace, crying out these words:
"Who has meat for sale? I wish to buy it. If anyone has meat, they shall receive gold as payment.
She searched every corner of the city but was unable to obtain any. Thereupon, the upāsikā took a knife herself and cut the flesh from her own thigh.
She made a soup by adding various fragrances and gave it to a sick bhikṣu; once the bhikṣu had consumed it, his illness was immediately cured.
At that time, this upāsikā suffered from a painful ulcer and, unable to endure the agony, cried out:
"Namo Buddhāya! Namo Buddhāya! I was then in Śrāvastī and heard her voice. Regarding that woman—
Giving rise to a heart of great compassion, that woman soon saw me taking excellent medicine and applying it to her wound, whereupon she was restored to her original state.
I then preached various sublime Dharmas to her; hearing the Dharma, she rejoiced and resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Good son, at that time, I did not actually go to the city of Vārāṇasī to bring the medicine."
