"Good son, you should know that the anointing of that upāsikā’s body was entirely due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness,
which caused that woman to see such things. Furthermore, good son,
because the evil man Devadatta was greedy and lacked contentment, he consumed much ghee, and consequently suffered from headaches and abdominal pain."
Experiencing great suffering and unable to endure it, he uttered these words: "Namo Buddhāya! Namo Buddhāya!
At that time, I was staying in the city of Ujjayinī; hearing his voice, I immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
Thereupon, Devadatta soon saw me; I went to his side, rubbed his head and belly with my hands, and gave him salted broth to drink.
Once his injuries had healed, I said, "Good son, I did not actually go to Devadatta's place to stroke his head and belly or give him medicine to drink.
Good son, you should know that it was entirely through the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness that Devadatta perceived such things."
Furthermore, son of good family, in the kingdom of Kośala there was a band of five hundred thieves whose plundering and violence were exceedingly great.
King Prasenajit, distressed by their lawlessness, dispatched troops to pursue and capture them;
having apprehended them, he gouged out their eyes and banished them to a dark thicket of forest. These thieves had already planted many roots of virtue under previous Buddhas.
Having already lost their eyes, they suffered great anguish and each cried out: "Namo Buddhāya! Namo Buddhāya!
We now have no protector! As they wailed and lamented, I was staying at the Jetavana Monastery;
hearing their voices, I immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*). At that time, a cool breeze blew from Mount Gandhamādana, carrying various fragrances.
Medicine filled his eye sockets, and he immediately regained his sight, no different from how it was before.
When the bandits opened their eyes, they saw the Tathāgata standing before them, preaching the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, the bandits conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Good son, at that time, I did not actually blow wind upon Mount Gandhamādana."

Various fragrant medicines stood before that person and preached the Dharma for them. Good son, you should know that it was all through the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion that caused those bandits to see such things.
Regarding the first part of the seventh matter, concerning "Kosala and Śrāvastī," some say these are alternative names for the same country, while others say that Kosala was a vassal state;
because there were bandits in that country, the King of Persia dispatched troops.
Furthermore, son of good family, because of his folly, Prince Vaidūrya deposed his father the king and established himself as ruler.
Recalling their former enmity, he harmed many members of the Śākya clan;

he took twelve thousand Śākya maidens, mutilated them by cutting off their ears and noses and severing their hands and feet, and cast them into pits. At that time, those women, suffering physical torment, spoke thus:
"Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Buddha! they cried out, wailing loudly as they said, "We now have no protector.
At that time, these women had already planted various roots of goodness under previous Buddhas.
While I was in the Bamboo Grove, I heard their voices and immediately gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness. Then, O women, you saw me arrive at Kapilavastu.

I washed their wounds with water and applied medicinal ointments, so that their suffering and illness were immediately removed; their ears, noses, hands, and feet were restored to their original state.
At that time, I briefly expounded the essential points of the Dharma for them, causing them all to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They then went to the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī and, according to the Dharma, left the household life and received full ordination.
"Good son, at that time the Tathāgata did not actually go to the city of Kapilavastu to wash the wound with water or apply medicinal ointment to stop the pain.
Good son, you should know that all this was due to the power of the roots of goodness of his loving-kindness (*maitrī-kuśalamūla-bala*), which caused that woman to see such things;
her feelings of sorrow and joy were likewise so. Good son, for this reason, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva..."
The cultivation of loving-kindness by a Bodhisattva through contemplation is itself reality and is not false.
Good son, this concludes the third section of praise.
Good son, as for "immeasurable," it is inconceivable; the conduct of Bodhisattvas is inconceivable. All...
The conduct of the Buddha is inconceivable, and this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise inconceivable.
That which is immeasurable is inconceivable; this is a general praise of the inconceivable conduct of the Bodhisattvas.
The sequential praise of the compassion practiced by all Buddhas is itself a praise of perfect compassion; that this is a Mahāyāna scripture is itself a praise of the teaching.
All are inconceivable, converging in a single perfection where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases—unspeakable and immeasurable.

The second fascicle begins, clarifying the fruits of the four minds, which is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying the fruit of the three minds as the stage of ultimate love;
second, clarifying the fruit of the mind of equanimity as the stage of empty equality. Regarding the former, there are two interpretations:

the first states that while the three minds are not yet perfected, they share a single fruit, but once one mind is perfected, it alone attains its own fruit; the second states that all three minds are equally existent.

The arguments that because they are "active" (*saṃskāra*) they share one fruit, or that while three minds act together they obtain one fruit while a single mind acts alone and obtains one fruit, are all untenable.

Furthermore, before the three minds have been established, how can there be the attainment of a fruit? Moreover, if four minds equally take sentient beings as their object, equally take dharmas as their object, equally possess "activity" (*saṃskāra*), or equally take the "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object and thus equally lack activity—since both existence and non-existence are the same, the three and the one should be equal. Now...

Furthermore, regarding the provisional distinction between the Separate (Byō) and Perfect (En) teachings: in the Separate teaching, the three minds of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are conjoined with attachment;
therefore, they are established as having a single fruit. Because the mind of equanimity supports emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it alone has a single fruit.

As for the Perfect teaching, the "one compassion" explained above is itself pity, joy, and equanimity. This perfect compassion is pervasive throughout all phenomena, encompassing every dharma without exception.

How could the fruit be separate? This is merely a matter of textual abbreviation, and it is also presented through mutual implication (as explained at length). Regarding the text of the *Ekabuddhabhūmi*, there are two parts: first, clarifying the fruit of the stage (*bhūmi-phala*);
second, the discussion of its meaning. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, stating the topical outline (*uddāna*); second, providing the explanation.
Furthermore, son of good family, once the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has cultivated loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy, he dwells in the stage of "Extreme Affection for an Only Son.
Regarding the first passage, the old commentary states: (1) it is the Stage of Nature (*gotrabhūmi*); (2) it is the eighth stage and above; (3) it is the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). Now...

To clarify that this is not so: first, it was clarified that "sage-conduct" (*ārya-caryā*) refers to one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), and it was stated that this occurs at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).

Now, it is clarified that "Brahma-conduct" (*brahma-caryā*) refers to transforming others (*parārtha*). Since one has already entered the first stage through one's own practice, how could transforming others be restricted merely to the stage of nature (*gotra-bhūmi*)?
How could it possibly skip ahead to the eighth stage or above? All such [interpretations] are either excessive or deficient; they are precisely [the errors of] the initial [stage].
The ground realizes the fruit of transforming others.
How is it that this ground is explained as having previously set forth these two chapters?
Noble son, why is this ground called "Supreme Love" and also named "Only Son"?
This means that although one loves an only son extremely, because it is "extremely loved" and because it is an "only son," these two aspects should not be distinct.
Yet, we now differentiate them: "extreme love" pertains to the mind, while "only son" pertains to the object. Since the son is not part of my internal self, he is called an "external object."
Next, in the explanation, five analogies are presented in total: the first analogy explains "extreme love," while the four subsequent analogies explain "the attachment to an only son.
The judgment is clear and distinct. First, as the text states:
"Good son, for example, when parents see their child safe and sound, their hearts are filled with great joy; so it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."
Abiding in this stage is likewise so: one regards all sentient beings as equal to an only child, and seeing those who cultivate goodness, one gives rise to great joy;
therefore, this stage is named "Supreme Affection" (Sudurjayā).
For example, it is like parents [who feel distress upon seeing their child fall ill]. Second, the Bodhisattva sees ordinary beings giving rise to evil causes and thus gives birth to compassion.
Good son, for example, when parents see their child encounter illness, their hearts give rise to suffering and affliction; they pity them with a sorrowful and bitter anguish. First...
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Aparityāga (Non-Abandonment) likewise dwells in this stage;

seeing all sentient beings tormented by the diseases of afflictions, his mind gives rise to sorrow, distress, and anxious concern as if they were his own son, and blood flows from every pore of his body.
For this reason, this stage is named "Only-Son."
It is like a person in their childhood who develops attachment while learning;
O son of good family, it is as if a person in their childhood were to pick up clods of earth, filthy objects, tiles, stones, dry bones, or wooden branches and place them in their mouth.
When their parents see this, fearing it will cause them harm, they grasp the child’s head with their left hand and pry the object out with their right hand. This Bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in this stage is likewise;

seeing sentient beings whose Dharma-body has not yet increased, or who perform unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, the Bodhisattva perceives them and uses the hand of wisdom to pull them out, desiring not to let them wander in birth and death or undergo various sufferings. For this reason, this stage is further named "The Only Son."
The clods of earth and so forth are metaphors for the five aggregates; the subsequent passage correlates them by stating that the body, speech, and mind constitute the karma.

The left side is a metaphor for real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), and the right side is a metaphor for expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Furthermore, the left side represents meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the right side represents wisdom (*prajñā*). Seizing the head to save the body is not like gouging out the eyes to save the mouth from its faults.

For example, it is like parents [who, as explained in the fourth section below, experience the fruit of suffering because sentient beings have evoked it, and thus it is said they are born together in hell].
Good son, it is like a beloved child of parents who dies after being abandoned; the parents are filled with grief and affliction, and they pray—
It is the same for me as it is for the Bodhisattva Samprajanya: when I see an icchantika falling into hell, I vow to be born together with them in that very hell.

Why is this? If, while suffering there, that icchantika should give rise to even a single thought of repentance, I shall immediately preach various teachings for them so that they may produce a single thought of wholesome roots. Therefore...
This stage is also called "The Only Son.
For example, parents—[this illustrates the fifth point on saving both cause and effect].
Good son, it is as if a father and mother have only one son; whether that son is asleep or awake, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, [the parents' minds...]

One should constantly keep them in mind; even if they commit offenses or faults, one should guide them with kind words rather than inflicting harm upon them. A bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this:

seeing sentient beings whether they have fallen into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, or are among humans or devas, performing good or evil deeds, he constantly keeps them in mind from the very beginning and never abandons them. Even if they commit various evils, he never gives rise to anger.
Because he treated him with such malice, this stage is further named "The Only Son.

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: [This concludes] the first round of the debate from the two rounds of question and answer regarding the second discourse; the first round was the debate, and the second round was the realization of understanding.
Regarding the first [round], there is first the question and then the answer. The initial question is divided into two parts: first, directly stating the lack of understanding.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has spoken, his words are esoteric;
my wisdom is shallow now, so how can I understand them?
Next, from 'If there are bodhisattvas' onwards is precisely the formal discussion of the doctrine; it is called the 'Five Difficulties' or the 'Three Difficulties. (1)
1. The difficulty of killing a Brahmin; 2. The difficulty of reviling Devadatta; 3. Citing Subhūti as an illustration.
Regarding the first, the killing of the Brahmin, there are three points: (1) Why did he kill him? (2) Should he not have been protected and remembered? (3) Why did he not fall into hell?
If bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of the "only son" (ekaputraka-bhūmi) can act in such a manner, why did the Tathāgata,
in the past when practicing the bodhisattva path as a king, take the lives of so many brahmins?
If he had attained this stage, he should have protected and remembered [the Buddha];
since he did not attain it, for what reason would he not fall into hell?
To regard him as equal [to the Buddha] is the second way of insulting Devadatta.
If he regards all sentient beings equally as his own son, just like Rāhula, why did he again speak such words to Devadatta, saying, "Foolish man!
You who eat the food of one who is no different from a spitter of snot"?
Having heard this, Devadatta gave rise to resentment and an unwholesome mind, shedding the blood of the Buddha. After Devadatta had committed this evil deed, [the Buddha said:]...
The Tathāgata further gave the prediction that [the person] would fall into hell and undergo punishment for one kalpa;
how is it that the World-Honored One’s such words do not contradict the meaning?
Thirdly, Subhūti raises the case of the Hīnayāna as an illustration for the Mahāyāna.
World-Honored One, Subhūti dwells in the realm of empty space; whenever he wishes to enter a city to seek food and drink by alms, he first observes the people.
If there is anyone who might conceive feelings of resentment or envy toward him, he stops and does not proceed.

This continues even until he is extremely hungry, yet he still does not go begging. Why is this? It is because Subhūti constantly reflects: "I recall that in the past, regarding the field of merit..."
"Because of the arising of even a single evil thought, one falls into the great hells and undergoes various sufferings due to such causes and conditions.
I would rather remain hungry and not eat for the rest of the day than allow that person to harbor resentment toward me and fall into hell to undergo all manner of suffering and distress.
He further reflected: "If there are sentient beings who resent me for standing, I shall sit upright for the entire day."
"If there are sentient beings who resent my sitting, I shall remain standing all day without moving from my place; the same applies to walking and lying down.
Subhūti, because he protects sentient beings, he still gives rise to such a thought; how much more so for a Bodhisattva?
If a Bodhisattva has attained the stage of regarding all beings as an only son, for what reason would the Tathāgata utter such harsh words as to cause sentient beings to give rise to grave malice?
The mind:

if even those of the Lesser Vehicle protect living beings in such a manner, how much more so for one who has perfected the fruit of Buddhahood? If there were still killing or reviling, how could that be called compassion?
For what reason would it cause people’s afflictions to increase?
"You should not now [answer] the second question. The Buddha answered the three preceding questions, yet he did not answer them in their original order;

rather, he first answered the difficult question, then the question regarding killing, and thirdly, the question regarding verbal abuse. Question: Why were they not answered in order? Was it merely to follow what was most immediate?
Why must there necessarily be an order? There are many such examples. However, the question regarding verbal abuse was the most severe of all. Why? Because the teacher who spoke it was absent.
Because his compassion did not extend to his disciples, he first sent them away and then rebuked them; however, it was improper for him to rebuke them collectively at the outset.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa: "You should not now raise such an objection, saying that the Buddha-Tathāgata acts thus toward all sentient beings."
They act as the causes and conditions for affliction.
Next, he rebukes them individually by citing seven matters:
"Good son, even if the proboscis of a mosquito could exhaust the depths of the ocean, the Tathāgata would never act as [a cause] for sentient beings."
Regarding the causes and conditions of afflictions:
as for the term "mosquito" (*maṅ*) mentioned at the beginning, that which has a bird-like beak is called a *maṅ*; since the mosquito's mouth resembles this, it is named after its likeness.
Good son, even if the great earth were entirely to become non-material, water were to take on the characteristic of solidity, fire were to take on the characteristic of coldness,
wind were to take on the characteristic of stillness, and the Three Jewels, the Buddha-nature, and space were to manifest the characteristic of impermanence,
the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.
Good son, even if one were to commit the four grave offenses or be an icchantika who slanders the true Dharma,
should they manifest in this very body the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics of a Tathāgata,
the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.
Good son, even if śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others were eternally abiding and unchanging,
the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.
Good son, even if bodhisattvas of the ten stages were to commit the four grave offenses, become icchantikas, or slander [the Dharma]...
The Tathāgata who slanders the True Dharma never acts as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.
Good son, even if all immeasurable sentient beings were to sever their Buddha-nature and the Tathāgata were ultimately to enter parinirvāṇa,
the Tathāgata would still never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.
The middle five are visible (and so forth).

Good son, even if one were to cast a snare capable of binding the wind, or have teeth capable of shattering iron, or claws capable of destroying Mount Sumeru, the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings; he would rather dwell together with a venomous snake than do so.
He placed his two hands into the mouth of a starving lion and used *khadira* charcoal to bathe his body;

he should not speak, for he knows that the World-Honored One acts as a cause and condition for the afflictions of all sentient beings. "Good son, the Tathāgata truly can sever the afflictions of sentient beings;
he never acts as a cause and condition for their afflictions."
In the final passage, there are further matters; therein it says: "It would be better to entrust oneself to a venomous snake," and so forth.

This section, in which Kāśyapa admonishes and restrains the ignorant, constitutes the first part of the second response to the "difficulty regarding killing," as mentioned in the phrase "O son of good family, as you have said. Now follows the initial [explanation].

Answer: Why is it that although [the Tathāgata] appeared to kill, in reality there was no killing? This is explained at length through the text of the six perfections, which is divided into three parts: first, restating the question; second, the formal answer;
and third, concluding that there was in fact no killing.
"Good son, as you have said, regarding the Tathāgata’s killing of the brāhmaṇa in the past..."
Good son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not intentionally kill even an ant, much less a brāhmaṇa.
The bodhisattva constantly employs various skillful means to bestow immeasurable life upon sentient beings through the gift of wisdom.
Good son, one who gives food is one who bestows life; when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), they constantly bestow it.
Sons of good family with immeasurable lifespans cultivate the precept of non-killing and thereby attain long life;
when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they bestow immeasurable lifespan upon all sentient beings.
"Noble son, by being careful with one's speech and committing no transgression, one attains a long life.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), they constantly exhort sentient beings not to give rise to thoughts of enmity; they attribute rectitude to others and take blame upon themselves, remaining free from dispute and litigation, thereby attaining a long life.
For this reason, when a Bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience, they have already bestowed [this gift]."
Sentient beings who diligently cultivate wholesome qualities obtain long life;

when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the *vīrya-pāramitā*, they constantly exhort sentient beings to diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas, and through such practice, those beings attain immeasurable lifespan.
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva practices the *vīrya-pāramitā*, they have already bestowed [this gift].
Sons of good family with immeasurable lifespans who practice the gathering of the mind attain long life.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the dhyāna-pāramitā, they exhort all sentient beings to cultivate a mind of equanimity;
once these beings have practiced it, they attain long life. Therefore, when Bodhisattvas practice the dhyāna-pāramitā, they have already bestowed immeasurable [benefits] upon sentient beings.
Noble son, those who are not negligent regarding wholesome dharmas attain a long life.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they exhort all sentient beings not to be negligent regarding wholesome dharmas;
having so practiced, by this causal condition, they attain a long life. Therefore, the bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom.
When practicing the pāramitās, he has already bestowed immeasurable life upon sentient beings.
Son of good family, for this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva never deprives any sentient being of life.
Regarding the two questions you previously asked, the response to your inquiry concerning protective mindfulness is likewise threefold; first, I restate your question:
"Good son, as you previously asked, when one kills a brahmin, does one attain this stage?"
Next, I shall now provide the correct explanation.
"Good son, at that time, because I cherished him with affection, I severed his life-faculty; it was not out of an evil mind.
Good son, it is like parents who have only one son whom they love very deeply; [if] he violates the laws of the state, at that time..."
If parents, out of fear, should exile or kill [their child], even though they exile or kill them, they harbor no evil intent;
likewise, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva acts similarly to protect the True Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who slander the Mahāyāna, he shall immediately punish them with lashes and harsh treatment, or even deprive them of life, desiring to cause them to reform their past ways and cultivate wholesome dharmas.
Sā always reflects thus: "By what causes and conditions can I cause sentient beings to give rise to faith?
I must act for their sake through whatever skillful means are appropriate. When the Brahmins pass away, they are reborn in the Avīci Hell, where they immediately have three thoughts:
first, they think to themselves, "From where have I come to be born here? and they know for themselves [the answer].
Second, those who come from among human beings think to themselves, "Where have I been born now? and immediately know for themselves that it is the Avīci Hell.
Third, they think to themselves, "By what karmic conditions have I come to be born here?

and immediately know for themselves that they have come to be born there because they slandered the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras, did not believe in causes and conditions, and were consequently executed by a sovereign.
Having formed this thought regarding these matters, he immediately conceived a heart of faith and reverence for the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras;
at that very moment, his life ended, and he was reborn in the world-system of the Tathāgata Amṛtadundubhi, where his lifespan was complete for ten kalpas.
When Upatiṣya (Kāśyapa) asked whether one who has not yet attained the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) could incur a breach of the precepts, the Buddha replied that they could.

Regarding this response, there are two interpretations: The first interpretation states that Upatiṣya’s question concerned both the attainment of the stage and the breach of precepts; the Buddha’s answer was that one who has already attained the "Stage of the Single Son" (*ekaputraka-bhūmi*) at the time of killing [a sentient being] would indeed incur such a breach.

The second interpretation states that Upatiṣya’s initial remark referred to those who have not yet attained the stage. (Note: This passage addresses the nuances of ethical transgression in relation to spiritual attainment within the Mahāyāna context.)

Regarding "attaining what was not yet attained" in the context of attaining the truth: the old interpretation states that because he killed [the person] upon seeing their spiritual capacity (mārga-darśana), there is no offense.
The Master of Hexi said: first, out of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), fearing that they would fall into hell;

second, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, since they had slandered the Dharma, he killed them so as to exempt them from the sin of slander; third, for the purpose of extinguishing false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); fourth...
If one gives rise to faith and performs this contemplation, it seems as though an actual killing occurs. Xinghuang said that these are manifestations of killing.
As with the previous instance of the boy eavesdropping, so too is the subsequent instance of reviling Devadatta. Now I ask:

if these were merely illusory killings, how could there be such matters as the hells, the three thoughts, the ambrosia, or the ten kalpas? If all of these were indeed manifestations produced by the Tathāgata, [how can they be explained?]
For whose benefit [is this]? If neither [of these two views] is the case, where would the transformed boy be reborn after death?
Therefore, one knows that the two interpretations cannot be applied exclusively; if one grasps the underlying meaning, the principle lies between them.
Third, the conclusion based on this principle:
"Good son, for this reason, even though I gave such a person a lifespan of ten kalpas in the past,
how could this be called killing?"
"Good son, if a person digs into the earth down to three *hastas* and does not fall [into the pit], there are again three questions:
first, a counter-question; second, Kāśyapa’s answer as recorded in the text.
Good son, if a person digs into the earth, cuts grass, hews trees, severs corpses, reviles others, or lashes them with a whip..."
"Would one fall into hell because of this karmic condition?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, according to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, such a person should indeed fall into hell.
Why is this? Because in the past, when the Buddha preached the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas, he said: 'O bhikṣus, regarding all grasses and trees...'"
"Do not give rise to an evil mind. Why? Because all sentient beings fall into hell due to an evil mind.
This is the third part of the Buddha’s praise, which consists of three sections: first, a laudatory description; second, a distinction between internal and external killing;
and third, a reconciliation with the question asked. This is the initial laudatory description.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, saying, "Excellent, excellent! What you have said should be properly upheld.
Son of good family, if one falls into hell because of an evil mind, a bodhisattva at such a time truly has no evil mind. Why is this?
Because a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to compassion for all sentient beings, even down to the smallest insects and ants."
It was because of a mind intent on benefit. Why is this? Because I well understood causes, conditions, and various skillful means (*upāya*).
By the power of these skillful means, I desired to cause sentient beings to plant roots of goodness.
Noble son, for this reason, although at that time I took his life through skillful means, it was not out of an evil mind.
If even killing grass with an evil mind incurs guilt, then if one kills a human being without an evil mind, there would be no guilt.
Following the Dharma of the Brahmins, the next section distinguishes between the internal and external; first, it distinguishes external killing as described in the text.
"Noble son, according to the Dharma of the Brahmins, if one kills ten wagon-loads of ants, there is no karmic retribution for sin;
likewise for mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, lice, kittens, lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, and other malevolent insects and beasts that can harm sentient beings—
if one kills ten wagon-loads of these, as well as ghosts, spirits, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, kālapūtanas, and those possessed by madness..."
If one slays mad spirits, withered ghosts, or various other demons who cause harm to sentient beings, there is no karmic retribution for taking their lives;
however, if one kills an evil person, there is karmic retribution. If, after killing, one does not repent, one will fall into the realm of hungry ghosts.
If one can repent and abstain from food for three days, the offense will be extinguished without remainder. If one harms one’s preceptor (upādhyāya) and...
Their parents, women, and cattle shall remain in hell for countless thousands of years.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas distinguish within themselves that there are three grades of killing—namely, inferior, middling, and superior. The "inferior" refers even to the killing of an ant.

Regarding all animals—with the sole exception of those born through the intentional manifestation of Bodhisattvas—good son, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by reason of their vows, manifest birth as animals, this is called "inferior killing.
Due to the causes and conditions of inferior killing, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, where they fully experience inferior suffering.
Why is this? Because these animals possess even a slight degree of goodness.

Because of these roots, the killer fully receives the retribution for the sin; this is called "inferior killing. As for "middling killing," it refers to those from ordinary worldlings up to the stage of Anāgāmin;
this is called "middling. Due to these karmic causes, they fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, where they fully experience middling suffering;
this is called "middling killing. As for "superior killing," it refers to [the killing of] one's parents, up to Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas.

A Bodhisattva who is certain of Buddhahood is called "superior. Because of such karmic causes, one falls into the Avīci Great Hell and undergoes the full extent of supreme suffering; this is called "supreme killing."

Good son, if there is anyone capable of killing those of the third assembly mentioned below, good son, if there is anyone capable of killing an icchantika, they shall not fall into these three types of killing.
Good son, all those brahmins and others are entirely icchantikas; it is, for example, like digging the earth.
Mowing grass, felling trees, cutting up corpses, reviling others, or whipping them carries no retribution for sin;
likewise, killing an icchantika also carries no retribution for sin. Why is this? Because among the various brahmins, there is not even the presence of the five dharmas, such as faith;
therefore, although they kill, they do not fall into hell.

Regarding the statement that there is no sin in killing, the subsequent text says: "Bestowing gifts upon an icchantika yields a thousandfold reward; bestowing gifts upon a hungry ghost yields a hundredfold reward.
Yet here it is said that there is no sin in killing an icchantika. These two statements mutually clarify the principles of giving and taking:
according to the icchantika’s present lack of goodness, there is no sin in harming them; however, based on their past observance of the five precepts, they still receive karmic retribution.
Since the human body is superior to that of animals, the retribution is a thousandfold.

Regarding your previous statement, the third response below addresses the difficulty of his insults; this also consists of three parts: restating the question, providing the formal explanation, and concluding with a reconciliation.
The first is as in the text.
"Good son, as for what you said above regarding why the Tathāgata reviled Devadatta as a 'fool who eats spittle,' the subsequent explanation cites seven past events as evidence.
This is further divided into two parts: first, a general summary of the intent."
You also should not raise such an objection. Why? Because whatever the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, utter is inconceivable.
Good son, there may be true speech that is beloved by the world, yet if it is untimely or contrary to the Dharma and does not bring benefit, I never speak such words.
Good son, furthermore, there may be speech that is harsh or false...
If speech is false, untimely, or contrary to the Dharma, and if those who hear it do not find it pleasing and it cannot benefit them, I shall not speak it.

Noble son, if there is speech that, though harsh and rugged, is true and not false, and is timely and in accordance with the Dharma, capable of benefiting all sentient beings—even if hearing it brings no pleasure, I must speak it. Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are worthy...
Because the Perfectly Enlightened One knows the skillful means,
he next specifically cites seven matters, beginning with:
"Son of good family, at one time I was traveling through that wilderness village and staying beneath a grove of trees."
There was a spirit named Āṭavaka who subsisted solely on flesh and blood and killed many sentient beings; furthermore, he would eat one person every day in that settlement.
Son of good family, at that time I extensively expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma for that spirit.
However, being violent, evil, foolish, and lacking wisdom, he did not accept the instructions. I then manifested as a powerful spirit and shook him.
The palace was thrown into turmoil; at that time, the demon, taking his retinue with him, emerged from his palace intending to come and obstruct me.
When the demon saw me, he immediately lost his wits and fell to the ground in terror, fainting and gasping for breath like one who is dead.
Out of compassion, I stroked his body with my hand, whereupon he immediately rose up and sat, exclaiming: "How wonderful!"
That today I have regained my life and body is due to this great king, who possesses great majesty and virtue and has a heart of compassion;
he has pardoned my transgressions and immediately conceived a virtuous faith toward me.

I then restored myself to the body of a Tathāgata and further preached various essential teachings to that spirit, causing him to receive the precept against killing. On that very day, in the wilderness...
In the village there was an elder who was next in line to die. The villagers brought him to that spirit;
having received him, the spirit immediately bestowed upon me the name "Hand-Elder" for the sake of that elder.
At that time, the spirit addressed me, saying: "World-Honored One, I and my retinue rely solely upon flesh and blood."
"By what means shall you now sustain yourself after having received the precepts?
I replied, "From this day forward, I shall command my śrāvaka disciples that wherever the Buddha-dharma is practiced, they shall all provide you with food and drink."
"Good son, for these reasons, I have established this precept for the bhikṣus: 'From this day forward, you must always provide food for those wilderness spirits (āṭavika).
If there are those who reside in a monastery and fail to provide it, you should know that such people are not my disciples;
they are merely the followers and retinues of the celestial Māras. Good son, the Tathāgata has done this because he wishes to subdue [them]."
It is for the sake of sentient beings that I manifest such various skillful means; it is not to cause them to give rise to fear.
Good son, I have also struck the Dharma-protecting spirits with wood; furthermore, at one time on a mountain, I pushed the Goat-headed spirit so that he fell to the foot of the mountain;
again, I dashed the Monkey-protecting spirit from the top of a tree; and now the Wealth-guarding elephant sees these five.
The Lion dispatched the Vajra-gods to terrify Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha, and they likewise pierced the body of the Arrow-hair Ghost with needles;
yet even though they acted in this way, they did not cause those spirits and ghosts to suffer destruction,
but rather desired to establish them in the True Dharma, and thus manifested these various skillful means.
At that time, I asked this at the assembly of the three lower fetters (*trisaṃyojana*).
"Good son, at that time I did not truly revile Devadatta, nor was Devadatta foolish enough to eat human spittle and saliva,
nor did he ever take birth in the miserable destinies (*apāya*) or suffer in the Avīci hell."

Even if one commits the sins of causing a schism in the Sangha or shedding the blood of a Buddha for an entire kalpa, nor violates the four grave offenses, nor slanders the True Dharma and Mahāyāna sūtras, such a person is neither an icchantika, nor a śrāvaka, nor a pratyekabuddha.
Good son, Devadatta is truly not within the realm of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; he belongs only to the Buddhas.
Son of good family, you who possess knowledge and vision should not now raise the objection:
"For what reason did the Tathāgata reprimand and revile Devadatta? You should not give rise to such a web of doubt regarding the domain of all Buddhas.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha for the second time to express his understanding; this section has two parts: first, the expression of understanding, and second, the confirmation.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, it is like sugarcane, which, when repeatedly boiled and processed, yields various flavors.
I am likewise; having heard from the Buddha many times, I have obtained much of the flavor of the Dharma—namely, the flavor of renunciation and the flavor of detachment from desire."

The Blessed One relishes the flavor of the taste of tranquility. World-Honored One, it is like true gold that, having been repeatedly heated, beaten, melted, and refined, becomes increasingly bright and pure, harmonious, soft, and of subtle radiance;

its value is immeasurable, and only then is it held in high esteem as a treasure by humans and devas. World-Honored One, the Tathāgata is likewise: through earnest inquiry, one obtains the hearing and seeing of the profound.
By means of this meaning, let those who practice deeply receive, uphold, and cultivate it;
then, after immeasurable sentient beings have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they shall be honored, revered, and made offerings to by all humans and devas.

The "four flavors" refer to the flavor of the Four Truths: emergence is the flavor of emerging from suffering; detachment is the flavor of detaching from the origin [of suffering]; cessation and the path are as stated in the text.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, saying, "Excellent, excellent! It is because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva desires to benefit..."
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, you have inquired of the Tathāgata regarding such profound meanings. Son of good family, for this reason, I shall,
according to your wish, expound the profound and secret Dharma of the Mahāyāna Vaipulya, namely, the stage called "Supremely Cherished as an Only Son."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha. This second section, which clarifies the fruit of the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), is divided into two parts:

first, it clarifies the equality of emptiness; second, it distinguishes the reason for knowledge and vision. This is because [the nature of reality] is both quiescent and illuminating, both empty and existent, and both real and provisional.
The fruits of the aforementioned three minds are such that phenomena are simultaneously principle. Thereafter, it concludes by stating that the realm of all Buddhas is precisely phenomena.

Now, the principle and the present [text] mutually clarify the initial section, which further consists of three parts: first, clarifying the fruit of equality; second, establishing the meaning of emptiness; and third, clarifying the benefits.
Regarding the first of these, there is first a question and subsequently an answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if all bodhisattvas cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy, they attain the 'one-child' [mind]."
Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*), when one cultivates the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), what stage is further attained?
The answer consists of two parts: first, a brief clarification of the fruit of the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*); second, an extensive clarification of the fruit of the gate of emptiness.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You know the proper time; knowing that I wished to speak, you have then inquired."
Question: When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), they then abide in the stage of the equality of emptiness, just like Subhūti.
By praising Subhūti as the foremost among the śrāvakas in understanding emptiness, [the text] uses the small to illustrate the great in order to clarify [this point].

Regarding the nature of the stages (*bhūmi*), there have traditionally been two interpretations: first, that the seven stages are so called because a sūtra states, "The seventh stage is able to enter into quiescence";

second, that the eighth stage is so called because it simultaneously contemplates emptiness and existence, and is therefore "equal. Now, it is said that the first stage shares the same principle as the stage of the "only-child" (*ekaputraka*), yet their capacities differ;
thus, distinct names are established. How can one take this difference in depth to serve as an analogy for the precepts and meditative concentrations within the "Noble Practices" (*ārya-caryā*)?
These fruits are all present in the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Good son, the second section below extensively explains the fruits of the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dvāra*) through three parts: the teaching, the analogy, and the application.
Good son, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the stage of the equality of emptiness, he does not perceive the existence of parents or brothers.

One does not perceive younger brothers, sisters, children, kinsmen, acquaintances, enemies, or neutral persons; nor does one perceive the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense bases (*āyatana*), nor sentient beings or a life-principle (*jīva*).

First, the teaching of the Dharma clarifies both the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); the non-perception of parents and so forth is precisely the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Having seen that the aggregates (skandhas) and elements (dhātus) are themselves the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā), the text further mentions "sentient beings" and "life-span" to reiterate the previously established emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).
Next, the passage beginning with "For example, like space" cites the emptiness of things (vastu-śūnyatā) as an analogy.
Good son, it is like space, which has no father, mother, brothers, wife, or children, and even lacks sentient beings or life-span;
all phenomena are likewise subsumed within this.
All phenomena are likewise thus, having no father, mother, or even life-span.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives all phenomena as likewise thus, their mind is equanimous like space. Why is this?
Because they are well able to cultivate all dharmas of emptiness.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: This is the second section, a detailed exposition on the meaning of the gate of emptiness, which consists of two parts: first the question, and then the answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, what is meant by 'emptiness'?"
The answer is further divided into three parts: first, the enumeration of the eleven emptinesses; second, the detailed explanation of each;

and third, the conclusion. "Good son, as for emptiness, it refers to internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, beginningless emptiness, essential emptiness, non-existence emptiness, ultimate truth emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, and great emptiness."

Regarding the initial passage: while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) elucidates eighteen emptinesses or seven emptinesses, the present text speaks of them in a middle way, thus enumerating only eleven.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* expands upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*) while abbreviating intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), whereas this sūtra expands upon intrinsic nature while abbreviating emptiness;
in total, these two sūtras mutually manifest their respective excellences.
Regarding how the Bodhisattva explains the eleven kinds of emptiness, there were formerly two interpretations. Yecheng said:

"The first six kinds of emptiness are the emptiness of mutual non-existence and the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the latter five kinds of emptiness are the emptiness of abiding in principle. Abiding in principle refers to the emptiness of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while mutual non-existence refers to the emptiness of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Zangyan used this approach, whereas Kaishan held that all of them are emptinesses of principle, though he explained them more extensively.
The *Chich yecheng* (Exclusion of the Iron City) further divides [emptiness] into four categories: first, the six types of emptiness as provisional names;

second, the two types of emptiness regarding substantial dharmas; third, the one type of emptiness of equality; and fourth, the two types of emptiness regarding the fruit of Buddhahood. Because spiritual cultivation proceeds gradually, Master Guan stated that these eleven types of emptiness are all for the purpose of destroying afflictions.
He cited the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), which says: "It is like medicine having eleven [ingredients]."
The eleven "diseases" are destroyed by the eleven "emptinesses"; thus both the names and the emptinesses are attained, and the principles are all made clear.
It may be said that the first eight destroy diseases while the latter three reveal the truth. Now, it is clarified that the eleven realms are arranged with distinct divisions;

they are taught as the "worlds" according to what is appropriate for conditions, and they are spoken of as the "eleven" to give rise to goodness, serving as the treatment for the eleven types of people.

Illness is the remedy; upon hearing that each [phenomenon] is empty, one is able to perceive the principle. This is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), which universally and harmoniously integrates all things.
How could one rigidly adhere to private opinions claiming that the sūtras and śāstras differ?

They do not exceed the four *siddhāntas*, which encompass both gradual and sudden teachings and unify the exoteric and esoteric. How could anything surpass this? These eleven types of emptiness constitute eleven sections.
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate internal emptiness? A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that internal dharmas are empty.
This "emptiness of internal dharmas" refers to the absence of father, mother, enemy, friend, or neutral person; the absence of sentient beings, life-span, permanence, bliss, self, or purity;
and the absence of the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, or any material possessions. Although the Buddha-nature exists within these internal dharmas, it is not the [self].
The nature is neither internal nor external. Why is this? Because the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding and without change;
this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s contemplation of internal emptiness.
External emptiness is likewise: there are no internal dharmas.

At the beginning, when explaining internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), it is said there are no external phenomena; when explaining external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), it is said there are no internal phenomena. Yecheng called this "mutual non-existence emptiness" (*itaretara-abhāva-śūnyatā*).

When Kaishan explained external emptiness, he analogically interpreted that internal phenomena are also empty; when explaining internal emptiness, he likewise interpreted that external phenomena are also empty.

When one knows that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are empty, one analogically knows that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are also empty; when one knows [the former], one knows the latter. There is nothing else.
Regarding the statement that "conditioned time and conditioned phenomena are also empty," there are two interpretations evaluated by others:

Master Yecheng is said to have succeeded in the literal phrasing but failed regarding the underlying principle, while Master Kaishan is said to have succeeded regarding the principle but found it inconvenient for the literal phrasing. A certain master stated:

"If one waits for the internal to clarify the external, then since the external does not exist, the internal likewise does not exist. This [argument] actually supports Master Kaishan’s interpretation; his interpretation of "internal emptiness" is without flaw.
Regarding the passage on the "eternal and blissful Three Jewels" and so forth, the subsequent text further states: "The Tathāgata, Dharma, and Saṃgha do not exist within the two types of emptiness.

This explains that what was previously called "non-existent" refers to irrational, external, and arbitrary conceptualizations, whereas what is later called "not non-existent" refers to the True Dharma within the principle.
The emptiness of both the internal and external is likewise so, O son of good family. There is only the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, and the Buddha-nature;
these do not reside within the two kinds of emptiness. Why is this? Because these four dharmas are eternal, blissful, self, and pure; therefore, these four dharmas are not called empty.
This is what is termed the emptiness of both the internal and external.
If one explains internal and external emptiness as mutual non-existence, it is utterly inconsistent; however, if one takes it in the sense of mutual dependence, it is easily understood:

since one relies upon the internal and external to achieve their separation as two kinds of emptiness, once the internal and external no longer exist, there is no longer an "internal-and-external" combined into a single emptiness.

Good son, as for the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), all conditioned dharmas are entirely empty; that is to say, they are empty of the internal, the external, and the internal-and-external;
they are empty of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; they are empty of sentient beings, life-span, and the Tathāgata’s Dharma and Saṅgha;

and they are empty of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Within this, the Buddha-nature is not a conditioned dharma; therefore, the Buddha-nature is not empty of being a non-conditioned dharma. This is called [the emptiness of the Buddha-nature].
There is conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). Conditioned emptiness is as [explained in] internal and external emptiness.
Noble son, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)? All these unconditioned phenomena are entirely...
This emptiness refers to that which is called impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self; the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; the characteristics of sentient beings and life-span;
conditioned phenomena and outflows; internal and external phenomena; and among unconditioned phenomena, the four dharmas such as the Buddha.
Because their nature is wholesome, they are not unconditioned; because their nature is eternally abiding, they are not conditioned. This is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation.
The emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
Regarding the emptiness of the unconditioned, it is said that the four dharmas, such as the Buddha, are neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
this is the Middle Way, the True Dharma.

What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of that which has no beginning? It is when the bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives that birth and death have no beginning and are entirely empty and quiescent.
That which is called "emptiness" refers to the fact that permanence, bliss, self, and purity are all entirely empty and quiescent, without change or alteration;
this includes sentient beings, life-span, the Three Jewels, the Buddha-nature, and unconditioned phenomena. This is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of no-beginning emptiness.

First is beginningless emptiness (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*). Regarding "beginningless emptiness": first, it is said that because one refutes the heretics' notion of a primordial darkness (*ādikṛta*), it is called "beginningless";

second, it is said that when one traces its root back to the distant past, there is no point of origin from which it came, and thus it is not empty only of a beginning now. This first refutes ignorance (*avidyā*); since ignorance has no beginning, it is beginningless.
How does a bodhisattva contemplate the emptiness of intrinsic nature?

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely empty—namely, the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, whether they be permanent or impermanent, suffering or pleasure, pure or impure, self or non-self.
By contemplating all such phenomena in this way, he does not perceive an intrinsic nature; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

First, it is said that emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) means breaking through intrinsic nature to explain emptiness; second, it is said that all intrinsic natures are empty, like a poor person for whom everything is empty.
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of non-existence? It is like a man who has no son saying, "My house is empty."
Ultimately observing emptiness, there is no such thing as kinship or affection; the foolish say that all directions are secure, while those who are impoverished say that everything is empty.
Such reckonings may be either "empty" or "not empty. When a bodhisattva observes them, they see that, like a poor person, everything is entirely empty.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)?

Good son, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the ultimate truth, he sees that when this eye arises, it comes from nowhere; and when it ceases, it goes nowhere. It was originally non-existent and now exists;
having existed, it returns to non-existence. When one investigates its actual nature, there is no eye and no master. As with the eye, so it is with the others.
All dharmas are likewise thus. What is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)? There is karma and there is retribution, yet no agent is perceived;
such an empty dharma is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplating the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
The old [commentary] says: "From the arising and ceasing of the eye, one proceeds to clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) as the primary truth;

from what is it that one proceeds? One proceeds to clarify the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) as the primary truth. Kaishan asks: "How can one employ the two types of emptiness—the emptiness of birth and phenomena—as an explanation for the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which is so profound and remote?
Furthermore, in all other sūtras, the emptiness of birth (*jāti-śūnyatā*) is invariably clarified first; why is it that here [in this sūtra], the [emptiness of phenomena] is clarified first?"
The Master of the Contemplation of the Emptiness of Dharmas said: "When the eye arises, it comes from nowhere;
this is the meaning of non-arising. When it ceases, it goes nowhere; this is the meaning of non-ceasing. This is precisely the meaning of 'neither' from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.

If the eye were an existent thing, it would not be the case that what was originally non-existent now exists, and what already existed returns to non-existence. Upon investigating its actual nature, there is neither an eye nor a subject who perceives it; thus, one realizes the single [emptiness]."
All phenomena should likewise be questioned in this way regarding the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*): how can there be karma and its retribution?
To answer this, one relies on existence to clarify non-existence, and relies on non-existence to clarify existence; that which is neither existent nor non-existent is the ultimate truth.
Regarding the "emptiness of emptiness," there are three parts: the praise, the explanation, and the conclusion. As for the praise:
how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of emptiness? This emptiness within emptiness is precisely the place where śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others are lost and submerged.
This is the place where ordinary and inferior beings are deluded and submerged.
"Existence" and "non-existence" is the correct explanation.
Good son, "existence" and "non-existence" is called the emptiness of emptiness; "is" and "is not" is called the emptiness of emptiness. Good.
Even a bodhisattva of the tenth stage can only penetrate a small portion of this, like a mere speck of dust; how much less so for others?
One interpretation states that "it exists" and "it does not exist" are two thematic gates (*dvāra*); the subsequent "it is it" reiterates the two preceding "its."
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "neither is this," both "is" and "is not" are empty. First, it was clarified above that both objects—existence and non-existence—are empty;
now it is clarified that both wisdoms—the provisional and the real—are empty. "Is" refers to provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), and "is not" refers to real wisdom (*prajñā-jñāna*).

Now, we shall further examine this through three propositions to demonstrate their emptiness: the object designated as "empty" is called "emptiness-of-emptiness"; the coming of emptiness is called "emptiness-of-emptiness"; and the wisdom of emptiness is called "emptiness-of-emptiness."

If one brings emptiness forward and asks whether the dharma capable of emptying is called "emptiness-of-emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā), or if one takes direct emptiness as both object and wisdom, this is still partial and cannot yet be called "perfect.
If one brings emptiness forward to empty that very emptiness, this is the emptiness of the Perfect Middle Way.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "All dharmas are entirely empty; even this emptiness is empty. Regarding this, there are two masters who hold differing views.
Regarding the statement that all phenomena are empty: this emptiness was not yet ultimate. Now, one further brings emptiness to empty this very emptiness—this is called "the double emptiness.
It is not so; since all phenomena were already the wondrously empty, the present emptiness is also empty, such that even the dharma capable of emptying is itself empty.
Because the Master of Hexi (He-xi) agrees with the latter interpretation, he says: "Or it may be said that although the myriad dharmas are empty..."
The essence of wisdom is not empty because it dispels and destroys deluded attachments; therefore, it is called "emptiness of emptiness.

That which exists is also empty, and that which does not exist is also empty. The subsequent phrase states: "Since the prior conceptualizations are already empty, wisdom does not exist in isolation. In the principle of true awakening, there is no simultaneous illumination.

Although there is no simultaneous illumination, the meaning of "dispelling" can be understood. Among people, there are many who [distinguish between] the emptiness of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the emptiness of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The untainted emptiness regards the tainted emptiness as light; yet these two emptinesses are one in essence—how could they be light and heavy?
Since all phenomena are quiescent and the essence of wisdom is also empty, this is called "wondrous emptiness," which is beyond the reach of the Two Vehicles.
Good son, in this way, even this emptiness of emptiness is not the same as the samādhi of the emptiness of emptiness attained by śrāvakas;
this is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of emptiness.
Good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate great emptiness? Good son, as for what is called "great emptiness":
This refers to the Prajñāpāramitā, which is called "Great Emptiness" (mahāśūnyatā).

Some say that Great Emptiness is the emptiness of Prajñā itself; because form (*rūpa*) is great, Prajñā is great. The *Śāstra* explains Great Emptiness in terms of both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).
Regarding phenomena: it is the emptiness of the eastern direction, up to the emptiness of the ten directions. Regarding principle: it is Nirvāṇa.
In the "Great Chapter on the Emptiness of the Ultimate Meaning" (*Paramārtha-śūnyatā-mahāparivarta*) of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, Nirvāṇa and Prajñāpāramitā are mutually elucidated.

Now, explaining the eleven kinds of emptiness according to the three truths: "internal emptiness" (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) is the emptiness of the ultimate truth; "external emptiness" (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) is the emptiness of the conventional truth;

"internal-and-external emptiness" (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) is the emptiness of both together; "emptiness of the conditioned" (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) is the conventional emptiness of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); and "emptiness of the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)... [is the emptiness of Nirvāṇa].
Regarding "Nirvana is true emptiness" and "beginningless emptiness": because the three truths are mutually identical and no primordial source is perceived, it is called beginningless emptiness.
Regarding "emptiness of nature": because the essential nature of the three truths is originally and inherently empty, it is called emptiness of nature. Regarding "emptiness of the ultimate meaning":

because the True is the Middle and the Middle is the True, it is called emptiness of the ultimate meaning. Regarding "emptiness of emptiness": [it refers to the fact that even this emptiness is empty].
"Empty as one, all is empty. This "Great Emptiness" means that the Three Truths are simultaneously empty. The subsequent passage of praise also takes the Three Truths as its basis for praise.

Because the characteristics of the Three Truths are mutually identical, it is said that where ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas are deluded and submerged—regarding things as either existent or non-existent—the two truths are both illuminated simultaneously;
thus it is called "both are one. Because each truth fully contains the Real (the Ultimate) and the Middle, it is called "empty and empty."
That which is "is" and "is not" is simply the illumination of the single truth, which inherently possesses both emptiness and the provisional. Because it is "is," it is provisional;

because it is "not is," it is complete with the Middle Way. To speak of "emptiness-emptiness"—whether as dual, singular, triple, or unitary—it is all inconceivable, fully endowed and without deficiency;
thus, it is not something that can be deliberated upon by ordinary beings or those of the Lesser Vehicle.
Good son, this concludes the third section, the summary of praise.
Good son, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains such gates of emptiness, they then abide in the ground equal to space.
Now, in this third section below, I shall clarify the benefits, which further consists of two parts; the first clarifies the realization of emptiness:

"Good son, when I now, amidst this great assembly, expound such meanings of all forms of emptiness, there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers who immediately attain the stage of 'Equal to Space.'"
Regarding the second dwelling, the following explains its functional capacity:
"Good son, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this stage, they encounter no obstruction, bondage, or grasping among all phenomena, and their mind is free from delusion or distress;
for this reason, it is called the 'Stage Equal to Space. Good son...

Son, for example, just as space does not give rise to attachment toward pleasant forms nor gives rise to aversion toward unpleasant forms, so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in this stage;
his mind is free from greed and anger toward beautiful or ugly forms.
Good son, for example, just as space is vast, without opposition, and is able to contain all things, [so too is this stage].
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this stage, it is likewise vast and peerless, fully capable of containing all dharmas;
for this reason, it is further named the "Stage Equal to Space."
This refers to the meaning of the "subsequent attainment" (prsthalabdha) that follows the preceding "detachment" (viveka).
Good son, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they proceed from the second [stage] to extensively differentiate knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*);

that their knowledge and vision are vast and far-reaching is precisely due to emptiness and quiescence (*śūnyatā-śānti*). Furthermore, it is the illumination within quiescence itself. The text is divided into four parts: first, explaining knowledge and vision; second... [and so forth].

The "Non-attainment" [section] synthesizes the three assemblies and commends the four knots; because it is tranquil yet illuminating, one clearly knows that seeing is itself illumination and tranquility, and thus there is no attainment.
Since its nature is non-dual, these dharmas are unified as something extraordinary, and for this reason they are praised.
The first section has three parts: first, knowing the thirteen dharmas; second, attaining the eight kinds of knowledge and vision; third, [the concluding summary].
He attains the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
Good son, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this stage, he both sees and knows all phenomena (*sarvadharmāḥ*)—

whether their activity, their objective conditions, their nature, their characteristics, their causes, their conditions, the minds of sentient beings, their faculties, or their meditative concentrations.
One knows and perceives all such dharmas as meditative concentration, vehicles, spiritual friends, the observance of precepts, and acts of giving.
The initial passage states: "Practice is the mind; conditions are the objects; nature is the internal; and characteristics are the external."
Those that are proximate act as causes (*hetu*), while those that are remote act as conditions (*pratyaya*).

Furthermore, regarding "knowing but not seeing," the second section below clarifies the eight types of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*): first, knowing what is impossible; second, knowing what is possible;

third, knowing concurrent practice; fourth, knowing cause and effect; fifth, knowing the transformation of hindrances; sixth, knowing the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*); [seventh, ...]; eighth, [ ... ].
He knows the two truths and the eight knowledges; he possesses the two wisdoms.
Furthermore, good son, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this stage, he knows yet does not see. What is meant by "knowing"?

It is knowing those who practice self-starvation, those who throw themselves into abysses or leap into fire, those who cast themselves from high cliffs, those who constantly stand on one foot, and those who practice the five heats.
One should practice self-mortification by constantly lying upon ashes, soil, thorns, thatched rafters, leaves, weeds, or cow dung;
wearing coarse hempen garments, rags discarded in cemeteries, *kāṣāya* robes, *kambala* woolens, deerskins, or clothes made of straw;
subsisting on vegetables, fruits, lotus roots, oil dregs, cow dung, roots, and fruits; and restricting one's alms-seeking to specific limits.
If the head of a household says there is nothing [to offer], they depart immediately; even if called back, they never look behind them. They abstain from salt, meat, and the five products of the cow;
they constantly drink and consume grain-ash water and boiling water. They observe the "cow-vow" (*go-vrata*), the "chicken-vow," and the "dog or pheasant-vow.
They smear their bodies with ash and let their hair grow long as their outward marks. When sacrificing sheep to the gods, they first recite incantations and then slaughter them. (4)

If one were to serve fire for seven months, consume wind [as food] for seven hundred billion days, and make offerings to the various devas, such that all desired wishes are thereby accomplished—there is no possibility that such dharmas as these could serve as the cause for unsurpassed liberation.
This is called "knowing. Why is it called "not seeing"? Because one does not see a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, nor does one see a single person practicing such dharmas.
Attaining right liberation is called "not seeing.
Knowing the false dharmas of external paths is knowing what is not the proper place.
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva both sees and knows. What is meant by "seeing"? It is seeing all...
That sentient beings who practice these false dharmas will inevitably fall into hell is called "view. What is meant by "knowledge"?

It is knowing that when sentient beings are born from hell into the human realm, if they are able to practice the *dāna-pāramitā* and so forth until they are fully endowed with all the *pāramitās*, such persons will certainly attain right liberation; this is called "knowledge."
He knows the retribution for good and evil and knows these states.
Furthermore, son of good family, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has both seeing and knowing. What is meant by "seeing"?
To see the permanent and the impermanent, suffering and pleasure, purity and impurity, and the self and non-self—this is called "seeing. What is meant by "knowing"?
To know that all Tathāgatas certainly do not enter final nirvāṇa;
to know that the body of a Tathāgata is adamantine and indestructible, not a body produced by afflictions, nor a foul, putrid, or decaying body;
and furthermore, to be able to know that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature—this is called "knowledge."
To know the four virtues of permanence and impermanence, and so forth, is what is known as "knowing through shared practice.
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva also possesses both knowledge and vision. What is meant by "knowledge"?
It is knowing that this sentient being’s mind has achieved faith; it is knowing that this sentient being seeks the Mahāyāna; and it is knowing that this person is following the current.
This person goes against the current; this person dwells correctly. One knows that these sentient beings have already reached the other shore.

Those who go with the current are called ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); those who go against the current range from stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) up to the pratyekabuddhas; those who dwell correctly are the bodhisattvas and others;
those who have reached the other shore are the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. This is what is meant by "knowing. How so?
In order to see the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and practicing the holy life (brahmacarya),

he uses his purified divine eye to see all sentient beings who, having committed unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind— the three karmas— fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts;
and he sees those sentient beings who practice wholesome deeds and, at the end of their lives, will be reborn among gods or humans.
There are sentient beings who enter from darkness into darkness; there are sentient beings who enter from darkness into light;
there are sentient beings who enter from light into darkness; and there are sentient beings who enter from light into light—this is called "vision."
Seeking the Mahāyāna is knowing the cause; reaching the other shore is knowing the fruit.
Furthermore, good son, there are also Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who both know and see:

these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas know that although certain sentient beings have cultivated their bodies, cultivated their precepts, cultivated their minds, and cultivated their wisdom, they have nonetheless produced evil karma in this present life.
Furthermore, there may be karma arising from greed, hatred, and delusion that ought to result in retribution in hell;
yet, because such a person has cultivated their body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, they receive this retribution lightly in the present life rather than falling into hell.
How is it that such karma can yield retribution in the present? Having confessed and revealed all one's evils, once repented, one dares not commit them again.

Because they have accomplished a sense of shame and remorse, because they make offerings to the Triple Gem, and because they constantly reproach themselves, such persons—by virtue of these causes and conditions of wholesome karma—do not fall into hell, but instead experience retribution in the present life.
This so-called retribution consists of headaches, eye pain, abdominal pain, and back pain;

encountering untimely death, being rebuked and insulted, being flogged with whips and staves, being imprisoned and bound, and suffering from hunger and deprivation—all such hardships as these they shall undergo.
These [actions] receive light retribution in the present life; this is what is meant by "knowing. What is meant by "seeing"?

It refers to a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who sees such a person—one who is unable to cultivate bodily discipline, mental precepts, and wisdom—and who, having committed even a small evil deed, must receive its retribution in the present life due to the causes and conditions of that karma.
This person is unable to repent for their slight evil, does not reproach themselves, and gives rise to no sense of shame or remorse.
To have fear is the ground for the increase of karma that results in retribution in hell; this is called "viewing.
The precepts of body, speech, and mind, as well as wisdom, are the means by which one knows how to transform obstacles.
Buddha-nature is threefold: first, based on ordinary beings; second, based on those in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); and third, with respect to the Buddhas.
Furthermore, there is the case of "knowing but not seeing. What is meant by knowing but not seeing?
It means knowing that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, yet being unable to see it because it is shrouded and obscured by various afflictions; this is called knowing but not seeing.
Furthermore, there are Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the tenth stage who, though possessing knowledge, have limited vision;
they know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet their vision is not clear, being like what is seen in the darkness of night—indistinct and unclear.
Furthermore, there is that which is both seen and known— namely, that which all Buddhas and Tathāgatas see and know.
Furthermore, there is that which is both seen and known, yet not seen and not known, and which is nonetheless both seen and known—
namely, the worldly conventions of letters, speech, men, women, vehicles, jars, basins, houses, cities, clothing, food and drink, mountains, rivers, and gardens.
The life-span of sentient beings in the forest is called both seeing and knowing. What is it that is neither seen nor known?
The subtle and secret words of the Sages—that there are no men or women, and so forth, even up to gardens and groves—this is called neither seeing nor knowing.
Not knowing and not seeing is knowing the ultimate; both knowing and seeing is knowing the conventional.

Furthermore, there is knowing without seeing: knowing the wisdom of giving, knowing the place of offering, knowing the recipient, and knowing the retribution of cause and effect—this is called "knowing.
