What is "not seeing"? It is not seeing the gift, the place of offering, the recipient, and the [retribution].
The retribution is called "not seeing. That a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows these eight kinds is precisely what is known by the Tathāgata’s five eyes.
Bestowing wisdom and so forth is knowing the provisional; not seeing that which is bestowed and so forth is knowing the real.

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha. This concludes the third section, which clarifies the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*). It is divided into two parts: first the question, followed by the answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what benefit does a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtain by being able to know in this way?"
The answer consists of three parts: first, the topical outline; second, the explanation; and third, the analysis.
The first is as stated in the text. The Buddha said: "Good son, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to know in this way, they attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge:
unimpededness in meaning (*artha*), unimpededness in expression (*nirukti*), unimpededness in eloquence (*pratibhāna*)."
Next, the explanation is divided into five parts: first, the explanation according to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya); second, the explanation according to the supramundane;

third, the explanation according to non-attachment; fourth, the explanation by way of analogy; and fifth, the explanation by way of the causal basis. First, regarding the explanation according to the conventional truth:

The unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) is the knowledge of all phenomena and the meanings of their names; the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) is the knowledge of all the meanings possessed by all phenomena;
the unimpeded knowledge of linguistic expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) is the ability to provide definitions and terminology according to the names established for all phenomena;

and the unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is that which follows the treatises on phonology (*śabdavidyā*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), etymology (*chandas*), and worldly debate (*loka-vāda*), namely, the bodhisattva’s...
O son of good family, whatever the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva expounds is without obstruction, unshakable, fearless,
and difficult to subdue; this is called the Bodhisattva’s ability to see and know in such a way that he immediately attains these four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
"Dharma" refers to knowing the phenomena (*dharma*) themselves; "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to knowing the underlying significance of the phenomena and the underlying significance of the names;

"Phrasing" (*vyañjana*) refers to the clarity and elegance of the sounds, which are distinct and lucid; "Eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) refers to the ability to transform and adapt [the teaching] infinitely and inexhaustibly;

"Discourse on Letters" (*akṣara-śāstra*) refers to determining the written characters and having a thorough knowledge of their forms; and "Discourse on Correct Pronunciation" (*svara-śāstra*) refers to correctness.
The phonetics and terminology are distinct and clear. Regarding *khandha*, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* also states that it refers to "joined sounds," like the chanting of *saṃghāta*;

the Hexi region explains this as being equivalent to the melodic intonation used here [in China]. Furthermore, it is said that this term applies exclusively to non-Buddhist (external) teachings, but this is not necessarily the case;
rather, it is the sound of verses (*gāthā*) that is common to both internal and external traditions.
Furthermore, the following section explains [the term] from the perspective of world-transcendence.

Furthermore, son of good family, regarding "unimpededness in phenomena" (*dharmā-pratighāta*), it means that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva universally knows the teachings and meanings of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all buddhas.
Regarding "unimpededness in meaning" (*artha-pratighāta*), although there are three vehicles, one knows they ultimately converge into one, and never...
Regarding the unimpeded analytical knowledge of distinctions in characteristics: it is impossible for a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha to provide such an exposition—
that is, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to produce various names for a single dharma and speak of them without end throughout immeasurable kalpas—
whereas for a bodhisattva mahāsattva possessing unimpeded eloquence to do so for the sake of all sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas is entirely possible.
He expounds upon all phenomena through various distinct explanations of both names and meanings, such that they can never be exhausted.
He knows that the meanings of the three vehicles all ultimately converge into one.
Regarding the third [section], according to Wuzhuo’s commentary, it is divided into two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the discussion of the meaning.
Furthermore, noble son, regarding the absence of obstruction in phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*): although a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows all phenomena, he does not grasp at them.

Regarding the absence of obstruction in meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*): although a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows all meanings, he does not grasp at them. Regarding the absence of obstruction in expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*):

although a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows names and designations, he likewise does not grasp at them. Regarding the absence of obstruction in eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*): [he is] unhindered in his delight in teaching.
Although this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that such eloquence is supreme, he does not become attached to it. Why is this?
Good son, if one were to grasp at or become attached to it, one would not be called a Bodhisattva.
He said that this was an interpretation by Vasubandhu based on the intent of the objection;
however, according to the commentary of Asaṅga, from the passage beginning with "Kāśyapa," the discussion of the meaning first poses a question and then provides an answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if one does not grasp or cling, then one does not know the Dharma; yet if one knows..."
As for "dharmas," this refers to grasping; if one knows without grasping, then there is nothing known.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata say that one knows dharmas without grasping?
Kāśyapa’s initial objection implies that knowing itself is grasping.
The Buddha said, "Good son, one who grasps and clings is not called 'unimpeded. Only one who has nothing to grasp or cling to is called 'unimpeded.
Good son, for this reason, among all bodhisattvas, those who possess grasping and clinging have no unimpededness.
If they lack unimpededness, they are not called bodhisattvas; you should know that such persons are called ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Why do they grasp and cling?"
They are called ordinary persons; all ordinary persons cling to form, and so on, up to clinging to consciousness.
Because they cling to form, a mind of craving arises; because a mind of craving arises, they are bound by form, and so on, up to being bound by consciousness.
Because they are thus bound, they cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, great suffering, and all afflictions.
Therefore, grasping at names is called being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). For this reason, all ordinary persons lack the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva has, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, known and seen the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Because of this knowledge and vision, he knows their meaning; and because he sees the characteristics of phenomena and knows their meaning, regarding form (*rūpa*)...
One does not give rise to attachment even toward consciousness; it is likewise for all [the aggregates].
Because of this non-attachment, the bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of craving toward form, nor does he give rise to a mind of craving even toward consciousness.
Because there is no craving, he is not bound by form, nor is he bound even by consciousness. Because there is no bondage, he is able to attain liberation.
Because of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and all great sufferings and afflictions—for this reason, all bodhisattvas attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.

Good son, for these causes and conditions, I have taught within the twelve divisions of the scriptures for my disciples that those who are bound by attachment are called "bound by Māra," whereas those who do not attach themselves are liberated from the bonds of Māra. It is, for example, as if there were in the world...
A person who has committed an offense is bound by the king, whereas one who is innocent the king cannot bind. It is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
those who possess attachment are bound by Māra, while those who are without attachment Māra cannot bind.
For this reason, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is without any attachment.
The Buddha replied, "One knows through non-attachment.
Furthermore, noble son, regarding the unimpeded nature of phenomena (*dharmāsaṅga*), the bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully knows the retention of syllables (*akṣaradhāraṇī*) without forgetting them.
As for this "retention," it is like the earth, like a mountain, like the eye, like a cloud, like a person, and like a mother—indeed, it is all things.

All dharmas are likewise thus. Regarding "unimpededness in meaning": although a bodhisattva knows the names of all dharmas, they do not know their meanings. When one attains unimpededness in meaning, one then knows those meanings. How does one know the meanings? That which is called the "earth-sustainer" (dharaṇī) is like the earth, which universally sustains all sentient beings and non-sentient things; for this reason, it is called the "sustainer. because each is a *siddhānta*, each is a departure from [the ultimate], and each is a negation [of the others]. Thus, we know that while the four emerge, these four are each distinct.
The calculation is likewise fourfold, yet because it is neither four nor not-four, all are simultaneously neither four nor not-four; therefore, all eight instances are "thus.

Brief characteristics are taught as extensive, and extensive characteristics are taught as brief. The four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*) are taught as *sthūlātyaya*; *sthūlātyaya* offenses are taught as grave offenses.
What is not an offense is taught as an offense, and what is an offense is taught as not an offense. Minor offenses are taught as grave offenses.
Why is it that the offense is said to be light? It is because the Tathāgata clearly perceives the faculties of sentient beings.
Son of good family, although the Tathāgata speaks thus, there is ultimately no falsehood in his words. Why is this?
False speech is itself a transgression, and the Tathāgata has completely severed all transgressions; how, then, could there be false speech? Son of good family, although the Tathāgata—
There are no false words; however, if one knows that sentient beings will gain benefit from the Dharma through false speech, one employs appropriate skillful means and speaks accordingly.
To summarize the preceding intent:
knowing that saying "it exists" is not necessarily existence, and saying "it does not exist" is not necessarily non-existence, all such speech is for the sake of benefiting others.

None of these are fixed; they vary according to the country and the person, as their characteristics differ. Therefore, there are differences regarding what constitutes a light or heavy offense, and what constitutes a transgression or non-transgression.
Good son, this is the third summary and explanation concerning all conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Good son, all conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are, for the Tathāgata, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Why is this?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach conventional truths for the sake of the ultimate truth, so that sentient beings may also attain the ultimate truth.
If sentient beings were not to attain such an ultimate truth, the Buddhas would never have proclaimed it.
"Good son of the worldly truth, there are times when the Tathāgata expounds the worldly truth, yet sentient beings think the Buddha is speaking of the ultimate truth;
there are times when he expounds the ultimate truth, yet sentient beings think the Buddha is speaking of the worldly truth.
This is the profound realm of all Buddhas, which is not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
All take birth and death to be the mundane world and nirvana to be the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). At times, it is said that the mundane world is the ultimate truth;
at other times, it is said that the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena is itself birth and death, which is what is called the ultimate truth;
or it is said that the wondrous existence of eternal abiding is the ultimate truth. People say this is birth and death, yet the Tathāgata speaks of emptiness in order to clarify [this].
Amoghasiddhi speaks thus to clarify that it is not the case that all conditions produce the views of existence and non-existence.
Good son, for this reason, you should not raise the objection mentioned above. Third, the clarification of attaining through non-attainment has three parts:

Next, regarding the two parts within the inquiry—first the question and then the objection—the initial question is as follows: "If there is that which is attained, it must be impermanent.

Both the Way and *bodhi* are termed "eternal. This concludes the second section, the direct answer.
"Good son, the Way, *bodhi*, and even *nirvāṇa* are all termed 'eternal'; all sentient beings are eternal."
Because they are shrouded by immeasurable afflictions and lack the eye of wisdom, they are unable to see;
yet, because sentient beings desire to see, they cultivate morality, concentration, and wisdom. Through such cultivation, they perceive the path, bodhi, and nirvana.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the path, bodhi, and nirvana. The essential nature of this path is truly neither arising nor ceasing; it is for this reason.
Therefore, it cannot be grasped or held.

Now, to say that the Way is perfect, constant, and primordially present, yet merely covered by delusions, and that through severing these delusions one returns to the original state—this implies that what is attained is itself constant.
This is the meaning of the statement.

Next, "Good son, although the Path has no form or appearance" is the response to the subsequent objection; it consists of three parts: the analogy, the application, and the synthesis with the primary teaching.
Good son, although the Path has no form or appearance that can be seen, weighed, or known, it nevertheless possesses actual utility.
Next, as explained in the analogy regarding the minds of sentient beings:

"Good son, although the mind of a sentient being is not form, is neither long nor short, neither coarse nor subtle, neither bound nor liberated, and is not a dharma that can be seen, it nevertheless exists. For this reason, I spoke thus for the sake of Sudatta."
It is said that the mind is the lord of the city. If one does not protect the mind, then one does not protect the body and speech;

if one protects the mind, then one protects the body and speech. Because failing to properly protect this body and speech causes all sentient beings to reach the three evil destinies, whereas protecting the body and speech causes sentient beings to attain the human and celestial realms, nirvana, and is called "true," while failing to do so is not.
Names are not real.
Good son, the Way, Bodhi, and Nirvana are also like this: they both exist and are eternal.

One clearly perceives and knows this;
yet, although it is truly permanent, those who are able to practice will attain it, while those who do not practice will not.

Good son, there are two kinds of seeing. This concludes the third assembly’s comprehensive explanation, which is further divided into two parts: first, the comprehensive explanation; second, [the specific analysis].

Regarding the initial section on the reconciliation of the treatise’s arguments: it reconciles what was previously stated—that the dharmas such as knowledge and vision all possess semblances of the real and semblances of marks—and that these, being clearly manifest, are themselves the real.
This reality is further divided into two: first, the clear manifestation of the Bodhisattvas; second, the clear manifestation of the Tathāgatas.
From here to the end of the scroll, this constitutes the reconciliation of these two chapters, as per the text.
Good son, there are two kinds of seeing: first, seeing by signs; second, seeing with clarity. What is meant by seeing by signs?
It is like seeing smoke from afar and calling it "seeing fire," though one does not actually see the fire. Although one does not see the fire, it is not a false seeing.
It is like seeing a crane in the sky and saying one sees water; although one does not see the water, it is not a false seeing. It is like seeing the petals of a flower.
He then said: "To say one sees the root, though one does not actually see the root, is not false. It is like a person who, seeing the horns of an ox through a fence from afar, says they see the ox;
though they do not see the ox, it is not false. It is like seeing a woman pregnant and saying one sees desire;
though one does not see the desire itself, it is not false. It is also like seeing leaves growing on a tree and saying one sees water."
Although one does not see the water, it is not false; likewise, upon seeing clouds, one says "I see rain," and although one does not see the rain, it is not false.

Just as upon seeing bodily action (*kāyakarman*) and verbal action (*vākkarman*), one says "I see the mind," and although one does not see the mind, it is not false—this is called "seeing by way of signs" (*nimittadarśana*).
What is "clear seeing"? It is like the eye seeing forms, O son of good family.
Son, it is like a person whose faculty of sight is pure and unimpaired who clearly perceives an *āmalaka* fruit within the palm of his own hand;
the Bodhisattva’s clear perception of the Path, Bodhi, and Nirvāṇa is likewise so. Although he sees them in this way, from the beginning there is no characteristic of seeing.
Son of good family, for this reason, in the past I told Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, all the worlds..."

Should there be anything—whether among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or humans—that is not known, not seen, and not realized, it is only the Tathāgata who fully knows, sees, and realizes it; and the same is true for the bodhisattvas.
Śāriputra, whatever is known, seen, and realized by those in the world, I and the bodhisattvas also know, see, and realize that.

Regarding that which the beings of the world do not know, do not see, and do not awaken to—and which they do not even recognize as being unknown, unseen, and unawakened—the Tathāgata knows, sees, and awakens to it all;

yet he does not say of himself, "I know, see, and awaken to it. Śāriputra, regarding that which the beings of the world do know, see, and awaken to, the Tathāgata likewise knows, sees, and awakens to it all, yet he does not say of himself, "I know, see, and awaken to it. All bodhisattvas are also thus.

Why is this so? If one were to cause the Tathāgata to produce knowledge, vision, or the realization of marks, you should know that such a person is not a Buddha, a World-Honored One, but is called an ordinary person; the same applies to a bodhisattva.

The second volume begins: Regarding this discourse on doctrine, there are questions and answers. There are two types of questions: first, questions concerning what is known in the world;
second, questions concerning what is not known in the world.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said: "As the World-Honored One, the Buddha, spoke for Śāriputra regarding that which is known in the world, I likewise—"
"Attaining suchness":
as for the meaning of "the world does not know me, yet I know it all," what is it?

The answer is twofold: first, the direct response; second, the conclusion. The initial response is threefold: first, clarifying how it differs from the world; second, clarifying... [text fragment ends]
It is identical to the three types of worldly [dharmas], yet it is neither worldly nor supramundane.
Good son, all those in the world do not know, see, or awaken to the Buddha-nature;
if there were those who knew, saw, and awakened to the Buddha-nature, they would not be called worldly, but would be named Bodhisattvas. People of the world likewise do not know it.
If one does not perceive, understand, or awaken to the twelvefold canon, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four inversions, the four noble truths,
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and mahāparinirvāṇa— yet if one were to know, perceive, and awaken to them,
one would not be called a worldly person but should be called a bodhisattva. Good son, this is what is meant by a worldly person who does not know, perceive, or awaken.
Because they are different, the world does not know them; it does not know the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

What is it that the world knows, sees, and perceives? It refers to Brahmā, Maheśvara, the eight-armed deity, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), time, atoms, dharma and adharma, the Lord of Creation, and the two views of the beginning and end of the world, as well as annihilationism and eternalism. Thus they speak.
"From the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called 'nirvāṇa,' good son; this is what is known, seen, and realized by the world.
Alternatively, there are those who recklessly speculate that the world arises from atoms, or who reckon that the world has a limit and ends there."

The extremes are the absence of beginning and end, which all fall into the errors of nihilism or eternalism. Regarding the traditional phrase "without beginning and without end," there are two interpretations:

first, that beginningless ignorance is entirely devoid of both beginning and end; second, that beginningless ignorance has both a beginning and an end, for there is not a single beginning existing at the very outset of this beginninglessness.
Thus, one should know that while it has a beginning, it ultimately finds its end in Buddhahood.
If these two interpretations are identical in this context, they both recklessly speculate on permanence and annihilation;
within the eleven kinds of emptiness, the emptiness of no beginning is clarified precisely to refute this "beginning" and also to refute this "end."
Regarding such matters, the third section below clarifies that which is neither mundane nor supramundane.

if the world does not know, see, or realize it, then the Bodhisattva likewise should not know, see, or realize it.

"If there were nothing of the world, what difference would there be?

Third, it clarifies how the three dharmas mutually support one another.
Upon hearing this Nirvāṇa Sūtra, the bodhisattva already knows that there is a world, yet he does not yet know, see, or realize it;

Having attained knowledge, vision, and awakening, he further reflects: "I must cultivate and maintain pure precepts with a profound mind.
Son of good family, at that time, by virtue of these causes and conditions, wherever this bodhisattva is born in future lives, his precepts will always be pure.
Son of good family, because the precepts are pure, wherever this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born, he will always be free from arrogance and deviance.
Seeing through the net of doubt, one never says that the Tathāgata has ultimately entered parinirvāṇa; this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation and maintenance of pure precepts.
Once the precepts are pure, one next cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Because of this cultivation of concentration, in whatever place one is born, right mindfulness is never forgotten—namely, that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, as taught in the twelve divisions of the sūtras by the Buddhas of the world.

The Venerable One is eternally blissful, self, pure, and possesses all such qualities as the Bodhisattvas’ dwelling securely in the Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and their universal vision of the Buddha-nature;

recollecting these matters without forgetting, and by virtue of practicing meditative concentration, one attains the eleven kinds of emptiness—this is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of pure concentration.
Once concentration and precepts are fully prepared, one next cultivates pure wisdom; because of this cultivation of wisdom, from the very beginning one is not bound.
To conceive that "I am within the body" and "the body is within me," or that "this body is the self" and "that which is not the body is not the self"—
this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of pure wisdom.
The first section clearly elucidates that all three dharmas take precepts as their foundation.
Following the cultivation of wisdom, the second section clarifies how the three dharmas mutually support one another; as the text is concise, it mentions only two.

Because of the cultivation of wisdom, the precepts one upholds are firm and immovable. Good son, it is like Mount Sumeru... [text continues]... does not move.

Second, it clarifies that ethical discipline serves as the provision for wisdom.

Because the mind is hidden and at peace, one attains immovable concentration (*āniñjya-samādhi*). Because one attains immovable concentration, one attains true knowledge and vision (*yathābhūta-jñāna-darśana*).

Because one attains true knowledge and vision, one becomes weary of and detaches from birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Because one becomes weary of and detaches from birth and death, one attains liberation (*vimukti*).

Because one attains liberation, one clearly perceives the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*); this is called that which is known, seen, and realized by a Bodhisattva, and it is not of the mundane world. Good son, this is...

Kāśyapa, furthermore, in the second section below, there is an extensive differentiation of gain and loss, consisting of questions and answers.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "How does a bodhisattva cultivate and maintain pure precepts so that the mind is free from regret, and even comes to clearly perceive the Buddha-nature?
The answer is twofold: first, it raises the case of impure observance of the precepts which cannot mutually support one another; second, it clarifies pure precepts as the direct response.
The first section of the text also has two parts: first, clarifying impurity;
second, the mutual support of signlessness. The Buddha said: "Good son, worldly precepts are not called pure. Why is this?
Because worldly precepts are for the sake of existence, their nature is indeterminate, they are not ultimate, and they cannot extensively benefit all sentient beings."
For these reasons, it is called impure.

There are four kinds of impurity: first, possessing afflictions such as those of Nanda (and so forth); second, having an unstable nature, being at times able to maintain [the precepts] and at other times unable;
third, not being ultimate, being unable to maintain them perpetually from beginning to end.
Fourth, because one lacks the vast intention for the sake of sentient beings and remains self-centered without benefiting others, one possesses a mind of regret due to impurity.
Because of this regret, the mind lacks joy; because there is no joy, there is no gladness;
because there is no gladness, there is no tranquility; and because there is no tranquility, there is no immovable concentration.
Because they lack the immovable concentration, they lack true knowledge and vision; because they lack true knowledge and vision, they lack revulsion;

because they lack revulsion, they lack liberation; because they lack liberation, they do not see the Buddha-nature; and because they do not see the Buddha-nature, they can ultimately never attain Mahāparinirvāṇa.
This is called the impurity of the worldly precepts of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

The second section below clarifies pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) by correctly answering that question; it also has two parts: first, clarifying pure ethical discipline, and next, clarifying their mutual support.
"Good son, the pure ethical discipline of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is such that ethical discipline is not ethical discipline, because it is not for the sake of existence."
Because it is ultimately settled and for the sake of sentient beings, this is called the purity of the Bodhisattva precepts.
Within the first purity, the four purities correspond to the aforementioned four impure precepts; "non-precept" corresponds to the aforementioned precepts that lack beginning or end.
This "non-precept" is not the fivefold ethical discipline (*pañca-śīla-vinaya*) and so forth, but rather takes the absence of precepts and the absence of observance as the precept. This...
This is ultimate pure precept (*śīla*).
Within the purity of precepts, the second section clarifies the power of mutual support; it further divides into two parts:

first, the three dharmas that mutually support one another, and second, the five dharmas that assist and mutually support one another. Within this mutual support, the preceding phrases are explained in successive sequence. This section contains two parts.
First, based on the precepts, the absence of regret is explained; furthermore, there is a combination of dharma, analogy, and application.
"Good son, although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not intentionally desire to give rise to a mind free from regret within the pure precepts, a mind free from regret arises spontaneously."
Good son, it is like a person holding a bright mirror who does not expect to see their face, yet the reflection of the face appears of its own accord;
or like a farmer scattering seeds in a fertile field who does not expect sprouts to grow, yet the sprouts grow of their own accord;
or like lighting a lamp who does not expect darkness to be extinguished, yet the darkness is extinguished of its own accord.
There are three similes.
Son of good family, it is likewise with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who, firmly upholding the pure precepts, naturally gives rise to a mind free from regret.
Next, by virtue of pure precepts, the following section explains "joy" (*prāmodya*). This is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying the three characteristics;

second, clarifying the sense of delight. The initial passage is divided into three sections: first, clarifying the maintenance of joy; second, clarifying the grief over its violation; and third, clarifying both meanings together.
Each of the former two sections contains a teaching, an analogy, and a synthesis.
Because of pure precepts, the mind attains joy.
Good son, it is like a handsome person who, seeing his own face, feels joy in his heart;
one who maintains pure precepts is just the same.
Good son, a person who has broken the precepts sees their own impurity and their mind finds no joy,
just as one with a physical deformity feels no delight upon seeing their own face;
so it is with the person who has broken the precepts.
Regarding the third pair, which clarifies the observance and violation [of precepts], there are two parts: first the analogy, and second the application.
Good son, it is like two women herding cows; one carries a jar of curd and the other a jar of whey.
They travel together to the city intending to sell them, but on the road they stumble, and both jars break. One is filled with joy, while the other...
Then there is distress.

In this analogy, the cow at the beginning represents the teaching of the *Gomayapinda-sūtra*; the milk represents the recipient; the curd represents one who has broken the precepts; the whey represents one who maintains the precepts;
reaching the city and desiring to sell represents seeking the future fruit by trading the cause for the fruit (and so forth); and tripping over the feet represents [the resulting suffering].

The death of the two individuals is likened to both jars being broken; their physical bodies perish. Sorrow and joy are likened to the milk and the ghee contained within the jars. As for the one who held the jar of milk:
having already obtained the ghee, what remains is merely the value of the leftover liquid; thus, even if it is not obtained, it is of no consequence. This is like a person who maintains the precepts:
having already cultivated and attained the Path, what remains is only the residue of life. Whether that life persists or ceases is of no consequence. This is as with the jar of curd.

It is like losing butter before it has even been churned, or losing cream before the butter has been produced; this is analogous to a person who breaks the precepts and has not yet attained the cultivation of the Path—when such a life comes to an end, the Path is likewise lost, and for this reason, there is grief and fear.
Next, the section on upholding the precepts follows the text exactly.
Upholding the precepts and violating the precepts are likewise treated in this manner; one who upholds the pure precepts feels joy in their heart.
Next, because the mind is joyful, one then engages in reflection; the following section explains "delight," which is further divided into two parts, the first of which is the direct explanation.
Because the mind is joyful, one then reflects: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have declared within Nirvāṇa that those who can maintain pure precepts shall attain Nirvāṇa;
as I now practice such pure precepts, I too should attain it.
For this reason, the mind becomes delighted.
In the subsequent discussion of the treatise, the question is posed first and the answer follows.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "What is the difference between joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*)?
"Good son, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not commit evil, this is called the purity of the mind of joy through the observance of the precepts."
It is called "joy" for the son of good family, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, when contemplating birth and death;
it is called "great nirvāṇa" and "delight. That which is below is called "joy," and that which is above is called "delight.
To be free from worldly common dharmas is called "joy," and to attain uncommon dharmas is called "delight. Because the precepts are pure, the body becomes light and supple.
The Bodhisattva has no coarse transgressions in speech. At that time, whether seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, or cognizing, they are entirely free from all evils.
Because there is no evil, the mind attains peace and stability; because of this peace and stability, they attain tranquil concentration (*samādhi*);

because they attain tranquil concentration, they attain true knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*); and because they attain true knowledge and vision, they become weary of and detached from birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Because they are weary of birth and death, [they seek liberation].
Thus one attains liberation; because of attaining liberation, one perceives the Buddha-nature; and because of perceiving the Buddha-nature, one attains Great Nirvana.
This is called the pure upholding of precepts by a Bodhisattva, not worldly precepts.
In the answer, there are four layers of explanation showing that as one progressively enters deeper stages, the attainment of Great Nirvana is entirely dependent upon the precepts (*śīla*).
However, among the five faculties of feeling (*pañca-vedanendriya*), pleasure (*sukha*) is shallow and joy (*prīti*) is deep; within the dhyānas, joy is shallow and pleasure is deep.
Each has its own basis, yet here they are treated identically as factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*).
Next, to clarify the five factors that provide assistance:
For what reason, noble son, do the pure precepts received by a bodhisattva mahāsattva have these five assisting factors?

What are the five? First, faith; second, self-respect (*hrī*); third, shame (*apatrāpya*); fourth, virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); and fifth, increasing reverence for the precepts and being free from the five hindrances (*pañcanīvaraṇa*).
Therefore, what is seen is pure because it is free from the five views; the mind is free from the net of doubt because it is free from the five doubts:
first, doubt regarding the Buddha; second, doubt regarding the Dharma; third, doubt regarding the Saṅgha; fourth, doubt regarding the precepts; and fifth, doubt regarding heedfulness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately attains the five faculties—namely, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—and by attaining these five faculties, he obtains [the fruits].
The five kinds of nirvāṇa refer to liberation from form up to liberation from consciousness;

this is called the pure observance of precepts by a bodhisattva, which is not of the mundane world. Good son, this is what is unknown, unseen, and unrealized by the world, yet known, seen, and realized by the bodhisattva.

To speak of attaining the five nirvāṇas means that one attains nirvāṇa by being liberated from the five aggregates; it is not that there are five [separate] liberations. Being freed from the bonds of the five aggregates is called the five nirvāṇas.
Good son, if my disciples... [this concludes] the second section clarifying the protection of the Dharma; protecting the Dharma is precisely protecting the precepts.

When the guarding of the precepts is firm, that is precisely upholding the precepts; when the upholding of the precepts is not firm, it is due to the absence of a guarding mind. Furthermore, there are two parts:

first, the censure and disparagement of the dharma, and second, the exhortation to guard the dharma. Regarding the first (the censure), there are three sections: first, the formal censure of breaking the precepts;

second, the censure of performing actions for the sake of seeking existence (*bhava*); and third, the censure of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*). Now, among all extreme depravities, none surpasses the breaking of the precepts. First:

The previous passage states: "It would be better not to receive, not to uphold, and not to use [the precepts], rather than receiving and reciting them while violating the precepts. The questioner asks: "In the preceding text, it was said that one should serve as a servant to cause others to recite; yet in this current text, it says one should 'preferably not receive or uphold. Why are these two statements contradictory? Answer: Each of these has its own intended meaning. The former clarifies that one should employ a hundred expedient means to draw people in and lead them toward entry [into the path]. The latter clarifies that once they have entered, one should cause them to receive and uphold [the teachings]. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the former refers to those who have not yet received the precepts, while the latter refers to those who have already received them. This is why the two passages differ. Moreover, the former speaks of the Dharma for the sake of the person, whereas the latter speaks of the person for the sake of the Dharma. Thus, although the words appear to conflict, their underlying intent does not. It is like a physician prescribing medicine according to the specific illness; the treatment varies, yet both aim at curing the disease. How could this be considered a contradiction? Finally, the former speaks of the ultimate goal, while the latter speaks of the provisional means. Since the provisional and the ultimate are distinct, how could they be in opposition? One should understand that the Buddha’s teachings are subtle and profound; they are like the ocean, where the waves are vast and deep, and the currents are difficult to fathom. One must rely on the guidance of a master to discern their true meaning. Do not harbor doubts based on superficial appearances. If you can understand this, you will realize that the scriptures are indeed the gateway to liberation. If you do not understand, you will remain lost in the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, you should strive with all your might to seek the truth. Do not let the opportunity pass by. This is what is meant by "the Dharma is like a great ship; it carries those who board across the sea of suffering. You should take this to heart and apply it diligently. Do not merely read the words but contemplate their meaning. Only then will you attain true understanding. This is the essence of the Buddha's teaching. May you practice accordingly. Do not doubt. He admonishes his disciples to remain free from transgressions.

Good son, if among my disciples who uphold, recite, copy, and expound the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra there is one who violates the precepts, and someone should reproach, despise, or humiliate him, saying: "If the Buddha’s secret treasury..."
If the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* possessed true power, how could it allow you to destroy the precepts you have received?
If a person who upholds this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* violates the prohibitions, one should know that this sūtra lacks power. If it lacks power, then even though one recites it, it will be of no benefit.
Because of this slighting and disparaging of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it further causes immeasurable...
Those beings who fall into hell while upholding this sutra, yet violate the precepts, are great evil friends to sentient beings;
they are not my disciples but the retinue of Māra. Such persons as these, I do not permit to uphold this scripture.
It would be better for them not to receive, uphold, or practice it than to receive, uphold, and practice it while violating the precepts.

In the initial section on censure and reproach, the three types of karma are not yet distinguished; first is the censure of the body, next is the censure of the mind, and third is the censure of the mouth.
Regarding the first passage: if one is able to uphold the precepts, all disciples will likewise emulate their teacher;
yet if the teacher themselves is not upright, their commands will lack gravity.
Next, following "one should rectify body and mind," is the second section: Rebuking the Seeking of Existence.
"Good son, if my disciples receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or expound the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they should rectify their body and mind;

be careful not to be fickle or frivolous. To be fickle in physical movement is 'fickleness of body,' and to be light and restless in thought is 'restlessness of mind. Do not seek [existence through such means]."
The mind that clings to existence is called "lightness and agitation," and the body's performance of various karmas is called "restlessness and playfulness.
If my disciples seek existence and perform such karma, they should not uphold this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
If there are those who thus uphold this sūtra, people will deride them, saying: "If the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, the secret treasury of the Buddha, exists..."
Regarding "lacking power": why would you seek existence by performing karma? If those who uphold this sutra seek existence by performing karma, you should know that this sutra lacks power.
Because it lacks power, even if one receives and upholds it, there is no benefit;
for by thus slandering and despising the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, one further causes immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to fall into hell and undergo suffering.
To uphold this sutra while seeking existence and creating karma is for sentient beings to be a great evil friend; such a person is not my disciple but a member of Māra’s retinue.
To seek the three realms of existence is called frivolous; to seek the name of the fruit without seeking existence is called profound and deliberate cultivation.
Because of this, it is called "creating karma through existence.
This concludes the third censure regarding what is not the timely teaching.
Furthermore, son of good family, if my disciples receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and expound this *Nirvāṇa* [Sūtra]...

The sutras do not speak at improper times; they do not speak about improper countries; they do not speak unless requested; they do not speak with a contemptuous mind; they do not speak everywhere; they do not speak in self-praise;
they do not speak in disparagement of others; they do not speak to extinguish the Buddha-dharma; and they do not speak to inflame worldly dharmas.
"Good son, if my disciples uphold this sutra and preach it at improper times, or even preach it while the worldly dharmas are burning,
people will despise and revile them, saying: 'If the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, the Buddha’s secret treasury, possesses such majestic power,
why does it cause you to preach at improper times, and even to preach while the worldly dharmas are burning?'"
Those who uphold this sutra speak thus: "One should know that this sutra possesses no power; if it lacks power, then even though one upholds it, it is of no benefit.
Because they thus slight and revile the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, they cause immeasurable sentient beings to fall into hell.
They uphold this sutra by speaking at inappropriate times, even speaking while worldly dharmas are in full blaze.
These are great evil friends to sentient beings, not my disciples, but the retinue of Māra.
One must leave such places; one who can truly propagate [the Dharma] must strictly distance themselves from all such unrighteous places.

Even if there is no one to request it, one should nevertheless act in opposition to those who are uninvited friends. The commentary states that matters must be suited to the occasion; now is precisely the time.
Please do not speak of the destruction of the Dharma, nor speak of failing to uphold the precepts, nor speak of failing to protect the Dharma.
To speak of the destruction of the Dharma and to speak of "blazing worldly dharmas" means to seek existence and create karma while explaining it to others;

such people mostly supplement their teachings with worldly classics, poems, and books to cause others to lose faith—this is what is called "blazing worldly dharmas. Now, I am not like that regarding what I have taught.
The increase of suffering and its origination within the interim is a world-dharma that blazes.
Son of good family, if you wish to uphold the second exhortation to protect the Dharma,
which is inferior [to the first], son of good family, if you wish to uphold it, you must speak of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, speak of the Buddha-nature, and speak of the Tathāgata.

Those who preach the secret treasury, those who preach the Mahāyāna, those who preach the Vaipulya sūtras, those who preach the Śrāvaka vehicle, those who preach the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, those who preach liberation, and those who see the Buddha-nature should first purify their bodies.
Because the body is pure, they will be free from reproach; because they are free from reproach, they cause immeasurable people to give rise to purity regarding the Great Nirvāṇa.

Because they give rise to faith and confidence, they revere this sutra; if they hear even a single verse, a single phrase, or a single word, or if they listen to the Dharma-preacher, they shall immediately resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
You should know that such persons are true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to sentient beings and not evil associates; they are my disciples and not the retinue of Māra.
"O son of good family, this is called that which is not known, not seen, and not realized by the world,
but which is known, seen, and realized by the Bodhisattva."
He said: First, the ten wisdoms are enumerated; next, the purification of the mind is exhorted.

Regarding the first point, "those who wish to receive and uphold" refers to receiving through faith and upholding by not forgetting—this constitutes one's own practice (*sva-caryā*). "That which is spoken by the mouth" refers to transforming others.

As for the essence of the *Nirvāṇa* school, its practice is the teaching and its function is the fruit. Previously, Buddha-nature was taught as the essence (*śarīra*); subsequently, the realization of nature (*dṛṣṭi*) is taught.
To ensure that both paths toward the fruit result in the purification of the three karmas.

Furthermore, "Next, good son" and so forth—this third section clarifies the Great Chapter on the Six Mindfulnesses (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). Within it, the Ten Mindfulnesses and Eight Mindfulnesses are explained;
the Lesser Vehicle also possesses the Six Mindfulnesses, which are those chanted at dawn: first, mindfulness of the year, month, and day; second...

1. Mindfulness of the years, months, and days since ordination; 2. Mindfulness of the method for giving food; 3. Mindfulness of the three robes and the necessity to declare them pure (*śuddhi-ārocana*) when they exceed the limit;
4. Mindfulness of not eating separately from the community; 5. Mindfulness that those who are ill should be treated; each of these has its own purpose.

Now, these six recollections are for practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) dwelling in forests and wild places who harbor fear; they are taught so that they may cultivate the six recollections, the first three of which concern mindfulness of the years, months, and days since ordination.

Regarding the subsequent three reflections: self-restraint is the cause for birth in heaven; this is its own cause. Heaven is its own result. Restraint is wholesome conduct of cessation; generosity is wholesome conduct of performance.
Heaven has both proximate and remote results (and so forth). According to the text, there are two parts: first, stating the number and listing the chapters.
Furthermore, good son, what is meant by that which is not known, seen, or realized by any in the world, yet is known, seen, and realized by the Bodhisattva?

It refers to the six applications of mindfulness (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti-sthānāni*). What are the six? They are: mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of ethical discipline (*śīla*), mindfulness of generosity (*tyāga*), and mindfulness of the devas.
How is this explained? The explanation of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) consists of six chapters. In the chapter on the recollection of the Buddha, there are two parts:

first, the recollection of the Buddha’s fruition; second, the recollection of the Buddha’s causes. The recollection of the causes refers to the recollection of past causes; the recollection of the fruition refers to the recollection of present fruition.

As for the cause by which the present fruition was obtained, the recollection of the fruition is divided into four sections: namely, two chapters and two explanations. First, the ten titles and manifold virtues are established.
The two chapters—the section on the ten titles and the section on the various virtues—explain these two aspects.

The explanation of the ten titles clarifies the meaning of the "name," while the explanation of the various virtues clarifies the meaning of the "substance. First, the chapter headings for the ten titles are listed.
Good son, how does one practice the recollection of the Buddha— the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān?
In the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* and the *Āgamas*, the titles "Unsurpassed One" (*anuttara*) and "Tamer of Men" (*puruṣadamyasārathi*) are combined into a single epithet;

it is only upon reaching the tenth title, "World-Honored One" (*bhagavat*), that the number ten is fulfilled. In the present sutra and its commentary, however, "Unsurpassed One" and "Tamer of Men" are opened up as two distinct titles, so that by the time one reaches "Buddha," the ten names are already complete.
Thus, the summary concludes that he is fully endowed with these ten titles of supreme virtue and is honored by the world.
In this separate explanation, the term "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) is not used; instead, "Bhagavat" is employed as a general name for the Buddha, intended to replace "World-Honored One.
The phrase "constant and unchanging" introduces the following two sections which enumerate the various qualities of his virtues.
Eternal and unchanging, fully endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, he utters the great lion’s roar;
he is the Great Śramaṇa, the Great Brāhmaṇa, the Great Purifier who has reached the ultimate further shore.

He is invincible, his crown is invisible, and he is free from fear, unstartled, and immovable. Solitary and peerless, having awakened by himself without a teacher, he possesses swift wisdom and great wisdom.
Possessing sharp wisdom, profound wisdom, liberating wisdom, uncommon wisdom, vast and universal wisdom, ultimate wisdom, and the accomplishment of the jewel of wisdom;
a human elephant king, a human bull king, a human dragon king, a great man among men, a lotus *puṇḍarīka* among men,
a teacher who tames others, a great donor, and a great Dharma master.
Third, the section explaining the various virtues begins with "by knowing the Dharma.

One is called a Great Dharma Master by virtue of knowing the Dharma; one is called a Great Dharma Master by virtue of knowing the meaning; one is called a Great Dharma Master by virtue of knowing the time;
one is called a Great Dharma Master by virtue of knowing contentment; and one is called a Great Dharma Master by virtue of knowing the self.
One is called a Great Dharma Master because of knowing the great assembly; one is called a Great Dharma Master because of knowing the various dispositions of sentient beings;
one is called a Great Dharma Master because of knowing the sharpness, dullness, and mediocrity of the faculties; and one is called a Great Dharma Master because of preaching the Middle Way.
The preceding passages have all provided direct explanations; regarding the final matter of the "Great Dharma Master," it is explained by means of the aforementioned seven virtues.

One knows that one can uphold the precepts and can expound the Mahāyāna, and furthermore, one knows that the Middle Way is what constitutes a Great Dharma Master, whereas those who follow the partial paths of the Hīnayāna are not true Dharma Masters.

What is meant by the fourth of the ten titles of the Tathāgata? Why is he called "Tathāgata"? It means that he does not change from what was spoken by the Buddhas of the past. How is it that he does not change? Just as the Buddhas of the past taught the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) in order to deliver sentient beings, the Tathāgata is likewise; therefore, he is called "Tathāgata. What is the meaning of the word *tathā*? It means "thus" (*tathā*). What is the meaning of the word *āgata*? It means "come" (*āgata*). Because he has come in the same manner as the Buddhas of the past, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the state of reality exactly as it is, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the ultimate truth, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of reality, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of the Dharma, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of the world, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all phenomena, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all dharmas, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all things, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all realms, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all paths, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all stages, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all knowledges, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all wisdoms, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all attainments, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all realizations, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all fruits, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all results, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all causes, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all conditions, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all effects, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all functions, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all activities, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all practices, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all virtues, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all merits, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all qualities, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all perfections, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all liberations, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all concentrations, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all meditations, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all samādhis, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all dhāraṇīs, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all eloquence, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all unique qualities, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all dharmas, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all truths, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all suchnesses, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-falseness, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-erroneousness, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-deviation, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-perversion, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-delusion, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-confusion, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-obscuration, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-obstruction, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-hindrance, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-barrier, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-limitation, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-exclusion, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-separation, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-differentiation, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-distinction, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-duality, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-agitation, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-turbulence, he is called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the limit of all non-proliferation, he is called "Tathā
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, comes from the six *pāramitās*, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eleven emptinesses to reach Great Nirvāṇa;
the Tathāgata is likewise thus, and for this reason the Buddha is called the Tathāgata.

For the sake of sentient beings, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ skillful means as appropriate to reveal the three vehicles; their lifespans are immeasurable and incalculable, and the Tathāgata is likewise thus.
For this reason, the Buddha is titled "Tathāgata. In Sanskrit, it is called *tathāgata*.

While the old [translation] explains it solely by the single meaning of "coming according to the path of reality to achieve perfect enlightenment," the *Śāstra* (Treatise) explains "Tathāgata" through four meanings:
as one who has come thus (*tathā-āgata*), as one who has gone thus (*tathā-gata*), and as one who has understood thus (*tathā-vijñāta*).
As it is said: by studying the twelve divisions of the sūtras under the Buddhas of the three periods of time and cultivating the eleven kinds of emptiness, one attains Buddhahood;
therefore, one is called a Tathāgata. Having departed from birth and death and forever escaped all evils, one is thus a "Gone Thus" (Tathāgata).
To understand according to suchness and to speak according to suchness is also to speak of what I have understood and to explain what I have spoken; herein lies the threefold repetition.
Next, regarding the two subsequent sections, within the meaning of "as it was taught," one is the meaning of "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come), as in the case of "Well-Gone" (*sugata*);
"as it was understood" is as in the case of "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*).

Why is it called "that which should be countered" (*ārya*)? All worldly phenomena are termed "enemies" because the Buddha should destroy them; therefore, they are called "that which should be countered.
Furthermore, the four Māras are the enemies of Bodhisattvas, and when the Tathāgatas were Bodhisattvas, they were able to destroy these four Māras through wisdom;
for this reason, they are called "that which should be countered. Moreover, "that which should be countered" means "to be far removed from"; when he was a Bodhisattva...
One should distance oneself from immeasurable afflictions; therefore, he is called "Arhat" (the Worthy One). Furthermore, "Arhat" means "joy.

When the Buddhas of the past were bodhisattvas, although they underwent various sufferings for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they never failed to find joy in them, but always took delight in them. The Tathāgata is likewise; for this reason, he is called "Arhat. Moreover—
He is called "Arhat" because all humans and devas should honor him with various kinds of incense, flowers, necklaces, banners, flags, and music;
thus he is named Arhat. What is meant by "Arhat"?
In Sanskrit it is *arhan*, which has three meanings: slayer of thieves (*vadhaka*), non-arising (*ajanman*), and worthy of offerings (*pūjārha*).
In this context, it is simply stated that one should not say there are five kinds of *arhat* (worthy ones).

Furthermore, the first four are explained by the term "slayer of thieves" (*vadhaka-ghātaka*), while the last one is interpreted as "worthy of offerings" (*arhat*). The former "slaying of thieves" includes "non-arising" (*anutpāda*), because by destroying the māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), it is itself non-arising.
"What is 'Perfectly Complete Knowledge' (*samyak-saṃbuddha*)? This is the third title. It is further divided into two parts: first, the direct explanation;
second, the counter-explanation beginning with "Why is it not incomplete knowledge?

Regarding the first part: "What is Perfectly Complete Knowledge? "Perfect" (*samyak*) means non-erroneous; "Complete Knowledge" (*saṃbuddha*) means that regarding the four inversions, there is nothing that is not [fully known].
Furthermore, "thorough penetration" and "correctness" refer to asceticism; "comprehensive knowledge" means knowing that because of asceticism there will certainly be the fruit of suffering.

Furthermore, "correctness" refers to the world; "comprehensive knowledge" means definitively and ultimately knowing that by practicing the Middle Way one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, "correctness" is called being countable and measurable.
That which can be called "omniscient" (sarvajña) is incalculable, immeasurable, and inexpressible; for this reason, the Buddha is titled the "Perfectly Omniscient One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
Good son, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also possess omniscience, yet they do not possess [the full] omniscience. Why is this?
"Omniscience" refers to the five aggregates (skandha), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the eighteen elements (dhātu); śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also attain knowledge of these.
It is called "Universal Knowledge" (*saṃjñā*).
In Sanskrit, it is *Samyaksambuddha*, which has five successive meanings. The first four refer to the Buddha’s ability to know four dharmas, all of which are termed "universal" (*samantāt*).
These are: [1] that those who undergo ascetic practices will certainly obtain the fruit of suffering—referring to the asceticism of non-Buddhists; [2] the last one... [text fragment].
Refuting the Lesser Vehicle:

Why is it that they do not possess universal knowledge? Good son, even if those of the Two Vehicles were to contemplate a single aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) for immeasurable eons, they could not know it exhaustively.
For this reason, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas lack universal knowledge.
What is meant by "Vidyācaraṇasampanna" as the fourth epithet?
Regarding "Vidyācaraṇasampanna": "Vidyā" (knowledge) refers to the attainment of immeasurable wholesome fruits; "caraṇa" (conduct) refers to the feet;
"wholesome fruits" refers to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed perfect enlightenment); and "feet" refers to the vehicle of ethical discipline and wisdom.
Because one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the feet of precept and wisdom, he is therefore called "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (*vidyā-caraṇa-saṃpanna*).
Furthermore, "knowledge" (*vidyā*) means incantation (*mantra*); "conduct" (*caraṇa*) means auspiciousness (*śiva*); and "feet" (*saṃpanna*) mean fruit (*phala*).
Good son, these are the worldly meanings. Incantation is named liberation (*vimukti*); auspiciousness is named *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The fruit of enlightenment is called Great Parinirvāṇa; therefore, it is called the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*). Furthermore, "knowledge" (*vidyā*) is called light;
"conduct" (*caraṇa*) is called action; and "perfection" (*saṃpanna*) is called the fruit.
Good son, these are the worldly meanings: "light" refers to non-negligence; "action" refers to the six *pāramitās*; and "fruit" refers to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, that which is called "clear" regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is termed the Threefold Clarity: first, the clarity of the Bodhisattva; second, the clarity of all Buddhas;
and third, the clarity of non-clarity. The clarity of the Bodhisattva is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā; the clarity of the Buddhas is precisely the Buddha-eye;
and the clarity of non-clarity is precisely ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). For the sake of sentient beings, the practitioner has practiced throughout immeasurable kalpas.

"Born thus, he is one who has perfected all wholesome karmas" means that he clearly perceives the Buddha-nature; for this reason, he is called "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*).
In Sanskrit, this is *vidyācaraṇa*, which has four successive explanations: the first explains it in terms of the feet, while the latter three explain it in terms of fulfillment.
All of these first cite worldly analogies and subsequently apply them to the Buddha to clarify the meaning. This is what is called the "Mantra of Prajñā."

This is the Great Illuminating Mantra (*mahā-vidyā-mantra*). "Through the mantra one attains liberation" means that through it, one is immediately liberated. "Auspiciousness" (*śiva*) is a name for the fruit of *bodhi*;

because one attains *nirvāṇa* through *bodhi*, [it is so named]. Regarding the "Three Illuminations" (*tri-vidyā*): the illumination of the Bodhisattva is the cause, while the illumination of the Buddha is the fruit.

As for "the illumination of non-illumination" (*avidyā-vidyā*), there are three interpretations of its unity: first, non-illumination is delusion (*kleśa*) and illumination is liberation; by employing this illuminating liberation, [one attains the goal].
Because ignorance (*avidyā*) has been severed, it is called "neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance" (*na-vidyā-nāvidyā*).

Second, because the object of ultimate emptiness is neither illumination nor ignorance, yet it is capable of giving rise to both illumination and ignorance, it is called "neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance. Furthermore, there is another interpretation:

the preceding section regarding Bodhisattvas and Buddhas was explained as a distinction, whereas the subsequent mention of "neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance" is explained as non-distinction between Buddha and Bodhi.
"Sak" is non-ignorance (*avidyā*); non-ignorance is itself knowledge (*vidyā*) (and so forth).
What is the fifth name of the Sugata?
What is the meaning of "Sugata"? "Sugata" means one whose excellence is high; "Gata" means not high. O son of good family, this is the worldly meaning.
That which is "high" is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; that which is not "high" is the mind of the Tathāgata.
Son of good family, if the mind were high, it would not be called the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is named the Sugata.
Furthermore, "good" (*su*) refers to the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and "gone" (*gata*) refers to the fruit of the spiritual friend. Son of good family, this is what is meant.
In the worldly sense, a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra) refers to one who has attained the fruit of the initial resolve for enlightenment; this is called Great Parinirvāṇa.
Because the Tathāgata does not abandon his original resolve and has thereby attained Great Nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata is called the "Well-Gone One" (Sugata).
Furthermore, "good" (su-) means excellent, and "gone" (gata) means having proceeded. O son of good family, this is what is meant by "excellent" in the worldly sense.
To perceive the nature of nirvāṇa as existing is called the Great Nirvāṇa. Good son, the nature of nirvāṇa is in reality not existent;
it is only because of the world that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, speak of it as being existent.

Good son, it is like when people in the world who have no children at all say they have children, or when there is no path at all yet they say there is a path—nirvāṇa is also like this, [spoken of] due to [worldly conditions].
For the sake of the world, it is said that there are Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who have attained Great Parinirvāṇa and are therefore called Sugatas.

Their Sanskrit name is Anuttara; they are also called Sugata or Sugatu. There are three successive stages [of explanation], and in the final stage, there is a teaching consisting of the dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis.
Regarding the first, "good" (su) refers to one whose fame is high, as it distinguishes excellence.

Regarding the name "Victorious One" (Jina), though he has transcended birth and death, he does not abandon [sentient beings]; speaking from the perspective of the Buddha-mind, those who serve as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) are themselves the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
What is meant by his sixth title, "Knower of the World" (Lokavid)?
What is meant by "knower of the world"? "World" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). "Knower" refers to knowing all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
because they thoroughly know the five aggregates, they are called "knowers of the world. Furthermore, "world" refers to the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*). "Knower" means being unattached;
because they are unattached to the five desires, they are called "knowers of the world. Furthermore, "world" refers to the immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* [realms] in the eastern direction...
All the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in the Sahā world do not know, see, or understand [the nature of] the Buddhas; the Buddhas alone know, see, and understand them all.
It is the same for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir. For this reason, the Buddha is titled "Knower of the World" (Lokavid).
Furthermore, "the world" refers to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and "knowing" refers to knowing the causes of good and evil for these ordinary beings.
Because this fruit is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but can only be known by a Buddha, the Buddha is therefore titled "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*).
Furthermore, "World" (*loka*) is named "Lotus," and "Knower" (*vid*) is named "Undefiled. Noble son, this is the meaning of "Knower of the World.
The "Lotus" is the Tathāgata; "Undefiled" means that the Tathāgata is not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas.

Because he is unstained by what defiles, the Buddha is therefore titled the "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*). Furthermore, as for the term "Knower of the World," all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "Knower of the World.
Why is this? Because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perceive the world; for this reason, they are named "Knower of the World."
Good son, just as one is called "life" because it arises from food, so too are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
because they perceive the world, they are called "Knower of the World."
In Sanskrit, *lokāyata* refers to the "world. There are three types of worlds: namely, the five aggregates (*skandha*), sentient beings, and the physical realm.
Within these, there are six further categories. Alternatively, there are six kinds of worlds: first, the five aggregates; second, the five desires;
third, the physical realm; fourth, sentient beings; fifth, the designation of the Buddha as the world; and sixth, that which illuminates the world, called the world.
What is the seventh title, "Unsurpassed Being" (*anuttara-pudgala*)?
Why is one called an "Unsurpassed Being"? One who has severed that which was to be severed is called an "Unsurpassed Being.
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess no afflictions, there is nothing for them to sever; therefore, the Buddhas are titled "Unsurpassed Beings."
Furthermore, "the superior person" (uttama-puruṣa) is one who has disputes; "the unsurpassed person" (anuttama-puruṣa) is one who has no disputes.
Since the Tathāgata is without dispute, the Buddha is therefore called the Unsurpassed One. Furthermore, "the superior person" is one whose speech can be subverted;
"the unsurpassed person" is one whose speech cannot be subverted. Since all that the Tathāgata speaks cannot be subverted by any sentient being, he is therefore called the Buddha.
The "Unsurpassed One" (Anuttara) and the "Superior One" (Uttara) are called the Elder (Sthavira). The "Unsurpassed One" is called the Non-Elder (As-thavira).
Among all Buddhas of the three periods of time, there is none who surpasses him; therefore, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed One. "Superior" (Uttara) means new, and "One" (Tara) means old.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the essence of Great Nirvana, which is neither new nor old; therefore, the Buddha is so titled.
He is the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*).
In Sanskrit, he is called *Puruṣa*. There are five successive explanations regarding the meaning of severing or not severing the afflictions (*kleśa*). As the text states:
"The essence of Great Nirvāṇa is neither new nor old," because the Buddhas of the past have already achieved its realization; [and] sentient beings are... [the locus].
When one realizes that there is neither the newly formed nor the new, and thus no old, this is the penetration of the essence of the principle of "presently appropriate.
If one were to speak of conditions as having "new" and "old," this would merely be a matter of what is "already appropriate."
What is the eighth title, "The Tamer" (Damyasārathi)? First, the term *puruṣa* (Great Man) is clarified;
next, *dampasārathi* (Tamer of Men) is clarified. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, clarifying the capacity to tame, which opens the two topical sections.
What is meant by "the Tamer of Men" (purusa-damya-sārathi)? He is himself a man and further tames men.
The one who can tame is the Tathāgata; those who are tamed are sentient beings.
The subsequent explanation of these two sections clarifies that the Tathāgata is in reality not [merely] the one who tames.
Good son, the Tathāgata is truly neither a man nor not a man; it is because he disciplines men that the Tathāgata is called a "man.
He is truly not a man, yet through skillful means he manifests as one who is able to discipline men.
"O son of good family, among all men and women, those who are disciplined by the Śākyas are called 'great men' (puruṣa).
If all men and women possess four qualities, they are named 'great men. What are these four? First, having a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra);
second, being able to listen to the Dharma; third, reflecting upon its meaning; and fourth, practicing according to what has been taught. Son of good family, if..."
Whether man or woman, if one possesses these four qualities, they are called a "true man" (*puruṣa*) or a "good son.
If a man lacks these four qualities, he cannot be called a true man. Why is this? Although his body is that of a man, his conduct is like that of a beast.
Because the Tathāgata tames both men and women, the Buddha is therefore titled the "Tamer of Men" (*purusa-damya-sārathi*).
One who is endowed with four qualities is called a true man; if one lacks these four qualities, his conduct is the same as that of a beast.
The *Mahā-śāstra* also says: "A human-headed deer, or a deer-headed human," and so forth.
Furthermore, good son, there are four ways of driving a horse: first, touching its hair; second, touching its hide;
third, touching its flesh; and fourth, touching its bone. According to what it is touched, the horse obeys the driver’s will.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he tames sentient beings through four kinds of methods. The first is to speak so that they immediately accept the Buddha’s words, as if touching [the horse] by its hair.

1. When it is said that "the hair follows the will of the charioteer," one accepts the Buddha’s words upon hearing [the teaching on] birth and old age, just as the hair and skin follow the will of the charioteer.

2. When it is said that "one accepts the Buddha’s words upon hearing [the teaching on] birth and old age," it is like the hair and skin following the will of the charioteer. 3. When it is said that "one accepts the Buddha’s words upon hearing [the teaching on] birth, old age, and sickness," it is like the hair, skin, and flesh following the will of the charioteer.

4. When it is said that "one accepts the Buddha’s words upon hearing [the teaching on] birth, old age, sickness, and death," it is like the hair, skin, flesh, and bone [following the will of the charioteer].
A good son, just as a charioteer’s training of horses is not invariably fixed, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, tames sentient beings with absolute certainty and never in vain;
therefore, he is titled the Buddha, the Charioteer of Men.
