Just as a horse trainer uses these four methods of instruction to tame horses of differing capacities— whether swift or dull—
so too does the sharp-witted person explain birth to the dull-witted, while explaining old age and death to them; it is like the jackal in the *Mahāśāstra* (and so forth).
What is the ninth title, "Teacher of Gods and Humans"?
Regarding the Teacher of Gods and Humans, there are two kinds of teachers: first, those who teach well; second, those who teach evil.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas always teach all sentient beings by means of wholesome dharmas. What are these wholesome dharmas? They are the virtues of body, speech, and mind. The Buddhas...
The Bodhisattva instructs all sentient beings, saying: "Good sons, you should distance yourselves from unwholesome physical karma.
Why? Because unwholesome physical karma can be distanced, and through such distancing one attains liberation.
Therefore, I instruct you with this Dharma; had this unwholesome karma been impossible to distance for the sake of attaining liberation, I would never have instructed you."
It causes them to remain far removed. It is impossible for any sentient beings who have abandoned evil karma to fall into the three evil realms;
because they are far removed from such deeds, they achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attain Great Nirvāṇa.
For this reason, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly teach and transform sentient beings through this Dharma, and their speech and mind are likewise so. Therefore, they are called "Buddhas."
As an unsurpassed teacher, furthermore, having previously not attained the Way but now having attained it, he preaches to sentient beings the Way he has attained;
having from the beginning not practiced the holy life but now having completed its practice, he preaches to sentient beings the holy life he has practiced himself;
having himself shattered ignorance, he further shatters the ignorance of sentient beings; having himself attained the pure eye, he further [bestows it] upon sentient beings.
He destroys the blindness of sentient beings so that they may obtain pure eyes and personally realize the two truths; furthermore, he expounds the two truths for the sake of sentient beings.

Having attained liberation himself, he further teaches the Dharma of liberation to sentient beings; having crossed the boundless great ocean of birth and death himself, he causes all sentient beings to likewise cross over;
having attained fearlessness himself, he again instructs sentient beings so that they too shall be without fear.
Having personally attained nirvana, he further expounds the Great Nirvana for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed Teacher.
"Heaven" (deva) means day; in heaven, days are long and nights are short, hence it is called heaven.
Furthermore, "heaven" means being free from sorrow and affliction while constantly experiencing bliss, hence it is called heaven. Furthermore, "heaven" is named after the lamp of light.
Because they can destroy darkness and provide great illumination, they are called devas;
furthermore, because they can destroy the darkness of evil karma and are born in the heavens through the power of wholesome karma, they are called devas. Moreover, "deva" means auspicious (*śubha*);
because they are auspicious, they are named devas. Furthermore, "deva" means "sun" (*āditya*); because there is light every day, it is called the sun.
It is for this reason that they are called "devas" (heavenly beings). As for "humans" (*manuṣya*), they are so named because they are capable of much kindness and righteousness;
furthermore, humans are those whose bodies and speech are gentle and supple; furthermore, humans are said to possess pride; furthermore, humans are those who can destroy pride.
Good son, although the Buddhas are the unsurpassed Great Teachers for all sentient beings, it is stated in the sūtras:
Why is he the Teacher of Gods and Humans? Good son, among all sentient beings, only gods and humans are able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
are able to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action, and are able to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*,
the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, the fruit of *arhat*, the path of a *pratyekabuddha*, and [the attainment of] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because he has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddha is therefore titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*).
In the Sanskrit, this is *śāstā deva-mānuṣyāṇām*. There are twelve successive explanations for this: the first two successive explanations explain "Teacher" (*śāstā*);
the next five successive explanations explain "God" (*deva*), all using the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) to explain "God"; and the final four successive explanations explain "Human" (*mānuṣya*).
People say that pride is not evil pride; it is the desire to establish oneself as a great man, to extensively protect the Triple Gem, and furthermore, to be able to destroy arrogance.
Next, another point provides a general explanation of the Teacher of Gods and Humans, as in the text.
What is the meaning of the name "Buddha"? This is the tenth title. First the name is explained, and afterwards his virtues are praised.
What constitutes being a Buddha? "Buddha" means awakening; having awakened oneself, one is further able to awaken others.
Good son, it is like a person who perceives that there is a thief; once the thief is known, he can do no harm. In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to awaken to all things.
Having fully awakened to the immeasurable afflictions and rendered those afflictions powerless, one is therefore called a Buddha.
In Sanskrit, this is *buddha* or *buddhaka*, which translates as "the Awakened One" (*jùzhě* 覺者) or "Awakening to Prior Conditions" (*jùwù qián yuán* 覺悟前緣).
Since the term "Awakened One" carries the same meaning, "Awakening" (*jù* 覺) should be understood as the true [nature]. As for the Pratyekabuddha, it is translated as "Solitary" (*dú* 獨).
To say that awakening does not speak of itself alone but teaches others, saying it awakens both self and others, and further saying that others awaken—this is far too prolix.
Because of this awakening, one is neither born, nor grows old, nor falls ill, nor dies; for this reason, one is called a Buddha.
The Eleventh Section on the Explanation of *Bhagavat*. Some claim this refers to a distinction between "World-Honored One" (*Lokanātha*) and "Bhagavat.
Why? Because the preceding chapter states, "The World-Honored One," and the current chapter explains *Bhagavat*;
therefore, they know it must be so. However, this is likely not the case. "World-Honored One" is called *Lokanātha* in Sanskrit, while Nāgārjuna explained *Bhagavat*.

There are four [qualities]: first, the ability to destroy afflictions; second, possessing merit; third, skillful discernment; and fourth, having a good reputation. These four meanings are now fully presented.
First, one subsequent explanation clarifies the destruction of afflictions; next, one subsequent explanation clarifies the possession of merit;
then, one subsequent explanation clarifies skillful discernment; and finally, one subsequent explanation clarifies the good reputation. This is the first.

1. "Having destroyed the afflictions" (*prahīṇakleśa*) explains that [the Buddha] is visible (*dṛśya*). 2. Furthermore, "having accomplished the lower [qualities]" explains the accomplishment of virtuous dharmas (*guṇasampad*), which is precisely the third [attribute], "possessing merit.

3. Furthermore, "being well-versed in understanding" explains the fourth [attribute], "skillful discernment" (*vibhaktikuśala*). 4. "Possessing great renown" explains the fifth [attribute], "having fame.
Regarding the remaining three [attributes], they belong to the subsequent explanation of merit (*guṇa*); one should know that [this refers to] the Blessed One (*bhagavat*).

There are immeasurable merits; as for the "World-Honored One" (*Lokanātha*), this refers to being honored within [the spiritual community], whereas here it refers to being honored by the world at large.
Now, the term *Bhagavat* is used as a substitute for "World-Honored One," yet it is not simply synonymous with "World-Honored One. This passage contains two meanings:
the first seven explanations cover four meanings, while the subsequent one further exhorts practice.
Regarding the term *Bhagavān*: "Bhaga" means "to break," and "vān" means "afflictions. Because he is able to break afflictions, he is called *Bhagavān*.
Furthermore, because he has accomplished all wholesome dharmas; because he skillfully understands the meaning of all dharmas; because he possesses great merit that cannot be surpassed;
because he possesses great renown that pervades the ten directions; and because he bestows various kinds of great gifts.

Therefore, because they have cast off the female organ for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, O son of good family, whether male or female, those who are able to recollect the Buddha in this manner—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
whether by day or by night; whether in light or in darkness—will always be able to behold the Buddha, the World-Honored One, without being separated from him.
"Good son, why is it that following these two causes for recollecting the Buddha, one wishes to clarify the attainment of the fruit?
This is explained in two parts: first, the inquiry that introduces the topic; second, the formal explanation.
Good son, for what reason is he called the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, up to Bhagavat?"
Thus, he possesses immeasurable merit and great renown.
Within this explanation, there are two parts; first, it clarifies that the six perfections and the four immeasurables serve as the causes.
"Good son, in the past, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Bodhisattva reverently served his parents, preceptors, and [other teachers]..."
The Master, the Elder, the Sthavira, throughout immeasurable kalpas has constantly practiced giving for the sake of sentient beings, upheld the prohibitive precepts, cultivated patience,
diligently applied himself to vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and exercised great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity; therefore,
he has now attained the body of vajra endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Next, it clarifies that the fifty-four moments of mind serve as the cause.
Furthermore, in the past, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Bodhisattva cultivated the faculties of energy, faith, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
he reverently made offerings to his teachers and elders, always seeking the benefit of the Dharma rather than the benefit of food. If the Bodhisattva maintains...

Whether reading or reciting the twelve divisions of the scriptures, one should always act for the sake of sentient beings so that they may attain liberation, peace, and happiness, never acting for one's own sake.

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva constantly cultivates a supramundane mind, a mind of renunciation, an unconditioned mind, a mind free from contention, a mind free from defilement, a mind free from bondage, and a mind free from grasping and attachment.
A mind that is unenveloped; a mind that is not indeterminate; a mind that is not subject to birth and death; a mind free from the net of doubt;
a mind free from greed; a mind free from hatred; a mind free from delusion; a mind free from arrogance; a mind free from turbidity; a mind free from affliction;
a mind free from suffering; an immeasurable mind; a vast mind; an empty mind; a mindless mind; a mind that is neither with nor without mind; a mind that is not undisciplined.

A mind that guards, a mind free from concealment, a mind free from worldly concerns, a mind always in meditative concentration, a mind always practicing cultivation, a mind always liberated, a mind free from retribution,
a mind free from aspiration, a mind of virtuous vows, a mind beyond words, a supple mind, a non-abiding mind, a sovereign mind, an untainted mind,
a mind of the ultimate truth, a non-retrogressive mind, a mind of impermanence, an upright mind, and a mind free from flattery and crookedness.

The mind is pure and wholesome; the mind has neither increase nor decrease; the mind is without solidity; the mind is without the state of an ordinary person; the mind is without the state of a śrāvaka; the mind is without the state of a pratyekabuddha.
It thoroughly knows the realm of the mind, it knows the realm of the arising of the mind, it knows the realm of the abiding of the mind, and it knows the realm of the mastery of the mind.
For this reason, one now attains the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness—permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Therefore, one may be called a Tathāgata, up to and including a Bhagavat; this is what is meant by "a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the Buddha.
Within this context, the so-called "unconditioned mind" does not mean that it is eternally abiding; rather, it means being without activity and without [discursive] mind.

It is the simultaneous relinquishing of both "having no mind" and "no non-mind. Not only is there no mind, but there is also no non-mind, and no mind of indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta-citta*); this is the light.
Zhai says that there are two types of neutral (avyākṛta) states within the fruit of Buddhahood: first, the neutral of cognitive understanding, and second, the neutral of karmic retribution.

This contradicts the present sutra, which states that even while practicing the causes [of enlightenment], one is already without neutrality; how then could there still be neutrality in the fruit of Buddhahood?
As for "a mind without retribution," it means not seeking retribution; as for "a mind without dwelling," it means being free from attachment and fixation.
The mind of constancy has no fixed attachment; the mind of neither-much-nor-little does not favor this while disparaging that;
the mind that knows realms discriminates that all phenomena each have their own distinct boundaries; the mind that knows the realm of birth understands the realm of arising and ceasing;
the mind that knows the realm of abiding understands the realm of eternal, non-extinguishing permanence; and the mind of mastery has no [attachment] toward the permanent.
Those who always and entirely do not give rise to [delusions] regarding the realm of mastery over penetration know the mundane abiding realm;
they know the true mastery and they know the middle.
What is the second mindfulness, the mindfulness of the Dharma? Below is the second mindfulness.
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice the recollection of the Dharma?

A son of good family, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the teachings expounded by all Buddhas as most wondrous and supreme. Because of this Dharma, they are able to cause sentient beings to attain present fruits.
Only this True Dharma is without temporal limitations; it is seen by the Dharma-eye, not by the fleshly eye. Yet, it cannot [be grasped]...
Using analogies as comparisons, for that which is unborn, unarisen, non-abiding, non-ceasing, without beginning, without end, unconditioned, incalculable, and without shelter, he acts as a shelter;
for those without refuge, he acts as a refuge; for ignorance, he acts as illumination; for those who have not reached the further shore, he causes them to reach the further shore;
and for that which is odorless, he acts as an unimpeded fragrance; and for that which is invisible, unmoving, and non-turning—[he acts as such].
It is neither long nor short; it has forever severed all worldly pleasures yet is the bliss of peace and security; it is ultimately subtle and wondrous;
it is non-form yet severs form while still being form, and so on up to non-consciousness yet severs consciousness while still being consciousness;

it is not karma yet severs karma, not fetters yet severs fetters, not entities yet severs entities while still being entities, and not elements yet severs elements while still being elements; it is non-existence yet severs existence.

It exists, yet it is existence that does not enter into cessation; it enters, yet it is entry that does not enter into cessation; it is a cause, yet it is causality that does not enter into cessation;
it is a fruit, yet it is fruition that does not enter into cessation; it is neither empty nor real, yet it is the severance of all reality that constitutes its reality;

it is neither arising nor ceasing, yet it is the eternal severance of arising and ceasing that constitutes its cessation; it is neither characteristic nor non-characteristic, yet it is the severance of the one.
All characteristics are yet characteristics; neither teaching nor non-teaching, yet they are the Teacher; neither fear nor peace, yet they sever all fear and are peace;
neither patience nor impatience, yet they forever sever impatience and are patience;
neither cessation nor non-cessation, yet they sever all cessation and are cessation. They are able to forever [transcend] the summit of all dharmas.

It is the severance of all afflictions, pure and signless, eternally liberated from all signs, the ultimate dwelling place for immeasurable sentient beings, that which can extinguish the blazing fires of all birth and death, and the abode where all Buddhas roam and reside; it is ever-unchanging.
This is called the bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the Dharma.

The old interpretation stated that the first two [stages] involve recollecting dharmas of distinct entities, while only this "True Dharma" (saddharma) below involves recollecting dharmas of a single entity; however, this is not the case here.

The text says: "It is most supreme and most wondrous, able to cause sentient beings to attain present fruits. If one were to judge this by the standards of the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings (zàngtōng), attaining present fruits would not be considered "supreme and wondrous";
conversely, being "supreme and wondrous" would not entail attaining present fruits, as it would take an immeasurable period of time.
One should know that throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, only that which is perfectly sublime can attain manifest fruit; this is the dharma of the perfect single essence.
How does one recollect the Saṅgha? This is the third recollection, as follows.
What is the recollection of the Sangha? The noble Sangha of the Buddhas dwells in accordance with the Dharma, receiving and practicing the upright teaching.
They are invisible, ungraspable, indestructible, and incapable of being harmed; they are inconceivable.
They are the field of merit and blessing for all sentient beings. Although they are a field of merit, they receive nothing and are pure and undefiled.

The untainted and unconditioned is vast, universal, and boundless; its mind is harmonious and supple, equanimous and non-dual, free from turbidity, and eternally immutable—this is called mindfulness of the Sangha.
Traditionally, this is also divided into two parts: first, clarifying the distinct substance where the harmony of the Sangha cannot be seen as a physical entity; next, clarifying their oneness.
The principle of the essence is that harmony with the Saṃgha is not as [you] now explain. The text states: "One receives the upright Dharma.
Among the three teachings, it is not only the Perfect (Cakra) Saṃgha that constitutes the upright Dharma.
How then can the mindfulness of the precepts be the fourth mindfulness?
What is the bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the precepts? The bodhisattva contemplates that the precepts are unbroken, unimpaired, indestructible, and unmixed.
Although they have no form or color, they can be guarded and maintained; although they have no tactile contact, through the skillful cultivation of means, they can be brought to fulfillment.
They are free from fault and are praised by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas. This is the cause for the Great Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa, O son of good family.
Son, it is like the great earth, a ship, a necklace, a great clan, the great ocean,
lye, a house, a sword, a bridge, a skilled physician, a wondrous medicine, an *agada* elixir, a wish-fulfilling jewel, feet, eyes, parents, cool shade,
something that cannot be stolen by thieves, something that cannot be harmed, something that fire cannot burn, something that water cannot float away, and a great mountain ladder.
"O all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, regarding this sublime jewel banner of victory: if one abides in these precepts and attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*, I too have a share in that;
yet I do not require it. Why? Because if I were to attain this fruit of *srotāpanna*, I would be unable to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
However, if one abides in these precepts and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I [do require it]."

Furthermore, there is a portion that is what I desire. Why is this? Because if I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall extensively expound the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings and act as their refuge;
this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the precepts (*śīla-smṛti*).
Although it lacks form and color, those who uphold it may regard it as the "unmanifest precept" (*avijñapti-śīla*). Regarding this, there are three interpretations:
First, the Mahāsāṃghika school maintains that because there is no such thing as unmanifest matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), there is naturally no unmanifest [precept], nor is the unmanifest itself matter;
rather, it exists solely as a mental state, and thus it is said to be "upholdable. Second, the Sarvāstivāda school maintains that there is unmanifest [matter].
This matter of "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) is that which people of the Saṃmitīya school employ; thus, while it exists inherently without being produced, it is nonetheless a form (*rūpa*).
This form is not a material obstruction (*sapratigha*), yet because there is an unmanifest, provisional form (*prajñaptirūpa*), one must maintain it through restraint.

The Sarvāstivādins, such as those of the Mahīśāsaka school who rely on the *Abhidharmasamayapradīpikā-śāstra*, maintain that this unmanifest is neither form nor mind. These various explanations are all points of contention and are merely minor [disputes].
Since our own school’s treatises on the existence or non-existence of the Mahāyāna do not clarify this at all, the preceding passage states:
"Contaminated phenomena are of two kinds, namely, form and non-form. Non-form phenomena consist of the mind and mental factors;
form phenomena consist of earth, water, fire, and wind. When, then, could there be such a thing as "unmanifest form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*)?
What is the fifth mindfulness, the mindfulness of giving?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the mindfulness of giving? They deeply contemplate that this giving is the cause of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
that the Buddhas and bodhisattvas have personally approached and cultivated such generosity, and that they themselves shall do likewise.
If one does not practice the cultivation of close association through giving, one cannot adorn the fourfold assembly;
although such giving may not ultimately sever the fetters, it can eliminate and destroy present afflictions.

By virtue of the causes and conditions of giving, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is constantly praised by the sentient beings of immeasurable, boundless worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
When a Bodhisattva gives food to sentient beings, he bestows upon them their very life; through this karmic fruit, at the time he attains Buddhahood, he is eternally unchanging.
Because he bestowed happiness, when he becomes a Buddha, he attains peace and bliss.

When a Bodhisattva gives, he seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and does not encroach upon others' offerings; for this reason, upon attaining Buddhahood, he achieves pure Nirvana. When a Bodhisattva gives...

It causes all sentient beings to obtain [what they need] without seeking; therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, one obtains self-mastery. By the causal conditions of giving, one enables others to obtain power;
therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, one obtains the ten powers (*daśabala*). By the causal conditions of giving, one enables others to obtain speech;
therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, one obtains the four kinds of unhindered knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cultivate this giving as the cause for *nirvāṇa*.
I also practice giving in this same way as a cause for nirvāṇa, as explained at length in the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*.
Regarding the statement that one cultivates the causes of goodness, the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra* says:
"In the *Saṃpuṣpita*, I have already taught this for Samantabhadra, Bhadramukha, and others; in this land, there is no *Saṃpuṣpita* sūtra, but only the *Avataṃsaka*. Or...
This refers to the *Saṃpuṣpita* Sūtra, which does not come to this land; one version states that the *Saṃpuṣpita* is the *Avataṃsaka*.
How is it that "recalling the world" is the sixth recollection?
What is the recollection of the devas? There are the abodes of the Four Great Kings up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception.
If one possesses faith, one has a share in attaining the abode of the Four Great Kings;

if one possesses much learning, generosity, and wisdom, one has a share in attaining the abodes of the Four Great Kings up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception. Yet, these are not what I desire.
Why is this? Because the realms from the Four Great Kings up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception are all impermanent.
Because they are impermanent, there is birth, old age, sickness, and death. For this reason, these are not what I desire;
they are like magical illusions that deceive the foolish, but do not delude or entice those with wisdom. That which is like a magical illusion refers precisely to the Four Great Kings.
From the realms up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the foolish are all ordinary worldlings; I am not like these foolish ordinary worldlings.
I have heard that there is the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-deva*), namely the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who are eternal and unchanging.
Because they abide eternally, they are neither born, nor do they age, nor fall ill, nor die. For the sake of sentient beings, I exert myself with diligence.

To seek the ultimate celestial realm (*paramārtha-deva*). Why? Because the ultimate celestial realm enables sentient beings to eliminate and sever afflictions (*kleśa*), just like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*).
If I possess faith, up to and including wisdom, then I shall be able to attain this ultimate celestial realm.
I shall extensively analyze and explain the ultimate celestial realm for the sake of sentient beings; this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Son of good family, this mindfulness of the devas is called the supramundane Bodhisattva, not the mundane.
It is that which the world does not know, see, or awaken to, yet it is that which the Bodhisattva knows, sees, and awakens to."

Some claim that the "heaven of the ultimate fruit" (*paramārtha-deva*) refers to future fruition; however, we say this is not so. The general recollection of all heavens is simply the recollection of devas themselves;

it does not refer to future fruition. Since the heaven of future fruition is no different from the aforementioned fruit of Buddhahood, it is precisely the general recollection of the celestial realms of this world that is established as distinct according to their specific meanings, and thus is called "heaven."

"Good son," the following constitutes the second major section, which praises the text of the sūtra. This is divided into two parts: first, within this fascicle, praising the sūtra for its capacity to generate goodness;
second, in the subsequent two fascicles, praising its capacity to extinguish evil. Regarding the initial section on generating goodness, it consists of three parts:

first, a direct praise of the sūtra; second, a praise of those who propagate the sūtra; and third, a praise of its rise and decline. The sequence of these three is due to the Five Elements (*pañca-dhātu*).
To further manifest the Way, there are those who sacrifice their own bodies to propagate it; because people propagate it, the Way flourishes, and because they do not propagate it, it declines.
This first section, which formally praises the sutra, is divided into two parts: first, the Tathāgata’s praise, and second, Kāśyapa’s acceptance.

"Good son, if my disciples were to claim that there is no difference between upholding, reciting, copying, expounding, and explaining the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), and upholding, reciting, copying, expounding, and explaining the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, this is not so. Why is this?
Good son, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is, in fact, all [the teachings]..."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a most profound secret treasury;
because this profound secret treasury of all Buddhas is supreme, sons of good family, for this reason the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is most marvelous, most extraordinary, and inconceivable.

In the initial praise within the middle section, it says that which is not reached by the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) has two interpretations: first, it refers to the twelve divisions of the Hīnayāna;

second, it refers to the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna, yet even these do not reach the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, for the Mahāyāna Vaipulya is superior as it accords with the specific capacities of those to be taught.
Furthermore, within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* there are the twelve divisions, yet it is not necessarily the case that [the same applies] within the twelve divisions themselves.
Because there is nirvāṇa, it is superior. Now, it is clarified that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is superior to the twelve distinct [teachings] in twelve ways.
From "Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha" onwards is the second section, the Comprehension and Understanding.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I also know that this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is most extraordinary and most..."
Furthermore, the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are inconceivable; the Bodhisattva, Bodhi, and Great Parinirvāṇa are likewise inconceivable.
From this point, based on the meaning of why [the Buddha] did so, the second section—praising the propagation of the teaching—is divided into three parts, the first of which is a question.
The two responses and three inquiries are as stated in the text.
For what reason did the World-Honored One further state that a bodhisattva is inconceivable?
Next, the Buddha answered by praising the bodhisattva for having thirteen inconceivable qualities: first, the ability to resolve upon enlightenment; second, receiving...
1. Suffering from the three types of sensation within birth and death; 2. Suffering in the hells; 3. Returning to rescue others; 4. Never retreating; 5.
Crossing the ocean of birth and death; 6. Being able to weigh and measure birth and death; 7. Being able to preach the eternally abiding;
8. Not being troubled by birth and death; 9. Not being confused while in the womb; 10. Not being stingy with the Dharma; 11. Remaining far removed from the ten evil deeds. (10)
Regarding the third point, "inconceivable through the forgetting of effort": the old interpretation states that this means "that which people cannot fathom. This meaning is not correct;
for if all worldly matters were unfathomable, could they then be equated with the sages and worthies?
Here we clarify that the three truths are mutually identical and cannot be conceived as one, two, or three. Where the activities of the mind cease, they likewise cannot be constructed as three.
Secondly, it is said that the path of speech is cut off; although thirteen items are enumerated, they are not actually numbers, and this is called "inconceivable.
Good son, there is no teacher who instructs the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, yet he is able to spontaneously give rise to the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).

Having already resolved their minds, they diligently cultivate vigor; even if a great fire were to burn their bodies and heads, they would never seek rescue nor abandon their mindfulness of the Dharma.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas constantly reflect:
"Throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, whether in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, or devas, I have been consumed by the fires of the various fetters."
Throughout all that has been burned away, I have never once attained a single definitive dharma;
for "definitive dharma" is precisely Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall never cherish or spare my body, mind, or life;
for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, even if I were to be shattered into pieces...
His body is like a mote of dust, yet he never abandons diligent vigor. Why is this?
Because the mind of diligent vigor is itself the cause of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Son of good family, if such a bodhisattva is thus able to disregard even his own body and life before he has seen *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how much more so [will he do so] once he has attained it?
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva is therefore inconceivable.

Regarding the first inconceivability, it is said that there is no one who instructs them, yet they are able to resolve their minds on enlightenment spontaneously. If they resolve their minds on enlightenment by taking the ultimate truth as their object, they fall into the category of the Śrāvaka;

for that reason, instruction by another is required. If they resolve their minds on enlightenment by taking conventional reality as their object, they fall into the category of conceptual discrimination; for that reason, instruction regarding the objective realm is required.
None of these can be called "inconceivable. If one contemplates the Middle Way where the three truths are mutually identical, then it is neither the True nor the Conventional;
because it does not arise from the realm of persons, it is said that there is no person who teaches. Because one clearly realizes the Buddha-nature, it is said that it arises spontaneously.
Being unmixed, it is called "pure"; entering the stream, it is called "progressing. Hell here refers to the fruits of birth and death, while the various fetters refer to [the causes].
I cite the causes of birth and death: for kalpas on end, one has been burned by these causes and effects.

Now, to understand birth and death is itself nirvana; to understand all fetters is itself bodhi. Because these are no longer two extremes, they are called "one. Because movement and stillness are not destroyed, it is called "definitive.
Whether burning the body or breaking the head, there is nothing that is not the right path; internally one does not abandon the Way, nor externally.

Not seeking rescue refers to the clarification of the inconceivable arising of the mind based on the three truths; this is identical in meaning to the intention of arousing the mind within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Next is the second inconceivable.
Furthermore, the immeasurable faults and afflictions of birth and death perceived by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are inconceivable, as they are beyond the reach of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Although they know these immeasurable faults and afflictions of birth and death, for the sake of sentient beings, they undergo suffering therein without giving rise to weariness or detachment; therefore, they are further called "inconceivable."
The text states: "That which is seen—the immeasurable faults and afflictions of birth and death—is beyond the reach of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, who do not give rise to weary detachment.
This means that the Two Vehicles only know a small portion of the *pariccheda* (segmented) death, and do not know the faults of the *pariṇāma* (transformative) death;

because the Bodhisattva surpasses them, it is said they "do not reach" [this level]. Furthermore, "not reaching" refers to the conventional truth within the Middle Way, while "not giving rise to weary detachment" refers to the Middle Way itself.
Because of the ultimate and the conventional, it is said that they are not separate; regarding the illumination of the three truths, the wisdom of clarity is inconceivable.
This is identical in intent to the method of settling the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
For the sake of sentient beings, although a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva undergoes various sufferings and afflictions even while in hell, it is like being in the third dhyāna.
Because it is blissful, it is further called "inconceivable.
The third passage on the inconceivable states, "experiencing the suffering of hell as the bliss of the third dhyāna";
this text is extremely brief and should also state that "experiencing the suffering of the three realms as the bliss of nirvāṇa. This refers to the obstacles upon the three truths.
This "clarifying the inconceivable" shares the same intent as the "passage and obstruction" of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and is also like great compassion.
Good son, it is like an elder whose house has caught fire; having seen it, the elder has emerged from the house, but his children remain behind, not yet freed from the danger of the fire.
At that time, the elder certainly knows of the harm of the fire, yet for the sake of his children, he turns back.
Returning to provide rescue while disregarding the hardships, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise:
although he knows that birth and death abound with faults and evils, for the sake of sentient beings he dwells therein without weariness; therefore, he is further named "inconceivable."
The fourth inconceivable passage states: "Like the elder rescuing his children from the burning house. This refers to the Middle Way, hence it says "returning.
The burning refers to the conventional truth, hence it says "the fire breaks out. The exiting refers to the ultimate truth, hence it says "leaving the house.

This clarifies the inconceivable through the practice of the three truths; its intent regarding true and correct compassion is identical to that of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Calming and Contemplation).
"Good son, immeasurable sentient beings who have resolved upon bodhicitta may, upon seeing the many faults and evils within saṃsāra, immediately fall back or become śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
However, if there are bodhisattvas who hear this sutra, they will never lose their bodhicitta or become śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Thus, although such bodhisattvas..."
Furthermore, although they have not yet reached the first Immovable Bhūmi, their minds are firm and steadfast without any regression or decline; for this reason, it is further called "inconceivable.
The fifth inconceivable passage states: "Seeing all sentient beings weary of the faults of birth and death, they regress into duality."

The Bodhisattva’s vehicle is not like this: he understands that birth and death are eternal and does not perceive their faults; he knows that Nirvana is near and does not regress to take up the Lesser Vehicle.
This is demonstrated by means of the Three Truths as being inconceivable; its intent is the same as that of the "Chapter on the Path" in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
“Good son, if someone were to proclaim, ‘I am able to float across the waters of the great ocean,’ would such a statement be conceivable?
“World-Honored One, such a statement might be conceivable or it might not be conceivable. “For what reason?
If a human being were to cross over, that would be inconceivable; if an asura were to cross over, that would be conceivable. “Good son...”
"Son, I do not speak of asuras; I speak specifically of humans, World-Honored One.
Among humans, there are those who are inconceivable and those who are conceivable. World-Honored One, there are two kinds of people:
first, the noble ones (ārya), and second, ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana). Ordinary worldlings are inconceivable, while noble ones are conceivable. "Excellent!"
"Son of good family, I say that this applies to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), not to noble ones (*ārya*).
World-Honored One, if ordinary persons are truly inconceivable, then, son of good family, ordinary persons truly cannot cross the great ocean;
yet a bodhisattva can indeed cross that great ocean of birth and death. For this reason, they are further called 'inconceivable.'"
The sixth inconceivable passage states: "The supernatural powers of the sages are like the wisdom of the essence-dharma; the growth of the asuras is like sequential wisdom.
That humans, though lacking these two [types of power], are nonetheless able to attain deliverance is like the wisdom of the Perfect Teaching.

Being neither sequential nor gradual, it is precisely the perfect wisdom that effects deliverance. This explains the inconceivability in terms of the stages of the three truths, and it corresponds to *śamatha*.
The intent of this contemplation on successive stages is the same.
"Good son, if there were someone who could suspend Mount Sumeru with a single fiber from the root of a lotus, would that be conceivable?
"No, World-Honored One. "Good son, in a single moment of thought, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to weigh [the weight of] all things."
All of birth and death is therefore further named "inconceivable.

Regarding the seventh inconceivable, the text says: "Suspending a mountain on a lotus fiber and weighing birth and death in a single thought-moment" means that one measures the infinite within the one and the one within the infinite; it is neither one nor infinite. This is based upon...
The illumination of the Dharma of the three truths is inconceivable; this is identical in meaning to the wondrous object of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Good son, although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas constantly contemplated birth-and-death as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure, they nevertheless analyze and expound for sentient beings [the truths of] permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Although it is explained in this way, it is not a false view; therefore, it is further called "inconceivable.
The eighth inconceivable passage states: "That which is impermanent, non-blissful, non-self, and impure—I teach as permanent, blissful, self, and pure.

This is like prescribing medicine according to the illness to meet the needs of those to be trained. This refers to the inconceivability of the teaching of the Three Truths, and it corresponds to *śamatha*.
The intention behind the remedies within these contemplations is the same.
Good son, it is like a person who enters water but cannot be drowned by the water, or enters a great blazing fire but cannot be burned by the fire;
such matters are inconceivable. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: although he dwells within birth and death, [he is not defiled].
Because one is not afflicted or harmed by birth and death, it is further called "inconceivable.
The text regarding the ninth inconceivable state says, "neither drowning nor burning," meaning that although one remains within birth and death,
one is not harmed by them.
Good son, there are three grades of persons: superior, middling, and inferior. When a person of the inferior grade first enters the womb, they think:
"I am now dwelling in a latrine, a place where all impurities gather, amidst corpses, within a thicket of thorns, and in great darkness.
When they first emerge from the womb, they again think: "I have now emerged from a latrine, a place of various foul impurities."
Upon emerging from the midst of the great darkness, those of middling capacity think to themselves:
"I have now entered a grove of various trees, a river of pure fruit, and dwellings within houses and mansions; my emergence is likewise so. Those of superior capacity think to themselves:
"I have ascended a celestial hall, stayed amidst flowering groves, ridden horses and elephants, and climbed high mountains; my emergence is likewise so."
The time is likewise inconceivable: when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first enters the womb, he knows he is entering; while dwelling there, he knows he is dwelling;
and when leaving, he knows he is leaving. He does not give rise to thoughts of greed or hatred, yet he has not yet attained the stage of the first abiding.
For this reason, it is further called inconceivable.
The tenth inconceivable passage states, "Remaining undisturbed while in the womb. The former [passage] indicates that death cannot extinguish it;

this indicates that the womb cannot produce it. This is explained in terms of the retribution of the Three Truths as being inconceivable, and its intent is the same as that of "patience" (kṣānti) within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation).
"Good son, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi truly cannot be compared by means of analogies.
Good son, the mind likewise cannot be compared by means of any analogy;
yet it can be said that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, without having a teacher from whom to receive instruction, is able to attain this Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Having attained this Dharma, Bodhi has no stinginess in heart and constantly expounds it for the sake of sentient beings;
therefore, it is named "inconceivable.
The eleventh inconceivable passage states: "Bodhi and the mind are both ineffable; yet they are spoken of."

This lack of parsimony is explained in terms of the three truths; the silence [of the Buddha] clarifies that which is inconceivable. This is identical in intent to the principles of "stagnation" and "penetration" found throughout the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation).
Good son, there are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose physical seclusion is not their verbal seclusion, and those whose verbal seclusion is not their physical seclusion.

There is that which is neither of body nor speech, yet is a distancing from the body; this refers to abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, which is called distancing from the body.
Distancing from speech refers to abstaining from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter; this is called distancing from speech.
That which is neither of body nor speech, yet is also a distancing, refers to what is called distancing from greed and envy.
O son of good family, anger and wrong views are called "neither body nor speech," yet they are the distancing [from them].
O son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive even a single dharma as being the body, as being karma, or as a master of distancing; yet there is still distancing.
For this reason, it is further called inconceivable. Speech is also like this. O son of good family, from the body one distances oneself from the body.
"Departing from the mouth through the mouth and departing through wisdom—this is neither of body nor of mouth.
The twelfth inconceivable passage states, "departing from the body through the body," and so forth. This explains the inconceivable by means of the karma of the three truths;
its intent is identical to that of the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" (*pōfǎbiàn*) within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation).
"Noble son, although this wisdom truly exists, it cannot cause a bodhisattva to become detached. Why is this?
Noble son, there is not a single dharma that can destroy or create the nature of conditioned phenomena, nor can it cause them to arise differently or cease differently.
For this reason, this wisdom cannot bring about detachment. Noble son, wisdom cannot shatter; fire cannot burn; and water cannot rot."
The wind cannot move it; the earth cannot support it; birth cannot give rise to it; old age cannot age it; abiding cannot cause it to abide;
destruction cannot destroy it; greed cannot make it greedy; hatred cannot make it hateful; delusion cannot make it deluded.

Because conditioned phenomena are by nature different in their arising and different in their ceasing, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva never gives rise to the thought: "By means of this wisdom, I shall shatter all..."
While still possessed of afflictions (*kleśa*), one says of oneself, "I have destroyed the afflictions. Although one speaks thus, it is not false;
for this reason, it is further called inconceivable (*acintya*).
The thirteenth inconceivable passage states: "One never says, 'I have destroyed the afflictions. This refers to—
The three truths are without subject or object of illumination and are inconceivable; this is identical in intent to the "detachment from craving" found within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

This sutra clarifies that for a bodhisattva at the initial stage who has not yet entered the [bodhisattva] positions, the meaning of inconceivability corresponds to the ten contemplations of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) bodhisattvas in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* treatise. Therefore, to explain this passage, it is said: "Wisdom cannot shatter [it]."

Fire cannot burn it; thus, because the true dharma fundamentally employs true wisdom as a single mind, it cannot destroy the continuity of dharmas—namely, the two minds where the former ceases and the latter arises.

Therefore, it can destroy delusions and further strike down [false] wisdom. Once delusions have been severed, there is nothing further to attack or strike; thus, it cannot [further] act upon the true dharma.

To decisively address this, the praise of the Bodhisattva’s propagation of the sutra is not dependent on the provisional or the real; it is simply because wisdom is sought and yet cannot be apprehended.
Thus, it is said that wisdom cannot destroy [afflictions]. For example, because greed and delusion are sought and cannot be apprehended, there is neither greed nor delusion.

Furthermore, arising does not arise from arising, and ceasing does not cease through ceasing; because ceasing does not cease through ceasing, ceasing gives rise to arising, and arising cannot give rise to arising.
Furthermore, if birth were permanent, it should not cease; if cessation were itself ceasing, it should not cease.
All phenomena are likewise so. Herein, there is a direct praise that all phenomena are non-existent, and wisdom likewise does not abide in their marks.
The section concerning the three Kāśyapas follows the text as written.

Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is only now that I have come to know that the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the inconceivable Buddha-dharma, the Saṃgha, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, and those who receive and uphold it, as well as their bodhi and nirvāṇa, are [inconceivable]."
Contemplation.
This is the third section, "Praising the Arising and Decline of the World-Honored One’s Unsurpassed Buddha-Dharma," which contains four questions and answers: first, the Buddha-dharma of Śākyamuni;
second, the Buddha-dharma of Kāśyapa; third, all Buddha-dharmas; and fourth, a concluding summary of the Buddha-dharma of Śākyamuni.
The initial question and answer are as stated in the text. [The question asks:
"World-Honored One, for how long will the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma abide, and after how much time will it perish?
In the response, there are two parts: first, it clarifies that if one practices the five dharmas, [the Dharma] will flourish; if one frequently violates the precepts, it will perish.
Good son, if there is even one who possesses these five practices in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra— namely, the noble practice, the Brahma practice, the celestial practice,
the practice of illness, and the practice of an infant— and if my disciples are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, copy,
and explain its meaning for the sake of all sentient beings, they shall be honored, respected, praised, and provided with various offerings by them.
Know that at that time the Buddha-dharma has not yet perished.

Good son, when this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is fully circulated, my disciples at that time will for the most part violate the prohibitions and precepts, commit various evils, and be unable to respect or have faith in such a sūtra; because they lack faith, [they will reject it].
If one is unable to receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or explain its meaning, and is not respected or even provided for by the multitude,
yet instead sees those who do uphold it and treats them with contempt, slanders, and reviles them, saying, "You are one of the six heretical teachers,
not a disciple of the Buddha," you should know that the Buddha-dharma will soon perish.
Next, Kāśyapa again addressed [the Buddha] regarding the clarification of the Buddha-dharma, which also consists of a question and answer. The initial question has two parts:
first, acknowledging the intent; second, the actual inquiry. Regarding the first part:
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I have personally received this teaching from the Buddha. Kāśyapa—
The Buddha-dharma will remain in the world for seven days and then perish entirely.
The *Bhadra-kalpika Sūtra* states that the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha remained in the world for twenty years;

as for the present statement that it remains for seven days, during those seven days it is no different from when the Buddha was still present, but after the seven days, the Buddha-dharma will become corrupted and degenerate, unlike when he was alive.
At that time, the twenty-year-old Mingzhu asked about the duration [of the teaching].
Kāśyapa Tathāgata’s second question, which consists of two parts, first raises the difficulty regarding whether it exists or not:
"World-Honored One, does Kāśyapa Tathāgata possess this sutra?"
Next is the double refutation:
If it exists, how can you say it is extinguished? If it does not exist, why do you say that the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is the secret treasury of all Tathāgatas?
The Buddha replied in two parts: first, he generally clarified that there is both cessation and non-cessation; second, he directly answered the question asked.
Within the initial general response, there are again two sections: first, a concession; second, the actual general response. The Buddha said:
"Good son, I previously stated that only Mañjuśrī understands this meaning; now I shall explain it further."
It says: "Listen with a sincere mind.

Regarding the beginning and middle, the statement that "Mañjuśrī is the one who understands" refers to the verse on "that which originally existed but now does not," intended to clarify that extinction is non-extinction, and non-extinction is extinction.
Next, the internal characteristics of the response can be seen in general.
Son of good family, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess two kinds of dharmas: first, worldly dharmas; second, the dharma of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Worldly dharmas are subject to extinction, whereas the dharma of the ultimate truth is indestructible. Furthermore, there are two [other] kinds: first, the non-existent...
Regarding permanence, self, bliss, and purity: if one possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity, there is no destruction;

whereas if one possesses impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity, there is destruction. Furthermore, there are two kinds: that which is maintained by the Two Vehicles and that which is maintained by Bodhisattvas.
That which is maintained by the Two Vehicles undergoes destruction, while that which is maintained by Bodhisattvas... [does not].
When maintained, there is no destruction or cessation. Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, the external; second, the internal-external.

External phenomena are subject to destruction and cessation, whereas internal phenomena are not subject to destruction and cessation. Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Conditioned phenomena are subject to destruction and cessation, whereas unconditioned phenomena are without destruction or cessation. Furthermore, there are two kinds.
First, there is that which can be obtained and that which cannot be obtained. Phenomena that can be obtained are subject to destruction and cessation;

phenomena that cannot be obtained are without destruction or cessation. Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, common phenomena (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and second, uncommon phenomena (*asādhāraṇadharma*).
Common phenomena are subject to destruction; uncommon phenomena are without destruction. Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, among humans, and second, among devas.
Among humans there is destruction and cessation, whereas among devas there is no destruction or cessation. Furthermore, there are two kinds [of scriptures]: first, the eleven divisions of the sūtras;
second, the Vaipulya sūtras. The eleven divisions of the sūtras are subject to destruction and cessation, whereas the Vaipulya scriptures are not subject to destruction or cessation.
Good son, if my disciples receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain, and revere the Vaipulya scriptures...
One should know that when there is offering, respect, and praise, at that time the Buddha-dharma does not perish.
Next, son of good family, regarding your previous question, here follows the second part: the direct answer to the question, which consists of four sections:

first, clarifying that there were sūtras from previous Buddhas; second, clarifying that it is unnecessary to expound them further; third, the present Buddha’s comparative elucidation; and fourth, the Dharma itself.
In truth, this initial clarification does not negate it; there is indeed a sūtra from a previous Buddha.
"Good son, as to what you have just asked—whether the Tathāgata Kāśyapa possessed this sūtra or not—good son, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
Why is this? Although the Buddhas possess eleven [aspects]..."

The various divisions of the sutras do not speak of the Buddha-nature, nor do they speak of the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, nor that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not enter ultimate nirvana.
For this reason, this sutra is named the "Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata. Because it is not spoken of in the eleven divisions of the sutras, it is called a "treasury" (*kośa*).
It is like a person's seven treasures that are not brought out for external use; such is called a treasury. Well said.
Just as a man stores up these goods for the sake of future needs— namely, when grain is expensive, when enemies invade the country,
when one encounters a wicked king and must ransom his life, or when roads are treacherous and wealth is difficult to obtain—
he then brings them out and uses them; so too, O son of good family, is the secret treasury of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, when such evils appear in the world— such as wicked bhikṣus of future ages who possess impure things,
preach to the fourfold assembly that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate nirvāṇa, and recite worldly treatises while showing no respect for the Buddha’s sūtras— the Tathāgata,
desiring to extinguish these evils and cause them to distance themselves from wrong livelihood and gain, [acts as follows].

When this comes, it shall expound this sutra. If this treasury of secret teachings of the sutra were to perish and not appear in the world, you should know that at such a time the Buddha-dharma would have perished.
Son of good family, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is eternally unchanging;
how can you ask whether this sutra existed during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha?
Next, noble son, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the following two points clarify that there was no need for further exposition:
Noble son, at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, all sentient beings had attenuated desire and abundant wisdom;
the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were gentle and easy to transform, possessed great majestic power, and held total retention (*dhāraṇī*) such that they never forgot, like a great [ocean].
In the world-realm of Elephant King, all sentient beings clearly know that the Tathāgata will never ultimately enter parinirvāṇa, but remains eternally present and unchanging;
although this scripture exists there, it need not be expounded.
I shall now distinguish [the characteristics of] the sentient beings of this world for you, O Son of Good Family.
The sentient beings of this world have many afflictions, are deluded and forgetful, lack wisdom, and are ensnared by many doubts;
their faculty of faith is not established, and the world is impure. All sentient beings say that the Tathāgata does not exist.
Constantly undergoing transformation, it ultimately enters Great Parinirvāṇa; for this reason, the Tathāgata expounds this scripture.
Good son, Kāśyapa, the Buddha-dharma is in truth not extinguished. Why? Because it is eternal and unchanging.

Good son, if there are sentient beings who perceive a self where there is no self, perceive no-self where there is a self, perceive permanence where there is impermanence, or perceive impermanence where there is permanence—[for them, the Dharma is not extinguished].
To perceive pleasure as non-pleasure and non-pleasure as pleasure; to perceive the pure as impure and the impure as pure;

to perceive the non-extinguished as extinguished and the extinguished as non-extinguished; to perceive what is not a transgression as a transgression and a transgression as not a transgression; to perceive light offenses as heavy and heavy offenses as light;
to perceive vehicles as non-vehicles and non-vehicles as vehicles; to perceive the path as non-path and non-path as path—this is truly Bodhi.

To see what is not Bodhi as Bodhi, and to see what is truly not Bodhi as Bodhi, is Bodhi. To see suffering as not suffering, to see the origin as not the origin, to see cessation as not cessation, and to see reality as not reality—yet where reality is indeed reality—is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

To see the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as the conventional truth, and to see the ultimate truth as the conventional truth, is to take refuge in what is not a refuge; to see what is not a refuge as a refuge. That which is called "the Buddha’s true word" is, in fact, Māra.
To take the words of Māra as the words of the Buddha—this is precisely when the Buddhas preach the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
It would be better to speak of the four clarities (caturvidha-vidyā) found beneath the mosquito’s mouth; these are truly imperishable.
Noble son, one might as well say that mosquitoes and gadflies can exhaust the depths of the great ocean as say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata will perish;
one might as well say that a rope can bind and restrain a violent wind as say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata will perish;

one might as well say that one can blow upon Mount Sumeru with the mouth to scatter and destroy it as say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata will perish; one might as well say that lotuses grow within a fire of khadira wood.
One cannot say that the Tathāgata’s Dharma has perished; rather, one might as well say that an *agada* medicine is poison. One cannot say that the Tathāgata’s Dharma has perished;
rather, one might as well say that the moon can be made hot and the sun can be made cold. One cannot say that the Tathāgata’s Dharma has perished;
rather, one might as well say that the four great elements each abandon their own nature. One cannot say that the Tathāgata’s Dharma...

[The Buddha] said, "Extinction. Good son, when a Buddha first appears in the world, he expounds the third penetration, clarifying that all Buddha-dharmas consist of six pairs of contrasting categories:
those whose meaning is understood and those whose meaning is not understood."
Good son, if after the Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,

there were no disciples who could understand the profound meaning and the World-Honored One were to enter *parinirvāṇa* immediately, you should know that this Dharma would not abide long in the world.
Furthermore, good son, if after the Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...
First, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning; even though the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, one should know that this Dharma will long abide in the world.
Second, there are those with patrons and those without patrons.

Furthermore, son of good family, if when a Buddha first appears and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning but lack sincere faith, and there are no white-robed lay donors (*upāsaka*) who revere the Buddha-dharma, then the Buddha will enter parinirvāṇa;
you should know that in such a case, this Dharma will not abide long in the world. Furthermore, son of good family, if when a Buddha first appears...
Once you have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, your disciples will understand the most profound meanings,

and there will be many lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) with sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma; even after your parinirvāṇa, you should know that the Buddha-dharma will abide long in the world.
Third, for the sake of benefit rather than for the sake of profit.
Furthermore, son of good family, when a Buddha first appears in the world and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are already disciples who understand the profound meaning;
although there are lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) of sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, if the disciples who expound the Dharma preach for the sake of gain and offerings rather than for the sake of *nirvāṇa*, and the Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa, you should know that this Dharma will not remain long in the world.
Moreover, son of good family, if when the Buddha first appeared and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there were disciples who understood the profound meaning and possessed firm faith; yet...
When lay devotees revere the Buddha-dharma and its disciples, whatever they preach will not be for the sake of seeking gain or offerings, but for the sake of seeking nirvana;
even though the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, you should know that this Dharma shall long abide in the world.
Fourth, [the category of] giving rise to disputes and not giving rise to disputes.
Furthermore, son of good family, if when a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and there are also lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) of sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma;
Furthermore, when the disciples frequently engage in disputes and litigation, mutually asserting right and wrong, and the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa,
you should know that this Dharma will not long remain in the world. Moreover, son of good family, if at the time the Buddha first appears and attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
there are already disciples who understand the profound meaning, as well as lay donors of pure faith.
Those disciples who revere the Buddha’s Dharma and practice the dharma of harmony and respect— neither disputing nor contradicting one another, but instead honoring each other—
should know that even though the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, this Dharma will abide for a long time without perishing.
Fifth, the fault of speaking what should not be spoken.

Furthermore, son of good family, if when a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and there are also devout lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) who revere the Buddha-dharma; yet...
Those disciples, for the sake of the Great Nirvāṇa, preach the Dharma and treat one another with mutual respect, yet they do not give rise to disputes;
however, they store all manner of impure things and further praise themselves, saying, "I have attained the fruit of a Srotāpanna, up to and including the fruit of an Arhat.
When the Buddha has entered Nirvāṇa, you should know that this Dharma will not remain in the world for long. Furthermore, O son of good family:
If, my son, when a Buddha first appears in the world and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and there are lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) of sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma;
and if those disciples expound the sūtras and dharmas for the sake of the Great Nirvāṇa, skillfully cultivating harmony and respect, honoring one another, and not storing up any possessions—
Even those who possess impure things do not claim for themselves to have attained the stage of Srotāpanna up to Arhatship;
yet one should know that although that Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa, this Dharma shall long abide in the world.
Sixth, the teaching of diversity and the teaching of non-diversity.
Furthermore, son of good family, when a Buddha first appears in the world and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
he already has disciples who do not even keep impure things and do not themselves claim to have attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Even up to the Arhats, each adhering to their own views and various divergent doctrines, spoke thus:

"Venerable ones, regarding the four grave offenses established by the Buddhas, as well as the seven rules for settling disputes, these were either prohibited or permitted for the sake of sentient beings;
the twelve divisions of the scriptures are likewise so. Why is this? Because the Buddha knows that lands and seasons differ from one another."

Sentient beings differ in their faculties, being either sharp or dull; therefore, the Tathāgata sometimes prohibits and sometimes permits [certain practices], teaching with varying degrees of gravity.

Good son, it is like a skilled physician who prescribes milk for some illnesses but prohibits milk for others: he allows its consumption for feverish illnesses but prohibits it for cold-natured ailments.
The Tathāgata is likewise; observing the roots of the afflictions of sentient beings, he both permits and prohibits [practices]. Long...
"I, an old man, have personally heard such a teaching from the Buddha. Only I know its meaning; you cannot know it.
Only I understand the Vinaya; you cannot understand it. I know the various sūtras; you cannot know them.
When that Buddha has passed into extinction, you should know that this Dharma will not remain long in the world. Good son, if a Buddha first appears and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."

The Bodhisattva had various disciples, who did not even say, "I have attained the fruit of a Srotāpanna" up to "I have attained the fruit of an Arhat," nor did they say that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, for the sake of sentient beings, either prohibit or permit [certain things].
"Venerable One, I have personally heard such a meaning, such a Dharma, and such a Vinaya from the Buddha; Venerable One, you should rely upon the ten [powers] of the Tathāgata."
"Regarding this meaning in the two divisions of the sūtras: if it is the true Dharma, I shall uphold it; if it is not, I shall abandon it.
Know that even though that Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa, this Dharma shall long abide in the world."
Good son, when my Dharma is extinguished, this is the fourth section of the summary: the final sealing of Śākyamuni Buddha’s Dharma. This further consists of three parts:

first, clarifying how disputes arise as the Dharma is about to perish; second, clarifying how the Buddha-dharma in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī subsequently perishes; and third, the great assembly’s lamentation.
"Good son, when my Dharma is extinguished, there will be śrāvaka disciples who may say that there is a self (ātman), or say that the self is empty;
some may say there is an intermediate state (antarābhava), or say there is no intermediate state; some may say there are the three periods of time, or say there are no three periods of time;
some may say there are the three vehicles (triyāna), or say there are no three vehicles; some may say that all things exist, or say that all things do not exist."
Some say that sentient beings have a beginning and an end; some say that sentient beings have neither beginning nor end.

Some say that the twelve links of dependent origination are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); some say that dependent origination is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Some say that the Tathāgata undergoes the practice of illness and suffering;
some say that the Tathāgata does not undergo the practice of illness and suffering. Some say that the Tathāgata did not permit bhikṣus to eat the ten [types of food].
Regarding the ten types of meat, what are they? They are human, snake, elephant, horse, donkey, dog, lion, pig, fox, and monkey;
all others are permitted. Some say that none at all are permitted. Others say that a bhikṣu does not perform five things. What are these five?
Not selling living beings, weapons, wine, *loṣṭa* (salt), or sesame oil; all others are permitted. Or it is said that [certain things] are not permitted to enter.
What are the five kinds of households? They are the butcher’s house, the prostitute’s house, the tavern, the royal palace, and the house of a *caṇḍāla*.
Regarding other households, some say they are permitted; others say they are not. Regarding *kauseya* silk garments, some say everything else is permitted;
others say that the Tathāgata permitted the bhikṣus to possess clothing, food, and bedding, each worth one hundred thousand pieces of gold; yet others say he did not permit it.
Some say that *nirvāṇa* is permanence, bliss, self, and purity; others say that *nirvāṇa* is simply the exhaustion of the fetters and that there is no separate dharma called *nirvāṇa*.
It is like the case of woven threads which are called "clothing";
once the clothing has been destroyed, it is called "no clothing," yet there is actually no separate dharma called "no clothing. The essence of *nirvāṇa* is likewise so, O son of good family.

At that time, among my disciples, those who preach correctly will be few while those who preach erroneously will be many; those who receive the true Dharma will be few while those who receive false teachings will be many;
those who receive the words of the Buddha will be few while those who receive the words of Māra will be many.
The initial passage, as clarified in the Kāśyapa-parivarta, states that *loha* refers to what is produced from the *palaśa* tree;
the Hexi [translator] says that when the tree produces it, it consists purely of insects, which foreigners use to dye wool.
At that time, in Kauśāmbī, the second section clarifies how the Buddha-dharma eventually perished.
Good son, at that time there were two disciples in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī: one was an Arhat, and the other was a breaker of the precepts.
The followers of the breaker of the precepts numbered five hundred, while the followers of the Arhat numbered only one hundred. As for those who broke the precepts...
Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate parinirvāṇa, I have personally heard this teaching from the Buddha:
"If one maintains the four grave offenses (pārājika) prescribed by the Tathāgata, one may commit them and yet remain without fault.
Now, I too have attained the fruit of Arhatship and the four types of unimpeded knowledge; yet even an Arhat may commit these four grave offenses. Regarding these four grave offenses—
If the Dharma were such that an Arhat could truly commit an offense, then the Tathāgata would never have prohibited it while in the world, nor would he have commanded its firm observance;
yet at the time of his parinirvāṇa, he relinquished all [restrictions]. An Arhat bhikṣu said:
"Venerable sir, you should not say that the Tathāgata has entered final parinirvāṇa. I know that the Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging; the Tathāgata is present."

There is no difference between committing the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*) while in the world and after entering *nirvāṇa*. If one says that an Arhat can commit the four grave offenses, this meaning is not so.
Why? Because even a *srotāpanna* does not violate the prohibitions, much less an Arhat.
If an Elder says, "I am an Arhat," a true Arhat would never give rise to the thought, "I have attained Arhatship."
"An Arhat speaks only of wholesome dharmas and never of unwholesome ones. Whatever the Elder says is contrary to the Dharma.
If one were to see the twelve divisions of the scriptures, one would certainly know that the Elder is not an Arhat.
Good son, at that time, the assembly of precept-breaking bhikṣus then collectively took the life of this Arhat. Good son, at that time...
Because of this, the two assemblies, driven by hearts of wrath, all together harmed these six hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the ordinary people each said, "Alas! The Buddha-dharma is now utterly extinguished! Yet my True Dharma is, in fact, not extinguished.
At that time, there were one hundred and twenty thousand great bodhisattvas in that land who skillfully upheld my Dharma; how could it be [extinguished]?
Should one say that my Dharma has perished? At that time, there will not be a single bhikṣu within Jambudvīpa who is my disciple.
At that time, Pāpīyān will completely burn all existing sūtras with great fires;
whatever remnants may remain there, the brahmins will immediately steal them together, gathering them from various places and storing them away.
For this reason, when the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world, the various lesser bodhisattvas collectively believed and accepted the words of the brahmins.
Although those brahmins claimed, "I possess the fasts and precepts," the non-Buddhists truly did not have them.
Furthermore, although these non-Buddhists spoke of "bliss" and "purity of self," they in reality did not understand what bliss and the self are.

The followers of the "Pure Meaning" (Śuddhārtha) directly explained the meaning of the Buddhadharma using single characters, two characters, single phrases, or two phrases, asserting, "In my scriptures, there is such a meaning. Because of this,
they gave rise to disputes for six hundred years, harming one another until their school was extinguished.
At that time, following the third section on the Great Assembly’s Lamentation at Kuśinagara, there are again three parts: first, the Great Assembly’s lamentation;
second, Kāśyapa’s consolation; and third, the cessation of the assembly’s lamentation and their arousal of the resolve for enlightenment.

At that time, when the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable multitudes among the twin śāla trees at Kuśinagara heard these words, they all cried out together: "The world is empty! The world is empty!"
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the great assembly: "Do not grieve, lament, or weep;
the world is not empty, for the Tathāgata abides eternally without change, and the Dharma and Saṃgha are likewise."
At that time, having heard these words, the great assembly ceased their weeping and all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They said:
"To hear of extinction is sorrow;
to hear of non-extinction is the cessation of sorrow; to realize that which is neither extinction nor non-extinction is to give rise [to the resolve for enlightenment]."
Because of the mind, one knows that it is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished; yet, through extinction and non-extinction, it brings about great benefit.
