*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 16, Day East.
Translated by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Benzhun. Sectioned and Compiled.
Collected Commentary on the Southern Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Sixteen;
Collected Commentary on the Southern Edition of the Mahāpari-nirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Seventeen;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter on the Holy Life (Brahmacarya), Part Four (Scroll Seventeen).
Translated during the Northern Liang dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master from India, Dharmakṣema;
re-edited by the Śramaṇas Huiyan and Huiguan,
and Xie Lingyun of the Jin dynasty.
The Fourth Fascicle of the Chapter on the Holy Life begins here;
this is the second discourse extolling the power to extinguish evil. "Evil" refers to icchantikas, the four grave offenses, and the five heinous crimes—all of which can be extinguished.
The traditional interpretation holds that King Ajātaśatru committed actual heinous crimes, yet the power of the sutra was able to extinguish them; there is indeed merit in this view.
Furthermore, the Guhyakapada Sūtra states that King Ajātaśatru was a skillful manifestation [of a king] as a means to eliminate the consequences of parricide;

by this analogy, one knows that Devadatta’s schism of the Saṃgha was certainly not a real schism. This is just as Sunakṣatra appeared to be an icchantika but was not actually an icchantika, and Nandika committed a grave offense but did not actually commit one.
The power of this sūtra can eliminate heavy evils and cause those who have actually committed offenses [to be purified].
This passage definitively demonstrates taking refuge and clarifies that the holy life (*brahmacarya*) must be kept pure rather than becoming impure.

Emperor Liang, failing to see this, claimed that this section was not part of the sequential order of the sutra and labeled it the "Guest Chapter. However, if one attains the intention to purify what is impure, this is precisely the holy life and cannot be called the "Guest Chapter.
Regarding the text itself, it is divided into two parts: the first clarifies the arising of evil, and the second clarifies the cessation of evil; the former begins as follows:
The evil discourse consists of three parts: first, the evil cause.
At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, King Ajātaśatru was by nature cruel and wicked, delighting in slaughter;
he possessed the four faults of speech, and his mind was ablaze with greed, hatred, and delusion, perceiving only the present while failing to see the future.
He takes delight in slaughter and possesses the four verbal evils; his mind is fiercely burning, possessing the causes for the ten unwholesome deeds.
With these two evil conditions, he takes exclusively wicked people as his retinue.
He took only evil people as his retinue;
being greedily attached to this present life, he abandoned the three right practices and clearly engaged in evil deeds.
Because he was greedily attached to the pleasures of the five desires of this present world, he perversely committed the crime of regicide against his father, the King, though he was innocent.

Having already committed the act of harming his father, he departs; this is the second [section] clarifying the extinction of evil. Furthermore, there are three parts: first, the cause for extinguishing evil;

second, the conditions for extinguishing evil; third, the actual extinguishing of evil. Regarding the first, the cause for extinguishing evil, there are four further points: first, generating a profound sense of remorse and burning anguish.
Because he had killed his father, remorse and fever arose in his mind; he could no longer wear his bodily ornaments or enjoy music.
Due to this mental remorse and fever, sores broke out over his entire body, which were so foul-smelling and filthy that one could not approach them.
Second, he had deep faith in cause and effect.
He reflected to himself: "This body of mine has already received the 'flower-retribution' (the present signs), and the retribution of hell is now drawing near.
Third, his mother applied medicine to him.
At that time, Queen Vaidehī, his mother, applied various medicinal ointments to him, but the sores only increased and did not subside. Then,
[the King] felt deep self-reproach and lamentation.
The king then said to his mother: "A sore such as this arises from the mind; it does not originate from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
To say that there exists anyone among sentient beings who can cure it is impossible.
At that time, there was a great minister. This is the second [section] on the conditions for extinguishing evil, which first clarifies how evil persons act as conditions.

Later, it was explained that virtuous people serve as conditions for the cultivation of goodness; now, regarding the commission of evil, it was asked whether those who do evil can also serve as conditions. The present discussion concerns the eradication of evil:

why would one need those who do evil? The answer is: when an evildoer encourages one toward evil, if one does not follow their evil teachings, that evildoer also becomes a condition for the eradication of sin.

If this is so, then when a virtuous person encourages one toward goodness, if one does not follow their good exhortations and instead commits evil, the virtuous person likewise becomes a condition for the commission of evil.
First, it may be compared to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which is called both "ambrosia" and "poison. Second, it cannot be so compared;
for when one examines the Buddha’s original intent, he did not create conditions for affliction for sentient beings.

If you do not accept my exhortation, that itself constitutes an evil condition and an evil exhortation. That you do not accept it becomes a source of goodness for you; you should know this regarding all things.
All arise from the mind; based on the conditions of evil people, the six ministers are treated as six chapters, each divided into four sections:
first, a minister comes to court and reports; second, the two kings respond; third, they petition the king to clarify the place where the offense was extinguished;

fourth, they proclaim the return to the former state. Some say that this "Worldly King" (Lokarāja) is real, which is impossible; others say he is a manifestation (nirmāṇa), or a function of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). However...
All of these were the skillful means employed by the Holy One, the King of the World, who used strategic artifice to manifest the power of the sutra and its ability to extinguish all evils.
At that time, there was a great minister named Candravimala (Moon-Adornment) who went to where the king was, stood to one side, and addressed him, saying: "Great King," he said.
"For what reason is your countenance so haggard and your expression so displeased? Is it because of physical pain, or is it because of mental anguish?
The King replied to his ministers, "How could my body and mind not suffer such pain? My father was innocent, yet I have perversely committed the crime of regicide.
I have heard from the wise that there are five kinds of people in this world who do not escape hell: namely, those who commit the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*)."
"I now possess immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sins; how could my body and mind not suffer pain?
Furthermore, there is no skilled physician to treat my body and mind.
The minister said to the Great King, "Do not grieve so greatly," and then spoke this verse:
If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, that sorrow will only increase further. It is just as when a person delights in sleep, their sleep becomes more abundant;
so too it is with greed, lust, and the indulgence in alcohol.
As Your Majesty has said, there are five types of people in the world who do not escape hell; who has gone there to see them and returned to tell Your Majesty?
Regarding what is called "hell," those of great wisdom in the world say it is as Your Majesty has stated: that there is no good physician in the world who can cure both body and mind.
Now, however, there is a great physician named Pūraṇa, who possesses all-knowing vision and has attained mastery in meditative concentration;
he has ultimately cultivated pure brahmacarya and constantly expounds the unsurpassed [Dharma] for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
The path to Nirvana is taught by the Teacher to his disciples as follows: there is no black karma nor retribution for black karma;
there is no white karma nor retribution for white karma; there is no karma that is both black and white nor retribution for karma that is both black and white;
there is no superior karma nor inferior karma. This Teacher is currently in the city of Rājagṛha; we only pray that Your Majesty will deign to visit him.
"He can cause this master to treat both body and mind.
At that time, the king replied, "If he can truly eliminate my sins in such a manner, I shall take refuge in him.
Furthermore, another minister named Guṇagupta went to the king's presence and spoke these words: "Great King, for what reason..."
His face was haggard and his lips were parched; his voice was faint like that of a timid man who has encountered a great enemy, his countenance turning pale with distress.
What is he suffering from? Is it pain in the body, or is it pain in the heart?
The king immediately replied: "How could my body and mind not suffer pain now? I was a deluded blind man, lacking the eye of wisdom;
having drawn near to evil companions as my kin, I followed the words of the wicked man Devadatta and unjustly brought about the violent harm of the King of True Dharma.
I have heard in the past a verse spoken by a wise person:"
If one gives rise to unwholesome thoughts toward one’s parents, the Buddha, or his disciples, and commits evil deeds, such a karmic retribution occurs in the Avīci Hell.
Because of this matter, my mind is terrified and great suffering arises; there is no skilled physician to provide me with rescue and healing.
The minister spoke again: "I only pray that Your Majesty do not grieve or fear. There are two kinds of dharma: first, the dharma of renunciation;
second, the dharma of kingship. As for the dharma of kingship, it is said that if one harms one's father, one then rules the kingdom; though this is called a parricide, in reality there is no sin.
It is like the *kalala* worm, which must destroy its mother’s womb before it can come into being—the nature of birth is thus."
Although one may destroy the mother’s body, in truth there is no sin; the same applies to mules and other such creatures when they are pregnant.

According to the laws of governing a kingdom, this is how it ought to be: even if one harms a father or brother, there is no sin. However, as for the Dharma of renunciation, even killing a mosquito or an ant constitutes a sin.
I only pray that Your Majesty will broaden your mind and not grieve. Why is this? Because if one is constantly sorrowful and afflicted by grief...
Consequently, they increase just as when a person delights in sleep, their slumber becomes more abundant; so it is with lust, greed, and the craving for wine.

As Your Majesty has said that there is no good physician in the world who can cure both body and mind, there is now a Great Master named Makkhali Gosāla, who possesses all-knowing vision, who pities sentient beings as if they were his own infants, and who is already free from all afflictions.

He extracts the sharp arrows of the three poisons from sentient beings. While all sentient beings lack knowledge, vision, and awakening regarding all phenomena, this One Person alone possesses knowledge, vision, and awakening.
This Great Teacher constantly teaches such a Dharma to his disciples:
"All sentient beings possess seven constituent parts in their bodies. What are these seven? They are earth, water, fire, wind, suffering, pleasure, and life."
These seven dharmas are neither transformed nor created; they cannot be destroyed or harmed. They abide immovably like the *iṣīkā* grass and like Mount Sumeru.
They are neither abandoned nor produced, just as milk and curd [are distinct]. They do not contend with one another regarding suffering or pleasure, or the wholesome or unwholesome.
Even if cast into a sharp blade, they cannot be injured. Why is this? Because the seven parts do not exist within space.
Because there is no obstruction, even life itself is without harm. Why is this? Because there is neither one who harms nor one who dies;
there is no agent and no recipient, no speaker and no listener, and no one who remembers or who teaches.

This Dharma, when constantly preached, can cause all sentient beings to extinguish all their immeasurable and heavy transgressions. This Teacher is now in the great city of Rājagṛha; we only pray that—
"Great King, go to that place; if Your Majesty sees him, all your sins will be extinguished.
Then the king replied, "If it is truly possible to thus eliminate my sins, I shall take refuge in him."
Furthermore, there was another minister named Śuddhilābha who went again to the king’s presence and spoke these verses:
"Great King, for what reason Have you cast off your necklaces, And your hair is disheveled? Why has your royal body come to such a state?
Why do you tremble with unease, Like a flowering tree shaken by a fierce wind?"
"O King, for what reason is your countenance so haggard and withered, like that of a farmer who has sown his seeds but the heavens have not sent rain?
You are so full of grief; is this pain of the heart or pain of the body?"
The king replied: "How could my body and mind not suffer pain now? My late father, the former king, was compassionate and benevolent;
he showed me special pity and care, and I truly have no fault. I went to consult a physiognomist, and the physiognomist answered:
'Once this child is born, it is certain that he shall harm his father. Although I heard these words, I continued to look after him and nurture him. I have once heard the wise say this:"
If a person commits incest with their mother, defiles a bhikṣuṇī, steals the property of the Saṃgha, harms one who has resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta,
or kills their own father— such a person will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell;
how could my body and mind not suffer such pain?
The minister spoke again: "I only pray that Your Majesty will not grieve or suffer. If your father, the King, had practiced liberation, then killing would be a transgression;
if he governed according to the laws of the state, then killing would be without fault.
That which is contrary to the Dharma is called 'lawlessness,' and lawlessness is indeed called lawlessness. It is like having no son being called 'sonless,' or like having a wicked son."

It is also called "childless," yet though it is said to be childless, it is not actually childless. It is like food without salt being called "saltless food," or even food with a little salt being called "saltless.
It is like a river without water being called "waterless," or even a river with a little water being called "waterless.
Just as that which perishes moment by moment is called "impermanent," so too is that which endures for an eon called "impermanent."
Just as a person experiencing suffering is said to be "without pleasure," yet one who experiences even a small amount of pleasure is likewise said to be "without pleasure";

and just as one who lacks sovereignty is said to be "without self," yet one who possesses even a slight degree of sovereignty is likewise said to be "without self"—so too, Great King, when it is dark at night it is called "sunless," and during times of clouds and mist it is also said to be "sunless.
Although you say that a small amount of dharma is "no dharma," in truth this is not so.
"O King Dharmarāja, please lend your attention to what your servant says:

all sentient beings possess residual karma, and by the conditions of that karma, they repeatedly undergo birth and death. If Your Majesty has residual karma, what crime is there in your killing me now?
I only pray that Your Majesty will set your mind at ease and not grieve. Why is this?"
If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, that sorrow will only increase further. It is just as when a person delights in sleep, their sleep becomes more and more abundant;
so it is with greed, lust, and the indulgence in wine.
As the King has said, there is no good physician in the world who can heal both body and mind; yet now there is a Great Teacher named Sañjaya.
Vairāṭīputra is all-knowing and all-seeing; his wisdom is deep and vast like the great ocean.
Possessing great majesty and virtue, and endowed with great supernormal powers, he is able to cause sentient beings to leave behind all nets of doubt.
While all other sentient beings do not know, see, or awaken, he alone knows, sees, and awakens. He is currently residing near the city of Rājagṛha for the sake of his disciples.

In preaching such a Dharma to all the assemblies, if there is a king who acts with sovereign will according to his own desires—whether performing good or evil—he incurs no sin whatsoever despite committing many evils.
Just as fire burns objects without distinction between the pure and the impure, so too is the king; he shares the same nature as fire.
For example, the great earth universally supports both the pure and the impure; although it performs this task, it is from the beginning free from either anger or joy.
The King is likewise of the same nature as the earth; for example, though water washes both the pure and the impure, it feels neither sorrow nor joy in doing so.
The King is likewise of the same nature as water; for example, though wind blows equally upon both the pure and the impure, it feels neither sorrow nor joy in doing so.
The King is likewise of the same nature as wind; he is like a withered tree in autumn.
If it grows again in spring despite having been cut down, there is truly no fault; all sentient beings are likewise so.
When one dies here and is reborn here again, since they are reborn, what fault could there be?

The karmic causes for the retributive fruits of suffering and happiness for all sentient beings do not depend on the present life; rather, the fruit is received in the present based on causes existing in the past.
The present has no cause and the future has no fruit; yet because there is a present fruit, sentient beings maintain the precepts and diligently practice vigor to ward off evil fruits in the present.
By maintaining the precepts, they attain the outflow-free (*anāsrava*); by attaining the outflow-free, they exhaust all outflowing karma;
by exhausting karma, all suffering comes to an end; and with the ending of all suffering, they attain liberation. May Your Majesty grant this wish.
Go quickly to his location and have him treat the physical and mental suffering; if the King sees him, his many sins shall be eliminated.
*Śaṃjaya*—the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* explains that this is merely a variation in the pronunciation of the characters for "night" (*yè*) and "light/heavy" (*qīngzhòng*).
This is the same character used in the *Shānjī Dìnglǐ* (The Rituals of Poetry and Rites), borrowed for its sound. *Zhì* is pronounced *zhíchí*.
The king spoke with equanimity, saying, "If there truly is such a teacher capable of removing my transgressions, I shall take refuge in him.
Furthermore, there was a minister named Sarvajñārtha who went to the king's presence and spoke these words: "Your Majesty, why is it that your appearance is no longer dignified?
You are like one who has lost his kingdom, like a spring that has run dry, or a pond without lotuses and trees without branches and leaves."
“Does a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts suffer physical pain, or does he suffer mental pain?

The king immediately replied, “How could my body and mind not suffer pain now? My late father, the former king, was compassionate and full of concern for me, yet I was unfilial and did not know how to repay his kindness.
He constantly provided me with peace and happiness, yet I turned my back on that kindness.”
On the contrary, he has cut off my happiness; the former kings committed no transgressions, yet he has wantonly raised up this rebellious harm against us.
I have also heard the wise say that if one harms his father, he shall undergo great suffering and affliction for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Before long, I shall surely fall into hell, and there will be no skilled physician to cure me of my sin.
The minister then said, "I only pray that Your Majesty will abandon this sorrow and suffering. Does Your Majesty not recall?
In the past, there was a king named Rāma who, having slain his own father, succeeded him to the royal throne;
as did the Great King Bimbisāra, King Virūḍhaka, King Nahusa, King Kārtika, King Viśākha, King Candraprabha, and King Sūryaprabha."
Kings such as King Priya, King Bahuputra, and others all killed their fathers to succeed to the throne;

yet not a single one of these kings entered hell. Furthermore, there are kings currently existing now, such as King Vairāṭya, King Udayana, King Duṣṭa-svabhāva, King Mūṣika, and King Padma—all of whom killed their fathers, and not a single one of these kings has ever given rise to grief.
"O King, although it is said that [beings] exist in the hells, among the hungry ghosts, and in the heavens, who has ever seen them? There are only two realms, O Great King:
first, the human realm; second, the animal realm. Although these two exist, they do not arise without causes and conditions, nor do they die without causes and conditions.
If there were no causes and conditions, how could there be good or evil? I pray only that the Great King does not harbor sorrow or fear. Why is this?"
If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, the sorrow will eventually increase. It is like a person who delights in sleep; as they sleep, it becomes more abundant.
Greed, lust, and the indulgence in wine are likewise the same.
As Your Majesty has said that there is no good physician in the world to treat the body and mind, there is now a Great Teacher named Ajita.
Kāśyapa, one who possesses all-knowing vision regards gold and earth as equal and non-dual;

whether his right side is struck by a blade or his left side is anointed with sandalwood, his mind makes no distinction between these two. He views enemies and kin with equal regard, his mind free from any sign of difference.
This teacher is truly a skilled physician for the world; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he is always present in the three [times].
With a clouded mind and without distraction, he addressed his disciples, speaking these words:

"Whether one acts oneself or causes another to act; whether one cuts oneself or causes another to cut; whether one roasts oneself or causes another to roast; whether one harms oneself or causes another to harm;
whether one steals oneself or causes another to steal; whether one commits adultery oneself or causes another to commit adultery; whether one speaks falsehoods oneself..."
To teach others to speak falsehoods, to drink alcohol oneself or to teach others to drink it; to kill a village, a city, or a nation;

to slaughter all sentient beings with a wheel of swords; or to give alms to sentient beings south of the Ganges while slaughtering them north of the Ganges—none of these acts would incur either sin or merit, nor would there be any giving, morality, or meditative concentration. Now, you are close at hand before the King.
"O King, dwell in the city of Śrāvastī; may the King go there quickly. If the King sees [the Buddha] there, the multitude of his sins will be extinguished.
'Ajina' means a winged garment (*śāṭaka*); 'kambala' refers to a garment made of *karpāsa* (cotton)."
The king said to the great minister, "If you are truly able to thus eliminate my sins, I shall take refuge in you.
Furthermore, there was another great minister named Śrīguṇa who went to where the king was and spoke these words:
"O King, why is it that your face now lacks luster, like a lamp in the midday sun, like the moon during the day, like a ruler who has lost his kingdom, or like a desolate and ruined land?"
"Great King, the four quarters are now peaceful and free from all enemies; for what reason, then, do you grieve so?
Is this suffering of the body, or is it suffering of the mind? There have been princes who constantly harbored this thought:
'When shall I attain sovereignty? And now, Great King, you have already fulfilled that wish, ruling over Magadha as a sovereign king."
"The former kings possessed a treasury of jewels in abundance; they should have simply enjoyed themselves at their pleasure and indulged in delight.
Why then do you harbor such sorrow and suffering in your heart?
The King replied, "How could I not be distressed? It is like a foolish person who craves only its flavor."
I do not see the sharp blade as one who eats food mixed with poison, nor do I perceive its danger; I am just like this.
Like a deer that sees grass but does not see the deep pit, or like a rat that craves food but does not see the cat or wildcat, I am just like this.
Seeing the pleasure of the present, I do not see the unwholesome fruits of suffering in the future. I have heard these words from the wise: "It would be better for one day..."
"Having received three hundred spears, I did not harbor a single thought of ill will toward my parents; now that I am close to the blazing fires of hell, how could I possibly avoid being distressed?
The word "jing" (穽) has two pronunciations:
one is *jian* (賤) and the other is *jing* (淨); it is mostly pronounced with the latter tone. This character has two forms: one is the version on the right side of the radical "阜" (mountain).
"In the two lower orifices, the lower orifices are mostly used.
The minister spoke again: "Who came to deceive the King, saying there is a hell with thorns as sharp as needles? Who created it?
Who made the birds of such diverse colors? The nature of water is moist, the nature of stone is hard, and the nature of wind is movement—who is it that acts thus?"
Just as heat is the inherent nature of fire, all things arise and perish of their own accord; who could have created them?
What is called "hell" is merely a construction of words by the wise. To speak of "hell," what meaning does it possess? Your Majesty, I shall explain:
"earth" (*dha*) is named as such because it is "broken" (*naraka*). Since there is no karmic retribution for breaking the earth, it is called "hell" (*naraka*).
Furthermore, "earth" (*dhi*) refers to humans, and "hell" (*niraya*) refers to devas; because they harm their father, they reach the realms of humans and devas.
For this reason, the seer Vasu proclaimed: "By killing a sheep, one attains the joy of humans and devas"—this is called "earth-hell.
Furthermore, "earth" refers to life, and "hell" refers to length; because by killing living beings one obtains a long lifespan, it is therefore called "earth-hell."

"Great King, you should therefore know that in reality there is no hell. Just as one who sows barley obtains barley and sows rice obtains rice, so too does one who kills a being in hell receive hell in return, and one who kills a human being should receive a human being in return. Great King, you should now listen to what your minister says:
in reality there is no killing. If there were a self (*ātman*), there would truly be no killing; if there is no self, [there is likewise no killing]."
Furthermore, there is nothing that can be harmed. Why is this? If there were a self, it would be permanent and unchanging;
because it is eternally abiding, it cannot be killed, it cannot be broken, it cannot be destroyed, it is neither bound nor fettered, and it is neither angry nor joyful—just like empty space.
How, then, could there be the sin of killing? If there is no self, all phenomena are impermanent; because they are impermanent...
Because every thought-moment perishes and every thought-moment ceases, both the killer and the slain perish moment by moment. If they perish moment by moment, who would possess the offense?
Great King, it is like fire burning wood: the fire incurs no guilt. It is like an axe felling a tree: the axe incurs no guilt.

It is like a sickle reaping grass: the sickle truly incurs no guilt. It is like a sword killing a person: the sword is not actually a person. Since the sword— [is not a person, how can it incur guilt?]
Since there is no person, how can there be sin? Just as poison kills a person, yet the poison itself is not the person; and since the poisonous drug has no person within it, how can there be sin?
All things are likewise: in reality, there is no killing, so how can there be sin?
I only pray that Your Majesty will not give rise to sorrow and suffering. Why is this?
If one is constantly sorrowful and suffering, sorrow will only increase further. It is like a person who delights in sleep; the more they sleep, the more it increases.
Greed, lust, and the indulgence in alcohol are likewise the same.
As the King has said that there is no good physician in the world to cure those of evil karma, there is now a Great Master named Kāḷaka.
Vāgīśa Kātyāyana possesses all-knowing vision and clearly perceives the three periods of time;
in a single moment, he can see immeasurable and boundless worlds, and his hearing is likewise so.

He enables sentient beings to distance themselves from faults and evils, such that all transgressions—whether internal or external—are entirely purified, just like the Ganges. This great and excellent teacher is also like this.
It can eliminate the manifold inner and outer transgressions of sentient beings. For the sake of his disciples, he teaches this Dharma:
"If a person kills all sentient beings yet has no sense of shame or remorse in their heart, they will never fall into the evil realms, just as empty space does not receive dust or water.
One who possesses shame and remorse enters hell, just as great water moistens the earth of all sentient beings."
All these are created by Īśvara; when Īśvara is pleased, sentient beings experience peace and happiness, and when Īśvara is angry, sentient beings suffer affliction.
Whether sentient beings commit sins or cultivate merit, it is all brought about by Īśvara.
How can one say that people possess their own sin and merit? It is like a wooden automaton made by a craftsman, which moves, stands, and sits.
Those who lie down and are unable to speak are likewise like sentient beings. As for Maheśvara, he is like a master craftsman;
the wooden figure is like the body of a sentient being. Since such a creation is thus brought about, who could be held guilty? Great Teacher, you are currently staying near the city of Rājagṛha;
we pray that you will go there quickly. If we are able to see you, all our sins shall be extinguished.
The king replied, "If there truly is such a person who can extinguish my sins, I shall take refuge in them.
Then another minister, named Abhaya (Fearless), went to the king's presence and spoke these words:

"Great King, in this world there are foolish people who, within a single day, experience a hundred joys, a hundred sorrows, a hundred sleeps, a hundred wakings, a hundred alarms, and a hundred weeps; yet those who possess wisdom..."
"O Great King, none of these things exist for such a person. Why then do you grieve so? It is as if a traveler has lost his companions;
as if one has fallen into deep mud with no one to pull him out; as if a person, parched with thirst, cannot find water;
as if a lost man has no guide; as if a sick person has no physician to treat them; or as if a ship at sea has been wrecked with no one to rescue it. O Great King!"
"Is it now your body that aches, or is it your heart?
The king immediately replied, "How could my body and mind not ache? I have recently associated with evil friends and failed to guard my speech;
though the former king was without fault, I perversely rose up to harm him. I now know for certain that I shall enter hell, and furthermore, there is no skilled physician."
And he was seen to be rescued.
The minister then addressed him, saying: "I only pray that Your Majesty will not give way to grief and distress. One who is a Kṣatriya is called one of the royal lineage;
whether for the sake of the kingdom, or for the sake of śramaṇas and brahmins, or for the sake of securing peace for the people, even if one commits killing..."
There is no sin. Although the former king venerated the śramaṇas, he was unable to serve the brāhmaṇas;
his mind lacked impartiality, and because it lacked impartiality, he was not a true Kṣatriya great king.
Now, in order to make offerings to the brāhmaṇas, you have slain the former king—what sin could there be in this? Great King, you truly did not kill him; as for killing...
One who harms is one who kills the life-force and severs the vital breath; yet the nature of the vital breath cannot be severed or harmed.
How can there be sin in killing life? I only pray that Your Majesty will no longer grieve. Why is this so?
If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, that sorrow will only increase further. It is just as when a person delights in sleep, their sleep becomes more abundant;
so it is with those who lust after greed and indulge in wine.
As Your Majesty has said, there is no good physician in the world capable of providing a cure, yet there is now a Great Master named Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.

The Tathāgata is all-knowing and all-seeing; he has compassion for sentient beings, thoroughly understands the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, and masters all skillful means appropriate to each situation.
He cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas and practices the pure conduct of brahmacarya in tranquility.
For the sake of his disciples, he spoke these words: "There is no giving, there is no merit, there is no father, there is no mother, and there is no present life."
In this world and in future worlds, there are no Arhats, no cultivation, and no Path; all sentient beings, after eighty thousand kalpas, will naturally be liberated from the wheel of birth and death.
Whether they have committed offenses or are without offense, it is exactly the same for all.
Just as the four great rivers—the Sindhu, Gaṅgā, Vakṣu, and Sītā—all enter the great ocean without distinction, so it is with all sentient beings.
Birth is likewise thus; at the time of attaining liberation, there is no distinction whatsoever. This Teacher now resides in the city of Rājagṛha;
we pray that the Great King will go to his place with all speed. If you should behold him, all your transgressions will be eliminated.
The King replied, "If there truly is such a teacher who can eliminate my sins, I shall take refuge in him.
At that time, the Great Physician [Jīvaka]... [The second section clarifying the conditions for a virtuous person has two parts: first, the elder brother; second, the father.
The first part consists of four sections: 1. Jīvaka’s inquiry; 2. The King’s reply; 3. The exhortation to go to the Buddha’s presence; 4. The shame at not having followed yet. Section One.
Regarding the term "wen" (text/pattern):
At that time, a great physician named Jīvaka went to the king’s presence and said, "Great King, have you slept peacefully?
Jīvaka, translated here as Gùhuó (Solid Life), was a boy at birth who held a pouch of medicine in one hand and a needle in the other.
In the past, he vowed to be a physician and was well able to treat others; based on this virtue, he established his title, which is translated as "Guo-huo" (Firm Life).
He was the son of the woman Āmrapālī.
The second king replied with a verse consisting of seventeen and a half lines, which, when divided into prose sections, consists of three parts. The first...
The eleven and a half verses following generally clarify those who sleep peacefully; the next six verses generally clarify those who do not sleep peacefully;

and the third section, consisting of a brief prose passage, correctly clarifies that the King cannot obtain peaceful sleep. This first part further divides into four sections: first, four verses clarify that the Buddha obtains peaceful sleep;
second, five and a half verses clarify that the Bodhisattvas obtain peaceful sleep; third, one verse provides a conclusion.

The Buddha concludes with four verses on the Bodhisattva’s initial approach to the Buddha-nature. Of these, the first two verses clarify the departure from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the attainment of *nirvāṇa*;
the latter two verses clarify the departure from evil transgressions and the attainment of eternal abiding (*nityatva*).
The King replied in verse: If one is able to forever sever All afflictions and is not defiled by craving for the three realms, Then one attains peaceful sleep.
If one has attained Great Nirvana and expounds the most profound meaning, Such a person is called a true Brahmin; Then one attains peaceful sleep.
With no evil deeds in body, Free from the four faults of speech, And with no net of doubt in the mind,
One attains peaceful sleep. With body and mind free from feverish distress, Abiding in a state of tranquility,
One achieves unsurpassed bliss And attains peaceful sleep.
However, the Buddha is truly without sleep; because he dwells in the state of bliss free from afflictions, it is said that he sleeps peacefully.
The following five lines and a half clarify that the Bodhisattva attains peaceful sleep through a mind free of grasping.
With a mind free from grasping and attachment, far removed from all enmity and hostility, always harmonious and without dispute—one then attains peaceful sleep.
If one does not commit evil deeds, if the mind is constantly filled with shame and remorse, and if one believes that evil has its retribution—one then attains peaceful sleep.
By honoring and supporting one’s parents, one attains peaceful sleep.
Not harming a single living being, Not stealing another’s wealth, And taming the sense faculties— One shall sleep in peace.
Associating with virtuous friends And destroying the four hosts of Māra— One shall sleep in peace.
Seeing neither the auspicious nor the inauspicious, Nor suffering, nor pleasure, and so forth— One shall sleep in peace.
For the sake of all sentient beings, one revolves through birth and death; if one can act in this way, then one attains peaceful sleep.
(Verses three and four are as in the text.)
Who sleeps in peace? It is those who are the Buddhas; Deeply contemplating the samādhi of emptiness, their bodies and minds are secure and unmoving.
Who sleeps in peace? It is those who possess compassion; They constantly practice without negligence.
Regarding the phrase "viewing all beings as one's only child," while sentient beings dwell in the darkness of ignorance, they cannot sleep in peace; this second section provides a twofold analysis.
The first three lines explain the teaching through the Dharma, and the subsequent three lines provide an explanation through analogy.
Sentient beings are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance; They do not see the fruits of their afflictions. Constantly creating all manner of evil karma, they cannot sleep in peace.
If, for the sake of oneself Or for the sake of another’s body, one commits the ten non-virtuous actions, One cannot sleep in peace. If it is said to be for the sake of pleasure, [it is likewise].
Harming one’s father is no greater fault than following evil associates; one cannot sleep in peace.

Just as eating beyond moderation or drinking cold water in excess leads to the suffering of illness and prevents peaceful sleep, so too is it for one who commits an offense against the king or harbors illicit thoughts toward another’s wife.
And for one traveling on a desolate road, there can be no peaceful sleep.

As long as the fruit of observing the precepts has not yet ripened, and the Crown Prince has not yet ascended the throne, and the thief has not yet recovered his stolen wealth, there can be no peaceful sleep.

"That the Crown Prince has not yet ascended the throne" means that the former Emperor has already passed away, the successor has not yet been established, and the four quarters have not yet [been brought under order].
"It is not that the Crown Prince cannot sleep peacefully; rather, it means that I, Jīvaka, am now unable to sleep.
This third section on the minor prose passage clearly explains the inability to sleep. It is further divided into two parts: first, the heading, and second, the explanation.
Within the heading, there are again two sub-sections: first, the indication that the illness is grave.
"Jīvaka, my illness is now grave; I have given rise to evil and rebellious intent against the King of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, it is said that there is no physician—none of the skilled and expert physicians, nor their wondrous medicines, incantations, or treatments for the sick, can cure me."
Why is this? The following explains these two matters in two parts; first, it explains the gravity of the illness. Why is this?
My father, the Dharma King, ruled the country according to the Dharma and was truly without fault, yet I have perversely brought him harm.
Like a fish cast upon dry land, what medicine could there be? Like a deer caught in a snare, I have no joy at all, as one who knows his own life is ending.
I cannot endure this for even a day, like a king who has lost his kingdom and fled to foreign lands; like a person who hears that their illness is incurable;
or like one who has broken the precepts and hears their own transgressions described. I have heard wise men say in the past:
"If the actions of body, speech, and mind are not pure, know that such a person will surely fall into hell. Now that I am in this state, how can I find peace?
Is it because they are dormant?
Next, he explains "without a physician":
Now I am also without the Unsurpassed Great Physician who expounds the medicine of the Dharma to eliminate my suffering of illness.
Jīvaka replied: [Section Three: Jīvaka’s Consolation and Exhortation to Go to the Buddha’s Abode.

This section has two parts: first, responding to the king’s two previous points; second, exhorting him to go to the Buddha’s abode. Regarding the first, responding to the king’s intent, there are again two parts:

first, clarifying that the king’s offense is light; second, indicating the medicine for the king. Regarding the first of these, there are four points: first, because the king possesses five virtues, his offense is light. Second... [text continues]
Because he lacks the five virtues, his three fetters are heavy; one who lacks the five virtues is an icchantika.
The King possesses the five virtues and is not an icchantika.
Jīvaka replied: "Excellent, excellent! Although the King has committed a transgression, he has given rise to deep remorse and harbors a sense of shame."
"Great King, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have always said these words: 'There are two pure dharmas that can save sentient beings: first, shame (*hrī*); second, remorse (*apatrāpya*).
Shame means not committing offenses oneself; remorse means not instructing others to do so. Shame is internal self-reproach; remorse is confessing one's faults to others.
Shame is being ashamed before men; remorse is being ashamed before the heavens. These are called shame and remorse. The absence of these is called shamelessness.'"
One who lacks a sense of shame is not called a human being, but is termed a beast; because they possess a sense of shame and dread, they are able to revere their parents, teachers, and elders.
Because they possess a sense of shame and dread, it is said that they have parents, brothers, sisters, and so forth. "Excellent! Great King, you are fully possessed of a sense of shame and dread.
Great King, listen for a moment: I have heard the Buddha say that there are two kinds of wise persons: the first is one who does not commit any evil.
Second, having committed [an offense], one repents; this foolishness also has two aspects: first, committing the sin, and second, concealing it.
Although one previously committed evil, if one later can reveal it and repent, feeling shame and remorse, one will not dare to do it again.

This is like placing a bright pearl in turbid water: by the power of the pearl, the water immediately becomes clear. It is also like the moon becoming bright and clear when the clouds are removed. Thus it is with those who commit evil.
The ability to repent is likewise so. Great King, if you repent and harbor a sense of shame and remorse, your transgressions will be extinguished and you will become pure as before.
Great King, there are two kinds of wealth: first, various animals such as elephants and horses; second, various precious treasures such as gold and silver.
Although one may possess many elephants and horses, they do not equal the value of a single jewel. Great King, sentient beings are also like this; there are two kinds: first, ...

Between the two types of evil wealth, the wealth of doing many evils is not as [grave] as a single act of goodness. Your servant has heard the Buddha say that cultivating a single virtuous mind destroys a hundred kinds of evil.

Great King, just as a small amount of vajra can destroy Mount Sumeru, as a small fire can burn everything, and as a small dose of poison can harm sentient beings, so too does a small amount of goodness destroy great evil.
Although it is called "minor goodness," in reality it is great. Why? Because it destroys great evil. Great King, as the Buddha has said:
those who conceal [their faults] have outflows (*āsrava*); those who do not conceal them are without outflows. To reveal and repent one's errors is therefore to be without outflows.
If one commits various offenses and does not conceal or hide them, because they are not concealed, the offenses will become slight. If one repents with shame...
When one feels shame for one's transgressions, they are extinguished. Great King, just as drops of water, though minute, gradually fill a large vessel, so it is with the virtuous mind:
each single thought of goodness can destroy great evil. If one conceals a transgression, the transgression increases;
if one confesses it with shame and remorse, the transgression is extinguished. Therefore, the Buddhas have said that the wise do not conceal their transgressions. Excellent, Great King!
He is able to believe in cause and effect, to believe in karma, and to believe in retribution; I only pray that Your Majesty will not harbor sorrow or fear.
Regarding the five virtues mentioned at the beginning, there are only four here because the single matter of "associating with virtuous friends" is omitted.

This is because, when looking from the lower to the higher, the higher principle ought naturally to include it; however, since Jīvaka himself constitutes the role of a virtuous friend, he intentionally omits it and speaks only of the four.
Regarding virtue: the first king possesses a sense of shame (*hrī*); the second king is able to repent; the third king is able to disclose his faults.

Disclosure and repentance are largely similar in their force, though they are not without slight differences. "Repentance" (*chan*) means to apologize; "repentance" (*hui*) means to regret one's transgressions.
As for "disclosure," it means to speak of one's faults before others. Although the fourth Ming King possesses faith, the four matters have already been settled.

If one has not yet placed faith in Jīvaka’s words, yet were to do so with certainty, he would be a virtuous friend; because such certainty has not yet been established, only four [qualities] are mentioned.
If there are sentient beings who fall into the second [category], it is clarified that their transgression is grave because the other lacks the five virtues.
If there are sentient beings who commit various transgressions, conceal them without repentance, lack a sense of shame or remorse, do not perceive cause and effect or karmic retribution,
fail to consult those of wisdom, and do not draw near to virtuous friends— such persons cannot be cured by any skilled physician,
nor even by those who attend to the sick; they are like the disease of kāmalā, for which worldly physicians stand by with folded hands.
A person who covers over their transgressions with their hands is also like this:
by committing a sin, they lack the virtue of disclosure; by concealing it, they lack the virtue of repentance; by failing to confess, they lack the virtue of remorse;
by ignoring cause and effect, they lack the virtue of faith; and by being unable to seek instruction, they lack the virtue of spiritual knowledge.
Virtue.
What is meant by "sinful persons"? This refers to the third section, which concludes that those who lack the five virtues are icchantikas.
What is meant by "sinful persons"? It refers to the icchantika; an icchantika is one who does not believe in cause and effect and lacks a sense of shame and remorse.

Those who do not believe in the retribution of karma, who do not perceive the present or future worlds, who do not associate with virtuous friends, and who do not follow the teachings and precepts spoken by the Buddhas—such persons are called icchantikas. They cannot be cured even by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Why is this?
Just as a corpse in the world cannot be treated by a physician, so too it is with the icchantika. All [the Buddhas]... [are likewise unable to cure them].
Even the Buddha, the World-Honored One, could not cure him.
Great King, you have now descended to the fourth stage; as a king, you possess five virtues and are bound by fetters that are not those of an icchantika.
Great King, since you are not an icchantika, why do you say that he cannot be healed?

As the King has said, the second section below demonstrates the physician and the medicine for the King; it is divided into two parts: first, demonstrating the excellent physician, and second, demonstrating the wondrous medicine.
Regarding what the King has said concerning the inability to cure him: "Great King, you should know that there is a son of King Śuddhodana in the city of Kapilavastu."
He was of the Gautama clan and named Siddhārtha; having attained awakening without a teacher, he spontaneously realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and he was fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and all-knowing vision.
Possessing great kindness and great compassion, he felt pity for all beings as if they were his own son, Rāhula.

Rāvaṇa follows after virtuous beings like a calf follows its mother; he speaks at the proper time and remains silent at the improper time. He speaks truthfully, purely, excellently, meaningfully, and in accordance with the Dharma.
With a single word, he is able to cause sentient beings to forever leave afflictions behind.
First, the excellent physician is shown; within that, the name Siddhārtha is mentioned, which translates as "Accomplishing Benefit.
[The phrase] "skillfully knowing the faculties of sentient beings" indicates, secondly, the wondrous medicine.

Since the medicine is the supreme Dharma and the excellent physician is clearly present nearby, how can one say there is no medicine? The text is divided into two parts: first, clearly knowing the faculties.
He thoroughly knows the faculties, natures, and minds of sentient beings, penetrating all appropriate skillful means without exception.
His wisdom is as lofty and great as Mount Sumeru, and as deep, vast, and far-reaching as the great ocean.
This Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses diamond-like wisdom capable of destroying all the evil offenses of sentient beings; it is impossible that he would be unable to do so.
Next, twelve *yojana* from here is where he clearly expounded the Dharma. This section has two parts: first, a general summary, and second, a detailed explanation.
Now, twelve *yojana* from here, between the twin *śāla* trees in the city of Kuśinagara, he extensively expounded various teachings for an immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* assembly of bodhisattvas.
The initial passage is a general exposition of the Dharma;

the subsequent section, concerning "whether existent or non-existent," is a specific exposition of the Dharma. This specific exposition is further divided into two parts: the first concerns two dharmas, and the second concerns three dharmas.
Whether existent or non-existent, conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows, whether the fruit of afflictions or the fruit of wholesome dharmas—
among these, the first two categories,
existence and non-existence, are the two truths; the conditioned and the unconditioned are affliction and nirvana, respectively.

The outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) are the Four Noble Truths: the afflictions and their fruits are suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), while the fruits of wholesome dharmas are the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
Following this, the discussion of material (*rūpa*) and non-material (*arūpa*) dharmas concludes with the explanation of three types of dharmas.
Whether it be a phenomenon of form, a phenomenon not of form, or a phenomenon that is neither of form nor not of form;
whether it be self, or non-self, or neither self nor non-self; whether it be permanent, or impermanent, or neither permanent nor impermanent;

whether it be pleasure, or suffering, or neither pleasure nor suffering; whether it be a characteristic, or a lack of characteristic, or neither characteristic nor lack of characteristic; or whether it be cessation.
Whether it be non-abandonment or neither abandonment nor non-abandonment; whether mundane or supramundane, or neither mundane nor supramundane;
whether a vehicle or not a vehicle, or neither a vehicle nor not a vehicle;
whether self-performed and self-experienced, or self-performed and experienced by another—O Great King, regarding all that which is without action and without experience as heard from the Buddha:
Heavy offenses shall be immediately extinguished.
Regarding "form" (*rūpa*), "non-form" (*arūpa*), and "neither form nor non-form": some teachers say that "form" refers to the eleven kinds of form;
"non-form" refers to the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*); and "neither form nor non-form" refers to the fourteen dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The commentator says: "Form (*rūpa*) consists of fourteen kinds; non-form is merely mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*);
that which is neither form nor non-form is the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). The Meditation Master says: "Form is the dharma of form; non-form is the mind;
that which is neither form nor non-form is the Middle Way Dharma of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) characterized by the abandonment of both extremes. This abandonment of both extremes is...
If this conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) were [itself] the Middle Way, how could it be established? Now it is clarified that this is not so. Previously, the two truths were explained;

here, the three truths are explained: form (*rūpa*) is the conventional truth; non-form (*arūpa*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); and that which is neither form nor non-form is the Middle Way, the Truth of Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-satya*).

That "one performs the action and one receives the retribution" is easily understood. As for "one performs the action and another receives the retribution," the subsequent text states: "There is no self (*ātman*)."

The two passages—one stating that one performs the action while another receives the fruit, and the other stating the opposite—contradict each other, yet each has its own scriptural authority. For now, I shall clarify that it is not as the other [position] claims.
Regarding "another receiving the fruit," they say: for example, when various people resolve their minds so that a king’s transgressions are eliminated;

or when all the merits performed by Bodhisattvas are bestowed upon sentient beings, such that sentient beings obtain happiness—this too is "receiving the fruit by another. Now, I clarify that this is not so; it is [the result of] one's own [action].
To perform "self-reception" is to enter emptiness from the conventional; to perform "reception by another" is to emerge from emptiness into the conventional;
and "non-action and non-reception" is precisely the Middle Way. This pattern holds true for all such passages. Furthermore, the text below states:
"If one hears of non-action and non-reception regarding offenses in the presence of a Buddha, those offenses are immediately extinguished"; therefore, this is the Middle Way.
Your Majesty, please listen now to the second exhortation to go to the Buddha’s presence, which consists of three parts: first, a broad citation of thirteen past events to provide encouragement;
second, an explanation of the Buddha’s impartial mind to provide encouragement; and third, a comparative evaluation of merit to provide encouragement. Regarding the sequence:

those who were formerly evil all saw the Buddha and attained liberation; the Buddha’s mind was impartial, neither favoring the former nor the latter. This was true of the past, and it remains so from the beginning until now.
The thirteen matters are further divided into two parts;
first, the primary listing of the matters. Your Majesty, please listen for a moment: when Śakra Devānām-indra’s life is about to end, five signs appear: first, his garments become soiled and greasy;
second, the flowers upon his head wither; third, his body becomes foul-smelling; fourth, sweat breaks out from beneath his arms.

Fifth, when he does not delight in his own seat, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, may see a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa in a secluded place and immediately go to that person’s location, conceiving the thought that they are the Buddha.
At that time, the śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, seeing Śakra approaching, feels profound joy and says these words: "O Lord of the Devas, I now take refuge in you. When Śakra hears this, he rejoices.
Having realized this, he knew it was not the Buddha and thought to himself: "If that were not the Buddha, he would not be able to cure me of these five signs of decline.
At that time, there was a minister named Pañcaśikha who said to Śakra: "Kauśika, there is a Gandharva king named Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
that king has a daughter named Subhadrā. If the King [the Buddha] would allow me to see him with this girl..."
When he said, "I shall show the King the place where decay is eliminated," Śakra replied:
"O noble son, the daughter of Vemacitrī, the Asura King, named Śacī, is one whom I revere. If you can indeed show me the place where evil signs are extinguished, I would still give her to you;
how much more so, O Subhadra Kauśika, since there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, by that name?"
"Śākyamuni is currently in the great city of Rājagṛha. If you can go there to consult him regarding the signs of decline and extinction that you have not yet heard, they will surely be eliminated.
Good son, if the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can truly eliminate them, you may then turn your carriage back to his dwelling.
Following the command of the charioteer, he immediately turned the vehicle and arrived at Rājagṛha, where the assembly of elders...
Having gone from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to where the Buddha was, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, among devas and humans, who is bound? The Buddha replied:

“Kauśika, it is stinginess, greed, and jealousy. He asked again: “From what do stinginess, greed, and jealousy arise? The Buddha replied: “They arise from ignorance (*avidyā*). He asked again: “Ignorance...”
"By what cause does ignorance arise? He replied, "It arises from heedlessness. "Furthermore, by what cause does heedlessness arise?
He replied, "It arises from perversion. "Furthermore, by what cause does perversion arise? He replied, "It arises from doubt.
"Blessed One, it is indeed as the Buddha has taught that the dharma of perversion arises from doubt. Why is this? Because I have doubts."
Because the mind is characterized by doubt, it gives rise to perversion; regarding one who is not a World-Honored One, one conceives the notion that he is a World-Honored One.
Now that I have seen the Buddha, the net of doubt is immediately removed. Because the net of doubt is removed, perversion is also exhausted.

Because perversion is exhausted, there is no longer a mind of stinginess, up to and including a mind of envy. The Buddha said: "As for your statement that you have no mind of stinginess or envy, you have now already attained [the stage of] Arhat."
"Anāgāmin, as for one who is an Anāgāmin, they possess no mind of craving.
If there is no mind of craving, why would they come to my presence seeking life? One who is truly an Anāgāmin does not seek life. World-Honored One, those who possess inversion seek life;
those without inversion do not seek life. However, I now truly do not seek life; what I desire to seek is [the Dharma]."
"Kauśika, only the Buddha’s Dharma-body and the Buddha’s wisdom exist; those who seek the Buddha’s Dharma-body and the Buddha’s wisdom will certainly attain them in a future age.
When Śakra heard these words of the Buddha, the five signs of his impending death immediately vanished.
He then rose, prostrated himself, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I am now as if dead and then reborn; I have lost my life and regained it.
Having heard this prediction from the Buddha that I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is for me a new birth and a new gaining of life.
World-Honored One, how do all humans and devas increase, and by what causes and conditions do they suffer decrease? Kauśika, it is due to the causes and conditions of strife.”
When humans and devas decline, if they cultivate harmony and respect, they will attain increase.
World-Honored One, if decline occurs through strife and contention, from this day forward I shall no longer wage war against the asuras. The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach that the dharma of patience is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, Śakra Devendra immediately came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and then departed.
"Great King, because the Tathāgata is able to eliminate all evil signs, he is called the 'Inconceivable King.
If you go [to him], all your heavy sins will surely be eliminated. Great King, listen: there was a son of a brāhmaṇa named Ahiṃsaka."
Because he killed immeasurable sentient beings, he was named Aṅgulimāla. Furthermore, when the evil intent to harm his mother arose, his body moved in accordance with it;
this movement of body and mind constitutes the cause for the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*). Due to these causes of the five heinous crimes, he was destined to fall into hell.
Later, when he saw the Buddha, both his body and mind moved again as he intended to cause her harm; this movement of body and mind likewise constitutes the cause for the five heinous crimes.

Because of these contrary causes, one would have entered hell; however, this person encountered the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, and immediately extinguished the conditions for hell, giving rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, the Buddha is called the Unsurpassed Physician, and not the six teachers. Great King, furthermore, there was Prince Subhira; his father, out of anger, cut him—
His hands and feet were thrust into a deep well; his mother, moved by compassion, sent someone to pull him out.
When he reached the presence of the Buddha and beheld the Buddha, his hands and feet were restored. He then conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Great King, because you have seen the Buddha, you have obtained this present retribution. For this reason, the Buddha is called the Unsurpassed Physician, and not the six teachers.
Furthermore, Great King, suppose there were five hundred hungry ghosts by the side of the Ganges River who, for immeasurable ages, had never seen water.
Although they reached the riverbank, they saw only flowing fire. Driven by hunger and thirst, they raised their voices and wailed.
At that time, the Tathāgata was by the side of the river, sitting beneath a tree in the Utpala Grove. Then those hungry ghosts came.
They went to where the Buddha was and said to him, "World-Honored One, we are so hungry and thirsty that our lives will soon come to an end.
The Buddha asked, "Why do you not drink the flowing waters of the Ganges? The pretas replied, "The Tathāgata sees water, but we see fire.
The Buddha said, "The clear, flowing current of the Ganges is truly not fire. Because of your own evil karma, your minds are inverted, and you perceive it as fire."

"I shall eliminate your inverted perceptions for you so that you may see the water. At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded upon the faults of stinginess and greed for the sake of the hungry ghosts.
The ghosts spoke again, saying, "We are now parched with thirst; although we have heard these words of the Dharma, they do not enter our minds at all.
The Buddha said, "If you are parched with thirst, you should first enter the river and drink as much as you desire. By the power of the Buddha, these hungry ghosts...
Consequently, they immediately obtained water to drink; having drunk the water, the Tathāgata further preached the Dharma to them in various ways.
Having heard the Dharma, they all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, cast off their forms as hungry ghosts, and attained celestial bodies.
Great King, for this reason, the Buddha is called the Unsurpassed Physician, and not the six teachers. Great King, Śrāvastī—
In that kingdom, there were five hundred bandits whom King Prasenajit had plucked out of their eyes;
having no one to lead them, they were unable to proceed to the presence of the Buddha. Out of compassion, the Buddha went before them and comforted them, saying:
"Good sons, well-guard your body and speech; do not commit evil again. At that time, the bandits heard the Tathāgata’s voice, which was subtle, wondrous, and pure.
They immediately regained their sight and, with palms joined before the Buddha, prostrated to him and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we now know that the Buddha’s compassionate heart universally covers all sentient beings, not only humans and devas.
At that time, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for them; having heard the Dharma, they all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason—
The Tathāgata is truly the unsurpassed, excellent physician of the world, not like the six teachers.
Great King, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī there was a caṇḍāla named Āśvāsa who had killed immeasurable people.
Upon seeing the Buddha’s disciple Mahāmaudgalyāyana, he immediately attained the cause and condition for breaking out of hell and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Because it was thus...
Because he is a noble disciple, he refers to the Buddha, the Tathāgata, as the unsurpassed physician and not as one of the six teachers.
Great King, in the city of Vārāṇasī there was the son of an elder named Ajita. Through his liaison with his mother, he killed his father;
subsequently, having committed adultery with another woman, he killed her as well. There was an arhat who was his spiritual friend, and toward this spiritual friend, [Ajita] gave rise to—
Filled with shame and remorse, he immediately killed him. Having committed the murder, he went straight to the Jeta Grove Monastery seeking to leave the household life.
At that time, the bhikṣus fully knew that this man had committed three of the heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma) and none dared to grant him ordination.
Because his request was denied, his anger redoubled; that very night, he set a great and fierce fire, burning down the monastic quarters and killing many innocent people. Then...
He went again to the city of Rājagṛha to the place where the Tathāgata was, seeking compassionate permission to leave the household life.

The Tathāgata immediately granted it, expounded the essentials of the Dharma for him, causing his heavy transgressions to gradually diminish, and inspiring in him the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, the Buddha is called the Good Physician of the World, and not the six teachers. Great King, your original nature is violent and evil, yet you have faith...
The wicked man Devadatta released a large, intoxicated elephant, intending to have it trample the Buddha; yet as soon as the elephant saw the Buddha, it immediately regained its senses.
The Buddha then reached out his hand and stroked the top of its head, further preaching the Dharma for it until it all attained the resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Great King, even an animal, upon seeing the Buddha, can still break free from its state as a beast.
If even the fruits of one's birth karma can be transformed, how much more so for a human being? Great King, you should know that if one sees the Buddha, all heavy sins will surely be extinguished.

Great King, when the World-Honored One had not yet attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Māra arrived at the Bodhisattva’s dwelling with immeasurable and boundless retinues; at that time, the Bodhisattva destroyed them through the power of his patience.
The evil mind of Māra caused Māra to receive the Dharma and immediately give rise to the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha possesses such great power of merit. O Great King, there was a wilderness spirit (*kāntāra-ghoṣa*) who greatly harmed sentient beings;
at that time, for the sake of the elder Bhadra, the Tathāgata went to the village of Kāntāra and preached the Dharma for him, and when the wilderness spirit heard the Dharma...
With great joy, he immediately offered the elder to the Tathāgata and then resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Great King, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī there was a butcher named Viśālakṣa who slaughtered countless sheep every day;
however, upon seeing Śāriputra, he immediately received the eight precepts for one day and one night. By this cause and condition—
By virtue of his life ending, he was reborn as a son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Northern Heavenly King, and became a disciple of the Tathāgata;
such great fruits of merit as these still remain for him, let alone for the Buddha. Great King, in North India there is a city named Śilā;
in that city there was a king named Nāgamudrā, who, out of greed for the kingdom and its high position, murdered his father. Having killed his father, [he...]
Feeling regret in his heart, he immediately relinquished the administration of the kingdom and came to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek permission for ordination.
The Buddha said, "Welcome," and he instantly became a bhikṣu; his grave offenses were extinguished, and he gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Great King, you should know that the Buddha possesses such immeasurable fruits of great merit. Great King, the Tathāgata has a younger brother named Ti...
Devadatta committed three of the heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma) by causing schism in the Saṃgha, shedding the blood of the Buddha, and harming the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā;
yet the Tathāgata preached various essential teachings for him, whereby his grave offenses were immediately lightened and diminished.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is the Great Physician, and not the six heretical teachers.
Next, Great King, if you can summarize and verify the intended meaning:
if you can believe my words, I only wish that you would go quickly to the place where the Tathāgata resides; if you do not believe me, I pray that you will reflect upon this well.
Next, "O Great King, all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones... and so forth, clarifies for the second time that the Buddha-mind is impartial and without distinction.

O Great King, the great compassion of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, universally covers all without excluding a single person; the True Dharma is vast and expansive, encompassing everything without exception.
It treats enemies and kin with equality, its mind free from hatred or love, never favoring one person over others to cause them alone to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi cannot be attained by others; the Tathāgata is not merely the teacher of the fourfold assembly, but is universally the teacher of all devas, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, those in the hells, animals, pretas, and so forth.

All sentient beings should regard the Buddha with the thought that he is their father and mother. Great King, you should know that the Tathāgata does not act solely for the sake of the noble and the powerful.
King Ti-ka preached the Dharma for those of low station such as Upāli, not only receiving the offerings of the wealthy Sudatta and Anāthapiṇḍada;
he also accepted the food of the poor man Sudatta.
He did not preach the Dharma solely for those of sharp faculties such as Śāriputra, but also for those of dull faculties such as Cūḍapanthaka. Not only... [did he do so].

Not only did he permit those such as Mahākāśyapa, who possessed a nature free from greed, to leave the household life and seek the Way; he also permitted the highly greedy Nanda to leave the household life.
Furthermore, not only did he permit those with thin afflictions, such as Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and others, to leave the household life and seek the Way;
he also permitted even those with deep and heavy afflictions who had committed grave offenses, such as Śuddhodana, the younger brother of King Prasenajit, to leave the household life.
In his household, he sought the Way and did not fail to venerate and make offerings with *śara* grass, thereby uprooting the source of his anger.
To Aṅgulimāla, whose evil mind desired to kill him, he remained unperturbed and did not seek to rescue himself;

rather, he preached the Dharma not only for wise men, but also for women who were utterly foolish and destined for marriage. He did not merely cause those who had left the household life to attain [realization].
The four fruits of the spiritual path are also attained by householders;

it is not only for those such as Puṇḍravardhana who have abandoned all busy affairs to contemplate in quietude that he expounds the essential teachings of the Dharma, but also for those such as King Bimbisāra who govern state affairs and manage royal duties. Furthermore, it is not only for those who have renounced alcohol that [he does so].
It was not only for the sake of the householder Ugga, who was intoxicated by wine, that he spoke; nor was it only for the sake of Revata and others who had entered meditative concentration;
it was also for the sake of the Brahmin woman Vāseṭṭhī, whose mind was distraught by the loss of her son.
It was not only for the sake of his own disciples, but also for the sake of the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas. It was not only for those who were in the prime of their youth...
He speaks not only for those aged twenty-five whom he regards as already old and decayed, nor only for those eighty years of age;

he speaks not only for those whose faculties are fully matured, but also for those whose roots of goodness are yet unripened. He speaks not only for Queen Mallikā, but also for the courtesan Utpalavarṇā.
He accepts not only the superior delicacies and sweet flavors offered by King Prasenajit, but also [the food of] the long...
"O Great King, you should know that Śrīgupta’s food was mixed with poison; yet in the past,
Śrīgupta also committed the cause for a heinous crime, but upon encountering the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he immediately gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"O Great King, even if one were to measure merit by the third grade of comparison, it would be inferior.
O Great King, suppose for one month one were constantly to provide food, clothing, and offerings with reverence to all sentient beings;
this would not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit obtained by someone who recollects the Buddha for a single thought-moment. O Great King, suppose one were to smelt gold..."

To provide people with chariots and horses carrying a hundred treasures each for the purpose of giving is not as good as someone who resolves their mind toward the Buddha and takes a single step forward.
Great King, suppose one were to take a hundred elephant-drawn chariots filled with various kinds of rare treasures from the kingdom of Da Qin,
along with women adorned with necklaces, numbering a full hundred, and hold them forth for the purpose of giving— this would still not equal the former.
It is still not equal to taking a single step toward the Buddha after having resolved one's mind upon him; let us set that matter aside.

Even if one were to provide the four requisites of offering to all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm, it would still not equal taking a single step toward the Buddha after having resolved one's mind upon him;
let us set that matter aside as well. Suppose, Great King, you were to offer worship and honor to as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River...
"Immeasurable sentient beings are not as [fortunate] as those who go once to the twin śāla trees where the Tathāgata resides to listen to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
At that time, the Great King replied [as follows]; this is the fourth instance of his shame and refusal to believe or comply.
At that time, the Great King replied to Jīvaka: "The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is by nature already tamed and gentle;

therefore, he has obtained a retinue that is likewise tamed and gentle. Just as a sandalwood grove is surrounded exclusively by sandalwood trees, so too are all the pure attendants of the Tathāgata pure.
It is like a great dragon who is surrounded exclusively by dragons as his retinue."
As the Tathāgata is tranquil, his retinue is likewise tranquil; as the Tathāgata is free from greed, his retinue is likewise free from greed;
as the Buddha is without afflictions, his retinue is likewise without afflictions.
Since I am now an utterly evil person, my body is entangled by evil karma and fettered by foul impurities destined for hell, how could I ever attain [such a state]?
"As for going to where the Tathāgata is, were I to go there, He would surely not deign to look upon me or engage me in conversation.
Although you have exhorted me to go to the Buddha’s presence, today I feel a profound sense of self-contempt and regret; I have no desire at all to go."
At that time, a voice issued from the sky concerning the second father-king; this section consists of four parts: first, the voice issues from the sky; second, the king asks in return;
third, the father-king speaks the truth; fourth, the world-king laments in grief. The first part consists of three sections:
one, exhorting because the Buddha-dharma is about to perish.
At that time, a voice suddenly issued from the sky, saying: "The unsurpassed Buddha-dharma is about to decline and perish;
the profound river of Dharma is now about to dry up. The great lamp of the Dharma will soon be extinguished;

the mountain of Dharma is about to crumble, the ship of Dharma is about to sink, the bridge of Dharma is about to collapse, the palace of Dharma is about to fall, the banner of Dharma is about to topple, the tree of Dharma is about to break, and the virtuous friends are about to depart."
