Great terror is about to arrive; beings famished for the Dharma will soon be reached. The pestilence of afflictions is about to spread;
the time of great darkness has come, and the time of thirsting for the Dharma has arrived. King Māra rejoices and casts off his armor.

The sun of the Buddha is about to set behind the mountain of Great Parinirvāṇa. Once the Great King of the Dharma, the Buddha, has passed away, there will be no one left to cure the heavy evils of kings.
"Great King, you must now descend [to the lower realms]; because these grave offenses will inevitably summon rebirth in hell, I urge you.
Great King, you have already committed the most heinous evil that leads to the Avīci Hell; by the causal conditions of this karma, you will certainly undergo its retribution without doubt.
'Avīci,' Great King, means 'without interval' (*avīci*): because there is no momentary pleasure in between, it is called 'Without Interval' (*Avīci*)."
Great King, suppose a single person were to fall alone into this hell; his body would become eighty thousand yojanas tall, filling it entirely so that no empty space remains between them.
His entire body would undergo various kinds of suffering. Even if there were many people, their bodies would likewise fill the space without obstructing one another.
Great King, in the cold hells, they may briefly encounter a warm wind and take it for pleasure.
In the hot hells, even encountering a brief cold breeze is considered a pleasure;
in some hells, if one’s life has ended, upon hearing the sound of "revive," one immediately returns to life. However, in the Avīci Hell, none of this occurs.
Your Majesty, the Avīci Hell has gates on all four sides, and outside each gate there is fierce fire, with flames from the east, west, south, and north intersecting one another.
It extends for eighty thousand *yojanas*, surrounded by iron walls and covered above by an iron net; the ground is likewise iron, with fire penetrating from above to below and from below to above.
Great King, it is like fish on a griddle, their fat and grease sizzling; the sinners therein are just like this.
Great King, one who commits a single *ānantarya* offense will thus fully undergo such suffering for that one crime. If one were to commit...
Regarding the two offenses of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), the sin is doubled; for one who possesses all five such offenses, the sin is likewise fivefold.
Great King, I know for certain that you must urgently go there, as urged by the three pairs of fetters and the two matters.
"Great King, I now know for certain that Your Majesty’s evil karma cannot possibly be avoided; I only pray that Your Majesty will go quickly to the presence of the Buddha.
Aside from the World-Honored Buddha, there is no one else who can save me. It is out of compassion for you that I have exhorted you thus."
The two kings asked in return.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King was filled with fear; his entire body trembled and his five limbs shook like a plantain tree.
Looking upward, he asked: "Who is this 'Heaven'? Why do you not manifest a physical form, but only a voice?"
The father-king replied truthfully:
"Great King, I am indeed your father, Bimbisāra. You should now follow what Jīvaka has said, and not follow the words of the six ministers who hold false views."
The four kings of the world lamented in grief.
Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell to the ground; his bodily sores flared up, becoming twice as foul-smelling as before.
Although he applied cooling medicines to treat them, the toxic heat of the sores only increased and did not diminish.
All is as stated in the text. Having questioned his father, the King, as to how he could utter a voice after death, the answer was twofold:

first, it was said that although the father king had attained the Way, even if killed he would not die, and for this reason he was able to exhort; second, it was said that he was not the original father, but rather various sages who had manifested themselves as his father to speak these words.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Seventeen.
Translated by the Eastern Sun. Compiled by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Benzhun.
A Commentary on the Southern Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Seventeen.
Commentary on the Southern Text of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Fascicle 18;
Chapter on Brahma-Conduct of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Part 5 (Fascicle 18).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Revised by the Jin Dynasty *śramaṇas* Huiyan,
Huiguan, and Xie Lingyun:
Chapter Five on the Brahma-faring (*Brahmacarya*).

The third scroll begins, clearly explaining the eradication of offenses; this section is further divided into two parts: the first concerns remaining in the world, and the second concerns the eradication of offenses.
Within the former, there are again two sub-sections: the first concerning remaining in the world, and the second concerning doctrinal discussion.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing King Ajātaśatru fallen to the ground in a swoon between the twin trees, addressed the great assembly:
"I shall now remain in this world for the sake of this king until immeasurable kalpas have passed, and not enter parinirvāṇa."
In this discussion, there are two parts: first the question, then the answer.

Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, since the Tathāgata should not enter nirvana for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings, why do you specifically act for the sake of King Ajātaśatru?"
The answer is twofold: first, the direct response; second, the esoteric teaching.

The Buddha said: "Good son, among this great assembly there is not a single person who thinks that I will definitely enter parinirvāṇa, yet King Ajātaśatru certainly believes that I shall ultimately and forever perish. For this reason, he has fainted and cast himself down."
Regarding the first answer: while those present in the assembly at the Twin Trees all knew that [the Buddha] was not extinguished, King Ajātaśatru alone believed he had been extinguished;
therefore, it was necessary to say "for the sake of."
"Good son, as in my [previous] explanation, the second part clarifies the Tathāgata’s esoteric language. This further consists of three sections: first, the proclamation of the esoteric language;
second, its interpretation; and third, the concluding praise. The proclamation of the esoteric language is as it appears in the text."
"Good son, you have not yet understood the profound meaning of what I said—that for Ajātaśatru, there is no entry into nirvāṇa. Why is this?
When I say 'for,' it refers to all ordinary beings; when I say 'Ajātaśatru,' it applies universally to all who commit [evil deeds]."
Furthermore, those who commit the five heinous crimes are precisely all conditioned sentient beings;
I never abide in the world for the sake of unconditioned sentient beings. Why is this? For that which is unconditioned is not a sentient being.
One such as Ajātaśatru is one who is fully possessed of afflictions; furthermore, "one who acts" is one who does not see the Buddha-nature.
If sentient beings were to see the Buddha-nature, I would never remain in the world for long. Why is this? Those who see the Buddha-nature are not [ordinary] sentient beings.
As for Ajātaśatru, he is precisely all those who have not yet resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, "those who act" refers to the two assemblies of Ānanda and Kāśyapa, as well as Ajātaśatru.
"World" (*loka*) refers to the queens and concubines in King Ajātaśatru’s inner palace, as well as all the women of the city of Rājagṛha.
Furthermore, "to be" (*bhava*) is named Buddha-nature; "A-ja" is named non-arising, and "Loka" is named enemy.
Because the Buddha-nature does not arise, the enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*) arise. Because the enemies that are the afflictions arise, one does not see the Buddha-nature.
Because one does not give rise to afflictions, one perceives the Buddha-nature; because one perceives the Buddha-nature, one attains abiding in Great Parinirvāṇa.
This is called "non-arising. For this reason, it is said for the sake of Ajātaśatru, O son of good family:
*aja* means non-arising, and non-arising means Nirvāṇa. *Śatru* refers to worldly dharmas; being unsoiled by these eight worldly dharmas is what is meant by "unsoiled."
Because he cannot be defiled by dharmas, he will not enter nirvana for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas;
therefore, I say that for Ajātaśatru there will be no entry into nirvana for immeasurable billions of kalpas.
There are six points of interpretation. First, it clarifies that this term "many" (*bahula*) is inclusive, meaning it applies universally to all.

Second, [it states] it does not apply to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); regarding the unconditioned, there are three interpretations: first, those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward are unconditioned sentient beings;
second, those who have attained the stages and above possess true realization, which is itself unconditioned; third, this very text explicitly states they are unconditioned.
These are not sentient beings; one should know that it is only upon attaining the fruit of Buddhahood that they are designated as "unconditioned sentient beings.

Furthermore, it is taught that sentient beings within the realm of principle (*li*) are all unconditioned. However, not only do various masters differ on this point, but the scriptural texts themselves are also inconsistent.

One passage states that "for" (*wei*) means "for the sake of all," while another states that it refers to the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*). Thus, the five heinous crimes and "all" are not the same.
Furthermore, it says "for those who have not yet resolved their minds" (*cittotpāda*); later in the text, it says, "You have already resolved your mind under Vipaśyin Buddha.
Thus, there is a distinction between having resolved one's mind and not having resolved one's mind.

It also says, "King Śa is one who has not seen the Buddha-nature and is possessed of afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, it says, "King Śa is named 'Non-arising' (*anutpāda*)," and "Non-arising is named Nirvāṇa."
As for the term "pan" (vessel), does one not see its nature? Others say that regarding esoteric speech (*sandhyābhāṣā*), interpretations vary;
however, I maintain that how can the esoteric speech of the Tathāgata be definitively categorized as deep or shallow, distant or near?
The third section concludes with a praise of the inconceivable nature of the Tathāgata’s secret words.
"Good son, the Tathāgata’s secret words are inconceivable; the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha are also inconceivable;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are also inconceivable; and the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also inconceivable."
At that time, the World-Honored One [proceeds with] the second section, which is the formal text for the extinguishing of offenses;
it is divided into two parts: first the body, then the mind. Thus it says, "First treat the King’s body, and then his mind.

Because it was previously stated that there is no skilled physician who can treat both body and mind, he emits light to treat the body and preaches the Dharma to treat the mind. The initial text on treating the body is further divided into two parts. First:
Following the emission of light, the text next discusses the initial radiance. As the text describes:
at that time, the World-Honored One, the Great Compassionate Guide, entered the Moon-Love Samādhi for the sake of King Ajātaśatru. Having entered this samādhi, he emitted a great radiance;
this light was cool and refreshing, and as it shone upon the king’s body, the sores on his body were immediately healed of their feverish inflammation.
It is eliminated.
Next, from "The King awakens and the wound heals" onwards is the second question-and-answer. Regarding the discourse on light, there are five sections;

within these, there are further two parts: first, four rounds of the discourse on light, and second, one round explaining the Moon-Love [Sūtra]. Within the initial four rounds, each contains a question.
The answer to the first three points is as stated in the text.
When the King awoke, his sores had healed and his body felt cool and refreshed;

he said to Jīvaka, "I have heard it said that when the end of a kalpa is near, the three moons appear simultaneously, and at such a time, the sufferings and ailments of all sentient beings are entirely eliminated. Yet, that time has not yet arrived."
"From where does this light come that shines upon my body, healing the suffering of my sores and bringing peace to my person?

Jīvaka replied, "This is not the light of the three moons shining together at the end of an eon, nor is it the light of fire, the sun, the stars, medicinal herbs, precious gems, or celestial radiance.
The King asked again, "If this light is neither the three moons shining together nor the brilliance of precious gems, whose light is it?"
Great King, you should know that this radiance emitted by the God among Gods has no root and no limit;

it is neither hot nor cold, neither permanent nor subject to extinction, neither form nor formless, neither with characteristics nor without characteristics, and neither blue, nor yellow, nor red, nor white.
Yet, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, it is made visible, possessing characteristics and being describable, and having a root.
"O Great King, although this light has boundaries and possesses heat and cold, as well as blue, yellow, red, and white, it is in truth ineffable and invisible;
indeed, it is devoid of blue, yellow, red, and white."
The King said, "Jīvaka, for what reason has that God among Gods emitted this radiance?

Jīvaka replied, "This auspicious sign portends that it is for the sake of the Great King. Because the King previously stated that there is no skilled physician in the world to treat both body and mind, he has emitted this light to first treat the King’s body and subsequently his mind."
At the end of the session, the King again questioned first and then Jīvaka answered.
The King said, "Jīvaka, does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, also hold you in his thoughts?
Jīvaka replied, "It is like a man who has seven sons; among these seven sons, if one should fall ill, the parents' heart toward them is not unequal."
Nevertheless, his mind is biased toward the sick child; the Tathāgata is likewise:

he is not impartial toward all sentient beings, for his mind is biased toward those who have committed offenses, and he gives rise to thoughts of compassion for those who are heedless, while he remains equanimous toward those who are not heedless.
What is meant by "those who are not heedless"? It refers to Bodhisattvas dwelling in the sixth stage and above.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not regard the lineage, age—whether young, old, or middle-aged—wealth, poverty, time, seasons, days, months, stars, constellations, craftsmanship, low status, or whether one is a servant or slave when it comes to sentient beings; they regard only whether a sentient being possesses a virtuous mind.
If there is a virtuous mind, they then regard them with compassion.

In the response, regarding one among the seven sons who falls ill, there are three interpretations: first, it is explained generally as a metaphor for sentient beings of the six realms, with those who have committed offenses representing the one sick son;
second, it refers to the Bodhisattvas of the six stages together with the external ordinary persons (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) as the seven, where the external ordinary persons are the sick ones;
third, it refers to the four fruits of the *śrāvaka*, the *pratyekabuddhas*, and the Bodhisattvas as the six, while including the external ordinary persons within the category of the "sick."
Generally, there are seven sons. When one son encounters illness, it is compared to an ordinary person (bālapṛthagjana) giving rise to evil;
this is to clarify that the present case is not so. The text says, "Among the seven sons, one son encounters illness. How could it ever have been said that this is the illness of an ordinary person?
Furthermore, all sentient beings are my children. As in the various previous interpretations, whether advancing or retreating, the meaning is not fully encompassed.

Taking the root-natures of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya-mārga*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*) as the "seven-times-seven sons" who give rise to rebellious thoughts and encounter [the Buddha], the mind is then focused exclusively upon them (and so forth).

Regarding the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*), there are two interpretations of the two types of understanding: one says it is true understanding (*bhūta-jñāna*), while the other says it is semblance understanding (*pratibimba-jñāna*) at the sixth mind.
In the subsequent explanation, Yue’ai (Moon-Love) first pointed to the samādhi entered by the Tathāgata,
saying: "Great King, you should know that such an auspicious sign is the radiance emitted when the Tathāgata enters the Moon-Love Samādhi."
Next, he asked.
The King then asked, "What is called the Moon-Love Samādhi?
He then proceeded to explain it.
Jīvaka replied, “Great King, it is like the light of the moon, which can cause all the *utpala* flowers to bloom and become fresh and bright;
the Moon-Love Samādhi (*candrakānta-samādhi*) is also like this, for it can cause the wholesome minds of sentient beings to bloom. Therefore, it is called the Moon-Love Samādhi.
Great King, it is like the light of the moon, which can cause the hearts of all people traveling on the road to rejoice.”
The Moon-Love Samādhi (*Candrakānta-samādhi*) is likewise; it causes those who cultivate the path to nirvāṇa to give rise to joy in their hearts.

For this reason, it is further named the Moon-Love Samādhi. Great King, for example, from the first day until the fifteenth day, the form, color, and radiance of the moon’s light gradually increase; the Moon-Love Samādhi is also like this.
It causes the roots of goodness of those who have first resolved their minds to gradually increase until they are fully perfected in Great Parinirvāṇa;
for this reason, it is further called the Moon-Love Samādhi.
For example, from the sixteenth day to the thirtieth day, the form, color, and radiance of the moon gradually diminish; the Moon-Love Samādhi is likewise such that its light [diminishes].
It can cause all afflictions present in the places it illuminates to gradually perish; for this reason, it is further named the Moon-Love Samādhi (*candrakānta-samādhi*).

Great King, just as during times of intense heat, all sentient beings constantly long for moonlight, and once the moonlight shines upon them, their oppressive heat is immediately dispelled, so too is the Moon-Love Samādhi:
it can cause sentient beings to eliminate the feverish heat of greed and affliction. Great King, it is like this:
Just as the full moon is the king among the multitude of stars, a flavor of ambrosia, and beloved by all sentient beings,
so too is the Moon-Love Samādhi (Candrāloka-samādhi) the king among all virtues, a flavor of ambrosia, and beloved by all sentient beings; for this reason,
it is further named the Moon-Love Samādhi.
Within this, the moon is first cited as a metaphor in six instances, as per the text.

The King speaks to Jīvaka regarding the second [instance] of extinguishing the offense of the mind; furthermore, there are two parts: first, clarifying the conditions for extinguishing the offense, and second, the actual extinguishing of the offense.
The first section contains four points: 1) not having yet set out oneself; 2) going after being exhorted; 3) the Tathāgata’s praise...

Praising the Four [Truths] and Proceeding to the Buddha’s Abode: First, it clarifies that those who have not yet resolved their intent undergo two rounds of question and answer—first, that the King was unable to resolve his intent;
second, Jīvaka exhorted him to go.
The King said to Jīvaka, "I have heard that the Tathāgata does not dwell, sit, rise, speak, or converse with evil persons."

"Just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse, as the ruddy sheldrake does not dwell in a latrine, as Śakra-devānām-indra does not cohabit with ghosts, and as the garuḍa does not perch on a withered tree, so it is with the Tathāgata.
How could I possibly go to see him? Even if I were to see him, would my body not sink into the earth? Thus do I contemplate the Tathāgata."
"It would be better to approach a drunken elephant, a lion, a tiger, a wolf, or a fierce fire with its flames at their peak than to draw near a person of grave evil.
Therefore, as I now reflect thus, with what state of mind should I go to see the Tathāgata?"

Jīva replied, "Great King, it is like a thirsty person who hastens toward a clear spring, a hungry person seeking food, one in fear seeking rescue, a sick person seeking a physician, or one suffering from heat seeking coolness, or one suffering from cold seeking clothing.
Great King, your current quest for the Buddha should be understood in the same way.
Great King, the Tathāgata still expounds the essential teachings of the Dharma even for those such as the icchantikas; how much more so for Your Majesty?"
It is not that those who are icchantikas will fail to receive the salvation of compassion.
In the second section of the discussion regarding icchantikas, there is first a question and then an answer.
The King said, "Jīvaka, I have heard in the past that an icchantika is one who does not believe, does not hear, and is unable to observe."
If one does not understand the underlying principle, for what reason does the Tathāgata preach the Dharma?

In the answer, there is first a simile followed by its application (*yōjina*). Within the initial simile, four points are established: (1) the icchantika’s severance of the roots of goodness; (2) the conditions and causes that elicit the Buddha;
(3) the impossibility of generating goodness; and (4) the preaching of the Dharma. Regarding the first section, there are further two parts, the first of which clarifies...

Following the arising of the five dull [afflictions], the arising of the five sharp [afflictions] is explained. This section has two parts: first, the arising of evil; second, the loss of goodness. The first part [on the arising of evil] further has two sections:
first, the general arising of evil; second, the specific explanation of the five dull afflictions.
Jīvaka replied: "Great King, it is like a person who, having contracted a grave illness, dreams at night of ascending a hall with a single pillar.
Of the two initial lines, the first is a metaphor for the illness—the icchantika possessing heavy evil—and the second line speaks of 'dreaming at night.'"
This is analogous to ignorance; the mind ascending to a single-pillar palace is like an icchantika who has severed all present and future roots of goodness,
possessing only the retribution-body induced by a small amount of past merit— just as a great palace with only one pillar will soon collapse.
Next, while consuming ghee and oils, five dull afflictions arise separately:
consuming ghee and oils and smearing them on the body; lying in ashes or eating ashes; climbing up a withered tree or wandering and sitting or lying down with monkeys;
and sinking into water or submerging in mud.
Attachment causes stickiness, like clarified butter; the soaking of greed is like grease. When it is in the mouth, one swallows it; when on the body, one smears it.
When the mind pervades both body and mouth, it is as if lying in ashes or eating ashes—this illustrates the arising of the affliction of anger.
Anger shatters the physical frame; its agitation is like ashes. When anger is unleashed and moves the body, it is like lying in ashes while discharging poison.

"His mouth is like eating ashes while his mind pervades his entire body; his mouth and body cling to a withered tree above. This is a metaphor for giving rise to pride (*māna*), exalting oneself and looking down upon others, like clinging to a withered tree above.
Why not cling instead to a tree of lush blossoms? If a noble or sage exalts themselves, they may be compared to a tree of lush blossoms;
because one exalts oneself through evil, it is called a "withered tree. Or, as for the monkey below, this is a metaphor for giving rise to doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Doubt and indecision are like a monkey leaping from branch to branch, abandoning one to seize another;

they are like a doubting mind seeking the truth, calculating existence and non-existence, or whether there is a self or no self. Furthermore, the monkey resembles a human but is not actually a human, which is a metaphor for doubt:
it appears to have attained the truth but in reality has not. To sink into water or be submerged in mud is a metaphor for falling into non-existence.
To illustrate light [transgressions], it is like sinking in water; for heavy ones, it is like being submerged in mud.

Falling from the palace tower is explained next. Second, the loss of goodness is further divided into two parts: first, the loss of the three grades of goodness; second, the loss of the three vehicles.
Falling from towers, palaces, high mountains, and trees. Regarding the first passage:
"falling from the tower" is a metaphor for losing the tower of wisdom; "the high pavilion" is a metaphor for wisdom, which ascends and emerges to illuminate and penetrate;

that one now falls signifies the loss of the category of wisdom. "The high mountain" is a metaphor for the loss of the category of precepts; "the trees" are a metaphor for the loss of [the category of concentration].
Chapter on Concentration.
Next, the analogies of the elephant, horse, ox, and sheep illustrate the loss of the three vehicles.
Elephant, horse, ox, and sheep.

Examining the meaning of this passage, there should be a succession of four vehicles (*catur-yāna*), yet it merely states that "three vehicles are lost. The mention of "falling" applies to all four vehicles;
this is simply a case of textual abbreviation.

Regarding the phrase "the body is clothed in blue and yellow," the second section begins with the arising of the sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*). This further divides into two: first, the arising of the sharp afflictions; second, their mixed arising.
Inauspicious conditions:
wearing garments of blue, yellow, red, or black; laughing, singing, or dancing with delight; or seeing birds, vultures, foxes, wildcats, and the like;
having teeth and hair fall out; being naked; or lying on a dog as a pillow amidst filth and excrement.
First, the analogy of putting on clothes illustrates the arising of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); it is like people reckoning the self in four different ways:

the Brahmins reckon it as yellow, the Kṣatriyas as red, the Vaiśyas as blue, and the Śūdras as black. The analogy of laughter, song, and dance illustrates the arising of the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*);
it is like conceiving a sense of pleasure within what is not pleasurable, and giving rise to the notion of superiority within what is not superior.
For example, the birds that delight in laughter, the vultures, and the foxes represent those who give rise to wrong views; these four types all consume flesh.
Thus, they are likened to wrong views devouring one's roots of goodness. The falling out of teeth and hair represents the extreme views of eternalism and annihilationism;
here, we specifically mention the view of annihilationism. Being naked and using a dog as a pillow represents the clinging to precepts and rituals, specifically the observance of the dog-precepts.

Because faith is the foremost [of the faculties], it is said that he rests his head upon a dog; this refers to the complete reckoning of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), hence the phrase "lying amidst excrement and filth.
Furthermore, for the deceased, the second section describes the arising of adverse conditions: encountering evil associates (pāpa-mitra).
Furthermore, they walk, stand, sit, and rise together with the deceased, hand-in-hand eating and drinking; they pass through the midst of roads filled with venomous snakes;
or again, in dreams, they embrace women with disheveled hair who wear *tāla* leaves as clothing, riding broken donkey carts as they travel due south.
Having had such dreams, these people give rise to sorrow and distress in their hearts, and because of this sorrow and distress...
His physical illness increased further, and he died immediately.
This is like the analogy of severing all roots of goodness; it is said that in the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—no wholesome state arises.

Thus it is said: "While walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, as soon as a wholesome thought is about to arise, a perverse thought immediately follows," which is why it says they "hold hands with the perverse."
Because it sustains itself, it is called "eating"; the simile of the snake refers to one with much anger.

In my private view, because the mind’s sphere of activity is constantly accompanied by anger, it is said that he passes through the middle of a road full of them. The woman with disheveled hair represents a person with much craving.
Wearing leaves as clothing represents a person without shame or dread of blame. Riding a dilapidated donkey cart represents being driven by unwholesome dharmas. "Directly south" means—

Regarding the three interpretations of this [passage]: The first says that "South" represents *li* (the trigram for fire) and "North" represents *kan* (the trigram for water). To move from *kan* toward *li* is like losing what is good and giving rise to evil.
The second says this is spoken in terms of the various directions: "North" is the upper direction, which serves as a metaphor for a person who has severed their roots of goodness falling from above.
The third says that since the Son of Heaven faces south, where he holds the power of life and death, this person’s false views judge that there is no cause [for such power].
If this mind is not sovereign, bodily illness increases further, like various evils turning toward gravity.
Because the illness increases, the second section below clarifies how the sense-faculties and conditions invoke the Buddha.
Because the illness increases, the relatives of his household sent a messenger to invite a physician; the messenger thus dispatched was deficient and deformed in body.
With his faculties incomplete, his head covered in dust, wearing tattered and ruined clothing, and riding an old, broken cart, he spoke to that physician, saying:
"Quickly, mount the cart.

The increase of illness is a metaphor for the severing of the roots of goodness and the heavy burden of relatives and kin; this has three interpretations. One interpretation states it refers to past precepts.
First, it is said that this human body is produced by wholesome karma; since only this wholesome karma remains, it is likened to one's kinsmen.

Second, it is said that although icchantikas have severed all past and present wholesome roots, their future wholesome roots will eventually arise, and thus they shall all become Buddhas; therefore, the wholesome roots not yet arisen are considered their kinsmen.

Third, it is said that this is not so: some possess wholesome roots that lead to Buddhahood, while others possess unwholesome roots that lead to Buddhahood, whereas icchantikas lack any wholesome roots whatsoever.
To take that which is evoked by evil as one's kinsmen is equivalent to dispatching a messenger to invite a physician;
those whose physical forms are deficient and stunted are so because they take what is good as their messenger—yet this goodness is afflicted by evil, hence it is said they are "deficient and stunted.

Alternatively, if they take what is evil as their messenger, then according to the nature of that evil, they are inherently hirsute and ugly; because their roots of goodness are weak, it is said they are "deficient in faith and incomplete."
Therefore, it is said that they are "deficient"; this means that because faith and the other [faculties] are not complete, they are said to have "incomplete faculties.

That their heads are covered with dust and soil refers to being shrouded by the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*). That they wear tattered and ruined clothing refers to being clothed in shamelessness (*ahrī*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*).

That they ride a broken cart refers to relying on the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) from previous lives to produce this present human body, yet with its faculties impaired. (Private note: This refers to the profound triggering of the karmic mechanism through a hidden resonance.)
Therefore it is said that when one tells a physician, "Quickly mount the carriage," one stands waiting for a response.
At that time, the skilled physician [proceeds with] the third contemplation: that good [intentions] should not arise. This section has two parts: first, the observation;
second, the granting of the response. The first part also has two sub-sections: first, going to observe the capacity of the recipient; second, the repeated observation.
At that time, the skilled physician thought to himself: "Now, observing the appearance of this messenger, it is inauspicious;
I know that the patient will be difficult to treat.
Having first examined the capacity [of the patient] and finding no roots of goodness, yet because the Buddha did not wish to abandon him, he examined him once more.
Secondly, there is again this reflection, which follows below and constitutes a further contemplation; it is also twofold: first, contemplating the present, and second, contemplating the past.

The contemplation of the present is threefold: first, contemplating the sun as a simile for those of superior faculties; next, contemplating the stars as a simile for those of middling faculties; and third, contemplating time as a simile for those of inferior faculties.
Regarding "time," the mention of "night" refers to the most inferior *icchantikas*; the stars are inferior to the sun, representing the middling *icchantikas*.
Although Ti had severed his roots of goodness in all three grades, he further thought:
"Even though the *māra* is not auspicious, I should consult the calendar to see if it can be cured.
If it falls on the fourth, sixth, eighth, twelfth, or fourteenth day—on such days as these, the illness is also difficult to treat."

First, the four days from the middle of the month symbolize the four inversions (*viparyāsa*); the six days symbolize the six obscurations (*āvaraṇa*); the eight days symbolize the eight heterodoxies (*mithyātva*);

and the twelve days symbolize the denial of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), as well as the twelve views of self (*ātman*). The fourteen days symbolize the denial of the fourteen truths (*satya*);
these fourteen truths appear in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where their sixteen aspects are shown to demonstrate the arising and cessation of all phenomena.
He spoke of entering the path through the wisdom of the Tathāgata and so forth.
Furthermore, he thought: "Even if the day is not auspicious, one should again examine the stars to see if it is possible to treat the illness.
If it is during the time of Mars, the constellation Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, the constellation of Yama (Kṛttikā), Śukra, or Puṣya, then even such an illness will be difficult to treat."
Second, among the observations of the stars, six stars are generally consulted, which is like receiving instruction from six teachers.
He further reflects: "Even if the stars are not auspicious, one must still observe the time.
If it is autumn or winter, or at sunset, midnight, or when the moon sets, one should know that this illness will also be difficult to treat."
During the three periods of contemplation, there are generally five stages, or it is said that one severs the roots of goodness of the five vehicles.
Then, one further reflects on the past roots of goodness during the second contemplation.
Again, he thinks: "Although these various signs may be inauspicious, whether they are certain or uncertain, when observing a patient, if that person possesses merit and virtue, they can all be cured;
if they lack merit and virtue, what benefit is there even if the signs are auspicious?"

Contemplating that the virtues of both worlds are all devoid of roots of goodness—having reflected thus, the second section consists of two parts: first, the provisional acceptance and response, which itself has two parts:
first, the formal provisional acceptance and response; second, further investigation.
Having reflected thus, he immediately set out together with the messengers.

Regarding the initial statement that he went "together with the messengers," this was said because he provisionally consented to the meeting between the sender and the sent; thus they were said to be "together" while on the road.
Furthermore, he reflected again, which constitutes the second [section] of the lower part; this also has two parts: first, observing the present, and next, observing the future.
As he was traveling along the road, he thought again: "If that patient possesses the signs of longevity, he can be cured; if he possesses the signs of short life, he cannot be treated.
Then, on the path ahead, he saw two young children pulling each other in a quarrel, seizing each other by the head and plucking out their hair.
They saw tiles, stones, swords, and staves being hurled at one another; they saw fire held by people extinguish spontaneously;
they saw some people cutting down trees, or others dragging hides along the road;
they saw objects left behind on the path, or people carrying empty vessels, or śramaṇas traveling alone without companions.
Furthermore, he saw tigers, wolves, crows, vultures, and wild foxes; having seen these things, he again thought to himself:
"The messengers I have sent, as well as all the omens encountered along the way, are entirely inauspicious. One should know that this patient will certainly be difficult to treat.
He further reflected: "If I do not go, I am not a skilled physician; yet if I do go, there is no hope of saving him."
Again he thought to himself: "Although these various signs are inauspicious, I shall set them aside for now and go to where the sick person is.

Having reflected thus, it is said that in the first instance, the two young children present represent the views of eternalism and nihilism, existence and non-existence, and so forth, which carry fire.

"Extinction" refers to the loss of the faculty of wisdom, illustrated by the analogy of a fire that has lost its light and function; the cutting down of trees illustrates the exhaustion of meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

and dragging a hide illustrates the loss of the faculty of ethical discipline (*śīla*). Although those with *icchantika* tendencies may receive [the teachings], they do not accept or follow them, like a withered hide from which all substance has fallen away.
They have exhausted all mundane and supramundane virtues, possessing only the attachment to wife and children—a virtue abandoned by the Noble Ones—like an empty vessel.
Although such a person possesses a physical body, it lacks the Dharma that is worthy of affection; the śramaṇa walks alone, like the supramundane Dharma which is solitary and without companion.
Furthermore, seeing tigers and wolves—beasts that devour flesh—is like the present evil consumption where all goodness has been utterly exhausted.

Furthermore, on the path ahead, he performs the second contemplation regarding the future, which consists of two parts: first, contemplating the causes of the future, and next, contemplating the effects of the future.
Again, on the path ahead, he hears such sounds as these: "lost," "dead," "passed away," "collapsed," "destroyed," "shattered," "stripped," and "separated."
Having fallen into this state of burning, they cannot return; they are incurable and cannot be rescued.
As for those on the path ahead, their present bodies will soon perish and they have not yet produced wholesome roots.
Furthermore, one hears that in the south, they look downward at future fruits.
Furthermore, he hears the sounds of birds and beasts in the south—namely, the cries of crows, vultures, and śarabha birds, as well as dogs, rats, wild foxes, pigs, and rabbits.
Having heard these sounds, he again reflects: "One should know that this patient is difficult to cure."
The sounds of birds and beasts, which are the retributions of the three miserable realms, are likened to hearing the sounds of suffering.
At that time, one enters the second section, "The Correct Response," which also has two parts: first, the analogy for the correct response; next, further contemplation.
At that time, he immediately enters the patient’s residence.
The first analogy—entering the house and abandoning one's original ground—is called "entering the patient’s residence" because it represents entering the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Upon seeing that patient, the second section follows, which further involves observation; this is divided into two parts: first, observing the present, and subsequently, observing the past.
Regarding the four, one, three poisons, two, five faculties, thirty proclivities, four, three karmas, and the first three poisons:
when observing that patient,
one sees them frequently experience cold and frequently experience heat.
The freezing congealment is like delusion; the feverish agitation is like greed, with hatred being omitted for brevity.
Next, the pain in the joints and bones represents the five faculties.
The pain in the joints and bones is accompanied by red eyes and flowing tears, sounds heard from the ears, constriction and pain in the throat, and the tongue splitting and cracking.
The bones and joints are the body faculty (*kāyendriya*); the redness of the eyes is the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*); the sound in the ears is the ear faculty (*śrotrendriya*);
the throat is the tongue faculty (*jihvendriya*);
the nose faculty is briefly absent. Third, its color is pure black; below this are the ten proclivities (*daśānuśaya*).

Its color is pitch black; the head is so heavy it cannot support itself, the body is withered and lacks perspiration, and the excretions of both large and small intestines are obstructed and do not pass.
The body suddenly becomes abnormally swollen, red, and crimson.

The black color is a metaphor for the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of ignorance (*avidyā*); the head being unable to support itself is a metaphor for the latent tendency of pride (*māna*), as one wishes to lift oneself up through pride.

A body that is emaciated and lacks perspiration is like the latent tendency of hatred, which lacks any moisture; the obstruction of the flow of excrement and urine is like the two views of annihilationism and eternalism;
and a sudden swelling of the body is like the view of a self.
The fourth [type] is that whose voice is unmodulated and low, which is a metaphor for the three karmas.
The voice is unmodulated, being either coarse or faint; the entire body is mottled with various colors such as blue and yellow; the abdomen is distended and full;
and speech is indistinct.
The sound of his speech is vocal karma; his body being mottled all over is bodily karma; and his belly being distended is mental karma.
Having observed this, the physician further examines the past, first investigating the primary conditions of the sense faculties.
Having seen this, the physician asks the attendant: "How has the patient’s mental state been since yesterday?
Since he says "since yesterday," is this not the past?
Next is the correspondence of the faculties and their objects.
He replied: "O Great Master, this man originally revered and had faith in the Triple Gem and the various devas, but now he has changed;
his feelings of reverence and faith have ceased. Originally he delighted in giving alms, but now he is stingy. By nature he ate little, but now he eats excessively.
By nature he was harsh and evil, but now he is gentle and kind. By nature he was compassionate, filial, and respectful toward his parents, but now, regarding his parents..."
Lacking a mind of reverence. There are five phrases in total;
the first constitutes a loss of supramundane goodness, while the latter four constitute losses of mundane goodness: first, the loss of goodness toward the Triple Gem;

second, the loss of goodness regarding wise giving; third, the loss of goodness characterized by moderation in eating and integrity; fourth, [the loss of goodness regarding... (The text appears to be truncated here).

The loss of the goodness of wickedness constitutes the first loss; the loss of the goodness of compassion and filial piety constitutes the second. Since the Three Jewels are known to be supramundane, the remainder are mundane.

Regarding the four types of goodness: as for the nature of wickedness according to the text, that which is now harmonious and good is merely the goodness of pitying one's wife and loving one's children, or the goodness of purity;
whereas wickedness is the fierce and violent goodness of protecting the Dharma.
Having heard this, the physician proceeds to the fourth stage, wherein he preaches the Dharma in three parts: first, the preaching of the Dharma; second, the cessation of the transformation;

and third, the severance of the response. Within the preaching of the Dharma, there are two phases: the first is the initial exposition, and the second is the thorough, repeated exposition that traces the source.
Having heard this, the physician immediately stepped forward and smelled it;

he discerned the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, the scent of aloeswood blended with various incenses, the scent of *piṅka*, the scent of *tagara*, the scent of *tamālapatra*, the scent of saffron, the scent of sandalwood, the stench of roasted meat, the stench of grape wine, the stench of burned bones and sinews, the stench of fish, and the stench of excrement.
Having thus distinguished the fragrances from the stenches, [he proceeded].
Regarding the first passage: "smelling it" is illustrated by the initial teaching on the seven fragrances and five stenches;
the seven fragrances represent the seven outflows (*āsrava*), and the five stenches represent the five desires (*kāma*).
"Touching the body" below illustrates the second teaching, which exhausts the source [of suffering].
When he touches the body, he perceives that it feels as soft and delicate as fine silk, cotton, or *sā* flowers;
yet at other times it is as hard as stone, as cold as ice, as hot as fire, or as rough as sand.

At that time, having observed these various signs, the skilled physician knows for certain that the patient will surely die without doubt; nevertheless, he does not definitively declare, "This person shall die."
Moving closer again until they were as if touching his body, he saw only the three poisons.
He said to the attendant: "Lower the second breath.
He said to the attendant: "I have urgent business now and shall come again tomorrow; provide whatever is required according to your needs, allowing yourself full liberty and do not restrain me."

Even when returning home, those with urgent affairs may do so after the first watch of the night; as for those who intend to come again the following day, there is currently no favorable condition for their transformation, and thus [the opportunity] has ceased.
Furthermore, to point toward the distant future and allow them to act as they please without restraint is not a regulation established by the Buddha-dharma.
The messenger arrived the following day and delivered the second verse.
When the messenger arrived again the next day, he spoke to him, saying, "My condition is not yet resolved, and furthermore, the medicine has not yet taken effect.
A wise person should know that such a patient will certainly die; there is no doubt.
The messenger’s arrival is again compared to the Buddha’s manifestation of skillful means; because [the beings] have not yet produced wholesome roots, it is said, "My work is not yet finished.

Great King, the second section of the text, which correlates the analogy, consists of three parts: first, the direct correlation; second, the exclusion of icchantikas; and third, the rescue and deliverance from the three miserable realms.
This is the initial direct correlation, which briefly summarizes the general meaning; if one looks back at the preceding analogy, it is simply...
The latter two [cases] accord, while the former two do not. First, it accords with the fourth [case] regarding the preaching of the Dharma;
next, it accords with the third [case] regarding the observation that goodness cannot arise.
Great King, the World-Honored One is likewise: he thoroughly knows the faculties and natures of those who are icchantikas and preaches the Dharma for them accordingly. Why is this?
For this reason, if one were not to explain it, all ordinary beings would say that the Tathāgata lacks great compassion;
yet those who possess compassion are called "Omniscient Ones. If he lacked compassion, how could he be called an Omniscient One?
Therefore, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma for the sake of icchantikas.

"Great King, when the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, sees those who are ill, he constantly bestows the medicine of the Dharma; yet if the sick do not take it, this is not the fault of the Tathāgata.
This concludes the first section on the icchantikas; now follows the second section, which further examines the icchantikas."

"Great King, among those who are icchantikas, there are two categories: first, those who will attain roots of goodness in the present life; second, those who will attain roots of goodness in future lives.
The Tathāgata clearly knows that for those icchantikas capable of attaining roots of goodness in the present, he teaches the Dharma;
for those who will attain them in future lives, he likewise teaches the Dharma. Although it may be of no benefit now, it serves as a cause for future lives."
For this reason, the Tathāgata expounds the essential teachings of the Dharma for icchantikas. There are two kinds of icchantikas:

first, those with sharp faculties; second, those with middling faculties. Those with sharp faculties are able to attain roots of goodness in the present life, while those with middling faculties will attain them in a future life.
Thus, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not preach the Dharma in vain.
In this context, regarding the statement that birth occurs either in the present or in future lives: if spoken in terms of actual entities, there is no such thing in any of the three times;

however, if one looks forward from afar at the possibility of birth for the sake of the meaning of "wholesome" (kuśala), there are two aspects: first, transforming through causes, and second, delivering through results.
For example, it is like a pure person who has fallen into a latrine;
a good friend sees him, feels pity for him, and immediately goes forward, seizes him by the hair, and pulls him out.
Great King, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are also like this: seeing sentient beings fallen into the three miserable realms, [they likewise rescue them].
Because he provides skillful means to rescue those in the evil realms and enable them to attain liberation, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma for the sake of icchantikas.
The King spoke to Jīvaka [as follows], marking the second instance of accepting the exhortation and proceeding as described in the text.
The King said to Jīvaka, "If it is indeed as the Tathāgata has declared, then tomorrow I shall select an auspicious day and favorable stars before proceeding.
Jīvaka replied to the King, "In the Dharma of the Tathāgata, there is no selection of auspicious days or favorable stars.
Great King, just as a person with a grave illness does not choose an auspicious day or consider the timing or omens, but seeks only a skilled physician, so it is now for Your Majesty."
When one is gravely ill and seeks the Buddha as a skilled physician, one should not select an auspicious time or a favorable day.
Great King, it is like the fire of sandalwood and the fire of *eranda*—the nature of their burning is no different. So it is with auspicious days and inauspicious days;
if one reaches the presence of the Buddha, both are able to extinguish transgressions. I only pray that the Great King will go there swiftly this very day. At that time, the Great King...
He immediately summoned a minister named Śrī and addressed him, saying: "Great Minister, you should know that I now wish to go to the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
quickly prepare all the requisites necessary for the offering. The minister replied: "Great King, excellent, excellent!
All the requisites for the offering are already present. Then King Ajātaśatru, together with his consort, prepared their carriage and mounted it.
There were twelve thousand great powerful elephants, numbering fifty thousand in total;
upon each elephant were three men carrying banners, parasols, flowers, incense, music, and various kinds of offerings, all of which were complete.
There were one hundred and eighty thousand horsemen leading the procession, and five hundred and eighty thousand people from the kingdom of Magadha followed the king.
At that time, the entire great assembly in the city of Kuśinagara, numbering as many as filled twelve yojanas,
all saw from afar King Ajātaśatru approaching along the road with his retinue.
At that time, the Buddha spoke; this third section, "The Tathāgata’s Praise," is further divided into four parts: first, the king’s doubt; second, the Buddha’s definitive resolution;
third, the retention of all questions; and fourth, the Buddha’s response.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying: "For all sentient beings who seek the proximate causes and conditions for Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, there is no one more fundamental than a virtuous friend. Why is this?

If King Ajātaśatru had not followed the words of Jīvaka, he would have certainly met his end this coming seventh day and fallen into the Avīci Hell. Therefore, [a virtuous friend] is the proximate cause."
The Prince Ajātaśatru, having previously heard on the road that King Virūḍhaka of Śrāvastī died after encountering fire while traveling by ship at sea,
and that the bhikṣu Kokālika entered the earth alive to reach the Avīci Hell,
and that Sunakṣatra, despite committing various evils, had his multitude of sins extinguished upon reaching the Buddha— having heard these things...
Having spoken thus, he said to Jīvaka: "Although I have now heard these two words, I am still not yet certain.
Come, Jīvaka; I wish to ride upon the same elephant as you. Should I enter the Avīci Hell, I hope that you will hold me fast so that I do not fall.
Why is this? In the past, I have heard that those who have attained the Way do not enter hell."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying: "King Ajātaśatru still harbors doubts.
His initial doubt concerned whether the Buddha’s wisdom could eliminate them; he wondered whether his own transgressions could be removed or not."
Next, from "I now" onwards, the Buddha makes a definitive determination:
"I shall now form a resolute mind to eliminate,
by means of the wisdom capable of elimination, those offenses that are to be eliminated."
3. At that time, the section beginning with "Holding All Questions" follows.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Holding All, who addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha previously taught, all dharmas are without fixed characteristics;
that is to say, form has no fixed characteristic, and so on, up to and including nirvāṇa."
"Since all things lack fixed characteristics, how is it that the Tathāgata now speaks of creating a resolute mind for Ajātaśatru?
The Buddha teaches that everything is without fixity; why then does he make a definitive statement for the sake of the king?"
The four Buddhas spoke in response below:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! I shall now certainly bring about a state of certainty for King Ajātaśatru.
Why is this? If the king's state of doubt can be destroyed, you should know that all phenomena possess no fixed characteristics."
Therefore, I have brought about a state of certainty in King Ajātaśatru; you should know that this mind is a certainty of non-certainty.
Good son, if that king’s mind were a fixed certainty, how could the king’s crime of parricide be destroyed?
Because it lacks the characteristic of fixedness, his crime can be destroyed; for this reason, I have brought about a state of certainty in King Ajātaśatru.
The king himself said, "That which can be eliminated and that which cannot be eliminated, I shall eliminate for him; that which is indeterminate, I shall render determinate.
At that time, the great king descended from the fourth level and arrived at the Buddha's dwelling; thus, the king came for the fourth time.
At that time, the Great King went to the twin śāla trees where the Buddha was staying;
he gazed up at the Tathāgata’s thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, which were like a mountain of exquisite, pure gold.
The two Buddhas comforted him.
At that time, the World-Honored One uttered eight kinds of sounds and addressed the Great King, saying: "At this moment, O Great King, look around among this great assembly;
who here is the Great King? Since I am one who has committed a heinous crime and lack merit, the Tathāgata should not [address me]."
When he was thus addressed as "Great King," the Tathāgata then called out again, "Ajātaśatru, Great King.
Upon hearing this, the king’s heart was filled with great joy, and he spoke these words: "Today the Tathāgata has looked upon me with words of affection;
truly, I know that the Tathāgata’s great compassion and pity for all sentient beings are equal and without distinction. He then addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I..."
Now, with all doubt forever eliminated, I know for certain that the Tathāgata is truly the unsurpassed Great Teacher of sentient beings.
When addressed collectively, they were still confused; when addressed individually, they rejoiced.
Thus spoke the three Kāśyapas.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvadhārī, saying: "The Tathāgata has already brought King Ajātaśatru to a state of certainty.
The four kings presented their offerings as described in the text."

King Ajātaśatru again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, even if I were now to share a seat, rise, eat, and drink with Brahmā or Śakra Devendra, I would still not feel such joy as I do upon encountering a single word or glance from the Tathāgata; I am profoundly delighted and celebrant.
He then took the banners, parasols, incense, flowers, and musical instruments he held and offered them as worship, prostrating at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulating him to the right.
Having circumambulated three times and completed his prostrations, he withdrew and sat to one side.

At that time, the Buddha spoke to him. This second section, which is precisely on the extinction of offenses, is divided into two parts: first, a brief exposition of the Dharma, followed by a detailed exposition of the Dharma.

Within the initial brief text, there are again two sections: first, the brief exposition; second, the comprehension and acceptance [of that teaching]. The brief exposition further consists of three parts: first, the granting of permission; [the subsequent parts follow].
Following the admonition, he proceeded to explain the three fetters.
At that time, the Buddha addressed King Ajātaśatru, saying: "Great King, I shall now expound for you the essentials of the True Dharma;
you should listen with single-minded attention, listen and listen carefully."
In the formal exposition, first twenty matters are indicated and then explained.
An ordinary person should always bind their mind to contemplate that the body possesses these twenty matters.

Within the explanation, they are arranged as ten pairs: first, it clarifies the absence of untainted (anāsrava) true dharmas; next, it clarifies the absence of tainted (sāsrava) semblances of understanding.
This constitutes a pair consisting of the real and the semblance:
first, that this body of mine is empty within and lacks the outflow-free [dharmas], and second, that it is devoid of all roots of goodness.

Next, the first part generally clarifies the existence of the evil causes of birth and death, while the latter clarifies the falling into the evil effects of the three miserable realms; these form another pair.
Third, this cycle of birth and death of mine has not yet been brought under control; fourth, having fallen into a deep pit, there is no place where I do not fear.
First, it clarifies the lack of wisdom and skillful means prior to the Path; next, it clarifies the power of meditative concentration cultivated prior to the Path—these two form a pair.
Fifth, by what skillful means can one see the Buddha-nature? Sixth, how does one cultivate meditative concentration to see the Buddha-nature?

First, it clarifies that the four inversions of birth and death consist only of suffering and impermanence; subsequently, it clarifies that liberation from the eight difficulties is treated as a pair with the difficulty of inversion.

Seventh, birth and death are constantly characterized by suffering, lacking permanence, selfhood, or purity; eighth, it is difficult to escape the hardships of the eight inopportune states (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*).
Ninth, the five enemies form a pair;
tenth, there is not a single dharma capable of obstructing the various realms of existence (*bhava*).

Sixth, they cannot escape the bitter fruits of suffering in the three miserable realms in the beginning, nor can they escape the seeds of suffering in the end; these two bonds of cause and fruit constitute one pair.
Eleventh, they have not attained liberation from the three evil destinies; twelfth, they are fully possessed of various kinds of evil and false views.
Seventh, beginninglessness and endlessness form one pair.
Thirteenth, likewise, they have not been created or established; they cross over the ford of the five heinous crimes. Fourteenth, birth and death are boundless, and their limit has not been attained.
The eight [points on] emptiness and existence constitute one pair.
Fifteenth: not performing various karmas and thus not obtaining retributive results; sixteenth: there is no "I" who acts and another who receives the results.
The ninth [point on] cause and effect constitutes one pair.
17. If one does not create the causes for happiness, there will ultimately be no fruit of happiness. 18. If one has created karma, its fruit will never be lost.
19. Delusion and negligence form a pair;
because of ignorance one is born, and because of it one dies. 20. One constantly practices negligence throughout the past, future, and present.

Now, based on the three truths, the twenty contemplations are explained as follows: 1. "There is none who lacks the outflow-free [dharmas] or the roots of goodness" refers to the true and semblance dharmas within the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha-satya*).
2. "Those whose birth-and-death is not yet tamed and who fear the deep pit" refers to the cause and effect involving fear within the Truth of Conventional Reality (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
3. These two phrases concerning the Buddha-nature refer to the wisdom and concentration of the means (*upāya*) prior to the Path, which constitute the path within that absence [of fear].

The four perversions are the path of affliction (*kleśa-mārga*); the eight difficulties are the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*); and enemies and the various realms of existence (*bhava*) are the path of karma (*karma-mārga*).
[As stated] at length.
This concludes the third section concerning ordinary persons, which summarizes the gains and losses.
"Great King, an ordinary person should constantly perform these twenty kinds of contemplations upon this body.

Having performed these contemplations, one will find no delight in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Finding no delight in birth-and-death, one then attains *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. At that time, one sequentially contemplates the characteristics of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the mind;
the same applies to concentration, wisdom, diligence, and morality. Once one has known the arising, abiding, and ceasing [of these], [one attains liberation]."
From the characteristics of the mind up to the characteristics of ethical discipline, one ultimately commits no evil and has no fear of death or the three evil realms;
however, if one does not bind the mind to observe these twenty matters, the mind will become heedless and there is no evil that will not be committed.
Regarding the statement, "To perform twenty kinds of contemplation is a loss, for one fails to attain non-contemplation," this is as stated in the text.
Under the words "Ajātaśatru said," the second section follows:
Ajātaśatru said, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, from the past until now, I have never contemplated this."
Due to twenty matters, one frequently commits various evils; because one commits various evils, there is the fear of death and the fear of the three evil realms.

[This concludes] the second section, "The World-Honored One Himself Brings Calamity Upon Himself," followed by an extensive explanation. Furthermore, there are three parts: first, the king gives rise to a misconception;

second, the Buddha extensively refutes it; third, the king receives the teaching and acts accordingly. Regarding the initial arising of the misconception, there are four points: first, the misconception regarding grave offenses; second, the misconception regarding... [text fragment].
"O Father King, you have thrice declared me innocent, yet four times you have declared that I am certain to fall.
World-Honored One, I myself have invited this calamity by committing such a grave evil.
O Father King!
To unjustly inflict harm upon the innocent—
these twenty matters, whether one contemplates them or not, will inevitably lead to rebirth in the Avīci Hell.
Because these four [categories] are stubbornly clung to and obstruct entry into the Path, they must be destroyed.

The Buddha told [the following], which constitutes the second section: "The Buddha’s Refutation. This is further divided into three parts: first, the individual refutations; second, the general refutation; and third, the summary exhortation.

Regarding the initial individual refutations, these refute the four aforementioned attachments without following their original order; first, the refutation of the fourth [attachment], "Necessarily Falling," is presented in three parts.
First, the actual refutation.
The Buddha told the Great King: "The nature and characteristics of all dharmas are impermanent and lack any fixed certainty.
Why, then, do you say that you will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell?
Killing lacks a fixed characteristic; as the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* says, 'All sinful karmas arise from deluded thoughts.'"
Sitting upright, contemplate the true nature of reality; all transgressions are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can dispel.
If one penetrates the nature of delusive thoughts, then karmic offenses are released and cleared away; because there is no karma, there is no falling.
Next, regarding the reign of King Ajātaśatru, the king addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if all dharmas lack a fixed characteristic, then my sin of killing should also not be fixed.
If killing were fixed, then all dharmas would not be unfixed."
The Tathāgata confirmed this, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Great King! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach that all dharmas are entirely without fixed characteristics.
Since you further understand that killing is also not fixed, you should therefore know that killing has no fixed characteristic."
Great King, as you have stated, this is the second section, refuting the second [type of] attachment to the father-king.

Although both [arguments] cite the innocence of the father-king, the first refutes the father-king by clarifying that he exists only as a provisional designation based on causes and conditions, and thus there is no father;
the second clarifies that because [the self] arises and perishes moment by moment, there is no father.
"Great King, regarding what you have said—that your father king was innocent and yet you perversely committed the act of regicide—who, then, is your father?

It is merely within the five aggregates (*skandha*) of a conventionally designated sentient being that one falsely gives rise to the notion of 'father. Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*), which one is the father?
If form (*rūpa*) were the father, then the other four aggregates would not be; if the four aggregates were the father, then form would likewise not be."
There is no possibility for form and non-form to combine to constitute a father. Why is this? Because the natures of form and non-form do not conjoin.
Great King, ordinary sentient beings falsely give rise to the notion of a "father" regarding this aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Furthermore, this aggregate of form cannot be harmed. Why is this? Because there are ten kinds of form; among these ten, only the single category of "form" [is subject to such considerations].
One may see that things can be held, weighed, measured, led, or bound;

yet, when one investigates and scrutinizes each and every phenomenon from the beginning, a father cannot be found. If one approaches from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the nature of heaven and the relationship between father and son are clearly manifest;
however, if one approaches from the perspective of ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), all phenomena are equal and without distinction.
Since there is no distinction between father and son, how could there be the duality of "the one who kills" and "the one who is killed"?

Regarding the ten kinds of *dharmas*, these consist of the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) and the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Furthermore, there must also be the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*); though the text is abbreviated, they are likewise mutually inclusive.

The five sense objects constitute the four great elements, and the four great elements constitute the five sense organs. Thus, the four great elements constituting the five sense organs means that the ten [categories] are subsumed within the four great elements.
Form consists of the five sense objects and the four great elements; since these ten types of form subsume the four great elements, they are not explained in detail.
Although it is visible, it is bound [to suffering]; below this, the second section clarifies that because it arises and perishes moment by moment, there is no fault.
Although it can be seen, its nature does not abide; because it does not abide, it cannot be seen, it cannot be grasped, it cannot be measured, and it cannot be bound.
Since the characteristic of form (*rūpa*) is thus, how could it be killed?
If form were the father who, when killed or harmed, would incur the retribution of sin, then the other nine [elements] would not be so; if the other nine were not so, then there would be no sin.
Great King, there are three kinds of form: past, future, and present. That which is past and that which is present cannot be harmed. Why?
Because the past has already passed away, and the present perishes moment by moment. One speaks of "killing" only by way of obstructing the future.
Thus, regarding this single form, some may be subject to killing while others are not; such is the nature of form, whether it can be killed or cannot be killed.
If the physical form is indeterminate and the killing is also indeterminate, then because the killing is indeterminate, the retribution is also indeterminate.
Why, then, do you say that one is certain to enter hell?
Great King, this [teaching] causes all sentient beings to abandon their third [type of] attachment—the first being the fixed adherence to gravity.
"Great King, the sinful karma committed by all sentient beings is of two kinds: first, light; second, heavy.
If it is committed through mind and speech, it is called light; if it is committed through body, speech, and mind, it is called heavy.

Great King, if you have thought of it in your mind and spoken of it with your mouth, but did not act upon it with your body, the retribution you receive will be light. Great King, in the past, you did not command others to kill with your mouth, but merely spoke..."
"Great King Prasenajit, if you had commanded your attendants to execute the king's head while he was seated, and you had executed it then, you would still not have incurred sin;
how much less so when you did not command it? How could you incur sin? If you were to incur sin, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, would also incur sin.
Why is this? Because your father, the former king Bimbisāra, once planted various roots of goodness under the Buddhas."
Therefore, that I am able to occupy the throne today is because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, accepted his offerings; had he not done so, I would not be king.
Had I not been king, you would not have been able to bring harm upon the state. If there were sin in your killing your father, then we Buddhas should also be guilty of sin.
Since the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are without sin, why is it that you alone are so?
And thus one incurs offense.

By blending the mind that distinguishes high and low and extinguishing the view of discrimination, King Bimbisāra’s fourth [section] below refutes his third attachment to the notion of innocence; this further consists of two parts, the first of which cites...
Regarding a past event:
In former times, King Bimbisāra, while wandering about Mount Vipula with the intent to hunt, traversed the entire wilderness but found nothing at all;
he saw only a single seer endowed with the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Upon seeing him, the king immediately conceived a feeling of malice.
With a mind of malice and hatred, he thought, "I am now out hunting; it is because of this man that I could not sit properly, as he drove me away.
He immediately commanded his attendants to kill him. As the man approached death, a hateful and malicious mind arose within him, and he lost his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
He then made a vow: "I am truly innocent, yet you have wantonly subjected me to slaughter through both heart and speech. In a future life, I shall likewise—"
"When you were thus returning [to life] by means of mind and speech, yet your life was taken, the King heard this and immediately gave rise to a heart of regret;
he made offerings to the corpse of the former king and thereby received only a light retribution, not falling into hell.

How much more so for a king who does not act in such a way—how could he receive the fruit of retribution in hell? The former king acted himself and must receive it himself; how could he cause the current king to..."
One incurs the sin of killing.
Next, I shall cite your position and refute it:

if, as Your Majesty says, the father king was innocent, how can you say he is not? If one has a husband, there is a sin; if one does not, there is no sin. Therefore, [the father] must have committed a sin.
If there were no evil karma, there would be no retribution for offenses; yet your father, the former king, was without offense—how then could there be retribution?
Bimbisāra obtained both good and evil fruits within his present life. Therefore, the former king’s case was also not fixed;
because it was not fixed, killing was also not fixed; and because killing was not fixed, how could [the act of killing]...?
It is said that one will certainly enter hell.
Great King, sentient beings are deluded and confused. [This concludes] the second section, the general refutation, which is further divided into three parts:

first, citing the four types of madness and so forth to dispel the fixed attachment to the real existence [of karma]; second, starting from "Just as in the royal palace," refuting the lack of compassion and inequality; third, the analogies.

As in the section on *nirvāṇa* below, this refutes the error of being stuck in extreme views; first, regarding the four types of madness, there are two parts: first the teaching (*dharma*), then the analogy.
"Great King, sentient beings who are deluded by madness are of four kinds: first, madness from greed; second, madness from medicine;
third, madness from incantations; and fourth, madness from the conditions of past karma. Great King, among my disciples there are these four types of madness, and though they are many..."
"I shall never record that this person has broken the precepts; what this person has done will not lead to rebirth in the three evil realms.

If he regains his mind, I shall not say he has committed an offense. Since the King originally coveted the kingdom and incited this rebellious harm, acting out of a mind maddened by greed, how could he incur guilt?"

Among these, the madness of craving is most violent and its delusive confusion is even more extreme than the madness of medicine, the madness of spells that causes one to lose one's mind by rushing headlong into water or fire, or the madness of karma that seizes and distorts the mind through unrighteous deeds. Of these three types of madness, the King possesses none;
he has only the madness of craving. What is produced by this madness of craving is merely the fault of craving itself.
Next, within the two analogies—first intoxication and then illusion—the section on intoxication further consists of two parts: first the analogy, then the application.
"Great King, it is like a man who, having become intoxicated with wine, harms his own mother; once he has sobered up, remorse arises in his mind.
You should know that for such karma, no retribution will be received."

To begin with, the analogy of the intoxicated person is as follows: if one was originally angry and, after consuming wine, continues to revile another, this is not called being "intoxicated" [in the sense of lacking responsibility].

If one commits an offense based on this principle, one incurs the karmic retribution for that offense. However, if after becoming intoxicated one is entirely without awareness and has no sense of avoidance or engagement, committing an offense in such a state constitutes no offense at all.
"Your Majesty, you have now fallen into error.
Your Majesty is currently intoxicated by craving and acts not from your original mind; if one acts not from their original mind, how can they be guilty of an offense?
Your Majesty is likewise, just like a drunken man."
Next, Great King, it is like a magician; [the text] next cites nine analogies, such as magical illusions and so forth, to refute their substantial existence.
In each case, there is first the analogy followed by the application (*yoga*). In the first analogy, the text specifically cites magical illusion to refute substantial existence.
