"Great King, it is like a magician who, at a crossroads, conjures various men, women, elephants, horses, necklaces, and garments through illusion.
A foolish person says they truly exist, whereas a wise person knows they are not real. Killing is likewise:
ordinary people regard it as real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it is not real."
Great King, it is like the sound of an echo in a mountain valley: a foolish person takes it to be a real sound, whereas a wise person knows it is not real.
Killing is also like this: ordinary people take it to be real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it is not real.
Great King, it is like a person who harbors enmity but feigns intimacy; a foolish person regards this as true, while one of wisdom understands and realizes it is a deception.
Killing is likewise: ordinary people regard it as real, whereas the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be unreal.
"Great King, it is like a person who takes up a mirror and sees the reflection of his own face; a foolish person calls it a real face, while a wise person understands and knows it is not real.
Killing is likewise: ordinary people call it real, whereas the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it is not real."
"Great King, it is like a mirage in the heat; a foolish person calls it water, but a wise person thoroughly understands that it is not water.
Killing is likewise: ordinary people call it real, but the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be unreal."
"Great King, it is like the city of the gandharvas: those who are foolish and ignorant claim it to be real, while the wise understand and know it to be unreal.
Killing is likewise: ordinary worldlings claim it to be real, whereas the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be unreal."
"Great King, it is like a person who experiences the pleasures of the five senses within a dream; a foolish person deems it real, while a wise person thoroughly understands that it is not true.
Killing is likewise: ordinary people deem it real, whereas the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be unreal. Great King, such is the nature of killing."
I fully understand the act of killing, the killer, the fruit of killing, and liberation; thus, there is no sin. Although Your Majesty knows of killing, how could there be sin?
Great King, it is like a person who is the master in charge of wine: if he does not drink, he will not become intoxicated. Even though...
One knows that fire does not burn;
the king is likewise, for although he knows of the killing, how could there be sin?
Great King, there are sentient beings who commit various kinds of offenses when the sun rises, and they further act [sinfully] when the moon rises.

Just as when the sun and moon are stolen away and do not appear, one does not commit a transgression; although it is because of the sun and moon that one commits a transgression, these sun and moon themselves are truly not guilty.
Killing is also like this: although it may depend upon a king, the king is truly without guilt.
This is like the second point of refutation [concerning] the lack of compassion and impartiality within the royal palace.
Great King, if within the royal palace you constantly command the slaughter of sheep without the slightest fear in your heart, why do you alone feel fear toward your father?

Although there is a distinction between humans and animals in terms of nobility and lowliness, there is no difference between the two when it comes to cherishing life and fearing death; for what reason is this so?
"Regarding the sheep, his heart was light and he felt no fear; regarding his father, the former king, he gave rise to heavy sorrow and suffering.

Great King, the people of this world are slaves to craving and lack self-mastery; driven by craving, they commit acts of killing. If there is a karmic retribution for this, it is the fault of craving.
Since the King himself lacked self-mastery, what fault could there be in him?"
Who is it that values death more than life? Since we do not speak of such a thing now, it must be because death is considered weighty.

Whether human or animal, all regard the suffering of death as weighty; thus it is said that preserving one's life is more important than death, and in this regard, humans and animals are no different.

However, if we proceed according to the established precepts (*śīla*), a human commits a grave offense while an animal commits a light one; this is discussed in terms of the distinction between the goodness or evil of their respective past karmas.
They may be considered analogous; if one approaches this from the perspective of giving food, it is equal to this because both give rise to a mind that takes the true reality as its object.
This is further discussed separately.
Great King, for example, like nirvāṇa... [The third section] below refutes the error of being stuck in extremes; it consists of two parts, the first of which presents the argument.
Nirvāṇa serves as the analogy.
Great King, it is like this: for example, nirvāṇa is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is also existent.
Next, bringing the act of being led to execution into conjunction with the analogy, there are three such applications as set forth in the text.
Killing is also like this: although it is neither existent nor non-existent, it is nonetheless existent.

Those who possess a sense of shame and remorse are said to be "existent," while those without shame and remorse are said to be "non-existent. One who experiences the retribution of karma is called one who holds the view of existence;
one who does not experience it is called one who holds the view of non-existence. Furthermore, one who holds the view of existence is also called...
For what reason? Because those who hold the view of existence obtain karmic retribution, whereas those who hold the view of non-existence have no such retribution.
One who holds the view of eternalism regards things as non-existent [in their true nature], while one who holds the view of non-eternalism regards them as non-non-existent.

Why is it that one who holds the view of eternalism cannot regard things as non-existent? Because one who holds the view of eternalism possesses the fruit of evil karma; therefore, they are eternally [bound by it].
One who sees [this] cannot say it is non-existent; for this reason, although it is neither existent nor non-existent, it is nevertheless existent, Great King.
Now, "sentient beings" is a name for the inhalation and exhalation of breath; because the inhalation and exhalation of breath are severed, it is called "killing.
Even the Buddhas, following worldly convention, also speak of it as killing.
Having finished the threefold refutation, he concludes by exhorting him to practice contemplation (as follows):

"Great King, form is impermanent... and so forth. This third section, which concludes with the exhortation to practice contemplation, is further divided into two parts: first, the exhortation to perform the contemplation of impermanence and so forth.
Great King, form is impermanent; the causes and conditions of form are also impermanent. Since form arises from impermanent causes, how could it be permanent? This applies even unto consciousness:
consciousness is impermanent, and the causes and conditions of consciousness are also impermanent. Since consciousness arises from impermanent causes, how could it be permanent?
Because it is impermanent, it is suffering; because it is suffering, it is empty; because it is empty, it is non-self. If...
Regarding this impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self: what is it that kills them? By killing impermanence, one attains the permanence of nirvana;
by killing suffering, one attains happiness; by killing emptiness, one attains reality; and by killing non-self, one attains the true self.
Next, by stating "if one kills the impermanent," he exhorts [the king] to cultivate the contemplations of permanence, bliss, and so forth.
"Great King, if you kill that which is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, then you are the same as I;
I too have killed this impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and thus do not enter hell—how could you possibly enter?"

At that time, King Ajātaśatru descended to the third section on "Practicing the Teaching. This section further divides into two parts: first, clarifying contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), and second, distinguishing the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Within the first part on contemplative practice, there are three sections: (1) correctly performing the contemplation, (2) consulting the Buddha, and (3) self-congratulation.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru contemplated form as taught by the Buddha, up to and including contemplating consciousness.

In the initial passage, it clarifies both treating [phenomena] as impermanent and treating them as permanent. Why is this? If one does not treat them as permanent, one will not understand the contemplation of impermanence;
by realizing both permanence and impermanence, one penetrates that which is neither permanent nor impermanent.
Having made this contemplation, he then addressed the Buddha.
Having made this contemplation, he said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, it is only now that I have come to know that form is impermanent, and so on, up to consciousness being impermanent.
Had I been able to contemplate in this way from the beginning, I would not have committed these offenses."
"O World-Honored One, I have heard this in the past and am filled with joy and self-congratulation. Furthermore, the first of these three [sections] clarifies how he was sheltered by the Buddha:
"O World-Honored One, I have heard in the past that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always act as parents to sentient beings," though I had heard this...
This statement was not yet fully understood, but now it is known with certainty.
Next, below the King of Mountains, Sumeru, it clarifies that [the understanding] is identical to the Buddha’s own explanation:
"World-Honored One, I have also heard that the King of Mountains, Sumeru, is composed of four jewels, namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and..."
Just as when various birds gather in a particular place, they take on the same color as that location, so too, although I have heard this teaching, I have not yet attained definitive certainty;
yet now that I have come to the Buddha’s Mount Sumeru, I have become the same color as it.
By becoming the same color as it, I realize that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Third, "I have seen the world" is precisely an expression of self-congratulation.
World-Honored One, I have seen that from an *eranda* seed an *eranda* tree grows, but I have never seen an *eranda* tree grow from a sandalwood tree.
Now, for the first time, I see an *eranda* seed produce a sandalwood tree; this "eranda seed" is my own body.
This sandalwood tree is precisely my own mind’s rootless faith.
It is called "rootless" because, in the beginning, I did not know how to revere the Tathāgata and lacked faith in the Dharma and the Saṃgha; this is what is meant by being rootless.
"Those with rootless faith" refers to those whose five faculties were not yet established at the outset, yet have now attained faith; hence they are called "rootless.

World-Honored One, if I had not encountered [the Buddha]—this second section distinguishes the arousal of the mind, which further has three parts: first, a general clarification of the King’s arousal of the mind;
second, the arousal of the mind by the Queen and her retinue; third, the King’s departure and arousal of the mind, which further has three parts: first, the King’s arousal of the mind...
[My] mind:
"World-Honored One, had I not encountered the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, I would have been undergoing immeasurable suffering in the great hells for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Now I am fortunate to have seen the Tathāgata; it is by virtue of seeing the Buddha that I have obtained this."
It completely destroys the afflictions and evil minds of sentient beings.
This is the second Tathāgata Seal.
The Buddha said, "Great King, excellent, excellent! I now know that you will certainly be able to destroy the evil minds of sentient beings."
The three kings again resolved their minds with gravity:
"World-Honored One, if we are truly able to destroy the various evil minds of sentient beings, we would rather remain forever in the Avīci Hell for immeasurable kalpas,
undergoing great suffering and affliction on behalf of all sentient beings without regarding it as suffering."

Second, at that time, King Adhastātprabhāsa of the Mahāvedalya kingdom and his retinue developed the aspiration for enlightenment; this further consists of three parts: first, the development of the aspiration;
second, making offerings and offering praise; third, the Tathāgata’s description of how they have correctly developed the aspiration.
This also consists of three parts: first, the people of the country; second, the king’s consort; third, the king’s joy.
At that time, immeasurable people in the kingdom of Magadha all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because such immeasurable people had thus developed the great resolve, King Ajātaśatru’s grave offenses were immediately lightened and diminished.
If the people of the country resolve their minds so that the king’s offense may be lightened, it serves as a remote condition for the extinction of his sin. Why is this?
Because when sentient beings are ill, the Bodhisattva is ill; when the illness of sentient beings is cured, the Bodhisattva is also cured.
According to this text, one who resolves their mind from the time of Vipaśyin Buddha will not fall [into evil realms]. According to the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*, by means of...
In the presence of seventy-two billion buddhas, he resolved his mind upon bodhi.
The king, along with his queen, the ladies of the inner palace, and the court attendants, all likewise resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to Jīvaka: "Jīvaka, although I have not yet died, I have already attained a celestial body;
I have abandoned a short life and obtained a long life, and I have abandoned an impermanent body and obtained an eternal body.
Causing all sentient beings to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is itself the celestial body, the long life, and the eternal body."
These are all the disciples of the Buddhas.
Having spoken these words, the second section on offering and praise begins; it is further divided into two parts, the first of which is the brief prose description of the bodily act of offering.
Having spoken these words, he immediately made offerings to the Buddha with various jeweled banners, flags, canopies, incense, flowers, necklaces, and exquisite music.
Next follows the oral offering in verse; there are fifteen and a half lines, divided into two parts. The first nine and a half lines consist of praises.
The eulogy consists of six lines; the aspiration for practice consists of nine and a half lines, further divided into three parts:

the first seven and a half lines eulogize the secret of speech (*vāg-guhyaka*), the next one line eulogizes the secret of mind (*manoguhyaka*), and the final one line eulogizes the secret of body (*kāyaguhyaka*). Within the initial section on the secret of speech, there are again three parts:
the first three lines eulogize truthful speech (*satya-vāk*), the next one and a half lines eulogize gentle speech (*mṛdu-vāk*), and the final three lines eulogize meaningful speech (*arthavād-vāk*).
Again, he praised him with these verses:
"Your truthful speech is most subtle, Skillful in its words and meanings. For the sake of the multitude, you have revealed The profound and secret treasury.
All those vast and extensive teachings, You have summarized for the sake of the multitude."
Possessing such speech as this, he is well able to heal sentient beings.
If there are any sentient beings who hear these words—whether they believe them or do not believe them—they will certainly know that this is the Buddha’s teaching.
The Buddhas always speak with gentle words; yet for the sake of the multitude, they may speak harshly. Thus there are both harsh expressions and gentle words.
All return to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore, I now take refuge in the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, whose speech is of a single flavor, like the waters of the great ocean.
Because it is called the ultimate truth, there are no words therein that lack meaning. Thus, the various and immeasurable dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata now [all converge in this].
Whether men or women, great or small, upon hearing this, all alike attain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Without cause and without fruit, without arising and without cessation—this is called Great Nirvāṇa (*mahāparinirvāṇa*). Those who hear it shall shatter all [false] fruits:
truthful speech counters false speech; gentle speech counters harsh speech; meaningful speech counters frivolous speech; and there shall be harmony.
Regarding the phrase "absence of divisive speech," the text is abbreviated; furthermore, truthful speech includes harmonizing speech.
Second, the Tathāgata praises for all beings the virtue of his great compassion in mental action.
The Tathāgata acts as a compassionate father and mother for all; one should know that all sentient beings are the children of the Tathāgata.
This single line praising the Great Compassion of the World-Honored One shows how he manifests his body for the sake of beings.
The World-Honored One, with great compassion, practiced austerities for the sake of the multitude; like one possessed by a malevolent spirit, he acted with much agitation.
Now that I have been able to see the Buddha—this marks the beginning of the second section of six verses on making vows and repentance, which embodies the meaning of the five types of repentance.
The Single Practice of Dedication:
Now that I have been able to behold the Buddha, Whatever goodness I have attained through the three karmas,
I vow to dedicate this merit toward the Unsurpassed Way.
The next line clarifies the exhortation:
"I now make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; by virtue of this merit, may the Triple Gem endure forever in the world."
The next line clarifies sympathetic joy:
"Whatever various merits I am now to obtain, may they serve to destroy the four kinds of Māra for all sentient beings."
The next line clarifies the confession:
"Having encountered evil associates, I have committed sins throughout the three periods of time; now, before the Buddha, I repent and vow never to commit them again."
The latter two lines express the vow; the first line expresses the initial aspiration:
"May all sentient beings alike All give rise to the bodhicitta, And with focused minds, constantly keep in mind All Buddhas of the ten directions."
Next, by practicing this, one will see the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, may all sentient beings forever destroy all afflictions and clearly perceive the Buddha-nature,
just like Mañjuśrī and others.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in the third section on "Explanatory Confirmation," further divided it into three parts, the first of which describes his manifestation in the present world.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised King Ajātaśatru, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
If there is anyone who can resolve to attain Bodhicitta, you should know that such a person serves as an adornment for the great assembly of all Buddhas."
Second, you have already described your past lives below.
Great King, from the time you first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* under Vipaśyin Buddha until my appearance in the world,
you have never again fallen into hell during that interval.
"O Great King who Endures Suffering, you should know that the bodhicitta yields such immeasurable fruits and rewards.
Thirdly, from this point forward, I shall describe its future [rewards], which likewise serves as an exhortation to practice."
"Great King, from this day forward, you should constantly encourage the cultivation of the bodhicitta. Why is this?
Because by means of these causes and conditions, you shall attain the eradication of immeasurable evils."

In the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, it is explained that when the Buddha spoke for the sake of King Śrīmālā and Mañjuśrī spoke for his sake, the king’s grave offenses—as vast as Mount Sumeru—were all extinguished.
That which was not extinguished was only the size of a mustard seed; yet even this entered the Bhaṇḍa hell.
Although he remained therein, he experienced no suffering. Furthermore, he received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood under the name Viśuddhamati.
Śāriputra, these words purify that which is illuminated.
The threefold salutation and withdrawal are as stated in the text.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru and all the people of the kingdom of Magadha rose from their seats and circumambulated [him].
The Buddha circumambulated him three times, took his leave, and returned to the palace.
As for the "Chapter on Celestial Conduct" (*Devagati-parivarta*), it is as explained in the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*.
The term "celestial conduct" points directly to the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-one: The Practice of the Infant. This chapter is the third that clarifies the practice of the infant.
Some teachers say that it derives its name from a metaphor and takes provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) as its essence.
Transforming beings is its function; now it is clarified that *nirvāṇa* is neither small nor large, yet one may still discuss smallness and largeness.
"Small" refers to the practice of an infant, while "large" refers to the practice of the Tathāgata. With expedient wisdom as its essence, it can be likened to the [use of] yellow leaves;

this cannot be categorized within the practice of the Tathāgata. The text is divided into three parts: first, clarifying the infant; second, explaining the meaning of the infant; third, concluding the section on the infant.

The child is indeed a supreme sage; both the Brahma and Śrāvaka practices are likewise so, and thus he cannot be without them. Taking the first [practice] as twofold: first, clarifying the infant of perfect practice;

second, clarifying the infant of partial practice. As for the interpretation that "not arising" and "not speaking" refer to the infant of the original stage (*mūla-bhūmi*), this meaning is not correct.
You say the infant is the practice for transforming others; yet, in the original stage, whom would he transform? Now...
It clarifies that the fundamental stage is neither great nor small, yet it can give rise to both great and small transformations.
Regarding the manifestation as a great or small infant, there are two parts: first, the analogy; second, the application of the analogy, which consists of four points: first, the inability to arise;
second, the inability to abide; third, the inability to come; and fourth, the inability to speak.
"Good son, what is called 'infant-like conduct'? Good son, one who is unable to arise, stand, come, go, or speak is called an infant.

'Not arising' is a metaphor for the eternal non-arising of the characteristics of all phenomena, whether at their extremes or in their center. 'Not abiding' is a metaphor for purity and non-attachment."
The fact that birth-and-death and nirvana neither come nor go is like my not proceeding from the shallow to the profound;
the absence of movement between this and that is like the silence of one who delights in the quiescence of nirvana, which is ineffable.

This "Perfect Infant" has, from the first moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment, constantly contemplated the four virtues of nirvana while practicing the Way; therefore, it is said that he cannot arise, abide, come, go, speak, or call out.

The "Infant" refers to the Tathāgata’s practice; when the Buddha performs this practice, it guides those of superior faculties so that both the transformer and the transformed practice the four virtues, all of which are the Tathāgata’s practice. Therefore, it is called the "Tathāgata Infant Practice.

Regarding the two practices of the Superior and the Holy, the sequence of gradual practice was explained first, followed by the perfect practice. In this present chapter, the perfect practice is clarified first, followed by the gradual practice.
This refers to the mastery of responding to conditions in succession;
from "the Tathāgata is also like this" onwards, these are combined with the four preceding similes to form three sets as in the text. "The Tathāgata is also like this...
unable to arise" means that the Tathāgata ultimately does not give rise to the characteristics of any phenomena.
That which cannot abide means that the Tathāgata does not cling to any phenomena.
That which cannot come means that the bodily activity of the Tathāgata is without movement or agitation. That which cannot go means that the Tathāgata has already reached Great Parinirvāṇa.
Next, within the category of "not speaking," there are four points: first, because one has reached ultimate completion and attained Great Nirvāṇa, one is unable to speak;
second, it clarifies that since speaking is itself non-speaking, one is unable to speak.
Regarding those who cannot speak: although the Tathāgata expounds all dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings, in reality there is nothing spoken.
Why is this? That which can be spoken is called a conditioned dharma (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is not conditioned.
Therefore, there is no speaking.
Because sentient beings do not understand the words of the three secrets, they cannot speak them.
Furthermore, those who have no speech are like infants whose language is not yet developed; although they may utter sounds, in reality they have no speech.
The Tathāgata is also like this: that which is not yet fully articulated is precisely the secret language of all Buddhas, even though it is something that is spoken.
Because sentient beings do not understand it, it is called "speechless.

The fourth [explanation] clarifies that, according to the different categories [of beings], one follows their respective speech and sounds; since this is neither speech nor non-speech from my perspective, one is unable to speak.
Furthermore, an infant is called by various names for objects and does not yet know correct speech;
although it is called by various names for objects and does not yet know correct speech, it is not that it cannot recognize objects because of this. The Tathāgata is also like this:
the species of all sentient beings differ, and their speech is not the same, yet the Tathāgata employs skillful means to teach according to them, so that all may likewise gain understanding thereby.
Explanation:
This ultimate eloquence (*pratibhāna*) is precisely non-eloquence; it is the eternal secret. Not understanding it is purity; following [the capacities of] beings is the self;
and being unable to speak is that which yet fully possesses the four virtues. The other three metaphors should also be understood in this way.
Next, regarding the infant who is able to speak large characters: this is the second section clarifying the partial practices of the infant, which consists of five parts:
(1) the infant of large characters, (2) the infant of ignorance, (3) the infant of non-action, (4) the infant of yellow leaves, and (5) the infant of joy and aversion.
Within the first, the infant of large characters, there are two sections: the analogy and the application.
Furthermore, an infant is able to utter "great words.

To take the initial analogy, the "great word" refers to *bha-va*; specifically, taking the character *ba* (和) as the "great word," this refers to the Bodhisattva-infant of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
This Bodhisattva has cultivated the marks [of a Buddha] throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred *kalpas*.
The aspiration to seek to become a Buddha refers to a Buddha who is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), consisting of half-syllables (*ardhākṣara*), and impermanent;

therefore, one knows that this is the "half-syllable" (the character *he*) and the "infant" (the character *er*), which together form the compound. The self-explanation of the text is extremely clear.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he speaks of the "Great Letter," which is *bha* and *ho*. *Bha* refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and *ho* refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is called the "infant. *Ho* is named impermanence, and *bha* is named permanence.
When the Tathāgata speaks of permanence, sentient beings, having heard it, take it to be the dharma of permanence and thereby sever impermanence; this is called the conduct of an infant.
Second, from the passage "Furthermore, an infant does not know suffering or pleasure" onwards, there is an analogy regarding an ignorant infant followed by its application.
Furthermore, an infant does not know suffering or pleasure, nor day or night, [nor] his parents.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: for the sake of sentient beings, he perceives neither suffering nor pleasure, nor the distinction between day and night;
because his mind is impartial toward all sentient beings, he has no perception of distinctions such as parent or child, or kin and stranger.
In the analogy, the six characters "neither suffering nor pleasure" represent non-acceptance and non-rejection; "neither day nor night" represents the absence of hatred and love.

Examining the text of this analogy, it appears to illustrate the Buddha’s own practice (*svayam-caryā*). In the section on application (*yoga*), the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others (*parārtha*) is illustrated.

This should be understood as a mutual manifestation: while the beginning and end employ the Tathāgata to correspond with the analogy, the two middle types employ the Bodhisattva to correspond with the analogy—this too is a mutual presentation.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who emerge [from this state] are all able to fully practice the various "infant" practices. As the subsequent text states:

"Kāśyapa and the ninety-three thousand people all attained these five practices" (and so forth). This "ignorance" refers to the infant-like Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śikṣā*) who have realized that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations;
they perceive suffering and pleasure as equal, and view enemies and kin as non-dual. The combined meaning of the text is clear.
Third, as for the infant being unable to perform actions, this is the "non-action" [of the infant]. There is both an analogy and a formal application.
Furthermore, an infant is unable to perform various tasks, whether great or small.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise; he no longer creates the karma of birth and death.
This is called "not performing great deeds," which refers to the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*). The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva never commits the minor offenses of the five heinous grave sins.
"Minor matters" refers to the mind of the Two Vehicles; the Bodhisattva never regresses from the *bodhicitta* to become a Śrāvaka.
Regarding the Pratyekabuddhayāna:

in the initial analogy, it says, "not committing great transgressions and not practicing the Lesser Vehicle"—this refers to the infant-like stage of the Bodhisattva according to the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao).
Subsequently, the corresponding text states, "having no mind for the five heinous crimes or the Two Vehicles," which means neither [remaining in] saṃsāra nor [fixating upon] nirvāṇa.
The practice of the Bodhisattva’s middle way is practiced therein.
Fourth, regarding the infant who cries—this section below concerns the yellow leaves; there is both a simile and its application.
Furthermore, when a practitioner who is like an infant cries out, his parents immediately take yellow leaves from a *śiṃśapā* tree and say to him, "Do not cry, do not cry;
I will give you gold. Upon seeing this, the infant conceives the notion that it is real gold and stops crying;
yet these yellow leaves are not actually gold. It is like a wooden ox, a wooden horse, a wooden man, or a wooden woman.
When a female infant sees this, she likewise gives rise to the perception that it is male or female; she immediately stops crying.
Although it is not actually male or female, because she forms such perceptions of male and female, she is called an "infant."

The Tathāgata is likewise. If there are sentient beings who wish to commit various evils, the Tathāgata speaks for them of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, which is characterized by permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity;
where beings are upright and self-sufficient, enjoying the five desires within wondrous palaces, and where nothing encountered by the six sense faculties is not pleasure.
Because sentient beings hear of such pleasures, they conceive a desire for them and cease from committing evil.
The diligent cultivation of wholesome karma in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is, in reality, subject to birth and death, impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity;
yet, as a skillful means to deliver sentient beings, it is spoken of in words as permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

In the initial parable, the willow tree represents false permanence, the yellow leaves represent false purity, the wooden oxen and horses represent false bliss, and the wooden men and women represent false self.
In the subsequent section on the application of these analogies, the text correlates these with the permanence, bliss, self, and purity found in the heavens;

by extension of this principle, one should understand that there are likewise the four inversions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity among human beings, though they are not explicitly mentioned in the text for brevity’s sake.
Fifth, regarding the "infant": this refers to those who delight in the lower [realms] and feel aversion toward them. The text on the direct teaching of the Dharma for infants consists of two parts:
first, a brief indication; second, an explanation.
Furthermore, as for the "infant": if there are sentient beings who feel aversion toward birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the Tathāgata then teaches them the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
When one feels weary of birth and death, the teaching of the two vehicles serves as the heading (*uddāna*).

However, "in reality there are none" is the explanation (*vyākhyāna*). Furthermore, this explanation has two parts: first, a brief explanation; second, an extensive explanation. Regarding "in reality there are none":
because of the two vehicles, one perceives the faults of birth and death and sees the bliss of nirvāṇa; yet, in reality, there is no such reality of the two vehicles.
The first summary is as follows: knowing the faults of birth and death is the recognition of suffering and its origin; seeing the bliss of nirvana is the recognition of the path and its cessation.

By means of this vision, one is then able to know for oneself whether there is abandonment or non-abandonment, whether there is the real or the unreal, whether there is cultivation or non-cultivation, and whether there is attainment or non-attainment.

Next, regarding "extensive," there is that which is severed and that which is not severed; this refers to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), wherein the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) may be severed while the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not.

There is that which is real and that which is not real; this refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), wherein if there is no nirvana within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is not real;

whereas if there is nirvana apart from birth and death, it is truly real. There is that which is cultivated and that which is not cultivated; this refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) concerning the four inverted delusions (*viparyāsa*).

"Not cultivating" refers to not practicing the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), while "cultivating" refers to practicing them; whether one attains [the fruit] or not depends on this. This is explained in terms of the sharp and dull faculties regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
What is termed "not attaining" refers to those with dull faculties, while what is termed "attaining" refers to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

However, in this context, the Path is explained first and Cessation second because, for followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) with dull faculties who cultivate causes in view of the fruit, cessation occurs before the Path; whereas for those of the Middle Vehicle (*madhyayāna*), it is otherwise.

Regarding the sharp-facultied path, there is neither extinction prior nor existence subsequent; this too has no location. Question: In this context, you specifically clarify the five kinds of infant-like conduct (*pañca-śiśu-carita*);

why do you not also clarify the five Brahma-conducts (*pañca-brahma-carya*) and the five noble conducts (*pañca-ārya-caryā*)? Answer: Those two types of conduct are non-existent according to the literal text, yet they exist when inferred through their meaning.
As for what is meant by "meaning," it refers to cultivating the three grades [of practice] by means of the mind of Great Nirvāṇa; thus, they are distinct.
When the Buddhas have expounded the noble practices of the Bodhisattvas, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are then able to practice them; these are thus the noble practices of the two vehicles.

Since the two vehicles are already able to practice them, it may be known by analogy that the six perfections are likewise accessible to humans, devas, and others, who can also practice them according to their respective capacities and as they are taught.
Therefore, they do exist. Within the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*), there is the cultivation of the nine grades of increase. That is to say:
This is the distinct Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) of the Bodhisattva, wherein compassion serves as the root of all wholesome dharmas.

It naturally encompasses the six perfections of the Śrāvakas, the common teachings for humans and devas, and the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), which constitute all Brahma-conduct. How is this known?
Because this "infant-like practice" is distinct from other minor virtues, and since minor virtues are not uniform, the five partial infants are enumerated in detail.
The child practices the holy conduct (*ārya-caryā*), which is precisely self-practice; however, because it clarifies only the sequential and non-sequential [stages], other practices are not listed.
Pure conduct (*brahma-caryā*) is pure practice for the sake of transforming others; thus, only the sequential and non-sequential stages of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are listed.

Although the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) generally encompass both self-benefit and benefiting others within the teachings, they are not "pure" for two reasons: first, they involve the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*); second, they involve the partial presence of afflictions. Therefore, they are not considered pure.
Because they practice the Brahma-faring, the two vehicles and the realms of humans and devas are not listed; since they lack the capacity to transform others, they are likewise not included.
The general meaning of the significance of their presence or absence is as follows.
From the passage beginning with "Good son, like that infant," the second section, which explains the meaning of the analogy of the infant, consists of three parts.
First, the citation of the analogy; second, the application; third, the explanation.
"Good son, just as that infant conceives the notion of gold within what is not gold, so too does the Tathāgata speak of purity within the impure.
Because the Tathāgata has attained the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he is without falsehood."

Just as that infant perceives what is not an ox or a horse as being an ox or a horse, so too, if there are sentient beings who perceive what is not the Path as being the true Path, the Tathāgata also speaks of the non-Path as the Path.

Although in reality there is no Path within the non-Path, because it can produce the subtle causes and conditions for the arising of the Path, he speaks of the non-Path as the Path; it is like that infant’s perception of wooden figures of men and women.
They give rise to the notion of male and female.
First, the gold is cited as a metaphor for false purity; the wooden ox and horse are metaphors for false bliss; the non-path is a metaphor for false permanence;
and the wooden man and woman are metaphors for the false self.
The second pair is as follows:
The Tathāgata is likewise; he knows that what is not a sentient being is spoken of as having the notion of a sentient being, yet in reality there is no notion of a sentient being.
The Tathāgata is likewise: it is merely the joining of wood [to form] male and female with a single intention; the remaining three cases can be understood accordingly.
Third, the explanation below regarding "if the Buddha, the Tathāgata":
If the Buddha, the Tathāgata, were to say that there are no sentient beings, then all sentient beings would fall into false views; therefore, the Tathāgata says that there are sentient beings.
Those who, among sentient beings, form the conception of "sentient beings" will be unable to destroy that conception of sentient beings.
Since one already knows this to be false, how could it deceive those sentient beings? If one does not lead them away from falsehood by means of falsehood, there is no way for them to escape.
Now, by leading them away from falsehood through the use of falsehood, one breaks their attachment to false causes; thus, the conceptual fetters that bind sentient beings are shattered.
To shatter those false fruits is to shatter the notion that fruits bind sentient beings; this is called shattering the mark of a sentient being.
Once the mark of a sentient being is shattered, those deluded people who lead others among gods and humans are like infants. Since their intent is thus, the rest can be understood by implication.
Regarding sentient beings, the third section clarifies the fruit of the practice of the infant.
If one eliminates the notion of "sentient being" with respect to sentient beings, one is then able to attain Great Parinirvāṇa;
because one has attained such Great Nirvāṇa, one ceases weeping—this is called the practice of the infant.
If one perceives sentient beings as sentient beings, this is merely the state of an infant; it is not the practice of an infant.
Because one does not perceive sentient beings as sentient beings, one is able to shatter the mark of "sentient being";

this is the accomplishment of the practice of an infant. Because the practice is accomplished, one ceases crying; because the fruit is accomplished, one attains the fruit of Great Nirvana. This concludes the section on the text.

How extraordinary it is that such clarity has not been seen since antiquity! While the former sages practiced the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) and established their fruits as being proximate to the First Ground (*prathamā-bhūmi*), this infant now practices it and establishes his fruit by reaching *nirvāṇa* from afar. These manifestations of the near and the far should not give rise to biased attachments.
Furthermore, the First Ground itself also possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and is likewise called "Great *Nirvāṇa*" (and so forth).
"Good son," and so forth, constitutes the third major section: the single summary of the sequential prose. This consists of three parts: first, the general summary;
second, Kāśyapa’s acknowledgment; and third, the Buddha’s exposition, as found in the text.
Good son, if there are men or women who receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and explain these five practices,
you should know that such persons will certainly attain these five practices.

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, according to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, I too shall certainly attain these five practices. The Buddha said:
"Good son, it is not only you who will attain these five practices; there are ninety-three [bodhisattvas] in this assembly [who will do so as well]."
Ten thousand people likewise all attained these five practices, just as you have.

Yao Liang states: "The Five Practices are concise; the Ten Merits are extensive. The first and second merits expand upon the Holy Practice."
Regarding the "Ninety Virtues" (*navati-guṇa*), Guangchang says that from the first to the sixth, the three preceding practices are expanded;

these primarily correspond to [the *dharmas*] of correspondence (*saṃprayukta*). The latter four expand the final two, which are entirely non-corresponding (*viprayukta*). Guangchang further states that the five practices and ten virtues are identical in essence but differ in meaning;
they are all wholesome causes that arise from the stage of ordinary beings (*bālapṛthagjana*) and culminate in the ultimate stage of the learner (*śaikṣa*), resulting in [spiritual] resonance.
The subsequent practice-fruit is called "action" (xing), while the recompense for prior practice-causes is called "virtue" (de). Thus, action is the cause and virtue is the fruit.
Kaishan (Kai-she) says that the five actions pertain to the shallow and the ten virtues pertain to the deep. The five actions begin with hearing the sutras and end at the first stage (bhūmi);
the ten virtues begin at the first stage and end at the diamond-mind (vajra-citta). Therefore, at the beginning of this chapter, there is a praise.
The sixth merit, which is not heard by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, is one of wonder and marvel. Its essence is the golden mind;
the Master of Hexi says that the five practices (*pañca-kṛtya*) are *nirvāṇa*. Because its destination is profound and distant, people fear it and do not practice it;
therefore, ten virtues are cited as adornments to encourage and exhort them toward study. Now, none of these [previous views] are correct; the two preceding schools have been overly expansive.
Briefly stated, the meaning of the mutual correspondence between subject and object is as follows.

As it has been said, Guangzhai claimed that "the cause of habituation and the fruit of habituation" pertain to the stage of the Bodhisattva and do not concern the Buddha-vehicle. Kaishan, however, stated: "The practice is shallow while the virtue is profound.
The text says that at the ninth stage of merit, the initial five matters are all fully accomplished; this should not be considered a profound holy practice, for by means of Great Nirvāṇa...

With a settled mind, one cultivates the practice of an infant; how can this lead to the attainment of Great Nirvāṇa? This [interpretation] is considered shallow by He Xi. He Xi says these are words of exhortation; since exhortation is universal, where would there not be exhortation? Examining his surviving writings, they do not accord with the sūtras, so none of them are used here. Now, according to the sūtra text, a bodhisattva should cultivate five kinds of practices. These practices are as follows: [The text continues with the list of the five practices. ...the practice of an infant. What is meant by "infant"? It means that one does not harbor resentment toward others. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors resentment, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor resentment. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor anger. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors anger, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor anger. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor malice. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors malice, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor malice. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor conceit. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors conceit, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor conceit. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor arrogance. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors arrogance, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor arrogance. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor jealousy. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors jealousy, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor jealousy. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor stinginess. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors stinginess, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor stinginess. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor deceit. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors deceit, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor deceit. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor guile. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors guile, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor guile. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor flattery. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors flattery, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor flattery. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor hypocrisy. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors hypocrisy, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor hypocrisy. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor pride. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors pride, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor pride. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor arrogance. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors arrogance, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor arrogance. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor haughtiness. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors haughtiness, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor haughtiness. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor impatience. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors impatience, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor impatience. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor stubbornness. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors stubbornness, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor stubbornness. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor attachment. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors attachment, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor attachment. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor aversion. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors aversion, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor aversion. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor craving. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors craving, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor craving. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor grasping. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors grasping, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor grasping. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor clinging. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors clinging, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor clinging. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor obstruction. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors obstruction, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor obstruction. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor hindrance. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors hindrance, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor hindrance. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor delusion. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors delusion, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor delusion. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor ignorance. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors ignorance, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor ignorance. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor doubt. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors doubt, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor doubt. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor hesitation. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors hesitation, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor hesitation. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does not harbor fear. Why? Because an infant has no sense of self. If one harbors fear, it is because one perceives a self. If one perceives a self, one will surely harbor fear. Therefore, the sūtra says: "One should cultivate the practice of an infant. Furthermore, an infant does
The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) states: "When a bodhisattva cultivates the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, they obtain ten kinds of merit.
Is this not a proof that the preceding three noble practices each have their respective fruits of cultivation? Furthermore, it is also a proof of those [fruits].

Although the text regarding these is brief, the subsequent ten merits are not unclear in demonstrating that through cultivation one attains realization; because the text is extensive and the matters therein are manifest, the practices are judged to be 'cultivation' (*bhāvanā*)."
The virtue serves as the testimony; the text consists of three parts: first, the Buddha clarifies the ten merits; second, the noble ones’ understanding and realization;

third, the general conclusion. The first part further has two sections: first, the general proclamation of the number ten; second, the detailed explanation. The initial proclamation of the number has three sub-sections:
the address, the proclamation of the number, and the praise.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāsa-vyūha-udāra-guṇa-rāja, saying:
"The one first addressed is Prabhāsa-vyūha, who expounds upon external transformation; Udāra-guṇa-rāja, who distinguishes the profundity of internal practice.
Furthermore, 'Prabhāsa' (Radiance) is Prajñā, 'Udāra' (Noble) is the Dharmakāya, and 'Guṇa-rāja' (King of Virtues) is Liberation—liberation."
Because it encompasses all dharmas, it is like a king; because its principle is all-pervasive, it is a universal illumination; because its Dharma-nature is most supreme, it is noble and exalted.
Possessing these three virtues, it is used to designate a single person; named after its virtues, it is called "Dharma," and named after the person, it is titled as a "Chapter."
Next, regarding the enumeration of the numbers:
Good son, if there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra in such a manner, they shall obtain ten kinds of meritorious qualities.
The ten numbers are recited directly without listing them individually; in the subsequent detailed explanation, each name is mentioned one by one.
Regarding the three praises:
they are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they are inconceivable, they cause wonder and astonishment in those who hear them, and they are neither internal nor external.
It is neither difficult nor easy, neither with characteristics nor without characteristics; it is not a worldly phenomenon and possesses no marks, being something that does not exist in the world.
He Xi (Hexi) says: "The Sanskrit original says 'rare and extraordinary. Those of dull faculties and small wisdom will be startled and find it strange upon hearing this. It is translated [thus].
This is briefly marvelous, consisting of only nine phrases; it is the exclusive domain of the Buddha, not shared with the Lesser Vehicle.
Because the path of language is severed and the sphere of mental activity has ceased, it is inconceivable. Because it is profoundly bottomless, it is startling;

because it is infinitely vast, it is strange. Because it is not real, it is not internal; because it is not contrived, it is not external. It is that which cannot be known by discriminative wisdom. Thus it is not... [the end].
It is difficult because it is not reached by the wisdom of *nirvāṇa*; it is not easy because it is formless; it is not a characteristic because it is mindless;
it is not a non-characteristic because it is devoid of past, future, and present; it is not a worldly phenomenon because it is boundless and without center;
and it is that which does not exist in the world because its appearances are severed from the four extremes and detached from the hundred [delusions].
What are the ten? Following this, the second section provides a detailed explanation by enumerating them individually. First, there is the inquiry: "What are the ten?

Next is the formal explanation, which consists of ten chapters. The old [commentaries] divide these differently; according to Yecheng, they are divided into two cycles, with the initial effort [of the first cycle] being as follows.
Regarding the "Virtue Not Heard and Now Heard," from the shallow to the deep, up to the sixth virtue, the Vajra Samādhi, constitutes one cycle;
the seventh virtue, from the initial arousal of the mind up to the tenth virtue, cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and seeing the Buddha-nature, constitutes another cycle.
Kaishan establishes three cycles: the first cycle is as previously described; the seventh [virtue] and... [the subsequent cycles follow].
The eighth [week] constitutes two cycles, meaning that arising from a virtuous friend is the external condition (*bāhya-pratyaya*).

The ninth and tenth constitute one cycle, meaning that attaining it through faith is the internal cause (*adhyātma-hetu*). Now, if we refer to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the meaning of the three cycles is clarified:

first the Dharma, next the parable, and finally the causes and conditions; since these all reiterate the preceding meanings, they are called the "three cycles. This is the present function [of this teaching].

The meanings of the names "Virtue" (德) and "Name" (名) are eternally distinct; how could they be the same as the three cycles? Now, for the first of the ten sections, the text is divided into three parts:

first, clarifying the five matters; second, discussing the meaning; third, the conclusion. The first part is further divided into three: first, indicating the five chapters; second, listing the three distinctions; third, the detailed explanation.
The first consists of five. What are these five?
First, being able to hear what one has not previously heard; second, being able to derive benefit once having heard it;
third, being able to sever the mind of doubt and confusion; fourth, possessing a mind of wisdom that is upright and free from crookedness; and fifth, [the fifth].
To be able to know the Tathāgata’s secret treasury constitutes five matters.

The traditional explanation of these five matters as three types of wisdom is as follows: the first one is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); the next one is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and the final three are the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Some say that the first two are the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, while the middle two are the functional applications of hearing and reflection, and the last one is [the wisdom of cultivation].

This [interpretation] is the view of Xiu Hui of Xinghuang, who holds that the first is the root and the latter four characteristics constitute its fulfillment; that one gains benefit through hearing, and because of this benefit, doubt is severed;
and because doubt is removed, there is directness, and because of directness, one knows the secret. Now, we clarify that this is not so. These three types of wisdom are merely semblances of the Path.
This text clearly demonstrates that by cultivating the Great Nirvana, one attains ten merits, yet even such true realization remains manifestly incomplete.

If one explains [the path] by distinguishing it from the true path, why bother with a minor explanation based on what merely resembles the path? Such an approach moves further and further away from the text.

Furthermore, Xinghuang’s interpretation that the five dharmas are mutually dependent is likewise incorrect. For when entry into realization is held within one's grasp, it is no longer a matter of sequential explanation;

this is already not the case during the time of practice, let alone at the time of realization. Since the sequence is clearly evident in the scriptures, how can one interpret the attainment of realization as being a process of cultivation?
The civilizing influence is not shared, yet it produces shared understanding; the civilizing influence is unheard, yet hearing it produces understanding derived from others;
the civilizing influence is inconceivable, yet it produces conceivable understanding; the civilizing influence is secret, yet it produces manifest understanding;

the civilizing influence is perfectly complete, yet it produces partial and deficient understanding; the civilizing influence is marvelous, yet it produces ordinary understanding; the civilizing influence is without differentiation, yet it...
In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, the middle way is explained through the analysis of distinctions; yet if one relies solely on the literal text, there are ten faults.
Not knowing why [the opponent] resists the Buddha’s sūtras (and so forth), I privately consult my junior students: please examine the passage on the five dharmas by the Elder [Asaṅga].
That which was not heard before is heard now, like participating in the causal characteristics; once heard, the four benefits and so forth are entirely present.

Since the first [of the ten stages] is established with many names based on the fruition (*phala*), even though the remaining nine seem to concern the cultivation of causes (*hetu-bhāvanā*), they are nonetheless placed within the chapter on "Practice" (*caryā*) among the realizations (*sākṣātkriyā*).
The intent behind the expressions regarding the quantity [of these stages] is likewise so.
Even upon closely examining the text of the nine phrases, all are consistent with both cultivation and realization; thus, one knows that in general, when interpreting the sūtras, if...

If one seeks the meaning by following the text and judges the text based on the meaning, it will not be so; otherwise, the text will become a mere phantom, and failing to interpret it correctly will inevitably lead to many errors.

Regarding the three interpretations of the five dharmas, the text itself constitutes five parts: first, the explanation of "not hearing what is heard," which is divided into three sections: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
What is it that is "not heard yet able to be heard"?

That which is designated as "hearing what was not heard" refers to the perfect realization and wondrous awakening; to give rise to understanding is called "hearing," for it is not receiving from another.
If one were to hear it from another, that would be "hearing what is heard"—how could that be "hearing what was not heard"?
Next, regarding what is called "profound" (*gambhīra*) and below, this is the explanation.
This explains that hearing the one is hearing all; it cannot be fully described, so three types are briefly cited: first, hearing what was not heard regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

second, hearing what was not heard regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); and third, hearing what was not heard regarding true reality (*bhūta-tattva*). These three truths and three dharmas are of one mind, not something prior.
Because it is neither posterior, nor shallow, nor deep, it is said that it is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Since those of the two vehicles never realize the Middle Way, it is not shared with them; nor is it shared because they do not realize the conventional.

Furthermore, although they may realize the ultimate truth, they do not know the secret of that truth, and thus it is not shared with them. It is for this reason that it is "not shared" in such a manner.
This is truly marvelous! It is not merely that which is praised and extolled by the world; rather, it concerns the primary meaning of "hearing what has not been heard.
This section is divided into two parts: first, a general enumeration, followed by a general explanation.
The meaning of what is called the profound and subtle mystery is that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
there is no distinction between the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. The nature and characteristics of the Three Jewels are eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
Among all Buddhas, there is none who enters ultimate *parinirvāṇa*; the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa* is eternally abiding and unchanging.
First, the five items listed in the introduction: 1) Buddha-nature; 2) the single essence of the Three Jewels; 3) the four virtues; 4) the permanence of nirvāṇa;
and 5) the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
This is followed by a general explanation.
It is neither existent nor non-existent; neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
neither with outflows nor without outflows; neither form nor non-form; neither name nor non-name; neither characteristic nor non-characteristic; neither existent nor non-existent;
neither thing nor non-thing; neither cause nor fruit; neither dependent nor independent; neither light nor darkness; neither emerging nor not emerging.
It is neither eternal nor non-eternal, neither annihilated nor non-annihilated, neither beginning nor end, neither past nor future nor present;

it is neither the aggregates (*skandha*) nor not the aggregates, neither the sense-bases (*āyatana*) nor not the sense-bases, neither the elements (*dhātu*) nor not the elements, neither the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) nor not the twelve links of dependent origination. Such dharmas as these are profoundly deep and subtle, never before heard.
Yet one is able to hear them.
In each and every matter, there is nothing that is not the profound Middle Way; these comprise twenty phrases in total, and other instances are likewise so.
Next, from the passage "Furthermore, there is hearing what was not heard regarding all the scriptures of the non-Buddhists" onwards, this is the second "hearing what was not heard."
Regarding what is heard concerning conventional truth, there are two parts: first, a listing of conventional dharmas; second, an explanation of the secret [teachings].

Furthermore, there is that which is not heard, namely: all the scriptures of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the four *Vedas*, the *Vyākaraṇa* (grammar), the *Vaiśeṣika* treatises, the *Kāpila* (Sāṃkhya) treatises, all incantations, medical prescriptions, arts and crafts, astrology, and the calculation of auspicious days for eating.
Regarding such scriptures as those on the movements of the constellations, *túshū* (diagrams), and prophetic records (*chènjì*), their secret meanings have never before been heard.
As for the initial worldly methods, there are fundamentally three root non-Buddhist paths (*bāhyatīrthika*), each possessing its own scriptures;
here, only Kāpila and Ulūka are listed, while the Leśaśa (Pāśupata) is omitted for brevity. Furthermore, the Kāpilas reckon that [the self] is one.
The view that the aggregates (*skandha*) are the self is the position of the Ulūka; the view that the aggregates are not the self is the position of the Ṛṣabha.

Since these two views are essentially the same as those of the two [previously mentioned] groups—namely, that they are both identical to and different from the aggregates—they are not mentioned separately.
One may now know this from this very sutra.
Furthermore, there are eleven classes of sutras that follow this third category; they concern the truth of hearing what has not been heard, which is twofold:
first, hearing the true dharma, and second, hearing the secret [dharma].
Furthermore, among the eleven divisions of the scriptures, excluding the Vaipulya, there is likewise no such profound and secret meaning;
it is now through this sutra that one comes to know them.
When it is said that "one hears them because of this sutra," this refers to the meaning of perfect realization within the Vaipulya.

The clarity that the Three Jewels are of one essence, that the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding, and that there is *nirvāṇa*—which are absent in the Lesser Vehicle—is therefore excluded [from their teachings].
The three fetters are as stated in the text.
Good son, this is called "being able to hear what one has not previously heard."
Next, the explanation of the benefits derived from having heard [the teaching] is presented in three parts: the heading, the exposition, and the conclusion.
Regarding "the benefits derived from having heard":
this indicates the benefit of actual realization, rather than the benefit of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). As the text says: "One attains proximity to *sambodhi* through reflection."
Since wisdom has not yet arisen, how could it be close to the ultimate meaning?

Next, the explanation is divided into two parts: first, the brief; second, the detailed. Within the brief section, there are again two parts: first, the presentation of the causal conditions, hence the statement "listen and receive."
If one can hear and receive this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one will be able to fully understand the profound meaning and flavor of all Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.
Next, the true realization is revealed.
For example, when men and women behold their own reflections in a bright, clear mirror, they see them with perfect clarity;
the mirror of the Great Parinirvāṇa is likewise. When Bodhisattvas hold it, they clearly perceive the profound meanings of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
It is also like a person in a dark room who, holding a great torch, sees all objects; such is the torch of the Great Parinirvāṇa.
It is likewise with the Bodhisattva who, by grasping it, attains insight into the profound and subtle meaning of the Mahāyāna.

Just as when the sun rises, its thousand rays can illuminate the dark recesses of all mountains, enabling all people to see distant objects clearly, so too is this pure sun of wisdom of the Great Parinirvāṇa;
it likewise illuminates the deep and profound places of the Mahāyāna.
The reason why those of the Two Vehicles are enabled to see the Buddha-way from afar is that they are able to hear and receive this subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.

This single mind and threefold wisdom are illustrated by three analogies: true wisdom illuminating principle is like the purity within a mirror; conventional wisdom [illuminating phenomena] is like... [the reflection in the mirror].
The wisdom that illuminates phenomena is like a torch that clarifies external objects; the middle wisdom that illuminates all is like the sun that shines everywhere.
These three stages are explained in this way to make them easy to understand; at the moment of realization, one attains all three wisdoms within a single mind.
Second, as for the Bodhisattva departing from this, there is a broad explanation of the benefits, which further consists of two parts. First, the account of the causal conditions:
"Good son, if there is a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva who hears and receives this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, he will come to know the names of all dharmas."
Next, the benefits of the four dharmas are clarified.

If one can copy, read, recite, master, extensively explain to others, and contemplate the meaning [of this teaching], then one will know the principles and meanings of all dharmas, O son of good family.
As for those who merely listen and receive it, they know only the names but do not know their meaning. If...
If one is able to transcribe, receive and uphold, read and recite, and extensively explain to others [this sutra], and contemplate its meaning, then one will be able to know its meaning.
Furthermore, son of good family, those who hear this sutra may hear that there is Buddha-nature but have not yet been able to see it;

however, by transcribing, reading and reciting, extensively explaining to others, and contemplating its meaning, they shall come to see it. Those who hear this sutra hear the name of *dāna* (generosity).
If one has not yet been able to see the *dānapāramitā*, nor has transcribed, recited, extensively explained it to others, or contemplated its meaning, then one cannot see the *dānapāramitā*;
this applies likewise up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Son of good family, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can hear this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they will know the Dharma and know its meaning.
Possessing the two kinds of unimpeded knowledge, among all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, brahmās, and the entire world, they attain fearlessness;
they reveal, analyze, and distinguish the twelve divisions of the sūtras, expounding their meanings without error.
Without hearing them from others, they are able to know them for themselves, drawing near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
As the text states, not hearing [the teaching] from another is the benefit of true realization, for one is thereby able to attain *sambodhi* in the near future;
thus, it is clear that this is not the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are as stated in the text.
Good son, this is called "having heard it, it is able to bring benefit.
Third, regarding "arising from the severance of doubt": this constitutes three headings, explanations, and a conclusion. As for the headings, they are as stated in the text.
Regarding "severing the mind of doubt": [the explanation follows].
The former benefit is internal realization; the severing of doubt is external discourse. It is also termed "separation" and called "the severance of ignorance through the arising of wisdom.

Although the preceding and succeeding sections clarify these points alternately, they equally manifest the merit of perfect realization. The old [commentary] states that this is the function of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī prajñā*).
However, if one asks whether this refers to the hearing and reflection of the Hīnayāna, how could they have ever heard or reflected upon the meaning of Buddha-nature? If it refers to the Mahāyāna...
Relying on the wisdom of hearing and reflection, one has not yet seen the Buddha-nature; therefore, establishing the meaning of "separation" now is conducive to the meaning of "realization.

Next, the explanation of the text is divided into two parts: first, a brief explanation of separation, and second, an extensive explanation of separation. The brief explanation has three sections: first, separating the doubts regarding name and meaning;
second, separating the doubts regarding the eight inversions; and third, separating the doubts regarding the provisional and the real. First, name and meaning:

It can be seen that there are two kinds of doubt: first, doubt regarding the names; second, doubt regarding the meaning. Those who listen to this sutra sever the mind of doubt concerning names, while those who contemplate its meaning with their minds sever the mind of doubt concerning the meaning.
Next, there is doubt regarding the eight inversions.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are five kinds of doubt: first, doubting whether the Buddha has definitely entered nirvana;
second, doubting whether the Buddha is eternally abiding; third, doubting whether the Buddha is true bliss; fourth, doubting whether the Buddha is true purity.
Regarding the five things not to be doubted: one doubts whether the Buddha is truly the Buddha if one does not listen to this sutra;

one doubts whether the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa results in eternal cessation if one copies, recites, reads, explains it extensively to others, and contemplates its meaning—these four doubts are eternally severed.
It says: "The doubt regarding the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* as being impermanent is an inversion;

next, it clarifies that the principle of the inversion of permanence must possess eight [factors], though the text is abbreviated, matching three single [factors] against one pair—these are the five kinds" (and so forth). My private commentary states: there is a distinction between the general and the specific regarding the four inversions of *nirvāṇa*.
There are three doubts concerning the three vehicles: first, doubt regarding whether the provisional and the ultimate exist or do not exist.

Furthermore, son of good family, there are three kinds of doubt: first, doubt as to whether the Śrāvaka vehicle exists or does not exist; second, doubt as to whether the Pratyekabuddha vehicle exists or does not exist;
third, doubt as to whether the Buddha-vehicle exists or does not exist. Those who hear this sutra [will resolve] these three [doubts].
