When doubt is forever extinguished without remainder, and one copies, recites, reads, extensively explains to others, and contemplates its meaning,
one will then be able to understand that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

The doubt regarding the three vehicles is a doubt concerning the provisional; that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is the true principle. While this [Buddha-nature] ought to be listed in full, here it is presented only in mutual relation.
Furthermore, the following two sections are extensive expositions on detachment, while the third section is the detachment from numerous doubts, beginning with impermanence.
This refers to departing from doubt regarding substantial dharmas. Next, furthermore, the statement "form is my self" refers to departing from doubt regarding conventional designations.
The four heavy offenses and the five heinous crimes refer to departing from doubt regarding the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary.

Regarding the four heavy offenses and the five heinous crimes, in terms of primary retribution, there is the question of whether there is Buddha-nature; in terms of primary retribution, there is also the question of what constitutes ultimate goodness.
Whether the world is finite or infinite is a matter of dependent retribution (*niṣyanda-vipāka*).
Furthermore, son of good family, if there are sentient beings who have not heard this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they harbor many doubts, namely:
whether it is permanent or impermanent, whether it is blissful or not blissful, whether it is pure or not pure, whether there is a self or no self, and so forth.
Life and non-life; sentient beings and non-sentient beings; the ultimate and the non-ultimate; the next world and worlds beyond;
existence and non-existence; suffering and non-suffering; the origin and non-origin; the path and non-path;
cessation and non-cessation; the Dharma and non-Dharma; the wholesome and the unwholesome; emptiness and non-emptiness.
Those who hear this sutra will have all such doubts forever severed.
This is as stated in the text.
Furthermore, good son, there are those who have not heard such a sutra, and they possess various and numerous doubts.
Does the mind consider that form is the self, or that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self? Is it the eye that sees, or am I who sees? And so on, up to:
is it consciousness that cognizes, or am I who cognizes? Does form experience retribution, or do I experience retribution? And so on, up to:
does consciousness experience retribution, or do I experience retribution? Does form go to another world, or do I go to another world?
Even up to consciousness, is this dharma of birth and death with a beginning and an end, or without a beginning and without an end?
Those who hear this sutra shall likewise forever sever such doubts.

Next, regarding provisional designations, it is said that the phenomena of birth and death have a beginning and an end; this notion of having a beginning and an end is what heterodox outsiders calculate, yet it is also found within our own tradition.
One view holds that birth and death are entirely without end or beginning, revolving through the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) without limit.
Another view holds that a single thought-moment of ignorance (*avidyā*) is its beginning, while the final moment of the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) is its end.

This refers to its "end. Third, it is said that there is an end despite being beginningless. A sutra states that "beginningless ignorance" (anādikālikāvidyā) is precisely this beginninglessness, whereas the "Buddha-fruit" is precisely this having an end.
If one dogmatically adheres to these three [positions], it constitutes a contentious argument;
at the time of true realization, one immediately becomes free from them.

Furthermore, there may be those who doubt whether icchantikas, those who have committed the four grave prohibitions, those who have committed the five heinous crimes, or those who slander the Vaipulya sutras—beings such as these—possess the Buddha-nature or do not possess the Buddha-nature; by hearing this sutra, all such doubts shall be forever severed.
Furthermore, there may be those who doubt whether the world is finite or infinite, or whether the ten directions exist.
Is it this world, or are there worlds in the ten directions?
Listen to this sutra; as stated in the text, the three lower fetters are abandoned.
For one who listens to this sutra, such doubts as these are also forever severed; this is called being able to sever the mind of doubt and confusion.
Fourth, the explanation of the wisdom-mind being upright and without crookedness also has three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. First is the heading:
"The wisdom-mind is upright and without deviance.

Previously, it was explained that one internally realizes the three types of knowledge and externally remains free from all doubts; however, it was not yet specified which knowledge this refers to. Now, the heading indicates "uprightness."
Because wisdom is not either of these two extremes, both the chapters on "uprightness" and "crookedness" are presented together.
Next, this is explained:
if the mind harbors doubt, then what is perceived will not be correct; all ordinary worldlings, if they do not hear this Great Nirvana...
In this subtle and wondrous sūtra, it is said that what is seen by those who follow heterodox paths is crooked, and even what is seen by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is likewise crooked.
Why is it called "the crookedness seen by all ordinary beings"?

It refers to perceiving permanence, bliss, self, and purity within that which is subject to outflows (āsrava), while perceiving impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self in the Tathāgata; and it refers to perceiving a sentient being, a life-span, and a soul.
To perceive and reckon that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is *nirvāṇa*, to view Īśvara as possessing the Eightfold Noble Path,
or to hold views such as those of eternalism or nihilism— such views as these are called crooked and deviant.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and practices the noble conduct (*āryacaryā*), they will then be able to sever and eliminate such crookedness.
What are called the deviant views of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s descent from Tuṣita, his transformation while riding a white elephant, and his entry into the mother’s womb—the father was named Śuddhodana and the mother was named Māyā.
When he was fully ten months in the womb of Kapilavastu and was born, before he had even reached the ground, Śakra received him in his arms, as did the Nanda Dragon King.
Pāṇḍaka spat out water to bathe him; the great ghost-king Maṇibhadra stood behind him holding a precious parasol;
the earth goddess manifested flowers to receive his feet; he walked seven paces in each of the four directions;
he went to a celestial temple where all the divine images rose to welcome him; and the seer Asita took him in his arms to examine his marks. Thus it was.
Having had his physiognomy examined, he conceived great compassion and sorrow, grieving that he would never again behold the appearance of a Buddha.

He went to a teacher to study writing, arithmetic, calculation, archery, horsemanship, divination, portents, and the arts. While residing in the inner palace, he enjoyed himself with sixty thousand court ladies.
Upon going out of the city for an excursion, he saw on the road an old man, and even a śramaṇa walking along in dharma robes.
Returning to the palace, he beheld the court ladies whose bodies and features were like withered bones; the palaces themselves were no different from burial mounds.

Disgusted, he left the household life at midnight and went beyond the city walls to the great seers such as Udraka Rāmaputra, where he heard the teachings on the sphere of consciousness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having heard this, [he departed].
Contemplating this state as impermanent, suffering, impure, and non-self, he abandoned it and went beneath a tree where he practiced asceticism for six full years.
Realizing that such asceticism could not bring about the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
he then proceeded to the river Ajitavatī to bathe and accepted the offering presented by a cowherd girl.
Having received [the milk-rice], the Bodhisattva proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree,
where he defeated Māra Pāpīyān and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. From his first turning of the Wheel of Dharma for the five bhikṣus at Vārāṇasī,
until his entry into parinirvāṇa here in the city of Kuśinagara— such views as these are called the crooked views of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Good son, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas hear and receive this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they will completely sever and eliminate views such as these.
If they can further transcribe, read, recite, master it thoroughly, expound it for others, and contemplate its meaning,
they will attain upright views free from all crookedness and deviation.

Having recognized the two extremes, the rectitude manifests of itself; when a Bodhisattva cultivates the noble practices (*ārya-caryā*), they are already able to eliminate the deviant crookedness of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
One should know that the five practices are the cultivation [of this rectitude]. Once the crooked views have been eliminated, what is seen becomes correct;
one should know that the ten virtues are the realization and proof thereof. The explanation of the crooked views of the Śrāvakas is as stated in the text.
The third section on practice is thus concluded and may be understood accordingly.
Good son, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, he truly knows that from immeasurable kalpas ago,
the Bodhisattva did not descend from Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb, nor did he enter parinirvāṇa at the city of Kuśinagara.
This is called the upright view of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Regarding the five explanations of the secret meaning, there are also three parts: the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. First, "one who is able to know" is the introduction.
One who is able to know the profound and secret meaning of the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom of the straight Middle Way, which is free from the two extremes and all crookedness;
this wisdom is able to know the profound and secret meaning.

Next, the explanation of "profound secrecy" (samdhā) is divided into three parts: first, profound secrecy regarding the fruit; second, profound secrecy regarding the cause; and third, profound secrecy regarding the inconceivable.
Regarding the first, as stated below, it refers to the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, which is profound secrecy regarding the fruit.
That which is thus described is precisely the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Next, "all [beings] below" refers to the cause.
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; through repentance for the four grave prohibitions, one eliminates the mind that slanders the Dharma and exhausts the five heinous crimes.
Only after extinguishing the icchantikas can one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
this is called the profound and secret meaning.
Thirdly, the following section concerns the inconceivable.
Furthermore, good son, what is meant by the meaning of "profound"? It is knowing that although sentient beings truly have no self, they do not lose the fruits of their karma in the future;
knowing that although the five aggregates are extinguished here, the karma of good and evil never perishes;
and though there are various karmas, there is no agent who performs them; and though there is a destination reached, there is no one who goes.
Although there are fetters, there is no one who is bound; although there is nirvāṇa, there is also no one who attains extinction.
In reality, there is no self, yet in the future, the fruits of karma are not lost. The first two phrases rely on "non-existence" to speak of "existence";
next, the four phrases beginning with "all karmas" rely on "existence" to speak of "non-existence," and rely on both "existence and non-existence" to speak of "neither."
There is that which is neither non-reliance nor existence, neither existence nor non-existence, yet is spoken of as existence and non-existence;
it is inconceivable, inconceivable again, and inconceivable once more; it is profound and yet further profound, and is discussed as being deep and secret by way of the inconceivable.
This is called the meaning of the profound secret.

At that time, the second section on the exposition of the Dharma concerning the descent of light is divided into four parts: (1) the Exposition of King of Virtue, (2) the Exposition of Lapis Lazuli Light, (3) the Exposition of Fearlessness, and (4) the Re-exposition of King of Virtue.
The first exposition is further divided into two: first, the inquiry; second, the praise. The inquiry is as follows:
The two [versions] initially received the instruction with reverence for what was not [the case].
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantaraśmivikrāntagāmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of 'hearing' and 'not hearing' as explained by the Buddha, this meaning is not so."
Second, the formal refutation (*samyak-codya*). Although five matters were previously mentioned, we now formally refute the first matter by means of three pairs of arguments:

first, the "denial-gate" (*apahāra-mukha*); second, the "concession-gate" (*anujñāna-mukha*); and third, the "analogy-gate" (*upanyāsa-mukha*). The initial denial-gate is divided into two parts: first, the application of the principle (*dharma*), and second, the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The application of the principle is further divided into three: first, a general denial based on existence and non-existence; second, a specific denial regarding what is not heard and what is heard.

Regarding the three fetters, the first existence is both negated and excluded; furthermore, of the two [sections], the first negates while the second excludes. First, the text of the negating section establishes two parts.
Why is this? If a phenomenon exists, it must necessarily exist; if a phenomenon does not exist, it must necessarily not exist.
Next, "There should not be... refutes that non-existence should not be produced and existence should not cease, thereby preventing them from being treated as one.
Next, "Just as... refutes the notion of hearing what has not been heard by means of the analysis of its non-hearing.
If one hears it, then that constitutes hearing; if one does not hear it, then that constitutes not hearing. How can you say that one hears what was not heard before?
O World-Honored One, if you do not provide a correct conclusion here, the previous conclusion will necessarily result in a contradiction.
World-Honored One, if it is not heard, that is non-hearing; if it has already been heard, then it is no longer hearing. Why?
Because it has already been attained through hearing.
Next, how can the subsequent [statement] "below" conclude that they should not be one?
How can it be said that one hears what has not been heard?
To illustrate this, the following is the second analogy, which first presents the simile and then provides the application. For example, as it is said:
"One who has already gone does not go; one who is going does not arrive; likewise, that which has already arisen does not arise, and that which has not yet arisen does not arise."
Once non-arising has been attained, there is no further attainment, nor is there non-attainment.

To illustrate this, three analogies have been presented in succession; now we arrive at the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*). For what reason would there be going? Since that which has already gone has not yet arrived, it must go.
Because that which has already arisen has already arisen, it does not arise again. If it were non-arisen, it simply would not arise.
The cases of "not arising," "not obtaining," and "non-obtainment" are all likewise determined as pairs.
Following the passage "Having heard... and below, the application of the analogy cannot be treated as a single unit;
for "having heard and not hearing" and "not hearing and not hearing" are also thus.
Within the analogies, there is nothing that is not an analogy; they merely manifest through mutual opening and closing.
From the passage "If, O World-Honored One, one hears what has not been heard," the second pair follows. This constitutes a series of three successive challenges (*zhòngnán*):
first, the challenge regarding sentient beings; second, the challenge regarding the three [realms]; and third, the challenge consisting of a single inquiry.
World-Honored One, if those who have not heard were to hear, then all sentient beings who have not yet attained Bodhi should immediately possess it;
those who have not yet attained Nirvana should also attain it; and those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature should see the Buddha-nature.
Why, then, do you say that although Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see the Buddha-nature, they have not yet attained clear realization?
Furthermore, regarding the fruit of Buddhahood, there is one concession and one challenge:
World-Honored One, if it is "hearing what has never been heard," from whom did the Tathāgata hear it in the past?
If one says that he did hear it, why does the Tathāgata state in the Āgamas that he was "without a teacher"?
[The text continues as follows: "Three times he tied two strands together," as written.
If one says he did not hear it, then how could the Tathāgata have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? First.
If all sentient beings who have not heard [this teaching] were also to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
and if the Tathāgata were to see the Buddha-nature even without hearing this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*,
then all sentient beings who have not heard this sūtra should likewise be able to see it.
From the passage beginning with the World-Honored One’s words, "Whatever is form," the third pair of dyads follows.
This section first uses form and sound as analogies, and subsequently uses the three periods of time as analogies. Regarding the initial text:
the World-Honored One stated that whatever is form is either visible or invisible; sound is likewise, being either audible or...
Whether it is heard or not heard, this Great Nirvāṇa is neither form nor sound; why then do you say it can be seen or heard?
Internal forms that are obstructed can be seen, while external forms cannot; coarse things can be seen, while subtle things cannot. [This is like] a solid pillar.
If even the forms of the world can be seen from one side while not seen from another, how much more so is it that Nirvana is subtle and inconceivable—how could it be seen? The same applies to sound.
Regarding the three periods of time:
the World-Honored One has already passed away in the past, and thus cannot be heard; the future has not yet arrived, and thus cannot be heard;
and while one is listening to the present, it is not yet called "heard"; once it has been heard, the sound has ceased and can no longer be heard. This Great Nirvana is also not [like that].
If the past, future, and present were not the three periods of time, they could not be spoken of; if they cannot be spoken of, they cannot be heard.
How then can it be said that a bodhisattva, by practicing this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, hears what has never been heard before?
"If even conditioned phenomena of the three periods of time cannot be seen, how can nirvana, which is unconditioned,
be seen or heard? At that time, the World-Honored One gave his second response by praising the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhāsa-Āryaguṇarāja, saying, "Excellent!"
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You now well understand that all dharmas are like illusions, like mirages, like the city of the Gandharvas, and like the tracks left by a painting on water;

they are also like foam, bubbles, and the plantain tree—empty and without substance, neither life nor self, and devoid of suffering or pleasure, just as is known and seen by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages."
The former [commentators] said that praising [the Buddha] is not an answer; now it is clarified that this is indeed an answer.

Since he uses the fixed characteristics of phenomena to challenge the Buddha’s clarification of illusions and so forth, how could those characteristics be fixed? Thus, all doubts are stilled; this is what constitutes "praising as an answer.
When the light of Vairocana comes, one does not see blue as blue nor yellow as yellow; is this not hearing what was previously unheard? This is precisely an auspicious omen.
Answer: The subsequent response by Vairocana-prabha to the questions simultaneously answers the doubts of King Guṇaratna, who raised them on behalf of the assembly;
thus, these three responses clarify the three faculties [of the listeners]. The Master of Hexi also stated that this is a general answer, while what follows is a specific answer.

At that time, within the great assembly, the second [section] concerning the debate on the meaning of the *Vaiḍūryaprabha* (Lapis Lazuli Light) is divided into two parts: first, those who come from afar; second, having arrived, they engage in the debate.
The first part is further divided into two: first, manifesting the signs of arrival; second, the actual explanation of the arrival.
Within the manifestation of the signs, there is first the emission of light, followed by questions and answers. First, regarding the emission of light:

At that moment, amidst the great assembly, in an instant, there appeared a great radiance: it was not blue yet appeared as blue, not yellow yet appeared as yellow, not red yet appeared as red, not white yet appeared as white;
it was not form yet appeared as form, not light yet appeared as light, and it was seen though there was no seer.
At that time, having encountered this light, the great assembly experienced physical and mental bliss, like a bhikṣu entering the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*.
This was indeed extraordinary; it further explained the previous question as an auspicious response, manifesting a sign of what was to come, for the emission of light is...
When the great assembly of the luminous essence encounters light, it is the function of light; the lion-king’s concentration is precisely the concentration of mastery.
Once mastery is attained, the inconceivable nature of the luminous essence is revealed (and so forth).

At that time, there are two sections of questions and answers following Mañjuśrī’s descent. Furthermore, these are divided into two parts: first, clarifying the fundamental essence (*mūla*); second, clarifying its traces (*liṅga*).
Within the first part on the essence, there are again two sections: first, clarifying the essence through wordlessness; second, clarifying the essence by means of words.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, who has emitted this radiance now?
At that time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not speak. Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again asked Mañjuśrī:
"For what cause and condition does this radiance exist, illuminating the great assembly? Mañjuśrī remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra again asked the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, "Whose light is this?

The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa remained silent and did not speak. The Prince Viśuddhavāsin Bodhisattva then asked the Bodhisattva Anantagātra, "By what cause and condition does this light appear within this great assembly? The Bodhisattva Anantagātra remained silent.
It is not said that these five hundred bodhisattvas were likewise silent; although they questioned one another, there was no one who answered.
That the first four bodhisattvas remained silent when questioned serves two purposes: first, to manifest that all phenomena are beyond words;

second, to manifest that this doubt should be resolved by Mañjuśrī, which is why the others did not answer. When Mañjuśrī questioned the Buddha, the Buddha remained silent, and so too did the assembly.
Seeing that the Buddha answered with silence, everyone concluded that Mañjuśrī had understood the profound mystery.

When Kāśyapa questioned Mañjuśrī again, Mañjuśrī remained silent once more, and the assembly concluded that Kāśyapa had already understood. Thus it was passed along from one to another until it reached five hundred people.
At that time, the World-Honored One—this marks the second section on entrusting words to clarify the original source—first asked:
"At that time, the World-Honored One asked Mañjuśrī: 'By what causes and conditions does this radiance appear within this great assembly?'"
Next, the response consists of seven sections; the first six all refute fixed characteristics.
Mañjuśrī said: "World-Honored One, this radiance is called wisdom. Wisdom is itself eternally abiding.
Since the eternally abiding Dharma has no causes or conditions, why does the Buddha ask what causes and conditions give rise to it?"
This radiance—this radiance is called Great Nirvāṇa; Great Nirvāṇa is termed the eternally abiding. The eternally abiding Dharma does not arise from causes and conditions.
Why, then, does the Buddha ask by what causes and conditions this radiance exists?
This radiance is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is that which is eternally abiding.
Since the eternally abiding Dharma does not arise from causes and conditions, why does the Tathāgata inquire about causes and conditions?
Radiance is called Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion; Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion are called the eternally abiding.
Since the eternally abiding Dharma does not arise from causes and conditions, why does the Tathāgata inquire about causes and conditions?

Radiance is precisely the mindfulness of the Buddha; that which is the mindfulness of the Buddha is called the eternally abiding Dharma. This eternally abiding Dharma does not arise from causes and conditions;
why then does the Tathāgata inquire about causes and conditions?
Radiance is precisely the unique path of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

the unique path of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is called the eternally abiding dharma of eternal abiding, which does not arise from causes and conditions. Why then does the Tathāgata inquire about causes and conditions?
Next, one point clarifies the causal conditions:
the World-Honored One also has causal conditions; by extinguishing ignorance, he attained the blazing lamp of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

I maintain that this response by way of cause and condition consists of both refutation and establishment: the extinction of ignorance is the refutation, as in the preceding [passage] where all remained silent;

the blazing of bodhi is the establishment, as in the subsequent [passage]. Furthermore, the former constitutes refutation and establishment for one’s own practice, which is why the assembly remained silent;
the latter constitutes refutation and establishment for the sake of others, which is why he responded regarding the causal conditions of light. Thus it is known.
The essence of light is nothing superior to the lamp of Bodhi;

therefore, this light is not a manifestation of form, yet it manifests form by arising from the True as a response, coming forth from that source to emit radiance and summon those with karmic affinity. Thus, it is a manifestation without manifesting. Question:
When a Bodhisattva emits light, is it eternally abiding? First, some say it exists because of the power of that Buddha, thus possessing constant light. Second, others say... [text ends]
The Bodhisattva is a Buddha; he naturally possesses this light.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī: "Next, I shall distinguish the traces of this light. Therein is also a dialogue.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī, you should not now enter into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of all phenomena, which is exceedingly profound; rather, you should..."
He explains this according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The Buddha said, "Do not enter," thereby halting its fundamental source; yet, as it is appropriate to clarify its traces through conventional truth, the textual traces are divided into three parts, the first of which describes that land.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One, to the east of here, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of twenty Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha-world named Acalā.
The dwelling place of that Buddha is exactly twelve thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
its ground is composed of the seven treasures, without soil or stone, level and even, soft and supple, and free from all ditches or pits."
The various trees there are composed of the four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and their flowers and fruits are so lush and abundant that they exist at all times.
If any sentient beings smell the fragrance of these flowers, their bodies and minds become peaceful and blissful, like a bhikṣu who has entered the third dhyāna.
Surrounding it are three thousand great rivers, whose waters are exquisite and endowed with the eight excellent qualities.
If there are sentient beings who bathe therein, the joy and bliss they obtain are like those of a bhikṣu who has entered the second dhyāna.
That river abounds with various kinds of flowers:
utpala, padma, kumuda, puṇḍarīka, fragrant flowers, great-scented flowers, exquisite-scented flowers, and ever-blooming flowers; all sentient beings [enjoy them] without end.
The riverbanks were also covered with various flowers, namely: *atimuktaka* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *pāṭala* flowers,
*vārṣika* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, *mahāmālikā* flowers, *navamālikā* flowers,
*sumana* flowers, *yūthikā* flowers, *tāmarakalī* flowers, and *nityaprasūna* flowers.
All sentient beings therein are not obstructed or harmed; the ground is spread with golden sand and features four staircases of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and variegated *vaiḍūrya*.

Many birds flock and gather upon them, and there are immeasurable tigers, wolves, lions, and other predatory beasts whose hearts regard one another as if they were their own infants; in that world, no transgressions whatsoever exist.
Regarding the grave prohibitions, such as slandering the True Dharma, the icchantikas, and the five heinous crimes—none of these exist in that land.
It is temperate and harmonious, free from the sufferings of cold, heat, hunger, or thirst; there is no greed, anger, negligence, or jealousy.
There are no sun or moon, nor day, night, or seasons; it is just like the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa. The inhabitants of that land all possess their own radiance.
None among them harbored a mind of pride; they were all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had attained supernatural powers and were endowed with great merit.
Their minds all held the True Dharma in high esteem; they rode upon the Mahāyāna, cherished the Mahāyāna, delighted in the Mahāyāna, and protected the Mahāyāna.
Having perfected great wisdom, they attained the Great Dhāraṇī, and their hearts were constantly filled with compassion for all beings.
For all sentient beings, that Buddha’s name is Pūrṇacandraprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Wherever he dwells and whatever he proclaims,
there are no sentient beings in that land who do not hear it, for the sake of the Bodhisattva Vaidūryaprabha.
Śākyamuni preached this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, saying: "Good sons, if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas can practice the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they shall hear all that they have not previously heard.
That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vaidūryaprabha questioned the Buddha Pūrṇacandraprabha in the same manner as [the Bodhisattva] Guangmingbianzhao gaogui de here."
The questions posed by the Bodhisattva King were identical and without difference.
Next, he described this land.
That Buddha, Pūrṇacandraprabha, then addressed the Bodhisattva Vaidūryaprabha, saying: "O son of good family, to the west..."
Beyond these twenty Ganges-sands of Buddha-lands, there is a world named Sahā.

That land abounds with mountains, hills, mounds, earth, sand, gravel, thorns, and sharp brambles, which fill it everywhere; it is constantly filled with the sufferings of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and affliction.
The people of that land are unable to show reverence toward śramaṇas, brahmins, parents, or teachers.
Long indulging in attachment to unrighteous desires, practicing unlawful and deviant teachings while lacking faith in the True Dharma, one’s lifespan becomes short.
When kings govern with such deceit and fraudulence, though they possess a kingdom, they know no contentment;

giving rise to greedy and covetous thoughts toward the possessions of others, they raise armies to wage war, resulting in a great many who die unjustly. Kings who practice in this manner do not follow the righteous path.
Because the four heavenly guardian deities were not joyful in their hearts, they sent down calamities and droughts;

the five grains did not ripen, and the people suffered immeasurable illness and affliction. Within that realm was a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha.

Out of great compassion and profound pity for sentient beings, the World-Honored One, between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara, has expounded this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the great assembly.
There was a bodhisattva there named Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja who had already inquired about this matter no differently than you; the Buddha has now answered him. You should go there at once.
"You shall surely hear it yourself.
For the third time, he described how that bodhisattva wished to come.
Upon hearing this matter, the World-Honored One, that Vaidūryaprabha Bodhisattva, together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
Because that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva wishes to come here, he first manifested this auspicious sign;
for this reason, there is this radiance, which is called both a causal condition and a non-causal condition.
At that time, the second [section], "The Descent of Prabhāsa," begins as that Bodhisattva truly approaches.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vairocana, together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, each carrying various banners, canopies, incense, flowers, necklaces,
and all kinds of musical instruments— surpassing those previously mentioned— came together to this place between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara.
With the offerings they had brought, they made worship to the Buddha, prostrating their heads at his feet.
With palms joined in reverence, he circumambulated him three times to the right. Having completed his acts of veneration, he withdrew to sit on one side.

It was not that those Buddhas were unable to answer or show him the Way; rather, they shared the desire for him to be born in this land, to thoroughly extinguish the evils of this land, and to see his nature and attain the Way.
For this reason, they sent him here to inquire. If all Buddhas follow the same path, then those lands would likewise send him.
This person should be sent to provide an answer, and that person should also be sent; however, it is omitted here for brevity.

Furthermore, following the example set by the Master of Transformation—just as this Buddha raised up that Bodhisattva—that Bodhisattva came here, and he too should have been raised up here; yet, it is omitted here for brevity. Question:
Why was this sutra not taught during the Age of Goodness? Answer: Because in this present evil age, the Buddha teaches it as an antidote to impermanence.
Question: Since the Tathāgata Nityapūrṇacandra also appeared in a good world, why is it that the questions and difficulties [posed there] are all the same as those of King Guṇarāja?

Answer: He constantly governs the impermanent; his land should therefore be without permanence. However, because he encounters beings with dispositions for permanence, he teaches according to the principle [of their needs].
For this reason, it is said they are the same. Furthermore, the statement that "what was previously unheard is now heard" cannot fail to be a form of remedial teaching (*pratipakṣa*).
Furthermore, Kāśyapa Tathāgata also possessed constant capacities [for teaching]; why then did he not speak [of this]? Now we understand it is not so;
although that land lacks the teaching of antidotes, he nevertheless taught through the three *paryāyas*. Kāśyapa was also like this.

At that time, the World-Honored One asked [the second question]. Having reached this point, the discussion of the meaning is divided into two parts: first, the incidental discussion on coming and going;
second, the formal inquiry into the meaning of the "upper" [section]. Regarding the first part: the sequence of questions and answers varies according to circumstances and is not fixed.
Here, the Buddha asks first, followed by the Bodhisattva asking. This incidental discussion differs from that of Cunda; whereas in the preceding text, he addressed the Buddha.
However, Mañjuśrī’s side-by-side challenge is that while the person is side-by-side, the Dharma is not;
herein, one should properly ask about "hearing what has not been heard," whereas asking about coming and going is side-by-side with the Dharma but not side-by-side with the person.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked that bodhisattva, "Good son, have you come, or have you not come?
The Buddha’s intention in asking was this: "Do you see all dharmas as having coming and going, and thus come; or do you see them as being without coming and going, and thus come?"
In the first two of the ten responses given by Vairocana, he clarifies that there is no coming with respect to the preceding objects.
The Bodhisattva Vairocana said: "World-Honored One, even if [the Tathāgata] arrives, there is no coming; even if he does not arrive, there is no coming.

As I contemplate this meaning, there is absolutely no coming. World-Honored One, if all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were permanent, they would likewise not come; if they were impermanent, they would likewise not come."
There is no coming.
The subsequent eight sections concern delusion and awakening: in awakening there is no going or coming, whereas in delusion there is going and coming.
If a person perceives that there is a fixed nature of sentient beings, they would perceive coming or not-coming; however, I do not now perceive a fixed nature in sentient beings.
How can one say that there is coming and no coming? Those who possess pride perceive coming and going; those without pride have neither coming nor going.
Those who practice with grasping perceive coming and going; those without grasping have neither coming nor going.

If one perceives the Tathāgata as having entered ultimate nirvāṇa, then there is coming and going; if one does not perceive the Tathāgata as having entered ultimate nirvāṇa, there is neither coming nor going.
Then there is no coming or going; if one does not hear of the Buddha-nature, there is coming and going, but for those who hear of the Buddha-nature, there is no coming or going.
If one perceives that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have a nirvāṇa, there is coming and going;
if one does not perceive that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have a nirvāṇa, there is no coming or going. If one perceives śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas...
If there were permanence, bliss, self, and purity, then there would be coming and going; if these are not seen, then there is no coming and going.

If one perceives the Tathāgata as lacking permanence, bliss, self, and purity, then there is coming and going; if one perceives the Tathāgata as possessing permanence, bliss, self, and purity, then there is no coming and going.
The principle of the luminosity of lapis lazuli neither comes nor goes, yet its manifestations appear to come and go; delusion and awakening are likewise so.
This also answers the noble [inquiry] regarding hearing what has not been heard.

World-Honored One, setting aside the mundane for a moment, the formal discussion of the meaning below consists of four parts: first, the request for permission; second, the question and answer; third, the repeated investigation; and fourth, the conclusion.
The fourfold objection and the granting of the request are as stated in the text.
"World-Honored One, let this matter rest for now; I wish to ask something, and I only pray that you will look upon me with compassion and grant me a brief hearing.
The Buddha said, "Good son, ask whatever you wish. Now is precisely the right time; I shall analyze and explain it for you."
Why is this? Because Buddhas are difficult to encounter, as rare as the udumbara flower; the Dharma is likewise difficult to hear.
Among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) is even more difficult to encounter. Therefore, you should listen and receive it with single-minded devotion.
Next, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vairocana asked.
At that time, having received the Buddha’s permission as well as his instructions, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vairocana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, how is it that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to practice the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and hear its teachings?"
"I have not heard it.
If one were to ask in full detail, it should be as in the *Śrīdevarāja-paripṛcchā*, which consists of three pairs and six items;

here, the direct questions concern what has been heard and what has not been heard, and there are generally three differences: first, the question by Śrīdevarāja is extensive while that by Prabhūtaratna is concise; second, the question by Śrīdevarāja concerns realization.
Ryūkō asks about the cultivation of the three virtues; Ōtokū asks about hearing what has not been heard.
Ryūkō asks how one can hear what was previously unheard. How are these two inquiries reconciled? The explanation states: Ryūkō, while in his original land, also posed these two pairs of questions.

Since the assembly had already heard them in detail, [Ōtokū] merely summarizes them. Ōtokū’s inquiry concerning the verification of the five practices refers to internal realization; such verification does not depend on external conditions.

Because one hears what was previously unheard, it is said that "one hears what was not heard. In the *Liu guang* (Flaming Light), it is asked: "The cultivation within realization is precisely the 'heavenly practice' (*devayāna*).

Since heavenly practice functions spontaneously, increasing in clarity with every thought-moment, it is said that 'one hears what was not heard. Though the phrasing differs, the principle is the same," and so forth.

The Buddha’s response consists of two parts: first, the introductory narrative (*nidāna*), and second, the formal reply. Within the introductory narrative, there are two sections: the praise and permission, and the exhortation to listen.
At that time, the Tathāgata praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You now wish to exhaustively [inquire about] such a great..."
Riding upon the ocean of the Great Nirvāṇa, you have now encountered me, who am well-able to explain for you the poisonous arrows of the net of doubt that you currently possess;
I am a great physician, able to skillfully extract them. Regarding the Buddha-nature, you are as yet not clearly enlightened;
I possess the torch of wisdom, able to provide illumination for you. Now that you wish to cross the great river of birth and death, I can act as your great vessel.
"Disciple, you should regard me as your parent; I, too, shall regard you as my own child.
Since your mind now craves the treasure of the True Dharma and you have encountered me who possess it in abundance, I am able to bestow it upon you with wisdom."
I permit six propositions that resemble the six perfections, though they do not follow their usual order: you wish to exhaust the ocean, which I can explain well; this refers to diligence.
You wish to extract the poisoned arrow, which refers to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*). You wish for the illumination of the wisdom-torch, which refers to *prajñā*.
You wish to ask about what has not been heard, yet you have already heard it; I permit this, for you have not yet attained clear realization of the Buddha-nature.
"I possess the torch of wisdom that can provide illumination; you should know that this refers to the detailed exposition on 'hearing what has not been heard'—that is, the Buddha-nature—and so forth.
Why? Because 'hearing what has not been heard' means attaining the hearing of the eternal, blissful, self, and pure; this is its further meaning.
If the inquiry of Ratnaprabha is the same as that of King Śrīkūṭa, then Ratnaprabha’s attainment of the *gotra* (cause) is likewise noble and sublime, as stated in the subsequent passage."
Because of this matter, I immediately attained awakening and understanding through a single phrase or half-phrase, whereby I beheld the Buddha-nature and entered Great Nirvana.
Regarding the three phrases: "hearing what is not heard" is the Buddha-nature; "not hearing what is heard" is the *nirvedha-hetu* (the cause of penetration);
"neither hearing nor not hearing" is the *samyak-hetu* (the true cause); and "hearing what is heard" is the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Furthermore—
This is the nature of the cause; hearing and not hearing are the nature of the cause of causes (and so forth).

Examples such as coming and not coming, birth and non-birth, reaching and not reaching, and so on, are likewise thus. Acting as a boatman refers here to the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
allowing the arising of the mind of a child refers here to the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); allowing wisdom and giving refers here to the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
"Next, listen attentively"—this is an exhortation to listen. It has two parts: first, an exhortation for those who have not yet heard; second, an exhortation for those who have already heard.
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Son of good family, for one who wishes to hear the Dharma, now is precisely the right time."

The admonition for those who have not yet heard consists of three points: listen attentively so that the vessel is not turned upside down; reflect well so that the vessel does not leak; and maintain mindfulness so that the vessel is not defiled.
Because it is not turned upside down, one is able to receive [the teaching]; because it does not leak, one does not lose it; and because it is not defiled, it is fit for drinking.

The admonition for those who have already heard also has three parts: the first three matters admonish against turning the vessel upside down; the next two matters admonish against leaking; and the final five matters admonish against defilement.
The first section on "defilement" (āvaraṇa) provides the heading; the second section on "concealment" (saṃvṛti) provides the explanation.
Having heard the Dharma, one should give rise to reverent faith and listen with a sincere mind, honoring and respecting it.
One should give rise to a reverent mind toward the Dharma, listen with a sincere mind, and, having so listened, honor and respect the teacher.
Regarding the True Dharma, do not seek out its faults; do not harbor thoughts of greed, hatred, or delusion;
do not examine whether the lineage of the Dharma teacher is noble or base.
Do not seek out their faults; set aside the Dharma and do not give rise to the three poisons. Having set aside [the pursuit of faults], do not examine their lineage.
If the teacher lacks three things, the vessel is not covered.
From "Once you have heard the Dharma" onwards, the next two points concern the prevention of leakage.
Having heard the Dharma, do not give rise to arrogance; do not act for the sake of respect, reputation, or gain; rather, you should strive for transcendence.
Regarding the benefit of the Dharma of the Deathless, do not give rise to the thought: "After I have heard the Dharma, I shall first deliver myself and then deliver others;
first liberate myself and then liberate others; first establish myself in peace and then establish others in peace;
first attain nirvana for myself and then cause others to attain nirvana."
Do not give rise to arrogance when departing from this; do not leak into saṃsāra. Do not give rise to conceptualization when departing from that; do not leak into nirvāṇa.
To be free from these two extremes is precisely what it means to be without leakage (*anāsrava*).
Departing from the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, one is cautioned not to defile them.
One should conceive the notion of equality toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; one should conceive the notion of great suffering within birth and death;
and regarding Great Nirvana, one should conceive the notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. One should first act for the sake of others and only then for oneself;

one should practice for the sake of the Mahāyāna and not for the sake of the two vehicles. Regarding all dharmas, one should have no dwelling place, nor should one be dogmatically attached to the characteristics of any dharma.
Among all phenomena, do not give rise to thoughts of craving, but always cultivate the thought of knowing the Dharma and seeing the Dharma.
Son of good family, if you can listen to the Dharma with such a sincere mind as this, it is called "hearing what has not been heard before."
First, do not defile the single essence; second, do not defile the four virtues; third, do not defile the Mahāyāna; fourth, do not defile non-abiding;

fifth, do not defile the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). If one treats [the teacher] as a separate entity, this is a defilement that prevents one from honoring the teacher. If one gives rise to the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*), this is a defilement that prevents one from honoring the Dharma.
If one gives rise to the attachment and craving of the Hīnayāna, this is a defilement that prevents one [from honoring it].
Since the Honored One himself is free from these five faults, he is untainted; thus, the ten dharmas for ordinary conduct constitute the ultimate sincerity (and so forth).

Question: The *Ratnaprabhāsa* emits light, and that light is eternally abiding; how then can it be subject to such admonitions? Answer: The striking of a hammer against an anvil and the clashing of objects serve as a means to entrust the admonitions of the sages to the ordinary person.

Good son, regarding the second correct answer concerning "hearing what has not been heard," it is divided into two parts: first, the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) of "hearing what has not been heard" based on its application;

second, the extensive opening of two successive sets of fourfold analyses regarding "the arising of the unarisen. According to the old Southern interpretation, the first fourfold analysis is an explanation of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*), while the latter two fourfold analyses are analogies (*upamā*).
According to the *Dìlùn* (Treatise on the Stages) school, the first fourfold analysis pertains to the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*).

The next two [sections] concern the contemplation of the characteristics of realization (*pratyakṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The Master says that the fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are not different; they are taught in three successive rounds to accommodate the three levels of capacity.
Regarding the first round of the fourfold propositions, the interpretations of various masters differ. One master explains them in terms of the two truths (*satyadvaya*):

"Hearing what is unheard" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while for the sake of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), the ultimate is said to possess hearing. "Neither hearing nor not hearing" refers solely to the ultimate truth.

There is absolutely no seeing or hearing; that which hears what is not heard takes the conventional as the real, such that there is nothing heard. That which hears hearing is merely the conventional; within this conventional, there exists seeing and hearing.
One Master explains this in terms of the Real and the Responsive: "Not hearing what is heard" refers to the Dharma-body arising as the Responsive-body;

"not hearing what is not heard" refers to the Dharma-body remaining majestic and unmoved; "hearing what is not heard" refers to the Responsive-body being gathered back into the Real; and "hearing what is heard" refers to the Responsive-body itself.
I have heard from one master that regarding birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa—wherein nirvāṇa is true stillness—one neither hears nor hears;

yet there is response whenever there is resonance, such that though not hearing, one hears. When the entanglements of birth-and-death are present, if one can cultivate the Way, then one hears what is not heard;
if one does not cultivate the Way, one is always merely hearing what is heard. This master says that the four propositions concerning "hearing what is heard" are not the primary intent.

Later, one must again investigate the four propositions regarding non-arising; only then does one grasp the correct meaning. One should explain it through [the perspective of] non-arising and so forth:
"Not hearing and not hearing is nirvana, which is without beginning and without end. "Non-arising while giving rise is nirvana, which begins though without beginning.
"Non-arising while arising is nirvana, which ends though without end. The same applies to birth-and-death: "Arising while giving rise is birth-and-death."
"Without beginning and without end, non-arising yet arising is 'without beginning,' while arising yet non-arising is 'without end' (and so forth).
To claim that these meanings are all incorrect—why? Because these three sets of four propositions encompass all phenomena without exception.
Since the Perfect [Teaching] uses these to explain the sutras, one fears that others will not understand; how then could one unilaterally treat them as if they were merely provisional teachings?"
Is this realization of the Dharma through analogy and interpretation? Not only does it fail to accord with the Perfect [Teaching], but it further dismembers and injures the essence of the body.
Furthermore, although another master relies on the single essence to explain the four propositions, the more he speaks of intimacy, the more remote he becomes;

how much more so when the complications of the two truths are multiplied? The same applies to the dualities of the True and the Responsive, and of birth-and-death and nirvana; how much more so, then, in other cases?
To interpret the three phrases as "producing production" and so forth results in a profound loss of the essential meaning;

moreover, to interpret them as mutual non-existence is merely the partial view of the Hīnayāna and has no bearing on the Great Way, so none of these [interpretations] are to be used now. Furthermore, all ten of these matters are qualities realized within;

King Dharanindhara’s difficulty was that he could not hear what is heard, while Prabhūtaratna’s difficulty was that he could hear what is not heard—though the two expressions differ, [the underlying principle is the same].

Within the "Questioning the Witness" section, the four propositions are explained in detail. Were one to attempt to interpret them, there would be a thousand paths and ten thousand tracks, all equally revealing this witness;

yet even then, one might still fear falling short of the mark. Consequently, various masters—like wild grasses blown by the wind beyond the fields or duckweed drifting on the surface of the sea—rely exclusively on specific phenomena, clinging to a single point to the detriment of the whole.
Not only do they deviate from the Perfect Teaching, but they never truly relate to the witness.
Good son, there is that which is heard by not hearing, that which is not heard by not hearing, that which is not heard by hearing, and that which is heard by hearing.
If one explains all meanings through these four propositions, they apply universally to every point of contact. To understand the first four propositions, one should rely upon the Buddha’s words.

Although the Buddha’s answer concerns realization, his underlying intent lies in the universal application of cultivation. When one first enters the path of realization, the path of cultivation may suddenly cease; [therefore, one must rely on the teachings].
That which can be called "not hearing" refers to the true illumination that is opened wide and shines upon everything; because this is indeed hearing, it is called "not hearing.
Hearing the realization of such Great Parinirvāṇa—wherein Great Parinirvāṇa has no characteristic of hearing—it is therefore called "not hearing.
The arising of delusion through "not hearing" is extinguished by hearing, yet this "not hearing" is quiescent and eternal.

To respond according to whatever is struck by illumination is called "hearing what is heard. Now, taking the Buddha’s own interpretation, these four lines are explained within the context of "non-arising arising":

since this is the Buddha’s interpretation, it is not a mere fabrication. The first line clarifies the realization of wisdom (*jñāna*); the second line clarifies the realization of principle (*tattva*);

the third line clarifies the realization of cessation (*prahāṇa*); and the fourth line clarifies the realization of response (*pratipatti*). Whether in terms of phenomena or principle, whether in terms of wisdom or cessation, [these constitute the realization].
This realization, which self and others possess in its entirety and without deficiency within the initial attainment, is not shared with the Lesser Vehicle;
it is inconceivable and would provoke astonishment upon hearing. This single, wondrous realization explains the doubts of both types of persons and exhausts the ocean of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, hearing what has not been heard is the realization of the holy practice (*ārya-caryā*); hearing what has been heard is the realization of the Brahma practice (*brahma-caryā*);

neither hearing what has not been heard nor hearing what has been heard is the realization of the celestial practice (*deva-caryā*); and hearing what has been heard is the realization of the infant practice (*bāla-caryā*).
Because these practices realize one through all and are perfectly realized and complete, the Buddha told Kāśyapa in the passage above: "It is not only you who have attained these five practices."
The meaning is this: that all five hundred and thirty thousand people within this assembly have now attained these five kinds of hearing is precisely what is intended.
Furthermore, "hearing what was not heard" is the evidentiary cause of realization (*pratyaya-hetu*); "not hearing what was heard" is the evidentiary condition-cause (*pratyaya-hetu*);

"not hearing what was not heard" is the evidentiary true cause (*samyag-hetu*); and "hearing what was heard" is the evidentiary object (*viṣaya*). Therefore, the Buddha answered Liangguang (Prabhāsa): [as follows].
The meaning is this: "You are not yet clearly aware of the Buddha-nature; I possess the torch of wisdom that can illuminate it for you.
Furthermore, "hearing what has not been heard" is the realization of perfected purity (*pariśuddhi*); "not hearing what has not been heard" is the realization of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-śuddhi*);

and "hearing what has been heard and hearing what has not been heard" is the realization of the purity of skillful means (*upāya-śuddhi*). Therefore, the Buddha answered Liangguang (Prabhāsa), saying: "You now desire to exhaust [all phenomena]..."
The meaning is this: "I am able to provide you with a complete explanation of the great ocean of *mahāparinirvāṇa*.
If one grasps this intent, one can freely and extensively expound upon a single realization (and so forth).
The second section extensively clarifies the fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). From the perspective that "the unborn arises from the like," it elucidates two types of fourfold propositions.

Good son, the unborn does not arise from the like; the non-arising does not arise from the non-arising; the non-arising arises from the arising; and the like does not reach the like. It does not reach the like; it does not reach the like; it does not reach the like; and it reaches the like.
What is meant by "the meaning of non-difference"? It is because these four propositions regarding self and other cannot be differentiated.

Within those four propositions, further names and meanings are established to mutually clarify and explain them; this method of categorization can be applied broadly. To briefly cite two types as examples to illustrate the scope of this extensive meaning, it universally encompasses all internal and external phenomena.
Why, then, does he say that these four are "illustrative explanations" (*paryāya*)? They are so called because they arise [from conventional usage].
The Imperial Precedent uses these four lines to explain the verses on "originally existing but now non-existent" and "cutting flesh from the Snow Mountain," and so forth:

"Non-arising arising" refers to that which was originally non-existent but is now existent; "arising non-arising" refers to that which was originally existent but is now non-existent; "arising arising" refers to dharmas that exist throughout the three periods of time;
and "non-arising non-arising" refers to that which has no such place of existence. Thus, arising and non-arising mean that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are non-existent.

That which is eternally non-arising is arising; this arising is the dharma of arising and ceasing. That which arises is precisely arising and ceasing; once arising and ceasing have ceased, there is no further arising.
This non-arising is quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), which is bliss. Non-arising arising is the Tathāgata’s realization of *nirvāṇa*;
arising non-arising is the eternal severance of birth and death. Birth and death are themselves arising. If one can listen with a sincere heart, one will always attain the Unconditioned.

The measure of bliss is precisely non-arising and non-non-arising. Now, to clarify: first, regarding the fundamental realization of the Perfect [Vehicle], once this principle is established, it universally penetrates all phenomena, both internal and external.
How could it apply only to the various Mahāyāna sūtras? It also applies to the Hinayāna vinayas.
"Arising" refers to the production of all evils; "non-arising" means not to commit them. "Non-non-arising" refers to the cultivation of all virtues.
"Practice non-arising and non-arising; this is to purify one's own mind" (and so forth).
This applies not only to the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and vinayas, but also extends to the Bodhisattva-śāstras. "Arising and arising" refers to dharmas produced by causes and conditions.
"Arising and non-arising," I say, is itself emptiness. "Non-arising and arising" is also called the provisional designation (*prajñapti*). "Non-arising and non-arising" [is the ultimate reality].
This is also called the meaning of the Middle Way (and so forth).
Why does the World-Honored One ask, "How is it that non-arising arises?

This third layer of inquiry is posed because the meaning of "not hearing what is heard" and so forth remains difficult to understand; thus, he further investigates "non-arising arising" and so on to provide additional clarification. If this is understood...

Since "not hearing what has been heard" and so forth do not involve repeated investigation, nor does "not being born from what has already been born" and so forth, we now wish to apply these analogies universally to all cases;
therefore, we shall investigate them repeatedly. This is further divided into two parts: first, regarding the four internal propositions; second, regarding the four external propositions.

“World-Honored One, why is it called ‘non-arising arising’? Son of good family, when one abides in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and first emerges from the womb, this is called ‘non-arising arising.
Why is it called ‘non-arising non-arising’? Son of good family, this Great Nirvāṇa has no characteristic of arising;
this is called ‘non-arising non-arising. Why is it called ‘arising non-arising’? Son of good family, at the time of death according to conventional truth, this is called [‘arising non-arising’].”
"What is meant by 'birth and non-birth' and 'the birth of birth'? Good son, all ordinary worldlings are called 'the birth of birth. Why?
Because their 'birth of birth' is uninterrupted, and because all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) arise moment by moment; therefore, they are called 'the birth of birth.
Bodhisattvas of the four stages of abiding are called 'birth and non-birth. Why? Because their birth is sovereign; therefore, they are called 'birth and non-birth,' good son."
This is called the internal dharma.
Within each of the four internal propositions, there is first a question followed by an answer. Regarding "abiding in the conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are two meanings:
if it refers to external dharmas within the cycle of birth and death, then from the very first moment of entering the womb, it is called abiding in the conventional truth. If...
The stage of practicing the skillful means within the internal dharmas of *nirvāṇa* is called "abiding in conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

From this practice, realization arises and ignorance is suddenly shattered; this is like the first moment of emerging from the womb. While *nirvāṇa* is without beginning, speaking of a "beginning" here serves as a general analogy for such cases, including "hearing what has not been heard" and so forth.
Thus, the meaning of its perfect realization becomes increasingly clear, and conventional death is likewise transcended.

At that time, there are also two meanings: if one considers external dharmas outside of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), when both merit and lifespan are exhausted, it is called "death according to conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

if one considers internal dharmas within *nirvāṇa*, it is called "death according to conventional truth" at the moment ignorance is exhausted. This is also the "end of the endless" regarding birth-and-death.
Among the four stages of abiding for a Bodhisattva—formerly called the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)—this corresponds to the fourth, the Stage of Noble Birth (*janma-vaṃśa-viśuddha*).

Regarding mastery over birth, it is further stated that within the ten stages (bhūmis), at the fourth stage, one exhausts the afflictions of the truths of seeing (darśana-heya) such that one is no longer born in the three miserable realms;

yet, by means of supernormal powers (ṛddhi), one can manifest mastery over birth. Now, observing these two interpretations—one appearing to be a specific meaning and the other a general meaning—I have not yet reconciled this passage.

Upon investigating the intent of this meaning, it simply intends to ensure that the Bodhisattva’s afflictions of the four abodes (catuḥ-vihāra-kleśa) are exhausted. It is not [the case that they are exhausted] otherwise.
These fetters and karmic actions draw one into birth within the three realms, yet they are able to manifest as being born in self or others.
In other sutras, there is the meaning of the six stages of abiding (*ṣaḍ-vihāra*); the fourth stage corresponds to this meaning, as fully cited in the fifth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
It also cites proofs regarding "non-arising arising" and so forth.
The second [section] concerns external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*) in four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
What are external phenomena that have not yet arisen, those that have arisen, those that have not yet arisen but will arise, and those that have arisen?
Good son, it is like a seed: when the sprout has not yet arisen, it obtains the harmony of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and human labor; only then does it arise.
This is called "the unborn arising from the unborn. What is the unborn arising from the unborn? It is like a rotten seed or one that has not encountered the necessary conditions;

such cases are called the unborn arising from the unborn. What is the arisen arising from the unborn? It is like a sprout that has already emerged but has not yet grown; this is called the arisen arising from the unborn.
What is the arising arising from the arisen? It is like a sprout that continues to grow. If there were no arising, then there would be no [growth].
The increase of all such outflows (āsrava) is called the "arising of arising" of external phenomena (bāhyadharma).
As for the expression "the arising of what has not yet arisen," the terms "not yet" (wei) and "not" (bu) are used interchangeably according to the requirements of the context.
In the fourth section following the *Vaidūryaprabha*, the refutation of the fourfold [analysis] is presented;

specifically, within the three and four [sections], there is a refutation of "non-arising arising" and so forth, which is equivalent to "non-arising non-arising" and so forth. Among these four propositions, there is a refutation of "arising arising. To explain these various propositions in detail according to the text, there are three parts:
first, the refutation; second, the explanation; third, the acceptance. Regarding the refutation, there are six sections: three single [refutations] and three pairs. First, [the single refutation]:

The refutation concerning permanence and impermanence is followed by the refutation of arising from self and arising from other; thirdly, there is the refutation of prior existence and prior non-existence.

These all refute arising, because if arising were permanent, it would be impermanent; and because arising would then be arising from self, arising from other, arising from prior existence, or arising from prior non-existence.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vairocanaprabha addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the dharmas of outflows (*āsrava*), if there is such a thing as their arising, are they permanent or are they impermanent?
If the arising of these dharmas of outflows were permanent, then the dharmas of outflows themselves would have no further arising;
if that arising were impermanent, then the dharmas of outflows would be permanent."
Regarding the first passage: as for "the permanent and the impermanent," if birth were permanent, then contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena would not have this "birth of birth" (*jāti-jāti*).
If birth were impermanent, then since the contaminated would be permanently born, and that which is impermanent perishes and cannot sustain itself, how could it give rise to the contaminated?
Since the contaminated is thus not produced by birth, it must therefore be...

[The interlocutor asks: "It is constant. Next, World-Honored One, if arising gives rise to itself, and from that second arising it gives rise to others, then World-Honored One, if arising is able to give rise to itself, since it lacks self-nature, for what reason would it not [also] give rise to others?
Arising is without outflow (*anāsrava*).
Regarding arising: if arising itself arises, it has no self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Since that which is called "arising" is what is produced by itself, it cannot further produce [itself];
because it lacks the nature of being a producer, it is said that arising has no self-nature. Second, arising is fundamentally dependent on conditions and does not yet exist [prior to them].
How can intrinsic nature produce itself? If there is no intrinsic nature, how can it produce another?

If it can produce another, then insofar as it produces another, why is it able to produce only that which is "other" in the sense of being contaminated (*sāsrava*), and not that which is "other" in the sense of being uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
For both the contaminated and the uncontaminated are equally "other" in relation to themselves.
The third objection regarding the time before the Blessed One was born:
If there was birth when the Blessed One had not yet been born, how is it that he is only now called "born"?
If there was no birth when he had not yet been born, why do you not say that empty space is what is born?
If birth were already existent when it had not yet arisen, then since it was already in the state of arising, why is it only now designated as "arising"?
Now is precisely the time when conditions converge. If that which was originally without birth could nonetheless arise, then since space is non-existent, why not say that space arises?

The Buddha’s words below constitute the second section, the "Exegesis," which is divided into three parts: first, the negation of the six questions; second, the explanation of the six negations; and third, the answers to the six questions.
Altogether there are six negations, which form seven topical headings. First, regarding the negation of the six questions:
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! 'Non-arising arising' cannot be spoken of;
'arising arising' also cannot be spoken of; 'non-arising non-arising' also cannot be spoken of; 'arising' cannot be spoken of;
and 'non-arising' also cannot be spoken of."

If it were as you have asked regarding these fixed positions, then all would be inexpressible: first, that "the arising of the unarisen" is inexpressible does not mean that the difficulty regarding the arising of the eternal is resolved;
second, that "the arising of the arisen" is inexpressible does not mean that the difficulty regarding the arising of the impermanent is resolved;
and third, that "the non-arising" is inexpressible does not mean that the difficulty regarding self-arising is resolved, for [in that case] self-nature would be lost. Therefore, this is so.
It cannot be said that "arising" arises; it cannot be said that "non-arising" arises. This is not the fourth [objection], which is the difficulty regarding the arising of another:
as stated previously, if it can give rise to another, why does it not give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*)?

Therefore, it is said that "non-arising" does not arise, and it cannot be said that "arising" arises either. This is not the fifth [objection], the difficulty regarding intrinsic existence (*svabhāva*): non-arising...
It may be said that this is not the difficulty of the sixth [sense-faculty] being fundamentally non-existent;
because there are causes and conditions, it can also be explained.
Furthermore, the fact that the final fetter has causes and conditions can also be explained; this is precisely to reveal the causes and conditions of the four *siddhāntas*.
It can be explained.
How is it that "non-arising arising" is inexpressible? This is the second explanation of the six preceding headings regarding non-existence.
How is it that "non-arising arising" is inexpressible? That which does not arise is called "arising. How can this be explained? Why is this so?
Because it arises. Regarding the first [point], the commentary states:
"To say it is itself arising and yet also not arising—since non-arising is permanence, these two matters are mutually contradictory;
therefore, it cannot be spoken of."
Why is it that "the arising of arising" cannot be spoken of? Because it is the arising of arising, and because it is the arising of the arising of arising, it is non-arising;
thus, it also cannot be spoken of. The second chapter explains arising: if arising were impermanent, then arising would give rise to further arising.

Since the entire substance of arising is produced by arising, it is entirely arising; yet since the entire substance of arising is extinguished by extinction, it is entirely extinction. Because it is the arising of arising, arising itself is its entire substance.
Because arising arises, non-arising occurs; since the entire substance is extinguished, it cannot be spoken of.
How can arising and non-arising be unspeakable? Arising is precisely what is called "arising arising"; because it does not arise by itself, it cannot be spoken of.
The Third Chapter: Explaining that birth does not arise from itself, fundamentally taking up birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
How is it that non-arising is non-arising and cannot be described? That which is non-arising is called *nirvāṇa*.
Because *nirvāṇa* is non-arising, it cannot be described. Why? Because it is attained through the cultivation of the path.
The commentary on the fourth chapter: Nirvana also possesses the sense of "arising," so it cannot be definitively stated that nirvana does not arise.

As to the previous objection—asking why others do not arise [in the same way] as these [conditioned phenomena]—it is because the untainted (*anāsrava*) is precisely nirvana, and nirvana also possesses the sense of arising;
yet, since it is attained through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is further characterized as "arising. Is this not arising? It is indeed arising.
Because that which is extinguished by cessation is such that its arising would be eternal, it cannot be said [to exist].
Why is arising also unspeakable? Because arising does not exist.
The fifth chapter clarifies that there is fundamentally no arising; how could one say that what has not yet arisen already exists?
Why is it that non-arising cannot be described? Because there is attainment.
This explains the sixth chapter’s gateway: one cannot definitively state that non-arising exists, yet there is also the matter of attainability.
Therefore, arising occurs again; it is not the same as space, which is unilaterally without arising.
How is it that, by virtue of causes and conditions, one may also say that the ten links of dependent origination act as the cause for birth?
For this reason, one may also say: "Good son, you should not now enter the profound concentration of emptiness. Why?
Because the great assembly is dull-witted."
Regarding the ten causes and conditions in the seventh chapter on "The Gateways of Discourse": excluding the final two branches, the preceding ten serve as causal conditions for arising;
therefore, they can be so described. This merely serves to resolve the text. In the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation), the explanation of the four propositions is somewhat more extensive.

My private opinion is that, according to the intent of that explanation, it accords perfectly with the elegant principles of the current *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and deeply harmonizes with its textual structure. That text contains nothing [that contradicts this].
The contemplation of arising accords entirely with the gate of *nirvāṇa*—non-arising. "Do not enter the concentration on emptiness" is explained in two ways by the assembly, as they are dull-witted:
first, it means that because the assembly is truly dull and does not understand the concentration on emptiness, it says "do not enter";

second, it means that if one were to speak of entering the concentration on emptiness, the understanding of the assembly would be slow, for the meaning of emptiness is profound and hidden, making it difficult for them to grasp.
