To say it is difficult to explain would be dull; however, since the sūtra text proclaims six phrases that are all "inexpressible," yet because there are causes and conditions, they can also be explained.
The Buddha, having finished explaining the "inexpressible" through six rounds, further pointed to the causes and conditions, thereby concluding that they can indeed be explained.
This meaning is still brief; now, I shall explain it again in two rounds: because there are causes and conditions, everything can be explained, as is fully possessed [by these factors].
A single phrase is explained as four propositions: namely, non-arising arising, arising non-arising, non-arising non-arising, and arising arising.
All four propositions are explained in this manner. This is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which may also be described as "having causes and conditions.
Yet it should also be said that because they have causes and conditions, all are ultimately ineffable. Why? Because a single phrase contains all four; how could one treat them as merely one?
If one explains these causes and conditions as two, three, or four, they cannot be so described;

even when all four phrases are complete, how can any single phrase—whether the first, second, third, or fourth—be taken alone as the cause and condition? All such descriptions are ultimately ineffable.

Furthermore, within the four phrases, phenomena are identical to principle, yet that principle is entirely ineffable. Moreover, within the four phrases, principle is identical to phenomena, and thus all phenomena are fully manifest.
To explain why: the subsequent text states, "If one knows that the Tathāgata never preaches the Dharma, this is called 'much learning' (bahuśruta).

Following this principle, if one knows that the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are such that the phenomenon (*dharma*) is itself the principle (*dharmatā*), this is precisely the stage of non-preaching.

Regarding the names of the masters, the first three types of four propositions concern the teaching, practice, and realization; while it is not that these meanings do not exist when speaking in a general sense, [the present intent] now wishes to...
Analyzing these six phrases, they appear as combinations of single and multiple, and general and specific [distinctions] regarding afflictions (*kleśa*) and understandings (*jñāna*).
The first two phrases clarify general and specific afflictions; the next two phrases clarify general and specific understandings. "Non-arising from arising" refers to specific afflictions (single);

"arising from arising" refers to general afflictions (multiple). "Non-arising from non-arising" refers to general understanding (single); "non-arising from non-arising" refers to specific understanding (multiple). Furthermore:
The phrase "arising" concludes the preceding section on the single and multiple arising of afflictions (*kleśa*), as both are equally the arising of delusion.
Next, the phrase "non-arising" concludes the preceding section on the single and multiple non-arising [of liberation], as both are equally the cessation of delusion.

Thus, while these single and multiple instances of affliction and liberation cannot be explained [in terms of their own nature], their causal conditions can be explained, as has been fully demonstrated previously (etc.).
"Good son, regarding the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), the third section below provides the direct answer to the six questions.
The preceding six phrases are divided into two parts: first, the answer to the first two questions; second, the answer to the latter four questions.

The answer to the former is further divided into two: first, treating the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) individually; second, treating the four characteristics collectively. First, treating the four characteristics individually consists of four parts."
Good son, regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), arising (*utpāda*) is also permanent, while abiding (*sthiti*) is impermanent; arising is likewise impermanent.
As for the initial statement that arising is permanent, it is because at the moment of its differentiation, it maintains its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and thus it is termed "permanent.
As for the statement that it is impermanent, from the time it comes to abide, as soon as it arises, it undergoes change; therefore, it is also impermanent.
Abiding is also permanent because it is produced by production; yet abiding is also impermanent.
Abiding is likewise [impermanent], for that which is produced by production cannot be permanent.
Change is also permanent because phenomena are impermanent; yet change is also impermanent.

The same applies to "difference" (*anyathātva*). Regarding the statement that all phenomena are impermanent (*anitya*): if it was previously said that there is "abiding" (*sthiti*) within the process of arising, then if abiding were impermanent, arising would also be impermanent.
Now, by taking "phenomena" (*dharma*) as the counterpart to "difference," it is shown that this very abiding within the prior arising is an impermanent phenomenon;
thus, difference also possesses the sense of being both permanent and impermanent, exactly as in the case of arising and abiding.
Destruction is also permanent because it was originally non-existent and now exists; yet destruction is also impermanent.

Regarding the statement that "destruction is likewise [impermanent]—that which was originally non-existent and now exists is the meaning of 'arising'—once arisen, whether arising further or undergoing destruction, it cannot be permanent; that which was originally existent and now no longer exists... [is the meaning of destruction].
This is impermanent.
Good son, because they arise, [the text] below explains the four characteristics in conjunction.
Good son, because of their nature, arising, abiding, change, and destruction are all eternal; yet because they perish moment by moment, they cannot [be so].
It is said that because the Great Nirvana is eternal and capable of severing [defilements], it is termed "impermanence.
Each, by maintaining its own nature and portion, attains this eternity. However, due to two meanings, it does not attain this eternity:
viewed closely, it undergoes moment-to-moment transformation; viewed from afar, it is not eternal as it is severed by Nirvana. Therefore, it is not [eternal].
"Constantly.
Good son, regarding the dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*), the answer to the second [question] below addresses the latter four difficulties, which is further divided into two parts:

first, directly answering the fifth while concurrently answering the sixth; second, directly answering the fourth while concurrently answering the third. This is the initial response to the first [difficulty]."
Regarding the five questions:
"Good son, because the dharmas with outflows already possess the nature of arising even before they have arisen, arising is able to produce them.
To the previous question, "If they exist fundamentally, why are they now called 'arising'?", the present answer is: "They exist fundamentally."
The principle of arising is not that what already exists is now being born; this simultaneously answers the sixth [point] and others regarding why non-arising is not mentioned.
Furthermore, as for why space is not said to be "arising," our current answer is that only where there is the principle of being capable of arising can there be actual arising.
Since space lacks the principle of being capable of arising, how can it be said that space constitutes arising?
Regarding the fourth difficulty answered below concerning the dharmas free from outflows (*anāsrava-dharma*):

as for the initial passage consisting of the dharma, the analogy, and the application, because the dharmas free from outflows are fundamentally without the nature of arising, arising cannot produce them.

The initial objection states: "If [arising] could produce another, it should produce the untainted (*anāsrava*). Now, the response is that there is no principle by which the untainted can be produced;

therefore, it cannot produce tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena, because tainted phenomena possess the nature of arising. This also answers the third objection regarding the production of that which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*):
if there were intrinsic nature, arising would be able to produce it; since there is no intrinsic nature, [production does not occur].
How could it be possible for [the mind] to arise? This simultaneously answers both points and naturally resolves them from afar.
For example, fire has an inherent nature that is ignited when meeting with conditions; likewise, the eye has a nature of seeing which sees because of form, light, and the mind.

Next, in the analogy, the mention of fire and the eye each having their own nature—where the nature of fire is to produce heat and the nature of the eye is to see—is used here to show that because there is the "nature of production," that which produces is precisely the refutation of the concept of "nature. Only after this is it said that "nature" exists;

thus, there is no contradiction with what was previously stated regarding the refutation of the clinging to nature, where it was subsequently stated that [things arise] when there are causes and conditions.
Thus it can be explained.
The union is as stated in the text.
The arising of sentient beings is likewise: by virtue of an inherently existing nature (*prakṛti*), meeting with karmic causes and conditions and the union of father and mother.
Then there was birth.
At that time, regarding the third section on the descent of *Ratnaprabhā*, there are two parts: first, the narrator’s account of the signs; second, the actual presentation of the understanding.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vairocana and eighty-four thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having heard this Dharma, leaped up into the air to a height of seven tala trees;
with palms joined in reverence, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
Chen Jie further addressed the assembly twice:
"World-Honored One, having received the Tathāgata’s earnest instruction, it is only through the Great Nirvāṇa that I have finally attained awakening and understanding,
hearing what I had never heard before."
He also caused eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas to deeply understand that all dharmas are neither produced nor non-produced.

Initially, he spoke for himself, saying "hearing the unheard," and then spoke for the assembly, saying "the production of the unproduced. This was precisely to present the gateway through which they attained understanding;
because there were those who had not yet reached the fourfold negation of "reaching" and "not reaching," Vimalakīrti asked again whether they were produced or not.
King Devarāja further discusses "the non-arrival of arrival" and so forth.

[The King says: "World-Honored One, I have now understood. This concludes the third section on the meaning of the fearless discourse, which is divided into three parts: first, requesting permission; second, the discourse itself;
and third, requesting an answer to King Devarāja’s question. The request for permission is as stated in the text.
“World-Honored One, I have now understood and severed all nets of doubt. However, there is a bodhisattva in this assembly named Abhaya who wishes to further inquire and receive instruction;
may you deign to grant him your attention. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Abhaya:
“Good son, ask whatever you wish. I shall analyze and explain it for you.”

Regarding the second section on the discourse of fearlessness, there are three questions and answers. Within the inquiry for understanding, there are two parts: first, the question regarding how this [life] gives rise to that;
second, the question regarding those of sharp faculties.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Abhaya, together with sixty-four thousand bodhisattvas, rose from their seats once more.
Adjusting his robes, kneeling with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what karma must the sentient beings of this land perform in order to be reborn in that Immovable World?"

How do the bodhisattvas in that land achieve the perfection of wisdom? They are like elephant-kings among men, possessing great majestic power, fully cultivating all practices, and endowed with sharp and swift intelligence such that they can understand immediately upon hearing.
These two aspects are established in mutual relation; their distinction lies in their shifting perspectives.

Regarding the question of how to reconcile the sutra’s statement that Bodhisattvas in the pure and impure lands have mutual superiority and inferiority with the present explanation: if viewed in terms of direct opposition, the Pure Land is superior;
if viewed in terms of the provisional versus the real, the Real Pure Land is superior when entering it, whereas the Provisional Impure Land is superior when entering it.
Next, the Buddha provides the direct answer to the first question while simultaneously dispelling the subsequent question; this consists of twenty-one lines of verse, divided into two parts.
The first ten lines concern the excellence of *śamatha*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Not harming the lives of sentient beings, Firmly upholding all the prohibitions and precepts, And receiving the Buddha’s subtle and wondrous teachings, one will be born in the Immovable Land.

Not seizing the wealth of others, Constantly bestowing gifts upon all, and constructing *caityas*, monasteries, and vihāras for the Saṅgha, One will be born in the Immovable Land. Not violating the wives of others.
One’s own wife does not engage in unseasonable conduct; one gives bedding and requisites to those who uphold the precepts—then one will be born in the Immovable Land.
Not for one's own sake nor for the sake of others, one seeks neither profit nor intimidation;
being careful of the mouth and refraining from false speech, one will be born in the Immovable Land. Do not destroy virtuous friends, and keep far away from evil associates.
With speech that is always harmonious, one will be born in the Immovable Land (*Acalā*).
Like the various Bodhisattvas, who are always free from harsh speech, what they say is pleasant for others to hear; thus one will be born in the Immovable Land.
Even in jest, one does not speak at an improper time, but speaks with restraint and at the proper time.

One will be born in the Immovable Land: Seeing others receive gain and offerings, Always giving rise to a heart of joy, Without producing the fetter of envy— Then one will be born in the Immovable Land.
Not troubling sentient beings, Always giving rise to a heart of loving-kindness, And not producing evil through expedient means— Then one will be born in the Immovable Land.
Those with wrong views claim that one should give offerings to one's parents and to those who have departed or yet to come;
by not giving rise to such views, one will be born in the Immovable Realm (Akaniṣṭha).
The following eleven lines clarify the practice of wholesome conduct.
Whoever digs a fine well on a desolate road, plants groves of fruit trees, and constantly gives food to beggars shall be born in the Immovable Land (*Acalā*).

If one makes an offering of even a single incense stick or lamp, or even presents a single flower to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, one shall be born in the Immovable Land. If, for the sake of fear...
If one seeks gain and merit, by writing even a single verse of this sutra, one will be born in the Immovable Land (Akṣobhya’s realm).
If, for the sake of rare gain and fortune, one can recite this scripture for even a single day, one will be born in the Immovable Land.
If, however, it is for the sake of the Unsurpassed Way, [one should recite] for a full day and night.
By observing the eightfold precepts of the fast, one will be born in the Immovable Land (Akṣobhya’s realm).

One shall not dwell in the same place as those who have violated the heavy prohibitions, nor with those who revile and slander the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) sūtras; such a person will be born in the Immovable Land.
If one can give even a single fruit to the sick, looking upon them with joy, [one will likewise be born there].

One will be born in the Immovable Land: By not misappropriating the property of the Saṅgha, By properly guarding the Buddha’s wealth and offerings, and by sweeping and cleaning the grounds of the Buddha and the Saṅgha, One will be born in the Immovable Land.
By fashioning images and stūpas even as small as a thumb, And by always giving rise to a heart of joy, One will be born in the Immovable Land.
If, for the sake of this sutra, one gives one’s own body and material wealth to the teacher of the Dharma,
one will be born in the Immovable Land (*Acalā*). If one can listen to, transcribe, uphold,
and recite this secret treasury of all Buddhas, one will be born in the Immovable Land.
However, the practice for the Pure Land is none other than the bodhicitta; the present treatise on its specific application is thus not different from the general [teaching].
The threefold understanding of this is as stated in the text.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Abhaya addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have now understood what has been established."
Through karmic conditions, one is born in that land.
This "The Universal Radiance Shines Throughout" section concludes the third request for an answer to the questions of King Devarāja; the preceding middle section has already been explained.
For those who have not yet attained full realization, he requests further clarification by first posing his questions, followed by the Buddha’s answers to those questions, as set forth in the text.
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhā-vairocana-āryaguṇarāja has universally out of compassion for all sentient beings inquired of the Tathāgata;
if [the Tathāgata] were to speak, it would bring benefit, peace, and happiness to humans,
devas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others.
The Buddha answered in two parts: first, he praised [the bodhisattva] and exhorted him to listen; second, he gave the formal answer.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Prabhāpāramitā-Abhyudgata-Guṇarāja: "Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son, you should now listen with a sincere mind; I shall analyze and explain this for you.
In the response, he first presents the categories of "not yet arrived" and "not arrived," followed by the citation of "hearing" and "not hearing. Regarding the former, there are two parts:
first, the headings for the chapters on "arrived" and "not arrived"; second, the detailed explanation.

There are conditions by which that which has not yet arrived does not arrive; there are conditions by which that which has not arrived arrives; there are conditions by which that which has arrived does not arrive;
and there are conditions by which that which has arrived arrives.
The meaning of this explanation is as follows: King Guṇa first asked about three kinds and six kinds, and the Buddha spoke six parables and...
Guangrui has already answered "not-hearing hearing" and subsequently answered "not-arising arising" following the discussion on the meaning of *Li-guang*.

Now, he restates this once more as "not-arriving arriving," which refers to the conditions for the object of perception. First, the four propositions regarding "not-hearing hearing" were understood by those of superior capacity;

next, the four propositions regarding "not-arising arising" were realized by those of middling capacity; now, for the sake of those of inferior capacity, he explains the conditions for "not-arriving arriving."
It is appropriate that these appear alternately before and after; regarding these four phrases, the first two clarify whether Nirvana is reached or not:
if one cultivates the path to eliminate delusions, it is reached; otherwise, it is not. The latter two phrases clarify whether Saṃsāra is reached or not:
if one turns away from and detests it through the cultivation of the path, it is not reached; otherwise, it is reached. Thus, they are repeated in reverse order.
This completes the preceding phrases.
For what reason has the noble son not yet reached it? Good man, that which is "not yet reached" is the Great Nirvana;
ordinary people have not yet reached it because they possess greed, anger, and delusion, and because their physical and verbal actions are impure.
Furthermore, because of accepting all impure things, committing the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*), slandering the Vaipulya sutras, being an icchantika,
or committing the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), for these reasons, one has not reached, nor will reach, [the state of non-retrogression].
However, in explaining this, one must still refer back to what preceded it: that "non-arising non-arising" is itself Great Nirvana.

This statement regarding "not arriving" (*apratisthita*) is itself non-arising and has no further distinction from it. If this is so, why is it not explained as "not arriving at not arriving" as was done previously?
The answer is: for the sake of the single and the multiple conditions; "not arriving" refers to those ordinary beings who are incapable [of such realization].
As for why the practice does not reach [its goal]:
Good son, by what causes and conditions does it fail to reach it? That which fails to reach it is called Great Nirvana. For what reason does it reach it?
Because it has eternally severed greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the evils of body and speech, it does not accept any impure things.

Therefore, because they do not violate the four grave offenses, do not slander the Vaipulya sutras, do not become icchantikas, and do not commit the five heinous crimes—for these reasons—they are called those who have "not yet reached the ultimate.
Those who have reached the stage of *srotāpanna* will [attain] it after eighty thousand kalpas;

those who have reached the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, after sixty thousand kalpas; those who have reached the stage of *anāgāmin*, after forty thousand kalpas; and those who have reached the stage of *arhat*...
Those who reach the stage of a Pratyekabuddha after twenty thousand kalpas do so after ten thousand kalpas; for this reason, it is called "reaching the non-reachable.
As for "the non-reachable reaching," this is also referred to in contrast to the initial time of emerging from the womb as "birth not being born.
Herein, the expressions "not reaching" and "reaching" regarding birth-and-death each cite one side of the duality.
"Good son, for what reason is it called 'the reached' and 'the unreached'? That which is 'reached' refers to the twenty-five existences (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
All sentient beings are constantly shrouded and obscured by immeasurable afflictions and fetters; they come and go without ceasing, like the turning of a wheel—this is called 'the reached.
Because the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have already attained permanent liberation from these, it is [called] 'the unreached.'"
It is called "non-arrival" because, for the sake of transforming and delivering all sentient beings, it manifests as being present within them; thus it is also called "arrival.

As for "arrival" and "non-arrival," one must also look back to the previous world of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); at the time of death, it is termed "birth" or "non-birth," which are likewise mentioned interchangeably.
Good son, for what reason is it called "the arrival at the arrival"? That which is called "the arrival at the arrival" refers to the twenty-five existences (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Because all ordinary beings, from the *srotāpanna* up to the *anāgāmin*, possess the causes and conditions of afflictions (*kleśa*), it is therefore called "the arrival at the arrival."

Regarding "the ultimate reaching the ultimate," one must also look back to the preceding "life giving rise to life" as being uninterrupted; since this section still discusses birth and death, it is the same as what preceded it.
Next, the phrase "hearing what was not heard before" is cited, which again consists of two parts, with the four chapters listed first.
Good son, hearing what was not heard is likewise thus: there is not-hearing-and-hearing, there is not-hearing-and-not-hearing, there is hearing-and-not-hearing, and there is hearing-and-hearing.
In the subsequent explanation, only one phrase is explained.
What is meant by "not hearing what is heard"? Good son, that which is "not heard" is called the Great Nirvana. Why is it not heard?
Because it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because it is not sound, and because it is ineffable. How, then, is it also "heard"? It is because the name "hearing" is attained;
that is to say, it is permanence, bliss, self, and purity. For these reasons, it is called "not hearing what is heard."

This has already been explained previously; I do not wish to burden the text with further elaboration. Although the people of the *bhūmi* distinguish between the differences in the depth of the teachings and their scriptural proofs, the intended meaning of the present passage is simply that there are three explanations according to what is appropriate for the occasion.
This concerns only the sequence of realization and has nothing to do with the depth of the Dharma. Why? Because although the expressions differ, the meaning is the same.

At that time, following the fourth section on "The Radiance," the King of Virtue (Guṇarāja) again discusses the subject in two parts: first, a single inquiry regarding the fruit; second, a dual inquiry regarding both cause and fruit.
In the first part, there are three inquiries: first, an inquiry as to whether Nirvāṇa exists only at the beginning, which would mean it is impermanent;
second, an inquiry as to whether it is also impermanent because it is adorned by causes; third, an inquiry as to whether Nirvāṇa is also impermanent if it exists.
Within the third question, there are further four sections; otherwise, one would simply pose seven questions:

first, questioning that it is impermanent because what was originally non-existent now exists; second, questioning that it is impermanent because it is adorned by causes; third, questioning that it is impermanent because it exists as such;
fourth, questioning that it is impermanent because it is visible; and fifth, questioning that it is impermanent because it is unequal.
Sixth, because it must depend on conditions, it is impermanent; seventh, because it possesses a name, it is impermanent. Regarding the first question, there are again three parts:
the inquiry that receives the essential meaning, the brief inquiry, and the extensive inquiry.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantāloka-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
As the Buddha has taught, the Great Nirvana cannot be heard;
why then do you say that it can be heard as characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
He asked extensively about the existence of this dharma and answered with analogies.
Why is this? World-Honored One, one who has severed the afflictions is said to have attained *nirvāṇa*, whereas one who has not severed them is said not to have attained it.
For this reason, the nature of *nirvāṇa* is originally non-existent and now existent. If a worldly phenomenon is originally non-existent and now existent, it is called impermanent.
For example, jars and the like are called impermanent because they did not exist originally but now exist, and having existed, they return to non-existence.
If nirvāṇa were likewise, why do you say that it is permanent, blissful, self, and pure?
The second, third, and fourth [sections] are as in the text.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, whatever is accomplished by means of adornment is entirely termed impermanent. If that were so, then *nirvāṇa* would also be impermanent.
For what reason? That is to say: the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the six *pāramitās*, and the four...

Contemplating the skeletal form with a measuring mind, the practice of *ānāpāna*, the six objects of mindfulness (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), the analytical breakdown of the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*), and other such dharmas are all causes and conditions for accomplishing *nirvāṇa*; therefore, they are called "impermanent."
Furthermore, World-Honored One, there is that which is called "impermanence. If nirvāṇa were existent, it too would necessarily be impermanent.
As the Buddha previously stated in the Āgamas: "The śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, all possess nirvāṇa.
For this reason, [if it were existent], it would be termed impermanent.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, that which is a visible phenomenon is called impermanent, as the Buddha previously taught:
"One who perceives nirvāṇa shall then sever all afflictions.
This fifth section contains two layers of analogies and their applications.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, for example, space is called "constant" because it is equal toward all sentient beings and possesses no obstruction.
If nirvāṇa were likewise constant, why would some sentient beings attain it while others do not?
If that were so, being unequal toward sentient beings, it could not be called "constant."
World-Honored One, it is like a hundred people who share a single enemy: if this enemy is slain, many will experience happiness.
If Nirvana were an impartial dharma, then when one person attains it, many should attain it;
when one person severs the fetters, many should also sever them. If it were not thus, how could it be called permanent?
The sixth [section] contains analogies, applications, and citations from the past:
For example, if someone reveres, makes offerings to, respects, and praises a king, a prince, their parents, or their teachers, they will obtain gain and support;
yet this is not called "permanent."
Nirvana is likewise not called "permanent. Why? As the Buddha previously stated in the Āgama Sūtras to Ānanda:
"If there is anyone who can venerate Nirvana, they will sever the fetters and experience immeasurable bliss.
For this reason, it is not called permanent.
The seventh point is as stated in the text:
"World-Honored One, if there were names such as permanence, bliss, self, and purity within nirvāṇa, it would not be called 'permanent.
If they do not exist, how can they be spoken of?"

At that time, the World-Honored One—this marks the second section where the Buddha answers three questions, beginning with the first answer concerning "that which was originally non-existent now exists"—responded by providing a simile and a synthesis regarding the existence of dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva King of Universal Radiance and Noble Virtue: "The essence of nirvāṇa is not..."

"Originally non-existent but now existent": if the essence of *nirvāṇa* were originally non-existent but now existent, it would not be an outflow-free (*anāsrava*) and eternally abiding (*nitya*) dharma.

Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, the characteristics of its nature remain eternally abiding. Because all sentient beings are shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), they do not see *nirvāṇa* and thus claim it does not exist.
When Bodhisattvas diligently cultivate their minds through the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and sever their afflictions, [they then perceive it].
Upon seeing this, one should know that Nirvana is an eternally abiding dharma; it is not something that was previously non-existent and now exists, and for this reason it is eternal.
Good son, it is like a well within a dark room containing various kinds of the seven treasures. Although people know they exist, they do not see them because of the darkness.
A person of wisdom, however, who well understands skillful means, takes a great bright lamp and goes there to illuminate it, whereupon they see everything clearly.
Such a person would never give rise to the thought that the water and the seven treasures—which were originally non-existent—have now come into being.
Nirvāṇa is likewise: it exists inherently from the beginning and is not something that has only recently appeared. Because of the darkness of afflictions, sentient beings do not see it;
the Tathāgata of Great Wisdom, through skillful means, kindles the lamp of wisdom, enabling all bodhisattvas to behold nirvāṇa.
Because [Nirvana] possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity, the wise should not say that this Nirvana was originally non-existent and now exists.

The followers of the *Dìlùn* (Treatise on the Stages) explain it through the dual cultivation of the "True" (*zhēn*) and the "Conditioned" (*yuán*), stating that the True cultivation is originally existent while the Conditioned cultivation begins to exist.

The masters of the Three Treatises (*Sānlùn*) use the "Principal Cause" (*zhèng yīn*) and the "Conditioning Cause" (*yuán yīn*) as their explanation, asserting that the Principal Cause is originally existent while the Conditioning Cause begins to exist.
In response to your statement that "because it is adorned by causes, Nirvana must be impermanent," I shall now answer the second point regarding the existence of phenomena and provide an analogy.
"Good son, your claim that Nirvana must be impermanent because it is accomplished through adornment is also not so.
Why is this? Good son, the essence of Nirvana is neither born nor produced; it is neither real nor empty."
The arising of karmic activity is not a contaminated or conditioned phenomenon;
it is neither hearing nor seeing, neither falling nor dying, neither a distinct characteristic nor a common characteristic; it does not go nor return, nor does it come, stay, or depart;
it is neither one nor many, neither long nor short, neither round nor square, neither pointed nor crooked; it is neither a characteristic nor a perception, neither a name nor a form.
Because it is neither cause nor fruit and is not the self, for this reason Nirvana is eternal, constant, and unchanging;
therefore, after adorning oneself by practicing wholesome dharmas for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one finally beholds it.
The three layers of analogies within the parable are combined as they appear in the text.
Good son, it is like the water of eight flavors beneath the earth, which all sentient beings cannot obtain;
yet, if a person of wisdom exerts effort to dig, they will immediately find it.
Nirvana is also like this.

For example, it is as if a blind person cannot see the sun and moon; when a skilled physician treats them, they are then able to see them, yet these sun and moon were not newly created at that moment.
Nirvana is likewise so: it has existed from the beginning and is not something acquired only now.

Good son, it is like a person who, having committed a crime, is imprisoned; after a long time he is released and returns home, where he is able to see his parents, brothers, wife, children, and kinsmen.
Nirvāṇa is likewise.
Following your statement regarding causes and conditions, the third point below answers that Nirvāṇa exists. This initial exchange of questions and answers seems inconsistent;
had you simply stated that Nirvāṇa exists, it would follow that it must be impermanent. Therefore, I now set forth five reasons.

The explanation that *nirvāṇa* differs from the five causes is followed by citing both "arising" (*jāti*) and "cognition" (*vijñapti*), yet further distinguishing arising so as to equate it solely with cognition;
answering this specific question thus implicitly includes the remaining four.
"Good son, as for your statement that because it is produced by causes and conditions, the dharma of nirvāṇa must be impermanent—this is also not so.
Why? Good son, there are five kinds of causes. What are these five? First, the cause of production; second, the cause of conjunction;
third, the cause of abiding; fourth, the cause of growth; and fifth, the remote cause. What is the cause of production?"
The cause of arising refers to karma, afflictions, and so forth, as well as external seeds such as those of grasses and trees; these are called the cause of arising.

What is the cause of conjunction? It is when the wholesome conjoins with a wholesome mind, the unwholesome conjoins with an unwholesome mind, and the indeterminate conjoins with an indeterminate mind;
this is called the cause of conjunction. What is the cause of abiding? It is like having a pillar beneath [a structure].

Just as houses do not fall because they rest upon the great earth, and mountains, rivers, trees, and forests likewise stand firm by virtue of the great earth, so too do sentient beings with their four elements and immeasurable afflictions abide;
this is called the cause of abiding. What is the cause of growth?
It is due to conditions such as clothing, food, and drink that sentient beings grow, just as external seeds are not consumed by fire nor destroyed by birds.

If one does not eat, one attains growth, just as various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas attain growth by relying upon preceptors and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), or as a child attains growth by relying upon its parents; this is called the cause of growth. What is the remote cause?
For example, it is like how, by means of incantations, demons cannot cause harm and poisons cannot take effect, or by relying upon a king, [one is protected from] fear.
There are thieves such as the sprout, which depends on the causes of earth, water, fire, and wind; there are proximate causes such as the drilling tool and human effort for the production of ghee;
there are remote causes such as light and form for consciousness, and the physical body of the parents for sentient beings;
and there are remote causes such as the seasons—all these are termed remote causes. Son of good family, the essence of Nirvāṇa is not produced by these five kinds of causes.
How can it be said that these are causes of impermanence?

The five causes previously cited correspond to the four conditions; the three causes—namely, the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*), which is the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), and the cause of growth—which is the cause of conjunction (*sāmagrī-hetu*), corresponds to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The cause of abiding, which is the natural similarity of good and evil, corresponds to the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Thus, they are increased.
The long-term cause is the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); the distant cause is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), but it lacks the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, son of good family, there are two other types of causes: first, the producing cause (*kāraka-hetu*); second, the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*).
For example, a potter, a wheel, and a string are called the producing cause; for example, lamps and candles that illuminate objects in the dark are called the revealing cause. Son of good family...
My son, Great Nirvāṇa does not arise from a producing cause (*kārana-hetu*); it arises only from a revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*).
What is called the revealing cause refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and the six perfections (*ṣat-pāramitā*); these are termed the revealing causes.
Good son, the practice of giving (*dāna*) is a cause for nirvāṇa, but it is not a cause for Great Nirvāṇa; only the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is named Great Nirvāṇa.
Because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are causes for nirvana, but not causes for Great Nirvana;
only the immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* factors that assist awakening can be called the cause of Great Nirvana.
Regarding the latter two causes, they differ from the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and are similar to the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*), as noted in the private commentary on the text.
This is because the latter two causes distinguish themselves from the preceding five causes, all of which are efficient causes.

In the passage beginning with "At that time, the light... and following, the second pair of questions concerns cause and effect; within this, first, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are... [text continues].
Question: Since the subsequent question concerns *nirvāṇa*, it is a question concerning the fruit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhāsa-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, why is giving not called *dānapāramitā*? Why is giving called [the perfection of giving]?”
How is it that from the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā* do not receive the name "perfection of wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*), while others do?
What is called "nirvāṇa," and what is called "great nirvāṇa"?
The Buddha answered in two parts: first, answering cause and effect together; second, answering cause and effect separately. Regarding the initial answer together, it is as stated in the text.
The Buddha said: "Good son, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa, he does not hear of giving nor see giving;
he does not hear of the dānapāramitā nor see the dānapāramitā, and so on..."
They do not hear of prajñā nor see prajñā; they do not hear of the prajñāpāramitā nor see the prajñāpāramitā;
they do not hear of nirvāṇa nor see nirvāṇa; they do not hear of mahāparinirvāṇa nor see mahāparinirvāṇa.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates mahāparinirvāṇa, they know and see the dharma-realm and fully comprehend the true mark as empty and non-existent.

When there is the characteristic of the cognition of the conjunction of existence and non-existence, the characteristic of the untainted (*anāsrava*), the characteristic of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*),

the characteristic of being like an illusion or a magical creation (*māyā-vaśya*), the characteristic of a mirage (*marīci*) in the heat, and the characteristic of a city of the Gandharvas (*gandharvanagara*) in empty space— at that time, the Bodhisattva attains such characteristics.
Being free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and neither hearing nor seeing [these things], this is called the true characteristic of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in the true reality knows for himself: "This is giving;
this is the perfection of giving," up to "this is wisdom; this is the perfection of wisdom"; and "this is nirvāṇa;
this is the Great Nirvāṇa."
Good son, what is the giving of the lower two? This is answered separately regarding cause and effect, which is further divided into two:

first the cause, then the effect. Within the initial section on the cause, there are again two parts: first, explaining the conforming causes; second, explaining the opposing causes. The first text is further divided into two:

first, the direct answer; second, praising the sūtra. The direct answer consists of six parts: distinguishing between that which is a perfection (*pāramitā*) and that which is not. The first five are the *parīttanirvāṇa* (limited nirvāṇa).
The last of these, "discrimination," is precisely the judgment of the degrees [of practice].
Good son, what is giving that is not a pāramitā? When one sees a beggar and only then gives, this is called giving, but not a pāramitā.
If there is no beggar and one opens the heart to give spontaneously, this is then called dāna (generosity).
Regarding the pāramitās:
if one practices giving only from time to time, it is called "giving" but not a pāramitā; if one cultivates constant giving, it is then called dānapāramitā.
If, after giving to another, one subsequently gives rise to a mind of regret, this is called "giving," but not the *pāramitā* of giving.
Giving without regret is what is called the *dānapāramitā*.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva develops a sense of fourfold dread toward material wealth—fearing kings, thieves, water, and fire—they give with joy.
When one gives in this manner, it is called the *dānapāramitā*.
If one gives with the expectation of a reward, it is called giving, but not the *pāramitā* of giving; if one gives without expecting a reward, it is then called the *dānapāramitā*.
If one practices for the sake of fear, fame, profit, or offerings; for the continuity of family traditions; for the five desires of the heavens;
out of pride; out of arrogance toward others; for the sake of acquaintances; or for the sake of karmic retribution—this is like the practice of bartering in a marketplace.
Noble son, it is as if a person plants a tree for the sake of obtaining shade, flowers, fruit, and timber; if a person practices cultivation in such a manner, [it is likewise].
Giving such as this is called "giving," but it is not a *pāramitā*.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices this Great *Nirvāṇa*, they do not perceive a giver, a recipient, or material wealth; they do not perceive time or season;
they do not perceive fields of merit or non-fields of merit; they do not perceive causes, conditions, or karmic retribution; and they do not perceive an agent.
The recipient does not perceive much or little, purity or impurity; they do not disparage the giver’s own body or wealth.
They do not perceive a seer nor a non-seer; they make no calculation of self or other.
They practice giving solely for the sake of the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Vaipulya, which is eternally abiding, and for the benefit of all sentient beings.
They practice giving for the sake of severing the afflictions of all sentient beings;
they practice giving so that all sentient beings may not perceive a recipient, a giver, or material wealth. Good son, it is like a person who has fallen into the great ocean;
by clinging to a corpse, they are able to cross over and be liberated. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the Great...
When practicing giving for the sake of *nirvāṇa*, it is also like this, just as that corpse [was].
Son of good family, it is as if there were a person imprisoned in a deep dungeon with doors and gates firmly secured, who escapes through a latrine hole and reaches an unobstructed place;
when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices giving while cultivating the Great *Nirvāṇa*, it is also like this, son of good family.
Son, it is like a person of high status who, in the midst of terror and urgent distress, having no other support or reliance, takes refuge in a *caṇḍāla*.
It is the same when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the path of the Great Nirvāṇa and performs acts of giving.

Good son, it is like a sick person who, in order to eliminate the suffering of illness and obtain peace and happiness, consumes impure substances; so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the Great [Nirvāṇa].
The practice of giving within *nirvāṇa* is also like this, son of good family.

Just as a Brahmin, encountering a time when grain has become exceedingly expensive, might eat dog meat for the sake of his life, so too is the practice of giving by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivating the Great *Nirvāṇa*.
Son of good family, such matters within the Great *Nirvāṇa* arise from the immeasurable.
Having not heard them for kalpas, one now hears of śīla and the śīlapāramitā, up to prajñā and the prajñāpāramitā,
as explained in detail in the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*.
If there are signs and attainment, it is not the meaning of "crossing over" (pāramitā); only when there are no signs and no attainment is it called "crossing over.
Within this, the first of the six perfections, dāna (generosity), is explained in detail, while the remaining five are all referred to as being in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
How is it that a bodhisattva hears what was not previously heard? Regarding the *Hantan jing* (Sutra on Praise), first the bodhisattvas are praised, and subsequently the three vehicles are praised.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing the Great Nirvāṇa, hear what was not previously heard? [He asks about] the twelve [links of dependent origination].
The meaning of these various sūtras is profound; though we have not heard it since time immemorial, through this present sūtra we now hear it in its entirety.
Although we previously heard them, we heard only the names; it is only now, through this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, that we finally hear their true meaning.
Regarding the statement in the opening text that "the meaning of the twelve scriptures is profound": formerly, the twelve divisions [of the canon] merely clarified emptiness;

compared to [this], birth-and-death was considered deep, yet not profound. This scripture clarifies that arising-arising is precisely non-arising, arising is precisely non-arising, and non-arising is precisely non-non-arising;
therefore, it is profound. It is also that existence is precisely non-existence, and...
"Emptiness and non-emptiness are neither emptiness nor non-emptiness; therefore, it is profound... [and so forth].
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have heard only the names of the twelve divisions of the scriptures but have not heard their meaning; now, in this sutra, they hear them in their entirety.
This is called "hearing what was not previously heard. Good son, for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, [this is] the scripture...

"In the past, I never heard that the Buddha possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity; that there is no ultimate extinction; that the Three Jewels and the Buddha-nature possess non-differentiated characteristics;
or that even those who have committed the four grave offenses, slandered the Vaipulya sutras, committed the five heinous crimes, or are icchantikas all possess Buddha-nature.
Now, having heard this in this sutra, it is called 'hearing what was not previously heard.'"

Chapter on the Virtuous King, Part Two.
Volume One: The Questions of King Śrīgarbha. Regarding the second section, "Clarifying the Violation of Causes," it is divided into three parts:

the questions and answers, the summary of understanding, and the treatment [of the views]. There are six questions directed at the Yecheng [Temple] school and five questions directed at the Kaishan [Temple] school;

these consist of only three underlying intentions: first, two questions concerning the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*); second, two questions concerning the icchantika; and third, one question concerning the indeterminate. The initial question concerns the four grave offenses.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāsa-vyūha-udgata-guṇa-rāja addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if those who have violated the grave prohibitions,
slandered the Vaipulya sutras, committed the five heinous crimes, or are icchantikas, all possess the Buddha-nature, how can it be that these individuals..."
World-Honored One, if those who fall into hell possess the Buddha-nature, why do you further say that there is no permanence, bliss, self, or purity?
If they possess the Buddha-nature, they should not fall into hell; if they do fall away, it is because the Buddha-nature does not sustain them. This is the second [point].
Question: If there is buddha-nature, why do you further say it is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure? If these four virtues do not exist, how can there be buddha-nature?

World-Honored One, if those who have severed their roots of goodness are called icchantikas, then at the time when they sever their roots of goodness, what of their buddha-nature? What does it become?
If the Buddha-nature is not severed, how can it be severed? If it were severed, why would you further speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
If it is not severed, for what reason is one called an icchantika?
The third question asks whether the icchantika, having severed their roots of goodness, should also sever the Buddha-nature; the fourth question asks why the Buddha-nature is not severed.
They are called icchantikas.

World-Honored One, those who commit the four grave prohibitions, those who slander the Vaipulya sutras as being indeterminate, those who commit the five heinous crimes, and the icchantikas—all these are termed "indeterminate.
If such individuals were fixed [in their nature], how could they ever attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi?
The attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, as well as the stages from *srotāpanna* up to *pratyekabuddha*, is also called "indefinite.
If the stages from *srotāpanna* up to *pratyekabuddha* were definite, then one would not be able to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
World-Honored One, if those who have committed the four grave offenses are indefinite, then [the same applies to] from *srotāpanna* up to... [pratyekabuddha].
Pratyekabuddhas are likewise not fixed; these various Buddhas and Tathāgatas are also not fixed.
If the Buddha is not fixed, the essence of his nirvāṇa is also not fixed; even reaching all dharmas is likewise not fixed. Why is it not fixed?
If an icchantika, by abandoning the state of an icchantika, then attains the Buddha-way, so too do the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
If one were to enter *nirvāṇa* in this manner and then subsequently emerge from it rather than remaining in *nirvāṇa*, then the nature of *nirvāṇa* would be unstable and indeterminate.
Since this would be the case, one should know that there is no permanence, bliss, self, or purity.
How then can it be said that those such as the icchantikas shall attain *nirvāṇa*?

The fifth question concerns the difficulty regarding the four grave offenses and the icchantikas being indeterminate: whether they will definitely return to produce bodhi and nirvana, or whether they will definitely return to become ordinary worldlings.
The text is slightly expanded here. If, after entering nirvana, one were to emerge again, then a sage would become an ordinary person once more.
If that were so, the Buddha would lack the four virtues; if it were not so, then even the icchantika would have no possibility of attaining buddhahood.
Regarding the previous objection that *nirvāṇa* must be impermanent, the Buddha replied that it is not impermanent. Herein, one raises the objection of "inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntika*):
if everything that is inconclusive were impermanent, then since *nirvāṇa* is also included within the limit of "everything," it too should be impermanent.
This objection challenges everyone, causing them all to turn back [from their position] (and so forth).

The Buddha’s response consists of two parts: first, he praises the question, and second, he answers the question. The initial praise of the question is fourfold; the first is the praise of his manifested virtues.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva King of Universal Radiance and Noble Virtue, saying: “Excellent, excellent!”
"Noble son, it is because you desire to benefit immeasurable sentient beings and bring them peace and happiness; out of compassion and loving-kindness for all the world;
and because you wish to increase and inspire those bodhisattvas who have resolved upon bodhicitta—that you have asked such a question."
Second, praising his past causes:
"Good son, you have already drawn near to immeasurable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past;
under those Buddhas, you have planted various roots of goodness and long ago accomplished the merits of Bodhi, subduing the hosts of Māras and causing them to retreat and disperse."
He has taught immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing them all to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
he has long since thoroughly mastered the profound and secret treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
and he has already inquired of past Buddhas, World-Honored Ones as numerous as the sands of immeasurable and boundless Ganges Rivers, regarding such profound and subtle mysteries.
A third time he praised the question, saying: "It transcends that of humans and devas.
I do not see anyone in all the world—whether among humans or devas, śramaṇas or brahmins, Māras or Brahmās—who is able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding this meaning."
The four admonitions and the permission to speak are as stated in the text.
Now, listen attentively, listen attentively with a sincere heart; I shall analyze and expound them for you.
Good son, the first part of the answer regarding the icchantika consists of three sections: the first answer, the fifth indefinite question, and the [subsequent] section.
The second response addresses the third question regarding the severance of the roots of goodness, while simultaneously answering the first and second questions concerning sinners;

the third response further answers the fifth question on the indeterminate, while also addressing the fourth question. Within the initial response to the fifth question, three points are first set forth.
"Good son, the icchantika is likewise not fixed.
Next, he answers:
"If it were fixed, an icchantika would ultimately never be able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Tīṣya: Because the three fetters are not fixed,
one is able to attain [liberation].
From "As you have said" onwards is the second part, the direct response to the third [question], which consists of three sections: first, concerning the internal and external;
second, concerning the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*); and third, concerning the permanent (*nitya*) and impermanent (*anitya*).
Regarding what you have said—that the Buddha-nature is uninterrupted—how can it be that an icchantika severs their roots of goodness?
Good son, there are two kinds of roots of goodness: first, internal; second, external. The Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external;
for this reason, the Buddha-nature is uninterrupted.
Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, those with outflows (*sāsrava*), and second, those without outflows (*anāsrava*). The Buddha-nature is neither with outflows nor without outflows;

therefore, it is not severed. Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, the permanent (*nitya*), and second, the impermanent (*anitya*). The Buddha-nature is neither permanent nor impermanent; therefore, [it is not severed].
It is not severed.
Because the Buddha-nature and the Middle Way are neither of these two extremes, they cannot be severed. The human and heavenly realms are good; the three miserable paths are evil.
Mundane phenomena are external; sacred phenomena are internal. The worldly is with outflows (*sāsrava*); the world-transcending is without outflows (*anāsrava*). The conditioned is...
Since the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and the impermanent are both the eternal Buddha-nature, and since [the nature] is entirely beyond these two extremes, it cannot be severed.
If it were subject to severance—this also answers the questions of the first and second types of offenders mentioned below.
If it were something that could be severed, then it should be possible to recover it; if it cannot be recovered, then it is called "unseverable. If it were severed, one would be called an icchantika.

Although such a person commits offenses, they ultimately do not sever their nature; this clarifies that offenses are not fixed. Because they are not fixed, one attains supreme enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
If one has already severed what was originally taken up, it is called the nature of an icchantika; since this has not yet been attained, how can it be severed?

Furthermore, if it does not exist as a fixed certainty, how can its falling away be prevented? In response to the first question: if it does not exist as a fixed certainty, the second question is also dispelled.
Moreover, it is only when something has been severed and then attained that it is termed an icchantika; since this nature has not yet been attained, the fourth question is also dispelled.
Regarding the third section following the four grave offenses, the answer to the fifth question is divided into three parts:

first, a general explanation of the indeterminate; second, a detailed explanation of the indeterminate; and third, a conclusion on the indeterminate. The first part further consists of four sections: first, explaining the indeterminacy of evil persons; second, explaining the indeterminacy of all phenomena;
third, explaining the indeterminacy of virtuous persons; and fourth, explaining the indeterminacy of the Tathāgata. This is as follows:
Evil persons are not fixed in their nature.

Those who have committed the four grave offenses are likewise not fixed; if they were fixed, those who have violated the four grave prohibitions would never be able to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Those who slander the Vaipulya sūtras are also not fixed; if they were fixed...
Those who slander those who uphold the True Dharma will ultimately never attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;

yet even for one who commits the five heinous crimes, [the result] is not fixed. If it were fixed, then a person who has committed the five heinous crimes would ultimately never be able to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Regarding "Form and the characteristics of form," the second section clarifies that all phenomena are not fixed. First, the explanation of the phenomena follows the text. Form and the characteristics of form—both are indeterminate.
This applies to the characteristics of odor, taste, and touch; the characteristics of arising and ceasing; up to the characteristics of ignorance, the aggregates, bases, and elements;
the twenty-five states of existence; the four modes of birth; and indeed all phenomena, which are likewise all indeterminate.
Next, in the section on analogies, there are three analogies and three applications as found in the text.
"Good son, it is like a magician who, in the midst of a great assembly, conjures by magic the four divisions of the army— chariots, infantry, elephants, and cavalry—
as well as various necklaces and ornaments for adorning the body, cities, towns, villages, mountains, forests, trees, springs, ponds, rivers, and wells."
Among that assembly were some children who lacked wisdom; when they saw this, they all took it to be real.
The wise people among them knew it was a deceptive illusion, for by the power of magic, it deluded the eyes of men.
Good son, it is likewise with all ordinary beings, up to and including śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who perceive fixed characteristics in all phenomena;
the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, however, do not perceive fixed characteristics in any phenomena.
Good son, it is like a small child who, during the midsummer months, sees a mirage and calls it water.
A person of wisdom, regarding this mirage, never gives rise to the thought that it is actual water;
they know it is merely a false mirage that deceives the eyes, and is not actually water.
All ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas likewise perceive all phenomena in this same way, asserting them all to be real;
however, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas do not perceive any fixed characteristics in any phenomena.
Good son, it is like a mountain ravine where an echo arises due to sound;

when a child hears it, he thinks it is a real sound, but a person of wisdom understands that it has no fixed reality, for there is only the appearance of sound that deceives the auditory consciousness.
Good son, it is likewise for all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas regarding all phenomena:
they perceive fixed characteristics. However, bodhisattvas and others understand that all phenomena are entirely without fixed characteristics;
they are characterized by impermanence, emptiness, quiescence, and so forth, and are without the characteristics of arising or ceasing. For this reason, bodhisattvas see all phenomena as impermanent.
Furthermore, son of good family, there is also a fixed characteristic. What is this fixed characteristic? It is permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Where do these reside?
They are said to be in nirvāṇa.
As for the statement that there is also a fixed characteristic—namely permanence, bliss, self, and purity—it is because the previous objection was not definitive.

If the Tathāgata, having entered [the state of non-determination], were also to emerge from it—becoming a sage and then an ordinary person—he would be impermanent and lacking bliss; however, the present answer is that this is not so.

Within the midst of non-determination, there is also the characteristic of determination, namely, that the Tathāgata is permanent, blissful, self, and pure; therefore, it is said that there is also the characteristic of determination.
Below the section on the *srotāpanna*, the third part clarifies that the virtuous person is not fixed.
Good son, the fruit of *srotāpanna* is likewise not fixed;
because it is not fixed, after eighty thousand *kalpas*, one attains the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* is likewise not fixed and not determined.
Because it is fixed, one attains the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after sixty thousand *kalpas*;
the fruit of *anāgāmin* is likewise not fixed, and because it is not fixed, one attains the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after forty thousand *kalpas*;
the fruit of *arhat* is likewise not fixed, and because it is not fixed, one attains [the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*] after twenty thousand *kalpas*.
Having attained the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the path of the *pratyekabuddha* is likewise not fixed;
because it is not determined, one attains the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after ten thousand *kalpas*.
The Tathāgata now, in the fourth section below, clarifies that the Tathāgata is not fixed. "Good son,
the Tathāgata is now manifesting between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara, reclining upon a lion’s couch,
desiring to enter parinirvāṇa, so as to cause all those disciples who have not yet attained the fruit of arhatship and..."
The Mallas were filled with great sorrow and suffering, and they caused the devas, asuras, gandharvas,
garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others to make extensive offerings, desiring to wrap the body in a thousand pieces of fine cloth,
place it in a coffin made of the seven precious gems filled with fragrant oil, pile up various kinds of fragrant wood, and cremate it with fire.
Except for two instances where it cannot be burned: first, that which is worn next to the body;

second, that which is on the very outermost layer for the sake of all sentient beings, so that the śarīra may be distributed into eight portions. All the śrāvaka disciples say that the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa;
you should know, however, that the Tathāgata does not necessarily enter nirvāṇa. Why is this? Because...
Because it comes and abides eternally without change, for this reason the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is likewise not fixed.
Within the path of skillful means, the Tathāgata is not fixed; the fundamental ground (*dharmakāya*) is fixed and is certainly not an ordinary thing—this is what is called "fixed.
Regarding the two ends that cannot be burned, there are two interpretations: first, the undergarment is used as a metaphor for the fundamental ground being situated on the outside.
The analogy of the footprints corresponds to these two [aspects]: the non-extinction of the two. The inner layer of clothing represents the Buddha’s wisdom observing capacities;
that which is outside represents the supernatural powers responding to phenomena. Since objects and capacities are inexhaustible, the supernatural powers are likewise never-ending.

Therefore, the fact that the inner garment is not burned does not mean it is not being responded to; rather, this garment is called the "intimate" garment because it is worn next to the body. Good son, you should know this.
In the second section below, "The Tathāgata," the various phrases of the "Indeterminate" (aniyata) are explained in detail.

The old commentaries treat these phrases as either "one exists and one perishes"—where "not a ghost" leads to the perishing of the *dharmakāya*, and "not not a ghost" leads to the existence of the *nirmāṇakāya*—or they interpret them differently.

Now, I maintain that the division between the *dharmakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* remains fixed definitions; how could they be indeterminate? Xinghuang says: "Not a ghost" refers to the *dharmakāya*; the "indeterminate *dharmakāya*" then...
To say "non-extinction" is not non-extinction, and "non-ghost" is the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is indeterminate. If the response-body is not existent, then it is not existent;

yet its existence is not [simply] existence. It can be a ghost and it can be a non-ghost; "non-extinction" is not extinction, and it can be a non-ghost and it can be a ghost. Now, we say that none of these avoid indeterminacy. Why?
Because if a ghost were determinately able to be a non-ghost, and a non-ghost were determinately able to be a ghost—then even if one says they are indeterminate, they are still called [determinate].
To establish the present point: that the ghost is neither a ghost nor not a ghost, and neither not a ghost nor not-not a ghost;

that the non-ghost is a ghost and also neither a ghost nor not a ghost, and that neither a ghost nor not a ghost is also a ghost and not a ghost—wherein one is three and three is one, and where oneness, threeness, and unity are indeterminate—this is true indeterminacy.

The meaning of the remaining phrases is likewise; now, first, I shall state the topical outline. Good son, you should know that the Tathāgata is also not fixed. The Tathāgata is not a deva. Why? Because there are four kinds of devas: first, worldly devas; second, devas by birth; third, pure devas; and fourth, devas of ultimate meaning. Worldly devas... [text continues]... Worldly devas refers to those who possess sovereign power over the world, such as Śakra, Brahmā, and the like. Devas by birth refers to those born into the heavens through the maturation of the fruits of their karma, such as the devas of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. Pure devas refers to those who have attained liberation from afflictions through the power of the path, such as the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas. Devas of ultimate meaning refers to those who have realized the ultimate truth, namely the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Why? Because they are the masters of all dharmas and have transcended all worlds. Therefore, the Tathāgata is not a deva. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he has abandoned the three types of existence, whereas devas are still bound by the three types of existence. Moreover, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he has severed the continuity of birth and death, whereas devas are still subject to the cycle of birth and death. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), whereas devas have not yet exhausted all outflows. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he has attained the ultimate fruit, whereas devas have not yet attained the ultimate fruit. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he has attained the supreme, unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, whereas devas have not yet attained the supreme, unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the teacher of gods and humans, whereas devas are themselves students. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the refuge for all beings, whereas devas are not the refuge for all beings. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the protector of all beings, whereas devas are not the protectors of all beings. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who bestows fearlessness upon all beings, whereas devas do not bestow fearlessness upon all beings. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain peace and happiness, whereas devas do not cause all beings to attain peace and happiness. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to transcend suffering, whereas devas do not cause all beings to transcend suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to enter the path to nirvāṇa, whereas devas do not cause all beings to enter the path to nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to dwell in the Dharma, whereas devas do not cause all beings to dwell in the Dharma. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to abide in the ultimate truth, whereas devas do not cause all beings to abide in the ultimate truth. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to realize the nature of reality, whereas devas do not cause all beings to realize the nature of reality. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the unconditioned, whereas devas have not yet attained the unconditioned. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the eternal, whereas devas have not yet attained the eternal. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain bliss, whereas devas have not yet attained bliss. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain selfhood, whereas devas have not yet attained selfhood. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain purity, whereas devas have not yet attained purity. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain liberation, whereas devas have not yet attained liberation. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain awakening, whereas devas have not yet attained awakening. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the Way, whereas devas have not yet attained the Way. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the fruit, whereas devas have not yet attained the fruit. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the ultimate goal, whereas devas have not yet attained the ultimate goal. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the finality, whereas devas have not yet attained the finality. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the end of suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the end of suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the cessation of suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the extinction of suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the extinction of suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the exhaustion of suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the exhaustion of suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the transcendence of suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the transcendence of suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the departure from suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the departure from suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the liberation from suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the liberation from suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the release from suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the release from suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the freedom from suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the freedom from suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the cessation of suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the end of suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the end of suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the ultimate end of suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the ultimate end of suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the finality of suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the finality of suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the exhaustion of suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the exhaustion of suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the transcendence of suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the transcendence of suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the departure from suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the departure from suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the liberation from suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the liberation from suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings to attain the release from suffering, whereas devas have not yet attained the release from suffering. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a deva because he is the one who causes all beings

Regarding the "Intermediate Devas" (antaradeva), these are like the various kings. Regarding the "Devas by Birth" (upapattideva), these range from the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (naivasamjñānāsamjñāyatana).
Regarding the "Pure Devas" (śuddhideva), these range from the Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to the Pratyekabuddha.

Regarding the "Devas of Meaning" (arthadeva), these are the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi). For what reason are the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes called "Devas of Meaning"? It is because they are able to skillfully... [text ends]
Because he understands the meaning of all dharmas, what is meant by "meaning"? It is seeing that the meaning of all dharmas is emptiness.
Good son, the Tathāgata is not a king, nor is he the gods of the Four Great Kings, up to and including the gods of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception;
from the Srotāpanna up to the Pratyekabuddha and the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes, for this reason, the Tathāgata is not a natural being among the various multitudes.
Birth also likewise refers to the Buddha as the God among Gods; therefore, the Tathāgata is not a god, nor is he a non-god;

he is not a human, nor is he a non-human; he is not a ghost, nor is he a non-ghost; he is not a denizen of hell, an animal, or a hungry ghost, nor is he a non-denizen of hell, an animal, or a hungry ghost;
he is not a sentient being, nor is he a non-sentient being; he is not a phenomenon (dharma), nor is he a non-phenomenon; he is not form, nor is he a non-form.
It is neither long nor non-long, neither short nor non-short, neither characteristic nor non-characteristic,
