neither mind nor non-mind, neither with outflows nor without outflows, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither illusion nor non-illusion,
neither name nor non-name, neither fixed nor non-fixed, neither existent nor non-existent, neither expressible nor non-expressible.
It is said that he is neither the Tathāgata nor not the Tathāgata; for this reason, the Tathāgata is indeterminate.
Next, twenty topical sections (dvāra) are explained, yet only sixteen are expounded while four sections remain unexplained.
"Good son, for what reason is the Tathāgata not called a 'worldly deva'? A worldly deva refers to various kings;
the Tathāgata has long since relinquished the royal throne throughout immeasurable kalpas, and is therefore neither a king nor a non-king.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata was born in the city of Kapilavastu into the household of King Śuddhodana, and is therefore neither a non-king nor one born as a celestial deva. The Tathāgata...
Because he has long since departed from all states of existence (*bhava*), he is neither one born in heaven nor one not born in heaven.
Why? Because he ascends to Tuṣita and descends to Jambudvīpa. Therefore, the Tathāgata is neither "not born in heaven" nor a "pure god.
Why? Because the Tathāgata is not a *srotāpanna*, nor even a *pratyekabuddha*. Therefore, the Tathāgata is not [any of these].
This Pure Heaven is not "not-non-pure. Why? Because it cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas, just as a lotus flower does not receive dust or water;
therefore, the Tathāgata is not "not-non-pure" heaven. Nor is he the "Meaning Heaven. Why?
Because the Tathāgata is not a bodhisattva of the ten stages; therefore, the Tathāgata is neither the Meaning Heaven nor "not [the Meaning Heaven]."

Why is it that the Tathāgata is not *Anartha-deva* (Non-Righteous God)? Because the Tathāgata constantly cultivates the meaning of the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*), for this reason the Tathāgata is not *Anartha-deva*.
Why is it that the Tathāgata is not a human? Because the Tathāgata has long been free from the state of being human throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Therefore, he is neither a non-human nor a non-non-human. Why? Because he was born in the city of Kapilavastu; for this reason, he is not a non-non-human.
The Tathāgata is not a ghost. Why? Because he does not harm any sentient beings; for this reason, he is neither a ghost nor a non-ghost.

He is not a ghost; why? Because he also manifests in the form of a ghost to transform sentient beings, therefore he is not "not a ghost. The Tathāgata is also not a denizen of hell, an animal, or a hungry ghost; why? Because the Tathāgata has long since abandoned all evil karma, therefore he is not a denizen of hell, an animal, or a hungry ghost. Yet he is also not "not a denizen of hell, an animal, or a hungry ghost. Why? Because he manifests in those forms to deliver those who are to be saved. Therefore, he is neither identical to nor different from them. This is called the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not a woman, why? Because he has forever transcended the characteristics of female form; therefore he is not a woman. Yet he is also not "not a woman," why? Because he manifests as a woman to transform women. Therefore, he is neither a woman nor not a woman. The Tathāgata is also not a man, why? Because he has forever transcended the characteristics of male form; therefore he is not a man. Yet he is also not "not a man," why? Because he manifests as a man to transform men. Therefore, he is neither a man nor not a man. The Tathāgata is also not a śrāvaka, why? Because he has forever transcended the stage of a śrāvaka; therefore he is not a śrāvaka. Yet he is also not "not a śrāvaka," why? Because he manifests as a śrāvaka to transform śrāvakas. Therefore, he is neither a śrāvaka nor not a śrāvaka. The Tathāgata is also not a pratyekabuddha, why? Because he has forever transcended the stage of a pratyekabuddha; therefore he is not a pratyekabuddha. Yet he is also not "not a pratyekabuddha," why? Because he manifests as a pratyekabuddha to transform pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, he is neither a pratyekabuddha nor not a pratyekabuddha. The Tathāgata is also not a bodhisattva, why? Because he has already attained the ultimate fruit; therefore he is not a bodhisattva. Yet he is also not "not a bodhisattva," why? Because he manifests as a bodhisattva to transform bodhisattvas. Therefore, he is neither a bodhisattva nor not a bodhisattva. The Tathāgata is also not a Buddha, why? Because he has forever transcended the characteristics of Buddhahood; therefore he is not a Buddha. Yet he is also not "not a Buddha," why? Because he manifests as a Buddha to transform sentient beings. Therefore, he is neither a Buddha nor not a Buddha. This is called the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not subject to birth, why? Because he has forever transcended the characteristics of birth; therefore he is not born. Yet he is also not "not born," why? Because he manifests birth to transform sentient beings. Therefore, he is neither born nor not born. The Tathāgata is also not subject to death, why? Because he has forever transcended the characteristics of death; therefore he does not die. Yet he is also not "not dying," why? Because he manifests death to transform sentient beings. Therefore, he is neither dying nor not dying. The Tathāgata is also not subject to aging, why? Because he has forever transcended the characteristics of aging; therefore he does not age. Yet he is also not "not aging," why? Because he manifests aging to transform sentient beings. Therefore, he is neither aging nor not aging. The Tathāgata is also not subject to sickness, why? Because he has forever transcended the characteristics of illness; therefore he is not ill. Yet he is also not "not ill," why? Because he manifests illness to transform sentient beings. Therefore, he is neither ill nor not ill. The Tathāgata is also not subject to dwelling, why? Because he has forever transcended the characteristics of dwelling; therefore he does not dwell. Yet he is also not "not dwelling," why? Because he manifests dwelling to transform sentient beings. Therefore, he is neither dwelling nor not dwelling. The Tathāgata is also not subject to movement, why? Because he has forever transcended the characteristics of movement; therefore he does not move. Yet he is also not "not moving," why? Because he manifests movement to transform sentient beings. Therefore, he is neither moving nor not moving. The Tathāgata is also not subject to cessation, why? Because he has forever transcended the characteristics of cessation; therefore he does not cease. Yet he is also not "not ceasing," why? Because he manifests cessation to transform sentient beings. Therefore, he is neither ceasing nor not ceasing. This is called the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not the same as the Dharma, why? Because the Dharma is unconditioned, while the Tathāgata is not unconditioned; therefore he is not the same as the Dharma. Yet he is also not different from the Dharma, why? Because the Tathāgata is the Dharma and the Dharma is the Tathāgata; therefore he is not different from the Dharma. This is called the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not the same as the Sangha, why? Because the Sangha is a conditioned phenomenon, while the Tathāgata is not conditioned; therefore he is not the same as the Sangha. Yet he is also not different from the Sangha, why? Because the Tathāgata is the Sangha and the Sangha is the Tathāgata; therefore he is not different from the Sangha. This is called the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not the same as the world, why? Because the world is a false and illusory phenomenon, while the Tathāgata is true and real; therefore he is not the same as the world. Yet he is also not different from the world, why? Because the Tathāgata is the world and the world is the Tathāgata; therefore he is not different from the world. This is called the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not the same as emptiness, why? Because emptiness is non-existent, while the Tathāgata is not non-existent; therefore he is not the same as emptiness. Yet he is also not different from emptiness, why? Because the Tathāgata is emptiness and emptiness is the Tathāgata; therefore he is not different from emptiness. This is called the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not the same as form, why? Because form is a conditioned phenomenon, while the Tathāgata is not conditioned; therefore he is not the same as form. Yet he is also not different from form, why? Because the Tathāgata is form and form is the Tathāgata; therefore he is not different from form. This is called the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not the same as sensation, perception, volition, or consciousness, why? Because these aggregates are conditioned phenomena, while the Tathāgata is not conditioned; therefore he is not the same as them. Yet he is also not different from them, why? Because the Tathāgata is these aggregates and these aggregates are the Tathāgata; therefore he is not different from them. This is called the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not the same as the eye, why? Because the eye is a conditioned phenomenon, while the Tathāgata is not conditioned; therefore he is not the same as the eye. Yet he is also not different from the eye, why? Because the Tathāgata is the eye and the eye is the Tathāgata; therefore he is not different from the eye. This is called the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not the same as the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, why? Because these faculties are conditioned phenomena, while the Tathāgata is not conditioned; therefore he is not the same as them. Yet he is also not different from them, why? Because the Tathāgata is these faculties and these faculties are the Tathāgata; therefore he is not different from them. This is called the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not the same as form, why? Because form is a conditioned phenomenon, while the Tathāgata is not conditioned; therefore he is not the same as form. Yet he is also not different from form, why? Because the Tathāgata
For this reason, the Tathāgata also manifests by assuming bodies within the three evil realms to transform sentient beings;
therefore, he is not non-hell-being, non-animal, and non-ghost.
Yet he is also not a sentient being, because he has long since abandoned the nature of a sentient being. Therefore, the Tathāgata is not [a sentient being].
Sentient beings are also not non-sentient beings. Why? Because at times he expounds the characteristics of sentient beings;
therefore, the Tathāgata is not non-sentient.
The Tathāgata is not the dharmas. Why? Because all dharmas each have their own distinct characteristics, whereas the Tathāgata is not like that. Only...
There is one characteristic; therefore, it is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Why? Because it is the Tathāgata’s *dharmadhātu*;
therefore, it is not non-dharma. The Tathāgata is not form (*rūpa*). Why? Because he is not subsumed within the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*); therefore, he is neither form nor [non-form].
It is not form. Why? Because the body possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
therefore, it is not non-form. The Tathāgata is not long. Why? Because he has severed all forms; therefore, he is neither long nor is he non-long.
For this reason, because no one in all the world is able to see the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on his crown, he is not "not long.
The Tathāgata is not short; why? Because he has long since abandoned the fetter of pride; therefore, he is not short. Nor is he "not not short"; why?
Because for the sake of the householder Ghoṣila, he manifested a body of three feet; therefore, he is not "not [short]."
Short. Regarding the ninth section on "the short and the non-short," it says: "He manifested a body three feet tall. He of Hexi said: "In his family there was no son;
a child was born measuring three feet in length and then died. His parents were so overcome by grief and suffering that they lost their sanity. The Buddha then manifested as the child."
It is like parents seeing their son return and regain his original mind; they say to him, "I said you were dead; from where have you come?

He replies, "I have come from the place of death. Because of the temporary meeting of causes and conditions, the body belongs to manifold conditions and is a provisional combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Upon universally observing these manifold conditions, he realizes that none of them are the self. Through various teachings on the Dharma, his deluded mind is immediately severed, and he then manifests the three [bodies].
When Śākyamuni Buddha’s radiance and physical marks appeared long, those who perceived them attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
Yet the Tathāgata is not a mark; why? Because he has long since distanced himself from all marks and characteristics.
Therefore, he is neither a mark nor a non-mark; why? Because he thoroughly understands all marks. Therefore, he is also not a non-non-mark.
The Tathāgata is not mind. Why? Because his nature is like empty space. Therefore, he is not mind; yet he is also not non-mind. Why?
Because he possesses the ten powers, which are mental factors, and because he is able to know the minds of other sentient beings. Therefore, he is not non-mind.
The Tathāgata is not conditioned; why? Because he is eternal, blissful, self, and pure. Therefore, he is also not unconditioned; why?
Because he manifests coming and going, sitting and reclining, and the entry into nirvāṇa. Therefore, he is not unconditioned.
The Tathāgata is not eternal. Why? Because his body has constituent parts; therefore, he is not eternal. How is it that he is not eternal?
Because he possesses cognition. An eternal dharma is without cognition, like empty space; the Tathāgata possesses cognition, and is therefore not eternal.
How is it that he is not eternal? Because he possesses speech. An eternal dharma is without speech, also like empty space; the Tathāgata possesses speech, and is therefore... [not eternal].
Therefore, because impermanence has a clan name, it is called the "Dharma of Impermanence with a Clan Name," which is termed "impermanent.
Because space is permanent, it has no clan name. The Tathāgata has a clan name—the clan name Gautama;
therefore, because impermanence has parents, it is called "impermanent. That which has no parents is termed "permanent"; because space is permanent, it has none.
The Buddha has parents; because he has parents, he is impermanent. That which possesses the four modes of deportment is called impermanent;
that which lacks the four modes of deportment is called permanent. Because space is permanent, it lacks the four modes of deportment. The Buddha possesses the four modes of deportment;
therefore, he is not permanent. A dharma that abides eternally has no location; because space is permanent, it has no location, just as [the Buddha].
He appears in the land of East India, dwelling in Śrāvastī or Rājagṛha; therefore, he is impermanent.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent. Why? Because birth has been eternally severed.
That which possesses the nature of birth is called impermanent, while that which is without birth is called permanent. Since the Tathāgata is without birth, he is [neither permanent nor impermanent].
That which is a permanent phenomenon is called "without lineage," whereas phenomena that possess a lineage are called "impermanent.
Because the Tathāgata is unborn and without lineage, he is eternally constant. This eternal dharma pervades all places, just as space exists everywhere;
likewise, the Tathāgata also pervades all places. Therefore, he is eternal. Regarding the dharma of impermanence, some say:
In this case, some might say that while [the world] exists here, the Tathāgata does not exist there; however, it is not so. One cannot say that he exists in one place and is absent in another.
Therefore, as for phenomena that are both permanent and impermanent, they sometimes exist and sometimes do not exist. The Tathāgata is not like this;
he is neither sometimes existent nor sometimes non-existent. Therefore, he is the eternally abiding phenomenon, which is without name and without form.
Because space is eternal, it is without name and without form; the Tathāgata is likewise without name and without form. Therefore, he is the eternal, ever-abiding Dharma.
Because space is eternal, it is without cause and without fruit; the Tathāgata is likewise without cause and without fruit.
Therefore, he is the eternal, ever-abiding Dharma. He is not encompassed by the three periods of time; the Tathāgata is likewise so.
Because it is not encompassed by the three periods of time, it is eternal.
The Tathāgata is not illusion; why? Because he has forever severed all deceptive minds.
Therefore, he is neither illusion nor non-illusion. Why? Because the Tathāgata may at times divide this single body into immeasurable bodies.
His body again becomes a single body that passes straight through mountains and walls without obstruction; he treads upon water as if on land and enters the earth as if it were water;
he travels through space as if on land; his body emits smoke and flames like a great mass of fire, and clouds and thunder shake with a terrifying sound.
He may become cities, villages, dwellings, mountains, rivers, and trees; or he may assume a massive body, or...
Because there are small bodies, male bodies, female bodies, and the bodies of boys and girls, the Tathāgata is likewise not non-illusory.
The Tathāgata is not fixed; why? Because the Tathāgata manifested entry into parinirvāṇa here between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara.
Therefore, he is neither fixed nor non-fixed. Why? Because he is eternal and blissful.
Because the self is pure, the Tathāgata is likewise neither non-fixed.
It is neither with-outflows (*sāsrava*) nor without-outflows (*anāsrava*). This is the twelfth chapter, yet it is placed at the very end. Why is this?
Because the Buddha wished to provide an extensive explanation of this chapter, he left it for last. Furthermore, among the various categories, if there were no outflows...

Because ordinary persons with outflows find it easy to understand when they hear this, there are two parts: first, clarifying that it is not "with outflows" (*sāsrava*), the text for which is extremely extensive;
second, clarifying that it is not "without outflows" (*anāsrava*), the text for which is very brief. This contrast between the extensive and the brief should also be evident.

Regarding the first section on its not being "with outflows," the text is divided into two: first, clarifying the three outflows (*traya āsravāḥ*); second, clarifying the seven outflows (*sapta āsravāḥ*).
The Tathāgata is not subject to outflows (*āsrava*). Why? Because he has severed the three outflows; therefore, he is not subject to outflows. As for the three outflows:

all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), are called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*); all afflictions of the form and formless realms, excluding ignorance, are called the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*);
and ignorance of the three realms is called the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). The Tathāgata has eternally severed these.
Therefore, they are not [themselves] outflows (*āsrava*).

Question: Why are the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms not taken as the three outflows, while form and formlessness are taken as the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), and ignorance is taken universally as the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*)?
Answer: The Buddha’s teaching is not fixed; he may transform the three outflows [into others].
Regarding the four floods (*ogha*), they are treated as three outflows (*āsrava*) because desire is so predominant that it is made into one category alone;
while form and formlessness are minor and thus combined into one. Ignorance is the root common to all, and thus is made into one.

While the school of enumeration calls these "falling into birth and death" (*saṃsāra-patana*), the school of treatises calls them "leaking away of principles" (*naya-prasravana*). According to the intent of this sutra, they are simply afflictions (*kleśa*).
These are called outflows (*āsrava*).
Furthermore, for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), [the text] next explains the seven outflows: first, view; second, reflection; third, the faculties;

fourth, evil; fifth, association; sixth, sensation; and seventh, mindfulness. Of these, the first two constitute the essence of the outflows, while the latter five are the conditions for the outflows.
"Viewing" refers to the sharp fetters (*tīkṣṇa-nīvaraṇa*); "thinking" refers to the dull fetters (*mṛdu-nīvaraṇa*). "Roots" refers to the five internal faculties;

"evil" refers to external unwholesome dharmas; "near" refers to evil persons; "receiving" refers to the appropriation of dharmas such as form and desire; "mindfulness" refers to the continuity of thought-moments throughout day and night without interruption.

In the present text, there is no mention of the outflows of thinking (*cintā-āsrava*) or the outflows of evil (*pāpa-āsrava*). Regarding the term "leaving-outflows" (*vairāgya-āsrava*): that which is able to leave them is the Path; that which is left behind is [the defilements].
Regarding the first interpretation of "evil": although the outflows of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*) should include all ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), only doubt and views are mentioned here.

This is intended to clarify that while the four proclivities of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride (*māna*) pertain to both the outflows of views and the outflows of thought (*vitarka*), when categorized within the gates of the truths of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), they are subsumed under pride.
Furthermore, the text is divided into two parts: first, a detailed explanation of the mind of doubt; second, a specific explanation of the proclivity of views.
Furthermore, all ordinary persons do not perceive outflows (*āsrava*). How is it that ordinary persons do not perceive outflows?
All ordinary persons harbor doubts regarding the future life: "In the future life, will I obtain a body, or will I not obtain a body?
In past lives, did this body fundamentally exist, or was it fundamentally non-existent? Regarding this body in the present life..."
Does this body exist, or does it not exist? If there were a self, would it be form, or non-form, or both form and non-form, or neither form nor non-form?
Would it be perception, or non-perception, or both perception and non-perception, or neither perception nor non-perception?
Does this body belong to another, or does it not belong to another, or both belong and not belong, or neither belong nor not belong?
Is there life without a body? Is there a body without life? Is there both body and life?
Is there neither body nor life? Are the body and life eternal? Are they non-eternal? Are they both eternal and non-eternal? Are they neither eternal nor non-eternal?
Are the body and life created by a self-existent lord (*īśvara*)? Are they created by time? Are they created without cause? Or are they created by primordial nature (*prakṛti*)?
Is it created by atoms? Is it created by dharma or adharma? Is it created by a person (*puruṣa*)? Is it created by afflictions (*kleśa*)?
Is it created by parents? Does the self abide in the mind? Does it abide in the eye? Does it pervade the body? From where does it come?
To where does it go? Who is born? Who dies? Was I a Brahmin by caste in the past? Or was I a Kṣatriya...?
"Am I of the Kṣatriya caste? Am I of the Vaiśya caste? Am I of the Śūdra caste? What caste shall I obtain in the future?
Regarding this body of mine, was it a male body in the past, or a female body, or the body of an animal?
If I take life, will there be sin, or will there be no sin? And so on, up to: if I drink alcohol, will there be sin?"
"Is there sin? Is there no sin? Did I create it myself? Was it created by another? Do I receive the retribution? Does the body receive the retribution?
Such views of doubt and immeasurable afflictions shroud the minds of sentient beings.
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is not itself a view (*dṛṣṭi*), but because it is closely associated with views, it is referred to as "doubt-view.
Regarding the arising of the six types of mind, this enumerates all the various views.
Due to these doubt-views, six types of mind arise: the certainty that there is a self, the certainty that there is no self, the view of a self, and the view of a self within a self.
To perceive non-self as self, or to perceive self as self—thinking "I act" and "I receive"—and to claim "I know," is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The Tathāgata has forever uprooted such infinite roots of the outflows of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*); therefore, it is not an outflow.
Son of good family, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who practices the noble path toward Great Nirvāṇa likewise attains the permanent severance of all such outflows. Thus do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas...
Because one constantly cultivates noble conduct throughout one's life, it is therefore "without outflows" (anāsrava).
Regarding the "adornment" (vyūha), it is simply the five views expanded by adding the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, hence they are called six.

Master Kai-shan says that "deciding there is a self" and "deciding there is no self" do not yet constitute the number six; rather, these are merely general declarations of decisiveness derived from the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
The six [views] immediately following "I" are: (1) seeing a self in what is not-self; (2) seeing non-self in what is not-self;

(3) seeing a self in what is non-self; (4) the notion that "I act"; (5) the notion that "I experience"; and (6) the notion that "I know. Regarding these six: first, because one calculates a true self within a conventional self, it is called "seeing a self in what is not-self.
Second, because one calculates the absence of such a self upon a conventional self, it is called... [the view of non-self].
The view of selflessness (*anātman-dṛṣṭi*) is threefold; because one falsely imagines a true self within the aggregates (*skandha*), it is called the view of selflessness.

Regarding the "view of self" (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and "the self as agent" (*ātmakāraka*), these three types below constitute three of the sixteen speculative views (*ṣoḍaśa-saṃjñā-dṛṣṭi*). According to the Hexi [commentary], existence and non-existence are determined as the two [extremes].
As for the "view of self," one originally conceives of a self; when entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one perceives wondrous light, as if...
For example, the sun and moon are used as metaphors for those who, based on what they have witnessed and realized, are certain that a self exists, and thus say, "I see the self.
Those who say, "I see no-self," calculate that there is a self in the present but no-self in the past and future; this is the view of annihilationism held by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Those who hold the view of no-self and yet claim to see a self say that all sentient beings are entirely without a self, and perceive a self existing separately outside the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), like sesame or wheat.
To claim that "I am the agent" and "I am the experiencer," asserting that these exist eternally from beginning to end, is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
This refers to the notions: "I am the cause of action," "I am the experiencer of the fruit," and "I am the knower.

Furthermore, regarding the inability of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to properly restrain the three faculties of the lower [realms] and the outflows (*āsrava*), there are three further points: first, to clarify the cause of being an ordinary being; second, to clarify the result of being an ordinary being; and third, to clarify the means for transcending the state of an ordinary being. First, to clarify the cause of being an ordinary being: [text continues].
The arising of outflows from the faculties is explained in two ways; it is clarified that Bodhisattvas are not like this, whereas the Tathāgata is free from outflows regarding the three fetters.
Good son, if ordinary people cannot properly restrain the five faculties, they will have the three outflows and be led by evil to unwholesome places.
Good son, it is like a wicked horse whose nature is fierce and unruly; it can cause its rider to reach a place of peril.
It is likewise for one who cannot properly restrain these five faculties: such a person causes oneself to depart from the wholesome path to *nirvāṇa* and reach various evil destinations.
Just as when a person mounts a wild elephant whose mind is not yet tamed, it does not go according to their will, but departs from cities and towns to reach desolate wildernesses;
so too is it for one who cannot properly restrain these five faculties.
In this way, they lead people away from the city of Nirvāṇa and into the wilderness of saṃsāra.

Noble son, it is just as a sycophantic minister teaches a king to commit evil; the sycophantic ministers of the five sense-faculties are likewise always teaching sentient beings to create immeasurable evils.
Noble son, it is just as a wicked child does not accept the instructions of teachers, elders, or parents.

Thus, there is no evil that they do not commit; their five faculties are likewise undisciplined. They do not accept the kind words, instructions, or admonitions of their teachers, and there is no evil they will not do.

Good son, ordinary worldlings who do not restrain their five faculties are constantly harmed and plundered by the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts, just as enemies and thieves harm and plunder virtuous people. Good son, ordinary...

Now, when a person does not restrain the five sense-faculties and rushes toward the five objects of desire, it is like a cowherd who fails to guard his cattle and allows them to trespass upon another's crops.
In this way, ordinary persons who do not restrain their five sense-faculties constantly dwell within the realms of existence and undergo much suffering and affliction.
The passage regarding ordinary persons is as previously explained.

Regarding the two lower sections concerning bodhisattvas: although they do not give rise to outflows (āsrava) due to their faculties, noble son, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the holy conduct of the Great Parinirvāṇa, they are always able to skillfully discipline themselves.
Guarding and restraining the five sense-faculties means fearing greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and envy, for the sake of attaining all wholesome dharmas.
Good son, if one can skillfully guard these five sense-faculties, one can then collect the mind;
if one can collect the mind, one then guards the five sense-faculties. It is like a person who, by protecting a king, protects the kingdom. Guarding...
Just as a country is protected by its king, so too it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: if he hears this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, he attains wisdom;
because he attains wisdom, he attains focused mindfulness regarding the five faculties, and if his mindfulness is scattered, he is able to bring it to rest.
Why is this? Because it is mindfulness and wisdom. Good son, it is like a skilled herdsman who, having set out his oxen...
Just as one who sees others devouring their crops will immediately stop them and prevent such plunder, so too is it with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva:
by reason of mindfulness and wisdom, they guard and restrain the five sense faculties so that they do not wander or scatter.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who possesses mindfulness and wisdom perceives neither the mark of a self nor the mark of "mine," and perceives neither sentient beings nor what belongs to them.

In their experience, they see that all phenomena are identical in their arising from the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), appearing as mere forms of earth, stone, tiles, and rubble—just as a house arises from a multitude of conditions and possesses no fixed nature.
Seeing that all sentient beings are composed of the four great elements and the five aggregates, they infer that these too lack a fixed nature;
because they lack a fixed nature, the Bodhisattva does not give rise to any craving or attachment toward them at all.
Because ordinary beings perceive the existence of sentient beings, they give rise to afflictions;
however, because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas cultivate the Mahāparinirvāṇa and possess mindfulness and wisdom, they do not give rise to greedy attachment toward sentient beings.

Furthermore, those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who cultivate the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra do not cling to the marks of sentient beings, but rather produce various marks of dharmas. Good son, it is like a painting...
The master uses various colored pigments to paint many images—whether male or female, oxen or horses.

When ordinary people who lack knowledge see them, they give rise to perceptions of male, female, and so forth. Yet the painter clearly knows that there are no such males or females. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this:
regarding the diverse characteristics of phenomena, he contemplates their single characteristic and ultimately never gives rise to the notion of a "sentient being."
What is the characteristic of this? It is because they possess mindfulness and wisdom.

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the Mahāparinirvāṇa, even if he occasionally beholds a beautiful woman, he never gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment. Why is this? Because he skillfully observes the characteristics [of phenomena].
Good son, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that the dharmas of the five desires contain no joy and cannot be obtained even for a moment.
It is like a dog gnawing on a dry bone; like a person carrying a torch walking against the wind;
like charcoal, a venomous snake, or fruit from a roadside tree obtained in a dream and cast away by many people; like a piece of meat pursued by competing birds;
like bubbles on water or the tracks of writing upon water; like the end of a woven thread; and like a prisoner heading to the marketplace—their strength is merely borrowed and cannot endure.
Having long observed that desire possesses such manifold faults and evils, furthermore, the Bodhisattva contemplates all sentient beings:

for the sake of the causes and conditions of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, they have constantly undergone suffering and affliction from time immemorial throughout countless and immeasurable kalpas.
Within a single kalpa, the bones accumulated by each and every sentient being would equal Mount Vipula in Rājagṛha; the milk they have drunk...
The milk produced by all women is like the waters of the four oceans; the blood shed from their bodies is even more than that.
The tears shed by parents, brothers, wives, children, and kinsmen when they weep at the death of a relative exceed the waters of the four great oceans.

If one were to take all the grasses and trees on the earth, cut them into inch-long tally-sticks, and count one stick for every instance of parental grief throughout immeasurable kalpas—even including time spent in the realms of hell and animals—the tally would never reach the end.
The suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) experienced by hungry ghosts is beyond measure;
even if this great earth were rolled up like dates, it would be easy to reach its end, yet the immeasurable cycle of birth and death can never be exhausted.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas contemplate all sentient beings in this way, they see that because of the causes and conditions of desire, they undergo immeasurable suffering. It is because of this suffering of conditioned existence within birth and death that Bodhisattvas [arouse great compassion].
Son of good family, one who does not lose mindfulness and wisdom is like this:

suppose there were a great multitude of people filling twenty-five *li* of the world, and a king commanded an official to carry a bowl of oil through their midst without spilling a drop; he was told that if even a single drop were lost, his life would be taken.
Furthermore, the king sent another man following behind him with a drawn sword to terrify him. Having received the king’s command, the official...

Exerting his utmost heart and maintaining firm resolve throughout that assembly of great beings, although he saw various agreeable objects of the fivefold perverse desires, his mind constantly thought:
"If I were to become negligent and become attached to those perverse desires, I would abandon what I hold; my life would not be fully sustained.
Because of this cause of fear, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva did not spill even a single drop of oil.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: within the cycle of birth and death, he does not lose mindfulness or wisdom. Because he does not discharge [the arrow], although he sees the five desires, his mind does not become attached to them.
If he sees pure forms, he does not give rise to the perception of form, but contemplates only the characteristic of suffering;

this applies likewise up to the characteristic of consciousness. He does not create the perception of arising, nor the perception of cessation, nor the perception of causes, but contemplates their conjunction.
When a Bodhisattva’s five faculties are thus purified, they fulfill the precepts for guarding the faculties.

All ordinary persons have impure faculties and cannot maintain them well; this is called "leakage of the faculties. The Bodhisattva has forever severed this, and is therefore without leakage (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), there are two interpretations: first, that it refers specifically to the *saṃskāra-duḥkha* among the three types of suffering, as this suffering is the most pervasive;

second, that "conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra*) means impermanence and suffering, yet it cannot be said that the retribution alone constitutes [the entirety]. The twenty-five *li* (miles) are a metaphor for the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
The bowl is a metaphor for form and mind (*nāmarūpa*). The oil is a metaphor for the precepts (*śīla*). Not discarding even a single drop is a metaphor for not [violating them].
Violating even one precept is like a king; the ministers are like the practitioner. The drawn sword held behind represents impermanence.
The Tathāgata has pulled out the third lower fetter; this refers to the Tathāgata’s state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
The Tathāgata has pulled them out and severed their root forever; therefore, they are not outflows (*āsrava*).

Furthermore, there is a fourth explanation regarding the separation from outflows: [the term] "evil outflows" refers to the essence of evil itself, while "separation" is named from the perspective of the path of remedy.

This is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying the path that effects the separation; second, clarifying the evil that is separated. The first part is further divided into two, beginning with...
The Bodhisattva’s practice subsequently cites the past to verify the present.
Furthermore, son of good family, there is another way for a Bodhisattva who has abandoned outflows (*āsrava*) to abandon evil outflows for the sake of the unsurpassed nectar of the Buddha-realm.
How does one abandon them? If one can practice, copy, receive, and uphold the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, this is how one abandons them.
To read, recite, explain, and contemplate its meaning is called "detachment. Why is this?
Good son, among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, I do not see any that can bring about detachment from evil outflows (*āsrava*) as effectively as this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Good son, it is like a brilliant teacher instructing his disciples; among those disciples, there are some who receive the teaching and whose minds do not engage in [unwholesome] actions.
It is the same for an evil bodhisattva who cultivates this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra: his mind does not produce evil.
Good son, it is like a skillful incantation in the world; if one hears it even once, for twenty years thereafter they will not be struck by any poison, nor can snakes bite them.
For those who recite it, there shall be no [harm] until the end of their lives.
O sons of good family, the Great Nirvāṇa is likewise: if there are sentient beings who hear it but once, they shall not fall into the evil realms for seven kalpas thereafter;
if they copy it, read and recite it, explain it, or contemplate its meaning, they will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and clearly perceive the Buddha-nature, just like that holy king.
"O son of good family who has attained the taste of the Deathless, this Great Nirvāṇa possesses such immeasurable merits as these.
Son of good family, if there be anyone who can copy this sutra, read it, recite it, explain it, expound it for others, and contemplate its meaning,
you should know that this person is truly my disciple, one who has well received my teaching, and is seen by me as my own."
Regarding those people who think, "I truly know that he does not enter parinirvāṇa," wherever such people may dwell—
whether in cities, towns, villages, mountain forests, wildernesses, houses, fields, residences, towers, or palaces— I likewise abide there permanently and do not move.
Toward these people, I constantly manifest as a recipient of offerings, appearing either as a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, or an upāsaka.
Sai, regarding these upāsikās, brahmins, śramaṇas, the poor, and beggars—
how may such people come to know that the Tathāgata accepts their offerings? Good son, such people may, while sleeping at night, see the image of a Buddha in a dream,
or see the images of various devas, śramaṇas, sovereign kings, noble monarchs, lion kings, or lotuses.
If one sees images such as the udumbara flower, or a great mountain, or the vast ocean,
or the sun and moon, or white elephants and white horses, or sees one's parents, or obtains flowers, fruits, or treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal,
or the five products of the cow— at that time, one should know that the Tathāgata has accepted their offering; this occurs upon awakening.
With joy and ease, they find all manner of necessary things; their minds do not dwell on evil, and they delight in cultivating wholesome dharmas.
Good son, this Great Nirvāṇa is fully capable of accomplishing such immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, inconceivable, and boundless merits.
Good son, you should now believe and accept my words. If there is a good son...
O son of good family, if you wish to see me, wish to revere me, wish to see me as identical to the *dharmatā*,
wish to attain the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), wish to see the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), wish to practice the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and the *Siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*,
and wish to shatter the eight māras— the eight māras being namely: impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity— [you should do so].

Those who have attained the bliss of humans and devas, upon seeing one who upholds the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra—whether by copying it, reciting it, explaining it to others, or contemplating its meaning—should approach, attend upon, seek instruction from, provide for, honor, revere, respect, and praise them;
they should wash their hands and feet, prepare beds and mats, and provide the four requisites so that they lack for nothing. If...
One should come from afar for ten *yojanas* to welcome [the teacher] in person for the sake of this sutra; whatever precious things one possesses should be offered as tribute.
If one has nothing, one should sell one's own body. Why? Because this sutra is difficult to encounter, even more so than the *udumbara* flower.

The initial passage contains five types of Dharma-preachers. Regarding the statement that "if [the teaching] passes through one's ears once, one shall not fall for seven kalpas," the preceding *Names and Merits* chapter states:
"If one hears even two characters of 'eternal abiding,' one shall not fall in every birth.
There are many ways of hearing: if one can contemplate deeply and practice according to the teaching, then one shall not fall in every birth; if one cannot...

For one who practices deep reflection and mental stillness, only slight benefit is obtained. Regarding the "eight māras," the old translation states that there are four, such as impermanence (*anitya*), each having its own cause;

these constitute the eight māras. Alternatively, another interpretation holds that the four beginning with afflictions (*kleśa*) and the four beginning with impermanence together constitute the eight.
"Good son, I recall the past. (This marks the second section, citing the past to corroborate the present.
"Good son, I recall that in the past, immeasurable, boundless, nayuta-kalpas ago, there was a world named Sahā.
In that world, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and Vidyācaraṇasampanna."
When the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfectly Complete One, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One,
was proclaiming this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the great assembly,
I heard from a virtuous friend that the Buddha was about to preach the Mahāparinirvāṇa to the multitude. Upon hearing this, my heart was filled with joy.
Desiring to make an offering, he found himself living in poverty with nothing to give. He traveled about selling his own body, but due to his meager merit, no one would buy it;
thus, he was about to return home when he saw a man on the road and spoke to him, saying, "I wish to sell my body; will you buy it?
The man replied, "The work performed at my house is such that no one else is capable of doing it. If you can perform it for me, I shall buy you. He then asked:
There was a man who could not endure his labor, and he replied, "I have a grievous illness;
a skilled physician has prescribed that I must take three *liang* of human flesh daily. If you can provide me with three *liang* of your own body's flesh every day, I shall give you five gold coins.
When I heard this, my heart was filled with great joy, and I immediately spoke again, saying:
"Give me money; I shall employ you for seven days, and once my business is finished, you may return to me. That man replied, "Seven days is too long;
if you can truly do it in one day, I will grant you permission. "Noble son," he said, "at that time I immediately took the money and returned to where the Buddha was.
I prostrated myself at his feet with my head and face touching them, and offered him everything I possessed. Thus he spoke.
Later, with a sincere heart, I listened to and received this sutra; though I was dull-witted at that time, having heard the sutra, I was only able to uphold the words and phrases of a single verse:
"The Tathāgata has realized nirvāṇa / And forever severed the cycle of birth and death / If there be one who listens with a sincere heart..."
"May I always obtain immeasurable pleasant sensations.
Having recited this verse, he immediately returned to the house of that sick man.

"Good son, although I gave him two or three pieces of meat every day, because of the causal conditions of recollecting this verse, he did not feel any pain; day after day, his condition was not neglected and he remained sufficient."
After one full month, son of good family, by these causes and conditions my illness was cured and my body was restored to health, free from all sores and wounds.
At that time, seeing my body complete and whole, I immediately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If even the power of a single verse can bring about such a result, how much more so when one fully receives, maintains, reads, and recites it? This is what I have witnessed.
This sutra possesses such benefits that one should further redouble their resolve and aspiration to attain the path of Buddhahood in the future, bearing the name Śākyamuni.
Son of good family, by the power of the causal conditions of this single verse, I am today, amidst this great assembly, fully proclaiming it for the sake of all devas and humans.
Son of good family, by these causal conditions, this is the Great Nirvāṇa.
The *pāṇa* is inconceivable and accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merit; it is the profound and secret treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
For this reason, those who are able to receive and uphold it sever and abandon evil outflows (*āsrava*).
Regarding this, there is a verse. The traditional commentary explains that the first half clarifies the fruit (*phala*) and the second half distinguishes the cause (*hetu*).

Realizing *nirvāṇa* is the fruit; listening with a sincere mind is the cause. Within these two matters—attainment (*prāpti*) and detachment (*visamyoga*)—realizing *nirvāṇa* is attainment, while eternal severance is detachment.
The cause also has two aspects: a sincere mind is the practice, and immeasurable bliss is the attainment of the fruit. This is what is meant by "attainment."
Regarding the "fruit of pleasure," it is not a fruit of eternal pleasure; rather, it is the fruit of pleasure within the cause obtained through the cause of practice.
Someone has critiqued this, saying: "This is far too narrow and restricted, being utterly devoid of reason. If there were only this matter, how could one sell one's own body?
Furthermore, how could one hear this and thereby attain Buddhahood? Master Guan said: "The meaning of the verse is immeasurable and cannot be grasped."
The scope of what is encompassed here is exceedingly vast and its profound meaning inexhaustible; for now, ten topics will be presented: first, the Three Jewels; second, the Four Noble Truths;
third, the three virtues; fourth, the four virtues; fifth, the fourfold tetralemma of arising and non-arising; sixth, the verse on "originally existing but now absent";
seventh, the verse on the Snowy Mountains; eighth, the intent of the four *siddhāntas*; ninth, the fourteen types of Buddha-nature as found in the verses of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
Regarding the statement that the verse contains the Three Jewels: the phrase "only the Tathāgata realizes nirvāṇa" constitutes the two jewels of the Buddha and the Dharma.
The person who is able to realize it is the Tathāgata, which is the Buddha Jewel; the dharma that is realized is nirvāṇa, which is called the Dharma Jewel.
The phrase "permanently severed" is merely auxiliary language. If one can [practice] with a sincere heart, this is it.
The Sangha Jewel being able to listen with a sincere heart is precisely the assembly that upholds and practices [the Dharma]; how could this not be the Sangha Jewel?
Furthermore, this single phrase yields two perspectives: "sincere heart" is also the Dharma Jewel, and "at the appointed time" is where one listens to the Dharma.
For now, it belongs to the Sangha, whereby one obtains immeasurable joy; this is also an auxiliary phrase for clarifying the Three Jewels. It is simply this.
Setting aside the two phrases for a moment, regarding the statement that the four truths do not take the meaning of "truths" (satya) but rather take the meaning of "practice and realization":
one who realizes this Dharma is a Buddha who has realized *nirvāṇa*, which is precisely the realization of cessation (*nirodha*). How is this known?

Since *nirvāṇa* is the antonym of "extinction" (*kṣaya*), is it not the truth of cessation? To eternally sever birth and death is precisely to eliminate the origin (*samudaya*). The origin consists of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and...
Karmic formations and present birth-and-death are likewise afflictions and karmic formations. If one can listen with a sincere heart, this is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Because one listens with a sincere heart, one realizes the Path and constantly attains immeasurable bliss; this is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Why is this?
Once the fruit of suffering has been dispelled, one immediately obtains the retribution of bliss. The threefold virtue is precisely the *māra*... [text fragment].

The three eyes of Śiva are also the three dots of the syllable *I*. The Tathāgata’s realization of the Dharma-body of *nirvāṇa* is the virtue of eternally severing birth and death, which is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*).
Listening with a sincere mind is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*). These must each be explained individually.
In the "Chapter on the Four Reliances," these three virtues are clarified as: first, the Dharma-body; second, liberation; and third, wisdom.
If, in the "Chapter on the Four Characteristics," it were not as stated—that there are three: first, *nirvāṇa*; second, liberation;
and third, *prajñā*—then one would be taking *nirvāṇa* as a substitute for the *dharmakāya*. Now, since it is said here that "it is *nirvāṇa*," how could this not be the *dharmakāya*?
That which eternally cuts off birth and death is liberation. If there were birth and death, there would be bondage and no release; now, since [birth and death] have been cut off...

To eliminate [afflictions] is itself to be free from entanglement; how could this not be liberation? To listen with a sincere mind is itself Prajñā (wisdom), for it is through hearing the Dharma that one is able to generate wisdom.

Once wisdom has been generated, how could this not be Prajñā? One who does not listen with a sincere mind may fail to generate it, but now that you listen with a sincere mind, you are able to generate wisdom and further attain the joy of the Dharma to delight yourself. Is this not so?
Furthermore, regarding the worldly happiness described as the "four virtues," these are permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*).
When the Tathāgata realizes *nirvāṇa*, this is the virtue of permanence. One may ask: is it the Tathāgata who is permanent, or is *nirvāṇa* that is permanent?

Here, it is clarified that both person and dharma are permanent; therefore, the preceding text states: "Because the dharma is permanent, the person is also permanent. The eternal severance [of afflictions] constitutes the virtue of purity.
Death is loathsome and filled with impurity; once impurity is removed, one attains purity. Is this not the virtue of purity?
To listen with a sincere mind is itself the virtue of the self; for if there were no self, who would listen? Thus one constantly attains immeasurable bliss—this is the virtue of bliss.
It is also said that this further clarifies the fourfold negation regarding the permanence of the self: arising, non-arising, and so forth.
This has already been explained in detail and fully resolved above; it need not be further expounded here (etc.). Regarding the verse concerning "that which originally existed but now does not":
when the Tathāgata realizes *nirvāṇa*, this is "originally non-existent but now existent"; prior to realizing *nirvāṇa*, it is "originally non-existent";
now that realization is complete, it is "now existent"; and the permanent severance of birth and death is "originally existent but now non-existent. As for...

When one has not yet severed birth and death, because afflictions exist, this is the meaning of "inherently possessed" (*mūla-vidyamāna*). Once the *dharmakāya* is realized, afflictions no longer exist;
how could it be that the two phrases "now they do not exist" (*idānīṃ na santi*) are not inseparable?

It is precisely because these three periods [of time] cannot possibly exist [as such] that the statement "it is impossible for there to be dharmas existing throughout the three periods" must be taken as a single, unified whole. Why would it be otherwise?
Is this the dharma of the three periods of time? To realize this dharma as the eternal fruit of *nirvāṇa*—that is simply impossible.

Regarding the verses from the *Himavat*, the phrasing is somewhat disordered and must be carefully distinguished; the first half does not correspond to the meaning of the present text, so one should take only the second half, yet even that is incomplete.

It should now be [restated] as four lines, and it should indeed be as follows: [Verse: The Buddhas of the past have all entered *parinirvāṇa*; The Buddhas of the future will likewise enter *parinirvāṇa*; The Buddhas of the present also enter *parinirvāṇa*; Yet, the nature of *nirvāṇa* is eternally abiding. This is what should be used here.
The two lines "when birth and death have ceased" mean that one has eternally severed the cycle of birth and death; "nirvāṇa is bliss" means that one eternally attains immeasurable bliss.
When these two verses are compared with one another, each lacks what the other possesses:
this verse lacks the line "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, they are dharmas of birth and death," while that verse lacks the line "the Tathāgata realizes nirvāṇa."
If one can listen with a sincere mind, it should also accord with the four *siddhāntas*. That the Tathāgata realizes *nirvāṇa* is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Sometimes *nirvāṇa* is explained as the ultimate truth because it eternally severs birth and death; this is the discourse on the therapeutic remedy (*pratipakṣa*). It is said therein:

"One treats the three outflows (*āsrava*) by means of the three contemplations. Since we are now precisely severing birth and death, is this not indeed the therapeutic remedy? If one can [listen] with a sincere...
Listening with the mind is itself the world. Within this world, some say there is a self (*ātman*) and some say there is no self;
one should receive these teachings on self and non-self with a sincere heart, thereby constantly attaining immeasurable bliss.

Thus, within each of the *pudgalavāda* (discourses for individuals), a single dharma is divided into two types of explanation: that which is taught as the "proponent of self" (*ātmavādin*) and that which is taught as "non-self."

Those who calculate that there is no self actually speak of attachment to a self; those who speak of suffering while attached to pleasure, or speak of pleasure while clinging to suffering—now, for the purpose of eliminating those who calculate that all is impermanent and suffering, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* clarifies the dharmas of permanence and bliss. The verse states:

"Phenomena produced through causes and conditions are precisely the Nirvāṇa realized by the Tathāgata. Nirvāṇa is merely a dharma produced through causes and conditions; if it were not produced through causes and conditions, [it would not be Nirvāṇa].

The meaning that conditions (*pratyaya*) constitute nature (*svabhāva*), which I declare to be emptiness (*śūnyatā*), is the eternal severance of birth and death; because birth and death are severed, one attains this emptiness.
That which is also called "provisional designation" (*prajñapti*) refers to listening with a sincere mind; for it is only through a provisional self that one can listen and receive [the teaching].
This is also the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*); it is the constant attainment of immeasurable bliss. The Middle Way is...
This is neither existence nor non-existence, and it is neither impermanence nor permanence; when these are unified, they constitute permanence.
There is no suffering and no pleasure, which, when unified, constitutes great bliss. This present permanence and bliss is precisely the permanence and bliss of the Middle Way.

Regarding the four kinds of Buddha-nature, excluding the nature of the primary cause (*dharmatā-hetu*), one takes the nature of the fruit-fruit, the fruit-cause, and the four conditions as the Buddha-natures of the Tathāgata.
Realizing *nirvāṇa* is the nature of the "fruit of fruits" (*phala-phala*), for the text below states: "The fruit of fruits refers to Great *Nirvāṇa*.
Samsara is the nature of the "cause of causes" (*hetu-hetu*), for the text below states: "The cause of causes refers to the phenomena produced by the twelve links of dependent origination;

furthermore, for one who has severed the afflictions of the twelve links of dependent origination and gives rise to the liberating understanding of contemplative wisdom—is this not the cause of causes?"

Those who listen with a sincere mind will immediately realize that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the six perfections, and the four immeasurables are all the nature of the "cause of realization.
They constantly obtain immeasurable bliss, which is the fruit of Bodhi. Since it is characterized by constant bliss, how could it not be the nature of the fruit?
Master Guan said: "If one reflects even briefly, one can immediately grasp the great meaning of these ten chapters. Therefore, one should know this."
The principle is immeasurable and cannot be fully described. What was previously referred to as "feeling" (*duḥkha*) within the context of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is here called "non-feeling.
The ancient commentary states that this is merely a matter of depth and shallowness, and so forth.
Next, the evils to be avoided are explained.

These so-called evils are: wild elephants, wild horses, wild oxen, wild dogs, dwellings inhabited by venomous snakes, thorny ground, precipices, steep cliffs, violent waters and whirlpools, wicked people, wicked countries, wicked cities, wicked houses, and evil associates.

Regarding such persons as these: if they act as a cause for outflows (*āsrava*), the Bodhisattva immediately distances himself from them; if they cannot so act, he does not distance himself. If they increase outflows, he then distances himself from them;
if they do not increase them, he does not distance himself. If they perform unwholesome dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*), he then distances himself from them;
if they can perform wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), he does not distance himself. What constitutes distancing oneself? It is not bearing weapons or staves.
One should always distance oneself from these through right wisdom and skillful means; therefore, this is called "distancing through right wisdom.

To give rise to wholesome dharmas, one must abandon unwholesome dharmas. A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates his own body as a disease, as a sore, as an abscess, as an enemy, and as an arrow piercing the body—a great mass of suffering that is the root of all good and evil.
Although the body is thus impure, such a bodhisattva nevertheless continues to look after and nourish it.
Why? It is not for the sake of craving the body, but for the sake of wholesome dharmas; it is for the sake of nirvāṇa and not for the sake of saṃsāra;

it is for the sake of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and not for the sake of impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity; it is for the sake of the path to bodhi and not for the sake of the path of existence; it is for the sake of the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
He does not seek the subtle body of the three vehicles, nor the body adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
he does not seek even the body of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He does not seek to be a Wheel-Turning King of the Dharma, nor a worldly Wheel-Turning King.

Good son, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva must always protect his body. Why is this? If he does not protect his body, his life will not be preserved. If his life is not preserved, [he cannot fulfill his vows].
If one is not complete [in these], one will be unable to copy this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain it extensively for others, or contemplate its meaning.
For this reason, a bodhisattva should skillfully protect their body. By means of this principle, a bodhisattva becomes free from all evil outflows (*āsrava*).
Good son, it is like one who wishes to cross water and carefully protects their boat or raft, or like a person on the road who carefully protects themselves.
Just as a fine horse, a farmer, or one planting crops carefully guards against excrement and filth; just as one carefully guards against a venomous wasp or a poisonous snake;
just as a person guards against a *caṇḍāla* for the sake of wealth; just as one maintains a valiant general to destroy bandits;
and just as a person suffering from the cold cherishes fire, or a leper seeks out poisonous medicine—so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. Although...
Seeing this body as being filled with immeasurable impurities, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva—out of a desire to uphold the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra—still cherishes and protects it so that it does not fail.

Why is there no distinction between a wicked elephant and a wicked spiritual friend? Because both destroy the body; therefore, the bodhisattva has no [aversion] toward the wicked elephant and the like.
One feels fear and trepidation toward evil associates (*pāpamitra*). Why is this?
Because while those evil elephants and the like can destroy only the body and not the mind, evil associates destroy both.

Those evil elephants and the like destroy but a single body, whereas evil associates destroy immeasurable virtuous bodies and immeasurable virtuous minds. Those evil elephants and the like can only...
Those who destroy the impure, foul-smelling body are evil associates (*pāpamitra*); they can destroy the pure body as well as the pure mind.
While evil elephants and the like may destroy the physical body, evil associates destroy the *dharmakāya*.

Those killed by evil elephants do not necessarily fall into the three miserable realms (*durgati*), but those killed by evil friends will certainly go to the three miserable realms. Evil elephants and the like are merely enemies of the body; evil associates are [enemies] of the Dharma.
The wise know that consciousness is an enemy of wholesome dharmas; therefore, a bodhisattva should always remain far removed from evil associates.
Such outflows as these are not abandoned by ordinary persons, and thus they give rise to outflows. Because the bodhisattva abandons them, outflows do not arise.
If even a bodhisattva has no such outflows, how much less so for a Tathāgata? Therefore, it is not an outflow.

This refers to wicked elephants, wicked horses, various wicked beasts, and so forth, which are capable of harming people and giving rise to evil thoughts, as well as the physical and verbal misconduct of the body and speech.
But how could inanimate things—such as wicked cities or wicked houses—be capable of doing evil?
It is like a border city where those who hold bows and carry arrows stand guard along the roads; would they not give rise to the intent to kill and harm people? Wicked houses are also like this.
These are evil conditions and evil associates who speak with sweet words, feign flattery, and employ clever speech and artful countenances to lead others toward evil;
therefore, one must distance oneself from them.
Next, the fifth point, "associating with those who have outflows," is explained according to the text.

What is the "outflow" (*āsrava*)? It refers to all ordinary worldlings who, for the sake of physical and mental pleasure, associate with [such things] and accept clothing, food, bedding, and medicine;
seeking these objects, they commit various evils without knowing their faults and afflictions, thereby cycling through the three realms of existence. For this reason, it is called an "outflow.
When a Bodhisattva perceives such faults, he immediately distances himself from them. However, when there is a need for clothing, he accepts it at once.
For the sake of the Dharma alone and not for the sake of the body, one does not cultivate a mind of arrogance but remains constantly humble;

one does not seek adornment but seeks only shame [as a restraint]. Though enduring cold, heat, and the biting of evil winds, rain, insects, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and venomous stings, one has no greedy attachment toward food and drink.
One acts always for the sake of the True Dharma and never for the sake of the physical form. Not for the sake of the skin or body, but only...
It is for the sake of sentient beings, not out of pride; it is for the sake of physical strength, not for the sake of harming others; it is for the sake of treating the wound of hunger.
Even when obtaining superior flavors, the mind remains free from attachment. Receiving and taking up dwellings is likewise so: the fetters of greed and pride are not allowed to dwell in the mind.
One accepts houses because they serve as a dwelling for Bodhi, warding off the thieves of the fetters and blocking the winds and rains of evil. One seeks medicine for this same purpose.
This person’s mind is free from greed and pride; they act solely for the sake of the True Dharma, not for the sake of physical life, but for the sake of eternal life.
Good son, it is like a person with a festering wound who applies ghee and parched grain flour and wraps it with cloth to draw out pus and blood;
he applies the ghee and flour to heal the wound, scatters medicine upon it to ward off evil winds, and stays within a deep chamber. Thus it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

The Bodhisattva likewise contemplates the body as a wound; thus, he covers it with clothing because of the leakage from its nine orifices, seeks food and drink because of the harsh winds and rains, and accepts dwellings because of the outbreak of the four poisons.
He seeks out medicine for the sake of the path to enlightenment, not for the sake of his own life. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva reflects thus: "If I do not accept these four offerings, my body will perish and fail to attain stability.
If it lacks stability, I shall not be able to endure suffering. If I cannot endure suffering, I shall be unable to cultivate wholesome dharmas.
If I can endure suffering, I shall be able to cultivate immeasurable wholesome dharmas. If I am unable to withstand [it]..."
When enduring various sufferings, one gives rise to a mind of hatred toward painful sensations; when experiencing pleasant sensations, one gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment;

and if one seeks pleasure but does not obtain it, ignorance arises. Therefore, ordinary people give rise to outflows (*āsrava*) regarding the four types of offerings, whereas Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to observe them deeply and do not give rise to outflows.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas are called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
Regarding "outflows" (*āsrava*): how could the Tathāgata be called one who possesses outflows? Therefore, the Tathāgata is not called one who possesses outflows.
Furthermore, [this is] the sixth explanation from among all ordinary beings regarding the outflow of sensation (*vedanā-āsrava*).
Furthermore, good son, although all ordinary beings well protect their bodies and minds, they still give rise to three kinds of evil thoughts.
For this reason, even though they sever their afflictions and attain birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they nevertheless fall back again into the three evil realms.
Good son, it is like a person crossing the great ocean who is on the verge of reaching the other shore.

Just as one who sinks into the water at the riverbank dies, so too it is with the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*): when their existence in the three realms (*trai-dhātu*) is nearly exhausted, they fall back into the three miserable destinies (*tri-apāya*).
Why is this? Because they lack wholesome awakening (*kuśala-bodhi*). What is this wholesome awakening? It refers to the six applications of mindfulness (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛty-upasthāna*).

The wholesome mind of the ordinary person is weak and inferior, while unwholesome states are rampant. Because the wholesome mind is weak, the mind of wisdom (*prajñā-citta*) is meager; because the mind of wisdom is meager, [they are lost].
Therefore, as they increase the various outflows (*āsrava*), the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s faculty of the eye becomes pure.

He perceives the faults of the three types of awakening (*trividha-bodhi*) and knows that these three awakenings possess manifold afflictions. They constantly act as enemies to sentient beings within the framework of the Three Vehicles (*tri-yāna*).

It is due to the causes and conditions of these three awakenings that immeasurable ordinary beings fail to see the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and for immeasurable kalpas they give rise to inverted thoughts, regarding the Buddha as... [a mere phenomenon].
The World-Honored One is impermanent, without bliss, without self, and possesses only one purity; the Tathāgata has ultimately entered parinirvāṇa.
All sentient beings are impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity; yet because of their inverted minds, they claim there is permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
In reality, there are no three vehicles; it is only because of their inverted minds that they speak of the three vehicles. The single true path is real and not false.
Because of a perverted mind, one says that there is not a single reality; these three evil thoughts are constantly censured by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
These three evil thoughts constantly harm oneself or may also harm others.
These three thoughts are followed by all manner of evils. Those who possess these three thoughts are bound by the three fetters that enchain sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantajanma constantly performs such contemplation on the three types of awakening.
At times, due to certain causes and conditions, he may encounter the arising of sensual thoughts; however, he remains silent and does not accept them.
This is like a person who is handsome and pure, who will not accept any filth or impurities; it is like a red-hot iron ball that no one would take up; it is like a Brahmin.
The nature of the gate is not to accept beef, just as a person who is full does not accept foul food;

it is like a Wheel-Turning King who does not sit on the same couch as any outcaste (caṇḍāla). In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva detests and despises the three types of awakening, neither accepting nor savoring them.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva reflects that sentient beings know him to be a worthy one.
"O Field of Merit, how shall I receive these evil dharmas? If I were to receive such evil thoughts, I would no longer be fit to be a field of merit for sentient beings.
I do not claim to be a virtuous field of merit; rather, because sentient beings perceive my outward appearance, they say, 'He is [a field of merit].
If I were now to give rise to such evil thoughts, I would be deceiving all sentient beings. In the past, I have deceived..."
Because of such deception, one wanders through birth and death for immeasurable eons and falls into the three evil realms.
If I were to receive the faithful offerings of others with an evil mind, all devas, humans, and seers possessing the five supernatural powers would bear witness to it and rebuke me.
If I were to receive the faithful offerings of others while harboring evil thoughts, I might cause the donor’s karmic fruit to diminish or even render it fruitless. If I...
To receive the offerings of a donor with an evil mind is to become an enemy and adversary to that donor.
Since all donors constantly regard me as their own infant, how could I deceive them by harboring thoughts of enmity? Why is this?

Because it may cause the donor to fail to obtain the fruit of their merit, or to obtain only a small portion of it, while I constantly claim for myself the title of one who has left the household life.
A person who has left the household life should not give rise to evil; if one gives rise to evil, then one is not a renunciant.
A renunciant’s body and speech must be in accord; if they are not in accord, then one is not a renunciant.

That I have abandoned my parents, brothers, wife, children, kinsmen, and friends to leave the household life and cultivate the Way is precisely the time for practicing all wholesome states of mind, not for practicing unwholesome ones.
When one habituates oneself to unwholesome thoughts, it is like a person who enters the ocean seeking jewels but takes up crystal instead of pearls;
or like a person who abandons exquisite music and play to wallow in filth; or like discarding a precious woman to cherish a maidservant;
or like casting away a golden vessel to use a clay bowl; or like rejecting nectar to consume poison; or like abandoning one's own kin.

Just as an old, virtuous, and skilled physician would instead seek medicine from those he hates and loathes to cure himself, so too have I abandoned the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, and his nectar-like flavor of the Dharma, only to consume the various evil perceptions of the Māra-enemy.
Human birth is difficult to obtain, as rare as the *udumbara* flower; I have now obtained it, and the Tathāgata, who is even rarer to encounter than the *udumbara* flower, I have now [met].
The pure Dharma-treasure is difficult to encounter and hear; I have now heard it, like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log.
Human life does not stop, passing faster than a mountain torrent. Though one exists today, even tomorrow’s light is difficult to guarantee.
Why do you indulge your mind, allowing it to dwell in unwholesome dharmas? Vigorous physical form does not endure, like a galloping horse; how can you rely upon it to give rise to arrogance?
Pride is like a malevolent spirit that waits to seek out the faults of others; the four great malevolent spirits are likewise always coming to seek out my own failings.
How can I allow unwholesome thoughts to arise? My life is like a dilapidated house on the verge of collapse;
how can I give rise to evil? I am called a śramaṇa, and one who is a śramaṇa is named for awakening to what is wholesome.
"I realize that I have now given rise to unwholesome thoughts. How can I be called a śramaṇa? I am one who has gone forth;
those who have gone forth are said to cultivate the path of goodness. Yet I now practice evil—how can I be called one who has gone forth?
I am now called a true brāhmaṇa; a brāhmaṇa is one who cultivates pure conduct. But I now..."
How can one who practices impurity and unwholesome thoughts be called a *brāhmaṇa*? I am now also called a member of the great clan of the *kṣatriyas*.
Those of the *kṣatriya* lineage are able to eliminate enemies; yet I am unable to eliminate my evil enemies—how then can I be called a *kṣatriya*?
My name is Bhikṣu. A person named a bhikṣu is one who has shattered the afflictions (*kleśas*), yet I am not [now]...
Regarding the destruction of evil thoughts and afflictions: how can one be called a bhikṣu? There are six things in the world that are difficult to encounter, which I have now attained;
how then could I allow evil thoughts to dwell in my mind? What are these six? First, a Buddha is difficult to encounter in the world;
second, the True Dharma is difficult to hear; third, a sense of dread is difficult to arouse; fourth, birth in a central land is difficult; fifth, a human body...
