It is difficult to obtain the six sense faculties, and it is likewise difficult to be fully endowed with these six things. Having obtained them, one should therefore not give rise to evil thoughts.
At that time, a bodhisattva practicing this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra constantly and diligently observes these evil minds;
because all ordinary people do not see the faults and afflictions of such evil minds, they receive the name of the "three perceptions."
When a Bodhisattva perceives the outflows of grasping (*upādāna-āsrava*), he does not accept them, does not cling to them, relinquishes them, and does not protect them;
relying on the Eightfold Noble Path, he pushes them away and cuts them off. For this reason, a Bodhisattva has no outflows of grasping.
How then could it be said that the Tathāgata has outflows? By this principle, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, is not one who possesses outflows.
The text states that "awakening to awakening" is precisely sensation (*vedanā*). The *Śrāvakabhūmi* (or *Śreṣṭha-caryā-paṭala*) says that sensation is the characteristic of awakening;

because the three afflictions arise subsequent to the three sensations, it is called the "outflow of sensation" (*vedanā-āsrava*). Within this, the names such as "śramaṇa" are further explained as having many meanings, so one must not adhere to a single fixed interpretation.
Here, the six difficulties differ from those concerning Cunda mentioned above; in the former case, *dāna* was [the subject].
In the "Chapter on Difficult Laments," the Arhat fruit is presented as difficult; here, it is the mind of fear that is presented as difficult.
Why is difficulty distinguished in three places while five are treated as identical? Because the *Cunda* chapter addresses the laity, it speaks of the difficulty of the final gift (*dāna*);

the "Chapter on Lamenting Decline" addresses the Path, thus it speaks of the difficulty of the Arhat. Here, it addresses both the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and those with existence (*bhava*), hence it speaks of fear.
The Difficulties of the Mind.

Chapter on the Virtuous King, Part Three, Scroll Seven:

Explaining the Contemplation of Outflows. This section has two parts: first, clarifying the characteristics of outflows; second, clarifying that the Bodhisattva is free from outflows and is able to sever the contemplation of outflows.
Furthermore, good son, if ordinary persons encounter physical or mental suffering and distress, they give rise to various evils;
whether they contract a physical illness or a mental affliction, they cause their body, speech, and mind to commit various evils.

Because they commit these evils, they transmigrate through the three realms of existence and undergo all manner of suffering. Why is this? It is because ordinary persons lack mindfulness and wisdom; therefore, they are born [into such states].
The various outflows (*āsrava*) are called the "outflow of mindfulness" (*smṛty-āsrava*).
When the mind engages in wrong mindfulness, it constitutes an outflow; logically, this should include the arising of mindfulness within all three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
However, here we specifically refer to the arising of the outflow of mindfulness within painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*), which gives rise to faults such as greed and hatred.
The second section below explains the bodhisattva’s state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*), further divided into three parts: the teaching, the analogies, and the conclusion.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly reflects: "From countless kalpas in the past, I have committed various evils with this body and mind;
by these causes and conditions, I have transmigrated through birth and death, undergoing all manner of suffering within the three evil realms."
Suffering thus causes me to distance myself from the true path of the Three Vehicles;
because of these evil conditions, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great fear within his own body and mind, abandons all evils, and seeks the way of goodness.

The initial brief explanation of the Dharma clarifies that a Bodhisattva’s contemplation can sever the outflows of mindfulness (*smṛty-āsrava*), whereas an ordinary foolish person lacks such contemplation and thus cannot extinguish those outflows.

From the passage beginning "Suppose there were a king" (*tadyathāpi nāma rājā...*) onwards, a second analogy is presented in two parts: first the simile, followed by its application (*yoga*). Regarding the first simile:
The explanations differ, being sometimes seven, eight, or nine; looking at the text below, they should be eight analogies: first, the four snakes; second, the five *caṇḍālas*;
third, the deceitful friend; fourth, the village; fifth, the six thieves; sixth, the great river; seventh, the raft of grass; eighth, reaching the shore. These eight are condensed into three:

the first six analogies illustrate the conditions for the Path (*mārga-pratyaya*); the next one illustrates the cultivation of the Path (*mārga-bhāvanā*); and the last one illustrates the attainment of the Path.
The first is an analogy for attaining the fruit.

Good son, it is like a king who places four venomous snakes in a single basket and orders a man to feed, care for, watch over, and attend to them—washing their bodies and following them as they move—saying:
"If you cause even one snake to become angry, I shall execute you according to the law."
At that time, when the man heard the king’s urgent command, his heart was filled with terror; he abandoned the chest and fled.
Regarding the initial mention of the "king," there are three interpretations: first, it refers to the Buddha’s teaching on the four great elements within the bodies of sentient beings;

second, it refers to ignorance, which constructs the physical body of the four great elements of sentient beings; third, it refers to this sutra’s exposition of the individual four great elements of sentient beings.
The analogy of mutual harm is like a snake in a basket; the analogy of nourishing the body is like washing and cleansing it.

Regarding the application of the law based on the gravity of the evil deeds committed: "execution in the marketplace" refers to the severing of the roots of goodness and the cutting off of the life-force of wisdom, as these matters are manifest.
Therefore, it is said to be "in the marketplace. The command to "exhort the evil not to be done and admonish the good to be practiced" is a solemn injunction.
If the fugitive were to attain true understanding and depart with it manifest, he would now first subdue the afflictions; therefore, it is said that he flees.
Subsequently, during the time of the King, he again dispatched the five lower *caṇḍālas*.
The king then again dispatched five caṇḍālas who followed him with drawn swords. When the man looked back and saw the five men behind him, he quickly abandoned his way and fled.

This is used as a metaphor for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); the swords represent impermanence and suffering; "looking back" represents delighting in *nirvāṇa*; and "fleeing" represents aversion [to the world].
Birth and death serve as the backward glance.
Third is the analogy of the five men at that time feigning intimacy;
at that time, the five men used an evil stratagem to conceal the knives they held and secretly dispatched one man to feign being a close friend.
And he said to him, "You may come back.
As for the one who hides the knife: by means of the false notion of "self," he conceals "non-self"; by means of the false attachment to pleasure, he conceals suffering.

He secretly dispatches a single person—this person is a metaphor for craving (*tṛṣṇā*) within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Because this craving can delude sentient beings, it is called "fraudulent."
"Father, there is one person who has faith, comparable to a lowly village.
This person, lacking faith, seeks to hide himself by entering a certain village; having entered the village, he peeks into the various houses."
He saw no people at all; all the earthenware vessels were empty and contained nothing. Seeing no one and failing to find anything he sought, he sat down on the ground.
This is analogous to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*); the five faculties are the dwelling place of consciousness, just as a person resides in a village with jars and vessels.

The term "zhě" (者) was formerly translated as "heavy-mouthed jar," which serves as a metaphor for the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) being layered together; in the dictionaries, it is given the phonetic reading "hóng.

Since no person is seen, this is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); since one seeks an object and does not find it, this is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); and as for sitting on the ground, this is settling the mind in the empty realm.
Fifth, hearing a voice from the sky; this is the analogy for the six bandits.
He hears a voice from the air saying: "Alas, O man! This place is desolate and empty, with no inhabitants.
Tonight, six great bandits will come here. If you encounter them, your life will not be spared. How will you manage to escape them?"
At that time, the man’s terror increased further, and he abandoned [the place] and departed.
This is like the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) being able to plunder one's wholesome wealth; the empty sound is like hearing it said within the Buddha's teaching that the six sense-objects exist.
When night comes, ignorance darkens the mind and obscures these six sense-objects.
The sixth path encounters a river below, which is a metaphor for encountering the flow of afflictions.
On this path, one encounters a river whose current is swift and turbulent, and there are no boats or rafts;
because of this fear, sentient beings remain constantly within the afflictions (*kleśa*), yet they suddenly encounter this [river] while having not cultivated the Path at all.

Unaware of the faults of delusion until now, one only begins to feel remorse upon realizing that these are obstacles; thus they are called "encountering," as they strike at the extremes of permanence and annihilation.
This is likened to being adrift in a swift current, for lacking the raft of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Seventh, taking various kinds of rafts as a metaphor for the cultivation of the path:

one takes various kinds of grass and wood to make a raft, and further reflects, "If I remain here, I shall be endangered by the venomous snakes, the five *caṇḍālas*, the one who feigns intimacy, and the six great thieves; therefore, I must cross this river."

Thinking, "This raft cannot be relied upon; I would rather drown and die than be harmed by those snake-thieves," he pushed the grass raft into the water, leaned his body against it, and moving his hands and feet, cut across the current.
Moving the hands and feet is like the application of the Way; one must not rely on the raft. If one’s wholesome thoughts are weak and feeble, they cannot carry one across to salvation.
When the body leans upon them, the mind relies on these virtues to cut through the stream and depart. Grasses and trees represent the various wholesome dharmas;
the two hands represent the two wisdoms of skillful means and reality; the two feet represent the two virtues of precepts and meditative concentration.
The eighth [point], "reaching the other shore," is a metaphor for attaining the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
It means reaching the other shore, being secure and free from affliction, with the mind at ease and terror eliminated.
While remaining within this flow, there is much to fear; but having crossed over and reached the fruit, one will certainly have nothing to dread.
Next, the eight similes are correlated: the first four snakes correspond to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas hear, receive, and uphold the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, they contemplate the body as being like a chest containing earth, water, fire, and wind, which are like four poisonous snakes—possessing the poison of sight, the poison of touch, the poison of breath, and the poison of the bite. All sentient beings encounter these four...
Because of poison, one loses their life; the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of sentient beings are also like this.
Whether seen as evil, touched as evil, encountered through breath as evil, or bitten as evil, by these causes and conditions, they remain far removed from all that is wholesome.
Furthermore, son of good family, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates that the four poisonous snakes have four kinds of natures, namely: the Kṣatriya... [and so forth].
The Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and [others] are likewise like these four great serpents; they possess four natures:

the nature of solidity, the nature of moisture, the nature of heat, and the nature of motion. Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates that these four great elements share the same essential nature as the four venomous snakes.
Furthermore, son of good family, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates these four great elements as being like four venomous snakes.
What is meant by contemplating these four venomous snakes as constantly watching for an opportunity—thinking, "When shall they look at me? When shall they touch me?
When shall they hiss at me? When shall they bite me?"? The four great poisonous snakes are likewise always watching sentient beings, seeking their vulnerabilities.
One who is killed by these four snakes will ultimately never fall into the three evil realms.
If one is slain by the four great elements, one will certainly fall into the three evil realms; of this there is no doubt.

Although these four poisonous snakes may be cared for and nourished, they still desire to kill people. The four great elements are likewise: although they are constantly provided for, they also constantly lead people to commit various evils.
If even one of these four poisonous snakes becomes enraged, it can kill a person; such is the nature of the four great elements.
It is just so: if even one of these becomes enraged, it can kill a person. Although these four poisonous snakes dwell in the same place, their four minds are each different;
the four great poisonous snakes are likewise. Although they dwell in the same place, their natures are each distinct.
Although these four poisonous snakes may be treated with respect, they are difficult to approach; the four great poisonous snakes are likewise.
Although they may be treated with respect, these four poisonous snakes are difficult to approach;
yet when they harm a person, there may be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who can treat them with mantras or medicinal herbs.

However, when the four great elements kill a person, even if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas with divine mantras and excellent medicines, none can cure it—just as one who takes pleasure in himself hears of the four poisonous snakes.

Just as one immediately distances oneself from a foul odor that is loathsome, so too do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; upon smelling the foul stench of the four great elements, they likewise distance themselves.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflects, giving rise to great fear toward the four great poisonous snakes, and turning his back on them, he hastens forth to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path.

In the Great Possession (Mahābhūta), there are internal and external aspects. Within the body, the four great elements are correctly joined like four snakes: the four great elements together produce the eye faculty, which is joined with the poison of sight;

they together produce the body faculty, which is joined with the poison of touch; they together produce the nose faculty, which is joined with the poison of air; and they together produce the tongue faculty, which is joined with the poison of biting.
Next, the combination of the five *caṇḍālas* is as stated in the text.
The five *caṇḍālas* are precisely the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). How does a bodhisattva contemplate the five aggregates as being like *caṇḍālas*?
A *caṇḍāla* constantly causes people to be separated from those they love and brings together those whom they hate; the five aggregates are likewise.
This causes people to greedily approach unwholesome dharmas and to distance themselves from all purely wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a *caṇḍāla* who adorns himself with various weapons—whether swords, shields, bows, arrows, armor, or spears—which can harm others;
the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are likewise, for they firmly bind one with the various afflictions (*kleśa*).

"Son of good family, just as a *caṇḍāla* may harm those who have committed transgressions and cause them to fall into various states of existence, so too do the five aggregates harm those who possess the faults of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Therefore, the Bodhisattva deeply contemplates the five aggregates as being like a *caṇḍāla*. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva observes the five aggregates as being like a *caṇḍāla*."
The caṇḍāla has no heart of compassion and harms both enemies and kin;
the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are likewise, having no heart of compassion, they harm both the good and the evil. Just as the caṇḍāla torments all people, so too do the five aggregates;
because the various afflictions (kleśa) constantly torment all sentient beings in saṃsāra, the bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates as being like a caṇḍāla.
Furthermore, Rāvaṇa, a bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates as being like a caṇḍāla.
Just as a caṇḍāla person always harbors a harmful mind, so too do the five aggregates always harbor minds of affliction and harm.
Just as a person who lacks feet, weapons, or attendants will surely be killed by a caṇḍāla, so too are sentient beings likewise without feet or [protection].

If a sword has no attendants, it will be harmed by the five aggregates; thus, the sword is named "precept," the attendants are named "wisdom," and the attendants are further named "all spiritual friends.
Because these three things are absent, one is harmed by the five aggregates.
Therefore, a Bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates as being like a *caṇḍāla*. Furthermore, O son of good family, a Bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva observes that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are more heinous than a *caṇḍāla*. Why is this?
If sentient beings are killed by the five types of *caṇḍālas*, they do not fall into hell; however, those killed by the five aggregates fall into hell.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva observes that the five aggregates are more heinous than a *caṇḍāla*. Having made this observation, he makes this vow: "I would rather [endure] until the end..."
A worldly *caṇḍāla* cannot be approached even for a moment; however, the *caṇḍāla* of the five aggregates can only harm those who are deluded within the desire realm.
This thief of the five aggregates universally harms all ordinary beings throughout the three realms.
A worldly *caṇḍāla* can only slaughter those who have committed crimes, whereas this thief of the five aggregates makes no distinction between whether sentient beings have committed a crime or not.

While a *caṇḍāla* can never harm the elderly, women, or children, these thieves of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) harm all sentient beings without exception—whether old or young, male or female.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva deeply contemplates that the faults of the five aggregates are worse than those of a *caṇḍāla*, and thus makes this vow:
"I would rather dwell near a *caṇḍāla* for the rest of my life than endure even a moment [of the suffering] caused by the five aggregates."
At that time, one remains close to the five aggregates. Furthermore, son of good family, a *caṇḍāla* harms only others and never harms himself;
the thief of the five aggregates harms both himself and others.
A *caṇḍāla* can be ransomed with kind words, money, or precious goods, but the five aggregates are not like that; they cannot be enticed or dissuaded by forceful kind words or wealth.
One may seek wealth and obtain release from a *caṇḍāla*, but the five aggregates do not necessarily kill one at all times;
the *caṇḍāla* does not constantly harm sentient beings in every moment as the five aggregates do.
While one might be able to escape a *caṇḍāla* by fleeing to another location, the five aggregates do not do so; they pervade all places, leaving no place of escape. Although the *caṇḍāla*...
To harm others and harm oneself is to follow the five aggregates; it is not otherwise. Once one has killed sentient beings, they pursue and never leave.
Therefore, a bodhisattva would rather remain close to a caṇḍāla for the rest of their life than associate with the five aggregates for even a moment.
A person of wisdom uses skillful means to escape the five aggregates; these skillful means are precisely the Eightfold Noble Path and the six pāramitās.

Through the *pāramitās* and the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), by means of these skillful means, one attains liberation; thus, body and mind are not harmed by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Why is this? Because the body is like a diamond (*vajra*) and the mind is like space (*ākāśa*); therefore, body and mind are difficult to destroy or corrupt.
For this reason, the bodhisattva contemplates the aggregates and perceives that they accomplish various unwholesome dharmas, thereby giving rise to great fear.
Fearing the cultivation of the Eightfold Noble Path, one proceeds like that person who, fearing the four poisonous snakes and the five caṇḍālas,
travels along the road without looking back or lingering—
yet there are three who feign intimacy.
To feign intimacy is called craving. Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas deeply contemplate the fetter of craving as being like a deceptive friend.
If one knows its true nature, it can do no harm; if one does not know it, one will certainly be harmed by it. Craving is likewise:
if one knows its essential nature, it cannot cause sentient beings to revolve in the suffering of birth and death; if one does not know it, [it will].
Those who wander through the six realms of saṃsāra undergo all manner of suffering. Why is this? Because craving is a disease that is difficult to abandon.
It is like a false friend who is difficult to distance oneself from; a false friend constantly watches for one's vulnerability to cause separation from what is loved and union with what is hated.
Craving is likewise: it causes one to depart from all wholesome dharmas and draw near to all unwholesome ones.
Because of this meaning, unwholesome dharmas are such that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva deeply contemplates craving as an enemy who feigns friendship;

it is that which is seen as not seen, and heard as not heard. Just as ordinary people see the faults of birth and death, yet although they possess wisdom, because it is covered by delusion, they later fail to see them again; the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are also like this, for although they see, they do not.
Although they have seen [the truth], they have not heard it. Why is this? It is because of the bond of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). What is the reason for this?
Because they see the faults of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they are unable to swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

For this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates this fetter of craving as an enemy disguised as a friend. What are the characteristics of an enemy disguised as a friend? They are like an enemy.

That which is unreal falsely manifests as real; its true nature is that it is not to be approached, yet it falsely manifests as being approachable. It is truly unwholesome, yet falsely manifests as wholesome.

It is truly not an object of affection, yet falsely manifests as an object of affection. Why is this? Because it constantly watches for a person's vulnerability, desiring to cause them harm. Affection is also like this:

it constantly acts toward sentient beings by falsely manifesting as real where there is no reality, falsely manifesting as approachable where there is no approachability, and falsely manifesting as wholesome where there is no wholesomeness.
Virtue is not [truly] desirable, while that which appears to be desirable is always deceptive to all within saṃsāra.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva views desire as an enemy. One who feigns friendship through body and speech does not perceive the mind;
therefore, such a person is able to deceive. Desire is likewise: it is merely empty deception and ultimately unobtainable; for this reason, it is able to delude all sentient beings.
One who is a born enemy feigning friendship has a beginning and an end, and thus can be easily avoided;

affection is not like this, for it has no beginning and no end, making it difficult to avoid. One who is a born enemy feigning friendship is difficult to recognize from afar but easy to perceive when near;
affection is not like this, for it is difficult to discern even when near, let alone when far away. For this reason, the Bodhisattva regards affection as worse than feigned enmity.
Because of the fetter of affection, all sentient beings distance themselves from Great Nirvāṇa and draw near to saṃsāra;

they distance themselves from permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and draw near to impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity. Therefore, in various sūtras, I have spoken of these as the three defilements.
Due to ignorance regarding present phenomena, they do not perceive their faults and are unable to abandon either attachment or enmity.
A false friend can ultimately never harm one who possesses wisdom; therefore, the Bodhisattva deeply contemplates this attachment and gives rise to great fear,
cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path just as that man, fearing the four poisonous snakes, the five outcastes, and the single false friend,
pressed on along the road without turning back.
"Affection" (*priya*) is merely love; it can flatter and entice sentient beings to their harm. However, among the [five] mental states, only the first three cannot produce affection;

it is only within the state of "conduct" (*caryā-citta*) that affectionate love can arise. Furthermore, although all five aggregates (*skandha*) are capable of committing evil, the arising of craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) necessarily depends on the mind of conduct;
therefore, it is said that "one enemy" [is concealed]. The text says: "An enemy feigning affection has a beginning and..."
The love of the end is not like this; it is without beginning and without end. Furthermore, there are two meanings:
first, just as the twelve links of dependent origination are like a wheel having neither beginning nor end, so too is the love of the end without beginning or end.

However, the twelve links of dependent origination do have a beginning and an end—namely, ignorance is the beginning and old age and death are the end—whereas [the love of the end] is said to be without beginning or end.

As for the meaning: seeking the place from which love comes, it can never be found; this is the meaning of being "beginningless. Seeking the place to which it goes, there is nowhere to go; this is further the meaning of being "endless.
This next point combines with the fourth.
The "empty village" refers to the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates these six sense bases as empty and non-existent, it is like an empty village;

just as that terrified person, having entered the village, does not see even a single inhabitant and searches everywhere through jars and vessels without finding a single thing, so too the Bodhisattva minutely observes the six sense bases as empty and devoid of anything real.

Because there is not even a single thing among sentient beings that possesses substantial reality, the Bodhisattva contemplates the six internal sense bases as empty and non-existent, like an empty village.
Good son, when a band of thieves gazes from afar at an empty village, they never conceive the notion that it is void;
ordinary people are just the same—they do not conceive the notion of emptiness regarding the village of the six sense bases.

Because they are unable to give rise to the perception of emptiness, they transmigrate through birth and death and undergo immeasurable suffering. Son of good family, when a band of thieves arrives, one then gives rise to the perception of emptiness;
the Bodhisattva is also like this, for he contemplates these six sense bases and constantly gives rise to the perception of emptiness.
Because he gives rise to the perception of emptiness, he does not transmigrate through birth and death to undergo suffering. Regarding these six sense bases, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
Because it is eternally free from inversion, and being free from inversion, one no longer transmigrates through birth and death.

Furthermore, son of good family, just as a band of thieves who enter this empty village find peace and security, so too do the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*) find peace and security upon entering these six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Just as the thieves dwelling in the empty village have no fear, so it is with the afflictions.
The bandits are likewise thus: dwelling within these six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), they have no fear.

Just as that empty village is the dwelling place of lions, tigers, wolves, and various other evil beasts, so too are these six internal sense bases the dwelling place of all manner of evil afflictions (*kleśa*) and evil beasts. For this reason, the Bodhisattva deeply contemplates the six sense bases.

Emptiness and non-existence are purely the dwelling place of all that is unwholesome. Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva contemplates the six internal sense bases as empty and non-existent, like an empty village.
Why is this? Because they are deceptive and unreal; because one forms the notion of existence regarding what is empty and non-existent;
because one forms the notion of pleasure regarding what is truly without pleasure; and because one forms the notion of a person regarding what is truly without a person.
Because of the perception of a person, the six internal sense bases are likewise thus: they are empty and non-existent, yet one forms the perception that they exist;
there is truly no pleasure, yet one forms the perception of pleasure; there is truly no person, yet one forms the perception of a person.
Only the wise person can know this and attain its reality. Furthermore, son of good family, it is like an empty village where, at times, there may be a person.
At times there may be no person, yet the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are not likewise entirely non-existent. Why? Because their nature is eternally empty;

this is what is known by the wise, not what is seen with the eyes. Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates that the internal six sense bases harbor many enemies and harms, and thus practices the Eightfold Noble Path without ceasing or resting, just like that man who feared the four poisonous snakes, the five *caṇḍālas*, and the one [ghost].
The six great thieves, feigning intimacy, terrify those on the right path.
The "empty village" refers to the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*); it is empty because the external world—the village where people dwell—is devoid of persons.

Thus, the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are empty, for they are the dwelling place of the "self," yet when sought, this self cannot be found. It is like a person looking for a house that is not there.

This means that when one searches internally for a person, even upon further investigation, no such bodhisattva is to be found; it is the same with observing the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), which are all empty and devoid of self.

These six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) constitute the six sense organs. Together with the six external objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), these twelve internal and external factors are also called the six passions (*ṣaḍ-rāga*) or the six consciousness-faculties (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-indriya*).
"Faculty" (*indriya*) is defined by its capacity to produce [consciousness], while "passion" (*rāga*) refers to its nature of attachment.
They derive their names from the arising of consciousness; yet while the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are insentient, they are termed "sentient" because they are capable of receiving [objects].
Thus, they are called the "six sentiments" (*ṣaḍvedanīya*). Because they bring together the faculties and their objects, they are able to generate consciousness.
Next, we combine this with the fifth [section].
As for the six great thieves, they are the six external sense objects (*ṣaḍ bāhyaviṣayāḥ*). A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates these six sense objects as being like six great thieves.
Why? Because they are able to plunder all wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*), just as the six great thieves are able to plunder everything.
The wealth and treasures of sentient beings are likewise like the six thieves of the sensory objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*); they can plunder the virtuous wealth of all beings.

Just as the six great thieves, upon entering a person's house, can plunder whatever is currently within the home regardless of its quality, causing even the most wealthy to suddenly become impoverished;
so too do these six thieves of the sensory objects, if they enter the sense-faculties (*indriya*) of a person.
Thus, they are able to plunder all wholesome dharmas; once wholesome dharmas are exhausted, one becomes impoverished, destitute, and solitary, acting as an icchantika.
For this reason, a bodhisattva carefully contemplates the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) as being like the six great thieves.

Furthermore, good son, when the six great thieves wish to plunder a person, they must rely on an "insider"; if there is no insider, they will simply turn back. It is the same with these six sense objects.

The bandits are likewise thus: they wish to plunder the wholesome dharmas, which requires that within there be sentient beings who perceive signs such as permanence, bliss, self, purity, and non-emptiness.
If there are no such signs within, then the evil bandits of the six sense objects cannot plunder any of the wholesome dharmas.

A person of wisdom has no such signs within, whereas ordinary people do; for this reason, [the six... (Note: The final character "六" appears to be a fragment of the original text's concluding phrase, likely part of a list or a structural marker.)
The sensory objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) constantly come to invade and seize the wealth of wholesome dharmas; because one does not guard them well, they plunder them.
One who guards them is said to possess wisdom; such a person of intelligence can guard them well and thus is not plundered.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates these six sensory objects as being no different from the six great thieves. Furthermore, son of good family, just as the six great thieves are able to...
The affliction of the body and mind of sentient beings is likewise caused by these six thieves of the sensory objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

While the six great thieves can only plunder the material wealth of people in the present life, these thieves of the six sense-objects constantly plunder the wholesome wealth of sentient beings across the three periods of time.
Furthermore, while the six great thieves find joy in the night, these evil thieves of the six sense-objects do the same.
In such a state, where the darkness of ignorance prevails, one finds joy; yet these six great thieves can only be restrained by kings.
Furthermore, it is likewise only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who can restrain these six great thieves.
Whenever they seek to plunder, they do not discriminate between the handsome and the ugly, the high-born and the low-born, the wise and the learned, the noble and the poor.

The base and evil thieves of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are likewise; they wish to plunder the wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*) without discriminating between the noble and the beautiful, or even the poor and the lowly.
Although various kings may cut off the hands and feet of these six great thieves, they are still unable to cause their minds to cease [their depredations].
The evil thieves of the six sense-objects are likewise; although the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, and *anāgāmin* may cut them off...
Their hands and feet likewise cannot prevent them from being robbed of wholesome dharmas; only a person of great courage and strength can subdue these six great thieves.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this, for they alone can subdue the evil thieves of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
It is just as when a person has many clans and a flourishing circle of kinsmen, they will not be plundered by those six thieves.
Birth is likewise: if one has a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one will not be plundered by the evil bandits of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
These six great bandits can steal and plunder the property of people whenever they see them; the six sense objects are not like this.
Whether seen, known, heard, smelled, touched, or perceived, they are all capable of plundering. These six great bandits can only plunder the wealth of those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
While the evil bandits who plunder the six sense-objects of the form and formless realms cannot compare to this, which can plunder all the jewels of goodness within the three realms;
therefore, the Bodhisattva carefully contemplates that the six sense-objects surpass those six bandits.

Having made this contemplation, he cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, proceeding directly forward without turning back, just as that terrified man fled from the four poisonous snakes and the five *caṇḍālas*.
Feigning intimacy, the six great thieves abandoned the deserted village and set out upon the road.

These six thieves are none other than the thieves of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); they come from without to plunder a person's resources, just as the thieves of the six sense-objects plunder a person's wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*).
However, these six sense-objects give rise to three kinds of dharmas; four matters among them can produce subtle afflictions (*sūkṣmakleśa*).

That which is produced from the four subtle elements (*tanmātra*) is called "gross," and thus is named the "four great elements" (*mahābhūta*). As for the "four things," these are visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility;
each of the four great elements possesses these four qualities, yet they are not complete in all five. That which is produced from the five things is called the "five desires.

As for the "five things," this refers to the five sense objects, adding sound as the sixth. That which is produced from the six things is termed the "six dusts" (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); "dust" (*rajas*) refers to that which is turbid and burdensome.
Name. Next, it joins with the sixth, a single river.
As for the "single river encountered on the way," this refers to affliction (*kleśa*). How does a bodhisattva contemplate this affliction as being like a great [ocean]?
Just as that swift river can sweep away fragrant elephants, so too is the swift river of afflictions (*kleśa*), which can sweep away *pratyekabuddhas*.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva deeply contemplates afflictions as being like a swift river, because it is deep and difficult to reach its bottom; thus it is called a "river.
Because its banks cannot be found, it is called "great. Within it there are many kinds of evil fish; such is the greatness of afflictions.
The river is likewise thus: because only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can reach its bottom, it is called "extremely deep";
because only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can find its boundaries, it is called "vast and great"; and because it constantly harms all deluded sentient beings, it is called "evil fish.
Therefore, a Bodhisattva contemplates these afflictions as being like a great river; just as the waters of a great river can cause growth—

All grasses, trees, thickets, and forests, as well as the great river of afflictions (*kleśa*), are likewise able to cause sentient beings to grow within the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
For this reason, the Bodhisattva contemplates these afflictions as being like a great river.

For example, just as there is no sense of shame or remorse when someone falls into a great river, so too it is with sentient beings who fall into the river of afflictions; they lack shame and remorse, just like one who has fallen into the river.
It is likewise with those who, before reaching the bottom, meet their end and fall into the river of afflictions;
they have not exhausted its depths and continue to revolve through the twenty-five states of existence. What is called the "bottom" is the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
If there are those who do not cultivate this characteristic of emptiness, it should be known that such persons cannot escape the twenty-five states of existence. All sentient beings [are thus].
Because they cannot skillfully cultivate emptiness and signlessness, they are constantly swept away by the swift river of afflictions.
Just as that great river can only destroy the body but cannot submerge all wholesome dharmas, the great river of afflictions is not like this;
it can destroy all wholesome dharmas of both body and mind. That great, violent river can only sweep away those within the desire realm.
The great river of afflictions can sweep away the worlds of humans, devas, and those in the three realms.
Just as one reaches the other shore by moving one's hands and feet across a great river, so too can a bodhisattva cross over the great river of afflictions only by means of the six pāramitās.
Just as it is difficult to cross a great river, so too is it difficult to cross the great river of afflictions.
Regarding "difficult to cross": why is it called difficult to cross? Even the great Bodhisattvas of the ten stages have not yet attained ultimate crossing;
only the Buddhas attain ultimate crossing. Therefore, it is called difficult to cross.
It is like a person being swept away by a river who cannot cultivate even a hair’s breadth of wholesome dharma; sentient beings are likewise.
Those who are swept away and submerged by the river of afflictions are likewise unable to cultivate wholesome dharmas.

Just as a person fallen into a river and drifting with the current cannot be rescued by others unless they possess sufficient strength, so too those fallen into the river of afflictions cannot be saved by icchantikas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even by all the Buddhas;
for this is the great worldly river that persists until the end of the kalpa.
At that time, even if seven suns were to shine simultaneously, they could only cause a great river of afflictions (*kleśa*) to dry up;
yet it is not so for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, for although they cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), they cannot dry them up.

Therefore, a Bodhisattva views all afflictions as being like a violent river—just as that person feared the four poisonous snakes, the five *caṇḍālas*, the one who feigned kindness, and the six great [elements].
The bandits abandoned the empty village and departed along the road.

The "rivers" refer to the afflictions (*kleśa*); however, as there are two rivers and six rivers [discussed elsewhere], it is not possible to describe them all here at once—namely, the river of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), the river of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa*), the river of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), and the river of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
(As stated above... However, within this sutra, three rivers are distinguished as being different.
In the *Siṃha*, the river of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is elucidated; in the *Kāśyapa*, the river of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa*) is elucidated; here, the river of afflictions (*kleśa*) is elucidated.
Having reached the riverbank, one takes grass to make a raft; this corresponds to the seventh analogy below.
Just as one who reaches the river takes grass to make a raft, so too is the Bodhisattva:

fearing the four great snakes of the four elements, the Caṇḍāla of the five aggregates, the deceptive intimacy of craving, and the evil bandits of the six sense-objects within the empty village of the six sense-bases;

upon reaching the river of afflictions, he cultivates the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—the six pāramitās and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—to serve as his boat and raft.
Relying on this raft, one crosses the river of afflictions;
taking precepts, concentration, and wisdom as its three components,
one reaches the other shore— this corresponds below to the eighth analogy of reaching the other shore, which is the eternal bliss of nirvana.
Having reached the other shore and constantly delighting in nirvana, the Bodhisattva who practices the Great Nirvana reflects thus:
"If I am unable to endure such physical and mental suffering, I shall not be able to enable all sentient beings to cross the river of afflictions.
Reflecting in this way, although there is such physical and mental distress, he endures it in silence.
Because they endure with patience, outflows do not arise.
Thus, if even a bodhisattva has no outflows, how much less could a Buddha-Tathāgata have any outflows?
Therefore, the Buddhas are not said to possess outflows.
What is meant by "the Tathāgata is not without outflows"? This is the second explanation of the half-phrase "not without outflows.
Why is it that the Tathāgata is not without outflows? Because the Tathāgata constantly acts within the realm of outflows;
these outflows are precisely the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*). Therefore, śrāvakas and ordinary worldlings say that the Buddha has outflows, whereas the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas...
It is truly untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the statement that "the Tathāgata constantly practices what is tainted," some scholars say that the distinction between the tainted and the untainted is determined by the object:
if one takes a tainted object as a condition, it is called tainted; if one takes an untainted object as a condition, it is called untainted. Within this context...
The explanation that the Tathāgata possesses outflows (*sāsrava*) is understood by some as referring to a specific number of people; why is this so? The text states:

"The Tathāgata constantly practices that which has outflows, and 'outflows' refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). Thus, we know it is named after the objective realm of the twenty-five states of existence.
When a person follows after objects with the mind, even though the essence of the self (*ātman*) is pure and free from afflictions (*kleśa*), one still conditions outflows when perceiving them.
The two interpretations—that objects and the mind do not constitute outflows—serve as the root of dispute. This passage clarifies both points:

that the Tathāgata is neither with outflows (*sāsrava*) nor without outflows (*anāsrava*). To say he is "not with outflows" clarifies that the Tathāgata no longer possesses any outflows; to say he is "not without outflows" clarifies that the Buddha still possesses these [outflows].
By stating he is "neither with outflows," it is intended to clarify that the Buddha is beyond being merely with outflows.
It is neither non-outflow nor outflow, nor is it both; how could it ever be said to be either with-outflow or without-outflow?
Good son, for these reasons, the third point below concludes that [the nature of] fetters is indeterminate.
"Good son, for these reasons, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess no fixed characteristics.
Good son, it is for this reason that those who commit the four grave offenses, those who slander the Vaipulya sūtras, and icchantikas are all indeterminate."
At that time, the third section on the realization [of the teaching] by King of Virtue (Guṇarāja) begins (as follows).
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Light-Pervading Noble Virtue King (Prabhāsa-vyūha-udāra-guṇarāja) said: "So it is, so it is;
it is truly as the Holy One has spoken. All dharmas are entirely indeterminate. Because they are indeterminate, one should know the Tathāgata."
Nor does he ultimately enter parinirvāṇa.
As the Buddha stated above, the second section on the "King of Virtue" further requests an answer to the previous question regarding the fruit;

since that prior question was distant, it is restated here. Within this second section where cause and effect are asked about together, the response first answers both cause and effect simultaneously.

Next, the specific response concerning cause and effect: within this specific response, the Tathāgata has already extensively answered regarding the cause; now, King Guṇarāja further raises a question concerning the fruit.
The text is divided into two parts: first, the restatement of the question regarding the fruit.

As the Buddha has previously taught, among the "hearing the unheard" practiced by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the Great Nirvāṇa, there is both nirvāṇa and great nirvāṇa. What is nirvāṇa? What is great nirvāṇa?
At that time, the Buddha praised [the assembly]. This second section, the Tathāgata’s response, is further divided into two parts: first, praising the question; second, the actual answer.
At that time, the Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāpāla-Ābhāsvara-Guṇarāja, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! If there is a bodhisattva who attains the *dhāraṇī* of mindfulness, they will be able to inquire as you have done."

Regarding the initial praise and inquiry, there are two meanings. First, it praises his power of mindfulness and dhāraṇī, in that even after a long period of time has passed, he still remembers his previous question and is able to request the Buddha’s answer.

Within this nirvana there is much that is contained; since you now wish to grasp it all together and maintain it, it is for this reason that it is further called "attaining the dhāraṇī of mindfulness.
This concludes the second part, the formal answer, which is divided into two sections. The first section presents a comparison between the Great and Small [Vehicles].
The answer to the two [questions] is given from the perspective of relative meaning; the answer to the question regarding the Great Nirvāṇa is given from the perspective of absolute meaning.
First, the relative aspect is clarified, which consists of ten pairs. As for the absolute meaning, it is as stated in the following text:
"For example, space is not called 'great space' because of a small space; Nirvāṇa is likewise not called 'the great characteristic' because of a small characteristic."
Within the context of mutual dependence, there are two parts: first, ten pairs are presented as ten analogies, followed by their synthesis.
"Good son, it is as people of the world say: there is a sea and a great sea; there is a river and a great river;

there is a mountain and a great mountain; there is earth and great earth; there is a city and a great city; there are sentient beings and great sentient beings; there is a king and a great king; and there is a person and a great person."
There is the human Dharma and the Celestial Dharma among humans; there is the Way and the Great Way.

Combining these, they form two [sections]. First, there is a general combination, followed by specific illustrations and applications. Furthermore, within the general combination, there are first two headings:
the Great Chapter and the Small Chapter.
Nirvāṇa is likewise twofold: there is nirvāṇa and there is great nirvāṇa.

Next, regarding the question "What is nirvāṇa?", the following explains these two chapters; first nirvāṇa is explained, then great nirvāṇa. In the initial explanation of nirvāṇa, there are again two parts:
first, it is raised that five matters, in their limited sense, possess the meaning of extinguishing suffering and are thus called nirvāṇa, yet they are not great nirvāṇa.
...Parinirvāṇa.
What is Nirvāṇa? Good son, it is like a person who, being hungry, obtains a small amount of food and calls this "peaceful bliss";
such peaceful bliss is also called Nirvāṇa. It is like one who recovers from illness and thereby attains peaceful bliss; such peaceful bliss is also [called Nirvāṇa].
It is called *nirvāṇa* because, just as a person who is terrified finds peace and happiness upon finding a place of refuge, such peace and happiness is also called *nirvāṇa*.
It is called *nirvāṇa* because, just as a poor person obtains the seven treasures and finds peace and happiness, such peace and happiness is also called *nirvāṇa*.
It is called *nirvāṇa* because, just as a person contemplates a skeleton and does not give rise to craving, they find peace and happiness; such peace and happiness is also [called *nirvāṇa*].
That which is called "nirvāṇa" in this way cannot be called "Mahāparinirvāṇa. Why?
Because it is characterized by hunger and thirst, by illness, by fear, by poverty, and because of the arising of craving and attachment; therefore, it is called nirvāṇa, not Mahāparinirvāṇa.
If ordinary persons [attain] the cessation through the suppression and abandonment [of defilements], this is called nirvāṇa.
First, the two general categories of ordinary persons and noble ones are presented. Good son, whether they be ordinary persons or śrāvakas—
Next, in the explanation, there are two parts: first, the explanation itself; second, the establishment of that explanation.
Whether by means of worldly convention or by means of the Noble Path, one severs the fetters of the desire realm and thereby attains peace and happiness.
Such peace and happiness is also called *nirvāṇa*, but it cannot be called "Great *Nirvāṇa*. This [path] can sever [the fetters] up to the first dhyāna, and so forth.
The fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) lead to peace and happiness;
such peace and happiness is also called nirvāṇa, yet it cannot be called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
First, [the text] explains the "ordinary person" (pṛthagjana) above by means of either the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) or the supramundane path (*āryamārga*).

They hear that "worldly" refers to those of external paths who have attained dhyāna and subdued their afflictions, while "noble path" refers to those of the Hīnayāna who have severed their afflictions. Why is this?
The following two explanations establish the preceding two points.
Why is this? Because afflictions arise again due to the presence of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). What is meant by "afflictive habitual tendencies"?
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess the residual traces of affliction, namely: "I am the body," "I am the robe," "I go," "I come," "I speak," and "I hear.
When the Buddhas and Tathāgatas enter *nirvāṇa*, the nature of that *nirvāṇa* is without self and without pleasure; it possesses only permanence.
Purity is what is called the habit-energy of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*). There are distinct characteristics between the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha;
yet, the *nirvāṇa* attained by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Tathāgatas is ultimately equal and without distinction.
For this reason, that which is attained by the two vehicles is not the Great *Nirvāṇa*. Why? Because it lacks permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Because they are purified.
The phrase "giving rise to afflictions once again" explains those ordinary persons who possess residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

The subsequent passage fully sets forth the meaning of these habitual tendencies; according to a general discussion, all ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) possess habitual tendencies, as illustrated by Śāriputra’s objection.
Dhāpiṅgala and others (as detailed above) now specifically address the view of self to clarify the practice of non-self and non-bliss,

asserting that only permanence and purity exist, and that what is non-self and blissful is precisely their permanence and purity. To refute this, [it is shown that] they are all actually impermanent, non-blissful, non-self, and impure.
The three phrases "permanence, bliss, self, and purity" below—comprising twelve characters in total—explain the preceding topical outline of the Great Nirvāṇa.
It is precisely because of permanence, bliss, self, and purity that it is named the Great Nirvāṇa.

Good son, it is like the second illustration below. Regarding the ten illustrations presented above for comparison and application, seven are applied separately, while the remaining three are combined.
These three matters—the royal city, the earth, and the person—are combined into one;

these three matters are mutually inclusive, such that the king possesses the city and the city possesses the earth, their meanings and implications following one another. Furthermore, humans and devas are also combined therein.
In the section on "Separate Unions," the union with the ocean is explained first.
Noble son, just as there is a place capable of receiving all streams that is called the great ocean,
so too is Great Nirvāṇa named after the places entered by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgatas— namely, the four dhyānas and the three samādhis.
The eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the ten totalities— those who are able to encompass such immeasurable wholesome dharmas as these are called Great Nirvana.
Next, the confluence of rivers.
Good son, it is like a river whose bottom cannot be reached even by the foremost of fragrant elephants;
such is called the "Great Nirvana" of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. When bodhisattvas up to the tenth stage do not see the Buddha-nature, it is called nirvana, not the Great Nirvana.
If one can clearly perceive the Buddha-nature, then it is called the Great Nirvana. This is the Great Nirvana.
Only the Great Elephant King can fathom its depths; the "Great Elephant King" refers to the Buddhas.
Regarding the Mountain of Three Unions:
O Son of Good Family, even those such as Mahānāga and the great strongman Pāñcika, though they have passed through a long period of time...
That which cannot be ascended is called the Great Mountain;
that which cannot be seen by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are like great nāgas and mighty warriors—this is what is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Regarding Mahānāga-pakṣanti, the *Mahā-śāstra* states it means "Great Dragon," "Great Elephant," or "Wrestler among the Gods.
Emperor Liang Wudi translated it as "Supreme Bull.
This follows the fourth section on minor kings, which combines three similes: the Great King, the Great City, and so forth.
Furthermore, son of good family, wherever a minor king resides is called a small city; where a wheel-turning sage-king (cakravartin) resides is called a great city.
Where śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or those with eighty thousand, sixty thousand, forty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand [followers] reside is called nirvāṇa;
however, only where the Supreme Dharma-King, the Sage-King, resides can it truly be so named.
Because it is for the sake of the Great Parinirvāṇa, it is therefore named Great Parinirvāṇa.
This concludes the fourth section on the fourfold army; the fifth section combines with the preceding seventh analogy of sentient beings and great sentient beings.
Good son, it is like a person who, upon seeing the fourfold army, does not give rise to fear; you should know that such a person is called a "great being.

If there are sentient beings who do not give rise to fear toward the afflictions and evil karma of the three evil realms, and are able to extensively deliver sentient beings therein, you should know that such persons have attained Great Nirvana.
If there is anyone who can set aside the six [types of persons] and combine them with the two previous examples— the Great Man (mahāpuruṣa) and the Great Deva (mahādeva)—
if there is anyone who can make offerings to their parents, show reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, cultivate wholesome dharmas,
speak words that are truthful and free from deception, endure all evils, and practice generosity toward the poor and destitute, such a person is called a Great Man.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: possessing great compassion and pitying all beings as if they were his own parents, he is able to deliver sentient beings from the river of birth and death.
He universally shows sentient beings the single reality—the Great Path that leads downward [to liberation]—which was previously mentioned.
To universally demonstrate to all sentient beings the Way of the Single Reality is what is called Mahāparinirvāṇa. The term "Great" (Mahā) signifies the inconceivable.
This is the second [section], the explanation of Mahāparinirvāṇa, which is an explanation by way of transcending all dependencies (*atyantika-vyākhyā*).

It is further divided into two parts: first, the general explanation, and second, the specific explanation. Within the general explanation, there are again two parts: first, clarifying that it is ineffable.
Good son, its great name is inconceivable; that which is inconceivable cannot be believed in by any sentient beings, and it is therefore called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
It is seen only by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and for this reason it is named Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Next, it may be explained:
for what reasons and conditions is he further called "Great"? Because he attains [this state] only after immeasurable causes and conditions, he is called "Great.
Good son, it is like those people in the world who are called "great" because they have obtained something through many causes and conditions.
Nirvāṇa is likewise called "Great" because it is attained through many causes and conditions.

In the subsequent detailed explanation, only the three virtues (*triguṇa*) are mentioned without reference to "permanence" (*nitya*); this has two meanings: first, because permanence was already extensively clarified when the doctrine was established in the preceding section, it is omitted here;
second, as stated in the *Mingzi-pin* (Chapter on Names): "That which is called 'Great' is named..."
Regarding this "constancy," it further clarifies the "Great" (mahat) without further mentioning "constancy. Within the three virtues (triguṇa), each also has two aspects.

First, within the Great Self (mahātman), there are two: first, the inconceivable explanation of the Great; second, the explanation of the Great through manifold causes and conditions, which refers to that which is both expressible and inexpressible.
Why is it further called the Great Nirvāṇa? Because it possesses the Great Self (mahātman), it is called the Great Nirvāṇa.
Since Nirvāṇa is without self, its great sovereignty is termed the "Great Self. What is meant by "great sovereignty"?
There are eight kinds of sovereignty, which are then called the Self. What are these eight? First, the ability to manifest a single body as many bodies, according to the number of bodies [required].
The size [of these bodies] is like that of minute atoms, filling immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions;
yet the body of the Tathāgata is truly not composed of atoms, for by virtue of his sovereign mastery, he manifests a body of atoms. Such sovereignty is the Great Self (mahātman).
Second, he demonstrates a single atom-sized body filling the trichiliocosm; yet the body of the Tathāgata is truly not limited to filling it.
Why is it that the trichiliocosm [is filled]? Because it is unobstructed and because of its very sovereignty, it fills the trichiliocosm. Such sovereignty is called the "Great Self.
Third, one is able to take this body—which fills the trichiliocosm—and lightly lift it to fly through the air, passing beyond as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in twenty Ganges Rivers.
The body of the Tathāgata is unimpeded throughout all realms; in reality, it has neither lightness nor heaviness. Because of his sovereignty, he can manifest as either light or heavy.
Such sovereignty is called the "Great Self. Fourth, because of sovereignty, one attains mastery. What is meant by mastery?
It is that while the Tathāgata dwells with a single mind in immovable concentration, the various forms and types he manifests through transformation are each [innumerable].

The Tathāgata, possessing mastery over the mind, may at times perform a single act that causes sentient beings to each perceive the body of the Tathāgata as eternally abiding in a single land, yet visible in its entirety in all other lands;
such sovereignty is called the "Great Self. Fifth, because of mastery over the faculties (*indriya*), what is meant by mastery over the faculties? The Tathāgata, with a single...
The sense faculties are also able to see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, distinguish tastes, feel tangibles, and cognize dharmas.

However, the Tathāgata’s six faculties do not see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, distinguish tastes, feel tangibles, or cognize dharmas; because they possess mastery, they cause the faculties to be masterful.
Such mastery is called the "Great Self. Sixth, because of this mastery, one attains all dharmas as they truly are.
The mind that comes also has no notion of attainment. Why? Because there is nothing to be attained. If something existed, it could be called "attainment";
but since in reality nothing exists, how can it be called "attainment"? If the Tathāgata were to conceive a notion of attainment, then all Buddhas would not attain *nirvāṇa*.
It is because there is no attainment that one is said to "attain" *nirvāṇa*; it is because of mastery that one attains the One.
Because all phenomena attain all phenomena, it is called the "Great Self. Seventh, because of the teaching on mastery:
when the Tathāgata expounds the meaning of all things, even after immeasurable eons, the meaning is not exhausted.

That is to say, whether it be regarding precepts, concentration, generosity, or wisdom, at that time the Tathāgata does not give rise to the thought, "I am speaking" or "He is listening," nor does he produce even a single verse.
Regarding this perception: if worldly people compose four lines as a verse, they call it a "verse" (gāthā) merely in accordance with worldly convention.
The nature of all dharmas is such that there is no speaking; yet, because of his sovereign mastery, the Tathāgata expounds them, and because of this exposition, he is called the "Great Self.
Eighth, the Tathāgata pervades all places, just like space; [the nature of] space—
The nature [of reality] cannot be perceived; the Tathāgata is likewise truly invisible. Because of his sovereign mastery, he causes all to see him.
This sovereignty is called the "Great Self" (mahātman). This Great Self is called Great Nirvāṇa.
For this reason, it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
In the present text, it is stated that because there is a "Great Self" (mahātman), it is called Great Nirvāṇa;

yet elsewhere it is said that Nirvāṇa is without self (anātman). Regarding this, there have been two traditional interpretations: The first states that "without self" means that names are severed and one merges with the True [Suchness];

therefore, Nirvāṇa is without self. Because conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) employs provisional names, Nirvāṇa possesses a self. The second states that "without self" means that within Nirvāṇa, there is no self. There is nothing [there].
Regarding the deluded self of birth and death, those who hold to a "self" claim there is a self of permanence and bliss. The Master refutes these two interpretations:
if one were to sever names and merge with the True (the *tathatā*), then that which is called "non-self" (*anātman*) would likewise involve severing names and merging with the True;

consequently, it should be called "impermanence. His [the opponent's] explanation states: "One cannot attain impermanence, for Nirvana is permanent; therefore, because the four [attributes] are severed within the merging with the True, it is called 'non-existence' (*abhāva*)."

I further maintain that because the self is simultaneously dark and identical with the ultimate reality (zhen), it is beyond the four extremes; therefore, there is no impermanence [in the self] (and so forth). The opponent then objects:

"If you say there is neither birth nor death [for the self], then the self within birth and death must also be permanent. To this, I counter-objection: "Where could there be permanence within birth and death?
He should then be asked in return: "How can there be a self within birth and death? If he attempts to explain: "Birth..."
Regarding the claim that while there is no true self (*ātman*) at death, there is a provisional self (*prajñapti-ātman*), this is likewise untenable.

If [the self] were eternally unchanging or eternally continuous, then not only would there be no self that undergoes birth and death, but there would also be no continuity of birth and death; both [self and continuity] would be non-existent and infinite.
As for the eight masteries (*aṣṭa-vaśitā*): first, manyness; second, smallness; third, greatness; fourth, lightness and heaviness; fifth, form and mind; sixth, the sense faculties... [and so forth].
The attainment of the seven and the exposition of the eight views are as stated in the text.
Furthermore, it is like a treasure trove; this is the second explanation of how it is called the "Great Self" due to many causes and conditions.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a treasure trove that contains many rare and extraordinary things and is fully endowed with all varieties; therefore, it is called "Great."
The profound and secret treasury of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas is likewise thus: it contains many wonders, is complete and without deficiency, and is named Great Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, son of good family, that which is boundless is called Great Nirvāṇa;
because it is boundless, it is called "Great."
Next, regarding "Great Bliss," there are two parts: first, explaining the ineffable Great Bliss; second, from "The Worldly" onwards, explaining the Great Bliss of manifold causes and conditions.

In the initial passage, four types of bliss are explained. Within that, regarding the first type of bliss, there are three successive expositions clarifying the bliss that is neither suffering nor pleasure.
Furthermore, son of good family, because it possesses great bliss, it is called Great Nirvāṇa (*mahānirvāṇa*).
Nirvāṇa has no [ordinary] bliss; it is called Great Nirvāṇa by virtue of four kinds of bliss. What are these four? First, because all [worldly] pleasures have been severed.

That which does not sever pleasure is called suffering. If there were suffering, it would not be called Great Bliss. Because pleasure has been severed, there is no suffering. Since there is no suffering, [it is Great Bliss].
The absence of suffering and the presence of bliss is called the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). Since the nature of *nirvāṇa* is neither suffering nor bliss, *nirvāṇa* is named Great Bliss.
For this reason, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa. Furthermore, good son, there are two kinds of bliss:
first, that of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and second, that of the Buddhas. The bliss of ordinary beings is impermanent and subject to decay; therefore, it is not true bliss.
The Buddhas always delight in that which is unchanging; therefore, it is called Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). Furthermore, son of good family, there are three kinds of sensation (*vedanā*):
first, painful sensation; second, pleasant sensation; and third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation. This neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation is also considered suffering.
Although *nirvāṇa* is likewise neither-painful-nor-pleasant, it is called Great Bliss because it is Great Bliss.
It is called Great Nirvana.
Second, "great tranquility" (mahā-śānti) refers to the absence of both clamor and stillness; this is clarified as being called "tranquility" and designated as "bliss."
Second, because it is great tranquility, it is called the nature of Great Bliss Nirvana. Why is it great tranquility?
Because it is far removed from all clamorous phenomena; thus, through this great tranquility, it is named Great Nirvana.
Third, because it is neither knowledge nor non-knowledge, it is called "Great Knowledge," and this knowledge is termed "Bliss.
Thirdly, because it possesses all-knowingness (*sarvajñatā*), it is called "Great Bliss"; that which does not possess all-knowingness is not called Great Bliss.
Since the Buddhas and Tathāgatas possess all-knowingness, they are called Great Bliss; and because they possess Great Bliss, they are called Great Nirvāṇa.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the indestructible body:
because the four bodies are indestructible, they are called the Body of Great Bliss (*mahāsukhakāya*). If something were destructible, it would not be called bliss;
the Tathāgata’s body is adamantine and indestructible. It is not a body of afflictions nor a body of impermanence; therefore, it is called Great Bliss. Because it is great...
Because it is blissful, it is called Great Nirvāṇa.
It is precisely this body that is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa; therefore, its indestructibility is termed "Great Bliss.
Next, following the section on "worldly names," the second explanation concerns having causes and conditions, which is contrasted with being without conditions.

To explain this, the text is divided into two sections: one on having causes and conditions, and the next on being without causes and conditions. First, it clarifies that Nirvana possesses causes and conditions;
subsequently, it distinguishes that Nirvana is likewise without causes and conditions. This latter point is identical to the previous meaning of "transcending all dependencies."
Good son, worldly names are either based on causes and conditions or are without causes and conditions. Those with causes and conditions are, for example, Śāriputra:
his mother’s name was Śārī, and because he was named after his mother, he is called Śāriputra. Or like Maudgalyāyana:
he was born into the Maudgalya clan in the kingdom of Maudgalya, and because he was named after the kingdom, he is called Maudgalyāyana. Or like Maudgalyāyana [the disciple].
Maudgalyāyana is his clan name; because the name is established based on the clan, he is called Maudgalyāyana.

Just as I was born into the Gautama lineage and am called Gautama because the name is established based on the lineage, or as the practitioner Viśākha—Viśākha being the name of a lunar mansion—is named Viśākha because the name is derived from the asterism—or as one who has six fingers [is so named] because of that physical trait.
One is called "Six-Fingered" because they have six fingers; one is called "Buddha-Slave" or "Deva-Slave" because of the Buddha or the Deva;

one is called "Moisture-Born" because of moisture; and one is called "Kakara," "Kukura," or "Tatara" because of sound—such names as these are names based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-nāman*).
In the initial section on causes and conditions, it says: *kāka* is the sound of a crow; *kūku* is the sound of a rooster;
*tata* is the sound of a pheasant.
Regarding those without causes and conditions: they are like the lotus, earth, water, fire, wind, and space; they are like the *mandapa*, which has one name but two [meanings].
In reality, one thing has two names: it is called a "hall" and also a "drinking-hall. Even if one does not drink there, it is still appropriately named "Mandapa.

Just as that which is called a "serpent-canopy" (*sarpacchattra*) is actually not a serpent-canopy—this is an instance of establishing a name without a basis—it is like calling *Cilāpāyī* "oil-eater," even though she does not actually eat oil; this is merely a name established by force.
To call oil "food" is to forcibly establish a name where there is no cause;
good son, this Great Nirvāṇa is also like this—it has no causes or conditions, yet a name is forcibly established for it. Good son, it is like space:
one does not call it "great space" because of a small space. Nirvāṇa is likewise: it is not called "Great Nirvāṇa" because of small characteristics.
Next, regarding the "man-da" and others mentioned in the section on the absence of causes and conditions:
He Xi (the Master from Hexi) stated that *mandapā* is a single sound in the Sanskrit original referring to two things: first, a high seat or a dilapidated hall; second, medicinal decoctions.
Those who produced the sūtras refer to them as halls and grain-drinks. In the *Sarvāstivāda* tradition, it is said to resemble *qín* (celery); it is a single sound with two names: *dīrgha* and *pā*.
The *yī* (夷) is like the *myna* (*píngquè*); it is a single sound with two names.
Next, regarding the passage "There is a dharma that cannot be measured," the third section explains purity by way of the immeasurable.
"Good son, for example, there is a dharma that cannot be measured and cannot be conceived; therefore, it is called Great Nirvāṇa."
The term *parinirvāṇa* is likewise so called because it is immeasurable and inconceivable;
although there are many causes and conditions for this explanation in the initial commentary, the text here is merely abbreviated.
Next, it is called "Great" because of its absolute purity;
because of this absolute purity, it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
The meaning of "purity" will be explained later.
What is meant by "pure purity"? There are four kinds. What are the four? First, the twenty-five existents are called impure;
because they can be permanently severed, they are termed "pure. This purity is *nirvāṇa*.

Although this *nirvāṇa* may also be termed "existent," in reality, *nirvāṇa* is not existent. It is only in accordance with worldly convention that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas speak of *nirvāṇa* [as such].

There is an analogy for this: just as people in the world may call one who is not their father "father" or one who is not their mother "mother," speaking of them as parents when they are actually not, so too is *nirvāṇa*.
It is spoken of in accordance with worldly convention, saying that all Buddhas possess the Great *Nirvāṇa*.
Second, because the karma of all ordinary beings is impure, they lack *nirvāṇa*, whereas the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, [possess it] due to the purity of their karma.

First, because karma is pure, it is called "Great Purity"; because it is Great Purity, it is called "Great Nirvana. Second, because the body is pure, it is called "Great Purity"; if the body were impermanent, it would be called impure, but since the Tathāgata’s body is eternal, it is called Great Purity; because it is Great Purity, it is called Great Nirvana.
