The second volume begins, clarifying the second merit. Regarding the individual explanations of the ten merits, it is said that while the first merit has five matters as its essence, this present merit has the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) as its essence. Now, it is stated that this is not so;
since this text says, "Because of the majestic power of having attained Great Nirvāṇa," one should know that all ten merits have [that same essence].
Taking *nirvāṇa* as its essence, it is differentiated into various distinct bodies according to specific circumstances; these bodies should correspond to the fundamental [nature].

How could one speak of the ten virtues and five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) based on mere branches and offshoots? Whether they be ten or five, these are all discussed in terms of differentiation within the state of non-differentiation.
As for the old claim that the first virtue is profound while the second virtue is shallow, this should not be so.
The Master [Zhiyi] expanded upon this using four propositions, which people consider profound; herein, he speaks directly, which people consider shallow.

If one wishes to expand this into four propositions, it is not "attaining" or "not attaining," nor is it "neither attaining nor not attaining," but rather "attaining through neither attaining nor not attaining.

This applies to all other chapters as well—how could there be anything shallow about it? (And so forth. The ancients said that the Mahāyāna differs from the Hīnayāna, and only the Buddha [can fully realize it].

A Bodhisattva who possesses the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is so designated because of their causal basis; thus, they possess only the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and are not said to have the exhaustion of outflows.
This is a provisional way of yielding the fruit to the cause. However, in a complete discussion, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses the true divine eye (*divyacakṣus*);

he does not perceive the Buddha-lands through two [limited] marks. Regarding the knowledge of others' minds and past lives, these ultimately reside in the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Since this is so...

If one has attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), why does it not say that one has attained the untainted (*anāsrava*)? Although this text lists five chapters, the six supernormal powers are implicitly complete within them.
Previously, "attaining what was unattainable" was used as a general heading for the five supernormal powers; now it is said that this is not so.
"Attaining what was unattainable" refers to attaining Great Nirvāṇa (*mahāparinirvāṇa*). Great Nirvāṇa is the Middle Way Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), which is not tainted (*anāsrava*).

Because it is not the "outflow-free" (anāsrava) of the outflow-free [in the conventional sense], the text states that what is not of the non-Buddhists is not "with outflows" (sāsrava), and what is not of the Two Vehicles is not "outflow-free";
yet, by saying one attains Great Nirvāṇa, it refers to that which is neither with outflows nor outflow-free—the outflow-free [in its ultimate sense]. The commentary explains:
"What is called 'supernatural power' (abhijñā) is not like the supernatural powers of the eighteen transformations of the Lesser Vehicle; 'shen' (神) is the name for [this] power."
The "Heavenly Mind" is generally termed the "nature of wisdom"; this innate wisdom is precisely the Middle Way, free from the two extremes and untainted, and is named Great Nirvana.
Pointing to this as the universal state of being untainted, I privately remark that by examining these ten virtues, they all testify to the initial passage.
Since there is already knowledge of the secret treasury, how could one be unable to partially realize the six supernatural powers? Thus, we know these are indeed virtues.
The texts all interpenetrate one another, being distinct yet not separate; thus, while the ten characteristics differ, they are non-different.

They are identical within *nirvāṇa*, and therefore there is no error even when correlating them with the stages (*bhūmi*). How much more so regarding the meaning of the ten stages, which is common to both the Perfect (*yuan*) and the Separate (*bie*):
they are non-different yet distinct, which is the meaning of the Separate; they are not distinct yet distinct, which is the meaning of the Perfect. If one relies upon this...

Explaining the four fetters:
Furthermore, good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa so as to achieve and fulfill the second merit?
Good son, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the Great Nirvāṇa, that which was previously unattained is now attained;
that which was previously unseen is now seen; that which was previously unheard is now heard;
that which was previously unreached is now reached; and that which was previously unknown is now known.
Since the names of these two sets of six differ from those of the Hīnayāna, one should know that these six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are not shared with them.

Although the individual names are explained differently in this text, they are nonetheless referred to here as the "six supernormal powers. That which is attained where there was nothing to attain is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*);

that which is heard where there was nothing to hear is the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-abhijñā*); and that which is seen where there was nothing to see is the [supernormal power of the divine eye].

The supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-abhijñā*) reaching what is not reached is the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-vidhi-abhijñā*); knowing what is unknown is the two supernormal powers of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) and recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).
Third, the explanation of the text consists of five parts; however, the arrangement of the headings and the explanation do not quite follow the sequence, as the context requires it.

It is precisely because they are not the same that it is so. Regarding the first [section], the chapter on "Attaining What Was Not Previously Attained," there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the detailed clarification and manifestation;
third, the conclusion.
What is meant by "attaining now what was not previously attained"? It refers to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) which were not previously attained.
Now it is only here that [the true meaning] is attained.
"Manifestation" (*biao*) refers to the manifestation of spiritual powers (*abhijñā*); these spiritual powers are the natural principle of the Great Parinirvāṇa.

Because this principle is pervasive, sovereign, and unimpeded, it is called "spiritual power. Although the names are the same, the underlying principles are eternally distinct; therefore, [the former] is excluded for the sake of clarification.
Since all small [attainments] manifest the Middle Way as complete and sovereign, one knows that only when the outflows are exhausted is it called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
From this power, there are two kinds of "going"; these are distinguished and clarified, and thus constitute the two headings for the explanation.
There are two kinds of penetration: first, the internal; second, the external. In the explanation, there are two parts:
first, the exclusion of what is not [the path]; second, the manifestation of what is.

Regarding that which is called "external," it is shared with non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Furthermore, the "internal" is twofold: first, the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas); second, bodhisattvas.
The supernormal powers attained by a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Why are they said to be not shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas? Because the supernormal powers and transformations produced by those of the two vehicles are performed with a single mind to produce a single result, and cannot produce many.
First, the non-middle is excluded; this immediately excludes the outsiders and those of the two vehicles, as the text states.
To reveal what it is, there are two points: first, it clarifies that within a single mind, supernatural powers are perfected and fully complete, as the text states.
The Bodhisattva is not like that; within a single moment of mind, he is able to fully manifest bodies in the five realms of existence.
Why is this? It is because he has attained the majestic spiritual power of this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra. This is what is called "that which was previously unobtainable, now obtained."

Second, the manifestation of the perfection of mastery over body and mind: its essence is explained through the completeness of its perfection, and its function is clarified through the excellence of its mastery.
Within the text concerning mastery, there are further two parts; first, the exclusion of that which lacks mastery.
Furthermore, what is it that was previously unattained but is now attained—namely, mastery over the body and mastery over the mind? Why is this so?
Because all ordinary beings lack mastery over their own body and mind; either the mind follows the body, or the body follows the mind.
What is meant by "the mind following the body"? It is like a drunken person whose wine has entered his body.
At that time, when the body moves, the mind also moves accordingly; likewise, when the body is weary, the mind also becomes weary accordingly—this is called the mind following the body.
Furthermore, it is like an infant whose body is small and its mind also follows as small; when an adult’s body is large, the mind also follows as large.
It is also like a person whose body is coarse and rough, yet whose mind constantly thinks of desiring to obtain unguents.
To soak [the body] with oil and moisture so that it becomes supple is what is called "the mind following the body. What is meant by "the body following the mind"? It is as follows:
when one who practices going, coming, sitting, lying down, giving, morality, patience, diligence, or who is afflicted by grief and distress, the body becomes emaciated;
when one is joyful, the body becomes plump and radiant; and when one is terrified, the body trembles. This is focused [on the mind].
When the mind hears the Dharma-body, it becomes joyful; when it encounters those in sorrow and suffering, tears flow profusely. This is what is called "the body following the mind.
Next, the mastery [of this] is explained.
The Bodhisattva is not like that; he attains mastery over both body and mind.
The third concluding sentence is easily understood:
this is what is called "that which was previously unattained but is now attained."

Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of bodily forms, the following two explanations do not reach the section on "reaching the non-reachable. This refers to the textual passage on the supernormal power of the body (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*), which consists of three parts:
first, manifesting arrival at a distance.
Furthermore, son of good family, the bodily forms manifested by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva are like motes of dust. By means of this...
With a subtle body, one is able to reach all immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges without any obstruction,
yet the mind remains constantly in samādhi, never shifting; this is called "the mind does not follow the body," and it is also called "that which was previously unreachable is now reached."
Second, distinguishing it from the two vehicles.
Why is it further called "that which was previously unattainable but is now attainable"?
Because all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others cannot reach it, whereas bodhisattvas can reach it; therefore, it is called "that which was previously unattainable but is now attainable."

Although all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others cannot transform their bodies into subtle atoms to pervade immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges through their supernormal powers—and when the bodies of these śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas move, their minds move along with them—the Bodhisattva is not like this;
although his mind does not move, there is nowhere his body does not reach. This is called a Bodhisattva.
The mind does not follow the body. Furthermore, son of good family, a Bodhisattva’s transformation body may be as vast as the trichiliocosm;
yet when this great body enters into a single atom-sized body, his mind at that time does not likewise become small.
Although a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha can manifest a transformation body as large as the trichiliocosm, they cannot [do so] with such a [vast] [mind].
When the body enters into a minute particle, even within such a state the body itself cannot remain so; how much less could it prevent the mind from moving along with it?
This is called the Bodhisattva’s mind not following the body.
The mastery of the three knowledges (*trividyā*) is as described in the text.
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, with a single sound, to cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to hear it;
yet his mind never thinks of making that sound pervade all worlds so that...

Sentient beings have not heard what they have never heard before, yet now they hear it; however, this bodhisattva does not say from the very beginning, "I have caused sentient beings to hear what they have not heard before.

If a bodhisattva were to say, "By means of my teaching of the Dharma, I have caused sentient beings to hear what they had not heard," one should know that such a person will ultimately never attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Regarding the three types of awakening (*trividhabodhi*): why is it that sentient beings do not hear me preach? Such a thought is the mind of birth-and-death (*saṃsāracitta*).
All bodhisattvas have already exhausted this mind; for this reason, the body and mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva do not follow one another.
Good son, the body and mind of all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) follow one another, whereas those of a bodhisattva do not.
It is not so; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, although he manifests a small body, his mind is not small.
Why? Because the nature of the minds of all Bodhisattvas is always vast and great. Although he manifests a large body, his mind is not large.
What is meant by a "large body"? A body such as that of the trichiliocosm. What is meant by a "small mind"? Practicing the conduct of an infant. For this reason...
Because of this principle, the mind does not follow the body. A bodhisattva has, for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, abstained from drinking alcohol;
yet their mind may still be stirred. Their mind may feel no sorrow or suffering, yet tears may flow from their body. They may truly have no fear, yet their body may tremble.
For this reason, it should be known that the body and mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are sovereign and do not follow one another.
Śāriputra manifests only a single body, yet all sentient beings each perceive it differently.
Furthermore, good son, the following three explanations clarify how one hears what was not previously heard; this refers to the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*).

The text is divided into two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the discussion of the meaning. The explanation consists of four sections: first, cultivation; second, attainment; third, discernment; and fourth, non-attachment.
The first two points are as stated in the text.
Good son, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa such that what was previously unheard is now heard?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva first grasps the characteristics of sounds—namely, the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and humans.
One practices by means of the sounds of conchs, drums, flutes, pipes, songs, and other such instruments.
Through this practice, one is able to hear all the sounds of the hells throughout immeasurable trichiliocosm worlds.
Furthermore, through further cultivation, one attains a divine ear-faculty that is distinct from that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?

The pure supernormal power of the ear attained by those of the Two Vehicles, if based upon the pure and subtle four great elements of the first dhyāna, hears only the first dhyāna and does not hear the second, third, or fourth dhyānas;
it is likewise for all others. Although they can at one time hear throughout the three thousand [great thousandfold worlds],...
One cannot hear any sounds within a thousand-world system, nor can one hear the sounds of worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable and boundless Ganges Rivers;
for this reason, what the Bodhisattva attains regarding the faculty of hearing differs from that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Because of this difference, what was previously unheard is now heard.

The third passage states: "Furthermore, by further cultivating practice, one attains a distinct faculty of hearing. This clarifies that what is attained through cultivation is entirely distinct from that of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
"Further cultivation" refers precisely to the mind of Great Nirvāṇa—a cultivation characterized by non-obstruction and sovereign mastery.

Furthermore, although sounds are heard, there is no characteristic of sound; this is called "attaining a distinct faculty of hearing through further cultivation," as it does not accord with the Lesser Vehicle.
Together.
Although they hear sounds, their minds from the very beginning possess no characteristic of hearing sound;
they do not form notions of existence, permanence, pleasure, self, purity, lordship, dependence, agency, causality, fixedness, or result. For this reason, [it is called "together"].
The various bodhisattvas, who had not heard this before, now hear it for the first time.

In the fourth section on "Non-attachment," it says: "Regarding the characteristics of the substratum and the supported, they differ from the *dravya* (substance) and *guṇa* (quality) of the non-Buddhists, which do not function as the characteristics of producing effects.

This means that [in our system] meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is not treated as the cause and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as the effect, thereby distinguishing [the Buddhist view] from [the non-Buddhist].
The remaining minor details can be seen in the text.
At that time, following the descent of the light, the second section on doctrinal discussion consists of two rounds of question and answer; the first question is divided into two parts:
the first is the reception of the essential meaning and the subsequent expression of dissent.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of High and Noble Virtue, Universally Radiant, said:
"As the Buddha has taught—that one should not form fixed notions of characteristics nor notions of results—this meaning is not so."
Why is this? Below, two difficulties are raised. The first difficulty concerns "wholesome sound.

Why is this? Previously, the Tathāgata stated that if a person hears even a single phrase or a single word of this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; yet now the Tathāgata further says there is no such certainty.
If one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* when there is no fruit, that itself is a mark of certainty and a mark of fruition;
why then do you say there is neither certainty nor fruition?
The two difficulties and evil sounds both constitute obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because one hears evil sounds, an unwholesome mind arises; because an unwholesome mind arises, one reaches the three miserable realms (*trāya*).
If one reaches the three miserable realms, this is the fruit of meditative concentration. How, then, can you say that there is no concentration and no fruit?
The Buddha’s response consists of two parts: first, praising the question; second, the actual answer.
At that time, the Tathāgata praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You are able to ask such a question. The answer also has two parts:
first, a general response; second, a detailed response. Regarding the first, the general response, there are again two sections: first, [the teaching that] all are indeterminate; second...

Furthermore, it clarifies that concentration (*samādhi*) is indeed concentration within the indeterminate; in the first two sections, there are two layers, each of which first presents the principle (*dharma*), then provides an analogy, and finally offers a conclusion.
If the Buddhas were to say that various sounds possess the characteristics of a fixed fruit of concentration, then they would not be the World-Honored Buddhas.
Characteristics are the characteristics of the Mara-king and the characteristics of birth-and-death; they are far removed from the characteristics of Nirvana. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas, in whatever they proclaim, do not have fixed characteristics of fruition.
Son of good family, it is like a person’s reflection appearing in a blade of steel: if held vertically, one sees it as long; if held horizontally, one sees it as broad. If...
If there were fixed characteristics, how could it be that when viewed vertically one sees length, yet when viewed horizontally one sees breadth?
For this reason, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught that all phenomena lack fixed resultant characteristics.
Good son, as for nirvāṇa, it is truly not the fruit of sound. If nirvāṇa were the fruit of sound, you should know that nirvāṇa would not be an eternal dharma.
Good son, for example, in the world, dharmas produced from causes exist when there is a cause and do not exist when there is no cause.
Because the cause is impermanent, the fruit is also impermanent. Why is this? Because the cause also acts as the fruit, and the fruit also acts as the cause.
For this reason, all phenomena possess no fixed characteristic.
If Nirvana were produced from a cause, then because the cause is impermanent, the fruit would also be impermanent; yet Nirvana is not produced from a cause, for its essence is not [conditioned].
Because it is a fruit, it is therefore permanent.
Son of good family, for this reason, the essence of nirvāṇa is neither fixed nor a fruit.
Son of good family, as for nirvāṇa, it may be called "fixed" and it may also be called a "fruit. What is meant by "fixed"? First:
All Buddhas possess nirvana, which is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, it is certain. It is free from birth, old age, and decay;

therefore, it is certain. Even those such as icchantikas who have committed the four grave offenses, slandered the Vaipulya sutras, or committed the five heinous crimes will certainly attain it once they abandon their original [evil] intentions; therefore, it is certain.
Next, as you have requested, I shall provide a separate answer in two parts; first, I shall answer regarding the "wholesome sound.

Good son, as you have said—that if a person hears even a single word or a single phrase of my teaching on the Great Nirvāṇa and thereby attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—you have not yet fully understood this meaning. You now...

Listen attentively; I shall further explain this for you in detail. Good son, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing even a single word or a single phrase of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, do not form a perception of words, do not form a perception of phrases, do not form a perception of hearing, do not form a perception of the Buddha, and do not form a perception of the teaching—if such is their understanding, it is called the "mark of marklessness. Because it is markless, it is so named.
One attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of signs.
Next, he answers regarding evil sounds:
"Good son, as for what you have said—that because one hears evil sounds one goes to the three miserable realms—that is not the case."
For this reason, one should know that it is not because of evil sounds that one arrives at the three miserable realms; rather, these fruits are the result of an evil mind.
Why is this so? Because there are sons and daughters of good family who, even upon hearing evil sounds, do not give rise to an evil mind.

Therefore, one should know that it is not because of evil sounds that one is born within the three lower destinies, but rather that sentient beings are [born there] due to the fetters of afflictions and an evil mind.
It is not because of evil sounds that many are born into the three evil realms;

rather, if sound possessed a fixed characteristic, then all who heard it would necessarily give rise to an evil mind. Yet some do so while others do not. Therefore, one should know that sound has no fixed characteristic.
Because it lacks a fixed characteristic, even though one encounters it, an evil mind is not produced.
To clarify the underlying cause, it is not that a malicious mind is unrelated to malicious sounds;
rather, since the World-Honored One’s voice is not fixed [in its nature], the second round of question and answer follows as in the text—first the question, then the answer.
“World-Honored One, if sound were not determinate, how could it be that what Bodhisattvas have never heard before is now heard?
Good son, because sound has no fixed characteristic, that which was not heard by Bodhisattvas in the past is now heard by them.
For this reason, I say: ‘That which was not heard before is now heard.’”
Good son, the following four sections explain "seeing by not seeing," which refers to the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). The text consists of six parts:
first, cultivation; second, attainment; third, distinction; fourth, non-attachment; fifth, clarifying the distinct knowledge; and sixth, the conclusion.
"Good son, what is it that was not seen before but is now seen by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who cultivates the subtle and wondrous Sutra of the Great Nirvana?
It is first the appearance of light, namely: the light of the sun, moon, stars, and constellations;
the light of courtyard lamps, lanterns, candles, pearls, fire, and medicinal herbs."
Through cultivation, one attains a distinct faculty of the eye.
How does this differ from what is attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas?

It differs in that the pure divine eye attained by those of the two vehicles cannot see the first dhyāna if it relies on the eye-faculty derived from the four great elements of the desire realm, nor can it see higher stages if it relies on the first dhyāna.

Even with their own eyes they cannot see; yet if they wish to see more extensively, up to the extent of a trichiliocosm, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have not cultivated the divine eye perceive all those with exquisite physical forms as being entirely skeletal in appearance.

Although one sees the forms and appearances of worlds in other directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one does not perceive them as forms, nor as permanent phenomena, nor as signs of existence, nor as substantial objects, nor as names and such, nor as signs of causes and conditions, nor as signs of perception.

One does not say that this eye is a subtle and pure phenomenon; rather, one perceives only the signs of conditions and non-conditions. What are the causal conditions for form being the object-condition of the eye?
If this form were not conditioned by causes and conditions, then all ordinary beings would not give rise to the perception of the appearance of form.

For this reason, form is said to be conditioned by causes and conditions. That which is not conditioned by causes and conditions means that although a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees form, they do not give rise to the conceptual mark of form;
therefore, it is not [subject to] conditions. For this reason, the pure celestial [vision] attained by the Bodhisattva—
The eye of the Bodhisattva differs from that attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;

because it is thus different, they simultaneously see all the Buddhas currently present throughout the worlds of the ten directions—this is called what the Bodhisattva has not seen before but now sees.
Because it is thus different, they are able to see even a single mote of dust, which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot see. Because it is thus different, although they see themselves...

The eye initially lacks the characteristic of seeing; it sees the characteristic of impermanence and sees that the body of an ordinary person is filled with the impurities of the thirty-six constituents, as if viewing an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand. For this reason, what was previously unseen is now seen.
If one perceives the physical forms of sentient beings, one knows their capacities for the Great or Small Vehicles;
by a single touch of their robes, one also knows the distinctions between their wholesome and unwholesome faculties.
For this reason, that which was previously unknown is now known through this single vision; that which was previously unknown is now known through this single vision.
In several instances here, it is clearly understood that this is not "subsequent knowledge" (*pṛṣṭhajñāna*), but rather "borrowed knowledge" (*prajñaptijñāna*) used to clarify what is seen.
Because of this borrowed knowledge, that which was previously unseen is now seen.
The concluding passage subsequently borrows the phrasing of "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*) to assist in the conclusion, because [the former] is not shared [with other types of knowledge].

Good son, how is it that the five lower explanations of "not knowing yet knowing" constitute the two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of reading others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) and recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), forming four sections?
First, knowing others' minds; second, knowing past lives; third, a further clarification of knowing others' minds; fourth, the conclusion based on these meanings.
Regarding the first, knowing others' minds, there are again two parts: first, the preliminary knowledge of others' minds.
Good son, how is it that a bodhisattva knows now what was previously unknown?

Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the minds of greed, anger, and delusion of ordinary beings, he does not initially form the conceptualization of mind or mental factors, nor does he form the conceptualization of sentient beings or of things;
he cultivates the mark of the ultimate emptiness of the primary truth. Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas are constantly...
Because one has well cultivated the characteristics of emptiness and practiced emptiness, that which was previously unknown is now known. What is this knowledge?
It is the knowledge that there is no self and nothing belonging to a self.
Next, one knows the Buddha-nature (and so forth).

Knowing that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and because of this Buddha-nature, even those such as icchantikas who have abandoned their original resolve shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; all such [teachings] belong to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
That which the Śrāvakas cannot know, the Bodhisattvas can know; for this reason, what was previously unknown is now known.
Furthermore, regarding the two types of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), there are two parts: first, the actual explanation of the knowledge of past lives.
Furthermore, good son, how is it that what was previously unknown is now known? It is when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva,
practicing the subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, recollects all sentient beings of the past,
including their various castes, parents, brothers, wives, children, kinsmen, friends, and enemies.
Next, one contemplates the past; this is distinguished from what precedes it and may be understood by analogy, so it is not explained in full detail here.
Within a single moment of thought, one attains a distinct and extraordinary wisdom that differs from the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. How does it differ?
The wisdom possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas consists of recollecting the lineages, fathers, and mothers of all sentient beings in the past.
Even regarding those who are hateful or hostile, one might conceive of them as having the characteristics of a lineage or as being objects of hatred; however, a bodhisattva is not like this.
Although they contemplate their past lineage, parents, and even those who are hateful or hostile, they never give rise to the conceptual signs of lineage, parents, or hostility.
They constantly cultivate the sign of the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena. This is called that which the bodhisattva did not previously know, but now knows.
Furthermore, how does one explain the three lower levels of knowing the minds of others? This is further divided into two parts: first, knowing the six realms of existence horizontally;
second, "Good son, how is it that what was previously unknown is now known?
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtra, he attains the knowledge of others' minds, which differs from that attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

What is the difference? When Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas employ the wisdom of a single thought-moment to know the minds of human beings, they are unable to know the minds of those in the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, or devas. It is not so for the Bodhisattva;

within a single thought-moment, he universally knows the minds of sentient beings throughout the six realms of existence. This is called that which the Bodhisattva did not previously know, but now knows.
Next, one sequentially knows the sixteen moments of mind.

Furthermore, son of good family, there is another way of knowing: the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows within a single moment of mind the initial mind of a srotāpanna, proceeding sequentially through to the sixteenth moment of mind.

This passage clarifies the meaning of the "sixteen moments of mind" (*ṣoḍaśa-citta*) as explained in the *Fushun Shu Yi Lun* (Treatise on the Sequence of Supportive Accordance), which states that the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) consists of immeasurable moments of mind;

yet because these moments are swift and sharp, they are termed "uninterrupted moments" (*ānantarya-citta*). The *Cheng Lun* (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya) further explains: if a Śrāvaka wishes to know the third moment of mind, he must perceive all sixteen moments;
if a Pratyekabuddha wishes to know the third moment of mind, he must perceive up to the seventh moment; only a Bodhisattva is capable of knowing them all at once.
Knowing that the faculties of those in the Hīnayāna are dull, one wishes to know the coming and going of the third mind and intends to infer the subsequent minds;
having already reached the sixteenth mind, the person of the Hīnayāna who possesses slight benefit knows the departure of the third mind,
whereas the Bodhisattva does not do so, knowing them all simultaneously as they follow one another, such that there is not a single mind that is not known.
To know this is the common doctrine of the Three Vehicles; yet while there are three distinct types of persons, they all share these same sixteen moments of mind.

This, however, is not the intended meaning of the present sutra. Prior knowledge of the six realms of existence constitutes knowing the finite; the subsequent sixteen moments of mind constitute knowing the infinite.
It is through the essence of the Middle Way—neither existent nor non-existent—that one is able to know both existence and non-existence.
For this reason, that which was previously unknown is now known.
This constitutes the second merit fully accomplished by a bodhisattva practicing the Great Nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, the following clarifies the third merit. The old translation states: "This section explains how loving-kindness (*maitrī*) fulfills the aforementioned Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*)," and so forth.
Within this, there is first a formal statement and then an explanation.
Furthermore, good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa so as to achieve and fulfill the third merit?
In the explanation, there are two parts: first the explanation, then the conclusion. Regarding the first, the explanation: the meaning here is that the merits within this context should be complete.

Regarding the clarification of the four immeasurable minds, while the text specifically clarifies loving-kindness (*maitrī*), there are two interpretations: first, it is said that this is merely a textual abbreviation and the meaning should be understood as including all four;
second, since loving-kindness is the very root of all wholesome dharmas, for what reason could it not be identical to the other three minds?

As for the statement that "equanimity (*upekṣā*) alone attains perfection," by citing one, the other three are known; thus, they are omitted in brief. The commentary on the text is divided into two parts: first, the proclamation of what is abandoned and what is attained.
Second, the sequential explanation of the gateways:

Good son, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the Great Parinirvāṇa, he abandons compassion and attains compassion; at the time of attaining compassion, it does not arise from causes and conditions.
In the commentary, first the inquiry is raised and then it is explained.
What is meant by "abandoning loving-kindness and attaining loving-kindness"?
In the explanation, there are five sections in total; the first concerns the two truths (*satya*).

Good son, "compassion" refers to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas relinquish compassion as conventional truth, they attain the compassion of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
This compassion of the ultimate meaning is not obtained through conditions.
Next, [the classification] is made according to ordinary beings and sages.
Furthermore, how is it that one abandons loving-kindness and attains loving-kindness? If loving-kindness could be abandoned, it would be called the loving-kindness of an ordinary being;
if loving-kindness can be attained, it is called the objectless loving-kindness (*anālambana-maitrī*) of a bodhisattva.
Third, regarding the icchantikas in contrast to the Tathāgata, these are categorized as good and evil:

the compassion that abandons the icchantika; the compassion that violates the grave prohibitions; the compassion that slanders the Vaipulya sutras; the compassion that commits the five heinous crimes; the compassion that attains pity;
the compassion that attains the Tathāgata’s compassion; the World-Honored One’s compassion; and compassion without causes or conditions.
Fourth, regarding the contrast between the base and the Bodhisattva, this constitutes the distinction between the inferior and the superior.

Furthermore, what is meant by "abandoning compassion and attaining compassion"? It means abandoning the compassion of eunuchs, the compassion of those without sexual organs or those with dual sexual organs, the compassion of women, the compassion of butchers, slaughterers, hunters, poultry-raisers, pig-breeders, and so forth; it also means abandoning the compassion of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
They attain the objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) of all bodhisattvas.
They are free from the five attachments:

they do not perceive their own compassion, nor do they perceive the compassion of others; they do not perceive those who maintain the precepts, nor do they perceive those who break them—even when perceiving their own pity.
One does not perceive sentient beings, nor does one perceive a feeler of suffering, even though such feeling exists. Why? Because one has cultivated the supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The subsequent conclusion follows the text.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Great Nirvāṇa, achieving and fulfilling the third merit.
Next, the fourth merit is explained in two parts: first, the explanation of the merit; second, the discussion of its meaning. The first part has four sections: first, the heading;
second, the listing of the topical gates; third, the explanation; and fourth, the conclusion.
Furthermore, good son, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the Great Parinirvāṇa so as to achieve and fulfill the fourth merit?
Good son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the Great Parinirvāṇa to achieve and fulfill the fourth merit.
There are ten matters. What are these ten? First, the roots are deep and difficult to uproot. Second, one gives rise to the thought of certainty within oneself.
Third, one does not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit. Fourth, one cultivates the purification of Buddha-lands.
Fifth, one eliminates what remains. Sixth, one severs the conditions of karma. Seventh, one cultivates a pure body. Eighth, one realizes...

9) Knowing all conditions; 10) being free from all adversaries; and 11) severing the two extremes. Yecheng says: "The first two refer to the stages prior [to the first bhūmi], while the latter eight correspond to the eight bhūmis. The preceding statement regarding 'deep roots' refers to the stage of nature (xingdi), which is also the mind of certainty regarding the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) upon entering the initial reliance. The latter eight refer to the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā). Regarding the first [of these eight]: *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The following is a reconstruction based on the context of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* or similar treatises on the ten stages.* [The first stage] is characterized by the realization that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature, thereby transcending all conceptual proliferation. It is the foundation for the subsequent stages, wherein one cultivates the path of non-duality and attains mastery over the dharmadhātu. By severing the bonds of ignorance and attachment, one enters the stream of the noble ones and becomes irreversible from the ultimate goal. This stage is called the "Joyful" (*pramuditā*) because it marks the beginning of the bodhisattva's true engagement with the Mahāyāna path, where one rejoices in the liberation of all sentient beings. Through this realization, one transcends the mundane realms and establishes oneself firmly in the supramundane state. Thus, the practitioner who has attained this stage is said to have "entered the first reliance," having fully integrated the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena into their very being. This is the essence of the first bhūmi. As for the remaining seven stages, they represent the progressive refinement of this initial realization, culminating in the perfection of all qualities and the attainment of omniscience. Each stage corresponds to a specific set of practices and purifications, ensuring that the bodhisattva remains steadfast in their commitment to the welfare of others while maintaining unshakable concentration and insight. Together, these stages constitute the complete path to buddhahood.

Therefore, one should understand that the cultivation of the ten stages is not merely a sequence of meditative states, but a comprehensive transformation of one's entire mode of existence, rooted in the profound conviction of the two-fold emptiness. This is the definitive teaching on the progression through the ten bhūmis. Thus concludes the exposition of the first stage. As for the second stage, it is characterized by the purification of ethical conduct and the removal of all subtle defilements that obscure the light of wisdom. It is here that the bodhisattva truly masters the dharma of discipline and becomes a model of virtuous conduct for all beings. This stage is called the "Immaculate" (*vimalā*). [The text continues in this manner through the remaining stages. *Note: The original Chinese fragment appears to be a commentary on a summary of the ten stages, specifically addressing the transition from the preparatory stages to the formal bhūmis and the significance of the two types of emptiness.*
The view that "observing the field of merit" corresponds to the first bhūmi where *dāna* is perfected, and "severing the two extremes" corresponds to the eighth bhūmi, is incorrect;
rather, both are now explained as merits of true realization.
Why is the root deep? Below this is the third explanation, wherein the fifth and sixth [sections] are combined into a single exposition.
The commentary on the first chapter is divided into three parts: the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion.
It asks: "Why is the root deep and difficult to uproot?
Regarding the first matter, five meanings are fully present: first, the root is fundamental; second, the root is deep; third, the root is broad; fourth, the root is long.
The five faculties and supreme heedfulness are the very root.
That which is called a "faculty" is named heedfulness (*apramāda*).
If discussed in general terms, all the practice of wholesome deeds is heedfulness; if discussed specifically, it consists of first examining the mind as heedfulness.
Heedlessness takes these two intentions as its root.
Next, regarding the root of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this is a deep root.
What is the root of heeding (*apramāda*)? It is the so-called root of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because it profoundly exhausts the true nature (*dharmatā*) and reaches its ultimate limit, it is truly the root of *bodhi*; thus it is called "profound.
Because all roots of goodness of all Buddhas consist in non-negligence (*apramāda*), it is the "extensive" root.
Good son, the roots of all goodness of all Buddhas consist entirely of non-negligence (*apramāda*).
Because it causes growth— just as when a root grows—
through non-negligence, all other roots of goodness increase progressively.
That which is supreme among all virtues is the supremacy of the roots, for it is able to increase all roots of virtue; thus, among all virtues, it is the most distinguished.
Noble son, just as the elephant’s footprint is the foremost among all footprints, so too is the dharma of heedfulness the foremost among all wholesome dharmas.
O noble son, just as among all lights the radiance of the sun is supreme,
so too is the dharma of heedfulness (apramāda) the most excellent among all wholesome dharmas. O noble son,
just as among all kings the Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin-rāja) is the foremost, so too is the dharma of heedfulness the foremost among all wholesome dharmas.
"Good son, just as among all flowing waters the four great rivers are supreme,
so too is the dharma of heedfulness (apramāda) supreme and foremost among all wholesome dharmas. Good son, just as among all mountains Mount Sumeru,
the king of mountains, is the very first and most excellent, so too is the dharma of heedfulness the very first and most excellent among all wholesome dharmas."
