Just as among all beasts the lion is the foremost, so too is the dharma of heedfulness the most supreme and excellent among all wholesome dharmas,
O son of good family. Just as among all flying birds the king of golden-winged birds is the most supreme and excellent,
so too is the dharma of heedfulness the most supreme and excellent among all wholesome dharmas, O son of good family.
Just as Rāhu, the Asura King, is the foremost and supreme among those with great bodies,
so too is the dharma of heedfulness the foremost and supreme among all wholesome dharmas. Son of good family, just as the Tathāgata is the foremost among all sentient beings—
whether they have two feet, four feet, many feet, or no feet— so too is the dharma of heedfulness the foremost.
Just as, among all assemblies, the Buddha and the Sangha are supreme, O son of good family,
so too is the dharma of heedfulness supreme among all wholesome dharmas; just as, within the Buddha-dharma,
the dharma of Great Nirvana is supreme, O son of good family, so too is the dharma of heedfulness supreme among all [wholesome dharmas].
Because wholesome dharmas are supreme and unsurpassed, O son of good family, for this reason the root of heedfulness is deep and firm,
difficult to uproot.
In all, thirteen similes are cited to illustrate its superior characteristics.
What is meant by "non-negligence"? Briefly stated, there are ten roots; to explain these roots in detail:

how does one achieve growth through non-negligence? It is said that it is through the root of faith, the root of ethical discipline, the root of generosity, the root of wisdom, the root of patience, the root of learning, the root of diligence, the root of mindfulness, the root of meditative concentration, and the root of virtuous friends. Through such roots as these, one is not negligent.
Because they have escaped [the previous stage], they increase; because they increase, they become deep-rooted and difficult to uproot.

These ten meanings constitute being "deep-rooted and difficult to uproot. I privately maintain that since Changsheng has already explained this through many meanings, the three [remaining] stages are likewise so;
the other four [stages] all possess these ten [meanings], and each consists of thirteen [factors].
For this reason, it is said that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s cultivation of the Great Nirvāṇa has roots so deep they are difficult to uproot.
How is this explained regarding the body? The second chapter is divided into three parts: the heading, the exposition, and the conclusion.
What is the formation of the perception of certainty regarding the body?
The heading is as in the text;
the explanation is twofold: first, the concentration of the body, and second, the concentration of the mind.
One develops a resolute mind regarding oneself, thinking: "In future lives, this body of mine shall certainly become a vessel for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
In the body of the first dhyāna, one contemplates the body as being existent, which is the vessel of birth and death; one contemplates the body as being non-existent, which is the vessel of nirvāṇa.
Now, contemplating the body as neither existent nor non-existent clearly reveals the Middle Way, which is the vessel of the three types of bodhi; this is called the "certainty of the body."
The mind should likewise not be narrow, nor subject to change;

it should not be the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, nor the mind of Māra, nor the mind that seeks its own pleasure or delights in birth-and-death (saṃsāra). It should constantly seek the mind of compassion for the sake of all sentient beings.
This is called the bodhisattva generating a resolute mind within himself, thinking: "In a future life, I shall become [enlightened] for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The vessel for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, if the mind is likewise narrow and small, it undergoes transformation through two meanings:

if one discusses the cultivation of causes characterized by arising and ceasing and impermanence, it is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*); if one discusses the experience of results, it is called "transformative birth-and-death" (*pariṇāma-saṃsāra*).
For those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who undergo transformation, they direct their minds toward human beings; this belongs to the side of the unconditioned and is the mind of Māra.
The mind that seeks self-delight belongs to the Heaven of Māra; the mind that seeks the pleasures of all heavens is the mind that clings to birth and death throughout the three realms.
These three types of mind are finite and not definitive. To practice loving-kindness (*maitrī*) by seeking nothing, and compassion (*karuṇā*) within existence—this is what is definitive.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa, gives rise to the thought of certainty regarding his own person.
How is it that he does not regard the field of merit? [The following] explains the text of the third chapter, which is divided into three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
How does a bodhisattva not regard fields of merit or non-fields of merit?
What constitutes a field of merit? From the heterodox practitioners who observe the precepts up to the Buddhas—these are called fields of merit.
If one should harbor the thought, "These types of persons are true fields of merit," know that such a mind is base and inferior for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

He contemplates that all immeasurable sentient beings are none other than fields of merit. Why is this? Because they have skillfully cultivated the distinct applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Those who have skillfully cultivated these distinct applications of mindfulness observe that among sentient beings there are neither those who uphold the precepts nor those who violate them;
they constantly observe that the four kinds of giving taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, all yield pure retribution.
What are the four? First, the donor is pure while the recipient is impure; second, the donor is impure while the recipient is pure;
third, both donor and recipient are pure; fourth, both are impure. What is meant by the donor being pure while the recipient is impure?
It refers to a donor who possesses ethical discipline, learning, and wisdom, and who understands that there is the merit of giving and its karmic fruit.

When the recipient breaks the precepts, is exclusively attached to false views, and holds that there is no giving and no retribution, this is called "the purity of the gift and the impurity of the recipient.

What is meant by "the purity of the recipient and the impurity of the donor"? It refers to a donor who breaks the precepts, is exclusively attached to false views, and claims that there is no wisdom in giving nor any karmic fruit thereof;
whereas the recipient upholds the precepts, possesses extensive learning and wisdom, and knows that there is wisdom in giving.
As for the fruit of giving, this is called "the donor is impure while the recipient is pure. What is meant by "both donor and recipient are pure"?
It refers to when both the donor and the recipient possess ethical discipline, extensive learning, and wisdom;

they know that there is the merit of giving and the fruit of giving—this is called the purity of both donor and recipient. What is meant by "both are impure"? It refers to the donor... [text fragment]... the donor.
The recipient breaks the precepts and holds wrong views, claiming that there is no giving nor any fruit of giving.
If this were so, how could one further say that a pure fruit of retribution is obtained? Because there is neither giving nor retribution, it is called "pure.

Good son, if there is someone who does not see giving or the retribution of giving, you should know that such a person is not called one who has broken the precepts; they are merely attached to wrong views. If one relies on...
The Śrāvakas say that not seeing the gift and the karmic retribution of the gift is called breaking the precepts and holding wrong views;
however, according to this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, not seeing the wisdom-gift and the karmic retribution of the gift is called upholding the precepts and holding right views.
Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have different bases of mindfulness (*anyathā-manasikāra*) through their cultivation, they do not perceive sentient beings as being possessed of [precepts].

Regarding the giving of those who observe the precepts and those who violate them, as well as the recipient and the karmic fruit of the gift—it is for this reason that one is said to possess "upholding the precepts and right view.

In the preceding "Chapter on the Four Reliances," which upholds the Buddha-dharma, it was necessary to distinguish between what is upheld and what is violated; here, in one's own cultivation, one should employ equanimity.

Furthermore, whereas the previous exhortation directed monastics to follow the practice of the precepts, the present exhortation directs laypeople to cultivate *dāna* (generosity) free from marks of self-reference.
The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) differ from the two extremes; they are the correct contemplation of the Middle Way.

As for non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika), they not only observe the precepts but also attain superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*). As the text below states: "Non-Buddhists who practice giving and sever the fetters surpass the bhikṣu who merely observes the precepts.

This means that while the bhikṣu who observes the precepts suppresses the evils of the desire realm, the practitioner who excels in giving is said to be superior. Although there are four types [of practitioners], all obtain purity.
As for retribution, it is through non-giving and non-requital that there is pure retribution.
For this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit.
"How does one purify the Buddha-fields? This explains the text of the fourth chapter; it also consists of three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
"What is meant by 'purifying the Buddha-lands'?
This is the heading, as in the text.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate this subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings,
they abandon all intent to kill. By means of these roots of goodness, they vow to share them with all sentient beings,
desiring that all beings attain long life, possess great power, and obtain great supernormal faculties.
By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age,
all sentient beings within his land shall obtain long life, possess great power, and acquire great supernormal faculties. Furthermore, son of good family,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous scripture of the Mahāparinirvāṇa for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi...
In order to deliver sentient beings through the three types of enlightenment, one abandons the mind of stealing; by means of these roots of goodness, one vows to share them with all sentient beings.
One prays that the lands of all Buddha-fields shall consist entirely of the seven treasures and that sentient beings therein shall be wealthy and abundant, freely enjoying all they desire.
By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, when one attains Buddhahood in a future life...
He attains a land that consists purely of the seven treasures, where sentient beings are wealthy and prosperous, and may indulge their desires at will.

Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he abandons the mind of lustful desire; by means of these roots of goodness, he vows to [share them] with all sentient beings.
I make a vow that all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands shall be free from desire,
hatred, and delusion, and shall have no suffering or affliction of hunger or thirst; by the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, when I attain Buddhahood in a future age,
the sentient beings of my land shall be far removed from lust, anger, and delusion, and none at all shall suffer from hunger.

The Suffering of Thirst. Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he abandons the mind of false speech.
By means of these roots of goodness, he makes this vow: "May I share them with all sentient beings; may there always be abundant flowers and fruits in all buddha-lands."
By the power of this causal condition of his vow that all sentient beings dwelling among the fragrant trees of the forest shall obtain wondrous voices,
when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, all the lands of his realm will always possess flowers, fruits, lush forests, and fragrant trees,
and all sentient beings therein shall obtain pure and sublime voices. Furthermore, son of good family, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...

For the sake of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and for the purpose of delivering sentient beings, I shall distance myself from divisive speech while reciting this subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
By means of these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings.
I pray that all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands may always live in harmony and together expound the True Dharma. By virtue of this vow, [may it be fulfilled].
By the power of these conditions, at the time he attains Buddhahood, all sentient beings within his land will gather together in harmony to discuss the essentials of the Dharma.

Furthermore, son of good family, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he remains far removed from harsh speech.
I dedicate these roots of goodness to all sentient beings together with them.
May the lands of all Buddhas be as level as the palm of a hand, free from sand, gravel, thorns, and harsh brambles; and may the minds of all sentient beings therein be impartial.
By the power of these vows and causal conditions, when I attain Buddhahood in a future age, may the land of my realm be as level as the palm of a hand.
Toward all sentient beings who dwell among sand, gravel, thorns, and harsh brambles, his mind remains impartial.

Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and delivering sentient beings, he refrains from meaningless speech.
By means of these roots of goodness, he vows to share them with all sentient beings.
He forms the vow that all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands shall be free from suffering and affliction.
By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, all sentient beings within his land shall likewise be free from suffering and affliction.
Furthermore, son of good family, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
I, as a Dharma-preacher, for the sake of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and delivering sentient beings, have distanced myself from greed and envy.

By means of these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings. I pray that in all Buddha-lands, all sentient beings shall be free from greed, envy, affliction, harm, and false views.
By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, may [this merit] be accomplished in future ages.
At that time, all sentient beings within the Buddha’s land were entirely free from greed, envy, affliction, harm, and false views.

Furthermore, son of good family, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he remains far removed from affliction and harm; by means of these roots of goodness, he makes this vow:
I share this with all sentient beings and vow that all sentient beings within all Buddha-lands shall together cultivate great loving-kindness and great compassion,
attaining the stage of regarding all as one's only child. By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, when I attain Buddhahood in a future age,
all sentient beings throughout that world shall likewise together cultivate great loving-kindness and great compassion and attain [the stage of regarding all as one's only child].

The Stage of the Only Son. Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he remains far removed from false views.
By means of these roots of goodness, he makes a vow to share them with all sentient beings, wishing that all sentient beings throughout all lands may likewise [be so].
Having attained the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, by the power of these causes and conditions of their vow,
when they attain Buddhahood in a future world, all sentient beings therein shall be able to receive, uphold, and maintain the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
In the preceding explanation, it was stated that the karma for the Pure Land has bodhicitta as its foundation.

Here, the "ten wholesome actions" (*daśa-kuśala*) do not merely refer to practicing the ten virtues in conjunction with the mind of enlightenment—as in the previous answer regarding the question on fearlessness.

Rather, these ten wholesome actions clarify the principle of "corresponding causes yielding corresponding fruits. For instance, the statement that one attains "flower-like fruits" by abstaining from false speech clarifies that delusion is non-existent.

Just as a flower that lacks fruit is not false, so too, when one does not speak falsely, there is a real karmic retribution; at the time of receiving that retribution, one experiences excellent flowers and fruits.
This is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of a pure buddha-field.
How are the meanings of the fifth and sixth chapters eliminated and explained together as a single interpretation? There are differing views among commentators.
One says: herein the opening of the chapters clarifies three kinds of "remnants" (*śeṣa*).
The first two matters explain the elimination of the remnants in the fifth chapter, while the final matter explains the severing of karmic conditions in the sixth chapter.
Regarding the explanation of the remaining retribution of afflictions as "extinguishing what remains" and the explanation of the remaining residual karma as "severing the conditions of karma above":

there is one further matter that is merely set forth in excess; according to the text, this consists of three parts: first, the proclamation of the three topical headings; second, their sequential explanation;
and third, the conclusion.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva eliminate the remaining traces of existence? There are three kinds of remaining traces: first, the remainder of afflictions;
second, the remainder of karma; and third, the remainder of existence.
In the second explanation of the three chapters, the first explains afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Good son, what is meant by the residual retribution of afflictions? If there are sentient beings who habitually indulge in sensual desire, when that retribution ripens, they fall into hell.
Upon emerging from hell, they receive the body of an animal, namely a pigeon, a sparrow, or a mandarin duck."
If one is born as a male parrot, a *śiva-śiva*, a *śarika* bird, a blue jay, a fish, a turtle, a monkey, a roe deer, or a stag;
or if one obtains a human body but takes on the form of a eunuch, a woman, one with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), one without sexual organs (*avyañjana*), or a *ṣaṇḍha*;

or if one leaves the household life and violates the first grave precept—these are called residual retributions. Furthermore, good son, if there are sentient beings who, with a heart of profound sincerity...
Habitually associating with anger is the ripening of this retribution: one falls into hell;

upon emerging from hell, one receives the body of an animal, such as a venomous snake possessing four kinds of poison—poison by sight, poison by touch, poison by bite, and poison by breath—or among those such as lions, tigers, wolves, bears, badgers, cats, foxes, hawks, and falcons.
If one obtains a human body, one is fully possessed of the twelve types of evil observances.
If one has left the household life and violates the second grave precept, this is called a remaining retribution.
Furthermore, son of good family, if there are those who practice foolishness, because that retribution ripens, they fall into hell.

Upon emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals—namely, the forms of elephants, pigs, cattle, sheep, water buffaloes, fleas, lice, mosquitoes, gadflies, ants, and so forth. If they should obtain...

If one is born as a human being but is deaf, blind, mute, crippled, or hunchbacked—possessing incomplete faculties and unable to receive the Dharma—and yet manages to leave the household life, but has dull and darkened faculties and frequently violates the heavy precepts, even down to [stealing] five coins, this is called a residual retribution (*avaśeṣa-vipāka*).
Furthermore, son of good family, if there is a person who cultivates arrogance, when that retribution ripens, they fall into hell. From...
Emerging from hell, one receives the body of an animal—namely, a dung-worm, a camel, a donkey, a dog, or a horse.

If born among humans, one receives the body of a slave or a servant, remaining impoverished and begging for alms; or, even if one manages to leave the household life, one is constantly held in contempt by sentient beings.
This is called the residual retribution for violating the fourth precept. Such as these are termed the residual retributions of afflictions. These are the residual retributions.
Because the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa, all [afflictions] are completely eliminated.

If one distinguishes between the categories of "habituation" (*vāsanā*) and "retribution" (*vipāka*), then habituation is the cause of affliction (*kleśa*) and retribution is the result of karma (*karma*).

Now, because this section distinguishes between the differences of habituation and retribution, it says that while afflictions give rise to retribution through karma, they are merely able to nourish it.
Regarding "moistening this karma," if, as stated in the *Mahāśāstra*, even those who merely indulge in afflictions can obtain retribution, how is it that other karmas [do not]?
Second, the explanation above removes the conditions for karma. What are these "other karmas"?
They refer to all the karma of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and all the karma of *śrāvakas* up to the stage of stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
There are those with seven more births, those with karma for two more births who are Sakṛdāgāmins, and those who are Anāgāmins receiving karma for the realm of form;
these are called "remaining karma. Such remaining karma, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva completely eliminates and severs by virtue of being able to practice the Great Nirvāṇa.

This generally clarifies the karma of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Regarding the statement that a *srotāpanna* undergoes seven existences (*sapta-bhava*):
although a *srotāpanna* has exhausted all views (*dṛṣṭi*), they still possess the moisture of conceptual thought (*vitarka*) that nourishes rebirth in the human or celestial realms.

When counting the combined cycles of seven human and seven celestial rebirths, the total is merely seven existences; however, when counting the individual instances of these cycles, there are fourteen existences. This refers to the *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Regarding the statement that "the *sakṛdāgāmin* undergoes two existences (*bhava*)," this means that the *sakṛdāgāmin* has exactly one birth each among humans and devas;
thus, these two births are separated when counted individually. However, if they were combined as a single count, it would constitute only one existence (*bhava*). Question:

Why is the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) counted together [as one existence], while the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*) is separated? Answer: This is merely a matter of alternating presentation. For the *anāgāmin*, there is the experience of the form-existence (*rūpa-bhava*).

The practitioner who is an Anāgāmin has exhausted all karma for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), yet because residual delusions regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) still remain, it is said that they "possess karma for existence in the form realm" (*rūpabhava*).
Now, there are five types of Anāgāmins, but only one among them—the "Upstreamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*)—is mentioned here. Regarding the upstreamer, there are two kinds:

first, those who go as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven; second, those who go to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Those who delight in discussing the meaning [of the Dharma] are born [there]."

Those who delight in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) are born in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). However, one who is born in the Nirodhana [heaven] traverses all four dhyānas:
if cessation is not attained in the first dhyāna, one is reborn in the second; if not attained in the second, one is reborn in the third;
and if not attained in the third, one is reborn in the fourth, where one finally attains cessation. Within this process, there is also the "threefold leap" (*tri-saṃkrānti*) and the "half-leap."

Transcending and pervading [the form realm], if one is born in the formless [realm], it is called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the formless" (ārūpyopapadya-parinirvāyī), and so forth. If one is born in the formless realm, one does not take birth again;
moreover, upon being born, one ceases immediately. This differs from taking birth through the four dhyānas of the form realm;

therefore, it is omitted here to mention the experiencing of karma in the formless realm, and only the experiencing of karma within the form realm is mentioned. Because one is not born there, it is also said that birth occurs with or without application of effort (*sābhisaṃskāra* or *anabhisaṃskāra*).
Because it is the same as [the case of] form (*rūpa*), it is also not mentioned.
How is it that there are other remaining states of existence? This third explanation clarifies the exclusion of existence mentioned above.
How are there other remaining states of existence? An Arhat attains the fruit of Arhatship; a Pratyekabuddha attains the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood.
To transform into two fruits without karma or fetters is called "remaining existence" (*śeṣa-bhava*).

Regarding "transforming into two fruits without karma or fetters," Zhuangyan states that an Arhat transforms into a Bodhisattva of the sixth stage and a Pratyekabuddha transforms into a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage;
thus it is said they "transform into two fruits. Now, this is clarified as follows:
Regarding the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya*), Kaiśan stated that there is no such thing as "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) in this sutra;

he claimed that those who were originally Arhats of dull faculties transform into Pratyekabuddhas of sharp faculties, and likewise, through repeated practice, they transform into the [first] two fruits.

However, what is clarified here is that these still belong entirely to the Two Vehicles and are not the teaching of this sutra. Hexi said: "The first phrase refers to attaining the Way and attaining the [first] two fruits."

Regarding the stages of the candidate for Arhatship and the attainment of the fruit of Arhatship, as well as those of the Pratyekabuddha—the text itself states "attainment" and "fruit"—how could one not provide this interpretation?
Now, to clarify: this still pertains to the meaning of the Two Vehicles and is not the intent of the present sutra.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: although the causes of affliction are exhausted and the fruits of retribution have perished, that which does not perish here is simply...
This is the residual momentum of saṃsāra; once karma has been eliminated, only these two fruits remain as a burden for the Bodhisattva.
Therefore, it is said that "turning" (parāvṛtti) means "abandoning. This is the interpretation of others and does not pertain to the present sutra. Xinghuang says:
"Turning the two fruits" means that the bodies of the two vehicles still possess cold, heat, hunger, and thirst; because these fruits are now eliminated, it is called "turning."
The two fruits also belong to the meaning of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Now it is clarified that these fruits do not arise; when they are exhausted by their own nature, they simply cease.

Why then is there a need for the sūtras to transform them? The answer is: although the fruits within the three realms are exhausted, the fruits outside the realms are precisely what arise. To speak of "transforming the fruit" refers to transforming the fruits outside the realms.
It is now clarified that this is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna), and it is not the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna).
These three kinds of dharmas with remainder are eliminated by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva through the cultivation of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra;
this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s eradication of what remains.

"How does one cultivate the pure body? This marks the beginning of the commentary on Chapter Seven, which likewise consists of three parts: the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. The initial introduction is as stated in the text:
"How does a bodhisattva cultivate the pure body?"
Next, in the explanation, the *Siṃhadvāra-parivarta* clarifies that either one karma produces one mark, or one karma produces two or three marks;

herein it is clarified that one hundred merits produce one mark. The text is divided into two parts: first, the clarification of the karma for the marks, and second, the clarification of the karma for the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the precept of non-killing, there are five kinds of mental states: namely, the inferior, the intermediate, the superior, the superior-superior, and the superior-intermediate.
This applies likewise up to right view. These fifty mental states are called the "initial resolve" (prathamacittotpāda) which is fully endowed with certainty.
To accomplish these fifty mental states is called "fulfillment. Such a hundred mental states are called the "fulfillment of a hundred merits."
One hundred merits complete one mark; thus, by successive accumulation, the full accomplishment of the thirty-two marks is called the "Pure Body.

For what reason, then, does he further cultivate the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*)? Among the sentient beings in the world, there are those who serve eighty kinds of deities. What are these eight?
The ten, twelve, and twelve great devas; the five great stars; the Great Dipper; the Deva of Horses;
the Deva of the Path; the Deva Varadvara; the Deva of Merit; the twenty-eight lunar mansions; the Deva of Earth; the Deva of Wind; the Deva of Water; the Deva of Fire; the Deva Brahmā;
the Deva Rudra; the Deva Indra; the Deva Kumāra; the Eight-Armed Deva; the Deva Maheśvara; and the Deva Apara.
The Śarā devas, the Kumbhāṇḍī devīs, the Cāturmahārājika devas, the Lekhakas devas, and the Vasus devas—these are called the eighty [deities].
For the sake of these sentient beings, the Bodhisattva cultivates the eighty minor marks (aśīty-anuvyañjana) to adorn himself; this is called the pure body of a Bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings have faith in and submit to these eighty deities; therefore, the Bodhisattva...
Cultivating the eighty minor marks, he remains unmoving in his body, causing those sentient beings to each see him according to their respective inclinations;
having seen him, they honor and revere him, and each gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates a pure body. Good son, it is like a person who wishes to invite a great king.
One must adorn all one's dwellings and make them utterly pure, preparing various kinds of food and delicacies of a hundred flavors;
only then may the King proceed to the place where he has been invited.
It is the same for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who wishes to invite the Dharma-Wheel King of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi: first, one must cultivate the body and make it utterly pure.
The Unsurpassed Dharma King shall indeed establish him therein; for this reason, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva must cultivate a pure body.
Good son, it is like a person who wishes to consume ambrosia (amṛta) and must first purify their body;
so too is it with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to consume the flavor of the unsurpassed ambrosial Dharma, the Prajñāpāramitā.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practicing the *pāramitās* must first purify his body with the eighty minor marks (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*).
Good son, it is like a fine vessel of gold or silver filled with pure water; both the vessel and the water appear pure. The purity of the body of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise so:
when filled with the water of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, both the vessel and its contents appear pure.
"O pure son of good family, it is like a cloth from Vārāṇasī that is naturally white and easily takes dye.
Why? Because its nature is pure and white. In the same way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, because his body is pure, swiftly attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The various objects of worship for non-Buddhists each consist of but a single characteristic, whereas the Buddha gathers all characteristics and possesses them fully within a single body.

As for the "twelve days," these refer to the twelve days beginning with Zi and Chou; the Hexi [master] says there are twelve auspicious days in a year suitable for ancestral sacrifices and seeking blessings.
Furthermore, cultivating the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) is also according to the four intentions (*catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu*): first, the body of the Dharma King ought to be so.

Adorning one's own body with the primary and secondary marks—this is the case for all Buddhas; this constitutes the world-aspect (*loka-dharma*), causing those who see it to give rise to faith and cultivate goodness.
This constitutes the person-aspect (*pudgala-dharma*): possessing manifold excellences in a single body to counteract the non-Buddhists.
This constitutes the aspect of remediation (*pratipakṣa-dharma*): because form is pure, prajñā is pure; because prajñā is pure, form is pure. This is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
Citing four analogies, it may be that [the Buddha] presides over this (and so forth).
For this reason, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the pure body.
How does he fully understand all conditions? This concludes the eighth chapter. Herein there are also three parts: the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. First, as follows:
The text says:
How does a bodhisattva thoroughly understand all conditions?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not perceive the mark of form, does not perceive the conditions of form, and does not perceive the essence of form.
In birth one does not see form; in cessation one does not see a single characteristic nor a different characteristic; one does not see a seer, nor does one see marks, nor does one see a receiver.
Why is this? Because of the thorough understanding of causes and conditions. As it is with form, so it is with all phenomena.
Regarding the explanation, others claim that knowing the harmony of causes and conditions is itself the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); this interpretation is incorrect.
Not seeing the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) is the cessation of the link of formations (*saṃskāra*); not seeing the conditions for form is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*);

not seeing the essence of form is the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling; and not seeing the arising of form is the cessation of craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and so forth.
Not seeing the cessation of form is the cessation of old age and death; not seeing a single characteristic is not seeing the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination;
not seeing a seer is not seeing that causes and conditions are provisional, such that both the ultimate and conventional truths are simultaneously extinguished, and even the Middle Way is not seen.
To thoroughly penetrate and understand dependent origination in this manner—how could it be anything less than this? How could it merely be a matter of cessation?
All phenomena are likewise according to worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*).
This is called the bodhisattva’s thorough knowledge of all conditions (*pratyaya*).
How does the bodhisattva [know this]? The commentary on the ninth chapter is divided into three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
How does a bodhisattva remain free from all enemies?

As indicated by the text, the explanation is divided into two parts: first, clarifying freedom from enmity; second, identifying what constitutes an enemy. Regarding the first—freedom from enmity—it is further divided into two sections, the first of which concerns [freedom from enmity] within oneself.
Regarding the first section on "being free from enmity toward others" following "being free from enmity oneself":
all afflictions (*kleśa*) are the enemies of a bodhisattva; because a bodhisattva mahāsattva is constantly far removed from them, this is called a bodhisattva destroying all hostile adversaries.
To distance oneself from afflictions (*kleśa*) is to distance oneself from enemies.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas dwelling in the five stages do not regard afflictions as enemies. Why? It is because it is due to afflictions that Bodhisattvas undergo birth;
and because they undergo birth, they are able to successively transform and teach sentient beings. For this reason, [afflictions are not regarded as enemies].
They are not called enemies.
The next five stages refer to being free from enmity toward others.
What follows, beginning with "What is an enemy?", distinguishes and identifies the actual adversary.
What is meant by an enemy? It refers to one who slanders the Vaipulya sūtras.
A bodhisattva does not fear falling into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts as much as he fears such a slanderer of the Vaipulya.
All bodhisattvas have eight kinds of māras called "enemies"; to distance oneself from these eight māras is called "being free from enemies."
The Śramaṇa Bamo of Hexi [states that] slandering the Vaipulya and other such [teachings] constitutes these four evils, which are the four māras:
namely, the māra of birth-and-death, and the four [māras] of impermanence, non-self, and so forth, which are the māras of nirvāṇa (and so on).
This is called the bodhisattva’s freedom from all enemies.
What is meant by "how he remains far removed"? This is the tenth chapter, which likewise contains the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion, as found in the text.
What is meant by "how the bodhisattva remains far removed from the two extremes"?

Regarding the "two extremes," this refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) and the affliction of craving (*tṛṣṇā-kleśa*). A bodhisattva constantly remains detached from these twenty-five states of existence and the affliction of craving.
In the commentary on the text, these twenty-five states of existence and the affliction of craving are identified as the two extremes, which are precisely cause and effect.

I, [the author], privately maintain that because one destroys the three kinds of delusions within the twenty-five existences (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), one thereby departs from the two extremes (*antadvaya*).

Regarding the "West River" (Hexi) school’s interpretation of karma and afflictions as the two extremes, I maintain that if one speaks of three kinds of delusions, it is only when there are three kinds of karma that it accords with the present meaning.
To simply take the delusions and karma within the realms (*dhātu*) as the two extremes is entirely not the present meaning; since this has already been established.
This principle applies to all dharmas: existence and non-existence, impermanence, annihilation, defilement and purity, bondage and liberation—all these are dual extremes.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s distancing from the two extremes.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s cultivation of the Great Nirvāṇa, fully accomplishing the fourth merit.
At that time, following the second section on the exposition of the Dharma concerning the light, there is a dialogue.
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra-Ābhāsa-Ucchraya-Guṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Buddha has taught, if there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa and fully perform these ten kinds of meritorious deeds, for what reason does the Tathāgata [speak thus]?"
"One only cultivates the nine matters and does not cultivate the Pure Land.
The intent of the question is: "If a bodhisattva fully cultivates the ten matters, for what reason does the Tathāgata not cultivate the Pure Land?
The Buddha answers with four points: first, "I have fully cultivated the ten matters because the assembly of sages has done so as well."
The Buddha said, "Good son, in the past I also constantly cultivated these ten matters.
Among all bodhisattvas and all Tathāgatas, there are none who do not cultivate these ten matters."
Second, if one were to disparage his question by claiming that it is impossible for Buddhas,
World-Honored Ones, to appear within a world-system that is filled with impurities, such a thing could never be.
"Good son, you should not now think that the Buddhas appear only in impure worlds; you should know that such a mind is unwholesome and narrow-minded.
You should now understand that I do not actually appear [only] within the Jambudvīpa realm.
For example, it would be like someone saying that this world alone possesses the sun and moon, while other world-systems have no sun or moon—such a statement is baseless."
There is a principle: if a bodhisattva should speak these words, "This buddha-world is defiled and impure;
the buddha-lands of other directions are likewise pure and adorned."
Third, the passage below indicates that there is no superior pure land [to the West].
"Good son, to the west of this Sahā world, passing through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of thirty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a world named *Anabhibhūta* (Unconquerable).
For what reason is that land named 'Unconquerable'?"

All the adornments of that land are entirely equal and without distinction, just like the Western World of Peace and Bliss (Sukhāvatī) and the Eastern World of the Full Moon; I shall appear in that land in the world.

The fourth is for the sake of sentient beings; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he manifests the turning of the wheel of Dharma within this world-system of Jambudvīpa in a defiled land, exactly as described in the text.
It is for the purpose of transforming sentient beings that he manifests the turning of the wheel of Dharma here in Jambudvīpa;
it is not only my own body that manifests the turning of the wheel of Dharma herein, for all Buddhas likewise turn the wheel of Dharma within this realm.
For this reason, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not fail to practice these ten matters.
Son of good family, because of his vow, the Bodhisattva Maitreya shall cause this world to be pure and adorned in a future age.
For this reason, there is no world belonging to any of the Buddhas that is not adorned and purified.
Furthermore, the fifth section on the merits is divided into three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. The heading is as stated in the text:
"Furthermore, son of good family, how does a bodhisattva who cultivates this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra fully accomplish the fifth merit?"

In the commentary, there are two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the discussion of the meaning. Regarding the first explanation, there are three traditional interpretations of the five matters.

Yecheng says that it applies to both ordinary worldlings and those in the thirty stages of mind; since it states that they are not born in borderlands and possess all faculties intact, this serves as proof.
Second, it is said that these virtues are not shallow. Why? Because from the attainment of the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) upward, all rely on the actual phenomena.
The statement regarding the "perfection of the faculties" does not refer to the ear-faculty and so forth, but rather to the supreme faculty of faith that transcends the world.
The term "borderlands" does not refer to geographical frontiers where the Buddha-dharma is absent, but rather to being free from the extremes of nihilism and eternalism.
"Being protected by the devas" means taking the Buddha as one's deity; "being revered by the fourfold assembly" means serving as a field of merit for all beings. (3)
Kaishan says: "This refers to bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (bhūmi) yet still take birth in the desire realm; therefore, it speaks of being 'fully endowed' and so forth.
If one discusses the attainment of the outflow-free (anāsrava) transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), this bodhisattva still possesses outflows (sāsrava);
thus, although he undergoes birth now, these five [faculties] exist, yet he harbors no attachment. He takes non-attachment as his very essence. Now, let us evaluate Kaishan’s position.

All of these pertain to the meaning of the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka. According to the first school, this applies generally to those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*); however, this is the distinct teaching (*biejiao*) and does not accord with the intent of the sutra.

The intermediate stage, the ascent to the stages, represents the intent of the path of realization (*sākṣātkriyāmārga*). Taking the text as our basis, there are two parts: first, clarifying the merits; second, discussing the meaning.
Regarding the first, the merits, there is the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. The heading is as stated in the text.
Good son, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the Mahāparinirvāṇa, he fully accomplishes the fifth merit through five matters.
What are these five?
First, the faculties are complete; second, one is not born in a borderland; third, [one is born among] the devas...
Regarding the four types of loving-kindness: first, one is always revered by celestial Māras, śramaṇas, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others;
second, one attains the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).
The commentator explains that of these five, the former four are fruits of retribution (*vipākaphala*), while the latter one is a fruit of cultivation (*niṣyandaphala*).
By the power of the causes and conditions of this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, the Bodhisattva is fully endowed with these five kinds of meritorious qualities.
Next, in the section on the discussion of the meaning, a question is first posed.
The Bodhisattva Guangming Bianzhao Gao-gui De-wang said: "As the Buddha has taught, if there is a son of good family..."
If a virtuous woman practices giving, she will fully accomplish five kinds of meritorious qualities;
why then do you now say that these five things are obtained because of the Great Nirvana?
Next, the Buddha’s response has two parts: first, he praises the question, and second, he provides the formal answer.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! Such matters as these have distinct meanings;
I shall now analyze and explain them for you.

In the response there are two parts: first, the chapter on superiority and inferiority; second, from "Son of good family" onwards, the section revealing the characteristics of superiority and inferiority.
The five things obtained through ordinary giving are indeterminate, impermanent, impure, inferior, non-distinctive, and not untainted;

they cannot benefit, bring peace and happiness to, or have compassion for all sentient beings. However, the five things obtained by relying on this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra are determinate, permanent, pure, superior, distinctive, and untainted; they are thus able to benefit, bring peace and happiness to, and [compassionately aid] all sentient beings.
Compassion for all sentient beings;
first, the five chapters establish that this is the excellence of bliss, the self, permanence, purity, and visibility—these are the uncommon, untainted [qualities] of the Middle Way.
This realization of the Middle Way, including its benefits and peace, and so forth, constitutes the transformation of others.
Good son, as for giving (*dāna*), it enables one to be free from hunger and thirst;
yet the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* can cause all sentient beings to completely distance themselves from the disease of craving within the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).

While the conditions of giving cause birth and death to continue in succession, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* can cause birth and death to be severed so that they do not continue. Because of giving, one receives the dharmas of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
By means of the Great Nirvāṇa, one becomes a bodhisattva; through the causal conditions of giving, one is able to sever all suffering and affliction of poverty.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* can sever all unwholesome dharmas. Regarding the causal conditions of giving, there are both portions and fruits;
by means of the Great Nirvāṇa, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which is without portion and without fruit.
The subsequent text states: "Being free from craving and thirst" explains *niyata* (certainty); "releasing the continuity of birth and death" explains *sukha* (bliss);
"attaining the state of a bodhisattva" explains *śubha* (purity); "severing all poverty and unwholesome dharmas" explains *viśeṣa* (excellence);
"having no portion and no fruit of self" explains *anātman* (non-self); and "attaining the uncommon [qualities] while simultaneously benefiting sentient beings" explains *anāsrava* (the untainted).

The Buddha taught that through five matters, by means of the Great Nirvāṇa, one attains the understanding of a Teacher of Men (*śāstṛ*). This occurs when one has passed beyond the thirty minds of the outer ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).

One should know that prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), this is not called "attainment. The Buddha himself stated that this is untainted (*anāsrava*); yet the Kai-sǎn school claims it is tainted (*sāsrava*).
Since they openly contradict the Buddha’s words, how can they be considered free from misleading later generations? Thus, we know that the interpretations of men are entirely untrustworthy.
In the future, practitioners should simply rely upon the sutras themselves;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fully accomplishing the fifth merit.
Good son, this concludes the sixth merit. Regarding the traditional interpretation of the *Vajrasamādhi*: if discussed in terms of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it is the final ultimate mind;

if discussed in terms of the three patiences (*kṣānti*), it is the "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). It is not called a Bodhisattva because it does not regress, yet it is not called the "wondrous enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) because it has not yet advanced.
This is the Vajra-mind of the Bodhisattva. One explanation states that it possesses both the understanding of emptiness and the understanding of existence. II. Two.

It is said that one should only take up the understanding of illuminating existence and not the understanding of emptiness; for the understanding of emptiness alone is insufficient to adorn the Golden Mind (*suvarṇa-citta*).

This passage is cited because, when Mount Gandhamādana was illuminated by seven suns simultaneously, everything was completely incinerated; thus we know that at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), the afflictions are entirely severed.
The Kai-shan school interprets the Golden Mind as merely suppressing ignorance, reaching its culmination only at the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
At that time, the Buddha severed this single thought of slight delusion and immediately attained Buddhahood. The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "The Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom can sever [delusion].

This text speaks of subduing it as being for the sake of its total exhaustion. When the gold-like mind is resolved, the understanding is fulfilled; the understanding of the void is not yet sufficient.

To extensively discuss this meaning, one may cite the *Twenty-two Wanderings Sūtra* (*Dvāviṃśaty-avakramaṇa-sūtra*) and the *Queen Sūtra* (*Devī-sūtra*). Master Guanding said: "This cannot be [otherwise]."
It should be definitively judged that its stage is analogous to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, which penetrates all stages (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) are too high;
moreover, what stage would the "fifth merit" belong to? They should not differ so vastly. It is sufficient that it corresponds with samādhi, regardless of whether it is high or low.
An old commentary further explains that one must first attain one hundred samādhis within the Ten Stages before attaining the Śūraṅgama-samādhi.

To claim that one who has just entered the Vajra-samādhi neither advances toward the fruit of Buddhahood nor regresses to lower stages, but remains solely at the limit of learning (*śaikṣa*), is also incorrect.
This single samādhi also possesses both specific and general aspects: specifically, it refers to the limit of learning;

generally, it interpenetrates all stages and even extends to the "semblance path" (*tadākāra-mārga*). How does this differ from the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, which pervades both the initial and final stages? Since Prajñā already pervades [all stages], [so too does this samādhi].
How can samādhi be distinguished? It is because the entire body is as firm as a vajra, the entire body is as concentrated as samādhi, and the entire body is as sharp as prajñā.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that the Vajrasamādhi has three names; as it is further stated below, the Buddha-nature has five names.
If one says that at the ultimate end there is both cessation and non-cessation, this is merely the mutual entanglement of two schools.
It is for the sake of benefiting others that one speaks of "severance" or "non-severance," yet in its actual principle, it is neither severed nor unsevered (and so forth).
Now, regarding the analogy of Mount Yugandhara cited by the *Vyākhyāyukti* school, why is this? For when the seven suns appear, they do not merely burn Mount Yugandhara;
rather, everything becomes completely incandescent (*prajvalita*), yet here [in this context] it is not said to be "completely incandescent."
As for the analogy of burning only the grass while leaving the mountain intact: this is not a metaphor for the severance of delusions at the final moment of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
Rather, it takes the first light emitted by the sun when it first rises over Mount Gandhamādana to illuminate the grass;

this illustrates that this samādhi is a merit of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), as it is the very first severance of delusions. Thus, the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion regarding the "burning of the grass" are as stated in the text.
Furthermore, good son, how does a bodhisattva cultivate the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra so as to fully accomplish the sixth merit?
The subsequent explanation consists of three parts: first, a brief clarification of samādhi; second, an extensive clarification of samādhi; and third, an explanation of its name.

Within the brief explanation there are again two parts: first, clarifying one's own virtue; second, distinguishing the transformation of others. Regarding one's own virtue, there are again two parts: first, clarifying the ability to sever [afflictions];
second, citing what is not [the case].
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the Great Nirvāṇa and attains the Vajra-samādhi, dwelling securely therein, they are fully able to...
They shatter and disperse all phenomena,
seeing that all dharmas are impermanent, characterized by motion, causes of terror, suffering from illness,
and plundered by the kalpa; they perish and decay moment by moment, possessing no reality, and are entirely the realm of Māra, having no visible characteristics whatsoever.
Being able to completely shatter and disperse [all views] is "the ability to sever [wrong views]"; "viewing all phenomena as being raised up" is "refutation.
Abiding in this samādhi while bestowing gifts upon the multitude is the second [section], clarifying the transformation of others.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, although they give to sentient beings, they do not perceive even a single sentient being as truly existing;
yet for the sake of sentient beings, they diligently cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), and likewise cultivate up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
It is also thus: if a bodhisattva perceives that there is even one sentient being who cannot ultimately fulfill [these perfections], [they continue to practice].
He accomplishes the dāna-pāramitā up to the fulfillment of the prajñā-pāramitā.

For example, as explained extensively below in the second section, there are two parts: first, the extensive explanation of one's own practice (sva-caryā), and second, the extensive explanation of transforming others (para-caryā).

Regarding the extensive explanation of one's own practice, there are three parts: first, the ability to sever; second, the ability to see; and third, the triple explanation of the ability to sever. First, the ability to sever.
In this section, eight analogies are presented in total; the first illustrates that which is capable of severing.
"Good son, for example, wherever a diamond is applied, there is nothing it does not shatter or destroy, yet the diamond itself suffers no fracture or loss.
The Diamond Samādhi is also like this: whatever dharmas it is applied against, there are none it does not shatter or destroy."
This samādhi is indestructible.
The seven subsequent similes offer praise:
"O son of good family, just as among all jewels the diamond is the most supreme, so too is the diamond-like samādhi attained by the bodhisattva."
Furthermore, it is thus the most supreme among all samādhis. Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates this samādhi, all other samādhis come to be subsumed within it.
Son of good family, just as all minor kings come to be subsumed under a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*), so too do all samādhis come to be subsumed within the Vajra [Samādhi].
"Good son, it is like this: suppose there is a person who is hated and oppressed by the enemies of his country, and someone kills him;
all the people of the world will praise that person's merit without exception. The Vajra-samādhi is also like this:
when a bodhisattva cultivates it, he can destroy all the enemies of sentient beings; therefore, it is always [the foremost] among all samādhis."

The object of veneration for those in ignorance, good son, is like this: suppose there is a man whose strength is so robust that no one can equal him, yet there is another person who is able to subdue him.
You should know that such a person is what the world calls "gold. The Vajra-samādhi is also like this;
its power is able to crush and subdue dharmas that are otherwise difficult to subdue. For this reason, among all samādhis—
All come to take refuge and submit. Son of good family, it is like a person who bathes in the great ocean;
you should know that this person has already used the waters of all rivers, springs, and ponds. So too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
when practicing this vajra-samādhi, you should know that they have already practiced all other samādhis. Son of good family, it is as follows:
In the Fragrant Mountains there is a spring named Anavatapta; its waters possess the eight excellent qualities, and whoever drinks from it is free from all suffering and illness.

The Vajra-samādhi is likewise thus: it possesses the Eightfold Noble Path, and when Bodhisattvas cultivate it, they sever all afflictions, which are like festering sores and grievous diseases. Good son, it is like a person making offerings to Mahākāla.
Śūra, you should know that such a person has already made offerings to all the devas; the Vajrasamādhi is likewise so.
You should know that if someone practices this, they have already practiced all other samādhis.
Good son, if there is a bodhisattva who dwells securely in the second lower stage, it extensively clarifies the first analogy for being able to see.
Good son, if there is a bodhisattva who dwells securely in this Vajra-samādhi, they see that all phenomena are non-existent.

There are obstructions, such as when one views an *āmalaka* fruit within the palm of the hand; although a bodhisattva attains such vision, they ultimately do not form the conceptual notion that they "see all phenomena.
The next three analogies are offered by way of praise.
Good son, it is as if there were a person sitting at a crossroads who sees all sentient beings coming and going, sitting and lying down;
the Vajra-samādhi is also like this, for one sees the arising and ceasing, the appearing and disappearing of all dharmas.

Good son, it is as if there were a high mountain upon which a person has climbed, and from which they gaze afar at all directions and see them all clearly; the mountain of Vajra-concentration is also like this.
In this way, when a bodhisattva ascends [the mountain] and gazes afar, there are no phenomena that are not clearly understood.
Good son, it is like the month of spring when the heavens send down sweet rain; its drops are fine and dense, with no gaps between them. A person with clear vision sees them with perfect clarity.
The bodhisattva is also like this: having attained the eye of purity through the vajra-samādhi, they see all worlds in the eastern direction from afar.
Within those realms, there may be lands undergoing formation or destruction; all of these are seen clearly and without obstruction, and it is likewise so throughout the ten directions.
Son of good family, just as beneath Mount Yugandhara, the third layer of light called "Able to Sever" also has three analogies.
The first analogy refers to that which is capable of severing.
Good son, just as when the seven suns emerge from Mount Yugandhara, all the trees, thickets, and forests upon that mountain are completely consumed by fire;
so too it is with a bodhisattva who cultivates the Vajra-samādhi—all things [are likewise destroyed].
The forest of afflictions is instantly extinguished.
Next, two analogies illustrate the absence of self-conceit.
Good son, for example, although a vajra can shatter all material things, it never gives rise to the thought: "I..."

The Vajra-samādhi that can shatter [all things] is also like this: once a bodhisattva has cultivated it, they are able to destroy afflictions, yet they never give rise to the thought, "I am able to destroy the fetters.
Good son, for example, the great earth can support all things, yet it never gives rise to the thought, "By my power I can support them";
fire does not think, "I can burn things"; and wood does not think, "I can..."
Moisture and wind do not think, "I can move things," nor does space think, "I can contain them.
Nirvāṇa likewise does not give rise to the thought, "I cause sentient beings to attain liberation. The Vajra-samādhi is also like this:
although it can eliminate all afflictions, from the beginning there is no thought that says, "I can eliminate them."
If there is a bodhisattva who dwells securely in the second lower stage, which extensively clarifies transforming others into four aspects— first, transforming the body to be like that of a Buddha—
if such a bodhisattva dwells in this vajra-samādhi, they can transform their body to be like that of a Buddha in a single thought-moment.
Their number is immeasurable, filling Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
Although these bodhisattvas perform such transformations, their minds are from the very beginning free from any thought of pride. Why is this? Because bodhisattvas constantly reflect:
"Who possesses such a samādhi that they can perform such transformations? Only a bodhisattva dwelling securely in this Vajra-samādhi can do so."
They are able to act as ears.
The two [hands] return to their original places.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells securely in this Vajra-samādhi, in a single thought-moment they pervasively reach the ten [directions].
Even though he possesses the power to return as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges to their original places, he does not think, "I am able to do such a thing.
Why is this? It is because of the power of the causal conditions of this samādhi.
Third, severing the afflictions of others:
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this Vajra-samādhi, they are able, within a single thought-moment,
to sever all the afflictions of sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, yet their own mind never at first severs those beings.
Why does the thought of affliction arise? It is because of the power of the causal conditions of this samādhi.
Furthermore, there are four manifestations of the three secrets: first, the manifestation of the secret of speech.
When a bodhisattva abides in this vajra-samādhi, whatever they proclaim with a single voice,
all sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind.
Second is the secrecy of body.
Manifesting a single color such that all sentient beings each perceive various forms and appearances while remaining in one place without their bodies shifting;
this is the third clarification of the secret of speech.
It enables sentient beings to each see and hear the exposition of a single dharma— whether it be a realm (*dhātu*) or an entrance (*āyatana*)—
according to their respective directions, such that all sentient beings hear it in accordance with their own individual capacities for understanding.
Previously, it was explained that a single sound adapts to various [capacities]; now, it is clarified that a single dharma adapts to various [capacities].
Regarding the fourth, the secret intention of the bodhisattvas:
although a bodhisattva abiding in such samādhi perceives sentient beings, their mind from the outset is entirely free from the mark of "sentient beings."

Although one sees men and women, there is no characteristic of man or woman; although one sees form (*rūpa*), there is no characteristic of form, and so on up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), where there is also no characteristic of consciousness;
although one sees day and night, there is no characteristic of day or night; although one sees all things, there is no characteristic of "all";
although one sees all afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*), there is also no characteristic of any affliction; [thus one] sees the Eightfold Noble Path.
There is no characteristic of the Noble Path, yet one sees Bodhi; there is no characteristic of Bodhi, yet one sees Nirvana; there is no characteristic of Nirvana.

Why is this? Good son, because all dharmas are fundamentally without characteristics, the Bodhisattva, by the power of this samādhi, sees all dharmas as they are, fundamentally without characteristics.
For what reason is it called the third [section], "Explaining the Names and Similes"? There are three parts to this; first, the simile of indeterminacy and signlessness.
For what reason is it called the Vajra-samādhi? Good son, for example, if a vajra is placed in the sunlight, its color is indeterminate;
the Vajra-samādhi is also like this: when it is among a great assembly, its appearance is likewise not fixed.
Therefore, it is named the Vajra Samādhi.
Next, the analogy of being beyond appraisal refers to its namelessness.
Good son, for example, just as no person in the world can appraise the value of a vajra, so too is the Vajra Samādhi.
Furthermore, because all such merits cannot be measured by any humans or devas, it is therefore also called the Vajra Samādhi.
Its subsequent freedom from the poison of suffering is likened to fearlessness.
Good son, it is like a poor person who, upon obtaining a vajra jewel, immediately becomes free from poverty, suffering, affliction, evil spirits, and malevolent poisons.

In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who attains this samādhi is able to remain far removed from the various sufferings of afflictions and the malevolent poisons of Māras. For this reason, it is further named the Vajra Samādhi.
The conclusion is as in the text.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, fully accomplishing the sixth merit.

The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Five: The Bodhisattva Noble Virtue King (Scroll Twenty-Three).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty;
revised by the Śramaṇas Huìyán and Huìguān of the Jìn Dynasty.
Xie Lingyun: Re-edited by the King of Virtue, Chapter Five, beginning from Scroll Seven;
the opening of the seventh merit, "Utilizing Skillful Means," wherein the following two merits constitute the second cycle.
By virtue of approaching virtuous friends and first hearing the True Dharma, one’s stage is shallow;

however, the eighth merit has the nine matters as its essence, and its meaning—discriminating the mind, wisdom, liberation, and illumination—is profound and ultimate. Now, it is said that this is not so;
all of these are merits obtained at the time of first realizing what was previously unheard. The Buddha explained the seventh and eighth items to clarify their penetration.
The Dharma that constitutes the proximate cause for realizing Nirvana is capable of serving as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for sentient beings;
why then do you abandon its internal virtue and its power to transform others, instead forming the view that one must seek an external teacher for one's own practice?

Even if one were to seek a spiritual friend for oneself, it would still be a case of using a provisional phenomenon to symbolize the ultimate principle, just as Vimalakīrti’s "recollection of the Buddha" [was used].

At that time, Siṃhanāda and others all came to preach the Dharma; having finished preaching, they departed. Regarding such spiritual friends who hear, contemplate, and practice the Dharma, how could their realization be shallow?
Taking the text as a basis, it is divided into three parts: first, the presentation of the chapter title; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
Furthermore, good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra fully accomplish the seventh merit?
[The heading is as in the text.]

The subsequent explanation is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying the four matters; second, discussing the doctrinal points. The first part is further divided into two: first, stating the headings; second, providing the explanation.
Stating the headings is further divided into three: first, clarifying what is correct; second, citing what is incorrect; third, formally listing the names.
Good son, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, he reflects:
"What dharmas can serve as the proximate causes for Mahāparinirvāṇa? The bodhisattva then knows that there are four kinds of dharmas that serve as the proximate causes for Mahāparinirvāṇa.
The clarification is as stated in the text.
If it is claimed that the diligent practice of all ascetic austerities is the proximate cause for Great Parinirvāṇa, this meaning is not correct.
Why is this so? Because it is impossible to attain Nirvāṇa apart from the four dharmas.
Next, regarding the two interpretations concerning asceticism as being neither [the middle way] nor [the correct path]: the first states that the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists are useless;

the second states that even within the Buddha’s own teaching, one cannot attain the Way by practicing asceticism directly, but must take the category of wisdom as primary, with other practices serving as its support.
The names of the three categories are as stated in the text.
What are the four? First, associating with virtuous friends; second, listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion; third, reflecting with focused mindfulness;
and fourth, practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
For example, there is a person... [This constitutes] the second explanation, which is divided into two parts: first, a general explanation, and second, a detailed explanation.
Within the initial general section, three analogies are presented: the first two analogies refer to Bodhisattvas, and the last one refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Regarding the first analogy for the Bodhisattva, the first part concerns their own practice (*svacaryā*), which likewise possesses four elements. Although the Bodhisattva abides in the causal stage where the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) are not yet perfected, they must still cultivate goodness.
"Friends, listen to the Dharma and practice it... (and so forth). Next, one parable illustrates the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others; this transformation of others also possesses four elements:
the Buddhas initiate [the teaching], and [the disciples] practice according to the instruction... (and so forth). Finally, a parable illustrates ordinary beings;
because the offenses of ordinary beings are heavy, it says they are "like lepers"... (and so forth). Thus, each of these three parables has its respective application.
Good son, it is like a person who encounters various ailments—whether feverish heat, cold chills, exhaustion, dysentery, malaria, or the poisons of malevolent spirits—who goes to a skilled physician.
The physician immediately prescribes medicine according to the specific illness.

That person, with a sincere heart, properly receives the physician’s instructions, compiles the medicine according to those instructions, and takes it as prescribed. Having taken it, the illness is cured and the body attains peace and happiness.

The initial fever is a metaphor for craving (*tṛṣṇā*); the chill is a metaphor for ignorance (*moha*); the exhaustion is a metaphor for pride (*māna*); the downward [symptoms] are a metaphor for anger (*dveṣa*); and the malaria is a metaphor for doubt (*vicikitsā*).

The various delusions are collectively likened to the five [types of] sharp faculties (*pañca-tīkṣṇendriya*), and so forth. Question: Since the bodhisattva’s both sharp and dull [afflictions] are exhausted, how can such illnesses exist? Answer: This is merely using the general to indicate the specific. The specific delusions of the bodhisattva are only exhausted upon reaching Buddhahood; how then could they be free from illness? (My private opinion: *** **Note on Terminology:** * *Tīkṣṇendriya*: "Sharp faculties" refers here to the five types of sensual desire associated with the five sense objects.

* *Pañca-tīkṣṇendriya*: In this context, it refers to the five types of afflictions corresponding to the five sense objects. * *Māna*: Pride. * *Dveṣa*: Anger or hatred. * *Vicikitsā*: Doubt. * *Tṛṣṇā*: Craving. * *Moha*: Ignorance. * *Bodhisattva-viśeṣa-kleśa*: The specific delusions of a bodhisattva. * *Buddhatva-prāpti*: Attaining the state of Buddhahood. * *Aroga*: Free from illness. * *Svamatam*: My own private view or interpretation.
The delusions of both the pervasive and the specific are termed "identical in essence yet distinct.
The person with the illness is likened to the bodhisattvas; the great physician is likened to the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*);

the physician’s instructions are likened to the Vaipulya sutras; properly receiving the physician’s teachings is likened to skillfully contemplating the meaning of the Vaipulya sutras; and applying medicine according to those instructions is likened to practicing accordingly.
For example, practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is like the curing of a disease;
being free from afflictions and attaining peace and happiness is like attaining the eternal bliss, selfhood, purity, and nirvana.
"Good son, it is like a king who, wishing to rule according to the Dharma so as to bring peace and happiness to his people, consults his wise ministers as to what that method should be.
The ministers then explain it to him by means of the ancient laws of former kings. Once the king has heard this, he practices it with sincere faith and governs the country according to the Dharma;
thus, there are no enemies or adversaries, and he causes his people to be peaceful, happy, and free from affliction."
Good son, the king is like the bodhisattvas; the wise ministers are like the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The methods of governance taught by the wise ministers to the king are like the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).

Once the king has heard them, his sincere faith and practice are like the bodhisattvas who focus their minds to contemplate the profound meanings contained within the twelve divisions of the scriptures. His governing the kingdom according to the Dharma is like [the bodhisattvas]... [governing sentient beings].
Bodhisattvas practice according to the Dharma, namely the six pāramitās; because they are able to cultivate these six pāramitās, they have no enemies.
This is like bodhisattvas who, having already abandoned all fetters, afflictions, and evil thieves, attain peace and happiness.
It is like bodhisattvas who have attained great nirvāṇa—eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
"Good son, it is like a person who contracts a malignant leprosy and is told by a good spiritual friend:
'If you can go to the edge of Mount Sumeru, your illness may be cured. Why is this? Because there is an excellent medicine there whose flavor is like nectar;
if one can take it, there is no illness that will not be cured. Having developed sincere faith in these words, that person immediately—"
Going to that mountain to gather and consume the ambrosia (amṛta), their illness was cured and their bodies attained peace and happiness.
Those with the foul disease of leprosy represent ordinary worldlings; the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) represent the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas;
wholehearted faith and acceptance represent the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa); Mount Sumeru represents the Eightfold Noble Path; and the flavor of ambrosia represents [the Dharma].

This is likened to the Buddha-nature; the healing of leprosy is likened to the extinction of afflictions and the attainment of peace and joy; and the attainment of peace, joy, selfhood, and purity is likened to the realization of *nirvāṇa*.
