This concludes the first section, which briefly explains the four matters, followed by a second section that provides a detailed exposition. First, the brief explanation; subsequently, the extensive one. Initial [section].
A brief explanation of knowledge further has four parts; first, there is the praise, which includes both the simile and the application, as in the text.
"Good son, it is like a man who keeps disciples who are clever and of great wisdom; this man teaches them day and night, never wearying."
The bodhisattvas are likewise in this regard: though all sentient beings may have faith or lack faith, they constantly teach and transform them without ever becoming weary.
This concludes the second section on the emergence of such individuals as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Good son, those who are spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) are those among the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas who believe in the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] scriptures.
There are five distinctions among persons: first, Bodhisattvas; second, Buddhas; third, Pratyekabuddhas; fourth, Śrāvakas; and fifth, those among people who believe [in the Mahāyāna].
Why is this called "The Third Section Below: Discerning Their Stages"? First, it clarifies the five stages: (1) teaching the abandonment of evil and the practice of good;
(2) acting according to what has been taught; (3) cultivating bodhi; (4) practicing precepts and giving; (5) not acting for one's own sake, but for the sake of others.
He may sometimes associate with the aforementioned five types of people, though it is not strictly necessary.

Why is he called a "good friend" (kalyāṇamitra)? A good friend is one who can teach sentient beings to distance themselves from the ten unwholesome actions and practice the ten wholesome actions; for this reason, he is called a good friend.
Furthermore, a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) teaches in accordance with the Dharma and acts as they teach. What is meant by "teaching in accordance with the Dharma and acting as one teaches"?
It means that one does not kill oneself and teaches others not to kill, and so on, up to practicing right view oneself and teaching others right view.
If one can do thus, one may be called a true spiritual friend.
One who cultivates enlightenment for oneself and is also able to teach others to practice enlightenment is, for this reason, called a "good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*).
One who is personally able to practice faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom, and is also able to teach others faith,
precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom, is likewise, for this reason, called a "good spiritual friend."
A spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) possesses wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*). What are these wholesome qualities?
They do not seek their own pleasure in whatever they do, but always seek peace and happiness for sentient beings; when they see the faults of others, they do not proclaim their shortcomings;
and their mouths constantly proclaim matters that are pure and virtuous. For these reasons, they are called spiritual friends.
As in the sky, the fourth benefit of obtaining a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is now explained.
Good son, just as the moon in the sky gradually waxes from the first day until the fifteenth day, so too is it with the spiritual friend;
he causes all students to gradually distance themselves from unwholesome dharmas and to increase wholesome dharmas.

If a man associates with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), even if he originally lacks morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, he will come to possess them;
and that which was not yet complete shall be further increased and expanded. Why is this?
Because he associates with virtuous friends, and by virtue of this association, he further attains a profound mastery of the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-buddhavacana*).
Regarding this meaning:

although the first day of the moon cannot be seen, one cannot say it does not exist; likewise, though those with limited knowledge may claim that [the teaching] has not yet been beneficial, it has in fact already moistened them.

If one is able to listen to the following, this is the second explanation regarding those who listen to the Dharma. Furthermore, there are two aspects: first, listening to the three sūtras, and subsequently attaining the three understandings.
If one is able to listen to the profound meaning of these twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is called "listening to the Dharma. One who listens to the Dharma is...
This Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtra states that hearing the name of a Vaipulya sūtra is truly hearing the Dharma; truly hearing the Dharma means receiving and upholding the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Within the Mahāparinirvāṇa, one hears that there is buddha-nature and that the Tathāgata ultimately does not enter parinirvāṇa;
therefore, this is called listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion.

Regarding the three sūtras, they refer to the twelve divisions of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna. According to the intent of this text, it appears that this sūtra is like the *Ekavyavahārika* (One Transformation), encompassing the teachings of the beginning, middle, and end (*yathāpūrvam ādimadhyāntadeśanā*). (And so forth.)
Next, "listening to the Dharma with a concentrated mind" below clarifies the three types of understanding.
Listening to the Dharma with a concentrated mind refers to the Eightfold Noble Path; because the Eightfold Noble Path can sever greed, hatred, and delusion, it is called "listening to the Dharma.
Furthermore, one who listens to the Dharma is said to practice the eleven kinds of emptiness, for these various forms of emptiness [apply] to all phenomena.

One should not manifest such appearances. Those who listen to the Dharma are said to possess the initial resolve for enlightenment, up to and including the ultimate mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It is by means of this initial resolve that one attains Great Nirvāṇa;
it is not through mere hearing that one attains Great Nirvāṇa, but rather through cultivation and practice.
This refers to the Eightfold Noble Path, the eleven kinds of emptiness, and Great Nirvana. Some people correlate these three interpretations with the first three teachings;
however, it is clarified here that this is not necessarily the case for all of them. Within each individual teaching, all three interpretations are fully present.
Because one practices them, one attains Great Nirvana. If there is anyone capable of practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, they will immediately see their Buddha-nature and attain Great [Nirvana].
If one merely hears of nirvana but does not practice it, how could one possibly attain perfect enlightenment (sambodhi)?
This concludes the third reflection, illustrated by the analogy of a sick person.
Good son, it is like a sick person who, though hearing the physician’s instructions and the names of medicines, cannot be cured of the illness;
it is only by taking them that one may achieve recovery. Likewise, though one hears the twelve profound dependent origination dharmas, one cannot sever all afflictions;
it is only by binding the mind in mindfulness and through skillful reflection that one can eliminate and sever them. This is called the third binding.
Furthermore, for what purpose is "contemplative reflection" (manasikāra) called "bound contemplative reflection"? It refers to the three samādhis:
the emptiness samādhi, the signless samādhi, and the wishless samādhi. Regarding "emptiness," one does not perceive a single reality among the twenty-five existences.
Regarding "wishlessness," one does not form aspirations or seek after those twenty-five existences. Regarding "signlessness," there are no ten signs, namely:

To cultivate these nine marks— the mark of form, the mark of sound, the mark of fragrance, the mark of taste, the mark of touch, the mark of arising, the mark of abiding, the mark of cessation, the mark of male, and the mark of female—
through these three samādhis is called a bodhisattva’s focused mindfulness and contemplation.

In the following passage, the ten characteristics are defined as the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and the four marks of impermanence (*catur-lakṣaṇa*); here, they are defined as the five sense objects, the three marks, and male and female.
This difference is merely due to a distinction in pedagogical methods (*upāya-mukha*).
Regarding the question "What is meant by 'in accordance with the Dharma' (*yathādharma*)?", the subsequent explanation of the fourth point follows the text.
What is called "practicing in accordance with the Dharma"? Practicing in accordance with the Dharma means practicing the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*;
it means knowing the true characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*);
and it means knowing that the *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and all Buddhas equally enter parinirvāṇa through a single path—that which is the Dharma of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Born, yet neither aging, nor ill, nor dying, nor hungry, nor thirsty, nor suffering, nor distressed, nor retreating, nor sinking—
the son of good family who understands the profound meaning of the Great Parinirvāṇa knows that the Buddhas never ultimately enter into parinirvāṇa.
"Good son, following the first 'True Reality,' this second section provides a detailed explanation of the four dharmas, which also consists of four parts.

This is the first [section], clarifying the person who is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); the text is concise while the explanation is extensive. First, it is explained through the Dharma; next, seven similes are presented."
Good son, the foremost and true spiritual friend is the Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Why is this?
Because they always skillfully discipline others through three modes. What are these three? First, ultimate gentle speech;
second, ultimate reprimand; and third, both gentle speech and reprimand. For this reason, the Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas [are the true spiritual friends].
This is precisely the true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Within the initial discourse on the Dharma, there are three types of speech, all of which are the Tathāgata’s skillful mastery of the faculties and dispositions of beings:
he speaks with gentle words when it is appropriate; he speaks harsh and cutting words when it is necessary to reprove; and he employs both methods when it is required. Thus it is.
Used together.
Furthermore, son of good family, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*) because they are great physicians. Why is this?

Because they know the illness, they know the medicine, and they administer the medicine according to the illness. It is, for example, like a skilled physician who is proficient in the eight branches of medical science and first examines the illness.
There are three types of symptoms; what are the three? They are wind, heat, and water. To one with a wind disorder, one administers clarified butter (*sarpis*);
to one with a heat disorder, one administers rock honey (*śarkarā*); to one with a water disorder, one administers ginger broth.

Because one knows the root of the disease and administers medicine so that recovery is attained, they are called a skilled physician. The Buddha and the Bodhisattvas are also like this; they know all ordinary beings... [and so forth].

There are three kinds of illness: first, greed and desire; second, anger and hatred; and third, ignorance and delusion. For those with the illness of greed and desire, one teaches the contemplation of the characteristics of bones;
for those with the illness of anger and hatred, one teaches the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion;

and for those with the illness of ignorance and delusion, one teaches the contemplation of the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination. For this reason, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "good spiritual friends. Good son, it is like this:

Because the boatman skillfully ferries people across, he is called a Great Boatman; the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise so, for they ferry all sentient beings across the great ocean of birth and death.
For this reason, they are called "Good Friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Furthermore, son of good family, because it is due to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas that all sentient beings are enabled to fully cultivate and attain the roots of wholesome dharmas, son of good family, it is like this: [the analogy follows].
Just as the Snowy Mountains are the source of various subtle and superior medicinal herbs, so too are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas the source of all roots of goodness;
for this reason, they are called "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Noble son, within the Snowy Mountains there is a superior fragrant medicine named *Saha*; if anyone sees it, they shall attain longevity.
It possesses immeasurable power to eliminate the suffering of illness; though one may be afflicted by the four poisons, they cannot inflict harm.
Should anyone come into contact with it, their lifespan will increase to a full one hundred and twenty years. Should anyone bring it to mind, they shall attain the knowledge of past lives.
Why is this? It is due to the power of the medicine. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise: should anyone behold them, they immediately attain the severance of all afflictions.

Although there are four afflictions, the Māras cannot disturb or confuse one; if there is such contact, life cannot be cut short prematurely, and one will neither be born nor die, neither fall back nor sink.
That which is called "contact" refers to listening to and receiving the sublime Dharma in the presence of a Buddha.
If there is mindfulness, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For this reason, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are so named.
"Good friend, good son, it is like the Anavatapta Lake on Mount Gandhamādana;
because of this lake, there are four great rivers, namely the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Sītā, and Vakṣu. The beings of the world often say:
'If one has committed offenses, by bathing in these four rivers, all sins will be extinguished. You should know that such words are false and empty."
Truly, having set this aside, what else is real? The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are indeed the reality. Why is this?
If one draws near to them, one shall extinguish and eliminate all transgressions; for this reason, they are called "virtuous friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like the great earth, where all medicinal herbs, trees, forests, and the hundred grains [grow].

When sugarcane, flowers, fruits, and their like encounter a celestial drought and are on the verge of withering away, the Nanda and Upananda Dragon Kings, out of compassion for sentient beings, emerge from the great ocean and pour down sweet rain;
all the thickets, forests, grains, grasses, and trees are moistened and restored to life. All sentient beings are likewise so: when all their roots of goodness are about to...

They extinguish the [afflictions] of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, give rise to great compassion, and from the ocean of wisdom, let fall the rain of nectar, causing all sentient beings to become fully endowed with and regain the ten virtuous dharmas.
For this reason, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Good son, it is like a skilled physician who is proficient in the eight branches of medicine; when he sees various patients, he does not discriminate among their castes.
Whether they are of noble lineage or of lowly appearance, whether they possess wealth and treasures or not, he treats them all; for this reason, the world calls him a great physician.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise: seeing that sentient beings suffer from the disease of afflictions, they do not regard their lineage, their physical beauty or ugliness, nor their wealth and treasures, but give rise to a heart of compassion and preach the Dharma to them all. When sentient beings hear it...
Since the disease of afflictions has already been removed for this reason, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra);
by virtue of the causal condition of associating with such virtuous friends, one attains proximity to Great Parinirvāṇa.
Among the seven similes, some serve as preceding analogies and others as subsequent analogies (and so forth).

Regarding the section "How to Listen to the Dharma," the second part provides a detailed explanation of listening to the Dharma, which is further divided into two: first, the explanation itself; second, the citation of scriptural evidence.
Within the explanation, there are both the doctrine (*dharma*) and the similes.
How does a bodhisattva, through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, draw near to Great Parinirvāṇa? Because all sentient beings hear the Dharma, they become endowed with the faculty of faith.
Because they possess the faculty of faith, they delight in practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
They thereby attain the fruit of a srotāpanna, up to and including the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, one should know that by hearing the Dharma, one attains all virtues.
All dharmas are the power of the causes and conditions for hearing the Dharma.

Good son, it is like an elder who has only one son; he sends him to another country to trade for what is needed, showing him the places where the roads are passable and where they are obstructed, and further admonishing him: "If you encounter a courtesan, be careful not to become intimate with her or harbor affection."
When those dear to him have lost their bodies or perished in life, as well as their wealth and treasures, even wicked people will no longer associate with them;
yet their son, being respectful and obedient to his father’s instructions, remains peaceful in body and mind and acquires much wealth.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva expounds the essentials of the Dharma for all sentient beings, demonstrating it to all beings and the fourfold assembly.
The opening and closing of the various paths—these multitudes, by virtue of hearing the Dharma, distance themselves from all evils and become fully endowed with wholesome dharmas.
For this reason, through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, one attains proximity to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Good son, it is like a bright mirror that reflects the features of a person’s face clearly and without exception; the bright mirror of hearing the Dharma is also like this.
When a person illuminates it, good and evil are seen clearly and without obscuration; for this reason, through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, one attains proximity to Great Parinirvāṇa.
Good son, it is like a merchant who wishes to go to a treasure island but does not know the way;
if someone shows him the path, that person follows the instructions and immediately reaches the treasure island, obtaining many precious jewels beyond measure.
It is likewise for all sentient beings who, desiring to reach the place of goodness and seeking the treasure of the Dharma, do not know the signs of whether the path is passable or obstructed.
The Bodhisattva shows it to them, and the sentient beings, following him, reach the place of goodness and obtain the supreme treasure of Great Nirvana.
For this reason, through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa, noble son, it is like a drunken elephant that is wild, unruly, violent, and evil, and is intent on killing many.
There is a tamer of elephants who, using a great iron hook, hooks the top of its head; immediately it becomes disciplined and its evil mind is entirely exhausted.
All sentient beings are also like this: because they are intoxicated by greed, hatred, and delusion, they desire to commit much evil. [This is so for] all Bodhisattvas.
By means of the hook of hearing the Dharma, one alone is drawn and made to abide, so that one may no longer give rise to various evil thoughts;
for this reason, through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
There are four analogies within this section.
Therefore, in the second part below, I cite scriptural evidence in two stages: first citing various sutras, and subsequently citing two specific instances.
For this reason, in various sutras, I have stated that my disciples listen to and receive the twelve divisions of the scriptures with single-minded devotion.
Thus, by abandoning the five hindrances and cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa through this cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment.
This first section generally cites various sūtras.
Second, regarding the attainment of the fruit of *srotāpanna* through hearing the Dharma, two matters are cited as evidence to first clarify the affairs of the initial fruit.
Because of hearing the Dharma, those who have attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* are free from all terrors. Why is this so?

When the householder Sudatta was afflicted by a grave illness, his mind was filled with great sorrow and fear; however, upon hearing Śāriputra explain that there are four merits of a *srotāpanna*, [he was relieved].
Having heard these ten kinds of consolation, one’s fear is immediately dispelled.

For this reason, through the causal conditions of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa. Why is this? Because it opens the eye of the Dharma. There are three types of people in the world:
first, those who are blind; second, those with one eye; and third, those with two eyes. The person who is blind never hears the Dharma.

Consider these three types of people: the first hears the Dharma for a brief moment, yet their mind does not abide in it; the second listens with single-minded devotion and practices according to what they have heard;
and the third, by virtue of listening to the Dharma, comes to understand the nature of the world.
For this reason, through the causal conditions of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.

This refers to when Sudatta fell ill and, upon hearing the fourfold consolation and admonition of Śāriputra, was immediately cured of his illness. These four types are the four dharmas mentioned herein.

Regarding the "tenfold consolation and admonition," the old translations state it refers to the Eightfold Noble Path and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

However, since those in the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) do not possess both of these knowledges, they offer this defense: that for them, the vision of the truths constitutes the knowledge of exhaustion, while the vision of the truths [regarding future non-arising] constitutes the knowledge of non-arising.
"Arising is itself non-arising wisdom"—this statement lacks a scriptural basis. Hexi (Dharmarakṣa) says: "The Eightfold Path, Right Wisdom, and Right Liberation.

This is derived from the Āgamas and must not be interpreted otherwise. "No eyes" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). "One eye" refers to the Dharma-eye. "Two eyes" refers to the Dharma-wisdom.
Furthermore, "no eyes" refers to ordinary worldlings with distracted minds; "one eye" also refers to the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
The second point refers to celestial wisdom (and so forth).
Regarding the two instances concerning Śāriputra mentioned below, starting from "As I formerly...
[it is said]: "O son of good family, when I was formerly in the city of Kuśinagara, the body of Śāriputra encountered the suffering of illness, and I..."
At that time, as the Buddha was entrusting his final instructions to Ānanda and preaching the Dharma extensively, Śāriputra, having heard of this matter, told his four disciples:
"Carry my bed to where the Buddha is; I wish to hear the Dharma. Then the four disciples, obeying his command, carried him there, and he immediately heard the Dharma.
By the power of hearing the Dharma, his suffering was alleviated and his body attained peace and comfort. It is for this reason [that it is said].
Therefore, through the causal conditions of hearing the Dharma, one attains proximity to Great Parinirvāṇa.

The Buddha dispatched Ānanda to preach the Dharma for him; since Ānanda had attained the first fruit and was not inclined to listen to teachings on lower fruits, the man was made to carry his bed to the Buddha’s presence to hear the Dharma, whereupon he was immediately healed.
How does one contemplate? Third, the detailed explanation of contemplation is divided into five parts: first, detachment from the five desires; second, detachment from the four perversions;
third, detachment from the four sufferings; fourth, knowing past causes; and fifth, understanding the nature of permanence.
How does a bodhisattva, by contemplating causes and conditions, draw near to Great Parinirvāṇa? Through this contemplation, the mind attains liberation.
Why is it that all sentient beings are constantly bound by the five desires, yet through contemplation they all attain liberation?
For this reason, by means of the causes and conditions of contemplation, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
Nirvana. Regarding the first passage: when the mind contemplates the Dharma, how could it again have thoughts conditioned by the five desires?
Furthermore, good son, all sentient beings are constantly deluded by the four dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
By means of correct contemplation, one perceives that all phenomena are impermanent, without pleasure, without self, and without purity.
Having seen them thus, the four inversions are immediately severed. For this reason, through the causal condition of contemplation, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
If one has not heard the Dharma and recklessly conceives of a self as permanent, once that thought of a permanent self has been considered, the perversion is then dispelled.
Furthermore, son of good family, all phenomena have four characteristics. What are these four? First, the characteristic of birth;
second, the characteristic of aging; third, the characteristic of illness; and fourth, the characteristic of cessation. By means of these four characteristics, [they] cause a single...
All ordinary beings, from the lowest up to those who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, experience great suffering and distress;

yet, if they can fix their mindfulness and engage in right reflection, even when encountering these four [conditions], they will not give rise to such manifold sufferings. For this reason, by reflecting upon causes and conditions, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
In this context, "the extinction of illumination" refers solely to death.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are no wholesome dharmas that are not attained through such reflection. Why is this?
Because even if someone were to listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, if they do not reflect upon it...
Ultimately, one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
for this reason, by contemplating causes and conditions, one draws near to *mahāparinirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, good son, if there are sentient beings who, with faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha that is unchanging, give rise to reverence, you should know that this is entirely due to the power of the causes and conditions of focused mindfulness and contemplation.
By means of this, they are able to sever all afflictions. For this reason, through the causes and conditions of contemplation, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.

How is it that the fourth section, the detailed explanation of practicing in accordance with the Dharma, is further divided into three parts? First, clarifying the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding). Second, [clarifying] the excellence [of the practice].

How does a bodhisattva practice in accordance with the Dharma? Good son, severing all unwholesome dharmas and cultivating wholesome dharmas is called a bodhisattva practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
Second, the explanation of emptiness and impermanence.
Furthermore, how does one practice in accordance with the Dharma? One perceives that all phenomena are empty, non-existent, impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity.
Because of this vision, one would rather sacrifice body and life than violate the prohibitive precepts; this is called a bodhisattva.
Practicing in accordance with the Dharma.

Regarding the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and the seven kinds of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*), there are further three [sections]: first, the presentation of the headings; second, the explanation of the three [knowledges];
and third, the critical analysis (*viniścaya*). Furthermore, what is meant by practicing in accordance with the Dharma? There are two types of cultivation: first, the real; second, the unreal.
Those who lack reality do not know the true marks of nirvāṇa, the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and space;
this is called unreality. How is it that those who possess reality can know the true marks of nirvāṇa, the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and space? This is called reality.

First, the headings are presented; next, within the brief enumeration, the two chapters on the real and the unreal are raised. "The real" consists of seven [knowledges], while among those that are "unreal," there is no such thing as "knowledge.
What is meant by "knowledge"? This is the second part, the explanation. Regarding the first, knowledge of *nirvāṇa*, it is further divided into two: first, the brief [explanation].
Regarding the explanation following the emergence from the three types of *nirvāṇa*: first, the *nirvāṇa* of a Buddha; second, that of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); and third, that of *śrāvakas*.
Of these, the latter two are merely partial cessations. First, to clarify the *nirvāṇa* of a Buddha:
What is called "knowing the characteristics of nirvāṇa"? There are eight matters that constitute the characteristics of nirvāṇa.
What are these eight? First, exhaustion; second, the nature of goodness; third, reality; fourth, truth; fifth, permanence; sixth, bliss; seventh, self; eighth, purity. These are called nirvāṇa.
Although the Buddha is endowed with ten thousand virtues, they are briefly summarized as eight;

"exhaustion" refers to the exhaustion of all afflictions, and "wholesome nature" means that all actions performed by the Tathāgata are wholesome, truly non-false, and truly non-deceptive. The remaining four are as stated in the text.
Furthermore, there are eight matters. What are these eight? First, liberation; second, the nature of goodness;
third, unreality; fourth, lack of truth; fifth, impermanence; sixth, absence of bliss; seventh, absence of self; eighth, impermanence.
Regarding the eight matters concerning the *nirvāṇa* of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): if it refers to those with distracted minds, such non-Buddhists do not engage with this text.

Here, however, we take up those who have attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which can liberate them from the afflictions of the lower stages; therefore, it is called "liberation.
While it possesses the nature of goodness, it is not ultimate, true, permanent, blissful, self, or pure; for this reason, it is said to be "non-existent" [in that sense].
Furthermore, there are six characteristics: first, liberation; second, a virtuous nature; third, unreality; fourth, lack of truth;
fifth, peace and bliss; and sixth, purity.
Regarding these six matters of the śrāvakas, because they involve mutual giving and taking, they do not equal the Buddha; thus, their [notions of] permanence and self are negated, leaving only...
Because these six matters surpass those of the non-Buddhists, they provide them with bliss and purity; this is based on *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder).

Because the eightfold noble path is free from outflows (*anāsrava*), it is called "blissful"; because the body and wisdom still remain, it is called "peaceful"; and because the bonds of the "son" [i.e., the afflictions] have been severed, it is called "pure."

If there are sentient beings who interpret the preceding chapter-gate [of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*] according to the latter two [interpretations], they do not explain the former one but only explain the latter two.

This is because the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* is extensively discussed in this sutra and requires no further elaboration; however, the latter two must be explained. Herein, the first explains the *nirvāṇa* of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
If there are sentient beings who, relying on the mundane path, sever their afflictions, such nirvana consists of eight factors and its liberation is not real.
Why? Because it is not eternal; because it is impermanent, it lacks reality. Because it lacks reality, it lacks truth.
Although they have severed the afflictions, they arise again; therefore, it is impermanent, selfless, and without bliss.
The absence of purity is called the liberation of nirvāṇa through eight matters.
What are the six characteristics? Below, these explain the two vehicles.
Why are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas called "liberated"? Because they have severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), yet they have not yet attained [the ultimate state].
Because *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is not real, it is called unreal; because it is unreal, it is called untrue.
Because one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a future age, it is called impermanent;
because one attains the untainted Eightfold Noble Path, it is called pure, blissful, and good. Son of good family, if one knows thus, this is—

Knowing that *nirvāṇa* is not designated as the Buddha-nature, nor as the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, the true mark (*dharmatā*), or empty space—this passage clarifies that it is neither truly existent nor substantially real because one attains the untainted Eightfold Noble Path;
it is called "pure" and "blissful" because one shall attain Great *Nirvāṇa* in the future. Therefore, it is impermanent, and subsequently, the text concludes by distinguishing it [from permanence].
Next, the second chapter, "Knowing the Buddha-nature," is explained.
How does a bodhisattva know the Buddha-nature? The Buddha-nature has six aspects. What are these six? First, permanence;

second, purity; third, reality; fourth, goodness; fifth, that which is to be seen; and sixth, truth. Furthermore, there are seven matters: first, that which is to be realized; the remaining six are as follows...
The above is called the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of the Buddha-nature.
In the following *Kāśyapa-parivarta*, five distinct types of nature are clarified: First, the Buddha-nature of the Buddhas has seven attributes:
(1) permanence, (2) self, (3) bliss, (4) purity, (5) truth, (6) reality, and (7) goodness. Second, the Buddha-nature of those in their final existence (*paścima-bhavika*).

There are six [aspects]: first, permanence; second, purity; third, truth; fourth, reality; fifth, goodness; and sixth, being easily perceived. Regarding the three [categories] of the nine abodes of Buddha-nature, they also consist of these six;

the first five are no different from those mentioned before, while the sixth is "being easily perceived. What is clarified here is that neither of these two is the Buddha-nature of a Buddha, because the meaning of the mind differs.
Kaishan says: "These two are both the Buddha-nature of the ninth stage (*navabhūmi*). If it were...
The "Chapter on Leaves" (*Patra-varga*) distinguishes the stages (*bhūmi*): from the first to the fifth stage there are five natures;
from the sixth to the seventh stage there are five natures; the eighth and ninth stages have six natures; the tenth stage also has six natures;

and the Buddha-nature of the final mind has seven natures—this is the detailed classification. However, this present text does not explain them by way of stages, as the six and seven natures apply universally.
According to the causal stage of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), they cannot be distinguished and assigned to each individual ground;

however, one must directly understand that they collectively characterize the Ten Grounds as being both visible and realizable, and that—prior to attaining Buddhahood—all stages down to the fourth, fifth, and sixth grounds are described in this general manner.
Fourth, from the eighth dwelling (*vihāra*) down to the sixth, there are five matters that do not differ from their usual names. Fifth, the fifth...
From abiding in the first stage up to the initial dwelling, there are five matters that differ only in being wholesome or unwholesome.

Next, in explaining the third point—the knowledge of the Tathāgata’s marks—it is shown that he possesses both a single essence and distinct essences; first, the essence of permanence and bliss is clarified.
How does a bodhisattva know the marks of the Tathāgata? The Tathāgata is the mark of awakening, the mark of excellence, and the reality of permanence, bliss, self, purity, and liberation.
It is further stated that the manifestation of the path as visible refers to a distinct essence.
To demonstrate that the Way can be seen is called the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of the marks of the Tathāgata.
Next, the fourth chapter on the knowledge of dharmas is explained.
How does a Bodhisattva know the marks of dharmas? As for dharmas: whether they are wholesome or unwholesome, permanent or impermanent, blissful or...
Not delighting in such things as self and non-self, purity and impurity, knowledge and ignorance, understanding and lack of understanding,

reality and unreality, cultivation and non-cultivation, teacher and non-teacher, or truth and falsehood— this is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

It also possesses two meanings: first, it is said that "permanence, bliss, self, and purity" constitute the single essence (*ekakāya-dharma*), while "impermanence and so forth" constitute the distinct essences (*pṛthagkāya*).
Next is the explanation of the fifth chapter, "Knowing the Sangha."
What is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the characteristics of the Saṃgha? The Saṃgha is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity;

these are the characteristics of the disciples, visible characteristics that are skillful yet not ultimately real. Why is this so? Because all śrāvakas shall attain the Buddha-way. For what reason is it called "real"?
Because they have awakened to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). This is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the characteristics of the Saṃgha.
The Sangha of the One Body is that which always delights [in the Dharma], while the Sangha of Distinct Bodies consists of those who possess the characteristics of disciples.
Next, the sixth point, the knowledge of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), is explained:
How does a bodhisattva know the true mark? As for the true mark, whether it be permanence or impermanence, pleasure or suffering, or...
Whether it be self or non-self, pure or impure, wholesome or unwholesome, existence or non-existence, nirvana or non-nirvana,
liberation or non-liberation, knowledge or ignorance, abandonment or non-abandonment, realization or non-realization,
cultivation or non-cultivation, seeing or non-seeing— these are called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and they are not the Nirvana, the Buddha-nature, or the Dharma of the Tathāgata.

The Sangha and space are called the causes for a bodhisattva; because they cultivate this Great Parinirvāṇa, they come to know the distinct characteristics among the dharmas of nirvāṇa, the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the reality-mark of space.

The essence of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is neither cause nor fruit, neither existent nor non-existent; however, if one relies on its functional activity, it pervades all fruits and possesses various distinct meanings.
Next, the seventh [knowledge] regarding space is explained; although this was not previously discussed, there are again three phrases concerning "practice" and "conclusion."

First, clarifying the emptiness of true reality; second, distinguishing the emptiness of phenomena; third, clarifying the emptiness of nirvana. These three are not different in substance, but are established as three from the perspective of their respective dharmas.
Furthermore, there are only two types of emptiness, because nirvana itself is inherently included within the first.
Good son, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, he does not perceive empty space. Why is this?
Although Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess the five eyes, that which they do not see can only be seen by the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
Because there is no dharma to be seen within what the wisdom-eye perceives, it is called "seeing. If it were a non-existent thing, it would be named...
Regarding space: such space is called "real. Because it is real, it is termed "eternally non-existent.
Because it is eternally non-existent, there is no pleasure, self, or purity.
This first clarifies true emptiness; thus it is said that the wisdom-eye sees this seeing of non-seeing.
"Good son, 'emptiness' refers to the non-existence of phenomena; this is the second [section] clarifying emptiness as the cessation of things.
Good son, 'emptiness' refers to the non-existence of phenomena, and the non-existence of phenomena is called emptiness. For example, in the world, that which has no substance is called empty space;
the nature of empty space is likewise such, and because it possesses nothing, it is named empty space."
This is raised as an analogy.
Son of good family, the nature of sentient beings is inferior, yet it is empty of nirvāṇa.
Son of good family, the nature of sentient beings and the nature of space both lack any substantial nature. Why is this? It is like a person...
It is said that one must first eliminate existing things and only then create emptiness; however, this empty space is truly not something that can be created. Why? Because it is nothing at all.
Because it does not exist, you should know that there is no "emptiness" [as a created thing]; rather, the nature of empty space is emptiness itself.
If it were something that could be created, it would be called impermanent; if it were impermanent, it could not be called empty space. Son of good family, it is like people in the world...
It is said that space is formless, unobstructed, eternal, and unchanging; therefore, the world refers to the nature of space as the "fifth great element.
Son of good family, however, this space actually has no inherent nature; it is called "space" only because of luminosity.
In truth, there is no such thing as space, just as worldly convention (saṃvṛti-satya) has no inherent nature, yet is spoken of for the sake of sentient beings.
The essence of nirvāṇa for a virtuous son of the world is likewise thus: it has no place of abiding;
it is simply the place where all Buddhas sever their afflictions, and is therefore called nirvāṇa. Nirvāṇa is itself permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The text states that space is called "empty" because it possesses luminosity; there are two interpretations of this.
First, some say that space is invisible and exists only as the functional capacity for the passage of light. If it were merely a void, there would be no luminous color;
yet, because color depends upon space, color becomes visible. If there were obstructions, one would not see color; because space is unobstructed, one perceives light and color.

Second, it is said that empty space is not what the discerning mind sees; rather, the discerning mind perceives light, which guides the arising of the active mind, and only then does one come to see space.

Although *nirvāṇa* is blissful—this concludes the third section, the "Discrimination," which analyzes the preceding four types [of views]—it is divided into four parts, the first of which is this discrimination.
Nirvāṇa. Although nirvāṇa is blissful, it is not the experience of sensation; rather, it is the bliss of supreme, wondrous quiescence.
Because it is a distinct quality, it is exclusively the bliss of quiescence.
Next, [the text] distinguishes that the Buddha is a human being.
All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess two kinds of bliss: first, the bliss of cessation (nirvāṇa); second, the bliss of awakening and knowledge.

Because humans collectively [strive for] the Dharma, they possess these two kinds of bliss: there is the bliss of cessation realized through the attainment of nirvāṇa, and there is the bliss of the illumination of wisdom.
Regarding the objects of perception, there is the pleasure of conscious awareness.
To distinguish this from the true nature (dharmatā):
the essence of the true nature consists of three kinds of pleasure—first, the pleasure of sensation; second, the pleasure of cessation; and third, the pleasure of conscious awareness.
Because it is already pervasive, there are three kinds of bliss.
Fourth, [it distinguishes] the Buddha-nature as the Middle Way.
The single bliss of the Buddha-nature is attained because it is to be seen; thus, at the time one realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is so named.
Regarding "the joy of bodhi": because it will be visible in the future, there is the joy of bodhi; this is stated with reference to the true nature (*dharmatā*).

At that time, the light [descends]; second, the discussion of the meaning is divided into two parts: first, the formal question, and second, the resolution of the difficulty. First [is the formal question].

The formal inquiry consists of three parts: first, an inquiry as to whether the place where afflictions are severed is nirvana; second, an inquiry as to whether the place where afflictions are severed is not nirvana;
and third, a repeated inquiry as to whether the place where afflictions are severed is indeed nirvana. The initial section further divides into two:
first, acknowledging the underlying principle while expressing disagreement; second, the actual critique.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Noble Virtue King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if the place where afflictions are severed were Nirvāṇa, this would not be so."
The objection is twofold: first, it is based on the response to Māra; second, it is based on the fact that Bodhisattvas also sever these delusions.

This objection follows from the previous statement that Nirvāṇa is so named precisely because it is the locus where all Buddhas sever afflictions (*kleśa*). According to reason, one should have merely objected that while the severing of afflictions is appropriate, the *locus* itself is not Nirvāṇa.
[To argue otherwise] would be to fear that the Buddha might shift his position, and thus to preemptively obstruct the Buddha’s intent by taking "locus" as the point of contention.
Regarding the initial response to Māra when difficulties arose:

Why is this? When the Tathāgata first attained the Way of Buddhahood in the past and went to the banks of the Nairañjanā River, at that time the King Māra arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling with his retinue and spoke these words: "World-Honored One, the time for your parinirvāṇa has arrived."

Therefore, he did not enter. The Buddha told the Māra King: "I do not yet have many learned disciples who well maintain the prohibitive precepts and possess wisdom, sharp faculties, and transformative intelligence to benefit sentient beings; for this reason, I do not enter."
If the severing of afflictions constitutes nirvāṇa, then since he had already severed the afflictions at the time of his initial attainment of the Way, he would have been in nirvāṇa immediately;
for what reason, then, did he wait until he had many learned disciples before entering nirvāṇa, and why did he say that it would be after three months?
One should know that the initial severing of the afflictions was not yet nirvāṇa. This is the speech uttered by Māra.
In the *Dīrgha Āgama*,
it is further cited that bodhisattvas raise an objection:
if one were to say that the point at which afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed is nirvāṇa, then since bodhisattvas have already severed them for immeasurable eons...
For what reason can afflictions not be called nirvāṇa, since both are places where [defilements] are severed?
By what cause is it said that only Buddhas possess this while Bodhisattvas do not?
If the severance of afflictions must constitute nirvāṇa, then Bodhisattvas also sever them and should therefore possess nirvāṇa.
If the cessation of afflictions were not nirvana, this would constitute the second objection:
"If the cessation of afflictions were not nirvana, for what reason did the Tathāgata formerly tell the Brahmin named Jāti,
'This very body of mine is now nirvana'?"
This merely precludes the Buddha’s intention; it is not a valid objection, and thus the text is not extensive.
If the severance of afflictions were not *nirvāṇa*, why did the Buddha formerly tell the brahmin: "This very body of mine is the *nirvāṇa*-body"?
If that were so, then the severance would not be *nirvāṇa*; if that were the case, then the location of the body would not be [the state of] non-existence.
Furthermore, at another time, the Tathāgata descended to the third level of difficult-to-sever obstacles, which is Nirvana. This is also threefold; first, it refers to the response given to Māra.
Furthermore, at another time, while the Tathāgata was in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, Māra again requested that the Tathāgata [reveal] why he had previously had no younger brothers.
"My son is widely learned, upholds the precepts, and possesses brilliant and sharp wisdom; he transforms sentient beings and does not enter nirvana.
Now that he is fully endowed with these qualities, for what reason does he not enter [nirvana]? At that time, the Tathāgata immediately addressed Māra, saying:
"Do not now give rise to thoughts of dejection or delay. Three months from now, I shall enter nirvana. "World-Honored One, if extinction were not nirvana, then why [would he not enter it]?"
Therefore, the Tathāgata himself designated that he would enter parinirvāṇa after three months.
As for the expression "three months," the lunar calendars differ; it may also be said to be two, three, or four months from now.
Four months refers to the time according to the Zhou dynasty; three months refers to the time according to the Yin dynasty; and two months refers to the time according to the Xia dynasty.
Regarding this, one tradition states that "three months" refers to the calendar system of the Yin dynasty;

another tradition says it is not so, but rather refers to the eleventh month of this year, when Māra urged the Buddha to depart, and the Buddha replied, "Three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
Second, regarding the time when he was at the site of enlightenment:

if Nirvana were the severance of afflictions by the World-Honored One, then since the Tathāgata severed his afflictions when he first sat beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment in the past, that would already be Nirvana.
For what reason, then, did he further say, "Three months hence, I shall enter Parinirvāṇa"?
Regarding *nirvāṇa*:
thirdly, based on the words of the Mallas and others, they raise an objection:
"If, World-Honored One, you had entered *nirvāṇa* at that time, how could you have gone to the city of Kuśinagara for the sake of the Mallas?"
The monks said, "At the end of the night, he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Regarding this "at that time," there are two interpretations: first, it refers to the time at the site of enlightenment;
since he has already entered nirvāṇa at that time, why would he need to enter nirvāṇa again tonight? Second, it refers to the morning of the fifteenth day of the second month.
If he has already entered nirvāṇa, for what reason do you now say that he entered nirvāṇa at midnight?
How could the Tathāgata, who is truthful, utter such a false statement?
The Buddha replied by first directly answering and then summarizing the fault of [the objection].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhijñābhirūpa-guṇarāja, saying:
"Good son, if it is said that the Tathāgata possesses a broad and long tongue, you should know that throughout immeasurable kalpas the Tathāgata has already abandoned all false speech;
whatever words are spoken by all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas are truthful and without falsehood."
This is indeed a word of truth and sincerity; it is already not false, let alone when uttered with the broad and long tongue—how could it possibly be deceptive?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata skillfully discerns the capacities and conditions of beings, providing benefit according to the occasion:
sometimes he speaks of cessation as *nirvāṇa*, and sometimes he speaks of cessation as not being *nirvāṇa*. All such teachings of the Buddha are nothing other than reality.

Subsequently, he provides the formal answers to the three difficulties, though not in the same order as the initial responses: the first answer addresses the final difficulty, and the third answer addresses the intermediate difficulty.
The response to the first [difficulty] is divided into two parts: first, the answer to Māra.
"Good son, as you have said, in the past Pāpīyān requested that I enter nirvāṇa.
Good son, this Māra King truly did not know the definitive characteristics of nirvāṇa. Why is this?
It is because Pāpīyān thought that not transforming sentient beings and remaining in silence was itself nirvāṇa. Good son, it is like people of the world..."
Seeing a person who does not speak and performs no actions, one might say that this person is no different from the dead; Māra Pāpīyān is also like this,
for he thinks that because the Tathāgata does not transform sentient beings and remains silent without speaking,
the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
Māra does not recognize *nirvāṇa*, taking silence to be extinction; the Buddha accords with his disposition, yet how could this be the essence of *nirvāṇa*?
"Good son," the latter two answers resolve the Bodhisattva’s objection.
Good son, the Tathāgata does not say that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha are identical in their lack of distinction;

he speaks only of the identity between the two dharmas of permanence and purity. Good son, the Buddha also does not say that the Buddha, the Buddha-nature, and nirvāṇa are identical in their lack of distinction;
he speaks only of the identity between the eternal, constant, and unchanging. Good son, the Buddha also—
It is taught that the true nature of nirvāṇa is characterized by non-differentiation; it is merely said to be eternally existent, real, and unchanging, and thus devoid of differentiation.
To clarify the similarity and difference between Buddhas and bodhisattvas: Buddhas possess nirvāṇa, whereas bodhisattvas do not—this is the distinction within the Saṃgha.

Because they are "Treasures," it is said that while the Three Jewels each have their own distinct characteristics, there is no difference between them regarding the two matters of being eternally abiding (*nitya*) and pure (*viśuddha*);
the same applies to the latter two explanations.
"Good son, at that time I... [and so forth] is the second response to the third repeated objection; first, it clarifies the point of severance regarding the question.

To extinguish evil, he proclaims the latter part of *nirvāṇa*; to give rise to goodness, he proclaims the beginning of *nirvāṇa*. Within the extinguishing of evil, he first speaks by means of the Dharma:
"Good son, at that time, my śrāvaka disciples gave rise to disputes, such as those among the people of Kauśāmbī."
Evil bhikṣus violate my teachings and frequently transgress the prohibitions, accepting impure things and greedily seeking gain and offerings.
They praise themselves before laypeople, claiming, "I have attained the outflows-free state," ranging from the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the fruit of an arhat.
They disparage others and show no reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, the precepts, or their preceptors.
"You previously said to me that such things as these were permitted by the Buddha to be kept, yet you now say that such things as these are not permitted by the Buddha to be kept.
I then spoke to him, saying: 'Such things as these are indeed not permitted by me;
you have contradicted my words, for such things as these are truly permitted by the Buddha. Because such evil persons do not believe my words, for their sake, I have addressed Pāpīyān."
"Do not be distressed or delayed; in three months' time, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.

Son of good family, it is because of such evil bhikṣus that my śrāvaka disciples who are learning from me do not see my body nor hear my Dharma, and thus they say that the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa.
Only the bodhisattvas are able to see my body and constantly hear my Dharma."
Therefore, I do not say that I have entered nirvāṇa. Although my śrāvaka disciples may speak of the Tathāgata’s entry into nirvāṇa, in reality, I have not entered nirvāṇa.

Good son, if any of my śrāvaka disciples should say that the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa, you should know that such a person is not my disciple, but is a companion of Māra and possesses false views.

An evil person does not possess right view; if one says that the Tathāgata does not enter *nirvāṇa*, you should know that such a person is truly my disciple and not a companion of Māra. One with right view is not an evil heretic.
Good son, from the beginning I have never seen among my disciples anyone who says that the Tathāgata does not transform sentient beings but remains in silence, which they call *parinirvāṇa*.
...it is so. Next, five analogies are set forth in detail.
"Good son, it is as if a householder who has many children were to depart for another land and not yet have returned."

Just as sons may think their father has already passed away while that elder is actually not yet dead, and those sons, being deluded, all conceive the notion of his death; so too it is with the śrāvaka disciples.
Because they do not see me, they say that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees at Kuśinagara, yet I have truly not entered parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, O son of good family, regarding those śrāvaka disciples who conceive the notion that they have attained nirvāṇa: it is like a bright lamp that someone covers;
those unaware of this might say the lamp has been extinguished, yet the radiant flame has not actually ceased. Because they do not know, they give rise to the perception of extinction.
The śrāvaka disciples are just the same; although they possess the eye of wisdom, it is shrouded by afflictions.
Causing their minds to become inverted, they fail to see my true body and thus falsely conceive the thought of my parinirvāṇa;
yet I have not, in fact, entered final extinction. Good son, it is like a person born blind who does not see the sun or moon;

because he does not see them, he does not know the characteristics of day and night or light and darkness. Because he does not know them, he says that the reality of the sun and moon simply does not exist. In truth, [the sun and moon do exist].
Just as those born blind do not see the sun and moon, and because they do not see them, give rise to perverted conceptions, saying that the sun and moon do not exist;
so too it is with the śrāvaka disciples. Like those born blind who do not see the Tathāgata, they claim that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
In reality, the Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa; yet due to their perverted conceptions, they give rise to such a thought. This is good.

Good son, it is like clouds and mist that obscure the sun and moon; a foolish person then says, "The sun and moon do not exist," yet the sun and moon truly exist, and it is only because they are obscured that sentient beings do not see them. The śrāvaka disciples are also like this:
with their eye of wisdom obscured by various afflictions, they do not see the Tathāgata and thus say, "The Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa. Good son...
My son, this is simply the Tathāgata manifesting the conduct of an infant; it is not his final nirvāṇa. Good son, it is like when the sun sets over Jambudvīpa:
sentient beings do not see it because it is obscured by the Black Mountains (Kṛṣṇaparvata), yet the nature of the sun truly does not sink away.
It is only because sentient beings do not see it that they conceive the thought that it has set. The śrāvaka disciples are just like this: for the sake of all afflictions... [text truncated]
Because they were obstructed by the mountain of afflictions, they did not see my body; because they did not see it, they conceived the notion that the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa.
Yet, in truth, I have not undergone ultimate and eternal extinction. Therefore, in the city of Vaiśālī, I said to Pāpīyān:
"Three months hence, I shall enter nirvāṇa."
Next, son of good family, because the Tathāgata foresaw that this was the time for generating wholesome roots, he proclaimed "Nirvāṇa.
Son of good family, the Tathāgata foresaw that in three months the roots of goodness of Kāśyapa Bodhisattva would ripen;
he also foresaw that Subhadra of Mount Gandhamādana, having completed his summer retreat, would come to my presence. For these reasons, I spoke thus to Māra.
"King Pāpīyān, three months from now I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Good son, there are five hundred Mallas who, at the end of those three months, shall likewise resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, I said to Pāpīyān: 'Three months from now I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Good son, it is as follows..."
Because the roots of goodness for the supreme path will mature in three months for Cunda and the five hundred Licchavis,
as well as the Āmra-fruit girl, I have told Pāpīyān that in three months I shall enter parinirvāṇa for their sake.
"Good son, Sunakṣatra was closely associated with the heterodox Nirgranthas and others;
I taught the Dharma to him for a full twelve years, yet that man held wrong views and neither believed nor accepted it.
Because such a person has the roots of wrong view firmly planted, they shall certainly be uprooted after three months. For this reason, I said to Pāpīyān: 'After three months, I shall [act]...'"
"O son of good family, for what reason did I, in the past, by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, tell Māra Pāpīyān:
'I do not yet have many disciples of great learning; therefore, I cannot enter parinirvāṇa'?
At that time, I wished to turn the wheel of Dharma in Vārāṇasī for the sake of the five bhikṣus. And so forth, for the sake of the five bhikṣus...
The World-Honored One first intended [to teach] for Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimalakīrti, Gavāmpati, and Subāhu;
next, he intended for the fifty people including the householder Ugga;
next, he intended for the immeasurable humans and devas including King Bimbisāra of Magadha; and finally, he intended for the gate of Uruvilvākāśyapa.
I first intended to turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma for my five hundred bhikṣus; next, I wished to do so for the two brothers, Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa, along with their five hundred disciples;
and subsequently, I wished to do so for Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the other two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
For this reason, I told the Māra Pāpīyas that I would not enter parinirvāṇa.
Good son, there is that which is called "Nirvāṇa" [Section Three: Answering Intermediate Difficulties]. It clarifies that the point of severance is not itself Nirvāṇa;
it shows that there is both "is" and "is not. If one does not see the Buddha-nature and merely severs afflictions, it is termed "Nirvāṇa," but not "Mahāparinirvāṇa.
If one sees the Buddha-nature while severing afflictions, that is Mahāparinirvāṇa. Since this distinction is thus established:
How can one categorically distinguish between the two at the outset?
Good son, there is that which is called *nirvāṇa* but is not *mahāparinirvāṇa*. Why is it that this *nirvāṇa* is not *mahāparinirvāṇa*?
Because one has not seen the Buddha-nature while severing the afflictions; this is called *nirvāṇa*, not *mahāparinirvāṇa*, because the Buddha-nature has not been seen.
Therefore, where there is impermanence and non-self, there can only be suffering and impurity. For this reason, although one may sever the afflictions, it cannot be called Great Parinirvāṇa.
If one perceives the Buddha-nature and is thus able to sever the afflictions, then this is called Great Parinirvāṇa.
Because one perceives the Buddha-nature, it is designated as permanent, blissful, self, and pure. For this reason, one eliminates the afflictions...
Affliction (*nir*) may also be called *mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Second, the extensive explanation of *mahāparinirvāṇa* consists of eleven successive sections.
"Good son, *nir* means 'not,' and *bana* means 'weaving. The meaning of not weaving is called *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore—
"Nibbāna" signifies the meaning of covering and non-covering; thus it is named Nibbāna. "Nibbāna" signifies that which has neither coming nor going, neither departing nor arriving;
thus it is named Nibbāna. "Nibbāna" signifies the meaning of grasping and non-grasping; thus it is named Nibbāna. "Nibbāna" signifies the absence of fixedness and non-fixedness;
thus it is named Nibbāna. "Nibbāna" signifies the absence of newness and antiquity; thus it is named Nibbāna. "Nibbāna."
To speak of the meaning of obstruction and non-obstruction is what is called *nirvāṇa*, son of good family.
There are disciples of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa who say that "nir" signifies the meaning of having marks and being without marks; this is called *nirvāṇa*, son of good family.
"Nir" signifies the meaning of existence and non-existence; this is called *nirvāṇa*. "Nir" signifies the meaning of conjunction and non-conjunction.
This is called *nirvāṇa*. "Nir" signifies suffering; "vāṇa" signifies the meaning of the absence of suffering—this is called *nirvāṇa*.
Good son, the cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*) is not called *nirvāṇa*; rather, the non-arising of afflictions is called *nirvāṇa*.
Good son, when the afflictions do not arise in the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, this is called *nirvāṇa*. All their wisdom is unimpeded regarding all phenomena; this constitutes [it].
The Tathāgata, the Tathāgata—neither an ordinary person, nor a śrāvaka, nor a pratyekabuddha, nor a bodhisattva—is called the Buddha-nature.
The body, mind, and wisdom of the Tathāgata pervade immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable lands without any obstruction;
this is called space. The Tathāgata is eternally abiding and without change; this is called the true mark (dharmatā). For these reasons, the Tathāgata...
In truth, they do not enter ultimate *parinirvāṇa*.
This is because people have cited the opening passage of this text, which states that *pari-nir* means "to weave" (*puna*) and *nir* means "to extinguish" (*na*).
However, upon examining the text, there is no mention of the term *pari* at all; furthermore, the two characters "shi" (識) and "zhi" (織) do not appear in the original scripture.
The remaining ten characters are to be understood according to the text.
The third conclusion is as stated in the text (and so forth).
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fully accomplishing the seventh merit.
The explanation of the eighth merit has three parts: the heading, the exposition, and the conclusion; the first is as in the text.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by practicing this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fully accomplish the eighth merit?"
Next, the explanation of the nine matters is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the merits; second, discussing the meaning. The first part is further divided into two:
first, listing the topical headings for the nine matters; second, explaining them in sequence. The listing of the topical headings is as in the text.
Good son, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the Mahāparinirvāṇa, he eliminates five things, distances himself from five things, accomplishes six things,
practices five things, protects one thing, draws near to four things, and with a mind that faithfully accords with the single reality,
attains liberation through faith and liberation through wisdom.

The first explanation concerns the removal of the five things to be abandoned, which are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Although the Bodhisattva has not yet completely eliminated the five aggregates, he is nevertheless not covered by them.
Regarding the initial explanation of the aggregates, there are two parts: first, a general explanation, and second, a detailed explanation.
Good son, how does a bodhisattva eliminate and sever the five things? These are the so-called five aggregates: form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
What is the meaning of the term "aggregate" (skandha)? It refers to that which causes sentient beings to continue in the cycle of birth and death, never laying down their heavy burden;

it involves dispersing and reassembling, being encompassed by the three periods of time, and when one seeks its actual reality, it is utterly unfindable. By means of these various meanings—[the bodhisattva eliminates them].
Therefore, they are called "aggregates" (skandha).
Although the initial general statement mentions "aggregates," "burdens," and "heavy loads" and so forth,
the second section provides a specific explanation for each aggregate.

Although a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), he does not perceive its characteristics. Why? Because when one investigates its nature within the ten types of form, it is entirely unobtainable;
yet, for the sake of the world, it is spoken of as an "aggregate" (*skandha*) that undergoes existence with its hundred and eight [sensations].

Although he perceives the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), from the beginning there is no characteristic of sensation. Why? Because although sensations number one hundred and eight, in principle they have no fixed reality.
Therefore, it is likewise for the Bodhisattva that he does not perceive the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva deeply perceives that the five aggregates are the root of all evil and the source of the arising of afflictions, he employs skillful means to bring them to cessation.

The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) consists of the five sense faculties and the five sense objects, making ten forms; because these are all produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), they are said to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Regarding the "one hundred and eight feelings" (*vedanā-aṣṭottara-śata*), there are two interpretations: first, it is said that within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) there is no mention of "one hundred and eight," but rather that within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) there are the various afflictions (*kleśa*), namely the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) together with the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), which together constitute the one hundred and eight. Second, [it is based on] the second [interpretation].

The *Śāstra* explains that within the aggregates (*skandha*) themselves there are one hundred and eight [afflictions]. Generally speaking across the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), since there are three [types] for each base, this constitutes eighteen.
Furthermore, within each single base, there are both wholesome and unwholesome [states], which constitute thirty-six.
Finally, when calculated across the three periods of time (*tryadhvan*), they total one hundred and eight.
What is the second chapter on the gate of distancing oneself?
How does a bodhisattva distance themselves from the five things? These are the so-called five views. What are the five? First, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);

second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); third, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); fourth, adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and fifth, adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). It is because of these five views [that one must distance oneself].
The sixty-two views arise from these [five] views; because of these views, birth and death are never severed. For this reason, the Bodhisattva guards against them and does not approach them.
This means being free from the five views. Furthermore, it is said that "from these five views, the sixty-two [views] arise. Regarding these two interpretations, one says they are combined.
Regarding the two types of "extremes" (*anta*), there are sixty-two views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). There are fifty-six views of self and six views of extremes. As for the fifty-six views of self:
in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), each of the aggregates (*skandha*) has four views—namely, the views of identity (*ekatva*) and difference (*anyatva*)—making twenty.

It is the same in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), making forty. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are only four [aggregates], each with four views, making sixteen. When added to the previous total, [the count is complete].
Regarding the sixty-two views, there are six because each of the three realms has both the view of annihilationism and the view of eternalism, making six.

Second, it is said that these sixty-two are established solely by way of the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), without considering the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). By distinguishing the three periods of time—present, past, and future—in terms of whether there is a self or no self, four views are established.
By applying these to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), twenty views are established. Regarding the future, there are twenty views concerning whether the world is finite or infinite.

The twenty views regarding whether the Tathāgata exists after death or does not exist after death constitute sixty positions when combined with those that do not depart from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism;
these, together with the four positions concerning the state of the Buddha after his parinirvāṇa, form the sixty-two views.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, in the "Examination of Nirvāṇa" chapter, clarifies that regarding the period after the Buddha’s passing, one gives rise to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism based on the Buddha; this is discussed in terms of the past and the future, and does not involve calculations concerning the present.
The sixty-two [views] are formed by taking the five aggregates as twenty— dividing each into the permanent and the impermanent—
and adding twenty for the future limit being finite or infinite, and twenty for the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
How does one achieve [the qualities]? This explains the third chapter.
How does a bodhisattva achieve the six matters? They are called the six bases of mindfulness (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). What are the six? First, mindfulness of the Buddha; second, mindfulness of the Dharma;
third, mindfulness of the Saṃgha; fourth, mindfulness of the devas; fifth, mindfulness of generosity (*dāna*); sixth, mindfulness of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
This is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the six matters.
The accomplishment of the six mindfulnesses is the same as that in the Chapter on Pure Conduct (*Brahmacarya-varga*), differing only slightly in its sequence.
How should one practice? This explains the fourth chapter.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the five matters, namely the five concentrations? First is the concentration of knowledge; second is the concentration of tranquility;
third is the concentration of experiencing physical and mental bliss; fourth is the concentration of non-bliss; and fifth is the Śūraṅgama concentration.
By cultivating these five kinds of concentrated mind, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa; therefore, the bodhisattva exerts himself.

Cultivating the mind means cultivating the five concentrations (*samādhi*): the former four are *dhyāna*, while the latter is *prajñā*. "Knowing concentration" refers to the first *dhyāna*, because it possesses vitarka and vicāra;
"tranquil concentration" refers to the second *dhyāna*, because it is without vitarka and vicāra, and is thus called the noble silence.
The concentration of experiencing the bliss of tranquility refers specifically to the third dhyāna, because it is the ultimate state of the feeling of bliss within meditative concentration.

The concentration that is without bliss refers to the fourth dhyāna, because suffering and bliss have been abandoned there, and it consists of the feeling of equanimity. Regarding the Śūraṅgama [Samādhi], there are both general and specific aspects.
Generally, it interpenetrates all ten stages as well as the stages prior to them. Specifically, within the ten stages, one further cultivates the one hundred and eight samādhis.
Only then does one attain this samādhi.
How does one guard [it]? This explains the fifth chapter’s section on guarding.
What is the single thing that a bodhisattva guards? It is the bodhicitta; the bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly and diligently guards it.

Guarding this bodhicitta is like a worldly person protecting an only son, or like a blind person protecting his remaining eye, or like one traveling through a wilderness protecting their guide; the Bodhisattva’s guarding of the bodhicitta is likewise so.
Because of guarding such bodhicitta, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one is fully endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
this is precisely the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa. Therefore, a bodhisattva protects a single dharma.

This refers to protecting the bodhicitta so that whatever wholesome deeds one cultivates are all bodhisattva practices; this includes the presentation of the teaching, the analogy, and their synthesis.
How does one draw near? The following explains the sixth chapter, namely, the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
What are the four matters to which a bodhisattva draws near? They are the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
What are the four? First, great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*); second, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); third, great sympathetic joy (*mahāmuditā*); and fourth, great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).
Because these four minds enable immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to give rise to the bodhicitta, the bodhisattva fixes his mind upon them and draws near to them.
What is meant by "faithful compliance"? This explains the seventh chapter.
What is meant by "the Bodhisattva’s faithful compliance with the One Reality"? It means that the Bodhisattva understands that all sentient beings ultimately return to the Single Path.
This Single Path refers to the Mahāyāna. For the sake of sentient beings, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have divided it into three.
Therefore, the bodhisattva believes and complies with it without opposition;
this is precisely the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). The One Vehicle is the true Dharma, as the Lotus Sūtra says: "This alone is the one true reality;
the other two are not real."
