What is the "mind well-liberated"? This explains the eighth chapter’s section.
What is the Bodhisattva’s mind well-liberated? It is because the mind has eternally severed and extinguished greed, hatred, and delusion; this is called the Bodhisattva’s mind being well-liberated.
Regarding the distinction between mind and wisdom: there are two interpretations. First, Yizheng says that when the mind takes conventional truth as its object, it is free from greed and hatred;
this is liberation of mind (*citta-vimukti*). When the mind takes ultimate truth as its object, it is free from ignorance; this is liberation by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).

Second, he says that because greed, hatred, and so forth are severed, there is liberation of mind; because ignorance is eradicated, there is liberation by wisdom. As the *Śāstra* quotes: "The afflictions..."
The mind inclines toward ignorance, while wisdom inclines toward [the truth].
What is the wisdom that is well-liberated? This explains the ninth chapter.
What is the bodhisattva’s wisdom that is well-liberated? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses unobstructed knowledge regarding all phenomena.
This is called the cause for the Bodhisattva’s wisdom of skillful liberation. Through this wisdom of liberation, that which was previously unheard is now heard;
that which was previously unseen is now seen; and that which was previously unattained is now attained.
Regarding the three phrases mentioned above in the commentary—"the wisdom-liberated one who has heard what was never heard before," and so forth—there are two interpretations.

The first states that "hearing" refers to the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), "seeing" refers to the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), and "attaining" refers to the supernormal power of the body (*kāyābhijñā*).

The second states that the nine stages (*navabhūmi*) constitute "hearing and seeing the Buddha-nature," while the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*) constitutes "seeing the Buddha-nature with the eyes," perceiving it fully and clearly; it is now because of this wisdom-liberation [that these qualities are realized].
Transcending to the ninth bhūmi is "hearing what was not heard"; because of the ninth bhūmi, one reaches the tenth bhūmi, which is "seeing what was not seen";
from the tenth bhūmi to the Buddha-bhūmi is "reaching where there is no reaching."
At that time, following the second section on the Discourse on Light, this is the eighth chapter of the preceding discourse, "Liberation of the Mind.

First comes the question, followed by the answer. The initial question has three parts: first, a refutation based on the premise of non-existence; second, a concession based on the premise of existence;

and third, a refutation based on the premise of indeterminacy. All of these aim to resolve the bondage. The first of these sections further consists of two parts: first, acknowledging the intent and expressing disagreement; and second...
[The formal inquiry:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantāloka-guṇarāja addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught regarding 'liberation of the mind,' that meaning is not so."
The meaning of the question is as follows: If the mind inherently possesses afflictions (*kleśa*), this is untenable; if it inherently lacks afflictions, this is also untenable.
It is untenable for afflictions to be definitively existent, and it is also untenable for them to be definitively non-existent.

Regarding the first point—that [the mind] is inherently without [afflictions]—there are nine difficulties raised within the inquiry. The World-Honored One addresses three points of intent; the first pair clarifies that the mind is neither bound nor unbound.
Regarding liberation, there are five points: first, it is exclusively clarified that there is no bondage; second, it is exclusively clarified that there is no liberation.
This is the primary text’s formal refutation of both non-bondage and non-liberation.
Why is this? Because the mind is fundamentally unconditioned. For what reason? Because the intrinsic nature of this mind is not subject to desire or hatred.
If one were bound by the fetters of anger, ignorance, and delusion, how could it be said that the mind is "well-liberated" when there was originally no bondage?

Furthermore, within the second of the five sections, the absence of bondage is specifically clarified; moreover, in the first two of the preceding four [sections], that which is to be bound is shown to be non-existent.
World-Honored One, if the intrinsic nature of the mind is not bound by the fetter of greed, by what causes and conditions can it become bound?
It is like the horn of a cow, which originally lacks the characteristic of milk; even if one applies effort, milk cannot be produced. This is not the case for a cow with respect to milk:
though little effort is applied, much milk flows forth. The mind is likewise originally without [greed].

How can there be greed now? If greed did not exist originally and only came into being later, then all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—who were originally devoid of the characteristic of greed—should now all possess it.
World-Honored One, it is like a barren woman who originally lacks the characteristic of having a child;

even if she applies effort and countless causes and conditions, a child cannot be obtained. The mind is also like this: it originally lacks the characteristic of greed, and thus even if one creates manifold conditions, [greed cannot arise].
“World-Honored One, greed has no basis for arising. Just as fire cannot be produced from drilling wet wood, so it is with the mind:
though one drills and seeks it, greed cannot be found. How then can the fetter of greed bind the mind? World-Honored One, it is like pressing sand to extract oil;
the mind is likewise: though one presses it, greed cannot be found. One should know that such is the nature of the greedy mind.”
The two principles are each distinct; even if [the former] were to exist, how could it defile the mind?
The latter clarifies that there is nothing capable of binding.
World-Honored One, it is as if someone were to try to drive a stake into space—it would never find a place to stay; attempting to fix greed within the mind is likewise.
In this way, various causes and conditions cannot cause greed to bind the mind.
To use the analogy of a wooden stake: it is like trying to lift a wooden post into the air; it has no cause for remaining suspended there (and so forth).

If a mind free from greed is what is called liberation—this is the third section, which specifically clarifies that [liberation] is not [attained through] understanding—it is divided into three parts.

First, it clarifies that it is not [attained through] understanding: "World-Honored One, if a mind free from greed is named liberation, for what reason do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not extract thorns from empty space?"
Second, clarifying that there is no liberation through attainment:
The World-Honored One’s mind in past lives is not called "liberated," nor is his mind in future lives liberated;
his mind in the present life does not coexist with the Path. Of which temporal mind, then, can it be said that it attains liberation?
The three types of clear knowledge (vidyā) do not consist in attaining a path of liberation.
World-Honored One, just as a lamp of the past cannot extinguish darkness, a lamp of the future will not extinguish darkness, and a lamp of the present likewise does not extinguish darkness.
Why is this? Because light and darkness cannot coexist; the mind is also like this.
How can it be said that "the mind attains liberation"?
World-Honored One, greed also exists [in the present]. This second section, based on the existence of the fundamental [defilement], poses a concessionary question with two further points:
first, to clarify that if it were fundamentally existent, there would have to be greed within a wholesome mind; second, by means of the analogy of drilling for fire, to clarify that [it must exist].
Regarding the presence of desire within the objective field, there are two parts to its initial discussion: first, an explanation by way of the Dharma, followed by two similes.
The World-Honored One [taught that] desire also exists; if desire were non-existent, then when one perceives the form of a woman, desire should not arise.
Since desire arises because of the form of a woman, one should know that this desire truly exists. Because desire exists, one falls into the three [realms].
The Evil Realms.
Regarding the intent of the first discourse on the Dharma: if one says that desire is inherently present in the mind, this is also untenable;

for if it were inherent, it would not arise from causes and conditions. Since desire arises by borrowing external forms, one should know that it does not truly exist. Furthermore, as for the mind being inherently...
If greed could not be made non-existent, one should not attain liberation from the mind, and the mind should be constantly greedy.
World-Honored One, it is as if someone, upon seeing a painted image of a woman, also gives rise to greed; because greed has arisen, they incur various kinds of offenses.
If there were originally no greed, how could greed arise upon seeing a painting? If the mind has no greed, how [could it arise]?

The Tathāgata has said that when the mind of a bodhisattva attains liberation, if there is still poverty of mind, how can one perceive signs such that they subsequently arise, whereas for one who does not perceive signs, they do not arise? I now see directly that there are evil retributions;
one should know that it is likewise with greed, hatred, and delusion. World-Honored One, it is as if sentient beings possess bodies but lack a self.
While ordinary beings recklessly conceive the notion of a self, and though they possess this notion of self, do not fall into the three miserable realms,
why is it that those who are lustful give rise to the perception of a woman where there is no sign of a woman, and thereby fall into the three evil destinies?
“World-Honored One, it is like drilling for fire; although fire is produced, that nature of fire does not exist within the various conditions.

By what causes and conditions is it then produced? World-Honored One, craving is also like this: craving does not exist within form, nor does craving exist within sound, smell, taste, or mental phenomena (*dharma*).
How then is craving produced with respect to form, sound, smell, taste, and mental phenomena? If [craving] does not exist within the various conditions...”
If all are entirely without greed, why is it that sentient beings alone give rise to greed, while the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not?
Next, one may raise this same objection by contrasting the object with the mind.
Section Three: Refutation Based on the Indeterminacy of the Mind. Furthermore, this section has three parts; first, it clarifies that the mind is indeterminate.
The mind of the World-Honored One is also not determinate. If the mind were determinate, there would be no greed, hatred, or delusion. If...
If one is in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), why is it said that "the mind attains liberation"?
Next, it clarifies that greed is not fixed.
If greed is also not fixed, how can it cause one to be born in the three evil destinies?
The three types of craving and their objects are likewise both indeterminate.
Why are both the craver and the object indeterminate?
Because with respect to a single form, one may give rise to craving, or give rise to hatred, or give rise to delusion. Therefore, both the craver and the object are indeterminate. If...
Since both are indeterminate, for what reason does the Tathāgata say that when a bodhisattva cultivates the Great Nirvāṇa, the mind attains liberation?
At that time, the World-Honored One [proceeds to] answer the second question; it is said that he answers them in successive order, providing three distinct responses to the three preceding questions.
First, he answers the question regarding "original non-existence. [The passage beginning with] "There are various heterodox paths... answers the second [question].
Regarding the question: "O son of good family, the Buddhas ultimately do not definitively provide answers," this addresses the third previous question concerning indeterminacy.

Furthermore, it is said that this is not so; although the sequential arrangement appears to involve a correspondence between subject and object, upon examining the meaning of the text, they are entirely unrelated.
Rather, the three sections follow the logic of the meaning: first, establishing the correct principle; second, refuting attachments; and third, providing an extensive analysis.
The Middle Way of Causality.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantāloka-Āryaguṇarāja, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! The mind is neither bound by the fetter of greed, nor is it unbound; it is not this [and it is not that]."
Liberation is neither non-liberation, nor existent, nor non-existent, nor present, nor past, nor future.
Why is this? Son of good family, it is because all dharmas lack intrinsic nature.
This is precisely the first [point]: clarifying that the substance of the mind is neither existent nor non-existent, neither mind nor non-mind, neither greed nor non-greed;
since it is a dual negation of every phenomenon and a relinquishing of both extremes, how could it not be the correct meaning of the Middle Way?

Next follows the second section, which refutes fixed attachments regarding meditative concentration; this is further divided into two parts: first, the refutation of the attachment to existence, and second, the refutation of the attachment to non-existence.
If you claim that the mind definitely possesses desire or definitely lacks desire, this is identical to the first passage concerning the Nirgranthas.
This section is again divided into two: first, the detailed presentation of what is being asserted.
Good son, there are certain non-Buddhists who speak thus: "When causes and conditions combine, a fruit arises.
If that which was originally devoid of the nature of arising within the various conditions could nevertheless give rise to it, then empty space—which does not arise—should also produce a fruit.

Since empty space does not arise because it is not a cause, [we conclude] that the nature of the fruit must already exist inherently within the various conditions; therefore, through their assembly, it is obtained."
Why is this so? It is because, for example, when Devadatta wishes to build a wall, he takes clay and earth rather than pigments;
when he wishes to create a painted image, he gathers pigments rather than grass or wood; when making clothing, he takes thread rather than clay or wood;

and when building a house, he takes clay rather than thread or cord. Because people take what is appropriate for each purpose, one should know that within these things, each possesses its own specific capacity.
Because a produced fruit is capable of being produced, one should know that its nature must necessarily exist within the cause.
If this nature were absent, then from a single object all things whatsoever ought to be produced.

Furthermore, if something is to be grasped, fashioned, or brought forth, one should know that the fruit must necessarily already exist therein; for if the fruit were absent, a person would not grasp it, fashion it, or bring it forth. Only...
Because space is without grasping and without action, it is able to give birth to all myriad things; because there is a cause,
just as a nyagrodha seed resides within the nyagrodha tree, as clarified butter exists within milk, cloth within thread, and a jar within clay.
All ordinary beings are blinded by ignorance; [the Buddha] rebukes them for the faults of the two lower fetters.
"Good son, all ordinary beings, blinded by ignorance, make this definitive statement: 'Form has the meaning of attachment,' and 'The mind has the nature of greed.
Furthermore, they say that although the minds of ordinary beings have the nature of greed, they also have the nature of liberation; when they encounter the conditions of greed, the mind..."
Thus, greed arises; yet if one encounters a mind of liberation, one is liberated. Although this is said, the meaning is not so.
There are various ordinary persons—this is the second [section], which refutes their attachment. This also has two parts: first, presenting what they grasp.
Furthermore, there are some ordinary worldlings who speak thus: "Within all causes, the effect does not exist at all.
There are two kinds of causes: first, the subtle; second, the coarse. The subtle is eternal, while the coarse is impermanent.

From the subtle cause it transforms into a coarse cause, and from this coarse cause it subsequently transforms to produce the effect. Since the coarse [cause] is impermanent, the effect is likewise impermanent."
"Good son, there are certain ordinary people who further say: 'The mind has no cause, and desire also has no cause;
it is simply due to the passage of time that the desirous mind arises.

Regarding such individuals, the following section is precisely for the purpose of censuring them and establishing the faults of their views, employing both doctrinal exposition (*dharmadeśanā*) and illustrative parables (*upamādeśanā*)."
Those of such a kind, because they are unable to understand the causes and conditions of the mind, transmigrate through the six destinies and fully undergo birth and death.
Good son, it is like a dog tied to a pillar by a collar; though it circles the pillar all day long, it cannot escape.
All ordinary worldlings are likewise bound by the collar of ignorance to the pillar of birth and death, circling through the twenty-five states of existence.
Good son, it is impossible for them to achieve liberation. It is like a person who has fallen into a latrine and, having emerged, enters it again;
or like one whose illness has been cured yet returns to the cause of the disease; or like one traveling on a road who, upon reaching an open wilderness, turns back after having passed through it;
or like one who has washed clean yet smears himself with mud once more. All ordinary beings are likewise.

Furthermore, having thus attained liberation from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) but not yet being liberated from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), they return once again to the three evil destinies.
Why is this? Because all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) contemplate only the fruit and do not contemplate causes and conditions;
just as a dog chases a clod of earth rather than the person who threw it, so too are ordinary beings: they contemplate only...

Regarding the fruit, one does not contemplate its causes and conditions; because of this lack of contemplation, one falls from the Realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception back into the three evil destinies.
Son of Good Family, in the third section of this extensive exposition on the meaning of the Middle Way’s causes and conditions, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have no fixed attachments whatsoever.
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, it clarifies that all dharmas of cause and effect are neither existent nor non-existent, yet they exist by virtue of causes and conditions.
Second, it is explained that the mind’s possession of desire also exists neither as being nor as non-being due to causal conditions. Regarding this, the first section has three parts:
first, clarifying the departure from the four extremes.
"Good son, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never definitively state that the effect exists within the cause, nor that the effect does not exist within the cause..."
There is the case where the effect is neither existent nor non-existent.
If one says that the effect is already definitively present within the cause, this is refuted by the second fixed position.
If one says that the effect is either definitively present within the cause, definitively absent, both present and absent, or neither present nor absent—[these are likewise refuted].
One should know that those who lack the fruit are all companions of Māra, belonging to Māra, and are indeed lovers of craving.
Such lovers of craving cannot permanently sever the fetters of birth and death, nor do they understand the characteristics of the mind or the characteristics of greed.
The third section below, concerning the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, correctly reveals the Dharma of the Middle Way.
Good son, why do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas reveal the Middle Way? Although they teach that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, they do not remain fixed [in that position].
Why is this? It is because of the eye, because of form, because of light, because of the mind, and because of mindfulness.
When consciousness arises, this consciousness is definitively not found within the eye, nor within forms, nor within light, nor within the mind, nor within mental attention;
it is neither in between, nor existent, nor non-existent. Because it arises from conditions, it is called "existent";
because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is called "non-existent. Therefore, the Tathāgata has said that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent.
Good son, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never definitively state that [the mind] is inferior.
Chapter Two correctly clarifies that the mind possesses greed, being neither existent nor non-existent, because it exists due to causes and conditions. This section further divides into two parts:

first, clarifying that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, indeterminate, and neither existent nor non-existent; second, clarifying that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure and devoid of conjunction. The first passage:
There are three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
Good son, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never definitively state that the mind has a pure nature or an impure nature, because the pure and impure mind has no fixed abode and arises from conditions.
Thus, it is said that it is not that there is no basis, yet there is no inherent nature of greed.
It is said that they do not exist.
In the commentary, there are again three parts; first, the topical outline is proclaimed:
"O son of good family, due to causes and conditions, the mind gives rise to greed; due to causes and conditions, the mind attains liberation."
There are two topical gateways: that which arises from conditions through greed and that which is liberated from conditions.
Regarding the second, the explanation of these two gateways, there are two kinds of causal conditions:

first, those that follow saṃsāra; second, those that follow Mahāparinirvāṇa. Good son, there are two kinds of causal conditions: first, those that accord with birth and death; second, those that accord with Great Nirvāṇa.
There is a cause and condition for this; the following third set of four phrases provides a detailed analysis.
Good son, due to causes and conditions, the mind arises together with greed and perishes together with greed;
it may arise together with greed and perish without greed; it may arise without greed and perish together with greed; and it may arise without greed and perish without greed.
What is cessation? It is when the mind arises together with greed and ceases together with greed, noble son.
If there is an ordinary person who has not yet severed the mind of greed and cultivates the mind of greed, such a person’s mind arises together with greed and the mind ceases together with greed.
All sentient beings who have not severed the mind of greed have minds that arise together with greed and cease together with greed, just like those sentient beings in the desire realm.

All [beings] possess the flavor of the first stage of dhyāna; whether they cultivate it or not, it is always accomplished, and upon encountering the appropriate conditions, they immediately attain it.
What are called "conditions" refers to the calamity of fire. All ordinary worldlings are likewise:
whether they cultivate it or not, their minds arise together with greed and their minds perish together with greed. Why is this? Because they do not sever greed. How so?
There is a state where the mind arises together with greed but does not cease together with greed:

when a śrāvaka disciple, due to certain conditions, gives rise to a greedy mind and, out of fear of that greedy mind, practices the meditation on the white bones (śvetāsthi-saṃjñā). This is called the mind arising together with greed but not ceasing together with greed.

Furthermore, there is a state where the mind arises together with greed but does not cease together with greed, as in the case of a śrāvaka who has not yet realized the four fruits [of the path], due to certain conditions.

When one born with a mind of greed realizes the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], that mind of greed is extinguished; this is called "the mind arising together with greed, but not extinguishing together with greed.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi), the mind arises together with greed but does not extinguish together with greed.
How is it that [the mind] does not arise together with greed, yet is extinguished together with greed? It is when the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has already severed the mind of greed.

For the sake of sentient beings, he manifests the appearance of having desire; by manifesting this, he enables immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to inquire about and receive the wholesome Dharma, thereby fully accomplishing it.
This is called "not arising together with desire, but ceasing together with desire.
What is meant by "not arising together with desire and not ceasing together with desire"? It refers to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas—excluding those in the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi).
The remaining bodhisattvas are said to be "not born together with greed" and "not extinguished together with greed.
For this reason, the subsequent causal conditions are concluded.
For this reason, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas do not definitively state that the nature of the mind is inherently pure or that its nature is inherently impure.
Good son, this mind does not associate with the lower [states], because the second point clarifies that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure and thus lacks association.
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, it clarifies the absence of association; next, it clarifies that because of the association of causes and conditions, there is bondage and liberation.
Good son, this mind does not unite with the fetter of greed, nor does it unite with hatred or delusion.
Good son, it is like the sun and moon: although they are obscured by smoke, dust, clouds, mist, and Rāhu, because of these conditions, sentient beings are unable to see them;
yet, though they cannot be seen, the nature of the sun and moon remains unchanged.
It never unites with those five obscurations; the mind is also like this. By reason of these causes and conditions, the fetter of greed arises.
Although sentient beings say that the mind unites with greed, the nature of the mind in reality does not unite with it.
If it is a greedy mind, it is the nature of greed; if it is a non-greedy mind, it is the nature of non-greed. A non-greedy mind cannot become greedy.
The mind bound by the fetter of greed cannot fail to be free from greed; noble son, for this reason, the fetter of sensual desire cannot defile the mind.
This is the first passage, clarifying that because it is ultimately pure, there is no conjunction.

In the section following "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas," secondly, it clarifies that bondage and liberation are obtained through the harmony of causes and conditions. This further divides into two parts:

first, it clarifies the objects of bondage and liberation; second, it clarifies the persons who experience bondage and liberation. Within the section on the objects, there are again two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have forever shattered the fetter of greed; therefore it is said that their minds attain liberation.
All sentient beings give rise to the fetter of greed due to causes and conditions, and their minds attain liberation due to causes and conditions.
The chapter on identifying the objects of perception distinguishes that freedom from greed is the state of liberation, while possessing greed is the state of bondage.

Next, under the heading "For example, like the Snowy Mountains," the two sections of the chapter are explained; this section has two parts: first, an explanation of the state of bondage, which begins with a simile followed by its application.
Good son, it is like this: for example, in places where the Snowy Mountains are steep and precipitous, neither humans nor monkeys can travel;
in some places, monkeys can travel while humans cannot; and in other places, both humans and monkeys can travel.
Good son, those places where both humans and monkeys can travel are like the hunters who exclusively use...
[Shu*Dao] glue was placed upon a table to catch a macaque. Because the macaque was foolish, it went and touched it with its hand;
having touched it, its hand became stuck. Desiring to free its hand, it stepped on it with its foot, but its foot likewise became attached.
Desiring to free its foot, it bit it with its mouth, but its mouth likewise became stuck. Thus, at all five places, it could not escape. Thereupon, the hunter took a staff...
Guanzhi carried it back home.

The "initial parable" refers to Zhongshan; the "steep precipice" is a metaphor for the Eightfold Noble Path; the "difficult terrain" is a metaphor for those who practice the difficult path of asceticism;
the "monkeys" are a metaphor for non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), all of whom are unable to traverse it and fail to cultivate the Noble Path. That the monkeys are able to traverse it is precisely this.
Those who have attained the higher realms cannot practice this; it is only those dwelling in the realm of Māra in the desire realm who can practice both.
Thus, the hunter represents the demonic and heterodox; the *shu-dao* (glue) represents the objects of craving and desire;
placing it upon the table represents the five desires; and placing it upon the fruit of retribution is used to deceive sentient beings.
The analogy of touching with the hand refers to the contact of the eyes, ears, and so forth with forms, sounds, and so forth;

"the hand being sticky" means that within the mind of formations (*saṃskāra*), one gives rise to attachment, becoming stuck in all five locations—that is, the five sense faculties give rise to defilement. "Pierced by a staff" means being transformed by the demonic and heterodox;
"carrying it back home" means being led into the three miserable realms (*apāya*).
The perilous regions of the Snowy Mountains are a metaphor for the right path attained by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; the monkeys are a metaphor for all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*);
and the hunter is a metaphor for Māra Pāpīyas. The sticky resin is a metaphor for the fetters of greed and desire.

That humans and monkeys cannot proceed together is a metaphor for how ordinary worldlings and the demon king Māra Pāpīyas cannot proceed together; whereas that monkeys can proceed while humans cannot is likewise a metaphor.
Those who are capable are like the non-Buddhists who possess wisdom; even though various evil Māras use the five desires to attempt to bind them, they cannot do so.
Those who can practice together with the monkey are all ordinary worldlings and Māra Pāpīyas, who constantly dwell in birth and death and are unable to cultivate the path.
Ordinary people are bound by the five desires, which allow Māra Pāpīyas to act with sovereign power over them.
He departs like that hunter who captures a monkey with a trap and carries it home;
the analogy is as explained in the text.
For example, the King descends to the second explanation for attaining understanding of the objects of focus, namely the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
Good son, it is like a king who dwells securely within his own realm and enjoys peace and happiness of body and mind;
yet when he enters another’s realm, he encounters manifold sufferings. All sentient beings are likewise: if they can abide securely within their own domain, they attain peace and happiness;
but if they enter another’s domain, they encounter evil Māras and undergo various afflictions. As for "one's own domain," it refers to...
The "objects of others" regarding the four foundations of mindfulness refers to the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

How are they bound? Second, the following clarifies the persons who are bound and those who are liberated, divided into two parts: first, the clarification of the person who is bound; second, the clarification of the person who is liberated.

Regarding the person who is bound, there are four aspects: first, being bound because of giving rise to perversions; second, being bound because of grasping at signs (*nimitta*); third, [being bound because of] the self...
They are bound by views and bound by the four unrighteous things, as stated in the text.
What are they called that belong to Māra? There are sentient beings who perceive the impermanent as permanent, the permanent as impermanent;
who perceive suffering as happiness, happiness as suffering; who perceive the impure as pure, the pure as impure; and who perceive non-self as self.
To perceive a self where there is no self is not true liberation; to perceive liberation where there is no liberation is a false view of liberation.
To perceive what is not liberation as liberation, what is not a vehicle as a vehicle, or a vehicle as not a vehicle—such a person is said to be bound to Māra.
One who is bound to Māra has a mind that is not pure.

Furthermore, good son, if one perceives that all phenomena truly possess determinate characteristics of both generality and particularity, you should know that when such a person sees form, they construct the characteristic of form;
likewise, up to seeing consciousness, they construct the characteristic of consciousness;

they see a man as the characteristic of a man, a woman as the characteristic of a woman, a day as the characteristic of a day, a month as the characteristic of a month, a year as the characteristic of a year, and the aggregates (*skandha*)...

To perceive the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), to perceive the entrances (*āyatana*), and to perceive the elements (*dhātu*)—one who perceives in this manner is said to be bound to Māra.
One who is bound to Māra has an impure mind.
Furthermore, son of good family, if one perceives: "This is form (*rūpa*)," "I am within form," "Form is within me," or "Form belongs to me"—[this is likewise bound to Māra].
Those who perceive me as being within consciousness, or consciousness as being within me, or that consciousness belongs to me—such views belong to Māra; they are not my disciples.
"Good son, my śrāvaka disciples who distance themselves from the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras and instead cultivate various non-Buddhist treatises,
who do not practice the monastic vocation of quiescence but exclusively engage in worldly,
household affairs— what are these so-called household affairs? They consist of accepting and keeping all manner of impure things, such as slaves, servants, fields, and houses."
Elephants, horses, chariots, donkeys, mules, chickens, dogs, monkeys, pigs, sheep, and various kinds of grain and wheat;
they distance themselves from their teachers and monks and draw close to laypeople, violating the holy teachings. To the laypeople they speak thus:
"The Buddha permits bhikṣus to accept and keep all manner of impure things. This is called practicing the affairs of householders. Such are the disciples.
Not for the sake of *nirvāṇa*, but solely for the sake of gain and offerings, they draw near to listen to and receive the twelve divisions of the scriptures;

they covet and consume the property of the universal community (*saṃgha*) and the personal belongings of the monks as if they were their own; they are stingy regarding the households of others; they seek out fame and praise;
they draw near to kings and princes; and they practice divination of good and ill fortune, calculation of the movements of the heavens and the void, and games such as *weiqi* and *liubo*.
Those who gamble with dice or play pitch-pot; who associate with bhikṣuṇīs and various young maidens; who keep two śrāmaṇeras;
who constantly frequent places of butchery, hunting, wine shops, and the dwellings of caṇḍālas; who engage in various kinds of trade; who prepare their own food by hand;
and who act as messengers for neighboring kingdoms to convey messages and mandates—such persons should be known as the retinue of Māra.
Those who are not my disciples, by this cause and condition, have minds that arise together with greed and minds that cease together with greed;
even so it is for the mind arising and ceasing together with delusion. Good son, by this cause and condition, the nature of the mind is neither pure nor impure;
therefore, I say that the mind attains liberation.
The final passage states: "Regarding stinginess toward other families: if one's own family is most intimate with me, one does not permit others to go there;
regarding praise, one should only praise oneself and not permit the praising of others."
If there are those who do not accept or possess any impure things, and who for the sake of Great Nirvana uphold, recite, read,
transcribe, and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures— know that these are my true disciples and do not act according to evil Māras.

The realm of Pāpīyas is precisely the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; because they are cultivated, they do not arise together with greed, nor do they cease together with greed.
The text is abbreviated, mentioning only one [instance].
The subsequent conclusion is as in the text.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fully accomplishing the eighth merit.
