The first part clarifies that there is cause and there is effect; the second clarifies that which is neither cause nor effect; the third clarifies that which is both cause and effect and also neither cause nor effect.

Since it should only clarify that which is neither cause nor effect, how can it be said to be "cause and effect"? If cause and effect were not clarified, what would there be to distinguish as "neither"?
The initial passage contains both the thesis (*dharmin*) and the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Good son, the Buddha-nature has causes and the causes of causes; it has fruits and the fruits of fruits.
That which is the cause is the twelve links of dependent origination; that which is the cause of the cause is wisdom;
that which is the fruit is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and that which is the fruit of the fruit is the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa.

In the *Dharmaparyāya-madhyamaka-śāstra*, it speaks of two causes and two effects. The "two causes" refer to the cause of the cause and the cause; the "two effects" refer to the effect of the effect and the effect.

Examining the intent of this passage, one must not take the cause belonging to the category of causes as the "cause of the cause," nor take the effect belonging to the category of effects as the "effect of the effect.
Rather, one takes the effect belonging to the category of causes as the "cause of the cause," and takes the cause [belonging to the category of effects] as the "effect of the effect."
Regarding the fruit of the family of fruits as the "fruit of fruits": why is this so? A single cause is the objective realm (*viṣaya*); a double cause is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
A single fruit is *bodhi*; a double fruit is *nirvāṇa*. The objective realm is merely a cause; one does not proceed from cause to cause through the cause itself, for the cause is not the cause.
It is through the wisdom of contemplation that one proceeds from cause to cause; therefore, it is obtained as the "cause of causes" which is *bodhi*.

However, a fruit does not proceed from fruit to fruit; rather, it is because a fruit that is not a fruit—the Nirvana of fruits—proceeds from fruit to fruit that it is attained as the "fruit of fruits.
Good son, for example, ignorance is the cause and the various formations (saṃskāra) are the fruit; with formations as the cause, consciousness (vijñāna) is the fruit. It is by this principle...
Therefore, the essence of that ignorance is both a cause and a cause-cause; consciousness is both a fruit and a fruit-fruit; and the Buddha-nature is likewise.
This is not the intended meaning in the illustrative analogy. In the analogy, ignorance is taken as the cause;

since the very essence of ignorance is the cause and it further acts as the cause for formative action (*saṃskāra*), it is a "cause-cause. Consciousness, in its own essence, is the fruit, and furthermore—

Because it functions as the fruit of practice, this "fruit-fruit" (phala-phala) is established by means of an analogy. Since the object (*ālambana*) is the cause of causes, Bodhi should be the fruit-fruit;
yet it is not so analogized because the essence of the object is not a cause—it does not proceed from a cause to a cause, being merely a cause that is not a causal cause.
Furthermore, the essence of the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) is not a fruit—it does not proceed from a fruit to a fruit. If this were the case, then the analogy [would fail].
The Dharma contradicts [the opponent's] response, which takes only a partial analogy; it is said that this is not a complete adoption [of the analogy].
Taking ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the objects and wisdom (*jñāna*) as the subject is merely an analogy for bodhi and nirvāṇa.

This is because one first cites ignorance, formations, consciousness, and so forth, which also possess the designations of cause and effect, and the cause of the cause and the effect of the effect; therefore, in the subsequent text, all four permutations are fully cited regarding the Buddha-nature and nirvāṇa.

The *paryaṅka* (cross-legged posture) constitutes the first two phrases, and the twelve links of dependent origination constitute the third phrase. As for the term "partial" (*pradeśa*), it refers to cases where the names are identical but the meanings differ;

thus it is called "partial. If one intends to take the object and wisdom as the two causes, and enlightenment and nirvāṇa as the two fruits, then the essence of the object is itself a cause and further serves as the cause for wisdom;
therefore, it is termed the "cause of the cause" (*hetu-hetu*). This refers to the essence of wisdom.
This cause further serves as the cause for two effects; the two effects are likewise to be understood by analogy with the cause.
For this reason, the second section below clarifies that which is neither cause nor effect, namely, the Middle Way and the True Nature.
Good son, for this reason, the twelve links of dependent origination neither arise nor cease; they are neither eternal nor discontinuous;
they are neither one nor two; they neither come nor go; and they are neither cause nor effect.
Within these ten [categories], there is nothing superfluous.

In the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, following the section on "that which is neither cause nor effect," the third [section] clarifies that which is both cause and effect, as well as that which is neither cause nor effect.
Good son, wholesome roots are causes but not fruits; the Buddha-nature is a fruit but not a cause; Great Nirvana is both a cause and a fruit.
The dharmas produced by the twelve links of dependent origination are neither cause nor fruit; that which is neither cause nor fruit is named the Buddha-nature.
Because it is neither cause nor fruit, it is eternal, constant, and unchanging.
Kaishan posits five natures: that which is cause but not fruit is the nature of the objective realm (*viṣaya*); that which is fruit but not cause is the nature of the fruit;

that which is both cause and fruit is the causal-enlightenment factor (*jñāna-hetu*); that which is fruit but not cause is the fruit of *bodhi*; and that which is neither cause nor fruit is the true nature (*bhūta-tathatā*).
However, in that school’s system, they take sentient beings to be the true nature, which is inconsistent with the meaning of being "neither cause nor fruit."
The Adornment (Śrīmalādevī-siṃhanāda-nirdeśa) establishes four natures: that which is a cause but not an effect is the revealing cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*), and its effect is *nirvāṇa*;

that which is a cause but not an effect is the true cause (*tathatā-hetu*), and its effect is *bodhi*. That which is neither cause nor effect is not a nature at all; it merely negates the preceding meanings. The Master Guan also establishes five natures:
that which is a cause but not an effect is the objective nature (*ālambana-svabhāva*); that which is an effect but not a cause is the fruit-nature (*phala-svabhāva*).
The nature of the fruit is the cause; that which is the fruit is precisely the nature of the clarifying cause (*vyañjana-hetu*) and the nature of bodhi.
Regarding the "clarifying cause": in relation to the objective realm it is the fruit, but in relation to bodhi it is the cause. If this is so, then the nature of bodhi should also be twofold:
in relation to the clarifying cause it is the fruit, and in relation to the fruit it is the cause. That which is neither cause nor fruit is the True Nature (*bhūtatā*), as stated by Xinghuang.

It is only the "Right Dharma" (*saddharma*) and the "Right Nature" (*samyaktva*) that are permitted; the "Right Cause" (*samyaghetu*) is not allowed as a designation. Yet, since the term "Right Cause" appears within this sutra, why is it not permitted?
This is because these five natures are merely differences resulting from the opening and closing [of categories]. The Right Nature is non-dual, whereas the causal nature is dual.
These two are cause and effect: when the cause is opened, the cause emerges from the cause; when the fruit is opened, the fruit emerges from the fruit; and when the fruit is closed, they merge.

The four [categories] become two, namely cause and effect; these two are combined into one, and the conditions are integrated into the "correct" (samyak), such that there is no longer any further enumeration.
For this reason, the third section below concludes by praising its profundity. This, in turn, consists of three parts: first, a brief praise; second, an extensive praise;
and third, a summary conclusion. First, regarding the brief praise:
For this reason, I have stated in my sutras that the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination is exceedingly profound;
it is without knowledge or vision, beyond conceptual thought, and is the domain of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, not something accessible to Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
The ordinary person of limited capacity cannot see it; only a Buddha can see it. For what reason?
The following two sections provide a detailed explanation of its profound depth, which has six aspects: first, clarifying the profundity of causes and conditions;

second, clarifying the profundity because it is not seen by ordinary persons; third, clarifying that only a Buddha can see it; fourth, again clarifying the profundity of difficulty; [fifth, ...]; sixth, ...].
Seeing the fivefold clarity, one is able to see the six pairs of clarity—both seeing and non-seeing.
For what reason is it so profoundly deep? It is because the karmic actions of sentient beings are neither permanent nor discontinuous, yet they obtain retribution;
although they perish moment by moment, nothing is lost; although there is no agent, there is the performance of action; and although there is no recipient [of the fruit].
Regarding the recipient of the retribution: although the fruit has perished, it is not destroyed or lost; there is no conceptual cognition, yet it exists through a combination [of conditions].
As for the statement at the beginning that it is "neither eternal nor annihilated," this applies to all subsequent phrases as examples of the Middle Way to clarify its profound depth:
although it perishes moment by moment, it is not eternal; yet because nothing is lost, it is not annihilated. Thus, it is neither annihilated nor eternal.
That is to say, although the profound Middle Way has no agent, it is not non-existent; although it performs activities, it is not non-void.
This inconceivable and profound Middle Way is such that all ordinary beings fail to perceive it—this is the second point clarifying how ordinary beings do not see it.
Although all sentient beings act in conjunction with the twelve links of dependent origination, they do not perceive or know them;
because they do not perceive or know them, there is no beginning or end.
Only those in the lower three stages of the Ten Abodes and the Buddha himself can see this.
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see only the end but do not see the beginning; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, see both the beginning and the end.
For this reason, the Buddhas clearly perceive the Buddha-nature.
Bodhisattvas see the Tathāgata only slightly; yet, since they have fully seen the end of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), they should likewise see its beginning only slightly.
Now, as for the mutual omission [of one or the other], it is said that at the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), with a single turn, one immediately becomes a Buddha;

because the distance to the point of the end is near, it is said that "one can see the end. Since the beginning is then utterly remote (*yāran*), it is said that "one does not see it. This is what was stated by the ancients.
In the "Chapter on Breaking the Source" of the *Ten Abodes*, it is said that because the future results of ignorance do not arise, one knows the end of birth and death;

its beginning is difficult to know. Xinghuang said: "That intrinsic nature is non-existent is easy [to understand]; that what is produced by causes and conditions is non-existent yet exists is difficult.
Now, it is said that at the stage of the Ten Abodes, because there is the path of cultivation capable of partial severance, one partially perceives its [beginning].
In the end, one is unable to discern its beginning; it is like a strong man who defeats bandits but does not know the origin from which they arose.
I privately maintain that it may also be said that what is severed at the initial stage severs its very beginning; therefore, it is called "seeing the beginning.

Since both the seeing and the severing occur simultaneously at the beginning, it is also called "seeing the beginning. Thus, we know that in the stage of the worthy (the *śaikṣa*), one not only fails to see the Middle Way, but also...
Because one does not see [the final stage] within ignorance, from the initial severance of the beginning-limit, it is called "seeing the beginning.

For those Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*) who have only one grade remaining, they are called "those at the end" because they have not yet severed the end; because they do not see the end of that which is to be severed at the end, they are also said to "see the end.
Thus, one should know that Equal Enlightenment not only fails to see the ultimate *tathatā*, but also...
Because ignorance is seen in the final chapter, only the Buddha severs it and only the Buddha perceives it;

the Buddhas perceive the beginning and perceive the end, for they ultimately know that there is neither beginning nor end and ultimately discern their beginning and end. In the text, "arising from self" constitutes an extreme;
therefore, reversing this, the "beginning" refers to the primary chapter and the "end" refers to the final chapter, as these are the coarsest and most manifest. Thus, it is called "seeing."

Because one knows and perceives that there is wisdom capable of counteracting [defilements], it is called "seeing. Since the wisdom of the first stage is shallow and sees only the end, it is said to be "seeing the end.
Because there is as yet no wisdom capable of counteracting the fundamental category [of afflictions], it is said to be "not seeing."
All sentient beings are unable to see the fourfold clarity;
good son, because all sentient beings cannot perceive the twelve links of dependent origination, they revolve in saṃsāra.
Good son, just as a silkworm makes a cocoon and is born and dies within it, so too it is with all sentient beings—they do not see [the truth].
Because of the Buddha-nature, one creates karmic bonds through one's own actions and transmigrates through birth and death like a bouncing ball.
For this reason, I shall now explain the five levels of being able to see.
Good son, for this reason, I have taught in various sutras that if there is anyone who sees the twelve links of dependent origination, they immediately...
This seeing of dharmas by one who sees dharmas is itself the seeing of the Buddha; the Buddha is none other than the Buddha-nature.
Why? Because all Buddhas take this as their nature.

The wisdom that contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination—hereafter, the six pairs clarify what is seen and what is not seen. Furthermore, there are two [sections]: first, the four topical headings are proclaimed.
Good son, there are four kinds of wisdom for contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination: first, the inferior; second, the middling;
third, the superior; and fourth, the supreme.
Next, I shall explain these four chapters.
Those with inferior wisdom contemplate and do not see the Buddha-nature; because they do not see it, they attain the path of the Śrāvaka.

Those with middling wisdom contemplate and do not see the Buddha-nature; because they do not see it, they attain the path of the Pratyekabuddha. Those with superior wisdom contemplate and see it, yet not clearly;
because their vision is not clear, they abide in the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Those with the highest wisdom see it clearly; because their vision is clear, they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is not seen by three [levels];

only the highest of the high (*uttamottama*) can see it. By extending this principle, it is clear that the previous three—the fixed stage (*niyata-bhūmi*), the stage of joyful practice (*sukha-caryā-bhūmi*), and so forth—do not perceive the meaning.
Regarding the question of those who "see slightly" in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*): does this refer only to the tenth stage?
Regarding the statement that "the [Bodhisattvas] from the ninth abode down to the first abode see only a small portion," the traditional commentaries offer two interpretations:

First, some say that only those in the tenth abode see a small portion of the nine abodes down to the first, while those in the lower abodes do not see them at all. Second, others say that from the first abode through the tenth, all see only a small portion;

however, this must be understood in two ways: first, compared to the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), seeing even a small portion constitutes "seeing a small portion" for those in the first through ninth abodes.

Regarding the view that the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*) do not involve seeing a person, the previous explanation stated: "The two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) each attain their own *bodhi* without seeing [a person];
yet since they do not see it at the Ninth Abiding, what kind of *bodhi* would they attain? Advancing, they are not equal to a Buddha; retreating, they are not the two vehicles.
They must separately attain a distinct *bodhi*. (And so forth. Now, it is clarified that if one refers to the "Abidings" as being the "Stages" (*bhūmi*), [the following applies].
That all ten dwellings (*daśa-vihāra*) involve partial vision (*pradeśa-darśana*) is a distinct meaning.
That if the dwellings were not the stages (*bhūmi*), one would see the ten dwellings but not the ten stages, is also a distinct meaning.

If it is said that the ten dwellings are themselves the ten stages, and that both stages and dwellings involve partial vision, this is the perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) meaning. If it is said that the ten dwellings are not the ten stages, yet the ten dwellings also involve partial vision, this—

This also carries the sense of being "perfect" (yuan). If one says that the ten abidings (daśabhūmi) are not the ten stages (daśabhūmi), yet claims that the nine abidings do not see the tenth abiding while the [tenth] sees it only slightly—this refers to the meaning of the "separate teaching connecting to the sudden" (bie-jie-tong-zhi). If people do not recognize this, they will frequently fail to penetrate the text and its meaning (and so forth).
For this reason, the third section below concludes that [the Dharma] is profoundly deep.
For this reason, the twelve links of dependent origination are called Buddha-nature; Buddha-nature is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā);
the emptiness of the ultimate truth is called the Middle Way; the Middle Way is called the Buddha; and the Buddha is called Nirvāṇa.

"Pan. That which is called the Buddha-nature—namely, the five Buddha-natures and the twelve links of dependent origination—is the "causal nature" (yin-xing) which concludes with the primary emptiness (di-yi-yi kong).

The "middle way" (zhongdao) within the causal nature is the "correct cause nature" (zheng-yin-xing), which is precisely what is named the Buddha. The "resultant nature" (guo-xing) is the fruition itself.
This conclusion, which fully encompasses both the words and their meaning regarding the nature of the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, is most excellent.
At that time, the second section of the discourse concludes.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if there is no difference between a Buddha and Buddha-nature..."
As for the distinction: if all sentient beings were [already identical to the Buddha], what would be the use of practicing the Path?
This point arises from the preceding conclusion that the karmic activities of sentient beings are profoundly deep and profound.

If sentient beings and the Buddha are equal and non-dual, what need is there to practice the Path? At first glance, this appears to be a single question, but the Buddha provides two answers, thus forming two points.

In the response to the question, the Buddha provides two answers: first, that the Buddha and *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) are equal; second, that one must cultivate the path (*mārga-bhāvanā*). Thus, we know there are two questions.

Those who follow the *Dilun* school say that sentient beings are already fully possessed of Buddhahood within their delusions and therefore need not cultivate the path; this precisely constitutes the objection [addressed by the first answer].

If one follows the *Shelun* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) school, they would say that the fruit of Buddhahood exists in the future, and thus they would not face this objection. However, [the present text] does not [agree with them].
One may say that this very [attainment] is the Buddha; to this, one should give the answer that there is no distinction between them.

Because there is no distinction, it is the Buddha; because there is a distinction, it is not yet fully perfected. Just as when a father begets a son, their lineage has no distinction, yet because the capacities are not yet perfected, they must be adorned.
Through adornment, they subsequently become perfected. However, this merely clarifies the Buddha-nature; what does it have to do with [the present matter]?
Regarding the fulfillment or non-fulfillment [of the Buddha-nature]: if fulfillment depends upon conditions, then the Buddha-nature must likewise depend upon conditions to be fulfilled.
If one says the Buddha-nature exists in the future, this refers to the nature of the fruit and the nature of the fruit-of-fruits;

if one says the Buddha-nature exists in the present, this takes up the nature of the cause and the nature of the cause-of-causes; if one says the Buddha-nature is neither future nor present, this takes up the fundamental [nature].

If each were to take their own causal nature as being correct, it would be like blind men touching an elephant; if one perceives this intention, there will be no dispute regarding the present manifestation.
The Buddha’s answer consists of three parts: first, the non-question; second, the direct answer; and third, the citation of evidence. The "non-question" is as stated in the text.
The Buddha said: "Good son, that which you have asked is not so.
To answer correctly, there are two parts: first, that there is no difference and yet there is a difference; second, what is the use of practicing the path? The first answer has three parts:
first, the direct answer; second, citing a verse; and third, using milk and curd as an analogy for this meaning."
In terms of their essence, they are not different, yet in terms of their objects of perception, they are distinct; the first passage contains both the subject and the illustration.
Although there is no difference between the Buddha and buddha-nature, all sentient beings have not yet fully realized it.
In the *Dharmaparyāya*, it is said that those who are "not fully endowed" (a-paripūrṇa) lack only the application of principle and function;
thus, they are called "unendowed," not because they are entirely devoid of them.
For example, as in the two preceding similes, first the simile and then the application. In the initial simile, there are again two parts: first, the presentation of the negative simile.
Next, the initial passage citing the analogy of good and evil is as follows:
"Good son, it is like a person who, with an evil mind, harms his mother; having harmed her, he gives rise to remorse.
Although his three karmas are now virtuous, this person is still called a 'person of the hells. Why? Because this person is certain to fall into hell. This person—
Although they lack the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of hell, they are nevertheless still called "hell-beings.

It is certain that they will eventually fall, just as one who has killed his mother will—though their bodies have not yet fallen into hell, they will certainly go there without doubt. Sentient beings are likewise:
they possess the principle of Buddha-nature and will inevitably attain it in the future.
Good son, for this reason, I have said in various sūtras that if one sees someone practicing wholesome deeds, it is called seeing devas and humans;
if one sees someone practicing unwholesome deeds, it is called seeing hell-beings. Why is this? Because they will certainly receive their retribution.
Next, the Buddha further cited that those who practice the ten wholesome actions are said to see the heavens, while those who practice the ten unwholesome actions are said to see the hells;
these are also [cases of] retribution in the present life.
This is the combined analogy for all sentient beings in the two lower realms.
"Good son, because all sentient beings will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; yet, in reality,
no sentient beings currently possess the thirty-two marks or eighty secondary characteristics."

All sentient beings have not yet possessed the marks and signs because they are "to be attained" (dangde). One interpretation states that they are "to be attained" as the fruit of the marks and signs;
another interpretation states that they are "to be attained" as the Buddha-nature (foxing) which is the fruit. What is this Buddha-nature that is "to be"?
If it were "to be," it would be subsumed within the three periods of time, and being thus impermanent, one should not say it is the "fruit to be attained" (dangguo) Buddha-nature.
Second, the response by means of a cited verse:
For this reason, I have spoken this verse in this sutra:
"Existing originally but now non-existent; Non-existent originally but now existent— That such dharmas exist throughout the three periods of time Is an impossibility."
Good son, that which exists is of three kinds: first, the future; second, the present; and third, the past.
All sentient beings shall, in a future life, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
this is called the Buddha-nature. All sentient beings currently possess all afflictions and fetters; therefore, in the present...
There are no beings among the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics who, in past lives, have severed their afflictions;

therefore, they now perceive the Buddha-nature. For this reason, I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, even including icchantikas and the like. As for these icchantikas and the like—
Although there are no currently existing wholesome dharmas, the Buddha-nature is also wholesome because it will exist in the future;
thus, even icchantikas and others all possess Buddha-nature. Why is this? Because icchantikas and others will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The brief explanation of the verse’s meaning is as previously stated. This verse appears four times: first, it answers the question of permanence and impermanence;

second, it answers the question of attainment and non-attainment; third, in the following twenty-six [verses], it answers the refutation of fixed natures; and now, it answers the question of existence and non-existence as indeterminate, thereby elucidating the Middle Way.

If one attempts to interpret it solely through the distinction between existence and non-existence, neither [interpretation] accords with the intent of the verse; the same applies to permanence, impermanence, and so forth.

One should interpret this passage according to the sūtra as follows: "There is difference, non-difference, both difference and non-difference, neither difference nor non-difference, neither one nor different—inconceivable.
Only through such an explanation does one grasp the intent of the verse. Other cases, such as permanence and impermanence, are likewise treated.
Now, the prose commentary on the original text states that all three times are fundamentally existent (*mūla-bhūta*), as the text reads.
Judging by this, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa should each have been inherently present and each should now be absent.
If saṃsāra were inherently present, it would be fully replete with immeasurable afflictions; if saṃsāra were inherently absent, then nirvāṇa would have been inherently absent from the beginning.
If nirvāṇa were inherently present, then nirvāṇa would have existed from the beginning and not merely arrived at the present; if nirvāṇa were inherently absent, then it has long been so.

One who has already attained Buddhahood is free from all afflictions and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Although these [afflictions and birth-and-death] originally existed but now do not, and originally did not exist but now do, they are all collectively categorized as "existence" when viewed in relation to *nirvāṇa*, because birth-and-death is something that can be apprehended.

Although *nirvāṇa* itself originally existed but now does not, and originally did not exist but now does, it is all collectively categorized as "non-existence" when viewed in relation to birth-and-death.

Because there is nothing to be attained, that which is originally existent is precisely what is now non-existent; one does not discuss non-existence apart from existence. That which is originally non-existent is precisely what is now existent;
one does not discuss existence apart from non-existence. These first three phrases are subsumed within the distinctions of the three periods of time.

The existence of original existence is not [ultimate] existence, and the non-existence of present non-existence is not [absolute] non-existence; it is neither existent nor non-existent, and neither non-existent nor non-non-existent.
The phrase "it is impossible for dharmas to exist throughout the three periods of time" refers to that which is without differentiation and is not subsumed by the three periods.
To further clarify the four propositions based on the primary and the secondary, there are two versions of the primary and two versions of the secondary;

one version of the primary and one version of the secondary; the secondary without the primary; the primary without the secondary; and that which is neither primary nor secondary. As stated in the preceding text: "provisionally dwelling in one."

The son leaves his master and the master drives him away; is this realm not rooted in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*)? The single son practices correct contemplation; is this not taking *nirvāṇa* as the ultimate end?
The text says that Great Parinirvāṇa is inherently present, and that the Tathāgatagarbha serves as its support and foundation;
is this not taking *nirvāṇa* as the root? When one is deluded regarding principle and gives rise to afflictions, is this not birth-and-death?
If each end has its own root, then each root has its own end; for this reason, there are two roots and two ends.
Furthermore, since birth-and-death has no end, it takes the beginning of nirvana as its end;
and since nirvana has no beginning, it takes the end of birth-and-death as its beginning. Thus, the two rivers face one another, mutually constituting end and beginning.

This constitutes the "one end and one root. Furthermore, whether regarding birth-and-death as the root or the end, both are collectively termed the "end," because it is false and illusory and lacks a fundamental basis;
thus, it is an end and not a root. Whether regarding nirvana as the root or the end, both are termed the "root," because it is true and without deception;
thus, it is a root and not an end. Thus, the end is not the root, and the root is not the end.

Neither the branch nor the root; not subsumed within the three periods of time. Having established these four propositions regarding the distinction between the root and the branch, the same pattern applies to all else:
attainment and non-attainment, permanence and impermanence—all are entirely indeterminate.
This inconceivability of the indeterminacy of the four propositions is precisely the Three Truths: they are neither concurrent nor distinct, as in the case of the analogy.
As previously stated:
for example, it is like a person who, having set aside the third illustration of milk and curd, uses it to prove that [the self] exists in the future.
Son of good family, it is as if there were a person in a house with milk and curd, and someone asked him, "Do you have ghee? He replied:
When I say that I possess curd, it is not because there is actually butter; rather, because it will certainly be obtained through skillful means, I say that there is butter.

Sentient beings are also like this: they all possess the mind, and since all who possess the mind will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for this reason I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
This means that while it is said that there is Buddha-nature in relation to the existence of mind, the mind itself is not identical to Buddha-nature.
How does this differ from the principle that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature? When one later attains Buddhahood, one does not take the sentient being to be the Buddha-mind;
the Buddha-mind is likewise described simply as "having mind" being Buddha-nature, yet the mind itself is not identical to Buddha-nature.

Ultimately, there are two kinds [of answers]. Second, one must explain that the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) must be practiced as a correct response to the prior question, "What is the use of cultivating the path?
Sentient beings and others possess the single vehicle’s true nature (*ekayāna-bhūtatā*); therefore, they must cultivate the adornments of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
If one does not practice them, one will not attain this true nature. Others say that the single vehicle consists of the myriad virtues; however, in this present text, it is by means of...
The One Vehicle is the Middle Way and the True Nature; because this single path is pure and can transport sentient beings to Buddhahood, it is called the One Vehicle.
How could it be the same as the "Ten Thousand Good Deeds"? In the text, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the topical outline (*chāngmén*); second, the explanation.
Good son, there are ultimately two kinds: first, the ultimate of adornment; second, the ultimate of culmination.
Furthermore, there is the mundane ultimate and the supramundane ultimate.
The first section contains two pairs, making four items.
In the subsequent explanation, there are two parts: first, explaining that the six perfections serve as adornment and the One Vehicle constitutes the ultimate goal;
second, explaining the mundane and the supramundane.
That which is ultimately adorned is the ultimate perfection of the six pāramitās; that which is ultimately perfected by all sentient beings is the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
This One Vehicle is called Buddha-nature. For this reason, I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
All sentient beings possess the One Vehicle, yet because it is shrouded by ignorance, they are unable to see it.
Good son, just as the inhabitants of this world cannot see the inhabitants of Uttarakuru or the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven because their karmic retributions conceal them,
so too is the Buddha-nature: because it is concealed by the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), sentient beings do not see it.
The initial six perfections and the One Vehicle have no distinct essence; they differ only according to their respective meanings.

Within this, there are both analogies and applications. The first analogy states: although the retributive fruits of the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens are superior, humans cannot see the Buddha-nature therein.
Because it is shrouded by ignorance, it cannot be seen; therefore, one must cultivate the Path.
Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the latter two lines of the *Buddha-nature* (*buddhadhātu*) section, there are two parts: first, the individual explanation of the ultimate transcendence;

second, the combined explanation of both worldly and transcendent ultimates. The first part [the individual explanation] further has three sections: first, defining the essence; second, explaining the name; third, citing examples.
The first [defining the essence] is as the text states.
Furthermore, good son, the Buddha-nature is the nature of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; it is like clarified butter (*ghṛta-maṇḍa*) and is the mother of all Buddhas.
By the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, all Buddhas possess the qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
All sentient beings likewise possess the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, yet because they do not practice it, they are unable to realize it.
Because one attains this vision, one cannot yet achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Good son, the *śūraṅgama-samādhi* has five names: first, the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*;
second, the *prajñā-pāramitā*; third, the *vajra-samādhi*; fourth, the *siṃhanāda-samādhi*; and fifth, the *buddha-dhātu*.
It receives its name according to its various functions in different contexts.

In the subsequent explanation of the names, it is stated that *śūraṅgama* is translated as "firm and solid" (*jiāngù*) and *aśvalī* (or *aśvali*) is translated as "cultivating the mind" (*xiūzhìxīn*).
This samādhi has both general and specific aspects: specifically, it resides in the final stage of the mind; generally, it pervades all stages.
Just as with one samādhi, the three subsequent exhortations are to be understood by analogy.
Good son, just as one samādhi receives various names— such as being called "dhyāna," "the four dhyānas," "the faculty of concentration" (samādhīndriya),

"the power of concentration" (samādhibala), "the awakening factor of concentration" (samādhisambodhyaṅga), "right concentration" (samyaksamādhi), or "the awakening factor of concentration among the eight factors of the great person"— so it is with this.
The Śūraṅgama-samādhi is also like this.

"Awakening" (bodhi) is called the awakening of concentration; this is precisely the factor of concentration within the seven factors of awakening (saptabodhyaṅga) and is correctly termed right concentration (samyaksamādhi) within the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga).

Furthermore, "awakening" is called the awakening of concentration; this is the awakening of concentration among the eight qualities of a great man (mahāpuruṣadharma), and the Śūraṅgama is likewise so.
There are five kinds of names (and so forth).
Good son, for all sentient beings, [the text] first explains the two pairs: the ultimate of the mundane and the ultimate of the supramundane.
Regarding these, the lower and middle [levels] are the ultimate of the mundane, while the upper concentration is the ultimate of the supramundane. Within this, the first two are fully explained.
Following the three concentrations, the preceding concentrations are explained again:
"Good son, all sentient beings are fully endowed with the three concentrations—namely, superior, middling, and inferior. 'Superior' refers to the Buddha-nature;
for this reason, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. 'Middling' refers to all sentient beings being endowed with..."
When there are causes and conditions for the first dhyāna, one is able to practice it; if there are no causes and conditions, one cannot practice it.
There are two kinds of causes and conditions: first, the calamity of fire; second, the breaking of the fetters of the desire realm.

For this reason, it is said that all sentient beings are fully endowed with the intermediate dhyāna. As for the lower dhyāna, it consists of the concentration among the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*). For this reason, it is so called.
All sentient beings fully possess the lower concentration (*samādhi*).

First, among the three concentrations, the higher concentration is explained; this refers to the Buddha-nature, also called the "revealing cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*) or the "direct cause" (*dharmatā-hetu*), wherein concentration is the concentration of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).
The lower concentration refers to the concentration of mental factors (*caitta*). Some teachers say there are ten such factors.
Arising together, they are called the "Great Earth" (mahābhūmi) and comprise five categories: namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, the indeterminate, the non-common, and the defiled.

The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states: "The arising of dharmas consists of ten numerical categories; thus they are explained as ten. Alternatively, it is said that the ten abodes of the desire realm constitute these ten numbers:
the three miserable destinies, humans, and the six heavens.
"All sentient beings possess [it]" is further explained as the transcendence of the world, which is the *Śūraṅgama*.
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet because it is shrouded by afflictions, they are unable to see it.

Although Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes perceive the One Vehicle, they do not know that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma; for this reason, it is said that [this is known by] Bodhisattvas of the Ten Grounds.
"Although one sees the Buddha-nature, it is not yet clear. Good son, 'śūraṅgama' means the ultimate perfection of all things;
'vyūha' means being firm in all that is ultimately perfected and attaining steadfastness. It is named Śūraṅgama-vyūha for this reason.
Therefore, the Śūraṅgama-samādhi is called the Buddha-nature."
The commentary names this the "Samādhi of the Mark of Vigor.

Good son, at one time—[this concludes] the third citation of evidence in response [to the question]. This clarifies that when the Tathāgata observes the capacities of beings, he may speak without error;
sometimes he speaks of no difference between the Buddha and Buddha-nature, sometimes he speaks of them as distinct, and sometimes he speaks of the cultivation of the path.

Regarding the statement "not practicing cultivation," it is like knowing that for the capacity of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), one must speak of a self (*ātman*), whereas for those who should be taught, one must speak of non-self (*anātman*), and so forth.
The text is divided into two parts: first, the formal citation of past proofs; second, the subsequent reconciliation and integration. The first part, citing past proofs, is further divided into two:
first, citing the past; second, proving the present. The citation of the past is further divided into three: first, explaining the ritual bathing; second, the discourse of the non-Buddhists.
The assembly benefited at three times.
"Good son, on one occasion while I was dwelling by the Nairañjanā River, I said to Ānanda: 'I now wish to bathe;
you may take my robe and the bathing powder. Once I had entered the water, all the birds and creatures of the air, water, and land [gathered around]."
"Come all to behold me.
At that time, there were also five hundred brahmins who came to the riverbank and approached my location;
they said to one another, "How can one obtain a vajra-body? If Gautama does not preach the view of annihilationism, we shall follow him."
The Master received the rules for the fast and said, "Good son, at that time, by means of the knowledge of others' minds, I knew what was in the mind of this brahmin and addressed him, saying:
'What do you mean when you say that I preach the view of annihilation? The brahmins replied:
'Gautama, you have previously stated in various sūtras that all sentient beings are entirely without a self. Since you say there is no self, why...'"
Why do you say it is not the view of annihilationism? If there were no self, who would be the one observing the precepts and who would be the one breaking them?
The Buddha said: "I do not say that all sentient beings are entirely without a self.
I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature. Is this buddha-nature not the self? For this reason, I do not say that [the self] is annihilated."
Because all sentient beings do not see the Buddha-nature, they are impermanent, without self, without bliss, and without purity;
this is what is called the teaching of the view of annihilationism.
At that time, when the various brahmins heard it said that the Buddha-nature is precisely the self, they immediately resolved upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, those with the three types of bodhicitta left the household life to cultivate the path to enlightenment;
even all the birds and aquatic creatures likewise gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi, and having so resolved their minds, they immediately attained the relinquishment of their bodies.
This is the second proof regarding the Buddha-nature below.
Good son, this Buddha-nature is truly not the self; it is for the sake of sentient beings that it is spoken of as "self.
To speak correctly, the Buddha-nature is not the self, yet it is called the self; one should not dogmatically cling to this when answering questions concerning the cultivation of the path.
The Tathāgata has causes and conditions for the latter two [teachings] which serve to reconcile them.
Good son, it is because of causes and conditions that the Tathāgata says "no-self" is "self"; although he speaks thus, there is no falsehood in it, for in truth there is no self.
Good son, it is because of causes and conditions that he says "self" is "no-self," yet in reality...
Because there is a self for the sake of the world, although he speaks of non-self, there is no falsehood. The Buddha-nature is non-self;
the Tathāgata speaks of self because it is eternal. The Tathāgata is the self, yet he speaks of non-self because he has attained mastery.
The Tathāgata, in his sovereign mastery, may regard the self as non-self and the non-self as self;

furthermore, there is one interpretation which states that he speaks of "non-self" because of the Buddha-nature in the causal stage, and speaks of "self" because of the Buddha-nature in the resultant stage (and so forth).
At that time, the third response from the Lion [of the Śākyas] to the fourth question above is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the question; second, the formal answer.
First, the presentation of the question:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said to the World-Honored One, "World-Honored One, if all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature..."
For what reason can all sentient beings not see the Vajrapāṇi?
There is a long discourse by the Vajrapāṇi.
The direct answer consists of two parts: first the direct answer, followed by a concluding eulogy. Within the initial direct answer, seven analogies are generally presented.
Regarding the three intentions, the first three analogies illustrate that [the object] exists yet is not seen; the middle analogy illustrates that it is equally present in all;
and the third set of three analogies illustrates that it is seen because it depends upon conditions. These three intentions follow one another in sequence:

although it is said to exist, it is nonetheless not seen—because it is not known for certain whether it exists, nor is it known for certain whether it is non-existent. Next follows the single [analogy].
The analogy shows that since it definitely exists, and since it definitely exists, why is it not seen? The subsequent answer is that it must wait for causes and conditions before it can be seen.
Of the first three analogies, each first presents the analogy and then provides the application; the first is the analogy of the blind man.
The Buddha said, "Good son, it is like the phenomenon of form (*rūpadharma*): although there are qualities such as blue, yellow, red, white, long, and short, a blind person does not see them.
Yet, even though they do not see them, one cannot say that the qualities of blue, yellow, red, white, long, and short do not exist. Why?
Because although the blind person does not see them, those with eyes do see them."
The Buddha-nature is also like this: although all sentient beings cannot see it, the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see a small portion of it, while the Tathāgata sees it in its entirety.
What the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see of the Buddha-nature is like seeing forms at night;
what the Tathāgata sees is like seeing forms by day.
For example, base ordinary beings are like the blind who do not see forms; this is how the followers of the *Saṃkhyā* school explain the nature of form (*rūpa*).
They maintain that there are twenty kinds of form: blue, yellow, red, white, high, low, oblique, square, round, long, short, shadow, light, brightness, darkness, smoke, cloud, dust, and mist;
or, including space, they add "space" as the eleventh manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*).
"Son of good family, it is like the disease of a cataract in the eye:
just as one with a cataract sees forms indistinctly, yet when a skilled physician treats them with medicine,
they see clearly through the power of that medicine, so too are all bodhisattvas illustrated."
Just as one with a slight film over the eyes cannot see forms, so too the bodhisattvas, because they possess afflictions (*kleśa*), do not see the Buddha-nature;
this is not the same as the blind person mentioned previously.
The bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are likewise: although they see the Buddha-nature, they cannot perceive it clearly because of the *Śūraṅgama*.
By the power of samādhi, one is able to attain clear understanding.

Good son, if there is a person who perceives all dharmas as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure, yet perceives that which is not "all" dharmas as impermanent, without bliss, selfless, and impure—such a person does not see the Buddha-nature. "All" refers to birth-and-death; "not all" refers to...

The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Triple Gem perceive all phenomena as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure, yet they do not perceive that which is not all phenomena as being likewise impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure; for this reason, they do not see the Buddha-nature.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes perceive all phenomena as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure, but they do not [perceive] that which is not all phenomena as such.
Because one perceives permanence, bliss, self, and purity through the partial analysis of phenomena (*dharma-prabheda*), one perceives but one part out of ten.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perceive all phenomena as impermanent, non-self, without bliss, and without purity; they do not perceive all phenomena as permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
For this reason, they perceive the Buddha-nature as clearly as observing an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of one's hand.
For this reason, the Śūraṅgama-samādhi is called "ultimate.

In the section on analogies, first the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are mentioned, followed by four types of individuals: ordinary worldlings, those of the two vehicles, those at the stage of the ten abidings, and the Tathāgata.
Regarding these, the Tathāgata sees them completely, while the Bodhisattva sees them only partially; thus, there is a distinction between seeing them fully and not seeing them at all.
The third simile is like the new moon.
Good son, for example, although the new moon cannot be seen, one cannot say it does not exist.

This also illustrates that sentient beings who have not yet severed their afflictions do not see them, whereas those who have severed their afflictions see them, just as one sees the moon on its first day.

That which is invisible can gradually become visible; the Buddha-nature is likewise. This principle has existed from the beginning, yet sentient beings, due to their afflictions, are unable to perceive it.
As delusions gradually diminish, one gradually gains the ability to see it.
The Buddha-nature is also like this: although all ordinary beings do not perceive it, one cannot say that they lack the Buddha-nature.
Good son, the Buddha-nature refers to the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness.
All sentient beings possess these three; only after destroying their afflictions can they perceive it. As for those such as the icchantikas, [they must first] destroy...
Only after an icchantika attains the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness can they do so;
for this reason, I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

The text states: "Regarding the claim that all sentient beings possess the nature [of Buddhahood] through Great Compassion, the Ten Powers, and so forth—the old translation says 'will have' (*dang you*), implying that the reality does not yet exist.
It further cites a passage from below which says: "Only after destroying the icchantika can one then attain the stages (*bhūmi*).

A commentator explains: "The true spirit of Buddha-nature is like gold wrapped in tattered rags; it possesses the characteristics of Great Compassion, the Ten Powers, and the marks and signs of physical perfection."

The reality is that it is shrouded by conditioned afflictions; if those afflictions are removed, one immediately attains the vision of it. Once the coarse cloth has been stripped away, one immediately obtains the gold.
The Master [Hui]shi said: "These two interpretations contradict one another. If you say that [the Tathāgatagarbha] exists [only potentially], this scriptural passage states:
'Great Compassion, the Ten Powers, and the Four Fearlessnesses—sentient beings possess these. Since it says they 'all possess' them, how could they possibly attain [it] [only later]?"
Regarding the statement that it "exists as if" or "is present as if" gold covered by impurities: if the Buddha-nature is so powerful and fierce, why does it not dispel delusions?

To insist on its being either "future" or "present" is merely a point of contention; it is simply this principle that one cannot be pushed toward the future, for it is through the cultivation of the path that it is attained, nor can it be said to be presently manifest.
These three interpretations are each partial and do not accord with the perfect meaning. Why is this so?
The Buddha-nature is neither one, two, nor three, yet for the sake of sentient beings it is distinguished by four gates:

some say it is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), like the city of Kapilavastu being empty; some say it is not empty, which is like the jewel in the forehead of a poor man’s treasury or his wisdom;
some say it is both empty and existent, like a water-jar or a wine-jar; and that which is said to be neither existent nor non-existent is called...
The Middle Way seeks to cause one to awaken to "non-four" by means of the "four," thereby abandoning attachment to the four to achieve thorough understanding.

When discussing people, this refers to those who grasp at these [extremes]; for such people, delusion obscures this very grasping. As the Master Guān (觀) has explained, this grasping is both existent and non-existent.
Now, in clarifying Buddha-nature, it is like a king seeing an elephant: what all the various masters perceive is entirely the same.

Regarding the phrase "the blind touch" (and so forth) in the final analogy, concerning the statement that there are three types of afflictions to be destroyed, there were two traditional interpretations:
first, that the afflictions of the three realms consist of the afflictions of views and thought;

second, that the afflictions of the defiled lands within the realms are the residual habits (*vāsanā*), the afflictions of the pure lands between the two realms are ignorance, and those of the realms beyond are the [afflictions] of the seven stages.
Regarding the statement that "the Bodhisattva cuts off the afflictions between two realms as an adornment," there are two interpretations.

One interpretation holds that seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*) constitutes the first affliction, while contemplation (*bhāvanā*) constitutes the second. As for the third, it is the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions;

because the fundamental grades of ignorance (*avidyā*) are identical to these habitual tendencies, they are not mentioned separately. From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the third stage, one cuts off the afflictions of seeing the truths.

From the fourth stage through the sixth stage, one abandons conceptualization (*vikalpa*); at the seventh and eighth stages, one simultaneously abandons the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

This is the interpretation of Kaishan. Furthermore, another master critiques these two interpretations, stating that while the text says "the three types [of wisdom] destroy the afflictions," it does not actually explain the intent behind destroying the afflictions;
it merely lists the names of the three types, which deviates from the meaning of the sutra. If we were to discuss the actual intent of destroying them:

One should understand that the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) serve as remedies for the three types of afflictions, as explained in the *Śāstra*. Furthermore, according to the *Neixiang benye jing* (The Sutra on the Original Acts of the Necklace), entering from the conventional into emptiness is called the contemplation of the two truths;

entering from emptiness into the conventional is called the contemplation of equality. These two contemplations serve as the skillful means (*upāya*) for entering the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the Middle Way.
By employing these three contemplations, one is able to destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*). Moreover, this applies to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The breaking of the disease of substantiality and the breaking of the disease of the provisional—these two truths are taught merely as means for subduing [afflictions] so that they may be severed.
If something is neither real nor existent, it is the Middle Way; observing the simultaneous removal of both the diseases of substantiality and the provisional is called the severance of afflictions.

Now, it is clarified that this interpretation is incorrect. The previous two explanations deviate from the sūtras. The Master of Contemplation refuted their deviation from the sūtras; now, their underlying meaning is challenged.

This is biased. If one has already destroyed the three kinds of afflictions and seen the Buddha-nature, then having destroyed the afflictions of the defiled land of *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*, as well as the afflictions of the intermediate pure land, one should either see the nature or not see it.

If one sees the nature, then since the followers of the Two Vehicles also destroy *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*, why do they not see it? If they do not see the nature, this contradicts the Sūtras. [The Master] explained:

The first is the thorough destruction of *dṛṣṭi* (views), and the second is the destruction of *kleśa* (afflictions). From the stage of a *srotāpanna* up to the fourth fruit, all have destroyed both views and afflictions.
This is because [the nature of views] is not [identical to] the nature of views; if it were the nature of views, this principle would not exist.

Furthermore, if one does not see [this], it contradicts the sūtras. Moreover, the contemplation of the two truths and the contemplation of equality are all skillful means (*upāya*) and do not enter the Middle Way.
Furthermore, not seeing one's nature contradicts the sutras; the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) refutes intrinsic nature, while the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) refutes the provisional.

This is merely a suppression [of afflictions] rather than their total eradication. Moreover, not seeing one's nature also contradicts the sutras, for it is only by eradicating both the true and the conventional that one attains the vision of one's nature.
Although three types of refutation of afflictions are proclaimed, if one speaks of only two types of refutation, then one does not see one's nature; there is only one [true way].
Regarding the statement in the *Zhongpo dejian jing* (Sūtra on Attaining Vision through Severing) that those who sever the three types of afflictions all see the Buddha-nature:
if it were the case that one who severs one type sees [it] while one who severs two types does not, how could this be consistent?

Here, we clarify that when one cultivates skillful means in the seventh stage and the path and contemplation flow together in the eighth stage to sever ignorance and see the Buddha-nature, this represents the "connecting the distinct to the universal" (*bie tong jie*).
There is one type of breaking through afflictions to perceive the Buddha-nature: if one enters the wisdom of principle (*yulig prajñā*), it is called "abiding" (*vihāra*);

if one breaks the four abiding delusions (*catur-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*) and gives rise to meritorious qualities, it is called the "ten practices" (*daśa-caryā*); if one breaks the delusions of dust and sand (*reṇu-saikatā-kleśa*) but has not yet seen the Buddha-nature, it is the "ten transferences" (*daśa-pratipatti*);

by subduing ignorance (*avidyā*) and ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*), one breaks through ignorance and perceives the Buddha-nature. This is the sequential breaking [of delusions] according to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*).
Furthermore, there is another way to destroy afflictions and see the Buddha-nature:

if one practices the perfect contemplation of the Dharma-realm, then afflictions are themselves bodhi, and at the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening and enters the stage of the copper wheel.

Upon ascending to the first bhūmi, one destroys ignorance and sees the Buddha-nature. These three ways of destroying delusion have their meanings clearly elucidated, and in each case, one sees the Buddha-nature.
The sutra text states that the assembly of virtuous ones should know that "one emptiness is all emptiness" and that the three truths are all empty;

this contemplation destroys the delusions of the five abodes and enables one to see the Buddha-nature. Furthermore, "one provisionality is all provisionality" and the three truths are all provisional;
this contemplation likewise destroys the delusions of the five abodes and enables one to see the Buddha-nature. Furthermore, "one middle is all middle" and the three truths are all... [middle].

In this contemplation, one also destroys the delusions of the five stages and is able to see the Buddha-nature; thus, these three types, both in their enumeration and their meaning, accord precisely with the Sūtra.

Furthermore, the various virtuous ones have not yet understood that the first three types of destroying delusions are based on the distinct (pṛthagjana) perspective, while the latter three types of contemplation are based on the perfect (pariniṣpanna) perspective.

Good son, regarding the twelve links of dependent origination, the final two have one analogy that illustrates their equality. All [links] first present the analogy and then provide the application (*yōjaku*).
The preceding analogy pertains to the external, while the current analogy pertains to the internal; thus, there are four parts: first, proclaiming equality;
second, revealing the substance of the causes and conditions; third, clarifying whether the factors are complete or incomplete; and fourth, concluding with equality.
Good son, the twelve links of dependent origination are equally shared by all sentient beings; they are both internal and external.
To clarify that they are equally present in all, it is said they are "both internal and external. This refers exclusively to human beings and does not mean external objects.
The mind is considered internal and form is considered external; because both form and mind are possessed, they are called internal and external. Furthermore, [it is as follows:]...

"Clouds are internal while within the womb and external once they have emerged from it. I personally maintain that the text itself speaks of "internal and external seeking" as well as "internal and external matters.
However, this passage does not mean that the twenty causal conditions (*nidāna*) are taken as the objects of contemplation;
rather, it takes the twelve [links] as the Buddha-nature, just as each individual link of the twelve causal conditions is distinct.

The analysis is intended to enable sentient beings to recognize the characteristics of saṃsāra throughout the three periods of time; how could it be that at the time of ignorance there is only ignorance?
Therefore, one should know that from birth through old age and death, all twelve links are constantly present. Thus, the subsequent passage states: "The Buddha-nature is also like this;
how could it be that while in the state of a sentient being it is merely a sentient being? This is because all sentient beings are, in fact, one.

Because every single thought-moment is fully endowed with the ten realms and the hundred realms as the conditions for the dependent and the primary causes, there is nothing within each realm that is not Buddha-nature;
thus, the terms "internal" and "external" carry multiple meanings.
What are the twelve? They are the twelve factors that emerge from below and fully explain the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*).
What are these twelve? Ignorance (*avidyā*) refers to the afflictions of the past; karmic formations (*saṃskāra*) refers to the actions of the past;

and consciousness (*vijñāna*) refers to the initial entry into the womb in the present life, during which the five stages of fetal development and the four sense organs have not yet been fully formed.

The state of being endowed with name-and-form and the four sense-faculties, prior to the arising of contact, is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The state of not yet distinguishing between suffering and pleasure is called contact (*sparśa*).
The cultivation and habitual attachment to craving is called feeling (*vedanā*). The frequenting and proximity to the five desires is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The internal and external seeking and grasping is called clinging (*upādāna*). The arousal of bodily, verbal, and mental karma regarding internal and external phenomena is called becoming (*bhava*).

The consciousness of the present life is called "future birth"; name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling of the present are called "the future life's old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
This is what is known as the twelve links of dependent origination.
Since the past possesses both cause and effect, why are two causes taken and not the result?

Because the result of the past itself repays its preceding cause, it is therefore not taken. Thus, the two causes produce the five present results, and the three present causes produce the two future results.
Regarding the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*), there are two interpretations: one states that the first seven days after conception constitute consciousness.

At that time, although there is form (*rūpa*), the meaning of consciousness (*vijñāna*) has not yet manifested; because the aspect of feeling (*vedanā*) has already manifested, it is given the name "consciousness.

Second, [it is argued] that it refers only to the initial moment of entering the womb (*pratisandhi*). Although at that moment there is form, the form is not yet complete; yet it is called "consciousness" because consciousness is the master of retribution (*vipāka*).
Therefore, it is termed "consciousness. Furthermore, by the second moment, it becomes the constituent of form (*rūpāṅga*). This interpretation is somewhat superior.
The fourth section of the *Womb-Entry Fivefold Exposition*, explaining the branch of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), also refers to the "five vesicles":
the two hands, the two feet, and the head. At this stage, the four sense-faculties are not yet complete; there is only the body and the mind, but no eye, ear, nose, or tongue.

Regarding the term "name-and-form," there are two interpretations: first, that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is "form," while the other four aggregates are "name"; second, that it refers simply to this [embryonic] matter together with...
Because of the designation "sentient beings," it is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Next, the fulfillment of the four sense organs constitutes the fifth link;

since these four organs are present, all six sense bases are complete, and thus it is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). From this point onward, there arises the production of coarse and subtle states.
If it is the production of subtle states, then within the womb, consciousness and mind have not yet developed ideation or feeling. If it is the production of coarse states, then it is as follows:
At the time of first emerging from the womb, one is unable to grasp fire or touch poison, like a small infant of one or two months who has not yet distinguished between suffering and pleasure;
this refers to the sixth link, contact (*sparśa*). If the subtle aspect of arising is considered, it is the conceptual mind within the womb that does not yet know suffering or pleasure;
if the coarse aspect of arising is considered, then at one or two years of age, one is already able to grasp fire and touch poison, yet still lacks true cognition.
Holding something in the hand yet unable to distinguish its value, one is permeated by a single craving; this is the seventh link, the branch of sensation (*vedanā*), which follows the five fruits.
If the signs arise subtly, it refers to the sensations and mind within the womb. Regarding "a single craving": when a single pleasant object arises, one conceives a conceptual attachment.
If the signs arise coarsely, as in the case of three or four years of age, one knows only the craving for food and does not yet know the five desires.

Habitually associating with the five desires constitutes the eighth link, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which is the first of the three causes. If analyzed in terms of subtle arising, it corresponds to the initial stage of mental formations within the womb.
In terms of the sequence of mental formations, there are three stages: the first is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the middle is called grasping (*upādāna*), and the last is called existence (*bhava*).

If analyzed in terms of coarse arising, it refers to the ninth link, occurring when one is eight or nine years old and begins to understand sensual desire, engaging in internal and external covetous seeking.

That is, from about ten years of age until one gradually grows older and becomes increasingly capable of craving and seeking—during which conduct slightly increases—this constitutes the tenth link, the arising of internal and external phenomena.

That is, from about ten years of age until the body has fully grown and belongs entirely to the hundred-year span of the present life, this constitutes the eleventh link, the consciousness of the present existence.
This is identical to the present in being the beginning of the two future fruits.
The temporal stage of the consciousness-link (*vijñāna-aṅga*) is precisely that single moment of initial conception in the present;

the twelfth link, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), likewise corresponds to the time of the present name-and-form and so forth. That is to say, future old-age-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and so on, are all future results.
These two future results, in turn, correspond to the present consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense-bases.
Entering [into these categories] merely involves changing the names by which they are designated.
Regarding the presence or absence of the three [factors] among all sentient beings,
O son of good family, although there are such twelve links of dependent origination, some may not be complete.
If one dies at the stage of *kalala*, the twelve links from birth through old age and death cannot be fully realized.

Sentient beings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) lack the three types of feeling, the three types of contact, and the three types of craving; they also lack old age and illness, yet they may still be said to possess the twelve links.
Sentient beings of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) lack form and so forth, up to and including old age and death, yet they may also be said [to possess them].

To complete the twelve [factors], regarding the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), it is said that there are no three types of feeling (*vedanā*). There are two interpretations: first, among the three feelings, because the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) is not present, it is said that there are no three;
second, because there is no perception (*saṃjñā*) of the category of suffering, it is said that there are no three kinds of contact (*sparśa*), nor is there [suffering].
Because they proceed from the basis of painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*), it is said that there are no three kinds of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
If [beings] in the form and formless realms do not possess the twelve [links], how can the text state that they are also called "complete with the twelve"?

Although those who die as an embryo (*kalala*) or those born in the form and formless realms do not possess the twelve, the wheel of suffering (*duḥkhacakra*) has not yet ceased; they continue to wander through the three realms until the end.

The twelve [links] are complete based on the fourth dhyāna; however, from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) upward, there is no longer suffering or pleasure, nor is there the equanimity that is neutral between them;
therefore, it is said that the three types of feeling (vedanā) do not exist there. Since the formless realm lacks form, the twelve [links] are not complete.
Because they are definitely attained, the fourth section below concludes that all possess the twelve [links].
Because they are definitely attained, it is said that sentient beings equally possess the twelve links of dependent origination.
Because they have not yet ceased the wheel of suffering and have long gazed toward its beginning and end, it is said that "all possess" it.
Buddha-nature is also like this; this is the second analogy.
"Good son, Buddha-nature is also like this: all sentient beings will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Because of this Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The six destinies and the four modes of birth all possess it; like the twelve similes, all sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature.
In the Snowy Mountains there is a herb; [the third section of the third analogy clarifies that it is only through dependence on conditions that it is seen]. This is divided into three parts:
first, the analogy and its application.
"Good son, in the Snowy Mountains there is a herb named 'Patience. If a cow eats it, it produces *sarpis* (clarified butter), and further..."

There is a different kind of grass that, if eaten by an ox, yields no clarified butter (*ghṛta*); yet, although there is no clarified butter [from it], one cannot say that the *kṣānti-grass* does not exist within the Snowy Mountains.
This consists of two parts: first, the formal application (*upanaya*), and second, the elucidation of the principle (*nyāya*).
The Buddha-nature is also like this. The Snowy Mountains represent the Tathāgata; the "patience-grass" represents the Great Nirvāṇa;

and the "other grasses" represent the twelve divisions of the scriptures. If sentient beings can listen to, receive, inquire about, and study the Great Parinirvāṇa, they will then see the Buddha-nature.
Although within the twelve divisions of the scriptures one does not hear it explicitly stated, one must not say that there is no Buddha-nature.
The Clarification of Principles has three parts. First, the proclamation of the nine chapters:
"Good son, the Buddha-nature is both form and not-form, neither form nor not-form; it is both characteristic and not-characteristic, neither characteristic nor not-characteristic;
it is both one and not-one, neither one nor not-one; it is neither eternal nor annihilated, neither non-eternal."
It is neither non-cessation, nor both existence and non-existence, nor neither existence nor non-existence; it is neither exhaustion, nor non-exhaustion, nor neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion;
it is neither cause nor fruit, nor neither cause nor fruit; it is neither meaning nor non-meaning, nor neither meaning nor non-meaning;
it is neither syllable nor non-syllable, nor neither syllable nor non-syllable.
Each gate contains three phrases, totaling twenty-seven phrases.
Second, the explanation:
Why is it the color-form vajra-body? Because it is not non-color-form; because it is not the eighteen non-color-form dharmas.
Why is it neither form nor non-form? Because form and non-form lack a fixed characteristic. Why is it a characteristic? Because of the thirty-two marks. Why is it not a characteristic?
Because the characteristics of all sentient beings do not manifest. Why is it neither a characteristic nor a non-characteristic?
Because characteristics and non-characteristics are not determinate. Why is it "one"? Because all sentient beings are entirely of the One Vehicle.
Therefore, why is it not one? Because it teaches the three vehicles. Why is it neither one nor not one? Because it consists of innumerable dharmas. Why is it not eternal?
Because it is seen as arising from conditions. Why is it not annihilated? Because it is free from the view of annihilation. Why is it neither eternal nor annihilated?
Because it has no beginning or end. Why is it said to exist? Because all sentient beings possess it.
Why is it that one attains vision through skillful means that do not originate from anything? Why is it that the nature of space is neither existent nor non-existent?
What is meant by "attaining the perfection of the Śūraṅgama-samādhi"? Why is it not "exhausted," because it is eternal?
Why is it neither exhausted nor non-exhausted, because all marks of exhaustion have been severed? Why is it called the "cause," because it is through this that [all things] are understood?

Why is it called a cause? Because it is the cause of results. Why is it a result? Because its fruition is certain. Why is it neither cause nor result? Because it is eternal. Why is it called a meaning?
Because it can encompass all meanings. Why is it unimpeded regarding meanings? Because there is no obstruction to meanings. Why is it not a meaning? Because it is ineffable.
Why is it neither a meaning nor a non-meaning? Because it is ultimately empty. Why is it called a letter? Because it possesses a name.
Why is it not a word? Because it is nameless. Why is it neither a word nor not a word? Because it has severed the first syllable.
Why is it neither suffering nor pleasure? Because it has severed all sensations. Why is it not self? Because one has not yet fully attained the eight masteries.
Why is it not non-self? Because it is eternal. Why is it neither self nor non-self? Because it does not act.
Because it is not grasped, how can it be empty? It is empty because it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). How can it be non-empty? Because it is eternal.
How can it be neither empty nor non-empty? Because it can serve as the seed for wholesome dharmas.
In the commentary, three additional matters are set forth, which, when combined with those listed in the main text, total thirty-six phrases.
