How can it be said that milk possesses the nature of curd?
If their colors were different— milk being white and curd yellow— and if their tastes were different— milk being sweet and curd sour— and if their medicinal properties were different—
milk treating heat and curd treating cold— since none of these distinctions exist, how could there be curd?
For example, it is like taking clarified butter (*sarpis*) to eliminate the third knot of affliction.
Good son, it is just as if there were a person who was to take clarified butter tomorrow but already suffers from its foul odor today;
to say that the nature of curd (*dadhi*) definitely exists within milk is likewise so.

"If one is to consume *sarpis* (clarified butter) tomorrow, yet already suffers from its odor today; and if one is to enjoy rich wine tomorrow, yet is already satiated today—how could it be possible to obtain and eat *dadhi* (curd) [in advance]?
This is like a certain person... [The second section, "Showing the Correct Meaning," is divided into four parts: First, citing a simile to show the correct meaning.

Second, citing verses as proof; third, applying [the analogy] to sentient beings below; fourth, elevating [the discussion] to the realm of the Buddha above. First, three analogies are presented, which are further divided into two parts:
first the analogy, then the application.
"Good son, it is like a person who possesses a pen, paper, and ink, which combine to form characters; yet within that paper, [the characters were] originally..."

There are no characters because they are originally non-existent; they are formed through the conjunction of conditions. If they were originally existent, what need would there be for manifold conditions?
For example, when blue and yellow combine to form green, one should know that these two are originally devoid of the nature of green.

If it were originally existent, what need would there be for them to combine? Son of Good Family, for example, sentient beings obtain life by means of food, yet within this food there is truly nothing [of the nature of life].
If there were a life-force such that this life-force existed from the very beginning, then food should be the life-force itself before it has been eaten.
In the first analogy, it is shown that although things lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they exist through the conjunction of conditions, as illustrated by the text.
All dharmas are summarized by means of analogies.
Son of good family, all dharmas are fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For this reason, the second section below cites verses to establish this proof.
For this reason, I have spoken these verses:
"Non-existent in the beginning, now existent; existent in the beginning, now non-existent— that there should be such a thing as a dharma existing throughout the three periods of time is impossible.
Son of good family, all dharmas arise because of causes and conditions, and they cease because of causes and conditions.
We take only the first two lines as proof that there is no inherent nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

If an inherent nature were determinately existent, it should not be the case that what was originally non-existent now exists, nor should it be the case that what was originally existent now ceases to exist; for what was originally existent should always exist, and what was originally non-existent should always be non-existent.
Since [existence] is thus indeterminate, how can you say that milk possesses the nature of curd? The following two lines follow in succession from this point.
This verse is the fourth citation used to prove the present meaning.
Regarding "all sentient beings," the third section—concerning the emptiness of the bodies of sentient beings—is presented to demonstrate the correct principle;
it consists of the thesis, the reason, and the example, with the example further divided into the primary illustration and its detailed application.
"Good son, if all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature within, then all sentient beings should have a Buddha-body just as I do now.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither broken nor destroyed; it cannot be dragged away, seized, bound, or fettered."
Just as there is space within all sentient beings— since all sentient beings possess space without obstruction,
each does not perceive that they possess this space— if sentient beings were devoid of space, there would be no coming or going,
walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, nor would there be birth or growth. For this reason, I have said in my sutras that all sentient beings [possess space].
There is the realm of empty space; that which is the realm of empty space is called "emptiness.
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are able to see it slightly, like a diamond jewel.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is the realm of all Buddhas; the fourth section below, "Exalted Only in the Buddhas," is as stated in the text.
Good son, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is the realm of all Buddhas, which is not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Because all sentient beings do not see the Buddha-nature, they are constantly bound by afflictions and wander through birth and death. Thus it is said: [text continues].
Because of the Buddha-nature, one cannot be bound by the various fetters and afflictions; one is liberated from birth and death and attains Great Nirvana.

Having finished the refutation through the method of "affirming and then negating" (*yǒng-duò*) based on the preceding scriptural passage, it is clarified that the Buddha-nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Next, three analogies are presented to clarify that the Buddha-nature is provisional (*prajñapti*).
Following this, a verse is cited to testify that the Buddha-nature is both emptiness and provisional. Finally, the emptiness of the sentient beings' bodies is explained.
This is analogous to how the Buddha-nature pervades all places and leads to the realm of all Buddhas; it clarifies that the Buddha-nature is precisely the Middle Way.

This text is highly consistent with the meaning of the preceding passage, which states that "Buddha-nature is named the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)," and that "emptiness is named wisdom," and so forth.
I privately maintain that Master Zhǎng'ān, relying on the sūtras, fully understood that the Buddha-nature pervades all places.
Yet he was unwilling to speak openly, for people of the time had not yet believed that there is peace.

To demonstrate this, he showed that since the Buddha-nature is fully endowed with the three meanings of emptiness and so forth, these are the three truths (*trisatya*). Thus, all dharmas are none other than the three truths, and none other than the Buddha-nature.
If it were not so, how could one say that within the bodies of sentient beings there exists the void?
Since empty space already exists elsewhere, how could it not exist here? If it did not exist, it would not be called "empty space. Reflect on this, reflect on this!
[This concludes] the third section of the *Siṃhanāda*, which establishes that conditions can produce results from within causes.
Furthermore, there are five rounds of question and answer.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said, “World-Honored One, all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature; this nature is like the quality of curd within milk.
If milk lacked the nature of curd, why would the Buddha say there are two kinds of causes:

first, the direct cause (*dharmatā-hetu*), and second, the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*)? As for the conditional cause, it consists of fermentation and warmth. Since empty space lacks these qualities, it has no conditional cause.”

The intent of the first question is as follows: If milk lacks the nature of curd, what use would there be for auxiliary causes? Since space lacks such a nature, it does not depend on two types of causes.
The Buddha said: "Good son, if there were a fixed nature of curd within milk, why would it require auxiliary causes?"
The answer is as stated in the text.

In the second turn of the discussion, the condition as a cause of transformation (*pariṇāma-hetu*) is designated as the cause of actualization (*kāraṇa-hetu*); within this inquiry, there are three analogies, followed by the analogy of milk, with the application (*yoga*) as in the text.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said, “World-Honored One, because there is an inherent nature (*svabhāva*), one requires contributory causes (*pratyaya-hetu*).
Why? It is for the sake of clear perception. A contributory cause is precisely a revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*). World-Honored One, it is like when various objects already exist in the darkness;
for the sake of seeing them, one uses a lamp to illuminate and reveal them. If they did not originally exist, what would the lamp illuminate? It is as with clay [in which the form already exists].”

Just as a jar requires a person, water, a wheel, a rope, and a staff as its efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*), or as the seed of a *nyagrodha* tree requires earth, water, and manure as its efficient causes;

so too is the fermentation and heat within milk: they likewise require efficient causes. Therefore, although the nature [of the effect] exists beforehand, it necessarily depends upon [these conditions].
One perceives [the result] only after the cause of perception (*jñāna-hetu*) has been realized; for this reason, it is certain that the nature of curd (*dadhi-bhāva*) already exists within milk.
The Buddha’s answer consists of four points: first, clarifying that the nature itself is the cause of perception; second, clarifying that what is perceived should be self-evident;
third, clarifying that what is perceived should be capable of both perceptions; and fourth, citing the direct cause to reach a definitive conclusion.
Good son, if there were a fixed nature of curd within milk, it would be a revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*). If it is a revealing cause, why would it need to reveal anything?
To say that the original nature is itself the revelation means that the revelation reveals what was originally revealed and causes it to emerge. If the nature already exists of its own accord...

If this [nature] is already manifest, why must it be manifested by something else? Since milk already possesses the nature of curd, and that nature is itself manifest, why must it be brought forth through the manifestation of yeast and heat?
Next, as for "if it were a cause of manifestation" (*vyakti-hetu*)...
Good son, if the nature of the clarifying cause were itself the clarification, it should always clarify itself;
if it cannot clarify itself, how can it clarify another?
To speak correctly, the yeast and warmth that act as the clarifying cause should be able to clarify themselves; if they do not clarify themselves, how can they serve to clarify milk?
If the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) were initially self-manifesting, it should be able to manifest itself and emerge as curd without needing to manifest the milk to produce the curd.
If one says that there are two types of efficient causes, then according to the third [point], it should be able to manifest both.
If it is claimed that the revealing cause has two natures—the first being self-revealing and the second being revealing others—this meaning is not correct. Why?
Because how can a single dharma that serves as a revealing cause have two [natures]?
The fermenting agent alone, through its own warmth, is able to bring about the production of curd; furthermore, it is able to discern that curd comes from milk.
If there were two [distinct causes], this would be the fourth point raised for the sake of a definitive resolution:
"If there were two, then milk should also have two [causes]. If there are no two characteristics within the milk, how can there be a discerning cause?"
Yet there are only two [conditions].
To clarify that the fermenting agent and warmth can both act as the efficient cause, milk should likewise be able to act as both;
it would then be acting as the efficient cause for itself to become curd, and simultaneously acting as the efficient cause for the fermenting agent and warmth.
Regarding the intent of the third question: although four objections were previously raised, the core point of attachment was the third—that [consciousness] is self-cognizing and cognizes others.
Thus, Siṃhanāda said: "World-Honored One, just as people in the world say, 'I together with eight people,' so too is the cause of cognition; it is both self-cognizing and cognizes others."
When it is said, "I am with eight people," this is like counting others as seven and oneself as the eighth; this is counting oneself and counting others.
It is likewise for counting others and counting oneself, as well as for perceiving oneself and perceiving others.
The Buddha replied by first refuting the attachment to duality and then demonstrating the correct meaning; the initial refutation consists of two parts. First, the refutation:
the Buddha said, "Good son, if the cause of manifestation were such as you describe, it would not be a cause of manifestation."
If that were so, it would not be a revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*).
Next, the passage beginning with "For what reason" provides the explanation.
For what reason? Because a counter (*saṃkhyā*) can count both its own color and other colors, one may say there are "eight"; however, as for the nature of this color itself—
Because that which lacks the characteristic of discernment cannot discern itself, it must rely upon the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*) to enumerate both self and other;
therefore, the cause of discernment (*vibhāva-hetu*) cannot discern itself, nor can it discern others.
Indeed, while wisdom can enumerate its own form as well as the forms of others, form cannot enumerate itself or the forms of others.

If form is such as it is, how could it cognize itself and also cognize others? Since there is another distinct dharma that cognizes both itself and others, it is called the "cause of cognition" (*jñāpaka-hetu*);
yet, this so-called cause of cognition is not actually a cause of cognition.
This concludes the first section; the following second section demonstrates the correct meaning for all sentient beings.
"Good son, if all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, for what reason do they cultivate immeasurable merits?

If you say that cultivation is the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*), it would be the same as [the case where] curd has already turned into butter. If you say that the fruit definitely exists within the cause, then precepts, concentration, and wisdom would not increase.
I observe that people in the world originally lack prohibitive precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom; from [these causes], they..."

Once the teacher has received [the teaching], it gradually increases. If you say that the teacher’s instruction is the "revealing cause" (vyākaraṇa-hetu), then at the time the teacher instructs, the recipient does not yet possess precepts, concentration, or wisdom.
If it were a revealing cause, it should reveal what is as yet unmanifest; how then could it reveal precepts, concentration, and wisdom so as to cause them to grow?
To clarify that things do not inherently exist but can exist by depending on conditions,
the fourth turn of the argument further raises an objection, citing the Buddha’s own words to demonstrate that because there is milk and there is curd, one knows they exist.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said, "World-Honored One, if the cause of manifestation (*vyakti-hetu*) does not exist, how can one say that there is milk and there is curd?
The Buddha replied in two parts: first, a general presentation; second, a specific answer.
Good son, there are generally three ways of answering difficult questions in the world: first, the answer by turning [the question back], as explained above:
"For what reason does one uphold the precepts? Because of freedom from regret," and so on, up to "for the sake of attaining great *nirvāṇa*";
second, the answer by silence, such as when a certain Brahmin came and asked me, "Am I eternal? and at that time I remained silent; third, the answer by means of doubt.
In this sutra, if there were two causes for manifestation, why could there not be two [lactants] in milk?

To answer by turning the question back is an answer that follows the inquiry; to answer with silence is an answer that sets the matter aside; to answer by questioning in return is an answer that is indefinite.
Subsequently, he provides a formal response by way of turning the argument, as in the text:

"Good son, I now respond by turning the argument: just as people in the world say 'there is milk' or 'there is curd' because they will certainly obtain them, and thus receive the names 'having milk' or 'having curd,' so too it is with the Buddha-nature.
There are sentient beings who possess the Buddha-nature because they shall [attain it]."
Because it is observed.

Since the fifth section of the *Siṃhanāda* refutes the claim that [the Tathāgata] will exist in the future, this objection is formulated; it consists of two parts, the first of which is a refutation by means of an appeal to authority (*āptāgama*).
The Lion’s Roar said: "World-Honored One, that which the Buddha has taught is not so.
Furthermore, [your argument] consists of three parts: the question, the analogy, and the application.
If the past has already ceased and the future has not yet arrived, how can they be called 'existent'? If you claim that what is 'to be' is called 'existent,' then..."
This interpretation is not correct.
For example, when people in the world see that they have no children, they say they have no children.
How then can it be said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, given that there are some sentient beings who lack Buddha-nature?

The Buddha answered with two parts: first the analogy, and second the application of the analogy, which consists of four sections. First, he clarifies that there was existence in the past. The Buddha said:
"Good son, 'existence' in the past is like planting an orange tree. When the sprout arises, the seed perishes;

yet the sprout is also sweet, and so it continues until the fruit is produced, the flavor of which is likewise [sweet]. Once it has fully ripened, it becomes sour. Good son, as for this sour flavor..."

From the seed and sprout up to the production of the fruit, all are devoid of [inherent existence]; yet at the time of ripening, a sour taste arises according to the original form, color, and characteristics.
Although this sour taste was originally non-existent and now exists, its present existence does not occur without depending on the original [cause].
Because this original cause, though having passed away, is still designated as "existent," for this reason the past is called "existent."
Second, explaining that the future exists.
Why is the future called "existence"? It is like a person who plants sesame seeds. Someone asks him, "For what purpose do you plant these?
He replies, "Because there is oil. Although the oil does not yet exist, once the sesame has ripened, one takes the seeds and roasts or steams them.

One must pound and press [the seed] before it can sprout; one should know that such a person is not speaking falsely. For this reason, it is called "existence in the future. To further clarify "existence in the past" three times: why, moreover, is it called "existence in the past"? Good son, it is like a person who, in private, reviles the king. After a long time has passed, the king hears of it and dispatches an official to arrest him. Upon being arrested, the man says: "I did not revile the king; I was merely talking to my wife. The official replies: "The king’s majesty is all-knowing; how could you have spoken thus without his hearing it? You are indeed a liar. The man says: "I spoke in private, and no one else heard me. Why do you call me a liar? The official replies: "If you had not reviled the king, why would the king have dispatched an official to arrest you? Because he heard your words, he sent for you. This proves that you did revile the king; you are indeed a liar. The man says: "I spoke in secret, and no one heard me. How can you say I am a liar? After many years, the king heard of this; having heard it, he immediately asked, "For what reason did you revile me? He replied, "Great King, I did not revile you. Why?
Because the one who reviles has already perished. The king said, "The reviler and I both exist;
how can you say he has perished? For this reason, I would lose my life. "Good son, these two are in reality non-existent."
The non-extinction of the fruit is called "existence in the past.
There are four further explanations of "existence in the future.
What, then, is meant by "existence in the future"? It is, for example, like a person who goes to a potter’s workshop and asks, "Is there a jar?"
He replied: "There is a jar, though the potter has not yet actually produced it; because the clay exists, one says there is a jar.
You should know that this person is not speaking falsely when he says there is curd within the milk."
Regarding the question of whether "future existence" is indeed "present existence," the answer is sufficient in itself;

yet, to further clarify the past, it must be understood that this arises from the differing views and various calculations of different schools. The Sarvāstivādins maintain that all three time periods exist:
there has been [the past], there will be [the future], and there is [the present]. The Dharmaguptakas maintain that the past and the future do not exist, and only the present exists.
The above concludes the refutation of existence. Now, if one employs [these concepts], they are merely provisional names used in accordance with worldly convention;

furthermore, since these are the deeds of the Dharma King, how could they be fathomed by mere human sentiment? It was previously stated that when an orange seed is planted, its sprout is sweet while its mature fruit is sour.

This subsequent sourness proves that the prior sweetness existed in the past. Conversely, if this present orange were initially sour and subsequently sweet, [it would likewise prove the existence of the future].

Whether it be due to differences in the land or the substance, or because it is taken at a time when it has fully ripened and its flavor is sour, this serves as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature within sentient beings.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this:
if one wishes to see the Buddha-nature, one should observe the timing, the season, and the form and color.
Therefore, I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; this is truly not false.
This correctly clarifies that they "shall have" [it], meaning that sentient beings shall attain it.

Following the "Lion’s Roar," the fourth section—based on the primary cause (hetu)—maintains that [Buddha-nature] exists, consisting of four question-and-answer exchanges. In the first of these, there are again four parts.
First, the principle; second, the analogy; third, the application;
fourth, the conclusion. The Lion’s Roar says: "If all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature, how could they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Because of the true cause, sentient beings are enabled to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
What is the primary cause of the three types of bodhi? It is what is called buddha-nature.
In the initial teaching, that which is termed the "primary cause of buddha-nature" is precisely the true nature of the Middle Way.
The passage beginning with "The nyagrodha tree" provides an analogy; furthermore, there are four parts, the first of which is the formal presentation of the analogy.
World-Honored One, if there were no *nyagrodha* tree for the *nyagrodha* seed,
why would it be called a *nyagrodha* seed and not a *khadira* seed?
Secondly, he mentions the Gautama clan by way of comparison:
the World-Honored One, being of the Gautama clan, cannot be called of the Atiya clan,
and one of the Atiya clan likewise cannot be called of the Gautama clan.
The third is the analogy of combination.
A seed of the nyagrodha tree is likewise not to be called a seed of the khadira tree,
nor can a seed of the khadira tree be called a seed of the nyagrodha tree.
The fourth [point] is like using the following analogy to raise an objection regarding the *gotra* (clan/lineage):
just as the World-Honored One cannot abandon his *Gautama* lineage, the intent of the objection is:
"If the seed of a *nyagrodha* tree lacks the nature of a tree, how can it be called a 'seed of a *nyagrodha* tree'?"
It should be called "the milk of the *khatāra* fruit," which lacks the nature of curd; it should not be called milk, as it would produce something entirely different.
The Buddha-nature is likewise analogous to this.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
For this reason, you should know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The Buddha’s answer is twofold; first, he cites eight matters that cannot be seen.
The Buddha said: "Good son, if one says that the nyagrodha tree exists within the seed, this meaning is not so."

Why is it that some good men do not see [the truth], even though it exists? It is because, like worldly objects, it cannot be perceived due to causes and conditions. What are these causes and conditions?
It is like being unable to see what is too distant, such as the tracks of birds in the sky; it is like being unable to see what is too near, such as one's own eyelashes;
it is like failing to see due to impaired faculties, such as those with diseased organs; and it is like failing to see due to distracted thoughts, such as when the mind is not concentrated.
First, because it is subtle, it is not seen; second, because it is obstructed by minute particles, it is not seen, like stars behind clouds;
third, because it is numerous, it is not seen, like hemp within a heap of rice; fourth, because it is similar [in appearance], it is not seen, like a bean within a heap of beans;

fifth, because it is different [in nature], it is not seen, as in the case of a *nyagrodha* tree [not being perceived as such when its fruit is consumed]. For what reason are these eight kinds of causes and conditions not seen, even though they exist?
If the *nyagrodha* seed possesses the nature of a tree, why is it not seen?

Next, regarding the statement that it is "subtle" and "obstructed," this is further refuted in two parts: first, a general negation; second, the formal refutation beginning with the words "Why is this so? and following.
If it is argued that [the tree] is not seen because of subtle obstruction, this interpretation is incorrect.
In the refutation, there are two parts: first, the refutation of subtlety, and second, the refutation of obstruction. First, regarding the refutation of subtlety: Why is this so?
Because the characteristics of a tree are coarse; if its nature were subtle, how could it grow?

Now, if the characteristics of the tree were originally coarse, how could they not remain so? If they were originally fine, they should not become large later; and if they are large later, they should have been large at the beginning as well. Next, the refutation of the obstacle [to growth]: The text states: "If the tree's characteristics were originally coarse, why would they not be seen as such?
If they were originally fine, they should not become large later; and if they are large later, they should have been large at the beginning. Next, the refutation of the obstacle.

If you say that it cannot be seen because of obstructions, then it should never have been seen; yet since there was originally no coarse form, but now a coarse form is seen, one should know that this coarseness was originally without its own nature.
Since there was originally no seeing-nature, but now seeing is possible, one should know that this seeing was also originally without its own nature.
It is the same with the son: if originally there was no tree, but now there is one, what fault could there be?
If the seed of a nyagrodha tree were to obstruct the nyagrodha tree such that it could not be seen, then the permanent [self] should likewise be obstructed,
and the permanent [self] should likewise be invisible.
This is the second round of question and answer.
Siṃhanāda said: "As the Buddha has taught, there are two kinds of causes: first, the direct cause (hetu); second, the revealing cause (vyañjana-hetu).
Because the seed of the nyagrodha tree uses earth, water, and manure as its revealing cause, it causes the minute to become coarse."

In the question, the two causes—the producing cause (*janaka-hetu*) and the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*)—are again raised. Regarding the revealing cause, it is asked: "If there is nothing to be revealed, how can it be said that there is none?
This is because the subtle is made manifest and thus becomes visible.
The Buddha’s answer has five stages; the first clarifies that both original existence and original non-existence do not require a revealing cause.

The Buddha said: "Good son, if it existed from the beginning, what need would there be for a revealing cause? If it lacked the nature [of existence] from the beginning, what would be revealed by a revealing cause?
As for the two examples of the nyagrodha tree cited below, they raise the objection that these are not fruits."
If within the nyagrodha tree there was originally no coarse characteristic, yet a coarse one arises by virtue of a revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*), why does it not likewise produce a khadira tree?
For both are equally non-existent [within the nyagrodha].
Since the *nyagrodha* seed is originally non-existent and the gross form of the *nyagrodha* tree is also non-existent,
and likewise the gross form of the *khadira* tree is non-existent, why does the *khadira* tree not arise?
If the subtle [embryo] were as difficult to see as the three lower [stages], then the coarse [embryo] should be visible.
Good son, if the subtle is invisible, the coarse should be visible. For example, a single mote of dust is invisible, yet when many motes are combined, they become visible.
In this same way, the coarse [form] within the embryo should be visible. Why is this?
Within this, there are already sprouts, stalks, flowers, and fruits; within each fruit there are immeasurable seeds, and within each seed there are immeasurable trees.
Therefore, it is called "coarse existence. Because it is coarse, it ought to be visible.
Fourth, the analogy of burning is presented together.
Good son, if the *nyagrodha* seed possesses the nature of a *nyagrodha* tree and yet grows into a tree, then one sees with one's own eyes that this seed is burned by fire;
likewise, this nature of being burned should have existed inherently from the beginning. If it existed inherently from the beginning, the tree should not [arise].

If the tree already possesses its nature at the beginning and only later grows, then it should likewise possess the characteristic of being burned at the beginning, and could only be burned later; furthermore,
the seed-nature that is burned should not be able to produce a tree.
In the fifth watch of the night, one grasps the essential meaning to refute the notion that arising comes first and ceasing follows later.
If all phenomena inherently possessed arising and ceasing, why would arising come first and ceasing later rather than occurring simultaneously?
For this reason, one should know that they lack intrinsic nature.
Wenju, regarding the fact that the arising and ceasing of all phenomena occur simultaneously— taking specifically the case of the arising and ceasing of a *nyagrodha* seed as an example—
how could it be that it arises first and only subsequently ceases? Since arising and ceasing are simultaneous, just as one might say it arises first and then ceases,
it would likewise follow that it ceases first and then arises.
The third question and answer.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said: "World-Honored One, if the seed of the nyagrodha tree originally lacks the nature of a tree yet produces a tree, why does this seed not produce oil?
For both [the tree and the oil] are equally absent."
"By raising the objection that seeds lack the cause for oil-production, you ask why they do not produce oil if they are devoid of its nature.
Son of good family, it is just so: although oil is not inherently present within the seed, it can nevertheless be produced from it due to the presence of causes and conditions."
Next, the Buddha replied: "One can also extract oil from the pressed pulp; the extracted juice is itself the oil.
For the fourth time, he asked again: "Should it also be called sesame oil?"
The Lion’s Roar asked, "Why is it not called sesame oil? "Good son, it is because it is not sesame," [the Buddha replied].

"Good son, just as fire arises from the condition of fire and water arises from the condition of water—though both arise from conditions, they cannot exist within one another—so too it is with the seed of the nyagrodha tree and sesame oil. Though...
They both arise from conditions, yet they do not produce one another. The nature of the *nyagrodha* fruit is capable of curing cold, while the nature of sesame oil is capable of curing wind.
Good son, it is like how sugar and dark honey are produced through the same conditions of sugarcane;
although they share a single cause, their appearances differ, such that sugar cures heat while dark honey cures cold.
The Buddha replied: "Names differ according to their respective conditions; thus, one cannot call it 'sesame oil' while calling it 'nyagrodha oil.

It is the same with the buddha-nature of sentient beings: within sentient beings there is buddha-nature, whereas within grasses and trees there is no buddha-nature, though they possess the nature of grasses and trees."
Following the Lion’s Roar, the second section refutes the attachment to the view that the effect does not exist within the cause.

Since this is not an external doctrine, it consists of a single round of question and answer, which is divided into three parts: first, receiving the essential point; second, the formal refutation; and third, the conclusion of the refutation.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said, “World-Honored One, if there were no nature of curd within milk, no nature of oil in sesame seeds,
no nature of a tree in a nyagrodha seed, and no nature of a jar in clay— and if all sentient beings likewise lacked the Buddha-nature—
then the World-Honored One’s previous statement that ‘all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature’ would be incorrect; therefore, they should not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The meaning of *samyaksambodhi* is not as you have stated.
To "receive the intent and look up to what is non-existent" means to receive the principle that there is no fruit [in the cause] and thus no longer harbor doubts;
since a fruit cannot exist within the cause, there is likewise no Buddha-nature within sentient beings—this principle is credible, and sentient beings thus cling to it.
Since it is certain that [the self] does not exist as a reality, and because it is certain that it does not exist, one can no longer say that all things possess intrinsic nature;
therefore, to claim this meaning is incorrect. Is it not the case that what is "not so" constitutes an adherence to non-existence?

Why is this? Below follows the second section, the "Proper Refutation," which is further divided into two parts: first, the refutation, and second, the response. In the initial text, there are seven general points:
(1) based on karmic action; (2) based on the severance of roots of goodness; (3) based on the arousal of the bodhicitta; (4) based on regression and non-regression;

(5) based on the cultivation of the ten thousand practices and the six perfections; (6) based on the regression from the ten thousand practices; and (7) based on the Sangha Jewel. First, regarding [the first point]:
Regarding the difficulty of karmic action:

why is this so? Because humans and devas have no fixed nature; because they lack a fixed nature, a human can become a deva and a deva can become a human, due to the conditions of karma and not due to a fixed nature.
Thus, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the conditions of karma.
[They attain] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Humans and devas have no inherent nature; there are only karmic conditions. By observing the five precepts one becomes a human, and by practicing the ten wholesome deeds one becomes a deva.
A deva can become a human, and a human can become a deva. It is the same for Bodhisattvas: they attain Buddhahood solely through karmic conditions, and not otherwise.
Regarding the Buddha-nature:
next, as for the objection raised concerning the severance of the roots of goodness—
If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, by what causes and conditions do those such as the icchantikas sever and destroy their roots of goodness?
If one falls into hell, and if the bodhicitta were the buddha-nature, then icchantikas and the like should not be able to sever it.
If it can be severed, how can it be said that the buddha-nature is eternal? If it is not eternal, it cannot be called the buddha-nature.
If sentient beings possess an inherently good nature that cannot be severed, yet they fall into hell, it must be by the power of their Buddha-nature that they are restrained from remaining in hell.
Since this Buddha-nature is eternal, how could it be severed? If it were severed, one would know it to be impermanent;
if it were impermanent, then there would be no Buddha-nature.
Third, regarding the objection concerning the difficulty of the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*):
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), why is it called the "initial arousal of the mind"?

If this nature were inherently present from the beginning, the mind should have already been aroused; yet since the mind is only now being aroused for the first time, we know that the nature was originally absent. Furthermore, [this applies to] the Buddha-nature...
Non-arising is non-arising, and thus it is not a nature.
Regarding the fourth point, which raises an objection based on falling back or not falling back:

how can one say that this person is a *vibhavati* (one who falls back), an *avibhavati* (one who does not fall back), or a *vibhavati-avibhavati* (one who both falls back and does not fall back)? One should know that such a person...
They lack the Buddha-nature.

If the nature were inherently present, they would not be subject to *vibbhamati* (falling back); they would only be subject to *avivbhamati* (not falling back) and would necessarily be non-retrogressive.
Since they do indeed fall back, and since they do indeed fall back, it is known that they lack the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the fifth point, the difficulty of the myriad practices:
the World-Honored One [taught that] a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva single-mindedly directs himself toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
perceiving through great kindness and great compassion the faults and afflictions of birth, old age, and death, and contemplating Great Nirvāṇa as being free from birth, old age, and death.
The various faults of afflictions, faith in the Triple Gem and the retribution of karmic results, and the upholding of the prohibitive precepts—such dharmas as these are called the Buddha-nature.
If there were a Buddha-nature apart from these dharmas, why would these dharmas be required to serve as causes and conditions?
World-Honored One, just as milk does not necessarily become curd without relying on conditions, whereas fresh butter does so require causes and conditions.
It is said that just as a water jar, a drill, and a rope require human effort, so too do sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
those who possess it should attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* apart from causes and conditions.

If Buddhahood-nature existed inherently from the beginning, why would it be necessary to cultivate the myriad practices? Those who engage in the myriad practices must realize that there is no inherent Buddhahood-nature.
Sixth, regarding the objection based on the possibility of regression from the myriad practices:
if [Buddhahood] were fixedly existent, for what reason would practitioners develop a mind of regression upon seeing the sufferings of the three evil realms, or birth, aging, sickness, and death?
Furthermore, it is not necessary to cultivate the six *pāramitās* in order to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
one should be able to achieve it just as milk becomes curd without external conditions.

Yet, it is not that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is attained without depending upon the six *pāramitās*. For this reason, one should know that all sentient beings are entirely non-existent [in essence].
Buddha-nature.
Since Buddha-nature is eternal, how could there be any regression? That one sees regression upon encountering the three evil realms is known to be the absence of Buddha-nature.
Seventh, regarding the objection based on the Three Jewels:
As the Buddha stated above, the Jewel of the Sangha is eternal; if it is as eternal as that, then it is not impermanent.
If it is not impermanent, how could it attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Furthermore, if the Sangha were eternal, how could it... [continue]?
It is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
As the Buddha has taught, the Three Jewels are eternal; since the Sangha is eternal, it should abide eternally. How then can one advance in practice to attain Buddhahood in the future?
If there is advancement in practice, then it is impermanent; because it is impermanent, it would lack inherent nature. Why, then, do you say they are "one"?
All sentient beings possess it.
World-Honored One, if sentient beings were to lack the bodhicitta and the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the very beginning and only acquire them later,
then the buddha-nature of sentient beings would likewise be originally non-existent.
Subsequently, based on this principle, it would follow that all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature.
Next, the Buddha’s words below provide the direct answers to the seven challenges, though not in their original order: first, the answer to the question regarding karmic activity;
second, the answer to the third question concerning the arousal of the bodhicitta; and third, the answer to the sixth question regarding the regression from the myriad practices.
The fourth [section] answers the second question regarding the severance of the roots of goodness; the fifth answers the fifth question regarding the ten thousand practices;

the sixth answers the seventh question regarding the Jewel of the Sangha; the seventh answers the fourth question regarding falling away or not falling away; and this [eighth section] answers the first question.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have long understood the meaning of the Buddha-nature;
for the sake of sentient beings, you ask such a question. All sentient beings truly possess the Buddha-nature."
The answer consists of eight characters that fully address the intent of the question: it states that humans and devas arise from karma and have no relation to Buddha-nature;

likewise, they should attain Buddhahood through karma and have no relation to Buddha-nature. The Buddha’s response was that humans and devas do not require Buddha-nature, but attain rebirth and return solely through karma, having no relation to Buddha-nature.
Since Buddha-nature is eternal, one should also know that becoming a Buddha likewise occurs [through its presence].
Regarding "Buddha-nature":
Your statement below provides a second, transcendent response to the third question concerning the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*). You first restate the question:
"If sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, one should not say that there is an initial arousal of the mind."
Next is the formal response:
"Good son, the mind is not the Buddha-nature. Why? Because the mind is impermanent, whereas the Buddha-nature is permanent.
To your question, "For what reason is there regression? this is the third direct answer to the sixth point regarding the regression from the myriad practices.
As for your question regarding why there are those with regressive minds: in reality, there is no such thing as a regressive mind.
If the mind were truly subject to regression, one would ultimately never attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is only because of the slowness of attainment that it is termed "regression."

It is clear that there is truly no regression; it is merely a matter of being slow to attain what is called "regression. Thus, the response regarding the myriad practices as inferior is a fitting answer.
This section on the Bodhicitta not being the Buddha-nature is the fourth successive response to the second question concerning the severance of the roots of goodness.
This bodhicitta is truly not the Buddha-nature. Why? Because those such as the icchantikas, having severed their roots of goodness, fall into hell.
If bodhicitta were the Buddha-nature, then the class of icchantikas could no longer be called icchantikas, nor could bodhicitta be called impermanent. Therefore, one knows for certain that bodhi—
The *icchantika*’s mind is truly not the Buddha-nature.
This clarifies that the bodhicitta is not the Buddha-nature, yet even though the *icchantika* does not give rise to bodhicitta, the Buddha-nature is never severed.
Good son, your statement [regarding] the fifth answer to the fifth question concerning the ten thousand practices is divided into two parts: first, the direct [explanation]; second...
Answer:
"Good son, as for what you say—that if sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, they should not depend on conditions, just as milk becomes curd—this meaning is not so.
Why is this? If one says that the five conditions produce fresh butter (*navanīta*), you should know that Buddha-nature is likewise."
Furthermore, it is like this: for example, among various stones there may be gold, silver, copper, and iron;

though they all equally derive from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and share the same name and substance, that which is produced from each is distinct. Only by relying on various causes and conditions—the merit of sentient beings, the furnace and bellows, and human labor—do they subsequently emerge.
Therefore, one should know that fundamentally there is no intrinsic nature of gold within the stone, and likewise, there is no [intrinsic] Buddha-nature within sentient beings.

One is not called a Buddha merely by that; rather, it is through the convergence of the causes and conditions of all merits that one perceives the Buddha-nature, and only thereafter does one become a Buddha.
Second, taking the meaning further to raise an objection:
Your statement that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature yet do not see it is incorrect. Why is this so?
Because the various causes and conditions have not yet converged, O son of good family, it is for this reason that I speak of two kinds of causes:
the direct cause and the conditional cause. The direct cause is called the Buddha-nature; the conditional cause is the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Through these two causes and conditions, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, just as gold is extracted from stone.
Regarding the statement "there was no such question previously," there are two interpretations: first, it is said that this question ought to have been present before, but the translator omitted it;
second, it is said that there was originally no such question, and this is merely a summary of the intended meaning.
"Good son, as for what you say regarding the Sangha-jewel... [This concludes] the sixth answer to the seventh question, which contains four successive sections. First:
There are two kinds of harmony.
Son of good family, as for your statement that the Saṃgha is permanent while all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature:
son of good family, the name "Saṃgha" signifies harmony, and there are two kinds of harmony: first, worldly harmony; second, harmony in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). Worldly...
"Harmony" refers to the meaning of the Sangha of Śrāvakas; "harmony" also refers to the Sangha of Bodhisattvas. The worldly Sangha is impermanent, whereas the Buddha-nature is permanent.
Just as the Buddha-nature is permanent in its meaning, so too is the Sangha.
Next, the twelve divisions of the sūtras are in harmony.
Furthermore, there is the Saṃgha, which refers to the harmony of the Dharma and the harmony of the Saṃgha; this means that the twelve divisions of the sūtras are eternal.
For this reason, I say that the Dharma and the Saṃgha are eternal.
The thirty-two factors of dependent origination are in harmony.
Good son, the name "Saṃgha" signifies harmony; that which is called harmony refers to the twelve links of dependent origination.

Within these twelve links of dependent origination there is also the Buddha-nature, and the twelve links of dependent origination are as constant as the Buddha-nature. For this reason, I say that the Saṃgha possesses the Buddha-nature.
Nature.
Furthermore, the Sangha is the harmonious assembly of all Buddhas; therefore, I say that the Sangha possesses the Buddha-nature.
All clarify that the "monks of the eternal" are the monks of the single essence, not the monks of the present age.

Good son, regarding your statement, "If sentient beings possess Buddha-nature," and so forth—this concludes the seventh section, which is a retrospective response to the fourth question concerning retrogression and non-retrogression.
The text is divided into two parts: first, restating the question and admonishing the listener; second, the formal response to the difficulty. The question asks: "If..."
If all possess Buddha-nature, how could it be appropriate for there to be a distinction between those who regress and those who do not?
Good son, as for your question regarding how it can be that sentient beings have Buddha-nature yet some regress while others do not—listen attentively, listen attentively;
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

The answer consists of four parts: first, clarifying regressive practice; second, clarifying non-regressive vows; third, clarifying both the regressive and non-regressive persons; and fourth, again clarifying non-regressive practice.
The Buddha’s intent in answering is that regression or non-regression does not depend on the presence or absence of *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature);
rather, it results solely from differences in the strength of one's resolve and vows. Although there is regression, it is not a loss; it is merely a delay.

Regarding the title "The First Treatise on Regression," regression of practice is further divided into four sections: first, an explanation of the thirteen dharmas; second, an explanation of the six dharmas; third, an explanation of the five dharmas;
and fourth, an explanation of the two dharmas. The first section, concerning the thirteen dharmas, is as explained in the text.
Noble son, there are thirteen dharmas by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva regresses.
What are these thirteen? First, lack of faith in the mind; second, not applying the mind; third, a doubting mind; fourth, stinginess regarding one's body and wealth;
fifth, giving rise to great fear toward nirvāṇa, thinking, "How can one cause sentient beings to be eternally extinguished? Sixth...
1. The mind being unable to endure; 2. The mind being unpliant; 3. Sorrow and affliction;
4. Lack of joy; 5. Heedlessness; 6. Self-deprecation; 7. Seeing one’s own afflictions as incapable of being destroyed; 8.
Not delighting in the dharmas that lead toward enlightenment. Good son, these are called the thirteen factors that cause [the decline of the bodhisattva].

Regarding the regression of bodhisattvas from enlightenment, within the subsequent six dharmas, there are further six dharmas that destroy the bodhicitta. What are these six? First, stinginess regarding the Dharma; second, [toward all...]
Sentient beings give rise to unwholesome thoughts through three factors: first, associating with evil friends; second, failing to exert diligent effort;
and third, being conceited and arrogant. Furthermore, the sixth factor is engaging in worldly occupations. These six dharmas are able to destroy the bodhicitta.
Good son, there are those who hear that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are the teachers of devas and humans for all sentient beings.
Among all, he is the most supreme and peerless, surpassing the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
with the clear and unobstructed Dharma-eye, he perceives all phenomena and is able to deliver sentient beings from the great ocean of suffering. Having heard this, he immediately makes a great vow:
"If there is such a person as this in the world, may I also attain it. By means of these causes and conditions, he resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Third, they may generate the bodhicitta either through their own resolve or by being exhorted by others;
or, upon hearing that a bodhisattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* only after practicing austerities for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), they reflect:
"I am currently unable to endure such hardships; how then could I attain this? For this reason, there are [those who do not generate it].
[The Buddha] withdrew.
There were those who managed worldly affairs who left the household life to study the Way; however, managing secular laws greatly hindered their practice.
What is called "secular law" refers to everything outside of true cultivation, all of which is termed "secular. Among the statesmen of the Spring and Autumn period, Zang Wenzhong had three failings.

Your benevolence has caused your maidservant to weave reed mats and sell them in foreign lands, while you, a high official of your state, neglect your virtue and compete with the common people for profit.
If ordinary folk still warn against greed, how much more so should those who drive oxen for plowing or engage in trade? They ought to abandon worldly paths;

as for your urging me to rebuke and scold [others], what need is there to even mention it? Furthermore, every sentence should be examined through wisdom; the text is verbose, so I shall not record it here.
O Master of Mastery of Mind, one who contemplates and understands should know that it is not merely wielding the plow or handling the axe that constitutes mundane affairs;

rather, to sit idly while the mind races after the five sensory objects and the six desires is itself a worldly concern. Furthermore, to be single-mindedly preoccupied with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) is also a worldly concern.

Moreover, to constantly dwell on sentient beings, smear oneself with ashes, or offer compassionate consolation and rescue is likewise a worldly concern. If one can remain without such thoughts, [this is liberation].
Within the single mind that is neither thought nor non-thought, awakening is precisely what is not worldly affairs.

My private view is that when the Great Master explained the sutras, although he followed the literal text to complete his exegesis sentence by sentence, his contemplative understanding of each sentence was not dependent on the words alone;
rather, he clarified this everywhere so that practitioners of the Dharma might give rise to contemplation in accordance with the language.
Good son, there are further five dharmas that cause one to regress from the bodhicitta. What are these five? First, delighting in leaving home as a renunciant among non-Buddhist paths;
second, not cultivating a mind of great compassion; third, taking pleasure in seeking out the faults and transgressions of Dharma masters;

fourth, constantly delighting in dwelling within the cycle of birth and death; and fifth, having no joy in receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, copying, explaining, or elucidating the ten [perfections].
These two categories of sutras are called the five dharmas that cause one to regress from the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, there are two other dharmas that cause one to regress from the bodhicitta. What are these two? First, being greedily attached to the pleasures of the five desires;
second, being unable to revere and respect the Triple Gem. Due to such various causes and conditions as these, one regresses from the bodhicitta.
First, what is meant by the second section, which clarifies the vow of non-retrogression?

Furthermore, what is called the mind of non-retrogression? There are those who, upon hearing that the Buddha is able to deliver sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death—attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through natural cultivation without following a teacher—[if such a person...]
Thinking, "If this Way is attainable, I shall practice it and surely cause it to be attained," one generates the bodhicitta through these causes and conditions.
Whatever merit has been performed, whether much or little, all is dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One makes this vow: "May I always be able to draw near to the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas. Always...
Hearing the profound Dharma, my five faculties remain intact; even when encountering hardships and calamities, I do not lose this mind.
Furthermore, I vow that all Buddhas and their disciples shall always give rise to a heart of joy toward me and be endowed with the five roots of goodness.
If any sentient beings were to hack at my body, severing my hands, feet, head, eyes, or limbs and joints, I would instead conceive a heart of great compassion for those people.
I rejoice that such people as these increase the causes and conditions for my awakening;
if there were no such as these, by what means could I achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Furthermore, I make this vow:
may I never obtain the body of a woman who is rootless or possesses dual organs, nor may I be dependent on others, nor encounter an evil king.
May I not be subject to evil kings nor born in an evil land; may I obtain an excellent body of noble lineage and great wealth, yet never give rise to arrogance.
May I always hear the twelve divisions of the scriptures, receiving, upholding, reciting, copying, and explaining them.
When I preach for the sake of sentient beings, may those who receive my teaching have respectful faith and no doubt, always regarding me with reverence.

If one does not give rise to evil thoughts, would it not be better to hear little but understand much of the meaning and flavor [of the teachings], rather than wishing to hear much while failing to comprehend the meaning?

One should wish to be a teacher to one's own mind rather than a slave to the mind; one's actions of body, speech, and mind should not associate with evil; one should be able to bestow peace and happiness upon all sentient beings;
and one's physical discipline, precepts, and mental wisdom should be as immovable as a mountain, in order to receive and uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma.

One does not give rise to stinginess regarding one's body, life, or wealth; one does not perform meritorious deeds with impure things; one sustains oneself through right livelihood with a mind free from deceit and flattery;

one constantly remembers kindness received and repays even small favors with great gratitude; one is well-versed in all worldly arts and crafts; one understands the various dialects and customs of sentient beings;
and one recites, copies, and studies the twelve divisions of the scriptures without falling into indolence.
If sentient beings possess a mind of indolence and do not delight in hearing the Dharma, one should employ skillful means to guide and attract them so that they may take pleasure in hearing it.
One’s speech should always be gentle and soft; one should not utter evil words, and one should be able to bring together those who are discordant.

For those who suffer from grief and fear, one should cause them to be free from grief and fear. In an age of famine, one should cause abundance to be attained; in an age of pestilence, one should act as a great king of physicians.
He possesses mastery over the wealth required for medicines and the needs of the sick, causing all who are ill to be completely healed.
During the kalpa of weapons, he wields great power to sever their violence so that none remain.
He can eliminate the various fears of sentient beings—namely, the fear of death, imprisonment, beatings, fire, water, kings, thieves, poverty, breaking the precepts, ill repute, and the evil realms.
One should sever all such fears as these: cultivate profound reverence for one's parents, teachers, and elders; give rise to great compassion toward those who harbor enmity or hatred;

constantly practice the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), the gate of the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi-mukha*), and the contemplations on the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*);

[practice] the out-breath and in-breath (*ānāpāna*), the celestial conduct (*divya-caryā*), the Brahma-conduct (*brahma-caryā*), and the noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*); and [cultivate] the Vajra-samādhi and the Śūraṅgama-samādhi.
In places where the Three Jewels do not exist, may I personally attain a mind of tranquility.
When my body and mind undergo great suffering, may I never lose the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta; may I not give rise to contentment through the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
In places where the Three Jewels do not exist, may I always go forth as a renunciant within the teachings of non-Buddhists solely to destroy their false views, yet without practicing their paths.

Having attained mastery over the Dharma and mastery over the mind, one clearly perceives conditioned phenomena as they truly are, which inspires a sense of dread regarding the fruits of the paths of the Two Vehicles.
For the sake of sentient beings, one fears the sacrifice of one's own body as much as one fears for one's life;

thus, one joyfully dwells in the three evil realms just as all sentient beings delight in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and for the sake of even a single person, one undergoes the sufferings of hell for immeasurable kalpas.
One’s mind shall not give rise to regret; seeing others gain benefit, one shall not harbor envy but always feel joy as if one had gained happiness oneself.
If one encounters the Triple Gem, one should offer worship with clothing, food and drink, bedding, dwellings, medicine, lamps, flowers, incense, music, banners, parasols, and the seven treasures.
If one receives the Buddha’s precepts, one shall protect and uphold them firmly, never giving rise to...
Regarding the thought of transgression: if one hears of the difficult practices and ascetic austerities of a bodhisattva, the mind feels joy and no regret arises;
one naturally recognizes the events of past lives and never again creates karma of greed, hatred, or delusion;

one does not cultivate causes and conditions for the sake of karmic retribution, nor does one give rise to craving attachment toward present pleasures. Noble son, if there is anyone who can thus resolve their mind...
This vow is called the Bodhisattva’s never-retreating from the bodhicitta;

it is also called being a donor who can perceive the Tathāgata, clearly understand the Buddha-nature, skillfully tame sentient beings, deliver them from birth and death, and be well able to protect and uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma. Good son, for these reasons, one does not retreat.
A mind that does not possess this [awakening] is not called Buddha-nature.
Regarding the vow to "be a teacher of the mind," there are two interpretations. The first states: it refers simply to the preceding and succeeding moments of mind;

if the preceding mind gives rise to evil and the succeeding mind follows its flow, this is not being a teacher of the mind. If the preceding mind gives rise to evil and the succeeding mind is able to stop it, then—

Regarding the phrase "the mind takes the teacher": there are two interpretations. First, one constrains the mind by means of a person who serves as its teacher; the mind does not act according to its own whims, but follows the instructions of this person who is its teacher.
Now, to clarify what is most proximate: the preceding text states that "that which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma.
When the mind takes the Dharma as its object, the Dharma becomes the teacher of the mind, and the depth or shallowness [of realization] is entirely within one's own control.

"Good son, you must not [speak] based on the third pair [of categories]. This clarifies the two types of persons—those who regress and those who do not—and directly answers your question with both a simile and its application, as the text states:
'Good son, you must not say that all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature simply because they possess a regressive mind. This is the simile."
Suppose two people hear that in another land there is a mountain of seven treasures, upon which is a clear spring whose water is sweet and delicious;
those who can reach it will forever sever poverty, and those who drink its water will increase their lifespan by ten thousand years.
However, the road is remote, perilous, and full of many hardships. At that time, both individuals desire to go together; one person prepares various kinds of travel equipment, while the other...

Thus they set out empty-handed, carrying nothing with them, and as they proceeded forward, they encountered a man on the road who was carrying a great abundance of treasures and possessed all seven kinds of precious jewels.
The two men went up to him and asked, "Virtuous one, does that land truly have mountains of the seven precious jewels?
The man replied, "It is indeed so; it is not false. I have already obtained the jewels and drunk its water, yet I only regret that the road is perilous and long."
There are robbers, sand, gravel, and thorns, and a scarcity of water and grass; of those who go, there are thousands of millions, but those who reach their destination are very few.
Having heard this, one person immediately felt regret and spoke these words: "The road is both remote and difficult in many ways;
of those who go, there are countless, but those who reach it are but few. How could I possibly arrive there? My current property is sufficient for my needs."
Having provided for themselves, if they were to travel this path, they might lose their lives; if their lives were not preserved, where would long life be found?
One person spoke again, saying: "If there is someone who can pass beyond me, I too shall pass beyond.
If we reach the goal, we shall obtain our wishes, gather precious jewels, and drink sweet water. If we do not reach it, let death be our limit. At that time, these two people—
Then, while one regrets and retreats, the other advances alone until he reaches that mountain, where he acquires abundant wealth and jewels;

as he wishes, he drinks the water, takes much of his possessions, and returns to his dwelling to support his parents and provide for his kinsmen. At that time, the one who had regretted and turned back sees this occurrence, and his heart again grows feverish with regret:
"He has already gone and returned, while I remain here—what am I doing staying? He then immediately prepares himself and sets out.
They departed by way of the road.
The mountain of seven jewels is a metaphor for the Great Nirvāṇa; the sweet-tasting water is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature;
the two men are metaphors for the two Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds; and the perilous and evil road is a metaphor for saṃsāra. As for the person encountered...
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, having thieves is a metaphor for the four Māras; sand, gravel, and thorns are metaphors for the various afflictions (*kleśa*);
the absence of water and grass is a metaphor for not cultivating the path to Bodhi; the one person who returns is a metaphor for a regressive Bodhisattva;
and the one person who goes forward is a metaphor for a non-regressive Bodhisattva. Good son, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is eternally abiding.
It is unchanging, like that perilous path which cannot be said to be impermanent simply because a person regrets their journey and returns;
the Buddha-nature is likewise. Good son, within the path to Bodhi, there is never anyone who regresses.

Good son, it is as when the one who previously regretted his way sees his former companion returning with treasures, possessing sovereign power, making offerings to his parents, and providing for his kinsmen.
Having experienced much peace and happiness and witnessed these things, his heart was filled with fervor;

he immediately adorned himself again and returned by that same path, disregarding his own body and life and enduring all manner of hardships until he finally reached those mountains of the seven treasures.
The Bodhisattva who regresses is also like this, O son of good family: all sentient beings shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, in my sutras I have taught that all sentient beings— even those who commit the five heinous crimes,
violate the four grave prohibitions, or are icchantikas— all possess the Buddha-nature.
In the fourth section following the Lion’s Roar, the practice of non-retrogression is further elucidated through a sequence of questions and answers.
The Lion’s Roar asked: "World-Honored One, why is it that some bodhisattvas retrogress while others do not?"
Good son, if there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata,

they receive the name "Non-retrogressive," the name "Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva," the name "Immovable," the name "Compassionate toward all sentient beings," and the name "Superior to all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Good son, if a bodhisattva...

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva maintains the precepts without wavering, his mind of generosity remains unshakable, and he abides in truthful speech as steadfast as Mount Sumeru, through these karmic conditions he attains the mark of soles that are level like the bottom of a casket.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva provides for and makes offerings with wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma to his parents, preceptors, teachers, elders, and even down to the animals... [through these]... [he attains this mark].
Through karmic conditions, one attains the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the feet.
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva refrains from killing and stealing, and always gives rise to joy toward parents and teachers, by these karmic conditions they attain three marks:
first, the fingers are slender and long; second, the heels are long; third, the body is square and straight. These three marks arise from the same karmic conditions.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather in sentient beings, through these karmic conditions they obtain fingers joined by webs like those of a white goose king.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, when their parents, teachers, or elders are suffering from illness, wash and wipe them with their own hands, support them, and massage them, through these karmic conditions they obtain soft hands and feet. When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas...

By upholding the precepts, hearing the Dharma, and practicing the wisdom of giving without weariness, through these karmic conditions, one obtains well-proportioned ankles and calves, with body hairs that grow upward.
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva listens to the Dharma with single-minded devotion and expounds the true teaching, through these karmic conditions, one obtains the *eṇeya* deer’s shanks.
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not give rise to a harmful mind toward sentient beings regarding food and drink...
By the karmic conditions of being contented and always joyful, practicing wise generosity, and providing medicine to the sick, his body becomes perfectly proportioned like a nyagrodha tree;
his hands reach below his knees, he has a fleshly protuberance on the crown of his head (uṣṇīṣa), and his cranial topknot is invisible to others.
Furthermore, by the karma of providing protection for those who are terrified and giving clothing to those who are naked and barefoot, [he attains these marks].
By virtue of attaining the mark of the sheathed organ (*kośagatavastiguhya*), if a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws near to the wise,

stays far away from fools, delights in skillful inquiry and response, and sweeps and repairs roads, through these karmic conditions his skin becomes fine and soft and the hairs on his body curl to the right.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly gives clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, incense, flowers, and lamps as offerings, [he attains this mark].
By virtue of these karmic conditions, a person obtains a golden-colored body that is constantly radiant with light.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when practicing giving, is able to relinquish their most cherished possessions without stinginess, and does not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit, by virtue of these karmic conditions they obtain the mark of the seven rounded protuberances.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives alms, their mind... [does not waver].
One who gives rise to doubt [regarding this] will, through these karmic conditions, obtain a soft and supple voice.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and uses it for giving, through these karmic conditions, they will obtain well-filled collarbones, an upper body like that of a lion, and long, slender arms and elbows.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva stays far away from divisive speech, harsh words, and a mind of malice, through these karmic conditions, they will obtain...

Forty teeth, white, clean, even, and closely set: if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates great loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, by virtue of these karmic conditions, he attains the mark of two fangs.

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly makes this vow—that those who come to him for anything shall be given according to their wishes—by virtue of these karmic conditions, he attains the mark of lion-like jaws. If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
Sā [the Bodhisattva] provides all beings with whatever food and drink they require; by these karmic conditions, he obtains the supreme flavor among all flavors.
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva personally cultivates the ten wholesome paths and simultaneously transforms others through them, by these karmic conditions, he obtains a broad and long tongue.
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not speak of others' shortcomings and does not slander the True Dharma, by this...

By the karmic condition of obtaining a Brahma-like voice, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to a heart of joy upon seeing those who are hostile or hateful, by this karmic condition they obtain eyelashes of deep blue.

By the karmic condition of not concealing the virtues of others and praising their goodness, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices, noble son, by this karmic condition they obtain the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*). Noble son, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates...
When practicing the karmic causes and conditions for these thirty-two marks, one attains the non-retrogressive mind of bodhi.
Generally speaking, all six perfections constitute non-retrogressive conduct; here, however, we specifically cite the karma for the thirty-two marks in relation to the aspiration for Buddhahood.
In the preceding text, it was explained that one hundred merits produce a single mark; in the present text, it is sometimes stated that a single karma produces a single [mark].
Regarding the statement that "multiple characteristics are produced by multiple karmas," this is spoken in terms of similar causes and effects.

To demonstrate that cause and effect do not deviate, it is shown that one karma produces one characteristic and multiple karmas produce multiple characteristics. Although the Buddha actually possesses four canine teeth, the text mentions only two;
this is because the two larger canines are white, and these two whites are treated as one, while the two large ones are treated as one. Some say there are two [pairs of] canines.
Furthermore, another interpretation is that if one discusses the "teeth" (danta), there are four; if one discusses the "edges" (pārśva), there are two.
Now, because it clarifies the teeth at both edges, it says "two teeth.
"Good son, all sentient beings... [This marks] the third section, concluding with a praise of the Buddha-nature.
Good son, the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas, the karmic fruits of all sentient beings, and the Buddha-nature are likewise inconceivable.
Why is this? Because these four dharmas are all eternal; because they are eternal, they are inconceivable.
Yet, because they are obscured by the afflictions of all sentient beings, they are termed "eternal-interruption" (śāśvata-uccheda); because their afflictions are eternal, [they are thus described].
It is called impermanence. If one were to say that all sentient beings are permanent, why would they cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path to sever all sufferings?
If all sufferings are severed, that is called impermanence; the bliss thus received is what is called permanence.
Therefore, I say that all sentient beings are shrouded by afflictions and do not see the Buddha-nature; because they do not see it, they [do not attain liberation].
