no one can prevent this physician from treating one ailment while setting aside another. The path of the noble ones and the Buddha-nature are also like this.
The Buddha replied: "The Buddha-nature is one; as many people cultivate it according to their own practice, each attains it without mutual obstruction.
This was the third question. Siṃhanāda said:
"World-Honored One, the meanings of the various analogies you have cited are not as they seem. Why is this? Because in the preceding [analogy],..."
If a path obstructs what lies behind it, how can you say there are no obstructions? The same applies to all other cases.
If the Noble Path and Buddha-nature were like this, then when one person practices them, they should obstruct others.
"Just as many people on a road hinder those behind them, so too does the Buddha-nature function; when one person before practices, it hinders those behind.
The Buddha said, "Good son, what you have said is not consistent with the meaning. The path I used as a metaphor is only a partial one."
This is an analogy for that which is not all-encompassing. Noble son, the worldly path is characterized by obstructions, distinctions between this and that, and a lack of equality.

The untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is not like this; it enables sentient beings to be without obstruction, equal and non-dual, and free from spatial distinctions or differences between this and that. Such a true path can serve as [the means] for all.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings acts as a revealing cause (*vyakti-hetu*) and not as a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), just as a bright lamp illuminates objects.
Good son, all sentient beings are equally subject to the causal condition of ignorance (*avidyā-pratyaya*) for the formations (*saṃskāra*);
it cannot be said that because one person’s formations arise from the causal condition of ignorance, others should be without them, for all sentient beings possess the causal condition of ignorance.
Because they are conditioned by formative activities (*saṃskāra*), it is said that the twelve links of dependent origination are all equal.
The untainted right path cultivated by sentient beings is likewise so; it equally severs the afflictions of sentient beings and the various realms of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).
For this reason, it is called "equality. Those who realize this possess knowledge and vision regarding both self and others that is free from obstruction.
Therefore, it is named "the wisdom of omniscience" (sarvajñajñāna).
As for the Buddha’s answer, it is like a road, a bridge, or a physician—all of which are but partial paths of the noble way;
it is not as with these bridges and such, which are likewise [limited].
The fourth objection:
The Lion’s Roar says that the bodies of all sentient beings are not of a single kind;

there may be celestial bodies, human bodies, or the bodies of animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings. Since there are such many different types of bodies and they are not one, how can it be said [that all are equal]?
"Buddha-nature is one;
yet the characteristics of the six realms of existence—gods, humans, and so forth—are not one. How can they all share a single Buddha-nature?
The Buddha said, "Good son, it is like a person who places poison in milk; even when it has transformed into *tīruma* (clarified butter), the poison is present throughout."
Poisoned milk is not called curd, and curd is not called milk; even up to *sarpis* (clarified butter) and *haviḥ* (ghee), it is likewise so.

Although the names change, the poisonous nature is not lost throughout all five flavors; it is exactly thus in every case. If one consumes *haviḥ*, it can still kill a person, yet one has not actually placed poison into the *haviḥ*.
The Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) of sentient beings is also like this: although it abides within the five [flavors/states],...
Although the path receives distinct and separate bodies, the Buddha-nature is eternally one and unchanging.
The Buddha answered: "If poison is placed within milk, that poison is able to kill everywhere according to the five flavors [of the milk];
the Buddha-nature is likewise pervasive in all places," and so forth.
Section Sixteen: The Lesser Section on the Sixteen Great Countries, Part Two: Elucidating the Causes and Conditions for Cultivating the Path. This section is further divided into two parts:

first, elucidating the conditions for the path; second, elucidating the causes of the path. Regarding the first, the conditions for the path, there are three: first, the condition of place; second, the condition of time; third, the condition of persons.

Since one cannot attain [the path] through improper places, improper times, or unwholesome spiritual friends, it is said that one must wait for the right place, wait for the right time, and wait for companions. Thus it is stated.

Furthermore, there are two types of locations: first, city locations; second, tree locations. Regarding city locations, there are again two: first, the question, and second, the answer. Siṃhanāda said:
"World-Honored One, among the sixteen great kingdoms, there are six great cities, namely:
the city of Śrāvastī, the city of Vārāṇasī, the city of Campā, the city of Vaiśālī, the city of Rājagṛha, and the city of Pāṭaliputra. Thus it was said.
Among the six great cities in the world, for what reason did the Tathāgata abandon them and enter parinirvāṇa here in this frontier land, this wretched,
evil, most humble, narrow, and small city of Kuśinagara?
The intent of the question is as follows: Since there are six great cities in the sixteen great kingdoms, why has the Tathāgata come to this small city?
The answer consists of two parts: first, a preliminary reprimand, and second, the formal explanation. Regarding the initial reprimand, the questioner asks: [Why do you say so?]
"Good son, you should not say that the city of Kuśinagara is a borderland, wretched, most base, narrow, and small;
rather, you should say that this city is adorned with subtle and sublime merits. Why is this? Because it is the place where all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have practiced.
Good son, it is like the house of a lowly person: if a king should pass by it, one ought to praise that house as being magnificent and beautiful."
"By the accomplishment of this merit, may you, Great King, turn your carriage back to visit us. Good son, it is like a person with a grave illness who takes foul and inferior medicine;
once the illness is cured by taking it, that person should rejoice and praise the medicine, saying: 'This is the most supreme and wondrous medicine, capable of curing my disease.
Good son, it is also like a person traveling by boat upon the great ocean whose vessel suddenly breaks apart and leaves them with no [refuge]."
Relying upon and depending on this corpse, one attains the further shore; having reached the further shore, one should feel great joy and praise this corpse, saying:
"I have attained peace and security by virtue of encountering it. Kuśinagara is also like this;
it is the place where all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas practice. How can you say it is a remote, wicked, narrow, and inferior small city?
One should not say that the dwelling place of the Buddha is small;
as illustrated by three similes, the abode of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the most honored among men, is itself honorable. When a gentleman resides there, how could it be considered humble?
I recall the past... [The second part of the main explanation consists of two sections: first, repaying the debt of gratitude to the ground; second, expelling the faction of heterodoxy.

Regarding the first (repaying the debt of gratitude), there are three parts: first, repaying the initial resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); second, repaying the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); third, repaying the great vows—as per the text.
"Good son, I recall that in the past, beyond kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was an eon named Suvijñāpta.
At that time, there was a noble king of the Kauśika clan who possessed the seven treasures and was endowed with a thousand sons.

This king was the first to establish this city, which was twelve yojanas in circumference and breadth, adorned with the seven treasures. The land abounded in rivers, the waters of which were pure, gentle, and soft."
There were soft and sweet rivers, namely the Nairañjanā River, the Airāvatī River, the Hiraṇyavatī River, the Ikṣumatī River, and the Vipāśā River;
such rivers numbered five hundred. On both banks, trees grew in profusion, their flowers and fruits fresh and pure.
At that time, the lifespan of the people was immeasurable, and there appeared the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings.
When the king had passed a hundred years, he made this proclamation: "As the Buddha has taught, all phenomena are entirely impermanent;
if one can cultivate the ten wholesome dharmas, one can sever such great suffering of impermanence.
When the people heard this, they all together reverently practiced the ten wholesome dharmas. At that time, I heard the name of the Buddha and received and upheld the ten [wholesome precepts].
Through skillful reflection and cultivation, he first gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having given rise to this mind, he further used these teachings to instruct immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, saying:
"All phenomena are impermanent and subject to decay; therefore, I now continue here as well to speak of the impermanence and decay of all phenomena. He spoke only of the Buddha.
This body is a dharma of permanence. I recall the causes and conditions of my past practices; therefore, I have now come here to enter nirvana.
Furthermore, I wish to repay the past kindness of this land. For this reason, I have said in my sutras that those who are my kinsmen are able to receive kindness and repay it.
Furthermore, son of good family, in the past when the lifespan of sentient beings was immeasurable, there was a city named Kuśāvatī, fifty yojanas in circumference and breadth.
At that time, the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa lived so close together that a rooster could fly from one to another.
There was a wheel-turning king (cakravartin) named Sudarśana, who possessed the seven treasures and was endowed with a thousand sons; he ruled over the four [continents].

When the world’s foremost crown prince contemplated the True Dharma and attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha, the Wheel-Turning King saw that his son had become a Pratyekabuddha, his majestic deportment composed and his supernormal powers rare and marvelous.

Having witnessed this, he immediately renounced the royal throne like spitting out phlegm and went forth into homelessness; for eighty thousand years, he practiced and cultivated himself amidst these *śāla* trees.
For eighty thousand years each, he dwelt in the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Good son, you who wish to know:
the noble King Sudarśana at that time was none other than myself. Therefore, I now always delight in dwelling within these four dharmas.
These four dharmas are called samādhi; for this reason, the body of the Tathāgata is eternal, blissful, self, and pure, good son.
For these reasons, I have now come here to this city of Kuśinagara, among the śāla trees, to enter into samādhi.
Good son, I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable kalpas, this city was named Kapilavastu.
At that time, there was a king named Śuddhodana; the king’s queen was named Māyā, and the king had a son.
Named Siddhārtha, at that time the Prince, without relying on a teacher’s instruction, attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through natural contemplation.
He had two disciples: one named Śāriputra and the other named Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
His attendant disciple was named Ānanda. At that time, the World-Honored One was between the twin trees, expounding the Dharma as follows...
At that time, while I was present in this assembly at the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, I was privileged to participate in these events and heard that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Having heard this, I immediately attained non-retrogression regarding Bodhi and promptly made a vow:
"In a future age, when I attain Buddhahood, may my parents, country, name, disciples, and attendants be such as they are described in the teachings of the Dharma."
The transformation is now no different from that of the World-Honored One; for this reason, he has come here to expound and proclaim the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.

Next, regarding the expulsion of the heterodox faction, there are two parts: first, his journey through the six great cities; second, the account of his arrival here and the subsequent subjugation of the opponents. This concludes the section on the subjugation.
When the heterodox is exhausted and the orthodox is perfected, that is quiescent nirvana. These six cities represent the six stages, and upon reaching the first, one arrives at the royal city.
"Good son, when I first left home and had not yet attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, King Bimbisāra sent an envoy who said:
'If Prince Siddhārtha becomes a holy wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), I shall become his subject.'"

"If you do not delight in the household life and have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I pray that you come here first to this city of Rājagṛha to preach the Dharma, deliver sentient beings, and accept my offerings. At that time, I remained silent and accepted his invitation.
Son of good family, when I had first attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I was heading toward the country of Kāśī.
On the banks of the Nairañjanā River, there was a brahmin of the Kāśyapa clan with five hundred disciples who were seeking the unsurpassed path.
For their sake, I went there and preached the Dharma. Kāśyapa said, "Gautama, I am now advanced in years, being one hundred and twenty;
all the people of the kingdom of Magadha, as well as its great king Bimbisāra—"
The Śālas all thought: "I have already realized the fruit of Arhatship.
If I were now to remain before you to listen to the Dharma, the people would all develop perverted views, thinking, 'Is the Venerable Kāśyapa not an Arhat?
We pray that Gautama will quickly go elsewhere; for if these people come to know for certain that Gautama’s virtues surpass mine, [we shall suffer]."

Having no other means to further provide for my needs, I replied, "Kāśyapa, if you do not harbor toward me excessive resentment or intense hatred, I ask that you grant me the use of this lodging for one night;
I shall depart early tomorrow morning. Kāśyapa said, "Gautama, my heart has no ill intent and I hold you in deep affection and respect.
However, there is a venomous dragon in my dwelling whose nature is violent and evil; I fear it might endanger you."
“Kāśyapa, you have harmed me by saying that among all poisons, none surpasses the three poisons; yet I have now severed these worldly poisons, and thus I have nothing to fear.
Kāśyapa spoke again: “If you truly have no fear, then it is well; noble son, listen as I remain here.
At that time, I intentionally manifested the eighteen transformations for Kāśyapa, as described in the sutra. Then, Kāśyapa—
When his retinue of five hundred and others saw and heard this, they realized the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, Kāśyapa had two younger brothers—one named Gayākāśyapa and the other named Nadīkāśyapa—whose disciples and retinues also numbered five hundred;
they too all attained the fruit of Arhatship. These were the followers of the six teachers in Rājagṛha.
Having heard this matter, they immediately conceived a great evil mind toward me. At that time, having accepted the King’s invitation out of faith, I proceeded toward Rājagṛha;
before I had reached the midpoint of the road, the King came with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of followers to welcome me.
When I preached the Dharma for them, eighty-six thousand devas of the desire realm, having heard the Dharma, resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
King Bimbisāra and his retinue of one hundred and twenty thousand attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*;
immeasurable sentient beings accomplished the mind of patience (*kṣānti*).

Having entered the city, [the Buddha] led Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, along with their retinues of two hundred and fifty, to renounce their original intentions and leave the household life to study the Dharma.
I heard that the six heretical teachers, who had been receiving royal offerings while I was staying there, gathered together and went to the city of Śrāvastī.
Since those heretics were in disarray and were seducing sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms, they must come here to be driven out.
The King sent him away again; however, because the Buddha did not refuse the King’s request, he went to the city.
There, the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) realized his own arts were shallow and fled to Śrāvastī. While the Buddha was there, he converted the three Kāśyapa brothers and the two men of supernatural wisdom.
At that time, there was an elder in that city, who was the second person to go to Śrāvastī to pursue the non-Buddhists.
The text is divided into two parts: first, the causal origin of his departure; second, the formal discussion of their mutual testing of supernatural powers as they proceeded there.
At that time, there was an elder in that city named Sudatta who went to Rājagṛha to seek a wife for his son.
Having arrived at that city, he stayed at the house of the elder Sandhāna. Then, this elder rose in the middle of the night.
He addressed his kinsmen, saying, "O virtuous ones, arise! Quickly together adorn and sweep the house, and prepare the various delicacies.
Having heard this, Sudatta immediately reflected to himself: "Is it that he wishes to invite the King of Magadha?
Or is there a marriage celebration? Having reflected thus, he went forward and asked: "Great King, do you wish to invite the King of Magadha?"
"Bimbisāra, do you have a wedding feast or some joyful celebration? Why are you so preoccupied and unsettled?
The householder replied, "No, layman. Tomorrow I have invited the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Dharma King.
When the Elder Sudatta first heard the name of the Buddha, the hairs on his body stood on end. He then asked again, "What is meant by 'Buddha'? The householder replied:
"Do you not hear? In the city of Kapilavastu, there is a son of the Śākyas named Siddhārtha, of the Gautama clan, whose father’s name is Śuddhodana.
Not long after his birth, physiognomists prophesied that he would certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
Yet, like an *āmra* fruit already held in the palm of his hand, his heart had no desire for it; he renounced the world and went forth as a monk, spontaneously and without a teacher."
He perceives that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is the exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion;

it is eternally abiding and unchanging, neither arising nor ceasing, and free from sorrow or fear. Toward all sentient beings, his mind is impartial, regarding them as equally as parents view their only child.
Although he is the most excellent among all beings in terms of body and mind, he is without pride, even when subjected to being smeared with filth or cut and sliced.
In these two matters, his mind is non-dual; his wisdom penetrates all phenomena without obstruction;

he is fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the five knowledges, the samādhis, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness; therefore, he is called the Buddha. He has accepted my invitation;
for this reason, he is in such haste that he has no leisure to look upon me. Sudatta said: "Excellent, Great Being! What you have said—"
"The Buddha’s merit is unsurpassed; where is he now? The elder replied, "He is currently here in the great city of Rājagṛha, dwelling at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery.
At that time, Sudatta single-mindedly called to mind all the Buddha's merits:
his ten powers, fearlessnesses, five wisdoms, samādhis, great kindness, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness. Having done so, he—

As he was reflecting, suddenly it became brilliantly bright; the light was so fierce and intense that it was like the midday sun. He immediately followed the light and emerged, arriving beneath the city gate.
By the Buddha's spiritual power, the gate opened spontaneously. Having exited the gate, there was a celestial shrine along the road which Sudatta passed by, bowing in worship and paying his respects.
Immediately, he was plunged back into darkness, and a heart of terror arose within him as he wished to return to his dwelling place.
At that time, a deva residing at the city gate addressed Sudatta, saying:
"Venerable sir, if you go to the place where the Tathāgata is, you will obtain great benefit. Sudatta asked: "What is this great benefit? The deva replied:

"Householder, suppose there were someone who possessed a hundred swift horses adorned with genuine jewels, a hundred fragrant elephants, a hundred jeweled chariots, and [a hundred] figures of cast gold..."
If one were to provide for a single person a hundred sets of garments, a hundred ornaments of upright and beautiful women adorned with necklaces and inlaid with various jewels,

and a hundred magnificent palaces, halls, and dwellings carved and engraved with intricate patterns, along with a hundred golden platters filled with silver grain and a hundred silver platters filled with golden grain—
were this to be done repeatedly until it covered the entire continent of Jambudvīpa, the merit obtained thereby would not equal [the merit of the former].
There was a person who, having resolved his mind, took a single step toward the place where the Tathāgata was. Sudatta said, "Good man, who are you?
The deva replied, "Householder, I am the son of the Brahmin Viśākha; I was your virtuous friend in a former life.
Because I saw Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana on a previous occasion, my heart gave rise to joy, and by relinquishing my body, I attained this state."
"I am the son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North, specifically charged with guarding this city of Rājagṛha.
Because I gave rise to a heart of joy upon prostrating to Śāriputra and the others, I have already obtained such a wondrous and excellent body;
how much more so would I obtain it were I to behold the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, to prostrate to him, and to make offerings? When the Elder Sudatta heard these words, he immediately returned.
He came to where I was, and having arrived, he bowed his head at my feet in respectful salutation. I then preached the Dharma to him as was appropriate.
Having heard it, the householder attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. Once he had realized this fruit, he further entreated me, saying: "The Tathāgata is greatly compassionate;
I pray that you will deign to visit the city of Śrāvastī and accept my humble offering. I then asked him: "What is your house?"
"In the city of Vaiśālī there are several monasteries that can accommodate [the community].

Sudatta said, "If the Buddha, out of compassion, would deign to visit, I shall exhaust my own resources to provide for and establish [a monastery]. "Noble son," at that time I accepted his invitation by remaining silent.
Once the Elder Sudatta had received my consent, he addressed me, saying, "Since ancient times, I have never done this..."
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will dispatch Śāriputra to instruct me in the proper rites. I then looked back and commanded him to assist in the construction.
At that time, Śāriputra and Sudatta traveled together in a single carriage toward the city of Śrāvastī;
through my supernatural power, they arrived at their destination in a single day and night. Then Sudatta said to Śāriputra, "Venerable One, this..."

"Outside the great city, where is there a place that is neither too near nor too far, abounding in springs and ponds, with fine groves of trees and lush, flourishing flowers and fruits—a pure, secluded, and spacious spot where I may build a vihāra for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the community of bhikṣus?
Śāriputra replied, "Prince Jeta’s Grove is neither too near nor too far; it is pure, tranquil, and secluded."
"There is a spring with flowing water, trees, flowers, and fruits available throughout the seasons; this place is most excellent and suitable for establishing a vihāra.

Having heard these words, Sudatta immediately went to the great elder Jeta and said to him, "I now wish to construct a monastic dwelling for the Unsurpassed Dharma King; only your noble grounds are fit for its construction."
"Now I wish to purchase it; will you grant me this? Jeta replied, "Even if one were to cover the entire ground with pure gold, I would still not give it.
Sudatta said, "Excellent! Since the forest land belongs to me, you may take the gold.
Jeta replied, "My garden is not for sale; why then do you speak of taking gold? Sudatta said, "If your mind is not yet resolved..."
They went together to the place where the arbitrators were. When the two elders arrived together, the arbitrator said, "The park belongs to Sudatta;
Jeta must take the gold. Elder Sudatta immediately dispatched people with carts and horses to carry and transport [the gold], spreading it over the ground as they gathered.
Within a single day, only five hundred paces remained where the gold had not yet been fully laid out. Then Jeta said: "Elder..."
When he said this, if [Gṛdhrakūṭa] were to regret it, he would listen; however, Sudatta replied, "I do not regret it.
He thought to himself, "From which treasury shall I draw forth enough gold? Then Jeta thought, "The Dharma-King Tathāgata is truly supreme;

because the wondrous Dharma he teaches is pure and untainted, it has caused this man to regard wealth so lightly. He then said to Sudatta, "As for the remaining areas that have not yet been covered..."
Furthermore, he required gold to be provided for him to personally construct a gate-tower for the Buddha, so that the Tathāgata might always pass through it when entering or leaving.
The Elder Jeta himself constructed the gatehouse, while the Elder Sudatta established a great residence within seven days consisting of three hundred rooms,
with sixty-three secluded meditation halls, each having a winter house and a summer hall.
Each separate kitchen, bathhouse, place for washing the feet, and large and small latrines were fully prepared;
once these arrangements were complete, he took a censer and, facing toward Rājagṛha, spoke from afar: "The preparations are finished;
I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion and pity, will accept this dwelling place for the sake of all sentient beings. At that time, I knew this beforehand.
The householder’s mind immediately joined with the great assembly to depart from Rājagṛha;
like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, they reached the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Sudatta in Śrāvastī.
Once I had arrived, the householder Sudatta offered what he had prepared to me, and having accepted it, I took up residence therein.
However, the various non-Buddhist teachers did not dare to oppose him while in Rājagṛha; they traveled on to Śrāvastī, where they sought a formal debate.
Sandhāna was a native of Rājagṛha—this translates as "Humi"—and Jeta was a native of Śrāvastī—this translates as "Victorious Clan.
Sudatta was also from Śrāvastī—this translates as "Good and Warm. They asked about the Buddha, whose fame resounded throughout the ten directions.
Sudatta was also one of the six great lay devotees; why then did he only hear the name of the Buddha for the first time when he was invited to stay the night?

The answer is that it was not that he had not heard of him before, but rather that his hearing had been superficial and fleeting. Now, as the conditions of his spiritual capacity have matured, upon hearing [the name], his hair stands on end all over his body.

Chapter Four of the *Siṃhanāda-bodhisattva-parivarta* of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty. (Fascicle Twenty-Eight)
Revised by the Jin Dynasty *śramaṇas* Huìyán,
Huìguān, and Xiè Língyùn;
the Fourth Chapter on the Lion’s Roar.
The second fascicle begins: The section on the mutual testing of supernatural powers upon arriving at the city consists of three parts:

(1) the occasion for the test, (2) the actual test, and (3) the benefit to the multitude. The first [part] further has four sections: (1) the request for the test, (2) the King’s refusal, (3) the repeated request, and (4) the King’s permission.
As for the reason for the request: previously, he had been expelled from the royal capital; now, having come again to Śrāvastī, he seeks this.
Having been deprived of their fame and lost their advantage within the city, they could not bear it and petitioned the king for a trial.
Initially there were two, but one used flattery and artful speech to praise the king.
At that time, the six teachers became jealous and all gathered together to go before King Prasenajit, speaking to him as follows:
"Great King, you should know that the realm of Your Majesty is pure, peaceful, and tranquil; it is truly a place for renunciants to dwell.
For this reason, we have come here. Great King, you govern with the True Dharma and eliminate the sufferings of your people."
Second, they disparaged and slandered the Buddha’s every gesture with extreme vituperation, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is both young in years and shallow in his studies; he has no mastery of the arts or doctrines to offer this country.

There are already elders and venerable sages here who, relying on their own status as descendants of the royal lineage, do not show him respect. If one is of royal descent, the law dictates that he should govern the people."
If he has left the household life, he should respect those of senior virtue. Great King, listen well:
the śramaṇa Gautama was truly not born from a royal lineage. As for this śramaṇa Gautama, if he had parents, how could he have stolen away the parents of others?
Great King, in my sūtras it is said that after more than a thousand years, a certain demonic, auspicious, and illusory being appeared, namely:
The śramaṇa Gautama says this is so; therefore, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has neither father nor mother.
If he had parents, how could he say that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and that there is no agent and no recipient?
By means of illusory arts, he deceives and deludes sentient beings; the foolish believe and accept it, while the wise reject it. O Great King, the Queen is a ruler.
"To all parents in the world, you are like a scale, like the earth, like the wind, like fire, like the path, like a river, like a bridge, like a lamp, like the sun, and like the moon.
You settle matters according to the Dharma without discriminating between enemy and kin. Yet, Śramaṇa Gautama does not permit me to live;
wherever I go, he pursues me without ceasing. I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me leave to compete with him in the power of their respective paths."
"If he defeats me, I shall belong to him; if I defeat him, he shall belong to me.

Since he was still a youth, and the Buddha had already attained enlightenment at thirty—at that time [the prince] would have been only thirty-some years old, and his ascetic practices had lasted for only six years—it is said that his learning was shallow and that he was not truly born of the royal lineage.
He says: "The Buddha is a mere illusion; he certainly does not belong to the royal lineage.
One who seizes the parents of others—namely, the Buddha’s teaching that leads people to leave secular life and become renunciants—is precisely one who robs his parents of their son.
Furthermore, by severing the progeny of others' parents and disallowing marriage, he is likewise one who robs the parents of other families," and so forth.
The king said, "Venerable sirs, the following two points are not permitted by me.
The king said, 'Venerable sirs, each of you has your own rules of conduct and your own places of residence, which are likewise different.
I now know for certain that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, will cause no hindrance to you.'"
The six teachers replied, "How can there be no harm? This was the third request.
The six teachers replied, "How can there be no harm? The śramaṇa Gautama uses the methods of illusion to entice and deceive people and brahmins until they have all submitted to him.
If Your Majesty would permit me to compete with him in the power of spiritual paths, it would bring great renown to Your Majesty."
"It shall be spread throughout the eight directions; if it is not so, evil reports will fill the roads.

The King said, "Virtuous ones, it is because you do not yet know that the Tathāgata’s power of the Way and his majestic spiritual authority are so sublime that you seek to challenge him to a contest. If you knew for certain, you would likely be unable to do so.
Great King, have you now already accepted the illusion of Gautama? I only pray that Your Majesty will pause to listen and examine this, and not treat us with contempt."
"Rather than our constructing these empty words, it would be better to verify them through reality.
The King said, "Excellent. [This concludes] the fourth instance of the King's consent.
The King said, "Excellent, excellent! At that time, the six teachers and their followers departed with joy, and then King Prasenajit immediately—

The King issued a strict command for his carriage to come to where I was; he prostrated himself with his head at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed me, saying:
"World-Honored One, the six teachers came earlier seeking to compete in spiritual power. Without weighing the matter, I ventured to grant them permission."
Although the king had privately given his consent, he still had to consult the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Excellent! This is the second formal trial, which consists of two parts: first, the command for the king to construct many [monasteries].
The Buddha said, "Great King, excellent, excellent! You should simply establish monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) here throughout every part of this kingdom."
Why is this? If I were to compete with him in the display of supernatural power, those among his assembly who would be converted would be many;
yet this place is narrow and small—how could it accommodate them?
Second, he manifested a supernormal transformation.
"Good son, at that time, for the sake of the six heretical teachers, from the first day until the fifteenth day,
I manifested great and rare supernatural transformations and miraculous powers,
as described in detail in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (and so forth)."
The assembly benefited at the three times.
At that moment, immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to faith in the Three Jewels without doubt; and the followers of the six heretical teachers, numbering in the immeasurable, were defeated.
Those with wrong views who had left the home life for the True Dharma attained the non-retrogressive mind toward Bodhi;
immeasurable sentient beings attained dhāraṇīs and various gates of samādhi; and immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruits from srotāpanna up to arhatship.

In this context, there was no explicit exchange of debate; rather, it was simply shown that the heterodox practitioners (tīrthikas) beheld a rare and extraordinary marvel, realized for themselves that they were unable to match it, and consequently fled to the city of Vārāṇasī. When asked why they did not engage in debate, they replied:

"Among the three wheels [of Dharma], the Wheel of Supernatural Powers (ṛddhi-cakra) is appropriate. At that time, the assembled multitude as well as the followers of the heterodox practitioners [were present].
Although they had benefited from this, the teachers of the non-Buddhists still did not believe or submit.
At that time, the six teachers felt shame within their hearts; this was the third instance of the Buddha proceeding toward that city.
Then, with the six teachers feeling ashamed in their inner minds, they surrounded him and went together to the city of Vārāṇasī to teach those people.
"The people have come to believe and accept false teachings; Gautama the Śramaṇa speaks only of empty matters.
Good son, at that time, for the sake of my mother, I was dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven under the Pārijātaka tree, practicing the retreat and preaching the Dharma.

At that time, the six heretical teachers were filled with great joy and cried out, 'Excellent! Gautama’s magical arts have now been extinguished,' and they further led immeasurable and innumerable multitudes."
At that time, when wrong views were increasing among those born [in this world], King Bimbisāra, King Prasenajit, and the fourfold assembly addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Venerable One, the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa who increase in wrong views are pitiable; they walk in great darkness.
We pray only that the Venerable One will go to that heavenly realm and prostrate before the World-Honored One, reporting our words as follows: 'It is like a calf...'"
"If this child has not been born for long and does not receive milk, he will surely die; we sentient beings are likewise so.
We only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on us and return to dwell here. At that time, Maudgalyāyana silently gave his consent.
In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he went to that heavenly realm, reached the place where the World-Honored One was, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
All the fourfold assemblies within Jambudvīpa long for the Tathāgata, yearning to see him and hear his Dharma.
King Bimbisāra, King Prasenajit, and the fourfold assemblies bow their heads at your feet.
All sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa have increased in wrong views and walk in great darkness; they are truly to be pitied, like a calf that has been born but not long ago.
"If we do not obtain milk, we shall surely die; of this there is no doubt. We are just like that;
we only pray that the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, will return here to Jambudvīpa. The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Return quickly now to Jambudvīpa and inform the various kings and the fourfold assembly: 'Seven days from now, I shall descend again for the sake of the six heretical teachers.'"
Furthermore, after seven days have passed since arriving at that city of Vārāṇasī, the Buddha— surrounded before and behind by Śakra,
Brahmā, Māra, and immeasurable sons of gods, as well as all the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven—
will arrive at the city of Vārāṇasī and utter a great lion’s roar, saying: "Only within my Dharma alone are there true śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas."
He proclaimed that all phenomena are impermanent, selfless, and that nirvāṇa is tranquil and free from all afflictions. He declared:
"It is impossible for there to be any other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who possess permanence, a self, or nirvāṇa.
At that time, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the six teachers said to one another, "If there were truly no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas within our own teachings, how could we receive the offerings of the world?
They asked, "The Buddha possesses great compassion and does not afflict sentient beings; why is it that he pursues us six teachers everywhere and yet does not catch us?"

To pause and answer [this] is intended to destroy heterodox views, to rescue immeasurable beings so they may emerge from false deliverance, to sever the bonds of birth and death, and to enable them to attain Great Nirvana.
If this is not compassion, what else could be considered mercy? What else could be considered loving-kindness?
Thereupon, the six teachers again gathered together; this was the fourth journey toward Vaiśālī.
Thereupon, the six teachers again assembled and proceeded to Vaiśālī. "Good son, at one time I was staying in the Āmra Grove in Vaiśālī.
At that time, the woman Āmrapālī, knowing that I was there and wishing to come to my place—"
At that time, he addressed the bhikṣus: "You should practice mindfulness of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and cultivate wisdom well;
according to what you practice, do not let the mind be negligent. What is meant by 'contemplating the foundations of mindfulness'?

If a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body and does not perceive a self or what belongs to a self, and contemplates the external body and the internal-external body, and does not perceive a self or..."
According to my observation, feeling, mind, and mental phenomena are likewise thus; this is called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
What is meant by "cultivating wisdom"? If there is a bhikṣu who perceives truly the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, this is called a bhikṣu cultivating wisdom.
What is meant by "the mind being non-negligent"? If there is a bhikṣu who recollects the Buddha, recollects the Dharma, and recollects...
"Mindfulness of the Sangha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of relinquishment, and mindfulness of the heavens—this is called a bhikṣu’s time when the mind is not negligent.

At that time, the woman Āmrapālī came to where I was, prostrated with her head at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, and having completed her respectful salutations, withdrew to sit to one side.
"Good son, at that time I preached the Dharma to Āmrapālī according to what was appropriate for her. Having heard it, the woman gave rise to the aspiration for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

At the time when [I] set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there were five hundred sons of Licchavis in that city who came to where I was, prostrated with their heads at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, and having completed their acts of reverence, withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, I further preached the Dharma to those sons of Licchavis as was appropriate for them: "O noble sons, as for those who are heedless..."
What are the five results? First, one does not obtain mastery over wealth and profit; second, an evil reputation spreads abroad;
third, one takes no pleasure in giving to the poor and destitute; fourth, one takes no pleasure in seeing the fourfold assembly; fifth, one does not attain the bodies of the various devas.
Sons of good family, it is because of non-negligence that one can give rise to both mundane and supramundane dharmas, provided they exist.
Those who wish to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should diligently cultivate the dharma of heedfulness (*apramāda*).
Furthermore, those who are heedless shall obtain thirteen kinds of retributive fruits. What are these thirteen? First, delighting in performing worldly tasks;
second, delighting in speaking useless words; third, always delighting in long sleep and slumber; fourth, delighting in speaking of worldly matters.
1. Constantly delighting in associating with evil friends; 2. Being indolent and lazy; 3. Constantly being held in contempt by others; 4.
Forgetting what one has heard as soon as it is heard; 5. Delighting in dwelling in remote borderlands;
6. Being unable to subdue the sense faculties; 7. Not knowing moderation in eating; 8. Not delighting in emptiness and stillness; 9. Having views that are not correct.
"O sons of good family, those who are heedless, even though they may be near the Buddha and his disciples, are nevertheless far from them.
The Licchavis said: 'We ourselves know that we are heedless people. Why is this?
If we were not heedless, the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, would have appeared in our land. At that time, within the great assembly, there was a brāhmaṇa..."
The gatekeeper named Ajitasena addressed the Licchavis: "Excellent, excellent, as you have said!
King Bimbisāra has already attained great benefit. The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has appeared in his kingdom like a wondrous lotus born from a great pond;
though it grows in the water, the water cannot defile it. O Licchavis, the Buddha is likewise. Though...
Those born in that land are not obstructed by worldly dharmas. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, neither emerge nor enter;
yet for the sake of sentient beings, they appear in the world, unobstructed by worldly dharmas.
You, sirs, are yourselves deluded, indulging in the five desires and not knowing to draw near to the Tathāgata. Therefore, you are called heedless people, and not [virtuous ones].
The Buddha appeared in the kingdom of Magadha, named Prahlāda. Why was this?
Because the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is like the sun and the moon; he does not appear in the world for the sake of only one or two people.
When the Licchavis heard these words, they immediately resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and further said: "Excellent, excellent! There is none superior!"
When the youth had thus spoken these excellent and sublime words, each of the Licchavis removed a garment from their own bodies and offered it to Ajita.
Having accepted them, Ajita in turn presented them to me, saying: "World-Honored One, I have obtained these garments and articles from the Licchavis;
I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings, will accept what I offer."
At that time, out of compassion for those Licchavis who were without a superior protector, I accepted their invitation. Then all the Licchavis simultaneously joined their palms and spoke these words:
"We pray only that the Tathāgata will dwell in this land for a single season and accept our humble offerings.
At that time, I remained silent and accepted the Licchavis' request.
The Tathāgata further went to preach various teachings for Āmrapālī and the Licchavis;
this was the mother of Jīvaka, Queen Vaidehī, who, possessing great beauty, instructed the bhikṣus in the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Subsequently, he preached non-negligence to the Licchavis to shatter their arrogance. According to the laws of the kingdom, those of intelligence were regularly selected [for such duties].
Because he presided over the deliberations of the remaining ministers, he was translated as "Border-Lord" (Biandi); he is also called "One Who Transmits and Participates in State Affairs.
At that time, the six heretical teachers arrived once more at the city of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, having heard of these matters, the six teachers and their followers went together to Vārāṇasī.
At that time, I also went to Vārāṇasī and stayed by the banks of the Varanā River.

In Vārāṇasī there was the son of an elder named Ratnayaśas, who was addicted to the five desires and ignorant of impermanence; because of my arrival, he spontaneously attained the contemplation of white bones.
Dharma saw that the palace buildings, the queens, and the handmaidens were all white bones;
his heart was filled with terror as if he had encountered a sword, a venomous snake, a thief, or fire. He immediately left the palace and came to where I was, speaking along the way:
"Śramaṇa Gautama, I am now being pursued by thieves and am greatly terrified; I pray you will rescue me. The Buddha said, "Excellent."
"O man, the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are secure and free from fear. The son of the elder said, "If within the Three Jewels there is nothing to fear, then I too shall now attain fearlessness.
I immediately permitted him to leave the household life to practice the Way.
At that time, the son of the elder had fifty companions; hearing from afar of Baocheng’s weary detachment and renunciation, they immediately joined him.
In harmony and accord, they went forth from the household life together.
Having heard this, the six teachers descended and proceeded further to the city of Campā.
Having heard this, the six teachers traveled on in succession until they reached the great city of Campā. At that time, all the people of the kingdom of Campā...
They all together served the followers of the Six Teachers and had never before heard the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
many people were committing extremely evil deeds. At that time, for the sake of sentient beings, I went to the city of Campā.
At that time, there was a great elder in that city who had no heir; he served the Six Teachers in hopes of obtaining a son, but after a short while, [he failed].
When his wife became pregnant, the elder learned of it and went to the six teachers, saying with joy, "My wife is pregnant;
will it be a boy or a girl? The six teachers replied, "It will certainly be a girl. Upon hearing this, the elder’s heart was filled with sorrow and distress.
Furthermore, a friend came to him and asked, "Why are you so distressed? The elder answered:
My wife is pregnant, and as it was not yet known whether the child would be male or female, I questioned the six heretical teachers.

When they saw me, they said, "According to our methods of physiognomy, the one born will certainly be a girl. Hearing these words, I reflected upon myself: I am advanced in years, yet my wealth is immeasurable;
if this child is not a son, there will be no one to whom I can entrust it. This is why I am sorrowful. My friends further said to me, "You lack wisdom; have you not heard before?"
"Of whom were the brothers Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his followers disciples—the Buddha or the Six Heretics?
If the Six Heretics were all-knowing, for what reason did Kāśyapa abandon them to become the Buddha’s disciple?
Furthermore, [why did] Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, as well as kings such as Bimbisāra and the queens such as Queen Mallikā [do so]?"
"Are the elders of various countries, such as Sudatta and others like them, not disciples of the Buddha?

Are the wilderness spirits, King Ajātaśatru, the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla, and Aṅgulimāla—whose malevolence was so intense that he sought to harm his own mother—not those who were tamed by the Tathāgata?
O Elder, [it is so] for the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One."
Because he possesses unobstructed knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena, he is called a Buddha; because his speech is non-dual, he is called a Tathāgata;
and because he has severed the afflictions, he is called an Arhat. What the World-Honored One says is ultimately without duality, whereas the six teachers are not so—how could they be trusted?
The Tathāgata now dwells nearby; if you wish to know the truth, you should go to where the Buddha is.

At that time, the elder immediately accompanied this person to where I was, prostrated with his head at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, joined his palms, knelt for a long time, and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One, you are impartial toward all sentient beings without distinction; to enemies and kin, you regard them as one and the same.
Yet I am bound by the fetters of craving, and among enemies and kin, I have been unable to maintain equanimity. Now, I..."
Desiring to ask the Tathāgata about the matter of his wife’s pregnancy, he felt deep shame and fear, and did not dare to speak.

He said, “World-Honored One, my wife is pregnant, and the six teachers have declared that she will certainly give birth to a girl. What do you say to this? The Buddha said, “Elder, there is no doubt that your wife is carrying a son;
once the child is born, his merit and virtue will be beyond compare. When the elder heard these words, he was filled with joy.

Filled with great joy, he immediately returned home. At that time, the Six Heretics, hearing my prediction that the child to be born would certainly be a boy and possess great merit, felt jealousy in their hearts.
They mixed poison with mango fruits and took them to his house, saying to the elder:
"How wonderful! Gautama has skillfully described the signs. When your wife is near her month, she may take this medicine. "Take it," they said.
When this medicine was administered, the child born was handsome and the mother suffered no harm; the elder was delighted. However, he gave her a poisonous drug and had his wife take it.
Once she had taken it, she died immediately. The six heretical teachers were overjoyed and, traveling throughout the city, cried out in a loud voice:
"The śramaṇa Gautama predicted that the elder’s wife would give birth to a son whose merit and virtue would be unsurpassed in the world. Now—"
Before the child was born, his mother had already passed away;

at that time, the elder further conceived a lack of faith in me and, following worldly custom, encoffined her, sealed the lid, and sent her to the outskirts of the city where he piled up a great quantity of dry wood and cremated her with fire.
I clearly beheld this matter with my eye of the Path and, turning to address Ānanda, commanded him to bring my robe, saying: "I wish to go there to destroy [his merit]."
When he was extinguishing wrong views, Vaiśravaṇa addressed the Great General Maṇibhadra, saying: "The Tathāgata now wishes to go to that cemetery;
you should go quickly to level the ground, sweep and sprinkle it, prepare a lion throne, and seek out exquisite incense and flowers to adorn the site.
At that time, the six heretical teachers saw me from afar as I was departing, and they said to one another: "The śramaṇa Gautama..."
"Have you come to this cemetery intending to devour flesh?
At that time, many upāsakas who had not yet attained the Dharma-eye felt shame and fear, and said to me, "That woman has already died; we pray that you need not go there.
Then Ānanda said to the people, "Wait but a moment; before long, the Tathāgata will extensively expound and reveal the realm of all Buddhas."
When I arrived, I sat upon the lion throne. The elder challenged me, saying, "Your words are not inconsistent; you may be called a World-Honored One.
Yet, your mother has already passed away—how could you have fathered a son?

I replied, "Elder, at that time you did not ask about the length of your mother's life, but only whether the child she carried was male or female. The speech of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is never inconsistent."
"Therefore, you should know that he will certainly obtain a son. At that time, the corpse was consumed by fire;

its belly split open and a child emerged from within, sitting upright amidst the flames like a ruddy sheldrake upon a lotus pedestal. When the six heretical teachers saw this, they spoke again, saying, "A marvel!
Gautama is skilled in the arts of illusion. When the elder saw this, his heart rejoiced once more, and he rebuked the six teachers.
"If you say it is an illusion, why do you not do so yourself? At that time, I immediately said to Jīvaka, "Go into the fire and bring this child here.
Just as Jīvaka was about to go, the six heretical teachers pulled him back and said, "The illusory arts performed by the śramaṇa Gautama are not necessarily always successful;
they may sometimes fail. If he fails, he might even be able to harm you."
"How can you now believe and accept his words? Jīvaka replied, "The fierce fires of the Avīci Hell, sent by the Tathāgata, cannot even burn him, let alone the fires of the world.
At that time, Jīvaka stepped forward into the mass of fire as if entering the cool waters of a great river;
he took the child in his arms, returned to my place, and handed the child to me.
Having received the child, he said to the elder: "The lifespan of all sentient beings is uncertain, like a bubble upon the water.
If a sentient being has heavy karmic retribution, fire cannot burn them and poison cannot harm them. This child’s karmic retribution was not created by me.
At that time, the elder said: "Excellent, World-Honored One! If this child may fulfill his natural lifespan..."
"May the Tathāgata establish a name for him. The Buddha said, "Elder, this son was born from within a fierce fire;

the fire is named Jyotiṣka, so he should be named Jyotiṣka. At that time, witnessing my spiritual transformation, immeasurable sentient beings in the assembly resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the six heretical teachers traveled throughout the six cities; the following two sections clarify how they were pursued all the way to Kuśinagara until they did not know where to go.
[The text states: "Kuśinagara is narrow and small; let us stay here for our own protection. Unexpectedly, the Buddha arrived there. This passage consists of three parts:
first, the false teaching; second, the true teaching; third, the debate between the false and the true.
At that time, the six teachers, having failed to find a place to set foot throughout the six cities, felt ashamed and lowered their heads; they returned once more to this city of Kuśinagara.
Having arrived there, they cried out these words: "All people, you should know! The śramaṇa Gautama is a great master of illusion who deceives and deludes the world.
Throughout the six great cities, he is like a magician who conjures the fourfold army by means of his illusions."
That is to say, he creates illusory chariot troops, cavalry, elephant troops, and infantry;
furthermore, he creates various kinds of necklaces, city walls, palaces, houses, rivers, ponds, trees, śramaṇas, and so forth. Śramaṇa Gautama is also like this:
for the sake of preaching the Dharma, he creates illusory bodies as kings, or as śramaṇas and brahmins, male bodies and female bodies, small bodies and large bodies, or even as animals.
Taking birth in the bodies of ghosts or spirits, they may sometimes speak of impermanence or speak of permanence; sometimes they speak of suffering or again speak of pleasure;
they may speak of a self or speak of no-self; they may speak of purity or speak of impurity; and sometimes they speak of existence or non-existence.
Because their actions are false and deceptive, they are called "phantasms. It is like a seed: according to the seed, one obtains its corresponding fruit.
Indeed, the śramaṇa Gautama is just like this. Since his mother Māyā gave birth to him through illusion, one cannot claim that the śramaṇa Gautama lacks true knowledge and vision.

Even though the various brāhmaṇas have practiced asceticism and maintained prohibitive precepts for many accumulated years, they still say they do not yet possess true knowledge and vision; how much less so for Gautama, who is young in age and brief in study?
How could one who does not practice asceticism for even a short time possess true knowledge and vision?
If, after practicing asceticism for a full seven years, one still possesses no such insight, how much less so for one whose practice does not even reach six years?
O son of good family, fools lack wisdom and thus accept his teachings; they are like a great magician who deceives the ignorant—the śramaṇa Gautama is just the same.
In this manner, these six teachers greatly increased false views among sentient beings within this city.
First, a non-Buddhist arrived at the city of Kuśinagara and spoke extensively of the Buddha's faults, causing people to give rise to heterodox views. His text stated:
"If the mother is an illusion, the son cannot be anything other than this; what is the meaning of this? The intended meaning was that the nature of human birth exists inherently.
"According to the constant custom, for what reason was he born from the right armpit? Is this not the birth of an illusory son from an illusory mother?
When the two Buddhas arrived and spoke the truth, O Good Man, I saw these things and felt compassion in my heart; by means of my supernatural power, I summoned the Buddhas of the ten directions."
A great multitude of Bodhisattvas has gathered in this grove, filling it completely for forty yojanas on all sides. Now, within this assembly, he utters the Great Lion’s Roar.
Good son, although one may speak much in a solitary place, it cannot be called a "Lion’s Roar.
Only within this assembly of wise people can it truly be called the Great Lion’s Roar of a Lion.
The Roarer proclaims that all phenomena are entirely impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure, whereas he alone teaches that the Tathāgata is eternal,
blissful, self, and pure.
By repudiating the heterodox and returning to the orthodox, the heterodox and the orthodox shall each proceed along their own paths.
At that time, the six heretical teachers again presented the third section, "A Combined Discussion of the Erroneous and the Correct," consisting of seven rounds of question and answer.
Of these, the first six rounds constitute the formal discussion, while the final round constitutes the subjugation. This is the first round, wherein the heretical position is first established.
At that time, the six teachers spoke again as follows: "If Gautama has a self (ātman), I too have what belongs to a self (ātmīya).
When it is said 'I,' the seer is the self. Gautama, it is like a person who sees an object within a mirror; I am likewise so.
The mirror is a metaphor for the eye, and the seer is a metaphor for the self."
To regard the seer as the self is one of the sixteen speculative views.
The Buddha’s refutation of this has three parts; first, he causes the six sense faculties to function simultaneously.
The Buddha said to the six teachers: "If you claim that the seer is named 'self,' this meaning is not so. Why? Because of what you have cited..."
By way of analogy, when a person is facing toward something, all six sense faculties are simultaneously engaged.

If there were a fixed self that sees through the eye, why would it not likewise perceive all objects within a single faculty? If a single faculty cannot simultaneously hear and see the six types of sensory objects, one should know that there is no self.
Regarding the previous argument you raised as an analogy, I shall now refute it: when a person is within a carriage, they see forms and hear sounds, perceiving all six sense objects.
You claim that because I am within the eye, I can only see forms and cannot perceive all sense objects;
you should know that this is not the case.
Next, it follows that there would be no distinction between the young and the old.
Although the analogy of the drawn-out [image] remains unchanged after a hundred years, the observer’s perception of it does not differ;
if the visual faculty were likewise [unchanging], then even as one grows old and the faculties mature, they should likewise remain without difference.
If, as in the case of the ear, one sees external objects clearly even after a hundred years,
then I too should see objects clearly with my eyes after a hundred years. If my aged eyes are not as capable as those of my youth,
how can you use the ear as an analogy?

Third, it would follow that both the internal and external are seen simultaneously, because the person facing [an object] is different [from the eye]. If the eye-faculty were such, it should likewise see both the internal and external at once.
If it does not so see, how can there be a self?
When a person faces toward the center, they see both the interior and exterior; yet why do they not see the "self" within their own eyes?
The six masters spoke again, and thus began the second round of inquiry.
The six teachers spoke again: "Gautama, if there is no self, who is it that can see?
This is not a valid objection, as it is merely a restatement of their previous argument; they ask about the "self" once more. The Buddha replied: "There is form... [and so on].
The answer below consists of three parts: first, demonstrating the causes and conditions; second, refuting the false self; third, establishing the correct [view].
"I. The Buddha said, "There is form, there is light, there is mind, and there is the eye; because these four are in combination, it is called 'seeing.
Within this, there is truly no seer and no experiencer. Sentient beings, through perversion, speak of a seer and an experiencer. Thus it is.
From the perspective of ultimate meaning, that which all sentient beings perceive is inverted, while that which all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perceive is true reality.

This first demonstrates that the perception of form is obtained by relying upon various causes and conditions; it has never been a vision of a self, but is merely a horizontal perception that asserts existence.
Second, refuting their heterodox views: first, stating that it is not so.
If the six masters say that form is the self, this is also not so.
Next, as for the passage beginning with "For what reason," it specifically sets forth various faults.
For what reason? Form is truly not the self. If form were the self, one should not incur an ugly appearance;
why, then, are there distinctions among the four castes rather than all being of one kind, such as Brahmins? Why, furthermore, would one be subject to another?
If those who have attained mastery over their faculties were to be born with defects or lack physical completeness,
why would they not manifest as the bodies of devas instead of receiving the various bodies of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts? If one cannot act according to one's will,
one should know that there is certainly no "self" (ātman).
If "self" (ātman) is defined as sovereignty, it ought to belong exclusively to the Brahmin caste; why, then, does it receive the various different forms of the six destinies?
Furthermore, since there is no self, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all devoid of self.
Because of the fault of the three lower fetters being without self, they are called impermanent;
because they are impermanent, they are suffering; because they are suffering, they are empty; because they are empty, they are inverted.
Because they are inverted, all sentient beings revolve through birth and death; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

The sixth section, "The Six Teachers and the Tathāgata," has three parts; the third is the summary and indication of the correct self, which further consists of two parts: first, a brief indication, and second, a comparative analysis.
The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, has eternally severed the bonds of form, up to and including the bonds of consciousness; therefore, he is named Constant, Blissful, Self, and Pure.

The meaning of the initial passage is as follows: Since the preceding section has already refuted that form, sensation, and so forth are self, he now asks whether the Tathāgata is these very things, such as form.
Anticipating this intent, the response is given: "The self of the Tathāgata is no longer bound by form, nor is it bound by sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
it is endowed with the four virtues. The 'self' you speak of does not escape [bondage]."
The four bonds.
Next, the subsequent fetters are also distinguished in contrast to the external.
Furthermore, form (*rūpa*) is itself dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); that which is dependent origination is called non-self (*anātman*); that which is non-self is called...
The body of the Tathāgata Duḥkhapraśamana (Suffering-Emptiness) is neither caused by conditions nor not caused by conditions; therefore, it is called "having a self.
That which has a self is eternal, blissful, and pure.
The non-Buddhists say that the self arises from causes and conditions, and for that reason it is impermanent; however, the self of the Tathāgata does not arise from causes and conditions.
Thus, one attains permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The six teachers say: "Gautama, this is the third external deviation from our original tenets. The six teachers say:
"Gautama, form (*rūpa*) is not the self, and so on up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is also not the self; the self pervades all things."
The locus [of the self] is like empty space.
Some other schools claim that the self is omnipresent throughout all places and does not take form (rūpa) as the self.

Regarding the Buddha’s refutation of this below, there are two intentions: first, he directly refutes it by means of its omnipresence; second, he further refutes it by means of the singular [unitary nature].
Examining the initial passage further, there are two successive sections.

In the first section, he questions the notion of pervasiveness. The Buddha said: "If it were pervasive, one should not say, 'I have never seen it before. If one has never seen it before, then one knows that this seeing was originally non-existent and now exists.
That which was originally non-existent and now exists is called impermanent. If it is impermanent, how [can it be pervasive]?"
What is meant by "pervasive"?
If I am pervasive, I should not fail to see at the beginning, and I should see constantly.
If [the self] were pervasive, it should possess a body within all five realms of existence; if it possessed a body, it should each receive its own retribution.
If each receives its own retribution, why do you say that one "successively receives" the states of humans and devas?

Furthermore, you should challenge me on this point of pervasiveness: if it were pervasive, why would one fear the three evil realms and instead maintain precepts and wholesome deeds for the sake of obtaining a human or deva body?
Next, regarding identity and difference, there are two parts; first, the two topical headings are announced:
"As for what you call 'pervasive,' is it one or many?
Second, each is explained individually, with the critique of the position of oneness following the text.
If the self were one, there would be no distinction between father and son, enemy and friend, or neutral person.
If the self were many, then the five faculties possessed by all sentient beings should all be equal, and their karma and wisdom should likewise be so.
If this were the case, why speak of some having complete faculties and others incomplete?
Regarding the distinction between good and evil karma and between the foolish and the wise,

if one were to emphasize the multiplicity [of selves], then since there is a distinct "self" within each individual body that acts as its own sovereign, why would there be such inequality in their faculties—
some being sharp and others dull, some wise and others foolish?
Gautama, regarding the "self" among sentient beings, there is no limit;
however, for phenomena that are either Dharma or non-Dharma, there are distinct boundaries.
Sentient beings who practice the Dharma obtain a good body, whereas those who engage in non-Dharma obtain an evil body. For this reason, sentient beings... [are so designated].
The fruits of karma cannot fail to be non-differentiated;
yet, while the self is one and also eternally pervasive throughout all sentient beings, the cultivation of karma is inherently differentiated, and thus the fruits of karma are not the same.
The Buddha said: "If the dharmas and non-dharmas of the six teachers were such as you describe, then my [dharmas] would not be all-pervasive.

If they were all-pervasive, then they should reach everyone. If they reached everyone, then those who cultivate goodness should also have evil conduct, and those who commit evil should also have goodness.
If this is not the case, how can you say they are all-pervasive?"

The Buddha refuted this, saying: "Since the self is both pervasive and eternal, how could it be that good and evil merely alternate? It would follow that both sin and merit must coexist simultaneously.
Therefore, one who performs evil deeds must possess goodness, and one who performs good deeds must possess evil; if they did not coexist, [the self would be impermanent]."
"This [self] is not omnipresent, and furthermore, as a sovereign being, I should be able to perform good or evil deeds myself" (and so forth).
Gautama, it is like a single room; the following is the fifth section, wherein the non-Buddhists again offer the analogy of lighting a lamp as a rebuttal.
"O Gautama, it is like a single room where a hundred thousand lamps are lit; each illuminates itself without obstructing the others.
It is the same with sentient beings and the self: when practicing good or performing evil, they do not intermingle."

"Although they share the same illumination, the substances of the lamps are each distinct; the 'Self' is ultimately all-pervasive, yet its functions of good and evil differ, just as one might light hundreds or thousands of lamps within a single room (and so forth)."
The Buddha refutes this again in two ways, first declaring it to be incorrect:
"If you say that 'I' am like a lamp, this meaning is not so.

Next, he refutes it in three ways: first, by refuting [the self] as arising from conditions; second, by refuting [the self] as being distinct from light and moving to another place; and third, by refuting [the self] in relation to light and darkness.
It is destroyed when it ceases to coexist.
Why is this? The light of that lamp exists in dependence upon conditions; as the lamp increases, the light also increases.
It is not so, however, with the "self" (*ātman*) of sentient beings.

The first refutation states: "If you take the lamp as an analogy for the dharma and the light as an analogy for the self, then since the light depends upon the lamp, and the lamp’s brilliance is great when there is much oil and a wick, it follows that the self depends upon karma.
When karma ceases, the self dies; since karma is limited, the self would not be all-pervasive."
Regarding the second point of censure:
it clarifies that while a sentient being’s self might emerge from a lamp and abide in a different location, it cannot likewise emerge from the body and abide in a different location.
If it is argued that light emerges from the lamp, then by analogy, the self must emerge from karma; thus, karma would possess the self rather than the self possessing karma.
Thirdly, it clarifies that at the initial moment of the lamp, it coexists with darkness.
How can that lamp-light coexist with darkness? Why is this so? For example, when a single lamp is lit in a dark room, the illumination is not yet clear;
it is only when many lamps are used that clarity is attained. If the first lamp had destroyed the darkness, there would be no need for subsequent lamps.
Since subsequent lamps are required, one should know that the initial light coexisted with the darkness.
If that were so, your eternal self would have to exist within the impermanent self,
and the impermanent self would likewise have to exist within the eternal self.
Gautama, if there is no self, [then] please inquire further beyond the sixth section below.
"Gautama, if there is no self, who is it that performs good and evil?
The Buddha answered in two parts: first, he refuted the false self.
The Buddha said: "If the self were the agent, how could it be called permanent? If it were permanent in this way, how could it ever come to exist [only at certain times]?"
If one performs good at certain times and performs evil at others, and if it is said that one performs both good and evil at times, how can one further claim, "I am infinite"?
If I were the agent, for what reason would I continue to practice unwholesome dharmas?

If I were the agent and the knower, why would doubt arise regarding sentient beings? Because there is no self, for this reason, within the teachings of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), [the notion of a self] is definitively non-existent.
If there is a self, and that self is eternal, how could it act? If it were eternal, what action could it perform?
Even if it were to act, why would it not always do good, yet instead performs evil? Since its actions are not fixed as either good or evil, it must be impermanent.
Next, the true self is elucidated.
If one speaks of the "self," it is the Tathāgata. Why? Because his body is boundless; because he is free from the net of doubt;

because he neither acts nor receives [karmic results], he is called "eternal"; because he is neither born nor extinguished, he is called "blissful"; and because he is free from the defilements of affliction.
It is called "pure" because it is devoid of the ten marks; it is called "empty" for this reason. Thus, the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity are empty and free from all marks.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding, which is beyond doubt.
The seventh section, concerning the submission of the foremost non-Buddhists to the Tathāgata, concludes as in the text.

The various non-Buddhists said: "If you say that the Tathāgata is permanent, blissful, self, and pure, yet is empty because he is signless, then one should know that the Dharma taught by Gautama is not truly empty.
Therefore, we now receive and uphold it with our heads bowed. At that time, the non-Buddhists...
Their number was immeasurable, and they left the home life out of faith in the Buddha-dharma.
Good son, by these causes and conditions, he descended to the second tree-place. Furthermore, this section has two parts: first, connecting the preceding with the following;
second, the actual explanation of the place. The first is as stated in the text.
Good son, for these reasons, I have uttered the Great Lion’s Roar here between the twin *śāla* trees.
That which is called the "Lion’s Roar" is the Great *Nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the twin trees of the east, there are three points to clarify their location: first, they symbolize the principle; second, they protect the Dharma.
The benefit of the flavor of the three dharmas first expresses the underlying principle:
"Good son, the 'pair' in the east destroys impermanence and attains permanence, and so on,
until the 'pair' in the north destroys impurity and attains purity."
The principle (*li*) consists of the four virtues; for what reason is the east used as a metaphor for permanence and impermanence, etc.?
One interpretation states that it is taken up as a single matter without a specific location, and thus the east can also serve as a metaphor for bliss and non-bliss. Second, Master He says:
"The two withered trees represent the extinction of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*; the two flourishing trees represent the eternal persistence of the *dharmakāya*. However, regarding bodhi..."
The tree likewise sprouts in one branch and withers in the other; when the Buddha-dharma is extinguished, both branches will wither.
If this is so, why must it necessarily refute [the views of] permanence and impermanence? However, the Buddha transforms according to conditions, and there must be a reason for this.
As He Xi said: "The two pillars facing east symbolize permanence and impermanence; this refers to Maheśvara, whom the non-Buddhists worship, who resides in the eastern direction."
The teaching of Abiding (Vihāra) is practiced in the West; because the Buddha-dharma constantly overcomes impermanence, it is said that the "pair" in the East symbolizes permanence and impermanence.
The South symbolizes the self (*ātman*), for the South is the right side, and the right hand performs actions with ease, serving as a metaphor for the sovereignty of the self.
The West symbolizes bliss (*sukha*), for practicing the Buddhist teachings in the West results in bliss; thus it symbolizes the Buddha-dharma.
The north is considered the direction of purity and the place of renunciation; therefore, it symbolizes purity within the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, it is said that the god Īśvara faces east, with his right hand toward the south;
these assignments are all made to refute the four inversions of the non-Buddhists and to represent the four virtues of the Buddha-dharma.
