If there is a bodhisattva who diligently practices with vigor but has not yet attained the benefit of the bliss of nirvāṇa, and because of this lack of attainment gives rise to a mind of regret—
due to dull faculties being unable to subdue the five sensory organs and the powerful force of various defilements and afflictions— [this is the case].

If one suspects that one’s precepts have become weak or impaired, one should know that at such a time it is not appropriate to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*), but rather that one should cultivate wisdom (*prajñā*).
This is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the opportune and non-opportune times.

Good son, if for a bodhisattva the two dharmas of concentration and wisdom are unequal, one should know that at such a time it is not appropriate to cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*); if the two dharmas are equal, then it is appropriate to cultivate it.

Good son, one who knows the proper time and the improper time is called a bodhisattva. If a bodhisattva practicing concentration and wisdom gives rise to afflictions, you should know that at such a time it is not appropriate to practice equanimity (*upekṣā*). Instead, they should recite, copy, explain, and expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures;

they should practice mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of the heavens, and mindfulness of renunciation. This is what is meant by practicing equanimity.

In the response, when clarifying the three dharmas regarding the timely and the untimely: for those who are prone to conceit because they enjoy the four *siddhāntas* (the fourfold teachings) through their own practice, it is appropriate to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
this is the skillful application of the *puruṣakāra* (teaching for others). For those who give rise to remorse through diligence and so forth, it is appropriate to cultivate wisdom (*prajñā*);

this is the skillful cultivation of the antidote. For those for whom the two dharmas are equal, it is appropriate to cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*); this is the skillful cultivation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the arousal of afflictions, one should recite the Six Recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).

The *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra* states that by cultivating and accumulating the three marks, one achieves formless *nirvāṇa* through these causes and conditions. Since it speaks of "causes and conditions," this refers to skillful cultivation as the *siddhānta* (established tenet) which serves as the cause and condition for achieving Great *Nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, one should cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is the gate of existence (*yu-men*). It is appropriate.
Cultivating wisdom is the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); cultivating equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the gate of neither emptiness nor existence;

cultivating the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) is the gate of both emptiness and existence. Through these four gates and their causal conditions, one achieves Great Nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, one should skillfully employ the four *siddhāntas* to transform others. As the text would become too cumbersome, the practitioner must simply ensure that they possess [these qualities]. (End of quote)
[It is said:
"O son of good family, if there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the power and function of the third stage of the path of cultivation, this text is divided into two parts:

first, clarifying the attainment of bliss and nirvāṇa; second, clarifying the departure from suffering and the transformation of hindrances. The first part is further divided into two: first, clarifying..."
One attains nirvāṇa.
Son of good family, if there is a bodhisattva who cultivates these three marks of phenomena, by this causal condition he attains the markless nirvāṇa.
Next is the discussion on the meaning of the doctrine, which consists of two rounds of questions and answers. First, the question:
Lion’s Roar said, “World-Honored One, because it is devoid of the ten marks, Great Nirvāṇa is called ‘markless.
For what further reasons is it called ‘unborn,’ ‘unemerging,’ ‘unconditioned,’ the ‘household,’ the ‘island,’ the ‘refuge,’ the ‘peaceful extinction,’ and ‘Nirvāṇa’?”
Is it because it is quiescent, free from all suffering and illness, and devoid of anything [substantial]?

Because one can attain *nirvāṇa* by practicing three dharmas, the text asks about its characteristics; this section consists of two parts. First, it restates that being devoid of the ten marks is called "Great *Nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha has already finished answering this point, and since the intent has been grasped, what remains ununderstood will now be further explained.
Ten dharmas constitute the question. The Buddha said:
"Good son, because there is no cause or condition, it is called 'unborn' (*anutpanna*); because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called 'unemerging' (*anirgata*);

because there is no creation of karma, it is called 'uncreated' (*akṛta*); because it does not enter the five views, it is called a 'dwelling'; and because it is free from the four floods, it is called 'separation'."
Because it is water, it is called an island; because it tames sentient beings, it is called a refuge; because it destroys the thieves of the fetters, it is called peace and security;

because the fires of all fetters are extinguished, it is called *nirvāṇa* (extinction); because it is free from applied and sustained thought, it is called *nirvāṇa*; because it is far removed from clamor and bustle, it is called tranquility;
because it has forever severed the certainty of death, it is called freedom from illness; because there is nothing at all, it is called non-existence.
When a son of good family or a bodhisattva contemplates in this manner, they immediately attain the clear vision of the Buddha-nature.
Kaishan takes the extinction of these various fetters and fires to be "extinction" (nirvāṇa), while Zhuangyan takes the departure from all discursive thought and observation to be "nirvāṇa.
[The author] refutes Kaishan, saying: "The exhaustion of the bonds of the 'son' is called extinction."
The exhaustion of the bonds of fruition is called *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the passage on the "bonds of seeds," why is it translated as the "fruit of *nirvāṇa*"? Kaishan (Kai-shan) offers this defense:
In the foreign [Sanskrit] original, both the exhaustion of the bonds of seeds and the exhaustion of the bonds of fruition are termed "liberation" (*vimukti*).

Both the extinction with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirodha*) and the extinction without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirodha*) are termed "extinction and transcendence" (*parinirvāṇa*). Those who produced the Chinese translations skillfully varied their terminology; thus, while the exhaustion of the bonds of seeds is retained [as such], the exhaustion of the bonds of fruition is rendered as *nirvāṇa*.
This sound refers to the fruit of parinirvāṇa where all fetters are exhausted; that sound refers to liberation. Yet, among these ten answers, all respond to the perfect virtues of nirvāṇa.
These two masters each cling to a single phrase and give rise to contention;
this is because they have given rise to afflictions regarding the interpretation of the meaning. It is like the analogy of the blind men touching the elephant (and so forth).
Following the Lion’s Roar, the Lion’s Roar asks again.
The Lion’s Roar said: “World-Honored One, by accomplishing how many dharmas can a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive such signless nirvāṇa, up to the state of non-existence?”
Having heard these ten meanings, but not yet knowing how to practice, one asks: "By practicing how many dharmas does one attain *nirvāṇa*?
Next, the Buddha speaks; the meaning of his answer is that the aforementioned ten dharmas are merely different aspects of the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
If one wishes to practice, one must further possess ten dharmas, among which three are presented as headings, explained, and concluded.
The Buddha said, "Good son, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he is able to clearly perceive nirvāṇa—from its signlessness up to its non-existence.
What are these eleven? First, the fulfillment of faith. What is meant by the fulfillment of faith? It is having deep faith in the Buddha."
The Dharma and the Sangha are eternal; the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest through skillful means that all sentient beings, including even icchantikas, possess Buddha-nature.
They do not believe in the Tathāgata’s birth, old age, sickness, and death, nor in his practice of austerities;
they do not believe that Devadatta truly caused a schism in the Saṅgha, shed the blood of the Buddha, or that the Tathāgata would ultimately enter parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma would perish.
This is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of faith and fulfillment of the two types of pure precepts. What is meant by the fulfillment of pure precepts?

Good son, if there is a bodhisattva who claims his own precepts are pure, yet when he encounters a woman—even though he does not engage in union with her—he may look at her, or engage in banter, speech, and playful laughter; such a bodhisattva has fulfilled desire.
One who violates the pure precepts and defiles the holy life (brahmacarya), causing the precepts to become defiled and impure, cannot be said to be "endowed with the purity of precepts.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who claim their own precepts are pure;

yet, although they do not physically unite with those women, they engage in jesting, teasing, and laughter, and from outside a wall or screen, they hear the various sounds of women’s necklaces, bracelets, and bangles, and their hearts give rise to desire.

One who is attached to such things is a bodhisattva who has failed to achieve the dharma of desirelessness; they have violated pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and defiled the holy life (*brahmacarya*), rendering their discipline impure so that it cannot be called "endowed with pure ethical discipline.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who claim their own ethical discipline is pure, yet although they do not consort with women, nor engage in flirtatious speech, nor listen to their voices, they nevertheless watch men pursuing women.
At times, when he sees a woman following after a man, he immediately gives rise to greedy attachment. Such a bodhisattva has accomplished the dharma of desire;
he violates pure precepts, defiles the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and makes his conduct impure, such that he cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts.

Furthermore, there is another type of bodhisattva who claims his own precepts are pure, yet even though he does not engage in physical union with women, he engages in flirtatious conversation and jesting.
He heard their voices and saw men and women following one another, thinking, "They are being born in heaven to enjoy the five sensual pleasures.
Thus, such a bodhisattva accomplishes the dharma of desire, destroys pure precepts, defiles the holy life, and makes his morality impure;
he cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts. Good son, if there is a bodhisattva who maintains pure precepts and does not [act as described above]...

He observes the precepts not for the sake of the *śīlapāramitā*, nor for the sake of sentient beings, nor for the sake of gain and offerings, nor for the sake of bodhi, nor for the sake of nirvāṇa, nor for the sake of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
he guards and upholds the prohibitive precepts solely for the sake of the supreme, ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Good son, this is called the third way in which a bodhisattva is fully endowed with pure ethical discipline: being intimate with all virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Regarding the recognition of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*): if there is one who can teach faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom, causing others to receive and practice them, this is called a Bodhisattva’s spiritual friend. Fourth is delighting in tranquility;
"tranquility" refers to the tranquility of body and mind, observing the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) of all things—this is called tranquility. Fifth is diligence.
Vigor means binding the mind to contemplate the Four Noble Truths; even if one's head were on fire, one would never relinquish this—this is called vigor.

Sixth is the perfection of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃpanna*). The perfection of mindfulness means mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of ethical discipline (*śīla*), mindfulness of the devas, and mindfulness of renunciation (*tyāga*)—this is called the perfection of mindfulness. Seventh is gentle speech. Gentle speech means...
Truthful speech, excellent speech, greeting with kind words first, timely speech, and true speech—these are called gentle speech. Eighth is the protection of the Dharma.
As for the protection of the Dharma, it means to cherish and delight in the True Dharma, always enjoying its exposition, recitation, transcription, and contemplation of its meaning;
to proclaim and disseminate it widely so that it may circulate. Furthermore, if one sees someone transcribing, explaining, reciting, or praising [it]...

To praise those who contemplate the meaning [of the Dharma] by providing them with the necessities of life—namely, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—and to protect the Dharma by not sparing even one’s own body or life: this is called protecting the Dharma.
Ninth, when a bodhisattva sees fellow students or fellow precept-holders who are in want, they seek from others what is needed for incense bowls, dyeing robes, or caring for the sick.
One must provide them with clothing, food and drink, bedding, and housing. Tenth, one must be fully endowed with wisdom.
Wisdom refers to contemplating the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity; contemplating that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
and contemplating the two aspects of phenomena—namely, emptiness and non-emptiness, permanence and impermanence, bliss and non-bliss, self and non-self, and purity and non-purity.
That one pure phenomenon can be abandoned while another cannot; that one phenomenon arises from conditions while another arises from seeing conditions;
and that one phenomenon is the fruit of conditions while another is not the fruit of conditions—this is called being endowed with perfect wisdom.
"Good son, this is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of ten dharmas by which one can clearly perceive the signlessness of nirvāṇa.
Then the Lion’s Roar said: "As the Buddha previously declared... [This marks the second section, clarifying the departure from suffering and the transformation of obstacles.

It is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying the karmic obstacles to be transformed; second, clarifying the remedial paths that effect such transformation. Therein are two rounds of question and answer. First:

First, it is explained that because karma is indeterminate, hindrances can be transformed; next, it is explained that because karma is indeterminate, the Path can be cultivated. This consists of two parts:
first, the question and answer regarding wholesome karma, and second, the question and answer regarding unwholesome karma. Regarding the first inquiry on wholesome karma, there are five sections:
first, explaining its lack of limit; second, explaining its certainty; third, the triple lack of limit; fourth, the quadruple certainty; and fifth, concluding with an illustrative analogy.
The question consists of three parts: first, the opening statement; second, the reception of the essential meaning; and third, the concluding inquiry. Siṃhanāda said:

"World-Honored One, as the Buddha previously told Cunda, 'You have now attained the vision of the Buddha-nature, you have attained Great Nirvāṇa, and you have realized Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. What is the meaning of this?"
The initial address to Cunda was intended as a gradual introduction to the questions he wished to pose.
As the Buddha subsequently received his intent, the World-Honored One said:
"As stated in the Buddhist sūtras, if one gives to an animal, one receives a hundredfold reward; if one gives to an icchantika, one receives [a thousandfold reward]..."
A thousandfold is the reward for giving to one who maintains the precepts; a hundred-thousandfold is the reward if one gives to a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) who has severed the afflictions (kleśa).
One obtains immeasurable reward for giving to those on the four paths and the four fruits, up to the level of a Pratyekabuddha.
The merit and reward obtained from giving to a non-regressive Bodhisattva, to a Bodhisattva in their final birth, or to a Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is immeasurable.
It is immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and inconceivable.
Giving to animals yields a hundredfold [merit], while giving to an icchantika yields a thousandfold;

this is because the former (the animal) had evil causes in the past and thus receives a low retribution now, whereas the latter (the icchantika) had good causes in the past and thus receives a superior retribution now—hence the distinction of a hundred-thousandfold difference. As stated in the preceding text, killing an animal results in...

Regarding the question: "Is there an offense for killing an icchantika, or is there no offense? What does this mean? The answer is: An animal lacks the fault of severing the roots of goodness or slandering the Dharma, whereas an icchantika possesses such faults.
Thus concludes the inquiry of the Great Being Cunda.
If the Mahasattva Cunda were to receive such immeasurable retribution, that retribution would be inexhaustible;
when, then, would he attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi?
Next, in another sutra of the World-Honored One, it is further stated that regarding the certainty of the lower [karmic] inquiries, there are first two points to be acknowledged.

In another sutra of the World-Honored One, it is further stated: "If a person performs wholesome or unwholesome karma with a resolute mind, they will certainly obtain its retribution—whether to be experienced in the present life, in the next life, or in subsequent lives."
Next is the formal inquiry:
Since Cunda performed this good karma with a focused and earnest mind, one should know that this karma will certainly result in retribution.
If it is certain that he must undergo this retribution, how can he attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and how can he further behold the Buddha?
As for his nature:
although Cunda’s mind was grave, this karmic cause is superior; how could it be determined that he would not attain Buddhahood?
Furthermore, in the sutras of the World-Honored One of the three periods, it is repeatedly taught that even the gravest [karma] is ultimately inexhaustible.
Furthermore, in a sutra, the World-Honored One stated that making offerings to three types of persons yields inexhaustible retribution: first, the sick; second, one’s parents;
and third, the Tathāgata.
Fourth, in another sutra, the World-Honored One spoke of these again to clarify that [the result] is certain.
Furthermore, in a sutra, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:

"If all sentient beings were to have no karma pertaining to the desire realm, they would immediately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is the same for karma pertaining to the form and formless realms.
World-Honored One, as it is said in the verses of the *Dharmapada*: "Not in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean..."
Not entering mountains or rocks, nor is there any place on earth where one can escape and not receive [the results of] karma.
(5) Furthermore, Āniruddha, the following is raised as an illustration regarding the inquiry into fetters.
Furthermore, Aniruddha said to the World-Honored One, "I recall that in the past, by giving a single meal as an offering, I did not fall into the three evil realms for eighty thousand kalpas;
World-Honored One, if even the gift of a single meal can obtain such a reward, how much more so for Cunda,
who with a faithful heart gives to the Buddha and fully accomplishes the perfection of dāna?"
Next, the World-Honored One [addresses] the second point: if the fruits of good karma are inexhaustible, how can the four types of people who commit endless evil deeds attain Bodhi?

World-Honored One, if the retribution for good deeds cannot be exhausted, then those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, commit the five heinous crimes, or destroy the four [reliances]—[how could they attain it]?
How can the offenses of those who violate the heavy prohibitions and those who are icchantikas ever be exhausted?
If they cannot be exhausted, how can they perceive the Buddha-nature and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha spoke, providing the following answer in two parts: first, praising the question; second, answering it.

The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! There are only two kinds of persons who can attain immeasurable and boundless merit—merit that is incalculable and inexpressible—which can exhaust the violent river of drifting through birth and death and subdue all enemies."

Regarding the first point—that the Tathāgata, who crushes enemies and conquers Māra, is able to turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma—there is first the skillful question and second the skillful answer.

The answer is further divided into two parts: first, the introductory context (*nidāna*), and second, the formal response. The initial praise of the profundity of karmic power constitutes the introductory context for this response to the question.
Good son, among the ten powers of a Buddha, the power of karma is the most profound.
Yet, even within these ten powers, there is no hierarchy of superiority or inferiority; it is simply that such is their nature.
Furthermore, because the relative weight of karmic actions—whether they are determinate or indeterminate—is difficult to know and beyond the understanding of others, this power is called "great."

There are sentient beings who, regarding the conditions of karma, have little faith; for the sake of delivering them, [the Buddha] provides a fourfold correct answer: first, opening the provisional; second, revealing the real;
third, explaining the provisional; and fourth, explaining the real. First, regarding "opening the provisional":
Good son, there are sentient beings who, regarding the conditions of karma, have little faith; for the sake of delivering them, he therefore acts.
Thus it is said.
For those who lack faith, he proclaims with certainty:
"All karmic actions [bear fruit]. This second section reveals the reality.
Good son, all karmic actions are either light or heavy; these two types of karma, light and heavy, each further have two aspects:
the determinate and the indeterminate.
Since the nature of karma varies—being sometimes light, sometimes heavy, determinate, or indeterminate—how can it be said to be exclusively determinate?
Alternatively, there is someone who explains this as being provisional.

A son of good family might say: "If evil karma has no fruit, then how is it that a *caṇḍāla* by the name of Qi-xu was reborn in heaven, and Aṅgulimāla attained the fruit of liberation? It is for this reason [that one speaks of provisional teachings]."
Based on this meaning, one should know that while there is certainty regarding the performance of karma, there is no certainty regarding the attainment of its fruit.
In order to eliminate such false views, I have stated in the sūtras: "There is no action performed that does not result in a fruit."
It is simply because those who are heterodox do not believe this to be the definitive teaching.
Regarding the explanation of heavy karma being transformed into light, there are further two parts: first, the presentation of the two types of persons, the foolish and the wise.
"Good son, there may be heavy karma that can be made light, or light karma that can be made heavy; it is not otherwise."

All people possess only two qualities: folly and wisdom. Therefore, one should know that while it is not the case that all karma invariably yields its fruit, it is also not the case that it fails to yield fruit altogether.
From the phrase "from all sentient beings," two pairs emerge, resulting in two turns.
Good son, all sentient beings are of two kinds: first, those who possess wisdom; second, those who are ignorant.
A person with wisdom, by the power of their insight, can cause the most grievous karma of the hells to be experienced lightly in the present life.
An ignorant person, however, causes even light karma of the present life to be experienced heavily in the hells.
The wise transform what is heavy into light and what is determinate into indeterminate; the foolish transform what is light into heavy and what is indeterminate into determinate.
If this is so, the second round of question and answer below clarifies that karma which is indeterminate can be transformed through the cultivation of the Path.
The Lion’s Roar said: "World-Honored One, if this were so, then one should not seek the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*) nor the fruit of liberation.
The intent of the question is twofold: first, since evil karma is not fixed, what is the use of seeking nirvana through the holy life? Second, [the implication that]...
Since wholesome karma is not fixed, what need is there to seek nirvana through the holy life (*brahmacarya*)?
The Buddha’s response to this question is extensive; because the points of doubt and confusion to be refuted are numerous, they cannot be treated summarily.
If one does not understand this, the single practice will not be accomplished. Therefore, the phrasing of this passage is somewhat lengthy and is divided into four sections.

First, the actual clarification that because karma is indeterminate, one must cultivate the path; second, clarifying that there are many faults if karma were determinate; third, clarifying both the determinacy and indeterminacy of karma;
fourth, concluding that because it is indeterminate, one must cultivate the path. Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:

first, clarifying indeterminacy; second, the mutual sublation of good and evil. Regarding the first of these, there are two parts: first, if [karma] were determinate, there would be no need to labor in cultivating the path.
The Buddha said: "Good son, if all karma were to necessarily yield its fruit, then one should not seek the holy life or liberation.
Second, because [the timing of the fruit] is not fixed, one can cultivate the Path."
Because it is indeterminate, one practices the holy life and attains the fruit of liberation.
If one can remain far removed from inferior clarity, good and evil will not contend with one another.
Good son, if one can remain far removed from all unwholesome karma, one will obtain wholesome fruits; however, if one distances oneself from wholesome karma, then...
One obtains evil results because evil is not fixed;
it can become good. Because good is not fixed, it can become evil.
If all karma were fixed in its attainment of results, there would be many faults in the two following explanations of fixity. Furthermore, regarding these two, first is the explanation of fixity.

Since there would be no cultivation of the path because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) would already be clearly manifest, there would be many faults. Regarding the first [of these two], there are further two parts: the former is brief and the latter is detailed.
Within the brief section, there are two sub-sections; the first clarifies that if one is already in meditative concentration, there is no need for the cultivation of the path.
If all karma were necessarily to yield its fruit, then one would not need to seek the cultivation of the Noble Path.
Next, it is explained that if one does not cultivate the path, there is no liberation.
Since there is no liberation for any noble person who does not cultivate the path, noble persons cultivate the path in order to destroy determinate karma.
Because they receive light retribution, indeterminate karma has no [fixed] fruit of retribution.

If all karma were [determinately] inferior, there would be two ways of explaining it extensively; furthermore, there are two [aspects]: first, if determinate [karma] were explained extensively, then cultivation would not be necessary.
If all karma were necessarily to yield its fruit, then one should not seek to cultivate the Noble Path.
Next, if a person remains far removed from [the lower realms], it is explained at length that if one does not practice, there will be no prospect of liberation.
If there were a person who, having distanced themselves from the cultivation of the Noble Path, could attain liberation—that is impossible;
likewise, that one could not attain liberation and yet attain nirvana—that too is impossible.
Good son, all karma is determinate; this is the second [point] clarifying that determinate karma has many faults. Furthermore, there are two [aspects].

First, the fault of the certainty of karma is clarified; next, the fault of the certainty of person and time is clarified. The preceding text is further divided into two parts: first, the explicit demonstration of the fault.
"Good son, if all karma were to necessarily yield its fruit, then the purely wholesome karma performed in a single lifetime should..."
If one were to experience peace and happiness forever, then even the most grievous evil karma committed in a single lifetime would result in experiencing great suffering and affliction forever; thus,
the wholesome and unwholesome karma created in a single instance would lead to the eternal experience of good and evil without any end in sight.
Next, regarding the result of karma: "If it were so," this concludes the refutation of the path of cultivation.
If the result of karma were such [as you claim], then there would be no path of cultivation, liberation, or nirvāṇa.

"The person acts and the person receives" introduces the second section, which clarifies the fault of the fixed timing of the person; this further consists of two parts: first, the actual clarification of the fault, and next...
Regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*), there is no need to cultivate the path [to abandon them]. Furthermore, there are two points: first, clarifying the faults in the fixed nature of persons.

If a human acts as a human and receives [the fruit] as a human, and a Brahmin acts as a Brahmin and receives [the fruit] as a Brahmin—if this were so—then there should be no such thing as low-caste people or those of inferior status; humans should be eternally humans, and Brahmins should be eternally Brahmins.
If karma were fixed, then the six realms of existence— humans, devas, and so forth— and their status as noble or base, beautiful or ugly, would forever remain as they are and could never be changed.
This explains the fault of fixity regarding the karma created during childhood that manifests in later life.
Karma performed in childhood should be experienced in childhood; it should not be experienced in middle age or old age.
Evil karma committed in old age should not be experienced immediately upon taking birth in hell; rather, it should wait until one is old before being experienced.
If there were no longevity in middle age, how could one reach old age? [Without middle-age longevity,] what karma would there be to reach old age?
Because there is no loss [of karma].
Just as actions performed during childhood are experienced again during childhood, so it is for youth and old age.
Furthermore, if there were no loss of subsequent karma, there would be no need for the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) as a concluding summary.
If karma were not subject to loss, how could there be the cultivation of the path or nirvana?
Good son, there are two kinds of karma. [The third section] extensively explains that karma is both determinate and indeterminate. Furthermore, this section has two parts:
first, the presentation of the two chapters on determinate and indeterminate karma; second, their explanation.
Good son, karma is of two kinds: determinate and indeterminate.
Yet, there are four permutations of karma: first, determinate in retribution but indeterminate in time; second, determinate in time but indeterminate in retribution;

third, determinate in both; and fourth, indeterminate in both. Now, these are combined into two chapters: "Determinate in Retribution but Indeterminate in Time" and "Determinate in Both Time and Retribution."

When entering the chapter on "Certainty of Rebirth" (*niyata-pada*), both the certainty of meditative attainment (*samādhi-niyata*) and the uncertainty of the timing of retribution (*aniyata-kāla-vipāka*) are equally uncertain;
likewise, when entering the chapter on "Uncertainty of Rebirth," this is because the primary intent in all cases is based upon the certainty of the retribution itself as the standard.

Fixed karma has two types. [This concludes] the second section, the explanation of the headings, which is further divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the heading on fixed karma, which is very extensive;

and second, the explanation of the heading on non-fixed karma, which is extremely brief, consisting of only twelve characters. Within the first explanation of the fixed heading, there are two further sections:
first, fixed in both retribution and time; and second, fixed in retribution but not fixed in time.
Fixed karma is of two kinds: first, fixed as to retribution; second, fixed as to time. Alternatively, there is that which is fixed as to retribution but not fixed as to time;
when conditions converge, one receives it. This immediately explains what was previously explained regarding fixed retribution and unfixed time.

When conditions converge, one experiences [karmic results], which may be experienced in three periods: namely, experience in the present life, experience in the next life, or experience in subsequent lives. Regarding those whose timing is indefinite:

although they ought to be experienced during the three periods of the present, the next life, or subsequent lives, they are not experienced; such cases will never be experienced. As for those whose timing is indefinite but whose retribution is fixed:
the retributions for good and evil are complete, yet they must await the convergence of conditions; once the conditions converge, [the result is experienced].
The retribution received is without the slightest discrepancy.
Regarding the phrase "if the concentrated mind acts," there are two interpretations: first, both are determined; furthermore, there are three further explanations:

first, determination of retribution; second, determination of time; third, the double conclusion. The initial passage also has three parts: first, explaining determinate karma; second, returning to the state of being indeterminate; third, the explanation.
Regarding the proof of the transformation of doubt, this first section correctly clarifies meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Good son,
if one performs deeds such as wholesome or unwholesome actions with a concentrated mind, and having performed them, gives rise to deep faith, joy,
and the making of vows to make offerings to the Triple Gem, this is called "concentrated karma" (*samāhita-karman*).
Furthermore, there are four matters that adorn [the mind]: first, faith; second, joy; third, making vows; and fourth, making offerings.
This refers to adorning wholesome karma with these four matters; the same applies by analogy to unwholesome [karma]. Namely: first, faith in evil; second, joy; third, making vows;
and fourth, making offerings to evil factions—thus adorning evil with these.
Second, regarding the roots of goodness of the wise, this section clarifies that these karmic actions can again encounter conditions and be transformed, such that they remain indeterminate.
Furthermore, there are three points: first, the wise can transform the heavy into the light.
Good son, because the roots of goodness of the wise are deep and firm and difficult to shake, they are able to cause heavy karma to become light.
Second, fools transform light karma into heavy;
those who are deluded and lack wholesome roots can cause light karma to produce a heavy retribution.
Third, these fetters are indeterminate.
For this reason, all karmic actions are not termed "fixed.
This concludes the third section, which resolves doubts by providing scriptural proof for the transformation [of karma]:
"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has no karma for the hells; yet, for the sake of sentient beings, he makes a great vow to be born in the hells."
In the middle [of this passage], there is a concern that people might doubt the various sages and give rise to the view that they were born in hell because their karma was fixed;
therefore, it is now explained that in reality they possessed no such karma, but were born therein solely through the power of their vows in order to deliver sentient beings. Thus it is concluded.
It is said that what is not experienced in the present life or in a future life is not a karmic retribution.

Regarding what was called "the transformation through realization" (*pratyakṣa-parāvṛtti*): although the preceding text mentioned the transformation of karma by the ignorant and the wise, its proof had not yet been seen.

Now it is clarified that when a sage enters into evil states to transform sentient beings, if their karma were not transformed, they would be of no benefit there; since they are indeed beneficial, [it follows that their karma is transformed].
It should be known that within this there are further two parts: first, the brief, and second, the detailed.
Good son, in the past, when the lifespan of sentient beings was one hundred years, I saw countless beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges receiving retribution in the hells.
Having seen this, I immediately made a great vow to take on a body in the hells; at that time, however, the Bodhisattva truly possessed no such karma.

For the sake of sentient beings, I undergo the retribution of the hells; at that time, while within the hells for immeasurable years, I extensively expound and analyze the twelve divisions of the sūtras for all those who commit transgressions.
Once they have heard them, they destroy their evil karmic retributions, thereby emptying the hells—except for the icchantikas.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s non-reception of retribution in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.
Evil karma.
Furthermore, son of good family, I have seen that within this Bhadrakalpa, immeasurable sentient beings fall among the animals to undergo the fruits of their evil karma;
having seen this, I have again made a vow to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, and for that purpose, I sometimes manifest as a deer.

The bodies of deer, bears, pigeons, monkeys, dragons, snakes, garuḍas, fish, turtles, foxes, rabbits, oxen, and horses—O son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva truly has no such evil karma of the animal realm;
rather, by the power of their great vows, they manifest and receive these bodies for the sake of sentient beings.
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not experience this evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.
Furthermore, son of good family, within this Bhadrakalpa, there are again immeasurable and boundless sentient beings born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
They consume vomit, spittle, fat, flesh, pus, blood, excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva for an immeasurable lifespan of hundreds of thousands of myriads of years;
they have never even heard the name of water or gruel, much less having seen it with their own eyes and being able to drink it. Even if they see it from afar...
When the intention to produce water arises, it reaches its destination and transforms into fierce fire and thick blood;
or at times, it does not change, and many people holding spears and javelins appear to guard and seize it, preventing it from proceeding forward;
or when summer rains fall upon the body, they turn into fire—this is called the retribution for evil karma. Son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva truly has none of these things.
Because he wishes to transform sentient beings and lead them to liberation, he makes a vow to undergo such a body as a result of evil karma;
this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s non-experiencing of that evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.
Good son, during the Bhadrakalpa, I was born into a family of butchers, where I raised chickens, pigs, cattle, and sheep, and practiced hunting with nets and snares, fishing, and acting as a caṇḍāla.
To abandon [the path] and engage in robbery and plunder—such evil karma truly does not exist for a bodhisattva.

Rather, in order to liberate sentient beings, they assume such a body through the power of their great vows; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-experiencing of such evil karma in the present, future, or subsequent lives.
Son of good family, within this Bhadrakalpa, they may again be born in borderlands and frequently give rise to greed and hatred.

Hating, deluded, and ignorant, practicing unrighteousness, lacking faith in the Triple Gem or the retribution of future lives, and unable to honor their parents, elders, seniors, or those of long standing—good son, at that time a Bodhisattva truly possesses none of these karmic conditions;
yet, for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain liberation, he is born among them through the power of his great vows. This is called a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
"O son of good family, this evil karma will not be experienced in the present life, nor in a future life;

rather, within this Bhadrakalpa, you shall again receive a female body—an evil body, a body of greed, a body of hatred, a body of delusion, a body of envy, a body of stinginess, a body of illusion, a body of deception, and a body shrouded by the hindrances."

Good son, at that time, the bodhisattva likewise possesses no such karma; rather, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to liberation, through the power of his great vows he aspires to be born therein.
This is called the non-experiencing of evil karma in the present, future, or subsequent lives by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Good son, during this Bhadrakalpa, I have received the bodies of a eunuch, one without sexual organs, one with dual organs, and those of indeterminate gender.
Good son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva truly possesses no such evil bodily karma;
rather, for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain liberation, they vow by the power of their great vows to be born therein.

This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva not experiencing this evil karma in the present, future, or subsequent lives. Good son, during the Bhadrakalpa, I further practiced as a non-Buddhist ascetic (tīrthika).

The son of a dry-woman (khañja-putra) accepted that teaching with faith: there is no giving and no sacrifice; there is no retribution for giving or sacrificing; there is no karma of good or evil, nor any retribution for good or evil;
there is no present world nor a future world; there is no "this" and no "that"; there are no noble ones (ārya);
there is no transformation body (nirmāṇakāya); and there is no path or nirvāṇa. "Good son, the Bodhisattva truly has no such evil karma; it is only for the sake of..."
To cause sentient beings to attain liberation, they accept these false dharmas through the power of their great vows;
this is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s not experiencing the retribution of such evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.
I recall that in the past, when I was descending with Devadatta to the second heaven of the Śakras, there were again two [sections]: first, the explanation of the present retribution;
next, the double summary of rebirth. Regarding the present retribution, there are again two parts: the former clarifies how I was obstructed by Devadatta, which is a matter of the present life.
"Noble son, I recall that in the past, Devadatta and I were both caravan leaders, each with five hundred merchants in our retinue.
For the sake of profit, we went out to the great ocean to gather precious jewels.
Due to the conditions of our evil karma, we encountered a violent storm on the way that wrecked our ships, and all our companions perished. At that time, it was only I and Devadatta who remained."

Due to the karmic fruit of abstaining from killing, which results in longevity, when we were all blown by the wind onto dry land, Devadatta, out of greed and attachment for his treasures, fell into great sorrow and anguish and wailed aloud.
I then said to him, "Devadatta, there is no need to weep. Devadatta said to me, "Listen attentively, listen attentively! It is as if there were a person..."
A person in extreme poverty and distress went to a cemetery, grasped a corpse with his hand, and spoke these words:
"I pray that you now grant me the pleasure of death, and I shall grant you the life of poverty. At that moment, the corpse immediately sat up and said to the poor man:
"Good son, accept for yourself this life of poverty; as for me, I am now exceedingly happy."
"This death was indeed not a joy for you, as it occurred while you were in poverty;
yet today, since I have neither the joy of death nor am free from poverty, how could I help but weep? I then comforted him further, saying, "Do not grieve;
there are two pearls here of immeasurable value. I shall divide one of them to bestow upon you as a gift. I then divided and gave it to him.
He said to me, "A man who possesses destiny can obtain this treasure; if one lacks destiny, who could possibly obtain it?
At that time, I was exhausted and went beneath a tree to rest and sleep.

Devadatta’s greed was burning fiercely, and for the sake of the remaining jewel, he conceived an evil intent, gouged out my eyes, and plundered my treasure. Thereupon, I suffered from the outbreak of a wound.
While I was groaning and crying out, a woman came to me and asked, "Virtuous one, why are you groaning and crying out like this?
I then explained my past history to her in detail. Having heard it, the woman asked me again, "What is your name?
I replied, "My name is Satyavādin (Truth-speaker). She said, "How do you know yourself to be a truth-speaker?"
"I now make this vow: if I harbor any ill will toward Devadatta at this moment, may my eyes become thus forever blind;
if I have none, may they be restored. Having spoken these words, his eyes were restored to their former state.
"Good son, this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s teaching on retribution in the present life."
Next, he was oppressed by Karapu.
"Good son, I recall that in the past, I was born into a brahmin family in the city of Pūṇḍravardhana in South India.

At that time, there was a king named Karapu; his nature was violent and cruel, and he was arrogant and conceited. In the prime of his youth and possessed of a beautiful complexion, he was addicted to sensual pleasures."
While I was dwelling in the five desires, at that time, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, I was practicing silent meditation outside the city.
At that moment, the king—during the spring when the trees were in full bloom—went out of the city with his retinue, palace ladies, and handmaidens to sightsee.
While he amused himself with the five desires beneath the trees, those handmaidens left the king to play and came to where I was. I...
At that time, wishing to sever his greed, I was about to preach the Dharma for him when the King arrived.
Upon seeing me, he immediately conceived an evil thought and asked me, "Have you now attained the fruit of Arhatship? I replied, "I have not.
He asked again, "Have you obtained the fruit of Anāgāmin? I replied, "I have not. He then said, "If you have not yet attained..."
"These two fruits constitute the fulfillment of the affliction of sensual desire. How can you, being self-indulgent, look upon me as a woman?
I then replied, "Great King, you should know that although I have not yet severed the fetters of sensual desire, my inner mind is truly free from attachment.
The King said, "Foolish man! There are sages in the world who subsist on air and fruit; yet they still feel greed when seeing beautiful forms. How much more so for one like you!"
"You are in the prime of your youth and have not yet severed your greed for desire; how can you look upon forms and remain unattached?
I say, Great King, that your lack of attachment when seeing forms is truly not due to practicing breath control or eating fruits, but rather stems from fixing your mind on impermanence and impurity.
The King said, "If one treats others with contempt and gives rise to slander, how can they be said to be cultivating pure precepts? I replied, "Great..."
"If the King harbors a jealous heart, then he slanders me; if he has no jealous heart, why does he say he slanders me?
The King said, "Venerable Sir, what is called 'precept' (śīla)? The Great King replied, "Patience is called precept. The King said, "If patience is the precept, then I shall cut off your ears.
If you can endure it, I shall know that you uphold the precepts. He then cut off those ears. At that time, though my ears were severed, my facial expression remained unchanged.
When King Aśoka saw this occurrence, he immediately admonished his ministers, saying, "A great being such as this should not be subjected to harm.
The king asked his ministers, "How do you know that this is a great being? The ministers replied, "We see that when he undergoes suffering, his countenance does not change.
The king spoke again, saying, "I shall test him further to see whether he changes or remains unchanged," and he immediately had his nose cut off.

Their noses were severed and their hands and feet cut off. At that time, as the Bodhisattva had already cultivated compassion for immeasurable and boundless eons out of pity for suffering sentient beings, the Four Heavenly Kings, harboring anger and resentment, rained down sand, gravel, and stones.
When the King saw this, his heart was filled with great terror; he came before me, knelt on both knees, and said: "I only pray that you will take pity on me and grant me your hearing."
"I confess my words, Great King; my mind is free from anger, just as it is free from greed.
The King asked, "Virtuous One, how can you know that your mind is free from anger and resentment? I then made this vow:

"If it is truly true that I am free from anger and resentment, may this body of mine be restored to its former state. Having uttered this aspiration, my body was immediately restored. This is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Sāṃkhyāya says it is a retribution in the present life.

The *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā* calls him Kali; the *Sutra on the Wise and the Foolish* calls him Kali; and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* calls him Kāli—these are all the same person, differing only in their Sanskrit pronunciation.
As for the name "Patience" (*kṣānti*) being called "Precept" (*śīla*), this refers to the sequential inclusion of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), which are all [contained therein].
It is said that patience (*kṣānti*) is precept (*śīla*); why is it now stated that patience is called precept?

This is because precept and patience mutually support one another. If precept is internally clear and externally pure, it is merely patience; regarding killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, precept merely prevents these.
Therefore, patience possesses the power to constitute precept; thus it is said that patience is called precept. Now this is clarified.
Patience encompasses the entire dharma-realm and contains all dharmas; it cannot be fully described, but for the sake of illustration, one aspect is cited:
thus patience is called "precept. The scriptural text states: "To 'nose' (ni) is to cut off the nose; to 'foot' (yue) is to sever the feet."

Regarding the second pair that concludes the two types of retribution—namely, the retribution in the present life (*upapadyavedanīya*) and the subsequent retribution (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) for wholesome karma, as well as unwholesome karma—it is likewise for sons of good family. Wholesome karma entails both retribution in the present life and subsequent retribution; unwholesome karma is also exactly thus.
Regarding the third pair of concluding statements on the two certainties at the time of retribution when a Bodhisattva attains Bodhi: first, the paired conclusion;
second, the individual conclusion. As for the first passage:
"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all karmas..."

All receive retribution in the present life; those who receive retribution for unwholesome and evil karma in the present life are like a king who, having committed an evil act, causes the heavens to send down calamitous rain, or like a person who points out a bear to a hunter or a deer with the color of a jewel, causing their own hands to fall off—this is called receiving the fruit of retribution for evil karma in the present life.
Regarding retribution in the next life: it is as in the case of an icchantika who commits the four grave prohibitions and the five heinous crimes.
Regarding future retribution, it is like a person who upholds the precepts and makes a profound vow, wishing that in future lives they may always obtain such a body of pure discipline;
should there be sentient beings with a lifespan of one hundred years or eighty years, they would become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*) therein to transform and guide those beings.
Although the icchantika who commits the five heinous crimes cannot receive immediate retribution, they likewise cannot receive retribution in subsequent lives or in future births;
at this time, their retribution is fixed. A text states: "When one attains Bodhi, all karmas receive immediate retribution.
At this time, the Bodhisattva has severed all delusions and no longer receives retribution in subsequent lives; there is only the single remaining birth.

Because one attains the fruit of Buddhahood, it is said that "present retribution" (kṣipra-phala) is attained. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that if the term "one lifetime" were taken as identical to the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence), it would not be called present retribution;
for since the attainment of one grade of wisdom and the severance of one grade of afflictions constitutes "one lifetime," it is still termed present retribution despite being "one lifetime.
One view maintains that only the *dharmakāya* Buddha possesses this present retribution; another view maintains that it is merely a trace (*nirmāṇa*).
That the Buddha-body possesses this present retribution refers specifically to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
If karma were necessarily to yield results in the present life, then—secondly, regarding the fixed timing of the result—the text states:

"Good son, if karma were necessarily to yield results in the present life, one would not be able to obtain results in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) or in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*)."
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the karma for the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, he cannot obtain retribution in the present life.
This is because, as the timing is fixed, he obtains only retribution in a future birth;
furthermore, because the cultivation of the karma for the thirty-two marks is difficult to accomplish and must necessarily serve as the cause for Buddhahood, there is no present retribution at all.
[Answer:
If karma does not obtain the three kinds of retribution, these twelve characters [beginning with] "below" explain the section on the indeterminate.
If karma does not obtain the three kinds of retribution, it is called "indeterminate."
Since this can be understood from what precedes, it need not be stated.

If one were to say that all karmas necessarily result in the lower [realms], then the fourth fetter would become indeterminate; furthermore, since there is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the first two fetters would necessarily be determinate, which would constitute an error.
Good son, if one says that all karmas necessarily yield their retribution, then it would be impossible to cultivate the holy life, attain liberation, or reach nirvana.
You should know that such a person is not my disciple, but a follower of Māra.

If one says that some karmas are determinate while others are indeterminate—where the determinate are those with retribution in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives, and the indeterminate are those received when conditions converge, but not otherwise—[then this is correct].
Because they do not accept [these views], it should be understood that such persons will attain the holy life, liberation, and nirvāṇa;
they are truly my disciples and not the retinue of Māra.
Next, for all classes of beings, the remaining fetters are indeterminate as to whether they will be attained.
Good son, for all sentient beings, indeterminate karma is abundant while determinate karma is scarce.

For this reason, there is the cultivation of the Path and the cultivation that reverses the Path; thus, even determinate heavy karma can be made to be experienced lightly, whereas indeterminate karma is not necessarily experienced as retribution in the present life.

There are two kinds of persons. [This concludes] the second section, which clarifies the path that can transform obstacles. Furthermore, this is divided into three parts: first, the person who transforms obstacles;

second, the practice for transforming obstacles; and third, the characteristics of transformation. Within the first of these, there are again two sections: first, the explanation by way of principle (*dharmadeśanā*).

Good son, there are two kinds of persons: first, those who transform what is indeterminate into determinate, what is to be experienced in the present life into what is to be experienced in the next life or subsequent lives, and what is to be experienced as heavy retribution into what is to be experienced among humans rather than in hell;

and second, those who transform what is determinate into indeterminate, what is to be experienced in the next life back into what is to be experienced in the present life, what is heavy retribution into what is light, and what is to be experienced in hell into what is experienced lightly among humans. Such are these two types of persons.
The first is the ignorant and the second is the wise; the wise are treated lightly while the ignorant are made to bear heavy [punishment].
Next, twelve similes are presented: the first and last two have a corresponding application (*saṃyoga*), while the ten in between lack one.
"Good son, it is like two men who have committed an offense against a king; he whose retinue is large has his crime considered light."
For those with little [merit], what should have been light becomes heavy.
It is the same for both the foolish and the wise: because the wise have abundant wholesome karma, they experience heavy [retribution] as light;
because the foolish have little wholesome karma, they experience light [retribution] as heavy.
Good son, it is like two men, one stout and strong, the other emaciated and weak; both sink into deep mud, yet the stout one is able to emerge while the weak one perishes.
Good son, it is like two men who both consume poison; one possesses the power of mantras and *agada* medicine, while the other does not.
In those who possess medicinal spells, poison cannot cause injury; in those who lack medicinal spells, death occurs immediately upon ingestion.
Good son, it is like two people who both drink much liquid: one has a powerful digestive fire and the other is weak.
He whose digestive fire is strong can digest it, while he whose digestive fire is weak suffers from it as a malady.
Good son, it is like two men who have been imprisoned by a king: one is wise and the other is foolish.
The wise man is able to obtain liberation, while the foolish man has no prospect of release.
Good son, it is like two people traveling together on a perilous path: one has eyes, while the other is blind.
The person with eyes passes straight through without harm, whereas the blind man falls and tumbles into a deep and dangerous pit.
Good son, it is like two people who both drink wine; one eats much before drinking, while the other eats little.
The one who ate much experiences no suffering from the drink, whereas the one who ate little falls ill from it.
Good son, it is like two men who both oppose an enemy army: one is fully equipped and adorned with armor and weapons, while the other is bare-bodied.
The one possessing weapons can defeat the enemy, whereas the one who is bare cannot even save himself.
Furthermore, there were two people whose clothes were soiled by excrement and filth; one noticed it and immediately washed them, while the other noticed it but did not wash them.
The clothes of the one who immediately washed them became clean and pure, whereas the clothes of the one who did not wash them grew increasingly foul with grime.
Furthermore, there were two people riding together in a carriage; one had a spare axle and the other did not.
The one with a spare axle proceeded according to his will, while the one without a spare axle could not move from his place.
Regarding the ninth of the ten similes in the *Madhyama-āgama*, it states: "There is no spare axle. There are two interpretations:

first, that when traveling far by carriage, one must store an axle as a spare to prepare for breakage or injury, just as a sovereign driving a chariot has a spare ox to replace one that becomes weary;
second, that this character is an error and should be "spoke" (*ara*) rather than "axle" (*akṣa*), meaning that if one wishes to ride in a carriage, one requires these spokes and axles.
Furthermore, there were two people traveling together on a desolate road; one was provided with provisions while the other was not.
The one with provisions was able to cross the perilous terrain, whereas the one who went empty-handed could not pass through.
Furthermore, there were two men who were robbed by bandits; one possessed a treasure storehouse while the other had none.
The one with the treasure storehouse felt no sorrow or distress, whereas the one without the storehouse was filled with grief and affliction.
The same applies to the wise and the foolish: those who possess a treasury of merit receive heavy karma as light, while those who lack such a treasury receive light karma as heavy.
Following this, the second section clarifies the practice of transforming hindrances through a series of questions and answers; herein begins the initial question.
Second, first receiving the essential meaning and then posing the formal question:
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said, "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, it is not the case that all karma invariably receives its fixed fruit,
nor is it the case that all sentient beings invariably undergo [the results]."

"Bhagavān, how is it that sentient beings cause light retribution in the present life to become heavy retribution in hell, or heavy retribution in hell to become light retribution in the present life?
What kind of light karma results in heavy retribution, and what kind of heavy karma results in light retribution? This was the intent of the question.

The Buddha’s response further consists of three parts: first, he distinguishes between the foolish and the wise, showing that their relative gravity is not fixed; second, he presents six successive points;
third, he provides an exposition using fourteen similes of good sons and various miscellaneous metaphors. The initial section contains two parts: first, the identification of the persons;
second, the dharma-exposition which extensively clarifies their characteristics.
The Buddha said: "All sentient beings are of two kinds: first, those with wisdom; second, those who are ignorant and deluded.

If one can cultivate bodily discipline, verbal discipline, mental cultivation, and wisdom, such a person is called wise. If one cannot cultivate bodily discipline, verbal discipline, mental cultivation, and wisdom, such a person is called ignorant and deluded."
Regarding the phrase "cultivating body, precepts, mind, and wisdom," when these are combined into a single expression, they refer only to the two matters of precepts and wisdom.
If one cultivates these precepts and wisdom, they can cause heavy karma to become light; without these two, they cause what is light to become heavy.

When expressed separately, it is said: "cultivate the body, cultivate the precepts, cultivate the mind, and cultivate wisdom. The body refers to the sevenfold precepts (*saptāṅga-śīla*), which guard the mind.
To cultivate the mind through tranquility and to cultivate wisdom through focused concentration is *prajñā*.
What is meant by "not cultivating the body"? If one cannot restrain the five sensory faculties, it is called not cultivating the body.
If one cannot receive and uphold the seven kinds of pure precepts, it is called not cultivating morality (*śīla*). If the mind is not disciplined, it is called not cultivating the mind.
To cultivate noble conduct while not cultivating wisdom is [a deficiency].
Regarding the sevenfold pure precepts, these are the seven branches of morality (*śīla*).

Not cultivating the mind refers to not cultivating the three characteristics—namely, the three phases of entering, abiding, and exiting—and furthermore, being unable to contemplate the three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, as well as non-arising and non-abiding.

Regarding "those who do not cultivate wisdom despite not having extinguished [defilements]," this refers to those who do not cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*); within the holy life, three factors are complete, with wisdom as the primary one.
Next are the six successive stages.
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body cannot fulfill the essence of pure precepts;
one who does not cultivate the precepts accepts and keeps the eight kinds of impure things; one who does not cultivate the mind cannot practice the three marks;

and one who does not cultivate wisdom does not cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is unable to contemplate the body, nor is able to contemplate...

Regarding form and observing the characteristics of form, one does not observe the characteristics of the body, does not know the enumeration of the body, and does not know that this body moves from here to there.

One gives rise to the perception of a body within what is not a body, and produces the perception of form within what is not form. Therefore, one is greedily attached to the self-body and the enumeration of the body;
this is called "not cultivating the body" and "not cultivating precepts. If one receives the lower precepts, it is not called cultivation.

Regarding the limits of upholding the precepts: if one observes the precepts for the sake of self-interest, for the sake of self-discipline, or is unable to universally bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings;

if it is not for the purpose of protecting and upholding the unsurpassed True Dharma, but rather for the sake of being born in the heavens to experience the pleasures of the five desires, this is not called cultivating the precepts.
As for not cultivating the mind: if the mind is distracted and cannot be focused single-mindedly to guard its own sphere—that is, its own objective domain—[it is not cultivating the mind].

"Those" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness; "the objects of others" refers to the five desires. If one cannot cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, it is called not cultivating the mind.
Not skillfully guarding the mind amidst evil deeds is called not cultivating wisdom.
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is unable to deeply contemplate that this body is impermanent, non-abiding, precarious, and fragile, perishing and decaying moment by moment.
Those who do not cultivate the precepts within the realm of Māra cannot fulfill the śīla-pāramitā;
those who do not cultivate the mind cannot fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā; and those who do not cultivate wisdom cannot fulfill the prajñā-pāramitā.
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is greedily attached to the self-body and the body belonging to the self, holding that the self-body is permanent, eternal, and subject to no change.
One who does not cultivate ethical discipline performs the ten wholesome actions for the sake of their own body.

One who does not cultivate the mind is unable to restrain the mind amidst unwholesome karma. One who does not cultivate wisdom, because they cannot restrain the mind, is unable to distinguish between the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Furthermore, regarding these dharmas: one who does not cultivate the body does not sever the view of a self; one who does not cultivate ethical discipline does not sever the grasping for precepts;
one who does not cultivate the mind performs actions of greed and hatred, heading toward hell; and one who does not cultivate wisdom does not sever the mind of delusion.
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is unable to contemplate that although the body may be without fault, it is nonetheless a constant enemy.

Regarding the first "visible" [aspect] mentioned in the second section: "the enumeration of the body" refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and so forth.

As for "lower precepts," these refer to the precepts regarding chickens, pigs, oxen, pheasants, and the like; furthermore, it is said that one maintains these precepts for the sake of the five desires of the heavens.
"Those who observe the lower precepts and the peripheral precepts": He of Hexi (Daorong) says that the five precepts of the non-Buddhists are not within the Buddha-dharma;
because the internal dharma is called "middle," these are termed "peripheral.

Alternatively, it is said that those who observe the precepts of pleasure to the extreme reach the limit of pleasure, while those who observe the precepts of austerity reach the limit of suffering. The remaining four are as stated in the text.
Good son, it is like a man who has an enemy constantly pursuing him, seeking an opportunity to strike. Once a wise person has become aware of this, he fixes his mind on careful protection;
if he does not protect himself with such care, he will be harmed. The bodies of all sentient beings are also like this:
they must always be nourished and sustained with food and drink, whether warm or cold. If one does not thus protect and guard them with care, they will immediately disintegrate. Good son.
Suppose a man, like a brahmin serving the fire deity, constantly offers incense, flowers, praise, prostrations, offerings, and service for a full hundred years;
yet if he should touch it even once, it immediately burns his hand.
Although this fire receives such offerings, it never, in a single thought-moment, repays the kindness of its server. The bodies of all sentient beings are likewise; although...
For many years, they provided them with fine incense, flowers, necklaces, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness; yet,

when encountering various adverse internal or external conditions, those [objects] were immediately destroyed, and [the recipients] no longer remembered the kindness of the food and clothing provided by their former benefactors.
Regarding the second noble son, it says: "The Fire God (Agnideva) means that fire is the mouth of the gods.
If one makes offerings to him, there is no smell of smoke from fish or meat reaching the heavens; because the gods receive this fragrance, fire is their mouth.

Furthermore, non-Buddhists serve fire and take fire as their teacher; they also use this fire to make offerings to their teacher, and because they revere the teacher, they address fire [as the teacher]."
He is the mouth of the gods.
Good son, it is like a king who keeps four venomous snakes in a single basket and entrusts them to a man, commanding him to look after and nourish them.
If even one of these four snakes should give rise to anger, it can kill that man; thus, that man is constantly terrified.
Seeking food and drink while constantly guarding against the four great poisonous snakes of the sentient beings' four elements is likewise.
Good son, just as one who has been ill for a long time should seek treatment with a sincere heart—if one does not diligently seek rescue, death will surely follow without doubt;
so it is with the bodies of all sentient beings, which should always be [tended].
One should collect the mind and not allow it to become negligent; for if one is negligent, one will then be destroyed and ruined.

Good son, it is like an unbaked clay jar that cannot endure wind, rain, being struck, or being crushed; the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise unable to endure hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, rain, being beaten, binding, or harsh abuse.
Good son, just as one must always carefully protect an abscess before it has ripened, so too should one protect oneself.
It does not allow others to touch it, and if there is contact, it results in great pain; the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise so.
Good son, just as a mule that becomes pregnant destroys its own body, the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise so:
when wind or cold arises within them, the body is harmed. Good son, for example, just as a plantain tree withers when it bears fruit, [so it is with the body].
The bodies of sentient beings are also like this, O son of good family. Just as a plantain tree has no solid core within, so too is the body of all sentient beings, O son of good family.
Just as snakes, rats, and jackals harbor mutual feelings of enmity toward one another, so too are the four great elements of sentient beings, O son of good family.
For example, just as a king of geese takes no pleasure in burial mounds...
The Bodhisattva is likewise; he does not crave or delight in this body, which is a cemetery.
Good son, it is like a *caṇḍāla* who, for seven generations in succession, has not abandoned his trade and is therefore despised by others. The seed of this body is also like that;
its seeds—sperm and blood—are ultimately impure. Because they are impure, [this body] is [shunned] by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

"Reproachful son of good family, this body is not like Mount Malaya, which produces sandalwood, nor can it produce blue lotuses (*utpala*), white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), *campaka*, *mallika*, or *vārṣika* flowers.
Its nine orifices constantly leak impurities such as pus and blood; its place of birth is foul-smelling, filthy, ugly, and loathsome, and it is always accompanied by various worms."
"Good son, it is as if there were a most excellent and pure garden in the world;
yet when a corpse enters it, it becomes impure, and the multitude all abandon it, no longer conceiving any attachment. The realm of form (rūpadhātu) is likewise:
although it is pure and wondrous, because it involves a physical body, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas collectively abandon it. Good son, if there is..."
If one cannot contemplate in this way, it is not called cultivating the body nor cultivating the precepts. Good son,
if one cannot contemplate that the precepts are the staircase for all wholesome dharmas and the root of all wholesome dharmas—
just as the earth is the basis from which all trees grow, and the precepts are the foremost leader of all roots of goodness, like a merchant leader— [then one does not cultivate them].
The precepts that lead all merchants are the supreme banner of all wholesome dharmas, like the victory banner established by Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
These precepts can forever sever all evil karma and the three evil realms; they can cure evil diseases, just like a medicinal tree.
The precepts are the provisions for the perilous path of birth and death; they are the armor that crushes the evil thieves of the fetters; they are the extinguisher of the fetters.

The precepts are a potent incantation against venomous snakes and a bridge for crossing over evil karmic actions. Those who cannot contemplate in this manner are said to be those who do not cultivate the precepts.
One who does not cultivate the mind is unable to observe the mind; it is light, fickle, and shifting, difficult to grasp and difficult to tame.
It gallops and runs away like a great, wicked elephant, swift in every thought-moment like a flash of lightning, restless and never remaining still.
They are like monkeys, like illusions, and like mirages; they are the root of all evils. The five desires are difficult to satisfy, like fire encountering fuel.
They are like the great ocean swallowing all streams. Like Mount Mandara, where grasses and trees abound, one cannot discern the falsity of birth and death;
through indulgence and delusion, one brings about calamity. Like a fish swallowing a hook, [the senses] always lead one astray first.
All their karmic actions follow them like a mother oyster shell leading its young;
they are greedily attached to the five desires and take no pleasure in Nirvana, just as a camel eating honey will not look back at its fodder even until death.

Deeply clinging to present pleasures, they do not contemplate future faults, like an ox eating the sprouts of grain without fearing the whip. They rush to and fro through the twenty-five realms of existence like a swift wind.
Blowing upon the silk-cotton down (*tūla-piṇḍa*) is something one should not seek; to seek it without satiety is like an ignorant person seeking a fire that does not exist.
One constantly delights in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and does not delight in liberation (*mokṣa*), just as the *niṃba* insect delights in the *niṃba* tree.
One is deluded and attached to the foul stench of birth-and-death, just as a prisoner delights in the women of the jailers, or as a pig in a latrine delights in impurity.
If there are those who cannot contemplate in this way, they are called those who do not cultivate the mind and do not cultivate wisdom.
They do not perceive that wisdom possesses great power, such as that of the golden-winged garuḍa which can destroy evil karma; like the light of the sun, it can destroy the darkness of ignorance;
like water, it can uproot the trees of the aggregates; and like a fierce fire, it can incinerate false views. Wisdom is all of these.
The root of all wholesome dharmas and the seed of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— if there are those who cannot contemplate in this way, they are not said to be cultivating wisdom.
O son of good family, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), if one perceives the body, the characteristics of the body, the cause of the body, the fruit of the body, the collection of the body,

the oneness of the body, the duality of the body, this body and that body, the cessation of the body, the equality of the body, the cultivation of the body, or the cultivator— if any such [perceptions] exist, [they are merely conventional].
One who views it in this way is said to be not cultivating the cultivation of the body, O son of good family.
