If one views precepts—the characteristics of precepts, the cause of precepts, the fruit of precepts, the superior precepts, the inferior precepts, the collection of precepts, the singularity of precepts, the duality of precepts, these precepts, those precepts, the cessation of precepts, and so forth regarding precepts;
or if one views cultivation—the cultivator, the precept-perfection (śīla-pāramitā), and so forth—if there is such a view, it is called not cultivating precepts. If one views the mind, the mind...

The mind of characteristics, the mind of causes, the mind of results, the collection of minds and mental factors, the oneness of mind, the duality of mind, this mind and that mind, the cessation of mind, and so forth—the cultivation of these, the cultivator, the superior, middling, and inferior minds, and wholesome and unwholesome minds:

if one views them in such a manner, it is called not cultivating the mind, O son of good family. If one views wisdom, the characteristics of wisdom, the causes of wisdom, the results of wisdom, the collection of wisdom, and the oneness of wisdom...
Wisdom is twofold: this wisdom and that wisdom; the wisdom of cessation, and so forth; superior, middling, and inferior wisdom; dull wisdom and sharp wisdom;
the cultivation of wisdom and the cultivator of wisdom. Good son, if one holds such views as these, it is called "not cultivating wisdom.

If there is a person who does not cultivate the body, ethical discipline, mind, or wisdom, such a person will receive a great evil retribution for even a minor evil deed. Because of such terror, they are constantly...
He gives rise to this thought: "I belong to hell; I perform the deeds of hell. Although he hears the wise describe the sufferings of hell, he constantly thinks:
"It is like iron striking iron, stone striking stone, or wood striking wood; as fire-insects delight in fire, so too does the body in hell resemble hell itself.
If it is like hell, what further suffering could there be? It is, for example, like a fly.
Just as one stuck by saliva cannot extricate oneself, so it is with this person:

unable to emerge from even a minor transgression, their mind lacks initial remorse and they fail to cultivate goodness. Concealing their flaws, all their past wholesome karma is defiled by these sins;
thus, whatever light retribution they were to receive in the present is transformed into the extreme suffering of hell.
"Son of good family, the fruit of grave evil is like this: if one places one *śī* of salt into a small vessel of water, its taste will be so salty and bitter that it is difficult to drink;

the sinful karma of such a person is also like this. Son of good family, it is like a person who owes another a single coin and, being unable to repay it, has his body bound and undergoes manifold sufferings; the sinful karma of such a person is also like this."
This is so. In the final section on mixed metaphors, it says: "Tūla-wool" refers to the catkins; "the body" refers to the eight-footed form; "the marks" refer to the five aggregates (*skandha*);
"the cause" refers to food and drink and so forth; and "the fruit" refers to the past five precepts, which induce the body as their resultant accumulation.
"Body" refers to the aggregate of the form-skandha (*rūpa-skandha*). "The body as one" means that those [aggregates], whether provisional or substantial, combine to form a single body.

"The body as two" refers to this body obtained through the harmony of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and that other body. Furthermore, "this body" is that which is obtained through the power of karma, while "that other body" refers to the physical remains.
"The cessation of the body" means that it does not abide for even a single moment; "the body and so forth" refers to these various aspects.
There are those who contemplate the body as being equal to empty space; yet they also say that each of the six realms possesses a body, and thus speak of "equality of bodies.
When one speaks of cultivation, it refers to the dharmas that are cultivated, while the "cultivator" is the person who performs the cultivation. This is still a matter of persons and dharmas.
Subsequently, the examples of precepts and wisdom should be understood accordingly.
The Lion’s Roar says: "This person is inferior. Third, clarifying the characteristics of the transformation of karma through two rounds of question and answer.
First, the question: how does one transform light [karma] into heavy? Second, the question: how does one transform heavy [karma] into light? The answers are as in the text.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said, "World-Honored One, for what reason do you cause these people to undergo retribution in hell instead of their light karmic results manifesting here?
The Buddha said, "Good son, if all sentient beings possess five conditions, they will cause light retribution to manifest in hell instead.
What are these five? First, because of ignorance; second, because their roots of goodness are meager; third, because their evil karma is deep and heavy."
Therefore, there are five reasons for this: first, not repenting; second, not cultivating one's fundamental wholesome karma. Furthermore, there are five other matters:

first, practicing evil karma; second, lacking the wealth of precepts; third, distancing oneself from roots of goodness; fourth, failing to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom; fifth, associating with evil associates.
Son of good family, it is for these reasons that they cause retribution to be light in the present life.
"Rebirth in hell is experienced repeatedly.
The Lion’s Roar said, "World-Honored One, what kind of person can transform the retribution of hell so that it is experienced lightly in the present life?
"Good son, if there is one who cultivates the precepts of body, mind, and wisdom as described above, and is able to contemplate all dharmas as being identical..."
Just as in empty space, one does not perceive wisdom nor the wise person; one does not perceive ignorance nor the ignorant person;
one does not perceive cultivation nor the practitioner—this is called a wise person. Such a person is able to cultivate bodily discipline, mental discipline, and wisdom.
This person can cause the retribution of the hells to be experienced lightly in the present life, even if they have committed [extreme] deeds.
By reflecting upon and examining heavy evil karma, one can cause it to become light. One should think thus: "Although my karma is heavy, it is not equal to wholesome karma.
For example, even if there were a hundred catties of *tāla* flowers, they could never rival a single *liang* of pure gold.
It is like throwing one *sheng* of salt into the Ganges River; the water has no salty taste, and those who drink it do not perceive it. It is like a person of great wealth..."
Suppose a person owes another a thousand million treasures; no one can bind them to make them suffer as a great fragrant elephant can break iron chains and depart at will.
A person of wisdom is also like this, constantly reflecting:
"My power of goodness is great, while my evil karma is weak. I am able to reveal and repent of my evils, and I can cultivate wisdom."
Having reflected thus—that the power of wisdom is great and the power of ignorance is slight—one draws near to virtuous friends and cultivates right view;
one receives, upholds, recites, copies, and explains the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

Upon seeing those who receive, uphold, recite, copy, and explain them, one gives rise to a mind of reverence and provides them with clothing, food, dwellings, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, flowers, and incense.
One who makes offerings, praises, and respects [the Buddha], and wherever they go speaks of their virtues rather than their faults;
one who makes offerings to the Triple Gem and reverently believes in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra— that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging,
and that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature— such a person can cause heavy retributions from the hells to be experienced as light in this present life.
For this reason, O son, it is not the case that all karma has a fixed fruit, nor is it the case that all sentient beings must necessarily experience its results.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 29.

Xie Lingyun. Re-edited by Master Shizi Hou, Chapter Six, Volume Four:
Exhortation to Practice, divided into two parts: first, exhortation by citing the Dharma; second, exhortation by citing persons. First, [exhortation by citing the Dharma].

Within this teaching, there are first questions and then answers; the questions are threefold: first, since all possess the power of Buddha-nature, they should equally attain nirvana—why then are there the distinctions of the six realms?
Second, if one already possesses Buddha-nature, one should naturally attain bodhi—what need is there to cultivate the path?
Third, if one already possesses Buddha-nature, one should be able to draw forth and attain bodhi immediately. Of these, the first question is addressed first.
The essential points follow as in the text.

The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said: "World-Honored One, if all karma does not necessarily yield its fruit, and if all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, they ought to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path."
"For what reason do all sentient beings not attain this Great Parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One, if all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, they would certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
why then must they cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path?"

The second question from the World-Honored One consists of four parts: first, citing the sutra; second, providing an analogy; third, applying the analogy; and fourth, resolving the difficulty, as per the text.
In this manner, the World-Honored One states in the sutra that if a sick person obtains medicine, a caregiver, and treatment according to the illness...
Just as food and drink, if they cannot be obtained, fail to cure all ailments, so it is with all sentient beings:
if they encounter Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and hear them preach the Dharma and cultivate the Noble Path;
yet if they do not encounter or hear [the teaching] and do not cultivate the Path, they shall nonetheless all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is it that [one attains] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? It is because of the Buddha-nature.
World-Honored One, it is like the sun and moon: nothing can obstruct them from reaching the edge of Mount Aṭavī;
the four great rivers do not fail to reach the great ocean; and those of the icchantika nature do not fail to go to hell.
All sentient beings are likewise thus; there is nothing that can obstruct them from attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? It is because of their buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
World-Honored One, for this reason, although all sentient beings do not cultivate the Path,
they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by virtue of the power of the Buddha-nature, and not by the power of cultivating the Noble Path.
If an icchantika—this is the third question, which again consists of three parts: the dharma, the analogy, and the synthesis as in the text—[asks]:

"World-Honored One, if an icchantika who has committed the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, and so forth, does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they must nevertheless practice [the path], because by virtue of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), they will certainly attain it; it is not [attained] through causes."
"It is attained only after cultivation.
World-Honored One, it is like a magnet that, though far from iron, causes the iron to follow it by its power.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this; therefore, there is no need for diligent cultivation of the Path."

Next, the Buddha’s response is divided into two parts: first, the direct answer, and second, the summary conclusion. The first part consists of four sections: (1) answering the objection regarding the simultaneous attainment of nirvāṇa;

(2) answering the objection regarding the premature absorption into bodhi; (3) answering the objection that the cultivation of the path is unnecessary; and (4) a reiterated answer to the objection regarding premature absorption.
Regarding the first [section], there is an analogy, its application, and the conclusion. Within the analogy, first the general meaning is presented: the seven men by the riverbank.
All are fully endowed with hands and feet; yet although hands and feet are common to all, there are distinctions between those who possess the proper measure and those who do not.

Next, seven individuals are listed in order: the first two are ordinary beings outside the stages of cultivation (bāhyapṛthagjana); the next one is an ordinary being within the stages of cultivation (adhyātmapṛthagjana); and the final four are noble ones (ārya). Among the ordinary beings outside the stages, there are two types:
those who exhaustively commit evil, such as the icchantikas, and those who were about to enter [the path] but then retreated. As for the ordinary beings within the stages, there are three types.
If one considers the skillful means (*upāya*) to be identical as a single entity, then despite their relative superiority or inferiority, none have yet manifested true sainthood.

As for the fourfold classification: the Śrāvaka does not eliminate residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*); the Pratyekabuddha eliminates residual habit-energies; the Bodhisattva eliminates residual habit-energies while further transforming sentient beings;

and the Buddha has exhausted all habit-energies. If one does not adopt this interpretation, there would be no way to distinguish them from the previous statement that "all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature."
For what reason do sentient beings not all attain nirvāṇa simultaneously? To make this clear, another river is presented where seven people do not cross together.

Throughout the preceding and following sections of this sutra, six rivers are described in total: the river of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the river of afflictions and buddha-nature, and the river of wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas.
These are paired in twos to discuss, from the perspective of saṃsāra, those who attain deliverance and those who do not.
The Nirvāṇa discourse concerns whether one can enter or not enter; the afflictions discourse concerns whether they can be severed or not severed;

the Buddha-nature discourse concerns whether it can be seen or not seen; the evil dharmas discourse concerns whether they can be abandoned or not abandoned; and the wholesome dharmas discourse concerns whether one reaches the ultimate or does not reach the ultimate.
Among these, the Gaṅgā River parable here specifically clarifies saṃsāra, while the Kāśyapa Chapter takes the Great Nirvāṇa as its subject.
In this section on the "Seven Persons in the River," the combinations and separations differ. This text clarifies the seven persons; the subsequent chapter clarifies the seven sentient beings.
Here, the four fruits are combined into one, and the fourth [person] is separated into three vehicles, making three persons.

In the subsequent chapter, the four fruits are separated into four persons, and the *pratyekabuddha*, *bodhisattva*, and Buddha are combined into the seventh person. This shall be further explained below.
[The Buddha] analyzed this.

The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! Suppose there were seven kinds of people by the side of the Ganges who entered the river for bathing, out of fear of bandits, or to gather flowers."
Regarding "bathing," this is a metaphor for leaving the household life and receiving the precepts to purify oneself. Regarding "fearing bandits," this is a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding "gathering flowers," there are two interpretations: first, that the "seven flowers of purity" refers to seeking the causes;

second, that "wandering among the flowers of awakening" refers to seeking the fruit. Leaving the household life should mean exiting the river, yet the mention of "entering the river" is intended to... [text fragment ends]
It clarifies that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not separated by a vast distance; one must seek nirvāṇa within saṃsāra itself.
Regarding the first person among the seven individuals listed below:
he sinks as soon as he enters the water. Why is this? Because he is weak and lacks strength, and has not practiced swimming. First...

Although these two persons sink, they emerge; having emerged, they sink again. Why is this? Because their physical strength is great, they are able to emerge, but because they are unaccustomed to swimming, they sink after emerging.
As for the third person, having sunk, he emerges immediately and does not sink again.
Why is this? Because his body is heavy, he sinks; because his strength is great, he emerges; and because he was previously practiced in swimming, he emerges as soon as he surfaces.
As for the fourth person: having entered, he immediately sinks; having sunk, he emerges again; having emerged, he stands still and surveys the four directions.

Why is this? Because [the water] is deep, he sinks; because his strength is great, he emerges again; because he has practiced swimming, he stands still; and because he does not know where to exit, he surveys the four directions.
As for the fifth person: having entered, he immediately sinks; having sunk, he emerges again; having emerged, he immediately...
Having stood, he surveyed the directions; having surveyed them, he departed immediately. Why? Because of fear.
As for the sixth person, having entered, he departed immediately and stayed in shallow water. Why? Because he observed whether the bandits were near or far.
As for the seventh person, having reached the other shore, he ascended a great mountain; being free from all terror and separated from all enemies and bandits, he experienced great happiness.

The first person who sinks immediately represents those of icchantika nature: because their past virtuous causes from former lives have already weakened and they lack faith in the present, they do not practice swimming.
The second person, who stands up but then retreats despite having great physical strength, represents those whose past virtue was profound but whom they fail to cultivate in this life;

thus, they are called "those who do not practice swimming" and are capable of severing their roots of goodness. The third person, who remains standing, serves as a metaphor for those who have attained stability.

Regarding those who have passed away from the inner stage of ordinary beings (antarapudgala) and emerged: the "fourth person" mentioned in the sutras concerning those who had previously perished refers to the analogy of the four directions.
As for these "four directions," they are used as an analogy for the Four Noble Truths in the subsequent text, though that is not their application here.

The text states that [the person] did not know the place of emergence; therefore, one observes the directions because of the previous ignorance regarding the place of emergence, whereas now, having known it, one does not observe them.
Because they dwell [in that state], it is said they "observe the directions. Furthermore, because they do not know the source from which the Mahāyāna emerges, they take up the lesser fruit.

The fifth person is the *pratyekabuddha*, who is also said to "observe the directions"; having surpassed the four fruits, because of their sharp faculties, they do not take the four fruits but depart for the sake of personal realization.
Because they likewise fear birth and death, it is said they are "terrified. The sixth person is...
The Bodhisattva who departs does not abide; he does not abide in the shallow waters of birth and death.
Because his mind rests securely within birth and death, it is said that these are "shallow waters" from the perspective of his own mind. The seventh person is the Buddha.
Good son, regarding the second combined analogy within the great river of birth and death: first, the general analogy is combined.

Good son, this great river of birth and death is likewise like this: there are seven kinds of people who, out of fear of the thieves of afflictions, resolve to cross the great river of birth and death;
they leave the household life, shave their heads, and don the dharma robes.
Fearing the thieves of the afflictions corresponds to the previous "fear"; conceiving the resolve to cross over corresponds to the previous "entering the river";
leaving the household life and shaving the hair corresponds to the previous "bathing the body"; donning the dharma robes corresponds to the previous "gathering flowers."

Having already left the household life, the second section below provides a combined and individual analogy for the seven types of people. First, the analogy for those who are constantly submerged—namely, the icchantikas—is briefly combined here.
Having already left the household life, they associate with evil friends, follow their teachings, and listen to and accept false doctrines; that is to say, sentient beings.

The body is the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and the five aggregates are called the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) of sentient beings. If one dies, these five great elements are eternally severed;
because the five great elements are severed, why would there be any need to cultivate various wholesome or unwholesome karmas?

Therefore, one should know that there is neither good nor evil, nor the retribution of good and evil. This is what is called an *icchantika*. An *icchantika* is defined as one who has severed all roots of goodness.
Because their roots of goodness have been severed, they sink into the river of birth and death and are unable to emerge. Why is this?
Because their evil karma is heavy and they lack the power of faith; they are like the first person on the banks of the Ganges.
There are six causes and conditions for falling into and remaining in the three evil realms from which one cannot emerge.
Good son, those who are icchantikas have six causes and conditions for sinking into the three evil realms and being unable to escape them. What are these six?
First, because their evil minds are intensely blazing; second, because they do not perceive future lives; third, because they delight in practicing afflictions.
Therefore, there are five causes for the severance of the roots of goodness: first, the obstruction of evil karma; second, proximity to evil associates;

third, performing improper acts toward a bhikṣu; fourth, performing improper acts toward a bhikṣuṇī; and fifth, the unauthorized use of the Saṃgha’s property. Furthermore, there are five other matters by which one sinks into the three evil realms.

What are these five? First, committing an illegal act against a bhikṣu; second, committing an illegal act against a bhikṣuṇī; third, using the property of the Saṃgha for one's own private benefit; fourth, [acting improperly] toward one's mother...

Because they practice what is contrary to the Dharma at the borders [of the realm], and because mutual disputes regarding right and wrong arise among the five divisions of the Sangha, there are furthermore five matters by which one perishes into the three evil destinies. What are these five?
First, constantly teaching that there are no fruits of good or evil; second, killing sentient beings who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta;
third, delighting in speaking of the faults of Dharma-teachers; fourth, teaching the Dharma as non-Dharma; and fifth, teaching non-Dharma as the Dharma.

Because of the Dharma, there are five faults in seeking the Dharma; furthermore, because one listens and accepts [the teachings] with these faults, there are three matters that cause one to sink into the three evil realms.

What are these three? First, it is the notion that the Tathāgata is impermanent and has been eternally extinguished; second, it is the notion that the True Dharma is impermanent and subject to change;
third, it is the notion that the Jewel of the Saṃgha can be destroyed. For this reason, one constantly sinks into the three evil realms.
Regarding the "five groups of monks" (*pañca nikāyāḥ*), there are two interpretations. First, it refers to five assemblies of monks who mutually confess their transgressions before one another.

Second, it refers to the five divisions of the Vinaya; more than a hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, King Aśoka convened a great assembly, and because the Sthaviras and Mahāsāṃghikas could not reach an agreement on the established doctrines, they split into two schools. Subsequently...

The Sthavira school split into two branches: the Haimavata and the Sarvāstivāda. Later, the Haimavata ceased to exist, while the Sarvāstivāda further studied the Mahāsāṃghika and gave rise to three schools:
the Mahīśāsaka, the Dharmaguptaka, and the Kāśyapīya. Together with the Sarvāstivāda and the Mahāsāṃghika, these constitute the five schools.
The Tathāgata foresaw their mutual disputes and criticisms; this is also recorded in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.
The five schools are pre-indicated; as the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra* explains at length how they further divided into twenty, these are not cited here as they are not essential to the present text.
The second person below [the list] was about to establish [his position] but withdrew.
As for the second person, they have resolved to cross the great river of birth and death; however, because they have severed their roots of goodness, they sink and cannot emerge.
What is called "emerging" is to draw near to virtuous friends and thereby attain the mind of faith. This "mind of faith" consists of: faith in giving and the fruits of giving;

faith in the good and the fruits of the good; faith in the evil and the fruits of the evil; and faith that birth and death are suffering, impermanent, and subject to decay and destruction. This is what is meant by having attained faith.

Having attained faith, they cultivate pure precepts, receive and uphold them, read, recite, transcribe, and explain them; they constantly practice the giving of wisdom and skillfully cultivate insight.
Yet, because their faculties are dull and they encounter evil friends, they are unable to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom;

they listen to and accept false teachings, or meet with evil times and dwell in evil lands, thereby severing all roots of goodness. Because they have severed these roots of goodness, they remain forever...
"Sinking in birth and death" refers to the second person by the side of the Ganges;
that is, even an ordinary outsider (*bālapṛthagjana*) can sever their roots of goodness, yet they differ from the one who sinks forever.
The third person is one who falls below this [second type] and corresponds to those among the inner ordinary persons (*ābhyantarapṛthagjana*) who have attained abiding.
The third person is one who has resolved to cross the great river of birth and death but, because they have severed their roots of goodness, sinks within it;

yet by associating with virtuous friends, they are said to have emerged. They place faith in the Tathāgata as omniscient, eternal, and unchanging, and for the sake of sentient beings, they proclaim the unsurpassed path:
that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and that the Tathāgata does not perish.

The Dharma and the Sangha are likewise indestructible; even those with icchantika tendencies who do not sever their connection to the Dharma will ultimately never fail to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
However, they must first distance themselves from such states, and only then, by means of faith, cultivate pure precepts.
Having cultivated the pure precepts, they shall receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they widely proclaim and disseminate [the Dharma], delighting in the giving of wisdom and cultivating wisdom to sharpen their faculties;
thus they abide firmly in faith and wisdom with minds that never regress, like the third person by the side of the Ganges.
If both the small and great [vehicles] share the same stage, is this not because the three types of practitioners in the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) occupy a common position?
If one adopts a distinct interpretation, since the Mahāyāna teachings differ, they should not occupy the same stage. The text states:

"One should believe that the Tathāgata is omniscient, eternal, and unchanging, and that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. One interpretation says: "This refers to the initial practice of the Three Vehicles."
One should not be deluded regarding the Dharma as explained in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*; this passage has many points of relevance.
If one believes that the Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging and that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, then it appears to have a distinct meaning.

To cultivate skillful means with the mind of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* and enter the stage of skillful means—Subhadra’s attainment of the fruit mentioned in the following text is precisely its significance.
As for the fourth person: having resolved to cross the great river of birth and death, they had previously sunk within it because they had severed their roots of goodness;
however, by associating with virtuous friends, they have attained faith. This is called "emerging.

Because they have attained faith, they accept, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain, and expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures for the sake of sentient beings, widely proclaiming and disseminating them, and delighting in the giving of wisdom.
By cultivating wisdom for the sake of sharpening one's faculties, one dwells firmly in faith and wisdom with a mind that never regresses.
One surveys the four directions; the "four directions" refer to the four fruits of the śramaṇa.

The "fifth person" is like the fourth man by the Ganges River who resolves to cross the great river of birth and death, yet sinks into its midst because he has severed his roots of goodness; however, through associating with virtuous friends, he eventually emerges.
Attaining the mind of faith is called "emerging. Because of this mind of faith, one receives, upholds, recites, copies, explains, and elucidates the twelve divisions of the scriptures;

for the sake of sentient beings, one widely proclaims and disseminates them. Delighting in the giving of wisdom and cultivating wisdom, because of these sharp faculties, one remains firmly established in faith and wisdom.
With the mind never regressing, once non-regression is attained, one immediately advances forward.

"Progressing" refers to the pratyekabuddha; although they are able to deliver themselves, they do not reach out to sentient beings, and this is called "emerging," like the fifth person by the side of the Ganges.
As for the sixth person, he has resolved to cross the great river of birth and death, but because he had severed his roots of goodness, he sank within it.
By drawing near to virtuous friends, he obtained faith; because he obtained faith, he is so named.
In order to emerge [from suffering], they receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures out of faith;

for the sake of sentient beings, they widely proclaim and disseminate them; they delight in the giving of wisdom and cultivate wisdom; because their faculties are sharp, they abide firmly in faith and wisdom with minds that do not regress;
having attained non-regression, they advance further until they reach the shallow waters, and having reached the shallow waters—

Having reached that place, he remains there and does not depart; this "remaining without departing" refers to the Bodhisattva who, desiring to deliver all sentient beings, dwells in contemplation of the afflictions like the sixth man by the side of the Ganges.

As for the seventh man, he has resolved to cross the great river of birth and death, yet because his roots of goodness have been severed, he sinks within it; however, by drawing near to virtuous friends, he attains [salvation].
Having attained faith and confidence, one is said to have emerged through that faith and confidence;
thus, for the sake of sentient beings, one upholds, recites, copies, explains, and widely disseminates the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

Delighting in the giving of wisdom and cultivating wisdom, because of these sharp faculties, one remains firmly established in faith and wisdom with a mind that never regresses. Having attained this non-regression, one then...
Having advanced and reached the further shore, one ascends the great high mountain, becomes free from all fears, and experiences abundant peace and happiness.
Good son, the "further shore" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata; "experiencing peace and happiness" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s eternal abiding;
and the "great high mountain" is a metaphor for Great Nirvāṇa.
The fourth person combines the four [levels] into one; they sever only the *mūla* (fundamental) and do not invade the *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies).

The fifth person is the Pratyekabuddha, who invades only a small portion of the *vāsanā*. The sixth person is the Bodhisattva, who can invade much of the *vāsanā* while further transforming sentient beings.
The seventh person is the Buddha, for whom the *vāsanā* is ultimately exhausted. It is for this reason that the distinctions between these four types of persons are established.
This is the general meaning; since both textual passages are present, it cannot yet be determined as exclusively one or the other. For now, let us apply a single line of reasoning:
this is merely the general meaning. Specifically, taking *pariccheda-maraṇa* (segmented birth-and-death) as the river, one resolves to cross over by means of the mind of *mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Within this, there are seven distinct differences, yet they share the same principle of possessing Buddha-nature and the same principle of achieving *nirvāṇa*.
This also constitutes a response to the question; it should be explained in this way.

This third analogy regarding the one who sinks by the side of the Ganges River answers the inquiry about being identical to *nirvāṇa*. The statement that both hands and feet are complete answers that their Buddha-nature is the same.
The distinction between those who cross over and those who do not, based on whether they have practiced swimming or not, provides the answer.

Regarding the question of why they do not equally attain *nirvāṇa*, the text is divided into two parts: first, it clarifies that failing to attain it through non-cultivation is not the fault of the Tathāgata;
the analogy and its application are as in the text.
"Good son, all these people by the side of the Ganges were fully possessed of hands and feet, yet none of them could cross over."
It is the same for all sentient beings: there truly exist the Buddha-treasure, the Dharma-treasure, and the Sangha-treasure;
the Tathāgata constantly speaks of the essential meaning of all dharmas—the Eightfold Noble Path and Great Parinirvāṇa—and yet all sentient beings are unable to attain them.
This is not my fault, nor is it the fault of the Noble Path; rather, one should know that this is entirely the fault and evil of their afflictions (*kleśa*).
For this reason, all sentient beings do not attain nirvana.

Next, it clarifies that those who practice will certainly attain it, illustrating this with three analogies. This is further divided into two parts: first the analogy, then the application [to the teaching], as in the text.
Good son, it is like a skilled physician who knows the diseases and prescribes the medicines; if the patient does not take them, it is not the fault of the physician.
Good son, if there is a donor who gives whatever he possesses to all people, and there are those who do not accept it, it is not the fault of the donor.
Good son, it is like the rising of the sun, which illuminates all darkness; yet the blind and sightless cannot see the path.

The road is not at fault for not being traversed daily. Good son, it is like the waters of the Ganges which can eliminate thirst; if those who are thirsty do not drink, it is not the fault of the water.
Good son, it is like the great earth which universally produces fruits and grains with impartiality and without distinction;
if a farmer does not sow, it is not the fault of the earth.
Good son, the Tathāgata universally expounds and analyzes the twelve divisions of the sūtras for the sake of all sentient beings;
if sentient beings do not accept them, it is not the fault of the Tathāgata. Good son, if one cultivates the path, one will immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Regarding your statement that sentient beings of the lowest capacity skip the second question to answer the third: this has two parts, the first of which restates the question and offers praise or censure.

"Good son, as for your statement that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—just like a magnet—this is excellent, truly excellent! Because of the causal power of possessing Buddha-nature, they attain *anuttara*..."
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the claim that it does not require the cultivation of the Noble Path is incorrect.
If one is able to cultivate it, one will certainly attain it without doubt; therefore, such a person is praised.
Conversely, those who are unwilling to cultivate it and instead rely on their own innate potential to achieve absorption are disparaged as being wrong.

Next, "For example, it is like a person... and so forth, is the first of the two parts within the formal response; it answers that those who practice will necessarily attain [the result], and thus employs the analogy of drawing water from a well.
"Good son, for example, suppose there is a person traveling through a vast wilderness who, parched with thirst, encounters a well. Although the well is extremely deep..."
If one does not see water, one should know that there must be a person who, through skillful means, seeks it out and draws it up using a jar and a rope until they finally see it.

The well is a metaphor for the body composed of the five aggregates; thirst is a metaphor for the mind’s weariness with suffering and its seeking of happiness; the depth of the well is a metaphor for the profound nature of the self;
and although it is not seen, the fact that it must be drawn is a metaphor for how, through cultivation, one comes to perceive the nature.
The Buddha-nature is also like this; the following section corresponds to the text as it appears.
Although all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, they must necessarily cultivate the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) before they can perceive it.
Next, the simile of the sesame seeds illustrates that if one does not practice, one will not attain [the result].
Good son, if there is sesame, one can obtain oil; yet apart from various skillful means, one cannot see it.
It is the same with sugarcane, good son. Just as the thirty-three heavens and Uttarakuru in the north, although these are existing phenomena, if...
Without the power of the divine eye and the supernormal powers resulting from wholesome karma, one cannot see the roots of grass in the earth or the underground water;
because the earth covers them, sentient beings do not see them.
This is consistent with the text.
The Buddha-nature is likewise; because one does not cultivate the Noble Path, it cannot be seen.
As you have stated, there are patients in the world—this concludes the third part of the response to the second question. Furthermore, this section has two parts:
first, a rebuke for the error of citing a scripture.
“Good son, as you have said, that there are sick people in the world who, whether they encounter a skilled physician who cares for them, good medicine,
and appropriate food and drink according to their illness, or do not encounter these things, all recover— good son,
I have taught this meaning for the sake of bodhisattvas at the sixth stage.”

Regarding the explanation that the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭha-vihāra*) is not identical [to the sixth ground], one interpretation says it is the sixth of the ten stages (*daśa-vihāra*), while another says it is the sixth of the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*).
It is said that on this ground, *prajñā* is manifest before one, and there is the sense of self-curing. The Buddha rebuked this, saying:
"When I spoke of meeting or not meeting [the medicine] and the illness curing itself, I was speaking for the sake of the bodhisattva of the sixth stage, not for ordinary beings."
The person points out their deviation.
Next, from "It is like empty space" onwards, the formal answer is given, citing three analogies in total.
"Good son, it is like empty space; with respect to all sentient beings, it is neither internal, nor external, nor both internal and external."
The Buddha-nature of unimpeded sentient beings is also like this.
Some say that this uses the emptiness perceived by the eyes of worldly people as a metaphor; some take the emptiness of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) as the metaphor;
and others say it is precisely the emptiness that is neither internal nor external within the principle. The *Zhonglun* (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā) states: "Empty."
Emptiness is neither existent nor non-existent, neither internal nor external; this is an analogy for the Buddha-nature.
Good son, it is like a person whose wealth is in a distant land: although it is not present before them, they may enjoy it as they wish.
If someone asks about it, they say, "I have it," because it is certainly theirs. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
In this way, because it is neither this nor that, yet is attained with certainty, it is said that "all exists.
The subsequent passage states that regarding "wealth," although the wealth is in another land and not currently available for use, one obtains it by going there to fetch it;
likewise, although the Buddha-nature cannot yet be seen, one realizes it through cultivation.
Good son, it is like sentient beings who perform various karmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome; these are neither internal nor external.
Likewise, the nature of such karma is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it something that was originally non-existent and now exists, nor does it arise without cause.
Later in the text it says: "The agent" refers to the initial aspiration; "action" refers to cultivation; and "the fruit" refers to the realization of nature (*dharmatā*).
Within this, there are six negations: first, not internal; second, not external; third, not existent; fourth, not non-existent;
fifth, not being something that was originally non-existent and now exists; and sixth, not arising without cause.
It is not the case that one who does not perform this action will experience its result; rather, it is clarified below that one who performs it must necessarily receive it.

It is not the case that one who does not perform this action will experience its result, nor that one who performs this action will experience another's result, nor that one who performs another's action will experience its result. Without action and without experiencing [the fruit], the temporal conjunction of conditions brings about the retribution.
There are five propositions for sequential explanation. The first states: "It is not that this aggregate performs the action and this [other] aggregate receives the fruit.

If it were the case that this [same] one performs the action and this [same] one receives [the fruit], then there would be a single aggregate, and that which is one would be permanent. Furthermore, if there were no subsequent aggregate arising from this [prior] aggregate, then that would constitute annihilationism.
In the second proposition, the character "not" (非) from the first phrase is applied as a prefix to the following, such that it becomes: "It is not that this performs [the action]."
That experiencer is not the same as the one who performed the action within these aggregates; rather, it is those aggregates that experience the fruit. As the Master of Hexi (Hexi Shi) says:

"If it were the case that a human performs the action and a deva experiences the fruit, then there would be a cause without a fruit, or a fruit without a cause. To have a fruit without a cause is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*); to have a cause without a fruit is the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, one must also consider the possibility that another performs the action while yet another experiences the fruit; this [latter] position can be understood."

The first phrase concerns those who perform an action and experience its result; the fourth [phrase] concerns non-action and non-experience, wherein there is a total absence of cause and effect, which thus cannot be reconciled with time and conditions; this is the fifth phrase.
The first section of the analogy for the Buddha-nature of sentient beings consists of six phrases concerning the creation of karma.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: it is neither originally non-existent and now existent, nor internal, nor external, nor existent, nor non-existent.

It merely conforms to the five [categories] and does not conform to the non-existent; it emerges from the first combination of the fifth category, which is neither internal nor external, and conforms to the first pair, which is neither existent nor non-existent.
"Neither this nor that" introduces the second section, concerning the signs that a practitioner will inevitably attain the fruition of their practice.
"Neither this nor that": it does not come from another place, nor does it arise without causes and conditions; yet it is not the case that all sentient beings do not see it.

When the time, season, causes, and conditions for the Bodhisattvas to appear harmonize, those who perceive the time and season shall behold them—namely, the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path and attains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, at that time he attains vision;
this is not called "acting.
Of the five preceding phrases, they are now fully integrated: the first is "neither that nor this," which combines two phrases; "neither that" is "is."
It is not that what was done by one is experienced by another; it is not that this very thing is joined with itself; it is not that what was done by this is experienced by that;

it is not that [the result] comes from another place; it is not that what was done by this is experienced by another; nor is there joining without causes and conditions. Above, there is no agent and no experiencer;
yet, below, through the conjunction of all various factors, it arises at the preceding moment.

Good son, this is the fourth and final response to the third question. While the preceding questions and answers consisted of both doctrinal exposition (*dharmadeśanā*) and illustrative parables (*dṛṣṭānta*), here I respond directly with parables alone.
First, [the initial response] was not appropriate for the question; second, regarding the first [response], it was not appropriate.
"Good son, your statement that it is like a magnet is incorrect.
Indeed, a magnet cannot attract iron. For what reason?
Below, the meaning of why it does not attract is explained in two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the analogy. Regarding the first text:"
Why is this? Because stone does not attract iron. Why is that? It is because it lacks the activity of mind (*citta-karman*).
Noble son, because a different dharma exists, a different dharma arises; because a different dharma is absent, a different dharma perishes. There is no creator and there is no destroyer.

A stone has no consciousness; how could it possibly absorb [light]? Like the heliotrope, which has no mind yet follows the sun from east to west, or the plantain tree, which has no ears yet produces flowers upon hearing thunder—all these arise through the principle of "different dharmas" (visadṛśa-dharma). They are able to follow and they are able to hear.
The amber that absorbs mustard seeds is likewise so. How can this be used as an analogy for the Buddha-nature? Now, let us explain the arising of different dharmas.
Regarding the destruction of one phenomenon through another: because one phenomenon exists, another phenomenon arises; all phenomena arise conditioned by causes and conditions.
Causes and conditions are termed "other" (anya) with respect to phenomena. Because there are other causes and conditions, there are various phenomena;
thus it is said that because one phenomenon exists, another phenomenon arises. This is also like soil and water acting as conditions for a sprout, where the sprout [arises from them].
When do water and earth ever have a mind that understands and gives rise to phenomena? They do not think, "I shall give birth to you;
you may take birth. There is only this distinct condition, and thus the sprout arises. Likewise, due to the causal conditions of water, fire is extinguished;
yet neither water nor fire has any mutual understanding, such as "I arise" or "you cease."
Good son, it is just as a fierce fire cannot actually burn the wood; rather, when the fire arises and the wood is destroyed, it is called "burning the wood.

Good son, it is like the heliotrope that turns toward the sun; yet this heliotrope has no mind of reverence, no consciousness, and no karma—it turns of its own accord due to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Good son, it is like the plantain tree, which grows because of thunder.

This tree has long been without ears, without mind, and without consciousness; because of the presence of one dharma, another dharma grows, and because of the absence of that dharma, another dharma perishes.
Son of good family, it is like the Aśoka tree: when a woman touches its flowers, they bloom. This tree has no mind and no perception of touch;
yet, because of the presence of one dharma, another dharma arises, and because of the absence of that dharma... [it ceases].
Therefore, son of good family, it is through the destruction of one phenomenon that another arises: just as when a citron tree receives the fruit of a *śīrṣaka*, its yield becomes abundant;
yet the citron tree has neither mind nor sensation. Because one phenomenon exists, another phenomenon flourishes; because one phenomenon is absent, another phenomenon perishes.
Good son, it is like the pomegranate tree: because of bricks, bones, and manure, its fruit becomes abundant and lush. Yet the pomegranate tree has no intention or contact;
rather, because other dharmas exist, other dharmas arise, and because other dharmas cease to exist, other dharmas perish.
Next, the example of the mugwort and morning glory turning toward the sun as they face east or west: how could this occur without intention?
Therefore, further analogies are provided; in total, five analogies are presented.
Next, regarding the magnet attracting [iron], there are two parts: first, returning to the analogy to apply it to the point being illustrated.
Good son, the magnet attracting iron is also like this: because a distinct phenomenon exists, another distinct phenomenon arises;
because that distinct phenomenon is absent, the other distinct phenomenon perishes.
Next, from the passage "the Buddha-nature of sentient beings" onwards, the text further uses the Dharma to correspond with the analogy; that which is the Dharma itself is the Buddha-nature.

This consists of three parts: first, clarifying that the cause does not draw in the fruit; second, clarifying that the Buddha-nature has no fixed abode; and third, an extensive analysis of the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the first section, there are again three sub-parts, the first of which correctly applies the analogy of the magnet and the iron.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise such that it cannot "inhale" or draw forth *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Next, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are cited to clarify the meaning of this inability to inhale.
Good son, ignorance cannot absorb the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), nor can the formative forces absorb consciousness (*vijñāna*);
yet it is still said that "ignorance conditions the formative forces" and "the formative forces condition consciousness."
If ignorance is the cause and the various formations are the effect, and so on up to birth as the cause and death as the effect, how could ignorance possibly "suck in" the formations?
It is just as the Buddha-nature cannot "suck in" bodhi.
Regarding the third point, "There are Buddhas," this section below correctly demonstrates that [the Buddha-nature] does not inhale.
There are Buddhas; the Dharma-realm of the Buddhas is eternally abiding.
Next, "Good son, if one says 'Buddha-nature'... and so forth, the second part clarifies that the Buddha-nature has no place of abiding, yet there is the Dharma.
The analogy can be understood through this principle:
"Good son, if one says that the Buddha-nature dwells within sentient beings, good son, the eternal dharma has no dwelling place;
if it had a dwelling place, it would be impermanent."
As in the following analogy regarding the twelve links of dependent origination, there are first two parts: first, the actual presentation of the analogy.
"Good son, just as the twelve links of dependent origination have no fixed place of abiding—if they had a place of abiding, the twelve links of dependent origination could not be called 'eternal.'"
Next, the analogy of the Tathāgata is presented:
the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata likewise has no place of abiding; the Dharma-realm, the Dharma-sphere, the aggregates of phenomena, and empty space all lack any place of abiding.
"Tathāgata" refers to that which is manifest, while "Buddha-nature" refers to that which is hidden.
Next, following the section on Buddha-nature, there is the passage beginning with "For example" (*tadyathā*).
Buddha-nature is likewise entirely without a place of abiding.

Following the passage beginning with "For example, the four great elements" (*mahābhūta*), the third section extensively clarifies Buddha-nature through four points; the first clarifies that it is neither future nor present.
It is stated that there will be a second [type of existence], which is neither identical to nor separate from the third; this fourth section extensively elucidates its essential nature.

First, regarding "will-be-existence" (*bhaviṣyat*) as distinct from present existence: it is called "will-be-existence" because sentient beings are destined to attain it; this includes the analogy, the existence, and the application.

Good son, it is like the four great elements: although they are equal in their possession of solidity, heat, moisture, motion, lightness, heaviness, redness, whiteness, yellowness, and blackness, these four great elements also possess no karma, because they are not distinct from the dharma-realm;
thus, each is not similar to the others.
However, among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there is no single karma that can produce the earth element while another distinct karma produces the fire element;
the same applies to the other two. It is simply by hearing the conditions of karma that all [elements] can be produced. The Buddha-nature is also like this: when the time arrives, it manifests.
Therefore, the four great elements are used as a metaphor. As for the saying that some are light and some are heavy: wind and fire are light, while earth and water are heavy.
Furthermore, regarding the mention of red, white, yellow, and black: these correspond to their colors—fire is red, wind is white, earth is yellow, and water is black.
If corresponding to the five elements (*pañca-dhātu*), fire is red, metal is white, earth is yellow, water is black, and wood is green.

Furthermore, within the Hīnayāna it is taught that wind is formless (*arūpa*), whereas in the Mahāyāna it is taught that wind possesses form (*rūpin*). Among the five elements, gold is white; gold resides in the western direction.
The Master said: "Furthermore, Master, regarding the autumnal qi: because the autumn wind is whistling and rustling, it is called 'wind-white,' though this is not yet fully explained;
it should accord with the text as it stands.
Buddha-nature is also like this, for it is distinct from the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); when the time arrives, it manifests. Good son, all sentient beings..."
Because they do not regress from their Buddha-nature, they are called "non-retrogressive" (avaivartika);
because it will exist in the future, because it is certain to be attained, and because it is certain to be seen—therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
It is like a king who employs two illustrations to show that the Buddha-nature is neither identical to nor separate from existence, using the metaphors of "having" and "combining.
Son of Good Family, it is like a king who says to a great minister, "Lead an elephant before these blind men to show it to them.
At that time, having received the king’s command, the minister gathers many blind men and shows them the elephant. Then, each of those blind men—
When he had touched the minister with his hand, he withdrew and reported to the king, saying, "I have finished showing him.
Thereupon, the great king summoned the blind men one by one and asked each, "Did you see the elephant? Each of the blind men replied, "I have seen it.
The king asked, "What is the elephant like? The one who had touched its tusk said, "The shape of the elephant is like a radish root. The one who had touched its ear...
The one who touched its head said the elephant was like a winnowing basket; the one who touched its trunk said it was like a stone; the one who touched its legs said it was like a pestle;
the one who touched its feet said it was like a wooden mortar; the one who touched its back said it was like a bed;
the one who touched its belly said it was like a large jar; the one who touched its tail said it was like a rope. Good son, it was just as with that multitude.

The blind man does not describe the elephant's body, yet it is not that he does not describe it; for if all these various features were not the elephant, there would be no other elephant apart from them.
Regarding the "radish" mentioned in the first passage, the *Erya* calls it *lubu*; Guo Pu’s commentary explains it as *luofu*, which is [the same as] *luopo*.
Fú (the fungus) serves as the primary means by which one leads the blind; others explain this by saying that one aspect perishes while another remains.
That the head, feet, and so forth are not the elephant is their perishing; that they are not separate from the head, feet, and so forth is their remaining.
Thus, Buddha-nature is not the six dharmas—that is its perishing; yet there is no Buddha-nature apart from the six dharmas—that is its remaining. It is thus.
The commentator cannot emerge from the two positions of identity and difference; how much less could they transcend the four propositions and depart from the hundred negations?

This passage simultaneously refutes both identity and difference: that there is no elephant in the head and feet is the refutation of identity; that there is no elephant apart from the head and feet is the refutation of difference.
Since the elephant does not exist within the head and feet, it cannot be identical to them; since it does not exist apart from the head and feet, it cannot be separate from them.
Since there is no separate form apart from these [six dharmas] that can be set aside, it is neither identical to nor separate from them, neither internal nor external;
thus one can speak of "form. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise: it is neither identical to the six dharmas nor separate from the six dharmas, neither internal nor external;
therefore it is called the Middle Way and is named Buddha-nature. If one were to take the six dharmas as the Buddha-nature, [it would be a mistake].
This is the Buddha-nature of the blind; if one were to claim that Buddha-nature exists apart from these six dharmas, it would be like pointing to empty space as Buddha-nature.

As for the Brahmins who slandered [the Buddha], claiming he was killed by Śāṇḍilya, or those who take the Middle Way—neither identical to nor separate from [the dharmas]—to be Buddha-nature, this is like the Buddha-nature seen by the king’s minister. If one attains...

Neither identical nor separate, the meaning extensively traverses all dharmas, which are entirely Buddha-nature; the four immeasurables, the six perfections, and so forth are all as stated in the text.
Within the section on synthesis, there are again two parts: first, the general synthesis.
Good son, the king is like the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; the minister is like the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra;
the elephant is like the Buddha-nature; and the blind man is like all sentient beings who are shrouded in ignorance.

Next, regarding these various sentient beings, there is a separate synthesis within which there are again three parts: first, the formal synthesis; second, the further citation of the original analogy of the blind man for synthesis; and third, the conclusion.

Within the first part, the formal synthesis, there are six sections, each of which contains three sub-divisions: first, the synthesis of the six analogies; second, the citation of the analogy for application;
and third, the conclusion—all as stated in the text.
When these sentient beings have heard the Buddha’s teaching, some may say: "Form is the Buddha-nature. Why?
Although this form perishes, it continues in succession; therefore, one obtains the thirty-two marks of the unsurpassed Tathāgata.
The form of the Tathāgata is eternal, for the form of the Tathāgata is eternally uninterrupted. For this reason, form is said to be named the Buddha-nature."
For example, although the substance of pure gold may change its form, its color remains constant;

sometimes it is made into a bracelet, sometimes a snake, and sometimes a dish, yet its yellow hue never alters. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: although its substance is impermanent, its nature is eternal.
For this reason, it is said that form (*rūpa*) is the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
Some say that feeling (*vedanā*) is the Buddha-nature. Why? Because through the conditions of feeling, one attains the true bliss of the Tathāgata.
The "feeling" of the Tathāgata refers to ultimate feeling and the feeling of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Although the nature of the feeling of sentient beings...
Furthermore, although it is impermanent, its sequential continuity is uninterrupted; therefore, one attains the eternal experience of the Tathāgata.
For example, there may be a person whose clan name is Kauśika; although the person is impermanent, the clan name is eternal, remaining unchanged throughout thousands of myriads of generations.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
For this reason, it is said that sensation (*vedanā*) is the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, some say that perception (*saṃjñā*) is the Buddha-nature. Why? Because through the conditions of perception, one attains the Tathāgata’s true perception.
This "Tathāgata-perception" is called the "perception of non-perception. This "perception of non-perception" is neither the perception of sentient beings nor...

The perception of male and female, as well as the perceptions of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the perception of non-perception, and the perception of sentient beings— though these are impermanent,
because they continue in succession without interruption, one attains the perception of the Tathāgata’s permanence and constancy.
"Good son, it is like the twelve links of dependent origination for sentient beings: although the sentient beings perish, the dependent origination remains constant.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
For this reason, it is said that conceptualization is the Buddha-nature."
Furthermore, there are those who say that practice is the Buddha-nature. Why is this? Practice is called "life" because it is the causal condition for life;

by means of it, one attains the eternally abiding life of the Tathāgata. Although the life of sentient beings is impermanent, because life continues in succession without interruption, one attains the true, eternal life of the Tathāgata.
Good son, it is like the twelve divisions of the scriptures: although those who hear them and those who preach them are impermanent, these scriptures remain eternally and do not change.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
For this reason, it is said that conduct is the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, some say that consciousness is the Buddha-nature; because of the causes and conditions of consciousness, one attains the Tathāgata’s mind of equality.
Although the mental consciousness of sentient beings is impermanent, because consciousness continues in succession without interruption, one attains the state of a Tathāgata.
The true, eternal mind is like the nature of heat in fire: although the fire itself is impermanent, its heat is not impermanent. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
For this reason, it is said that consciousness is the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, there are those who say that apart from the aggregates (skandhas) there is a self (ātman), and this self is the Buddha-nature. Why?

Because by means of the conditions of the self, one attains the eight kinds of mastery of a Tathāgata. There are non-Buddhists (tīrthika) who say that going and coming, seeing and hearing, sorrow and joy, and speaking are the self.
Thus, although these characteristics of the self are impermanent, the self of the Tathāgata is truly eternal.
"Good son, just as the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are impermanent, yet their names are permanent, so too is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings.
Good son, it is like those blind men who each described the elephant; although they did not grasp the reality, it was not that they were not describing the elephant."
The Buddha-nature is likewise: it is neither identical to these six dharmas nor separate from them.
Good son, for this reason I say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is not form, yet not separate from form; and so on, up to:
it is not self, yet not separate from self.
There are various non-Buddhists; this third section distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox in two parts. First, it distinguishes the heterodox self as being non-existent.
"Good son, there are various non-Buddhists who, although they speak of a self, in reality have no self."
The calculations of the non-Buddhists—whether they claim [the self] is eternal and all-pervasive or that it is like a mustard seed—are both erroneous attachments.

Next, the true self is explained, which is twofold: first, the provisional self is explained; second, the ultimate self is explained. Regarding the first, the explanation of the provisional self, the text is divided into two parts:
first, the principle (dharma).
The "self" of sentient beings is precisely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); apart from the aggregates, there is no separate self. Next, the explanation of the analogies contains six parts:
the first and last contain the application (*yō*), while the middle four lack it. The school of Kaishan [Hui-ssu] holds that provisional names have function (*yō*) but no substance (*t'i*);
the school of Zhuangyan [Hui-kuan] holds that both name and substance exist. Both of these positions are untenable, whether one considers the name...

What is meant by saying that both substance and function exist? This refers to the provisional [designation]. Although the Kaishan school maintains that there is no substance, since names and functions do exist, they too cannot be considered provisional.
Master Guan cites the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*: "There is neither self nor non-self; the negation of self refutes eternalism, and the negation of non-self refutes nihilism.
It also refutes both identity and difference. For the sake of refuting these views, it is said that although "self" and "non-self" are spoken of...
Since both of these are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*), the text employs six similes to illustrate the conventional self (*pudgala*).
"Good son, it is like a lotus flower, which is formed by the combination of its stalk, petals, filaments, and base; apart from these, there is no separate flower.
The 'self' of sentient beings is also like this. Good son, it is like a wall, which is a combination of earth, grass, and wood."

It is designated as a "house," yet apart from these, there is no separate house. It is like the *khadira*, *palāśa*, *nyagrodha*, and *udumbara* trees which, when combined, form a forest; apart from these, there is no separate forest.
It is like chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry which, when combined, form an army; apart from these, there is no separate army.
An army is like a brocade made from a combination of five-colored threads; apart from these, there is no separate brocade.
Just as the four castes combined are called a "great assembly," and apart from these there is no separate assembly, so too it is with the self of sentient beings:
apart from the five aggregates, there is no separate self.
The second section, following "The Tathāgata is eternally abiding," clarifies the true self:
"Good son, the eternal abiding of the Tathāgata is called 'self. The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is boundless, unimpeded, unborn, and undying;
it has attained the eight masteries—this is called 'self. Sentient beings truly lack such a self as this, and I..."
Because what I have taken as the self is definitively and ultimately the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), it is called Buddha-nature.
This true self, which refutes the false self and is ultimately pure, is neither a self nor a non-self;
sentient beings should likewise attain this true self.

In the fourth section of the "Great Compassion" chapter, there is a broad exposition of Buddha-nature, which is further divided into three parts. First, it clarifies that Buddha-nature exists in eight ways.
Next, following what I have said above, it concludes by returning to these three points. Then, starting with "If I were to speak of form," it concludes by negating the five aggregates.
Good son, great loving-kindness and great compassion are called the Buddha-nature. Why is this?

Because great loving-kindness and great compassion always follow the bodhisattva like a shadow follows a form, and all sentient beings will certainly attain great loving-kindness and great compassion.
For this reason, it is said that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature. Great loving-kindness and great compassion are what is called the Buddha-nature, O Buddha.
"Nature" refers to the great joy and great equanimity of the Tathāgata; this is called Buddha-nature. Why is this?
Because if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot relinquish the twenty-five states of existence, they cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Since all sentient beings will inevitably attain it, for this reason it is said that all sentient beings [possess it].
That which possesses the Buddha-nature and great joy and great equanimity is itself the Buddha-nature; that which is the Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata.

The Buddha-nature is called great faith. Why is this? Because by means of faith, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to fulfill the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*, and all sentient beings shall certainly [attain it].
Because they have attained great faith, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
This great faith is itself Buddha-nature; Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata; and Buddha-nature is called the Stage of the Only Son.
Why is this? Because by means of the causal conditions of the Stage of the Only Son, a bodhisattva attains equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Because the minds of all sentient beings shall ultimately and certainly attain the stage of the only son, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The stage of the only son is precisely Buddha-nature; Buddha-nature is precisely the Tathāgata.
Buddha-nature is called the fourth power. Why is this? Because by means of the causal conditions of the fourth power, the bodhisattva then...

Because one is able to transform sentient beings so that all sentient beings will certainly attain the fourth power, it is therefore said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. This fourth power is precisely Buddha-nature; Buddha-nature is precisely the Tathāgata; and Buddha-nature is named the twelve links of dependent origination. Why is this? Because it is by means of causes and conditions. As it is said: [The original text continues: "By means of causes and conditions, suchness arises; By means of causes and conditions, suchness ceases. To see the arising and ceasing of suchness Is called seeing the Buddha. Thus, because of these causes and conditions, it is as stated above. Furthermore, the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings is the Tathāgata’s true nature. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all dharmas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all sentient beings. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all phenomena. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all things. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all realms. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all lands. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all worlds. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all Buddhas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all bodhisattvas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all dharmas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all afflictions. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all karmic retributions. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all nirvāṇas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all emptinesses. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-selfhoods. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all signlessnesses. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all wishlessnesses. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all unconditionednesses. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-arising and non-ceasing. Why is this?
