Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-clinging and non-releasing. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-grasping and non-rejecting. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-increasing and non-decreasing. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-growth and non-diminution. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-extinction and non-perishing. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-defilement and non-purity. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-bondage and non-liberation. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-obstruction and non-hindrance. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-attachment and non-detachment. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-discrimination and non-conceptualization. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-thought and non-mindfulness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-perception and non-cognition. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-knowledge and non-insight. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-wisdom and non-ignorance. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-suffering and non-happiness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-form and non-formlessness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-sound and non-silence. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-smell and non-odorlessness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-taste and non-flavorlessness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-touch and non-tangibility. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-phenomena and non-characteristics. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-dharmas and non-non-dharmas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-existence and non-non-existence. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-being and non-non-being. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-emptiness and non-non-emptiness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-mark and non-non-mark. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-desire and non-non-desire. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-form and non-non-form. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-feeling and non-non-feeling. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-perception and non-non-perception. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-volition and non-non-volition. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-consciousness and non-non-consciousness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-eye and non-non-eye. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-ear and non-non-ear. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-nose and non-non-nose. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-tongue and non-non-tongue. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-body and non-non-body. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-mind and non-non-mind. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-form and non-non-form. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-sound and non-non-sound. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-smell and non-non-smell. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-taste and non-non-taste. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-touch and non-non-touch. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-dharmas and non-non-dharmas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-eye-consciousness and non-non-eye-consciousness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-ear-consciousness and non-non-ear-consciousness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-nose-consciousness and non-non-nose-consciousness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-tongue-consciousness and non-non-tongue-consciousness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-body-consciousness and non-non-body-consciousness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-mind-consciousness and non-non-mind-consciousness. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-eye-contact and non-non-eye-contact. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-ear-contact and non-non-ear-contact. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is the nature of all non-nose-contact and non-non-nose-contact. Why
It comes to abide eternally within all sentient beings as these twelve links of dependent origination; therefore it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The twelve links of dependent origination are themselves Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata.
Buddha-nature is called the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catur-pratisaṃvid*); by means of the causes and conditions of these four unimpeded knowledges, the meaning of the words is explained.
Because the meaning of the unimpeded syllables is itself unimpeded, one is able to transform sentient beings. These four kinds of unimpededness are the Buddha-nature;
the Buddha-nature is the Tathāgata. Buddha-nature is called the "Crown Samādhi" (Mūrdha-samādhi).
Because one cultivates this Crown Samādhi, one is then able to encompass all Buddha-dharmas. Therefore, it is said that the Crown Samādhi is named "Buddha."
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages who cultivate this samādhi have not yet attained its full perfection;
although they perceive the Buddha-nature, they do not clearly understand that all sentient beings will certainly attain it. For this reason, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

The first four [powers] are as stated in the text. Regarding the fifth, it says: "As for the fourth power, one interpretation holds that this is the fourth of the ten powers, the faculty-power (*indriya-bala*), which knows the essential conditions for transforming beings according to their faculties.
A second interpretation holds that there is a distinct teaching: first, the power of faith; second, the power of patience; third, the power of concentration;
and fourth, the power of skillful means (*upāya-kuśala-bala*). This power of skillful means is so called because it facilitates the path of transformation."

Regarding the statement in the fourth power and the sixth section that the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are themselves Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), both of the two interpretations offered by others are unsatisfactory.
The first claims that the twelve links are contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*); how then could they possess the nature of an objective realm?
The second claims they are the nature of the fruit (*phala-dharmatā*); this is also untenable. Here, it is clarified that the twelve links of dependent origination are indeed Buddha-nature.
There is another source [for this statement] (and so forth). The remaining two cases are as stated in the text.
Good son, because all sentient beings will certainly attain all these various dharmas as described above, it is therefore said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
"Good son, if I were to say that form (*rūpa*) is the Buddha-nature, sentient beings, upon hearing this, would give rise to perverse inversion.
Because of this perverse inversion, at the end of their lives they would be reborn in the Avīci Hell. The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the purpose of severing the hells;
therefore, I do not say that form is the Buddha-nature. This applies even up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is likewise."
Good son, as for all those sentient beings who have fallen into the second [category], there is a summary that answers the previous question in three parts.
First, it summarizes the question regarding the lack of need to cultivate the path:
"Good son, if all sentient beings were to realize their Buddha-nature, they would not need to cultivate the path, even [the path of] the Ten Abidings Bodhisattvas."
If those who cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path see the Buddha-nature only to a small degree, how much less can those who do not cultivate it see it? Good son,
since Mañjuśrī and other bodhisattvas have cultivated the Noble Path for immeasurable eons and thus fully understood the Buddha-nature,
how could śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possibly know the Buddha-nature?
Next, if there are sentient beings who have not yet severed their fetters, they should be exhorted:

"If any sentient beings wish to clearly realize the Buddha-nature, they should single-mindedly receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain, offer worship, show respect, honor, and praise this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Upon seeing those who do so receive and uphold it..."
Furthermore, one should praise those who extol such a sutra as this, providing them with excellent dwellings, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness and infirmity;
moreover, one should praise, prostrate to, and inquire after them.
Good son, if there are those who, throughout immeasurable and boundless past lives, have personally approached and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas...
Only after planting roots of goodness can one hear the name of this sutra.
Regarding the three inconceivable Buddha-natures, the following is the concluding praise in two parts: first, the Buddha’s own praise:
"Good son, the Buddha-nature is inconceivable; the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is also inconceivable. All...
That all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature yet are unable to know it is inconceivable;
that the Tathāgata’s dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity are also inconceivable; and that all sentient beings are able to believe in this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is likewise inconceivable.
Next is the praise by Siṃhanāda.

The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, those among this great assembly who can believe in such an inconceivable Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra number eighty-five thousand."
Hundreds of millions of people do not give rise to faith in this sutra;
therefore, those who are able to believe in this sutra are called inconceivable sons of good family.
Such persons shall, in future ages, also certainly attain faith in this scripture, perceive the Buddha-nature, and realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The Lion’s Roar asked: "What is meant by 'not falling back'? Second, regarding those who have seen the Buddha-nature and are exhorted to practice, there is a question and an answer as stated in the text.
The Lion’s Roar said: "World-Honored One, how does a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva know for himself that he possesses the mind of non-retrogression and is certain [of his attainment]?"

The Buddha replied that there are three [reasons]: first, testing one's own mind; second, undergoing suffering for the sake of sentient beings; and third, transforming others through the six perfections.
The first is self-cultivation, while the latter two are the transformation of others.
The Buddha said, "Good son, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should test his own mind through ascetic practices.
For seven days he eats only one sesame seed per day; likewise with rice, mung beans, hemp seeds, millet, and white beans, each for seven days.
When eating only one sesame seed, he reflects thus: 'Such ascetic practices as these are all...'"
If one is able to perform even that which is neither beneficial nor purposeful, how much more so that which is truly beneficial? One should not fail to act accordingly.
Because the mind can endure what is not beneficial without wavering or turning back, one will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
While practicing such asceticism for these days, all his skin and flesh became emaciated, shriveled, and wasted away.
It was like a fresh gourd cut open and placed in the sun, its eyes sunken like stars at the bottom of a well;
its flesh wasted away until only the sinews remained, like a dilapidated thatched hut; its backbone appeared in succession like a string of beads;

and the place where it sat was like a horse's hoofprint—when it wished to sit, it collapsed, and when it wished to rise, it fell prostrate. Although it endured such useless suffering, it did not retreat from [the practice].
Regarding the Bodhicitta:

when one first attempts it, it is still a shallow practice; its profound virtue does not require further explanation. As for the character [序-予+禾], people read it with the sound "he" (hé), which is incorrect.
Others say it has the sound "li" (lí), and others say it has the sound "[序-予+禾]" (xù-yú-hé); however, upon searching and examining, this character does not exist.
Good son, a bodhisattva undergoes suffering for the sake of sentient beings in order to destroy the two lower [obscuration]s.

Furthermore, good son, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva bestows peace and happiness in order to destroy all sufferings, he is able to relinquish internal and external wealth as well as his own body and life, discarding them like blades of grass; if he can thus disregard this body—
O Life-possessor, in this way the Bodhisattva knows for himself that he is certain to possess the non-retrogressive mind, thinking, "I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, for the sake of the Dharma, the Bodhisattva carves his own body to serve as a lamp-wick;
he wraps his skin and flesh with cloth, pours ghee over it, and burns it as a wick. At that time, the Bodhisattva undergoes this great suffering himself.
He rebuked his mind, saying: "Such suffering as this does not even equal one-hundred-thousand-millionth part of the suffering in hell.
Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you have experienced great agony without any benefit.
If you cannot endure this slight suffering, how will you be able to rescue sentient beings from their suffering within hell?"
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, his body does not perceive suffering, and his mind does not retreat, waver, or turn back.
At that time, the Bodhisattva should deeply know within himself: "I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son, at that time, although the Bodhisattva is fully possessed of afflictions and has not yet severed them, these serve as the causal conditions for the Dharma.
If a bodhisattva is able to give their head, eyes, marrow, brain, hands, feet, blood, and flesh to sentient beings, and even when nailing their body with stakes,
throwing themselves from cliffs, or leaping into fire, their mind does not retreat, does not waver, and does not turn back at such immeasurable sufferings—
then a bodhisattva should know that they now certainly possess a non-retrogressive mind and shall attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

O Son of Good Family, for the sake of destroying the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who seeks *samyak-saṃbodhi* vows to take on the body of a coarse and large animal. He gives his own flesh and blood to sentient beings;
when they take it, he again manifests compassion as a Bodhisattva, at which time he holds his breath without gasping and displays the appearance of death so that they may take [the body].
One who does not give rise to thoughts of killing or the net of doubt is a bodhisattva; though such a one may receive the body of an animal, they ultimately never perform the karma of an animal.
Why is this? Good son, once a bodhisattva has attained the non-retrogressive mind, they will never perform the karma of the three evil realms.
If, in a future age, a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to encounter even so much as a speck of dust...
As for those who do not experience the retribution of evil karma in a fixed manner, they accept it all on behalf of sentient beings through the power of their great vows.

It is like a patient possessed by a ghost who hides within the body, yet by the power of a mantra, the spirit immediately manifests its form—speaking, rejoicing, becoming angry, reviling, weeping, or laughing. So too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva regarding the future...

The karmic actions leading to the three evil realms of this world are likewise so. When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas receive the body of a bear, they constantly expound the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
or, receiving the body of a *kapiñjala* bird, they expound the True Dharma for all sentient beings.
For this reason, they receive the bodies of a *gōṭa*, a deer, a rabbit, an elephant, a ram, a monkey, a white pigeon, and a *garuḍa*.
When the Bodhisattva receives such bodies as those of birds, dragons, and snakes among the animal realm, he never commits the evil karma of an animal;
rather, he constantly expounds the True Dharma for other sentient beings in the animal realm so that, upon hearing the Dharma, they may quickly attain liberation from their animal bodies.
One should know that at such times, although the Bodhisattva assumes an animal body, he does not perform evil deeds. It must be understood that...

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with resolute and non-regressing minds who, during an age of famine, seeing hungry sentient beings, manifest as the bodies of turtles and fish many *yojana* in length, and further make this vow:
"May all sentient beings, when taking my flesh, have it grow back immediately as they take it;
by eating my flesh, may they all be freed from the suffering of hunger and thirst and cause everyone to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Third, regarding the Bodhisattva’s aspiration for the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*):

"If there be anyone who, because of me, shall be freed from hunger and thirst, may they in future ages swiftly attain liberation from the suffering of hunger and thirst within the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
If a Bodhisattva undergoes such suffering of mind without retreating, one should know that they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva...
In an age of pestilence, seeing those suffering from disease, one should reflect:
"Just as the King of Medicine Trees heals all illnesses—whether one takes its root, stem, branch, leaf, flower, fruit, bark, or pith—may this body of mine be likewise.
May any who hear my voice, touch my body, or consume my flesh and blood be completely cured."

"May all illnesses, even those reaching the marrow, be completely healed. I vow that when sentient beings eat my flesh, they will not give rise to an evil mind as if eating the flesh of their own children.
Once I have cured their illness, may I always preach the Dharma for them; may they believe and accept it, contemplate it, and teach it to others."
Furthermore, good son, although a bodhisattva who is fully possessed of afflictions experiences physical suffering, his mind does not retreat, waver, or turn back;
you should know that he will certainly attain the non-retrogressive mind and achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, good son, if there are sentient beings afflicted by ghosts, as soon as the bodhisattva sees them, he immediately acts [to help].
He made this vow: "May I take on the body of a ghost—a large body, a robust body, and one with many followers—so that upon hearing or seeing me, their illnesses may be cured.
For the sake of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva diligently practices asceticism; though he possesses afflictions, they do not defile his mind.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s practice of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to transform others is as described in the text.
Furthermore, son of good family, although the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the six perfections, he does not seek the fruits of those six perfections.
While practicing the unsurpassed six perfections, he makes this vow, saying: "I..."
Now, with these six *pāramitās*, I give to all sentient beings;
once each and every sentient being has received my gift, may they all attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

I too shall personally practice the six *pāramitās* through diligent cultivation and asceticism, enduring all manner of suffering and affliction; while undergoing such suffering, I vow that I shall not retreat from *bodhi*.
Good son, when a bodhisattva contemplates in this manner, it is called the mark of non-retrogression from bodhi.
Furthermore, within the second major section of the "Lower Volume," there are three parts praising the teaching: first, praising the person who propagates the sutra, which is the bodhisattva;
second, praising the Dharma being propagated, which is the Nirvana teaching; and third, praising the exposition of the teaching.
The "Lord" is the Tathāgata; the teaching does not propagate itself, but its propagation depends on people; the teaching does not proclaim itself, but its proclamation proceeds from the Buddha.
Thus, they praise one another in succession. This is also a praise of the Triple Gem. The first section has two parts: first, a general and brief praise;

second, an extensive explanation. Within the initial brief praise, there are two parts: first, a general praise of the Bodhisattvas; second, a specific praise of those in their final birth (*caramabhavika*).
These great beings (*mahāsattva*) are praised because they labor with humility and diligence for the benefit of sentient beings;

they are praised specifically as those in their final birth (*ciopaccha*), who are about to succeed to the position of the Honored One. First, there are nine verses of specific praise; next, there is general praise as found in the text.
Furthermore, good son, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is inconceivable. Why?
Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva deeply understands that saṃsāra abounds in many faults and transgressions, and perceives that great nirvāṇa possesses great merit;
thus, for the sake of all sentient beings, they dwell within saṃsāra and undergo various kinds of suffering without ever regressing. This is called the inconceivability of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is inconceivable that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives rise to compassion without any external cause;
truly, they do not receive gratitude, yet they constantly bestow grace, and though they bestow grace, they do not seek recompense. For this reason, it is further called inconceivable.
Furthermore, son of good family, there may be sentient beings who practice various austerities for their own benefit.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices asceticism for the sake of benefiting others, this is called self-benefit;

therefore, it is further called inconceivable. Furthermore, when a bodhisattva who is still possessed of afflictions cultivates a mind of equanimity toward the various sufferings experienced by both enemies and kin in order to destroy them, it is for this reason further called inconceivable. Furthermore, if a bodhisattva...
When he sees sentient beings who are evil and unwholesome, he may reprimand them, speak to them gently, expel them, or simply let them be.
Toward those of a wicked nature, he manifests gentleness; toward those who are arrogant, he manifests great arrogance, yet in his inner mind there is truly no arrogance.
This is called the inconceivable skillful means (*upāya*) of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, the bodhisattva is fully endowed with afflictions...
When their wealth and possessions are meager, those who come to them for alms are many, yet their minds are not constricted; this is called the inconceivable nature of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when a Buddha has appeared in the world, the bodhisattva, knowing the Buddha’s merits, takes on a body in a remote borderland where no Buddha resides—like one who is blind, deaf, lame, or crippled—for the sake of sentient beings; this is called the inconceivable nature of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva deeply understands all the transgressions of sentient beings; for the sake of their deliverance, he always acts together with them.
Although he conforms to their inclinations, he is not defiled by the stains of their offenses. For this reason, he is further called "inconceivable.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva clearly perceives and sees that there is no characteristic of a sentient being, no defilement of afflictions, no path of cultivation, and freedom from afflictions.
Although such a person acts for the sake of bodhi, there is neither a practice of bodhi nor one who accomplishes the practice of bodhi;
yet, while there is no one who undergoes suffering or destroys suffering, they are nonetheless able to perform the practices of bodhi in order to destroy the suffering of sentient beings.
For this reason, it is further called inconceivable.
Next, regarding the reception of the final body, there are seven further sections of distinct praise.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva receives his final body in the Tuṣita Heaven, this too is called inconceivable. Why?
Because among the heavens of the Desire Realm, the Tuṣita Heaven is superior; those in the lower heavens have minds that are negligent and distracted.
Those who ascend to the heavens have dull faculties; therefore, this is called "superior cultivation. By cultivating generosity and morality, one obtains a body in the upper or lower realms;
by cultivating generosity, morality, and meditative concentration, one obtains a body in Tuṣita. All Bodhisattvas revile all states of existence (*bhava*) and destroy all states of existence;
they never perform the karma for Tuṣita Heaven to receive a body in that heaven. Why is this? Because if a Bodhisattva were to remain in any other [state],...
Furthermore, they are able to teach and bring sentient beings to maturity; though they truly possess no desire-mind, they are born into the desire realm.
For this reason, they are again called the inconceivable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. When born in Tuṣita Heaven, there are three things by which they excel:
first, life; second, physical form; and third, name. Although these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas truly do not seek after life, physical form, or fame, [they nevertheless possess them].
Seeking the mind and attaining what is superior, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva deeply delights in *nirvāṇa*, and their causal conditions are likewise superior;
for this reason, they are further called the inconceivable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Although these three matters are superior to those of the devas, the devas and others ultimately never give rise toward the Bodhisattva to thoughts of anger, envy, or arrogance.
The Bodhisattva constantly gives rise to a joyful mind and is not arrogant even toward the devas; for this reason, he is further called the inconceivable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
He does not create karma for his lifespan, yet his life-span in those heavens is ultimate—this is called "superiority of life.
He has no karma for form, yet his wondrous body is filled with pervasive radiance—this is called "superiority of form," O Bodhisattva.
The Mahāsattva dwells in that celestial palace, taking no pleasure in the five desires but engaging solely in Dharma activities;
therefore, his fame fills the ten directions, and he is called "Renowned" (Yaśasvin). For this reason, he is further called the "Inconceivable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
When he descends from Tuṣita Heaven, at that time the great earth trembles in six ways; for this reason, he is further called "Inconceivable."
For what reason? When the Bodhisattva descended, the devas of the desire and form realms all came to attend and escort him, raising a great sound to praise the Bodhisattva;
by the breath from their mouths, they caused the earth to tremble. Furthermore, among humans there is the Elephant King, and this Elephant King among humans is named the Dragon King.
When the Dragon King first entered the womb, various dragon kings were present upon this earth.
Some below may feel fear or trepidation; therefore, the great earth shakes in six ways. For this reason, he is further named the Inconceivable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
He knows the times of entering, abiding in, and emerging from the womb;
he knows his father and mother, yet remains unstained by impurity, like the indranīla-blue jewel of Śakra. For this reason, he is further named the Inconceivable.

In the second passage, it says that regarding the three matters of superiority: among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the life-span of these [Sudṛśa] gods is fixed; among humans, the life-span of the *Uttarakuru* is fixed;

and including the Brahmā-world as the seventh, this celestial abode is described in the text as being "either fearful or awakened. (The character previously read as *hé* [盍] is actually the phonetic for *jiào* [覺], meaning "awakened").
Regarding this, Master Seng’an questioned Wang Jian, who replied: [...]* *Note: The bracketed portion indicates the original text’s commentary on the reading of the character.*

This is the son of Sengda, who was widely learned and famous. Ancient scribes wrote the character for "teaching" (jiao) with a "cave" (穴) radical, a vertical "heart" (心) stroke, and the character "I" (吾) placed beside it;
nowadays, people have simplified the "cave" radical to a single "ear" (耳).
Good son, the following two sections praise the sutra in two parts: first the praise, then the detailed analysis. In the initial text, there are the Dharma, the parable, and the application.
The Dharma is visible.
Son of good family, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is likewise inconceivable.
Son of good family, for example, the great ocean has eight inconceivable qualities. What are these eight? First, it gradually deepens.
1. It is profoundly deep; 2. it is difficult to reach its bottom; 3. it has a single uniform salty taste; 4. its tides do not exceed their limits; 5.
it contains various treasuries of jewels; 6. large-bodied beings dwell within it; 7. it does not harbor corpses; 8.
when all the myriad streams and great rains pour into it, it neither increases nor decreases. Good son, as it gradually becomes deeper, there are three further matters: what are they?
These constitute three [points]: first, the power of the merit of sentient beings; second, proceeding with the wind; and third, because the river water flows into it.
Furthermore, regarding the fact that it neither increases nor decreases, there are likewise three [points].

In the subsequent analogy, it says, "deep and difficult to find its bottom. A person’s interpretation states: "In terms of vertical discourse, it refers exclusively to permanence, bliss, self, and purity."
It is not the case that [the teaching] is profound because it is difficult to fathom due to its cross-referential discussion of permanence, impermanence, and so forth;
this is also incorrect. The sutra merely says "profound"—why provide such a one-sided interpretation?
Now, I maintain that it is called "profound" because it is permanent yet not permanent, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither identical nor different, and inconceivable (and so forth).
It is as stated in the text.
This subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is likewise possessed of eight inconceivable aspects. The first is gradual profundity, namely:
the five precepts, the ten precepts, the two hundred and fifty precepts, the bodhisattva precepts, and the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

The fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of the Anāgāmin, the fruit of the Arhat, the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha, the fruit of the Bodhisattva, and the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—these dharmas are described in the Nirvāṇa Sūtra as being progressively deeper.
For this reason, this sūtra is called "Progressively Deep. Furthermore, these two depths are difficult to fathom; thus, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, [has spoken of them].
Because it is neither born nor extinguished, it does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, does not turn the wheel of Dharma, and does not practice the giving of wisdom through eating or receiving;
for this reason, it is called permanent, blissful, self, and pure. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

This Buddha-nature is not form (*rūpa*), yet it is not separate from form; it is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*), yet it is not separate from consciousness either.
One can always perceive that the revealing cause (*vyañjanahetu*) is not a producing cause (*kārakahetu*).
From the stage of a *srotāpanna* up to a *pratyekabuddha*, one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; yet there are neither afflictions (*kleśa*) nor a place of dwelling (*sthāna*).

Although there are no afflictions, this is not called "eternal" (*nitya*); therefore, it is called "profound. Furthermore, within this sutra, there is that which is even more profound: at times it speaks of a "self" (*ātman*), or...
He speaks of non-self, or at times speaks of permanence, or speaks of impermanence; at times he speaks of purity, or speaks of impurity; at times he speaks of pleasure, or speaks of suffering;
at times he speaks of emptiness, or speaks of non-emptiness; he speaks of the existence of all things, or speaks of the non-existence of all things;
he speaks of the three vehicles, or speaks of the one vehicle; or he speaks that the five aggregates are themselves the Buddha.
The Samādhi of the Nature-Vajra, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi of the Middle Way, the twelve links of dependent origination, the ultimate emptiness, compassion,
equanimity toward all sentient beings, the wisdom of the crown, faith, the knowledge of the faculties and powers, and the unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena—
though the Buddha-nature exists within them, it is not declared to be determinate; for this reason, these are called the three profound samādhis.
The single salty taste; all sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature; they are all of one vehicle, one liberation, one cause, and one fruit;
they shall all attain the same nectar of permanence, bliss, self, and purity—this is called the "single flavor.
Just as the four tides do not exceed their limits, so too in this sutra it is prescribed that bhikṣus must not accept or store the eight impure things.

If any of my disciples are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain, and analyze this subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtra, they would rather lose their bodies and lives than ever violate it; this is called "the tide not overstepping its limit.

There are various treasuries of jewels, and this sutra is precisely an immeasurable treasury of jewels. What is called "jewels" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
The four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
the conduct of infants, the noble conduct, the Brahma-conduct, and the celestial conduct; all skillful means; the Buddha-nature of sentient beings;
the merits of bodhisattvas, the merits of Tathāgatas, the merits of śrāvakas, and the merits of pratyekabuddhas; the six pāramitās; and immeasurable samādhis.
The measure of wisdom is called the treasury of jewels; it is the dwelling place of beings with great bodies.

"Beings with great bodies" refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. They are called "beings with great bodies" because of their great wisdom, their great mind, their great adornment, their great subduing, their great skillful means, their great preaching of the Dharma, and their great power. Great...

Because of their retinue, because of their great supernormal powers, because of their great compassion, because they are eternally unchanging, because they are free from all obstructions regarding all sentient beings, and because they accommodate all sentient beings—this is called the "Great Body. Where such beings dwell, seven things do not remain after death:
that is, corpses. By "corpses" is meant those who are icchantikas, those who have committed the four grave prohibitions, and those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution.
To commit the sin of slandering the Vaipulya sutras by declaring non-Dharma to be Dharma and Dharma to be non-Dharma; to accept and store the eight kinds of impure things;
to use the property of the Buddha or the property of the Sangha according to one's own whims;
or to commit unrighteous acts toward bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—these are called "corpses. This *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is free from such things; therefore, it is called "not harboring corpses."

The eighth [topic], the *śava*, is without increase or decrease because it is boundless, because it has no beginning or end, because it is not form, because it is unconditioned, because it is eternally abiding, because it is neither arising nor ceasing, because all sentient beings are entirely equal, and because all natures are of one and the same nature.
This is called "without increase or decrease. Therefore, this sutra possesses eight inconceivable qualities, just like that great ocean.
In the following two sections of the Lion’s Roar, there is a series of questions and answers. The Lion’s Roar said:

“World-Honored One, if you say that the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished and this is what is called ‘profound,’ then all sentient beings have four modes of birth—egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. Among these four modes of birth, humans...”

It should be known that among humans there are those born from eggs and those born from moisture, just as the bhikṣu Śiva, the bhikṣu Upaśiva, the householder Mṛgāra’s mother, the householder Nyagrodha’s mother, and the householder Pañcāla’s mother each had five hundred sons who were all born from eggs. Regarding this, the Buddha said: "In the past..."
When he was a bodhisattva, he was King Mūrdhaja and King Hastija, as has been related; he was also the daughter of the *āmra* tree and the daughter of the *kapittha* tree.
One should know that among humans there is moisture-born birth (*saṃsvedaja*). At the beginning of the eon, all sentient beings were entirely born by transformation (*aupapāduka*).
For what reason and by what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, who has attained the eight masteries (*aṣṭavaśitā*), not undergo birth by transformation?
"Yes. [The interlocutor] asks: "Is it that from the beginning, that which is profound and difficult to attain—neither arising nor ceasing—is not of three kinds of birth, but only of one kind?
The Buddha answers by first explaining in general that he does not undergo birth from eggs or moisture.
The Buddha said, "Good son, when all sentient beings born through the four modes of birth have attained the noble Dharma,
they can no longer be as they were originally— born from eggs or born from moisture. Next,
[the sūtra] specifically clarifies that they do not undergo transformational birth (upapāduka), and so forth."
Good son, at the beginning of the kalpa, all sentient beings were born by transformation; at that time, no Buddha appeared in the world.
Good son, when sentient beings encounter the suffering of illness, they require physicians and medicine.

Although sentient beings at the beginning of the kalpa were born by transformation and possessed afflictions, their illnesses had not yet manifested; therefore, the Tathāgata did not appear in the world during that initial kalpa.
Because the bodies and minds of sentient beings are not suitable vessels, the Tathāgata does not appear in the world.

Good son, the lineage, retinue, and parents of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, surpass those of all other sentient beings; because they are so preeminent, all who hear the Dharma he teaches believe and accept it.
For this reason, the Tathāgata does not undergo transformation-birth (*upapāduka*). Good son, [he is] the father of all sentient beings.

If a son performs the karma of a father, and a father performs the karma of a son, then if the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, were to receive a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), he would have no parents.
If he had no parents, how could he cause all sentient beings to perform various wholesome karmas? Therefore, the Tathāgata does not receive a transformation body.
Good son, within the Buddha’s True Dharma there are two kinds of protection: the internal and the external. The internal protection...
That which is called "external protection through the observance of precepts" refers to relatives and kinsmen;

however, if a Buddha or Tathāgata were to receive a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), there would be no such external protection. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not receive a transformation body. Good son, there are those who give rise to arrogance based on their clan;
in order to destroy such pride, the Tathāgata is born into a noble lineage and does not receive a transformation body.
"O son, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has true parents: his father is named Śuddhodana and his mother is named Māyā.
Yet sentient beings still say he is an illusion; how then could he receive a body born of transformation?

If he were to receive a transformed body, how could there be *śarīra* relics of fragmented bone? It was for the sake of increasing the merit and virtue of sentient beings that the Tathāgata fragmented his own body and caused [relics to remain]."
Because I have made offerings, the Tathāgata does not accept a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); all Buddhas are entirely without birth by transformation.
Why, then, should I alone be made to receive a transformation body?
At that time, the three verses beginning with "Lion's Roar" below praise the Lord of the Sūtra; the first two lines of these forty-line verses are as follows:
The Request to Speak.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and praised the Buddha in verse:
“The Tathāgata is a mass of immeasurable merit; I am now unable to proclaim it fully.”
Now, for the sake of sentient beings, I shall expound one portion; I only pray that you will compassionately listen as I speak these thirty-seven verses of praise.
Sentient beings wander in the darkness of ignorance, fully undergoing hundreds of boundless kinds of suffering.
The World-Honored One is able to cause them to distance themselves from it; therefore, the world calls him the Greatly Compassionate One.
Sentient beings wander back and forth within the ropes of birth and death, heedless, deluded, and devoid of peace and happiness.
The Tathāgata can bestow peace and happiness upon all; therefore, he forever severs the ropes of birth and death.
Because the Buddha is able to bestow peace and happiness upon all beings, he does not crave his own pleasure;
for the sake of all sentient beings, he practices asceticism.
Therefore, when the world offers him worship, he remains unmoved even when seeing others suffer, as if his body were trembling; though dwelling in hell, he feels no pain.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he undergoes great suffering; therefore, there is none superior and none equal to the Tathāgata.
For the sake of the multitude, the Tathāgata practices asceticism, accomplishing and fulfilling the six perfections.
His mind remains unmoved by the winds of heterodoxy; therefore, he is the Great Being who triumphs over the world.
Sentient beings constantly desire peace and happiness, yet they do not know how to cultivate the causes of peace and happiness.
The Tathāgata is able to instruct them so that they may practice these causes, just as a compassionate father loves his only son.
When the Buddha sees sentient beings afflicted by the maladies of the afflictions (*kleśa*), his heart suffers like a mother grieving for her sick child.
Constantly contemplating the various means to be free from illness, he understands that this body is subject to others and that all sentient beings undergo various sufferings;
yet their minds are inverted, taking these for pleasure.
The Tathāgata expounds upon true suffering and pleasure, and for this reason, he is titled the Greatly Compassionate One.
The world dwells entirely within the shell of ignorance; No intellectual beak exists that can break it open.
Only the Tathāgata’s beak of wisdom can shatter it;
Therefore, he is called the Greatest Son, Not encompassed by the three periods of time, Devoid of name or conventional designation.
Having realized the profound meaning of Nirvana, he is therefore called the Buddha, the Great Awakened One.
There is a river with swirling currents that submerges sentient beings; blinded by ignorance, they do not know how to escape.
The Tathagata, having crossed over himself, is able to deliver others; therefore, the Buddha is called the Great Captain.

Able to know all causes and effects, and likewise thoroughly penetrating the path to their cessation and extinction, you constantly bestow the medicine for the sickness and suffering of sentient beings;
therefore, the world calls you the Great King of Physicians.
Through the practice of asceticism taught by those of heterodox views, one may thereby attain unsurpassed bliss.
The Tathāgata expounds the practice of true bliss, enabling sentient beings to experience happiness;
the World-Honored Tathāgata destroys heterodox paths and reveals to sentient beings the path of true correctness.
Those who walk this path attain peace and joy; therefore, the Buddha is called the Guide.
Not created by self, nor by another, Nor produced by both together, nor without cause—
Such is the matter of suffering taught by the Tathāgata, Surpassing all those of the non-Buddhists.
Having fully perfected the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, He likewise teaches these dharmas to sentient beings.
When giving the Dharma, he is free from envy and stinginess; therefore, the Buddha is said to possess unconditional compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*).
It is unconditioned and without causal basis; thus he attains that which is neither cause nor karmic fruit.
For this reason, all the wise proclaim that the Tathāgata does not seek recompense.
Though constantly dwelling among those in the world who act with negligence, his body is never defiled by negligence;
therefore he is called the Inconceivable One. The eight worldly dharmas cannot defile him;
the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has neither enemy nor friend, and thus his mind is always equanimous.
[The section on] the three types of fetters (and so forth).
My lion’s roar praises Great Compassion; [this concludes] the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the Sutra of the Great Parinirvāṇa that can roar the immeasurable lion’s roar, Fascicle Thirty.

The Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-four: The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, Volume Thirty-one. Revised by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhìrén.

Revised by the Jin dynasty śramaṇas Huìyán,
Huìguān, and Xiè Língyùn;
the twenty-fourth chapter, the Kāśyapa Chapter.

This was a virtuous beginning for the inquiry; now, desiring to bring it to completion, he requests further clarification. Following the previous thematic headings according to their meaning, this section is titled after the person, thus "Kāśyapa.
As previously explained, Kāśyapa opens with skillful means by using this response concerning the nature of peace and bliss.

Regarding the "Stages" (Bhūmi), Master Anle [of the] Ci (慈) school provides the following exegesis on the section on "Skillful Abiding and Sustenance": [this is] the same as that of Xinghuang [Temple] in Hexi.
Regarding the gate of Buddha-nature, we now clarify the fifth [topic]: the function of *nirvāṇa*. This scripture discusses Buddha-nature comprehensively from beginning to end.
What are the similarities and differences between this chapter and the preceding one? Briefly stated, there are five points of difference: first, the meaning and function differ;

whereas the preceding chapter clarifies the Buddha-nature as the Middle Way and as the seed of *bodhi*, this chapter clarifies the supreme function of Buddha-nature, which is capable of encompassing all.
The extremely wicked icchantikas and the biased heterodox outsiders differ from those mentioned in the preceding chapter regarding the nature of causes;
there it was clarified that the nature of the cause resides in the cause and not in the fruit.

This chapter clarifies that all evil aggregates (*skandhas*) are the Buddha-nature. This is the nature of the cause; from these evil five aggregates, the wholesome five aggregates arise. This, too, is...
Regarding the nature of fruition (*phala-dhātu*), it is also said that Buddha-nature exists across the three periods of time, while the fruition-nature of the sages does not.

Some have traditionally interpreted this by claiming that the fruition-nature of fruition (*phala-phala*) pervades the three periods, whereas the Buddha-nature of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) does not;
however, this is incorrect. It simply states that the nature of fruition pervades the causal stage.
As for the fruit, why must one distinguish between the two bodies that correspond to the Dharma? If the five aggregates of a Buddha are wholesome, the Buddha-nature encompasses both cause and fruit.

The Buddha-nature within the cause is subsumed under the three periods of time, whereas the Buddha-nature of the fruit is not subsumed under the three periods of time. Regarding the distinctions of opening and closing:

in the preceding chapter, the river of birth-and-death combined the four fruits and separated them from the three vehicles; in this chapter, the river of nirvāṇa separates the four fruits and combines them with the three.

Building upon the fourfold distinctions made in the preceding chapter, which universally elucidated the five kinds of Buddha-nature—showing that gods, humans, and beings of the six realms all possess Buddha-nature—this chapter specifically clarifies the *dharmatā* (causal) Buddha-nature.
It demonstrates that even those with no aspiration for enlightenment (*icchantika*) can still give rise to wholesome roots by virtue of this causal nature.

While the preceding chapter specifically addressed the "understanding cause" (*parijñā-hetu*) of Buddha-nature based on the myriad wholesome deeds, this chapter addresses both good and evil as being equally [the basis of] it.
Because of the Buddha-nature, it is said that those with roots of goodness exist, while icchantikas do not; those who are not icchantikas exist, while those with roots of goodness do not.

In the previous chapter, one person was addressed; in this chapter, Kāśyapa is addressed again. Although the various differences are many, at the beginning of this chapter, the distinct functions are clarified.
Since the chapters were established from the original intent, it is said that Nirvāṇa functions [differently]. According to the text, there are two parts.

First, the subduing of the evil is clarified; subsequently, the subduing of the heterodox is clarified. Within the subduing of the evil, there are two parts: first, the function of Buddha-nature is clarified; second, the sutra is praised.
Regarding the clarification of the function, there are again two parts: first, the severance of goodness is clarified; second, the production of goodness is clarified.

Because of the power of false delusion, goodness is severed; because of the power of Buddha-nature, goodness is produced. The ancient commentary states: "There are two types of people: those who commit evil and those who produce goodness."
Furthermore, they occur in succession yet are not mutually related. Another teacher says: "It is simply one person who, being inverted at first, gives rise to evil;
later, encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), good arises. Now we clarify that this is not so; it may be one person or many people.

For example, the seven types [of beings] in the river refer to many people; if it were one person, then from the initial sinking [in saṃsāra] until the attainment of Buddhahood would constitute a single continuum.
This refers to a single individual—formerly described as one who "produces goodness" (*shansheng*)—who possesses the capacity for the reception of consciousness (*jieshi*).

Such a sentient being, having begun by arising from within the cave of ignorance and consciousness outside the realms (*jiewai*) with a single grade of ignorance (*wuming*), has not yet given rise to the four abidings (*sizhu*).

If a Buddha receives them and leads them away, they immediately attain Buddhahood. This interpretation presents a major obstacle; even if such a sutra existed, it would merely represent a case of reforming evil at a particular moment.
If this sūtra did not exist, one would be entirely unable to rely [on a path].

If you say that one must necessarily complete the five stages of abiding before being able to reform evil and practice good, there is not a single sūtra that definitively states this. Even if such a sūtra existed, it would merely take "a single moment" as the condition.
If that were so, once evil has reached its extreme, one would be spontaneously received [into the path] by itself; what need would there be for the cultivation of the path?
How does this differ from attaining the Way after eighty thousand kalpas? If you say that one comes from within the "cave of consciousness," then one comes from within ignorance (*avidyā*).
How then can you say that ignorance begins with the first grade? If no delusion has yet arisen, one should be born in another place.
If one comes from the cave and is received [into the womb] at the moment the first grade of ignorance begins, then for all subsequent grades...
If one is not received [into the higher stages] even upon reaching the fourth dwelling, why is one not received into the fourth dwelling once one has already been received into the cave of ignorance?
Therefore, this is difficult to believe. If that were so, there would be no need at all to cultivate the higher stages;
this refutes the old claim that if the power of the Buddha-nature allows one to attain Bodhi spontaneously without cultivation, then cultivation is unnecessary.

The claim that Sunakṣatra has no point of origin and is therefore a truly evil person is incorrect. Although this meaning is not explicitly seen in the sūtras, by inferring from the underlying principle, we know it is a provisional teaching (*upāya*).
Why? Because the Buddha’s two disciples each followed paths of good and evil—Ānanda practiced goodness and Devadatta committed evil—and all of these were provisional.
Now, by analogy with Rāhula practicing goodness and Sunakṣatra committing evil, we know they are likewise provisional.

The passage on the severance of the roots of goodness consists of three parts: first, identifying the person who severs the roots of goodness; second, identifying the characteristics of the severance of the roots of goodness;
and third, identifying the views that lead to the severance of the roots of goodness. Regarding the person who severs the roots of goodness, this refers to Śuklodana (Sunakṣatra).

Regarding the characteristics of the severance of the roots of goodness, it concerns those of indeterminate faculties who, upon hearing the indeterminate teachings, form fixed attachments to them. Regarding the views that lead to the severance of the roots of goodness, these consist of the analytical investigation into the principles of all phenomena.
Regarding the first section on humans, there are two parts: first, the question, and second, the answer. The question is divided into two:

first, the introductory context (*nidāna*), and second, the formal inquiry. Within the introductory context, there are two parts: first, clarifying that the Buddha possesses the virtue of being able to transform others; second, clarifying that Sunakṣatra possesses the conditions for being transformed.
Regarding the Buddha, there are again two parts: first, internally possessing compassion; second, externally possessing skillful means. As for the first passage:
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has compassion for all sentient beings.
'Compassion' (lián) refers to great kindness (*maitrī*), and 'pity' (cì) refers to great compassion (*karuṇā*).
Following this, the seven phrases beginning with 'the ability to tame those who are untamed' constitute the external skillful means."
He can tame those who are untamed, purify those who are impure, provide refuge to those without refuge, and bring liberation to those not yet liberated;
having attained the eight masteries, he acts as a great physician and a great king of medicine.
Section Two: Clarifying that there are conditions capable of being transformed. This section has two parts; first, clarifying that he was a son.
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was a son when the Buddha was a bodhisattva.
This circumstance regarding Rāhula’s elder half-brother was particularly grave;
after he left the household life, he received, upheld, recited, and expounded upon the twelve divisions of the scriptures, destroyed the fetters of the desire realm,
and attained the four dhyānas.
Following his renunciation of the household life, he possessed faith and upheld the precepts; his study of the twelve divisions of the scriptures constituted wisdom;
his destruction of the fetters of the desire realm and attainment of the four dhyānas constituted concentration. To be thus endowed with these three virtues—is this not the result of profound causes?
How is it that the Tathāgata poses the following correct questions? First, he presents two difficulties and subsequently provides two conclusions.

Regarding the first difficulty: why did he grant a prediction for this evil person? Regarding the second difficulty: why did he not first preach the Dharma for him? Furthermore, the first difficulty has two parts. The first part asks:
why did he grant a prediction for this icchantika, which is itself an evil cause?
Why did the Tathāgata declare that Sunakṣatra was an icchantika and a person of the lowest class? Furthermore,
why is it difficult to explain how dwelling in hell for an eon constitutes such an evil fruit—
that is, a person who dwells in hell for an eon and is incurable?
For what reason did the Tathāgata descend? This is the second difficulty regarding the gravity of the conditions for encountering a Buddha: why did he not first preach the Dharma for him?
Why did the Tathāgata not first expound the True Dharma for him before [converting] the bodhisattvas?
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, concludes the second dilemma by asking: "How can he be said to possess great compassion? He concludes the first dilemma by asking:
"If the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, cannot save the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, how can he be said to possess great compassion?"
If the Buddha possesses compassion, why does he remain for such a long time in this inferior kalpa? Since it is said that this [kalpa] is inferior, one should know that the Buddha lacks compassion.
Next, there is the section "Furthermore, there is great skillful means," which concludes the subsequent objection.
There is a great skillful means.
Since the Buddha did not first preach the Dharma for them, how can it be said that he possesses great skillful means?
If there were such skillful means, he ought to have preached the Dharma for them.

In the Buddha’s reply, he does not answer the question regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), but rather addresses two difficulties and two conclusions: first he answers the latter, then the former;
and within the latter, he provides seven analogies. Of these, the first six analogies clarify that because conditions have varying degrees of depth, there is a sequential order in their explanation.
The final analogy clarifies that the Buddha’s mind is impartial, teaching all things equally without bias. Within the first six analogies, there are examples [of this].
First, an analogy is raised as a question; second, a formal response is given by recounting the facts; third, the analogy is applied to form an understanding. The Buddha said:
"Good son, it is like a father and mother who have only three sons.
One of these sons possesses a mind of faith and compliance, respects his parents, has sharp faculties and wisdom, and is able to fully understand all worldly matters. As for the second..."
The first son does not respect his parents and lacks a mind of faith and obedience, yet he possesses sharp faculties and wisdom, enabling him to quickly understand worldly affairs.
As for the third son, he does not respect his parents, lacks faith, has dull faculties, and is without wisdom;
if the parents wish to instruct him, whom should they teach first? Whom do they love most? To whom should they first teach the knowledge of worldly affairs?

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, one should first instruct those who possess faith and obedience, who revere their parents, and who have sharp faculties, wisdom, and knowledge of worldly affairs; only after them should the second and third be taught.
Yet, although those two sons lacked faith, obedience, and a heart of reverence, you nevertheless instructed them next out of your compassionate concern for them."
Good son, the Tathāgata is also like this. His three sons represent, respectively: first, the bodhisattvas; second, the śrāvakas;

and last, the icchantikas. Just as in the sūtras among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, I have already explained the subtle meanings for the sake of the bodhisattvas, the shallow and proximate meanings for the sake of the śrāvakas, and worldly meanings for the sake of the icchantikas.

Regarding the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), although they offer no benefit in the present life, out of compassion I speak of them so as to plant the seeds of various virtues for future lives.
Good son, it is like three kinds of fields: the first is one where irrigation channels are easy to manage and free from saline soil, gravel, stones, and thorns.
First, for every one seed sown, one hundred are obtained; second, although there are no sand, teeth-like stones, gravel, thorns, or dangerous watercourses, the harvest is reduced by half;
third, where there are many dangerous watercourses, saline soil, gravel, stones, and thorns, for every one seed sown, only one is obtained because it becomes fodder for grass.
Good son, in the spring months, in which field does the farmer sow first?
The World-Honored One first planted in the first field, then in the second, and finally in the third.
The first is a metaphor for the bodhisattva, the next for the śrāvaka, and the last for the icchantika.
Good son, it is like three vessels: one is whole, the second is leaking, and the third is broken. If one wishes to place [anything] within them...
Regarding milk, curd, butter, and water, which should be used first?
The Blessed One replied: "One should use the complete first, then the leaking, and finally the broken.
The complete and pure is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva-saṃgha; the leaking is a metaphor for the Śrāvakas; and the broken is a metaphor for the icchantikas."
"Good son, it is like three patients who have come together to a physician: one is easily cured, the second is difficult to cure, and the third is incurable.
Good son, if the physician were to treat them, whom should he treat first?"
“World-Honored One, you should first treat those who are easy to cure, then the second group, and finally the third. Why is this? Because they are kinsmen.
Those who are easy to cure are a metaphor for the Bodhisattva Saṃgha; those who are difficult to cure are a metaphor for the Śrāvaka Saṃgha; and those who cannot be cured—”
It is like the case of an icchantika who, although lacking wholesome fruits in the present life, out of compassion plants the seeds for various wholesome offspring in future lives.
Good son, it is as if a great king has three kinds of horses: the first is well-trained, powerful, and strong; the second is... [the third is... not... [well-trained].
Regarding the three—well-trained, strong, and powerful horses—if they are not well-trained, emaciated, old, and lacking strength, which one should the King mount first?
World-Honored One, he should first mount the well-trained, strong, and powerful horse; next, the second; and finally, the third.
Good son, the well-trained, powerful stallion is a metaphor for the assembly of Bodhisattvas; the second is a metaphor for the assembly of Śrāvakas;
and the third is a metaphor for the icchantikas. Although they provide no benefit in the present life, out of compassion, they plant the seeds of various wholesome dharmas for future lives.
"Good son, suppose at the time of a great almsgiving three people come: first, one of noble birth who is intelligent and observes the precepts;

second, one of middle birth who has dull faculties but observes the precepts; and third, one of low birth who has dull faculties and violates the precepts. Good son, as the master of this great almsgiving, to whom should he give first?"
World-Honored One, you should first address those of noble lineage, sharp faculties, and who uphold the precepts; next, those of the second category; and finally, those of the third.
The first is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva Saṃgha, the second for the Śrāvaka Saṃgha, and the third for the icchantikas.
Why is there this sequence of three? The explanation is as follows: When the Buddha first taught the five precepts for humans and devas to Trapusa, Bhallika, and the blind dragon, he did so next;
subsequently, he went to the Deer Park to turn the Dharma of the Four Truths for those of the Two Vehicles;

and later, he clarified the Vaipulya teachings for the various Bodhisattvas. This constitutes one approach, which takes the Small Vehicle as the beginning. Alternatively, if one considers the time of his initial attainment of Buddhahood...
The Way, through the teaching of Śākyamuni, first illumined Mount Sumeru and subsequently illumined the level plains; this is one perspective that takes the Great [Vehicle] as the beginning.

However, the intention of this current text encompasses the beginning, middle, and end, taking Mount Sumeru as the beginning, the scales of the dragon as the middle, and the Twin Trees (Śāla grove) as the end.
Thus, although the third son was extremely wicked, because their essence is identical, he must therefore...
Although the lower field is infertile, it is not abandoned because of one's family estate; although the lower vessel is broken, it is preserved for urgent use;
although the lower patient is destined to die, they are not forsaken because of kinship; although the lower horse is old, it is kept to relieve fatigue;
and although the lower person is base, they are given equal gifts.
Good son, it is like a great lion: when it kills a fragrant elephant, it exerts its full strength; likewise, when it kills a rabbit, it does so without giving rise to a thought of contempt.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are also like this: when they preach the Dharma for the sake of bodhisattvas and for icchantikas, their functional effort is no different.

Although the meaning was answered with distinctions within the first six similes, the underlying intent of non-distinction had not yet been fully revealed. In the seventh simile, however, the meaning becomes even clearer:
it cites the lion king who neither values the elephant nor despises the rabbit, exhausting his full vigor in both cases.

This illustrates how the Buddha does not treat the virtuous with partiality nor the wicked with contempt, but extends great compassion to all equally—whether viewing them as "great" or "small," the elephant is no more than sufficient and the rabbit is no less.
There are others who, observing according to their own capacity, hold that the elephant must move swiftly while the beast-king (the lion) must move slowly; yet these two are in no way different.
When observed in terms of conditions, the Bodhisattva teaching is profound and subtle, while the Śrāvaka teaching is shallow and near.
The teaching for icchantikas is worldly, whereas the Buddha’s [teaching] is neither two nor three, being equal through great compassion.
At one time, while residing in Rājagṛha, I answered two successive questions regarding that inquiry, which consisted of two parts:

first, the answer concerning the icchantika; second, the answer concerning the underlying intent. Regarding the first answer on the icchantika, they themselves claim to possess faith, wisdom, and meditative concentration, yet these are not what was asked.

By not admitting their existence, it is clarified that they lack faith. Furthermore, there are three aspects to this lack of faith: first, they do not believe in the Buddha as being the One Who Has Nothing [to Attain].
Fearing that people might [misunderstand] me, at one time when I was in Kāśī— this second section clarifies that the Buddha is not a person of false speech—
at another time, together with Sunakṣatra— this third section clarifies that the Buddha is not a person of jealousy.
Regarding the first passage:
"Good son, at one time I was staying in the city of Rājagṛha, and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra served as my attendant.
During the first watch of the night, I expounded the essential Dharma for Śakra, Lord of the Devas. According to the law of disciples, they should sleep after their teacher;
however, at that time, because I had sat for so long, Sunakṣatra conceived an evil thought. At that moment, the young boys and girls of Rājagṛha..."
When his weeping did not cease, his parents said to him, "If you do not stop, we shall hand you over to the spirit Bakula.
At that time, Sunakṣatra was instead seized and restrained, and he spoke to me, saying, "Enter the meditation chamber quickly; Bakula is coming!
I said, "Foolish man, have you not always heard that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is free from fear? At that moment, Śakra...
He said to me, "World-Honored One, can such people as these also enter into the Buddha-dharma?
I replied, "Kauśika, such people as these can indeed enter the Buddha-dharma; they possess the Buddha-nature and shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Although I preached the Dharma for this Sunakṣatra, he had no faith at all.
Receive this into your heart.
You said that leaving home signifies the presence of faith; however, I shall now reveal through three matters how he lacks faith.
Son of good family, at one time, while I was in the city of Śivapura in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra.
When I was on my alms-round and wished to enter that city, immeasurable sentient beings, with hearts empty and yearning, desired to see my tracks.
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra followed closely behind me and attempted to erase them;
yet, being unable to erase them, he instead caused the sentient beings to give rise to unwholesome thoughts. After I had entered the city, I saw a Nirgrantha at a tavern.
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, having seen [the Buddha] crouching on the ground with his spine arched, eating fermented rice mash, said:
"World-Honored One, if there be any arhats in this world, this man is the most excellent among them. Why? Because what he teaches is that there is neither cause nor effect.
I said: "Foolish man, have you not always heard that an arhat does not drink alcohol and does not harm living beings?"
One who deceives others, does not steal, and does not commit sexual misconduct—how can such a person, who kills his parents and devours fermented grain mash, be called an Arhat?
When this person casts off the body, he will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell.
How can one who has eternally severed the three evil paths be called an Arhat? Sunakṣatra then spoke of the four great elements.
Even their nature could still be transformed; it is impossible that this person must fall into the Avīci Hell.
I say, "Foolish man, have you not always heard the non-dual, truthful words of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas?
Although I have preached the Dharma for this Śunakṣatra, he is utterly devoid of any mind to believe or accept it."
When the second Buddha was walking, his feet remained four inches above the ground, and the marks of the thousand-spoked wheel appeared upon the tracks he left.

People all desired to see them, yet they were unable to erase them. Consequently, they took dead earthworms and placed them within the Buddha’s footprints, causing immeasurable people to give rise to thoughts of malice and harm (and so forth).
"Good son, at one time I was staying in the city of Rājagṛha together with the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra.
At that time, there was in the city a Nirgrantha named Duḥkha who constantly spoke thus: 'The afflictions of sentient beings have no cause and no condition;
the liberation of sentient beings likewise has no cause and no condition. The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra then spoke again, saying: 'World-Honored One, in this world...'"
"If there were any who were arhats, I would say that for you, 'attaining suffering' is supreme. "Foolish man," I said, "the Nirgrantha Kṣāntivādin is certainly not an arhat;
he is unable to understand the path of an arhat. Sunakṣatra spoke again:
"For what reason do arhats give rise to jealousy toward other arhats? I said: "Foolish man, I do not give rise to jealousy toward arhats. And so on.
"You have merely given rise to evil and false views yourself. If you say that Kṛtaka is an Arhat, then seven days from now he shall suffer from abdominal pain caused by indigestion and die;
having died, he will be reborn among the ghosts who consume vomit.
His fellow students shall carry his corpse to the cold forest. At that time, Sunakṣatra immediately went to where the Nirgrantha Kṛtaka was and said:
"Venerable sir, do you know this? The śramaṇa Gautama has prophesied that in seven days you shall suffer from abdominal pain due to indigestion and die;
having died, you shall be reborn among the *udumbara* (vomit-eating) hungry ghosts. Your fellow students and teachers will carry your corpse to the cold forest.
Venerable sir, reflect well and employ every means to cause Gautama to fall into falsehood."
At that time, having heard these words, Kṛtaka immediately ceased eating from the first day until the sixth;
when the seventh day was completed, he ate black honey. Having eaten the black honey, he drank cold water. Once he had drunk the water, his belly ached and he died.
After he had died, his fellow students carried his corpse to the cold forest (*śmaśāna*) and placed it there, whereupon he immediately began to eat.
Beside the corpse was the form of a hungry ghost vomiting its food;
having heard of this matter, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra went to the Śītavana forest and saw Duḥkhaprapta with that body of one vomiting food, crouching on the ground in distress.
Sunakṣatra said, "Venerable sir, are you dead? Duḥkhaprapta replied, "I am already dead. [Sunakṣatra asked], "How did you die? [Duḥkhaprapta] answered, "Because of..."
"Who removed your corpse when you died of abdominal pain? He replied, "A fellow student removed it. "In what place was it placed?

He replied, "You fool, do you not know this is the Cold Forest (Śītavana)? "What kind of body did you obtain? He replied, "I obtained the body of a *vāntāśinī* (vomit-eating) hungry ghost (*preta*). "Sunakṣatra, listen attentively!
The Tathāgata speaks words that are good, true, timely, meaningful, and in accordance with the Dharma. Sunakṣatra, such are the words from the mouth of the Tathāgata."

"By this true speech, how could you not believe at that time? If there are sentient beings who do not believe the Tathāgata’s true words, they too shall receive a body just like mine. At that time, Sunakṣatra immediately returned to me and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One, after the death of the ascetic Kṛṣṇa, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
I said, "Foolish man! An Arhat has no place of rebirth; how can you say that Kṛtaka was born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three?
"World-Honored One, it is indeed as you have said: Kṛtaka the Nirgrantha was not truly born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
he now receives the body of a *preta* who eats vomit. I said, "Foolish man! The words of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are truthful."
"There is no duality; it is impossible for there to be two words from the Tathāgata.
Sunakṣatra then said, "Tathāgata, although you spoke thus at that time, I did not give rise to even a single thought of faith regarding this matter.
"Good son, I have also constantly taught the true Dharma to the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, yet he utterly lacked any heart of faith or acceptance."

Regarding the third passage: although the human and ghostly realms are distinct in their retributions, that they could see one another so clearly and engage in mutual inquiry and response—how could this truly be something an evil person would be capable of doing?
It is verified as being a provisional manifestation (expedient means), and so forth.
Although Sunakṣatra recited and chanted the two lower types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*),
he lacked wisdom. Good son, although the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra recited the twelve divisions of the sūtras and attained the four dhyānas,
he did not understand the meaning of even a single verse, a single phrase, or a single word.
To merely acquire the words without understanding their meaning is not wisdom.

The third section, "Associating with Evil Friends," clarifies the absence of concentration; it is further divided into two parts. First, it explains that although one may initially attain [concentration], one subsequently loses it, and thus it is said to be without concentration.
By associating with evil friends, he fell away from the four dhyānas.

Next, having fallen from the dhyānas, the text concludes by summarizing the reasons for his arising of wrong views, recording that after falling from meditative concentration, he gave rise to evil and false views, saying: "There is no Buddha, there is no Dharma, and there is no nirvāṇa."
"The śramaṇa Gautama is well-versed in the dharma of marks; therefore, he is able to know the minds of others.
At that time, I said to Sunakṣatra, "The Dharma I teach is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end;
its words are skillful, its syllables and meanings are authentic, and what is spoken is unadulterated, fully accomplishing the pure brahmacarya. The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra then spoke again as follows:
"Although the Tathāgata has preached the Dharma for me, I truly maintain that there is no cause and no effect.

"Good son, if you do not believe this," [the Buddha said]. This is the second part of the answer to the preceding question, which clarifies the intent of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). It is further divided into two sections:
first, clarifying the intent of the prediction; second, clarifying that he is incurable. Regarding the first section:
“Good son, if you do not believe such matters, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra is currently nearby at the Nairañjanā River;
we may go together to question him. At that time, the Tathāgata immediately went with Kāśyapa to Sunakṣatra’s location.
When the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra saw the Buddha coming from afar, as soon as he saw him, he gave rise to an evil and heterodox mind; because of that evil mind, [he was reborn in hell].
His body fell into the Avīci Hell;
