because he was certain to enter it, I predicted this to manifest the signs of his inevitable entry. When [the Buddha] went to see him, he gave rise to malice toward the Buddha upon seeing him and immediately entered hell;
thus his certain entry was made clear. As for the reason for going to where Sunakṣatra was, some say it was to cite past events.
Or, by the power of inconceivable might, one may proceed without moving [the body] (and so forth).
Although Sunakṣatra entered the Buddha-dharma, the second answer holds that such an incurable person cannot be healed because of his negligence;
out of compassion for him, there is a teaching consisting of the dharma, the analogy, and their application.
"Good son, although the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra entered the Buddha-dharma— a boundless treasury of jewels—
he obtained nothing at all and did not gain the benefit of even a single dharma, because of his negligence and because of evil associates."
It is like a person who, though having entered the great ocean and seen many kinds of jewels, obtains nothing because of negligence;
or like one who, having entered the sea and seen a heap of treasures, kills himself, or is killed by rākṣasas and evil spirits.
In these two sections, each consists of two parts: first the formal application (*yōgā*), and second the application by means of a simile.
It is the same with the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra; having entered the Buddha-dharma, he was killed by evil associates who were like rākṣasa demons.
Therefore, O son of good family, out of compassion, the Tathāgata has always said that Sunakṣatra is [a person of] much [evil].
O sons of good family, regarding those who are negligent: although one may give rise to compassion for a person who was originally poor, that mind of compassion is slight;
however, if one gives rise to compassion for a person who was originally wealthy but later lost their wealth, that mind of compassion is profound.
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was likewise in this regard: he upheld, recited, and studied the twelve divisions of the scriptures and attained the four dhyānas, yet he subsequently fell away from them;
he is truly to be pitied. For this reason, I say that the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra is full of negligence;
because of his great negligence, he has severed all roots of goodness. Among my disciples, those who have seen or heard of him should [avoid] such a person.
There was no moment when I did not give rise to profound compassion.
Just like one who was once immensely wealthy but later lost all their fortune, I constantly followed after Sunaksatra for many years;
yet he himself gave rise to evil and heterodox thoughts, and because of those heterodox views, he would not abandon his wrong perspectives.

From the phrase "Since ancient times" onwards, there are two responses to the two preceding points. The first response addresses the initial point—the lack of a compassionate heart—and this is further divided into two parts:

first, the direct response; second, the analytical clarification. Within the direct response, there is the presentation of the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*).
"Good son, since the distant past, I have seen that this Sunakṣatra possessed not even a hair’s breadth of roots of goodness;
therefore, I never predicted that he was one who had severed his roots of goodness, an icchantika, a lowly person destined to dwell in hell for kalpas.
It was only because he proclaimed that there is no cause and no effect, and that there is no such thing as karmic action, that I then predicted he had forever severed his roots of goodness."
Icchantikas and those of the lowest station shall dwell in hell for kalpas.
Good son, it is like a person who has fallen into a cesspool;
a good friend reaches in with his hand, and if he finds a hair, he wishes to pull him out, but after searching for a long time without success, he finally desists.
I have likewise sought out even the slightest roots of goodness in Sunakṣatra, desiring to rescue him;
yet though I searched all day long, I could not find so much as a hair’s breadth of them. Therefore, I am unable to deliver him from hell.
The second section consists of questions and answers for clarification, which is divided into two parts: first the question, and then the answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said: "World-Honored One, for what reason did the Tathāgata record that he would fall into the Avīci Hell?"
In the answer, there are two parts; first is the direct response:
"Good son, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra has many followers who all claim that Sunakṣatra is an arhat and one who has attained the fruit of the Path.
Because I wish to destroy their evil and heterodox minds, I have declared that Sunakṣatra will fall due to his negligence."
Regarding the hells:
next, the "Good Son" section below cites the past to reveal the reality.
"Good son, you should now know that what the Tathāgata speaks is true and non-dual. Why is this? If the Buddha..."
Regarding those who have been prophesied to fall into hell, it is impossible that they should not fall;
as for the prophecies made by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, there are two kinds: either false or true.

For example, when Maudgalyāyana was in the kingdom of Magadha, he proclaimed to all the people, "Seven days from now, the heavens shall send down rain," yet in the end no rain fell. Later, he further prophesied that a cow would...
One gives birth to a white calf, yet at the time of delivery, a brindled calf is born; one records the birth of a son, yet later a daughter is born.
Within these accounts, the records concerning Maudgalyāyana are cited, which are not entirely without error: they see the preceding rain but do not see the subsequent connection;
they see the white head but do not see the brindled body (and so forth). The Tathāgata is not like this; therefore, there is no duality.
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra constantly provides immeasurable inferior answers and subsequent expedient conclusions.
Son of good family, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra constantly proclaims to immeasurable sentient beings that there are no fruits of good or evil;
at that time, he eternally severs all roots of goodness until not even so much as a hair’s breadth of goodness remains.
"Good man, I have long known that this bhikṣu Śunakṣatra was destined to sever his roots of goodness;

yet I continued to dwell with him for a full twenty years, supporting and associating with him. Had I cast him far away and not kept him by my side, he would have taught immeasurable sentient beings to commit evil deeds.
This is called the Tathāgata’s fifth power of understanding."
I clearly intend to keep them constantly at my side and not allow them to go far away, fearing they might commit evil.
What is this fifth power of resolution, which is the power of aspiration (*chanda-bala*), that knows the inclinations and understandings of sentient beings? It is the lack of skillful means.

In the second section of the *Bhagavat-icchantika* chapter, "The Characteristics of Severing the Roots of Goodness," the text is divided into three parts: first, the formal explanation of severing the roots of goodness;

second, the explanation of severing the roots of goodness because the nature of the faculties is indeterminate; and third, the explanation of severing the roots of goodness because the teaching is indeterminate.
The first part consists of five rounds of questions and answers; this is the first round, beginning with the question.
"Bhagavat, by what causes and conditions do those who are icchantikas lack wholesome dharmas?
In the Buddha’s subsequent answer, he said:
"Good son, because those who are icchantikas have severed their roots of goodness, [whereas] all sentient beings possess the five faculties, such as faith."

Because those who are icchantikas have eternally severed [the roots of goodness], for this reason, although one incurs the sin of killing even by slaying an ant, there is no sin of killing in killing an icchantika.

This is because they have severed their roots of goodness; thus, there is no basis for goodness. According to the interpretation of the Saṃmitīya school, an icchantika is one who gives rise to evil and false views.
The severing of these roots of goodness is like the abandonment of afflictions by the unobstructed path (*anāvaraṇa-mārga*) of the untainted (*anāsrava*);
if this were so, one should know that the roots of goodness would never arise again. How, then, could they ever be produced once more? This interpretation is incorrect.
Within the bodies of icchantikas, there exist heavy obstacles of evil such that goodness and [evil] do not coexist; it is designated as "obstructed goodness" because it cannot arise in the future.
Because evil is gradually extinguished and good is once again able to arise, it is said that "one regenerates the roots of goodness. Question:

Does an icchantika possess goodness that can be severed, or goodness that cannot be severed? Answer: Both meanings apply. Since they previously performed wholesome deeds but later encountered evil friends who caused those virtues to be severed and extinguished, it is said that there is goodness that can be severed.
As for the claim that there is no goodness to be severed, this refers to the evil they committed in the past.
There is not yet any goodness at all, yet evil karma is about to be extinguished; while wholesome karma ought to arise, obstacles instead re-emerge, preventing it from arising.
Thus, there is no goodness that can be severed. The text states: "All sentient beings possess the five faculties, such as faith.

Regarding the claim that *icchantikas* have eternally severed [these], the traditional interpretation explains: "Sentient beings within the principle (the Buddhist fold) possess the five faculties such as faith, whereas those outside the principle are perverted."
The claim that because [icchantikas] are inverted and deluded they lack the five faculties such as faith is incorrect; for even outside this principle, there exist faith and the others.
Since icchantikas are outside this principle, they give rise to evil and sever these five faculties;

yet, as beings who commit evil still possess Buddha-nature, they ought to give rise to these five faculties. Because they do not yet manifest them in actual fact, it is explained according to the principle that they must possess them. Thus it is said:
It is stated that all sentient beings possess [the Buddha-nature], yet the text says: "Killing an icchantika is without fault; killing mosquitoes or ants is a transgression.

This means that because an icchantika possesses grave evil within their person, killing them incurs no fault; whereas because mosquitoes and ants lack such grave evil, killing them constitutes a transgression.
Furthermore, the text states: "Giving to animals yields a hundredfold reward; giving to a single icchantika yields a thousandfold reward."
Regarding the icchantika: the merit derived from giving to one who has observed the five precepts in the past and thus inspires human rebirth is heavy;
the merit derived from giving to one who, due to evil karma in previous lives, has received this animal body is light.
This concludes the second round of questions and answers concerning the definitive tenet regarding the icchantika, as established by the World-Honored One.
“World-Honored One, since those who are icchantikas ultimately possess no wholesome dharmas, they are called icchantikas.
[The Buddha] replied, “It can be seen so;
the Buddha said, ‘It is so, it is so.’”
The World-Honored One’s third round of question and answer concerning all sentient beings:

The World-Honored One has stated that all sentient beings possess three kinds of goodness—past, future, and present—and that even those among the icchantikas cannot sever their future wholesome dharmas.
How then can it be said that one who severs all wholesome dharmas is called an icchantika?
Yes. In the question, it is clarified that although icchantikas do not sever their future [roots of goodness], how is it that they sever their roots of goodness?
Good son, there are two kinds of severance: first, extinction in the present; second, obstruction in the present regarding the future. Regarding the first, the icchantika—
Because these Icchantikas possess these two kinds of severance, I say that they have severed all roots of goodness. Good son, it is like a person who has fallen into a latrine;

although there is but a single hair’s breadth of his head that has not yet sunk, even though that single hair’s breadth remains unsunk, that single hair cannot support the body. The Icchantikas are also like this; although they have not yet... [future...]
In this world, there may be those with roots of goodness who cannot be saved from the sufferings of hell;
although they may be rescued in future lives, there is nothing that can be done for them in the present life. Therefore, they are called "incurable.
Yet, by means of the causal conditions of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), they can be saved. This Buddha-nature is neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present. Therefore—
The Buddha-nature cannot be severed, just as a rotten seed cannot produce a sprout; the icchantikas are likewise so.

The Buddha replied that there are two kinds of severance: first, the cessation of what is presently manifest; second, the obstruction of what is yet to come. This refers to when evil dharmas arise and obstruct wholesome dharmas.
Because [the unwholesome] does not arise, it is currently extinguished; yet, having manifested as evil, it further obstructs the arising of future goodness.
Thus, while severing the future, it also entails the severance of the three periods of time. Although past evil was committed, the failure to repent means that no further goodness can arise.
While there is still the possibility for goodness to arise again in the future, it is merely weak and cannot save itself.
The fourth round of questions and answers from the section on the icchantikas clarifies that the Buddha-nature is never severed.
World-Honored One, since the icchantikas do not sever their Buddha-nature and the Buddha-nature is itself wholesome, why is it said that they have severed all goodness?
Good son, if sentient beings possessed the Buddha-nature in the present life, they could not be called icchantikas.
Just as in the world, the self-nature and Buddha-nature of sentient beings are eternal and are not subsumed within the three periods of time;
if they were subsumed within the three periods, they would be called impermanent. Because the Buddha-nature will be seen in the future, it is said that all sentient beings [possess it].
Because there is the Buddha-nature for this reason, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes must be fully adorned with merit before they can perceive it even slightly.
This Buddha-nature is good; because this goodness is uninterrupted, it is called the "uninterrupted nature. Furthermore, the Buddha-nature is eternal and real, and thus cannot be severed.
Regarding what is said about the "self-nature" of worldly sentient beings and the Buddha-nature, there are three interpretations. First, some say it is borrowed.
Regarding the outsiders (*tīrthika*), I take this as an analogy because they have no false self at all; thus, the true self is not subsumed within the three periods of time and is eternal.
Second, [the opponent] says it is not so, but rather that the nature of the self of worldly sentient beings is itself the Buddha-nature;
because it is the Buddha-nature, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time. Third, [the opponent] says it is indeed the true self, as the force of the argument leads to this conclusion.

The statement that the Buddha-nature is eternal contradicts the later passage which says that the Buddha-nature is not subsumed within the three periods of time, while the earlier passage states it is "future.
These two statements must now be reconciled. The earlier claim that it is not subsumed within the three periods refers to the essence of the Buddha-nature itself;
the later reference to it as "future" concerns the cultivation of sentient beings—that all sentient beings will, in the future, attain its purity.
Because it pertains to the body, it is said to be "future.
Kāśyapa spoke; this is the first of five successive question-and-answer sessions concerning the Buddha-nature. First, the Buddha-nature is questioned; next, the icchantika is questioned.
Regarding the first inquiry:
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said: "World-Honored One, the Buddha-nature is eternal, just like empty space. For what reason does the Tathāgata speak of it as being 'in the future'?
Since the Buddha-nature is not encompassed by the three periods of time, why do you say it is in the future?"
If the Tathāgata says "next," he asks about the icchantikas.

If the Tathāgata says that those who are icchantikas possess no wholesome dharmas, then do these icchantikas not give rise to feelings of love and affection toward their fellow students, their teachers, their parents, their kinsmen, and their wives and children?
If they do indeed give rise to such feelings, [how can it be said they have no wholesome dharmas?]
Is this not excellent?
If one says that icchantikas are entirely devoid of wholesome dharmas, how can they possess a mind of compassion and affection?
If such a mind exists, then they must possess wholesome qualities.

The Buddha spoke, providing the following answers in response to the initial question. This section has two parts: first, the answer to the question; second, the discussion of the meaning. Within the first part (the answer), there are two sub-sections.
First is the praise for the question. The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have asked this question most skillfully."
Next is the formal response:
Buddha-nature is like empty space; it is neither past, nor future, nor present.
All sentient beings possess three kinds of bodies, namely those of the past, future, and present sentient beings; [the body] of future sentient beings is fully endowed with adornments.
Because the pure body attains Buddhahood, I say that the Buddha-nature is future.
Son of good family, for the sake of sentient beings, I sometimes speak of cause as effect, and sometimes speak of effect as cause.
Therefore, it is said in the sutras that life is food, seeing forms is called contact, and because the future body will be pure, it is called the Buddha-nature.
The nature [of phenomena] does not belong to the three periods of time; it is said to be "future" because it is attained in the future. Therefore, below, examples are cited:

the cause is spoken of as the effect, and the effect is spoken of as the cause. Buddha-nature is also like this; when it is called "future," the effect is being spoken of within the context of the cause.
As for "food" and "contact": food is visible, while contact has different names—sometimes consciousness is designated as contact, and sometimes the sense-faculties are designated as contact.
Now, because it possesses both meanings, the treatise states: "Since contact (*sparśa*) is indeterminate, there is no separate dharma.

If consciousness abides in its object, this is called contact; if this contact resides in consciousness, and one speaks of "eye-consciousness" or "eye-contact," this contact exists within perception (*saṃjñā*).

Now, when we say "seeing form is called contact," this refers to the mind of consciousness (*vijñāna-citta*) taking that as contact. Form is the external sense-field (*viṣaya*) capable of producing [consciousness].
"Because consciousness contacts it, one refers to form as 'contact'; this is also stating the effect within the cause.
The World-Honored One [proceeds with] the second section of the discussion, first posing a question and then providing an answer:
"World-Honored One, if the meaning is as the Buddha has explained, for what reason do you say that all sentient beings possess [it]?"
Regarding the Buddha-nature:
Question—since the Buddha-nature that arises from prior causes does not belong to the three periods of time, why do you say that sentient beings possess it?

Good son, although the Buddha-nature of sentient beings does not exist in the present, one cannot say it is non-existent, just as the nature of empty space, though not existing [as a substantial entity], cannot be said to be non-existent.
Because there is no present [state], one cannot say that all sentient beings do not exist. Although they are impermanent, their Buddha-nature is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Therefore, in this sutra I have said that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither internal nor external, just as space is neither internal nor external.
If space were to have an interior or exterior, it would not be called "space."
First, although it is eternal, one cannot say that space exists everywhere; yet, while it is neither internal nor external, all sentient beings possess it.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
The Buddha replied that this nature is neither internal nor external, being like empty space, yet all sentient beings certainly possess this nature;
the text states that "all have it.
Regarding what you said [in the previous question], the following response addresses the second question: first, he restates the question and then refutes it.
As for what you have said—that those who are icchantikas possess wholesome dharmas—this meaning is not so. Why?
[The following provides] the correct answer, consisting of the thesis, the example, and the application.
Why? Because if those who are icchantikas possess bodily action, vocal action, mental action, the karma of grasping, the karma of seeking, or the karma of giving...
Regarding "karma, understanding karma," and so forth—all such karmas are indeed perverse karma. Why? Because they do not seek cause and effect.

Although the Dharma speaks of virtues such as filial piety and compassion, the texts state that these are all perverse karma; although there is seeing and hearing, these are all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Since there is neither right nor good, they are all termed perverse and evil karma. As for "seeking karma," this is the opposite of the aforementioned.
Within the wholesome, first the wholesome desire arises, followed by the wholesome volition;
now, although both are termed "wholesome" when contrasted with the wholesome desire for action and the wholesome volition for action, they are nonetheless indeterminate (avyākṛta).
"Good son, it is like the harītakī fruit, whose roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all bitter.
Next, he provides an analogy, saying: 'Just as the taste of the harītakī is exclusively bitter while its color and fragrance are not bitter, how could it be that the icchantika has no goodness?
Since the presence of even a trace of compassion or affection is what is called 'goodness,' the Buddha replied: 'All [is bitter].'"
The Zhe-ye (Zhengyuan) school maintains that these are "adornments of evil" and that no supramundane goodness exists;

the You-lan-ai (Lian'ai) school maintains that even if such affection were present, it would be exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and cannot be called good, just as skills such as chess or calligraphy are indeterminate in their craftsmanship.

The Kai-shan school maintains that for one who has severed the roots of goodness and commits evil, even if affection were present, it would belong entirely to the category of evil and perversion; how then could there be any goodness?
Master Guan, in agreement with Kaishan, said: "When grave evil dwells within one's person, it is like planting a bitter gourd; its roots and leaves are all bitter.
The karma of an icchantika is also like this.
This is consistent with the text.

"Good son, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with [the knowledge of] the second [of the four analytical knowledges], which clarifies that the nature of the faculties (*indriya*) is indeterminate—being either evil or good.

Furthermore, this section has two parts: first, the formal clarification of indeterminacy; second, further questions and answers regarding the meaning. The first part also has two sections: first, clarifying indeterminacy;
second, severing the roots of goodness. Clarifying indeterminacy also has three parts: first, knowing the indeterminate faculty; second, bringing it forth..."
The characteristics of concentration are fixed, while the three fetters are not; the first is as stated in the text.

Good son, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of knowing the faculties of all beings; therefore, he is well able to distinguish the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of sentient beings.
As for the subsequent passage:
it states that one can know this person transforms the lower into the middle; one can know this person transforms the middle into the upper;
one can know this person transforms the upper into the middle; and one can know this person transforms the middle into the lower.
Through repeated practice, the sharp faculty transforms from inferior to middling or superior; through lack of practice, the dull faculty transforms from superior to middling or inferior.
Regarding the three fetters, it is as stated in the text (*etc.*).
Therefore, one should know that the spiritual faculties and natures of sentient beings are not fixed.

Because there is no fixed [nature], the following two sections clarify the lack of fixity; therefore, one severs the roots of goodness. Furthermore, there are three parts: first, clarifying the indeterminate severance of the roots of goodness.
Because there is no fixed nature, one may sever the roots of goodness, and having severed them, they may arise again.
Next, it is explained that if [the faculties] were fixed, this would not be so.
If the root-natures of sentient beings were fixed, they would never first sever [the roots of goodness] and then have them arise again;
nor should it be said that those of the icchantika class fall into hell for a lifespan of one kalpa.
Third, for this reason, the following establishes that [the nature of phenomena] is indeterminate.
"Good son, for this reason the Tathāgata says that all dharmas have no fixed characteristics.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, initiating the second section of the discussion (as detailed below); the question may be seen therein.

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of knowing the faculties of others and certainly knows that Sunakṣatra will sever his roots of goodness;
for what reason and by what causes and conditions did you permit him to leave the household life?"
The Buddha’s response is twofold: first, he answers concerning Sunakṣatra, and second, he answers concerning other people.

This shows that he not only knows the spiritual faculties of Sunakṣatra but also knows the faculties of others. The first part further has three sections; the first clarifies that even while occupying the royal throne, [Sunakṣatra] was able to bring about destruction.

The Buddha said, "Good son, in the past when I first left the household life, my younger brother Nanda, my nephew Ānanda, Devadatta, Rāhula, and others like them all followed me to leave the household life and practice the Way.
Had I not permitted Sunakṣatra to leave the household life, that man would have succeeded to the royal throne by right of succession; his own power was such."
Because he was about to destroy the Buddha-dharma for these reasons, I permitted him to leave the household life and practice the Way.
Whether Sunakṣatra had attained the two types of clear knowledge or not, whether he left the household life or not, he would have been able to sever his roots of goodness;

however, by leaving the household life, he increased his respect for his elders and fulfilled the various virtues such as recitation and the cultivation of meditative concentration, as described above.
Good son, if the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra had not left the household life, he would have severed his roots of goodness and brought no benefit whatsoever for immeasurable eons.

Now that he has left the household life, although he has severed his roots of goodness, he is able to receive and uphold the precepts, and he makes offerings to and reveres those who are aged, senior, and virtuous;
he cultivates the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna—this is called a "wholesome cause. As it is said:
This wholesome cause can give rise to wholesome dharmas; once wholesome dharmas have arisen, one can cultivate the Path;
having cultivated the Path, one shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, I permitted Sunakṣatra to go forth as a monk.
If I did not permit the three lower fetters to be abandoned through the power of the faculty of knowledge,
O son of good family, and if I had not permitted the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra to go forth and receive the precepts,
then I could not be called a Tathāgata endowed with the ten powers.

Next, the Buddha observes the sentient beings and provides an answer concerning the remaining people, which is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying those of indeterminate destiny; second, distinguishing between those who ascend and those who sink. The first part is further divided into two:

those who sever the roots of goodness and those who produce the roots of goodness. Regarding the first, the severing of the roots of goodness, there are three sections: first, the actual severing of the roots of goodness.
"Good son, the Buddha observes that sentient beings are endowed with both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas;
although such persons possess these two types of dharmas, they will before long sever all roots of goodness and come to possess only roots of unwholesomeness."
Next, as for the passage beginning "For what reason," it sets forth the conduct that severs the roots of goodness.

For what reason? It is because such sentient beings do not associate with virtuous friends, do not listen to the true Dharma, do not engage in proper reflection, and do not act in accordance with the Dharma.
Third, from "By these causes and conditions" onwards, he concludes the severance of the roots of goodness.
By these causes and conditions, one is able to sever the roots of goodness and become fully possessed of the roots of non-goodness.

Next, from "Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows" onwards, the second section clarifies the dharma for producing the roots of goodness; the analogy and its application to the meaning can be understood accordingly.
"Good son, the Tathāgata further knows that whether in the present life or in future lives, during youth, middle age, or old age,

when such a person draws near to virtuous friends and hears and receives the True Dharma of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, they will then be able to regenerate their roots of goodness."
Good son, it is like a spring not far from a village whose water is sweet and possesses the eight meritorious qualities.

Suppose there is a person suffering from heat and thirst who wishes to go to that spring; a wise person observes this thirsty man and knows for certain, without doubt, that he will reach the water. Why? Because there is no other path.

The analogy of the spring represents the Buddha-nature; the village represents the aggregates (skandhas); the heat and thirst represent the oppression of suffering; the desire to go represents the mind seeking happiness;
and the wise man at the edge [of the water] represents the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the combined analogies, first the two [initial ones] are combined.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, observes all sentient beings in this very same way.
Next, he binds the power of knowing the faculties (indriya-jñāna-bala).
For this reason, the Tathāgata is said to be fully endowed with the power of knowing the various faculties.

At that time, the World-Honored One took a small amount of earth from the ground; first, he lowered it and then raised it, showing that their sinking and rising were different, with the sinking being much greater than the rising.
Furthermore, thirdly, he first cited this event to pose a question:
At that time, the World-Honored One took a small amount of earth and placed it upon his fingernail, saying to Kāśyapa, "Is this earth more?"
"Is the earth and soil of the worlds in the ten directions much?
Next, receiving this instruction, he offered his reply:
"Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, the soil upon the tip of Your fingernail cannot be compared to all the soil that exists throughout the ten directions.'"
Furthermore, regarding the third conjunction, there are three initial points concerning the conjunction with the fruit.
Good son, there are those who, having abandoned their bodies, regain human bodies; having abandoned the bodies of the three evil realms, they receive human bodies.
Those who possess intact faculties, are born in a central land, and are endowed with right faith, are able to cultivate the path; having cultivated the path, they are able to practice the true path;
having practiced the true path, they are able to attain liberation; and having attained liberation, they are able to enter nirvāṇa.

They are like the soil on a fingernail compared to the soil of the great earth: having abandoned a human body, they obtain the bodies of the three evil realms; having abandoned the bodies of the three evil realms, they obtain the bodies of the three evil realms again.

Those who are deficient in their faculties, born in borderlands, who believe in heterodox and inverted views, and who practice false paths— failing to attain liberation and the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa—
are as numerous as all the dust motes upon the earth throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Next, regarding the conjunction of causes:
good sons who uphold the prohibitive precepts with diligent and tireless effort, who do not commit the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes,
who do not misappropriate the property of the Sangha, who do not become icchantikas, and who do not sever their roots of goodness— such as those who believe in sūtras such as this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Those who treat the scriptures as mere dust on their fingernails, who violate the precepts through negligence, commit the four grave offenses, or the five heinous crimes;

those who misappropriate the property of the Sangha, act as icchantikas, sever all roots of goodness, and do not believe in this sutra— such people are as numerous as all the soil of the lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The third is the faculty of knowing the faculties (*indriya-jñāna-bala*).
Good son, the Tathāgata thoroughly knows such superior, middling, and inferior faculties of sentient beings; therefore, the Buddha is said to be endowed with the faculty of knowing the faculties.

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: "The Tathāgata is fully endowed with [the following]. Third, it clarifies that the teaching is not fixed: the Buddha perceives that roots [of capacity] differ, and thus his teachings vary.
Sentient beings do not understand the distinction between faculties and teachings; they cling to them and give rise to contentious arguments.
Those who can sever these two views regarding Bodhi first ask a question and then receive an answer. The initial question has three parts: first, clarifying the faculties; second, clarifying..."

Regarding the inquiry on the three fetters that give rise to contention: why was an indeterminate teaching given, which leads to the arising of dispute? First, it clarifies the faculty of knowing faculties (*indriya-jñāna-bala*).
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with this power of knowing faculties;
therefore, he is able to know the distinctions between superior, middling, and inferior faculties, as well as sharpness and dullness, among all sentient beings in the present world."
The faculties also know the faculties of future sentient beings;
they should also know those of the past, though this is merely an abbreviation.
Following this, the passage beginning "such sentient beings" next clarifies the grasping of disputes.
Thus, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, these sentient beings will speak as follows: that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate parinirvāṇa, or that he has not entered ultimate parinirvāṇa;
or they will say there is a self, or that there is no self; or that there is an intermediate state (antarābhava), or that there is no intermediate state;
or they will say there is falling back (parihāṇi), or that there is no falling back; or they will say that the body of the Tathāgata is conditioned (saṃskṛta).

Some say that the body of the Tathāgata is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); some say that the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*);
some say that dependent origination is unconditioned; some say that the mind is eternal, while others say that the mind is impermanent;
some say that the enjoyment of the five sensory pleasures can obstruct the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), while others say it does not obstruct it; and some speak of the worldly stages (*laukikabhūmi*).
One dharma is said to belong exclusively to the desire realm; or it is said to belong to all three realms. Some say that giving is exclusively mental action (*manas-karman*);
others say it is the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Some say there are three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*);
others say there are no three unconditioned phenomena. Furthermore, some say there is derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*); others say there is no derived matter. Or...
Some say that there is unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), while others say that there is no such unmanifest form;

some say that there are mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), while others say that there are no mental factors; some say that there are five kinds of existence (*bhava*), while others say that there are six kinds of existence;
and some speak of the eightfold precepts of the fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) and the complete precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka-śīla*).

Regarding the reception [of the precepts], some say it is received incompletely; others say that even after a bhikṣu has committed the four grave offenses (pārājika), the bhikṣu-precepts still remain, while others say they no longer remain.

Some say that those who have attained the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat all attain the Buddha-way, while others say they do not. Others say that buddha-nature is itself the assembly [of sentient beings].
Regarding the existence of the Buddha-nature within sentient beings, some say it is distinct from them;
others say that even those who have committed the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, or those who are icchantikas all possess the Buddha-nature, while others say they do not.
Some say there are Buddhas of the ten directions, while others say there are no Buddhas of the ten directions.
From this point, the characteristics of the various controversies are extensively set forth: Kaishan says there are twenty controversies, while Yecheng says there are twenty-one (and so forth).
Thirdly, as for the passage beginning "Just as the Tathāgata," it concludes the refutation (and so forth).
If the Tathāgata is fully accomplished in the power of knowing the faculties (*indriya-jñāna-bala*), why does he not provide a definitive teaching today?
In the subsequent answer, the Buddha fully answers the three questions: within this fascicle, he answers the first two, and at the beginning of the next fascicle, he answers the third.
The answer to the first [question] is twofold: first, it correctly clarifies that the teaching is not fixed; second, it extensively explains its lack of fixity.

The opening section of this Dharma discourse consists of four parts: first, clarifying that the principle is profound and difficult to understand; second, distinguishing between the two types of people—the ignorant and the wise;
third, explaining the necessity of indeterminate teaching; and fourth, concluding with the power of knowing faculties, which corresponds to the intent of the four *siddhāntas*.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "Good son, such a meaning is not known by eye-consciousness, nor indeed by consciousness up to mental consciousness;
it is that which can be known only by wisdom."

Regarding the initial statement that "the principle is profound": it is because this principle is not known by the consciousnesses of the six classes of ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-gati*) but is understood only by the wisdom of the noble ones (*ārya-jñāna*) that it is called "profound.
This is the meaning of the first point.
Within the subsequent discussion of the ignorant and the wise, there are again two parts: first, the presentation of the wise, and second, the presentation of the ignorant.
If there is a wise person, I shall never treat them as two, nor do I speak with a dualistic discourse regarding them.

When a wise person first hears "existence," they know it as existence; when they hear "non-existence," they know it as non-existence; when they hear "both existence and non-existence," they know it as both existence and non-existence; and when they hear "neither existence nor non-existence," they likewise know it as neither existence nor non-existence, and so forth for all such categories.
To those who lack wisdom, I speak with indeterminacy, yet those lacking wisdom likewise claim that I have spoken indeterminately.

Furthermore, when the foolish hear of "existence," they reject "non-existence"; hearing of "non-existence," they deny it as being "existent"; hearing of both "existence" and "non-existence," they cling to their simultaneous preservation;
hearing of the abandonment of both, they become attached to dualistic renunciation. If this is the case even when faced directly, how much more so in the degenerate age?
This further aggravation arises from not understanding the complete intent of the remedies.

Third, regarding all that the Tathāgata has taught as "undetermined" (aniyata), this is stated generally based on the existence of undetermined phenomena; it consists of the analogy and its application, beginning with the phenomenon itself.
Good son, all the virtuous deeds of the Tathāgata are for the purpose of taming all sentient beings.
To deliver sentient beings, he must teach that which is indeterminate; this is intended to bring them benefit and not to cause them to cling to the indeterminate as a basis for dispute.
For example, all the medical prescriptions of a king of physicians are intended solely for the treatment of all forms of illness and suffering.
In the subsequent analogy, it is like a physician who uses medicine primarily to cure a disease; he never wishes that the patient’s taking of the medicine should result in further illness.
Good son, for the sake of the land, for the sake of the season, for the sake of the words of others, for the sake of individuals,
and for the sake of the various faculties of beings, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, makes two kinds of explanations regarding a single dharma.

In the section on analogies, it is stated that because the territories and boundaries of nations differ, they cannot be treated as a single category; if they were treated as a single category, it would be of no benefit to the nation.

Regarding "the land," this refers to a very cold country where one uses woolen mats and wears leather boots. Regarding "the season," this refers to a time of famine when, when begging, one can obtain only meat.
Regarding "speaking for another," this is like a person at the ninth stage saying they do not see [the tenth], while one at the tenth stage says it is slight.
To see that which is for the sake of people according to their individual faculties is precisely the intention regarding people.
The fourfold summary of knowing the power of the faculties is the worldly intention (and so forth). There is a scriptural passage where the summary is absent;
this must be a textual omission.

Under the first heading, two points are extensively set forth regarding the indeterminate dharmas (*aniyata-dharma*): first, the formal explanation of the indeterminate dharmas; second, the citation of scriptural evidence;
and third, the conclusion that these are not known by the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*). Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the indeterminacy of names and meanings;

second, the indeterminacy of extensive and abbreviated [explanations]. Within the first part on names and meanings, there are two sections: first, the listing of the topical headings; second, the explanation.
Regarding a single dharma-name, one speaks of immeasurable names; regarding a single meaning, one speaks of immeasurable names; and regarding immeasurable meanings, one speaks of immeasurable names.
In the initial listing, three topical headings are set forth as in the Sūtra: "If one wishes to clarify them in correspondence, there should be six propositions for each one."
Regarding the statement "an immeasurable name is taught," it should be said "in contrast to an immeasurable name, one name is taught.
Regarding "one name is taught in contrast to one meaning," it should be said "an immeasurable name is taught in contrast to one meaning.

Regarding "an immeasurable name is taught in contrast to immeasurable meanings," it should be said "immeasurable meanings are taught in contrast to an immeasurable name. The present text briefly cites only one side [of these possibilities].
How is it that a single name is explained by many? Having first explained the three categories of gates, we now re-explain the second gate.

How is it that one name expresses immeasurable names? It is like *nirvāṇa*, which is called *nirvāṇa*, and also called "non-arising," "non-emergence," "non-action," "unconditioned," "refuge," and "abode."
It is also called liberation; it is also called radiance; it is also called the light of a lamp; it is also called the further shore; it is also called fearlessness;
it is also called non-retrogression; it is also called a secure dwelling; it is also called tranquility; it is also called signlessness;
it is also called non-duality; it is also called the single practice; it is also called coolness; it is also called darkness-free; it is also called unobstructed; it is also called non-contention.
It is also called "unturbid," it is also called "vast," it is also called "ambrosia," and it is also called "auspiciousness.
Thus, what is a single name is made into immeasurable names.
This concludes the first chapter. Master Dàliàng states that the single name "Nirvāṇa" contains all names and possesses eight flavors.
The name "Nirvāṇa" is a collective designation for manifold virtues; this is the intended meaning here.
As for the various translations of "nirvāṇa" by different masters, their disputes also arise solely from this point.
Next, I shall explain how a single meaning is expressed by immeasurable names.
How is it that a single meaning is expressed by immeasurable names?
For example, Śakra is also named Śakra, also named Kauśika, also named Vāsava, also named Purandara, also named Maghavan, and also named Indra.
Dhara is also named Thousand-Eyed, also named Consort of Śacī, also named Vajra, also named Jewel-Crest, and also named Jewel-Banner;
these are called the immeasurable names spoken for a single meaning.
Regarding the mention of Śakra, how does this differ from what preceded? The former was an allegory for the Dharma, while the latter is an allegory for the person.

Within the subsequent detailed explanation, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are again employed as an allegory; this is another way of explaining the resultant Dharma, though it is given many names and various distinctions to facilitate understanding.
The Master of Hexi translated *vibhūṣaṇa* as "fine adornment," referring to the fine garments of former times.
As for the reward obtained now from practicing generosity, it is the "Lifesplendid" (Purandara), which is translated as "Subduer of the Senses.
He is a celestial king who externally adorns his appearance with splendid robes and internally disciplines his mind with wholesome dharmas.
"Makha" is translated as "Unconquerable," because he transcends all other devas and is without peer. "Indra" is translated as "Radiance," for his radiance is supreme among the thousands.
The "Eye" (cakṣus) knows a thousand meanings and severs a thousand matters in a single moment; the "Vajra" has a physical form that is firm and solid.
Regarding the third explanation—expounding immeasurable meanings and speaking immeasurable names—how does one speak immeasurable names for immeasurable meanings?
For example, the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is called "Tathāgata," yet the meanings [of these terms] differ.
He is called by different names; he is also called Arhat with a different meaning, and also called Samyaksaṃbuddha with a different meaning,
and also called Ship’s Captain, and also called Guide, and also called Perfectly Awakened One,
and also called One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, and also called Great Lion King, and also called Śramaṇa, and also called Brāhmaṇa, and also called Tranquil.

The donor is also called "One Who Has Reached the Other Shore," "Great King of Physicians," "Great Elephant King," "Great Dragon King," "Giver of Eyes," "Great Malla," "Great Fearless One," "Mass of Jewels," "Caravan Leader," "One Who Has Attained Liberation," "Great Man," and "Teacher of Gods and Humans."
Puṇḍarīka is also named "Solitary and Without Peer," also named "Great Field of Merit," also named "Ocean of Great Wisdom," also named "Formless," and also named "Endowed with the Eight Knowledges.
All such variations in meaning and variations in names are what is meant by "expounding immeasurable names within immeasurable meanings."
To explain how the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten thousand virtues: it is the single meaning within immeasurable meanings, and the single name within immeasurable names.
Regarding the eight knowledges (*jñāna*), there are three interpretations: first, that the eight consist of [knowing] the eternal and so forth as impermanent and so forth;

second, that there are eight by taking each of the Four Truths (*catuḥsatya*) as having both dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*); and third, that from the perspective of persons, they are discussed in terms of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
The logicians argue that by taking the present as the basis for inference, one infers the past and future;
thus, it is said that the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* contains eight knowledges and seven suchnesses, wherein the seven wholesome dharmas within the holy life are supplemented by the faculty of knowledge.
Fourth, there is another meaning: the following provides a further explanation of two chapter-headings.
Furthermore, there is another meaning that explains them by means of immeasurable names;

that is to say, just as the aggregates (*skandha*) are called "aggregates," they are also called "perversions" (*viparyāsa*), "truths" (*satya*), "the four foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*), "the four nutriments" (*āhāra*), and "the four stations of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*).

It is called existence (*bhava*), it is called the path (*mārga*), it is called time (*kāla*), it is called sentient beings (*sattva*), it is called the world (*loka*), and it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It is also called the three cultivations—namely, body, precepts, and mind; it is called cause and effect (*hetu-phala*);

it is called afflictions (*kleśa*); it is called liberation (*vimukti*); it is called the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*); and it is also called the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas.
The names "hell-beings," "hungry ghosts," "animals," "humans," and "devas" are also called "past," "present," and "future.
This is what is meant by "one meaning expressed through immeasurable names.

The preceding section, concerning Śakra, was restricted to the sense of "wholesome" (kuśala) and thus possessed immeasurable names; however, those names did not extend to the unwholesome (akuśala). This [current section] is presented to clarify that point.
The "aggregates" (*skandha*) are primarily defined by the five aggregates; these are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and are further called the "inverted aggregates.

They are the objective domain of the Truth of Suffering and are what is contemplated by the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). One contemplates form as impure, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as suffering, non-self, and impermanent.

These are also called the four applications of mindfulness. Excluding the aggregate of form, the remaining four aggregates are precisely the abodes of the four consciousnesses. The aggregate of form also pervades the internal.
Because they are external, they are called the four nutriments; because they can penetrate [to the ultimate], they are called the cause of the Path.

Since provisional names exist based on real dharmas, it is said that the substance of time is itself signless (animitta), which is the primary truth (paramārtha). The three cultivations—namely body, precepts, and mind—are precisely the afflictions within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha);
liberation is conditioned liberation (saṃskṛta-vimukti), and what is also called the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) is...
Taking the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the substance of causes and conditions is also called the "Three Vehicles," because they can bring about the bodies of the Three Vehicles;
the rest is intelligible and need not be explained (etc.).
"Good son, regarding the second section, 'The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One,' which explains the brief, the extensive, and the indeterminate, it is divided into three parts:
first, the listing of the four topical headings; second, the explanation beginning with 'How so...'; and third, the conclusion."
Good son, for the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, explains the extensive in brief and the brief in detail;
he explains the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and explains the phenomena of conventional truth as the ultimate truth.
What is meant by "expounding the brief within the extensive," as when it was said to the bhikṣus: "I now proclaim the twelve links of dependent origination"?
What are called the twelve links of dependent origination? They are cause and effect. What is meant by "expounding the extensive within the brief," as when it was said to the bhikṣus:
"I now proclaim suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path"? Here, "suffering" refers to immeasurable varieties of suffering.
"Accumulation" refers to the immeasurable afflictions; "extinction" refers to the immeasurable paths of liberation; and "expedient means" refers to the immeasurable skillful methods.
Why is it that what is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is spoken of as conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)? It is as when [the Buddha] addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this body of mine now, there are old age, sickness, and death. How is it that what is spoken of as conventional truth is called the ultimate truth?
As it was said to Kauṇḍinya: "Because you have attained the Dharma, you are named Ajñāta-Kauṇḍinya.

The commentary explains that regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): *A-jñāta* means "non-existent" (*a*), and *jñāta* means "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

This refers to his attainment of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). This is explained in terms of the conventional truth to indicate the ultimate truth; other points may be inferred accordingly.
Third, there are two subsequent summaries following the preceding section; first, the summary of the indeterminate [powers].
Therefore, because they follow persons, intentions, and times, it is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowing the faculties of others.
Next, regarding my power of knowing the faculties (*indriya-jñāna-bala*) in relation to the lower [stages], there are two parts; first, the explanation of the Buddha’s knowledge:
"Good son, if I were to provide a definitive exposition on such matters as these, I could not be called a Tathāgata endowed with the power of knowing the faculties.
Good son, a person of wisdom should know that this is like the load carried by a fragrant elephant."
That which cannot be surpassed by a donkey— the immeasurable conduct of all sentient beings— is why the Tathāgata expounds immeasurable teachings in various ways.
This clarifies that it is for those with wisdom, and is not something known by those of shallow understanding.
Next, why is it that the following section clarifies that being a person is not fixed?
For what reason? Because sentient beings possess many afflictions (*kleśa*).

If the Tathāgata were to teach only a single practice, he would not be called a Tathāgata who has fully accomplished the power of knowing the faculties (*indriya-jñāna-bala*). Therefore, in other sūtras, I have taught five [faculties].
For these five types of sentient beings, one should not preach the five corresponding dharmas: for those who lack faith, one does not praise right faith;

for those who violate the precepts, one does not praise the observance of the precepts; for those who are stingy and greedy, one does not praise giving; for those who are indolent, one does not praise extensive learning;
and for those who are ignorant, one does not praise wisdom. Why is this? Because if a wise person were to act toward these five [in such a manner]...

Regarding these five types of people who speak thus, it should be known that such speakers cannot possess complete knowledge of the powers of the faculties (*indriya-bala*), nor can they be called compassionate toward sentient beings.
Why is this? Because when these five types of people hear these matters, they give rise to lack of faith, malevolence, and anger;
by reason of these causes and conditions, they will undergo the retribution of suffering for immeasurable eons. Therefore, [they are not so].
He is named "One Who Pities Sentient Beings and Possesses the Knowledge of the Faculties and Powers.
He does not preach five kinds of dharmas to the five types of people because he does not employ antidotes;

rather, he teaches only those who are stingy—namely, precepts, patience, meditation, and wisdom—so that they may spontaneously practice giving, and cause those who break the precepts to spontaneously cultivate meditation, wisdom, and so forth.
They are able to uphold the precepts.
For this reason, I previously cited the second scriptural proof.
Therefore, in another sutra, I first told Śāriputra: "Be careful not to [teach] for the sake of those with sharp faculties."
"To those of dull faculties, he expounds the Dharma extensively; to those of dull faculties, he expounds the Dharma in brief.
Śāriputra said, "World-Honored One, I have spoken only out of compassion, not because I possess the power of complete faculties."
Regarding the third section, which concludes that the teaching of the Dharma in its extensive and abbreviated forms is not known by those of the two vehicles:
"Good son, the teaching of the Dharma in its extensive and abbreviated forms is the realm of the Buddha; it is not known by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
"Good son, as you have said, this is the second answer to the second question regarding conflicting disputes; it is further divided into two parts:
first, a brief answer, and second, a detailed answer.
Good son, as you have said, that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his disciples each gave different explanations—this refers to..."
All people, due to inverted causes and conditions, fail to attain right view; for this reason, they are unable to benefit themselves or others.
Good son, these sentient beings do not possess but a single nature, a single practice, a single faculty, a single land, or a single spiritual friend.
Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims various essential teachings for them. For these reasons, throughout the ten directions...
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the three periods of time, for the sake of sentient beings, reveal and expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Good son, when the Tathāgata speaks these twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is not for his own benefit, but solely for the benefit of others.
Therefore, the fifth power of the Tathāgata is called the power of understanding; by means of these two powers, the Tathāgata deeply knows this person’s present [state].
Because there are those who can sever their roots of goodness in future lives, those who can sever their roots of goodness in the present life,
and those who can attain liberation in future lives, the Tathāgata is therefore called the Unsurpassed Hero.

In the initial summary, it is stated that the fifth power is the power of understanding (*adhimukti-bala*), also called the power of desire (*chanda-bala*); this refers to knowing the dharmas according to the desires and understandings of sentient beings.
Furthermore, the text states: "These two powers arise from the fourth power, which is named the power of the faculties (*indriya-bala*), and the fifth, which is named the power of understanding;
thus they constitute two powers."
"Good son, as for the statement 'The Tathāgata descends,' this refers to the second part of the extensive response, which clarifies that the Buddha’s manifestations differ according to conditions;
because sentient beings do not understand this, they give rise to polemical disputes. There are twenty-one such points in total.

First, regarding whether there is parinirvāṇa or no parinirvāṇa, one must understand the differences between the various schools: the Sarvāstivāda school explains ultimate parinirvāṇa based on actual phenomena, while the Mahīśāsaka school..."
Furthermore, the Mahāsāṃghikas, relying on reason, state that [the Tathāgata] does not enter ultimate nirvāṇa.

Traditional critiques have claimed that the Sarvāstivādins are wrong because they are deficient in virtue, while the Mahāsāṃghikas are right because they are extensive in merit; both of these views miss the Buddha’s intent. As the text says:

"If one claims that the Tathāgata either enters ultimate nirvāṇa or does not enter ultimate nirvāṇa, these are both contentious arguments and do not capture my meaning. How could such a critique be considered anything other than false?
The Chief Judge [Heshan] said: "Ultimately, is this cessation or is it permanence? To speak of 'cessation' or 'permanence'—how could these be mere cessation or permanence?
They are rather non-cessation and non-permanence, yet capable of both cessation and permanence. To say 'cessation' does not contradict permanence; to say 'permanence' does not contradict cessation.
Cessation and permanence do not differ from one another; cessation and permanence are both complete. Master Guan said: "The Buddha..."

To preach according to the specific capacity [of the listener] while asserting "this is right" or "that is wrong" loses the Buddha’s intent; it is like a physician treating illnesses where the administration of medicine differs according to the case.
If disciples do not understand this and instead harbor false attachments, they lose the essential meaning. This initial debate has two parts: first, the general thesis.

"Good son, if one says that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate parinirvāṇa or has not entered ultimate parinirvāṇa, such a person does not understand the intention of the Tathāgata and therefore speaks in this way.
Next, in the explanation of the commentary, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the attachment to fixed nirvāṇa; second, the explanation of the attachment to non-fixed nirvāṇa."
The preceding passage also consists of two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the conclusion. Regarding the first part, the Buddha spoke of *nirvāṇa* for five reasons:
first, for the sake of the sages; second, for the sake of the Mallas; third, for the sake of Cunda; fourth, for the sake of Subhadra;
and fifth, for the sake of King Brahmadatta. First, regarding the sages:
"Good son, in this Fragrant Mountain there are fifty-three thousand sages who, in the past, cultivated various merits under the Buddha Kāśyapa;

yet they have not yet attained the Right Path. Having approached the Buddhas and heard the True Dharma, the Tathāgata, wishing to act for the sake of such people as these, addressed Ānanda, saying: 'After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.'"
Having heard this, the sound was passed on in succession until it reached the various seers on Mount Gandhamādana. Upon hearing it, they immediately felt remorse and spoke these words:
"How is it that we, though born among human beings, have not drawn near to the Buddha?
The appearance of a Buddha, a Tathāgata, in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower. We shall now go to the presence of the World-Honored One to hear and receive the True Dharma."
"Son of a noble family, at that time fifty-three thousand sages came to where I was.
I then taught them the Dharma as was appropriate for them, saying: 'Great beings, form is impermanent. Why is this? Because the causes and conditions of form are impermanent.
How could form produced from impermanent causes be permanent? This applies likewise up to consciousness. At that time, the sages heard this.
As soon as the Dharma was taught, he immediately attained the fruit of Arhatship.
However, Xiansheng (Born-of-the-Mountain) spoke of "successive transformation," meaning that from the various heavens one transforms and arrives at the mountain dwelling of the rishis;
having attained Arhatship, there is both the provisional and the real, for by destroying their adherence to permanence, he taught impermanence.
In Kuśinagara, the second [group] were the Mallas.
Good son, in Kuśinagara there were three hundred thousand Mallas who were without any master or affiliation;
they relied on their own pride and arrogance, and were crazed and distracted in mind by their physical strength, vitality, and wealth. Good son, I acted for the sake of subduing these Mallas.
The Licchavi then said to Maudgalyāyana, "You must subdue such a strongman.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana, out of respect for and compliance with my instruction, engaged in various forms of teaching and conversion over the course of five years; yet he was unable to cause even a single strongman to receive the Dharma or be subdued.
Therefore, I again spoke to Ānanda regarding those strongmen, saying: "After three months have passed, I shall..."
"Nirvāṇa, son of good family! At that time, when the Mallas had heard these words, they gathered together and leveled the road.
After three months had passed, I then departed from the city of Vaiśālī for the city of Kuśinagara.
Seeing the Mallas from afar along the way, I immediately transformed my body into the likeness of a śramaṇa and went to where the Mallas were."
"What work are these youths doing? When the Mallas heard this, they were filled with resentment and spoke thus:

"Śramaṇa, why do you now call us 'youths'? We, a great assembly of three hundred thousand people, could not move even this tiny stone by exerting all our physical strength; how [could we be called youths]? At that time, I said to them:
"If you, a great assembly of three hundred thousand people, cannot move this minute stone even with the full force of your bodies, why [do you call yourselves youths]?"
"Are you not called a youth? The Mallas said, "If you consider us to be youths, you should know that you yourself are a great man.
"Good son, at that time I dug up this rock with two toes of my feet.
When those Mallas saw this, they immediately conceived a sense of inferiority toward their own bodies and further thought:"
He said, "Śramaṇa, can you now move this rock aside to clear the path?
I asked, "Young man, for what reason have you adorned and prepared this road? The Mallas replied, "Do you not know, Śramaṇa?
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni shall travel by this very road to the Śāla grove to enter parinirvāṇa; for this reason, we have leveled it."
While I was being treated, he praised me, saying: "Excellent, young man! Since you have already given rise to such a virtuous mind, I shall remove this rock for you.
At that time, I lifted the rock with my hand and hurled it high until it reached the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
When the Mallas saw the rock suspended in the air, they were all struck with terror and immediately sought to scatter in the four directions. I then addressed them again, saying: "O Mallas!"
"You should not now give rise to a heart of fear and each wish to disperse. The Mallas said, "If you, O Śramaṇa, can protect us, we shall remain settled here.
At that time, I again caught the stone with my hand and placed it in my right palm.
When the Mallas saw this, their hearts were filled with joy, and they spoke thus: "Śramaṇa, is this stone permanent?"
"Is it impermanent? At that time, I blew upon it with my mouth and the stone immediately crumbled and fell apart like fine dust.
When the Mallas saw this, they cried out, "The śramaṇa! This stone is impermanent!

They were immediately filled with shame and reproached themselves, saying, "Why do we rely on our sovereign physical strength, life, and wealth to give rise to such arrogance? I knew their thoughts and...
Having relinquished his transformation body and returned to his original form to preach the Dharma, when the Mallas saw him,
they all conceived the aspiration for Bodhi.
Among them was a craftsman, the third from the bottom, named Cunda.
"Good son, in Kuśinagara there was a craftsman named Cunda. This man had previously made a great vow before Kāśyapa Buddha, saying:
'When the Tathāgata Śākyamuni enters parinirvāṇa, I shall be the last to offer him food and drink.
For this reason, in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, he entrusted the bhikṣu Upamāna with [this matter]."
"Three months from now, I shall enter parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees at Kuśinagara;
you should go and inform Cunda so that he may know this."
The fourth [disciple] below those from Rājagṛha was Subhadra.
Good son, in the city of Rājagṛha there was a seer possessing the five supernatural powers named Subhadra, who was one hundred and twenty years old and constantly claimed himself to be omniscient.
Having given rise to great arrogance, he had previously planted [roots of merit] under immeasurable Buddhas of the past.
"Out of my desire to discipline those who possess various roots of goodness, I have told Ānanda: 'After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
When Subhadra hears this, he will come to me and give rise to a mind of faith and reverence;
I shall then preach various teachings to him, and upon hearing them, he will attain the exhaustion of the outflows."
In the fifth section concerning Rājagṛha, there was a world-ruling king.
Noble son, King Bimbisāra of Rājagṛha had a crown prince named Ajātaśatru.

Due to the causal conditions of his past karma, he conceived a mind of perversity and rebellion, desiring to harm his father; yet, he could find no opportunity. At that time, there was an evil man, Ti... [text continues]
Devadatta, likewise due to the causal conditions of his past karma, again conceived an unwholesome mind toward me with the desire to harm me;
he then cultivated the five supernormal powers and before long attained them.
He became close friends with Prince Sudarśana and, for the sake of the prince, manifested various kinds of miraculous feats, such as exiting through what was not a gate and entering through a gate.
Emerging from the gate rather than entering through it, he at times manifested the forms of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, men, and women.
Upon seeing this, Prince Sudarśana immediately conceived feelings of affection, joy, and reverent faith.
For this reason, he prepared various kinds of offerings and made them, further addressing him, saying: "O Great Master, O Holy One!"
When I now wish to see the *mandārava* flowers, Devadatta immediately went to the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*) and sought them from the devas there;
however, because his merit was exhausted, no one gave him any. Having failed to obtain the flowers, he thought to himself:
"The *mandārava* trees have neither 'I' nor 'mine. If I were to take them myself, what would it matter?"
As soon as he committed this offense, his supernormal powers were lost;
he saw himself once again in Rājagṛha and felt deep shame and remorse, unable to look upon Prince Sudarśana. He then thought to himself:
"I shall now go to the Tathāgata and request the great assembly. If the Buddha grants permission, I shall instruct and command Śāriputra according to my will."
At that time, Devadatta came to me and spoke these words: "I pray only that the Tathāgata entrust this great assembly to me;
I shall preach the Dharma in various ways to instruct and transform them, so as to bring them to subdual.
I said: "Foolish man! Śāriputra and the others are brilliant and possess great wisdom; they are trusted and revered by the world. I would not even [entrust them] to them."
"How much more so for you, foolish men who feed on spittle! At that time, Devadatta conceived an even greater malice toward me and spoke these words:
"Gautama, although you now subdue the great assembly, your power shall not last long;
you shall soon see them destroyed. As soon as he had spoken these words, the great earth immediately shook in six ways. Deva...
Devadatta immediately fell to the ground, and a great, violent wind arose from his side, blowing dust and dirt to defile him.
Having seen these evil omens, Devadatta spoke again, saying:
"If this body of mine must enter the Avīci Hell in this very life, I shall surely take revenge upon such a great enemy. Thereupon, Devadatta rose at once.
He went to where Prince Sudarśana was; having seen him, Sudarśana immediately asked, "O Noble One, why is your countenance so haggard and why do you have such a look of sorrow?
Devadatta replied, "I am always like this; do you not know it?
Sudarśana answered, "I pray you, tell me its meaning; by what cause and condition is it so? Devadatta said, "I am now extremely close to you."
"O outsider, you revile me as being unrighteous; hearing this, how could I not be grieved?
Prince Sudarśana spoke again, saying, "How is it that the people of the country insult and humiliate me? Devadatta replied, "The people of the country call you 'Ajātaśatru' (Unborn Enemy).
Sudarśana asked again, "For what reason am I called 'Ajātaśatru'? Who made this name?"
He was named Devadatta, who said: "Before you were born, all the physiognomists made this prediction:

'Once this child is born, he shall kill his father. For this reason, outsiders all call you 'The Unborn Enemy' (Ajātaśatru), while those within the palace, wishing to protect your heart, call you 'Good Vision' (Sudarśana).
When Queen Viḍūḍabha heard these words, she gave birth to you."
When you threw your body from the high terrace to the ground and broke off one of your fingers, for this reason people further called you Bhallika.
Having heard this, my heart was filled with grief and distress, yet I could not speak of it to you.
Devadatta has instructed you in various such evil deeds, commanding that you kill your father. If you...
"My father died, and I too shall be able to kill the Śramaṇa Gautama.
Prince Sudarśana asked a great minister named Varṣākāra, "Great King, for what reason was my name made 'Unborn Enemy' (Ajātaśatru)?
The minister then explained its origin and details to him exactly as Devadatta had described them. Having heard this, Sudarśana immediately [ordered] the minister to seize him.
The father-king confined her outside the city and stationed the fourfold army to guard her.
When Queen Mṛdvī heard of this matter, she went immediately to the king’s location; however, the guards stationed there blocked her and would not allow her entry.
At that time, the queen gave rise to a mind of resentment and began to revile them. Then the guards informed the prince, "The Great King’s wife wishes to see you."
The father king, having failed to listen with discernment and having formed improper views and perceptions, gave rise once more to anger and resentment.
He went immediately to his mother’s quarters, seized her hair from the front, drew his sword, and was about to strike her when Jīvaka addressed him, saying:

"Great King, since you have possessed this kingdom, though a crime may be of the utmost gravity, it does not extend to women, much less to one who is your own biological mother. Upon hearing these words, Prince Sudarśana [intervened] for Jīvaka...
Because of this, [the father] immediately abandoned him and cut off his access to clothing, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions;
after seven days had passed, the King’s life came to an end. Upon seeing his father’s funeral rites, Prince Sudarśana finally gave rise to a mind of remorse.
However, the minister Vṛṣṭika again expounded various evil and heterodox doctrines to him, saying: "Great King, all karmic actions..."
"Since there is no sin whatsoever, why do you now give rise to a mind of regret?
Jīvaka replied again, "Great King, you should know that such an act of karma carries a twofold gravity of offense: first, the killing of your father, the king; second, the killing of a *srotāpanna*.
As for such a sin, none other than the Buddha has the power to eliminate it. King Suprabuddha said, "The Tathāgata is pure."
"Being defiled by our own sins, how could we, who are such offenders, have been able to see [the Buddha], O son of good family?
It was because I knew this matter that I told Ānanda: 'After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Having heard this, Sudarśana immediately came to my presence;
I preached the Dharma for him, whereby his heavy offenses were lightened and he attained rootless faith."
Having lost his supernatural powers and fallen [from his celestial state], he did not die because of the remaining force [of his merit].
King Bimbisāra—also called Piṅsā—is from the country of Magadha, also known as Māgadha; Rājagṛha is translated here as "King’s House City" (Wángshèchéng).
The concluding summary that follows is easy to understand.
"Good son, when my disciples hear this teaching, they fail to comprehend my intention and thus speak these words:
'The Tathāgata definitively teaches ultimate nirvāṇa.'"

The second section, "The Two Kinds of Bodhisattvas," provides an explanation of the insistence that [the bodhisattva] definitely does not enter nirvāṇa. This is further divided into two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the conclusion.

Regarding the first part: "Good son, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas: first, those who exist in reality; second, those who exist as designations. When a bodhisattva who exists as a designation hears...
When they heard that I was to enter parinirvāṇa in three months, all of them gave rise to thoughts of retreat and spoke thus:
