"If the Tathāgata is impermanent and does not abide, for what purpose should we strive? For this reason, throughout immeasurable ages, we have endured great suffering and affliction.
Even though the World-Honored Tathāgata has fully accomplished and perfected immeasurable merits, he cannot even overcome such a death-demon; how much less could we?"
"Could we possibly destroy it, O son of good family? For this reason, I speak thus for the sake of such bodhisattvas:
'The Tathāgata is eternally abiding and undergoes no change.'"
For those who are called "bodhisattvas" by way of conventional designation, one does not say they enter nirvāṇa; for true bodhisattvas, one speaks neither of nirvāṇa nor of non-nirvāṇa.
Such a bodhisattva is able to know that the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent; how could they hold a biased understanding of him as either permanent or impermanent?
"Good son, when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and definitively claim that the Tathāgata will never ultimately enter parinirvāṇa. Good son,
there are various sentient beings who, having fallen into the second type of contentious debate regarding the existence or non-existence of a self, must..."
The school of the Saṃmitīya (formerly known as the Śāriputrābhidharma) follows the tenets of the Sarvāstivāda;

it exclusively elucidates non-self (*anātman*) to refute the heterodox views of external paths regarding a "false self" (*mithyātman*), and maintains that there is no provisional designation of a self (*prajñapti-ātman*).

While it clearly explains non-self, it does not conclude with the doctrine of impermanence (*anitya*) alone to enter the Path, differing from the theorists of external paths; it is similar to the Dharmaguptaka in its explanations.

There is a provisional self that refutes the various non-Buddhist schools, which assert a continuous provisional self existing either within the aggregates or apart from the aggregates; this provisional self is established through causes.
Furthermore, it is said that while real dharmas perish moment by moment, there is no longer a provisional name for a continuous provisional self established through causes.
Furthermore, it is said that because real dharmas perish moment by moment, there is no self, yet the provisional name of continuity remains uninterrupted.
Therefore, some speak of a self, while others say that in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) there is no self, but in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) there is a self.
This is a one-sided clarification of the doctrine of a self; yet, as these two schools do not grasp the Buddha’s intention, they fall into contentious debate. Jiatixie explains:
"These two passages clarify both self and non-self in order to remedy two maladies. To say 'there is a self' is to refute the false notion of non-existence."
I do not say that "self" is provisional; rather, I say "non-self" in order to refute those who hold the views of self and permanence.
To speak directly of non-self is also not to say it is provisional. A true seeker might raise this objection:

"If both 'self' and 'non-self' are refuted, then there is a principle here—whether it is accepted or not—if one cannot find either self or non-self, then one should likewise be unable to employ them."

If the sicknesses of "self" and "non-self" are mutually sublated within the midst of birth-and-death, then the sicknesses of "permanence" and "impermanence" should likewise be mutually sublated within nirvana.
If nirvana possessed only permanence and could not possess impermanence, then within birth-and-death one could only possess non-self and could not possess self. As the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says:
The Buddhas sometimes speak of a self and sometimes speak of non-self; yet within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither self nor non-self.
One should apply this principle to all points of contention. Regarding the text, there are two parts: first, clarifying the existence of a self;

second, clarifying the absence of a self. The first part also has two sections: first, clarifying the provisional self of the continuum (*saṃtati-prajñapti-pudgala*) in order to refute false views regarding non-self.
"Good son, there are sentient beings who give rise to the view of annihilationism and speak thus:
'After the bodies of all sentient beings have perished, there is no one who experiences the retribution of their good and evil karma. For these people, I say:
'The retribution of good and evil truly has one who experiences it. How do we know this exists? Good son, in a past age, at Kuśinagara..."
In the kingdom of Rājagṛha there was a king named Sudarśana. When he was a youth, eighty-four thousand years passed;
as a crown prince, eighty-four thousand years passed; and likewise, while occupying the throne, eighty-four thousand years passed.
Seated in solitude, he reflected thus: "Sentient beings have meager merit and short lifespans; they are constantly pursued by four enemies."
Because he does not realize this and remains thus negligent, I shall now leave the household life to practice the Way and sever the four enemies—birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Thereupon, he commanded his officials to construct a hall of seven treasures outside the city.
Once it was finished, he addressed his ministers, high officials, palace ladies, consorts, sons, and kinsmen: "You should know that I intend to depart."
"If my householder [request] may be granted," at that time the great minister and his retinue each spoke these words: "Excellent, Great King!
Now is precisely the right time. Then, King Sudarśana took a single attendant and went alone to the hall;

for another eighty-four thousand years, he cultivated a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). By reason of this cause and condition of loving-kindness, in the subsequent eighty-four thousand lifetimes...

For thirty lifetimes he attained the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin rāja*), for immeasurable lifetimes he was Śakra Devānām Indra, and for countless lifetimes he was various minor kings.
"Good son, do not entertain the thought that the one who was King Sudarśana at that time was anyone else;
it was none other than myself. Good son, when my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed:
The Tathāgata definitively teaches that there is a self and that there is what belongs to a self (*ātmiya*).

Next, from "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) onwards, it clarifies the establishment of the self through causes; this section has two parts: first, the actual clarification of the establishment of the self through causes;
second, the clarification of that which is established by those causes. Regarding the first part:
Furthermore, at one time I spoke for the sake of all sentient beings, saying that what is called "self" is precisely "nature"— namely, internal and external causes and conditions,
the twelve links of dependent origination, sentient beings, the five aggregates, the mind-realm, and the world.

The text states: "As for 'self,' there are two traditional interpretations regarding its nature (*xing*). First, it refers to the nature of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), as cited from the preceding passage:
'Among the twenty-five existences (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), is there not a self? (and so forth). Second, it takes the nature of conventional designations (*prajñapti*) as the nature of the self;

this nature is the essence (*tattva*), and this essence is that which is constituted by causes. Among the three types of conventional designations, only that which is constituted by causes is the essence."
Continuing to await this application: internally it refers to the four aggregates (*skandhas*), and externally it refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūtas*).

"Twelve links of dependent origination" is a general designation for form and mind; "sentient beings" is a provisional name for their nature. These things that constitute the body are what is termed "provisional existence through causes.

If one were to take this as the meaning of Buddha-nature, then sentient beings possess it as that which is accomplished by the five aggregates; Buddha-nature is precisely defined in relation to these [aggregates].

The five aggregates within the living body are the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Regarding the "mind-element" (*citta-dhātu*), it is the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*) among the five aggregates.
Following this, the virtues, karma, and practices clarify the relationship between the cause and that which is accomplished by the cause.
"In the world of the Īśvara of meritorious karmic actions, that which is called 'self' is precisely what I mean by 'self.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and say, 'The Tathāgata definitively asserts that there is a self.'"
Karmic activity is the cause, while Īśvara is the result; it is said that by cultivating the cause one attains the result.

The term "Īśvara" does not merely designate the specific deity Īśvara; it is a general term for all devas who possess mastery over ascending and soaring. The term "worlds" refers to the other four realms of existence (*gati*).
Furthermore, at another time, the second [section] follows, which clarifies non-self. This is further divided into two parts: first, the Buddha’s teaching; second, the arising of attachments.
The first part consists of three sections: 1) a provisional question; 2) a provisional answer; and 3) the benefit gained from contemplating non-self. Regarding the question, there are three points:
first, asking what is meant by the name "self. What is the designation for "self"?
"Good son, at another time, there was a bhikṣu who came to me and asked this question:
'World-Honored One, what is called "self"?
He asked a second time: "'What is the substance that is the self?'"
"Who am I? He asked this three times: "For what reason am I?
For what reason am I?"
At that time, I immediately provided provisional answers for the latter two [questions], answering them in three parts: first, a general response to the overall meaning; second, a specific response;
and third, a conclusion stating there is no answer. The general meaning is divided into two sections: first, the presentation of the topical outline (*uddāna*).
At that time, I spoke to the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus, there is no self (ātman) nor anything belonging to a self (ātmīya).
I then proceeded to explain this in detail (*yathāvistaraṃ*).
As for the eye: it is originally non-existent and now exists; having existed, it returns to non-existence. At the moment of its arising, it comes from nowhere.
At the time of its cessation, it likewise goes nowhere; although there are karmic fruits, there is no agent, and there is no one who discards the aggregates or takes up new aggregates.
As for your questions, the three have already been answered in substance by the two preceding specific responses; why then is it necessary to provide separate answers? Nevertheless...
The general discussion on non-self is followed by a specific response concerning provisional names, provisional entities, and provisional causes and conditions.
Regarding your question, "What is the self? the self is precisely *jī* (the life-principle).
In the initial response concerning provisional names, it says that *jī* is what Hexi [Daoxuan] described as being like a person making a pact; one responds to the appointed time.

"Coming" has the meaning of conjunction; "not being expected" has the meaning of non-conjunction. Because the aggregation of the five aggregates constitutes a provisional name, it carries the meaning of expectation.
Next, karma is cited to answer the question regarding substance; subsequently, craving is cited to answer the question regarding conditions.
That which is "who am I" is precisely karma.
For what reason? That which is "I" is precisely craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Since karma is that which truly brings about the formation of results, it has the sense of being the "substance" (*bhāva*); craving is the affliction that moistens karma and causes it to be reborn. Furthermore, it is...
The meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*).

For example, it is like two hands [clapping]; because the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are absent, and furthermore, because the four [factors] are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*), they exist. This consists first of the analogy and subsequently of the application (*upanaya*).
"O Bhikṣu, it is like two hands clapping together; from their meeting, sound arises.
The two hands represent the conditions for producing the sound, the sound represents the substance [of the self], and the clapping represents craving.
I am also like this: because of the three causes and conditions of sentient beings' karma and craving, they designate it as 'self.'"
"O Bhikṣu, in all things below the second illumination, both 'separation' and 'non-existence' are absent.
O Bhikṣu, for all sentient beings, form is not the self, and within the self there is no form; within form there is no self.
This applies likewise up to consciousness."
The third section below, concerning the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), serves as a distinction.

Although the various classes of non-Buddhists claim that there is a self (*ātman*), they ultimately do not depart from the aggregates (*skandha*). It is impossible for them to say that there is a self existing separately apart from the aggregates.
The text states that "one never departs from the aggregates" because non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) give rise to the conceptualization of identity with or separation from them.

Here, the statement "it is impossible to depart from the aggregates" is explained in two ways: first, it is said that fundamentally all [non-Buddhists] reckon the aggregates themselves to be the self, and thus have no reckoning of departing from them;
second, regarding the reckoning of a self in grasses and trees, the Buddha refutes that the aggregates are the self, and furthermore... [the text continues].

Regarding the calculation that there is a self apart from the aggregates (skandhas) which currently exists within them, this is refuted; therefore it is said: "If there were a self apart from the aggregates, such a case would not exist.
Second, since even the Hinayana of the Buddha's Dharma contains the view that the self is identical to the aggregates, this is also refuted;
thus one must not calculate that there is a self apart from the aggregates.
All sentient beings have severed the fourth fetter of selflessness.
All sentient beings practice like an illusion or a mirage in the heat; O Bhikṣu, the five aggregates are all impermanent, without pleasure, without self, and without purity.
At that time, many— this is the third contemplation on non-self and the resulting benefit—
O son of good family, at that time there were immeasurable bhikṣus who, by contemplating these five aggregates as being without self or belonging to a self,
attained the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, it was explained that those present at this assembly had attained benefit;
later, however, they clung to this and gave rise to disputes (and so forth).
"Good son, when my disciples heard this teaching, they failed to understand my intention and proclaimed: 'The Tathāgata has definitely [said... "
It speaks of non-self.

Son of good family, in my sūtras, during the debate concerning the existence or non-existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within the third realm of existence, the *Vibhāṣā* states that Bhadanta Deva said that for one being born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is certainly an intermediate state; [this is] the *Vibhajyavādin*.
It is said that there is definitely no intermediate state (*antarābhava*). The Sarvāstivādins also say it definitely exists.

The masters of the treatises further state that it exists, citing the sharpness or dullness of one's karma—just as when a drill-point is pulled away from the hand, those with powerful evil karma enter hell directly, while those with powerful wholesome karma are born straight into the human or celestial realms, with neither case involving an intermediate state.
In the preceding text, it was first stated that it definitely exists, followed by three successive arguments.
It is taught that there are definitely four further points.
Son of good family, in the sūtras I have also said this: "Through the coming together of three things, one receives this body:
first, the father; second, the mother; third, the intermediate state (antarābhava). Through the coming together of these three, one receives this body. At that time, I further spoke of the *a-*...
An Anāgāmin may manifest parinirvāṇa, or enter parinirvāṇa within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, it is said that the sense faculties of the intermediate state body are fully complete and lucid; all of this is due to past karma, like refined clarified butter (*sarpis*).

Good son, at times I speak of the intermediate state experienced by evil beings as being like coarse, rough woolen cloth in this world, while that of those who are purely virtuous is like [refined] silk.
The intermediate state experienced by sentient beings is like the white cotton cloth produced in Vārāṇasī;
when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim, "The Tathāgata says that an intermediate state exists."

"Good son, I have further spoken these words for the sake of those sentient beings who commit the five heinous crimes: 'One who commits the five heinous crimes will, upon casting off the body, enter directly into the Avīci Hell.
I have also said: 'The bhikṣu Dharmaruci, upon casting off the body, will enter directly into the Avīci Hell;
there is no place to stay or rest in between. I have also [spoken] for the sake of that Brahmā Vatsa..."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "If there were an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for a brahmin, then there would be six types of self-existence. Furthermore, I have also said that for formless beings (*ārūpya-sattva*), there is no intermediate state.
Son of good family, when my disciples heard these teachings, they failed to understand my intention and proclaimed:
'The Buddha has definitively stated that there is no intermediate state.'"
If one asserts that there is an intermediate state (antarābhava), then there are six states of existence; yet these six states are merely the six realms of rebirth.
When the Buddha separately opened up the asuras for Śakra, the asuras were simply part of the realm of hungry ghosts (preta); thus, there would be only five, not six.

Furthermore, there are those who maintain that there is falling away from the fourth [fruit], arguing that there is falling away from the untainted (anāsrava) state, as in the case of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).

For one who has seen the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*), there is never any falling away; however, for those who have entered the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and attained the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*) by abandoning defilements through conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), there is indeed the sense of falling away.

As for the Arhat, it is logically certain that there is no falling away from the untainted state. The falling away of the two preceding fruits is cited here to imply the possibility of falling away for the Arhat.
The analogy of the sand-well is that there are bricks above and below with sand in between; when the middle sand collapses, it falls both upward and downward.
The proponents of the Abhidharma (the *lun-jia*) say that while the untainted (*anāsrava*) is non-retrogressive, meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is subject to retrogression.

One may attain the "thunderbolt-light" concentration of the desire realm through cultivation, but because this concentration is difficult to maintain and may sometimes be lost, it is called "retrogression. The untainted is without retrogression. In the text, first...

The explanation of falling back (parihāṇi) consists of three parts: first, the falling back from what is attained; second, the falling back from what was not yet attained; and third, the analogy and its application to the dharmas. Within these, there are again three sections:

first, a general explanation of the falling back of bhikṣus; second, a specific explanation regarding arhats; and third, a general enumeration of six types of persons. Within the first section on the general explanation, there are two further parts, the first of which is the general explanation itself.
"Good son, I have further stated in the sūtras that there is regression. Why is this?
It is because of the immeasurable number of bhikṣus who are indolent and lazy, and thus do not cultivate the Path."
Next, the conditions for regression are explained through five causes and conditions.
Five types of regression are taught: first, delighting in many affairs; second, delighting in discussing worldly matters; third, delighting in sleep;
fourth, delighting in associating with householders; and fifth, delighting in frequent wandering. By these causes and conditions, [the practitioner] is caused to regress.
The Master [Kātyāyanīputra] withdraws.
Next, there are two further types; the following section specifically clarifies the Arhat, which is divided into two parts: first, it states directly that the Arhat is subject to regression.
There are two kinds of causes and conditions for falling away: first, internal; second, external.
Although an Arhat is free from internal causes, he is not free from external causes. Due to external conditions, afflictions arise; because afflictions arise, he then falls away.
Next, the Arhat known as Gautamī, who possessed the perception of death, is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu named Gautamī who six times fell back from his attainment; out of shame and remorse, he practiced again and attained it for the seventh time.
Having attained it, he feared losing it and took his own life with a blade.
Furthermore, I have sometimes spoken of those who fall back by referring generally to six types of persons.
Again, I have sometimes spoken of "occasionally liberated" ones, or of the six kinds of Arhats.
When my disciples hear these teachings, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim: "The Tathāgata has definitively stated that there is falling back."

First, those who regress; second, those who do not regress; third, those with wisdom; fourth, those possessing both; fifth, those for whom it is timely; sixth, those for whom it is untimely. Those who are dull-witted when it is timely are prone to regression, while those who are sharp-witted when it is untimely do not regress.
Next, the passage beginning with "Good son" provides an analogy.
Good son, the sūtra further states: "For example, once charcoal has been burned, it cannot become wood again; likewise, once a jar is broken, it no longer serves the function of a jar.
The three afflictions are also like this. The following is the application of the analogy.
The afflictions are likewise; once an Arhat has severed them, they never arise again. It is also said that there are three causes for the arising of afflictions in sentient beings:
first, the non-abandonment of afflictions; second, the non-interruption of their causal conditions; and third, unwholesome reflection.
"Causal conditions" refers to external adverse conditions.
Here, the Arhat and the two lower stages clearly demonstrate non-retrogression.
Furthermore, the Arhat is free from these two causal conditions: namely, the severance of afflictions and the absence of unwholesome reflection, O son of good family.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has definitively stated there is no falling back.
They claim there is no falling back because internally there is no cause for evil and externally one cannot be disturbed.
"Good son, in my sutras, the fifth section on the debate concerning whether the Buddha-body is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states:

the Sarvāstivādins say it is conditioned; the Mahāsāṃghikas say it is unconditioned; and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* contains two views—the view that it is beyond verbal expression, thus unconditioned, and the view that it can be expressed through words, thus conditioned.
Regarding the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it is conditioned; regarding the true body (*dharmakāya*), it is unconditioned. In this passage, the conditioned is explained first."
"Good son, in the sūtras I have taught that there are two kinds of the Tathāgata’s body: first, the birth-body (*janma-kāya*); second, the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
What is called the 'birth-body' refers to the body of expedient means and transformation. Such a body may be said to be subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death;
it has length or shortness, black or white; it is this or that; and it is [the state of] training or no-more-training (*śaikṣa-aśaikṣa*)."

Having heard this teaching, the disciples did not understand my intention and proclaimed that the Tathāgata had definitively stated that the Buddha-body is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*),
followed by an explanation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Dharma-body is precisely that which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure; forever free from all birth, old age, sickness, and death;
neither white nor black, neither long nor short, neither this nor that, neither a learner (*śaikṣa*) nor one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*);
whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, it remains eternally abiding and immovable, without change or alteration. "Good son, when my disciples have heard this teaching," [they...]
Failing to understand my intention, they proclaim that the Tathāgata definitively taught that the Buddha-body is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma.

Son of good family, in my sūtras I have explained the twelve links of dependent origination. Regarding the sixth section on disputes, first I clarify the tenets held [by various schools], and subsequently I provide an explanation.
As for the initial passage: the Sarvāstivādins maintain that the links of dependent origination are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), whereas the Mahāsāṃghikas maintain that they are unconditioned.

To say that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) means that the cycle of cause and effect throughout the three periods of time revolves without end; how could this not be conditioned?

To say that the conditioned is unconditioned means that the principle of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) is unconditioned; although its causes and effects are impermanent, its underlying principle is unconditioned.
Regarding the initial adherence mentioned in the text, there are two parts: first, the adherence to the conditioned.
"Good son, in my sūtras I have explained: what is called the twelve links of dependent origination?

From ignorance arise volitional formations; from volitional formations arises consciousness; from consciousness arise name-and-form; from name-and-form arise the six sense bases; from the six sense bases arises contact;
from contact arises feeling; from feeling arises craving; from craving arises grasping; from grasping arises becoming; from becoming arises birth."
"From birth there arise old age, death, sorrow, and suffering, O son of good family. When my disciples hear this teaching, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata has taught that the twelve links of dependent origination are definitively conditioned.'"
Next, I shall address the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

On another occasion, I instructed the bhikṣus, saying: "Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, the intrinsic nature and characteristics (*dharmatā*) of the twelve links of dependent origination remain eternally present."
Next, in the explanation, first the topical outline is stated: "Good son,
there are twelve-fold dependent origination that does not arise from conditions, there is that which arises from conditions but is not twelve-fold dependent origination,
there is that which arises from conditions and is also twelve-fold dependent origination, and there is that which neither arises from conditions nor is twelve-fold dependent origination."
There are twelve links that are not produced by conditions; this refers to the twelve factors in the future life. There are those produced from conditions that are not the twelve links;
this refers to the five aggregates possessed by an Arhat. There are those produced from conditions that are also the twelve links;

this refers to the five aggregates possessed by ordinary worldlings. Regarding the twelve causes and conditions, there are those that are neither produced by conditions nor [constitute] the twelve links.

Regarding the two conditions, they are space and nirvana. Son of good family, when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim, "The Tathāgata has definitively taught that the twelve links of dependent origination are unconditioned."
The initial commentary on the first phrase states: "Not arising from conditions refers to the twelve links in the future.

However, since there are only two links—birth and death—in the future, how can one speak of twelve? Although the actual phenomena have not yet come into being, the cycle of transmigration is necessarily present;
thus, even without [actual] conditions, the meaning of the twelve links is complete. Is this not the use of the term "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) to provide proof for this?
The remaining three phrases of the "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) section then proceed to explain the second phrase.

It states that "that which arises from conditions but is not [part of] the twelvefold [causal chain]" refers to an Arhat who has already destroyed the three causes and is no longer subject to birth and death; this means he has already severed the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*).

Yet, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of this present body were obtained through the twelve links of dependent origination (and so forth). The explanation of the final two phrases can be understood accordingly.
(As stated above). In my sūtras, it is taught that for all sentient beings, the seventh *vijñāna*—the mind—is always subject to dispute as to whether it is permanent or impermanent.

The Sarvāstivādins (*Sarvāstivāda*) say that because the mind lacks continuity, it is impermanent; the Mahāsāṃghikas (*Mahāsāṃghika*) say that because the mind possesses continuity, it is [permanent].
The *Sāṃmitīya-śāstra* maintains that because the mind has continuity, it is eternal. This text consists of two parts:
first, the attachment to the eternity of the mind; second, the attachment to its impermanence.
"Good son, in my sutras I have said that when all sentient beings perform good or evil deeds and cast off their bodies, there are four..."
At that very moment, [the body] disintegrates and perishes. For those who perform purely wholesome deeds, the mind moves upward;

for those who perform purely unwholesome deeds, the mind moves downward. Good son, when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim, "The Tathāgata says that the mind is definitely permanent."
First, they cling to the notion of permanence, claiming that when the four great elements disperse and perish, this is the destruction of the body;

yet they assert that the mind of one who performs wholesome deeds ascends upward and is reborn in a good realm, and that by leading this very mind to a good realm, it is indeed the principle of permanence. They say the same applies to those who commit evil.
"Good son, at one time I spoke these words to King Bimbisāra: 'Great King, you should know that form is impermanent.
Why? Because it arises from causes that are themselves impermanent.
If form arises from impermanent causes, how could a wise person say it is permanent? If form were permanent, it should not undergo destruction.'"

"Various sufferings and afflictions arise; now that this form is seen to be dispersed, extinguished, and destroyed, one should therefore know that form is impermanent, and so it is for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including consciousness itself.
Son of good family, when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim, 'The Tathāgata says that the mind is definitively annihilated.'"
In my sutras, I have taught that the eighth [topic] is the dispute concerning whether the five desires obstruct the Path or do not obstruct it.

Good son, in my sutras I have said that my disciples, having received various perfumes, flowers, gold, silver, precious objects, wives, children, servants, and the eight kinds of impure things, attain the Right Path; and having attained the Right Path, they do not abandon me.
When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and declared: "The Tathāgata has said that experiencing the five desires does not obstruct the Noble Path.
Furthermore, at another time I made this statement: "It is impossible for a person living at home to attain the Right Path.
Good son, when my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed:
The Tathāgata taught that the experience of the five desires certainly obstructs the Right Path.
The Sarvāstivādins say they hinder the Path; the Mahāsāṃghikas say they do not hinder it; and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* maintains that there are arguments for both hindering and not hindering.

In my sūtras, it is taught that the "Distant" (dūre) stage, the ninth [of the aids to penetration], the "Controversial" (vivāda), and the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma) exist in the desire realm and pervade all three realms.
According to the Sarvāstivādins, the four fundamental dhyānas of the form realm can give rise to the Supreme Worldly Dharma.
The Dharmaguptakas maintain that both the form and desire realms can give rise to the five preparatory stages (pañca-prayoga), as there is no treatise clarifying that the formless realm lacks them.
Regarding the statement that "the five expedient means (upāya) arise across the three realms," only the Vātsīputrīya school asserts that they arise simultaneously across all three realms.

They claim that while still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one has already cultivated conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) to abandon the afflictions up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); subsequently, at a later time, one further cultivates untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) to abandon the afflictions up to the formless realm.
Because what was previously abandoned now gives rise to the expedient means, it is said that the expedient means arise simultaneously across the three realms.
The middle consists of three [realms], each of which adheres to one specific realm.

Good son, in my sūtras I have said that being free from afflictions yet not having attained liberation is like the cultivation of the "supreme worldly dharma" (laukikāgradharma) within the desire realm.
Good son, when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand it.
My intention was to proclaim that the "Supreme Dharma" taught by the Tathāgata exists only within the desire realm;

yet my disciples, upon hearing this, failed to understand my meaning and proclaimed that the Supreme Dharma taught by the Tathāgata exists within the form realm— specifically, that the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Worldly Dharma exist from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.

Furthermore, I have said that there are certain non-Buddhists who have already severed the afflictions of the four dhyānas and cultivated the stages of *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgradharma*, and by contemplating the Four Noble Truths, they attain the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim: "The Tathāgata says that the *laukikāgradharma* exists within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)."

Regarding the *dhātu* (elements). In my sūtras, I have taught four kinds of giving. [This concludes] the tenth section on the debate concerning whether giving pertains to the three types of action (*karman*) or does not pertain to them.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states that it exists only in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), because its primary essence consists of the volition (*cetanā*) associated with the relinquishing of wealth; it is also [considered such] for this reason.

The *Abhidharma* clarifies this through the Sarvāstivāda perspective regarding the three karmas of giving, concentration, and so forth; since the mental ground is wholesome, the bodily and vocal [karmas] are likewise wholesome.
The text is divided into two parts: first, the position that [wholesomeness] resides in the mind, and second, the view that it pervades all five aggregates.
"Good son, in my sutras I have taught that among the four kinds of giving, there are three types of purity:

first, the donor has faith in the cause, faith in the result, and faith in the recipient, while the recipient lacks such faith; second, the recipient has faith in the cause, the result, and the gift, while the donor lacks such faith;
third, both the donor and the recipient possess faith; and fourth, neither the donor nor the recipient possesses faith."

Faith constitutes four kinds of giving, the first three of which are pure; when my disciples hear this teaching, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata says giving consists solely of the mind.
"Good son, at one time I further spoke thus: 'When a donor gives a gift, they give by means of five things.
What are these five? First, giving form; second, giving strength; third, giving peace; fourth, giving life; fifth, giving eloquence.
Through such causes and conditions, the donor receives the retribution of these five things. My disciples heard this."
Having spoken thus, those who do not understand my intention proclaim that the Buddha taught that giving is itself the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
This clarifies the fourfold classification: the giver who believes in cause and effect and so forth is the mental ground;
subsequently, physical strength and so forth are explained as the body, speech as the mouth, and life-force as the mind.

"At one time, in the eleventh section on disputes concerning whether there are three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) or not, I, O son of good family, taught that *nirvāṇa* is precisely the distancing from afflictions, their eternal exhaustion and cessation until nothing remains, just as when a lamp is extinguished no further phenomenon arises;
*nirvāṇa* is likewise. That which is called 'space' (*ākāśa*) is—"

"Non-existence" is like the emptiness of the world; it is called "emptiness" because there is nothing there. It is not the cessation through the lack of conditions for cognition (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), which is simply non-existence.
If it were something that exists, it would have causes and conditions; because it has causes and conditions, it would consequently be subject to exhaustion and cessation.
Since it does not exist, there is no exhaustion or cessation. When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and cry out: [that it is annihilationism].
The Buddha said: "O son of good family, there are no three and no unconditioned phenomena. At one time, I spoke these words for the sake of Maudgalyāyana:
'Maudgalyāyana, nirvāṇa is precisely the scriptural phrases; it is the footprint; it is the ultimate state;
it is fearlessness; it is the Great Teacher; it is the Great Fruit; it is ultimate wisdom; and it is great forbearance.'"
The unimpeded samādhi is the great dharma-realm; it is the flavor of ambrosia, and it is difficult to perceive, Maudgalyāyana.
If one were to say that there is no nirvāṇa, how could those who give rise to slander fall into hell?
Good son, when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim, "The Tathāgata says there is nirvāṇa," and yet again [they say otherwise].
At one time, I spoke thus to Maudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, the eye is not solid; so it is with the body—all are not solid.
Because they are not solid, they are called 'space. The place where food is swallowed, turned over, and digested, as well as all sounds, are all called 'space.
When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my meaning."
The Master declared: "The Tathāgata definitively teaches that unconditioned space exists. Furthermore, on another occasion, he said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Maudgalyāyana, when a person who has not yet attained the fruit of a Srotāpanna dwells in the stage of patience (kṣānti), they sever the retribution for immeasurable births in the three evil realms;
you should know that this extinction does not occur through the conditions of wisdom. When my disciples heard this teaching, they... [did not understand].
To clarify my intention, I declare that the Tathāgata definitively taught that there is "cessation not through conditions" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).

However, since we do not see any school that maintains the non-existence of the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma), how could such a statement exist? This too has its own underlying meaning:
if a follower of the *Abhidharmakośa* were to say, "Since the three unconditioned phenomena are equally unconditioned, how could they have different natures? [this is the intent behind my statement].
This refers to those who calculate that the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are distinct entities;
since they speak of "three kinds," how could there not be distinct entities? This is precisely the sense of calculating that the three unconditioned phenomena exist.

Furthermore, at one time, for the sake of the twelfth dispute concerning whether there is derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) or no derived matter, I [discussed] the Abhidharma position that it definitely exists because it has the four great elements as its cause, whereas the *Abhisamaya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Formation of Form) lacks such textual evidence; thus, this constitutes the first [section].
Regarding the initial clarification of its existence, there are two parts: first, the clarification of the four great elements that act as the producers (*janaka*).
"Good son, at another time I spoke to the bhikṣu Bāpaka: 'If a bhikṣu contemplates form—whether past, future, or present;

near or far; coarse or subtle—and realizes that such forms as these are neither self nor belong to a self, then if a bhikṣu, having contemplated in this way, is able to sever craving for form. Bāpaka then asked: 'How...'"
"What is meant by 'form' (rūpa)? I say that the four great elements (mahābhūta) are form, and the four aggregates (skandha) are name (nāma).
When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed: 'The Tathāgata has definitively stated that form is the four great elements.'"

For example, just as blue, yellow, and so forth appear because of a mirror, these are derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*); and just as lightness, heaviness, roughness, and smoothness appear because of a mirror, these are derived tangibles (*upādāya-spraṣṭavya*).
Son of good family, I have further said that just as images appear because of a mirror, form (*rūpa*) is likewise dependent upon causes.

The four great elements produce what are called coarse and fine, rough and smooth, blue, yellow, red, and white, long, short, square, round, crooked, and angular, as well as lightness and heaviness, cold and heat, hunger and thirst, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist;
these are termed "derived matter" (*upādāya-rūpa*). It is like an echo.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim, "The Tathāgata says that because there are the four great elements, there is derived matter."
Regarding form (*rūpa*):
next, it is explained that there is no creation.
There may be the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) without the creation of derived form (*upādāyarūpa*).

The text is extremely concise and not extensive because it speaks in terms of functional phenomena (*vastu*). Since most [phenomena] arise from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), they possess the meaning of being "created" (*kṛtaka*);
therefore, it does not extensively clarify their non-existence.

In the past, at one time—this is the thirteenth section on the dispute regarding the existence or non-existence of unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*)—[the question is]: Is there unmanifest form, or is there no unmanifest form?
The Sarvāstivāda school maintains that *avijñapti* (non-informative action) is material (*rūpa*). The Dharmaguptaka school maintains that *avijñapti* is not material.

The Mahāsāṃghika school states generally that *avijñapti* cannot be said to be either material or non-material. In the text, it first addresses those who hold that [non-informative action] is material and not distinct from matter as cause and effect:
"distinct from matter" refers to mind (*citta*); they claim that *avijñapti* does not act as a cause for the mind. Furthermore...

Because it does not produce the fruit of mind, one knows this is form (*rūpa*). The Master He says: "It does not give rise to other forms. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, clarifying existence;
second, clarifying non-existence.
"Good son, at one time in the past, Prince Bodhi spoke these words: 'If there is a bhikṣu who maintains..."
If one who upholds the prohibitive precepts gives rise to an evil thought, you should know that at that moment the bhikṣu-precepts are lost. At that time, I said:
"The prince’s precepts are of seven kinds; they consist of non-manifesting form (*avijñaptirūpa*) arising from body and speech.

By reason of this non-manifesting form, even though the mind remains in an evil or neutral state, it is not called 'losing the precepts,' but is still called 'upholding the precepts. For what reason?"
"Conditioned by name, there is unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa), which is not a cause distinct from form, nor does it produce a result distinct from form.
Good son, when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim: 'The Buddha has said that unmanifest form exists.'"
"Good son, in other sūtras I have spoken thus: 'Precepts are that which restrain and prohibit unwholesome dharmas;
if one does not commit evil, this is called upholding the precepts. When my disciples hear this teaching, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata has definitively declared that there is no such thing as non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa).'"
In the fourteenth section of this treatise, "Disputes Regarding the Existence or Non-existence of Mental Factors (*caitta*) within the Sūtras," I clarify that according to the Sarvāstivāda,
mental factors exist as distinct entities separate from the mind and arise simultaneously; whereas the Mahāsāṃghika maintain that there are no mental factors,

and the Buddhatīva hold that while they are not distinct entities, they nevertheless arise sequentially, with what arises first being the mind and what arises subsequently being the mental factors— this is the position of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

Regarding the preceding section on the text, it is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the absence of mental factors (*caitta*), and second, clarifying the presence of mental factors. Within the clarification of the absence, there are two sub-sections;
first, citing the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as taught by the Sage.
"Good son, in the sūtras I have made this statement: 'The noble ones' aggregates of form up to the aggregate of consciousness all arise from the causes and conditions of ignorance.
Next, I shall correctly explain the twelve links of dependent origination for ordinary beings; herein there are two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the application of what preceded."
Since the preceding and succeeding lives are identical in their nature, they are one and the same; thus, there are no separate mental factors.
One should carefully examine the first passage for this.
All ordinary beings are likewise so: from ignorance arises craving; one should know that this craving is itself ignorance.
One should know that ignorance arises from craving and grasping; this grasping is itself ignorance. One should know that existence arises from grasping;
this existence is itself ignorance. One should know that feeling arises from birth and craving-grasping; this feeling is itself the formations and existence.
From the causal condition of feeling (*vedanā*), the following two [sections] clarify the sequence from prior to subsequent [birth].

From the causal condition of feeling arise name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), contact (*sparśa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and so forth;
therefore, feeling is itself the twelve links. Son of good family, when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not...
To explain my intention, I declare that the Tathāgata taught there are no mental factors (*caitasika*).

One must carefully investigate the explanation here: when it says "feeling" (*vedanā*), some might claim that this refers to the members of existence in a future life as feeling, rather than the members of the present life.
In the sūtras, I have spoken thus: "The two lower types of grasping possess mental factors (*caitasika*).
Son of good family, in the sūtras I have spoken thus: "From the four factors of the eye, forms, light, and unwholesome desire, visual consciousness arises.
Unwholesome desire is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). When there is a seeking of the nature of desire, it is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*); craving is the cause.
Conditioned by grasping, there arises becoming; conditioned by becoming, birth;
conditioned by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair arise.
Such phenomena as these are born from contact (*sparśa*). Yet, good son, when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention.
It is proclaimed that the Tathāgata has taught the existence of mental factors (*caitasika*).

Furthermore, by examining their characteristics through the lens of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), it can be seen that although these factors arise in succession, they do not coincide;
therefore, the mental factors exist as distinct entities, separate from [the primary mind].
At times, I have spoken of fifteen or sixteen forms of existence (*bhava*) to clarify the disputes regarding the five and six existences.
Good son, at other times I have said there is only one existence, or I have spoken of two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, up to twenty-five.
When my disciples hear these teachings, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim: "As [the Buddha] has said..."
Regarding this, some say there are five *bhavas* (existences), while others say there are six.
Most other schools speak of only five destinies (*gati*), whereas only the Vātsīputrīya school asserts that there are six destinies. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) also states that there are six;

however, regarding the single destiny of the *asuras*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* offers two explanations: first, that they are subsumed under the category of devas, and second, that they are *pretas* (hungry ghosts).

"First, regarding 'one existence' (*eka-bhava*): this refers generally to one *saṃskṛta-dharma* (conditioned phenomenon), though privately it is said to refer generally to one among the twenty-five existences (*bhava*).
As for what is called 'generally,' it is as follows: the three miserable destinies (*durgati*) are also collectively treated as one existence;

humans and devas are each separately divided into many existences; first, humans and the four [deva] realms constitute seventeen existences; second, cause and effect consist of the wholesome and the unwholesome; third, there are the three [realms]."

The four realms (*dhātu*) correspond to the four modes of birth; the five correspond to the five destinies (*gati*); the six correspond to the six paths of existence; the seven correspond to the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
The Master of Hexi says that by adding the realms of form and formlessness to the five destinies, they become seven. The eight correspond to the eight blessings (*puṇya*).

The Master of Hexi says that by adding the realms of form and formlessness to the six paths of existence, they become the eight blessings. This is not correct; how could the three miserable realms be considered blessings? The nine correspond to...
Regarding the "nine abodes of sentient beings" and the "twenty-five existences," He Xi (Heli) states that the nine consist of the eight dhyānas and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In the section beginning with "At one time in the past," the sixteenth point of debate concerns whether the five precepts and eight precepts are received in their entirety or not.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, they must be received in their entirety for them to be established; however, according to treatises such as the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, they may also be obtained even if not complete.
It is said that one who has directly received the three refuges but has not yet received even a single precept is called a "partial" (*amśika*) *upāsaka*.

There are likewise those who are "half-part," "majority-part," or "full-part. Furthermore, the Master [Vasubandhu] explains: "If one receives all five [precepts] but maintains only one or two, they are called 'one-part' or 'two-part,' and so forth.
This text is divided into two parts: first, it clarifies the non-observance of the five precepts; second, it clarifies the observance of the eight precepts. However, this is merely...
[They] appear interchangeably.
"Good son, once in the past, when I was dwelling in the Nyagrodha Grove at Kapilavastu, Śreṇika Bimbisāra came to where I was and spoke these words:
'What is called an upāsaka? I then explained it for him."
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who possess all their faculties and receive the three refuges, they are called upāsakas.
Śreṇika Bimbisāra asked, "World-Honored One, what is meant by a 'one-part' upāsaka?
I replied, "If one receives the three refuges and receives one precept, this is called a one-part upāsaka. My disciples—
Having heard this teaching, you did not understand my intention and proclaimed that the Tathāgata said one obtains the Upāsaka precepts even without receiving them in their entirety.
Good son, at one time I was dwelling by the side of the Huan River; at that time, Kātyāyana came to where I was.

He spoke thus: "World-Honored One, if I teach sentient beings to receive the precepts of the fast—whether for one day, one night, one period, or even a single thought-moment—does such a person accomplish the fast?
I replied, "Bhikṣu, such a person attains merit, but it is not called attaining the fast. When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed:
The Tathāgata said that the eightfold precepts of the fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) must be fully received to be obtained.
In the sūtras, section seventeen below clarifies whether one loses the precepts through a grave offense (pārājika) or not;

the four-volume Abhidharma states that losing them through a grave offense constitutes a forfeiture. Thus, the Abhidharma says that the restraint of the Vinaya (vinaya-saṃvara) is forfeited at five times.

First, when wrong views increase; second, when the Dharma is extinguished; third, when the life-faculty is severed; fourth, when a grave prohibition is violated; and fifth, at the time of renouncing the path.

According to the *Miśrakābhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā*, these are further increased or diminished; however, regarding the "defiled precepts," with the exception of the extinction of the Dharma and the violation of a grave prohibition, both are said to be not relinquished.
Furthermore, at the time of the arising of the two sexual organs, one does not enter the number of the Saṃgha, nor is one included among the nuns.
Other schools mostly state that the non-loss of the text constitutes the two [aspects of the offense]. First, they maintain that it is definitely lost.
"Good son, in my sūtras I have spoken thus: 'If a bhikṣu has committed the four pārājika offenses, he is no longer called a bhikṣu;
he is called a broken bhikṣu, a lost bhikṣu, one who can no longer produce the seeds and sprouts of the wholesome.'"
Just as a scorched seed does not produce fruit, and just as a *tāla* tree whose head is destroyed will not bear fruit, so it is with a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata has said that once bhikṣus have committed a grave transgression, they lose their bhikṣu precepts."
Next, I shall explain the non-forfeiture [of the precepts].
Good son, in a sutra I spoke of four kinds of bhikṣus for the sake of Cunda: first, those who have ultimately reached the Way;
second, those who show the Way; third, those who receive the Way; and fourth, those who defile the Way. Those who commit the four grave offenses (pārājika) are precisely those who defile the Way.
I say that when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata has said that even after committing the four pārājika offenses, bhikṣus do not lose their prohibitive precepts."
To "attain the Way" is true outflow-free realization (*anāsrava*); to "demonstrate the Way" is semblance outflow-free realization; to "receive the Way" is maintaining the precepts;
and to "suffer the Way" is violating the precepts.

In my sutras, chapter nineteen clarifies that Buddha-nature is neither separate from sentient beings nor identical to them; this is the view held by all schools, though it is a recent conception.

Regarding the text, there are two parts: first, the presentation [of the positions].
The six matters and the three clarifications reveal [the Buddha-nature].

Furthermore, son of good family, I have also said that the buddha-nature of sentient beings is like space. Space is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is neither internal nor external;
and it is not comprised of form, sound, smell, taste, or touch. The buddha-nature is likewise. When my disciples heard this...
Having spoken thus, they failed to understand my intention and proclaimed, "The Buddha says that the buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from sentient beings.

Good sons, I have further said that the buddha-nature of sentient beings is like a treasure trove within the house of a poor woman, a diamond jewel upon the forehead of a strongman, the nectar spring of a wheel-turning sage king; when my disciples heard this teaching...
Failing to understand my intention, they proclaim, "The Buddha said that the buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from the sentient beings themselves.

Son of good family, I have further stated that even those who commit the four grave offenses, icchantikas, those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, and those who commit the five heinous crimes all possess the buddha-nature.
Although such sentient beings lack any wholesome dharmas whatsoever, the buddha-nature itself is wholesome; this is what I have taught to my disciples.
Having heard this teaching, they failed to understand my intention and proclaimed that the Buddha taught that the buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from sentient beings,
whereas later he said that sentient beings are themselves the buddha-nature.
"Good son, I have also said that sentient beings are themselves the Buddha-nature. Why is this?
Because apart from sentient beings, one cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, I spoke to King Prasenajit using the analogy of the elephant:
although the blind men describing the elephant do not actually possess the elephant, they do not describe it apart from the elephant. When sentient beings speak of form..."
It is likewise with the teaching that consciousness is the Buddha-nature; although it is not the Buddha-nature, it is not non-Buddha-nature.
Just as I used the analogy of the lute for the king, so too is the Buddha-nature.
Good son, when my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and produce various interpretations, like a blind man asking about milk; such is the case with the Buddha-nature.
For this reason, regarding the twentieth section on whether those who have committed the four grave offenses possess the Buddha-nature or not:
Kaishan says that "the twentieth" still belongs to the nineteenth [section] concerning the meaning of the identity and separation of the Buddha-nature.
If Yecheng says "the twenty-first," this is actually the twentieth; why does it belong to the preceding? The preceding [section] states: "It is identical with sentient beings."
Apart from sentient beings, how can it be said that within this [nature], the presence or absence of the Buddha-nature in those who commit the five heinous crimes or grave offenses is identical?
For what reason is there a distinction?
Because of these causes and conditions, some may say: "One who violates the four grave prohibitions, slanders the Vaipulya sutras, or commits the five heinous crimes..."
Whether it is said that those such as the icchantikas all possess the Buddha-nature or that they lack it,
in various places— specifically in the twenty-first section below— I have clarified the positions of the Sarvāstivāda (which asserts there are no Buddhas in the ten directions),
the Mahāsāṃghika (which asserts there are Buddhas in the ten directions), and the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* (which asserts that there is only one world-system, whereas others assert there are many).
"Good son, in various sūtras I have stated that it is impossible for one person to appear in the world and benefit many people,
for two wheel-turning kings to appear within a single land, or for two Buddhas to appear in a single world-system.
Likewise, it is impossible for eight Cāturmahārājika devas, or even up to two Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, to appear [in a single world-system]."
I have taught that from Jambudvīpa down to the Avīci Hell and up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;
yet when my disciples heard this teaching, they failed to understand my intention and proclaimed, "The Buddha says there are no Buddhas of the ten directions.
However, I have also stated in various Mahāyāna sūtras that there are Buddhas of the ten directions.

This fascicle begins by responding to the third question posed in the previous section: "The Tathāgata skillfully knows the dispositions of sentient beings; for what reason does he give indeterminate teachings, thereby causing disputes?

The treatise is divided into two parts: first, praising the profundity of the principle; second, distinguishing and refuting doubts and attachments. The first part, praising the profundity, is further divided into two sections.
The first clarifies that these indeterminate teachings are the domain of the Buddha.
Good son, such disputes are the realm of the Buddhas and are not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Therefore, this principle is profound; it is not that the Buddha intentionally made contradictory statements to cause dispute.
Rather, because they do not understand the reason, they cling to their positions and argue.
If a person, regarding what follows here, is further exhorted and advised in two ways: first, one exhorts them to give rise to doubt; second, one warns them not to cling.
If one hears an indeterminate teaching and gives rise to doubt, it will necessarily lead to understanding; therefore, there is the exhortation.
If one hears an indeterminate teaching and clings to it as being correct, one will inevitably fall into delusion; therefore, there is the warning.
If a person conceives doubt regarding this, they can still destroy immeasurable afflictions as Mount Sumeru.
As for the first passage: generally, doubt is both a ford to liberation and the root of delusion.

If the "doubt" among the ten fetters (*daśa-ānuśaya*) refers to doubt regarding [wrong] views, then this doubt is not a ford to liberation and cannot destroy afflictions like Mount Sumeru. One interpretation states that "affliction" refers to...
The afflictions are as lofty and vast as Mount Sumeru; one doubts whether they can be shattered. Furthermore, it is said that the afflictions are as firm and solid as Mount Sumeru’s stable standing;
one doubts whether they can be uprooted. For these reasons, they are used as a metaphor.
If one gives rise to a fixed conviction regarding these matters, it is called attachment.

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: [The following] two sections distinguish between doubt and attachment as two distinct categories. The first two rounds of questioning concern attachment, while the subsequent four rounds concern doubt.
Each of the first two rounds contains both question and answer, as found in the text.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, what is meant by ‘clinging’?
The Buddha said, “Good son, if such a person— whether hearing it from another, seeking it out in the sūtras themselves, or being intentionally taught by another—
is unable to relinquish the object to which they are attached, this is called clinging.”
Kāśyapa spoke again: "World-Honored One, is such attachment as this wholesome or unwholesome?
"Good son, such attachment is not called wholesome. Why is that? Because it cannot destroy the web of doubts."
Kāśyapa spoke again: "World-Honored One, if such a person has fundamentally no doubt from the outset, why do you say that they have not destroyed the net of doubt?
The meaning of his later question was this: since he had not yet seen nirvāṇa, how could he suddenly doubt whether it exists or does not exist?"
"Good son, that which is called 'not doubting' is itself doubt.

The Buddha has taught that birth and death are suffering and Nirvana is not suffering; one must therefore doubt whether, by means of suffering, there can certainly exist a non-suffering that is able to sever suffering."
The second time, he raised a present instance to question a doubt:
"World-Honored One, if someone were to say that a srotāpanna does not fall into the three evil realms, would that person also be said to be attached to names and possessed of doubt?"
If one who perceives suffering were to doubt whether it is not suffering, then a person who has attained the first fruit would have to doubt that they have fallen into suffering.
In the Buddha’s response, the first four points of the middle section reprimand [this view]:
"Good son, this may be called 'certainty,' but it cannot be called 'doubt.'"

This is because it is logically inconsistent to harbor doubt regarding what has been definitively established; I have declared with certainty that this fruit does not fall [into the realms], and it is likewise stated that it will not fall.
Just as one says that the Buddha is definitively omniscient, how could there arise doubt regarding the indeterminate concerning that which has been definitively established?
Next, why is it that [the text] below sets forth the characteristics of a doubting mind in order to manifest the absence of doubt?
Why is this so? Good son, it is like a person who first sees a human and a tree;
later, while traveling at night, they see a pillar from afar and give rise to a doubtful thought: "Is it a person or a tree? Good son, it is as when a person first sees a bhikṣu... [and so on].
Later, while traveling on the road, he saw a bhikṣu from afar and immediately gave rise to a doubt: "Is this a śramaṇa, or is it a brahmin?
Good son, it is like a person who has previously seen both a cow and a water buffalo; later, seeing a cow from afar, he gives rise to a doubt:
"Is that a cow, or is it a water buffalo?"
Within this, there are three analogies, each stating that one first sees and subsequently doubts.
Third, regarding all sentient beings who first see two objects, the conclusion below definitively establishes their doubting attachment:
"Good son, all sentient beings first see two objects and subsequently give rise to doubt."
Fourth, as for the passage beginning "Why is this?", it explains the cause of the doubt.
Why? Because the mind does not understand. I also do not say that a *srotāpanna* falls into the three evil realms or does not fall into the three evil realms;
why, then, would such a person give rise to a doubting mind?
The third set of questions consists of two parts: first, a question regarding nirvāṇa, and second, a question regarding turbid water.

Kāśyapa said: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught that one must first see something before one can doubt it, there are those who also give rise to doubt even when they have not yet seen two kinds of things. What are these? They are what is called nirvāṇa."
World-Honored One, it is as if there were a person who encountered turbid water on the road; though they had never seen it before, doubt arose within them:
"Is this water deep or shallow? Since this person had not yet seen it, how could such doubt have arisen?
Since such principles and facts have never been seen before, one may still give rise to doubt; why must one first see them before doubt arises?
Good son, that which is nirvana is the cessation of suffering, and that which is not nirvana is suffering. I.
All sentient beings have two kinds of views regarding suffering: those who see it as suffering and those who do not see it as suffering.

Those who do not see it as suffering are those who experience hunger, thirst, cold, heat, anger, joy, illness, emaciation, well-being, old age, vigor, birth and death, bondage, liberation, separation from loved ones, and association with the hated.
Having perceived these, sentient beings immediately give rise to doubt, thinking: "There must be a way to ultimately distance oneself from such suffering."
Because this troubling matter is not [a matter of] falsehood, sentient beings give rise to doubt regarding nirvana.
The Buddha’s answer likewise first considers crossing over from nirvana and saṃsāra;
since saṃsāra is that which is to be remedied and nirvana is that which remedies it, he causes them to infer whether the remedy exists or does not exist.
If you think that the subsequent answer regarding turbid water first restates the question and then refutes it—
namely, that it is illogical for this person to have doubts if they had not previously seen turbid water— then that interpretation is incorrect.
Next, the passage beginning with "For what reason" provides the direct answer:
For what reason? Because this person has previously seen such things in other places; therefore, even regarding this place where he has never been before, doubt arises once again.
Having previously perceived that there were both deep and shallow [levels], one might doubt the depth and shallowness within this context.
The subsequent four rounds of question and answer are as stated in the text.
The World-Honored One said: "When this person previously perceived the deep and shallow places, they did not give rise to doubt; why then do they do so now?"
He gave rise to doubt.
The Buddha said, "Good son, it is because you have not yet practiced that doubt arises; therefore, I say that because of a lack of clear understanding, doubt occurs."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: This is the third major section, clarifying the views that sever the roots of goodness; it further consists of three parts: first, further identifying the person;
second, clarifying the arising of the view; and third, the ability to sever the roots of goodness.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, doubt is itself attachment, and attachment is itself doubt. To whom does this refer?
World-Honored One, it refers to those who have severed their roots of goodness. Kāśyapa asked: “World-Honored One, what kind of people are able to sever the roots of goodness? The Buddha replied:
“Good son, if there are those who are clever, wise, of sharp faculties, and capable of skillful discernment...”

One who stays far removed from virtuous friends, does not listen to the true Dharma, engages in improper reflection, and does not abide in accordance with the Dharma—such a person is able to sever their roots of goodness.
Although Sunakṣatra was already mentioned previously, he is mentioned again here because it is intended to clarify the arising of [wrong] views; thus, the person is cited once more.
Setting aside these four matters, the second section follows, which presents the arising of views in four parts: first, six "furthermore" sections explaining that there is no act of giving;
second, six "furthermore" sections explaining that there are no parents; third, three "furthermore" sections explaining that there is no cause and effect;
fourth, nine "furthermore" sections explaining that there are no noble beings (*ārya*). Now, merit arises from conditions; when the conditions of giver and receiver coincide, [merit is produced].
It can produce merit just as planting in fertile soil does; when the conditions of rain from heaven and water from the earth are fully present, sprouts can grow.
How could it be permissible for one who gives to the poor to receive the retribution of poverty? Poverty is an inferior fruit, whereas giving yields a superior reward.

It would be like sowing grain that turns instead into weeds, or a field so barren that the harvest is meager—these matters need not even be discussed. Yet, in my private opinion, if one gives to the poor and receives [the retribution of] poverty...
One who is poor should sow seeds in the earth to harvest water and soil in winter. As for those who give rise to views:

those who sever the roots of goodness are mostly found in the three continents of Jambudvīpa; the gods are weak and attached to pleasure, while those in the hells suffer so heavily that they all lack firm resolve, and thus this mind [to sever the roots] arises rarely among them.
Setting aside these four matters, one reflects within the mind: "There is no such thing as a gift. Why? Because the giver is precisely that which relinquishes material wealth.
If giving were to have a retribution, one should know that the donor would always remain impoverished;
why? Because the fruit resembles its cause. Therefore, it is said that there is neither cause nor fruit. If one speaks in this way of neither cause nor fruit, then—
This is what is called "severing the roots of goodness. Furthermore, one might think: "The donor, the recipient, and the material gift—these three things are impermanent and do not abide.
If they do not abide, how can it be said that 'this is the donor,' 'this is the recipient,' or 'this is the material gift'?
If there is no recipient, how can there be a fruit? For this reason, there is neither cause nor fruit. If [one thinks thus]...
One should know that such a person who speaks thus—that there is neither cause nor effect—is able to sever their roots of goodness. Furthermore, they entertain this thought:

"When a donor gives, there are five aspects to the giving; yet when the recipient has received it, they may at times perform good or perform evil, and the donor likewise does not obtain any fruit of good or evil.
This is like the worldly law where a fruit arises from a seed. The fruit...

If one were to claim that the son is the cause and the donor is the fruit, while the recipient is the one who receives it, yet the recipient cannot transfer these wholesome or unwholesome dharmas to the donor—on this basis, there would be neither cause nor fruit.
One should know that if such a person asserts that there is neither cause nor fruit, they are capable of severing their roots of goodness. Furthermore, they might think: "There is no gift."
For this reason, if the object of giving is neutral (*avyākṛta*), how can it yield a wholesome fruit? That which has neither wholesome nor unwholesome fruit is neutral.
If wealth is neutral, one should know that there will be no wholesome or unwholesome retribution.
Therefore, there would be no giving, no cause, and no fruit. If one speaks thus of no cause and no fruit, one should know that such a person is capable of severing [the roots of goodness].
The roots of goodness further form this thought: "The donor is the mind; if it is the mind, it is invisible and non-obstructive, and is not a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*).
If it is not a material phenomenon, how can it be given? Therefore, there is no giving, no cause, and no fruit.
If one speaks thus of no cause and no fruit, it should be known that such a person is capable of severing the roots of goodness. Furthermore, the donor forms this thought: [and so forth].
If one gives alms for the sake of images of Buddhas or deities, or for deceased parents, there is no recipient.
If there is no recipient, there should be no karmic fruit. If there is no karmic fruit, this constitutes the absence of cause. If there is no cause, this constitutes the absence of effect.
One who speaks thus of the absence of cause and the absence of effect should be known as a person capable of severing their roots of goodness.
In the first of the six sections, the first subsection clarifies the absence of a cause by means of the similarity between seed and fruit;
the second subsection shows that both the wealth bestowed and the recipient are non-existent;

and the third subsection demonstrates that when one bestows gifts upon another and that person subsequently performs good or evil deeds, since the performance of evil does not benefit the donor, the performance of good likewise does not.
If there is a benefactor who provides a sharp blade to someone, commanding them to kill another person, would this evil not accrue to the benefactor?
Fourthly, since the gift is merely the object given, and the object itself is ethically neutral (*avyākṛta*), how could a wholesome fruit be obtained?
Fifthly, the act of giving is an invisible process inferred through the intention; since the intention is invisible, how could the act of giving be visible?
Seeing only the fruits of good and evil; sixth, furthermore, if there is neither agent nor recipient, when one cultivates merit for a deceased person of the past, who is there to receive this merit?
Regarding the section "There is no father, there is no mother," the second part, number six, further clarifies the absence of father and mother as stated in the text.

Furthermore, one reflects: if there were no father and no mother, and if it were said that parents are the cause for the birth of sentient beings, then logically they should produce beings constantly without interruption.
Why? Because the cause would be ever-present. Yet, beings are not produced constantly. Therefore...
