Therefore, one should know that there are no parents. Furthermore, one might think: "There is neither father nor mother. Why? Because if the bodies of sentient beings were caused by parents, then every single person should possess both male and female sexual organs; yet there is no one who possesses both. Thus, one should know that sentient beings do not arise because of parents. Furthermore, one might think: "Sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if sentient beings were born without being caused by parents, then all sentient beings would be born simultaneously; yet this is not the case. Therefore, one should know that sentient beings are not born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born with the same physical form; yet they are not born with the same physical form. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born at the same time; yet they are not born at the same time. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born from eggs; yet they are not all born from eggs. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born from wombs; yet they are not all born from wombs. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born from moisture; yet they are not all born from moisture. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born spontaneously (*upapāduka*); yet they are not all born spontaneously. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as humans; yet they are not all born as humans. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as gods; yet they are not all born as gods. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as hell-beings; yet they are not all born as hell-beings. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as animals; yet they are not all born as animals. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as hungry ghosts (*preta*); yet they are not all born as hungry ghosts. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as asuras; yet they are not all born as asuras. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as humans; yet they are not all born as humans. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as gods; yet they are not all born as gods. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as hell-beings; yet they are not all born as hell-beings. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as animals; yet they are not all born as animals. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as hungry ghosts; yet they are not all born as hungry ghosts. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as asuras; yet they are not all born as asuras. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as humans; yet they are not all born as humans. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as gods; yet they are not all born as gods. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as hell-beings; yet they are not all born as hell-beings. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as animals; yet they are not all born as animals. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as hungry ghosts; yet they are not all born as hungry ghosts. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as asuras; yet they are not all born as asuras. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as humans; yet they are not all born as humans. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Furthermore, one might think: "It is not the case that sentient beings are born without being caused by parents. Why? Because if it were so, then all sentient beings would be born as gods; yet they are not all born as gods. Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that sentient beings
Therefore, when one sees sentient beings with the eye, they do not appear like one's parents; this is because their physical form, mind, deportment, and movements differ from those of the parents.
Thus, the parents are not the cause of the sentient being. Furthermore, one should consider that there are four kinds of non-existence (*abhāva*) in the world:

first, non-existence by way of not yet having arisen (*anutpanna-abhāva*), such as when a lump of clay has not yet become a jar and thus lacks the function of a jar; second, non-existence by way of having already ceased (*vinaṣṭa-abhāva*), such as when a jar has been destroyed.

The first is called "non-existence by way of difference," such as there being no horse within a cow and no cow within a horse. The second is called "non-existence by way of mutual absence," such as there being no horse within a cow and no cow within a horse.

The third is called "non-existence by way of ultimate non-existence," such as the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise; the parents of sentient beings are likewise like these four types of non-existence.
If one says that parents are the cause of sentient beings, yet when the parents die the child does not necessarily die—[how can this be so?]

Therefore, parents are not the cause of sentient beings. Furthermore, one reflects: "If it were said that parents are the cause of sentient beings, then sentient beings should be born constantly from parents;
yet there are also those born by transformation and those born from moisture. Thus, one should know that sentient beings are not born from parents.
Furthermore, one reflects: "There are sentient beings who exist independently, without depending on parents."
Their growth is like that of a peacock which, upon hearing the sound of thunder, immediately attains its body;
or like a blue jay which, by drinking the tears of a male jay, immediately attains its body; or like the *jīvajīvaka* bird which, seeing a male dance, immediately attains its body.
When one reflects in this way, if they do not encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), it should be known that such a person is capable of severing their roots of goodness.
Third, once again, it clarifies that there is no cause and effect.
Furthermore, one might think: "In all the world, there are no fruits of good or evil. Why is this?

There are sentient beings who possess the ten wholesome dharmas, joyfully practice wise giving, and diligently cultivate merit; yet such persons likewise suffer from diseases gathering within their bodies."
In some years there is death and loss of wealth, with much sorrow and suffering;

yet for those who commit the ten non-virtues, being stingy, greedy, envious, jealous, lazy, and indolent, and do not cultivate various virtues, they may live out their natural lifespan in physical ease and freedom from illness, possessing abundant wealth and treasures and being free from all grief and suffering.
Therefore, one should know that there is no fruit of good or evil. Furthermore, one might think: "I have also heard that..."

The Sages have said that there are those who, having cultivated merit, fall into the three evil realms at the end of their lives, and those who, having committed evil, are born among humans or devas at the end of their lives;
therefore, one should know that there are no fruits of good or evil. Furthermore, they form this thought:
all Sages have two kinds of teachings—some say that killing results in a favorable retribution, while others say that killing results in an unfavorable retribution.

Therefore, one should know that the Noble One’s teaching is not fixed; if the Noble One were not fixed, how could I be fixed? For this reason, one should know that there are no fruits of good or evil.

In the second passage, it says: "Those who practice good die and are reborn in the three evil realms, while those who practice evil die and are reborn among gods and humans. This is explained as follows: [The text continues with the refutation of such a view.]

It is said that all [beings] fall or ascend based on the single thought of good or evil at the moment of death; as for those with remaining [karmic debts] yet to be repaid, they do not perish in the end.
If one discerns this principle through the three periods of the present life and the two subsequent lives, it can be contemplated; everything else can likewise be seen.
The fourth [section], the ninth: furthermore, all is as in the text.
Again, he reflects: "In all the world there are no noble ones (ārya). Why?

If one says that a noble one should have attained the Right Path, then when all sentient beings cultivate the Right Path while still possessing afflictions (kleśa), it should be known that these persons are truly [noble]."
If the path and the afflictions exist simultaneously, one should know that the true path cannot destroy the fetters.
If one cultivates the path when there are no afflictions, what function would such a true path have?
Therefore, for one who possesses afflictions, the path cannot destroy them; for one who lacks afflictions, the path is useless. Thus, one should know that in all worlds...

In the interim, there would be no noble ones (ārya). Furthermore, one might think: "The twelve links of dependent origination—from ignorance conditioned by [volitional] formations, up to birth conditioned by [existence], leading to aging and death—are shared equally by all sentient beings.

Likewise, the Eightfold Noble Path, being equal in its nature, should also be such that when one person attains it, everyone should attain it; and when one person practices it, all suffering should cease."
"Why is it that although cessation exists, one does not currently attain it because of afflictions and the like? Therefore, one should know that there is no true Path.

Furthermore, they think: "The noble ones all share the same dharmas as ordinary people—namely, eating and drinking, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, laughing, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, sorrow, and fear. If these matters are the same as those of ordinary people," [then how can they be considered noble?]

One should know that if a noble one (ārya) has not attained the Noble Path, or if having attained the Noble Path they have not eternally severed such matters as these—namely, if they do not sever such matters—one should know that there is no Path. Furthermore, one might think:
"A noble one experiences the five sensual pleasures with the body, yet also reviles, strikes, and beats others; they harbor jealousy and arrogance, and experience both suffering and pleasure."
Because one performs good and evil karma, it is known that there is no sage. If there were such a thing as the Way, one should have severed these matters;
since these matters are not severed, one should know there is no Way. Furthermore, one reflects thus: "One who possesses great compassion is called a sage.
For what reason is he called a sage? It is because of the causes and conditions of the Way that he is called a sage. If the nature of the Way is compassion...
If one has compassion, one should simply have compassion for all sentient beings without waiting until after practice; otherwise, how could there be compassion?
For what reason would a sage, having attained the Path of the Sages, be able to feel compassionate pity? Therefore, one should know that the world lacks the Path of the Sages.
Furthermore, one should reflect: "All four great elements do not arise from causes; all sentient beings equally possess these four great elements."
By nature, one does not observe whether sentient beings belong to this side or that side, or whether they should go there or not;
if the nature of the Noble Path were such, it would be so, but now it is not. Therefore, one should know that there are no noble ones in the world. Furthermore, one reflects:
if all noble ones possessed a single nirvāṇa, then one should know that there would be no noble ones. Why? Because [such a nirvāṇa] cannot be found.
The principle of the eternally abiding dharma cannot be attained, nor can it be grasped or abandoned. If the nirvāṇa of the various sages were manifold, it would be impermanent;
why? Because it would be a countable phenomenon. If nirvāṇa were one, then when one person attains it, everyone should attain nirvāṇa simultaneously.
If it were manifold, it would have limits; how then could it be called eternal? If someone were to say that nirvāṇa—
If the substance of *parinirvāṇa* were one liberation and its manifestations were many—just as a single umbrella has many ribs, or a single tongue has many teeth—this would not be correct.
Why? Because what is attained individually is not the attainment of all; since it would have limits, it would necessarily be impermanent.
If it were impermanent, how could it be called *nirvāṇa*? If *nirvāṇa* did not exist, who would be an *ārya* (noble one)? Therefore...
One should know that no noble one (ārya) would again entertain such a thought as: "The path of the noble ones is not attained through causes and conditions.
If the path of the noble ones were not attained through causes and conditions, for what reason would everyone not become a noble one?
If all people were not noble ones, one should know that there would then be neither noble ones nor the noble path. Furthermore, the Noble One speaks thus: [text continues]
Right view has two causes and conditions: first, hearing the Dharma from others; second, internal reflection for oneself.

If these two causes and conditions arise from conditions, then that which arises from them must itself arise from further conditions. If this were to continue in such a succession, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress.
Conversely, if these two matters do not arise from conditions, why is it that all sentient beings do not attain them?
The third section, "When Making This Contemplation, One Can Sever the Roots of Goodness," is further divided into two parts;

first, it clarifies the severing of the roots of goodness: "Good son, if there are sentient beings who deeply perceive such [a view] that there is neither cause nor effect, these people can sever the five faculties, beginning with faith."
Next, let us briefly examine the distinction between those of sharp and dull faculties.
Good son, one who has severed the roots of goodness is neither a person of inferior, foolish, or dull capacity, nor is such a person among the gods or in the three evil realms;
the same applies to one who causes a schism in the Sangha.

All is as asked in the text. Regarding the icchantika: they once possessed wisdom and cultivated causes; since there must be fruits corresponding to those cultivations, why did they sever their roots of goodness?
The answer is: they possessed only mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*) and lacked supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*).

Because they used mundane wisdom to sever supramundane goodness, they were also able to sever the roots of goodness that lead toward transcendence. Such examples in the world are truly not few. Formerly, there was the official Xu... [text ends].
"Li Ren-shi was very capable as the Magistrate of Shangyu, yet he was unskilled in responding to questions;
Tianzhu Yu understood profound meanings to the utmost, yet he did not comprehend worldly speech. Such people of superior intelligence are ignorant of worldly affairs.
Furthermore, although an icchantika may possess worldly wisdom, how could they possibly know the supramundane Dharma? (and so forth).
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha. This is the second section within the larger division, clarifying the arising of wholesome states (*kuśala*).

It is divided into three parts: first, a dual clarification of how wholesome states arise through the Middle Way; second, a single clarification of the Middle Way; and third, a single clarification of the arising of wholesome states.

The first part consists of five rounds of question and answer, which may also be further divided into three: the first round clarifies the timing of the arising of wholesome states; the next round clarifies [the absence of]... [text truncated].
Regarding the three sets of three causes for severing the Buddha-nature and the arising of goodness from that nature: the first set of questions is as stated in the text.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, at what time will such a person be able to once again give rise to roots of goodness?"
In the Buddha’s response, there are two parts: first, he clarifies the timing, and second, he clarifies the arising of wholesome roots. Regarding the first part, the Buddha said:
"Good son, this person will regenerate wholesome roots at two times: when they first enter hell and when they emerge from hell."
Those who benefit others emerge first, while those of dull faculties emerge later; logically, there should be those of middling faculties emerging in between.
However, because they give rise to wholesome states in the intermediate state and undergo suffering in hell, they lack the leisure to develop [the path]; therefore, they are not mentioned.

There are three types of wholesome [roots]. Regarding the arising of further wholesome states, the discussion of the severance of wholesome roots concerns only the severance of present wholesome roots, not those of the past or future;
because these present wholesome roots exist, they enable further wholesome states to arise. Furthermore, first the three time periods are proclaimed, and subsequently the three fetters are explained.
Good son, there are three kinds of goodness: past, present, and future.
As for that which is past, its nature is inherently extinguished; although the cause has been completely extinguished, the retribution has not yet matured.

In the explanation, there are two [types]: first, the wholesome of the past; once it has already vanished and is no longer obtainable, it cannot be severed even though its causal conditions have been extinguished, because its fruit has not yet matured.
Second, that which has not yet arisen in the future cannot be severed either.
Third, for this reason, it is not termed the "lower double-knot. This section has two parts: first, clarifying that the past and future cannot be severed;
second, clarifying that present wholesome states can be severed. Regarding the first part:
for this reason, it is not termed the severance of past results.

The two periods of past and future are both incapable of being severed; "the past" refers to the fact that past fetters are not severed, and the word "fruit" refers to the fact that future fetters are not severed.
Next, regarding "severing the three periods," this correctly clarifies the severing of the causes of the three periods, which specifically means severing present wholesome causes.
It is called "severance" because it severs the causes of the three periods of time.
When present wholesome causes are extinguished, there is no longer any future wholesome [result]; the meaning of this non-arising of future wholesomeness is explained as "severance.

Since the present and future are absent, the past also ceases; this meaning is explained as "severance," which is the complete severance of the habitual causes of wholesomeness throughout the three periods of time.
Since [the seeds] are exhausted, they can no longer draw forth the fruits of habituation from the three periods of time.

The second round of question and answer clarifies that the Buddha-nature is uninterrupted. This section is divided into two parts: first, the question as to whether the Buddha-nature belongs to the three periods of time;
second, the question as to whether the Buddha-nature is subject to severance. First, the intent is acknowledged; next, the thesis is established; finally, the conclusion is drawn.
[This is] difficult.

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if severing the causes of the three periods of time is called 'severing the roots of goodness,' then within the established doctrine there are four questions which pertain to the general and specific aspects of the three periods of time."
If those who have severed their roots of goodness possess Buddha-nature, is this Buddha-nature past, present, or future?
Or does it pervade all three periods of time?
The objection merely raises a difficulty regarding the distinction between the three time periods.
If it were past, how could it be called the eternal Buddha-nature? Since the Buddha-nature is also eternal, one should know that it is not of the past.
The initial objection states: "If the Buddha-nature were past, and if it were eternal, it would not be past;
why then do you say it is severed in the past?
If it were future, how could it be called eternal? For what reason does the Buddha say that all sentient beings will certainly and inevitably attain it?"
If it is already definitely attained, why speak of "severing"?

If it pertains to the future, there are two difficulties: first, it would mean that which is not yet future must become so; second, it would mean that which is already in the future must remain there.
Since the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is certainly not something of the future. If it is not something of the future, then everything in the future ought to be already attained.
Is not the threefold awakening (trividha-bodhi) future?
If it were present, how could it be permanent? For what reason, then, is it said that it must necessarily be visible?
There are two difficulties regarding its being present: first, the difficulty of making it non-present because it is permanent; second, the difficulty of making it [present].
If the nature of that which is present can already be seen, how could it not be present?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata also spoke of the second question—whether [defilements] are abandonable or non-abandonable—in two parts:
first, six matters are raised, and subsequently, the formal question is posed.
The Tathāgata has also taught that the Buddha-nature possesses six aspects: first, permanence; second, truth; third, reality; fourth, goodness; fifth, purity; and sixth, visibility.

Regarding these initial six matters as the causal conditions for inquiry, there are two interpretations of their six meanings: the first states they are the "revealing cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*), while the second states...
Because the Dharma-nature (dharmatā) as viewed from the perspective of the primary cause is precisely the Buddha-nature of the ninth stage, their number corresponds.
Regarding the severance of the roots of goodness, among the three questions in the second section on "Correct Inquiry," the first question asks:
if an icchantika possesses Buddha-nature, they should not sever the roots of goodness.
If one who has severed the roots of goodness still possesses the Buddha-nature, then they cannot be called one who has severed the roots of goodness.
This arises from the fourth of the six matters: the Buddha-nature is good.
If there is no Buddha-nature, this is the second question below: if the Buddha-nature were severed, why would it be said that all possess it?
If there is no Buddha-nature, why further say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature?
This arises from the sixth [point] among the six; since all that is visible has already arisen, how can it be severed?
If one says that the Buddha-nature is [inherent], this is the third question, which anticipates the meaning of the answer to pose a challenge.
If one says that the Buddha-nature both exists and is severed, how can the Tathāgata further declare it to be eternal?
If one claims that what existed equally in the past is later severed of its own accord, then it would both exist and be severed; how then could it be called eternal?
This [view] arises from the first of the six [extremes], namely, the view of permanence.
The Buddha replied by dividing [the response] into two parts: first, he proclaimed the four categories of questions; second, he provided their explanations. The Buddha said:
"Good son, for the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has four ways of answering:

first, the categorical answer (ekāṃśavyākaraṇa); second, the analytical answer (vibhajyavyākaraṇa); third, the answer according to the question (paripṛcchāvyākaraṇa); and fourth, the answer by setting aside (sthāpanīyavyākaraṇa)."
In the explanation, first the three gates are interpreted, followed by a further interpretation of "discrimination" (*vikalpa*), and only then is "setting aside" (*sthāpanīya*) explained.
The explanation of the first three answers constitutes three sections.
"Good son, what is a definitive answer? If one asks whether evil karma results in a good fruit or an unwholesome fruit—"
One should give a definitive answer that "it results in an unwholesome fruit," and the same applies to wholesome [results].

If it is asked whether the Tathāgata’s omniscience is not such, one should give a definitive answer that "it is indeed omniscience. If it is asked whether the Buddha-dharma is not pure, one should give a definitive answer that "it is certainly pure.
If it is asked whether the disciples of the Tathāgata do not abide according to the Dharma, one should give a definitive answer that "there are those who abide according to the Dharma."

Abiding [in this] is called a categorical answer (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*). What is a discriminative answer (*vibhajyavyākaraṇa*)? It is as I have taught regarding the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. What are the four? They are suffering, origination, cessation, and the path.

What is the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*)? Because there are eight types of suffering, it is named the truth of suffering. What is the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*)? It is the cause of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

Therefore, it is called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). What is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*)? Because greed, hatred, and delusion are ultimately exhausted, it is called the Truth of Cessation.
What is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*)? The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are called the Truth of the Path. This is known as the detailed answer.
What is meant by answering in accordance with the question? It is as when I have said that all phenomena (*dharma*) are impermanent, and someone further asks:
"For what purpose did the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, teach impermanence? The answer is: "The Tathāgata taught impermanence for the sake of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The same applies to selflessness (*anātman*). Furthermore, as I have said that all phenomena burn others, someone else asks the Tathāgata: [and so forth].
"For what phenomena, World-Honored One, did you say that 'everything is burned'? He replied: "The Tathāgata said 'everything is burned' with reference to greed, hatred, and delusion.

This was a detailed explanation given in response to a specific inquiry; it was used to resolve the question by providing a precise answer. Therefore, he provided a further explanation of the previous answer in response to the subsequent question.

Answering the first question and subsequently answering the latter question, there are four parts. First, from "The ten powers of the Tathāgata" downwards, he enumerates the seven matters of Buddha-nature:
"Good son, the ten powers of the Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the three foundations of mindfulness, and the Śūraṅgama..."
The eighty trillion samādhi-gates such as the *Vajra* and others, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics,
the thirty-five thousand samādhi-gates such as the five wisdom-seals (*pañca-jñāna-mudrā*), the four thousand two hundred samādhi-gates such as the *Vajrasamādhi*,
the samādhis of skillful means, and other such dharmas that are immeasurable and boundless— these are the Buddha-nature of the Buddhas; such is the Buddha.
The nature [of the self] consists of seven matters: first, permanence; second, selfhood; third, bliss; fourth, purity; fifth, truth; sixth, reality; and seventh, goodness.
This is called the analytical answer.
Next, the six matters concerning the final body are raised.
"Good son, the Buddha-nature of a Bodhisattva in his final birth has six aspects: first, permanence; second, purity; third, truth; fourth, reality; fifth, goodness;
and sixth, being rarely seen. This is called the analytical answer."
Whether seven or six, all are the reasons for the answer.
As you previously asked regarding the three lower [stages], this is the direct restatement of the question.
It is as when you previously asked whether those who have severed their roots of goodness possess the Buddha-nature.
There are three questions; here, the first question is cited.
The passage beginning with "There is also the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata" provides the direct answer.
This refers to both the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata and the Buddha-nature of the future body; these two types of Buddha-nature are obstacles to the future.
It is called "non-existent" because there is no definitive attainment; it is called "existent" because there is [attainment]. This is called the "analytical answer.

First, it clarifies that although it exists, it is non-existent; subsequently, it clarifies that although it is non-existent, it exists. This constitutes the comprehensive answer to the preceding three questions.
The Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature is not of the past; this is the second section, a subsequent response to the previous questions concerning the three periods of time.

The preceding question held that if the Buddha-nature is eternal, it would not belong to the three periods of time. Now, in response, [the text] first distinguishes the differences in the Buddha-nature according to the nine, eight, and five stages of the Tathāgata’s dwelling, and so forth;
yet even those who have severed their roots of goodness all possess these seven or six types [of Buddha-nature].

Because the nature will be attained in the future, one cannot say it is not a dharma of the three periods of time. Its essential characteristic is that it is not subsumed under the three periods of time, yet it is attained in the future;
thus it is again called "future. The text consists of five parts: first, the *tathāgatagarbha* and the Buddha-nature of the subsequent body;
second, the Buddha-nature of the ninth stage (*navama-bhūmi*); third, the Buddha-nature from the eighth stage to the sixth stage; fourth, the [Buddha-nature] from the fifth stage to...

Regarding the first dwelling in the Buddha-nature, there are five points concerning the questions asked therein; the first of these has four parts. First: the nature of the Tathāgata is not of the three periods of time.
The Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata is neither past, nor present, nor future.
The nature of the final body exists across the three periods of time;
because the Buddha-nature of the final body can be partially seen in the present and the future, it is designated as "present," and because it is not yet fully seen,
it is designated as "future."
In the present one sees little, whereas in the future one sees completely.
The threefold clarity of the Tathāgata’s cause is such that there is right and wrong regarding the fruits of the three periods of time.
Even when the Tathāgata had not yet attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it was because of the Buddha-nature as a cause.
The fruits of the past, present, and future are not like that; some belong to the three periods of time, while others do not.
If the five aggregates are wholesome, they still belong to the three periods of time, but the fruit of Bodhi does not belong to the three periods of time.
The fourth point clarifies that the final body is visible throughout the three periods of time.
Because the Buddha-nature of the Bodhisattva in his final body is the cause, it likewise exists in the past, present, and future; its fruit is also thus.
This is called the analytical answer.
The Ninth Abode, Part Two: The Ninth Abode.
The Buddha-nature of a Bodhisattva in the Ninth Abode has six aspects: first, permanence; second, goodness; third, truth; fourth, reality; fifth, purity; and sixth, visibility.
Because it is the cause of Buddha-nature, it likewise pertains to the past, present, and future results. This is called "partial" (or "segmented").
A separate response:
the six matters merely state that they are "visible," which differs from what preceded.
In the third section of the eighth dwelling, it clarifies the progression from the eighth dwelling down to the sixth dwelling.
From the eighth stage of the Bodhisattva down to the sixth stage, the Buddha-nature possesses five attributes: first, it is true; second, it is real; third, it is pure; fourth, it is good;
and fifth, it is visible. Because these are the causes of the Buddha-nature, its fruits in the past, present, and future are likewise so.
This is called the analytical answer.
There are five matters for which it does not receive the name "constant.
The fifth dwelling explains the five dwellings down to the first dwelling.
Regarding the Buddha-nature of Bodhisattvas in the five dwellings, from the lowest up to the first dwelling, there are five matters: first, true; second, real; third, pure; fourth, [capable of...].
One perceives the five wholesome and unwholesome states.
There are only five matters referred to as wholesome and unwholesome; the distinction between the preceding and succeeding bodies constitutes six matters.

Regarding those who speak of "limited vision" (*parīttadṛś*), since their stage is already high, they are able to attain limited vision and perceive the nature [of reality] according to their capacity; thus they are called those of limited vision. From the ninth ground down to the first...
Since the stage of the Ground (bhūmi) is still low, its nature has not yet been seen; it ought to be seen, and therefore it is said that it "can be seen.

Regarding the fifth ground up to the first ground, the terms "wholesome" (*kuśala*) and "unwholesome" (*akuśala*) are used: "wholesome" carries the sense of being cultivated or uncultivated. That which is attained through cultivation is wholesome, while that which is not so cultivated is unwholesome.
It is further stated that both should possess "real" and "unreal" aspects. The explanation is that "reality" is the essence of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
That which does not exist yet exists is precisely the ultimate reality; it is for the sake of this reality that there is the distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome.
According to the old interpretation of the sixth stage, when prajñā manifests, one may at times lose mindfulness; losing mindfulness constitutes the unwholesome, while not losing it is the wholesome.
Regarding the question of the final body, it is the same as the ninth stage in possessing six matters; among these six matters, they are identical in possessing constancy.
Regarding the fact that these five matters from the eighth stage through the first stage are identical, why is it that the single matter of impermanence is not [present]?
Some explain this by saying that because the subsequent bodies are all high [in rank], while the nine stages are low, they possess permanence for a long time;

however, as this does not yet resolve the difficulty, one must further align the five stages through the first stage so that they are equally possessed of the single matter of impermanence, when viewed from the perspective of the subsequent body relative to the Buddha.

Furthermore, one should also [consider] impermanence. Someone might answer: "The Buddha spoke according to his own intention; it cannot be forcibly analyzed or challenged. This difficulty has not yet been resolved. Question:
Regarding the subsequent body (*paścātkāya*), why is it said to be permanent, pure, and selfless? Answer:

Because a Bodhisattva always possesses the two types of wisdom (*prajñā*) to transform sentient beings, it is called "permanent. Because both the object and the cognition are simultaneously luminous, it is called "pure. This is truly the real as opposed to the false.

This is because it relies on the void and non-existence, and perceives the aspect of evil as a portion of the good; thus, it lacks even a small measure of the eight masteries, and for this reason there is no self.

Since there is no self, there is no retribution body (*sambhogakāya*), and for this reason there is no bliss. Now, I maintain that this interpretation is not perfect; it shall be explained separately later.
These five kinds and six kinds [of Buddha-nature]—the latter five fetters (saṃyojana)—respond to the preceding question.

Good son, because these five kinds, six kinds, and seven kinds of Buddha-nature will certainly be attained by those who have severed their roots of goodness, it can be said that they "possess" them; this is called an analytical answer.
If there is one who says that the "setting aside" (sthāpanīya) answer is explained first and then the "direct" (viniścaya) answer is explained,

or if there is one who says that for those who have severed their roots of goodness, to state definitively that they possess Buddha-nature or definitively that they do not possess Buddha-nature is called the "setting aside" answer.
The following clarifies the question and answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said, "World-Honored One, I have heard that it is called 'setting aside' (sthāpanīya) when there is no answer;
for what reason and by what causes does the Tathāgata now provide an answer yet call it 'setting aside'?"
"Good son, I do not say that setting aside [a question] constitutes an answer; rather, I speak of the 'setting-aside answer' (*sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa*).
Good son, there are two kinds of such setting-aside answers: first, cessation (*pratiṣedha*), and second, non-attachment (*anabhiniveśa*). For this reason, it is called the 'setting-aside answer.'"
There are two types of *sthāpanīya* (setting aside): setting aside and not answering is *sthāpanīya*, and answering by means of a counter-question is also *sthāpanīya*.
[The author] privately explains that using "setting aside" as the answer is called *sthāpanīya-uttara*.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: The following constitutes the third section, clarifying how goodness arises from the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

This consists of three rounds of question and answer: first, clarifying the nature of cause and effect; second, correctly clarifying how the causal nature gives rise to goodness; and third, resolving doubts.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, what is meant by that which is a cause belonging to the past,
present, and future, yet its fruit belongs to the past, present, and future, while it is not itself [the fruit] of the past,
present, or future?”

The meaning of the first question is as follows: If the nature of the Tathāgata’s fruition is not subsumed within the three periods of time, yet the cause and effect within the causal stage of Buddha-nature are subsumed within the three periods of time, how can it be called Buddha-nature?

The Buddha’s response is twofold: first, the direct answer; second, the conclusion regarding the nature [of the latent dispositions]. Regarding the first, there are three parts: (1) the differentiation of cause and effect;
(2) the existence of nature, wherein some exist throughout the three periods of time while others do not; and (3) the exposition of the essential substance of the causal nature.
Third, the citation of scriptural proof, which itself has two parts: first, the presentation of the topical outline of cause and effect; second, the detailed explanation thereof.
The Buddha said: "Good son, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are of two kinds: first, cause; second, fruit.

Regarding the 'five aggregates having both fruit and cause' mentioned in the initial section: within the five aggregates, delusion and karma constitute the cause, while the wholesome aggregates are the fruit.
As for the cause, the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) pertain to the three periods of time; however, Great Bodhi does not."
The preceding passage concerning the three periods of time stated: "When the Tathāgata had not yet attained bodhi, the nature of the cause was itself the nature of the past and future results.
Otherwise, there would be this fault; it is not the case that what has not yet occurred is neither past nor future. Now, reaching this point, the matter is finally explained.
These five aggregates as causes belong to the past, present, and future;
these five aggregates as effects also belong to the past, present, and future, yet they are also neither past, present, nor future.
Next, to explain the cause: all ignorance, afflictions, fetters, karma, and the evil five aggregates are the cause of the Buddha-nature.

That which arises from ignorance, afflictions, and so forth as the wholesome five aggregates is the nature of the fruit. The five aggregates of unwholesome dharmas are exclusively of the nature of the cause;
the wholesome five aggregates pertain to both cause and fruit—the cause being the three periods of time, and the fruit being [the state beyond].

Regarding the passage in the preceding text stating that "the nature of the fruition of fruition is both of the three periods of time and not of the three periods of time," some interpret it as follows:

the nature of fruition of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) belongs to the three periods of time, whereas the nature of fruition of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) does not belong to the three periods of time.

"Good son, all ignorance, afflictions, and fetters are entirely the Buddha-nature. Why is this? Because the Buddha-nature... [The second section, "Revealing the Nature of Cause and Effect," is divided into two parts:
first, revealing the nature of the cause; second, revealing the nature of the effect. Regarding the first passage:
"Good son, all ignorance, afflictions, and fetters are entirely the Buddha-nature. Why is this? Because the Buddha-nature..."
Because of this reason:
to clarify that the nature of the Middle Way is identical to all phenomena, if one considers them in terms of afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called "causes.

From "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*) downwards, the second section presents the essence of the fruit; this further has two parts, the first of which clarifies that the nature of the fruit of the wholesome aggregates (*kuśalaskandha*) is universal.
The causes are the four fruits, and the fruits are the ten stages; these fruits are the three periods of time.
From ignorance, formative action, and all afflictions, one attains the wholesome five aggregates—this is called Buddha-nature.
Next, it is explained that the fruit of the aggregates exists solely as a fruit and is not comprised within the three periods of time.
This extends from the five wholesome aggregates up until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, in the third section of my citation from the sūtra, there are two parts: first, the proof that causes possess dharmas, followed by an analogy and its application.
Thus, in the sūtra, I first speak of the buddha-nature of sentient beings.
It is like milk mixed with blood:
"blood" refers to all afflictions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), while "milk" refers to the wholesome five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Therefore, I say that the two lower fruits of realization also possess both the teaching and the analogy.
Therefore, I say that one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from the various afflictions and the five aggregates of merit,
just as the bodies of sentient beings are all brought to completion through semen and blood.
The Buddha-nature is also like this: for a *srotāpanna* and a *sakṛdāgāmin*, who have severed a small portion of afflictions, the Buddha-nature is like milk;
for an *anāgāmin*, the Buddha-nature is like curd; for an *arhat*, it is like fresh butter;
from a *pratyekabuddha* up to a bodhisattva of the tenth stage, it is like clarified butter; and the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature is like the finest cream (*mṛdvīkā*).
Within the fruit itself are fully present both the fruit that existed within the cause and the fruit of bodhi.
Present afflictions constitute the second category of fetters; by nature they are delusions that obscure the luminous Middle Way, yet they are also covered by delusion.
Furthermore, this serves as a metaphor for the synthesis of the three dharmas.
Good son, because present afflictions act as obstacles, they cause sentient beings to be unable to behold the Tathāgata.
On Mount Gandhamādana there is a grass of forbearance that not all oxen are able to eat.
The Buddha-nature is also like this; this is called the analytical answer. Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"Regarding the five kinds and six kinds [of Buddha-nature]... This marks the second section, which correctly clarifies how the causal nature gives rise to goodness.
First, the question is posed; next, the answer follows. Within the question, the previously mentioned seven, six, and five types of Buddha-nature are first restated.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if the five kinds, six kinds, and seven kinds of buddha-nature exist only in the future,
why do you say that those who have severed their roots of goodness possess buddha-nature?"
Next, regarding the meaning within the formal inquiry: since the intention lies in the future, how can it be said that [the past] exists and is able to produce wholesome states?
The Buddha’s answer consists of three parts: (1) two pairs of analogies, (2) two pairs of applications, and (3) two pairs of conclusions. Within the first part, there are again two sections:
first, citing past karma as the reason for currently receiving pleasant retribution.
The Buddha said, "Good son, just as all sentient beings possess past karmic causes,
and because of these karmas they receive retributive fruits in the present;
so too, regarding future karma, because it has not yet arisen, it will ultimately not produce fruit."
There is future karma which, because it has not yet arisen, will ultimately not produce a fruit.
There are present afflictions; [the text] combines the latter two pairs and then the first phrase of the second pair with the preceding past karma and its present pleasant fruit.
There are present afflictions;
that is to say, by means of these present afflictions, one is able to sever the roots of goodness. This must necessarily be due to the past;
what is here called "present affliction" was originally past and has now come into the present.
Next, if there were no afflictions, this would correspond to the second analogy: future karma that has not yet arisen will never produce fruit.
If there were no afflictions, all sentient beings should clearly and directly perceive their Buddha-nature.
Because one unites with the causes and conditions of the future Buddha-nature, one is able to produce roots of goodness.
Therefore, regarding the three pairs of fetters of those who have severed their roots of goodness, it is as stated in the text.
Thus, by means of the causes and conditions of afflictions in the present life, those who have severed their roots of goodness are able to sever them for the future.
"By reason of the power and conditions of the Buddha-nature, one gives rise to roots of goodness once again.
Kāśyapa asks: "How will this be in the future? This concludes the third section, which clarifies a doubt. The doubt is as follows: "In the future, [the Buddha-nature] does not yet exist;
how then can roots of goodness arise?"
Kāśyapa asked, "World-Honored One, how can wholesome roots be produced in the future?
The Buddha replied in two parts: first by means of a simile, and then by application.
"Good son, it is just as a lamp or the sun: although they have not yet arisen, they are nonetheless able to dispel darkness; so too will that which arises in the future."
Regarding the birth of sentient beings:

the first passage cites the analogies of a lamp and the sun. Just as one who stubbornly clings to [the idea that] a lamp or the sun has not yet appeared cannot dispel the darkness, so too, when the lamp or the sun is merely a provisional name based on causes and conditions and has not yet arisen, it can nonetheless dispel the darkness.
Next, the passage beginning "The Buddha-nature is likewise" correlates [the teaching] with the fact that all sentient beings possess future goodness capable of generating Buddha-nature;
that future Buddha-nature is also like this, and this is called the "analytical answer."

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: "If it is said that the second section, which explains the Middle Way in isolation from the five aggregates below, is for the purpose of generating wholesome states in sentient beings—if there were no principle of the Middle Way, how could wholesome states be generated?

Because there is the Buddha-nature as a support and foundation, the text is divided into three parts: first, the Middle Way that is neither internal nor external; second, the Middle Way that is neither existent nor non-existent."

Third, regarding the extensive clarification of the Middle Way through all phenomena, it may be said that the first two [sections] correctly clarify the essence of the Middle Way, while the latter one extensively clarifies its function.
In the initial passage, there are two rounds of question and answer; the first round is as the text states.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, if it is said that the five aggregates are the Buddha-nature,
why do you say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither internal nor external?”
The Buddha said, "Good son, for what reason have you lost your composure in this way? Did I not previously state that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is the Middle Way?
In the subsequent turn, Kāśyapa himself explained that it was not his own intention, but rather he acted solely for the benefit of sentient beings.
Kāśyapa said, "World-Honored One, I truly did not lose my composure; it was simply because sentient beings cannot understand this Middle Way that I posed this question.
The Buddha answered in six successive stages:
first, he clarified the Middle Way by way of understanding and delusion; second, he clarified the Middle Way by way of internal and external paths.

Third, clarifying through the internal and external aspects of the fruit; fourth, clarifying through the internal and external causes and conditions; fifth, clarifying through the internal and external practices;
sixth, clarifying through the internal and external aspects of the body. Within these six, there are two parts:

the first briefly clarifies the general meaning by way of delusion and awakening, while the latter five extensively elaborate upon this. Regarding the first brief clarification, there are three further points.
This is the initial heading for the two explanations and three conclusions regarding the Middle Way.
"Good son, sentient beings do not understand that this very [state] is the Middle Way; at times they understand it, and at times they do not."
"Good son, for the sake of sentient beings, I provide this second explanation.
Good son, because I wish for sentient beings to attain understanding and liberation, I say that the Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external.
Why is this? Because ordinary sentient beings may say that the Buddha-nature dwells within the five aggregates, like fruit inside a vessel."
To say that it exists apart from the aggregates, like empty space, is why the Tathāgata speaks of the Middle Way:
the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither the six internal sense bases nor the six external sense bases; because it is the union of the internal and external, it is called the Middle Way.

This generally clarifies that [the self] is neither internal nor external: it is not internal because it is not the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), and it is not external because it is not the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
However, the latter five [points] are specifically presented to refute two types of attachment.
Therefore, the section beginning with "Thus the Tathāgata... constitutes the third conclusion.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has proclaimed that buddha-nature is precisely the Middle Way; because it is neither internal nor external, it is called the Middle Way.
This is known as the "analytical answer.
I [the author] say: this single sutra consists largely of five chapters, all of which refer to *nirvāṇa*; *nirvāṇa* is simply the Buddha.
The nature is three yet one, which is the nature of the True Cause; the nature is one yet three, which is the nature of the Three Virtues.
Now, when it is explained that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, these two meanings are fully present. Master Zhizhe (Zhang’an) calls this the Middle Way.
How could there be a Buddha-nature without being the center between the ultimate and the conventional? Therefore, Buddha-nature is the Middle Way, and Buddha-nature is all-encompassing.
Because it is pervasive, many passages throughout the preceding and following context discuss this pervasiveness; therefore, it is stated here that it is "neither internal nor external.
This "double negation" does not merely negate both sides, for there must also be a double affirmation; thus, subsequent passages state that it is "both internal and external.
If there were no double affirmation, how could one speak of pervasiveness? Therefore, the text rebukes [the opponent], saying: "Ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) sometimes say..."
The Buddha-nature within the five aggregates is like fruit within a vessel or like space;

when worldly people say that Buddha-nature exists only in sentient beings, it is merely like the fruit in a vessel and has not yet been reckoned as being like space—how then could they understand that it is neither internal nor external?

Furthermore, the sutra text itself explains that because the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are joined, this is called the Middle Way. As for the sense faculties and their objects...
If they are conjoined, are they not of one essence? Are they not mutually identical? Is their nature not all-pervasive? Are they not like the fruits of a vessel? Now I ask:
are these walls and partitions the sense organs, or are they the sense objects, or are they the conjunction of both, or are they neither?
If they are neither, they are also not the five aggregates; why then do you speak only of walls and partitions? Alas for the people of this world! How bitter is their discourse!

I request that you carefully employ these six gates to encompass this entire treatise, and that you use this treatise to unify the entirety of Śākyamuni’s teachings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
In principle, there is no duality; in fact, there is not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy. Since the loss [of the truth] would not be slight, I have been so earnest.
Furthermore, in the second section below, which extensively elucidates the Middle Way, there are five successive expositions, all of which clarify that [reality] is neither internal nor external;
among these, the first two successive expositions first set forth the two types of clinging.
Furthermore, good son, what is meant by "neither internal nor external"? Good son, some say that Buddha-nature is identical to the paths of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, throughout immeasurable kalpas, remain among the non-Buddhists to sever all afflictions (*kleśa*), subdue their minds, and transform sentient beings; only thereafter do they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is such that the Buddha-nature is itself the non-Buddhist path, or it is said that the Buddha-nature is itself the Buddhist path.

Why is this? Although a bodhisattva may practice the non-Buddhist paths for immeasurable kalpas, if they depart from the Buddhist path, they cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is itself the Buddhist path.
For this reason, the Tathāgata negates these two extremes by declaring that the Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external, yet it is also called both internal and external;
this is termed the Middle Way and is known as the analytical answer.
Next, the fourth section further correctly concludes the Middle Way.
Furthermore, son of good family, some say that the Buddha-nature is the Tathāgata’s vajra-body, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
why? Because it is not false or deceptive. Others say that the Buddha-nature is the ten powers.
The four fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the three foundations of mindfulness, the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, and all other samādhis—why is this?
Because it is due to these samādhis that the vajra-body with its thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics is produced.
Therefore, the Tathāgata refutes these two extremes by declaring that buddha-nature is neither internal nor external, yet it is also called both internal and external.
This is called the Middle Way.
Furthermore, son of good family, some may say that buddha-nature is precisely internal right reflection. Why?
Because apart from right reflection, one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore...
The Buddha-nature is precisely internal right reflection; some say that the Buddha-nature is the hearing of the Dharma from others. Why is this?
Because by hearing the Dharma from others, one is able to engage in internal right reflection; if one does not hear the Dharma, there is no such reflection.
Therefore, the Buddha-nature is precisely the hearing of the Dharma from others. For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks to block these two extremes.
To say that the Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external, yet is called both internal and external—this is termed the Middle Way.

Furthermore, son of good family, there are those who further say that the Buddha-nature is external, meaning that it is through the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving) that one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; for this reason, they say that the *dāna-pāramitā* [is the Buddha-nature].
Honey is itself the Buddha-nature; some say that the Buddha-nature is internal, meaning the five *pāramitās*. Why?

Because apart from these five things, one should know that there is no Buddha-nature, as they are its cause and fruit. Therefore, it is said that the five *pāramitās* are themselves the Buddha-nature.
For this reason, the Tathāgata refutes these two extremes and says that the Buddha-nature is neither internal nor [external].
To be neither external nor internal, yet both external and internal—this is called the Middle Way.
Furthermore, good son, some may say that the Buddha-nature is within, like a jewel on the forehead of a strongman. Why?
Because it is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity, just like that jewel; therefore, it is said that the Buddha-nature is within.
Some may say that the Buddha-nature is external, like a treasure trove belonging to a poor man; why? Because it is seen through skillful means (*upāya*).
They claim that the Buddha-nature is likewise outside sentient beings, yet is perceived through skillful means.

Therefore, the Tathāgata refutes these two extremes by declaring that the Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external, yet both internal and external; this is called the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
"Good son, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither existent nor non-existent. This second section below has two parts: first, clarifying the central thesis;

second, extensively refuting attachments. The first part, clarifying the central thesis, further has three sections: first, clarifying that it is neither existent nor non-existent; second, clarifying that it is both existent and non-existent;
third, concluding that it is neither existent nor non-existent. The first of these [three] also has three parts: first, stating the two negations.
Good son, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither existent nor non-existent.
Next, I shall explain these two negations.
Why is this? Although the Buddha-nature exists, it is not like empty space. Why? Because although the empty space of the world...
Because it cannot be perceived even through immeasurable skillful means, the Buddha-nature can nevertheless be seen;
therefore, although it exists, it is not like empty space. Although the Buddha-nature does not exist, it is not the same as a rabbit's horn. Why?

Because while a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horn cannot be produced even by immeasurable skillful means, the Buddha-nature can be produced. Therefore, although it does not exist [in that sense], it is not the same [as those things].
The horns of a rabbit;
three fetters and two negations.
Therefore, the Buddha-nature is neither existent nor non-existent.
Next, the passage concerning "both existent and non-existent" consists of three parts: the proclamation, the explanation, and the conclusion. The proclamation and explanation are as in the text.
Regarding "both existent and non-existent":
why is it called "existent"? Because all things exist; these sentient beings neither cease nor perish, being like the flame of a lamp.
Up until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is therefore called "existence. Why is it called "non-existence"?
Because for all sentient beings at present, none possess the eternal, blissful, self, and pure qualities of all Buddha-dharmas; therefore, it is called "non-existence."
There is neither existence nor non-existence regarding the lower fetters;
because existence and non-existence are unified, this is precisely the Middle Way.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that for the three lower fetters, both [existence and non-existence] are negated, as stated in the text.
For this reason, the Buddha taught that the buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither existent nor non-existent.
Good son, if someone asks about the two lower [stages], there is an extensive refutation of the adherence to deviation from the Middle Way, which relies largely upon parables.

This section consists of three parts: first, the refutation by means of the parable of the seed; second, the refutation by means of the parable of milk and curd; and third, the refutation by means of the parable of salt and salinity.
In the initial section on the seed, three analogies are combined and concluded:
"Good son, if someone were to ask whether the fruit exists within this seed or does not exist, you should answer definitively that it both exists and does not exist. Why?
Because apart from the seed, the fruit cannot be produced; therefore, it is said that the fruit exists within the seed."
Because the sprout has not yet emerged, it is called "non-existent"; for this reason, it is both existent and non-existent. Why is this so?
Because while the time periods differ, their essence is one.
[My] private opinion is that the text is divided into two parts: first the demonstration, followed by the explanation.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this. If one says that within sentient beings there exists a separate Buddha-nature, this meaning is not so.
In the initial exposition, it was stated that the claim that sentient beings possess a separate Buddha-nature is incorrect.
Why is this? Sentient beings are the Buddha-nature, and the Buddha-nature is sentient beings; it is only because of differences in time that there is purity or impurity.
The subsequent explanation states: "Sentient beings are the nature, and the nature is sentient beings. Since these are neither internal nor external, they are yet both internal and external.
The non-duality of the internal and external may also be stated as "form is itself Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is itself form"; thus, the second [point] follows from the preceding.

Furthermore, taking the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) as external power and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) and so forth as internal: if form and the like lack the marks and signs, then the latter three [categories] would also be absent.
The subsequent instances should be understood by analogy with this.
Good son, if someone were to ask, "Is it the seed that produces the fruit, or is it the fruit that produces the seed?
one should not definitively answer that it both produces and does not produce.
Next, in the analogy of milk and curd, there are two parts: first, the direct illustration using milk; second, further illustrating milk as the producer of consciousness.
First, within the three stages of establishing the correct Middle Way and subsequently refuting biased attachments, there are three sections concerning the nature of reality.
Regarding the first, the establishment of the correct Middle Way, there is first a question and then an answer:
"World-Honored One, as people in the world say that there is curd within milk, what is the meaning of this?"
In the response, there are three parts; first is the fixed determination:
"Good son, if one says that there is curd within milk, this is called attachment; if one says there is no curd, this is called falsehood."
Third, the explanation: regarding the two fetters, they are conventionally designated as both existent and non-existent;
apart from these two matters, one should definitively state that they are both existent and non-existent.
Third, the explanation.
Why is it called "existence"? From milk, curd is produced; the cause is the milk and the effect is the curd—this is what is meant by "existence. Why is it called "non-existence"?
Because color and flavor differ, and their applications are distinct: milk is consumed for feverish illnesses, while curd is consumed for ailments caused by cold-natured humors;
milk produces cold-natured illnesses, whereas curd produces feverish illnesses.
Good son, the following two sections refute biased attachments; they should also both refute existence and non-existence. Here, we only refute existence, which is divided into three parts:

first, raising the objection that cause and effect are simultaneous and mutually inclusive; second, clarifying that the example of "the effect existing within the cause" is equally subject to refutation;
and third, clarifying that the example of "the cause existing within the effect" is equally subject to refutation.
Good son, if one says that the nature of curd exists within milk, then milk is itself curd and curd is itself milk;
since their nature is one, for what reason does milk appear first and curd not appear first?
If there is a cause and condition, why do all people in the world not speak of it? If there is no cause and condition, why does curd not appear first? If curd [does not appear first]...

First, [one asks] who created the sequence of milk, curd, whey, fresh butter, clarified butter, and the finest essence (sarpis). Therefore, one knows that curd did not previously exist but now exists;
if it did not previously exist but now exists, it is an impermanent phenomenon.
First, it is clarified that since milk and curd are simultaneous, then butter, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and *maṇḍa* should also emerge all at once;
because they are simultaneous, one must further inquire: if they do not emerge simultaneously, who establishes their sequence?
Good son, if there is a second objection regarding the presence of the effect within the cause—that which is inferior—there are two parts:
first, establishing a parallel example, and second, demonstrating that the case at hand is not analogous. Regarding the initial establishment of the parallel:
good son, if someone were to say, "Milk possesses the nature of curd and is thus able to produce curd, whereas water lacks the nature of curd [and therefore cannot]."
The claim that curd does not arise [from milk] is incorrect. Why? Because water and grass also possess the nature of producing milk and curd. For what reason?
Because it is from water and grass that milk and curd emerge. To say that the nature of curd definitely exists within milk while it does not exist in water and grass is called a falsehood.
"Milk is the cause of curd and can produce it; likewise, water and grass, as causes of milk, should also produce milk" (and so forth).
Next, [the text asks] "For what reason?"—this is not an analogous case.
For what reason? Because the mind is not equal [to them], it is therefore called false.
Good son, if one says that there is a cause within the third fruit contained in milk, this is an analogy; yet it is difficult to say that the analogy holds.

If milk is the cause of curd and curd is the fruit of milk, and if milk is the cause of curd such that the fruit exists within the cause, then since curd is the fruit of milk, the fruit should possess its own cause.
Within this, there are two points: first, the formal refutation.
Good son, if one says that curd definitely exists within milk, then milk-nature should also definitely exist within curd.
For what reason, then, does curd emerge from milk, while milk does not emerge [from curd]?
Next, regarding the refutation within the middle [position], first one establishes that it did not exist originally.
If there were no causes and conditions, one should know that this curd would have been non-existent originally and only come into being now.
Next, one establishes that it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Therefore, the wise should say that within milk there is neither the nature of curd nor the absence of the nature of curd.
Good son, this concludes the third section on the principle of nature; it further consists of two parts: first, the conclusion that transcends partiality.
"Good son, for this reason, the Tathāgata has spoken these words in this sutra:
'To say that all sentient beings definitely possess the Buddha-nature is called attachment; to say that there is no Buddha-nature is called falsehood.'"
Finally, he concludes with the Middle Way.
The wise should say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings both exists and does not exist.

Next, "Good son, through the combination of four things... and below, two analogies are raised to illustrate the production of consciousness; these serve as metaphors for the illustration. Furthermore—
Second, first the primary illustration of the arising of consciousness:
"Good son, through the conjunction of four factors, eye-consciousness arises. What are these four? They are the eye, form, light, and attention.
The nature of eye-consciousness is not the eye, nor form, nor light, nor attention; yet, from their conjunction, it is produced. As it is said:
This visual consciousness was originally non-existent and now exists; having existed, it returns to non-existence. Therefore, one should know that it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Next, regarding the nature of curd within milk, the text again employs the analogy of milk and curd in two parts: first, the formal application of the analogy; second, the refutation of attachment.
The nature of curd within milk is likewise so.
Regarding the refutation of this attachment, first the attachment is restated, and then it is formally refuted:
If someone were to say that because water lacks the nature of curd it does not produce curd, therefore milk must certainly possess the nature of curd.

Regarding the refutation [of the opponent's position], there are first two topical headings (*dvāra*), followed by the explanation of those headings. First, the heading concerning distinct causes and distinct effects:
this interpretation is not tenable. Why? Because all phenomena have distinct causes and distinct effects.
Next, "it is not that all effects arise from a single cause, nor that all effects arise from a single cause"— this is the second section of the gateway. Furthermore,
it is neither the case that all effects arise from a single cause, nor that all effects arise from a single cause.
Regarding these four matters, the following two explanations clarify the two headings: first the explanation, then the heading.
Noble son, it cannot be further stated that visual consciousness arises from these four matters; rather, from these four matters, auditory consciousness should arise.
Noble son, apart from skillful means, one cannot obtain curd from milk, nor can one obtain clarified butter from curd.

In this way, O son of good family, one must rely on skillful means; for a wise person cannot see that butter can be obtained from milk apart from skillful means, nor should it be thought that cream can likewise be obtained apart from skillful means.
However, as for visual consciousness, once it has arisen, it cannot produce auditory, olfactory, or other types of consciousness;
how could a single cause produce all effects? It is the same with milk being able to produce curd: it must depend on various conditions.
That which arises from various conditions is precisely the gate of impermanence.
Next, for this reason, I shall now provide a retrospective explanation of the preceding chapter on "different causes and different effects.
Good son, it is for this reason that I have said in this sutra: "Because they arise from causes, phenomena exist; because they cease due to causes, phenomena do not exist."

Because it arises from causes, one calculates that there is existence; because it ceases due to causes, one calculates that there is non-existence. If there were no cessation, then cause and effect would be distinct.
Good son, as with salt—this is the third instance where salt is raised to illustrate the refutation of salinity. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the actual presentation of the analogy;
second, the further refutation of attachment.
