Good son, it is like the nature of salt, which is salty and can cause that which is not salty to become salty.

If things that are not salty already possessed a salty nature from the beginning, why would people seek salt? If they did not possess it from the beginning, you should know that what was previously non-existent now exists;
it has acquired its saltiness through other conditions.
Refuting the attachment [to the existence of salt] in two parts: first restating the attachment, then refuting it. In the initial restatement, there are generally two attachments restated:
first, the attachment that there is salinity within salt.
If one says that all non-salty things possess the nature of salinity but it is not perceived because it is subtle, then by virtue of this subtle nature...
Salt can cause something to become salty; if it lacked intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from the outset, even if salt were present, it could not make it salty.
Second, this restates the position that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) exist within the seed:
for example, the seed itself possesses the four great elements which, depending upon external great elements, undergo growth as sprouts, stalks, branches, and leaves.

Next, the nature of salt is also like this; the following section correctly refutes two attachments. This is further divided into two parts: first, refuting the notion that there is salt within what is not salty;
second, refuting the four great elements. Within the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the negation.
The claim that "the nature of salt is likewise" is incorrect.
Next, regarding the section beginning with "For what reason," there is a formal refutation in two parts: first, a reductio ad absurdum, and second, an analogy to other substances.
For what reason? If non-salty things possessed a pre-existing salty nature, then salt itself should also possess a subtle non-salty nature.
If this salt possessed these two natures, for what reason could it not be used alone apart from non-salty things?
Therefore, one knows that salt originally has no dual nature.
The intent of this challenge is that if salt were salty only when placed among non-salty things, one should know that it possesses no intrinsic nature at all.
If it was not salty before but is now salty, is this not because it was originally absent?

Furthermore, if one places a single sheng of salt into a large volume of water, it loses its original salinity, and the water likewise lacks the nature of salinity. Since both locations are devoid of it, how can there be a nature of salinity?
Next, this example applies to all cases in the same way.
Just as salt [renders] all non-salty things [salty], it is likewise here.

If one says that the four external elements are refuted by the two subsequent refutations of the four elements, then the latter attachment is also refuted in two stages, beginning with the first refutation.
Regarding the subsequent examples (and so forth):
if one were to say that the power of the external four great elements can increase the internal four great elements, this meaning is not correct. Why?
Because they are explained in sequential order; it does not proceed from expedient means.

Just as curds, fresh butter, and so forth are obtained from milk, yet all phenomena do not exist [independently] in that way, and cannot be obtained through improper means, so it is with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
If one speaks of the external four great elements increasing the internal four great elements, one does not see the internal four great elements increasing the external four great elements;
it is like the *śirīṣa* fruit, which has no form or substance beforehand, yet is seen when the constellation Puṣya appears.
Then there will grow fruits five inches long, which do not increase by depending on the external four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
As I have taught in the third section of the twelve-part [treatise], which extensively clarifies the Middle Way among all phenomena, it is also said that the function of clarity is threefold:
first, the function of arising the teaching based on principle; second, the function of clarifying the cultivation of causes and the pursuit of results; and third, the function of practice.
Regarding the function of dispelling delusions through the initial teaching, there are two parts: first, the heading, and second, the explanation.

"Good son, as I have taught in the twelve divisions of the sūtras, some are spoken according to my own intention, some are spoken according to the intentions of others, and some are spoken according to the intentions of both myself and others."

In the explanation, there are again two parts: first, a general clarification of the three types of speech; second, a specific clarification of the speech of one's own intention. The first part has two sections:

first, clarifying the three types of speech according to the former teachings; second, clarifying the three types of speech according to the present teaching. Regarding the former teachings, the detailed explanation of the three types of speech is divided into three sections.
What is meant by "teaching according to one's own intention"? For example, when five hundred bhikṣus asked Śāriputra:
"Venerable One, the Buddha spoke of the cause of the body; what is that? Śāriputra replied:
"Venerable ones, you yourselves have each attained right liberation and should know this for yourselves. For what reason do you ask such a question? A bhikṣu said: "Venerable One..."
"When I had not yet attained right liberation, I thought that ignorance (*avidyā*) was the cause of the body; while contemplating in this way, I attained the fruit of Arhatship.

Furthermore, some say: "Venerable Sir, when I had not yet attained right liberation, I thought that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance were the causes of the body; while contemplating in this way, I attained the fruit of Arhatship. Or again, it is said:
Volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, food, and the five desires are the causes of the body.
At that time, the five hundred bhikṣus each spoke of their own understanding;

having done so, they went together to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and after completing their salutations, sat down to one side, each [reporting] what they themselves had [understood] as above.
Having understood the meaning, they explained it to the Buddha. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, among these people, who speaks correctly and who speaks incorrectly?
The Buddha told Śāriputra, “Excellent, excellent! Not a single one of these bhikṣus speaks anything other than correctly.
Śāriputra said, “World-Honored One, what is the Buddha’s intention? The Buddha said, “Śāriputra, for my sake...”
The sūtras that state, "Sentient beings of the desire realm say that their parents are the cause of their bodies," and so forth, are called "teachings according to one's own inclination.

Regarding the first type, "according to one's own [inclination]": for example, when various bhikṣus each spoke of the cause of the body, the Buddha likewise spoke of it himself; this is "according to one's own [inclination]."
This is a statement of intention.
What is meant by "speaking in accordance with the intentions of others"? For example, when the householder Ghaṭila came to me and spoke these words:
"Gautama, do you know magic? If you know magic, you are a great magician; if you do not know it, [you are not]."
"It is not that I, the All-Knowing One, say that the elder knows a phantom person and calls him a 'phantom person.
The elder said, 'Excellent, excellent! A person who knows a phantom is indeed a phantom person.
The Buddha said, "Elder, do you know that within the kingdom of Śrāvastī there is a *caṇḍāla* named Qi xu? The elder replied, "Gautama..."
“Tāṇḍya, I have known this for a long time. The Buddha said, “If you have known this for a long time, can you then truly be a caṇḍāla?
The Elder said, “Gautama, although I know that he is a caṇḍāla, this body of mine is not a caṇḍāla.
The Buddha said, “Elder, you have grasped this principle: that one who knows a caṇḍāla is not a caṇḍāla. For what reason, then, am I not [a caṇḍāla] now?”
"Do you know that it is an illusion and not a non-illusion? "Householder, I truly know illusion; I know the person who knows illusion; I know the fruit of illusion; I know the technique of illusion.
I know killing; I know the person who kills; I know the fruit of killing; I know liberation from killing.
... [and so on] ... up to: I know wrong view; I know the person with wrong view; I know the fruit of wrong view; I know liberation from wrong view, householder. If...
"To call one who is not a person of delusion a 'deluded person' is not the speech of one with wrong views; to call one with wrong views a 'person of wrong views' incurs immeasurable sin.
The elder said, "Gautama, according to what you have said, I have committed a great sin. Whatever I possess, I now offer it all to you;
I pray that King Prasenajit may not learn of this matter of mine. The Buddha said, "Elder, this is indeed a sin."
It is not necessarily through the loss of wealth that one falls into the three evil realms; rather, it is because of this [transgression] that one shall fall into them.
At that time, having heard the name of the evil realms, the elder’s heart was filled with terror, and he said to the Buddha: "O Holy One, I have now lost my way and incurred a great sin.
O Holy One, you possess all-encompassing wisdom and should know how to attain liberation; how may I obtain it?"
Having been liberated from the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, I then preached the Four Noble Truths for you, O Householder.
Upon hearing them, you attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and felt shame and remorse; you then confessed before the Buddha, saying, "I was originally foolish;
the Buddha is no phantom, yet I called him a phantom. From this day forward, I take refuge in the Triple Gem. The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Householder!"
This is called speaking in accordance with the intentions of others.
For example, when a householder speaks of an illusory Buddha, his speaking in accordance with that illusion is speech that accords with the intentions of others.
What is meant by speaking in accordance with both oneself and others? It is as I have spoken, and as all wise people of the world speak.
When I say "there is a self," those with worldly wisdom say "there is no self";
when I say "there is no self," those with worldly wisdom say "there is a self. When I say that the pleasures of the five desires exist, they say they do not;

when I say they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self and should be abandoned, they say they are permanent, have a self, and are pure—this is impossible. I likewise say this is impossible. This is called conformity.
This is spoken according to the intentions of oneself and others; it may be understood accordingly according to the intentions of oneself and others (and so forth).
Good son, as I have explained below, there are three [points] based on the present teaching; the threefold phrasing of the text is also threefold, as the text itself indicates.
Good son, as I have taught, that Bodhisattvas in the ten stages see the Buddha-nature only slightly is spoken according to the intentions of others.
Why is it called "seeing slightly"? It is because Bodhisattvas in the ten stages attain samādhis such as Śūraṅgama and three thousand dharma-gates;
therefore, they clearly know for themselves that they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet they do not [yet] see it.
"All sentient beings will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
for this reason, I say that bodhisattvas of the ten stages see the Buddha-nature only partially.
Good son, I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature; this is called 'according with one's own mind'."
To say that all sentient beings are neither severed nor extinguished, and will eventually attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is called "teaching according to one's own intention.
I have taught thus: all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; because it is shrouded by afflictions, they are unable to see it.
Your statement is also like this; this is called "speaking in accordance with the intentions of oneself and others.

Son of Good Family, the Tathāgata sometimes explains next, in order, the speaking in accordance with one's own intention, which is divided into three parts: first, the speaking in accordance with one's own intention regarding the extensive and the concise;

second, the explanation of the seven kinds of speaking in accordance with one's own intention; and third, the explanation of the speaking in accordance with one's own intention regarding existence and non-existence. This is the first section.
"Good son, the Tathāgata sometimes, for the sake of a single dharma, teaches immeasurable dharmas. As it is said in the sūtras:
'The cause of all holy life (brahmacarya) is the spiritual friend. Although the causes of all holy life are immeasurable, when one speaks of them, they are summarized as the spiritual friend."
All unwholesome conduct and wrong views as causes, which I have described as being exhaustively subsumed, may be infinite in their specific causes;
yet, if one speaks of wrong view, they are already fully subsumed.
Alternatively, if one speaks of faith in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as the cause, although the causes of that bodhi are likewise infinite, if one speaks of faith, they are already [fully subsumed].
Good son, although the Tathāgata has taught immeasurable dharmas as the Buddha-nature, they do not depart from the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus).
To speak of it in terms of a single dharma is concise;
to speak of it in terms of immeasurable dharmas is extensive.
Therefore, these seven types are further divided into two [sections]: first their enumeration, followed by their explanation.
Noble son, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings through seven kinds of speech: first, speech concerning causes; second, speech concerning results;
third, speech concerning both cause and result; fourth, speech concerning analogies; fifth, speech that should not be spoken; sixth...
Regarding the seventh of the seven types of worldly conventional speech, it is "speech according to one's wish.
In the commentary, this is divided into seven sections. First, concerning the statement of the effect within the cause:
what is meant by "causal speech"? It refers to speaking of a future effect within the present cause, as when I say, "O son of good family."
"Good son, if you see sentient beings who delight in killing and even delight in practicing wrong views, you should know that such people are those of the hells.
Good son, if there are sentient beings who do not delight in killing and so forth up to wrong views, you should observe that such people are those of the heavens;
this is called the 'language of causes.'"
Those who practice good see the heavens, and those who commit evil see the hells; this is what is meant.
Next, regarding the explanation of causes within the context of effects:
how is it that effects are spoken of while referring to past causes? As stated in the Sūtra: "Good son, it is like this..."
When you see sentient beings who are impoverished, with ugly countenances and lacking self-mastery, you should know that these people certainly possess broken precepts,
a jealous mind, a mind of anger, and a lack of shame and remorse. When you see sentient beings who are immensely wealthy,
with all their faculties intact and possessing majestic power and mastery, you should know that these people certainly possess the precepts, generosity, diligence, shame, and remorse.
To have envy and anger is called "speech of the fruit";
this refers to knowing stinginess by seeing poverty and knowing generosity by seeing wealth.
The remaining five are as stated in the text.
What is the discourse on cause and effect? As it is said in the Sūtra: "Good son, the present six sense bases and contact of sentient beings are called the fruit of past karma.
The Tathāgata also says that these are called 'karma. Through the causal conditions of this karma, one obtains future fruit;
this is called the discourse on cause and effect."
What are these metaphorical expressions? They are as follows: "Lion King" is a metaphor for my own body;

likewise, the Great Elephant King, the Great Dragon King, the Pārijāta tree, the heap of the seven jewels, the great ocean, Mount Sumeru, the great earth, the great rain, the shipmaster, the guide, the charioteer of men, the strongman, the bull-king, the brāhmaṇa, the śramaṇa, the great city, and the tāla tree.
Such parables as these are called "figurative speech.
Why are they not [considered] "should-not-be-spoken"? In my sūtras it is said that heaven and earth may join, yet rivers do not enter the sea;

this was spoken for King Prasenajit. It is like the account of the four mountains closing in from the four directions, spoken for the laywoman Mṛgāramātṛ; or like the *śāla* tree, spoken for [the same].
If a tree could receive the eight precepts, it would obtain the pleasures of humans and devas.
Would one rather say that a Bodhisattva of the ten stages has a regressive mind, rather than saying that the Tathāgata has two kinds of speech?
Would one rather say that a Srotāpanna falls into the three evil realms, rather than saying that those in the ten stages have a regressive mind? This is called "inappropriate speech."
What is conventional worldly discourse as spoken by the Buddha? It refers to such things as male and female, large and small, coming and going, sitting and lying down, vehicles, houses, jars,
clothing, sentient beings, permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as armies, forests, cities, towns, illusions, transformations,
aggregations, and disintegrations— these are called conventional worldly discourse.
What is speech that accords with reality? It is speaking in such a way as to reproach those who violate the precepts so that they may feel self-reproach and maintain their observance of the precepts;
praising those who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* so that ordinary worldlings may give rise to wholesome thoughts;
praising bodhisattvas so that sentient beings may resolve to attain *bodhicitta*; and describing all the sufferings of the three evil realms so that [sentient beings] may cultivate [renunciation].
Because one practices all wholesome dharmas, it is said that "all is burned," which refers exclusively to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); the same applies to "non-self" (*anātman*).

Furthermore, the teaching that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is for the purpose of causing everyone to be diligent and not negligent; this is called "speech according to [the needs of] others" (*yathā-vadana*).

Third, there are further three points clarifying existence and non-existence according to one's own intent: first, a direct clarification of existence and non-existence; second, clarifying that sentient beings do not understand this;
third, making a fourfold classification based on existence and non-existence. This section has two parts:

first, regarding the existence and non-existence of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature; second, clarifying the existence and non-existence of the icchantika’s Buddha-nature. The first part, concerning the Tathāgata, is as follows:
Second, first clarifying existence and non-existence, followed by an analogical explanation. This section has two parts: first, clarifying non-existence;
second, clarifying that which exists within non-existence. Regarding the first passage:
"Good son, the Tathāgata further possesses speech according to his own intention. The Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature is of two kinds. First:
That which "exists" and that which "does not exist" refers to the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics,
the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the *Śūraṅgama* and other immeasurable samādhis,
the *Vajra* and other immeasurable samādhis, the immeasurable samādhis of skillful means, and the immeasurable samādhis of the five wisdoms. This is it.
This is called "existence.
The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth are all non-existent yet existent.
Next, that which exists but is non-existent is explained.

That which is called "non-existent" refers to the Tathāgata’s past wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate karmas, their causes and effects, retributions, afflictions, the five aggregates, and the twelve links of dependent origination; these are termed "non-existent."
All unwholesome and indeterminate afflictions and so forth were previously present but are now absent.
Next, as with the existence and non-existence of the wholesome and unwholesome, the following twenty-two pairs of dharmas are raised to categorize them according to the two preceding matters.
Good son, it is as if there were that which is wholesome and unwholesome, outflowing and non-outflowing, mundane and supramundane, noble and non-noble,
conditioned and unconditioned, real and unreal, tranquil and non-tranquil, contentious and non-contentious, a realm and non-realm, affliction and non-affliction,
grasping and non-grasping, prediction and non-prediction, existence and non-existence, and the three times and non-three-times.

Time and non-time, permanence and impermanence, self and non-self, bliss and suffering, purity and impurity; form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and that which is not form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
the internal bases and that which is not the internal bases, the external bases and that which is not the external bases;
the twelve links of dependent origination and that which is not the twelve links of dependent origination—these are called the existence and non-existence of the Tathāgata’s buddha-nature.

Regarding "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and "without outflows" (*anāsrava*): that which belongs to the category of "with outflows" exists, while that which belongs to the category of "without outflows" does not exist;

that which belongs to the category of "mundane" (*laukika*) exists, while that which belongs to the category of "non-mundane" (*alaukika*) does not exist. The same applies to all subsequent categories.
Next, from "The icchantika’s buddha-nature" onwards clarifies whether the icchantika possesses buddha-nature or not;
even down to the question of whether the icchantika possesses buddha-nature or not, it is likewise thus.
"All are reversed: where there is a Tathāgata, there is no icchantika; where there is an icchantika, there is no Tathāgata" (and so forth).

Although I have spoken thus, the following section clarifies that sentient beings do not understand these words of the Tathāgata. This further consists of two parts: first, the actual presentation [of their misunderstanding].
Regarding the failure to understand, the subsequent citation of ancient proofs for the first passage has two parts; first, the failure to understand:
"Good son, although I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, sentient beings do not understand this.
Such words as these are spoken by the Buddha according to his own intention."
Next, I shall use the profound to illustrate the shallow.
Good son, even Bodhisattvas in their final birth cannot understand such speech, let alone those of the two vehicles or other bodhisattvas.
If even Bodhisattvas of profound practice do not yet understand this, how much less so those of shallow capacity?
Next, the passage beginning with "Once, in the past, I went... is cited as scriptural evidence:
"Good son, once in the past, while I was on Vulture Peak Mountain, I engaged in discourse with Maitreya Bodhisattva regarding the world."
Śāriputra and the other five hundred śrāvakas were entirely ignorant of this matter, let alone the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) that transcends the world.

Regarding the Buddha’s teaching that the śrāvakas do not understand conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), there are two interpretations: one states that conventional truth consists of distinct categories and its phenomena are vast.

First, because the causes and effects of karmic actions are profound and hidden, they are difficult to understand. Second, it is said that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) exists for the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and thus the followers of the Two Vehicles do not comprehend it.
Regarding the question of where the Buddha spoke of conventional truth such that the five hundred [disciples] did not understand:

one interpretation says this was spoken in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and those five hundred were deaf and mute. Another interpretation says that while many scriptures exist in foreign lands, few of them have been translated here [into Chinese]. (And so forth. — Tiantai.
The Great Master explains that this has a specific significance (and so forth).
Regarding the line "There is the Buddha-nature," the third and fourth lines distinguish this into two parts: first, a formal application of the four-line tetralemma;
second, an exhortation to perform such discrimination.
Good son, there may be a Buddha-nature that the icchantika possesses while those with roots of goodness lack;
there may be a Buddha-nature that those with roots of goodness possess while the icchantika lacks; there may be a Buddha-nature that both possess;
and there may be a Buddha-nature that neither possesses.

The former commentators [state that] icchantikas possess the nature of evil and perverse objects, while those with the nature of good roots possess the ten thousand wholesome *liào-yīn* (causes of realization), which are also called *yuán-yīn* (causes as conditions).
Both types of persons possess these together, as well as the *zhèngxìng* (nature of correctness) or the *zhòngshēngxìng* (nature of sentient beings).
Those who lack both have no fruit and no nature of fruit. Hexi said: "Icchantikas possess the five *yīn* (aggregates) of evil."
Those of a virtuous nature and those with virtuous roots both possess the five aggregates of a virtuous nature;
those who both possess [them] have the five aggregates of an indeterminate nature; those who both lack [them] are identical to the nature of the wondrously transcendent fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
This differs from the old terminology, yet the meaning is the same. Xinghuang explains this from the first phrase to the seventh: the single phrase is simply the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

The first two phrases concern whether the *icchantika*’s Buddha-nature exists or does not exist as taught by the Tathāgata. The three phrases represent three types of speech: the first is the Tathāgata’s own words stating that the *icchantika* possesses the nature;
the second is the speech of others stating that the *icchantika* lacks the nature; and the third is the speech of both [the Tathāgata and others] stating that it both exists and does not exist.
The four phrases refer to the four sets of four phrases within this context, while the seven phrases refer to the two types of persons among the seven classes of living beings.
Regarding the explanation that the latter five types of persons who are evil become good and further perform three kinds of actions, there are three interpretations:

first, a general treatment concerning all meanings; second, a treatment concerning the internal and external according to principle; and third, a treatment concerning only the internal according to principle. As for the general treatment concerning all meanings: although principle itself is neither good nor evil, it possesses two functions—good and evil.
Persons possessing roots of goodness have the function of good, while persons who are icchantikas have the function of evil; both possess these functions.
Those who hold one side each have a partial view; those who hold neither side lack both views. Next, regarding the internal and external from the perspective of principle:

Buddha-nature is fundamentally neither "attainment" nor "non-attainment," yet it is spoken of as having attainment or non-attainment based on conditions. From the perspective of what is outside the principle, the icchantika has attainment;
from the perspective of what is within the principle, there is non-attainment. Those with good roots possess the nature of non-attainment, whereas the icchantika possesses [the nature of] attainment.
Regarding their natures, both the presence and absence [of these qualities] are as explained above. Next, to speak solely in terms of principle:

the icchantika within the category of principle is identical to Shanxing (Śrīgarbha), while the person possessing roots of goodness is identical to Rāhula. These represent the two modes of transformation—conformative and inverse.

The icchantika possesses the nature of unwholesomeness through inverse transformation, while the person with roots of goodness possesses the nature of wholesome dharmas through conformative transformation; thus, both the presence and absence [of these qualities] are as stated.
The aforementioned discourse refers to this as "the teaching that can resolve what is difficult to resolve. Now, to clarify how one may construct four propositions based on this text:

there are those who have only the state of being submerged (icchantikas), those who have only the state of emerging (those whose roots of goodness are severed), those who possess both states (both remaining together in the Ganges), and those who possess neither state (neither reaching the shore). One who wishes to contemplate this should act accordingly.
This should also be understood as immeasurable, though it is summarized here as follows (and so forth). Furthermore, with respect to the three truths:
those who are icchantikas possess [the cause] in the conventional truth, while those who possess roots of goodness possess the supramundane good cause.
Both possess the body that is the fruit of retribution in the conventional truth; both lack [the cause] in the Middle Way, and both lack the cause and fruit of the Middle Way.
Next, my various subordinates shall provide an exegesis as written in the text.
"Good son, if my disciples understand the meaning of these four propositions, they should not raise the objection:
'Does an icchantika definitely possess Buddha-nature or definitely lack it? If one says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature," [the following applies].

The name "Tathāgata’s speech according to his own intention" means that when sentient beings hear such speech from the Tathāgata according to his own intention, how could they not understand it with single-minded resolve?
Furthermore, the second stage of cultivating causes and proceeding toward the fruit within the Ganges River is also explained by way of analogy to clarify the Middle Way.
There is a parable with a summary and a detailed explanation of two types of analogies.
Good son, it is like seven kinds of sentient beings in the Ganges River:
first, those who are constantly submerged; second, those who emerge briefly and then submerge again; third, those who, having emerged, remain there; fourth, those who, having emerged...
1. Surveying the four directions; 2. Having surveyed them, proceeding; 3. Having proceeded, returning to a standstill; 4. Moving both on water and on land; 5.
Constantly submerged—this refers to the great fish that, having experienced great evil karma, have heavy bodies and dwell in deep waters, and for this reason remain constantly submerged; 6.
Emerging briefly and then submerging again—such great fish, because they have experienced evil karma, have heavy bodies and dwell in shallow waters, and thus are seen only momentarily.
Regarding the statement that "because of light, it briefly emerges from its depth and then submerges again;
having emerged, it remains"—this refers to the *timi* fish, which dwells in shallow water and, delighting in seeing light, emerges and remains there to survey the four directions.

Regarding the statement that "the *śiśumāra* surveys the four directions in order to seek food"—therefore, that which surveys the directions and, having surveyed them, proceeds, is called the *śiśumāra*.
The fish, seeing something from afar, thinks it is edible and hastens toward it; thus, having observed it, he moves, and having moved, he stops again.
This means that once the fish has approached and obtained what is edible, he immediately comes to rest; therefore, after moving, he stops again.
As for those who move both on water and on land, they are tortoises.
It is said that although the seven types of sentient beings differ, their Buddha-nature is one.

This subtle point is now illustrated through a simile. As in the preceding chapter, the river was used as a metaphor for birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); here, the river is used as a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*.
The initial general correspondence is as stated in the text.
Good son, within this subtle and wondrous great river of *nirvāṇa*, there are likewise seven kinds of sentient beings;
from the first who are perpetually submerged to the seventh, they either enter or emerge.

Next, regarding those who are "perpetually submerged," the following section combines the general and specific analogies. First, combining the analogy for those *icchantikas* who are perpetually submerged, there are four parts; first, combining the analogy for those who turn their backs on the wholesome:
"Perpetually submerged" refers to those people who, upon hearing this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, [realize that] the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and without change.
Those who delight in the notions of self, pleasure, and purity shall never ultimately enter parinirvāṇa. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
even those of icchantika nature who slander the Vaipulya sūtras, commit the five heinous crimes, or violate the four grave prohibitions, will certainly attain the path to Bodhi.
Those such as the Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, and Pratyekabuddha will certainly...
Upon hearing these words that they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
they give rise to a lack of faith and immediately think thus;
subsequently, they conceive thoughts that lead downward and accord with evil.
Having formed this thought, he then further thinks: "This treatise on nirvāṇa is merely a non-Buddhist text; it is not a Buddhist scripture.
At that time, such a person distances himself from virtuous friends and does not hear the true Dharma. Even if he should hear it at times, he is unable to contemplate it;
and even if he contemplates it, he does not contemplate what is wholesome.
Third, as with unwholesome dharmas, they abide in the lower [realms] and are conjoined with evil.
Because one does not contemplate the wholesome, they abide like unwholesome dharmas; those who abide in unwholesome dharmas have six types:
first, evil; second, the absence of goodness; third, defiled dharmas; fourth, increase; fifth, affliction and feverish distress; and sixth, the experiencing of evil fruits.
This is called "sinking. Why is it called sinking? Because there is no wholesome mind, because one constantly practices evil, and because one does not cultivate remedies;

therefore, it is called sinking. It is called evil because the noble ones censure it, because it gives rise to fear in the heart, because virtuous people distance themselves from it, and because it does not benefit sentient beings;
therefore, it is called evil. One who lacks goodness can produce immeasurable evil fruits.
Because they are constantly entangled by ignorance due to their past retributions; because they delight in associating with evil people as equals;
because they lack the skillful means for cultivating wholesome deeds; because their minds are inverted and perpetually erroneous;
this is called being defiled by unwholesome dharmas—constantly defiling body and speech, defiling pure sentient beings, increasing unwholesome karma, and remaining far removed from wholesome dharmas.

Therefore, these are called the defiled dharmas that increase existence (*bhava*). As with the three types of persons mentioned above, the dharmas they practice increase rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts;
they are unable to cultivate the dharmas of liberation, and their actions of body, speech, and mind do not weary of the various states of existence.
These are called the afflictions of heat that increase existence. Such a person fully practices the four aforementioned matters, which cause both body and mind—
Because it is far removed from the afflictions of worldly affairs and is tranquil, it is called the "Hell of Hot Suffering.
It is called "hot" because it scorches all sentient beings; it is called "hot" because it scorches all wholesome dharmas. Good son, the mind of faith is cool and refreshing;

because such a person does not possess this [faith], it is called "hot suffering. As for those who perform evil deeds, they are fully possessed of them and practice the highest [of unwholesome states].

Regarding the five matters that lead to death and falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals: son of good family, there are three kinds of evil things which are also called evil fruits:
first, the evil of afflictions; second, the evil of karma; and third, the evil of retribution. These are what is meant by "receiving the fruit of evil retribution."
The fourth is the person who possesses [the following]: combined with the above, such a person is one who severs the roots of goodness.

Good son, this person, possessing the six matters mentioned above, is able to sever the roots of goodness, commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), violate the four grave offenses, slander the Triple Gem, misappropriate the property of the Sangha, and perform various kinds of unrighteous deeds.
Due to these causes and conditions, they sink into the Avīci Hell, where the bodies they receive are eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in height and breadth.
Because the karmic actions of their body, speech, and mind are heavy, they cannot escape. Why is this?
It is because their minds are unable to give rise to wholesome dharmas; thus, even though immeasurable Buddhas appear in the world, they neither hear nor see them. Therefore, they are so named.
They are constantly submerged like large fish in the Ganges.

Although I have further explained that those who fall back correspond to the second type—those who emerge for a moment and then submerge—their initial engagement in practice being contrary to principle constitutes their "having cultivated goodness.
Next, why is it called "submergence"? This is the second [section], explaining emergence and submergence.
The meaning is this: although people believe [the former], the third point clarifies those who do not possess both practice and realization and thus sink back down;
the fourth point specifically identifies such individuals.
"Good son, although I have further stated that icchantikas and others are called 'perpetually submerged,' there are also those who are perpetually submerged who are not [icchantikas]."
Who is an icchantika? It is like a person who, for the sake of existence, practices the virtues of giving and precepts; this is called "perpetually submerged.
Good son, there are four wholesome deeds that result in evil fruits. What are the four? First, reciting and chanting the sūtras for the purpose of surpassing others;
second, upholding the prohibitive precepts for the sake of gain and offerings; third, [acting] for the sake of being subservient to others...
Fourth, one practices giving for the sake of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

by binding one's mindfulness to these four wholesome matters, one obtains an evil retribution. If a person cultivates and accumulates these four matters, this is called "sinking and then emerging, and having emerged, sinking again."
Why is it called "sinking"? Because one is submerged in the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*). Why is it called "emerging"? Because of seeing the light. What is this "light"?
It is precisely hearing, morality, generosity, and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Why does one sink back again? Because wrong views increase and arrogance (*māna*) arises.
Therefore, I have spoken these verses in the sutra:
If there are sentient beings who delight in the various realms of existence, And for the sake of existence perform good and evil deeds, Such people lose their way on the path to nirvāṇa;
This is called "emerging for a moment only to sink back again," Wandering in the dark ocean of birth and death.
Though they may attain liberation and be free from afflictions, [They remain bound by the craving for existence.]
This person again receives an evil retribution; this is called "temporarily emerging only to sink back.
Good son, it is like that great fish which, because it sees the light, temporarily emerges from the water, but because its body is heavy, sinks back down again.
These two types of people are just like this. Good son, furthermore, there may be someone who is attached to pleasure...
The three realms of existence are called "submergence. To hear this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and give rise to faith is called "emergence.
For what reason is it called "emergence"? Having heard this sūtra, to distance oneself from unwholesome dharmas and cultivate wholesome dharmas is called "emergence."
Regarding the lack of perfection in practice, there are again two parts: first, the actual presentation of the individuals; second, the summary and demonstration following the five matters.
First, as for the five matters: (1) lack of faith, (2) insufficiency in precepts, (3) learning, (4) generosity, and (5) wisdom. Faith can be understood [as previously explained].
Although this person has faith, it is not complete. For what reason is their faith incomplete?
Although they believe in the Great Parinirvāṇa as permanent, blissful, self, and pure, they say that the body of the Tathāgata is impermanent, non-self, without bliss, and without purity.
They claim that there are two kinds of nirvāṇa for the Tathāgata: first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). [They say] the conditioned nirvāṇa...
Nirvana, which is unconditioned, is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
yet, although one may believe that the Buddha-nature exists within sentient beings, it is not necessarily present in all of them. For this reason, such belief is called "incomplete faith.
Good son, there are two kinds of faith: first, faith; second, seeking. A person of such [incomplete] faith, even though they possess faith, does not...
Because one is able to infer this, it is called "incomplete faith. Furthermore, there are two types of faith: first, that which arises from hearing;
second, that which arises from reflection. This person’s faith arises from hearing and not from reflection; therefore, it is called incomplete faith.
Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, faith that the Path exists; second, faith that there is one who attains it. This person’s faith is merely...
To believe that the Path exists, yet not to believe in one who has attained the Path, is therefore called "incomplete faith.

Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, believing what is correct; second, believing what is false. To say that cause and effect exist, and that the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha exist, is called "correct faith.
To say that cause and effect do not exist, and to believe the various false doctrines of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others—that the nature of the Three Jewels is different—is [false faith].

One who is said to have "faith in the heterodox" is one who, though they believe in the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, does not believe that the Three Jewels share the same nature and characteristics;
or though they believe in cause and effect, does not believe in the attainment [of its fruit]. For this reason, it is called "incomplete faith."
This person fails to achieve fulfillment in their faith, and the precepts they receive are likewise not fulfilled. For what reason are they called "incomplete"?
Because the causes are incomplete, the precepts obtained are also incomplete. Furthermore, for what reason are they called "incomplete precepts"?
There are two kinds of precepts: first, the precept of deportment (*īryāpatha-śīla*); second, the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*). Although this person possesses [the former],...
The precepts of deportment and so forth are incomplete; because they lack the precepts derived from the [fundamental] precepts, this is called "incompleteness of precepts.

Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, the precept of action (*kriyā-śīla*); second, the precept of non-action (*avijñapti-śīla*). Although such a person possesses the precept of action, they do not possess the precept of non-action;
therefore, it is called "incompleteness of precepts. Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, that which is obtained from body and speech regarding correctness...

It is said that one fails to obtain right livelihood through body and speech; although such a person does not obtain right livelihood through body and speech, for this reason they are called "incomplete in precepts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, seeking the precepts, and second, relinquishing the precepts.
Although such a person may fully seek the precepts of worldly existence, they do not obtain the relinquishing of the precepts; for this reason, they are called "incomplete in precepts. Furthermore...

There are two kinds: first, that which accords with existence (*bhava-anuvartin*); second, that which accords with the Path (*mārga-anuvartin*). Although such a person possesses the precepts that accord with existence, they do not possess those that accord with the Path;
therefore, it is said that their precepts are incomplete. Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, wholesome precepts (*kuśala-śīla*);
second, unwholesome precepts (*akuśala-śīla*). Wholesomeness of body, speech, and mind is called wholesome precepts; the "ox-precepts" and "dog-precepts" are called unwholesome precepts. This is so.
People deeply believe that these two kinds of precepts both possess wholesome fruits; therefore, this is called "incompleteness of precepts.

Regarding the second kind of precept, the "precept of deportment" (īryāpatha-śīla) refers to having no genuine virtue within while outwardly proclaiming integrity and frugality, desiring people's respect and compliance with the precepts.
Such a person’s inner and outer states do not correspond; they do not attend to human affairs but merely seek actual gain, and yet—
One who upholds the precepts is one who follows the precepts from the precepts; one who seeks the precepts of existence seeks the three realms of existence;
one who abandons the precepts abandons the three realms of existence.
Such a person lacks both faith and the precepts, and their cultivated learning is likewise incomplete. How, then, can they be called [a practitioner]?
To lack the fullness of hearing refers to not believing in six of the twelve divisions of the *sūtras* taught by the Tathāgata while only believing in the other six;

for this reason, it is called "incomplete hearing. Furthermore, although one may receive and uphold these six divisions of the *sūtras*, if one cannot read, recite, or explain them to others so as to provide benefit, it is therefore called "incomplete hearing. Moreover, to receive these...

Because the six classes of scriptures have already been used for debate, for the sake of defeating others, for the sake of gain and offerings, and for the sake of various states of existence, one upholds, reads, recites, and explains them;
therefore, this is called "incomplete hearing. Good son, in the sūtras I have spoken of "complete hearing.
What is completeness? If there is a bhikṣu who is virtuous in body, speech, and mind, and who first can make offerings to his preceptor...
Those teachers and virtuous persons—because these teachers have conceived a heart of affection and regard for such a person, by this causal condition they instruct them in the sūtras and dharmas;
that person receives, maintains, recites, and practices them with a sincere mind; having recited and practiced them, they obtain wisdom;
having obtained wisdom, they are able to contemplate well and abide in accordance with the Dharma; and having contemplated well, then...
One attains right view; having attained right view, body and mind become tranquil; when body and mind are tranquil, a joyful mind arises; with joy as its condition, the mind attains concentration;
because of concentration, one attains right knowledge and vision; having attained right knowledge and vision, weariness and remorse arise toward all states of existence (*bhava*);
through this remorse for all states of existence, one is able to attain liberation. Such a person has no [further] existence.
These matters are therefore called "incomplete hearing.
Regarding the third type of hearing, it says: "believing six divisions [of the canon] and not believing six divisions.
Hexi (He Xi) states that these six are: Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Udāna, Itivṛttaka, and Upadeśa.
Because they are manifest and easy to understand, one has faith in these six; because the other six are profound, hidden, and difficult to understand, one does not have faith in them.
Furthermore, some say that among the twelve, one should believe in six and not believe in the other six, as the remaining ones are visible.
Such a person does not possess these three things, nor is their giving complete. There are two kinds of giving: first, the gift of material wealth; second, the gift of the Dharma.

Although this person may practice the gift of material wealth, they do so for the sake of seeking existence within cyclic birth; although they practice the gift of the Dharma, it is likewise incomplete. Why is this?
Because they withhold and do not teach exhaustively, fearing that others might surpass them. For this reason, it is called "giving."
The two types of giving—material and Dharma—are each twofold: first, noble; second, non-noble. The noble give and do not seek karmic retribution;
the non-noble give and do seek retribution. The noble give the Dharma for the sake of increasing the Dharma;
the non-noble give the Dharma for the sake of increasing existence (*bhava*). Such persons practice [giving] for the sake of increasing material wealth.
Because they practice the gift of Dharma for the sake of increasing existence through the gift of material wealth, it is called incomplete giving.
Furthermore, such a person receives the six classes of scriptures and provides for those who receive the Dharma, but does not provide for those who do not receive the Dharma;
therefore, it is called incomplete giving.
Such a person does not possess the wisdom cultivated through the four aforementioned matters, nor do they possess the nature of wisdom capable of discernment;
such a person cannot distinguish whether the Tathāgata is permanent or impermanent.
In this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Tathāgata has said: "The Tathāgata is liberation, and liberation is the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata...
That is itself nirvana, and nirvana is itself liberation; within this meaning, one cannot differentiate them.

The holy life (brahmacarya) is itself the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is himself loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are themselves liberation, and liberation is itself nirvana;
nirvana is itself loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; within this meaning, one cannot [differentiate them].
Because of such discrimination, it is said that one’s wisdom is incomplete. Furthermore, one is unable to discern that buddha-nature is the Tathāgata;
that the Tathāgata is all the unshared dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*); that the unshared dharmas are liberation (*vimukti*);
that liberation is nirvāṇa; and that nirvāṇa is the unshared dharmas. Regarding this meaning, one is unable [to understand it].
Because they engage in conceptual discrimination, they are said to be incomplete in wisdom.

Furthermore, because they cannot discern the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and because they cannot discern these four true truths, they do not know the noble practice.

Because they do not know the noble practice, they do not know the Tathāgata. Because they do not know the Tathāgata, they do not know liberation. Because they do not know liberation, they do not know nirvāṇa.
Therefore, this is called the non-fulfillment of wisdom.
Such a person does not fulfill the second lower fetter.
This person’s lack of fulfillment regarding these five matters is of two kinds: first, the increase of wholesome dharmas; second, the increase of unwholesome dharmas. What are they?
What is called the increase of unwholesome dharmas? It is when a person, though not seeing themselves as incomplete, claims to be complete and gives rise to a mind of attachment;
among those of similar practice, they consider themselves superior and thus associates with evil friends who are like themselves.

Having associated with them, they further hear the dharma of incompleteness; having heard it, their minds rejoice, and their minds become defiled and attached, giving rise [to further unwholesomeness].

Abounding in pride, they practice heedlessness; because of this heedlessness, they associate with householders and take pleasure in hearing talk concerning household life, while remaining distant from the pure dharma of renunciation.
Due to these causes and conditions, they increase unwholesome dharmas.
Because they increase unwholesome dharmas, impure karma arises through their body, speech, and mind. Since the three karmas are impure, they increase the realm of hell.
Animals and hungry ghosts are said to emerge for a moment and then sink back down.
As for those who "emerge for a moment and then sink back down" within my Buddha-dharma, who are they?
They are Devadatta, the bhikṣu Kokālika, the bhikṣu Hastaka, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, the bhikṣu Tiṣya, the bhikṣu Puṣya, and Maitreya.
The bhikṣuṇī Dì, the bhikṣuṇī Kuàngyě, the bhikṣuṇī Fāng, the bhikṣuṇī Màn,
the upāsaka Jìngjié Qiúyǒu, the Śākya upāsaka Shèlé, the upāsaka Xiàng, the upāsikā Míngchēng,
the upāsikā Guānmíng, the upāsikā Nántuó, the upāsikā Jūn, and the upāsikā Líng— such persons as these.
This is called "emerging for a moment and then sinking," like a great fish that emerges from the water because it sees the light, but sinks back down because of its heavy body.
Regarding the second person—logically, the one who belongs in the third category and is capable of attaining stability—one should refer to them as the third;
why then is he called the second person? The explanation is that this second person practices the conduct that ought to result in becoming the third.

Therefore, it is said that the second "Lion Chapter" encompasses all five stages of skillful means (*pañca-upāya*) and the twenty moments of mind (*viṃśati-citta*), all of which constitute the attainment of abiding.

Herein, however, we rely solely on the initial stage of attainment; specifically, according to the Hīnayāna, this refers to the first two stages of skillful means—the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
If one follows the system of seven stages of skillful means, this refers to the stages from "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) and "Patience" (*kṣānti*) upward.

Upon reaching the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one belongs to the category of those who practice contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). According to the Mahāyāna, this includes those within the thirty stages of mind (*triṃśac-citta*) as practitioners of contemplation;
from the first bhūmi (*bhūmi*) upward, they belong to the category of those who have reached the other shore (*pāramitā-prāpta*). This text is divided into four parts: first, the origin;

second, identifying these individuals; third, clarifying their attainment; and fourth, distinguishing the methods of practice. The first three are at the end of this fascicle; now, the first [part] is explained.
The Origin.
The second person, through deep self-knowledge and insight, realizes that their conduct is incomplete; because it is incomplete, they seek out virtuous friends.

Because they have approached virtuous friends, they delight in inquiring about what they have not yet heard. Having heard it, they delight in receiving it; having received it, they delight in skillfully reflecting upon it. Skillfully reflecting...
Only by being able to abide in accordance with the Dharma does one increase wholesome qualities; because wholesome qualities increase, one never again sinks back.
This is called "abiding.
It is not correct to say that the second [stage] preceding it becomes the third, or to alter the third to be so.
In my Buddha-dharma, I shall now set forth the second group of individuals.
Who are they in my Buddha-dharma? They are Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the other four bhikṣus, Yaśas and the other four bhikṣus, the youth Ānanda, and Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa, Daśabala-Kāśyapa, Kṛśa-Gautamī Bhikṣuṇī, Pāṭalā Bhikṣuṇī, Jitā Bhikṣuṇī,
Arthavatī Bhikṣuṇī, Manasvinī Bhikṣuṇī, Bhadrā Bhikṣuṇī, Śuddhā Bhikṣuṇī,
Avaivartikā Bhikṣuṇī, King Bimbisāra, the Householder Ugga, and Sudatta.
The elder Śreṣṭhi Śramaṇa, the poor Sudatta, the elder Mūṣika, the elder Siṃha, the elder Yaśas,
the elder Saṃpanna, General Siṃha, the elder Upāli, the elder Dīpa, the fearless upāsikā, the well-established upāsikā,
the dharma-loving upāsikā, the courageous upāsikā, the deva-attained upāsikā, and the virtuous [upāsikā].
The laywoman Jāti, the laywoman Kāyā, the laywoman Goniṣādhā,
the laywoman Āṭavikā, the laywoman Mahāsena, and others such as these— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
are said to be "abiding."

Regarding the statement that "those who possess semblance-understanding (*sādṛśa-adhimukti*) should emerge," while Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana are both currently those with true understanding (*bhūta-adhimukti*), there are two traditional interpretations:
First, it is said that the status of this third person extends upward to the level of an Arhat; therefore, the text refers to them collectively.

Second, it takes into account their original state: they were initially persons of semblance-understanding who, through cultivation, attained entry into true understanding, yet even now they still retain their original semblance.
This is why they are arranged in their respective positions.
What is meant by "abiding"? Thirdly, it clarifies attaining abiding. Why is it called abiding?
Because one constantly and joyfully beholds the sublime light; for this reason, whether a Buddha appears in the world...
If such persons as these did not appear in the world, they would never commit evil;
this is called "dwelling like the *ṛmī* fish, which delights in seeing light and neither sinks nor drowns. Such multitudes as these are also like this.
For this reason, I have spoken a verse in the sutra.
If a person is well able to discern the meaning, And with a sincere heart seeks the fruits of the śramaṇa,
If they can censure all forms of existence, Such a person is said to dwell in accordance with the Dharma.
If they can make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, Then they will be able to cultivate the path for immeasurable eons.
If one experiences worldly pleasures without negligence, such a person is said to dwell in accordance with the Dharma;
they draw near to virtuous friends, listen to the true Dharma, reflect well within, dwell according to the Dharma,
delight in seeing the light, cultivate the Path, and attain liberation to abide in peace and security.
Question: Regarding the river of *nirvāṇa*, four types of persons—Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas—equally attain *nirvāṇa*.
However, within the river of birth and death, only the Buddha alone is the "seventh person," while the other three have not yet crossed over.

Some explain this by saying that in the river of *nirvāṇa*, those of the Three Vehicles equally attain *nirvāṇa*, and for this reason, all are considered the seventh person; whereas in the river of birth and death, [only the Buddha has crossed].
Because those in the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] within the river have not yet escaped the river of birth and death, they cannot cross it.
Although an arhat has no further births after this life, because this present life still remains, they have not yet crossed.

Thus, while attaining nirvāṇa does not necessarily mean escaping birth and death, once one has crossed over birth and death, one will certainly attain nirvāṇa (and so forth). Now, I shall evaluate this interpretation; its terminology is clear.

The principle behind this appears to be unclear; I shall now inquire further: among the four people who attain nirvana together in the river of nirvana, do they all equally perceive the Buddha-nature?
If he answers that they equally perceive the nature, this would mean they have not yet seen the principle.
If he answers that they do not equally perceive it, then they likewise do not equally attain nirvana. Why, then, does the preceding text state that they attain it together?
Since the seventh [consciousness] is identical in its nature—whether it possesses the quality of seeing or not—it is known that *nirvāṇa* differs from *saṃsāra*.
Now, considering the intent of the sutra: the "river of *saṃsāra*" refers exclusively to the *pariṇāmi-śūnyatā* (transformative change), which only the Buddha can cross;
all others remain within its current. The "river of *nirvāṇa*" pertains specifically to the *paricchinna-śūnyatā* (segmented existence), which applies to all four types of practitioners. Thus:
Because there are seven types of persons in the Hīnayāna, the *Śāstra* states that the stage of the Arhat is called the stage of the Buddha;

furthermore, the fact that Kāśyapa shared the same liberation-seat as the Buddha conveys this very meaning. These general and specific designations are raised interchangeably to suit the occasion, and one must not adhere to them dogmatically.
