Those of middling capacity dwell in the Atapa Heaven; those of inferior capacity dwell in the Parīttaśubha Heaven.

Of these two types of persons, one delights in philosophical discourse (abhidharma) and the other delights in tranquility (śamatha). Those who delight in tranquility enter the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu);

those who delight in philosophical discourse dwell in the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa). Furthermore, there are two kinds: those who cultivate perfumed dhyāna (vāsita-dhyāna) and those who do not cultivate perfumed dhyāna. [Those who] cultivate...

When a practitioner of dhyāna enters the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) and does not cultivate the perfumed dhyāna (vāsita-dhyāna), they are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and attain parinirvāṇa at the end of their lifespan;

this is called "parinirvāṇa by upward-streaming" (ūrdhvasrotas-parinirvāṇa). If one wishes to enter the formless realm, one cannot cultivate the four dhyānas with their five distinctions (pañca-prakāra);
however, if one cultivates these five distinctions, one is able to censure the meditative absorptions of the formless realm.

From this, the stream branches out to give rise to two realms: those who delight in discussing the meaning of the Dharma are born in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, while those who delight in samādhi are born in the Ākiṃcanyāyatana (Sphere of Nothingness).
It is asked: Are there people who, from the first dhyāna, are immediately born in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and then enter parinirvāṇa?
Or are there people who must be born in the Ākiṃcanyāyatana before they can enter parinirvāṇa? There are indeed some who have not yet reached the Ānāgāmin stage [and yet do so].
"Tha" [the sound] ceases immediately; "not-yet-reached" (*anabhisamāpanna*) and "unrestricted" (*apranihita*) cease immediately. To whom does this belong? The answer says:

this belongs to those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and those who have attained faith-understanding (*śraddhādhimukta*); they are not called "upward-streamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*). There are four meanings contrasted here: first, based on the ease of concentration (*samādhi*) and the ease of wisdom (*prajñā*);

second, clarifying the cultivation of the five differences and the non-cultivation of the five differences; third, clarifying the delight in tranquility (*śamatha*) and the delight in discussion (*vibhāṣā*); fourth.
Regarding the four meanings—cultivating perfuming meditation (*vāsanā-dhyāna*) and not cultivating perfuming meditation—they resolve into two intentions:
the third resolves into the first, and the fourth resolves into [the distinction between] having five differences and lacking differences.
The first three are as stated in the text; regarding the "perfuming" mentioned in the fourth, there are two interpretations. First, the Sāṃkhya masters say: "The two..."
Regarding the point that an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) permeates a single tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*):
the masters of the treatise state that this meditative absorption is permeated by a mind of loving-kindness and compassion; therefore, they do not explain the latter two categories.

This is because the preceding six persons were originally added to those who manifest extinction (*nirvāṇa*), and since the category of those who manifest extinction has already been explained in the previous section, it is not explained here. Furthermore, the former seven persons were originally added [to the same group].

Since the explanation for the person of superior practice who reaches the cessation at the formless realm has been completed—thereby also concluding the discussion of the fifth type of person—it is unnecessary to further explain it.

In the third section of the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* concerning the analysis of the doctrinal debate, regarding the cessation [of the faculties], there is first a question and then an answer; within the question, there is...

Regarding the first of these two questions: since those who attain extinction in the intermediate state (*antarā-parinirvāyin*) possess sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), why do they not enter nirvana immediately in the present life?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state possesses sharp faculties;
if they possess such sharp faculties, why do they not enter parinirvāṇa in the present?"
Second, the question: Why is it that there is intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) but not in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
Why is it that there is intermediate nirvāṇa (*antarāparinirvāṇa*) in the desire realm but not in the form realm?

The Buddha’s answer consists of two parts. This first part answers the initial question through three reasons why [intermediate nirvāṇa] does not manifest in the form realm: first, because [the beings there] are weak and inferior;...
Second, they lack the necessary conditions; third, they take pleasure in mundane affairs and other such activities; the rest is as can be seen [in the text]. The beginning is according to the script.
The Buddha said: "Good son, this person’s four great elements are currently weak and inferior, and thus they are unable to cultivate the Path."
Second, the deficiency of necessary conditions.
Although there may be bhikṣus whose four great elements are healthy, they lack the various conditions such as dwellings, food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medical requisites;
therefore, they cannot attain parinirvāṇa in the present life. Good son, once in the past, at one time, I was...
At that time, a bhikṣu from the Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery in Śrāvastī came to me and spoke thus:
"World-Honored One, I constantly practice the Path, yet I am unable to attain the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat.
I then said to Ānanda: "You should now provide this bhikṣu with all his necessary requisites. At that moment...
Ānanda took this bhikṣu to the Jeta Grove and provided him with a fine dwelling.

At that time, the bhikṣu said to Ānanda, "Venerable One, I pray that you will adorn my dwelling for me, making it pure and clean, embellished with the seven treasures, and hung with silken banners and canopies.
Ānanda replied, "In this world, those who are poor are called śramaṇas; how could I possibly do such a thing?"
When that bhikṣu was preparing these things, he said, "Venerable sir, if you can do this for me, it would be well;
if you cannot, I shall go back to the World-Honored One. At that time, Ānanda immediately went to where the Buddha was and spoke thus:
"World-Honored One, just now a bhikṣu requested from me various kinds of ornaments, seven-jeweled banners, and parasols; I do not know [what to do]."
"What should be done about this matter? At that time, I again addressed Ānanda: "Go back now and prepare whatever items this bhikṣu requires according to his wishes.
Thereupon, Ānanda immediately returned to his quarters and prepared everything for that bhikṣu.
Having received these things, the bhikṣu applied his mindfulness to the practice of the Way and before long attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Noble sons, from the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, there are immeasurable sentient beings who ought to enter nirvana;
however, because they lack certain necessities, their minds are obstructed and distracted, and for this reason they cannot attain it.
This matter is derived from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. That text states: "The celestial Subhūti is not the same as the present Subhūti who understands emptiness.

Good son, there are further sentient beings who greatly delight in teaching and transforming others; because their minds are preoccupied with such activities and unable to attain meditative concentration, they cannot attain nirvana in the present life."

In response to your question, the answer to the second inquiry is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the distinction of objects (*ālambana*), and second, clarifying the distinction of faculties (*indriya*).

Within the section on the distinction of objects, there are further two points: first, clarifying that those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) mostly engage with objects; and second, clarifying that this is because their nature is courageous and robust.

"Good son, as to your question regarding the causes and conditions for why there is *nirvāṇa-without-remainder* (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) after casting off the body of the desire realm, yet none exists in the form realm:
Good son, this person contemplates that the causes and conditions of afflictions in the desire realm are twofold:
first, internal; second, external. Within the form realm, such external causes and conditions do not exist. Furthermore, in the desire realm, there are two kinds of craving: first—"
There are two kinds of craving: first, craving for sensual desire; second, craving for food. One contemplates these two cravings with a sincere heart and reproaches them.

Having reproached them, one attains entry into *nirvāṇa*. Within this realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), one is able to reproach the coarse afflictions, namely stinginess, greed, anger, jealousy, lack of shame, and lack of remorse.
By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to attain *nirvāṇa*.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), because there are no external sufferings, [the afflictions] cannot arise;

however, since the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) possesses external afflictions, one becomes weary of them and thus cultivates the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*). This cultivation is termed "courageous.

Regarding the numerical analysis, some masters maintain that the higher realms are entirely devoid of those who first enter the Path, while others say that they do exist, or alternatively, that they also exist in the higher realms.
Because there is an initial entry [into the path], the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance) states that eighty thousand devas attained the purity of the Dharma-eye;

this indicates that those in the higher realms also realize the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). As for the existence of this text, it is because practitioners who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) may initially be in the stage of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), from which they can emerge from contemplation and be reborn above;
thus, it says they "attain the fruit," rather than implying they are starting from the very beginning as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and proceeding to sainthood (*ārya*).
Next, the nature of the faculties (*indriya*) is explained as being courageous and robust.
Furthermore, why is it that the path of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is by nature courageous and robust? Because one attains the fruit of progress toward the goal (*phala-pratipannaka*).
For this reason, there is *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) within the desire realm, but not within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Next, there are three kinds [of persons] explained below to clarify the differences in their faculties (*indriya*), as in the text.
Among those who attain *nirvāṇa* while still a "good man" (*satpuruṣa*), there are generally three types: superior, middling, and inferior.

The superior type attains *nirvāṇa* after casting off the body, even before having departed from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The middling type attains *nirvāṇa* upon first departing from the desire realm, but before reaching the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding "descending from the disk" (*paryaṅka*): having already departed from the desire realm and reached the limit of the form realm, one then attains *nirvāṇa*.
This is illustrated by the analogy of a fish descending to the fourth [level]; having completed its movement, it then comes to rest.
It is like a fish that, having obtained food, remains still; this person is also like this. Why is it called "abiding"?

Because they reside in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and have obtained a body, it is therefore called "abiding. They do not receive [the bodies of] those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—humans, devas, hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts—and thus it is called "abiding.
Furthermore, because they have already severed immeasurable fetters of affliction (*kleśa-saṃyojana*) and only a small remainder remains, it is called "abiding."

For this reason it is called "abiding. Furthermore, for what causes and conditions is it called abiding? Because one ultimately never performs actions shared with ordinary worldlings, it is called abiding.
Because one is oneself without fear and does not cause others to fear, it is called abiding.
Because one remains far removed from the two types of craving, stinginess, greed, and anger, it is called abiding.
The one who has reached the other shore corresponds to the seventh person.
Good son, those who have reached the other shore—namely Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas—are likened to a divine tortoise that can travel both on water and on land.
For what reason are they compared to a tortoise? Because it well conceals its five [limbs]. Thus, these Arhats...
From the people of Han up to the Buddhas, it is likewise so: they skillfully conceal the five faculties. Therefore, they are likened to the turtle that moves both on water and on land;
"water" is a metaphor for the mundane world, and "land" is a metaphor for the supramundane. These noble ones are also like this:
because they are able to contemplate all evil afflictions, they reach the other shore; therefore, they are compared to one who travels both on water and on land.
Furthermore, there are four types of persons: first, the Arhat; second, the Pratyekabuddha; third, the Bodhisattva; and fourth, the Buddha.
The former three have all attained partial realization, while the Buddha has reached ultimate perfection.
This is like the third simile regarding the river Gaṅgā. Furthermore, this section has three parts: first, the actual simile; second, the clarification of gain and loss.
Third, distinguishing similarities and differences to reaffirm the preceding meaning. This section consists of three parts: first, a general conclusion regarding the seven types of persons;

second, further questions and answers on doctrinal points; and third, a specific conclusion regarding those who have reached the other shore (*pāramitā*). The first part [the general conclusion] further has two sections: first, concluding that the seven types of persons are those who see the Buddha-nature;
second, concluding that the seven dharmas are themselves the Buddha-nature. This initial passage clarifies the seven [types of persons].
All people are never apart from the water of the Buddha-nature; here are both the analogy and its application.
Good son, it is like the seven kinds of sentient beings in the Ganges River: although they have the names "tortoise" and "fish," they are never apart from the water.
Thus, within this subtle and wondrous Great Nirvana, although there are different names ranging from the icchantika up to the Buddhas, they do not depart from the water of the Buddha-nature.
This concludes the first section on the seven classes of beings;
the following second section clarifies the seven dharmas, which are precisely the Buddha-nature.
"Good son, whether these seven types of sentient beings possess wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas, whether they follow the path of skillful means,

the path of liberation, or the sequential path, and whether they consist of causes or fruits— all of these are the Buddha-nature. This is called the Tathāgata’s speech according to his own intention."

First, the wholesome; second, the unwholesome; third, the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*); fourth, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); fifth, the sequential path (*anukrama-mārga*); sixth, the cause; and seventh, the fruit.
These can be seen as preceding and succeeding one another, with the middle three being the "three paths" of the *Vibhāṣā*:

the path of preparation is the semblance of realization (*pratirūpaka-abhisamaya*), the path of liberation is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the sequential path is the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*). Thus, the *Śarīra-skandha* chapter of the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* states, "in this order."

Non-obstruction necessarily gives rise to liberation. Regarding these seven dharmas as the Buddha-nature, there are two interpretations: first, correlating them sequentially with the seven types of persons;
second, correlating them collectively. As for the sequential correlation: if one possesses wholesome dharmas, they correspond to the second type of person;
ordinary beings who possess even a small amount of wholesome roots correspond to this, whereas those with unwholesome qualities correspond to the first type, those who are perpetually submerged.
Because humans who are extreme icchantikas have no good qualities to discuss, they are said to possess "unwholesome skillful means.
This refers to the third stage, those who have attained abiding and are endowed with the four foundations of mindfulness and the two skillful means of the *uṣmagata* (heat) stage.

As for the path of liberation, it corresponds to the fourth stage, the person who contemplates the directions; from the *mūrdhan* (summit) stage up to the sixteenth moment of mind is the true liberation.
Because it liberates beings, it is called the "Path of Liberation. Regarding the "Successive Path," this refers to the fifth stage:

having combined one's own practice with the Path of Seeing Truths (*darśanamārga*), one subsequently enters the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and attains the state of *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner). Therefore, it is called "successive.

As for the "cause," this refers to having already practiced and now abiding [in that state] before yet attaining Arhatship; since one has just become a *anāgāmin* (Non-returner), it is called the "cause. As for the "fruit," it is...

These seven individuals—the one who has reached the seventh *pāramitā*, the Arhat, the intermediate vehicle practitioner, the Bodhisattva, and the Buddha—comprise four distinct types and two groups, totaling seven persons.
Because these include the aforementioned two types of people (the virtuous and the non-virtuous), they are constantly submerged and emerging within this river; having emerged, they submerge again.
If one relies on the causes, one attains stability from that point up to the stage of *Anāgāmin*. All of these are both cause and effect; specifically, the Arhat is the result.
The four individuals, including Han, are all those who have practiced the preparatory path prior to the fruition; thus, they are all at the stage of the cause.
Below this, the second section discusses the meaning through two rounds of question and answer. The first question has two parts:
[the first asks] how Nirvana can be designated as a "fruition" when it is without a cause.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said: "World-Honored One, if there is a cause, then there is a fruit; if there is no cause, then there is no fruit.
Nirvāṇa is called a 'fruit,' yet because it is eternal, it has no cause. If it has no cause, how can it be called a fruit?"
Next, it is asked: Why is nirvāṇa further called the fruit of the śramaṇa?
Since this nirvāṇa is called both "śramaṇa" and "fruit of the śramaṇa," what is a śramaṇa and what is the fruit of the śramaṇa?
The Buddha’s answer consists of two parts: first he answers the initial question, and subsequently he answers the latter question. This initial response further comprises two sections:
first, it clarifies that the seven fruits and nirvāṇa are the fruit of remoteness (*dūre-phala*).
Good son, there are seven kinds of fruits in all the worlds: first, the fruit of skillful means; second, the fruit of repaying kindness;
third, the fruit of intimacy; fourth, the fruit of remnants; fifth, the fruit of equality; sixth, the fruit of retribution;
and seventh, the fruit of detachment. As for the fruit of skillful means, it is like people in the world who, having harvested much grain in the autumn, [all] mutually...
It is said that one attains the fruit of skillful means (*upāya*). The "fruit of skillful means" refers to the fruit of karmic action (*karmasamudācāra-phala*).
Such a fruit has two kinds of causes: first, the proximate cause (*āsanna-hetu*); second, the remote cause (*viprakṛṣṭa-hetu*). The proximate cause is what is called the seed;
the remote cause refers to water, fertilizer, and human labor. This is termed the "fruit of skillful means. As for the "fruit of gratitude," it is like a person in the world making offerings.
The parents both said: "I have now obtained the fruit of being nurtured; that which can repay this kindness is called 'fruit.
Such a fruit has two kinds of causes: first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.
The proximate cause is the pure, wholesome karma of the parents in the past; the remote cause is the filial son who was born. This is what is meant."

Regarding the fruit of repaying kindness and the fruit of intimacy: for example, suppose there is a person who associates with a virtuous friend and attains the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of *arhat*.
That person proclaims, "I have now attained the fruit of intimacy.
As for such a fruit, there are two kinds of causes: first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause. The proximate is faith; the remote is...

A virtuous friend is called the fruit of association. As for the residual fruits: for example, by virtue of the cause of refraining from killing, one obtains a third body that extends the years and increases longevity;
this is called the residual fruit. Such fruits have two kinds of causes: first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.
The proximate is the purity of body, speech, and mind; the remote is the extension of years and increase of longevity.
What is called the "fruit of remnants" (*avaśeṣa-phala*) and the "fruit of equality" (*sabhāga-phala*) refers to the world-receptacle (*bhājana-loka*). Such fruits are also of two kinds of causes:
first, the proximate cause (*āsanna-hetu*); second, the remote cause (*dūre-hetu*). The proximate cause is what sentient beings cultivate through the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma*);

the remote cause is what are known as the three calamities (*trayo vipattayaḥ*). These are called the fruit of equality. As for the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*), it is like a person who attains purity.
When one has already cultivated the body and purified the karma of body, speech, and mind, that person says, "I have obtained this retribution.
Regarding such a fruit, there are two kinds of causes: first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.

The proximate cause refers to the purity of body, speech, and mind in the present; the remote cause refers to the purity of body, speech, and mind in the past. This is called the retribution of the fruit.
The fruit of detachment is itself nirvāṇa; freedom from all afflictions and all wholesome karma are the causes of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, the proximate cause, and second, the remote cause. The proximate cause is the three gates of liberation;
the remote cause is the wholesome dharmas cultivated over immeasurable lifetimes.
Next, the two causes are explained.
Good son, just as in worldly dharmas one speaks of either the producing cause (*janakahetu*) or the revealing cause (*paridīpanahetu*), so it is with supramundane dharmas:

they are likewise said to have both a producing cause and a revealing cause. Good son, the three gates of liberation... [thirty]... *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*
These seven categories can act as the non-arising cause for all afflictions and also serve as the revealing cause for nirvāṇa.
Son of good family, by distancing oneself from afflictions, one attains the clear vision of nirvāṇa;
therefore, nirvāṇa possesses only a revealing cause and no arising cause.
Regarding *nirvāṇa*, although it can be generally discussed as having a cause, it is also meaningful to explain that non-arising is called the "cause of arising.
In fact, the text states: "The three gates of liberation can act as the 'non-arising cause of arising' for afflictions.

This means they cause afflictions not to arise while allowing wholesome dharmas to arise; this is precisely what is meant by the "causes of penetration" (*prativedha-hetu*) of the three gates of liberation.
That it serves as the cause for birth and yet can also serve as the cause for realizing nirvāṇa is precisely the correct meaning.
As to what you asked previously, I have now answered that subsequent question.
"Noble son, regarding what you asked: 'What is a śramaṇa? What is the fruit of a śramaṇa?'—Noble son," [he continued].

The śramaṇa is the Eightfold Noble Path; the fruit of the śramaṇa is the ultimate and permanent abandonment of all greed, hatred, and delusion through that path—this is called the śramaṇa and the fruit of the śramaṇa.
He possesses three qualities: first, the elimination of poverty; second, the delight in tranquility; and third, being a superior person.
Kāśyapa’s speech follows the second round of question and answer; the initial question further elaborates upon the preceding meaning.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said, “World-Honored One, for what reason is the Eightfold Noble Path called *śramaṇatā*?
Worldly people say that *śramaṇa* means ‘exhaustion’ (*śrama*) and *tā* means ‘path’ (*mārga*). This path severs all exhaustion and severs all paths;
for this reason, the Eightfold Noble Path is named *śramaṇatā*. From this path...”
Because one attains the fruit therein, it is called the "fruit of the śramaṇa. Furthermore, son of good family, as for the term *śramaṇa*:
just as those people in the world who delight in tranquility are also called *śramaṇas*, so too is this Path.

It enables the practitioner to leave behind the evils of body, speech, and mind, as well as wrong livelihood and the like, and to attain the bliss of tranquility; therefore, it is named the *śramaṇa*.
Just as that son of good family who, like an inferior person of the world, can act as a superior person is called a śramaṇa, so too is this path;
because it enables inferior persons to become superior persons, it is therefore named "śramaṇa."
The Buddha replied: "To reverse 'na' is to speak of the name 'śramaṇa,' which means 'one who has severed other deprivations. Other paths are called the Eightfold Noble Path;
these two are not the intended meaning.
As for the Arhat, he is the third [fruit] among the four types of persons who have reached the other shore; furthermore, there are two categories regarding the prior fetters."
Regarding the next section on the Bodhisattva and Buddha following the Pratyekabuddha in the text of the *Han*:
"Good son, those Arhats who cultivate this path attain the fruits of śramaṇaship; for this reason, they are named 'those who have reached the other shore.
The fruit of Arhatship is precisely the fivefold Dharma-body of no-more-learning: precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation."
Liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation are attained by means of these five factors; therefore, it is called "reaching the other shore.

Because one has reached the other shore, one declares of oneself: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence.
Noble son, this is the Arhat, for he has forever severed the causes and conditions for birth throughout the three periods of time.
Therefore, he declared for himself: "My births are exhausted," because he had severed the body of the five aggregates within the three realms. For this reason, he further said:
"Birth is exhausted," because the holy life (*brahmacarya*) he cultivated has reached its ultimate consummation. Therefore, he proclaimed: "The holy life is established.

Furthermore, having relinquished the path of training, it is also called "established"; that which was originally sought has now been attained today. For this reason, he proclaimed: [the holy life is established].

Having completed what was to be done and having attained the fruits through the cultivation of the path, and because he has obtained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), he proclaims:
"I have exhausted all fetters of existence. For this reason, he is called an Arhat who has reached the further shore;
as it is with the Arhat, so it is also with the Pratyekabuddha.
Question: The Pratyekabuddha is a fruit that belongs to the "arrival at the other shore" (pāramitā); to what category does his "path toward it" (pratipannaka) belong? Answer:

Since it was previously stated that the *anāgāmin*-candidate (anāgāmipratipannaka) belongs to the fifth contemplation (*dhyāna*), he proceeds from the basis and takes abiding as the sixth. Within this stage of the candidate, he still practices the *anāgāmin* path;
thus, he does not belong to the fifth person (the *anāgāmin* fruit). Furthermore, this person is also based on the original fruit as the seventh person, and his candidate stage remains as such.
Because they belong to the sixth practice, they abide [therein].
When Bodhisattvas and Buddhas fully accomplish the six pāramitās, it is called "reaching the other shore.
Why is it that once these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they are said to be "fully endowed with the six pāramitās"?
Because they have thereby attained the fruit of the six *pāramitās*, and because they have attained this fruit, they are said to be "complete.
Question: Originally, one who has attained the fruit is the seventh person; since a bodhisattva has not yet attained the fruit, how can they be the seventh person?
Answer: The sutra explains: For what reason is a bodhisattva so called? It is because of practicing the six *pāramitās*. *Pāramitā*...

"Madhu" (honey) is translated as "crossing to the other shore. Furthermore, since the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) correspond to the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*), why would one not be a person who has crossed to the other shore?
Now, it is said that this answer does not resolve the objection; rather, there is another underlying meaning [to be understood] (as elaborated at length).
Regarding these seven types of sentient beings who do not cultivate the body, this second section clarifies gain and loss, which is further divided into three parts:

first, a restatement of the indeterminate nature of the middle way; second, the actual clarification of gain and loss; and third, a summary of the main thesis. Within the first of these [three], there are four sub-sections;
this first part clarifies the person who sinks.
Good son, these seven types of sentient beings do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate precepts, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom.

Being unable to practice these four matters, they are able to commit the five grave offenses of immediate retribution, sever their roots of goodness, violate the four heavy prohibitions, and slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
for this reason, they are called those who are eternally submerged.

Regarding the statement that "the seven types of people are all unable to cultivate body, precepts, mind, and wisdom": those who have attained the four fruits of the path are precisely those capable of cultivation.

Why, then, is it said they cannot understand? This is because initially none of them cultivated [these qualities], but later, through the cultivation of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they reached the other shore.
Those with *icchantika* tendencies cannot cultivate and thus do not reach the other shore; therefore, Buddha-nature is both existent and non-existent.
To claim that "attaining this" means both existing and not existing is to commit a dual negation (and so forth).

Now, I say that one should not interpret it in this way. For the seven types of persons, at the outset, none have yet practiced; while they have not yet practiced, they are not the seventh person. It is only after having practiced that one is called the seventh person.
Yet the scripture clearly states that all seven types of persons are unable to practice. How can you say that the initial state is not the seventh?
The seven persons now clarify this because they specifically refute the universal [view]; thus, none of these seven persons can cultivate the body, precepts, mind, or wisdom.
Herein, Nirvana is universally established as the river; since the textual evidence for this is clear, there is no need to harbor confusion.
Among these seven types of people, the second is explained as those who enter and emerge [from the path]. Good son, among these seven,
there are those who are able to draw near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), listen to and receive the Tathāgata’s true Dharma with a sincere heart,
reflect upon it well within, abide in accordance with the Dharma, and diligently cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom.
Therefore, one is said to have crossed the river of birth and death to reach the other shore.
If anyone should say that those who fall short [of the path]— the third point clarifying that such partial attachments are untenable—
or if anyone should say that an icchantika attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi:
It is called "defiled attachment"; if one says that [attachment] is not obtained, this is called falsehood.
Regarding these seven types of persons, the fourth section below correctly clarifies the Middle Way as indeterminate:
"Good son, among these seven types of persons, there may be one person who possesses all seven, or there may be seven persons each possessing one."

Alternatively, if one person possesses all seven [stages], this refers to the sequence from beginning to end; although they initially commit evil, they gradually practice cultivation until they achieve the second, third, and seventh stages.
Or, if seven people each possess one stage, these should be explained as distinct cases.

If one’s mind and speech are thus, the second section correctly clarifies gain and loss, which is further divided into two parts: first, a single clarification of loss; second, a dual clarification of both gain and loss.
The first part [the single clarification of loss] is further divided into two: first, clarifying loss with respect to the three dharmas; second, concluding on the nature of that loss.

Regarding the first [clarifying loss with respect to the three dharmas], there are three sections: first, regarding icchantikas; second, regarding the noble path; third, regarding the Buddha-nature—in each case, it is determined that [the practice] is impossible.
"Good son, if a person’s thoughts and speech differ, speaking with a divergent view that an icchantika attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
you should know that this person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. If a person’s thoughts and speech differ,
speaking with a divergent view that an icchantika does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this person likewise [slanders the Triple Gem]."
This is called slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Good son, if someone says that the eightfold noble path is attained by ordinary persons, that person also slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
If someone says that the eightfold noble path is not attained by ordinary persons, that person also slanders [the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha].
Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Good son,
if there are those who say that all sentient beings definitely possess the Buddha-nature, or that they definitely lack the Buddha-nature,
these people are also said to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Therefore, regarding the second summary of the meaning of the faults in the sūtras, there are four [points]. First, it proclaims that two types of persons are capable of slandering:
"Good son, for this reason, I have said in the sūtras that there are two kinds of persons who slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. First...
First, because of a mind of lack of faith and anger; second, although one has faith, one does not understand the meaning.
If the mind of faith is inferior, then for the second time, faith and wisdom are mutually absent.
Good son, if a person possesses the mind of faith but lacks wisdom, that person will increase ignorance.
One who possesses wisdom but lacks faith will be able to increase their wrong views.
The third concluding section below, concerning those who lack faith, is entirely slanderous.
Good son, because of a mind of anger, those who lack faith say that the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha does not exist. They do not believe...
Those who lack wisdom have perverted understandings of the meaning [of the Dharma], causing those who hear the teaching to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
For this reason, I say that the fourth fetter is mutually absent.
Son of good family, it is for this reason that I say that because of the mind of hatred in those who lack faith, there is no [hatred] in those who possess faith.
Because of their wisdom, such persons are able to slander the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
If there are those who speak thus, the second pair below clarifies gain and loss; furthermore, this is divided into two parts: first, regarding whether the icchantika attains Buddhahood or not;
second, regarding whether sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature or not. Each of these has three propositions, the first three of which are as follows.
"Good son, if there should be one who says that icchantikas and others who have not yet produced wholesome dharmas attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
this person is also said to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. Furthermore, if there should be one who says [that] an icchantika..."
If one says that an icchantika abandons their current body and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within another body,
such a person is also said to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. Furthermore, if one says that an icchantika can produce roots of goodness,
and having produced these roots of goodness, they continue in an uninterrupted succession until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, therefore [they are not called an icchantika].
One should know that an icchantika who attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is a person who does not slander the Three Jewels.
Of the three types mentioned, the former two are slanders while the latter one is not; why is this so? It is because each takes up only one side, grasping either at existence or at non-existence.

Therefore, two such statements constitute slander; however, if one understands them through the lens of the Middle Way’s accommodative tolerance (*anuloma*), then not a single statement is slanderous.
Some say that if an icchantika does not abandon their evil mind, they will immediately attain Buddhahood—this is slanderous.
Others say that an icchantika cannot attain Buddhahood in this very body, but will attain it in a future body—this too is slanderous.

Regarding the meaning [of "denial"], some say that if an icchantika reforms their evil ways to practice goodness such that the continuum of the virtuous mind is uninterrupted, this is not the meaning of denial;

the same applies to the meaning of Buddha-nature. Others say that if sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and already have within their bodies the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), as well as the perfection of permanence and bliss, and they can attain it simply by severing delusions, this too is the meaning of denial. If one says that sentient beings [possess it] entirely...
To say that there is no Buddha-nature is also called slandering [the Dharma]. Now, if someone says that the Buddha-nature is the future fruit, they fall into this same error.
Good son, if there is anyone who says, "All sentient beings definitely possess Buddha-nature, which is permanent, blissful, self, and pure;

it is not produced and does not arise through the causes and conditions of afflictions, and therefore it cannot be seen," you should know that such a person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Some say that all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature entirely, being like the horns of a rabbit;

they claim it arises from expedient means, being non-existent originally and existing now, and having existed, returning to non-existence. It should be known that such a person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
If one says that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is not existent like space, yet not non-existent like the horns of a rabbit—for what reason? Because space is eternal.

Because the rabbit’s horns do not exist, one may say they both exist and do not exist; because they exist [as a conceptual negation], the non-existence of the rabbit’s horns is refuted, and because they do not exist [as physical entities], emptiness is refuted.
One who speaks in this manner does not slander the Triple Gem.
Regarding the latter three phrases, the first two constitute slander while the last one does not, as the text explains.
Now, as for "Buddha-nature," it is not designated by a name; this third section provides a summary of the main thesis in four parts, the first of which clarifies the principle of Buddha-nature.
Good son, as for the Buddha-nature, it is not called a single dharma, nor ten dharmas, nor a hundred dharmas,
nor a thousand dharmas, nor ten thousand dharmas.
Before attaining bodhi— this second section clarifies that, regarding dharmas, the fruit is spoken of within the cause.
Before attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states are collectively termed "Buddha-nature.
Third, as proof by citation, it is like the Tathāgata’s speaking of the fruit within the cause, or speaking of the cause within the fruit.
The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of the effect within the cause, or speaks of the cause within the effect.
This is called the Tathāgata’s fourth type of speech according to his own intention (*svasaṃtaty-abhiprāya-vāk*).
Because it is speech according to his own intention, it is called the Tathāgata’s speech according to his own intention.
He is named Arhat because he speaks according to his will; therefore, he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Kāśyapa Bodhisattva spoke next—this is the third section, clarifying the similarities and differences [between the Buddha-nature and space]. It is further divided into three parts: first, clarifying that the Buddha-nature is the same as space;
second, clarifying that it differs from space; and third, refuting the heterodox attachments regarding space and the Buddha-nature. Regarding the statement of their similarity and difference:
Sengzhao said: "For those who favor sameness, I speak of sameness; though they are the same, they are different. For those who favor difference, I speak of difference;
though they are different, they are the same. The preceding section clarified that while Buddha-nature shares the same quality as empty space, it is not the same as empty space.
This is the true scripture of the Dharma King, which, through both sameness and difference, refutes the empty space of the non-Buddhists; this is the refutation of the worldly nature-eye.
Regarding the initial clarification that the nature of emptiness is identical [to the Buddha-nature], the text first poses a question and subsequently provides the answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said, "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space.
In what sense is it said to be 'like empty space'?"
In the response there are three parts: first, it clarifies that Buddha-nature is identical to empty space and is not encompassed by the three periods of time;
second, it clarifies that it is identical to empty space and is neither internal nor external; third, it clarifies that it is identical to empty space and is without obstruction.
Good son, the nature of empty space is neither past, nor future, nor present; the Buddha-nature is also thus.
Good son, why is empty space not past? Because there is no present. If a dharma were present, one could speak of it as past;
because there is no present, there is no past. Furthermore, there is no present. Why? Because there is no future.
Because [the future] has not yet come, if the dharma were future, it could be said to be present; however, since there is no future, there is neither present nor future.
Why is this? Because there is no present and no past. If there were a present and a past, then there would be a future.
Since there is no past and no present, there is no future. For this reason, such is the nature of space.
Good son, the three periods of time are not subsumed [within it] because empty space is non-existent; it is not that the three periods of time do not exist because [space] exists.
Just as a flower in the sky does not exist, and thus the three periods of time do not exist, so too is empty space:
because it is not an existing thing, the three periods of time do not exist. Good son, that which is without substance is precisely empty space, the Buddha-nature.

It is likewise, good son: because space is non-existent, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time; because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
Good son, the Tathāgata has already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and all his Buddha-nature and all Buddha-dharmas are eternal and unchanging.
For this reason, they do not exist within the three periods of time, just like space.
Emptiness.
The first section extensively clarifies that the three periods of time are non-existent because they exist only in mutual dependence;
since the three periods do not exist, empty space is not subsumed by them. The text states: "Because empty space is non-existent, it is not of the three periods."
Regarding the summary of its characteristics: how is it that emptiness is simply non-existence, while non-existence is eternal?

Because the Buddha-nature exists and is furthermore eternal, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time. Emptiness is non-existent yet eternal, and likewise is not subsumed by the three periods. Question:
If this is so, then the Buddha-nature would simply exist and not be subsumed by the periods; for what reason is it said to be eternal and not [subject to] the three?
Shiye’s commentary states: Because Buddha-nature is not fully present [in all], it is not said to exist.

Furthermore, because empty space does not exist, it is neither internal nor external. Below this, the second section concerns how Buddha-nature is identical to space, being neither internal nor external.
Good son, because space is non-existent, it is neither internal nor external; because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is neither internal nor external.
Therefore, it is said that the Buddha-nature is like space.
Just as in the world, the third category of the Buddha-nature is identical to space in being without obstruction; no further detailed analysis is required.

Good son, just as in the world that which is without obstruction is called space, so too the Tathāgata, having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, has no obstructions regarding any of the Buddha-dharmas;
therefore, it is said that the Buddha-nature is like space. For this reason, I say that the Buddha-nature is like space.
The second section, following the previous passage, clarifies the meaning of how [the Buddha-nature] differs from empty space through two rounds of question and answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Buddha-nature and Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata are not subsumed within the three periods of time, yet they are called 'existent.
Empty space is likewise not subsumed within the three periods of time; for what reason can it not be called 'existent'?"
Regarding this first question: it is argued that since Buddha-nature, nirvāṇa, and space are all not of the three periods of time—
whereas space is not of the three periods yet is called "existent," and nirvāṇa is not of the three periods yet is called "permanent"— and since both are alike in being beyond the three periods,
why is one not considered "existent" as well?
The Buddha’s answer consists of three parts: first, the topical outline; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion that responds to the initial inquiry.
The topical outline is as stated in the text. The Buddha said: "Good son, that which is not nirvana is called nirvana; that which is not the Tathāgata is called the Tathāgata;
that which is not buddha-nature is called buddha-nature."
What is meant by "next" [in the title]? This explains that all three sections have their respective reasons.
Why is it called "not nirvāṇa"? It refers to all afflictions (*kleśa*) and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). To destroy such conditioned afflictions is what is called "nirvāṇa.
Why is it not the Tathāgata? It refers to those ranging from icchantikas up to pratyekabuddhas.
The Pratyekabuddhas, having destroyed such icchantikas and others up to the stage of Pratyekabuddhahood, are called "Tathāgata" rather than "Buddha-nature.
That which is referred to as "all insentient things— walls, fences, tiles, stones, and the like"—
and that which is apart from such insentient things, is called Buddha-nature.
The three states, beginning with nirvāṇa, are spoken of in mutual relation for the sake of providing benefit; since emptiness provides no such benefit, it is not spoken of in relation to them.
To merely attain this "non-existence" is not what is called "permanence.

In my private view, "benefit" refers solely to protecting those of provisional capacity in the final age who would find it unsuitable to hear that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, or that the two vehicles are themselves the Tathāgata.

These rubble and debris are the Buddha-nature; when a karmic opportunity suddenly arises, one must not fail to speak of it. However, one should rely on the answer provided below, for those words have their source.
Since the *Lotus Sūtra* has already explained this, how could one stubbornly contradict it? Thus the Sūtra says: "The characteristics of the world are eternal.

Do not the worldly terms refer to nothing other than the five aggregates (*skandha*), the lands, and so forth? Furthermore, this applies to the aggregates, realms, and bases (*āyatana*) across both the Great and Small Vehicles regarding form (*rūpa*).
It is not only the primary retribution.
The third section concludes by responding:
"Good son, there is nothing in all the worlds that is not empty space; it stands in relation to empty space."
Because empty space has nothing upon which it depends, it is called "non-existent" (wu); because nirvāṇa has something upon which it depends, it is called "eternal" (chang). Question:
If nirvāṇa is contrasted with non-nirvāṇa, and empty space is likewise contrasted with non-empty space, why is it said that they do not depend on one another?

Answer: It is intended to manifest their mutual relationship. Nirvāṇa is fundamentally beyond all limits, yet it is spoken of as "dependent"; empty space is fundamentally dependent, yet it is spoken of as [non-existent].
Because it transcends the mutual dependence of nirvana, it attains being as "wondrous being" (miaoyou) and emptiness as "wondrous non-being" (miaowu);
because it transcends all dependencies, it is not comparable to [ordinary] examples.

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, even though there is nothing in the world that is not a counterpart to the four great elements, they are nevertheless called 'existent.
Why is it that space, which has no counterpart, cannot likewise be called existent?"

Later, Kāśyapa, following the Buddha’s previous answer, immediately proposed a parallel argument, saying: "The Tathāgata previously stated that because *nirvāṇa* has an opposite, it is therefore 'existent.
If [you claim] space is 'non-existent' because it has no opposite, then the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which also have no opposites, should likewise be non-existent.
Conversely, if the four great elements are existent despite having no opposites, then space should likewise be existent despite having no opposite."
Because the phrasing is not easily altered, there is nothing in the entire world that is not a counterpart to the four great elements; thus, they are still called "the four great elements.
Furthermore, whatever exists in the entire world—all things whatsoever—are the four great elements, and thus all are "existence" (sat).

There is nothing that is not a counterpart to the four great elements. Although [the opponent] continued to set them side by side, the Buddha ultimately did not answer, but merely took "empty space" (ākāśa) as a counterpart.
Regarding the question of why Nirvāṇa does not answer [the same], there is a profound intention. Kāśyapa’s original text states: "The four great elements have no counterpart;
therefore, they are called 'existent. Space, too, should have no counterpart; thus it is 'existent.

Here, we clarify that although the four great elements have no external counterparts, we do not deny that they come to face one another within the four great elements themselves; for example, earth has its own internal oppositions.
Water and the other elements each exist in relation to one another, yet within empty space there is nothing further that exists in relation to itself;
therefore, it is non-existent. Since these [questions] all arise from emptiness, the Buddha did not answer them.
The Buddha replied: "There are three [points]. First, he restates the question and refutes it.
The Buddha said: 'Good son, if you say that nirvana is not subsumed within the three periods of time and that space is likewise so, this meaning is not correct.'"
Why is this? The following two explanations clarify:
Why is it that Nirvana is existent, visible, and realizable; that it is the "footprint" and "chapter-and-verse"; that it is existence, characteristic, condition, and place of refuge;
and that it is tranquility, luminosity, peace, and the further shore? For these reasons, it is so named. It is not [non-existent].
The nature of space encompassed by the three periods of time does not possess such dharmas; therefore, it is called "non-existent.
It is clarified that *nirvāṇa* possesses fifteen phrases, whereas space lacks these fifteen phrases; therefore, it is non-existent.

If there were something apart from these, there would be five possible responses to the correct answer. First, it is clarified that if space existed, it should be included within the four great elements and the three periods of time.
If there were any phenomenon existing apart from such things as these, it should likewise be included within the three periods of time; if space were [such a thing], it would be the same.
That which is an existent dharma cannot be excluded from being subsumed within the three periods of time.
As worldly people say, [this applies] to the second point below, clarifying that if space were an existent, it would necessarily share the same three propositions as the mental factors (*caitta*).
Good son, as worldly people say that space is called formless, non-obstructive, and invisible— if it were formless,
non-obstructive, and invisible, it would then be a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*).
If space were the same as [the aforementioned categories], then according to the third section below, if there is any phenomenon, it must be subsumed within the three periods of time.
If space were the same as a mental factor (*caitta*), it could not fail to be subsumed within the three periods of time.

If that which is subsumed within the three periods of time is indeed the four aggregates (skandhas), as clarified in the fourth [section] below, then whatever is subsumed within the three periods of time is precisely the four aggregates.

It is simply that, being identical to the four aggregates with the single exception of form (rūpa), it is termed the "four aggregates"; yet the four aggregates are not vision, and empty space likewise is not.
If the aggregates are subsumed within the three periods of time, is space likewise so?
Therefore, apart from the four aggregates, there is no fifth aggregate;
thus, once the four aggregates are excluded, there is no such thing as space.

This passage precisely clarifies that if a phenomenon (*dharma*) were existent, one could discuss its dependent relativity; however, since emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is non-existent, what could it possibly depend upon?

Furthermore, regarding the statement "Next, the various non-Buddhists say," this is the third section, which refutes the non-Buddhist conception of emptiness. This section is further divided into two parts: first, the actual refutation.
Holding the sequence, the refutation of the identity and difference [of space] follows the main argument; this section also has two parts:

first, the individual refutation of the eight positions, and second, the general refutation by means of five major examples. First, the individual refutation of the eight positions: (1) refuting that space is light; (2) refuting that space is a dwelling place;
(3) refuting that space is sequential; (4) refuting that space exists in three locations; (5) refuting that space is something produced.

Sixth, the refutation of emptiness regarding the state of non-obstruction; seventh, the simultaneous refutation of both attachments; eighth, the repeated refutation of emptiness as the locus of abiding.
Regarding the first refutation of emptiness as luminosity: the Sarvāstivādins also maintain that among the twenty-one types of form, the form of emptiness belongs to the category of luminous form.
Within this, there are two parts: first, restating their position, and second, refuting it.
Furthermore, son of good family, the various non-Buddhists (tīrthika) say that space (*ākāśa*) is itself luminosity.
If it is luminosity, it is a phenomenon of form (*rūpadharma*). If space were thus a phenomenon of form, it would be impermanent;

being impermanent, it would be subsumed within the three periods of time (*trikāla*). How then can the non-Buddhists say it is not subsumed within the three periods? If it is subsumed within the three periods...
Thus, although space is non-existent, it may also be said that space is permanent.
When the text says, "it may also be said that space is permanent," it should in full read, "it may also not be said to be permanent";
however, because the text is abbreviated, the character "not" (不) is absent. Although space does not exist, it cannot be said that it is permanent; yet, in the end...
This impermanence is merely that these non-Buddhists do not understand the meaning of emptiness; they claim that emptiness is form (*rūpa*).

However, it is within emptiness that light and color are accommodated—how can one say that emptiness is form? If they could indeed say so, one should have said "it cannot," but this was simply omitted for brevity of expression.
Furthermore, there are those who say: [this begins] the second refutation of emptiness as a place of dwelling. First, the proposition is restated, and then the three fetters are refuted.
"Good son, furthermore, there are those who say that empty space is itself a place of dwelling."
If there were a place of abiding, it would be a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*); yet all places are impermanent, subsumed within the three periods of time.
Space (*ākāśa*), however, is permanent and not subsumed within the three periods of time.
If one speaks of a "place," one should know that space does not exist [as such].

Guangzhai says: Since it is stated that the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) has multiple layers and that space (ākāśa) has a location—just as when two rooms, one to the east and one to the west, are respectively full and empty—one should know that the existence of location is likewise refuted in this manner.
Furthermore, there is another explanation stating that the third [type of] refutation of emptiness is a statement of sequence. Regarding "sequence," it is like the following:
when counting people inside a house through a flute-like tube or a window opening, one first sees the space outside through the first window lattice, and then sees it through the second and third;
this is what is meant by sequence. This also first cites [the example].
Next, the refutation:
Furthermore, some say that space is sequential. If it were sequential, it would be a numerical phenomenon;
if it were numerable, it would be subsumed within the three periods of time; if it were subsumed within the three periods of time...
How can it be said that [the self] is permanent?
Furthermore, regarding the statement "below," the fourth section refuting emptiness within three locations consists of three propositions; there are also two parts:
first, restating the position, and second, refuting it.
Good son, if it is further said that space consists of three dharmas—first, emptiness; second, reality; and third, both emptiness and reality—then their reckoning of these three is as follows:

first, they claim that emptiness still resides within the locus of emptiness, yet there is no emptiness within the locus of existence; second, they claim that emptiness resides within the locus of existence.

If there were no place that is empty, how could one say that emptiness exists? A place that is currently decaying, such as a moist and rotting object, is called "having emptiness" while it is in the process of decaying but not yet fully decayed.
If one says that emptiness exists [as a substantial entity], one should know that space is an impermanent phenomenon. Why? Because it does not exist in a real sense. If...
If one says that [space] is real, one should know that space is also impermanent. Why? Because it is non-existent in the locus of emptiness.
If one says that space is real, one should know that space is also impermanent. Why? Because it is non-existent in both loci.
Therefore, space is designated as "non-existent."
The refutation of this attachment follows the text.
As it is said that "space can be produced," the fifth refutation of space as a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) first restates the opponent's position and then refutes it.
Good son, it is as if one were to say that space is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), or as if one were to say that by removing trees or removing houses one creates space,
or that one levels space, or that one covers space, or that one paints the color of space upon space like the waters of the great ocean;
therefore, space is a conditioned phenomenon.

Nowadays, the Sāṃkhya and other schools each maintain that such acts as digging the earth or cutting down trees all result in the attainment of space, and thus regard them all as the "creation of space.
They claim that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, like a clay jar; yet if space were likewise a product of such action, it too would necessarily be impermanent.
Regarding the sixth point, the refutation of the worldly claim concerning the state of non-obstruction: first, the position is restated.
"Good son, worldly people say that among all phenomena, the state of non-obstruction is called 'space'."
Next, to refute that [opponent's] attachment, the first two lines of the middle section establish the presence or absence [of the factors].
Is this state of non-obstruction possessed of all conditioned components in every action?
Next, if one possesses the following objection:
if space were to exist as a whole, one should know it would not exist in other places;
if it existed as parts, it would be a phenomenon that can be counted as "this" or "that," and if it can be counted, one should know it is impermanent.

If you ask whether that which is unimpeded is empty, is this emptiness fully capable of containing the emptiness of the ten directions, or is it not fully capable of containing the emptiness of the ten directions?
If it fully contains the emptiness of the ten directions, one should know that there is no emptiness within those ten directions;
if it does not encompass them all, then it would mean that what exists here is absent there.
If someone were to say that the seventh pair below refutes two attachments— the attachment to both emptiness and existence,
and the attachment to space being within things— this first restates those two attachments.
Good son, if someone were to say that unobstructed space coexists and merges with existing things,
or further claim that space resides within objects like a fruit inside a vessel—
neither of these is correct. Below, the text properly refutes these views, beginning with a general declaration that they are incorrect.
Neither of the two [positions] is tenable.

Next, regarding the passage beginning with "For what reason," the text refutes both attachments simultaneously. Furthermore, within the first section of the preceding refutation of emptiness and existence, there are two parts:
first, the establishment of the three topical headings (*dharmamukha*); second, the sequential explanation of these three topical headings.

Why is this? If one says they combine simultaneously, there are three possibilities regarding the combination of distinct actions: first, the combination of distinct actions is like birds gathering on a tree;
that is, the distinct actions combine like birds gathering on a tree, where only the birds come to roost in the tree while the tree does not come to roost in the birds.
It is also like when objects come together with space, yet space does not come together with objects.
The conjunction of two shared karmas is like two rams butting heads;
the mutual conjunction of two individual karmas is like two rams butting heads. Thus, space also conjoins with objects, and objects also conjoin with space.
Third, "already joined and mutually joined" is like two pairs of fingers joined together in one place.
Regarding "already joined and mutually joined," the function of a thing and the thing itself are already joined;

the substance is the thing, while its movement and activity constitute the function of the thing. When these two—substance and function—are already joined, the function of emptiness and emptiness itself [are likewise joined].

Having already united with emptiness, this is the very essence of emptiness; its function is also the capacity of emptiness to contain and receive. Having already united with this essence and function, one further unites with objects within emptiness, like two fingers that have already been joined and are then joined together again. If one speaks of "different activities," the following explains the three preceding chapters. First, the explanation of the first passage itself has three parts: 1. Regarding the phrase "if one says they are different activities": This means that although the mind and objects are originally non-dual, they are now perceived as distinct. Because they are perceived as distinct, one engages in various mental constructions, such as thinking, "I am here" or "that is there. Because these thoughts arise, one becomes attached to them. Because of this attachment, one gives rise to the karma of the three types of action (body, speech, and mind). Because one gives rise to this karma, one undergoes the retribution of the three realms of existence. Because one undergoes this retribution, one wanders through the cycle of birth and death. Because one wanders through birth and death, one experiences suffering. Because one experiences suffering, one cannot escape it. Thus, because of the initial perception of difference, one subsequently undergoes all manner of suffering. Therefore, it is said that "if one says they are different activities. 2. Regarding the phrase "if one says they are not different activities": This means that although the mind and objects are originally non-dual, they are now perceived as distinct. Because they are perceived as distinct, one engages in various mental constructions, such as thinking, "I am here" or "that is there. Because these thoughts arise, one becomes attached to them. Because of this attachment, one gives rise to the karma of the three types of action. Because one gives rise to this karma, one undergoes the retribution of the three realms of existence. Because one undergoes this retribution, one wanders through the cycle of birth and death. Because one wanders through birth and death, one experiences suffering. Because one experiences suffering, one cannot escape it. Thus, because of the initial perception of difference, one subsequently undergoes all manner of suffering. Therefore, it is said that "if one says they are not different activities. 3. Regarding the phrase "if one says they are both different and not different activities": This means that although the mind and objects are originally non-dual, they are now perceived as distinct. Because they are perceived as distinct, one engages in various mental constructions, such as thinking, "I am here" or "that is there. Because these thoughts arise, one becomes attached to them. Because of this attachment, one gives rise to the karma of the three types of action. Because one gives rise to this karma, one undergoes the retribution of the three realms of existence. Because one undergoes this retribution, one wanders through the cycle of birth and death. Because one wanders through birth and death, one experiences suffering. Because one experiences suffering, one cannot escape it. Thus, because of the initial perception of difference, one subsequently undergoes all manner of suffering. Therefore, it is said that "if one says they are both different and not different activities. Because they are perceived as distinct, one engages in various mental constructions, such as thinking, "I am here" or "that is there. Because these thoughts arise, one becomes attached to them. Because of this attachment, one gives rise to the karma of the three types of action. Because one gives rise to this karma, one undergoes the retribution of the three realms of existence. Because one undergoes this retribution, one wanders through the cycle of birth and death. Because one wanders through birth and death, one experiences suffering. Because one experiences suffering, one cannot escape it. Thus, because of the initial perception of difference, one subsequently undergoes all manner of suffering. Therefore, it is said that "if one says they are neither different nor not different activities. Next, the explanation of the sixth chapter: Regarding the phrase "if one says they are neither different nor not different activities": This means that although the mind and objects are originally non-dual, they are now perceived as distinct. Because they are perceived as distinct, one engages in various mental constructions, such as thinking, "I am here" or "that is there. Because these thoughts arise, one becomes attached to them. Because of this attachment, one gives rise to the karma of the three types of action. Because one gives rise to this karma, one undergoes the retribution of the three realms of existence. Because one undergoes this retribution, one wanders through the cycle of birth and death. Because one wanders through birth and death, one experiences suffering. Because one experiences suffering, one cannot escape it. Thus, because of the initial perception of difference, one subsequently undergoes all manner of suffering. Therefore, it is said that "if one says they are neither different nor not different activities. Next, the explanation of the seventh chapter: Regarding the phrase "if one says they are neither different nor not different activities": This means that although the mind and objects are originally non-dual, they are now perceived as distinct. Because they are perceived as distinct, one engages in various mental constructions, such as thinking, "I am here" or "that is there. Because these thoughts arise, one becomes attached to them.
