Because they are perceived as distinct, one engages in various mental constructions, such as thinking, "I am here" or "that is there. Because these thoughts arise, one becomes attached to them. Because of this attachment, one gives rise to the karma of the three types of action. Because one gives rise to this karma, one undergoes the retribution of the three
The three difficulties regarding permanence are: first, the difficulty of non-permanence; second, the difficulty of permanence;

and third, the difficulty of being both permanent and impermanent. If one says that distinct karmas combine with one another, then there would be two types: first, the karma of material objects, and second, the karma of empty space.

If the karma of empty space combines with a material object, then empty space would be impermanent; if the karma of material objects combines with empty space, then the material object would not be pervasive. If it were not pervasive, [it would contradict the nature of space].
This, too, is impermanent.

Now, first, regarding the objection concerning impermanence: it is stated that "the activity of substance (*dravya*) is itself the activity of motion," and "the activity of space (*ākāśa*) is itself the activity of emptiness.
If one asserts that the activity of emptiness is identical to the emptiness of substance, then substance is impermanent; and since substance is impermanent, [space is likewise so].
If space were to combine with its objects, would it not become impermanent? If the object combines with space, then the object would no longer be omnipresent;
since this [object] has combined with that [space], it should follow that space is also omnipresent, and furthermore, the object should follow space and thus be eternal.

In the *Śata-śāstra*, it is argued that consciousness and so forth are perceived by means of the perception of the self, and so on (as explained therein). However, the present statement differs slightly from that.
Returning here to this [position], you maintain that the substance of things is not pervasive;
how then can it be joined with the statement that "emptiness is impermanent"?
If you say that empty space is permanent, the second [section] below raises the objection regarding permanence, which is further divided into two parts: first, restating the position to refute it.
Next is the formal objection:
If it is claimed that space is eternal and its nature is immovable, yet it unites with moving objects, this is not logically tenable. Why?
Because if space were eternal, objects would also have to be eternal; if objects are impermanent, space must also be impermanent.
The intent of the objection is to demonstrate that both [space and the self] are simultaneously impermanent.
If one says that space is both permanent and impermanent, this constitutes the third objection regarding permanence and impermanence.
If one says that space is both permanent and impermanent, there is no such possibility.
Their intention may be to say that the emptiness of things that are conjoined is itself impermanent, while the emptiness of things that are not conjoined is eternally permanent;
yet they also claim it is both permanent and impermanent. To this, we now directly challenge them by saying:
such a position is untenable, for within the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there is not a single dharma that is half-permanent and half-impermanent.

If [it is argued that] it is produced by common karma, this is refuted at the beginning of the second chapter; furthermore, there are two parts to this, the first of which restates the opponent's position and rejects it.
"If it were produced by common karma, this meaning would not be so. Why is this?
The following section provides the formal refutation.
Why is this? Space is called "pervasive. If it were to combine with karma, karma would also have to be pervasive. If it were pervasive, it would have to be pervasive everywhere.
If it were pervasive everywhere, it would have to combine with everything. Thus, one could not speak of there being both combination and non-combination.

If it is argued that "if emptiness conjoins with karma, then karma should also be omnipresent," this means that if the essence of emptiness conjoins with its function, then the function should also be omnipresent.
If the function of emptiness were omnipresent, it would necessarily be omnipresently conjoined with all things; there could be no emptiness apart from things.
Thus, one should not speak of there being conjunction or non-conjunction.
If it is argued that "that which has already conjoined" conjoins with another, this first restates the third section’s heading and refutes it:
if one says that what has already conjoined conjoins with another— like two fingers joined together— this meaning is not so.
Why is this? Below, the text correctly refutes the existence of a "dharma" within that [space] by means of a syllogism consisting of the reason, the example, and the application.
Why? Because there was no prior application and only later does application occur; since it is non-existent before and existent after, it is an impermanent phenomenon.
Therefore, one cannot say that space has already been applied or is being applied together with something else.
Just as in worldly phenomena, that which first did not exist and subsequently comes into being is impermanent;
if space were likewise so, it too would be impermanent.
To say "first non-existent and subsequently existent" means that space and material objects were not conjoined at an earlier time, but are only conjoined at a later time.

If this were so, then that which was originally non-existent and now exists ought to be impermanent; however, this [argument] only refutes the subsequent conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and does not refute the prior conjunction.

The reason for this is that, regarding the preceding [case], the substance of emptiness and the functional activity of emptiness, as well as the substance of an entity and the functional activity of an entity, must either both be absent or both be present at the same time.
How could it be said that there was no conjunction at a prior time and only then a conjunction occurs at a later time?
Yet those of shallow understanding claim that emptiness is the substance and that its function of "coming" exists only when it arrives;

they say the same applies to objects, whose substance moves only when their function of "motion" occurs. This very [argument] is already included in the refutation of "that which was originally non-existent now exists.
As for the refutation of "that which was previously non-existent now exists," this itself fully subsumes the preceding [arguments].
The latter two [sections] combine to provide a direct refutation of the subsequent [position], while the pair combined provides a lateral refutation of the preceding single combination.
If it is claimed that space exists beneath objects, this refutes the latter attachment; it clarifies that space exists within objects. Furthermore, there are three parts:
first, restating the attachment and refuting it; second, the actual objection; and third, the concluding sentence. This is the first part: restating the attachment and refuting it.
If it is claimed that space exists within objects like fruit inside a vessel, this meaning is not tenable. Why?

Because the following constitutes a formal refutation, which is twofold: first, a logical critique, and second, a parallel refutation. The first [the logical critique] is further divided into three parts;
this is the initial formal critique.
Why is this? When such empty space did not yet possess a vessel, where did it abide?
If one says that when there is a vessel, space exists within the vessel, then when the vessel originally did not exist, where was the space?
If there were a place of abiding, the second objection would entail that there must be many voids.
If there were a place of abiding where space is abundant, then before the vessel existed there was already one void, and after the vessel exists there is yet another void; how could this not be many?
Empty.
Regarding the phrase "if it were manifold," this concludes the third section on refuting errors.
If it were manifold, how could one say it is permanent, or that a single sound is all-pervasive?

In general, there are three fallacies: first, one must not say it is permanent; for how could that which was previously the emptiness of no vessel now become the emptiness of a vessel and yet be permanent?
Second, one must not say it is one; this can be understood. Third, one must not say it is pervasive;
for when there is a vessel, the emptiness is not the emptiness of no vessel—how could the emptiness be pervasive?
If space were to abide apart from space, this would constitute the second simultaneous refutation:
if space were to abide apart from space, then material objects should likewise be able to abide apart from space.

If one were to claim that space when there is no vessel exists separately from space when there is a vessel, and that objects which occupy a location likewise exist separately from space at their location,
then one should know that the third concluding sentence below is evident [as a refutation].
Therefore, one should know that there is no such thing as empty space.
If someone were to say that the eighth layer below where the finger points is the place where space resides, this too would first be restated and then subsequently refuted.
Good son, if there were one who said that the place where a finger points to is called "space," you should know that space is an impermanent phenomenon.
Why? Because the finger has four sides; if it has four sides, you should know that space also has four sides.
All permanent phenomena are entirely devoid of sides; because [space] has sides, it is not permanent.
If emptiness is impermanent, it cannot be separate from the five aggregates; yet if it were to be separate from the five aggregates, it would be non-existent.

As for what is called the "abode," if one says that all abodes are the abode of empty space, since there are four directions, if these directions were distinct [from space], then space would have to abide within those four directions.

Regarding the dharmas that abide through causes and conditions: this second summary, which cites the five great elements as examples to refute [the notion of permanence], may be investigated accordingly.
"Good son, if a dharma abides by means of causes and conditions, you should know that such a dharma is called impermanent.
Good son, for example, all sentient beings and trees abide because of the earth; since the earth is impermanent, those things that abide upon the earth [are likewise impermanent]."
The sequence of all things is impermanent. Good son, for example, earth depends on water; because water is impermanent, earth is also impermanent.
Water depends on wind; because wind is impermanent, water is also impermanent. Wind relies upon space; because space is impermanent, wind is also impermanent.
If it is impermanent, how can you say that space is eternal, pervasive, and singular?

In all respects, because space (*ākāśa*) does not exist, it is not of the past. [This concludes] the refutation of the non-Buddhists' attachment to the middle. Next, the similarities and differences are summarized:
as for what is said to be the same, *nirvāṇa* and space are alike in being devoid of the three periods of time; as for what is said to be different, *nirvāṇa* is eternal.
Space is non-existent; furthermore, first it is clarified that space is not of the three periods of time.
Because space does not exist, it is neither past, future, nor present.
Next, it is shown that even a rabbit’s horn is likewise not [of the three periods].

Furthermore, just as a rabbit’s horn is a non-entity and therefore does not belong to the past, future, or present, I have thus explained the similarities and differences regarding the three lower fetters.

For this reason, I say that because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time; and because space is a non-entity, it is likewise not subsumed within the three periods of time.
Good son, I never grant the function of the third stage of practice within the intermediate illumination for the purpose of dispelling delusions;
it is also called the function of non-contention. Why is it able to eliminate delusions? Because one has already attained the contemplation of the Middle Way and is thus able to remove them.
If this contemplation were absent, by what means could they be severed? This is divided into two major sections: first, explaining how the Tathāgata’s practice and understanding are perfected.

Therefore, it is said that one does not contend with the world. This second point clarifies how bodhisattvas and others contemplate and resolve delusions. The preceding section further consists of three parts:
first, contemplative resolution; second, doctrinal discussion; and third, the conclusion establishing the function of non-contention. This is the first part.
"Good son, I never dispute with the world. Why is this? When worldly wisdom speaks of a self, I also speak of a self;
when worldly wisdom speaks of no-self, I also speak of no-self."
The worldly wise person explains the principle within their own being through both existence and non-existence;
the Buddha likewise does not contradict such explanations, for he has attained the Middle Way. Therefore, because he is in harmony with all things, he does not engage in dispute.
Is this not the function of the Middle Way’s contemplative understanding? The words spoken by worldly fools deviate from reason and do not accord with the true nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
It is said that there is no one who contradicts the Buddha’s intent, let alone those who dispute with the Buddha—how much less so ordinary people of the world.

Kāśyapa Bodhisattva spoke [as follows]; this is the second section on the discussion of principles, which consists of four rounds of question and answer. This first round begins with a question followed by an answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said, “World-Honored One, how many dharmas must a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva fulfill so as not to contend with the world and not be defiled by worldly dharmas?
In the answer, there are three parts; first, the ten dharmas are proclaimed.
The Buddha said: "Good son, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, he does not contend with the world and is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
He then enumerated the ten dharmas.
What are these eleven? First, faith; second, possessing ethical discipline; third, associating with virtuous friends;
fourth, internal reflection; fifth, being endowed with diligence; sixth, being endowed with right mindfulness;
seventh, being endowed with wisdom; eighth, being endowed with right speech; ninth, delighting in the true Dharma; tenth, having compassion for sentient beings.
Free from the three fetters and non-contentious,
son of good family, a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with these ten dharmas does not dispute with the world and is not defiled by worldly dharmas,
just like an utpala lotus.
In both instances where the two phrases for the formal act of binding (*karmavācanā*) are recited, the character "沾" (zhān) must be pronounced with the tone of "diǎn.
Next, the second round of question and answer discusses whether what is spoken by worldly wisdom exists or does not exist, which can be seen from the inquiry.

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, there are those of worldly wisdom who say 'there is a self' and also say 'there is no self,' and there are those of worldly wisdom who say 'there is no self' and also say 'there is a self.
What is meant by the existence and non-existence [of a self] according to worldly wisdom?"
In the answer, regarding the substance of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*), there are again two parts; first, it clarifies existence.

The Buddha said: "Good son, if worldly wisdom (*loka-jñāna*) says that form (*rūpa*) is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and so on up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is likewise—good son, this is called worldly wisdom speaking of existence, and I also speak of existence."
Next, the non-existence [of self] is explained.
Good son, worldly wisdom says that form (rūpa) lacks permanence, bliss, self, and purity; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Good son, this is called worldly wisdom speaking of no-self and also speaking of non-existence.
Next, within the third round of questioning, there are two parts; first, the actual formulation of the contradictory question.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, those who are wise in the world are precisely Bodhisattvas and all noble ones (*ārya*).
If for all these noble ones form (*rūpa*) is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, why does the Tathāgata speak of the Buddha?”
The physical body is eternal and unchanging; yet the wise of the world say that no such thing exists. How then can the Tathāgata say it exists?
The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, has spoken thus; how then can he also say that he does not contend with the world and is not defiled by worldly dharmas?
Next, there is the contradiction regarding the Buddha’s possession of inversion.

Since the Tathāgata has already abandoned the three kinds of inversion—namely, inversion of perception, inversion of thought, and inversion of view—it should be said that the Buddha’s physical form is truly impermanent;
yet now it is said to be permanent. How, then, can he be called one who is free from inversion and does not contend with the world?
The Buddha said, "Good son, the form of ordinary beings arises from afflictions; therefore, wisdom declares that form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
The form of a Tathāgata is far removed from afflictions; therefore, it is said to be permanent, eternal, and unchanging."

In the response, it is clarified that there is no contradiction, as each position has its own basis: because the form (*rūpa*) of sentient beings arises from afflictions (*kleśa*), such form is "without Buddha";
yet, because such [afflicted] form does not exist [in the ultimate sense], [the Buddha's] form exists.
Next, the fourth question and answer clarifies the characteristics of the permanence and impermanence of form (*rūpa*).
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said, "World-Honored One, how is it that form arises from afflictions?
This question contains two meanings: first, it asks how the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) arises from afflictions and yet attains this state of impermanence.
The second question asks: "How is it that form does not arise from afflictions and yet attains permanence? In the response, both meanings are fully explained;
however, as this question is abbreviated, it mentions only one side—that form arising from afflictions is impermanent.

The Buddha’s response has three parts: first, clarifying that contemplation and non-contemplation are the roots of permanence and impermanence; second, correctly clarifying the fruits of permanence and impermanence;
third, concluding by identifying the persons to whom these apply. The first section further divides into two: first, a general clarification of contemplation and non-contemplation;
second, a specific clarification of those who contemplate (which may also be described as first brief and then detailed). Within the detailed section, only one [type] is clarified.
The preceding text further contains four sections: first, it clarifies that the three outflows (*āsrava*) are the objects of observation, stating that "the wise person should immediately...
Second, it identifies the observer, stating "as if a person were leading a blind man... Third, it identifies those who cannot observe, stating "there are four kinds of people...
Fourth, it presents two types of persons together; the first two are as explained in the text.
Good son, there are three kinds of afflictions, namely: the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
A wise person should contemplate the faults inherent in these three outflows. Why is this? Because once one has recognized their faults, one is able to distance oneself from them.
It is, for example, like a physician who first examines the patient’s pulse to know where the illness lies, and only then administers the medicine.
Good son, it is like a person who leads a blind man into a thicket of thorns and abandons him there before returning;
the blind man will find it extremely difficult to escape from behind, and even if he does escape, his body will be utterly ruined. Worldly ordinary people are just like this:

if they cannot know and see the faults and afflictions of the three outflows (*āsrava*), they will follow them wherever they go; but if they can see them, they will be able to distance themselves from them and know [the way out].
Although one has already passed beyond [the stage] and receives retribution, the retribution is slight.
In the third passage, "those who do not observe" refers to people; the "blind" is a metaphor for the three outflows (*āsrava*); and the "thorns" are a metaphor for the evil realms (*durgati*).

This is intended to clarify that the three outflows drag all sentient beings and cause them to fall into the evil realms; even if they emerge from the evil realms, they remain within the *dharmakāya*.
Because the Dharma-body is destroyed, the three bodies are all utterly ruined.
Good son, there are four kinds of persons: first, those who perform heavy karma but receive light retribution; second, those who perform light karma but receive heavy retribution;
third, those who perform heavy karma and receive heavy retribution as well; fourth, those who perform light karma and receive... [light retribution].
The retribution is also light.
Among the four pairs of fetters and two types of persons, there are four propositions: the first two concern those who do or do not contemplate;
the latter two concern those who act according to their karma.

If a person can contemplate the faults and transgressions of afflictions, that person’s karma and the retribution they receive will both be light. Furthermore, there are two ways to contemplate: first, contemplating the person who contemplates, which is further divided into two; first, contemplating the person who contemplates alone.
Good son, if a person can contemplate the faults and transgressions of afflictions, the karma they create and the retribution they receive will both be light.
Next, the person is explained in detail, which is further divided into two parts: first, the general, and second, the specific. Within the general section, there are again two parts;
this is the first, which correctly explains the contemplation of outflows (*āsrava*) in six phrases.
"Good son, a wise person reflects thus: 'I should distance myself from such outflows as these. Furthermore—
Furthermore, one should not commit such base and evil deeds. Why?

Because I have not yet attained liberation from the retributions of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas. If I cultivate the Path, I shall, by the power of this practice, destroy all sufferings.
Having contemplated this, his greed, anger, and delusion become feeble; thus he perceives greed, anger, and delusion for what they are.
Having become light, his mind is joyful.
He further reflects as follows; the next two lines clarify that he himself is capable of diligent cultivation, which also consists of five phrases.
He further reflects: "Now, all this is due to the power of the causal conditions of practicing the path, which has enabled me to attain liberation."
By associating with unwholesome dharmas and approaching wholesome dharmas, one shall now behold the True Path;

therefore, one should apply oneself with diligence to its cultivation. Through this power of diligently cultivating the Path, such a person will distance themselves from immeasurable evil afflictions and escape the retributive fruits of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.
Therefore, in the second section below, the contemplation of outflows (*āsrava*) is specifically explained in two parts: first, the actual explanation of contemplating the outflows;

second, the explanation of being able to diligently cultivate [this practice] oneself. The preceding text has three sections; this is the first, wherein one first contemplates the phenomena that serve as causes for existence, using both scripture and analogy.
Therefore, in the sūtras I have said that one should contemplate all out-flowing afflictions (*āsrava*) as well as the causes of those out-flows. Why is this?
Because if a person of wisdom contemplates only the out-flows without contemplating their causes, they will be unable to sever those afflictions. Why is this?
Because the wise person observes that the out-flows arise from these causes; I shall now sever the causes so that the out-flows cease.
Then it will not arise.
Good son, just as that physician first eliminates the cause of the disease so that the disease does not arise,
so too is it for the wise one who first eliminates the causes of affliction.
A person of wisdom next contemplates the retribution of results.
A person of wisdom should first contemplate the cause and then contemplate the retribution of the result;

they know that from a virtuous cause a virtuous result arises, and they know that from an unwholesome cause an unwholesome result arises. Having contemplated the retribution of results, they distance themselves from unwholesome causes.
Having contemplated the karmic retribution, one next contemplates the gravity [of the afflictions] through the following three contemplations.
Having contemplated the retribution, one should then proceed to contemplate the gravity of the afflictions. Once the gravity has been contemplated, one first abandons what is heavy;
once the heavy has been abandoned, the light will depart of its own accord.
If a wise person knows these two lower types of clarity, they will naturally be able to diligently practice; this also includes the application of both dharma and analogy.

Son of good family, if a wise person knows afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retributions of afflictions, and the gravity or lightness of afflictions, that person at such a time will diligently cultivate the Way without ceasing or regretting it, drawing near to virtuous friends and listening to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
In order to extinguish such afflictions, noble son,
it is like a sick person who knows for himself that his illness is light and will surely be cured; even if he must take bitter medicine,
he does not regret it.
The person of wisdom is likewise: they diligently cultivate the Noble Path with joy, without sorrow, without ceasing, and without regret.
If one can know that afflictions lead to the two lower [results], this correctly clarifies the results of the eternal and the impermanent; furthermore, there are two points:
first, it clarifies that if one does not arise from afflictions, one will obtain the eternal result.
Good son, if a person can know afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the gravity of afflictions,
and diligently cultivates the Path for the sake of eliminating afflictions, that person does not give rise to form, feeling, perception, mental formations,
or consciousness from afflictions; it is likewise so for the others.
Next, it is explained that from afflictions arise impermanent fruits.
If one cannot know the afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the gravity of afflictions,
and does not diligently practice cultivation, then for such a person, form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness will likewise arise from afflictions.
One who knows afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the persons to whom the three lower fetters belong, and furthermore, those who have previously attained the fruit of permanence—
namely, the Tathāgata— is a son of good family. Such a person knows afflictions,
the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the lightness or heaviness of afflictions, for the purpose of severing them.
To afflict those who practice the Path is precisely what the Tathāgata does; for this reason, the form of the Tathāgata is eternal, and so on, up to consciousness being eternal.
Next, it clarifies that those who obtain the fruit of impermanence are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Good son, those who do not know afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retributions of afflictions, or the gravity of afflictions, and thus cannot cultivate the Path,

are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, for ordinary persons, form (*rūpa*) is impermanent, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are all impermanent.
Section Three: Returning to the Conclusion on the Utility of Non-Contention.
"Good son, what the world’s wise ones, all the sages, bodhisattvas, and buddhas call these two meanings, I likewise call these two meanings.
Therefore, I say that I do not contend with the world’s wise ones."
They are defiled by worldly dharmas.

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: [This concludes the second section, clarifying that the Bodhisattva’s elimination of delusion consists precisely in these Bodhisattvas practicing this contemplative understanding to sever all fetters and outflows.
If there were no power and function of the Middle Way, how could one cause the afflictions and latent tendencies to be eliminated?]

Furthermore, there are four [sections] for the complete exhaustion: first, contemplating the essence of the outflows (*āsrava*); second, contemplating the cause of the outflows; third, contemplating the fruit of the outflows; and fourth, concluding with the wisdom of contemplation.
Regarding the first, the contemplation of the essence of the outflows, there are three rounds of question and answer. This initial passage first asks about the essence of the three outflows.

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what the Buddha has taught concerning the three outflows (*āsrava*), how are they defined as the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*)?"

In the Buddha’s response, he explains that the three outflows (*āsrava*) constitute the first three [categories]. First, he clarifies the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), which is further divided into three parts: first, the definition of its essence; second, the citation of scriptural evidence;
and third, the conclusion of its name. Regarding the first, the definition of its essence, the Buddha said:
"Good son, as for the outflow of desire, it arises from internal unwholesome vitarka and vicāra, conditioned by external objects, thereby producing the outflow of desire."
The internal contemplation of evil refers to the internal mind, while its dependence on external conditions refers to the external objects.
Therefore, I previously cited a second scriptural proof, stating:
"In the past, while I was in Rājagṛha, I told Ānanda: 'Ānanda, you are now receiving this woman.'"
The verse that has been spoken was proclaimed by the Buddhas of the past. This verse appears in the *Udānavarga*:
Once, as the Buddha was walking with Ānanda, he saw a woman carrying her child to draw water.
Seeing a man, she immediately conceived a lustful mind and gazed at him without ceasing; consequently, she tied the child’s neck [with a rope] and pulled the child inside.
In the well, he then spoke a verse to praise himself, saying: "O Desire, I know your root; you arise from conceptual thought (*saṃkalpa*).
If I do not engage in such thought, you shall not arise. While the wording of this teaching may vary slightly, it clarifies that the three outflows (*āsrava*) differ in two respects.
In the preceding "Chapter on the Virtuous King," all afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) were excluded, with the exception of ignorance (*avidyā*).

It is explained that the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) consists of the afflictions of the upper two realms excluding ignorance; the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) comprises the ignorance of all three realms;
and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) consists of ignorance conjoined with the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

In the present text, that which is clarified is that craving within the desire realm constitutes the outflow of desire, craving in the upper two realms constitutes the outflow of existence, and ignorance combined with the view of self constitutes the outflow of ignorance.
Therefore, all that is inferior is designated as the third fetter.
Consequently, all internal evil thoughts and external conditions are called "desire" (*kāma*); this is termed the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsava*).
Next, regarding the explanation of the outflows with taints (*sāsrava*), there are also three parts. First, the essential nature of the outflows is set forth:
that which is "with outflows" refers to all unwholesome dharmas within the realms of form and formlessness, as well as external causes and conditions.
Next, it distinguishes these from the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
Excluding the external causes and conditions and internal applied and sustained thought within the desire realm,
the names of the three fetters are called "with outflows" (sāsrava).
Next, the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) is explained in two parts: first, its essential nature is set forth; second, how it gives rise to the various outflows is clarified.
Regarding the outflow of ignorance: that which is unable to discern "self" and "what belongs to self," and fails to distinguish between the internal and external, is called the outflow of ignorance.
The first line of this [passage] defines the essential nature [of the outflows], while the section from "From ignorance, all...
onwards is the second part, clarifying how they can produce the various outflows; this text consists of three sections: the citation, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Good son, ignorance is the root of all outflows (*āsrava*). Why is this?

Because all sentient beings, through the conditions of ignorance, give rise to conceptualizations and signs regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); these are called "sentient beings.

This is termed a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), a perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and a perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*). By means of these causes and conditions, all outflows are produced.
Therefore, in the twelvefold division of the scriptures, I have stated that ignorance is the cause of greed, the cause of hatred, and the cause of delusion.
Kāśyapa then asked: "The Tathāgata has previously provided a second round of questions and answers; why does he now speak differently?"

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the World-Honored One: “World-Honored One, in the past the Tathāgata spoke in the twelve divisions of the scriptures that greed, hatred, and delusion arise due to the causal condition of improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*); for what reason does he now say they arise from ignorance (*avidyā*)?”
Regarding these two dharmas, the Buddha’s response below consists of three parts; first, he proclaims the two topical headings:
"Good son, these two dharmas serve as cause and effect for one another and mutually increase each other."
First, mutual causality; second, mutual growth.
Regarding the second section of the chapter on explanation, which first explains mutual causality:
unwholesome reflection gives rise to ignorance, and with ignorance as a causal condition, unwholesome reflection arises.
It is able to produce and increase the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Good son, that which can produce and grow all afflictions (*kleśa*) is entirely called the causes and conditions of affliction.
To draw near to such causes and conditions of affliction is called ignorance (*avidyā*) and unwholesome reflection (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
"Like a seed producing a sprout" concludes the third analogy below.
Just as the seed is the proximate cause for the production of the sprout, while the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the remote causes, so too it is with the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha" introduces the third round of question and answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, according to what the Buddha has taught, ignorance itself is the outflow (*āsrava*);
why then do you further say that the various outflows arise because of ignorance?"

Question: The meaning of the question is this: Previously, before the Buddha, it was stated that the third outflow (*āsrava*) is ignorance (*avidyā*); how is it now said that [the other two] arise from ignorance?
The Buddha says: "As I have taught... [The Buddha answers: Furthermore, there are first mentioned two types of ignorance.
The Buddha said, "Good son, as I have taught, that which is the 'outflow of ignorance' (avidyā-āsava) is the internal cause of ignorance;
that which gives rise to various outflows from ignorance is the internal-and-external cause."
Regarding the second explanation of the two types of ignorance (*avidyā*) mentioned below: first, it clarifies that the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) is internal ignorance;
next, it explains that what arises from it is the external outflow.
If one speaks of the outflow of ignorance, it is called internal perversion—the failure to recognize impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
If one speaks of the causal conditions for all afflictions, it is called not knowing the external "self" and "what belongs to the self."
Not understanding within the inner mind is internal ignorance, while the further arising of afflictions externally is external ignorance.
If one speaks of the third fetter, the outflow of ignorance, it consists of these two fruits.

If one speaks of the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), it is called "without beginning and without end," for from ignorance arise the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

To say that the outflow of ignorance is without beginning or end means that one attains the fruit of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) which is itself without beginning or end;

herein, ignorance is the first [link] and is able to produce the fruits of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth. Such causal conditions [operate] throughout the three periods of time.

The cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) is said to be without beginning or end; yet, if one attains the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), it can burn away the conditions of dependent origination so that they come to have a beginning and an end, thereby turning back from birth and death toward the finality of *nirvāṇa*.

As for the statement "the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and so forth arise from ignorance," this means that from ignorance arise the various outflows (*āsrava*), which in turn bring about the fruit of the aggregates.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: [This concludes the second contemplation on the causes of outflows, which consists of two rounds of question and answer; this is the first question.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught that a person of wisdom knows the causes of outflows, what is meant by 'knowing the causes of outflows'?"
The wise should contemplate that the Buddha’s answer consists of four parts; this first section clarifies external causes. "Good son, the wise should contemplate:
by what causes and conditions do these afflictions arise? What actions are performed that give rise to these afflictions?
At what time do these afflictions arise? With whom does one dwell when these afflictions arise? What [is the cause]...?

Regarding the dwelling where one resides and where these afflictions arise: having observed what object has given rise to the affliction, and from whom—whether from the recipient of lodgings, bedding, food, clothing, or medicinal requisites—the affliction has arisen?
For what reason does that which was inferior transform into the intermediate-inferior? This second section clarifies the internal causes:

by what causes and conditions does that which was inferior transform into the intermediate, and that which was intermediate transform into the superior; how do inferior actions become intermediate, and intermediate actions become superior?
When the bodhisattva performs this contemplation— this is the third section, clarifying that through contemplation one attains the Way—
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while performing such contemplation, becomes far removed from the causes and conditions for the arising of outflows (*āsrava*). While contemplating in this way,
he prevents unarisen afflictions from arising and brings already arisen afflictions to their cessation.
Therefore, I shall cite a scriptural proof below in the fourth section.
Thus, in the sūtra, I said: "The wise should contemplate the causes from which afflictions arise.
Kāśyapa then spoke, beginning with the first question of the subsequent series of questions and answers concerning sentient beings having but one body.

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how can a single body of a sentient being give rise to various kinds of afflictions? The Buddha first provided an analogy and then applied it to the point at hand. **The Analogy:** It is like a single vessel into which [various substances] are poured. **The Application:** Similarly, within the single body of a sentient being, various afflictions arise.

Just as different flavors and essences manifest when diverse ingredients are placed into one container, so too do manifold afflictions emerge from the single basis of the body. Thus, although the physical form is one, the afflictions that arise are manifold. This demonstrates that the nature of the afflictions is not fixed; depending on conditions, they manifest in diverse ways. Therefore, even though the body is singular, the afflictions produced therein are varied. This concludes the response.
The Buddha said: "Good son, it is like various kinds of seeds within a single vessel that, having received water and rain, each sprout forth on their own.
In the initial analogy, the phrase 'like a single vessel' refers to a single spiritual consciousness (śubhāśaya), while 'various kinds of seeds' refers to the formations (saṃskāra)."

Regarding the statement that "the various afflictions arise individually upon obtaining [their objects]," this means that when one obtains the perception of characteristics, they each arise from themselves:
if one perceives favorable characteristics, greed arises; if one perceives unfavorable characteristics, hatred arises.
Next, the analogy is combined [with the teaching].
Sentient beings are also like this: although the vessel is one, it is due to the conditions of craving that various afflictions are able to grow.
As for saying that afflictions arise due to the conditions of craving, this refers to taking up signs (nimitta), which is called craving;
alternatively, it is said that craving does not necessarily imply the explicit grasping of signs.
Following Kāśyapa’s words, the third contemplation on the fruit of outflows (*āsrava-phala*) also consists of two questions and answers; this is the first question.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said: "World-Honored One, how does the wise one contemplate the retribution of the fruit?"
In the response, there are again two parts: first, clarifying the fruit of retribution; second, clarifying the fruit of habituation.
"Good son, the wise should contemplate that the causal conditions of the outflows (āsrava) can produce birth in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals;
yet, through these same causal conditions of the outflows, one obtains the bodies of humans and devas—which are themselves impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—within this vessel-like body."
Regarding the three kinds of suffering and the three kinds of impermanence within the fruit of retribution, there are two interpretations. One states:

the three sufferings are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); the three impermanences are first, arising and ceasing; second, flux and movement; and third, great destruction.
The second period states: "This refers to the three realms being the three types of suffering and the three types of impermanence," which means that the three realms are all impermanent.

These are the causes and conditions of outflows (*āsrava*) that enable sentient beings to commit the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), undergo various evil retributions, and sever their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Regarding those who commit the four grave prohibitions or slander the Triple Gem, the wise should contemplate:
"Since I have already received such a body, I ought not to give rise to such afflictions that would lead me to undergo these evil fruits."
Kāśyapa said, "The Buddha possesses the outflow-free [dharmas]. This is the second section, which distinguishes the retribution of the outflow-free.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the brief, and second, the detailed. Regarding the brief, there are three further points: first, the proclamation that there is the outflow-free fruit.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said, "World-Honored One, there is the fruit of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
The two types of wise ones possess the fruit of cessation.
Furthermore, it is said that the wise one cuts off all fruits of retribution."
The third question concerns the fruit of the cessation of outflows (*anāsrava-phala*).
Is the retribution of the fruit of outflowlessness contained within that cessation?

Among the various attainments of those who have entered the Path, this second section of extensive questioning also consists of three parts; herein, for the first time, it proclaims the existence of the fruit of outflowlessness.
All those who have attained the Way possess the fruit of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
According to that wise one, [the text] explains below in the second section how it is said that [defilements] are abandoned.
According to that wise one who seeks the fruit of outflowlessness, why does the Buddha say that all-knowing ones (*sarvajña*) should abandon the retribution of the fruits?
Regarding the phrase "if it were severed," the third question below asks: "How can one say it exists?
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "if it were severed," [the questioner asks]: "How could the various noble ones (āryas) now possess it? The intent of the question is this:
there are both tainted fruits (*sāsrava-phala*) and untainted fruits (*anāsrava-phala*); if the noble ones were to sever the untainted [fruit], how could they possess it?
Regarding the question of how one can obtain the retribution of the fruits of sainthood (*ārya-phala*), the Buddha’s answer contains two meanings:

first, speaking from the perspective of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), there is no retribution in that which is untainted (*anāsrava*); what is here called "having" refers to the fruit being spoken of within the cause.

Furthermore, the Buddha’s answer has three parts: first, he cites the mutual explanation of cause and fruit; second, he clarifies that the untainted has no fruit; third, he clarifies that it is non-existent.
Regarding the first of the three phrases concerning the fruit of afflictions in the preceding text, it was initially stated that the Tathāgata has two ways of teaching.
"Good son, the Tathāgata sometimes speaks of the fruit within the cause, and sometimes speaks of the cause within the fruit."
Next, the second section clarifies the assertions of worldly people.
As worldly people say that "clay is the jar" or "thread is the garment," this is called speaking of the effect within the cause or speaking of the cause within the effect—
such as saying "the ox is the grass and water" or "the person is the food."
I am also like this; here follows the third section, which sets forth the Tathāgata’s teaching.
I am also like this: within the causal state, one speaks of the result. Previously, in the sūtras, it was stated:

"From the mind-body [because the body moves according to the mind, therefore 'mind-body'], I reach the limits of the Brahma-world. This is called speaking of the result within the cause. Speaking of the cause within the result is as follows: [text continues].
The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are called past karma; this is termed "stating the cause within the effect.
To say that the body extends from the mind up to the limit of the Brahma-heaven is to state the effect within the cause;

that is, taking the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) as the body and the meditative concentration of the First Dhyāna as the mind—since concentration is mental action (*manaskarma*), it is called "mind," and for this reason, form is always [associated with] the mind.

The elements give rise to the mind, and this mind constitutes the body; this is what is meant by "concentration of the mind. Although the mind in reality is not the body, it is able to obtain a body, and thus it is called the "body.
This can be seen as an instance of expressing the effect within the cause, or expressing the cause within the effect.
The second section below clarifies that there is no outflow (anāsrava) result for all noble ones (ārya).
Good son, for all noble ones, there is truly no such thing as an outflow result;
because the results of the path cultivated by all noble ones do not give rise to further outflows, they are therefore called "outflow-free results."
This means that within the three realms, one receives retribution solely through tainted (*sāsrava*) karma; therefore, it is said that there is no untainted (*anāsrava*) fruit.
Although the subsequent phrase again mentions "untainted fruit," this is a case of designating the cause as the fruit.

Because this untainted [cause] can attain the fruit of Buddhahood, the cause—though not actually a fruit—is designated as the fruit because it is capable of attaining the fruit. Thus, the cause is called the fruit.
The third section, clarifying that there is no fruit of afflictions for those with wisdom, is further divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the severing of delusions:
"Good son, when a person of wisdom contemplates in this manner, they will attain the permanent extinction of the retribution of afflictions."
Next, the section beginning with "The wise one" clarifies the cultivation of the path (*mārga-bhāvanā*).
O son of good family, having observed thus, the wise one cultivates the noble path in order to sever such afflictions and their karmic retributions.
The section beginning with "The noble path" concludes the fourth [section] on the wisdom of observation.
The Noble Path is precisely emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; having cultivated this path, one is able to extinguish all afflictions and their karmic retributions.

The Fourth Chapter on Kāśyapa, Volume Three:
A Single Section Clarifying the Arising of Wholesome Roots, consisting of two rounds of question and answer. This section has three parts: first, the introductory context (*nidāna*);
second, the formal questioning; and third, the concluding summary of the questions. Within the introductory context, there is the teaching, the analogy, and their synthesis (as detailed below).
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all sentient beings obtain their retributions from afflictions (*kleśa*).
What is called 'affliction' refers to evil. The afflictions produced by these evil afflictions are also called evil.
Thus, there are two kinds of afflictions: first, the cause; second, the fruit. Because the cause is evil, the fruit is evil; because the fruit is evil..."
Therefore, the son is bitter.
Just as the *nimba* fruit—because its seeds are bitter, its flowers, fruits, stems, and leaves are all bitter—it is like a poisonous tree;
because its seeds are poisonous, its fruit is also poisonous.
The cause is sentient beings and the fruit is sentient beings; the cause is afflictions and the fruit is afflictions.
The cause and fruit of afflictions are precisely sentient beings, and sentient beings are precisely the cause and fruit of afflictions.
If one follows this meaning, there are two subsequent formal questions:
"According to this meaning, why did the Tathāgata previously use the analogy of the Snowy Mountains, which contain both poisonous herbs and subtle medicinal kings?"
If afflictions are taken as sentient beings, and sentient beings in turn are afflictions—
such that afflictions being sentient beings constitute the suffering of the cause while sentient beings being afflictions constitute the suffering of the effect—
and if both are thus unwholesome, how can wholesome dharmas arise? How could there even be a "wonderful medicinal king"?
If it is said that the three lower fetters are in question,
and if it is said that afflictions are themselves sentient beings and sentient beings are themselves afflictions,
how can it be said that there is a "wondrous king of medicines" within the body of a sentient being?

The Buddha’s answer consists of three parts: first, praising the question; second, correlating it with the preceding parable; and third, concluding with the person capable of cultivation, which is the power of the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the first, the praise is as stated in the text:
the Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! Immeasurable sentient beings all share this doubt, yet you are now able..."
"Since you have requested an explanation and seek its resolution, I am able to sever [your doubts]. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it;
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
'In the Snowy Mountains'—the following line combines with the preceding analogy."
Good son, the analogy of the Snowy Mountains refers to sentient beings; the poisonous herbs refer to afflictions (*kleśa*);
and the king of wondrous medicines refers to pure brahmacarya.

While the previous "wondrous medicine" was likened to the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), the present "king of medicines" refers to pure brahmacarya; thus, there is a slight difference in terminology.
It is different.
If there are sentient beings who have severed the first three fetters as described in the text...
Good son, if there are sentient beings who are able to cultivate such pure brahmacarya, this is called having [the Dharma] within one's body.
"O Wondrous Medicine King.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, initiating the second question and answer which correctly elucidates the conduct that arises therefrom.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how is it that sentient beings possess pure Brahma-conduct?"
This further asks what kind of sentient beings possess pure brahmacarya.
The Buddha answers in two parts: first, a general response to the question; second, a detailed response. Within the general response, there is first a simile.
Good son, it is just as in the world where fruit arises from a seed. Of these fruits, some are capable of acting as a cause for a seed while others are not.
That which is capable is called both "fruit" and "seed"; if it is incapable of doing so, it can only be called "fruit" and cannot be called a "seed."
Next, the synthesis.
All sentient beings are likewise of two kinds: first, those who possess the fruit of afflictions that are causes of afflictions;
second, those who possess the fruit of afflictions that are not causes of afflictions. Regarding those who possess the fruit of afflictions that are not causes of afflictions: [text continues].
This is what is called pure brahmacarya.
The Buddha’s intended meaning in answering was that sentient beings do not all possess this brahmacarya in its entirety;
it is like the fruit of a tree—though it is already a fruit, it does not necessarily produce seeds [if] eaten by birds, burned by fire, or rotted by water.
Those who are unable to give birth do not undergo the three matters, yet they are still able to give birth to children; sentient beings are also like this.
Those who are unable to cultivate are the fruit of afflictions, and upon that fruit, they further produce the causes of delusion.
If one cultivates goodness, there is only the fruit of delusion and no cause of delusion; this is what is meant by having pure *brahmacarya* within the body of a sentient being.
Section Two: A Specific Response on the Contemplation of Feeling by Sentient Beings, Explaining the Text on Cultivating Contemplative Understanding. This section is divided into five parts:

(1) contemplation of feeling, (2) contemplation of perception, (3) contemplation of desire, (4) contemplation of karma, and (5) contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). These five contemplations comprise two categories:

the first four contemplate the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), while the last one contemplates dependent origination. Within the contemplation of the five aggregates, what [is the nature of feeling]?

Therefore, one does not contemplate the two aggregates of consciousness and form. When consciousness first arises, it has not yet distinguished between suffering and pleasure. As the proponents of the person (pudgalavādin) say:
"Consciousness apprehends real dharmas, while perception apprehends provisional names; [at this stage] one is unable to differentiate.

For this reason, one does not contemplate the aggregate of form because it is coarse and shallow, nor does one contemplate the other three aggregates because they are violent and intense. Among these three aggregates, one specifically contemplates feeling and perception.

The opening of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is twofold; that is to say, desire and karma. The reason for this is that the faults of the aggregate of formations are particularly heavy, and therefore it is opened up.

Within each instance of the contemplation, there are four parts: first, contemplating the essence of sensation (*vedanā*); second, contemplating the cause of sensation; third, contemplating the fruit of sensation;
and fourth, clarifying the cultivation of the path. First is the contemplation of the essence of sensation.
Good son, sentient beings contemplate feeling (*vedanā*) and know it to be the proximate cause of all outflows (*āsrava*), namely the internal and external outflows.
Because they take feeling as their causal condition, they are unable to sever all outflows, nor can they escape the prison of the triple world (*tridhātu*).

Sentient beings, due to feeling, become attached to "self" and "what belongs to self," giving rise to perversions of mind, perversions of perception, and perversions of view. For this reason, sentient beings...
First, one should contemplate sensation (*vedanā*). Such sensation serves as the proximate cause for all craving (*tṛṣṇā*);

therefore, the wise who wish to sever craving should first contemplate sensation. Noble son, for all sentient beings, whatever good or evil is produced through the twelve links of dependent origination occurs precisely at the time of sensation.
For this reason, I said to Ānanda: "Ānanda, for all sentient beings..."
Whatever good or evil one has performed in this life is all experienced at the time of feeling; therefore, the wise should first contemplate feeling.
Having contemplated feeling, one realizes that feeling is merely the fruit of retribution. As for what is called the "proximate cause," it is because feeling is the final stage among the five fruits.
From this point, three further causes arise that produce all afflictions; these are called the "causes and conditions of contact.

Regarding the term "causes and conditions," the designation "contact" is not fixed, as it has no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); one may speak of consciousness (*vijñāna*) as contact, or one may speak of perception (*saṃjñā*) as contact.
This refers to the sequential causes and conditions, wherein "ignorance-contact" (*avidyā-sparśa*) is precisely the preceding state of mind that constitutes the affliction.

"Contact associated with clear knowledge" (vidyā-saṃsparśa) refers to the preceding moments of mind that are untainted (anāsrava); "contact associated with neither clear knowledge nor ignorance" (na-vidyā-nāvidyā-saṃsparśa) refers to the preceding moments of wholesome [states] that are tainted (sāsrava).
Furthermore, one should further contemplate the second contemplation below: the cause of feeling (vedanā-hetu).

Furthermore, one should further contemplate: from what causes and conditions does such feeling arise? If it arises from causes and conditions, from what do those causes and conditions themselves arise?

If it were to arise without a cause, why would that which lacks a cause not also give rise to the absence of feeling? Furthermore, one contemplates that this feeling does not arise from the creation of Īśvara, nor does it arise from a Puruṣa, nor does it arise from atoms, nor does it arise from the seasons.

Feeling does not arise from conceptualization, nor does it arise from intrinsic nature; it is not produced from itself, nor produced from another, nor produced from both self and other, nor is it produced without cause.
This feeling arises solely from the conjunction of conditions. That which constitutes the causal condition is craving.
Within this conjunction, there is neither feeling nor the absence of feeling. Therefore, I shall sever this conjunction; I shall sever the conjunction.
Therefore, feeling does not arise. When a wise son of good family has thus examined the cause, he first investigates that the cause of feeling arises from nowhere;
subsequently, he clarifies that it arises from a combination of conditions.
Next, he contemplates the fruit and retribution; this is the third contemplation of the fruit.
Next, one contemplates the retribution of sentient beings: how they undergo suffering in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm, and even throughout the three realms;

how they experience immeasurable afflictions due to the causes and conditions of their feelings; how they sever their roots of goodness due to the causes and conditions of impermanent pleasant feelings;
and how they attain liberation due to the causes and conditions of [certain] feelings. When contemplating in this way, one does not create the causes for feeling. What is this called?
"Not creating the cause for feeling" refers to the discrimination of feelings: what kind of feeling can act as the cause for craving, and what kind of craving can act as the cause for feeling?
Son of good family, if sentient beings can thus deeply contemplate the cause of craving and the cause of feeling, they will then be able to sever both "I" and "mine."
If a person can practice this fourth stage of the path of cultivation as described above,
noble son, if a person can perform such contemplations, they should then discern where craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are extinguished.
Upon seeing that there is even a slight place where craving and feeling are extinguished, one should know that there must also be ultimate extinction.
At that time, one gives rise to faith and confidence in liberation; having already given rise to such confidence, from what source is this state of liberation known?
It is known through the Eightfold Noble Path, which one then practices. What is called the Eightfold Noble Path?
This path contemplates that feeling has three aspects: first, suffering; second, pleasure; and third, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. These three types are all...
What causes and conditions enable the growth of both body and mind? It is the condition of contact (*sparśa*). This contact is of three kinds:
first, contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*); second, contact of clarity (*vidyā-sparśa*); and third, contact that is neither clarity nor ignorance (*naivavidyā-nāvidyā-sparśa*).

What is called "contact of clarity" is precisely the Eightfold Noble Path. As for the remaining two types of contact, they cause the growth of the body and mind, as well as the three kinds of feeling (*vedanā*).
"Therefore, I should sever the two kinds of causes and conditions for contact; once contact is severed, the three feelings will not arise.
Good son, such feelings are called both cause and effect. The wise should contemplate them as both cause and effect. Why are they the cause?
Because feeling gives rise to craving, it is called the cause. Why are they called the effect? Because they arise dependent upon contact, they are called the effect."

Because it is a fruit, this sensation (vedanā) is both cause and fruit. The wise, having observed this sensation in such a manner, next observe craving (tṛṣṇā), for craving is named as the retribution of sensation.
The wise observe that craving is further of two kinds: first, craving for food;
second, craving without food. Craving for food arises because of birth, old age, sickness, death, and all states of existence (bhava).
One who craves food must sever all craving for existence—including birth, old age, sickness, and death—by means of the wisdom of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Furthermore, such a person should reflect: "If I give rise to this craving for mixed food, I will be unable to sever birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Although I now crave the untainted path, if I do not sever the cause of sensation (*vedanā*), I shall not attain the fruit of the untainted path."
Therefore, one should first sever this contact; once contact is severed, sensation naturally ceases. Once sensation has ceased, craving also follows and ceases.

This is called the Eightfold Noble Path. Good son, if there are sentient beings who can contemplate in this way, although they possess poisonous bodies, within them there is also a subtle and wondrous King of Medicine, just as among the poisonous herbs in the Snowy Mountains, there is also the supreme medicinal herb.

There is also a wondrous medicine, son of good family: although such sentient beings obtain retribution from their afflictions, that retribution no longer serves as a cause for further afflictions; this is what is called pure brahmacarya.

The text states that there are three kinds of contact (*sparśa*): first, contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*), which refers to when the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) produce evil, such that the subsequent consciousness, perception, and feeling are termed contact of ignorance;
second, contact of knowledge (*vidyā-sparśa*), which refers to when the preceding three mental states arise from wholesome mental formations;

and third, contact that is neither knowledge nor ignorance (*naivavidyā-nāvidyā-sparśa*), which refers to when the mental formations are neutral—neither wholesome nor unwholesome—and thus the preceding three mental states are termed contact that is neither knowledge nor ignorance. Furthermore...
The explanation is as stated in the preceding text: "Clear contact" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path, while the other two types of contact increase all evils.
Furthermore, "Good son," and so forth, constitutes the second contemplation on perception (*saṃjñā*). Following the previous pattern, this is divided into four parts.

This term "perception" does not refer to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); rather, within the mind of formations (*saṃskāra*), there is specifically the inversion of perception, which is further termed the "inverted mind" within the process of reflection.

Among the inverted views regarding the truths, these are specifically termed "inverted views"; however, when discussed in general, they cannot be called "views" alone, but are collectively termed "perceptions" (*saṃjñā*).

Furthermore, it is said that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of all perceptions; yet within the formless realm there is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), so it is not the case that it comprises "all" perceptions.
Rather, it is because the [lower] two [spheres] constitute "all" [of those relevant here] that this name is applied. Thus, one should contemplate the essence of perception.
Within this, there are further two parts: first, the correct contemplation of the essence.
Furthermore, son of good family, a wise person should contemplate the two matters of sensation (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*): by what causes and conditions do they arise?
One should know that they arise from perception (*saṃjñā*). Why is this? When sentient beings see forms, greed does not arise; likewise, when contemplating sensation, greed does not arise.
If one gives rise to perverted perceptions regarding form—thinking that form is permanent, blissful, self, and pure;
or that sensation is eternal and unchanging—one produces greed, hatred, and delusion due to these perverted perceptions. Therefore, the wise should contemplate perception.
How should they contemplate it? They should reflect: "All sentient beings who have not yet attained the Right Path possess perverted perceptions."
What is perverted perception? It is to give rise to the perception of permanence within the impermanent; to give rise to the perception of pleasure within the unpleasant;
to give rise to the perception of purity within the impure; to give rise to the perception of a self within empty phenomena;

and to give rise to the perceptions of man, woman, large, small, day, night, year, month, clothing, house, and bedding within that which is not man, woman, large, small, day, night, year, month, clothing, house, or bedding.
These perceptions are of three kinds: first, small; second, large; and third, boundless.
Due to small causes and conditions, small perceptions arise; due to large causes and conditions, large perceptions arise; and due to immeasurable conditions, immeasurable perceptions arise.

Furthermore, there are small perceptions, which refers to not yet having entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*); there are large perceptions, which refers to having already entered meditative concentration; and there are immeasurable perceptions, which refers to...
The ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana) further comprise minor perceptions, namely all perceptions of the desire realm;
they also comprise major perceptions, namely all perceptions of the form realm; and they also comprise immeasurable perceptions, namely all perceptions of the formless realm.
Because these three types of perception cease, feeling naturally ceases. Because perception and feeling have ceased, it is called liberation.
Next is the dialogue (as follows).
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said: "World-Honored One, the cessation of all dharmas is called liberation.
Why does the Tathāgata say that the cessation of perception and feeling is called liberation?"

Regarding the initial question concerning the statement that "the cessation of feeling and perception is called liberation," some teachers say that those who attain liberation do not merely cease these two states of mind, but must cease all mental activity to attain liberation.
Now, the reason only these two states are specifically mentioned is because they involve many faults:

feeling involves the savoring of dhyāna, while perception involves the conceptualization of the formless realms; one becomes attached to the flavor of feeling-dhyāna and clings to the perceptions of the formless.
The proponents of the Nirvāṇa-as-form theory do not hold this view. According to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*) and "feeling" (*vedanā*);

according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*) and "mind" (*citta*). While the perception and mind of the conventional truth can be extinguished to attain liberation, the wisdom and mind of the ultimate truth cannot be extinguished, as they are largely identical to the [Abhidharma] numerical categories.
Therefore, Kāśyapa raised an objection: "If the extinction of all dharmas is called liberation, how could one possibly extinguish two minds?"
"Does one attain liberation?
The Buddha said, "Good son, the Tathāgata sometimes teaches by taking sentient beings as the cause, and those who hear it understand the Dharma;

sometimes he teaches by taking the Dharma as the cause regarding sentient beings, and those who hear it likewise understand. How is it that teaching by taking sentient beings as the cause is defined?"
Regarding the teaching that the listener understands the Dharma: as I previously explained to Mahākāśyapa, "Kāśyapa, when sentient beings perish, wholesome dharmas likewise perish.
This is called explaining the Dharma based on sentient beings, whereby the listener understands the Dharma.
What is explaining [the Dharma] based on the Dharma regarding sentient beings, whereby the listener also understands it? It is as I previously said to Ānanda: "I also do not..."
It is taught that one should associate with all dharmas, yet it is also taught that one should not associate with all dharmas.
If, having associated with a dharma, wholesome qualities decline and unwholesome qualities flourish, such a dharma should not be associated with.
If, having associated with a dharma, unwholesome qualities perish and wholesome qualities increase, such a dharma should be associated with. This is called the "dharma as cause."
It is said that among sentient beings, there are those who hear this and also explain it to others.

Good son, although the Tathāgata has spoken of the cessation of perception and feeling, he has thereby explained everything that can be abandoned by the wise. Once the wise have contemplated such perceptions as these, they proceed accordingly.
The Buddha replied: "One must extinguish everything in order to attain liberation. Sometimes the Buddha speaks in general terms, thereby encompassing all things;
sometimes he speaks specifically. Now, by speaking of the cessation of perception and feeling, one attains liberation.
This is a general discussion that already includes everything. In the text, it was previously stated: "Because of sentient beings, the listener understands the Dharma"—this refers to the cause.
It is said that by taking sentient beings as the basis, one explains dharmas such as good and evil, and upon hearing them, understanding is immediately attained;

furthermore, it is said that by taking dharmas as the cause, one explains sentient beings, and sentient beings attain understanding. First, regarding the explanation of good dharmas that must be cultivated and evil dharmas that must be abandoned, when sentient beings hear this, they are able to attain understanding.
These two points directly answer the previous question.
Next, one contemplates the cause of perception, which also has two aspects.

First, one correctly contemplates the cause. Then, regarding the cause of perception: from what does this immeasurable cause of perception arise? One knows that it arises from contact (*sparśa*). This contact is of two kinds:
first, contact due to afflictions (*kleśa-sparśa*); second, contact due to liberation (*vimukti-sparśa*). That which arises from ignorance (*avidyā*) is called contact due to afflictions.

That which arises from the contact of liberation is called the "contact of liberation"; from the contact of afflictions arises perverted perception, while from the contact of liberation arises non-perverted perception.
Having thus contemplated perception, one next contemplates the retribution.
Next, in the second round of question and answer, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, if it is because of these perceptions of affliction that inverted perceptions arise, then do all noble ones truly possess inverted perceptions while lacking afflictions? What is the meaning of this?"
The Buddha said, "Good son, how can a noble one have perverted perceptions?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva replied, "World-Honored One, all noble ones perceive a cow as a cow and likewise say it is a cow;
they perceive a horse as a horse and likewise say it is a horse. It is the same for men and women, large and small, houses, carriages, coming and going."
This is called inverted perception.
Good son, all ordinary beings have two kinds of perception: first, the perception of worldly convention; second, the perception of attachment.
All noble ones possess only the perception of worldly convention and lack the perception of attachment. All ordinary beings are evil...

Because of vitarka and vicāra, one gives rise to the notion of attachment toward worldly conventions; because all noble ones have skillfully mastered vitarka and vicāra, they do not give rise to the notion of attachment toward worldly conventions.
Therefore, ordinary persons are said to possess "perverted notions," whereas noble ones, though they know [these things], are not said to possess perverted notions.
Thus does the wise person contemplate the cause of perception.
Third, the contemplation of the fruit.
Next, one contemplates that the retribution of the fruit is the fruit of unwholesome perception (*saṃjñā*), which is experienced among the denizens of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.

Just as my cause for severing unwholesome thought and observation has ceased, so too has contact with ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*) ceased; therefore, perception ceases. Because perception has ceased due to its cause having ceased...
The karmic retribution is also severed.
The four paths of cultivation are all as stated in the text.
A wise person, in order to sever such conceptual causes, cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path. Good son, if there is anyone capable of acting in this way...
One who contemplates in this way is called a son of good family whose pure brahmacarya is perfected;

this is called having a king of wondrous medicines within the poisonous body of sentient beings, just as although there are poisonous herbs in the Snowy Mountains, there are also wondrous medicines therein.
Furthermore, the wise person contemplates desire as the third gate of contemplation on desire, which is also a gate of affliction; this too has four aspects.
First is the contemplation of the essence of desire.
Furthermore, son of good family, the wise person contemplates desire: "Desire" refers to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, son of good family.
"Son, this is the Tathāgata speaking of the fruit within the cause; it arises from these five things as what is perceived as desire, yet in reality it is not desire.
Good son, foolish people greedily seek to receive them, thereby giving rise to inverted perceptions regarding form, and even giving rise to inverted perceptions regarding touch."
It is precisely because external objects (*viṣaya*) can now give rise to mental desire that they are called "desire" (*kāma*);
this is a case of designating the effect by the name of its cause.
