Through the causal condition of inverted perception (*viparīta-saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*) subsequently arises. This concludes the second contemplation on the causes of desire.
With perverted perception as a causal condition, feeling arises;
therefore, the world says that because ten kinds of perceptions and desires arise from perverted perception, one remains in the world and undergoes evil retribution.
Because of these evil causes, one commits toward one's parents, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas what should not be done, even at the cost of body and life; for this reason, the wise person...
Observing that this mind of desire arises due to the causal conditions of these unwholesome perceptions, one thus observes the causes of desire.
Next, one observes the retributions of the three lower realms.
Then, one observes that these retributions of desire consist largely of various evil fruits, namely those of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.
In the human realm and the heavens, these are called the fruits of observation. If one can eliminate unwholesome perceptions, one will never give rise to such desires again.
Because there is no desire, one does not undergo unwholesome experiences; because there are no unwholesome experiences, there are no unwholesome fruits.
Therefore, I should first sever unwholesome perceptions. Once unwholesome perceptions have been severed, such dharmas as these will arise spontaneously.
It is extinguished.
Therefore, the four subsequent paths of cultivation are for this purpose.
Thus, when a wise person cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path in order to extinguish unwholesome perceptions, this is called pure brahmacarya.
This is called the presence of a sovereign medicinal king within the poisonous body of sentient beings; just as within the Snowy Mountains there are both poisonous herbs and marvelous medicines.
Furthermore, the wise person performs the fourth contemplation on karma, which also consists of four parts; first, one contemplates its essence.
Furthermore, son of good family, when a wise person has thus contemplated this desire, they should next contemplate karma.
Why is this? A wise person should reflect: "Sensation, perception, contact, and desire are themselves afflictions (*kleśa*).

Afflictions produce the karma of birth (*jāti-karma*), not the karma of sensation (*vedanā-karma*). When these afflictions operate together with karma, there are two types: first, [the affliction that produces birth]; second, [the affliction that produces sensation].
There are two types of karma: productive karma and experienced karma. Therefore, the wise should contemplate karma; this karma is of three kinds, namely those of body, speech, and mind.
Good son, the two karmas of body and speech are called both "karma" and "the fruit of karma.
The karma of the mind is called only "karma" and not "fruit," because it is the cause of karma; thus it is named "karma. Good son, as for the two [karmas] of body and speech—
Karma is termed "external karma," while mental karma is termed "internal. These three types of karma, because they proceed together with afflictions, constitute two kinds of karma:
first, karma that produces birth; second, karma that results in experience. Good son, "right karma" is precisely mental karma.
"Projecting karma" refers to bodily and verbal karma; it is called "mental karma" because it arises first, and it is called "bodily and verbal" because it is produced from mental karma.
Karma is intentional action; this is what is called "observing karma" by one of right knowledge.

The text states that sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), contact (*sparśa*), and desire (*chanda*) are afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding this, there are two interpretations from the Sāṃkhya school:

first, it is said that when the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*) arises as sensation, perception, contact, and desire, the *sāṃkhyas* (mental concomitants) arise accordingly. Herein, "sensation and perception" refers to the ten pervasive [factors].

Among the mental factors (*caitasika*), four factors—namely sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth—are included within the category of "suffering" (*duḥkha*). Since these belong to the universal mental factors that accompany all states of mind, they are common to both wholesome and unwholesome minds.

When these mental factors arise as wholesome, they are called wholesome mental factors; when they arise as unwholesome, they are termed afflictions (*kleśa*). Here, the discussion is based on their arising as unwholesome.

The *Śāstra* states that there is no difference between the sovereign mental factors (*adhipati-caitasika*) and those mentioned here; the four factors of sensation, perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth, are simply the four types of mind.

The contact of the formless aggregates (*ārūpya-skandha*) is itself consciousness (*vijñāna*); desire is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). If a formation gives rise to what is wholesome, it is called "wholesome";
if a formation gives rise to what is unwholesome, it is called "affliction" (*kleśa*). Here, the primary meaning clarified is that of committing evil.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that [the agent] can perform the karma of birth but does not perform the karma of experiencing [its results], there are two interpretations. One says: "Due to these causes and conditions of affliction..."

Because it is severed, it is said to produce the karma for rebirth; yet, because it cannot distinguish between the various feelings that are the retribution of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), it does not produce the two types of feeling.
Second, because these afflictions moisten karma so that rebirth may occur, they are said to be able to produce the karma for rebirth;

however, they cannot induce equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Within equanimity, there is the "equanimity of neutrality" (*madhyastha-upekṣā-citta*); since this is an affliction, how can it [produce such a state]?
Moistening arises from the experience of pleasant feeling; yet, while it is indeed a state of pleasure, the mind itself cannot moisten [the seeds].

This is discussed together with the meaning of how karma produces birth. Regarding the statement that there are "two kinds" which proceed together with karma: this intends to clarify the essence of karma.

When discussing karma, since afflictions (*kleśa*) still persist, it is said that they "proceed together with karma. However, because the nature of karma and the nature of phenomena (*dharma*) differ, [the latter] must be fully established for the sake of production.
Regarding the statement that the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—are both called "karma" and also called "fruit":

that which is capable of performing an action is termed "karma," while that which fully expresses the intention of speech and mind is termed "fruit. As for the mental [karma], it is exclusively karma and lacks the sense of self-expression;
therefore, it is not termed "fruit. Furthermore, it is said that right action is the mind, because the mind is the very essence of karma.

Therefore, "appointed karma" (*kṣaṇika-karman*) refers to the actions of body and speech; because these naturally correspond to one's intentions as if by a formal agreement, they are called "appointed karma.

Next is the contemplation of the causes of karma. The causes of karma are namely ignorance and contact (*avidyā-sparśa*); through ignorance and contact, sentient beings seek existence and seek [rebirth].
That which has conditions is precisely craving; because of the condition of craving, one performs the three types of karma of body, speech, and mind.
Son of good family, the wise person, having thus contemplated the causes of karma, [proceeds accordingly].

The third [section] is the contemplation of karmic retribution, which also has two parts: first, the correct understanding of the four types of karma; second, the analysis through two rounds of questions and answers.
The first is as in the text. Next is the contemplation of karmic retribution. There are four types of retribution: first, black-black retribution; second, white-white retribution.
Third is the variegated retribution; fourth is the neither-black-nor-white retribution. Regarding black-black retribution:

when the karma is performed it is defiled, and the retribution is likewise defiled. Regarding white-white retribution: when the karma is performed it is pure, and the retribution is likewise pure. Regarding variegated retribution:
when the karma is performed it is mixed, and the retribution is likewise mixed. [The neither-black-nor-white...]
That which is neither black nor white and has no retribution is called untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
The first set of questions is as in the text.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, you previously stated that the untainted has no retribution; why is it now [said otherwise]?"
"Is it said that there is neither white nor black karmic fruition (*vipāka*)?
The Buddha said, "Good son, this principle has two aspects: first, that which is both fruition and retribution; second, that which is only fruition and not retribution.
That which is black-black fruition is also called fruition and also called retribution, because it is produced from a black cause."
Because a fruit can act as a cause, it is further termed "retribution" (*vipāka*); the same applies to the pure and the mixed.

As for an untainted fruit, because it arises from tainted causes, it is termed a "fruit"; since it does not act as a cause for others, it is not termed "retribution. Therefore, it is called a fruit but not retribution.
In the response, it is stated that "the untainted (anāsrava) is called a fruit (phala), but not a retribution (vipāka). Sometimes it is said that "fruit and retribution are not different.
My personal judgment in distinguishing these here is as follows: because the untainted is a fruit of cultivation (abhyāsa-phala), it is simply called a "fruit" and cannot be called a "retribution."
The subsequent question is as stated in the text.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) is not a black dharma;
for what reason is it not called white?"
"Good son, because it has no retribution, it is not called white; because it counteracts the black, it is called white.

I now say that that which receives a fruit of retribution is called black-and-white. Because this untainted karma (anāsrava-karman) does not receive retribution, it is not called white, but is called 'quiescence.
Such karma has a fixed place where its retribution is received, just like the ten unwholesome paths of action."
The karma of the ten wholesome actions is fixed for rebirth among humans and devas; the ten unwholesome dharmas are fixed for rebirth in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.
Due to superior causes and conditions, one receives a body in the hells; due to middling causes and conditions, one receives a body as an animal;
and due to inferior causes and conditions, one receives a body as a hungry ghost. Furthermore, the human karma of the ten wholesome actions is of four types: first, the inferior... [and so forth].
Among these, those with the third grade of causes and conditions are born in Uttarakuru; those with the fourth grade are born in Pūrvavideha;
those with the superior grade are born in Aparagoyānī; and those with the superior-superior grade of causes and conditions are born in Jambudvīpa.
The answer states: Furthermore, it is said that the ten unwholesome dharmas have superior, middling, and inferior grades;

those of heavy suffering lead to rebirth in hell, those of light suffering lead to rebirth as a hungry ghost, and those that are neither heavy nor light result in rebirth as an animal. Regarding the four retributions of the ten wholesome dharmas, they exist within the four continents;
among these, the life-span and karmic fruit of Jambudvīpa are the most inferior, being the fruit of lower karma, yet they are referred to as "superior" because they are taken [as the standard].
In the cultivation of the path, one excels at the side of wholesome deeds.
Fourth, the wise person cultivates the path from the foundation.
Having made this observation, the wise person reflects: "How shall I sever this karmic retribution?"
Again, he reflects: "This karma arises from the causal conditions of ignorance and contact (*avidyā-sparśa*).

If I eliminate ignorance and contact, then such karmic fruits will cease and not arise. Therefore, the wise person, in order to sever the causal conditions of ignorance and contact, cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path;
this is called the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*). Good son, this is what is meant by the "poison of sentient beings."
Within the body there is a wondrous king of medicines, just as within the Snowy Mountains there are both poisonous herbs and wondrous medicines.
Furthermore, after the wise have contemplated karma and afflictions—this being the fifth section on contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination—there are four aspects:
namely, afflictions, karma, existence, and suffering. However, in the present text, following the previous [analysis of] feeling, perception, and so forth, all [links] possess these four aspects.

The current text of the *Mon* (Gate) merely states "afflictions, etc. [I, the private commentator, say: Within the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the three meanings of essence, cause, and karmic retribution are fully present.
The wisdom that contemplates this is precisely the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Furthermore, according to the present text, this refers to karmic retribution.
Inferring from this passage, afflictions result in suffering, and karma likewise results in suffering; one should not say that afflictions cannot [result in suffering].

The *Śālistambasūtra* (Ten Stages Sutra) divides the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) into three paths: namely, the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*), the path of karma (*karma-mārga*), and the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*).

Unknowing (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) constitute the path of afflictions; volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) constitute the path of karma; and consciousness (*vijñāna*) along with aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) constitute the path of suffering.

Within this framework, four [links] are extended from "existence" (*bhava*), specifically referring to the five fruits of the present life as "existence" (*bhava*) within the cycle of birth and death.

Regarding the statement that "suffering as suffering" and "existence" (bhava) are likewise not fixed, the preceding text explained the eight sufferings by not taking consciousness and name-and-form (nāmarūpa), but rather taking old age and death;
therefore, this statement was made. However, if these four propositions were fully present, their characteristics would be:
first, the arising of afflictions from afflictions; second, the arising of karma from afflictions; and third, the arising of existence from afflictions.
Fourth, suffering arises from afflictions; next, further categorized by karma: first, karma arises from karma; second, afflictions arise from karma;
third, [afflictions] arise from karma; fourth, suffering arises from karma. The latter two phrases are likewise [to be expanded], which would result in sixteen phrases;
however, the current text contains only nine phrases. There are also scriptural versions that state twelve phrases, yet [the standard version remains] only nine phrases.
It lacks twelve phrases; according to reason, there should be eleven. Why? Because the twelve links of dependent origination arise in succession:
conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise; conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness arises; and so on, up to: conditioned by birth, old age and death arise.
But if one does not know that old age and death lead back to further birth, what then? If that were the case, there would be only eleven phrases; yet this is precisely what appears in the sutras.
The twelve periods were established with the intention of manifesting the twelve links of dependent origination; what is currently insufficient here is merely a difference in expansion and brevity.
As for mutual generation, there is that which precedes and that which follows, as well as that which precedes in reverse order.
Furthermore, there is mutual generation that spans across sections. Thus, taking the first phrase: "affliction gives rise to affliction"—ignorance is the root, which is itself affliction.

The arising of craving and grasping is the arising of afflictions from karma; this is the arising of formations (*saṃskāra*) from ignorance (*avidyā*). The arising of existence (*bhava*) is the arising of afflictions from karma;
this is the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth from ignorance. The arising of suffering is birth, old age, and death; this is the arising of afflictions from karma.
Regarding the second phrase, "the arising of karma from karma": it is the arising of existence from formations, and the arising of afflictions from karma is the arising of ignorance from formations.

Regarding "existence arises from karma": this refers to consciousness arising from formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth. Regarding "suffering arises from karma": this refers to birth and old age and death arising from formations.
The third phrase, "existence arises from existence": this refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arising from consciousness, and so forth.

Regarding "afflictions arise from existence": this refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) arising from consciousness. Regarding "karma arises from existence": this refers to formations arising from consciousness. Regarding "suffering arises from existence": [this refers to the aforementioned sequence].
This refers to the fourth clause: "from birth arise old age and death. From suffering arises suffering;
this means that from birth arise old age and death. From suffering arise afflictions; this means that from old age and death arises ignorance. From suffering arises karma;

this means that from old age and death arise volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*). From suffering arises existence; this refers to the five fruits, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*). The text says: "internal and external craving."
Regarding the phrase "the suffering of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-duḥkha*), there are two textual passages: one says "craving is suffering" and the other says "suffering is craved.

The meaning of "craving" is somewhat weaker [in the latter], as both are generally understood to refer to "feeling" (*vedanā*). Because of this craving, one experiences suffering; thus, it is called "the suffering of craving.
In the sūtras, it is frequently stated that "affectionate attachment is suffering. Now, in examining causes and conditions, we shall also follow the previous four contemplations.
Within the section on "Identity" (*samatā*), there are four parts: first, clarifying how cause and effect arise from one another; second, contemplating that the five destinies are all suffering;

third, contemplating that the three realms are all suffering; and fourth, contemplating the eight sufferings. Regarding the first [of these four], there are two further sections: first, the formal analysis of how they arise from one another; second, the summary of the twelve meanings.
Furthermore, son of good family, once the wise person has contemplated karma and contemplated afflictions, they next contemplate the retributive fruits obtained from these two;
these two fruits are themselves suffering. Having known this to be suffering, they are then able to relinquish all rebirth.
The wise person further contemplates that afflictions arise through the causal conditions of afflictions, and that through the causal conditions of karma, afflictions likewise arise.
Affliction arises from the causal conditions of afflictions; from the causal conditions of karma, suffering arises; from the causal conditions of suffering, afflictions arise;
from the causal conditions of afflictions, existence (*bhava*) arises; from the causal conditions of existence, suffering arises; from the causal conditions of existence, existence arises;

from the causal conditions of existence, karma arises; from the causal conditions of karma, afflictions arise; from the causal conditions of afflictions, suffering arises; and from the causal conditions of suffering, suffering arises.
The nine phrases regarding mutual production are all interconnected as stated in the text.
Good son, if a wise person can perform such contemplation, you should know that this person is able to contemplate the suffering of karma. Why is this?
That which has been contemplated above is precisely the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) of birth and death. If a person can contemplate in this manner...
One should know that regarding the twelve links of dependent origination within birth and death, such a person does not create new karma and is able to destroy past karma.
A wise person contemplates the second stage beneath the earth: the suffering of the five realms of existence.
Good son, a person of wisdom contemplates the suffering of the hells;

they contemplate one hell up to the one hundred and thirty-six locations, seeing that each and every hell possesses various sufferings, all of which arise from the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma.
Having contemplated the hells, they next contemplate the sufferings of the hungry ghosts, animals, and so forth. Having made these contemplations, they further contemplate those of humans and devas.
There are various sufferings; all such manifold sufferings arise from the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma.

Good son, although there are no great sufferings or vexations in the heavens, when their bodies—which are soft, supple, and smooth—encounter the five signs of decay, they experience extreme suffering that is no different from the sufferings of the hells.
Within the five destinies, among the twelve links of dependent origination, the four hells are suffering;
afflictions are affliction; karma is karma; and the substance [of existence] is becoming. This pattern applies to the other destinies as well.
The wise deeply contemplate that the three realms are suffering. Third, they observe that all within the three realms is suffering.
Good son, the wise deeply contemplate that all sufferings within the three realms arise from the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma.
Good son, it is like an unbaked earthen vessel that is easily broken; the bodies received by sentient beings are just like this. Once received...

The body is already a vessel for manifold sufferings; it is like a great tree with abundant flowers and fruit that can be destroyed by flocks of birds, or like dry grass that can be consumed by a small fire.
When sentient beings receive a body, they are likewise destroyed by suffering in this very same way.
However, it is not necessarily the case that all three realms are suffering; only the three miserable paths are suffering.

From the human and celestial realms up to the third dhyāna are all pleasure, while the fourth dhyāna is equanimity. This is one perspective. Yet, according to when the Tathāgata first attained enlightenment, he pointed with his finger to the upper and lower realms, stating that all three realms are suffering.
If a wise person can apply the fourth contemplation to the eight sufferings,
son of good family, if a wise person can contemplate these eight kinds of suffering as they appear in the Noble Practice, you should know that such a person is able to bring an end to all sufferings.
The wise person deeply contemplates the second [aspect]: the cause of suffering.
Good son, after the wise person has deeply contemplated these eight sufferings, they next contemplate the cause of suffering. The cause of suffering is craving and ignorance.
This craving and ignorance is of two kinds: first, seeking the body; second, seeking wealth. Seeking the body...
Seeking wealth is suffering in both cases; therefore, one should know that craving and ignorance are the causes of suffering.
Good son, this craving and ignorance are of two kinds: first, internal; second, external. The internal can produce karma, while the external can cause it to increase.
Furthermore, the internal can produce karma, whereas the external produces the fruits of karma. Once internal craving is severed, karma is thereby extinguished.

Having severed external craving, one then attains the severance of internal craving; external craving can produce suffering in the present life, while [internal craving] can produce suffering in future lives.
The wise person contemplates that craving is the very cause of suffering; having thus contemplated the cause, [they proceed].
The text states that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are the causes of suffering. In the Hīnayāna, karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) are the causes of suffering;
in the Mahāyāna, it is craving, existence (*bhava*), and ignorance that constitute the causes of suffering. In the Hīnayāna, craving is the root of suffering while ignorance is secondary;
therefore, the text says that craving is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), as both systems take afflictions to be the fundamental cause of suffering. The text states: [as above].
Regarding the statement that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) have internal and external aspects, there are two meanings. First, concerning the internal and external aspects of craving:

when one perceives external forms and objects and gives rise to conceptual attachment, this is called external craving; when defilement arises from within one’s own mind, this is called internal craving.
Seeing the bodies of others is external craving; seeing one's own body is internal craving. As for ignorance, it is the lack of understanding within the internal mind.
What is termed "internal ignorance" does not refer to external phenomena as distinct from it;
rather, it is external ignorance itself. As the text states: "With craving as condition, grasping arises; with grasping as condition, craving arises.

This is like the forward order of the twelve links of dependent origination, where craving conditions grasping, and the reverse order, where grasping conditions craving. These two meanings are simply that grasping and craving are mutually causal.
Contemplate that ignorance conditions formations and formations condition ignorance as both cause and fruit; this is the third contemplation on the retribution of fruits.
Next, contemplate the retribution of fruits: the fruit of suffering is grasping (*upādāna*). Grasping is the fruit of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and craving is the causal condition for grasping.

That is to say, when there is internal and external craving, there is the suffering of craving. Good son, the wise person should contemplate that craving is the causal condition for grasping, and grasping [is the fruit].
Regarding the craving of causes and conditions: if I can sever both craving and grasping, I shall not create karma and will not undergo manifold sufferings.
As for the "four knowledges," the subsequent cultivation of the path is as described in the text.
Therefore, the wise cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path in order to sever the suffering of experience. Good son, if there is anyone who can thus...

This contemplation is called the pure holy life; it is called the wondrous King of Medicines within the poisonous bodies of sentient beings, just as although there are poisonous herbs in the Snowy Mountains, there are also wondrous medicines therein.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "How is it that the second part of the middle section of this sutra is divided into three:
first, praising the teaching; second, praising the practice; and third, praising the Buddha? Regarding the initial praise of the teaching:

it is able to give rise to the Middle Way Buddha-nature, thereby enabling even icchantikas to restore their roots of goodness. For this reason, the teaching is praised; and by relying on the teaching, one practices accordingly."
Because his practice is rare, he praises that practice; because the Buddha is the Teacher, he praises the Buddha. This is precisely the praise of the Three Jewels.
Within the initial teaching, there are two rounds of question and answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is meant by ‘pure brahmacarya’?
The intent of this initial question is to inquire about the conditions for brahmacarya; it is not a question regarding the essential nature of brahmacarya itself.”
The Buddha said, "Good son, all dharmas are [the cause].
The Buddha’s answer that "all dharmas are" is a general response indicating that all phenomena are capable of producing practice.
The intent of this passage lies in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, where the complete teaching encompasses all dharmas; the subsequent meaning will become manifest of itself.
The second round of question and answer precisely praises the sutra.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said: "World-Honored One, the meaning of 'all dharmas' is not fixed. Why is this?

The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of them as wholesome or unwholesome; at other times he speaks of them as the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness; and at other times he speaks of them as the twelve bases."
Some say it is the spiritual friend; some say it is the twelve links of dependent origination;
some say it is sentient beings; some say it is right view or wrong view; some say it is the twelve divisions of the scriptures; and some say it is the two truths.
Now the Tathāgata says that all dharmas constitute the pure Brahma-faring. What, then, are all these dharmas?
The intent of the question is: how can it be said that the sūtra is able to produce practice, given that all phenomena (*dharma*) are [empty]?
The Buddha’s answer consists of two parts: first, a praise, and second, the actual response.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is indeed the One..."
The treasury of all dharmas.
Regarding the meaning of the answer: this very *nirvāṇa* is precisely what constitutes all dharmas. Furthermore, first there is an extensive presentation of twenty-five parables;
subsequently, from the words "Good son" onwards, the text concludes by pointing to *nirvāṇa* and praising this sutra.
For example, just as the great ocean is a treasury of all jewels, so too is this Nirvāṇa Sūtra;
it is the secret treasury of the meaning of all syllables. Good son, just as Mount Sumeru is the root of all medicinal herbs, so too is this sūtra;
it is the very root of the bodhisattva precepts. Good son, just as space is that in which all things abide, [so too is this sūtra].
It is the same with this sutra; it is the dwelling place for all wholesome dharmas.
Son of good family, just as a fierce wind cannot be bound, so too are all bodhisattvas who practice this sutra not bound by any afflictions or unwholesome dharmas.
Son of good family, just as a vajra cannot be destroyed, so it is with this.
The sutra is likewise: although there may be those who are heterodox and of evil, perverse views, they cannot destroy it.
O son of good family, just as no one can count the sands of the Ganges River, so too the meaning of this sutra is such that no one can enumerate it.
Son of good family, this sutra serves as a Dharma-banner for all bodhisattvas, like the banner of Śakra. Son of good family...
This sutra is the caravan leader who leads the way to the city of Nirvana; it is like a great guide who leads merchants toward the great ocean.
Good son, this sutra can act as the light of Dharma for all bodhisattvas, just as the sun and moon in the world can dispel all darkness.
Good son, this sutra can act as a great [remedy] for sentient beings suffering from illness.
Good son, this sutra is like a supreme medicinal king among the subtle and wondrous medicines of the Fragrant Mountains, capable of curing all diseases.
Good son, this sutra serves as a staff for icchantikas, just as a weak person relies upon it to rise up.
Good son, this sutra serves as a bridge for all evil people, just as a worldly bridge enables one to cross over everything. Good son, this is so.
This sutra can provide cooling shade for those who wander through the five realms of existence and encounter the heat of the afflictions, just as a worldly parasol shields one from the scorching sun.
Noble son, this sutra is the King of Great Fearlessness;
it can destroy all afflictions and evil Māras, just as the lion king subdues all other beasts. Noble son, this sutra is a great divine mantra.
The Master can destroy all afflictions and evil spirits, just as a worldly sorcerer can expel malevolent ghosts.
Good son, this sutra is the supreme frost and hail that can destroy all the karmic fruits and retributions of birth and death, just as worldly hail and rain destroy all fruit-bearing crops.
Good son, this sutra serves as a great and excellent medicine for those whose eyes of precepts are impaired.
Good son, just as the medicinal ointment *añjana* in the world effectively cures eye pain, so too this sutra can cause all wholesome dharmas to abide.
Good son, just as the earth in the world can support all things, so too this sutra is the bright mirror for sentient beings who have violated the precepts.
Good son, just as a mirror in the world reflects all forms and images, so too this sutra can act as...
For those who lack shame and remorse, this sutra serves as clothing, like worldly garments that conceal the physical form.
Good son, for those who are poor in wholesome dharmas, this sutra can act as great wealth and treasure; it benefits the destitute just as the goddess Puṇyavatī benefits the poor.
Good son, for sentient beings who thirst for the Dharma, this sutra can act as nectar; it satisfies them just as water of eight virtues does.
O son of good family, this sutra can serve as a Dharma-couch for those afflicted by the defilements,

just as people of the world encounter a couch of peace and security. O son of good family, this sutra can serve as a necklace for Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth abode (*vihāra*),
providing them with pure lineages complete with incense, flowers, ointments, powders, and burning perfumes.
Riding upon this surpasses all six *pāramitās*; it is a place of sublime bliss, like the *pārijātaka* tree in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Good son, this sutra is a sharp vajra-axe capable of felling the great trees of all afflictions;
it is a keen blade capable of severing habitual tendencies; it is a courageous warrior capable of crushing the enmity of Māra. It is...
The fire of wisdom burns the fuel of afflictions; it is the treasury of causes and conditions from which pratyekabuddhas emerge,
the treasury of hearing from which śrāvakas are born, the eye of all devas, the right path for all humans,
the refuge for all animals, the place of liberation for hungry ghosts, and the unsurpassed [refuge] for those in hell.
This Honored One is the unsurpassed vessel for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions;
he is the father and mother of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present in the ten directions.

The twenty-fifth [chapter] states that "severing habitual tendencies" refers here to severing the lightest grade; it is now the severance of the most subtle ignorance, which is spoken of in terms of "habitual tendencies.
According to both the Tripiṭaka and the Shared Teachings, one first severs the primary afflictions and subsequently severs the habitual tendencies;

these are the primary and habitual afflictions within the realm of desire (the internal realm). If one follows the Distinct Teaching, one first severs the primary and habitual afflictions within the realm of desire, and subsequently severs those beyond the realm of desire.

Next, regarding the simultaneous severance of both the true afflictions (*samyak-kleśa*) and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) within and beyond the realms according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*):
the present text’s mention of "severing habitual tendencies" expresses the intent that the Perfect Teaching severs them simultaneously; it does not refer to the provisional teachings (*fangbian*).
Good son, for this reason, this sutra encompasses all dharmas.

As I previously stated, the second section, concerning conduct, is praised as being twofold: first, the elucidation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), and second, the elucidation of the ten perceptions (daśasaṃjñā).
This has two meanings: first, they are the essentials of conduct; second, both constitute great practice. Thus, it is said that these are the essentials of conduct.

If a bodhisattva should take the six perfections and the four immeasurables as the essentials of their practice, how can the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) and the ten perceptions (daśasaṃjñā) of the śrāvaka vehicle be considered essential?
This clarifies that the factors of the path pertain to the stage of attaining true understanding (*tattvārtha*), whereas the ten perceptions pertain to the stage of skillful means (*upāya*).

These [perceptions] constitute a semblance of understanding, while correct contemplation (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is the fundamental principle for entering the Path; how could they not be essential? Furthermore...
If one cultivates with the mind of Great Nirvana, it is not the Dharma of the Two Vehicles. It is said that those who practice the "Great Path" desire to encompass all virtues;

since there is nothing that is not the conduct of a Mahāsattva, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) are first clarified. Within this, there are two parts: first, the correct clarification of the essence of the factors of enlightenment;

second, the clarification of the causes and conditions of the factors of enlightenment. Regarding the essence, there are three further points; the first clarifies that true understanding constitutes the "is-ness" (*tathatā*).

Second, it clarifies that while those with outflows (*sāsrava*) are not [the ultimate], the three returns and the true knots are indeed the adornment of the path. As the *Dàodǐng pǐn* (Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment) states:

"Three and four are what the external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) contemplate; two and five are what the internal ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*) can contemplate; eight and seven are what the true sages (*ārya*) practice as contemplation. Kaishan said: "It is not so;

the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśadbodhipākṣikadharma*) apply to both internal and external ordinary beings, and both sets of three and four, as well as two and five, are [equally applicable]."
Regarding the contemplations of the inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) that resemble [noble] understanding: the eight and seven [factors] are all contemplations of true sages;

the eight are the contemplation of the truths (*satyadarśana*), and the seven are the contemplation of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Master Tan criticizes Zhuangyan, saying: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies that the thirty-seven factors are supramundane dharmas;
how can three or four be mundane ordinary beings? He also criticizes Kailian, saying: "This text refers to the 'worldly supreme' (*laukikāgradharma*)."
The Dharma is not itself the pure Brahma-conduct; rather, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment constitute the pure Brahma-conduct.

How can an external ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana) be able to contemplate them? Tiantai clarifies that there are many types of the path-factors (mārga-pakṣya-dharma), all of which are fully contained within the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation).

Zhiyan bases his [explanation] on the path-factors according to specific stages (*avasthā*), while Kaishan bases his on the path-factors as a general cultivation of the path; both are but single approaches. (And so forth.)
Regarding the first point, there are four clarifications. First, it clarifies that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment constitute the core of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
As I have previously stated, although this sutra encompasses all dharmas, I declare that the holy life is precisely these thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
If one is separated from these [factors], the second section clarifies that if one is separated from the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*),
one will not attain the fruit. Good son, if one is separated from these thirty-seven factors, one can ultimately never attain the correct fruit of a śrāvaka,
nor even the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor perceive the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) or the fruit of the Buddha-nature.
For these reasons, the third conclusion follows.
For these reasons, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is precisely the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Why is this? The fourth section below explains the meaning of this.
Why is this? Because the nature of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is not inverted, and thus it can destroy the nature of inversion;
its nature is not that of evil views, and thus it can destroy the nature of evil views; its nature is not that of fear, and thus it can destroy the nature of fear;
it is a pure practice that enables sentient beings to ultimately perform pure brahmacarya.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha: "Regarding the dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*), [the following] clarifies that they are not fourfold through a series of questions and answers.
In this first question, it is clarified that wholesome dharmas with outflows are not [of the same nature as those without outflows].
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, dharmas with outflows can also produce dharmas without outflows (*anāsrava*')."
For what reason does the Tathāgata not state that contaminated [phenomena] constitute pure brahmacarya?
The intent of the question is: since wholesome contaminated phenomena also serve as a support for the arising of the uncontaminated, why are they not described as brahmacarya?
"Good son, all that is with outflows (sāsrava) is precisely inversion; therefore, that which has outflows cannot be called pure holy conduct (brahmacarya).
The Buddha answered that because its essence is inverted, it cannot be said to be [otherwise]; as for 'inversion,' this does not clarify existence."

Regarding the perversions such as regarding what is with outflows (*sāsrava*) as being permanent or impermanent: since these are indeed with outflows, there is a mind of grasping (*sagrāha-citta*), and because one cannot be without attainment, they are called "perversions.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha concerning the first question and answer regarding that which is below the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, is the 'Dharma Supreme in the World' (laukikāgra-dharma) with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava)?
The intent of this question is to raise an objection based on worldly phenomena; therefore, he first establishes the definition of the thesis."
The Buddha said, "Good son, these are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Regarding what the Buddha called "with outflows," the Buddha answered Kāishan, saying: "The five expedient means (*pañca-upāya*) all involve the grasping of signs; they are indeed with outflows.
However, they are also similar to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Yet, they have not yet been able to sever the outflows and do not encompass the truly outflow-free."
Because it is a fruit, it is said to be "with outflows" (*sāsrava*); however, since its essence is in fact not grasped, the text of the objection states that "its nature is not inverted.
Although the World-Honored One [is] with outflows, this concludes the third question and answer.
Although the Blessed One possesses a nature that is subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), he is not inverted; for what reason, then, is he not called one of "pure holy life" (*brahmacarya*)?
The intent of this direct challenge is as follows: although he is said to possess outflows, he is able to generate understanding and his essence is not inverted;
since this is so, why is he not [considered] one of pure holy life?
The Buddha replied: "There are two reasons.

Son of good family, because the 'supreme mundane dharma' (laukikāgradharma) is the cause of the outflow-free (anāsrava), and because it resembles the outflow-free as it tends toward the outflow-free, it is not called a perversion."

This initial statement that it is not called an "inversion" because it is directed toward the untainted (*anāsrava*) clarifies that while this contemplation gives rise to the untainted and is therefore not termed an inversion,
its own essence still possesses grasping.

Son of good family, from the arising of the pure brahmacarya and the continuity of the thought of enlightenment, up until the ultimate stage of the Worldly Supreme Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), it is exclusively...
Because this consists of a single moment of mind, it cannot be called the "pure holy life" (*brahmacarya*).

Furthermore, when it was subsequently stated that the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) consist of only a single moment of mind, this was intended to mean that taking the stage immediately preceding the "patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkhadharmanidhyānakṣānti*) as the supreme dharma constitutes a single kṣaṇa of mind.
Now, the Buddha’s intention in his reply is to clarify that what I have taught is the foundation of the holy life.
It causes sentient beings to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment in a continuous succession; since worldly phenomena are thus nothing other than the single mind, they are not grasped.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha regarding the five consciousnesses of sentient beings. (This concludes the fourth question and answer.)

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the five consciousnesses of sentient beings are also with outflows (*sāsrava*), yet they are neither inverted nor a state of single-mindedness;
for what reason, then, are they not called pure brahma-conduct?"
In the question, the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are raised as the subject of inquiry, stating: "The five consciousnesses of sentient beings are not inverted.

Regarding this, various interpretations differ: some say that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has not yet grasped characteristics; others say that while the mind of consciousness possesses characteristics, these are slight compared to the latter three minds.
Now, the questioner states that the five consciousnesses are not inverted because they merely encounter their objects in a single, immediate stroke.
Because one has not yet discerned the distinct characteristics of the three provisional designations, it is said that there is no inversion; yet it is further stated that this is not a single mind.
For example, when the eye sees a form, the mind and its mental concomitants continue in succession. If this were the case, one could not help but practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Good son, although the five consciousnesses of sentient beings are not of a single moment, they are nevertheless outflowing (sāsrava) and inverted;

because they increase all outflows, they are called "outflowing. Their essence is not real, and because they involve attachment through conceptualization, they are inverted. Why is it said that their essence is not real and that they are inverted due to attachment through conceptualization?
It is because one gives rise to the perception of male and female within that which is neither male nor female, and so on, up to houses and vehicles.
Mounting upon a water-jar or clothing is likewise thus; this is called perversion (*viparyāsa*).
The Buddha answered, "Because these are tainted (*sāsrava*) and are also perversions, one should know that the mind already possesses grasping at signs.
Furthermore, it says, "Because the essence is not real, one is inverted by attachment to conceptualizations. The subsequent text explains: "To give rise to the perception of male or female..."

Regarding the perception of houses, jars, clothes, and so forth: it is because the consciousness-mind has not yet attained the mental state of male or female forms that one understands jars, clothes, and the like.
This passage concerning the "perceiving mind" (想心) is intended to clarify why attachment arises during the stage of perception;
it is precisely because the preceding consciousness-mind was already attached to forms and sounds that the present attachment to perceptions arises. This cites the effect to illustrate the cause.
Good son, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are these very things that conclude the third [section].
Good son, because the nature of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is free from inversion, they are called the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Good son, if there is a bodhisattva who, regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, understands the causes and conditions of the second section, the Chapter on the Path (Mārgavarga), they will be able to know nine meanings.
These nine meanings are precisely the functions of the path-factors. In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is explained that the path-factors possess nine natures;
this refers to their nature. If one discusses their substance (*tattva*), each has its own basis for being so designated. Thus, they are called the "nine natures."
These are: first, morality; second, concentration; third, wisdom; fourth, mindfulness; fifth, faith; sixth, diligence; seventh, joy; eighth, tranquility; and ninth, equanimity.
In terms of the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), there are only three [of these nine]: morality corresponds to right speech, right action, and right livelihood;

the eight [limbs] correspond to concentration, specifically the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) as the four concentrations, the five faculties of concentration, the faculty of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and right concentration—thus making nine types.
This wisdom consists of the four foundations of mindfulness as the four faculties of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena as the seventh;

it consists of right view and right thought as the ninth; and four kinds consist of mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and the enlightenment factor of mindfulness—these two types [each] being eightfold;
it consists of faith, the faculty of faith, and the power of faith—these three being eightfold; and it consists of diligence, the four right efforts as the four faculties and powers.
Regarding the six right efforts (*ṣaḍ-samyak-pradhāna*) and the awakening factor of effort (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), there are eight [categories]; for the remaining [factors], there is one each.

This passage consists of five parts: first, the enumeration of names; second, the clarification of their essence; third, the explanation of their meaning; fourth, the application to the dharmas; and fifth, the analytical investigation. This is the first: the enumeration of names.
Good son, if there is a bodhisattva who, regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, knows their roots, knows their causes, knows their inclusion, knows their increase,

knows their masters, knows their guides, knows their excellence, knows their reality, and knows their ultimate consummation— such a bodhisattva may be called one whose pure conduct (brahmacarya) is purified.
However, these nine meanings constitute three distinct categories: the first four are the causes of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*);

the middle three are the essence of the factors of enlightenment; and the final two are the fruits of the factors of enlightenment. Regarding the first four causes: "root" refers to desire; "desire" refers to the aspiration for awakening;
"cause" refers to clarity (*vidyā*) as opposed to ignorance (*avidyā*); "good cause" refers to clarity; and "bad cause" refers to ignorance.

"Clarity" (*vidyā*) refers to gathering [the mind] so as not to let it be scattered or lost; "increase" (*vṛddhi*) refers to wholesome reflection, for through such reflection one performs what is wholesome.

Thus, these four are the causes: mindfulness is the leader, concentration is the sovereign, and wisdom is the excellence. Since they are called mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, how could they not be the essence?
In reality, they are liberation—that is, the partial ultimate, which is the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. These two—[liberation and its fruit]—are...
Is this not the fruit?
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha. [This concludes] the second section, which clarifies the essence by first posing questions and then providing answers.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, what is meant by 'knowledge of the faculties' (*indriya-jñāna*) up to 'knowledge of the ultimate' (*atyanta-jñāna*)?"
Yes. The answer further consists of two parts: first, praising the question.
The Buddha said, "Good son, excellent, excellent! A bodhisattva’s posing of a question is for two purposes: first, for..."

"Because you know it for yourself, and because others shall know it—since you have now realized this, yet immeasurable sentient beings do not understand, you have requested an exposition of this matter.
Therefore, I now praise you again and again: Excellent, excellent!"
Next, the formal response:
"Good son, the root of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is desire;

it is called 'contact' when it is subsumed by clarity, 'feeling' when it increases, 'good volition' when it is predominant, 'mindfulness' when it guides, 'concentration' when it excels, 'wisdom' when it is real, and 'liberation' when it is complete."
Ultimately, it is named the Great Parinirvāṇa.
In the answer, it says that what is termed "contact through clarity" (*vidyā-sparśa*) is the condition of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
"Virtuous son" and "wholesome desire" constitute the third section below; this explains the nine meanings, which comprise nine passages, beginning with this one.
Desire is the root; this is explained in two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the analysis. Within the explanation, there are two sections: first, the response, and second, the analogy.
"Good son, wholesome desire is the root of the initial aspiration for the Way, up to and including *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, I say that desire is the root."
Good son, as it is said in the world: all suffering and affliction have craving as their root;
all diseases have undigested food as their root; all legal disputes have contention as their root; and all evil deeds have falsehood as their root.
Next, within the section on critical analysis, there are two rounds of question and answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata previously stated in this sutra that all wholesome dharmas have non-negligence as their root;
yet now you say that desire is [the root]. What is the meaning of this?"

The Buddha said, "Good son, if one says that wholesome desire is the generative cause (*janakahetu*), it is so; if one says that non-negligence (*apramāda*) is the revealing cause (*vyañjanahetu*), it is likewise.

It is as the world says that for all fruits, the seed is their cause; or again, as some say that the seed is the generative cause and the ground is the revealing cause—the meaning here is also like this."
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said, “World-Honored One, the Tathāgata previously stated in other sūtras that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the root and the meaning; what does this mean?
Good son, when the Tathāgata previously spoke of sentient beings first coming to know the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, he meant that the Buddha is their root.”
Self-realization has desire as its root.
World-Honored One, how do you clarify "contact" (*sparśa*)? [The second explanation of contact:
World-Honored One, why is "clear contact" (*vidyā-sparśa*) called a cause? Good son, the Tathāgata sometimes explains clarity (*vidyā*) as...
Wisdom is sometimes explained as faith; because a son of good family has faith in causes and conditions, he draws near to virtuous friends—this is called the condition of contact.

Through the condition of drawing near, one hears the True Dharma—this is called the condition of contact. Having heard the True Dharma, one purifies body, speech, and mind—this is called the condition of contact.
Through the purification of the three karmas, one attains right livelihood—this is called the condition of contact. Because of right livelihood... [the text continues].
Obtaining the purity of the faculties is due to the precept of pure faculties; delighting in secluded places is due to the purity of the faculties;
being able to contemplate well is due to delighting in seclusion; attaining dwelling in accordance with the Dharma is due to contemplating well;
and attaining the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment which can destroy immeasurable evil afflictions is what is called "contact."
There are many phrases [in the text] that, because they lack a fixed certainty, may all be explained according to the meaning of their respective applications.
The text states: "By means of right livelihood, one obtains the pure faculties and the precepts.

Since it was already clarified previously that right livelihood is the *prātimokṣa*—where *prātimokṣa* means "precepts"—how do we know that this passage does not further clarify the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*) or the path (*mārga-saṃvara*)? Regarding this, the subsequent text states:

He himself says: "Because of the precepts for purifying the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara-śīla*), one attains joy and tranquility; only then does one attain concentration (*samādhi*) and become able to contemplate well;
only then does one attain wisdom (*prajñā*). Since he has not yet clarified concentration and wisdom, how can there already be the "precepts of the path-concentration" (*mārga-samādhi-śīla*)?

Now, since the attainment of the *vimukti* (liberation) occurs after the path-concentration, why are the precepts for purifying the faculties mentioned before it? Regarding this, there are two interpretations. The first says: "The former..."

It clarifies that right livelihood is the *prātimokṣa* precept; it is precisely the firm maintenance of non-transgression. Furthermore, it clarifies the purification of the faculties (*indriya-pariśuddhi*):

this further clarifies that these precepts become increasingly subtle so that they can encompass and protect the five faculties, preventing them from giving rise to transgressions. Thus, it is called "purification of the faculties.

Second, it is said that this does not refer to purifying the five faculties, but rather that the Bodhisattva inherently possesses the various faculties such as faith and so forth, which constitute the precept.

The sense of being able to generate [wholesome qualities] is precisely that the precepts serve as the root; since these precepts, once purified, can generate dharmas such as concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they are called "purified roots" (*viśuddha-mūla*).
Both the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* contain this teaching on purified roots.
Regarding the term "appropriation" (*parigraha*), the third explanation below clarifies its inclusion.
Good son, "feeling" (vedanā) is named "gathering sentient beings. At the time of feeling, one is able to produce both good and evil;
therefore, feeling is called gathering. Good son, because of the conditions of feeling, various afflictions arise;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment can destroy them. Therefore, feeling is taken as gathering.
Previously, it was explained that feeling (*vedanā*) is the beginning of the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus feeling is said to "grasp" (*parigraha*) the afflictions;
now, it is explained that feeling gives rise to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), and therefore feeling is again called "grasping.
Regarding the phrase "due to wholesome reflection" (*samyakcintanāt*), the fourth [section] explains "increase" (*vṛddhi*): because of reflection, the mind’s understanding increases and progresses.
It is named "Increase" (*vṛddhi*); first it is proclaimed and then explained.
It is called "Increase" because through skillful reflection one is able to destroy the afflictions.
Why is this? Because by diligently practicing, one attains these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
If one contemplates that which can destroy [the afflictions], this is the fifth section explaining mindfulness (*smṛti*) through the method of thesis, example, and application.
If one contemplates that which can destroy all evil afflictions, it necessarily depends upon exclusive mindfulness; therefore, mindfulness is taken as the primary factor.
Just as all four divisions of the world’s armies follow the will of their commander-in-chief, so too are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; they all follow mindfulness as their leader.
Once one has entered meditative concentration, the sixth section, "Explanation and Guidance," follows.

Once one has entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) are able to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena;
therefore, concentration serves as the guide. This is because concentration can lead to the arising of wisdom (*jñāna*); thus, it bears the name "guide."
This is the seventh section of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which explains the analogy and its application regarding the excellence of dharmas.
Among these thirty-seven factors, the wisdom that discriminates the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is the most excellent; therefore, wisdom is considered supreme.
When this wisdom recognizes the afflictions (*kleśa*), through the power of wisdom, the afflictions are extinguished.
Just as in the world, among the fourfold army, either one or two brave and skillful warriors are able to defeat the enemy, so too it is with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
by the power of wisdom, they are able to destroy the afflictions. Therefore, wisdom is considered supreme.
Because the wisdom of mental discourse can correctly sever [afflictions], it is called "superior. Although it arises from the practice of the lower [stages],
the eighth [chapter] explains that while concentration first raises up and suppresses what is not real,
O son of good family, although one obtains the four dhyānas, supernormal powers, and bliss through the practice of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, it is still not the ultimate reality.
It is not called "real.
Next, the wisdom that correctly knows and abandons [defilements] is real;
it is only when one destroys the afflictions and realizes liberation that it is called "real."
This is the ninth section of the explanation of the "Ultimate" (*atyanta*) within the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).

First, it clarifies that although one attains the four fruits of the śramaṇa through the cultivation of the path by generating the resolve [for enlightenment], these are still not ultimate. Although one attains worldly happiness and supramundane happiness through these thirty-seven factors and the four fruits of the śramaṇa...
The fruits and liberation also cannot be called ultimate.
It is only when one subsequently attains Great Nirvana that it is truly the final goal.
If one can sever the practices associated with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, this is called Nirvana; therefore, I have said this.
"Ultimate" refers to Great Nirvāṇa.
As for the statement that one "eliminates and severs the practices of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment," this means that on the day one attains the fruit,
all conditioned wisdoms previously present within the causal stage are entirely relinquished.

Furthermore, next, "the mind of wholesome affection" (the fourth section) clarifies the application of the Dharma, which again has three parts: first, the application of the Dharma; second, the application of persons;
and third, the application of analogies. This first part clarifies it by means of the Dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family, the mind of wholesome affection is itself desire. Because of wholesome affection, one draws near to the wholesome.

Because of friendship, it is called "contact" (*sparśa*); this is named the "cause. Because one draws near to a virtuous friend, it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*); this is named the "appropriating cause.
Because drawing near to a virtuous friend enables one to practice correct reflection, it is called the "augmenting cause.

These four dharmas can bring forth and grow the Path—namely, aspiration (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—and these are therefore named the "predominant causes. It is by means of these three factors that [the Path] is attained.
The two liberations are as follows: because craving is eliminated, one attains liberation of mind; because ignorance is eliminated, one attains liberation through wisdom.
These are called the "real. When these eight factors ultimately attain their fruit, it is called *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is called "ultimate."
Among these, nine dharmas constitute the three intentions: the first four are the causes, the middle three are the essence, and the final two are the results.
Furthermore, "desire" refers to the arousal of the mind; this is the second section, which treats the subject from the perspective of the person.

Furthermore, son of good family: "desire" (*chanda*) is the arousal of the mind to leave the household life; "contact" (*sparśa*) is the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of motion and three proclamations);
this is called the cause. "Inclusion" (*saṃgraha*) is the reception of two kinds of precepts:

first, the *prātimokṣa* precepts; second, the *viśuddhendriya* (purified faculties) precepts; this is called receiving [the precepts] and this is called inclusion. "Increase" (*vṛddhi*) is cultivation and practice.
The "Lord" of the four dhyānas is the fruit of srotāpanna; the "Guide" is the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin;
the "Victorious One" is the fruit of anāgāmin; the "Fruit" is the fruit of pratyekabuddha;
and the "Ultimate" is the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Among these, nine factors constitute two groups: the first four pertain to the cause, while the latter five pertain to the fruit. Furthermore, within the cause, the internal ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is included;
within the fruit, both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are included.
Moreover, "desire" is termed "consciousness"; this third section proceeds by way of analogy.
Furthermore, good son, desire is called consciousness; contact is called the six sense bases; grasping is called feeling; increase is called ignorance;
the master is called name-and-form; the guide is called craving; the superior is called clinging; the reality is called becoming;
and the ultimate is called birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Regarding this, there are three interpretations and one opening [of the text]. First, Kaishan says: "This cites the twelve links of dependent origination as the object-domain of the nine dharmas;
the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) take these objects. Second: "That which is used here is explained through analogy;

it clarifies that the sequence of these nine dharmas is like the production of the twelve links of dependent origination, for these nine dharmas likewise arise in a sequential manner. Third: [The text continues: "However..."
These twelve links of dependent origination have three points that are difficult to understand: first, their incompleteness; second, the double appearance of the *vijñāna* link;
and third, their non-sequential arrangement. As for why they are incomplete, it is because they are intended to be both inclusive and abbreviated;
while the *saṃskāra* link is abbreviated, the *avidyā* link is not, because *avidyā* is the root of all causes and conditions. As for why the *vijñāna* link appears twice, the first is precisely...

Regarding the two aspects of the consciousness member (*vijñāna-aṅga*), namely contact (*sparśa*) as the basis for consciousness, the reason they are not presented in sequential order is precisely to clarify that the cycle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) revolves infinitely and lacks a fixed sequence.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said: "The fundamental cause increases... This is the fifth section of analysis, which first poses a question and subsequently provides an answer.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said, “World-Honored One, regarding these three dharmas—the root, the cause, and the increase—how can there be any difference between them?
The Buddha replied, “There are five further aspects.

Good son, that which is called the ‘root’ is the initial arousal [of the aspiration]; that which is called the ‘cause’ is its similarity [to the goal]; and that which is called ‘increase’ is its uninterrupted progression.”
That which has already ceased is similar to what is about to arise; furthermore, O son of good family, the faculty (*indriya*) is the cause of action and is itself the fruit.

"Increase" (*vṛddhi*) refers to that which is functional. Furthermore, O son of good family, although there is a retribution in future lives, it is called a "cause" because it has not yet been experienced;
at the time it is experienced, it is called "increase. Furthermore, O son of good family:
"Good son, in this sutra, 'roots' (mūla) refer to the path of seeing (darśanamārga); 'causes' (hetu) refer to the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga);
and 'increase' (vṛddhi) refers to the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga). Furthermore, good son, 'roots' are the direct cause (samyag-hetu);
'causes' are the causal conditions (upāya-hetu); and from these direct causes, one attains the name of 'increase' when the fruit (phala) is realized."
First, regarding the subsequent explanation: "Root" (mūla) refers to the initial arising, which is easily understood. "Cause" (hetu) refers to that which is similar;

this refers to the continuity of the two minds—the initial and the subsequent—without interruption. "Increase" (vṛddhi) refers to the cessation of the similar [preceding state] and the attainment of the similar [subsequent state].
"Similarity" (tulya) means that having ceased the preceding similar mind, one further attains a subsequent similar mind. However, among these, the three factors are excluded from within.
Regarding the teaching on the three paths: the path of seeing is the path of realizing the truths (*satyadarśanamārga*), and the path of cultivation is the path of reflection (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Excluding the fruit of arhatship, the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is simply the state of an arhat.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said: "As the Buddha has taught," [this concludes] the second section, which clarifies practice by means of the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*); first, he asks:
Next, the answer was given.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, that which is ultimate is precisely nirvāṇa.
How, then, can such nirvāṇa be attained?"
The answer consists of three parts: first, a general summary; second, an explanation; and third, a concluding summary. This first part is the general summary of the ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*).
"Good son, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, is able to cultivate the ten perceptions, you should know that such a person will be able to attain nirvāṇa."
Next, the enumeration follows. What are the eleven? First, the perception of impermanence; second, the perception of suffering; third, the perception of non-self;
fourth, the perception of revulsion toward food; fifth, the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in; sixth, the perception of death; seventh...
Eighth is the perception of many transgressions; ninth is the perception of detachment from liberation; tenth is the perception of cessation; and eleventh is the perception of non-attachment.

Son of good family, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās cultivate these ten perceptions, such persons will ultimately and certainly attain nirvāṇa; they do not follow the minds of others, but are able to [realize it] for themselves.
The discernment of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so forth is called the true meaning of a *bhikṣu*, and even extends to being called an *upāsikā*.

However, when considering its essential nature, it is actually wisdom (*prajñā*); it is spoken of by the name "perception" (*saṃjñā*) because at the initial stage of practice, one is still unable [to maintain it as wisdom].
Having clearly visualized the object, one contemplates its perfected state; because this name is established based on the preparatory means (*upāya*), it is also called "perception" (*saṃjñā*).
As for its stage, it extends through both shallow and deep levels; since it is practiced at the beginning, it is also called the "ten perceptions" (*daśa-saṃjñā*).

The commentary on the *Mahāvagga* states that what is practiced initially is called the "nine perceptions," while their accomplishment is called the "ten perceptions"; this refers to the enumeration of names.

The general outline is the same as this, with only two differences: first, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) adds the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) and the perception of cessation (*nirodha-saṃjñā*);
second, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* lacks the perception of many transgressions (*bahv-āpatti-saṃjñā*) and the perception of non-attachment (*anunaya-saṃjñā*).

Among these, the "perception of distancing from evil" is the "perception of distancing and liberation," and the "perception of exhaustion" is the "perception of extinction. Thus, these ten perceptions constitute two groups as previously stated.
Sixth, the explanation of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*); seventh, the explanation of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*). Based on the preceding six [contemplations], they are divided into two:

the first three constitute correct contemplation—namely, suffering (*duḥkha*), impermanence (*anitya*), and non-self (*anātman*)—while the latter three are merely mutually supportive conceptualizations. Regarding this, there have been two interpretations since antiquity. One states that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are primary and correspond as follows:
the contemplation of death establishes impermanence; the contemplation of the unattractive (*aśubha*) establishes suffering; and [the contemplation of] revulsion establishes dispassion (*virāga*).
Regarding the statement that "the perception of food leads to the realization of non-self" and "disgust for food leads to the realization of non-self":
it is because worldly people give rise to craving for food solely by conceiving of a self and desiring its beautiful appearance. Since the Buddha knows there is no self, he does not crave fine food;
thus, one knows that disgust for food accomplishes the perception of non-self. As for "perceiving what is unlovely as suffering," [it is explained as follows:]
Therefore, the *Śrī-mālā-devī-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (or *Sutra on Auspicious Responses*) states: "The three realms are all suffering; how can they be enjoyed?

Regarding the contemplation of death that establishes impermanence, this is the most easily perceived: because of death, there is impermanence. These two [contemplations] mutually establish one another: it is precisely because of the revulsion toward food, the lack of delight, and the inevitability of death that there is non-self;
and it is likewise because of the revulsion toward food, the lack of delight, and the inevitability of death that there is suffering—due to food.

Because one is weary of death as something undesirable, there is impermanence. Regarding the latter four perceptions: the perception of many faults and transgressions is common to both the perception of weariness toward the world and the perception of renunciation;
however, it differs from the perception of cessation (*nirodha-saṃjñā*). Regarding this difference, three explanations exist:

first, that "renunciation" (*vairāgya*) refers to the exhaustion of causes through their severance, while "cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the exhaustion of results through their severance; second, that "renunciation" refers to partial knowledge, whereas "cessation" refers to total extinction; third, that [the former] refers to suppression (*vibhava*).

Delusion is that which is to be abandoned; its cessation is extinction (*nirodha*). Since one who is free from the perception of craving has already abandoned and extinguished it, the mind is without attachment.
As the text says, "the meaning of *bhikṣu* can be known," and below it says, "it accords with the characteristics of a *śramaṇa*.
Kāśyapa asks: "What is meant by... This is the second [section], the explanation, which is further divided into three parts; first, the individual explanation of the six perceptions.

Next, there is a general praise of the six perceptions (*ṣaḍ-saṃjñā*) and a brief indication of the four perceptions (*catasraḥ saṃjñāḥ*). Regarding the first of these, the individual explanation of the six perceptions begins with impermanence (*anityatā*);
first a question is posed, followed by the answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said: "World-Honored One, what is meant by bodhisattvas, up to and including laywomen (*upāsikā*), practicing..."
The Perception of Impermanence.
In the response, the six perceptions are treated as six distinct sections; first, within the section on impermanence, there are two parts:

first the heading, and second the explanation. "Good son, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas: first, those who have newly resolved their minds, and second, those who have already practiced the path. As for the perception of impermanence..."
Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, the coarse; second, the subtle.
In the commentary, regarding the two [types of impermanence], the coarse comes first.
When a beginner bodhisattva contemplates the perception of impermanence, they reflect: "Generally, there are two kinds of things in the world."
There are two kinds of seeds: internal and external. Thus, internal things are impermanent and subject to change.

When I observe [the body], it is different at the time of birth, childhood, youth, adulthood, old age, and death; since these various stages are each distinct, one should know that internal things are impermanent.
Furthermore, one reflects: "I see sentient beings who are perhaps plump and fresh, endowed with physical beauty and strength, as they go about..."
