He observes some whose coming and going are free and unimpeded; others he sees suffering from illness, their physical strength ruined and wasted, their countenances emaciated and deprived of autonomy;
some he sees with wealth and treasuries overflowing; others he sees impoverished, lacking in everything; some he sees accomplished in immeasurable merit;
and others he sees possessed of immeasurable evil dharmas. Therefore, he knows with certainty that within...

The Dharma is impermanent; furthermore, one contemplates external phenomena through their various stages: the time of the seed, the time of the sprout, the time of the stalk, the time of the leaves, the time of the flower, and the time of the fruit.
These various stages are each distinct from one another. Thus, these external phenomena may be complete or incomplete;
therefore, one should know that all external things are certainly impermanent. Having thus contemplated and seen that phenomena are impermanent, one further—
Observing that I have heard the various devas possess and fully achieve most exquisite bliss and sovereign supernormal powers, they likewise have five characteristics;

therefore, one should know that these are impermanent. Furthermore, I have heard that at the beginning of the kalpa there were sentient beings, each endowed with supreme and wondrous merit, whose bodily radiance illuminated themselves without depending on the sun or moon; yet by the power of impermanence, their light [vanished].

Regarding the virtue of cessation and its decline: it is further heard that in the past there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King who ruled over the four continents, possessed the seven treasures, and attained great sovereignty;

yet he could not escape the mark of impermanence. Furthermore, observing the great earth, in times of yore it was peacefully settled and arranged such that there was no empty space even as large as a chariot wheel where beings did not grow and flourish in full abundance.
All the groves of exquisite medicinal herbs, trees, and fruits were once lush and flourishing;

however, due to the meager merit of sentient beings, this great earth now lacks power, and all things produced therein have consequently become depleted and wasted. Therefore, one should know that all internal and external phenomena are impermanent;
this is what is called coarse impermanence. Having thus contemplated the coarse, [one proceeds further].
Next is subtlety.

Next, regarding the observation of subtlety: why is it called subtle? When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas observe all internal and external things, even down to a single atom, they see that these have already been impermanent at the time of the future. Why is this? Because they have fully accomplished [this realization].
Because it possesses the characteristic of disintegration, if future form were not impermanent, one could not say that form has ten temporal distinctions.
What are these ten? First, the stage of the kalala; second, the stage of the arbuda; third, the stage of the peśī; fourth, the stage of the ghana;
fifth, the stage of limbs; sixth, the stage of infancy; seventh, the stage of childhood; eighth, the stage of youth... [and so on].

Regarding the nine stages: the stage of full vigor is the tenth, the stage of senility. The Bodhisattva contemplates that if the membrane-stage were not impermanent, it would not reach the bubble-stage;
likewise, if the stage of full vigor were not impermanent, it would never reach old age.
If these various stages did not perish moment by moment, they could never gradually grow; rather, they should grow to full completion all at once. For this reason, they are [impermanent].
Therefore, one should know that there is certainly a subtle impermanence moment by moment.

Furthermore, seeing some people with all their faculties complete and their complexions radiant, while seeing others emaciated and withered, one further reflects: "This person certainly possesses moment-by-moment impermanence.
Again, one contemplates the four great elements and the four postures, and contemplates the two internal and two external causes of suffering: hunger and thirst, and cold and heat.
If one contemplates these four [aggregates] as being momentary and subtly impermanent, one cannot say that these four sufferings do not exist.
If there is a bodhisattva who can form such a thought, this is called a bodhisattva contemplating subtle impermanence. It is the same for internal and external forms and mental phenomena.
Why? Because they proceed through the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). When proceeding through the six sense bases, either a mind of joy arises or...
The mind of anger may arise, or the mind of affection, or the mind of greed; as they arise successively in different ways, they do not remain of one kind.
Therefore, you should know that all phenomena of form and non-form are entirely impermanent.

Son of good family, if a bodhisattva can, within a single thought-moment, perceive the arising and ceasing and the impermanence of all phenomena, this is called a bodhisattva being endowed with the realization of impermanence.

It is said that when a wise son of good family has cultivated the perception of impermanence, he becomes free from the conceit of permanence and the inversion of perceiving what is permanent as such. Regarding the two causes of suffering: one interpretation states that internal suffering arises from internal causes, while external suffering arises from external causes; another interpretation holds that this is explicitly stated in the text, where hunger and thirst are internal, and cold and heat are external. As for the "six spheres of activity" (ṣaḍāyatana): 1. The six sense faculties (*indriya*) are the six spheres of activity. 2. The six objects (*viṣaya*) are the six spheres of activity. 3. The six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are the six spheres of activity. 4. The six contacts (*sparśa*) are the six spheres of activity. 5. The six feelings (*vedanā*) are the six spheres of activity. 6. The eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are the six spheres of activity. 14. The twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) are the six spheres of activity. 15. The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśadbodhipakṣadharma*) are the six spheres of activity. 16. The four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are the six spheres of activity. 17. The four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are the six spheres of activity. 18. The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are the six spheres of activity. 19. The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are the six spheres of activity. 20. The five powers (*pañcabala*) are the six spheres of activity. 21. The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are the six spheres of activity. 22. The eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) is the six spheres of activity. 23. The three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*) are the six spheres of activity. 24. The ten powers of a great Mahānārāyaṇa are the six spheres of activity. 52. The ten powers of a great Mahāmahānārāyaṇa are the six spheres of activity. 53. The ten powers of a great Mahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahāmahānārāyaṇa are the six spheres of activity. 68. These are the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
Next, one cultivates the perception of suffering; this concludes the second explanation of the perception of suffering.
Regarding the subsequent cultivation of the perception of suffering: for what reason does such suffering exist? One deeply realizes that the cause of this suffering is impermanence (*anityatā*).
Because of impermanence, one undergoes birth, old age, sickness, and death; because birth, old age, sickness, and death serve as conditions, they are called "impermanent.
Because of the condition of impermanence, one undergoes internal and external sufferings such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, flogging, and verbal abuse—all such sufferings are caused by impermanence.
Furthermore, the wise deeply contemplate that this body is a vessel of impermanence; being a vessel, it is...
Because suffering is a vessel for suffering, the phenomena contained within it are likewise suffering.
To contemplate deeply that this body is an impermanent vessel means that the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering are all contained within the body;

therefore, it is called a "vessel of suffering. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "because it is impermanent, it is suffering," the Śābdiya school (Śuṣṭhuvādins) says: "It is like the sword of impermanence."
Because all things are impermanent, they are suffering; if they were not oppressed by impermanence, they would not be suffering. The Master says: "That is not so.
Suffering is necessarily impermanent, but that which is impermanent is not necessarily suffering. For example, all grasses and trees are impermanent yet do not suffer.

Among the categories of sentient beings, those who possess suffering are necessarily impermanent. The three aggregates [of form, sensation, and perception] are material and indeterminate, and thus are all without [suffering]."
That which is permanent and not suffering is only the single matter of the mind; this is suffering.
From the perspective of the wise, one further contemplates the third [mark], the mark of non-self (*anātman*), as follows:
O son of good family, the wise further contemplate that arising itself is suffering and cessation itself is suffering; because there is the arising and cessation of suffering, it is [non-self].
These are impermanent, not-self, and do not belong to a self; the wise who cultivate the perception of non-self further contemplate that suffering is impermanent and impermanence is suffering.
If suffering is impermanent, how could the wise say there is a self?
Suffering is not the self, and impermanence is likewise so. Thus, these five aggregates are also suffering and impermanent; why, O sentient beings, do you say there is a self? Furthermore...
Next, one contemplates that all phenomena arise from various combinations and do not arise from a single combination;
furthermore, all phenomena are neither a single phenomenon nor the fruit of all these combinations.

All combinations lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), lack a singular nature, lack a differentiated nature, lack substantiality, and lack sovereignty. If all phenomena possess such characteristics as these...
How can the wise say that there is a self? Furthermore, they reflect: among all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is not a single phenomenon capable of acting as an agent.
If even a single phenomenon cannot act, then a combination of many phenomena likewise cannot act.
The nature of all phenomena ultimately cannot arise or cease independently; they cease through combination and they arise through combination.
Once these phenomena have arisen, sentient beings harbor perverted perceptions, claiming they are a composite and that they arise from a composite.
Since the perception of a "sentient being" is a perversion and lacks reality, how could there be a real self? Therefore, the wise contemplate non-self.
Furthermore, they carefully examine: for what causes and conditions do sentient beings say "this is my self"? If such a self existed, would it be one or many?
If the self were one, how could there be kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras;
gods, humans, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals; or the young, the old, and the middle-aged? Therefore, we know that the self is not one.
If the self were many, why would it be said that the self of sentient beings is one, all-pervading, and without limit? Whether it be one... [or many].
Regarding the two [types of] non-self, once one has contemplated non-self in this way, next the perception of revulsion toward food is explained.
This section also has three parts: first, the actual explanation; second, the discussion of the meaning; and third, the conclusion.
Next, one further contemplates the perception of revulsion toward food, reflecting thus:
"If all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and non-self, how can one give rise to the three kinds of unwholesome karma—of body, speech, and mind—for the sake of food?

If sentient beings, out of greed for food, give rise to these three kinds of unwholesome karma, the wealth they thereby acquire will be shared by the multitude, while they themselves must undergo suffering."

If there is no sharing of the fruit [of one's actions], O son of good family, the wise person further contemplates that all sentient beings undergo suffering of body and mind for the sake of food and drink.
If food is obtained through such manifold sufferings, how could I give rise to craving and attachment toward this food?
Therefore, one does not produce a mind of craving regarding food. Furthermore, the wise person should contemplate its cause.
"Food and drink cause the body to grow; yet I have now left the household life to receive the precepts and cultivate the Way, desiring to cast off this body.

Now, if I greedily crave this food, how shall I ever succeed in casting it off? Having contemplated thus, although he continues to receive food, he regards it as if eating the flesh of his own child in the wilderness;
his mind feels only revulsion and finds no pleasure in it at all, deeply contemplating that this food is merely a mass of matter."
Following this, one contemplates the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) as being like an ox that has been flayed and is being devoured by immeasurable worms.
Next, one contemplates the nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*) as being like a great mass of fire, and the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) as being like three hundred spears.

When the wise person has thus contemplated these four nutriments, they will never again give rise to thoughts of greed or delight regarding food. If greed should still arise, one should contemplate impurity (*aśubha*). Why is this?
Therefore, in order to become detached from craving and attachment, one should skillfully cultivate the perception of impurity regarding all food, making it correspond to its various impure aspects.
Having contemplated in this way, whether one receives excellent food or poor food, one should accept it as if applying medicine to a festering wound;
thus, no mind of craving or attachment will arise. Noble son, if a wise person...
One who can contemplate in this manner is said to have accomplished the perception of revulsion toward food (*āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñā*).

As stated in the text, regarding the four kinds of nutriment—edible food (*kavaḍīkāra*), contact (*sparśa*), volition (*manasikāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—"edible food" refers precisely to the meals of people today, as they can be divided into portions;

"contact-nutriment" refers to the clothing, bedding, and various tactile objects, both coarse and fine, which constitute the secondary environment (*upādāya-rūpa*); and "volition-nutriment" refers to...
These—the food of karma and the food of consciousness—are merely the food of mind.

Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, when a wise person contemplates food and forms the perception of it as impure, is this a real contemplation or a conceptual understanding?
If it is a real contemplation, then the food being contemplated is actually not impure; if it is a conceptual understanding, then..."
“What is this dharma called ‘wholesome perception’? The Buddha said, “Good son, such a perception is both a true contemplation and a conceptual understanding.
It is called ‘true’ because it can destroy the craving for food; it is called ‘conceptual understanding’ because one perceives insects where there are none.”
"Good son, all that is with outflows (sāsrava) is called 'empty,' yet one can also attain the real.
Good son, if there is a bhikṣu who resolves to beg for food, he premeditates thus: 'I shall beg for food; may I obtain what is good and not what is coarse or bad;
may I certainly obtain much and not let it be meager; may I obtain it quickly and not let it be delayed. Thus it is."
A bhikṣu who does not conceive a sense of revulsion toward food causes the wholesome dharmas he has cultivated to decline day and night, while unwholesome dharmas gradually increase.
Good son, if a bhikṣu wishes to go for alms, he should first make this aspiration:
"May all those who beg obtain full satisfaction; may those who give this food obtain immeasurable merit. If I..."
Food serves as an antidote for the body; one should cultivate wholesome dharmas to benefit the donor.
When making this aspiration, the wholesome dharmas one cultivates will increase day and night, while unwholesome dharmas will gradually be extinguished.
Good son, if there is a bhikṣu who can practice in this way, you should know that this person does not consume the offerings of faith from the country in vain.
Next, the perception of non-delight is explained as in the text.
Good son, a wise person who is endowed with these four perceptions is able to cultivate the perception of the world as being unsatisfactory, reflecting:
"There is no place in all the worlds where birth, aging, sickness, and death do not exist; yet there is no place where this body of mine has not been born.
If among all the worlds there were even a single place where one could escape birth, aging, sickness, and death, [I would seek it]."
How could one find pleasure in the world when there is no further attainment in all worlds and only decline?
Therefore, the world is certainly impermanent. If it is impermanent, why would a wise person take pleasure in the world?
Every sentient being, traversing throughout all worlds, fully experiences suffering and pleasure; even though they may attain the state of Brahmā...
Even those with the bodies of gods, up to the level of the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, when their lives end, fall back into the three evil realms;

though they may have been the bodies of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, at the end of their lives they are born into the animal realm, becoming lions, tigers, rhinoceroses, jackals, wolves, elephants, horses, oxen, or donkeys. Next, one contemplates the Universal Monarch who rules over the four continents.

When those of noble birth, high status, and sovereign power find their merit exhausted and fall into poverty such that they lack even food and clothing, the wise, having deeply contemplated such matters, conceive the perception that the world is not to be relished.
Furthermore, the wise contemplate that there are things in the world, namely:
houses, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, incense, flowers, necklaces, various kinds of music, wealth, and treasures.
Wealth and such things are all for the sake of escaping suffering; yet the very substance of such things is itself suffering. How can one seek to escape suffering by means of that which is suffering?
Son of good family, when the wise have contemplated in this way, they do not give rise to attachment or the notion of pleasure toward worldly objects.
Son of good family, it is like a person afflicted with a grave illness who, although possessing various [medicines],...
Various kinds of music, singing, dancing, flowers, incense, and necklaces—ultimately, one should never give rise to greedy attachment or delight within them.

When the wise observe this, they do so in the same way. Good son, the wise deeply contemplate that all worlds are not places of refuge, not places of liberation, not places of tranquility, not places of endearment, not the further shore, and are neither permanent nor blissful.
If I delight in this world through attachment to the dharma of self-purity, how shall I be able to leave it?

It is like a person who, disliking to dwell in darkness, seeks light but then returns again to the dark; "darkness" refers to the interval of ignorance, while "light" refers to the transcendence of the world.
If I take pleasure in the world, I increase the darkness and distance myself from the light; "darkness" is thus ignorance, and "light" is...
The clarity of wisdom is the cause of the clarity of wisdom; that is, the perception of the world as unlovely (*lokānabhirati-saṃjñā*).
Although all fetters of greed are indeed bonds, I now desire the clarity of wisdom and do not desire the world.
Having deeply contemplated such dharmas, the wise person fulfills the perception of the world as unlovely. Good son, a person of wisdom who has already cultivated the world...
Next is the contemplation of the perception of the unattractiveness of the interval.
Following that, the perception of death is explained in two parts: first, the explanation of death as the great terminal period;
second, the cultivation of the contemplation on death, wherein this life-span is constantly surrounded by immeasurable enemies and diminished moment by moment.

There is no growth; it is like a mountain torrent that cannot be stayed, or like the morning dew whose duration is brief, or like a prisoner heading to the market with death at every step, or like leading an ox or a sheep to the place of slaughter.
The subsequent section clarifies death in every thought-moment and consists of two parts: first, the question;
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said, "World-Honored One, how does the wise person contemplate the extinction of every thought-moment?
Next, the answer.
Good son, it is like four men, all skilled in the art of archery, who gather in one place and each shoot in a different direction.
They all think to themselves: "Our four arrows shall be released together and fall together. Then there is another man who thinks:
"These four arrows, from the moment they are released until they finally fall, I am able to catch them all at once with my hands. Good son, it is just so.
"Such a person may be said to be ill. Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said, "So it is, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "Good son, the illness of a terrestrial ghost is faster than that of such a person;
a flying ghost is faster than the terrestrial one; a terrestrial Cāturmahārājika deity is faster than the flying ghost;
a flying Sun and Moon deity is faster than the Cāturmahārājika; and a Cāturmahārājika deity of firm speed is faster than the flying Sun and Moon."

The lifespan of sentient beings is further swift, fragile, and fleeting, O son of good family. In a single breath and a single blink of an eye, four hundred births and deaths occur within the lifespan of sentient beings.
If a wise person can contemplate life in this way, it is called being able to contemplate the extinction of every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Son of good family, the wise person contemplates that life is subject to the King of Death; if I can distance myself from such a King of Death, then I shall attain [liberation].
To eternally sever impermanent life: furthermore, the wise contemplate this lifespan as being like a great tree on the edge of a steep riverbank;
like a person who has committed a heinous crime and faces execution with no one to show compassion;
like a lion king when he is severely famished; like a venomous snake inhaling fire and wind; and like a thirsty horse guarding its [water].
When the water [dries up], it is like the moment a great malevolent spirit gives rise to wrath; when all beings die, the King of Death is likewise so.
Good son, if a wise person can practice such contemplation, this is called cultivating the perception of death. Furthermore, good son, the wise person further contemplates:
"Now that I have left the household life, even if I were to obtain a lifespan of seven days and seven nights, I should, within that time..."

Diligently practicing the Way, upholding the prohibitive precepts, preaching the Dharma to transform and edify others, and benefiting sentient beings—this is called the wise person’s cultivation of the perception of death.
Furthermore, one may take seven days and seven nights as the maximum duration;
or six days, five days, four days, three days, two days, one day, one session, or even down to the interval of a single inhalation and exhalation. If, within that time, I...

To diligently cultivate the path, uphold the prohibitive precepts, preach the Dharma to transform others, and benefit sentient beings—this is called the wise person’s skillful cultivation of the perception of death.
A text states: "In one breath and one blink, there are four hundred births and cessations. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "In one thought-moment, there are sixty births and cessations."

Question: Why do these two passages not correspond? There are two interpretations. The first says: The *Abhidharmakośa* (Treatise on the Treasury) is of the Hīnayāna and explains impermanence in a general manner;
therefore, the *Ṣaṣṭi-saṃvartanī-kalpa-sūtra* (Sutra on the Sixty Cycles of Arising and Ceasing) is of the Mahāyāna and explains impermanence more precisely.
Thus, in the *Catuḥśataka-śāstra*, it says: "What is called 'one thought-moment' (*ekakṣaṇa*)? Because this moment is brief, it is merely... [the text continues].
The *Ṣaṣṭi-sūtra* states that because breaths are long, there are four hundred [breaths].
"The wise one is fully endowed" refers to the second general praise of the six perceptions (*ṣaḍ-saṃjñā*).
When the wise one is fully endowed with the aforementioned six perceptions, they are the cause for seven perceptions. What are the seven? First, constant cultivation.
The first is the perception of renunciation; the second is the perception of joy in cultivation; the third is the perception of non-anger; the fourth is the perception of non-envy;
the fifth is the perception of virtuous vows; the sixth is the perception of non-arrogance; and the seventh is the perception of mastery over samādhi.
Good son, if there is a bhikṣu who possesses these seven perceptions, he is called a śramaṇa, he is called a brāhmaṇa, he is called one who is tranquil, and he is called one who is pure.
This is called liberation; this is called a wise person; this is called right view; it is called reaching the other shore;

it is called the Great King of Physicians; it is called the Great Caravan Leader; it is called being well-versed in the secrets of the Tathāgata; and it is called knowing the seven kinds of speech of all Buddhas.
It is called right view because it knows how to sever the web of doubt arising from those seven kinds of speech.

It is said that one attains the seven perceptions from the six perceptions; furthermore, it is stated that "constantly cultivating the perception" does not mean contemplating a permanent object, but rather refers to constantly performing this cultivation.

Regarding "delighting in the cultivation of the perception," the term "desire" (yù) is used as a phonetic transcription for *praṇidhāna* (vow); it likewise signifies a constant delight in the desire to cultivate.
If a person is endowed with the six perceptions mentioned above— [the third section briefly designating four perceptions]— good son,
you should know that such a person is able to revile the three realms, distance themselves from the three realms,
extinguish the three realms, and does not give rise to attachment within the three realms.
The text states: "To be able to revile the triple world is the notion of transgression; to distance oneself from the triple world is the cessation of the notion of distancing;
to eliminate the triple world is the cessation of the notion of elimination; and to not give rise to attachment is the absence of the notion of craving."
This is called the third summary for the wise.
This is called the wise one being fully endowed with the ten perceptions; if a bhikṣu is fully endowed with these ten perceptions, he may truly be said to possess the characteristics of a śramaṇa.
At that time, Kāśyapa next offers praise in the following verses. Of these thirty-six verses of praise concerning the Buddha, there are three major divisions:
first, two lines that provide a general introduction; second, thirty lines that constitute the actual praise; and third, four lines that serve as a concluding eulogy.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva immediately praised the Buddha before him with these verses:
"Great King of Physicians who has compassion for the world, Whose body and wisdom are both utterly tranquil;
In the dharma of non-self, there is a true self— Therefore, I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One."
The initial resolve and the ultimate goal are ultimately not two; of these two states of mind, the former is more difficult to achieve.
To seek first to deliver others before one has delivered oneself—therefore, I pay homage to the initial resolve.
Having made this initial resolve, one becomes a teacher of humans and devas, surpassing both the śrāvakas and the pratyekabuddhas.
Thus, this resolve transcends the three realms; for this reason, it is named the Most Unsurpassed.
The World-Saviors seek [beings] before they can be found; the Tathāgata provides refuge without being requested.
The Buddha follows the world like a calf follows its mother; for this reason, he is named the Great Compassionate Ox.
The Tathāgata’s merits fill the ten directions; Those who are base and lacking wisdom cannot praise him.
I now praise his heart of compassion, To repay the two types of karma—of body and speech.
Those in the world who always delight in their own self-interest— The Tathāgata never acts for such purposes.
He is able to sever the worldly karmic retributions of sentient beings; for this reason, I pay homage to him who benefits both himself and others.
In the world, those who pursue kinship act with increasing intimacy and benefit; yet the Tathāgata’s benefit extends to all without distinction between enemy and kin.
The Buddha does not harbor such thoughts as worldly people do; therefore, his mind is equal and non-dual.
The world speaks of diverse actions and diverse results, yet for the Tathāgata, as he has taught, there is no discrepancy in karma.
Whatever practices he cultivates serve to sever all conditioned formations; therefore, he is named the Tathāgata.
Having already fully understood the faults of afflictions, he manifests dwelling among them for the sake of sentient beings.
Having long attained liberation within the world, you delight in dwelling within birth and death out of compassion;
though manifesting in celestial and human forms, your compassion follows you like a calf.
The Tathāgata is the mother of sentient beings, and the mind of loving-kindness is the little calf.
Reflecting on sentient beings while undergoing suffering myself, my mind felt no regret when contemplating compassion;
as the heart of pity grew intense, I was unaware of the pain. Therefore, I prostrate to the Tathāgata, the one who uproots suffering.
Though he has performed immeasurable merit, his actions of body, speech, and mind are ever pure.
Always acting for the sake of sentient beings and not for oneself, I therefore pay homage to the Tathāgata Viśuddhakarma.
Enduring suffering without perceiving it as pain, seeing the suffering of others as his own,
though he dwells in hell for the sake of sentient beings, he gives rise to neither the thought of suffering nor a mind of regret.
The various sufferings experienced by all sentient beings are entirely the suffering of the Tathāgata alone;
having realized this, his mind becomes firm and steadfast, and he is thus able to diligently cultivate the unsurpassed path.
The Buddha possesses a great heart of single-flavored compassion, regarding all sentient beings with pity as if they were his own children.
Sentient beings do not know that the Buddha can save them; Therefore, they slander the Tathāgata, as well as the Dharma and the Saṅgha.

Although the world is possessed of manifold afflictions And immeasurable faults and evils, The Buddha was already able to destroy these various fetters and transgressions From the very moment he first resolved upon enlightenment.
Only the Buddhas can praise the Buddha; Aside from the Buddhas, none can offer such praise.
I now praise him with but a single dharma: That he wanders through the world with a heart of loving-kindness.
The Tathāgata is a great mass of the dharma of loving-kindness; This loving-kindness is also able to deliver all sentient beings.
This is the unsurpassed, true liberation; liberation is itself the Great Nirvana.
Master Lingwei said: "The 'Lion’s Roar' praises the Buddha’s great kindness (*maitrī*), while this chapter praises the Buddha’s great compassion (*karuṇā*).
I say this is not so; for within the text it is stated that the Buddha possesses a single-flavored mind of great kindness, and further says, "that which is called the mind of kindness."

Saving the world is surely nothing other than great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); now it is said that one should be like the "Spiritual Flavor" (*lingwei*) lion’s roar, clarifying that Buddha-nature is itself great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) bestowing joy.
This chapter clarifies that the arising of wholesome roots in *icchantikas* is itself great compassion uprooting suffering.
Though explained separately, although it clarifies great kindness, it is not without great compassion; although it speaks of great compassion, it is not without great kindness.

Xie Lingyun’s Re-edition of the *Kauṇḍinya-varga*:
Kauṇḍinya is translated as "Fire-Vessel," which is his clan name; Ājñāta is translated as "Known-Without," meaning "Nameless. Its meanings are manifold.
Furthermore, there are four intentions regarding those who first attain the Way: they are the most senior elders; they sit to the left and right of the Buddha;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they uphold and lead the Dharma for the present and the future; and among the aged and virtuous, they are the foremost leaders.
Because the Buddha wishes to ensure a good beginning and a successful conclusion, he first turned the wheel of the Dharma by addressing these individuals and extensively propagating it before them.
After the turning of the Wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī, he again confronted them to reveal the secret treasury;

while the three versions of the *Tri-saṃyukta* primarily refute externalists, this [text] is the very first to do so. Now, because it targets these individuals at the very end to destroy externalism, it is named after the person.

First, he confronted them to enable the five bhikṣus to realize the Truth (*satyadarśana*); later, he confronted them to enable the ten ṛṣis to perceive the Principle. For this reason, it derives its name from the person. If...
Regarding the entrustment of the Dharma to Ānanda, if it concerns the reception of oral instructions, it should rest with Ānanda;

if it concerns the maintenance and succession of the lineage, it should rest with Kāśyapa; and if it concerns the broad exposition of the great purport, it should rest with Mañjuśrī. Yet, among the great disciples, some have already entered parinirvāṇa and others have not yet appeared.
As for the elders of long-standing virtue who witnessed the Buddha from beginning to end, they must certainly rely upon [the aforementioned].
Because it is capable of bearing the entrustment, it is addressed to the assembly for the purpose of circulating the final testament. Kaishan says: "The translation was not yet complete;
it consists of the Preface and the Main Text. The Main Text is further divided into three parts: first, the brief exposition opening the school; second, the extensive exposition defining the school;

and this present chapter is the third, which explains the subduing of the heterodox and returning to the orthodox. Guangzhai says: "Although the translation was not yet complete, it consists of three sections."
To be fully endowed with this chapter constitutes the section on the dissemination (*pravartana*). Furthermore, it is said that this chapter answers the thirty-seventh question.
Now, one might wish to ask: "I am questioning the various aggregates (*skandha*), yet I lack wisdom. Xinghuang remarked:

"If this were an answer to a question, one would obtain the preceding slight meaning but lose the subsequent texts; if it were intended as the dissemination, one would obtain the text addressed to Ānanda but lose its [original] purpose."

Regarding other matters, if one were to evaluate the various masters, each has grasped a particular point: some cite the words of Dharmakṣema, stating that while the meaning of this sutra is complete, the text is not;
others cite the *Gṛhapati-Prārthanā-bhikṣu-sūtra*, which mentions three categories of future [beings];
and still others cite the passage below where the Buddha commands Ānanda, noting two purposes therein: first, to transform Subhadra, and second, to entrust the teaching.
Although the [teaching] has already concluded and no formal entrustment (*parindanā*) has been seen, one should know that it is not yet exhausted.

As for the claim that there is a "circulation" (*pravartana*) section, there are two types: first, circulation through the gathering of the heterodox into the orthodox; second, circulation through formal entrustment. Although there is no textual passage concerning formal entrustment, because there is the gathering of the heterodox, it is said that there is a circulation section.
Now, it is clarified that this chapter is still the function of *Nirvāṇa*; its meaning is broad and manifest.
In this [text], there is the function of subduing the wicked and subduing the heterodox; in the future, there will be the function of rescuing the wicked and rescuing the heterodox.
If one wishes to propagate the correct teaching, both paths are attainable; if one wishes to compose a work that either exhausts or does not exhaust [the meaning], there is no hindrance.
Now, clarifying the function of *nirvāṇa*, the preceding chapter was the function of subduing the wicked, while this chapter is the function of subduing the heterodox. This is according to the text.

The first is the correct contemplation of practice (*samyag-darśana-pratipatti*), and the second is the refutation of various heterodox views. Among the essentials of spiritual cultivation, nothing surpasses these two:
correct contemplation is the superior seeking for one's own practice, while the refutation of heterodoxy is the downward transformation for the benefit of others.

Correct contemplation is the cultivation of wholesome action (*kuśala-karma*), while the refutation of heterodoxy is the cessation of unwholesome action. Correct contemplation is the arising of liberation, while the refutation of heterodoxy is the extinction of delusion. Correct contemplation...

This wisdom-virtue (jñāna-guṇa) destroys the heterodox, and this cessation-virtue (prahāṇa-guṇa) corresponds to the fourfold intent (*caturvidha-saṃgraha*). First, the correct contemplation is elucidated, which is further divided into two parts:
first, the formal exposition of the practice of contemplation; second, the concluding summary of praise and censure.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya: "Form is impermanent; by the cessation of form, one attains liberation in the eternally abiding form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise impermanent; by the cessation of consciousness, one attains liberation in the eternally abiding consciousness.
Kauṇḍinya, form is suffering; by the cessation of form, one attains liberation in peace."
The form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness of pleasure are also like this, Kauṇḍinya. Form itself is emptiness;
by the cessation of form through emptiness, one attains liberation. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are not empty are also like this, Kauṇḍinya.
Form is non-self; by the cessation of this form, one attains liberation. [The same applies to] true-self form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Consciousness is also like this, Kauṇḍinya. Form is impure; by the cessation of this form, one attains the pure form of liberation.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this, Kauṇḍinya. Form is the characteristic of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
by the cessation of this form, one attains the form of liberation that is free from the characteristics of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

"Kauṇḍinya, it is the same for perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Form is caused by ignorance; when that cause is extinguished, one attains liberation from form, which is no longer caused by ignorance.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, Kauṇḍinya.

Even so, form is caused by birth; when that cause is extinguished, one attains liberation from form, which is no longer caused by birth. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
Consciousness is also like this, Kauṇḍinya. Form is the cause of the four perversions;
when the cause of perversion is extinguished, one attains liberation from form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this, Kauṇḍinya.
Form is the cause of immeasurable unwholesome dharmas, namely: the body of a man, craving for food, craving for desire, and greed.

Anger, jealousy, malevolence, stinginess, the nutriment of physical food, the nutriment of sensory consciousness, the nutriment of volition, the nutriment of contact, birth from eggs, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation, as well as the five desires and the five hindrances—all such phenomena arise because of form (*rūpa*) and are extinguished by the cessation of form;

thus one attains liberation. There are no such infinite evil forms, and it is likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*). Pride... [is likewise].
"Kauṇḍinya, form itself is the cause of bondage; by extinguishing the form that is bondage, one attains liberation—the form that is free from bondage.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Kauṇḍinya, form itself is the cause of the stream; by extinguishing the form that is the stream, one attains liberation—the form that is not of the stream.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Kauṇḍinya, form is not a refuge."
By the cessation of this form, one attains the refuge of liberation; it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Kaccāyana, form is a festering sore; by the cessation of this form, one attains the form of liberation, free from sores;
it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Kaccāyana, form is not tranquil; by the cessation of this form, one attains [the state of tranquility].
The same applies to the form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness of the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding this initial pair that clarifies the contemplation of the permanent and the impermanent, the reason both rely upon the aggregates (*skandhas*) as their objects rather than other phenomena is due to four general meanings:

first, the beginning and end of the Buddha’s transformative teaching; second, what is appropriate for the capacities of sentient beings; third, the conclusion of the sūtra; and fourth, the consistency from beginning to end.
Fourth, regarding the beginning and end of all dharmas as a single path of transformation from start to finish:
the *Lotus Sūtra* states that in the past at Vārāṇasī, he turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths and analytically taught the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
These five aggregates—their arising and ceasing—are impermanent. Now, entering nirvāṇa, he causes these five forms of impermanence to cease, so that all five become eternal.
2. Regarding "according to what is appropriate for the object," this can be seen [in the text]. 3. Regarding "the three statements that conclude the beginning and end of the sutra":
at the very opening of this sutra, it says, "I now bestow upon you constant life, form, and strength.

Now, at the conclusion of this final sutra, it returns to conclude with this same intent, explaining that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are permanent, desiring to clarify that the security of life and form is precisely the five aggregates. 4. Regarding "concluding all... [the text continues].

Regarding the beginning and end of the Dharma: in the essence of all contemplative practice, there is none that does not first take the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its beginning and take the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) as its end.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other scriptures frequently speak of the emptiness of form (*rūpa*), the emptiness of sensation, perception, and so forth, up to the emptiness of the knowledge of all modes;
the five aggregates constitute the beginning, and nirvana constitutes the end, with the intermediate stages being omitted. [Some] interpret "form" (*rūpa*) as being obstructive.
The Dharma-mind takes dharmas as its object; because the Buddha is unimpeded and without objects, it has no form.

If the mind possessed form, it would have to be covered by a roof and clad in clothing. That which is called "form" refers to the clarity and purity of discerning wisdom, which is metaphorically likened to physical form.
Now, this explanation contradicts the sutra, for the sutra says: "By the cessation of this form, one attains the eternal form. This [explanation] should likewise [contradict it].
If one attains unimpeded form by extinguishing obstructed form, one should likewise attain a mind without objects by extinguishing the mind that takes objects;
how then could such a mind with objects still persist? Furthermore, why call a mind that takes objects "form"?

If you use form as an analogy for wisdom, what then would you use as an analogy for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? How could the ocean ever be contained within the hoofprint of a small-vehicle ox?
Furthermore, another master says: "According to the actual reality, it is not that there is no form or mind. He cites a sūtra, saying:

"At that time, having transcended the realm of consciousness (manodhātu), one dwells within the activity of wisdom (jñānakarma). Although he cites this sūtra, it actually works against his own position.

What is this "activity of wisdom"? Is it not the Buddha-mind? Furthermore, he says: "Ordinary beings are called aggregates (skandha); how could this apply to the Buddha? But the Buddha is called the "Five Parts" (pañcaskandha). Which [parts] are they?
The term "skandha" (aggregate) means "to cover and conceal"; because the Buddha has no such covering, he is not a skandha.

This is analogous to how the cause is called the "ten thousand practices" and the fruit is called the "ten thousand virtues"—this [interpretation] also contradicts the sutra. The sutra says: "One attains eternal form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
it is likewise for these as well. Is this not the case that the eternal skandhas are the eternal form and mind? The preceding passage states: "I now bestow upon you eternal life."
Physical power, tranquility, and unimpeded eloquence are the eternally abiding aggregates (*skandhas*) that pervade and cover the *dharmadhātu*.

What obstruction could there be in this, such that you would claim they are not aggregates? As for the *dharmakāya*, it is neither an eternal aggregate nor an impermanent aggregate; the same applies to the *dhātus* and *āyatanas*.

Yet, it is capable of being an eternal aggregate and capable of being an impermanent aggregate. Here, in response to Cūḍapanthaka, the previous argument is refuted by demonstrating that [the aggregates] do not exist.
If one attains permanent form, that very permanent form is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). How can it contradict the sūtra by saying there is no aggregate of form?

If explained comprehensively, even impermanent form is still permanent form; the same applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates—impermanent aggregates are themselves the permanent aggregates.

This is likewise true for the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*). Although there are two modes of explanation—the specific and the comprehensive—they both clarify that the aggregates, elements, and bases are permanent.
...entering [the stages], etc.
Second, the conclusion consisting of praise and censure:
"Kauṇḍinya, if there is anyone who can know in this way, they are called a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa; they are fully endowed [with these qualities]."
Ājñātakauṇḍinya, apart from the Buddha-dharma, there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor is there any dharma of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
All those of external paths are false and deceitful; they have no genuine practice at all.
Although they manifest signs and claim that these two exist, in reality they do not; such a thing is impossible. Why is this? If there are no śramaṇas...
"O Gatekeeper Brahmins, how can you say there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?
I have always uttered the lion’s roar within this great assembly; you, too, should likewise utter the lion’s roar within the great assembly."
The text is clear enough to refute heterodox views based upon it.
At that time, the second section, "Refuting Heterodoxy," begins; it is further divided into two parts: first, the introductory narrative (*nidāna*), and second, the formal refutation.

Within the introductory narrative, there are two sections: first, the deliberation, and second, the seeking of the Buddha to compete in supernatural powers. The deliberation consists of five rounds, as can be seen.
At that time, there were immeasurable followers of external paths who, having heard these words, conceived thoughts of anger and malice:
"Now Gautama says that among our assembly there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor is there any dharma of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
How shall we extensively employ skillful means to say to Gautama that within our assembly there are indeed śramaṇas?"
When there are those who follow the dharma of a śramaṇa and those who follow the dharma of a brāhmaṇa, a certain brahmin in that assembly proclaimed these words:
"O worthy ones, the words of Gautama are no different from those of a madman; how can they be scrutinized?
A madman in this world may sing, dance, weep, laugh, revile, or praise, whether toward enemies or kin."
The inability to distinguish [the true nature of] the śramaṇa Gautama is likewise: some say that I was born into the family of King Śuddhodana, while others say I was not born;
some say that after being born, I walked seven steps, while others say I did not walk;

some say that from childhood I practiced worldly affairs, while others say that I am an omniscient person (sarvajña); and at times it is said that I enjoyed pleasures within the palace and fathered a son.
At times he felt weary of and reviled [worldly life], at times he personally practiced austerities for six years;
at times he criticized the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists, or spoke of how he had received teachings not previously heard from Udraka Rāmaputra and Ārāḍa Kālāma;
at times he said they possessed no knowledge, and at times he said that he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* beneath the Bodhi tree.
"Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, at times he says, 'I did not go to the tree and obtain anything';
at other times he says, 'This very body of mine is now nirvāṇa,' or he says, 'The extinction of the body is nirvāṇa.
What Gautama has said is no different from the ravings of a madman; for what reason, then, do you grieve and lament? The Brahmins then—

He replied, "Great Being, why should we not be distressed? The śramaṇa Gautama has already gone forth and taught that all things are impermanent, suffering, empty, selfless, and impure. When my disciples heard this, they were struck with terror.
How can sentient beings accept such words—that all things are impermanent, suffering, empty, selfless, and impure? Now, Gautama has come here once again."
"In this Śāla grove, he is preaching to the great assembly the Dharma of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Having heard these words, all my disciples have abandoned me to go and accept the teachings of Gautama. Because of this, I am born into great sorrow and suffering.
At that time, there was another brāhmaṇa who spoke thus: "O worthy ones, listen attentively, listen attentively!"
The claim that the śramaṇa Gautama practices loving-kindness and compassion is false and not true.

If he possessed loving-kindness and compassion, why does he teach my disciples to receive his own dharma for themselves? If the fruit of loving-kindness and compassion consists in conforming to the intentions of others, yet now he violates my wishes, how can you say he possesses them?
Furthermore, if it is said that the śramaṇa Gautama does not act for the sake of the world...
That which is defiled by the eight worldly dharmas is likewise false. If you say, "Gautama has few desires and is content," how is it that he now robs us of our profit?
If you say, "As for his lineage, he is of a noble clan," this too is false. Why?
Because from time immemorial, we have neither seen nor heard of a great lion king harming a small mouse. If Gautama were [truly such a one]...
How can one of such noble lineage now trouble and disturb us? If you say that Gautama possesses great power, this too is false.
Why? Because from ancient times until now, we have neither seen nor heard of the King of the Garuḍas ever contending with a crow.
If you say his strength is great, for what reason would he fight with us? If you say that Gautama possesses [the power of] others...
The mind and its intellect are likewise illusory. Why is this? If one possessed such wisdom, for what reason and by what causal conditions would they not know my mind?
O worthy ones, in the past I heard from ancient sages that after a hundred years had passed, an illusory phantom would appear in the world;
it is this very same deceptive phantom, Gautama, who now appears here.
"In the Śāla grove, our passing will soon take place; you should not now be filled with grief and distress. At that time, another Nirgrantha said:

"Venerable sir, my present sorrow and suffering are not for the sake of myself or the offerings from my disciples, but rather because this world is shrouded in the darkness of ignorance and lacks eyesight, failing to recognize fields of merit and non-fields of merit, and abandoning the wisdom of the ancients."
"The Brahmin’s offering of food has caused me grief because I am young. The Śramaṇa Gautama is well-versed in incantations;
by the power of these incantations, he can cause one body to become infinite bodies, and infinite bodies to return to being one body.
Or he can transform his own body into the likeness of men, women, oxen, sheep, elephants, or horses. My power is such that I can destroy such incantations. Gautama said:
"When the magical arts of the śramaṇa Gautama have been extinguished, you shall all return to receiving abundant offerings and enjoy peace and happiness.
At that time, another brāhmaṇa spoke thus: "O virtuous ones, the śramaṇa Gautama is endowed with and has perfected immeasurable merits;
therefore, you should not contend with him. The great assembly replied: "Foolish man!"
"How can it be said that the śramaṇa Gautama possesses great merit? That his mother passed away seven days after his birth—can this truly be called a mark of merit?
The brāhmaṇa replied: "When reviled, he does not become angry; when struck, he does not retaliate.
Know that this is indeed a mark of great merit. His body is fully endowed with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics."
He possesses immeasurable supernormal powers; therefore, you should know that these are the marks of his merit. His mind is free from pride;
he greets others first with kind words, speaking with gentleness and never with harshness. Though both his age and vigor are at their peak, his mind is not impulsive or violent.

Possessing great wealth in the kingdom, he felt no attachment to it and renounced it to leave the household life, casting it away as if it were phlegm or saliva. For this reason, I say: "The Śramaṇa Gautama..."
The great assembly, endowed with immeasurable merit, replied: "Excellent, O worthy Gautama! Śramaṇa, it is indeed as you have said;
you possess immeasurable supernormal powers and transformations. We do not wish to compete with you in this matter.
The nature of the Śramaṇa Gautama is gentle and soft; he is incapable of ascetic practices, having been raised in the depths of the palace and never having engaged in worldly affairs."
One may only speak with gentle words; if he does not know the arts, scripts, or the principles of debate, one should invite him to discuss in detail the essentials of the True Dharma, stipulating:
"If he defeats me, I shall serve him; if I defeat him, he shall serve me."
At that time, there were many who, being of inferior rank, desired to compete in strength.
Then, a great multitude of immeasurable non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika) gathered together and went to the Magadhan King Ajātaśatru.
Upon seeing them, the King asked: "O worthy ones, each of you practices the noble path; you are renunciants who have abandoned [worldly life]."
"Free from wealth and household affairs, the people of my kingdom all provide for me together with hearts of reverence, gazing upon me without ever transgressing or offending.
For what reason have you come here in such a harmonious assembly? O worthy ones, each of you has received different teachings and different precepts;
your renunciations are not the same, and furthermore, each of you follows his own respective precepts to practice the Way as a renunciant. What is the cause [for this]?"
"For this reason, we have now gathered together with one mind, like fallen leaves driven by a whirlwind into a single place.
For what cause and condition have we come here? We shall always protect those who have left the household life, even at the cost of our own bodies and lives.
At that time, all the various groups of non-Buddhists spoke thus: "Great King!"
Listen attentively, Great King! This is the great bridge of Dharma, the great whetstone of Dharma, and the great scale of Dharma;
it is the vessel for all merit, the true nature of all merit, the path of the True Dharma, the fertile field for seeds, the root of all lands, and the illumination of all lands.
He is a mirror for the forms of all the devas and a parent to all the people of the land.
Great King, you are a treasury of merit for the entire world, and this very body of yours is that treasury. For what reason is he called the King Treasury of Merit?
Because when he adjudicates state affairs, he makes no distinction between kin and enemy; his mind is as impartial as earth, water, fire, and wind. Therefore, he is called the King.
"O Great King Guṇakara, although the lifespan of beings in the present age is short, your merit is like that of the long-lived and blissful kings of old—
such as King Mūrdhaja, King Sudarśana, King Kṣāntivādin,
King Nahuṣa, King Yajñadatta, King Śibi, and King Ṛkṣa— who were all endowed with wholesome qualities. So it is with you, Great King, now."
It is likewise so, Great King. Because of the King’s presence, the land is peaceful and prosperous, and the people flourish;
therefore, all those who have gone forth from home admire this country and joyfully uphold the precepts with diligence, practicing the Right Path.
Great King, in my sutras I have said that if a renunciant dwells in whatever country, they should uphold the precepts with diligence and practice the Right Path.
"It is said that Your Majesty also possesses the capacity for practicing virtue. Great King, you have already brought all thieves and robbers under control;
those who have left the household life no longer have any cause for fear. Now there remains only one great evildoer, the ascetic Gautama, whom Your Majesty has not yet investigated.
We are deeply afraid of this man; he relies on his own noble lineage and is endowed with a handsome physical appearance."

"In this way, O Brahmin, when asked whether the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* is eternal, the Buddha likewise replied, 'It is so. Yet, in ultimate discourse, how could *nirvāṇa* ever be definitively eternal?

Again, when asked whether the absence of afflictions (*kleśa*) constitutes *nirvāṇa*, the Buddha likewise replied, 'It is so. But how could the Buddha [ever have said that the absence of afflictions is the same as *nirvāṇa*]?"
If one asks, "Is the absence of afflictions what constitutes nirvana?"— the preceding text did not state that the severance of afflictions constitutes nirvana,
but rather that the non-arising of afflictions constitutes nirvana. This present explanation is made in response to these non-Buddhists,
as they are people who hold the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Vāsiṣṭha said: "Gautama, there are four kinds of things in the world that are called 'non-existent. First, a thing that has not yet emerged is called non-existent;
for example, when a jar has not yet emerged from the clay, it is called a non-existent jar. Second, a thing that has already ceased is called non-existent;
for example, once a jar has been broken, it is called a non-existent jar. Third, the mutual non-existence of distinct entities is called..."
"Non-existence" refers to that which is ultimately non-existent, such as the absence of a horse within a cow or the absence of a cow within a horse;

it is called "non-existence" because these things do not exist at all, like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. Gautama, if you define *nirvāṇa* as being merely the cessation of afflictions, then *nirvāṇa* would be non-existent.
If it were non-existent, how could you say it possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
However, prior to the third turn, you raised the four absences as an objection to the extinction of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*):
"If a phenomenon is extinguished and there is no extinction, how can there still be permanence and bliss? That which has not yet arisen is the absence of the future;
that which has been extinguished is the absence of the past.
The Buddha said, "Good son, such nirvāṇa is not a prior non-existence like that of a jar while it is still clay;

nor is it a non-existence through destruction like that of a broken jar; nor is it an absolute non-existence like that of a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns, which is a non-existence by way of difference.
Good son, as you have said, although there is no horse within a cow, one cannot say that the cow is also non-existent."
Just as one cannot say that a horse is non-existent simply because there is no ox within it, so too it is with nirvāṇa:
nirvāṇa is not present within the afflictions, nor are the afflictions present within nirvāṇa; therefore, they are said to be mutually exclusive.
The Buddha replied: "It is the same as [the case of] mutual non-existence; this was also spoken with reference to the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).

However, if one discusses the correct principle (nyāya), it is not a case of total mutual non-existence. Why is this so? Originally, 'mutual non-existence' is defined by the mutual absence of oxen and horses.
Now, it is clarified that within saṃsāra, nirvāṇa is inherently present; therefore, according to the correct principle, it is not a case of total mutual non-existence."

Vāsiṣṭha said: "Gautama, if you consider 'otherness' and 'non-existence' to be nirvāṇa, then since otherness and non-existence lack permanence, bliss, self, and purity, why do you, Gautama, say that nirvāṇa is permanent, blissful, self, and pure?"
Regarding the fourth point, that remains difficult to resolve: if they were mutually non-existent, then even impermanence would not exist.
Although there is no horse within an ox, it is likewise with the horse being absent within the ox; oxen and horses are fundamentally non-existent and only now exist.
Nirvāṇa is also like this: although there is no saṃsāra within nirvāṇa, the fact that nirvāṇa exists is precisely its fundamental nature.
That which exists now having been non-existent is also impermanent.
Although the Buddha’s current answer is the same in terms of mutual non-existence (*itaretara-abhāva*), it is not identical; there are three types of non-existence: first, mutual non-existence;
second, prior non-existence (*prāg-abhāva*); and third, the subsequent non-existence of what was previously existent (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). One should know that [this refers to] Nirvāṇa.
Since identity and difference are both absent, these three things do not exist; therefore, they are permanent and blissful. Within this passage there are three parts:
first, the explanation by way of the Dharma; second, the citation of the three illnesses and three medicines as a simile; and third, the citation of the simile to clarify the fruit.
The Buddha said, "Good son, as you have stated, there are three kinds of non-existence:

first, the non-existence of oxen and horses, which is called 'prior non-existence' (*pūrvābhāva*); second, that which was previously existent and has subsequently ceased, which is called 'non-existence through destruction' (*vināśābhāva*);

and third, the non-existence of distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇānyathābhāva*), as you have described. Good son, these three kinds of non-existence do not exist within *nirvāṇa*; therefore, *nirvāṇa* [is free from them]."
Permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
It is like a worldly patient who has three types of illness: first, fever; second, wind; and third, cold.
These three illnesses can be treated by three medicines: for those with fever, clarified butter (*sarpis*) can cure it; for those with wind, oil can cure it.
For those with cold-natured illnesses, honey can cure them; these three kinds of medicines can thus cure these three kinds of evil diseases.
Good son, there is no oil within the wind, no wind within the oil, and so on, up to: there is no cold within the honey, and no honey within the cold.
Therefore, they are able to cure all sentient beings; it is also like this. There are three kinds of diseases: the first is greed.
The second is hatred, and the third is delusion. For these three illnesses, there are three kinds of medicine: the contemplation of impurity serves as the medicine for greed;
the contemplation of loving-kindness serves as the medicine for hatred; and the wisdom that contemplates causes and conditions serves as the medicine for delusion.
Good son, one practices the contemplation of non-greed to eliminate greed, the contemplation of non-hatred to eliminate hatred, and [the contemplation of non-delusion] to eliminate delusion.
Therefore, one should intentionally observe that among the three types of diseases there are no three types of medicines, and among the three types of medicines there are no three types of diseases.
Furthermore, the subsequent text states: "Honey can treat cold-natured ailments; according to medical authorities, the nature of honey is indeed cold, as it is suited to the local climate."

Differences do not necessarily always follow this pattern; furthermore, it is stated in the analogy that "among the three kinds of illnesses there are no three kinds of medicines, and among the three kinds of medicines there are no three kinds of illnesses.

The ancient [commentators] used this passage to prove the absence of identity (asvabhāva). However, if ignorance were to exist as a medicine within wisdom, then illness would contradict this teaching.
Yet, according to the ancient interpretation of the *Vyavahāra-śāstra* (or *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha*), it clarifies that [ignorance does not exist therein].

Regarding the doubt as to whether there truly exists [a result] within the outflows (*āsrava*), this statement that it "does not exist" refers merely to the absence of delusions such as grasping at characteristics (*nimittagraha*).

If one were to interpret this according to the understanding of the *Jātaka* (or the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*), since true outflowlessness (*anāsrava*) cannot actually produce a retribution, there would be no need to speak of ignorance (*avidyā*) in order to enter into the realization of its essence.
However, in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, it is stated that the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) takes outflowless karma as its cause. This...
When we speak of "similar outflows-free" (*anāsrava*) and "outflows-free by guidance," we do not refer to the "true outflows-free.
Noble son, because the three medicines are absent within the three types of illness, and because the three illnesses are absent within the three medicines—
namely, impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity— one is therefore able to attain what is called permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Vāsiṣṭha said, "The Tathāgata has taught me regarding the permanent and the impermanent. This is the second instance of his submission.
Vāsiṣṭha said, "World-Honored One, Tathāgata, you have taught me regarding the permanent and the impermanent; what is permanent and what is impermanent?

The Buddha said, "Good son, form (*rūpa*) is impermanent, while liberation from form is permanent; this continues up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is impermanent [while liberation from it is permanent]."

"O son of good family who possesses the consciousness of eternal liberation, if there are sons or daughters of good family who are able to contemplate that from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*) these are impermanent, you should know that such persons have attained the eternal Dharma.
Vāśpaṭa said, "World-Honored One, I now already know the dharmas of the eternal and the impermanent.
The Buddha said, "Son of good family, how do you know the eternal and the impermanent?"
The Venerable Vāseṭṭha said, “World-Honored One, I now know that my form is impermanent; having attained liberation, it is permanent. This applies likewise up to consciousness.
The Buddha said, “Good man, you have done well. You have already repaid this body. Tell Kauṇḍinya and the others:
‘Vāseṭṭha has already realized the fruit of Arhatship; you may give him his three robes, bowl, and requisites.’”
Then, as Kauṇḍinya bestowed the robe and bowl according to the Buddha’s instructions, Vāśiṣṭha, having received the robe and bowl, spoke these words:
"Venerable Kauṇḍinya, by means of this wretched and evil body of mine, I have now obtained a virtuous fruit of retribution.
I pray that you, Venerable One, would deign to go to the World-Honored One on my behalf and fully declare my heart's intent, for I am indeed wicked."
"A person has offended the Tathāgata by addressing him by his clan name, Gautama; I pray that you will repent this transgression for me.
I, too, can no longer endure this poisonous body and shall now enter parinirvāṇa. At that time, Kauṇḍinya went to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One, the bhikṣu Vāsiṣṭha has given rise to a sense of shame and remorse, saying himself that he was obstinate and foolish to have offended the Tathāgata."
"O Nigaṇṭha Gautama, you cannot remain long in this body of a venomous snake; now I wish to extinguish my body and entrust myself to you for repentance.
The Buddha said, "Kauṇḍinya and the bhikṣu Vāsiṣṭha have already cultivated roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas of the past.
Now they accept my words and abide according to the Dharma. Because they abide according to the Dharma, they shall obtain the fruit of right attainment. You all—"
"One should make offerings to his body. At that time, having heard this from the Buddha, Kauṇḍinya returned to the place where the body was and prepared the offerings.
While Vāsiṣṭha was having his body cremated, he performed various miraculous feats (*ṛddhi-pāda*).
When the non-Buddhist practitioners saw this, they cried out in a loud voice, "This Vāsiṣṭha has already obtained the incantations and arts of the śramaṇa Gautama!"
"This person shall, before long, surpass that śramaṇa Gautama.
Regarding the phrase "form is impermanent, yet liberation from form is permanent," there are two interpretations:
first, since form is indeed impermanent, my liberation from form is such that form no longer exists; therefore, it is permanent. Second, liberation itself is...
Since form (*rūpa*) is itself eternal, the preceding text states that one attains the "eternally abiding form of liberation.
Here, the latter explanation is considered superior. Within this context, the text of Cunda’s confession refers to the clan name Gautama as "Ni" (禰).
This was because the old pronunciation was "Ni," meaning they called you "Ni. Thus it says, "The Gautama clan is Ni. Now, according to the West Wing of the Yecheng Monastery:
According to the Dharma Master’s explanation, the pronunciation is *nǎi*; however, when translated, it is simply the sound of *nǎi* (or *ní*) used by the people of the North.
It is also said to be the sound of *ní wǒ* (I). This character is also employed in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, where the text reads:
"Those of the Gautama clan—if a disciple of the Buddha addresses the Buddha as 'Gautama,' it is as previously described."
In the verse of the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness," it says: "O Gautama of great and holy virtue, we pray that you arise and expound the Dharma.

This is a word of praise, clarifying that although the Buddha has for seven generations descended from the royal lineage of the Śākya clan, his original family originated from the great clan of Gautama;
his ancestral lineage is exceptionally remote and does not begin only today. [This was said] if one were to harbor the views of the non-Buddhists.
To address him as "Gautama" does not refer to his virtues, but speaks merely of his clan; this is what is meant by being slighted or treated with casual disregard.
It is like when people in the world do not call someone by their title or position, but only by their clan name, thereby treating them with slight.

Furthermore, when he says, "I too cannot remain long in this poisonous body; I now wish to enter parinirvāṇa," it means that he possesses innate supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) which he can obtain at will.
Because the noble fruit employs the knowledge of the ultimate limit (*paryanta-jñāna*), one enters *nirvāṇa*.

As for the preceding passage stating that "one who has attained *arhatship* receives three robes," according to principle, once one has attained *arhatship*, one is already fully endowed with robes and bowl.

That it is said here [he] "has none" refers to the case of an *arhat* by birth (*svayam-āgata-arhat*); since he has already attained *arhatship* on his own, he requires robes. Furthermore, this person’s original...
How do we know that these renunciant non-Buddhists did not wait to have their hair shaved?

In the preceding text, Jāti is called a *brāhmaṇa*, whereas here Vāsiṣṭha is simply called a *brahmacārin*; since a *brahmacārin* is precisely a renunciant non-Buddhist, it was therefore necessary to further bestow upon him an alms-bowl.
At that time, there was also Śreṇika among the assembly; this Śreṇika, a third non-Buddhist teacher, was not merely one individual—just as among the Buddha’s disciples there were many named Kāśyapa.

This chapter consists of four sections: first, the introductory narrative (nidāna); second, the refutation of attachments; third, the discussion of doctrine; and fourth, the conversion and submission.
At that time, there was another brahmin in the assembly named Śreṇika who spoke again, saying: "Gautama, does the self exist?
The Tathāgata remained silent. "Gautama, does the self not exist? The Tathāgata remained silent. A second and a third time he asked in this same manner, and the Buddha remained silent each time.

However, the Buddha’s teaching is not fixed; there are times when he first clarifies the correct principle so that non-Buddhists may attain understanding, and there are times when he must first remain silent, waiting for the opponent to establish their own thesis before subsequently refuting it to set forth the correct principle.

Since it is appropriate to remain silent first in this instance, he did not answer the three questions. Generally, there are three reasons for not answering: first, what is suitable according to the faculties and conditions [of the audience].

Furthermore, although there is no verbal response, this silence itself constitutes an answer. This is because both types of definitive questions—those concerning existence and non-existence—are based on erroneous intentions.

Thus, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is stated that the Buddha did not answer the fourteen difficult questions, such as whether the world is finite or infinite, eternal or non-eternal, and whether the Tathāgata exists after death or does not exist after death. Thirdly, the Buddha intended to refute the opponent's own established positions.

The meaning emerges from the fundamental principles; only then can one refute [the opponent]. Thus, although the Tathāgata’s superior answers have consistently been subjected to their challenges, he has never succeeded in refuting them, and for this reason he remains silent. There are three reasons for this.
Śreṇika said: "If all sentient beings possess a self that is omnipresent and is the single agent"—this is the first of two parts for refuting the second misconception;
herein, first the thesis is established, and subsequently the refutation is properly carried out.
This section below is the establishment of the thesis. Śreṇika said: "Gautama, if all sentient beings possess a self that is omnipresent and is the single agent..."
For what reason, Gautama, do you remain silent and not answer?
There are three reasons: first, establishing that the self (*ātman*) is all-pervading; second, establishing that the self is singular; and third, establishing that the self is the agent.

Since the "self"—that is, the sentient being, the person (*pudgala*), the individual (*puruṣa*), and the life-principle (*jīva*)—has been refuted, [the self] is no more. And since the person and the individual have been refuted...
Now, since the self as "agent" and "knower" has already been refuted, that which "arises" is likewise of the same category as the agent and is thus also refuted.
I now ask those externalists: do you hold that the "self" is identical to the aggregates (*skandhas*), or do you hold it to be separate from the aggregates?

If you hold that the self is the agent, then "acting" is simply the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); if you identify the formation as the self, then if you further identify it as the knower...
Those who hold such views all reckon the aggregates themselves to be the self;
they reckon that this self is the agent, and although the karma performed differs from one case to another, it is nonetheless the same agent.

The Buddha said: "Srenika," etc. The second section, "Explaining the Correct Refutation," has two parts. First, the correct refutation of the previous three [views]; second, the specific refutation of the remaining three views:
the knower (*jñātṛ*), the perceiver (*vedaka*), and the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*). Regarding the first part, there are three sections: first, the refutation of the universal;
second, the refutation of the unitary; third, the refutation of the agent. Regarding the first of these, there are four sections; this is the first, which first establishes their position.
