The Buddha said, "Srenika, do you say that this 'self' of mine is omnipresent? Srenika replied, "Gautama, not only do I say so;
those who possess all-knowledge (sarvajña) also speak in this way."
The Buddha said: "If I were omnipresent, [this would be the second point of formal refutation].
The Buddha said: 'O son of good family, if I were omnipresent in all places, then one should receive retribution for the five destinies simultaneously.
If there were simultaneous reception of retribution for the five destinies, for what reason and by what causes and conditions, you brahmins, would not create [karmic] aggregates?'"
"Committing evil acts serves as a barrier against the hells, while practicing various wholesome dharmas serves to receive a celestial body.

Śreṇika said, "Gautama, in my teaching there are two kinds of self: first, the self that creates the body; second, the eternal self. By practicing the abandonment of unwholesome dharmas for the sake of the self that creates the body, one does not enter the hells;
by practicing various wholesome dharmas, one is born in the heavens."

[The Buddha said: "If the self were omnipresent, it should already exist within the five realms of existence; why then would one need to cultivate goodness in order to receive the retribution of rebirth in heaven and distance oneself from the evils of the miserable realms?
Since I [the self] should always exist for both the purpose of being born in heaven and the purpose of avoiding evil, there would be no need to cultivate goodness.
Pakṣilasvāmin (Śreṇika) said: "There are two kinds of self for me: first, the bodily self, and second, the eternal self. Śreṇika originally maintained the doctrine of an eternal self.
Because it has been refuted, it turns into two selves.
The Buddha said: "As you have stated regarding the self," and so forth; this is the third refutation by the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "O son of good family, as you say that the self is omnipresent, if such a self were to become the body..."

In this regard, one should know that conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*) is impermanent. If it were the self (*ātman*), how could you say, "O Gautama, the self established by me also exists within conditioned activity and is likewise an eternal dharma"?
O Gautama, it is like a person whose house is set on fire;
when the master escapes, one cannot say that because the house is burned, the master is also burned. My doctrine is also like this, yet this conditioned activity—
Although the body is impermanent, when it is constantly impermanent, the self then departs; therefore, the self is both pervasive and eternal.
If the self were eternal while residing within a body that acts, and that acting body were impermanent, then the self of that impermanent body would likewise have to be non-existent.

If the permanent self were not present within the body it has fashioned, then that body would lack the quality of pervasiveness. Consequently, Śreṇika further raised the analogy of a house and its owner:

the permanent body is likened to the house-owner, while the fashioned body is likened to the house. Just as when the house is set on fire, the owner immediately departs, so too when the fashioned body is impermanent, the permanent self departs.
The Buddha said, "As you have spoken, I shall now refute it from the fourth point downward.
The Buddha said, "Good son, as for your statement that 'I' am both pervasive and eternal, this meaning is not so.
Why? Because pervasiveness is of two kinds: first, eternal; second, impermanent. Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, form; second, formless."
Therefore, if one says that all things exist and are both permanent and impermanent, both material and immaterial;

or if one says that when the owner of a house departs, the house is not called "impermanent"—this meaning is not correct. Why? Because the house is not called the "owner" and the owner is not called the "house," since burning is one thing and departing is another.
Thus [the opponent] might attain [his conclusion], but I do not accept it as such. Why? Because the self is...

If this form is the self, then form is the self; if there is no form, then that is the self; and if the self is without form, how can it be said that when form is impermanent, the self attains liberation?
If the enlightened, eternal body and self are already omnipresent, then the eternal is non-eternal, and since the eternal is eternally present, the non-eternal is also eternal.
How could it be that impermanence does not exist within? Thus, it pervades both the material and the immaterial.

Since it exists within the immaterial as the immaterial itself, how could it not be identical to the material when existing within the material? It may be that the house and its owner are distinct, such that one burns while the other does not;
this can be clearly understood. However, for the eternal body to act as a physical body is not the case; how, then, can it be said to "act"?
If you say that the body is impermanent and that you have therefore departed, I shall now ask you: from where do you depart?
Since the eternal body is permanent and its substance is eternally pervasive, there is no place from which to depart.
If you intend to claim that all sentient beings [depart], this constitutes the first point of refutation; in total, there are eight such sections for refuting the notion of a single entity. This...
The first section of the lower part.
Good son, if you think that all sentient beings share one and the same self, this would contradict both worldly and world-transcending dharmas. Why?
Because worldly dharmas consist of parents, children, and so forth; if the self were one, then the father would be—
The son is the father, and the father is the son; the daughter is the mother, and the mother is the daughter;
the enemy is the kinsman, and the kinsman is the enemy; this is that, and that is this.
Therefore, if one says that all sentient beings share the same self, it contradicts both mundane and supramundane dharmas. Śreṇika said: "I do not say that all sentient beings..."

If you claim that because birth is identical there is but one self, and thus say each person has a single self, then since the self is one, how do the father-self and the son-self differ? Next, Śreṇika offers this defense:
"I mean that one person has one self, but it is not the case that all people share one and the same self; therefore, the two selves of father and son are distinct."
Having finished refuting this, he then shifts the tenet of his argument.
The Buddha says: "If one says that there is a single person, and then posits a second Buddha, I shall immediately refute it. The Buddha says:
"Good son, if you say that each single person has a self, does this mean there are many selves? Is this your position?"
However, for what reason? As you previously stated, "I am omnipresent. If I were omnipresent, then the karmic faculties of all sentient beings should be identical to the Buddha-nature (*buddhatā*).
When the *devatā-prāpti* (attainment of the gods) sees, the Buddha-nature should also see; when the *devatā-prāpti* acts, the Buddha-nature should also act;
when the *devatā-prāpti* hears, the Buddha-nature should also hear. All phenomena would be likewise. If the *devatā-prāpti* sees...
One who has not attained the vision of a Buddha should not say that the self (*ātman*) pervades all places;

if it does not pervade, then it is impermanent. Śreṇika said: "Gautama, the self of all sentient beings pervades all phenomena (*dharma*) and non-phenomena (*adharma*). It does not pervade everything.
For this reason, what the Buddha attains is different, and what Devadatta attains is different. Therefore, Gautama, you should not [say such a thing]."
It is said that when the Buddha sees, Devadatta should see; when the Buddha hears, Devadatta should hear.
If there were many selves for a single person, then, Kassapa, it could not be called permanent.

If you say that the karmic retribution of all sentient beings should be identical, yet you also claim that each person has a distinct self, then since the self is omnipresent, [there would be no distinction].

If Zhang’s self resides within Wang’s self, and Wang’s self likewise resides within Zhang’s self, then since these selves are mutually interpenetrating, there would be neither folly nor wisdom, neither nobility nor meanness.
It is just as when Tian obtained my self; since my self is already present within him, he can see the Buddha with his own eyes through the self that is the Buddha’s.
Furthermore, Devadatta’s self is obtained through heaven, while the Buddha’s self is obtained through Buddhahood;

since I have already seen through the eye that Devadatta’s self is obtained through heaven, I should likewise see through the eye that the Buddha’s self is obtained through Buddhahood. Such is the person named Śreṇika. Śreṇika then offers this defense:
"The self pervades all phenomena, yet these phenomena do not mutually pervade one another; therefore, the two acts of Devadatta and the Buddha are different."
The Buddha said: "Dharma and non-Dharma are not produced by karma. This is the third section where the Buddha further refutes [the opponent].
The Buddha said: "Good son, are Dharma and non-Dharma not produced by karma? Śreṇika replied: "Gautama, they are produced by karma."

Is it that dharma and non-dharma are not produced by karma? It may be that the word "karma" (業) in the passage concerning what Śreṇika or Śiśinaka conceived as the "self being the agent" should have been "self" (我);
such would be the meaning. However, there is no need to change the character.

Following the subsequent text, since the word "karma" is used and he conceives of the self as the agent, what is called "produced by karma" is precisely "produced by the self. Next, [the text continues with] "first..."
The answer of the nun may be seen [in the preceding text].
The Buddha said: "Dharma and non-Dharma" is the fourth section below, which further refutes [the opponent].
The Buddha said: "Good son, if Dharma and non-Dharma were the agent of karma, they would be identical to Dharma; how then could you say [they are different]?"
Why is this? Because when the Buddha-attainment (*buddhalābha*) exists, there is the celestial attainment (*devatālābha*); when the celestial attainment exists, there is the Buddha-attainment.
Since I am thus, when the Buddha-attainment acts, the celestial attainment also acts. Both the Dharma and the non-Dharma should likewise be understood in this way, O son of good family.
Therefore, for all sentient beings, if the Dharma and the non-Dharma are such as these, the retribution obtained will also be so.
It should not be otherwise that a fruit arises from a seed;
for that seed never thinks or discriminates, "I shall produce only the fruit of a Brahmin, and not the fruit of a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra. Why is this?
Because when a fruit arises from a seed, it is never obstructed. In the same way, the dharmas and non-dharmas of these four castes are also like this.

One cannot distinguish whether this [karma] will bear fruit for me as Buddhahood rather than as celestial attainment, or as celestial attainment rather than as Buddhahood. Why? Because karma is equal. Śreṇika said:
"Gautama, it is like a single room containing hundreds of thousands of lamps; although the wicks differ, there is no difference in their light, yet the wicks themselves remain distinct."
The analogy of Dharma and non-Dharma is as clear and without distinction as the analogy of sentient beings and the self.
Since both are equally "my actions," when Devadatta acts, it is simultaneously the Buddha who acts; since the two acts are identical, their retribution cannot differ.
Below, the equality of karma is raised, and thus the fruit should likewise be the same. Next, Śreṇika raises the example of a lamp’s light to offer a rebuttal.
The Buddha said: "Regarding your statement that the light of a lamp [illustrates my nature], this fifth point refutes that analogy.
The Buddha said: 'Good son, your claim that the light of a lamp serves as a metaphor for me is incorrect.
Why? Because the room is distinct from the lamp; while the light of this lamp exists near the wick, it also pervades the entire room. As for what you call the 'self'...'"
If it were so, then both the dharma and the non-dharma would each possess a self, and within that self there would likewise be dharma and non-dharma.
If dharma and non-dharma had no self, one could not say that they pervade all places.
If both exist [as having a self], how can you again use the analogy of the wick and the light? Good son, if you think that the wick and the light are truly...
If they are truly distinct, for what reason does the light increase and blaze when the wick increases, and why does the light perish when the wick withers?
Therefore, it is not appropriate to use *dharma* and *adharma* as metaphors for the wick, nor the light as a metaphor for the self (*ātman*). Why is this?
Because the three things—*dharma*, *adharma*, and the self—are one and the same. Śreṇika said: "Gautama, the analogy of the lamp you have cited is inauspicious."
Therefore, if the analogy of the lamp were auspicious, I would have already cited it; why then do you speak of it again if it is inauspicious?
You argue that just as light exists at the edge of the wick and further illuminates the interior of the room, so too the locus of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) must exist within me.
If I am pervasive throughout both the dharma and the non-dharma, then the dharma and the non-dharma should likewise be pervasive within me.
This would mean that [the two] are mutually co-extensive. Śreṇika said: "You have cited the analogy of the lamp, yet later you again defend that analogy.
"Good son, as for the analogies I have cited, they are not true analogies. Below this, the sixth section further refutes the analogy.
"Good son, the metaphors I have cited are neither auspicious nor inauspicious; they are spoken according to your own inclinations.
You may say that light exists apart from the wick, or that light exists within the wick itself, for your mind is inconsistent.

Therefore, I have used the metaphor of the lamp-wick to represent the Dharma and non-Dharma, while the light represents the Self (ātman). Thus, I am challenging you: is the wick itself the light, or does the light exist apart from the wick?"
"If there is a self, then there is a self; if there is a dharma, then there is non-dharma; if there is a self, then there is non-dharma; if there is a self, then there is non-dharma.
Why do you now accept only one side and not the other? Such a metaphor is inauspicious for you;
therefore, I shall now refute it for you, O son of good family. Such a metaphor is actually no metaphor, and because it is no metaphor, it does not apply to me."
"Then it would be auspicious for you and inauspicious for me, O son of good family. If you think that if I am not auspicious, you also must not be auspicious, this is not the case.
Why? Because one sees people in the world who use their own knives to harm themselves, yet use them for others;
the analogy you have cited is likewise so—it is auspicious for me, but inauspicious for you. Śreṇika said, "Gautama..."
"O Dharma, you previously reproached me for my mind being unequal; yet what you have now said is also unequal. Why is this?
Gautama, you now direct what is auspicious toward yourself and what is inauspicious toward me; by this inference, I see that it is indeed unequal."
Since such an analogy is itself not an analogy, we know that the light of a lamp cannot serve as an analogy for the self.
If it were to serve as an analogy for the self, it would be inauspicious for them, yet auspicious for the Buddha. Śreṇika said: "You first rebuked me, and now you defend the lamp;
even the Buddha is not impartial."
The Buddha spoke: "My speech is as I am not uneven; this concludes the seventh [section].
The Buddha said: 'Good son, just as my lack of unevenness can destroy your unevenness, therefore, your leveling of my unevenness is auspicious.
My lack of unevenness destroys your unevenness, causing you to attain evenness.'"
"Why is it that I am equal? It is because I have attained equality with all the noble ones. Śreṇika said, "Gautama, I am eternally equal;
why do you say that you destroy my inequality? Since all sentient beings are equal in possessing a self, why do you say that my self is unequal?"
To clarify my own lack of equanimity and to shatter your lack of equanimity so that you may attain equanimity is itself my equanimity.
Only when one attains equanimity together with all the sages is there "Great Equanimity. Śreṇika then offered this defense: "All sentient beings are equal;
that which possesses this [self] is my equanimity."
You also state that the eighth Buddha below further refutes the meaning of equality.
Son of good family, you also say: "One shall receive the hells, one shall receive the hungry ghosts, one shall receive the animals, and one shall receive humans and devas.
If I have already pervaded all five destinies, why do you now say that one "shall receive" various realms of existence?
It is also said that a child is born only after the union of father and mother; if the child already existed beforehand, why speak further of their union?

Therefore, for a single person to have bodies in the five destinies—if those bodies already existed in the five locations—by what cause or condition would one create karma for the sake of a body? Thus, [the theory] is inconsistent.
Since it has been stated that one must receive a body within the five realms of existence, how could I be equal [to you]?
If your intention is to claim that "I" am the creator, the following third section refutes the existence of such a creator in six parts.
This first passage refutes [the notion of a creator] by means of the experience of suffering.
"Good son, if you think that 'I' am the creator, this meaning is not so. Why?
If 'I' were the creator, for what cause and condition would I create suffering for myself? Yet now, sentient beings truly experience suffering;
therefore, one should know that 'I' am not the creator. If it is said that this suffering is not created by me and does not arise from causes, [it is entirely] false."
All phenomena should likewise be such that they do not arise from causes; for what reason, then, is it said that "I am the creator"?
If I were the creator, why would I create suffering for myself? If suffering is not created by me, then all phenomena should likewise not be created by me.
Regarding the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings, the second section below clarifies sorrow and joy.
Good son, the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings truly arise from causes and conditions; such suffering and pleasure can produce sorrow and joy.
When there is sorrow, there is no joy; when there is joy, there is no sorrow. Whether it be joy or sorrow, how could a wise person say that these are permanent?
In your statement that "I am eternal," you have explained the third point, clarifying that there are ten stages.
Son of good family, if you say that "I am eternal," then being eternal, how can you speak of these ten distinct stages?

This would differ from the nature of ordinary phenomena; for while even the eternal phenomenon of space does not possess even a single stage, let alone [possess] the stages from the *kalala* through to old age.
There are ten stages, O son of good family; the "self" is not the stage of the *kalala*, nor does it extend to the stage of old age.
How, then, can one speak of the distinctions between these ten stages?
If the self were the agent [of these changes], [this would be untenable]. (The fourth section below clarifies the presence of flourishing and decline.)
"Good son, if the self were a creator, then the self would have times of flourishing and times of decline;
sentient beings likewise have times of flourishing and times of decline. If the self were like that, how could it be permanent?"
Sentient beings also experience prosperity and decline; since sentient beings are identical to the self, the self must likewise experience prosperity and decline—how could it be permanent?
If the self were the agent [of action], the following fifth section clarifies why it cannot be so with respect to sharpness and dullness.
Good son, if I were the creator, why would one person be sharp in some matters and dull in others?
How could it be that this person is sharp at writing but dull at chess, while that person is sharp at chess but dull at writing,
and so on for all other examples?
"If I were the agent," this concludes the sixth section.
"Good son, if I were the agent, then I would be capable of performing bodily, verbal, and mental actions.
If I were that which performs the action, why do you say verbally that there is no self? Why do you doubt for yourself whether it exists or not?"
You yourself have stated that there is no self, yet you harbor doubts as to whether the self exists or not.
If your intention is to suggest that seeing exists apart from the eye—this second section refutes the remaining three positions; therefore, it is refuted individually.
Within this, there are three parts: first, the refutation of the seer; second, the refutation of the feeler; and third, the refutation of the knower. First, the refutation of the seer.
Furthermore, there are three [points] here; this first one is the direct refutation:
"Good son, if you think that seeing exists apart from the eye, this is not so. Why?
Because if seeing existed separately from the eye, what need would there be for this eye? This applies even to the body-faculty and the others. Your thought—
If you claim that although I am capable of seeing, I must see by means of the eye, this too is not so. Why?
It is like someone saying that *sumana* flowers can burn down a great village; how can they burn? It is because of fire that they burn.
Your proposition that "I" see is likewise the same.
If it is claimed that there is a seer apart from the eye, this refers to the "Self" (ātman) as the seer.

The Vaiśeṣika school maintains that the Self employs cognition (*buddhi*) to know, asserting that the Self is distinct from cognition; however, this position is identical to the Sāṃkhya calculation that the Self is itself the knower.
Therefore, the claim that there is a seer apart from the eye is incorrect. If there were a Self apart from the eye that could see, why would [the sense organs] be required?
If this eye could see while being detached from the view of a self, it would be like saying "the flowers can burn the village";
yet it is only because the flowers envelop fire and are thrown onto the roof that one says "the flowers burn. That the spirit sees by means of the eye is likewise so;
in the end, it is the eye that sees, and the spirit cannot see.
The second rebuttal by Śreṇika follows:
Śreṇika said, "Gautama, it is just as when a person grasps a sickle and is able to mow grass; my seeing, hearing, up to touching, through the five sense faculties, is likewise so."
It is said that just as a person holding a sickle is able to mow grass, so too, because of the eye, I am able to see forms.
Within the correct meaning, it is merely through the conventional designation of a "self" that the eye is made capable of seeing; there is certainly no real self that must depend on the eye to see.
"Good son, the sickle and the person are each distinct; this concludes the third layer of refutation.

Good son, because the sickle and the person are each distinct, it is the grasping of the sickle that enables action to be performed. Apart from the sense faculties (*indriya*), there is no separate self (*ātman*).
How then can you say that the self, by means of the sense faculties, is able to perform actions? Good son, as for your thought..."
If you say that the act of grasping a sickle can mow, it is the same with this "self. Does this self have hands, or is it handless?
If it has hands, why does it not grasp [the sickle] itself? If it is handless, how can you say, "I am the agent"?
Good son, that which is able to mow the grass is the sickle; it is neither the self nor the person. If it were the self or the person, for what reason [would it not grasp it]?
Good son, because of the sickle, a person has two functions: first, grasping the grass; second, grasping the sickle.
This sickle possesses only the efficacy of cutting. When sentient beings perceive dharmas, it is also like this: the eye can see forms through the arising of a combination [of conditions].
If seeing arises from the combination of causes and conditions, how could a wise person say that there is a self?
The sickle and the person are not analogous, for while one may cut grass, there is no separate self apart from the root; therefore, it cannot serve as a parallel case.
If your intention is to claim that the body acts and the self experiences—this second point refutes the notion that the experiencer is the self.
Good son, if you think that the body performs the action and the self receives the fruit, this meaning is not so. Why?
Because in the world, one does not see it being that Devadatta performs the action and Buddhadatta receives the fruit.

If you say it is not the body that acts and that the self is not the cause for receiving [the fruit], why do you seek liberation from causes and conditions? Your former body was not born from causes and conditions.
Once liberation has been attained, the body should likewise not arise again from a cause; all afflictions should be understood in the same way as the body.
The statement "the body acts is the self that acts" is made below to reveal this very point.
Śreṇika said: "I have two kinds [of selves]. Third, the refutation of the knower being the self:
therein he first clarifies his attachment.
Śreṇika said: "Gautama, I have two kinds [of selves]: one is conscious, and the other is unconscious. Regarding the unconscious...
"I am able to perceive that there is a self within the body, yet I am able to relinquish the body just as a clay jar, once fired, loses its original color and never returns to it again.
The afflictions of the wise are likewise; once they have been extinguished and destroyed, they will never arise again."
The Buddha said, "Good son, as for what you call 'knowing,' I shall now refute it.
The Buddha said, 'Good son, regarding what you call knowing: is it that wisdom knows, or is it that "I" am able to know?
If it is wisdom that knows, why do you say, "I am the knower"? If it is "I" who knows, why do you employ skillful means to further seek [a self]? "
I know your intention; if you think that I know through the knowledge of a self, this is like the analogy of a flower—it destroys [the notion of] a son of good family.
For example, a thorny tree has the nature of piercing by itself; one cannot say that the tree grasps the thorn to pierce. Knowledge is also like this: knowledge knows by itself.
How can it be said that "the self grasps knowledge to know"? Son of good family, according to your own dharma, there is no liberation for me.
If one knows "I know" or "I have attained," then if there were no knowing or attaining, one should know that one still possesses afflictions (*kleśa*).
If there is knowing and attaining, one should know that the five sensory faculties (*indriya*) already exist. Why? Because apart from the faculties, there is no separate knowing.
If one possesses all the faculties, how can one further be said to have attained liberation? If you say it is the nature of this "self"...
If you are pure and detached from the five sense faculties, why do you say that [defilements] exist pervasively throughout the five realms of existence?

For what reason and by what causal conditions do you cultivate various wholesome dharmas for the sake of liberation? Son of good family, it is as if someone were to pull a thorn out of empty space; you are just like this.
If I am already pure, why do you further speak of severing all afflictions? If your intention is that [afflictions] do not arise from causes...
If one has attained liberation from all states of animal existence, why is it that [the animal] cannot [attain it]?

Because I know through wisdom that those who are destroyed by the analogy of the flower are still subject to the same principle as before: the flower can envelop the fire, and the fire can burn the house;
thus, it is called "the flower burning. Although the spirit (*ātman*) is capable of knowing, it nevertheless requires further wisdom to act as the knower. Ultimately...

This wisdom is capable of knowing itself, whereas the self (*ātman*) cannot know it, as has already been refuted. Therefore, it is said that [the claim that] the Buddha’s true doctrine is destroyed by this analogy of the flower is false;
there is indeed a conventional self that governs the meaning of "knowing through wisdom," yet this is not the same as a real self that knows by means of wisdom.
Śreṇika said: "If there is no self," [this concludes] the third section of the discourse on the meaning.

Having refuted Śreṇika’s arguments point by point, the Buddha has eliminated his erroneous views. Now, he shall further debate this matter with the Buddha to determine whether the self definitely exists or definitely does not exist.
First, this is a challenge to the Buddha’s position that there is no self; second, it establishes the existence of a self as a counter-argument.
Regarding the Buddha’s teaching on non-self, the doctrine of a self is not established; rather, he clarifies the existence of the self through five successive rounds of questioning.
This is the first question of Śreṇika:
Śreṇika said, "Gautama, if there is no self, who is it that can remember?"
"If there were no self, who would be able to remember?
The Buddha told Śreṇika: "If there were a self, for what reason would one again forget?
Good son, if that which remembers were the self, by what causes and conditions would it remember evil thoughts, not remember what should be remembered, or fail to remember what has been remembered?"
The Buddha replied: "If you know there is a self because of memory, then since there is now forgetfulness, one should know that there is no self.
If you use the presence of recollection as proof that there is a self, then the occurrence of forgetfulness proves that there is no self.
If temporary recollection manifests a self, then temporary forgetfulness likewise manifests the absence of a self. Since the 'self' is supposedly autonomous, how can it be subject to recollection?"

If it is said that one does not contemplate the wholesome while contemplating the unwholesome, and furthermore, that one contemplates what should not be contemplated—when one is precisely in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one ought to reflect upon and recollect the object of that concentration; why then would one take other matters as objects?

Moreover, if it is said that one does not contemplate what should be contemplated, then while actually committing evil, one would still be maintaining wholesome dharmas; since there is thus a self, how could one not be in a state of concentration?
"Who sees and who hears? This was the second question posed by Śreṇika.
Śreṇika spoke again: "Gautama, if there is no self, who sees and who hears?
If there is no self, who is it that is able to see and hear?"
The Buddha said, "Good son, there are the six internal bases within and the six external objects without; when these internal and external factors combine, the six kinds of consciousness arise.
These six kinds of consciousness receive their names based on their causes and conditions. Good son, it is like a single fire: because it arises from wood, it is called a 'wood-fire';
because it arises from grass, it is called a 'grass-fire'; and because it arises from chaff, it is called a 'chaff-fire'."
Just as fire is named after cow dung because it arises from cow dung, so too is the consciousness of sentient beings:

because of the eye, because of forms, because of light, and because of desire, it is called "eye-consciousness. Good son, this eye-consciousness does not reside within the eye, nor does it reside within desire;
rather, it arises through the conjunction of these four factors. This applies likewise to the mental consciousness. If...
Because these causes and conditions combine, wisdom arises; one should not say that "seeing" is the self, up to and including "touching" being the self.
Good son, for this reason I say that from eye-consciousness to mind-consciousness, all phenomena are like an illusion.
Why are they like an illusion? Because they originally did not exist but now exist, and having existed, they return to non-existence. Good son, it is like, for example, clarified butter.
Flour, honey, ginger, black pepper, long pepper, grapes, pomegranate, and *karīra*—when these are combined, they are called "joy-pills" (*modaka*).
Apart from this combination, there are no joy-pills. Likewise, the six internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) are what constitute a sentient being, a self, a person, or an individual;
apart from the internal and external sense bases, there is no separate sentient being, self, person, or individual.
The Buddha’s intended meaning was that seeing and hearing arise from the conjunction of the sense faculties and their objects; they do not truly result from a self that is able to see and hear.
He offered two analogies himself.
Śreṇika then spoke the words, "If there is no self," which constitutes the third question.
Śreṇika said: "Gautama, if there is no self, why do you say: 'I see,' 'I hear,' 'I suffer,' 'I am happy,' 'I grieve,' or 'I rejoice'?
You use these names to question me: what is this 'self' that sees and hears? The people of the world all say, 'I see.'"
[If one says,] "I hear my suffering, pleasure, grief, joy,
and so forth," the Buddha said, "Good son, if one says that 'I see' and 'I hear' constitutes having a self, for what reason does the world further say,
'The sin you have committed was not seen or heard by me,' good son? It is, for example, like the combination of the four types of troops."
Just as an army composed of these four divisions of troops is not a single entity, yet one still says,
"My army is brave and strong" or "My army has defeated the enemy," so too it is with the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*): although they are not a single unity,
one can nevertheless say, "I act," "I experience," "I see," "I hear," "I suffer," or "I am happy."

The Buddha’s answer has two intentions: first, he employs a counter-question to respond, saying that those who claim to see, hear, or know a self are like one who says they neither saw nor heard another commit a crime;
thus, there should likewise be no self. Second, following the analogy of the fourfold army, he again cites conventional designations to demonstrate that it is the "self" which sees and hears.
Śreṇika said: "As you have stated," [he continued] with his fourth further question.
Śreṇika said: "Gautama, according to what you say, when the internal and external come together, who is it that utters the voice saying, 'I act' and 'I experience'?"
"If the internal and external [factors] are in harmony, who is it that produces the sound?
The Buddha said: "Śreṇika, from craving and ignorance as causes and conditions, karma arises; from karma, existence arises; from existence, immeasurable mental states arise;
from these mental states, vitarka and vicāra arise; vitarka and vicāra move the wind; and the wind, following the mind, strikes the throat, tongue, teeth, and lips."
Sentient beings, with their inverted perceptions, utter sounds saying, "I act," "I receive," "I see," and "I hear. Good son, it is like the bells atop a banner:
due to the conditions of the wind, they produce sounds; if the wind is great, the sound is great, and if the wind is small, the sound is small.
There is no agent therein. Good son, it is like hot iron cast into water, which produces various kinds of sounds within it.
In reality, there is no agent. Son of good family, because ordinary beings are unable to contemplate or discern such matters, they say:
"There is a self and what belongs to a self; I am the doer and I am the receiver."
The Buddha replied: "That which is caused by ignorance is precisely the body formed through the combination of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Because there is a body, there is vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), which move the wind; this wind strikes the lips and tongue to produce sound and speak of 'self.
As the Mahā-śāstra says: 'The wind named āyudha touches the navel and ascends upward to the teeth; because it agitates the lips and tongue, [speech arises].'"
The sounding of wind-bells and red-hot iron are likewise thus.
Śreṇika said: "As Gautama has taught in the fifth question below," Śreṇika said:
"If, as Gautama has taught, there is neither self nor what belongs to a self, for what reason do you further speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity?"
If clarity were to follow reason, there would be no self at all; for what reason, then, could the Tathāgata possess permanence and bliss?
It is because of the existence of a self that there are dharmas such as permanence; if there were no self, how could these dharmas exist?
The Buddha said, "Good son, I do not say that the six internal and external bases (āyatana) and the six consciousnesses are permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
Rather, I proclaim that the cessation of the six consciousnesses produced by the internal and external bases is called 'permanent.
Because it is permanent, it is called 'self. Because there is a permanent self, it is called 'blissful. Because there is a permanent, blissful self, it is called..."
O pure son of good family, when sentient beings weary of suffering, sever the causes of this suffering, and attain sovereign detachment from it, this is called "self.
For these reasons, I now proclaim the eternal, self, bliss, and purity.
The Buddha’s intended meaning was that those who attain the eternal self must do so only after the extinction of the body;
how could they attain the eternal self within this very body?
Śreṇika said, "I only pray for your great compassion... This concludes the fourth section on submission, which consists of four parts; this is the first request.
The Buddha said, "Śreṇika, the World-Honored One, I only pray that out of great compassion you will explain for me: how may I obtain such permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
The Buddha said, "Good son, all worlds have been complete with these from the very beginning."
Great pride can increase pride and furthermore creates the causes and karmic conditions for pride;
therefore, one now undergoes the retribution of pride and is unable to remain far removed from all afflictions to attain the permanence, self, bliss, and purity.
If sentient beings wish to remain far removed from all afflictions, they must first abandon pride.
The Buddha explained at length the causes and the meaning of pride (*māna*) in order to refute his underlying conceit.
When Śreṇika said, "So it is, so it is," this constitutes the second section: acknowledging the essential point.
Śreṇika said, “World-Honored One, it is so, it is so; it is truly as the Holy Teaching declares.

Previously I possessed pride, and because of that pride and its conditions, I addressed the Tathāgata by his name and by the clan name Gautama. Now that I have abandoned such great pride, I entreat you with a sincere heart to request the Dharma:
how may one attain the eternal, the blissful, the self, and the pure?”
The Tathāgata, for this reason, spoke again in two parts: first a warning and then an exposition.
The Buddha said, "Good son, listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall now analyze and explain it for you."
Good son, if one can [realize] that there is neither self nor other nor sentient beings, one remains far removed from these dharmas.
To say "neither self, nor other, nor sentient beings" clarifies that dharmas and sentient beings are identical and equal.
Śreṇika said, "I have understood. This concludes the third section: his own attainment of understanding.

Śreṇika said, "World-Honored One, I have already known and understood, and have attained the right Dharma-eye. The Buddha said, "Good son, how can you say that you have known, understood, and attained the right Dharma-eye?"
The Tathāgata, further questioning him, brought out the characteristics [of his understanding].
Regarding what the World-Honored One calls "form" (*rūpa*), the fourth section below presents his own interpretation in two parts; first, he describes it himself:
"That which the World-Honored One calls 'form' is neither self nor other, nor does it belong to any sentient being; this applies even up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is likewise."
"World-Honored One, through such contemplation as this, I have attained the eye of the True Dharma. Now I take great delight in leaving the household life to cultivate the Way;
I pray that you will grant me permission.
Thereupon, the Buddha commanded him, "Come, well-come," and he attained the purity of the eye of wisdom.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu," and immediately he became fully endowed with pure brahmacarya and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
What is called the "Dharma-eye" refers to the first fruit (Srotāpanna), while the "purification of the wisdom-eye" refers to the fourth fruit (Arhat).
However, at the time he conversed with the Buddha, he had already attained the first fruit; subsequently, upon being addressed as "Welcome," he attained the fourth fruit.

Among the assembly of non-Buddhists, there was another belonging to the Kāśyapa clan; this is the fourth non-Buddhist, whose text is divided into three parts: first, the introductory narrative (*nidāna*);
second, the discussion of doctrine (*dharmārtha*); and third, the conversion and submission.
Among the assembly of non-Buddhists, there was again a brahmin of the Kāśyapa clan who spoke thus: "The body of Gautama is itself..."

"Is the life-principle different from the body? and "Is the life-principle different [from the body] after death?"—to these questions the Tathāgata remained silent. A second and a third time he was asked the same, and each time he likewise remained silent.

Since he remained silent in response to these first three questions, they served as the causal basis for his not answering; the Tathāgata intended to lead them toward the realization of his own doctrine.
The brahmin spoke again. This second discussion consists of five sections; this is the first. The brahmin spoke again:
"Gautama, if a person has cast off the body but has not yet attained a subsequent body, in that interval, could it not be said that the body is one thing and the life-principle is another?
If they are different, Gautama, why do you remain silent and not answer?"

It is clear that the body and the life-force are distinct, just as when a person leaves the present body and has not yet received a subsequent body, during which time they exist in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
at that time, the body and life-force are different from those of the previous body and life-force, and are not obtained through causes.
Next, son of good family, I say that the body and life are inferior and are destroyed by the Tathāgata.
Son of good family, I say that the body and life both arise from causes and conditions and do not exist without causes and conditions;
as it is with the body and life, so it is with all phenomena.
It clarifies that all phenomena arise from conditions; not only is this true for the body and life, but it applies to all phenomena.
At the time of death within the aggregates, this life, relying on conditions, continues into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The Brahmin spoke again: "I see the world... This is the second instance of his presenting a formal proposition.
The brahmin spoke again: "Gautama, I see that there are phenomena in the world that do not arise from causes and conditions. The Buddha said:
"Brahmin, how do you see that there are phenomena in the world that do not arise from causes and conditions?"
The Tathāgata further rebuked him, saying that his assertion of a phenomenon existing that does not arise from conditions is untenable.
The Brahmin said: "I see a great fire burning trees; when the wind blows, the flames are extinguished and fall elsewhere. This is the third instance where he establishes a matter based on a cause.
The Brahmin said: "I see a great fire consuming trees; when the wind blows, the flames are severed and fall in other places."
"Is it not then called 'without causes and conditions'? The Buddha said, "Good son, I say that this fire also arises from causes;
it does not arise without causes.

To say that when light is extinguished and the flames are gone, it does not arise from conditions—this is what the Tathāgata further refutes; light also arises from conditions. Regarding that which is within [the text]:
Regarding the character for *zhēn* (hazel), some take its pronunciation as *zhēn*, while others take it as *chōu-shēn*. I now consider the pronunciation *zhēn* to be correct.

The *Shijing* says, "Planting hazels and chestnuts," and the *Zhuan* explains, "Hazels, chestnuts, jujubes, and dried meats. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the hazel resembles the *zǐ* tree, and its fruit is like a small chestnut.
When the brahmin’s speech ended, the flame went out. At that time, the fourth section was explained in detail to clarify that it did not depend on fuel or charcoal.
The brahmin said, “Gautama, when the flame goes out, it does not depend on fuel or charcoal; why then do you say it depends on causes and conditions?
The Buddha said, “Good son, although there is no fuel or charcoal, it goes out because of the wind; by reason of the wind as its condition, that flame ceases.”
"It is not extinguished.
The Buddha then refuted this, clarifying that it arrives due to the wind.
"Gautama, suppose a person casts off their body and is reborn in the fifth hell; even there, that difficulty would arise again."
"Gautama, when a person has abandoned this body but has not yet attained a subsequent body, what serves as the causal condition for their intermediate lifespan? The Buddha said:
"Brahmin, ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) serve as the causal conditions. Due to these two causal conditions—ignorance and craving—the lifespan is maintained.
Son of good family, because there are causal conditions, the body is itself the life, and life is itself the body; it is due to causal conditions."
Therefore, those who hold that the body and the life-principle are distinct should not categorically state that the body and the life-principle are distinct.
To clarify which serves as the cause and condition between the two bodies, the Buddha replied: "Ultimately, it is with afflictions (*kleśa*) as the condition.

He further stated that there is a causal relationship such that the body is itself the life-principle and the life-principle is itself the body; this refers to the fruit of a single lifetime (*eka-kalpa*).
Regarding the statement that body and life are distinct because they are obtained through the causal conditions of a single karmic retribution:
"life" refers to the continuity of form and mind, while "body" refers to the five aggregates; thus, their meanings differ.
The brahmin said, "I only pray that you will grant me the third refuge and submission. There are three such requests; this is the first.
The brahmin said, "World-Honored One, I only pray that you will analyze and explain it for me, so that I may clearly understand the cause."
[The section on] the fruit.
Next, the Buddha’s response also consists of two parts; first, he answers:
the Buddha said, "Brahmin, the cause is the five aggregates, and the fruit is likewise the five aggregates."
Next, the refutation of their calculation is set forth; this is also termed "sealing the exposition.
"Good son, if there are sentient beings who do not kindle fire, then there will be no smoke.
From "World-Honored One, I have already understood" onwards is the second section on receiving and understanding the teaching, followed by the Buddha’s further inquiry.
The brahmin said, "World-Honored One, I have known; I have understood. The Buddha said, "Good son, how have you known?
How have you understood?
Next, the World-Honored One [addressed] fire, which is none other than affliction. Thirdly, he detailed his own understanding in full.
World-Honored One, fire refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), which can burn within the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.
The smoke is the retribution of the afflictions—impermanent, impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome; therefore, it is called "smoke.
If there are sentient beings who do not produce afflictions, they will have no retribution of the afflictions; for this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of "non-[smoke]."
"When fire is lit, there is no smoke, World-Honored One; I have attained right view. I only pray that you will compassionately grant me permission to go forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Kauṇḍinya, "I permit this brahmin to go forth and receive the precepts.
Having received the Buddha’s command, Kauṇḍinya informed the harmonious Saṃgha, and they granted him permission to go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Five days later...
He attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Five days after attaining the fruit of Arhatship, he spoke of the distance or proximity of his realization and the early or late timing of his awakening.
Furthermore, among the assembly of non-Buddhists, there was Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, the fifth of the six heterodox teachers; that which he clung to was as follows:

Although the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) possess their own attachments, fearing they might cause confusion or stagnation, I have not dared to describe them; therefore, I shall briefly raise them as questions according to the text.
This section has two parts: first, the discussion of the doctrine, and second, the submission through conversion. Within this initial discussion of the doctrine, there are four rounds of inquiry;
this is the first round, which raises the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭidṛṣṭi*) as questions.
Among the assembly of non-Buddhists, there was again a brahmin named Pūraṇa who spoke thus:
"Gautama, having perceived that the world is an eternal phenomenon, do you declare it to be eternal? Is such a proposition real or false?
Is it eternal, non-eternal, both eternal and non-eternal, neither eternal nor non-eternal; or is it finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite?"
"Neither finite nor infinite; the body is the life-principle; the body is one thing and the life-principle another; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he exists;

he does not exist; he both exists and does not exist; he neither exists nor does not exist. The Buddha said, "Pūrṇa, I do not say that the world is eternal, nor that it is non-eternal, nor that it is both eternal and non-eternal, nor that it is neither eternal nor non-eternal, nor that it is finite."
The infinite is also finite; the infinite is neither finite nor infinite; the body is the life-force;
the body is one thing and the life-force another; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he exists; he does not exist; he both exists and does not exist;
he neither exists nor does not exist.
Regarding the sixty-two views, there are two interpretations. One says that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) together constitute the sixty-two.
Why? Because the view of a self-identity has fifty-six [aspects] and the view of extremes has six. Based on each of the five aggregates (*skandha*), there are four types of grasping:

that it is identical to form, distinct from form, both identical and distinct, and neither identical nor distinct. This applies analogously to the remaining four aggregates. Thus, these amount to twenty for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding the realms: in the form realm there are forty; in the formless realm, only four aggregates are mentioned, and since four times four makes sixteen, it is known that the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) consists of fifty-six [factors].
As for the six types of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), this refers to the presence of both annihilationism and eternalism within each of the three realms;
when added to the view of self-identity, they constitute sixty-two. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "For example, the view of self encompasses all six."

Regarding the twelve views, two are direct and six are derivative, totaling eighteen views concerning the past and eighteen concerning the future, making thirty-six; with the addition of the eighteen views concerning the present, they total sixty-two.

Within the present life, if one takes form (*rūpa*) as the self, then with the cessation of form, the self is annihilated. If one takes the self as distinct from form, then with the cessation of form, the self remains eternal.

Furthermore, there are views that it is both identical to and distinct from form, both annihilated and eternal, or neither identical nor distinct, thus being neither annihilated nor eternal. The same applies to the other four aggregates (*skandha*); thus, these views are established.
The twenty views regarding the past and future likewise constitute sixty. Although there are these sixty, they do not transcend the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism;
therefore, they are headed by annihilationism and eternalism as the sixty-two [views].

Now, when the present text speaks of "eternal" and "non-eternal," this refers to the finite and infinite [nature] of the past, while it refers to the future. This term "extreme" (anta) does not mean horizontal [spatial] limits.
The discussion of breadth and narrowness refers to the limits of the vertical [analysis]; thus, "that extreme" concerns whether the Tathāgata goes or does not go after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
To calculate that the Tathāgata is identical with form and that nirvāṇa is an ultimate and eternal extinction—this is "going.
If the body does not perish, this is "not going. Also, "both going and not going," and so forth (as detailed). This completes the preceding section.

When these sixty views are combined with the view that "this body is the life" (the eternalist view) and "the body is one thing and the life another" (the annihilationist view), they constitute the sixty-two views. Yet this text speaks of "after the Tathāgata has passed away.
Since others do not perceive this [distinction], and since it is not permitted to apply these twenty reckonings to the Tathāgata, he himself explains: "I am like form coming [into being]."
"Just as form goes, it does not go; therefore, it is said that 'it goes' and 'it does not go. The Buddha then replied to him, "I do not speak in this way.
The Brahmin then asked: "What fault or error do you see now? This is the second question.
Pūrṇa spoke again: "Gautama, what fault do you now perceive that you do not make such a statement? The Buddha said:
"Pūrṇa, if someone says, 'The world is eternal; only this is true, all else is false,' this is called a view (*dṛṣṭi*).
The locus where one sees and is seen is called the practice of views, the karma of views, attachment to views, and bondage by views."
This is called the view of suffering, this is called the grasping at views, this is called the dread of views, this is called the fever of views, and this is called the entanglement of views.
Purna, ordinary worldlings are entangled by such views and cannot distance themselves from birth, old age, sickness, and death;
they circulate through the six realms of existence and undergo immeasurable suffering. This is likewise true even regarding [the views] that "it is neither thus nor not thus. Purna, it is thus.
"If I were to hold this view, such faults would arise; therefore, I do not cling to it, nor do I teach it to others.
[The interlocutor asks: "What fault is there in this that you do not teach it? The Buddha answers: "Because this is the fault of *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views), I do not make such a statement."
"If, Gautama, you see such faults, why do you not cling to them nor speak of them? This concludes the third question.
Gautama, if you see such faults, why do you not cling to them nor speak of them?

What do you now perceive, what do you cling to, and what do you proclaim? The Buddha said: "Good son, that which is called 'perception' and 'clinging' is the dharma of birth and death. The Tathāgata has [already transcended this]."

Because he is free from the phenomena of birth and death, he does not cling; therefore, O son of good family, the Tathāgata is called one who "is able to see" and "is able to speak," but is not called one who clings.
What does the Tathāgata see and cling to? What does he speak of? The Buddha answered him by first dispelling the words "seeing" and "clinging."
The subsequent section clarifies that [the Buddha] is able to see and speak.
From "How, Gautama... onwards, there is a fourth round of interrogation regarding seeing and speaking:
"Gautama, how can you see? How can you speak?"
The Buddha then gave a detailed response in two parts, the first being the direct answer.
The Buddha said: "Good son, I am able to clearly perceive and analytically proclaim these Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Because I see them thus, I am able to remain far removed from all views, all cravings, all outflows, and all [defilements]."
Because of this pride, I have perfected the pure Brahma-conduct and attained unsurpassed tranquility and an eternal body;
yet this body does not belong to the east, west, south, or north.
Later, he further rebuked him to bring out its true nature.
Pūrṇa said, “Gautama, for what reason is the eternal body not [limited to] the directions of east, west, south, or north?
The Buddha said, “Good son, I shall now question you; answer according to your own understanding. What do you think? Suppose a great mass of fire were ignited before you;
when it was burning, did you know that it was burning? “Not so, Gautama. “When that fire was extinguished, did you know it? “Not so, Gautama.”
"It is not so, Gautama. Purna, if someone were to ask you: 'From where did that previous mass of fire come when it was burning, and to what place did it go when it was extinguished?
how would you answer? Gautama, if such a person were to ask, I would answer them:
'When this fire arose, it relied upon various conditions; once the original conditions were exhausted and new conditions had not yet arrived, the fire was extinguished. "If, moreover—"
If someone asks, "After this fire has been extinguished, to which direction does it go? how would you answer, Gautama? I would answer, "It is extinguished because its conditions have ceased;
it does not go to any location. Noble son, the Tathāgata is also like this.

If there is impermanent form, up to and including impermanent consciousness, they burn because of craving. That which burns is precisely the undergoing of the twenty-five states of existence; therefore, it burns.
At that time, it can be said that this fire—namely, the present craving—is extinguished; the retribution of the twenty-five states of existence does not burn.

Because it does not burn, one cannot say that there are directions such as east, west, south, or north. Son of good family, the Tathāgata has already extinguished impermanent form up to impermanent consciousness.
Therefore, the body is eternal. If the body were [merely] eternal in that sense, one could not say that it exists [as a conditioned entity].
"East, west, south, and north.
Pūrṇa said, "Please allow me to offer a parable," thus beginning the second section on conversion.
Pūrṇa said, "I wish to speak a parable; I only pray that you will listen and consider it. The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent! Speak as you please."

In the time of that World-Honored One, it was as if outside a great village there were *sāla* groves, and within one such grove there was a tree that had grown before the grove itself, reaching a full hundred years.
At that time, the owner of the grove watered it and maintained it according to the seasons;
the tree’s old and withered bark and foliage all fell away, leaving only the solid heartwood remaining. The Tathāgata is also like this: all that is ancient and worn away has likewise fallen away.
Having completely eliminated all [defilements], with only the truly real Dharma remaining, he said to the World-Honored One, "I now deeply desire to leave the household life to cultivate the Way.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu! As soon as these words were spoken, he immediately left the household life; his outflows were exhausted, and he realized the fruit of Arhatship.

The phrase "as if outside a great village" is a metaphor for the *nirvāṇa* of the Buddha-fruit. "There is a *sāla* grove" refers to a person, who is a metaphor for the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*).
Now, the metaphor of "there being one tree within the hearts of sentient beings" refers to the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
"A full hundred years" is the completion of a numerical cycle; it is a metaphor for the Middle Way, wherein the Buddha-nature is perfectly complete and upright.

The text states: "One tree was born before the forest. Since one tree serves as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), it may be said that the Buddha-nature exists prior to sentient beings;
yet, while there were no sentient beings, the Buddha-nature already existed, and once sentient beings exist, the Buddha-nature exists.

Why, then, does it say it was "born before the forest"? If one claims that the Buddha-nature and sentient beings have a temporal sequence of priority and posteriority, whether they are identical or distinct, both positions lead to logical fallacies.
None of these can be taken together; one must break through their inherent attachment to fixed natures. Once they have been broken, one may then provisionally speak of "before" and "after.
This sequence of before and after does not contradict one another. Since they do not contradict each other, it is permissible to explain the Buddha-nature as being prior.
Why is this? Because Buddha-nature is primordially existent (*prakṛti-siddha*). Because it is primordially existent, it is explained figuratively as being "first," and thus it is never lost.
The "master who cultivates and repairs the forest of principle" refers to the practitioner;

the tree being worn out and its bark completely stripped away is a metaphor for all afflictions and evils having been entirely exhausted, leaving only the enduring reality, which is the myriad virtues.
