The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter on Kauṇḍinya, Part Two (Fascicle Thirty-Six).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Revised by the Jin dynasty śramaṇas Huiyan, Huiguan,
and Xie Lingyun; from the *Cenrupu* (Chapter on the Questions of Candra), Part Two.
The sixth volume of the non-Buddhist texts begins with two parts: first, the discussion of doctrine, and second, the submission through conversion.
Within the discussion of doctrine, there are two rounds.
In the first round, there was a brahmin named Śuddha who spoke as follows: "Gautama, all sentient beings do not know what dharma [is]."
They perceive the world as eternal, as non-eternal, as both eternal and non-eternal, as neither eternal nor non-eternal, and so on, up to:
as neither thus-gone nor not thus-gone.
[The Buddha] asked: "By reason of what phenomena do sentient beings give rise to these sixty-two views, such as the views of eternity and non-eternity?"
The Buddha said: "Good son, because they do not know form (*rūpa*), and so on up to not knowing consciousness (*vijñāna*), they view the world as eternal, and so on up to neither going nor not going.

The Buddha answered: Because they do not know form, they give rise to views of permanence and impermanence; and so on up to because they do not know consciousness, they give rise to views of permanence and impermanence."
Those who commonly speak of "form" (rūpa) claim that past karma is its cause and the clothing and food provided by parents in this life are its conditions;

they falsely assert that it possesses a permanent nature through such deceptive combinations. Thus, they give rise to views of permanence, impermanence, and so forth, even extending their ignorance to consciousness (vijñāna), where they likewise give rise to various views.
Next, the brahmin said:
"Gautama, by knowing what dharma do sentient beings not see that the world is eternal,
or even that it neither passes away nor does not pass away?"
He asked further, "By knowing what form and by knowing what consciousness does one not give rise to various views?
The Buddha said, "Good son, by knowing form, and so on up to knowing consciousness, one does not see the world as eternal,
nor even as neither-going-nor-not-going."
The Buddha said, "To know that form is merely a combination of causes and conditions, without a master and without a self, is to be free from all views;
this applies even up to consciousness, which is likewise so.
The Brahmin said, "I pray only that you will [teach me] the two lower [stages]; I shall take refuge and submit."
The brahmin said, “World-Honored One, I only pray that you will analyze and explain for me whether the world is eternal or non-eternal.
The Buddha said, “Good son, if a person abandons the old and does not create new karma, such a person can know what is eternal and what is non-eternal.
The brahmin said, “World-Honored One, I have already understood. The Buddha said, “Good son, how do you see it? How do you understand it?”
Because one knows the World-Honored One, ignorance and craving are called "grasping" and "existence.

If a person distances themselves from this ignorance and craving and does not produce grasping and existence, that person truly knows the permanent and the impermanent. I have now attained the pure eye of the True Dharma;
I take refuge in the Triple Gem. I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me permission to leave the household life. The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya: "I grant you permission."
When the brahmin went forth and received the precepts, Kauṇḍinya, having received the Buddha’s command, led him into the midst of the Saṃgha and performed the *karmavācanā* for his ordination.
Fifteen days later, all his outflows were forever exhausted, and he attained the fruit of Arhatship.

The text states that "the old" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), while "the new" refers to grasping (*upādāna*) and becoming (*bhava*). Regarding this, there are two interpretations.
One says that ignorance and craving are called "old" because they belong to the past, whereas grasping and becoming are called "new" because they belong to the present.
As for craving, which is itself present, why is it called "old"? To this, some offer a forced explanation: "It is called 'old' because it is obtained through formative forces (*saṃskāra*)."
This interpretation is not correct. Second, it is said: "If based on the afflictions (*kleśa*), ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are considered 'new';
if based on karma, grasping (*upādāna*) and existence (*bhava*) are considered 'new'. This too is untenable; for if grasping is an affliction, why is it suddenly called "new"?

And if ignorance and craving are "new," why are they suddenly attributed to karma? This is most unacceptable. Furthermore, another interpretation says: "There is no need to mention the past and present..."
Regarding the afflictions and karma, it is discussed that ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) alone are the roots from which the body arises;

since [the body] originates from ignorance and craving, these are the branches and tips. Therefore, they are called "new" [afflictions], as there are no prior faults. As stated above: "Ignorance is the father and craving is the mother;
if one respects this [view], upon death one enters the Avīci hell. Furthermore, it says: "The ultimate limit of birth and death consists of all that exists..."
These two types of ignorance and craving—are these not the "causes"? Now, in relation to the three periods of time, looking back from the present toward past ignorance constitutes the cause;

thus, looking forward from the future toward present craving constitutes the effect. This is the same as the Master’s [Kumārajīva’s] view, and it does not contradict the text concerning the three periods which states:
"I have now attained the pure eye of the True Dharma," or "the purity of the Dharma-eye. This should be understood accordingly.

There is no difference [in their attainment], though there is a distinction between those on the left and those on the right; as for those who attain Arhatship fifteen days later, their realization simply comes sooner or later.
Section Seven: The Brahmin Gokulika. This section is divided into three parts: first, the narrative background (nidāna); second, the doctrinal discussion; and third, the conclusion.
He submitted.
The brahmin Vatsa spoke again, saying: "Gautama, I now wish to ask a question; if you will permit me to do so, I shall not remain silent.
He said this a second and a third time, and likewise each time.
Since remaining silent is also a form of causal origination (pratītyasamutpāda), it cannot be cited as a precedent for manifesting one's refined elegance;
therefore, he waited patiently and deliberately for the three parties to respond.
Vatsiputriya’s statement that "the following two are points of debate" [refers to the subsequent discussion].
The Vātsīputrīya spoke again: "Gautama, for a long time I have been your close friend; between you and me, there is no difference in principle.
I wish to inquire of you, so why do you remain silent? At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This brahmin is by nature refined, gentle, pure, good, and straightforward; he has always come to inquire and question for the sake of knowledge, not for [other reasons]."
"If anyone should disturb you by asking questions, you should answer them according to your own inclination. The Buddha said, "Vatsa, excellent, excellent!
Whatever questions you may have, I shall answer them for you.

This is because you are free from self-attachment and merely inquire after the true meaning. Consequently, the Buddha remained silent, first intending to observe the questioner's intent through his silence, and then reflecting upon it.
In silence, his mind was opened and he began the inquiry.

Next, following the words of the Vatsiputriya, the formal discussion of the meaning commenced; since there was no personal dogmatism, he merely inquired about the correct principle. Within this, there are two parts:

first, the inquiry concerning the Dharma, and second, the inquiry concerning the person (*pudgala*). In the initial inquiry concerning the Dharma, there are two sections: first, the question, and second, the Buddha’s response.
The Vatsīputra said: "Gautama, is there goodness in the world? Is there likewise, O Brahmin, evil in the world?
Gautama, I pray that you explain this to me so that I may come to know the dharmas of goodness and evil."
In the response, there are again two parts: first, the granting of permission.
The Buddha said: "Good son, I am able to analyze and explain its meaning in detail; I shall now provide you with a concise explanation."
Next, the correct answer regarding the three kinds and ten kinds is presented; herein, first both are explained together, followed by both being concluded together.
"Good son, desire is called unwholesome, while the desire for liberation is called wholesome. Hatred and delusion are likewise so.
Killing is called unwholesome, while non-killing is called wholesome, and this applies even up to wrong view."
In the commentary it says: "Liberation from desire" refers to the wholesome root of non-attachment.
Good son, I have now for your sake explained the three kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, as well as the ten kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
If my disciples are able to perform such a discrimination of the three kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas...
Regarding the ten kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, one should know that such a person is able to exhaust desire, hatred, and delusion,
sever all outflows (*āsrava*), and terminate all existence (*bhava*). Next,
he asks about the person who is able to cultivate the wholesome and sever the afflictions.
The brahmin said, "Gautama, is there perhaps even one bhikṣu within this Buddha-dharma who is able to exhaust such craving, hatred, and delusion—all outflows (*āsrava*) and all existence (*bhava*"?
The Buddha said, "Good son, within this Buddha-dharma, it is not one, two, three, nor even five hundred;
rather, there are immeasurable bhikṣus who are able to exhaust such craving."

"Gautama, among all those bhikṣus who have abandoned desire, hatred, delusion, all outflows (*āsrava*), and all modes of existence (*bhava*), is there perhaps even one bhikṣuṇī within this Buddha-dharma who can likewise exhaust such desire, hatred, delusion, all outflows, and all modes of existence?
The Buddha said: "Good son, within this Buddha-dharma, it is not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred."
There are indeed immeasurable bhikṣuṇīs capable of severing all such outflows of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all forms of existence.

The Vatsīputra said: "Gautama, setting aside one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī, is there perhaps even one upāsaka in this Buddha-dharma who maintains the precepts with diligence, whose pure conduct is stainless, who has crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, and who has severed [the fetters]?"

Regarding the net of doubt, the Buddha said: "Good son, within my Dharma, there are not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred, but rather immeasurable upāsakas who maintain the precepts with diligence, whose pure conduct is stainless, who have severed the five lower fetters to attain the stage of anāgāmin, who have crossed to the other shore beyond doubt, and who have cut through the net of doubt.
Vatsa replied: "Gautama, let us set aside one person."

"One bhikṣu, one bhikṣuṇī, and one upāsaka—among the teachings of the Buddha, is there perhaps even one upāsikā who maintains the precepts with diligence, whose pure conduct is stainless, who has crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, and who has severed the web of doubt?
The Buddha said, "Good son, in my Dharma, it is not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred; indeed, there are immeasurable upāsikās."

"Practicing the precepts with diligence, pure in holy conduct, having severed the five lower fetters, one attains the stage of *anāgāmin* and crosses to the further shore beyond doubt, severing the web of doubt.

Vatsa said: "Gautama, set aside one bhikṣu, one bhikṣuṇī, one upāsaka, and one upāsikā who practice the precepts with diligence, are pure in holy conduct, and have severed doubt, such that they have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*)."
"Is there, within the Buddha-dharma, any upāsaka who enjoys the five objects of desire yet has no net of doubt in his mind?
The Buddha said, "Good son, within this Buddha-dharma, it is not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred;

rather, there are immeasurable upāsakas who have severed the three fetters and attained the stage of Srotāpanna, and who have thinned greed, anger, and delusion and attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin."
It is the same for upāsakas and upāsikās.
Those who wish to practice should first seek out such persons; if there are high examples, I too shall follow and practice accordingly.
Here, one simply asks about the two groups of the ordained, which by extension includes the fourfold assembly who have severed all existence—this clarifies that these are arhats.

When those among the two groups of renunciants who had attained the stage of Anāgāmin questioned those among the two groups of householders who had crossed to the other shore beyond doubt, [the latter] replied that they had partially attained such crossing.
Herein, the term *upāsaka* (lay follower) is explained again: there are those who have abandoned desire and those who possess wives and children.
As the text says, the Buddha answered all those who, while experiencing the pleasures of the five senses, remained free from the net of doubt in their minds.
As for why it is not one, two, three, or even five hundred— as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that there are five thousand divisions—
yet many sūtras frequently mention five hundred disciples, this is merely a conventional expression regarding numbers.
"World-Honored One, I now wish to speak an analogy. This concludes the third section, "The Submission through Taking Refuge," which consists of five parts;
first is the request to speak.
"World-Honored One, I now wish to speak an analogy."
Next, the Buddha granted his permission.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent! Speak as you please.
Having spoken thus three times, [he ceased].
World-Honored One, it is as if the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda send down a great rain;
so too is the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata, falling equally upon upāsakas and upāsikās.
Fourth, the request for ordination.
"World-Honored One, if various non-Buddhists wish to come forth and leave the household life, I do not know for how many months the Tathāgata tests them.
The Buddha said, "Good son, all are tested for four months; it need not be of one kind. [The interlocutor asked,] "World-Honored One, if it is not of one kind, I only pray that the Great..."
"Compassionately grant me permission to leave the household life.
The Buddha ordered that he be tested for four months regarding his mastery of the *upāsaka* scriptures. Regarding the mention of "four months," it refers simply to a period of time;
this is because the faculties and natures of beings differ and are not of a single kind—having heard the teaching in one way, he immediately sought to leave the household life.
The five Buddhas permitted his ordination.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya, saying, "I permit this son of a cowherd (Vatsa) to leave the household life and receive the precepts.
Having received the Buddha’s command, Kauṇḍinya stood among the assembly of monks and performed the *karmavācanā* for him. Fifteen days passed after he had left the household life.
Having attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, and having already attained that fruit, he further thought: "If there is wisdom to be gained through training, I have now attained it;

I am fit to see the Buddha. He immediately went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and having completed his respectful salutation, he withdrew to stand to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as for all wisdom to be gained through training, I have now [attained it]."
“Now that you have attained this, I pray that you will explain it to me again in detail so that I may obtain the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna).
The Buddha said, “Good son, you must diligently apply yourself with vigor to cultivate two dharmas: first, śamatha; second, vipaśyanā.”
Good son, if there is a bhikṣu who wishes to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, he should also diligently cultivate these two dharmas.
If he further wishes to attain the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, or the fruit of arhat, he should likewise practice these two dharmas.
Good son, if there is a bhikṣu who wishes to attain the four dhyānas and the four immeasurable minds...

The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*), the knowledge of the summit (*mūrdhajñāna*), the ultimate knowledge (*atyantajñāna*), the four unhindered knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*),
the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)— these dharmas should also be cultivated. Good son,

if one wishes to attain the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*), the patience of signlessness (*animittadharmakṣānti*), and the inconceivable dharma, [one must cultivate these].

One should also cultivate these two dharmas: the noble conduct of patience, the holy life (*brahmacarya*), the divine conduct, the bodhisattva conduct, the Samādhi of Space, the Wisdom-Seal Samādhi, the Samādhis of Emptiness, Signlessness, and Wishlessness, the Ground Samādhi, the Non-retrogression Samādhi, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Vajra Samādhi, and the conduct of the Buddha of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus, one should practice these two dharmas.
Having heard this, the son prostrated and departed. He practiced these two dharmas within the Śāla grove and before long attained the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, there were also immeasurable bhikṣus who wished to go to where the Buddha was;
seeing them, the calf asked, "Venerable sirs, where do you wish to go? The bhikṣus replied, "We wish to go to where the Buddha is. The calf spoke again:

"Venerable sirs, when you reach the presence of the Buddha, please announce on our behalf that the brahmin Ghoṭaka, having practiced the two dharmas, has attained the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) and now, in order to repay the Buddha’s kindness, is entering parinirvāṇa. When the bhikṣus reached the presence of the Buddha, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the bhikṣu Ghoṭaka entrusted these words to us: 'World-Honored One, the brahmin Ghoṭaka has practiced..."
Having attained the wisdom of one beyond training through these two dharmas, he now repays the Buddha’s kindness by entering nirvana.
The Buddha said, “Good son, the Brahmin Vatsa has attained the fruit of arhatship; you all should go and make offerings to his body.
When the bhikṣus had received the Buddha’s command, they returned to the site of the corpse and made extensive offerings.

Regarding the statement that after leaving the household life one gains benefit through practice by means of the "two dharmas": some refer to these as *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, while others refer to them as *samādhi* and *prajñā*.

Although the pronunciations of *śamatha* differ—being either light or heavy—the way to repay the Buddha’s kindness is to practice in accordance with the Dharma; this is how one repays the Buddha’s kindness.

The eighth section, "The *Naiyāsika* Brahmin," concerns non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*). These are also renunciants who constantly wear this patched robe (*nāi*), and thus they are named after their garment.
In this land as well, there are those like Ma Ru and Bei Du who follow this style. This section is divided into two parts: first, the discussion of doctrine; second, their submission.

The discussion of doctrine is further divided into two: first, the presentation of their tenets; second, the refutation thereof. Regarding the presentation of their tenets, the Kai Shan school provides the initial analysis.
The text consists of eight further expositions: first, based on afflictions; second, based on the five great elements; third, based on bracelets and bangles; fourth, based on intrinsic nature;

fifth, based on the five sense objects; sixth, based on the five sense faculties; seventh, based on infants; eighth, based on existence and non-existence. This section [the *Zhao ti fen*] is divided into two parts:

first, the refutation of the correct meaning; second, the establishment of false meanings. Within the first part, there are again two sections. First: [The text continues with the specific arguments.]

Regarding the difficulty of the subsequent [stage] of non-karmic action, the Master divides the contemplation of afflictions (*kleśa*) into four parts: first, one section that further raises difficulties regarding the meaning of causes and conditions;
next, three sections that establish the meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); third, one section that re-examines the correct meaning; and fourth, three [sections].
Furthermore, to re-establish the intrinsic nature by merely dividing the text: who among men is right and who is wrong?

Moreover, according to Master Guan and most other masters, it is said that the beginning question concerns the origin of sentient beings flowing from the three realms; the final question concerns the vastness [of that flow];

the initial question concerning the resolution of the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa* is the beginning of the inquiry into the flow [of existence], while the final question is the inquiry into the reversal [of that flow].
The Master [Seng]guan, relying on three scriptural passages, deduces that the first [case] is Ājñātakauṇḍinya’s answer being extensive; it says:

"If someone comes and asks whether the permanent or the impermanent has a beginning or an end, the Buddha remains silent. As for the second, when Nādikā asked about the beginning, why did the Buddha answer?
First, it is difficult to say that sentient beings have performed good or evil deeds throughout immeasurable lifetimes and will yet again receive their retribution in the future.
Regarding the question of the retribution for wholesome and unwholesome deeds: what connection does the fruit of karma have to the initial inquiry?
Among these, concerning the first point regarding that which "flows in," the Buddha replied that it does not come from anywhere. Why?

Because when one first gives rise to a single thought outside the realms and it flows in, if one were to trace back where this flowing-in comes from, it can never be known. Therefore, the answer is: it does not come.
Because this question was not asked, the Tathāgata explained the meaning of how craving moistens and gives rise to existence through the proper inquiry into causes and conditions,
and how death due to evil causes and conditions leads to seeing hell, yet one instead generates craving and is reborn therein;
whereas death due to wholesome causes and conditions leads to seeing heaven, and one who generates craving is reborn therein— this numerical analysis is thus understood.
Some people say that prior to the arising of the *nirvṛtti-bhava* (the existence at birth), craving arises and moistens the body of the *upapatti-bhava* (the existence at rebirth);
since both craving and the body arise simultaneously, one immediately obtains the body. This implies that the afflictions exist first and the body follows later.

Other proponents of this theory say that after the cessation of the *maraṇa-bhava* (the existence at death), craving arises and moistens the next life; thus, the afflictions come first and the body exists only later.
Regarding the difficult conditions, there are two initial points concerning the failure to grasp the intended meaning.

Furthermore, the *Nāṭaputta* (Nigaṇṭha) ascetic spoke thus: "Gautama, as Gautama has stated—that throughout immeasurable lifetimes one performs good and evil deeds and consequently receives good and evil bodies in the future—this principle is not so."

The subsequent refutation of the passage on afflictions (*kleśa*) is further divided into four parts: first, receiving the essential meaning; second, the double refutation; third, the specific refutation;
and fourth, the summary conclusion. Why is this so? As Gautama has said: "It is because of afflictions that one obtains this body."
The following section cites what the Buddha taught regarding afflictions (*kleśa*) and the body (*deha*), hence it is titled "Receiving the Intent.

Regarding the passage beginning with "If [it arises] because of afflictions," the second part consists of a double objection, which further divides into three sections: first, two determinations; second, two objections;
and third, two conclusions. Of these, the initial two determinations are evident.
If the body is obtained because of the afflictions (*kleśa*), does the body come first or do the afflictions come first?
These are the two dilemmas.
If the afflictions come first, by whom were they created, and where do they abide? If the body comes first, how can it be said [that the body arises from the afflictions]?
It is said that afflictions are obtained through causes.
First, it is asked: if the afflictions existed prior [to the body], and the body did not yet exist at all, how could those afflictions be obtained?
Where would the afflictions abide? By what would the afflictions be produced? Furthermore, if afflictions were produced by further afflictions, then they would not be "prior."
Therefore, it is said that the objection regarding the impossibility of sequence— namely, that if the body existed first, it would not be obtained through afflictions,
and since the body would not arise from afflictions, afflictions likewise could not depend on the body— is in both cases untenable.
Therefore, if one says that the afflictions exist prior [to the body], this is untenable; if one says that the body exists prior [to the afflictions], this is also untenable.
If one says they exist simultaneously, it is difficult to resolve according to the three lower [positions].
If one says they occur simultaneously, that is also untenable.
Since it has already been stated that cause and effect should not be simultaneous,
the subsequent section on simultaneity— consisting of the four points below— is a summary of these three meanings.

The meanings of "prior," "subsequent," and "simultaneous" are all untenable; therefore, I say that all dharmas possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and do not arise from causes and conditions.
Since all three [temporal relations] are untenable, one knows that dharmas do not arise from causes and conditions.

Furthermore, Gautama, solidity is the nature of earth; next, moisture is the nature of water, heat is the nature of fire, and motion is the nature of wind. Herein lie three further instances establishing the meaning of false intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Gautama, solidity is the nature of earth, moisture is the nature of water, heat is the nature of fire, and motion is the nature of wind.
That which is unimpeded is the nature of space; the natures of the five great elements do not exist through causes and conditions.
If there were even a single dharma-nature in the world that did not exist through causes and conditions, then the natures of all dharmas would likewise not exist through causes and conditions.
If there were even one dharma that arose from causes and conditions, for what reason would the natures of the five great elements not arise from causes and conditions?

"Gautama, when sentient beings attain liberation through either virtuous or non-virtuous bodies, it is all due to their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and does not arise from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Therefore, I say that all phenomena exist by virtue of their intrinsic nature and are not produced from causes and conditions."
The nature of that luminous ground is firmness, up to the nature of emptiness as being unobstructed; such is not established by causes and conditions.
Since these five great elements are thus, so it is with all things; this is the meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, the worldly dharmas have fixed applications that serve as proof for the preceding argument.
Moreover, Gautama, worldly dharmas have fixed applications;
for example, a craftsman might say, "This wood is suitable for making a carriage," or "This is suitable for making a door, a bed, or a small table. It is also like the work produced by a goldsmith.
That which is on the forehead is called a *mālā* (garland); that which is below the neck is called a *hāra* (necklace); that which is on the upper arm is called a *kaṭaka* (bracelet);
and that which is on the fingers is called a *valaya* (ring). Because their respective positions are fixed, they are termed "fixed-natured. All sentient beings are likewise so:
because they possess the nature of the five destinies (*pañcagati*), there are those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.
If humans and devas are thus, why do you speak of them as arising from causes and conditions? Furthermore, Gautama, all sentient beings have distinct natures;
therefore, they are said to possess their own inherent natures (*svabhāva*). For example, a tortoise born on land can naturally enter the water;
a calf, once born, can naturally drink milk; and a fish sees a baited hook and naturally swallows it, as does a venomous snake.
Once born, they naturally consume earth; who could have taught them such things?
Just as thorns, once grown, are naturally pointed at their tips, and the plumage of flying birds is naturally differentiated in color, so too it is with the sentient beings of the world:

some are sharp-witted and others dull, some wealthy and others poor, some handsome and others ugly, some attain liberation and others fall into lower realms. For this reason, [it is not due to a creator].
One should know that within all phenomena there exists their respective intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the statement, "That which is on the forehead is called a *mālā* (garland) and so forth," this refers to the ornaments of this land;

thus, first citing the carpenter’s measuring of wood—taking what is straight for a bed and what is curved for a table—it further cites the five destinies as examples of such [intrinsic natures], thereby speaking of intrinsic nature.
Those born in the hells and so forth, as well as those born on land such as turtles who immediately enter the waters of the sea—by whom were the shells of these oysters and clams carved?
Thirdly, regarding the raising of the issue of desire: furthermore, the aforementioned reasoning based on causes and conditions is not the Buddha’s intent.
Furthermore, Gautama, you claim that greed, hatred, and delusion arise from causes and conditions, and that the causes and conditions for these three poisons are the five sensory objects;
this meaning is not correct.
[The opponent] subsequently raises this objection.
Why is this? When sentient beings sleep, they are far removed from the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), yet they still give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion;

it is the same while in the womb. At the moment of first emerging from the womb, they are not yet able to distinguish between the beauty and ugliness of the five sensory objects, yet they still give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Even when sages and noble ones dwell in secluded and tranquil places where the five sensory objects do not exist, they are still capable of giving rise to greed.
Regarding desire, hatred, and delusion, there are likewise those who, because of the five sense objects, give rise to non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion;
therefore, it is not necessarily the case that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, for they exist by virtue of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

There are four points of difficulty: first, it is difficult [to maintain] that craving does not confront objects, for even when a person is asleep and does not confront objects, desire and craving still arise;
second, it is difficult [to maintain] that an infant at birth, having no capacity for discrimination, likewise gives rise to craving;

third, it is difficult [to maintain] that noble ones dwelling in mountain forests, though separated from the five sensory objects, nevertheless give rise to craving; fourth, it is difficult [to maintain] that there is intrinsic confrontation [with objects].
Attachment to sensory objects and non-attachment to sensory objects are both intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
Fourth, there are three further instances where you repeatedly establish a false meaning.
Furthermore, Gautama, I observe that among people in this world, those who lack the five sense faculties yet possess abundant wealth and have attained great sovereignty [are numerous].
There are those who possess all their faculties yet are impoverished, lowly, and lack autonomy, serving as slaves to others; if there were causes and conditions, why would this be so?
Therefore, all phenomena each have their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and do not arise from causes and conditions.
First, it is explained that some lack the five faculties yet possess great wealth, while others possess all five faculties yet have meager fortune.

If one lacks the faculties, why would they have much wealth in this life despite having committed evil in the past? If one possessed the faculties, why would they be poor in this life despite having practiced virtue in the past?
In both cases, these are simply their inherent natures and are not related to causes and conditions.
Secondly, it can be seen again.
Furthermore, Gautama, even infants in this world are unable to distinguish the five sensory objects;
yet when they laugh, one knows they are joyful, and when they cry, one knows they are distressed. Therefore, one should know that all phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Third, furthermore, the objection regarding existence and non-existence is raised.
Furthermore, Gautama, there are two worldly phenomena: first, existence; second, non-existence. Existence is like space; non-existence is like the horns of a rabbit.

Of these two phenomena, that which exists does not arise from causes and conditions because it already exists, and that which does not exist likewise does not [arise from causes and conditions] because it does not exist.
Because of these reasons, since all phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they do not arise from causes and conditions.
For them, space is "existent" and the horns of a rabbit are "non-existent. Who created the existence of space? Who caused the horns of a rabbit to be non-existent?
Since these two cases are thus, so it is with everything else; all things are simply intrinsic nature.
The Buddha’s response below answers the questions; briefly, there are three differences between the questions and the answers:

first, presence and absence; second, gravity; and third, lack of sequential order. Regarding presence and absence: previously there were four difficulties, which formed eight "repetitions" (*punaḥ-kāra*); now there are only seven repetitions. Why is this so?
Because when the Buddha finished answering the seven difficulties, [the interlocutor] immediately attained realization; therefore, he did not answer an eighth.

The "Difficulties" (Nan) are treated with great gravity; this is the second response to the second difficulty. Why is this so? Because "nature" (xing) is the core tenet [of the opponent's position], it is refuted twice.
As for the lack of sequential order: the first response addresses the second [difficulty]; the second response addresses the third; the third response addresses the fourth;
the fourth response addresses the first; the fifth is a further response to the second; and the sixth is a response to the fifth.

The seventh [section] answers the sixth, and the eighth answers the seventh; the first [section] answers the second. Regarding the refutation and establishment of the meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*):
The Buddha said, "Good son, as you have stated—that all dharmas should be like the intrinsic natures of the five great elements—this is not so.
Why is this? Good son, in your doctrine, the five great elements are eternal."
Because of causes and conditions, all dharmas are entirely not eternal.

If worldly things are impermanent, for what reason would the nature of the five great elements (pañcamahābhūta) not be impermanent? If the five great elements were eternal, then worldly things should also be eternal.
Therefore, your claim that the nature of the five great elements possesses an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and does not arise from causes and conditions is untenable.
It is impossible that all phenomena are identical to the five great elements.

You [the opponent] use the fact that the five great elements do not arise from conditions as an analogy to claim that all phenomena likewise do not arise from conditions; the Buddha refutes this by asking:

"You establish that the five great elements do not arise from conditions, and therefore you name them 'permanent'; you then use this as an analogy to claim that all phenomena likewise [do not arise from conditions]."
That which arises from conditions should also be permanent.
Your statement that "the locus of activity is lower" is the second response; the third refutes its supporting argument.
Noble son, as for your claim that because the locus of activity is fixed, there must be an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this is not the case. Why is this so?
All names are obtained through causes and conditions; if a name is derived from a cause, its meaning is likewise derived from a cause.
What is meant by "a name being derived from a cause"? For example, when it is on the forehead, it is called a "crown";

when on the neck, a "necklace"; when on the arm, a "bracelet"; when on a chariot, a "wheel"; and when fire is in wood or grass, it is called "wood-fire" or "grass-fire. Good son, when wood first grows...

At that time, the nature of arrows and spears does not exist inherently; rather, they are fashioned by craftsmen due to causes and conditions as arrows, and fashioned by craftsmen due to causes and conditions as spears.
Therefore, one should not say that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature.

Regarding those bracelets and armlets, for what reason did the Buddha refute them? He said they are both designated by name through causes and conditions, and their meanings are also derived from causes and conditions.
To call them "garlands" or "necklaces" is to derive their names from causes; to say a craftsman makes arrows or spears is to derive their meanings from causes.
If their nature were already that of an arrow, there would be no need for a craftsman; how much less so when they are originally bracelets now being struck and fashioned [into something else]?
When a bracelet is changed into a ring, that which was curved for use as a rest becomes a bed when the rest is straightened;
and that which was straight for use as a bed is now used as a rest when the bed is curved by ironing. All of these are merely conditions and causes—what inherent nature could there be?
Regarding your statement that it is like a tortoise born on land, this is the third refutation of that fourth [point].
Furthermore, there are seven matters for the purpose of refuting seven matters; this is the first matter.

Noble son, as for your statement that a tortoise born on land naturally enters the water by its own nature, and that a calf, once born, naturally possesses the ability to drink—[this is likewise refuted].
This interpretation is incorrect. Why? If you say that entering water is not due to causes and conditions, then since both would equally lack causes and conditions, why does the calf not enter fire?
Furthermore, once born, the calf’s innate nature is to suckle milk; if this were not due to causes and conditions—being entirely without them—why does it not suckle its own horns?
Why not enter the fire and suck up the horn to overturn that school?
If it is said that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature, this is the second point below.
Noble son, if it is said that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature, there would be no need for instruction or practice, and no growth or increase would occur.

This interpretation is not correct. Why? Because we now see that there are teachings, and that these teachings increase through conditions; therefore, one should know that they have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, in the middle section above, this statement is entirely absent; it merely says: "Whoever possesses teachings, for them these [teachings] now exist."
Since the refuter has already stated that sharpness is the very nature [of things], dullness must likewise be so; how then could there be any teaching that is superior?
This concludes the third point regarding the claim that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Good son, if all dharmas possessed an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then none of the brahmins would ever act to purify their bodies by slaughtering sheep for sacrificial offerings.
Since they do perform such bodily sacrifices, you should know that there is no intrinsic nature."
It clarifies that a brāhmaṇa should not perform sacrificial offerings.
Regarding the worldly methods of speech, there are three [stages], with the fourth being the matter at hand.
Noble son, there are generally three kinds of worldly methods of speech: first, the intention to act; second, the time of acting; and third, [the completion of the act].
If all phenomena possessed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), why would there be these three verbal expressions in the world?
Because these three verbal expressions exist, we know that all things lack intrinsic nature.
The statement that all things possess "activity" (saṃskāra) cannot possibly be natural.
If one says that all phenomena (dharmas) possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), this is the fifth point below.
Son of good family, if one says that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature, one should know that each phenomenon would then have its own fixed nature.
If sugarcane were a single entity with a fixed nature, for what reason would it produce syrup, honey, candied sugar, wine, and sour gruel?
If there were a single nature, for what reason would such various things emerge from it?
Since such things emerge from a single object, one should know that all phenomena cannot possess a fixed, singular nature.
If [things] were fixed, they would necessarily be determined.
If all phenomena possessed a fixed nature—this is the sixth point below.
Noble son, if all phenomena possessed a fixed nature, why would the sages drink sugarcane juice, stone [gruel], and so forth?
Honey, black honey-wine, and vinegar are not drinkable at certain times, yet later they become sour wine and can be drunk again.
Therefore, one should know that there is no fixed nature; if there were no fixed nature, how could things not exist by way of causes and conditions?
Since clarity is not fixed, it must follow from conditions.
You have stated that all phenomena [possess] their own-nature; this is the seventh point below.
Son of good family, you say that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature—how can you provide an analogy for this? If there were an analogy, [it would be as follows:]...
One should know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; if they possessed intrinsic nature, one should know there would be no analogies.
The wise of the world all employ metaphors, so one should know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and possess no single, fixed nature.

Because the analogy is explained so clearly, one knows that there is no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). If [the listener] were already to understand it, then their nature would already be understanding; why labor to provide an explanation?
If they do not understand, their nature will remain non-understanding even if the analogy is repeated; thus, the benefit of establishing the point would be nil.
Good son, as for your statement that "the body comes first," this is the fourth point following the refutation of the first [position].
Furthermore, the original objection consisted of four parts: first, receiving the intent; second, the dual objection; third, the specific objection; and fourth, the summary conclusion.

Now, my response does not correspond to each of these individually, but rather provides a general reply. Moreover, these four points pertain specifically to the fundamental core of the primary objection.
Regarding the three ways in which [the body] might arise first: first, the difficulty that the body arises first; second, the difficulty that the afflictions arise first;

and third, the difficulty that the afflictions and the body arise simultaneously. Within these, there is no difficulty regarding the "knot" (*saṃyojana*) itself, but it exists within the difficulties.

Now, I shall answer these three: first, answering the difficulty that the body arises first; next, answering the difficulty of simultaneity; and finally, answering the difficulty that the afflictions arise first. Regarding the first:
Second, first the double negation:
"Good son, as for your statement that the body comes first or that afflictions come first, this meaning is not so.
Next, the formal response to the three difficulties; herein, the first response is that the body comes first.
Why is this? If I were to say that the body exists prior [to consciousness], you might object, "You are the same as me in that the body does not exist prior.
For what reason do you raise such an objection?

However, according to the Buddha’s fundamental meaning, he taught that afflictions (*kleśa*) are the cause of the body; therefore, one should properly challenge [the opponent] by asserting that afflictions must come first.
As for why they further challenge that the body comes first, this arises from a relative perspective and is not his original intent.

Now, wishing to provide a correct response, I first dismiss the incidental point, saying: "I have made no such statement, and your own position is likewise [unfounded]. Why do you suddenly raise this objection?"
What I originally intended as a refutation of my opponent has instead established my own position.
Good son, regarding the second answer concerning the objection that [the causes and effects] occur simultaneously, the text is divided into three parts:
first, clarifying simultaneity; second, clarifying succession; and third, providing a further response by restating the intent.
Good son, the bodies and afflictions of all sentient beings are devoid of priority or posteriority; they exist simultaneously.
As for the initial statement "simultaneously," this excludes that which they falsely conceive of as simultaneity.

If what they understand by "simultaneous" were truly so, it would be impossible [to speak of them as such]. What is here called "simultaneous" refers to a sequence of before and after, yet it is also simultaneous.
Although they exist simultaneously, there must first be the afflictions for a body to come into being; it is never the case that afflictions arise because of the body.
Regarding the phrase "its before and after" in the second passage: this refers to the before and after within a single moment;

there is no difference between before and after apart from the single moment, nor is there a difference in the single moment apart from before and after. Now, it is precisely within the meaning of a single moment that we speak of before and after:
namely, that the afflictions constitute the prior body, which belongs to the subsequent [result], while the afflictions are the causal body. This is what is meant.

Is it not the case that the fruit precedes the cause? If it is as clarified in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*—that things are established through conditions—then there is a specific intention behind [the claim] that "it exists by way of the fruit" (and so forth).
Personally, I maintain that when various Mahāyāna sūtras speak of "beginninglessness," they do not refer solely to the body, nor do they refer solely to afflictions.

If one were prior to the other, then the other would have a beginning. The present sūtra, however, speaks from the perspective of the pedagogical transformation of those to be trained (*vineya*) through the application of remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
Because it is taught that one must rely on afflictions (*kleśa*) for a body to exist, this is still spoken according to the principle (*yukti*). Thus it says, "although there is no before or after.
Although "although" is a term of incompleteness, incompleteness is a teaching of remainder (*śeṣa*).

Therefore, one knows that the true principle (*tattva*) is actually the remainder of the provisional path (*upāya*); speaking in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is not only the past that is said to be non-existent.
Prior and posterior exist only within the present afflictions; when these act as causes for the body, there is likewise no sequence of before and after.
Why is this? Because cause and effect are non-dual, and the substance of matter and mind is one. The three paths and the three virtues do not conflict within a single thought-moment;

the five aggregates and the five liberations are equal in principle at every instant. What is precious lies in wearing the patched robe and maintaining the practice of shattering attachments; once shattered, the nature of things is realized to be identical to emptiness.
"Emptiness has no before or after, nor inside or outside; who is it that bestows these thirty-six fascicles? They proceed solely from Nirvana.
The fifty-two assemblies all possess the Buddha-nature; until this is fully realized, one ultimately returns to forming karmic conditions.
These two segments of meaning consist of only two lines; the remainder of the sutra text is the essential explanation for dispelling doubts.

If you think that it is like a person who, having two eyes, takes a third [eye] as an object and thereby refutes [the necessity of two], or if you think that it is like a person whose two eyes are obtained simultaneously without depending on one another—where the left does not depend on the right and the right does not depend on the left—and that afflictions and the body are likewise, this meaning is not correct. Why? Because in the world...

In the interim, one observes with the eye that although the wick and the light exist simultaneously, the light must depend upon the wick; it is never the case that the wick exists by depending on the light.
If one were to say that afflictions and the body are simultaneous, they should not be sequential like the two horns of an ox, one on the left and one on the right.
It is not because of the right that there is the right, nor because of the left that there is the left; this matter is not so.
Just as the wick and the light exist simultaneously, yet the light exists because of the wick and never the wick because of the light, so it is with afflictions and the body.
The wick is merely the vessel of the lamp; it is because of the lamp that there is light, and what is called the "wick" is simply that which is consumed by the fire.
Before it has been burned, it cannot be called a wick (and so forth). This clarifies that the Buddha’s meaning here is precisely that of simultaneous cause and effect.
Former explanations mostly claim that this clarifies the beginning of sentient beings as being simultaneous cause and effect; however, I say this is not so.
This does not clarify the beginning of sentient beings, but rather clarifies that when sentient beings employ karma to obtain a body, it must necessarily arise from afflictions (*kleśa*).
Affliction (*kleśa*) itself is of two kinds: first, that which "intercalates" karma; second, that which "intercalates" birth. Regarding "intercalating karma," its bodily fruit is extensive;
what is clarified here specifically refers to that which "intercalates" birth. To explain according to the numerical analysis:

at the very beginning of the aggregates of birth, the defiled consciousness constitutes the affliction of intercalating birth. This very [consciousness] binds the retribution of a single lifetime; this is what is meant by affliction.
From the perspective of meaning, it is convenient to hold that [the intermediate existence] exists simultaneously with the body; however, we now rely on the latter interpretation.

If Master Lingwei also employs the "arising skandhas" (*upapattibhava-skandha*), he says that the arising of the "intercalary craving for birth" (*antarābhava-tṛṣṇā*) at the very beginning is extremely similar to the meaning of "number.

Other masters all say that within the "skandhas of death" (*maraṇabhava-skandha*), the arising of the "intercalary craving for birth" allows one to speak of cause and effect as being simultaneous. This was previously stated by Ka.
The *Yezhang* (Chapter on Leaves) states: "Due to the two causes and conditions of craving and ignorance, one obtains a lifespan. The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:

"With a mind possessed of outflows (*sāsrava*) and grasping (*upādāna*), the seeds of feverish affliction gradually become complete. The *Sūtra* states: "With a mind possessed of outflows and grasping, the seeds of outflows arise.
Although the distinction of "moistening birth" (*vṛddhi-janman*) arises earlier, it is precisely due to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because it is *sāsrava* (tainted), the craving that gives rise to rebirth binds it; this constitutes the "grasping-consciousness" (*upādāna-vijñāna*).
Once it is *sāsrava*, these three meanings—cause, effect, and their simultaneity—are present at one time. This point subtly adopts the explanation of Lingwei.
Regarding the previous objection which stated, "If one speaks of the meaning of simultaneity, that too is untenable," our current response is that there is indeed this principle of simultaneity.
This is because it can withstand the challenge of being turned toward error; therefore, it is said:

"If you think that it is like a person’s two eyes [which exist simultaneously], I shall refute that intention by clarifying that although they exist at the same time, there is truly a sense of mutual dependence, just as a wick and its light exist at once yet are mutually dependent."
If you think that the body does not exist prior [to the afflictions], this is the third response to the objection that the afflictions must precede it. Furthermore, there are two parts to this;
first, he restates that objection:
"Virtuous son, if you think that because the body does not exist prior [to the afflictions], one knows there is no cause—this meaning is not so."
Therefore, the following section provides a formal refutation.
Why? If you maintain that something is called "non-existent" because it previously lacked causes and conditions, you should not say that all phenomena possess causes and conditions.
However, within this passage there are two schools of interpretation. One says:

"If one claims that [things] are called 'non-existent' because they previously lacked causes and conditions, this merely restates the opponent's objection; 'you should not say so' is the refutation of that claim.
'You should not speak in such a manner' means that everything possesses causes and conditions, thereby clarifying that all phenomena [arise from them]."
While it is true that there are causes and conditions, one need not analyze the phrasing in such detail; one could simply say:

"You should not claim that all phenomena possess causes and conditions. However, that [position] refers to the meaning of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), which asserts that things exist without causes and conditions;
thus, when one says "you should not claim that all phenomena possess causes and conditions," these three teachers among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain that there are two [types of causes].
The fifteen truths (*satya*) all arise in mutual succession; this is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), yet it differs from the Buddha’s meaning of dependent origination.
In the Buddha’s teaching, the past is taken as the cause and the present as the fruit. In that [other] school, they take the mutual arising within a single present lifetime as dependent origination.

Furthermore, just as in the case of *Lakṣaṇa*, there are the "supporting truths" (*āśraya-satya*) and the "governing truths" (*adhipati-satya*), such as the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*).
The five faculties and the five great elements are the primary truths; the five faculties are the dependent truths, both of which function as causes and conditions.
For example, the fire element creates the eye, enabling it to see forms; form is a *guṇa* (quality) belonging to the fire element.
Likewise, the space element creates the ear, enabling it to hear sounds; sound is a *guṇa* belonging to the ear. (And so forth.)
If it is said that [the Tathāgata] does not see [them], the text refutes this by taking up that intention again.
If it is said that he does not speak because he does not see them, then why does he not speak [of the fact that] jars and so forth are now seen to emerge from causes and conditions?
Just as with the jar, the prior causes and conditions of its body are likewise thus. O son of good family, whether seen or unseen, all phenomena...
All phenomena arise from causes and conditions and possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If you claim that you do not speak [of the self] because you do not perceive its cause, then why do you not speak of the jar, which is currently perceived to emerge from clay?
To say you do not speak because you do not perceive it is contrary to your own experience; whether you see it or do not see it, this [point] is now made clear.
Whoever debates whether you see or do not see merely states that, according to the present discourse, all phenomena arise from causes and conditions. Son of good family,
if one says that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this concludes the fifth section,
which refutes the second major objection concerning the five great natures.
"Good son, if you say that all dharmas possess an intrinsic nature and have no causes or conditions,

for what reason do you say that the five great elements (mahābhūtas) are the very nature of the five great elements and that this constitutes their cause and condition? Good son, although the causes and conditions of the five great elements are thus,
one should not say that all dharmas are identical to the causes and conditions of the five great elements, as worldly people might say."
All those who have left the household life and diligently uphold the precepts—even outcastes and the like—should likewise diligently uphold the precepts.
Good son, as for your statement that the five great elements possess a fixed and solid nature, I observe that this nature is subject to transformation and is therefore not fixed.
Good son, in your own doctrine, butter, wax, and lac are called "earth"; yet this earth is not fixed, as it may become identical to [other states].

"Water may be identical to earth; therefore, its intrinsic nature cannot be defined as such. Son of Good Family, in your doctrine, white tin, lead, pewter, copper, iron, gold, and silver are called 'fire.
When this fire flows, it has the nature of water; when it moves, it has the nature of wind; when it is hot, it has the nature of fire;
and when it is solid, it has the nature of earth. How then can you say that it is definitively named the nature of fire?"
Good son, the nature of water is called "flowing. If water freezes, it is not called earth; therefore, for what reason and by what causal conditions is it still called water?
When it moves and waves, why is it not called wind? If movement is not called wind, then when it freezes, it should likewise not be called water.
If these two meanings both arise from causes and conditions, for what reason do you say that all dharmas [are without self-nature]?
"Good son, it is not so that the nature of the five faculties is able to see, hear, perceive, know, and touch by virtue of its own self-nature (*svabhāva*) rather than from causes and conditions.
This meaning is not correct. Why? Good son, the nature of self-nature is a nature that cannot be altered.
If you say that the nature of the eye sees, it should always be able to see; there should be no time when it sees and no time when it does not."
Since it is seen [in this way], one should know that seeing arises from causes and conditions, and is not without causes and conditions.
First, let us refute their notion of the "earth element" (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*). The Buddha reverses their meaning:

substances such as ghee and wax are what they call "earth," yet ghee and wax are not fixed; sometimes they become water, and sometimes they are called earth. Therefore, they are not fixed. Hereafter, we shall further refute them.

Regarding items such as white tin (*raṅga*), they are collectively raised as the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) [and so forth]. If one does not speak of three or four great elements, is this not indeed dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
Within this, there are two pairs: the former refers to your own doctrine which asserts the existence of the five great elements;

the latter asserts that fragrance constitutes earth (*pṛthivī*) and visible form (*rūpa*) constitutes fire (*tejas*). This is as clarified in the *Ālokakalāpa* chapter of the treatise regarding the Vaiśeṣika doctrine.
To say that fragrance is water and color is earth—is this not dependent origination? Regarding the latter pair:

the former refers to your position that a jar arises from clay and a garment arises from threads; is this not dependent origination? The latter refers to your position that what is moist is the water-element;
even if it freezes due to the condition of cold, you still maintain that it is water by virtue of the condition of moisture, not by virtue of the cold.
Because when earth freezes due to water, it is no longer called "earth" but is instead called "water," why then is it not called "wind" when it is in motion?
This is a "parallel difficulty" (*kaṇṭaka-samāna-paryanuyoga*). If one were to apply this same logic as a challenge, one should say:

"Water has the inherent nature of flowing; when it freezes and does not flow, it is still called 'water. Likewise, wind has the inherent nature of moving; [when it does not move,] it should likewise [be called 'wind']."

If even an unmoving object is not considered "wind," then according to this current text, if one intends that water—which by nature flows but does not flow when frozen—is still called "water," then wind, which by nature moves, must be called "wind-waves" since waves are already moving.
Yet, although waves are moving, they cannot be named "wind"; and since water does not flow [when frozen], it cannot be named [wind].

Water, moreover, provides an illustration for this objection: just as water is inherently flowing, yet encounters conditions of cold and freezes so that it no longer flows, it nevertheless remains fundamentally water;
likewise, wind is inherently moving, yet encounters conditions of water and is stirred into waves—should it not still remain fundamentally wind?
If the movement of wind were to follow conditions and become water, it would no longer be called wind or ice.
Time, too, should be established according to causes and conditions; earth is not water, yet the underlying intention is this:

if water is originally of a flowing and moist nature, when it freezes it lacks flow, yet because it maintains its original moist nature, it is still called "water. What difference is there between this and wind, which is originally of a moving nature?
When wind stirs to form waves, why is it still called "water" and not "wind"? It is no different from the case of water when it moves and waves. Why does it maintain [its identity] at that time?
Intrinsic mobility should be called wind; it is only when there is movement of waves that it is called water, and when it freezes, it is called ice.
Therefore, it is established that while motion is wind, the great element of water, when it forms waves, although it relies on wind as a condition, still follows its cause and belongs to water;
it does not follow the motion and become wind. How could this not be a matter of causes and conditions?
Regarding your statement that greed does not arise because of the five sense objects, this sixth section refutes that fifth point.
"Good son, your claim that liberation arises without being caused by the five sense objects is incorrect. Why is this?"

Good son, although the arising of greed and liberation does not depend on the causal conditions of the five sensory objects, it arises because of unwholesome mental application (*vitarka-vicāra*) that leads to greed, and because of wholesome mental application that leads to liberation.

Good son, greed and liberation arise due to internal causes and conditions, while they are further increased by external causes and conditions. Therefore, as you said, all phenomena each have their own [causes].
It is impossible for liberation to exist if one’s own nature gives rise to craving due to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

It is clear that the five sensory objects serve merely as external conditions; furthermore, it is due to the internal causes of vitarka and vicāra that greed and anger arise from wholesome or unwholesome vitarka and vicāra.
Regarding your statement that those who possess all faculties yet lack wealth and do not attain mastery,
while those with impaired faculties possess abundant wealth and attain great mastery— this is the seventh refutation of your sixth point. Noble son, you claim that because these conditions exist,
there must be an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and therefore things do not arise from causes.
This reasoning is not correct. Why? Good son, sentient beings possess retributive fruits according to their karma.
Such retributive fruits are of three kinds: first, retribution in the present life; second, retribution in the next life; and third, retribution in subsequent lives.

Whether one is poor or immensely wealthy, or whether one’s faculties are complete or incomplete—these karmas are each distinct. If there were an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) that possessed all the faculties, [then these distinctions would not exist].

Those who ought to possess abundant wealth and those who ought to possess all their faculties do not now do so; therefore, one knows for certain that there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and that all things arise from causes and conditions.
This clarifies that because the causes of karma differ, the resulting retributions vary accordingly.
As you have said, this refutes the seventh [point] by means of the worldly child as the eighth.
Noble son, as you have stated, even worldly children who are unable to distinguish the causes and conditions of the five sensory objects both cry and laugh;
therefore, the claim that all things possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is incorrect. Why is this? If [an intrinsic nature were] inherent...
If there were such a thing as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one should laugh always when it is time to laugh and weep always when it is time to weep; one should not laugh once and weep once.

If one laughs once and weeps once, one should know that all things arise from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Therefore, one should not say that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature and thus do not arise from causes and conditions.
If tomorrow there is weeping and laughter, one will know that there is a karmic affinity; furthermore, the eighth [consciousness] is not destroyed. Regarding this, there are two interpretations.
Kai-shan previously said: "The eighth is of two kinds of non-existence; since nothing does not arise from conditions, there is no need to refute it.
Yi-ch'eng said: "This refutation concludes with the seventh; since he immediately attains realization, the eighth is therefore not refuted."
The brahmin said: "If all dharmas are inferior to this, this is the second passage on taking refuge and submission. It consists of two parts:
first, he poses two questions in a general manner to seek an explanation.
The brahmin said: 'World-Honored One, if all dharmas arise from causes and conditions, from what cause does such a body as this arise?'"
The Buddha said, "Good son, this body has afflictions and karma as its causes and conditions.
The Brahmin asked, "World-Honored One, if this body arises from afflictions and karma, can these afflictions and karma be severed? The Buddha said, "It is so, it is so."
Next, from "I only wish that you would act for my sake" onwards is the section on correct submission.

The brahmin spoke again: "World-Honored One, I only wish that you would analyze and explain this for me, so that having heard it, I may not remain in this state but shall completely sever [these afflictions].
The Buddha said: "Good son, if one knows that there is no obstruction between the two extremes, this is..."
“A person is thus able to sever the karma of afflictions, World-Honored One; I have already understood and attained the right Dharma-eye.
The Buddha said, “How do you know this, World-Honored One? The two extremes are form and liberation from form; that which is between them is the Eightfold Noble Path.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent! Good son, you understand well.”

Having severed the afflictions and karma of the two extremes, he said to the World-Honored One, "I only pray that you will grant me permission to leave the household life and receive the precepts. The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
At that very moment, he severed the afflictions of the three realms and attained the fruit of Arhatship.

The Buddha, knowing their faculties to be sharp, spoke directly of the two extremes and the middle way, and they immediately attained realization. Indeed, the methods for refuting [false views] are manifold and not limited to a single kind;
the application of medicine according to the illness is not fixed as preceding or following. If one discards the general and follows the specific, one must discuss the sequence:
when first attaining the Way under the Bodhi tree, he primarily used dependent origination to refute intrinsic nature, followed by impermanence and suffering.
Emptiness is used first to refute dependent origination; next, the essence is used to refute analytical [reductionism];
next, discernment is used to refute the essence of emptiness; next, the Middle Way is used to refute the two extremes; and finally, the perfect and eternal is used to refute the partial and gradual.

Such meanings pervade the sutras and treatises; now, in the Great Nirvana Sutra, which is the ultimate teaching of the perfect and eternal, the function of dependent origination is employed to refute those who accept [the former].
Regarding the conceptualization of the robe's own nature (*svabhāva*), it is simply that one administers this initial medicine according to the specific ailment, and subsequently employs others;

since this is the case for the beginning and the end, it is likewise for the middle. In all instances, through the skillful means of wisdom—whether according to desire, suitability, treatment, or realization—one may employ these interchangeably without fault, yet the sequence remains perfectly distinct.
In my private view, the meaning of the four *siddhāntas* is inclusive of all these aspects.

Although the secret and indeterminate [teachings] are hidden and indeterminate, their sequential order remains perfectly distinct. If one grasps this intent, one should fully elaborate upon it so that the meaning of the text becomes clear.

Even though the causal conditions for refuting inherent nature are already present in the scripture, one must further develop the arguments for impermanence, analytical emptiness, up to the perfect and eternal meanings, so that the practice of the Dharma is perfected and its key points are manifest.
All of this accords with the Sūtras. If this meaning were established, it would refute the heterodox teachings and false attachments of all outsiders;
it would refute the correct teachings and right principles of all internal [Buddhist] schools; it would refute the teachings, practices, stages, and principles of all Hīnayāna worthies and sages;

and it would refute the teachings, practices, stages, and principles of all Mahāyāna worthies and sages. It encompasses the Buddha-dharma to its ultimate limit—how much more so, then, [regarding other matters]?
If one were to record each point in full within the "Ten Categories of the Heretics who Cling to Self-Nature" (Daśa-ṛṣi-vāda), the text would become overly cumbersome;

therefore, this intent is briefly set forth here in the chapter on the "Robe of Rags" (Pāṃsukūla). Having grasped the meaning of this inquiry, it may be applied as needed, both vertically and horizontally, throughout the preceding and following sections. (Et cetera.)
Furthermore, there was a brahmin named Hongguang (Vipula). This ninth section on the non-Buddhists is divided into two parts: first, the debate;
second, the submission.
At that time, there was another brahmin named Hongguang who spoke again, saying: "Gautama, you know me now."
The Buddha said to those who were so minded, "Good son, Nirvana is eternal; the conditioned is impermanent. That which is crooked is false view;
that which is straight is the Noble Path. The Brahmin asked, "Gautama, for what reason do you speak thus?

The Buddha replied, "Good son, it is because you always think that begging for alms is eternal and that special invitations are impermanent. That which is crooked is the door-bolt; that which is straight is the bolt-socket."
"Therefore, I say that Nirvāṇa is eternal and conditioned phenomena are impermanent. 'Crooked' refers to wrong views; 'straight' refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
It is not as you previously conceived it. The Brahmin said, "Gautama, you truly know my mind.
Does this Eightfold Noble Path cause all sentient beings to attain complete extinction? [The Buddha replied: "Not so. At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer.
The brāhmaṇa said, "Gautama, you already know my mind; for what reason do you remain silent and not answer what I have asked?
At that time, Kauṇḍinya spoke these words: "Great brāhmaṇa, if someone asks whether the world is finite or infinite, the Tathāgata always remains silent and does not answer.
The Eightfold Noble Path is the direct [path], and Nirvāṇa is the eternal. If one cultivates the Eightfold..."
The Noble One immediately attains extinction; if one does not practice, one cannot attain it.
O Great Brāhmaṇa, it is like a great city whose four walls have no openings whatsoever, but only a single gate.

The gatekeeper is intelligent and wise, capable of discerning well those who should be let in and those who should be barred. Although he cannot know the exact number of those entering and exiting, [he manages them all].

One who has attained even a slight degree of meditative concentration knows that all those who enter and emerge [from saṃsāra] do so by means of this gate. Good son, it is the same with the Tathāgata:
the city is a metaphor for nirvāṇa, the gate is a metaphor for the Eightfold Noble Path, and the gatekeeper is a metaphor for the Tathāgata.
Good son, although the Tathāgata does not now answer you as to whether there is an end or no end, those for whom there is an end must certainly practice this.
The Eightfold Noble Path.
He has no attachments and asks directly, knowing the thoughts in his mind. The Buddha does not know his thoughts and therefore makes a different statement;
its basis consists of four recollections of the Buddha, to which he also replies with four propositions: Nirvana is eternal, while conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
"Curved" refers to wrong views, while "straight" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path. Regarding these four meanings, the names and their intended senses differ;
therefore, he asked again. The Buddha then explained them, saying: "Begging for alms is constant, whereas special invitations are inconstant;
'curved' is a door-key, and 'straight' is the imperial banner. Thus, he silently tested the Buddha regarding the matter he had been contemplating.

The Buddha, knowing his intention, answered by transcending the literal meaning of the characters used to express it; because his answer went beyond the literal expression, [the interlocutor] requested further clarification.
Regarding the character "ran" (閻): its form should be written with "men" (門) inside "yue" (龠). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "han" (函) and "yue" (龠) refer to the lower pillars.
