At that time, the World-Honored One descended. Regarding the tenth section on the non-Buddhists, some say this chapter has three parts, which differ slightly from the preceding sections:
first, the conversion of outsiders; second, the subduing of Māra; and third, the conversion of Subhadra as an entrustment.

It is for the sake of entrustment that he speaks thus, for the sutra having been finished, he must entrust it to Ānanda. It is for the sake of subduing Māra, for Māra is an obstacle to the True Dharma.
Originally a celestial Māra, he has now been subdued by means of incantations so that the Dharma may flow without obstruction. As for the conversion of Subhadra:

previously, when the various non-Buddhists joined forces with their heterodox views to challenge the Buddha, the Buddha had already subdued them; yet Subhadra, relying on his own pride, did not come. The Buddha then commanded Ānanda to summon him, and upon doing so, he attained the Way.
This [account] clearly shows that it was not otherwise; all were conversions of non-Buddhists, though the phrasing differs while the meaning is the same. Why is this?
The Buddha’s great compassion is immeasurable; it not only shattered attachments at that time but also ensured the salvation of those with heterodox views in the future.

Therefore, he entrusted Ānanda with the mission of circulation. Since Ānanda was currently ensnared by Māra, and Māra could likewise create obstacles for the future, [the Buddha] used divine mantras to bind him, ensuring that there would be no hindrance for two generations. Subhadra, being obstinate by nature, manifested his intent...
The arrival of Subhadra to receive the teaching and the dispatching of Ānanda to summon him signify that the transmission of the Dharma must be propagated.

Subhadra’s arrival and attainment of the Way signify that all future generations shall be able to return to the orthodox path. To explain this passage according to its literary structure, it consists of four parts:

first, the final charge to Ānanda; second, further discussion of the doctrine; third, the formal charge to Ānanda; and fourth, [the conclusion]. (Note: The original text fragment ends with "third, the formal charge to Ānanda").
The fourth difficulty concerns the simultaneous conversion [of Subhadra]; the initial text has two parts: first the question, then the answer. The following is the question:
At that time, the World-Honored One, having known this, addressed Kauṇḍinya, saying, "Where is the bhikṣu Ānanda now?"
The intent behind entrusting this sutra and simultaneously transforming Subhadra was such that he looked back and charged Ānanda with the task;

the text of the two responses given by Cunda is divided into two parts: first, it clarifies how the various Māras caused disturbances; second, it clarifies how Ānanda was subjected to those disturbances.

Within the section on the disturbances caused by the various Māras, there are two further divisions: first, the disturbances caused by their verbal proclamations; second, the disturbances caused by their supernatural powers.
Kauṇḍinya said, “World-Honored One, the bhikṣu Ānanda is outside the śāla grove, twelve yojanas from this great assembly, where he is being harassed by sixty-four billion māras.
These hosts of māras have all transformed themselves into the likeness of the Tathāgata; some proclaim that all dharmas arise from causes and conditions.”

Some say that all phenomena do not arise from causes; others say that all causes and conditions are eternal dharmas, while those produced by causes and conditions are entirely impermanent. Some say that the five aggregates are real, while others say they are false;

the same applies to the entrances (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). Some say there are twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), while others say there is only the correct [path].
There are four conditions: some say that all phenomena are like illusions, like transformations, or like a mirage;
some say that one attains the Dharma through hearing; some say that one attains it through reflection; some say that one attains it through cultivation; some speak of the meditation on impurity;
some speak of the inhalation and exhalation of breath; and others speak of the four [dhyānas].
Regarding the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), some explain it as having three types of contemplation and seven kinds of skillful means;

others explain it as the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), as well as the stages of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and the Bodhisattva’s first through tenth abodes (*vihāra*).
Some speak of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); others speak of the Sūtras, Geyas, and Vyākaraṇas.

The Sūtras (sūtra), Geya (geya), Vyākaraṇa (vyākaraṇa), Gāthā (gāthā), Udāna (udāna), Nidāna (nidāna), Avadāna (avadāna), Itivṛttaka (itivṛttaka), Jātaka (jātaka), Vaipulya (vaipulya), Adbhutadharma (adbhutadharma), and Upadeśa (upadeśa);

or alternatively, the teaching on the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; or the teaching on internal emptiness.

The emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the emptiness of the beginningless, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of detachment,

the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of signlessness, the emptiness of the aggregates, the emptiness of the sense bases, the emptiness of the elements, the emptiness of the wholesome, the emptiness of the unwholesome, the emptiness of the indeterminate, the emptiness of awakening,
the emptiness of the path, the emptiness of nirvana, the emptiness of practice, the emptiness of attainment, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of emptiness, and the great emptiness.

Regarding what are called the "three contemplations," there are several interpretations. One says they are the contemplation of suffering, impermanence, and non-self.
Another says they are the contemplation of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), also known as the contemplation of the three poisons.

The Satyasiddhi-śāstra proponents say the first is the contemplation of form (rūpa).

The Western River (Hexi) commentator explains that there are five reasons why Ānanda was harassed by Māra:
first, because Cunda (Kāśyapa) was the one who should respond to and convert the various non-Buddhists, Ānanda was not [so appointed].

third, he desired to reveal the eight internal virtues of Ānanda; fourth, he intended to have Ānanda go and summon Subhadra; and fifth, he sought to humble Ānanda’s pride.

first, the question; second, the answer. Within the question, there are again two parts: first, the inquiry regarding those who are fully capable of circulating [the teaching] themselves as bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, within this great assembly there are bodhisattvas who have already, in a single lifetime, resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, up to those who have resolved their minds toward *bodhicitta* over immeasurable lifetimes;
they have been able to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, and their resolve is firm and complete."

Having sufficiently practiced the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, they have long since accomplished meritorious virtues, drawn near to immeasurable Buddhas, purified their brahma-conduct, attained the non-retrogressive mind of enlightenment, obtained non-retrogressive patience (*akṣānti*), and acquired the non-retrogressive retention (*dhāraṇī*).
They have attained the patience according to the Dharma (*yathābhūta-kṣānti*) and immeasurable samādhis such as the Śūraṅgama. Thus it is.

When such individuals hear Mahāyāna sūtras, they never give rise to doubt; they are well able to discern and proclaim that the Three Jewels share the same nature and characteristics, being eternally abiding and unchanging.
Hearing of the inconceivable, they do not feel alarm or wonder; hearing of the various aspects of emptiness, their minds are not terrified.
They clearly and thoroughly penetrate the nature of all phenomena, are able to uphold all twelve divisions of the scriptures, and provide extensive explanations of them.
Since he is also able to receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the sūtras of immeasurable Buddhas,
why worry about being unable to receive and uphold such a Mahāparinirvāṇa scripture?
For what reason was this question posed, and why was Ānanda alone favored with this inquiry?

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, and the following two answers are divided into three parts: first, a detailed account of the original circumstances;
second, praise in the present; and third, the direct answer to the two questions. This is the first part, the detailed account of the original circumstances.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, son of good family!
Since I attained Buddhahood, thirty years have passed while I have resided in the city of Rājagṛha. At that time, I said to the bhikṣus:
'Who among this assembly is able to receive and uphold for me the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures, and provide whatever necessities may be required for my personal service?'"
Furthermore, lest you lose your own opportunity for spiritual benefit, at that time Kauṇḍinya came from within that assembly and addressed me, saying:
"I am able to receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures and to serve as your attendant, never failing in the tasks necessary for my own self-benefit.
I said to Kauṇḍinya: "You have already grown old and infirm; you require someone to assist you. How then can you wish to serve as my attendant?"
At that time, Śāriputra spoke again, saying: "I am able to receive and uphold all the Buddha’s words, provide whatever is required, and ensure that my own work for self-benefit is not neglected.
I said to Śāriputra: "You are already advanced in years and require an attendant;
how then can you wish to serve as my attendant? This was true even for all five hundred arhats.
"I accept none of these. At that time, Maudgalyāyana was among the great assembly and had this thought:
"The Tathāgata now refuses the service of five hundred bhikṣus; whose service does he intend for them to perform?
Having reflected thus, he immediately entered meditative concentration and perceived that the Tathāgata’s mind rested upon Ānanda, like the light of the rising sun illuminating all.

Having seen this on the western wall, he immediately arose from his meditative concentration and said to the Venerable Kauṇḍinya, "I see that the Tathāgata wishes to have Ānanda serve as his attendant.
Then Kauṇḍinya, together with five hundred arhats, went to where Ānanda was and spoke these words to him:
"Ānanda, you should now act as an attendant for the Tathāgata; please accept this task."
Ānanda said, "Venerable sirs, I truly am not fit to serve the Tathāgata. Why is this?
The Tathāgata is as venerable as a lion king, as a dragon, or as fire; how could I, being now impure and weak, be able to attend to him?
The bhikṣus said, "Accept our words and serve the Tathāgata; you will obtain great benefit. A second and a third time, they spoke thus.
Ānanda said, "Venerable sirs, I do not seek great benefit; in truth, I am not fit to serve as an attendant.
Then Maudgalyāyana spoke again, saying, "Ānanda, you do not yet understand. Ānanda said, "Venerable sir, I only pray that you will explain it.
Maudgalyāyana said, "A few days ago, the Tathāgata sought an attendant from among the Sangha of five hundred [monks]."
"All the Arhats sought to do this, but the Tathāgata did not permit it. I immediately entered meditative concentration and perceived that the Tathāgata intended for you to perform it;
why then do you now refuse? Having heard this, Ānanda joined his palms, knelt down, and spoke these words:
"Venerable sirs, if such is the case, and if the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, grants me three vows, I shall comply with the Sangha."
The Buddha commanded an attendant to inform Maudgalyāyana on his behalf. Maudgalyāyana asked, "What are the three vows?

When the listeners were about to comply with the Sangha’s command, Kātyāyana and five hundred bhikṣus returned to my presence and spoke as follows:
"We have already exhorted the bhikṣu Ānanda; he seeks only three wishes. If the Buddha will grant them, he shall comply with the Sangha’s command.

"Good son, the Bhikṣu Ānanda is endowed with eight qualities that enable him to fully uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures."
These constitute the eight [qualities]: first, the faculty of faith is firm; second, the mind is upright and sincere; third, the body is free from the suffering of illness;
fourth, one is constantly diligent and energetic; fifth, one is endowed with mindfulness; sixth, the mind is free from arrogance;
seventh, one achieves concentration of mind; eighth, one is endowed with the wisdom born of hearing. Mañjuśrī, this is the *Vipaśyin* [Sūtra].
The Buddha’s attendant disciple was named Aśoka, who likewise possessed these eight qualities.
The attendant disciple of the Tathāgata Śikhin was named Kṣemakāra; the attendant disciple of Viśvabhū Buddha was named Upaśānta;
and the attendant disciple of Krakucchanda Buddha was named Bhadrika.
The attendant disciple of the Buddha Kāśyapa was named Sūti, and the attendant disciple of the Buddha Kāśyapa was named Upananda;
both were likewise endowed with these eight qualities. Now, Ānanda, I am also thus endowed with these eight qualities;

First, because one cuts off all afflictions by means of the wisdom of reality, it is said to be 'according to the place where they are extinguished.

Second, because this emptiness dispels conventional existence, it is said to be 'according to what is extinguished. Furthermore, it is called the 'ultimate truth' (paramārtha-satya) and the 'ultimate' (paramārtha)."

Regarding "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*), this term is also applied to the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, as was first stated in the "Lion’s Roar. However, in the present passage, it specifically clarifies that true emptiness (*tattva-śūnyatā*) is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Because those of inferior wisdom contemplate it, they attain the enlightenment of a *śrāvaka*; because those of middling wisdom [contemplate it], they attain the enlightenment of a *pratyekabuddha*.
Regarding this, there have been ancient interpretations suggesting that the three vehicles involve different modes of contemplation; however, in the present context...

The text clarifies that while the three vehicles equally contemplate the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), they differ according to the inferiority or mediocrity of their wisdom;
this is illustrated by the analogy of three animals crossing a river, where the depth of water reached depends on their respective sizes.

Similarly, when the three vehicles equally contemplate the Middle Way, those with profound wisdom attain unsurpassed *bodhi*, whereas those with shallow wisdom attain only the *bodhi* of a pratyekabuddha or a śrāvaka.
When this Dharma was being taught, ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the realization of one more birth;
fifteen thousand bodhisattvas attained the realization of two more births regarding the dharma-realm; twenty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained ultimate wisdom;
and thirty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained awakening. This second section clarifies the benefits obtained by the assembly at that time.
The ultimate truth is called the ultimate truth; it is also named the emptiness of the ultimate (paramārtha-śūnyatā), and it is also named the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Forty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the space-like samādhi (ākāśa-samādhi);

this space-like samādhi is also named the vast samādhi (vipula-samādhi) and the wisdom-seal samādhi (jñāna-mudrā-samādhi). Fifty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained non-retrogressive patience (avaivartika-kṣānti).
This non-retrogressive patience is also called "patience in accordance with the Dharma" and "patience in accordance with the Dharma-realm.
Sixty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained dhāraṇīs; these dhāraṇīs are also called "the mind of great mindfulness" and "unobstructed wisdom.
Seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the Lion’s Roar Samādhi; this Lion’s Roar is also called the Vajra Samādhi.
It is also called the Samādhi of the Seal of the Five Wisdoms. Eighty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the samādhi of equality;
this samādhi of equality is also called Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion.

Immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, resolved their minds toward the state of a pratyekabuddha.

Innumerable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka; twenty trillion human males, females, and goddesses manifested the transformation of their female bodies and attained male bodies.

As for the text stating that they "attained the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) in one lifetime and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in two lifetimes," this refers to the great bodhisattvas who are in their final birth before buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*) on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

To consider one lifetime as nine stages would constitute two lifetimes; however, if explained in full detail, it is as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the meaning of "diminishing birth" (*saṃjīvana*).
Third, following Subhadra, this section clarifies Subhadra’s realization of the Way.
Subhadra attained the fruit of Arhatship;
there ought to have been a formal entrustment [of the Dharma], yet the text does not conclude with it. Kaishan says: "From this point onward, how lamentable!
Nevertheless, as they have all already received the causal conditions for deliverance, they shall attain the Way after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa."

First, the teachings of this present sutra are complete and one should only encourage oneself to achieve liberation; yet, if one were to pass away without further encountering them, how could one endure such suffering?
Layman, you requested that monks recite from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "In the latter portion of the *Nirvāṇa*, there are further chapters on 'Burning the Body,' 'Erecting Stupas,' and 'Entrustment.
These three chapters have not yet arrived."
